title: Agentic inequality
authors: Matthew Sharp, Omer Bilgin, Iason Gabriel, Lewis Hammond
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01318-5

Sharp et al. investigate the implications of unequal access to AI agents and of differences in their quality and number, developing a conceptual framework to identify potential sources of inequality and suggesting a research agenda to help address the resulting societal challenge.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents could deepen societal inequality when people have unequal access to them or differ in the quality and number of agents they can use. The paper offers a conceptual framework for understanding these risks and a research agenda for addressing them.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a structured way to examine how unequal access to AI agents—and differences in their capabilities and availability—could create or reinforce inequality.
method: Develop a conceptual framework to identify potential sources of inequality involving AI agents.
Examine disparities in access, agent quality, and the number of agents available to different users.
Propose a research agenda to better understand and address the resulting societal challenges.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the paper highlights why agent access and distribution matter alongside technical performance. It encourages attention to who benefits from agentic systems and who risks being left behind.
visual_elements: Three-axis diagram showing access, agent quality, and agent quantity as dimensions of inequality.
Side-by-side illustrations of users with different levels of agent support.
Conceptual flowchart linking unequal agent resources to potential societal disparities.

infographic.paper_title: Agentic inequality
infographic.paper_authors: Matthew Sharp, Omer Bilgin, Iason Gabriel, Lewis Hammond

title: Lagrangian–Eulerian learning of flow field and trajectories with TrajectoryFlowNet
authors: Jingdi Wan, Hongping Wang, Bo Liu, Xiaolei Yang, Xiaodong Hu
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01316-7

Wan et al. introduce a physics-informed learning model that simultaneously predicts long-range particle paths and flow fields based on very limited trajectory measurements, validated in both simulations and blood-flow experiments.

infographic.key_insight: TrajectoryFlowNet learns both how particles move and the flow field carrying them from very limited trajectory measurements. Its physics-informed approach connects individual particle paths with the surrounding fluid motion.
infographic.problem_solved: Reconstructing flow fields and predicting long-range particle trajectories when only sparse measurements of particle motion are available.
method: Combine Lagrangian learning of particle trajectories with Eulerian learning of flow fields.
Use physics-informed learning to jointly predict particle paths and fluid motion from limited trajectory measurements.
Validate the approach in simulations and blood-flow experiments.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the work illustrates how physical knowledge can support learning from sparse observations. Joint trajectory and flow prediction could help analyze fluid systems where extensive measurements are difficult to obtain.

title: Physics-informed machine learning: a hybrid lens for fluid dynamics
authors: Kai Fukami, Romit Maulik
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01319-4

A neural network approach bridging Lagrangian and Eulerian perspectives transforms sparse observations into physically accurate, high-resolution maps of complex and chaotic fluid motions.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network combines two ways of describing fluid motion—following moving particles and observing flow at fixed locations—to turn sparse measurements into detailed, physically accurate flow maps.
infographic.problem_solved: Reconstructing complex, chaotic fluid motion at high resolution when only limited observations are available.
method: Bridge Lagrangian descriptions, which follow fluid particles, with Eulerian descriptions, which represent flow at fixed spatial locations.
Use a physics-informed neural network to connect sparse observations with physically consistent flow reconstructions.
Generate high-resolution maps of complex and chaotic fluid motion.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this illustrates how physical knowledge and complementary representations can support reconstruction from limited data. It highlights a hybrid approach to scientific machine learning beyond purely data-driven prediction.

title: VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Token
authors: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk

infographic.key_insight: VideoMaMa++ targets inconsistent foreground extraction between video chunks using a Preserve-and-Refine Token. The goal is to retain the generalization benefits of video diffusion models while making matting more temporally coherent.
infographic.problem_solved: Compute-heavy diffusion models process only 6–24 frames at a time. Independently matting these short chunks from coarse masks can produce inconsistencies at chunk boundaries.
method: Build on diffusion-based video matting, which uses pretrained video priors and coarse mask guidance to estimate foreground transparency.
Introduce a Preserve-and-Refine Token to address temporal consistency, as indicated by the title; the truncated abstract does not provide its implementation details.
infographic.impact: More consistent chunked matting could improve foreground extraction for video editing and compositing. The supplied excerpt does not establish measured quality gains or inference costs.

title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
authors: Xabier Martínez-de-Morentin, Sumeer A. Khan, Itziar Cenzano, Robert Lehmann, Alberto Maillo
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01311-y

This work studies the reusability of CORNETO, a previously developed framework for learning biological networks from multi-omics data. Robust network inference is found to depend on data availability, prior knowledge, regularization and biological context.

infographic.key_insight: CORNETO’s reliability when inferring biological networks from multi-omics data is not uniform: it operates in distinct robustness regimes shaped by prior knowledge and data availability. Regularization and biological context also influence how well the framework can be reused.
infographic.problem_solved: The study examines when a previously developed biological network inference framework remains robust across different data and biological settings.
method: Study the reusability of CORNETO for learning biological networks from multi-sample, multi-omics data.
Assess how data availability and prior biological knowledge relate to inference robustness.
Examine the roles of regularization and biological context in reliable reuse.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the findings emphasize that reusing a network inference framework requires checking its data, prior-knowledge and regularization requirements. Robustness in one biological setting should not be assumed to transfer to another.

title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
authors: Zehao Wang, Jianpeng Yao, Yuping Wang, Yiping Li, Jiaqi Li
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major chall

infographic.key_insight: CoopUQ proposes uncertainty-aware cooperative forecasting to help teams of robots navigate safely around people. The central idea is to account for uncertain predictions while cooperating, rather than treating each robot as an independent navigator.
infographic.problem_solved: Single-robot navigation strategies can become unsafe or inefficient when extended to robot teams, especially when occlusions hide hazards or unfamiliar situations make predictions unreliable.
method: Use reinforcement learning as the foundation for fast navigation decisions in human-shared spaces.
Introduce cooperative forecasting to address the limitations of individual robots' predictions.
Account for prediction uncertainty in multi-robot navigation; specific mechanisms and evaluation results are not available in the truncated abstract.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the paper highlights cooperation and uncertainty handling as important considerations when scaling navigation from one robot to a team. These ideas target safer, more reliable behavior under limited visibility and distribution shift.

title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
authors: Yu Zhou, Cheng-Fu Yang, Rui Sun, Di Wu, Sibo Peng
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retai

infographic.key_insight: Better visual AI requires access to the right evidence, not just more time to reason. A controlled study across 22 benchmarks found that increasing the base model’s inference budget delivered only modest gains.
infographic.problem_solved: Visual tasks often require grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements that a model cannot reliably obtain through internal reasoning alone.
method: Evaluate the benefits of increasing inference budgets across 22 benchmarks.
Use heterogeneous tools to obtain task-relevant visual evidence, external information, and measurements.

title: Towards understanding and monitorability of reasoning LLMs
authors: Unknown
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01333-6

Frontier LLMs are trained to solve problems in a step-by-step way, generating reasoning text in human-understandable language. However, these reasoning tokens are not accurate explanations of LLMs’ internal computations, raising challenges for monitorability.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM’s step-by-step reasoning text is not a faithful explanation of its internal computations. Human-readable reasoning alone therefore cannot guarantee reliable monitoring.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of understanding and monitoring reasoning LLMs when their visible reasoning may not accurately reflect how they produce answers.
method: Examines the distinction between generated reasoning text and internal model computations.
Considers how this gap limits understanding and monitorability.
The supplied abstract does not specify experiments, datasets, or a concrete monitoring method.
infographic.impact: AI/ML practitioners should not treat readable reasoning as definitive evidence of a model’s decision process. Reliable oversight requires validation beyond inspecting reasoning text alone.

authors: Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yu-Lun Liu, Kaipeng Zhang
abstract: Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset t

title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
authors: Wenqian Zhang, Yangyi Huang, Zigeng Xu, Weiyang Liu, Zhen Liu
abstract: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating

infographic.key_insight: A CAD mechanism that looks plausible may still fail to work. This paper studies AI-generated mechanisms through their physical function, rather than appearance alone.
infographic.problem_solved: How can AI agents turn underspecified requests into working CAD mechanisms—and verify success when different designs use different components, controls, and operating conditions?
method: Study functional CAD design, where agents interpret underspecified requests and construct mechanisms.
Iteratively revise candidate mechanisms to satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation.
Address the difficulty of verifying function across structurally different designs; the provided abstract is incomplete and does not specify the verification method.

title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
authors: Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Yue Zhao, Armin W. Thomas, Ehsan Adeli, Jiajun Wu
abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8+

infographic.key_insight: Halcyon shows that strong text-to-image generation does not require language pretraining. Trained from scratch, Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 while using 18.2× less pretraining compute.
infographic.problem_solved: Modern text-to-image systems typically rely on internet-scale language pretraining. This work tests whether models can generate high-quality images from text without that dependency.

title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
authors: Tianqi Liu, Hanfei Zhao, Qifeng Liang, Hui En Pang, Jiarui Xu
abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. infographic.key_insight: Ropedia W0 introduces a shared world model for anticipating movement and object-interaction outcomes across humans and different robot bodies. Its central idea is to combine large-scale first-person human experience with robot data.
infographic.problem_solved: Humans and robots have different action spaces, making it difficult to build one model that predicts both locomotion and manipulation across embodiments. Limited multimodal training data adds to this challenge.
method: Develop an egocentric world foundation model spanning human and diverse robot embodiments.
Curate Xp-Data with 10,000 hours of first-person human data and 3,000 hours of robot data.
Use unified multimodal annotations to support joint modeling of locomotion and manipulation.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang
abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. infographic.key_insight: The paper aims to make visual-reasoning feedback more trustworthy by distinguishing corrections grounded in visual evidence from those driven by language priors or response style.
infographic.problem_solved: Verifiable rewards evaluate overall task success but provide little guidance about where visual reasoning fails. Teacher-generated token-level corrections offer finer feedback, yet may mix genuine visual evidence with non-visual influences.
method: Use multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for task-level supervision.

authors: Dongyoon Hahm, Woogyeol Jin, Dennis Wei, Yi Zhou, Nathalie Baracaldo
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuning a language model for one behavior can bring out another, unintended behavior—a relationship called a behavioral coupling. This paper studies how these couplings form and behave, although the supplied abstract is too truncated to establish its specific findings.
infographic.problem_solved: Understanding why targeted fine-tuning can change seemingly unrelated behaviors, making model adaptation harder to predict and control.

title: Self-Building Labs
authors: Jiaru Bai, Yuchi Zhao, Han Hao, Miroslav Bogdanovic, Yang Cao
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setu

infographic.problem_solved: Existing self-driving laboratories are limited to procedures they were engineered to perform. Supporting new experiments requires extensive manual engineering, making laboratory flexibility a bottleneck for scaling scientific discovery.

authors: Kaixuan Ji, Zixiang Chen, Wenting Zhao, Cheng Qian, Heng Wang

title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
authors: Jiaming Xu, Hanzhen Wang, Tianlang Zhao, Jiewen Xiao, Chengze Yuan
abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique

infographic.key_insight: OmniVerifier-C1 replaces simple True/False judging with a graded verifier that breaks complex multimodal rules into smaller parts and scores them individually. This gives a more nuanced, informative critique of generated visuals in rule-governed settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional visual verifiers often struggle with complex prompts or environmental rules because they output only binary decisions and cannot explain partial compliance. This paper addresses the need for finer-grained evaluation in compositional multimodal tasks.
method: Automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components.
Assigns pointwise scores to each component instead of producing only a binary verdict.
Aggregates these graded judgments into a continuous, more informative verifier signal.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables more robust evaluation of generative visual models in complex scenarios where partial correctness matters. It can improve debugging, benchmarking, and training feedback for multimodal systems.

title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
authors: Dongxu Yang, Hongda Yan, Renxin Wang, Baoli Zhang, Haojia Zuo
abstract: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated cu

infographic.key_insight: FDE-Gym shifts AI evaluation from clean, predefined benchmarks to messy, real-world delivery work where requirements are ambiguous and constraints emerge during execution. It provides a realistic testbed for measuring how well agents handle the “last mile” of deployment and customer delivery.
infographic.problem_solved: Most agent benchmarks focus on well-specified tasks with clear instructions, but real forward-deployed engineering involves ambiguous goals, live systems, and hidden constraints. This paper addresses the gap between benchmark performance and the practical challenges of customer-facing AI delivery.
method: Built FDE-Gym as a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks drawn from 20 customer scenarios across 18 industries.
Tasks were adapted from real-world delivery projects by industry experts to preserve realism and complexity.
The benchmark simulates the interactive, uncertain conditions FDEs face when clarifying requirements and operating in live environments.
infographic.impact: FDE-Gym gives AI researchers and practitioners a more realistic way to evaluate agents for deployment-oriented work. It can help reveal whether models are truly ready for customer-facing delivery, not just narrow benchmark tasks.

title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
authors: Chenyuan Zhou, Yining Hong, Huang Huang, Yunfan Jiang, Wenlong Huang
abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying envi

infographic.key_insight: T2-Z improves robotic world models by learning a compact latent representation of hidden environmental factors at test time. This lets the model adapt its predictions to unseen physical conditions and human-defined rules without requiring explicit environment labels.
infographic.problem_solved: Robots often need to predict future outcomes in environments where important factors like friction, mass, or task-specific rules are not directly observable. Existing world models can fail when these hidden conditions differ from training-time assumptions.
method: Augment the robotic world model with a learnable environment latent variable that conditions future predictions.
Optimize this latent at test time using observed context so the model can infer hidden environmental properties on the fly.
Use the latent to capture compact, environment-specific information that improves prediction accuracy under changing conditions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to make robotic prediction systems more robust in real-world settings where environment details are incomplete or shift over time. It reduces reliance on explicit supervision for every physical or rule-based variation.

title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
authors: SeungJu Cha, Ye-Chan Kim, HyunGee Kim, Sungho Koh, Dong-Jin Kim
abstract: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background obje

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that token merging should not be guided only by text relevance: some background tokens are also important for preserving image quality. By using diffusion dynamics to decide which tokens to keep, the method aims to speed up generation without losing important visual details.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of choosing which tokens in diffusion-based image generation can be merged safely, so models can run faster while avoiding visible quality degradation.
method: Analyze diffusion dynamics to estimate token importance over the generation process.
Identify tokens that should be preserved even if they are not strongly aligned with the prompt, including important background regions.
Merge redundant tokens more selectively to reduce computation while maintaining image fidelity.
infographic.impact: This helps practitioners accelerate diffusion models with a more reliable token-merging strategy that better preserves both foreground and background content. It is useful for practical high-quality image generation where speed and visual consistency both matter.

title: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture
authors: Chen Yang, Jiemin Fang, Fanpeng Meng, Zihao Huang, Jichen Pang
abstract: Single image 3D generation aims to dress a given 3D mesh with relightable materials while faithfully preserving the visual details of a reference image. Existing methods either introduce artifacts when fusing inconsistent multi-view predictions or struggle to preserve fine details through implicit image-feature conditioning. To resolve these challenges, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, built on the principle of decoupling visible-material estimation, surface alignment, and observation-guided 3D completio

infographic.key_insight: SUPRA-Tex improves single-image 3D generation by separating material estimation, surface alignment, and 3D completion, so the final textured mesh stays both visually faithful and physically consistent. This helps preserve fine image details while avoiding the artifacts common in multi-view fusion approaches.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of dressing a 3D mesh with relightable textures from a single reference image without losing fine details or introducing inconsistencies across views.
method: Decouples the pipeline into visible-material estimation, surface alignment, and observation-guided 3D completion.
Aligns texture/material predictions to the target 3D surface to reduce cross-view mismatch and artifacts.
Uses observation guidance to complete unseen regions while preserving reference-image details.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more reliable way to generate textured 3D assets from minimal input, improving quality for graphics, virtual try-on, games, and AR/VR workflows. It also highlights a design pattern—explicitly separating alignment from completion—that can generalize to other 3D reconstruction tasks.

title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
authors: Tianjiao Yu, Zhilin Ou, Yifan Shen, Xinzhuo Li, Yuanzhe Liu
abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagn

infographic.key_insight: CoDA makes robot training smarter by letting the simulation environment and the policy learn from each other. Instead of generating any physically valid scene, it finds the environments and supervision that specifically fix the policy’s weak points.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between physically valid simulated environments and truly useful training environments. In robot learning, the hard part is identifying which environments expose policy failures and what feedback helps the policy improve.
method: Uses a co-evolution framework where a simulation data engine and an action policy improve together over time.
Shares a heterogeneous memory that stores environment constructions, policy failures, and learning progress.
Uses validated diagnostics from memory to guide the generation of more useful environments and supervision signals.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, CoDA offers a more targeted way to generate training data for robotics and embodied AI. This can improve sample efficiency, reduce wasted simulation, and produce policies that learn from the failures that matter most.

title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
authors: Hongchang Liu, Jian Liu, Yujuan Ding, Liang Peng, Xun Jiang
abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically,

infographic.key_insight: GeoState separates true scene geometry changes from camera/view effects, making 3D world state prediction easier and more stable. Instead of treating geometry features as directly predictive, it learns a view-decoupled representation of world evolution.
infographic.problem_solved: Many 3D world models rely on geometry foundation model features that change with the camera view, which mixes actual scene dynamics with observation-dependent variation. This makes future state prediction harder and less reliable.
method: Learn a geometry state representation that is explicitly decoupled from viewpoint changes.
Model scene-state evolution separately from camera-dependent observations.
Use geometry foundation model features as input while removing view-induced entanglement for predictive world modeling.
infographic.impact: This can improve the stability and accuracy of predictive 3D world models by giving them a cleaner notion of scene state. For practitioners, it means better long-horizon reasoning, more robust geometry prediction, and more reliable world modeling from changing viewpoints.

title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zhixu Li, Keqian Tang, Litian Gong, Jingyu Yao, Wenqian Zhang
abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings;

infographic.key_insight: LIBERO-PeRM introduces a controlled benchmark for personalized robotic manipulation, separating whether a robot completes a task from whether it satisfies a user's preferences. This makes it possible to measure true personalization in embodied agents rather than just task success.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing robotic manipulation benchmarks mostly test generic task completion and do not cleanly evaluate preference satisfaction. The paper addresses the lack of a standardized benchmark for studying personalized robotic manipulation in household settings.
method: Introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark designed to evaluate preference learning in embodied robotic agents.
Structure evaluation around key research questions about how policies follow preferences, including zero-shot preference compliance.
Provide a controlled setup that distinguishes task execution quality from user-preference satisfaction.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark offers a clearer way to measure progress in personalization for robots, which is crucial for real-world home deployment. It can improve the development and comparison of policies that are not only effective, but also aligned with individual user needs.

title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Zirui Wu, Chen Guo, Tianjian Jiang, Zeren Jiang, Zeming Li
abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a l

infographic.key_insight: P^3-WAM unifies three capabilities for egocentric dexterous manipulation in one model: understanding past motion, predicting future visual outcomes, and planning actions toward a goal. This lets the system connect perception and decision-making in a single framework instead of treating them as separate tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of learning a coherent model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that can infer 3D hand/camera motion from video, forecast what will happen under actions, and generate goal-directed action plans.
method: Perceive mode: reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from egocentric video.
Predict mode: generates future visual states conditioned on prescribed actions.
Plan mode: jointly produces action trajectories and their expected visual consequences from an initial image and goal context.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a unified foundation for training and evaluating manipulation agents that need both visual understanding and action planning. It can simplify pipelines for robotics, embodied AI, and human-centric manipulation by consolidating multiple capabilities into one model.

title: Feed-Forward Multi-View Feature Coding for 3D Gaussian Splatting
authors: Seungmi Choi, Ji-Hyoun Choi, Suhyun Jo, Tae-Gwon Park, Hui Yong Kim
abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods enable efficient reconstruction of 3D scenes from sparse multi-view images in a single forward pass, without scene-specific optimization. However, existing feed-forward scene-coding pipelines first generate a complete Gaussian representation and then encode its geometry and appearance attributes separately, often involving non-differentiable operations. The resulting 'generate-then-compress' pipeline requires complex attribute-specific codec desi

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues for a more direct, differentiable way to code 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes from multiple views, instead of generating a full 3D representation first and compressing it later. The goal is to make feed-forward 3D reconstruction simpler, more efficient, and better suited for learning-based optimization.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the inefficiency and complexity of existing feed-forward 3DGS pipelines that use a "generate-then-compress" design. These methods often require separate codecs for geometry and appearance, and may rely on non-differentiable steps that limit end-to-end training.
method: Uses multi-view feature coding to represent scene information directly from sparse input images.
Replaces separate geometry/appearance compression with a more unified feed-forward encoding pipeline.
Aims to keep the reconstruction-and-coding process differentiable end-to-end for easier learning and better integration.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this could simplify 3D scene reconstruction pipelines and reduce engineering overhead in codec design. It also points toward faster, more scalable 3D perception systems that can learn directly from sparse multi-view inputs.

title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal, Jialin Zhang, Yilin Chen
abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent beco

infographic.key_insight: Giving research agents more time, more parallel workers, or opportunities to collaborate eventually produces diminishing returns as their histories accumulate. The paper points to forgetting as a potential ingredient for sustained discovery, although the supplied abstract is incomplete.
infographic.problem_solved: How to keep automated research productive when additional computation and agent collaboration no longer yield continued improvements.
method: Use LLM agents to iteratively refine research candidates with feedback from scored verifiers.
Compare three scaling strategies: longer individual runs, independent parallel agents, and parallel agents that share and build on candidates.
Examine performance plateaus associated with accumulated history; the excerpt does not specify the forgetting mechanism or detailed results.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, simply increasing agent runtime or team size may not sustain progress. History management and selective forgetting are worth investigating alongside compute scaling.

title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong
abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore intro

infographic.key_insight: VITAL shows that action targets for driving can be derived directly from visual motion rather than from trajectory labels alone. This makes the learned action more tightly aligned with what the camera actually sees, improving precision beyond coarse maneuver reconstruction.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the mismatch between visual anticipation and trajectory-based action supervision in world-action models. Existing methods often learn from action targets that are detached from the underlying visual dynamics, which can leave small but important control errors.
method: Reconstruct future trajectories from recorded future images to test how much driving intent can be recovered from visual motion alone.
Use the reconstruction result as a bridge from visual dynamics to action targets, capturing the dominant maneuver while reducing dependence on hand-defined trajectory representations.
Refine the supervision to reduce centimeter-scale errors and better convert visual motion into precise driving actions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more grounded way to supervise driving models: learn actions from visual evidence instead of only from abstract trajectory labels. That can improve precision, robustness, and alignment between perception and control in autonomous driving systems.

title: Can Learning to Answer Spatial Questions Improve Novel-View Generation?
authors: Jahyeok Koo, Hyeonseo Yu, Seungho Jang, Jaewoo Jung, Jiwon Kang
abstract: Generating novel views from limited observations requires preserving both the appearance and spatial structure of a scene. Although recent approaches exploit fine-grained geometric cues, they do not explicitly model high-level semantic and spatial properties such as object identity, attributes, and inter-object relationships. In this work, we investigate whether 3D language understanding can provide complementary supervision for novel-view generation. We introduce Ask4NV, built on a pretrained u

infographic.key_insight: Learning to answer spatial questions can provide useful 3D semantic supervision that helps novel-view generation preserve object identities, attributes, and relationships—not just raw geometry. The paper suggests language-based spatial understanding can complement traditional geometric cues for better scene reconstruction from limited views.
infographic.problem_solved: Novel-view generation from sparse observations often struggles to maintain consistent spatial structure and semantic details across unseen viewpoints. This work addresses the gap by adding explicit high-level 3D language understanding to improve view synthesis quality and consistency.
method: Introduces Ask4NV, a framework built on a pretrained model to leverage 3D spatial question-answering as supervision for novel-view generation.
Uses spatially grounded language signals to model semantic properties such as object identity, attributes, and inter-object relationships.
Combines this complementary supervision with visual/geometric cues to improve the fidelity and structural consistency of generated novel views.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this shows that language supervision can strengthen 3D generation pipelines beyond purely geometric training. It offers a promising direction for improving robustness, semantic consistency, and interpretability in view synthesis systems.

title: Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
authors: Mingyu Ouyang, Yiran Wang, Siyuan Hu, Xingyilang Yin, Huiqiang Sun
abstract: Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Pla

infographic.key_insight: The paper suggests that agents can learn game-playing skills from synthetic experience instead of depending only on expensive human demonstrations. This opens a scalable path to training more capable computer-use and game agents in rich, dynamic environments.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of training game-playing agents when real demonstrations are limited and interactive environments are hard to scale. Existing pipelines often miss rare or dynamic states, making learning incomplete and inefficient.
method: Generate synthetic experience to expand training coverage beyond what human demonstrations provide.
Use this synthetic data to teach agents how to act in visually rich game environments with diverse mechanics.
Build a learning pipeline aimed at improving robustness in dynamic and hard-to-cover game states.
infographic.impact: This matters because it reduces reliance on costly, narrow demonstration datasets and makes agent training more scalable. For practitioners, it suggests a practical route to improving general-purpose digital agents in complex interactive settings.

title: DynThinker: Unifying Static 3D and Dynamic 4D Spatial Reasoning
authors: Qihang Cao, Haoyuan Li, Zihan Guo, Sensen Gao, Zihui Gao
abstract: Achieving general spatial intelligence requires a unified understanding of both static 3D and dynamic 4D. However, we find that existing models struggle to excel at both: 3D post-training can weaken dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models often lack strong static 3D reasoning. Our analysis reveals that this spatial--dynamic interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-laye

infographic.key_insight: DynThinker shows that strong spatial intelligence requires balancing static 3D and dynamic 4D reasoning instead of optimizing one at the expense of the other. The paper finds this tradeoff is not uniform across the network, with late-layer parameters being especially important for maintaining both abilities.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge that current models cannot reliably handle both static 3D spatial reasoning and dynamic 4D reasoning at the same time. Improving one often weakens the other, making it hard to build general-purpose spatial models.
method: Analyze where 3D-4D interference occurs across different parameter groups in the model.
Identify which layers are most sensitive to the static-vs-dynamic balance, especially in later layers.
Use this understanding to guide a unified evaluation and reasoning framework for both static and dynamic spatial tasks.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work provides a clearer roadmap for building spatial models that generalize across both worlds and motion. It can help avoid training strategies that accidentally degrade one capability while improving another.

title: CommerceGen-Studio: An End-to-End Framework for Commercial-Grade Main-Image Generation
authors: Xiaoli Xu, Zhengtao Wu, Zhengze Xu, Tao Liu, Yongchao Du
abstract: We present CommerceGen-Studio, an end-to-end framework for generating commercial-grade main images for e-commerce Stock Keeping Units (SKUs). Our framework is organized along a three-stage pipeline of information extraction, semantic rewriting, and multi-condition generation: Prompt-Eval-Refine-Loop Agent (PERL-Agent) distills heterogeneous SKU metadata into concise selling-point text lists through an iterative closed loop of VLM and LLM roles scored by a reference-free rubric. Layout Thinker Op

infographic.key_insight: CommerceGen-Studio turns messy SKU metadata into commercial-grade main images through a structured three-stage pipeline. Its core idea is to combine iterative vision-language refinement with multi-condition generation so e-commerce images are both faithful to the product and optimized for selling.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of generating high-quality, market-ready product main images from heterogeneous and incomplete e-commerce SKU data. Existing workflows often require manual prompt engineering and struggle to preserve product details, layout quality, and commercial appeal at scale.
method: Uses a three-stage pipeline: information extraction, semantic rewriting, and multi-condition image generation.
Introduces PERL-Agent, a Prompt-Eval-Refine-Loop system where VLM and LLM roles iteratively convert SKU metadata into concise selling-point text lists using a reference-free rubric.
Applies a layout-oriented generation module to produce final main images conditioned on the rewritten semantics and product constraints.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this framework shows how to move from raw product metadata to production-ready visual content with less manual intervention. It is especially relevant for applied generative AI systems that need controllability, consistency, and commercial quality in real-world deployments.

title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
authors: Kaixiang Zhao, Tianrun Yu, Shangzhe Li, Yuxiao Yang, Amanda Hughes
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the st

infographic.key_insight: The paper finds that standard on-policy distillation breaks when the student makes mistakes because the teacher can recognize errors but still fails to recover from them. CriticOPD fixes this by adding critique-based supervision, restoring the teacher’s ability to guide the student back to correct solutions.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the unreliability of supervision in on-policy distillation when training on the student’s own rollouts. The core challenge is that a teacher may not be recoverable from incorrect prefixes, which weakens training signal and harms learning.
method: Use the student’s own generated rollouts as training trajectories, as in on-policy distillation.
Have the teacher explicitly critique incorrect rollouts instead of only following them token by token.
Convert critiques into supervision signals that help the teacher recover to the correct answer path, improving training stability and correctness.
infographic.impact: This makes on-policy distillation more reliable on hard or error-prone trajectories, which can improve student learning from imperfect self-generated data. For practitioners, it offers a practical way to get stronger supervision without needing perfectly correct rollouts.

title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
authors: Haofei Yu, Yixing Chen, Yining Zhao, Xuyan Ye, Yuxiang Liu
abstract: Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that language agents can learn better from intermediate steps, not just final outcomes, by co-training two complementary abilities: acting in the environment and forecasting what will happen next. This makes long-horizon agent training more efficient and uses supervision that standard RL usually ignores.
infographic.problem_solved: Training language agents is expensive because long rollouts are costly, and traditional reinforcement learning relies mainly on a single terminal reward. This leaves most intermediate-step supervision unused and makes it difficult to build good per-step learning targets.
method: Co-evolve two objectives during training: acting, which performs actions in the environment, and forecasting, which predicts future outcomes or responses.
Use intermediate supervision more effectively than terminal-only RL by turning step-level signals into learning targets for both action selection and prediction.
Reduce reliance on manually constructed value targets or environment-response targets, which are often hard to define accurately.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this approach offers a more sample-efficient way to train language agents on long-horizon tasks. It can improve learning from sparse rewards and may lead to more robust agents that better anticipate consequences before acting.

title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen
abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations co

infographic.key_insight: GeoThinker-$F$ turns an MLLM’s own hidden states into predictive world representations, reducing dependence on external 3D encoders. This lets the model internalize spatial and temporal structure for faster, more efficient geometry-aware reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Geometry-aware MLLMs often need separate 3D encoder modules to inject spatial priors, which adds latency, memory cost, and inference complexity. The paper addresses how to preserve strong spatial intelligence without paying the overhead of extra encoder paths.
method: Transforms causal MLLM hidden states into endogenous latent world representations that carry spatiotemporal structure.
Uses predictive internal representations instead of external 3D feature extractors to support spatial reasoning.
Optimizes for efficiency by keeping perception and reasoning largely inside the main model pathway at inference time.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more deployment-friendly way to build spatially aware multimodal models with lower latency and compute. It is especially relevant for robotics, embodied AI, and real-time 3D understanding where speed matters.

title: A$^3$PreCore: Robust Rigid Registration for Native FLAIR-Space Brain-Mask Transfer
authors: Elmira Mirzabeigi, Zahra Khalilzad, Taylor Snowden-Richardson, Jesus Eduardo Lugo Arce, Jodie R. Gawryluk
abstract: Reliable brain-mask transfer into native fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) space can fail when T1-to-FLAIR rigid registration is unstable. We developed A$^3$PreCore, a six-degree-of-freedom rigid-registration strategy that aligns the full bias-corrected T1-weighted image to native FLAIR using normalized mutual information while preserving the established T1-space anatomical mask. We also introduced extended quantitative quality control (E-QC), which characterizes mask extent, field-of-

infographic.key_insight: A$^3$PreCore improves the reliability of transferring brain masks into native FLAIR space by using a more robust rigid-registration strategy that is less likely to fail than standard T1-to-FLAIR alignment. It preserves the original T1-space anatomical mask while better aligning the full T1 image to FLAIR.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard rigid registration between T1 and FLAIR images can be unstable, causing inaccurate brain-mask transfer in native FLAIR space. This creates quality-control and downstream analysis issues in neuroimaging pipelines.
method: Uses a 6-degree-of-freedom rigid registration between the full bias-corrected T1-weighted image and native FLAIR.
Optimizes alignment with normalized mutual information for improved robustness.
Retains the established T1-space anatomical mask while adding extended quantitative quality control (E-QC) to assess mask extent and field-of-view coverage.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners working with medical imaging, this improves preprocessing reliability and reduces failure cases that can propagate into training or inference. More stable mask transfer means cleaner inputs, better QC, and more trustworthy downstream results.

title: Any Time, Any Space: A World-State-Centric Framework for Agentic Video Generation
authors: Weijie Wang, Haomin Zhang, Ye Li, Akide Liu, Zeyu Zhang
abstract: Long-form agentic video generation must turn a screenplay into shots that remain spatially and temporally consistent across nonconsecutive requests. Passing prompts or recent frames between shots does not provide a shared spatial frame for revisiting a scene or a time-indexed record for replaying an earlier event. We present Any Time, Any Space (ATAS), which compiles a screenplay into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references. Before generation, it retrieves relevan

infographic.key_insight: ATAS reframes long-form video generation around a persistent world state, so the model can consistently revisit places, camera setups, and past events across nonconsecutive shots. This makes screenplay-driven video generation more coherent than simply passing prompts or recent frames forward.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of a shared spatial frame and time-indexed memory in agentic video generation, which causes inconsistencies when a scene is revisited later in the story.
method: Compiles a screenplay into shot requests with explicit references to location, camera, and event time.
Retrieves relevant world-state information before generation to provide continuity across shots.
Uses a world-state-centric framework so scenes can be revisited and replayed with spatial and temporal consistency.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical blueprint for generating longer, more coherent videos from scripted inputs. It is especially useful for applications that need continuity across scenes, such as storytelling, previsualization, and agentic video pipelines.

title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
authors: Shubhendu Trivedi, Jacob Eisenstein, Alekh Agarwal, Ian Gemp, Michael Kaisers
abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabi

infographic.key_insight: This paper studies how efficient first-price auctions are for allocating prompts in agentic AI markets. It characterizes the price of anarchy: how much social welfare can be lost when independent AI agents bid strategically rather than coordinate perfectly.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses prompt allocation in decentralized serving-time markets where multiple AI agents compete for each user query. It asks whether simple first-price auctions can reliably assign prompts while preserving efficiency despite private values, inference costs, and strategic bidding.
method: Model each agent’s bid as its expected value for a prompt: expected reward from the response minus inference cost.
Analyze first-price auctions as the allocation mechanism for prompts in a decentralized agentic market.
Derive price-of-anarchy bounds to quantify worst-case welfare loss from strategic behavior.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides theory for building scalable, transparent prompt marketplaces without needing a central controller to know each model’s capabilities or costs. It helps system designers anticipate efficiency losses and choose auction rules that better balance incentive compatibility and performance.

title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
authors: Weichen Lyu, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong, Long Xu, Shengjun Zhang
abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise

infographic.key_insight: PhySGA grounds 3D object composition in physical-space reasoning rather than relying only on static digital priors. This makes 3D scene assembly more generalizable, interactive, and better suited to challenging real-world constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of composing multiple 3D objects accurately in complex scenes, where prior methods struggle with precise placement, physical consistency, and generalization beyond simple layouts.
method: Uses a physics-space grounded agentic framework to reason about object composition in physically meaningful coordinates.
Combines agent-like decision making with 3D spatial constraints to improve placement quality and interaction support.
Targets generalizable composition across diverse scenes instead of depending on fixed coordinate prediction or image-synthesis priors.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more robust path to 3D content creation and robot simulation by aligning composition with physical reality. It can improve downstream tasks that need accurate, interactive, and transferable scene assembly.

title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
authors: Dennis Grinwald, Ankur Singha, Khaled Kahouli, Karl Jansen, Shinichi Nakajima
abstract: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion models for lattice field theories can be trained without access to real target samples by using the model's own generated configurations. This removes a major practical barrier and makes generative sampling more feasible for physics simulations.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the bottleneck of generating independent equilibrium field configurations in lattice field theory, where standard diffusion training appears to require samples from the very distribution one wants to learn.
method: Train the diffusion model using self-generated samples rather than true target samples.
Leverage the model's own outputs to replace the standard denoising score matching data requirement.
Use the resulting generative sampler to produce equilibrium-like field configurations for lattice field theory.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows a path to train generative diffusion models in settings where labeled or target data are unavailable or expensive to obtain. It broadens the use of diffusion-based sampling to scientific domains with severe data-generation costs.

title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
authors: Jiaru Zou, Yunzhe Qi, Sirui Chen, Federico Bianchi, Shang Zhu
abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturall

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid Reasoning Agents let an AI reason internally in a latent space when speed and efficiency matter, then switch back to text when it needs to use tools or communicate externally. This creates a single agent that can think beyond language without losing the flexibility of language-based interaction.
infographic.problem_solved: Current LLM agents are forced to reason and act through text, which is slow and inefficient, while latent reasoning is efficient but usually cannot directly access tools or provide transparent outputs. This paper addresses the gap by unifying both modes in one agent.
method: Introduce a hybrid agent architecture that dynamically switches between latent reasoning and text-based reasoning during one generation process.
Use latent space for internal computation and planning, while using text tokens for tool use, interaction, and interpretable outputs.
Coordinate both modes so the agent can reason efficiently without sacrificing external action capability or transparency.
infographic.impact: This approach could make AI agents more efficient, flexible, and practical for real-world workflows where both deep internal reasoning and clear external communication are needed. For practitioners, it offers a path toward agents that are faster than pure text-based systems yet still usable in tool-rich environments.

title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
authors: Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Xinxin Liu, Jiawei Zhou, Yuzhang Shang
abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once

infographic.key_insight: ChunkAct reduces repeated LLM reasoning in agentic robotics by grouping low-level actions into reusable action chunks. This keeps the flexibility of LLM-driven control while making robot episodes much more efficient.
infographic.problem_solved: Agentic robotics is powerful for generalization, but it is inefficient because the LLM must re-reason over the full history for every primitive action. The paper addresses the growing cost and latency of long-horizon robotic episodes.
method: Identify redundancy in step-by-step LLM control and replace repeated primitive-level reasoning with chunk-level execution.
Use action chunking so the agent can plan once and execute multiple actions before needing another reasoning pass.
Preserve the memory-guided, tool-using agentic framework while reducing the number of LLM calls per episode.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical path to make agentic robotics cheaper, faster, and more scalable without retraining the robot policy. It is especially valuable for long-horizon tasks where inference cost and latency become major bottlenecks.

title: EgoExplorer: A Vision-Motion-Touch Observatory for Human Loco-Manipulation In Situ
authors: Yunsong Zhou, Xuekun Jiang, Haiqi Shen, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi
abstract: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation from human demonstrations rests on observing how locomotion, posture, and object interaction evolve together as tasks unfold. Scaling collection across diverse environments, in turn, favors lightweight, portable capture systems. Yet, existing datasets provide only partial views of this coordination. Thus, we introduce EgoExplorer, a 100-hour vision-motion-touch observatory of human loco-manipulation built with a wearable system. With an emphasis on professiona

infographic.key_insight: EgoExplorer introduces a wearable, multi-modal dataset that captures human loco-manipulation as coordinated vision, motion, and touch events in real-world settings. This gives researchers a more complete view of how people move, stabilize, and interact with objects during tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of scalable, portable datasets that jointly capture locomotion, posture, and object interaction during human demonstrations. Existing datasets often miss one or more of these signals, making it hard to learn humanoid loco-manipulation from realistic in-situ behavior.
method: Built a wearable observatory system for collecting synchronized vision-motion-touch data during human loco-manipulation.
Recorded a 100-hour dataset spanning diverse environments and task contexts to improve realism and coverage.
Focused on capturing the coupled evolution of movement, body posture, and tactile/object interaction as tasks unfold.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this dataset provides richer supervision for training and evaluating humanoid robots and embodied agents in loco-manipulation. It can help improve policies that require coordinated perception, movement, and contact-rich interaction in everyday environments.

title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
authors: Xin Gao, Yifan Yang, Xin Li, Pan Wang, Yan Li
abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which gen

infographic.key_insight: AesCode improves aesthetic code generation by separating visual style learning from content fidelity, allowing models to produce more attractive and usable code-based artifacts. It bridges the gap between code models that understand structure and image models that understand design.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of generating visually appealing slides, posters, dashboards, and other rich visual artifacts as code without losing layout quality or misrepresenting the requested content.
method: Uses decoupled cross-modal rewards to separately optimize aesthetic quality and content correctness.
Leverages the strengths of code generation for structure and image-based feedback for visual design.
Targets generation of editable, verifiable visual artifacts while reducing common failures in spatial planning and rendering accuracy.
infographic.impact: This matters because practitioners can generate polished visual assets that remain editable and faithful to the prompt, making AI more useful for design-heavy workflows. It could improve automated slide creation, dashboard synthesis, and other content-rich generation tasks.

title: PixelMoE: Scaling Pixel-Space Diffusion with LLM-Style Mixture-of-Experts
authors: Ruixiao Dong, Jianmin Bao, Bozhi Luan, Zijie Meng, Xin Tao
abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models provide an appealing alternative to latent-space diffusion models by directly modeling raw images without relying on a learned tokenizer. However, scaling pixel-space models has predominantly followed dense strategies, tightly coupling model capacity with active computation. In this work, we show that standard LLM-style Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures can be effectively transferred to pixel-space diffusion. Building on this finding, we introduce PixelMoE, a pi

infographic.key_insight: PixelMoE shows that LLM-style Mixture-of-Experts can work effectively in pixel-space diffusion, letting these models scale capacity without making every inference step fully dense. In simple terms: you can make image diffusion bigger and stronger while only activating part of the model at a time.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the scaling bottleneck of pixel-space diffusion models, where increasing model capacity usually also increases active computation. This makes dense scaling expensive and limits efficiency compared with sparse expert-based designs.
method: Adapt standard LLM-style Mixture-of-Experts layers to pixel-space diffusion models.
Route image tokens/features to a subset of experts so only part of the network is active per step.
Build PixelMoE as a sparse, scalable diffusion architecture for raw-pixel generation.
infographic.impact: This matters because it offers a practical path to larger, more capable image diffusion models without proportional compute growth. For practitioners, it means better efficiency and a new architecture option for scaling high-quality pixel-level generative models.

title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
authors: Wenxuan Guo, Yingping Liang, Zhaoguo Wang, Ziyuan Li, Angyuan Ma
abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other dep

infographic.key_insight: LoopWAM shows that robot policies can improve from real deployment rollouts, not just expert demos, by learning from the full spectrum of outcomes: successes, partial failures, and outright failures. Instead of discarding bad data or copying everything blindly, it uses closed-loop learning to turn interaction consequences into training signal.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the limitation of imitation learning where expert demonstrations alone are insufficient for generalist robot policies to improve in the real world. It addresses the challenge of using noisy deployment rollouts without reinforcing poor actions or losing useful physical feedback from failed attempts.
method: Introduces a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from deployment rollouts.
Uses rollouts from both the policy itself and other policies, covering successes, suboptimal behaviors, and failures.
Trains on the full quality spectrum of interactions so the model can learn from action consequences rather than filtering them away.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a practical path to continual improvement after deployment using real robot experience. It can reduce dependence on expensive expert relabeling and make generalist policies more adaptable in complex, real-world settings.

title: What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study
authors: Mingxuan Yan, Litian Gong, Dihong Huang, Zhixu Li, Tianyu Zhang
abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Ac

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that not all ways of using demonstration quality help equally in VLA pretraining: the best gains come from choosing the right combination of weighting, filtering, or conditioning rather than simply using more data. It benchmarks these strategies across different reward definitions and label granularities to identify what actually transfers to downstream tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses how to exploit quality signals from suboptimal human demonstrations during vision-language-action pretraining so that models improve after fine-tuning on target tasks, instead of wasting noisy or low-value data.
method: Compare three quality-use strategies during pretraining: weighting demonstrations, filtering demonstrations, and conditioning the model on quality tags.
Evaluate these strategies across multiple reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations.
