title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
authors: Yuante Li, Junwei Quan, Kai Qiu, Kate Zhang, Yicheng Tao
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule p

infographic.key_insight: Larger rollout batches can make reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards learn more slowly per unit time, even if they preserve progress per sample. The paper’s “two clocks” view explains why the square-root batch/lr rule can still delay or align collapse and failure on schedule in multi-step training.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how to scale rollout batch size and learning rate in RLVR when model-generated responses are expensive. It explains the gap between theoretical progress-per-sample rules and practical multi-step training behavior, including slower learning and eventual collapse.
method: Introduces a two-clock framework that separates "progress time" from "collapse time" in RLVR training.
Analyzes training under a local quadratic approximation to understand how batch size and learning-rate scaling affect learning dynamics.
Uses the framework to interpret why square-root scaling can look stable in sample efficiency while still changing the wall-clock pace of learning and failure.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this provides a clearer rulebook for choosing batch sizes and learning rates in costly RLVR setups. It helps anticipate when larger batches will slow learning and when training may fail, improving scheduling, stability planning, and compute budgeting.

title: PLAYGROUND: Progressive Layout Generation with Render-Grounded Planning
authors: Jaeho Lee, Junhwan Heo, Junghyun Park, WonJun Moon, Eunju Yang
abstract: Generating editable graphic designs requires arranging visual and textual elements into a coherent composition while preserving their content and editability. Although recent MLLM-based approaches employ iterative generation and visual refinement to reflect the real-world design workflows, their high-level plans are predetermined prior to execution, limiting their adaptability as the design evolves. To address this limitation, we propose PlayGround, a progressive layout generation framework that

infographic.key_insight: PlayGround makes graphic layout generation more adaptive by planning progressively while looking at the rendered design, instead of locking in a fixed plan upfront. This helps layouts evolve in response to what the model has already created.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of generating editable graphic designs that stay coherent as visual and text elements are arranged, while avoiding rigid pre-planned workflows that cannot adapt during refinement.
method: Uses a progressive layout generation framework that builds designs step by step rather than all at once.
Grounds planning in rendered visual feedback, so later layout decisions can respond to the current state of the design.
Supports iterative generation and refinement to better match real design workflows while preserving editability.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this improves the practicality of design-generation systems by making them more flexible, interactive, and robust to changes during creation. It is especially useful for tools that need editable outputs and human-in-the-loop refinement.

title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
authors: Wenbo Hu, Shraman Pramanick, Krishna Kumar Singh, Nanyun Peng, Kai-Wei Chang
abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce

infographic.key_insight: Tev proposes a way to scale long-horizon agent training by turning sparse, hard-to-evaluate tasks into dense-progress learning problems. This gives open-source agents a more practical path to improving on hours- to days-long tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the lack of training data and effective rewards for long-horizon agentic tasks, where success is rare, verification is difficult, and scaling supervision is expensive.
method: Introduce Tev, an environment/training framework designed for long-horizon agentic tasks.
Use dense progress rewards instead of only end-of-task rewards to provide frequent learning signals.
Create a scalable recipe for generating, curating, and verifying complex tasks for agent training.
infographic.impact: This matters because it makes long-horizon agent training more feasible for open-source models. Practitioners can potentially build agents that learn more reliably on extended tasks with less dependence on sparse success signals.

title: Make It Flow: Animating Water in 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
authors: Kjell Keune, Florian Hahlbohm, Jannis Möller, Susana Castillo, Martin Eisemann
abstract: Explicit 3D scene representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently enabled high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. However, these methods assume static scenes, limiting realism in the presence of dynamic phenomena ubiquitous in real-world environments. While coherent motion (e.g., humans or vehicles) can be captured and reconstructed, high-frequency effects such as flowing water remain intractable under casual capture conditions, where dense multi-view, high-speed acquisi

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows how to animate flowing water in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, extending a typically static 3D representation to handle dynamic, high-frequency natural effects. In simple terms, it makes captured scenes look more realistic by letting water move convincingly in real time.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting on dynamic phenomena—especially fast, complex motion like water—under casual capture conditions where dense multi-view, high-speed data is unavailable.
method: Adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent dynamic water rather than treating the scene as fully static.
Uses a motion/animation strategy tailored to high-frequency fluid motion that is difficult to reconstruct directly from casual captures.
Preserves real-time rendering and novel-view synthesis quality while introducing plausible temporal changes in the water surface.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this expands the practical scope of neural scene representations from static environments to visually important dynamic effects. It improves realism in AR/VR, digital twins, robotics simulation, and content creation without requiring expensive capture setups.

title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark
authors: Xudong Cai, Ruijie Zhu, Haoliang Shang, Ruining Li, Marc Pollefeys
abstract: In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-fre

infographic.key_insight: This paper shifts 3D asset generation from making objects that only look correct to making articulated objects that also move and behave plausibly in the physical world. The proposed Artisan pipeline adds multi-agent coordination and simulation feedback to improve geometry, appearance, and functional articulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Current 3D generation methods often produce visually plausible objects but fail to capture physical realism, especially for articulated assets like doors, drawers, tools, or machinery. The paper addresses the gap between static appearance and physically grounded motion/functionality.
method: Builds on Articraft with a multi-agent generation pipeline for articulated 3D assets.
Uses physical simulation feedback to refine and validate motion, articulation, and interaction behavior.
Targets richer asset quality beyond geometry and appearance, including collision-free and physically plausible articulation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables more useful 3D assets for robotics, simulation, gaming, and digital twins, where motion and physical interaction matter as much as visual quality. It also provides a benchmark-oriented direction for evaluating generative 3D systems on functional realism, not just shape fidelity.

title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation
authors: Xiaomeng Ye, Krishna Jaganathan, Gyubeum Lim, Gunjan Chhablani, Muhammad Zubair Irshad
abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $π_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy

infographic.key_insight: Splat2Act personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific home or office using captured scene data, avoiding the need for expensive in-environment demonstrations. It bridges the gap between generalist manipulation policies and real-world deployment in user-specific spaces.
infographic.problem_solved: Generalist robot manipulation policies can fail completely in new, personalized environments because they do not know the layout, objects, and geometry of each user’s space. Collecting real demonstrations for every deployment scene is costly and impractical.
method: Capture the target environment and build a scene representation for simulation.
Use an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline to adapt a pretrained VLA policy to the user’s specific setting.
Transfer the personalized policy back to the real world for manipulation tasks like picking up objects from shelves, counters, and tables.
infographic.impact: This approach makes it more practical to deploy generalist robot policies in everyday environments without collecting large amounts of robot data on-site. For practitioners, it offers a scalable path toward personalized robot manipulation in homes and offices.

title: Revisiting the Task of Building Damage Assessment by Satellite Imaging
authors: Anthony Cioppa, Virgile Blua, Sébastien Piérard, Pietro Ceccato, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
abstract: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, tropical storms, and floods cause extensive damage to buildings, and rapid, reliable damage maps are essential to guide emergency response. Automating this task, referred to as building damage assessment (BDA), from satellite imagery, has become an active research topic at the intersection of remote sensing, computer vision, and machine learning, particularly since supervised deep learning methods were shown to outperform earlier handcrafted approaches. Yet

infographic.key_insight: This paper revisits building damage assessment (BDA) from satellite imagery and positions it as a practical AI problem for rapid post-disaster response. The key message is that modern supervised deep learning has made BDA far more effective than handcrafted methods, but the field still needs careful benchmarking and clearer task design.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of automatically identifying and mapping building damage after natural disasters using satellite images, so emergency teams can quickly estimate impact and prioritize response.
method: Reviews and re-examines the BDA task through the lens of recent deep learning advances.
Frames the problem at the intersection of remote sensing, computer vision, and machine learning.
Highlights how supervised models improve damage mapping compared with earlier handcrafted feature-based approaches.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work clarifies a high-stakes real-world application where model accuracy and speed directly affect disaster response. It also helps researchers understand the evolving benchmarks and assumptions behind satellite-based damage assessment.

title: Can Language Models Learn When to Abstain? Policy Learning and Calibrated Answer Selection
authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita Córdova-Esparza, Ruben Gomez, Carlos Miranda Rocha, Julio-Alejandro Romero-González
abstract: A useful language model should know when to answer and when to say "I don't know." Can we improve that decision by training the model itself or by training a separate component to check its answers? We study both approaches on Qwen3-14B for factual questions, using a score that rewards correct answers, penalizes mistakes, and allows abstention. Across three training seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds, a learned answer selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the original model

infographic.key_insight: Language models can be made better at knowing when to answer and when to abstain. In this study, a learned answer selector outperformed the base model by improving threshold-averaged utility on factual QA.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of calibration: helping a language model decide whether it is confident enough to answer or should say "I don't know" to avoid harmful mistakes.
method: Evaluate two strategies on Qwen3-14B: training the model to abstain directly versus training a separate component to select answers.
Use a utility-based score that rewards correct answers, penalizes wrong answers, and permits abstention.
Compare performance across three training seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds to test robustness and calibration.
infographic.impact: This work gives AI practitioners a practical path to reduce overconfident errors in factual QA systems. It is especially useful for deploying LLMs in settings where reliability and uncertainty awareness matter more than always answering.

title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
authors: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou
abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed c

infographic.key_insight: MC-EvoBench introduces a controlled way to test whether Minecraft agents truly learn reusable skills from experience, rather than just carrying over memories, resources, or lucky outcomes. It focuses on measuring genuine capability growth across tasks and worlds.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating recursive self-improvement in embodied agents: distinguishing real skill acquisition from superficial performance gains caused by saved state, unequal task exposure, or early execution failures.
method: Build MC-EvoBench, a controlled Minecraft evaluation benchmark designed to isolate experience-driven improvement.
Compare agent behavior across repeated and later tasks to determine whether gains transfer beyond the original world or context.
Separate capability change from confounders such as carried-over resources, prior exposure differences, and failures that happen before learning can occur.
infographic.impact: This benchmark gives researchers a more reliable way to audit whether agents are actually improving through experience. For AI/ML practitioners working on embodied agents, it helps prevent misleading conclusions from evaluations that overstate learning.

title: Designing Protein Structures from Natural Language
authors: Joseph Lee, Yanjing Li, Bo Qiang, Gregory Lau, Allyson Ettinger
abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a pa

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces Prompteina, a protein design model that can generate all-atom structures from natural language instructions. Instead of requiring a separate input format for each design goal, it lets users describe desired properties in plain text, making protein design more flexible and intuitive.
infographic.problem_solved: De novo protein design often depends on specialized representations for each structural or functional objective, which limits the range of design tasks a model can support. This work addresses the need for a more general, user-friendly way to specify protein design goals.
method: Build Prompteina, an all-atom protein structure generation model conditioned on natural language prompts.
Create Prompteina-Data to train the model on text-to-structure examples spanning broader design objectives.
Enable prompt-based control over protein properties, similar to text-to-image generation systems.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how generative models can move from narrow task-specific inputs to flexible natural-language control. It opens the door to more accessible and extensible protein design workflows for research and biotechnology applications.

title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems
authors: Yeonsung Jung, Zhiyuan Wang, Zifan Wang, Vítor Albiero, Benjamin Newman
abstract: Personal agents increasingly connect to services across the web and applications by using tools. As the effects of their actions accumulate and interact across services, unintended or harmful outcomes can arise when agents fulfill benign user requests. Proactively identifying these compositional failures requires systematically exploring diverse cross-service paths. Existing red-teaming methods often simply prompt LLMs to identify potentially harmful paths from task and environment descriptions

infographic.key_insight: X-AgentRed shows that red-teaming personal agents should not rely on static prompts alone: harmful behavior often emerges from how actions compose across multiple services over time. The paper focuses on systematically searching these cross-service paths to uncover failures that simple task descriptions miss.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of detecting unintended or harmful outcomes in personal agents that operate across many web and app services. The core issue is compositional failure, where individually benign actions combine into unsafe end states.
method: Systematically explores diverse cross-service action paths rather than only asking an LLM to imagine risks from descriptions.
Targets evolving multi-service ecosystems where agent actions accumulate and interact across tools and platforms.
Red-teams personal agents by searching for sequences that reveal unintended outcomes from otherwise benign user requests.
infographic.impact: This helps AI/ML practitioners evaluate agents more realistically in connected environments where small mistakes can cascade into serious failures. It provides a better way to test safety before deploying agents that can act across many services.

title: LapMerge: Differentiable Exact-Budget Token Merging in Linear Time
authors: Magdalena Trędowicz, Aleksandra Nowak, Tomasz Steifer, Łukasz Struski, Szymon Płotka
abstract: Modern vision and language models process ever longer token sequences, and reducing them is the main lever on downstream cost. Token compression, however, faces a fundamental trade-off: selecting tokens discards information, while existing merging methods preserve it only through pairwise token-to-token matching or $MN$ token-to-output interactions. We introduce LapMerge, a differentiable merging operator that resolves this trade-off for ordered sequences: a learned mass distribution partitions

infographic.key_insight: LapMerge introduces a differentiable token-merging method that can reduce sequence length while preserving information under an exact budget. It does this in linear time for ordered sequences, making token compression more practical for long-context models.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high cost of processing long token sequences in vision and language models. Existing token reduction methods either discard information when selecting tokens or rely on expensive pairwise/token-to-output interactions when merging.
method: Uses a learned mass distribution over an ordered token sequence to partition tokens for merging.
Provides a differentiable merging operator that preserves information better than hard token selection.
Achieves exact-budget compression in linear time, avoiding the quadratic costs common in prior merging approaches.
infographic.impact: LapMerge can help reduce inference and training cost for models that handle long sequences, especially in vision and language tasks. For practitioners, it offers a more efficient way to compress tokens without giving up as much information as traditional pruning or merging methods.

title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
authors: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu, Hao Xiao, Shuhan Xue
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks g

infographic.key_insight: RSI-Anything proposes a general framework for turning interaction experience into lasting system improvements using predictive world models. It combines observed feedback with selective model updates so the system can keep improving even when external supervision is limited.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses two core RSI challenges: costly external feedback and the risk that world-model predictions become unreliable as the policy changes over time.
method: Builds on JEPA-Anything to use predictive world models for guiding actions and selecting learning data.
Uses observed feedback to improve the policy or workflow and, when appropriate, adapt the world model conditionally.
Adds component and compatibility checks to reduce mismatch between evolving policies and model predictions.

title: On the Design Space of Continuous Diffusion Language Models
authors: Oscar Davis, Daan Roos, Alice Bizeul, Amitis Shidani, Victor Turrisi
abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) promise to bring the benefits of continuous flow modelling to language, including accelerated sampling and controllable generation. The field has grown rapidly, and the capabilities of CDLMs have begun to rival those of discrete diffusion. Yet, unlike for continuous modalities such as images or videos, our grasp of the levers that matter when training CDLMs remains limited. In this work, we focus on two of these levers, namely self-conditioning and em

infographic.key_insight: This paper maps out key design choices in continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs), showing that training performance depends strongly on specific levers such as self-conditioning. It helps clarify how to make continuous diffusion more competitive, controllable, and efficient for language generation.
infographic.problem_solved: CDLMs are promising, but researchers still lack a clear understanding of which training and architectural choices actually matter most. The paper addresses this gap by studying the design space and identifying the most influential factors for improving CDLM performance.
method: Systematically analyze the CDLM design space with a focus on self-conditioning and related training levers.
Compare how different settings affect model quality, sampling behavior, and controllability.
Use empirical evaluation to identify which choices improve continuous diffusion language modeling most effectively.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work provides a clearer roadmap for building stronger CDLMs without relying on trial-and-error. It can help accelerate progress toward faster and more controllable language generation systems.

title: TabMF: Learning Dataset Representations with Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Rafiq Kamel, Nicolas Atienza, Aziz Fouché, Nicola Cancedda, Josif Grabocka
abstract: Representations of supervised datasets support higher-level machine-learning tasks such as dataset retrieval and distribution-shift monitoring. However, existing approaches typically rely either on hand-crafted meta-features or on dataset encoders trained specifically for representation learning. We introduce TabMF, a framework that repurposes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) as encoders of supervised datasets. TabMF equips a predictive TFM with an architecture-aware dataset-level rea

infographic.key_insight: TabMF shows that pretrained tabular foundation models can be reused as strong dataset encoders, turning a model built for prediction into a representation learner for whole supervised datasets. This gives a more scalable alternative to hand-crafted meta-features or separately trained dataset-embedding models.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of effective, general-purpose representations for supervised datasets needed for tasks like dataset retrieval, similarity search, and distribution-shift monitoring. Existing methods often depend on manual feature engineering or specialized encoders that do not leverage large pretrained tabular models.
method: Repurpose pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) as dataset encoders instead of using them only for prediction.
Add an architecture-aware dataset-level representation mechanism to aggregate information from tabular samples into a single dataset embedding.
Use the resulting embeddings for higher-level dataset understanding tasks such as retrieval and monitoring.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, TabMF offers a practical way to generate meaningful dataset embeddings without designing meta-features from scratch. This can improve workflow for benchmarking, data discovery, and monitoring changes in real-world tabular data pipelines.

title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models
authors: Bahey Tharwat, Iman Nematollahi, Marvin Alles, Xingyuan Zhang, Akshay L Chandra
abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering mo

infographic.key_insight: This paper tackles continual learning for robot policies by using world models to steer a frozen generalist policy across tasks without repeatedly rewriting the policy itself. The core idea is to preserve earlier skills while still adapting to new tasks, reducing catastrophic forgetting in sequential robot learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Generalist robot policies improve from reinforcement learning, but fine-tuning causes forgetting of prior tasks and steering-based methods can still shift forgetting into shared steering modules. This work addresses how to continually adapt robot policies to new tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones.
method: Use a frozen generative robot policy rather than fully fine-tuning policy weights for each new task.
Train or leverage a world model to provide task-aware steering signals that guide the policy during execution or adaptation.
Apply continual/ sequential task adaptation so the system can learn new behaviors while minimizing degradation on previously learned tasks.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a path toward more scalable robot learning systems that can keep improving over time without expensive retraining from scratch. It is especially relevant for long-horizon deployment settings where robots must handle new tasks while retaining old capabilities.

title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
authors: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai
abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to

infographic.key_insight: SpatialASM argues that strong spatial reasoning in AI depends on Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM): proactively revisiting a scene from relevant viewpoints and rebuilding the spatial layout in mind. The paper introduces a scalable framework to internalize this human-like strategy in LVLMs.
infographic.problem_solved: Current large vision-language models struggle with complex spatial reasoning because they do not naturally re-imagine scenes from task-relevant perspectives. This work targets the gap between human-like mental reconstruction and model behavior in spatial tasks.
method: Introduces SpatialASM, a framework designed to teach LVLMs Active Spatial Mentalization for spatial reasoning.
Encourages viewpoint switching and internal scene reconstruction before answering spatial questions.
Aims to scale the process so it can be evaluated and applied across challenging spatial reasoning tasks.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests a path to improve LVLM performance on tasks requiring viewpoint awareness, object relations, and spatial transformations. It may lead to more reliable multimodal systems for robotics, navigation, and embodied AI.

title: Images Talk Back: Guiding MMDiTs by Suppressing Image-to-Text Feedback
authors: Yucheng Yang, Xiaoxiao Sun, Shusheng Yang, Jiakang Chen, Serena Yeung-Levy
abstract: Multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs) allow the evolving image to update internal text representations through joint attention. These representations then guide subsequent image updates, raising a question: does this feedback help correct deviations from the prompt, or preserve them? We find that image-to-text (I2T) feedback can preserve the objects and attributes already represented in the evolving image, including errors. Transplanting I2T messages can rescue failures or disrupt successes

infographic.key_insight: In multimodal diffusion transformers, image-to-text feedback does not always correct mistakes—it can also preserve them. The paper shows that the evolving image can feed back into text representations in ways that lock in both correct content and errors, and that transplanting these feedback messages can either rescue or ruin generations.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the unclear role of image-to-text feedback in MMDiTs: whether it helps the model recover from prompt deviations or unintentionally reinforces them during image generation.
method: Analyze the joint attention mechanism in MMDiTs to study how evolving image features update internal text representations.
Examine image-to-text feedback as a communication pathway that preserves objects and attributes already present in the image state.
Transplant image-to-text messages between generation runs to test whether the feedback can correct failures or propagate errors.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work reveals a previously underappreciated source of generation bias in multimodal diffusion models. Understanding and controlling image-to-text feedback could improve prompt adherence, reduce error reinforcement, and enable more reliable image synthesis.

title: Can machines reason non-verbally?
authors: Shaheer U. Saeed, Zion Tse, Gregory Slabaugh, Daniel C. Alexander, Yipeng Hu
abstract: Modern machines can solve equations, follow logic and reason through language, yet they still struggle with problems that require visual non-verbal reasoning. This is evident even in advanced systems such as DeepSeek, ChatGPT and Gemini, which remain limited on visual tasks such as completing abstract patterns or delineating ambiguous regions-of-interest. Unlike explicit intermediate steps in verbal reasoning which can be verified through logic or automated tests, visual reasoning involves impli

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that current AI systems are strong at language-based reasoning but still lack robust non-verbal, visual reasoning abilities. It highlights the gap between solving verbal logic and interpreting abstract or ambiguous visual patterns.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of whether machines can reason without language, especially on visual tasks like abstract pattern completion and identifying ambiguous regions of interest.
method: Analyzes the limitations of modern AI models on non-verbal visual reasoning tasks.
Contrasts explicit verbal reasoning steps with implicit visual reasoning processes that are harder to verify.
Frames visual reasoning as a distinct capability gap that requires new evaluation and modeling approaches.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work emphasizes that language competence does not imply general reasoning ability. It motivates better benchmarks and model designs for vision-based reasoning, beyond text-centric evaluation.

title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
authors: Danil Rudenko, Georgii Bulgakov, Nikolay Kartashev, Ivan Rubachev, Daniil Krasylnikov
abstract: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives

infographic.key_insight: This paper systematically re-checks which loss functions actually help deep regression on tabular data, instead of assuming Mean Squared Error is always the best default. It also shows that the widely used practice of global early stopping has important limits that can distort comparisons across objectives.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the lack of a fair, apples-to-apples comparison of regression objectives for tabular deep learning. Prior results were hard to trust because studies used different datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols.
method: Re-evaluate multiple regression objectives under a controlled, standardized benchmark setup.
Compare objectives across the same datasets, model backbones, and training/evaluation protocol.
Analyze the interaction between objective choice and global early stopping to isolate its effect on reported performance.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this helps identify when switching away from MSE is worthwhile and when it is not. It also encourages more reliable benchmarking, reducing the risk of overestimating gains from new regression losses.

title: InstantFusion: A Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators
authors: Xuanlang Dai, Jiazi Bu, Yujie Zhou, Yuhong Liu, Beichen Zhang
abstract: Diffusion/flow models have emerged as the de facto paradigms for image generation, giving rise to a diverse family of modern generators with increasingly heterogeneous architectures and representations. Despite their remarkable generation capabilities, the cross-model alignment of latent representations and the consistency of their underlying denoising dynamics remain underexplored. In this work, we uncover an intriguing cross-model compatibility: independently trained generators exhibit similar

infographic.key_insight: InstantFusion suggests that independently trained image generators can share compatible latent structures and denoising behavior, even when their architectures and representations differ. This opens the door to a shared latent interface that can connect heterogeneous models without fully retraining them.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of cross-model alignment between modern image generators, where different diffusion/flow models use incompatible latent spaces and denoising dynamics. This makes it difficult to transfer capabilities, compare models, or build unified systems across generators.
method: Identify and analyze latent compatibility across independently trained image generators.
Propose a shared latent interface that aligns heterogeneous generators in a common representational space.
Leverage consistent denoising dynamics to enable interoperability between models.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this could simplify model integration, enable reuse of generative capabilities across architectures, and reduce the need to train separate pipelines for each generator. It may also improve model comparison, composition, and deployment in multi-model generation systems.

title: OmniCapBench: A Deep-Structured Evaluation Framework for Fine-Grained Audio-Visual Captioning
authors: Zhongyu Yang, Jiale Tao, Ruitao Chen, Zuhao Yang, Yingfang Yuan
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly evolving toward continuous audio--visual reasoning, creating an urgent need for evaluations that expose their capability limits. Audio--visual captioning is an ideal diagnostic task, yet current benchmarks face a coupled trade-off: whole-caption scores provide coverage without localization, local probes provide localization without coverage, and unconstrained LLM judges introduce instability. We introduce OmniCapBench (Omni-Video Caption Bench

infographic.key_insight: OmniCapBench proposes a more precise way to evaluate audio-visual captioning by combining broad coverage with fine-grained localization. It helps reveal where multimodal models succeed or fail, instead of only giving a single overall score.
infographic.problem_solved: Current audio-visual caption benchmarks force a trade-off between global evaluation and local diagnosis: whole-caption metrics miss detail, local probes miss coverage, and LLM-based judges can be unstable. This paper addresses the need for a benchmark that can expose fine-grained capability limits in multimodal large language models.
method: Introduces OmniCapBench, a deep-structured evaluation framework for fine-grained audio-visual captioning.
Designs evaluation that balances whole-caption coverage with localized assessment of specific audio-visual details.
Uses a more structured benchmark setup to reduce reliance on unconstrained LLM judging and improve evaluation consistency.
infographic.impact: This benchmark gives researchers and practitioners a clearer diagnostic tool for understanding multimodal model behavior. It can guide better model development, targeted debugging, and more reliable comparison across systems.

title: Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization
authors: Hanyang Li, Shao Tang, Daniel Thomas Braithwaite, Gregory Dexter, Leonardo Neves
abstract: Quantizing AdamW's optimizer states reduces persistent storage, but quantization errors propagate through the moment recurrences and perturb subsequent adaptive updates. We redesign 4-bit optimizer-state quantization for AdamW from the perspective of \emph{rounding space}: the coordinate in which a quantizer chooses between adjacent reconstruction levels. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes 4-bit AdamW optimizer-state quantization in terms of "rounding space"—the decision space a quantizer uses to pick nearby reconstruction levels. This reveals that for the second moment, being locally close in mean error is not always enough to guarantee stable adaptive updates.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of compressing AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit precision without letting quantization noise accumulate through the moment recurrences and degrade training quality.
method: Analyze AdamW quantization from the perspective of rounding space rather than only reconstruction error.
Study the second-moment update locally near the zero-adjacent quantization cell to characterize how quantization errors propagate.
Redesign the 4-bit optimizer-state quantizer to better preserve the adaptive update dynamics of AdamW.
infographic.impact: This can make low-memory training more practical by reducing optimizer-state storage while maintaining better training stability and accuracy. It is especially relevant for large-scale model training where optimizer memory is a major bottleneck.

title: LEGO: A Lifting-Free Approach for Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
authors: Suhwan Cho, Yonwoo Choi, Soongjin Kim, Jicheol Park, Taegyu Lim
abstract: Generating an egocentric video from a single exocentric recording is a challenging case of novel view synthesis, as the two cameras share little overlap and much of the target view is unobserved. Current state-of-the-art methods reconstruct the scene explicitly by estimating depth, lifting the video into a point cloud, and re-rendering it from the egocentric camera to condition a video diffusion model. This deterministic mapping assigns each pixel to a single reprojected location, which preserve

infographic.key_insight: LEGO proposes a lifting-free way to generate egocentric video from a single exocentric recording, avoiding explicit 3D reconstruction. Instead of deterministically projecting pixels into a point cloud, it uses a more flexible conditioning strategy that better handles missing/occluded content.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles exocentric-to-egocentric video generation, where the source and target viewpoints have little overlap and large parts of the egocentric view are not directly visible in the input.
method: Removes the need for explicit depth estimation and point-cloud lifting used in prior pipelines.
Directly conditions a video diffusion model without re-rendering the scene through a reconstructed 3D representation.
Uses a lifting-free formulation to better preserve uncertainty and handle unobserved regions in the target view.
infographic.impact: This matters because it simplifies the pipeline and can improve robustness when viewpoint overlap is low. For practitioners, it offers a promising alternative to brittle reconstruction-based methods in view synthesis and video generation.

title: Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception
authors: Oskar J. Hollinsworth, Alex F. Spies, Tigist Diriba, Adam Gleave, Chris Cundy
abstract: Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and show

infographic.key_insight: Probes can effectively detect sabotage and hidden deception in LLM agents, even in frontier-style monitoring settings. The paper shows that white-box monitoring can scale up with a large deception dataset and a new probe architecture that aggregates signals across many layers and tokens.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how to monitor LLM agents for deceptive behavior and sabotage, especially when the model does not explicitly verbalize its intent. This is a major challenge for safely deploying powerful AI systems.
method: Collected the largest deception dataset to date for training white-box probes.
Designed a novel probe architecture that combines information across many layers and tokens.
Evaluated the approach in SHADE-Arena and compared it against a strong Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline.
infographic.impact: This work suggests that internal model signals can reveal deception more reliably than text-only monitoring. For AI safety and ML practitioners, it offers a practical direction for building stronger oversight tools for advanced agents.

title: DreamTrue: Action-Faithful Robot World Model with Counterfactual Post-Training
authors: Junyan Li, Ruizhi Li, Yu Liu, Xiangshuo Liu, Mingchao Sun
abstract: We present DreamTrue, a multi-view, cross-embodiment robot world model for action-faithful and physically plausible video prediction. Training such a model on existing robot datasets faces two obstacles: imprecise calibration can impair action following, while limited coverage of unsuccessful interactions can bias predictions toward successful outcomes. To improve action following across embodiments, we render action trajectories into image-space conditions and introduce offline geometric calibr

infographic.key_insight: DreamTrue makes robot world models follow actions more faithfully by turning action trajectories into image-space guidance and correcting calibration issues offline. It also learns from counterfactual post-training so predictions remain physically plausible even for failed or unusual interactions.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing robot video prediction models often struggle with inaccurate action following due to poor calibration across embodiments, and they tend to over-predict successful outcomes because training data contains too few failed interactions.
method: Render action trajectories into image-space conditions so the model can better align predicted motion with commanded actions across different robot embodiments.
Apply offline geometric calibration to reduce calibration errors and improve action-faithful prediction.
Use counterfactual post-training to expose the model to alternative, failure-like outcomes, improving robustness and physical realism.
Train a multi-view, cross-embodiment robot world model for video prediction that is both action-faithful and physically plausible.
infographic.impact: This work can improve robot planning, simulation, and policy learning by making predicted future scenes more trustworthy. For practitioners, it means better model-based robotics systems that generalize across robots and handle failures more realistically.

title: A Balanced Data Diet: Addressing the Exploration Bottleneck in Mega-Scale RL for Robot Control
authors: Octi Zhang, Mateo Guaman Castro, Patrick Yin, Ignacio Dagnino, Abhishek Gupta
abstract: General-purpose robots must perform a wide range of tasks from agile locomotion to dexterous manipulation. While sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has proven to be a useful tool for this goal, current RL pipelines depend on engineering-heavy, per-task structural priors such as shaped rewards and demonstrations. Recent work has shown that diverse simulator resets, combined with massively parallel simulation, can alleviate much of this engineering burden on several manipulation problems. How

infographic.key_insight: Mega-scale reinforcement learning for robot control is bottlenecked less by model capacity and more by the quality and balance of training data. The paper argues that diverse resets and a carefully balanced data diet can replace much of the task-specific engineering usually needed for sim-to-real robot learning.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the exploration bottleneck in large-scale robot RL: agents often fail to discover useful behaviors without hand-designed rewards, demonstrations, or other structural priors, especially across diverse control tasks like locomotion and manipulation.
method: Use massively parallel simulation with diverse environment resets to broaden exploration without relying on task-specific reward shaping.
Replace heavy per-task engineering with a balanced sampling strategy that keeps training data diverse and prevents the agent from overfitting to narrow state distributions.
Leverage mega-scale RL to learn general-purpose robot behaviors that can transfer from simulation to real robots.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more scalable path to robot learning: less manual reward design, fewer demonstrations, and better reuse of large simulation budgets. It points toward more general-purpose robot policies that can be trained efficiently across many tasks.

title: Hybrid Cinematography: Previsualizing and Managing Hallucination Risk in Generative Video Reshooting
authors: Nhan,  Tran, Neal Wadhwa, Abe Davis, Stefan Stojanov
abstract: On a film set, the camera move is committed during a take. Generative video reshooting lets filmmakers change it afterward, but may require hallucinating unrecorded content, a gap sometimes discovered only after leaving the set. We present Hybrid Cinematography, a workflow that bridges physical capture and generative reshooting to manage hallucination risk while filmmakers can still act on it. Using an editable 3D shot plan and a proxy of the take, our previsualization evaluates hallucination ri

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid Cinematography combines physical filming with generative video reshooting so directors can preview and manage hallucination risk before it becomes a costly problem. It turns a post-production uncertainty into something that can be evaluated and addressed while the crew is still on set.
infographic.problem_solved: Generative video reshooting can require inventing unseen or unrecorded content, and those hallucination gaps are often discovered too late, after leaving the set. This paper addresses the need to detect and mitigate that risk during production.
method: Uses an editable 3D shot plan to represent the intended camera move and scene structure.
Combines the shot plan with a proxy of the actual take to previsualize how reshooting will behave.
Evaluates hallucination risk during previsualization so filmmakers can adjust the plan while changes are still possible.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how generative video tools can be integrated into real production workflows with risk-aware feedback loops. It provides a practical framework for making generative systems more usable, controllable, and production-ready.

title: VersaCamVLA: Camera-Configurable VLA Policies for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Boyao Han, Chen Shi, Jingjing Qian, ZhuoTan Tian, Li Jiang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful foundations for robotic manipulation, but their reliance on fixed camera configurations during training makes them brittle to changes in camera count or pose during deployment. To overcome these limitations, we propose VersaCamVLA, a camera-configurable framework that decouples camera-set representation from action learning. VersaCamVLA learns a unified scene-token interface that maps an arbitrary, variable set of posed RGB views into

infographic.key_insight: VersaCamVLA makes robotic VLA policies adaptable to changing camera setups, instead of depending on one fixed training configuration. It learns a camera-agnostic scene representation so the same policy can work across different numbers, positions, and poses of cameras.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard VLA models for robotic manipulation are brittle when the camera configuration changes at deployment. This includes changes in camera count, viewpoint, or pose that were not seen during training.
method: Decouples camera-set representation from action prediction, so visual input handling is separated from control learning.
Learns a unified scene-token interface that converts an arbitrary set of posed RGB views into a consistent representation.
Uses this camera-configurable representation to support variable sensor setups without retraining a separate policy for each camera arrangement.
infographic.impact: This helps researchers and practitioners deploy manipulation policies in real-world robotics settings where camera setups are rarely fixed. It improves robustness and flexibility, reducing the need for expensive reconfiguration-specific training.

title: BrickBench: Evaluating Agentic Brick Design
authors: Peter Kulits, Yiqing Xu, R. Kenny Jones, Cordelia Schmid, Jiajun Wu
abstract: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding

infographic.key_insight: BrickBench introduces a new way to test whether an AI agent can design LEGO-like structures that are not only semantically on prompt, but also physically buildable. It highlights the need to jointly evaluate creativity, constraint reasoning, and real-world assembly validity.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap in evaluating agentic design systems for text-conditioned LEGO assembly. Existing benchmarks often miss whether generated designs are both aligned with the prompt and physically feasible under discrete part constraints.
method: Defines BrickBench, a benchmark with prompts that require agents to produce valid, buildable brick assemblies from a discrete part library.
Evaluates designs across three settings that vary in scale and part availability to test robustness under different constraints.
Scores outputs on three dimensions: validity, alignment to the text prompt, and overall design quality.
Provides BrickAgent, an environment for coding and testing agentic brick-design solutions.
infographic.impact: BrickBench gives researchers a clearer target for building agents that plan under combinatorial and physical constraints. For practitioners, it provides a practical evaluation framework for assessing whether generative design systems can succeed beyond surface-level text matching.

title: Dex-One2Many: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from a Single Human Demonstration
authors: Jusuk Lee, Sungha Kim, Yeonsoo Park, Jonguk Cheon, Yoonkyo Jung
abstract: While learning dexterous manipulation from a single human video offers a promising alternative to costly robot demonstrations, many recent methods predominantly imitate demonstrated motions. Such strict motion matching often limits generalization to initial object poses, goal poses, and grasps not shown in the video. Alternatively, discovering a policy via reinforcement learning (RL) allows for broad generalization, but without prior guidance, it struggles with high-dimensional exploration in co

infographic.key_insight: Dex-One2Many learns dexterous manipulation from just one human demonstration, but avoids overfitting to that single motion by using it as guidance rather than a strict template. This helps the policy generalize to new object poses, goals, and grasps.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of learning dexterous robot manipulation when only a single human video is available. Existing imitation methods often copy motions too rigidly, while RL alone is too hard to train from scratch in high-dimensional action spaces.
method: Use one human demonstration as weak prior guidance instead of exact motion matching.
Combine imitation-style initialization with reinforcement learning to discover better manipulation behaviors.
Aim for one-to-many generalization: one demo, many valid robot trajectories and grasps.
infographic.impact: This approach reduces the need for expensive robot demonstrations and makes dexterous manipulation learning more practical. For practitioners, it offers a path to train more adaptable manipulation policies from very limited demonstration data.

title: What 30,000 Hours of Ego-centric Video Does Not Teach
authors: Jiahua Dong, Anurag Bagchi, Yash Jangir, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov
abstract: World models offer a promising alternative to physics-based simulators, yet remain far from practical deployment. We ask how far scaling ego-centric human video takes them, using a dataset of 30,000 hours spanning over 1,000 scene types and 14,000 contributors. Rather than relying on opaque downstream metrics, we directly evaluate agent and object-interaction fidelity on a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark. Increasing training data by 100x improves both, but unevenly: the agent is modele

infographic.key_insight: Scaling ego-centric video to 30,000 hours does improve world-model fidelity, but the gains are uneven: the agent representation improves faster than object-interaction understanding. In short, more video helps, but it does not automatically teach robust, general physical interaction.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper asks whether massive ego-centric human video can serve as a practical substitute for physics simulators when building world models, especially for out-of-distribution scenes and interactions.
method: Train/evaluate world models using 30,000 hours of ego-centric video spanning 1,000+ scene types and 14,000 contributors.
Measure performance directly on a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark instead of relying only on downstream proxy metrics.
Compare how scaling data affects two capabilities: agent fidelity and object-interaction fidelity.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this paper clarifies the limits of data scaling for world models and shows where additional data still falls short. It helps researchers choose better evaluation targets and reveals that object dynamics may need new model designs, not just more video.

title: CSF: Contextual Safety Filtering for Motion Generators
authors: Lizhi Yang, Yiling Hou, Yao Tang, Junheng Li, Daniel Weng
abstract: Text-conditioned motion generators produce trackable whole-body motion, but they have no notion of scene-dependent safety: the same action may target an object or a person. Existing safeguards either inspect the prompt, require labeled motion data, or enforce geometric constraints; therefore, they do not directly account for how scene context changes a motion's meaning. We introduce contextual safety filtering (CSF), a training-free filter that grounds natural-language safety rules in safe and u

infographic.key_insight: Contextual Safety Filtering (CSF) adds scene awareness to motion generators, so the same movement can be judged differently depending on what is nearby or who is present. It filters unsafe motions without retraining the generator by grounding safety rules in the current context.
infographic.problem_solved: Text-conditioned motion generators can produce motions that are technically correct but unsafe in a specific scene, because they do not understand context-dependent meaning. Existing safety methods rely on prompts, labeled motion data, or fixed geometry rules, and they do not directly model how the surrounding scene changes safety.
method: Uses a training-free filtering stage rather than retraining the motion generator.
Grounds natural-language safety rules in the current scene context to decide whether a generated motion is safe.
Filters motion outputs based on contextual interpretation, not just the action text or generic spatial constraints.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, CSF offers a practical way to add safety checks to motion generation systems without expensive reannotation or model retraining. This is especially useful for interactive or real-world applications where the same motion may be safe in one scene and unsafe in another.

title: WorldGuide: Goal-Directed Video World Model for Procedural Task Execution
authors: Ankan Deria, Komal Kumar, Hisham Cholakkal, Fahad Shahbaz Khan, Salman Khan
abstract: Video generators and video-based world models can synthesize plausible visual trajectories, but long-horizon procedural tasks require generation to adapt to what has actually been produced. A model must determine the next action from its generated state, execute that action, and recognize when the task is complete. Open-loop generation cannot adapt to execution outcomes, while existing closed-loop systems often rely on pretrained executors or indirect verification. This leaves a gap between deci

infographic.key_insight: WorldGuide turns video generation into a closed-loop, goal-directed process: it does not just predict the next frame sequence, it decides the next action from the current generated state, executes it, and checks whether the task is finished. This makes long-horizon procedural task execution more adaptive and reliable than open-loop video generation.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between plausible video synthesis and actual task completion in long-horizon procedural workflows. Existing open-loop models cannot react to their own outputs, while many closed-loop methods depend on pretrained executors or indirect verification rather than a unified goal-directed world model.
method: Build a video world model that conditions generation on the current generated state and task goal.
Use a closed-loop cycle of action selection, execution, and completion checking to adapt to outcomes.
Support procedural tasks where each next step depends on what the model has already generated.
Reduce reliance on external executors or weak proxy signals for verifying progress.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more practical framework for agentic video generation and procedural planning, especially when tasks require feedback-aware execution over long horizons. It can improve robustness in simulation, robotics-like settings, and interactive content generation.

title: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems
authors: Anna Zimmel, Fleur Hendriks, Markus Holzleitner, Florian Sestak, Martin Weichselbaumer
abstract: Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems, from structural buckling to fluid and climate dynamics, yet they remain largely unexplored in deep learning. At a symmetry-breaking bifurcation, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption underlying most learned physical surrogates. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through la

infographic.key_insight: Bi-FORK tackles bifurcation problems where one input can lead to multiple valid outcomes, instead of forcing a single prediction. It learns the full set of possible trajectories in high-dimensional systems, capturing symmetry-breaking behavior that standard surrogates miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Most deep learning surrogates assume a one-to-one mapping from input to output, which fails for bifurcating systems with multiple equally valid solutions. This paper addresses the challenge of modeling one-to-many solution maps in complex physical dynamics.
method: Introduces Bi-FORK, a generative framework designed specifically for high-dimensional bifurcating systems.
Produces complete trajectories rather than a single deterministic output, representing multiple valid branches of the solution space.
Learns the structure of symmetry-breaking bifurcations so the model can generate diverse physically plausible outcomes.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this opens the door to more realistic surrogate modeling for systems with intrinsic ambiguity and branching behavior. It is especially relevant for scientific ML in physics, engineering, climate, and other domains where multiple outcomes can arise from the same conditions.

title: OuroWorld: Bringing Any 3D World Alive as Diverse, Endlessly Looping 3D Cinemagraphs
authors: You-Zhe Xie, Ting-Wei Chou, Yu-Hsuan Li, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang
abstract: Recent 3D world models generate photorealistic, explorable scenes that remain frozen in time. OuroWorld is a mask-free framework that turns any static 3D Gaussian Splatting scene into a 3D cinemagraph: a dynamic scene with vivid, diverse motion looping seamlessly from any viewpoint. A vision-language model infers plausible dynamics and guides a video model to synthesize a reference video, which we lift and complete into multi-view videos. To learn from this imperfect supervision, we propose Inco

infographic.key_insight: OuroWorld converts a static 3D Gaussian Splatting scene into a looping 3D cinemagraph, making any viewpoint feel alive with diverse, seamless motion. It does this without masks by using a vision-language model plus video generation and multi-view completion.
infographic.problem_solved: Most 3D world models create realistic scenes that are visually impressive but completely static. This paper addresses how to add plausible, viewpoint-consistent, endlessly looping motion to arbitrary 3D scenes.
method: Use a vision-language model to infer realistic scene dynamics and motion cues from a static 3D scene.
Guide a video generation model to synthesize a reference dynamic video that captures the desired motion.
Lift the reference video into multi-view supervision and complete missing views to support consistent 3D motion synthesis.
Train with imperfect supervision using a specialized learning strategy so the final animation loops seamlessly from any angle.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to animate existing 3D scenes without manual masking or artist-driven editing. It can improve interactive media, virtual environments, and content creation pipelines by adding natural motion to static 3D assets.

title: Agentic RSR: Real-to-Sim-to-Real through Scene Reconstruction and Execution-Grounded Robot Policies
authors: Yihan Li, Yating Feng, Shengjiu Sun, Jianing Chen, Hao Ren
abstract: A simulation of a real robot workspace must preserve task-relevant interactions, while policies developed in it must operate on observations available to the real robot. Yet scene reconstruction and policy development are often treated separately. We present Agentic Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Agentic RSR), a framework that links scene reconstruction, policy development, and real-robot execution through the same manipulation task. Given a workspace video, a task description, and a known robot model, an

infographic.key_insight: Agentic RSR connects scene reconstruction and robot policy learning into one loop, so the simulated workspace matches the real task and the learned policy can act using real-robot observations. In simple terms: it tries to make the sim look and behave like the real world in a task-aware way.
infographic.problem_solved: Most real-to-sim-to-real pipelines treat environment reconstruction and policy training separately, which can cause a mismatch between what is simulated and what the robot can actually perceive and do. This paper addresses the challenge of building task-relevant simulations and execution-grounded policies from the same real-world manipulation data.
method: Use a workspace video, task description, and known robot model to reconstruct a task-relevant simulation of the real scene.
Develop robot policies in simulation that are grounded in the observations and actions available to the physical robot.
Link reconstruction, policy learning, and real-robot execution through the same manipulation task to reduce sim-to-real gap.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it provides a more unified pathway from real-world data to deployable robot behavior. It can improve transfer reliability in manipulation tasks by aligning what is simulated, learned, and executed.

title: Emotional optimization by newsroom AI needs behavioural evaluation
authors: Bence Bago, Jean-François Bonnefon
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01315-8

When newsroom artificial intelligence (AI) engages in emotional packaging, it changes how a story feels, shaping whether people approach, trust and share it. As these systems are designed and deployed, AI and behavioural researchers should work together to test whether emotional packaging helps accurate information reach readers, an

infographic.key_insight: Newsroom AI can influence not just what people read, but how they feel about the information—affecting trust, approach, and sharing. The paper argues that these emotional effects must be tested behaviorally, not assumed to improve communication.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the risk that AI systems used in newsrooms may optimize emotional packaging without knowing whether this actually helps accurate information reach readers. The paper highlights the need to evaluate whether emotionally tuned presentation improves or harms reader trust and engagement.
method: Review and frame newsroom AI emotional packaging as a behavioral optimization problem.
Call for controlled behavioral evaluation of how different emotional framings affect reader responses such as trust, willingness to read, and sharing.
Encourage collaboration between AI researchers and behavioral scientists to test real-world communication outcomes rather than relying on proxy metrics.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means optimizing for engagement alone is not enough when systems shape public information exposure. The paper pushes teams to measure downstream human behavior and information quality before deploying emotionally adaptive AI in news settings.

title: Never Look Back: Understanding Persistence in 3D Object Memory from Egocentric Videos
authors: Shravan Chaudhari, William Paul, Suchi Saria, Rama Chellappa, Homanga Bharadhwaj
abstract: As we move through the world and carry out everyday tasks, we encounter objects that may become relevant only later. We are capable of recalling where we left something or what was inside a container, even without knowing we would need it later. Here, we study how an embodied assistant can build a similar memory from egocentric videos, by observing a person's day-to-day activities. We present Ledger, a persistent 3D object memory that combines object locations, their histories, and contextual de

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces Ledger, a persistent 3D object memory that helps an embodied assistant remember where objects are, what happened to them, and how their context changes over time from egocentric video. The key idea is to move beyond short-term perception toward human-like long-term memory for later retrieval.
infographic.problem_solved: AI assistants often perceive objects only momentarily and forget them once they leave view, making it hard to answer later questions like where an item was left or what was inside a container. This paper addresses the challenge of building durable, queryable object memory from everyday first-person videos.
method: Builds a persistent 3D memory representation that stores object locations across time.
Tracks object histories and contextual cues from egocentric video to support later recall.
Integrates observations into a structured memory so the assistant can retrieve past object states and placements.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners working on embodied AI, robotics, and personal assistants because it enables more reliable long-horizon reasoning about the physical world. It also provides a practical direction for memory systems that support real-world retrieval, planning, and interaction.

title: QuadTok: Quadtree Visual Tokenizer for Autoregressive Image Generation
authors: Yucheng Mao, Zeyuan Chen, Xiaojun Shan, Xiang Zhang, Divyansh Srivastava
abstract: We introduce QuadTok, a novel framework for visual tokenization and autoregressive image generation. Compared to traditional approaches using 2D grids or 1D token sequences, we propose a hierarchical quadtree structure, bridging the gap between 2D spatial binding and 1D sequence-level flexibility. The QuadTok tokenizer dynamically allocates representational capacity to visually intricate areas while leaving homogeneous regions at a coarse resolution. Compared with a fixed 256-token grid, our Ima

infographic.key_insight: QuadTok replaces fixed-grid image tokens with a quadtree-based tokenizer that adapts token density to image complexity. This preserves fine detail where needed while keeping simple regions compact, improving the balance between spatial structure and sequence modeling.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional image tokenization for autoregressive generation often uses either rigid 2D grids or flat 1D sequences, which can waste tokens on simple regions and fail to efficiently represent variable visual detail. QuadTok addresses the challenge of creating a tokenizer that is both spatially aware and flexible enough for sequence-based generation.
method: Builds a hierarchical quadtree representation of images, splitting regions more finely only when they contain complex visual content.
Allocates more representational capacity to detailed areas and fewer tokens to homogeneous regions, rather than using a fixed token budget everywhere.
Bridges 2D spatial locality and 1D autoregressive ordering, making images easier to model as sequences without losing structure.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, QuadTok offers a more efficient way to tokenize images for generative models, potentially improving quality, token efficiency, and scalability. It is especially useful for autoregressive image generation tasks where preserving detail and spatial organization both matter.

title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
authors: Python Song, Zhixuan Liang, Kelsey Fu, Mengdi Wang, Junfeng Yang
abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving a

infographic.key_insight: EmbodiedRSI makes robot learning more adaptive by actively choosing which code and skill changes to test, instead of wasting robot trials on unguided self-improvement. It uses hypothesis-guided co-evolution to update both the robot’s behavior and the harness that guides learning.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the brittleness of robot foundation models when object positions or task instructions change, and the high cost of improving them through large-scale post-training data collection. It also tackles the inefficiency of current self-evolving systems that spend robot trials poorly when exploring new code and skill updates.
method: Uses a self-evolving framework that iteratively improves robot control performance through active continual learning.
Introduces hypothesis-guided co-evolution to prioritize promising code and skill modifications before spending real robot trials.
Reduces wasted experimentation by selecting adaptation steps based on expected utility rather than brute-force trial-and-error.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, EmbodiedRSI offers a more sample-efficient path to continual robot adaptation in changing environments. This could lower the cost of deploying robot foundation models in real-world settings where tasks and object layouts frequently shift.

title: Best Arm Identification for Bandits with Shifting Means
authors: Lukas Zierahn, Wouter M. Koolen, Shubhada Agrawal, Christina Katsimerou, Dirk van der Hoeven
abstract: We study the best arm identification problem in a stochastic environment with a novel form of adversarial perturbations, which we coin Shifting Means. While classically the mean rewards of the $K$ arms are stable in time, in Shifting Means only the gaps $\boldsymbolΔ$ between mean rewards are stable, while their common shift may be determined adversarially in each round. The objective of the learner is to identify the best arm with high probability while minimizing sample complexity (the fixed c

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a new bandit setting where arm gaps stay fixed but all means can shift adversarially over time. This lets the learner focus on identifying the best arm reliably even when the overall reward level keeps moving.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses best arm identification in stochastic bandits under "Shifting Means," a nonstandard perturbation model where the relative differences between arms remain stable but a shared time-varying shift can change adversarially each round.
method: Formulate a best-arm identification problem under shifting common means rather than fixed arm rewards.
Develop sampling and decision strategies that exploit the stability of the gaps between arms.
Analyze sample complexity for identifying the best arm with high probability despite adversarial shifts.
infographic.impact: This work broadens best-arm identification to more realistic nonstationary settings where absolute rewards drift but relative arm quality remains meaningful. It is useful for practitioners building robust bandit-based decision systems in changing environments.
