title: Long-WAM: Scaling the Context of World-Action Models
authors: Wei Huang, Bohan Zhang, Chenzhi Liu, Isabella Liu, Shuai Yang
abstract: Real-time robot control demands enough visual history to infer motion and task progress, but processing that history can delay action. We present Long-WAM, a model-system framework for scaling the context of causal world-action models under real-time control constraints. Our central finding is that access to history is not the same as using it: longer histories pay off far more when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively (AR). We first learn causal prediction from robot and egocentr

infographic.key_insight: Longer visual history only helps robot control when the underlying video model is pretrained autoregressively (AR). Long-WAM shows that careful model-system design can extend context length without breaking real-time action.
infographic.problem_solved: Real-time robot control needs enough past visual context to understand motion and task progress, but processing long histories can introduce latency and slow action decisions.
method: Build a model-system framework for causal world-action models that can use longer context while staying within real-time control limits.
Pretrain the video foundation autoregressively so the model learns to better exploit extended visual history.
Learn causal prediction from robot and egocentric video data, then evaluate how context length affects control performance under latency constraints.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in robotics, this work shows that scaling context is not just an engineering issue—it depends on how the backbone is pretrained. It provides a practical path toward more temporally aware robot policies without sacrificing responsiveness.

title: Tetris3D: 3D Scene Generation With Objects That Fit Together
authors: Jaeyeong Kim, Jinhyuk Jang, Jongmin Lee, Kyehong Park, Seungryong Kim
abstract: We propose Tetris3D, a generative framework for single-image 3D scene reconstruction that recovers objects which are physically and geometrically coherent as a scene. Existing methods often generate objects independently or couple them implicitly, providing limited guidance for ensuring fine-grained spatial compatibility between neighboring objects that interact with one another. To address this, we explicitly condition the generation of each object on the geometry of surrounding objects and the

infographic.key_insight: Tetris3D improves single-image 3D scene reconstruction by generating objects that physically and geometrically fit together, rather than placing each object in isolation. The key idea is to condition each object on its neighbors so the reconstructed scene is more coherent and realistic.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of fine-grained spatial compatibility in 3D scene generation from a single image. Existing methods often fail to enforce how neighboring objects should align, interact, or fit together in a physically plausible way.
method: Generates 3D scene objects with explicit conditioning on surrounding object geometry.
Encourages local spatial compatibility so adjacent objects better match in shape, placement, and interaction.
Reconstructs a complete scene from one image while aiming for physical and geometric coherence.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners because it can produce more realistic 3D reconstructions that are better suited for downstream tasks like robotics, AR/VR, and scene editing. It also shows a practical direction for improving generative models by incorporating local geometric constraints.

title: Label-free cell counting and viability prediction with brightfield imaging and deep learning
authors: Amir Reza Vazifeh, Christian Zeigler, Sornanathan Meyyappan, Richard Jeske, Jason W. Fleischer
abstract: Cell viability assessment is a core requirement in cell culture systems, with critical applications in biopharmaceutical manufacturing and drug development. Conventionally, it is measured by adding membrane-impermeable dyes to a sample (a process called staining), which allows compromised cell membranes to be distinguished from intact ones. However, staining has several limitations: (a) chemical agents can perturb normal cellular processes of the cells being measured, (b) it is often ambiguous t

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that deep learning can estimate cell count and viability directly from brightfield images, removing the need for fluorescent staining. In simple terms, it enables label-free, non-destructive quality checks for cell cultures.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional viability assays rely on dyes that can alter cells, add workflow complexity, and create ambiguity in some cases. The paper addresses the need for a faster, less invasive, and more scalable way to count cells and assess viability.
method: Use brightfield microscopy images as input, instead of stained or labeled samples.
Train a deep learning model to predict cell count and viability from image patterns visible in standard imaging data.
Evaluate the approach as a label-free alternative to conventional staining-based cell viability measurement.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this demonstrates how computer vision can replace expensive or disruptive lab assays with non-invasive inference from routine images. It is especially relevant for biomanufacturing and drug development workflows where speed, scalability, and sample integrity matter.

title: GRACE: Generation-aware latent compression for efficient video generation
authors: Jiyoung Kim, Paul Hyunbin Cho, Jisu Nam, Donghoon Lee, Hyunsung Go
abstract: Highly compressed video autoencoders offer an effective way to accelerate video diffusion models, as the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) operates on far fewer tokens. However, such autoencoders are challenging to train, since a higher compression ratio degrades reconstruction quality and recovering it requires more channels, which is known to slow the convergence of the DiT. The compressed latent also differs from the one the DiT was trained on, so the pretrained DiT must be either retrained from sc

infographic.key_insight: GRACE shows how to make video generation faster by compressing video latents more aggressively without breaking the pretrained Diffusion Transformer. It introduces generation-aware compression so the model can keep quality while operating on far fewer tokens.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the tradeoff between high latent compression and video quality: stronger compression speeds up diffusion models, but it usually hurts reconstruction and creates latents that pretrained DiTs were not trained to use.
method: Learns a generation-aware latent compression scheme tailored for video diffusion, rather than only optimizing reconstruction.
Aligns the compressed latent space with the pretrained DiT so the generator can be reused with minimal retraining.
Uses a highly compressed video autoencoder to reduce token count, improving efficiency while preserving visual fidelity.
infographic.impact: This makes video generation more practical by lowering compute and memory costs without a major quality drop. For practitioners, it offers a path to faster inference and more efficient training when working with diffusion-based video models.

title: EngramEdit: Decoupled Knowledge Updates in LLMs through Conditional Memory
authors: Hongru Cai, Ran Wei, Wenjie Wang, Chengfa Wu, Ning Song
abstract: Conditional memory architectures such as DeepSeek Engram use input n-grams to look up learned embeddings, expanding the capacity of large language models (LLMs) with limited additional computation. Beyond model scaling, this architecture has demonstrated the potential to decouple factual knowledge storage from general-purpose computation, offering a promising route to updating factual knowledge while keeping the Transformer backbone fixed. Realizing this potential is challenging because differen

infographic.key_insight: EngramEdit shows that factual knowledge in an LLM can be updated through a conditional memory module instead of retraining the whole Transformer. This decouples knowledge storage from general computation, making targeted edits more efficient and controllable.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of updating factual knowledge in large language models without costly full-model fine-tuning or risking unwanted changes to general capabilities. It targets the difficulty of making precise knowledge edits when memory and computation are tightly coupled.
method: Use a conditional memory architecture that maps input n-grams to learned embeddings for factual retrieval.
Introduce an editing mechanism that updates stored knowledge directly in memory while keeping the Transformer backbone fixed.
Design the system to preserve general model behavior while enabling efficient, localized factual updates.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical path to maintain and patch LLM knowledge without expensive retraining. It can improve deployment workflows by making factual updates faster, cheaper, and less disruptive to model performance.

title: RoboJEPA: Scaling Robotic Latent World Models
authors: Artem Zholus, Nicolas Beltran-Velez, Jianhao Yuan, Sarath Chandar, Tushar Nagarajan
abstract: Latent world models have shown a remarkable ability to predict future states and to plan in the real world. In practice, however, we lack a principled way to estimate how their capabilities scale with model size, data, and compute, an open problem that slows progress in the field. In this work we present RoboJEPA, a world model based on the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and trained on a large-scale dataset spanning 12 robotic embodiments. We show that RoboJEPA's imagination erro

infographic.key_insight: RoboJEPA is a scalable latent world model for robotics that learns to predict and plan in compact representations rather than raw observations. The paper shows how model size, data, and compute affect robotic imagination, helping turn world-model scaling into something measurable and actionable.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of a principled way to evaluate how robotic latent world models improve as they grow with more parameters, more data, and more compute. This makes it hard to know how to build stronger planning and prediction models for real-world robots.
method: Trains a JEPA-based latent world model called RoboJEPA on a large-scale dataset covering 12 different robotic embodiments.
Learns predictive representations of future states for planning and imagination in latent space instead of pixel-level forecasting.
Studies scaling behavior to understand how performance changes with model size, dataset scale, and compute budget.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical framework for building and scaling robot world models more systematically. It can guide model design and training decisions for more capable robotic prediction, planning, and generalization across embodiments.

title: Before They Can Solve: Predicting Post-Training Coding-Agent Performance from Base Models
authors: Tan Yu, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Jennifer Williams, Zirui Liu
abstract: How can we predict which base checkpoint is worth an expensive round of agentic post-training? End-to-end pass@$K$ tests whether successful behavior already appears in a base model's distribution, but it is a poor fit for agentic coding: many base checkpoints cannot reliably produce the well-formed tool invocation required to complete a task end-to-end. Single-shot or short-horizon tasks avoid these tool-calling failures by collapsing a multi-step interaction into a fixed prompt and a single pat

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that you can predict whether a base model is worth expensive agentic coding post-training before you actually train it. Instead of relying on end-to-end pass@K alone, it focuses on signals that better reflect whether the model can support multi-step tool use and coding behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of choosing promising base checkpoints for costly agentic post-training in coding tasks. Standard pass@K-style evaluation is a poor predictor because many base models fail at reliable tool invocation, even when they may contain useful coding competence.
method: Compare base checkpoints using evaluation signals designed for agentic coding, not just end-to-end success rates.
Use short-horizon or single-shot task formulations to reduce failures caused by multi-step tool-calling breakdowns.
Predict which checkpoints are most likely to benefit from post-training, enabling better checkpoint selection before expensive training runs.
infographic.impact: This helps practitioners spend compute on the base models most likely to improve after agentic training. It can reduce wasted training runs and make model development for coding agents faster and more efficient.

title: SciExam for ENSO: Can AI Agents Build Climate Models?
authors: Yinling Zhang, Langchen Liu, Dongbin Xiu, Xueyan Zou, Xu Kuang
abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out open-ended scientific research, yet their results are usually graded against a known answer, a rubric, or a language-model reviewer, none of which can tell whether a new scientific model is valid. The AI Science Exam for El Nino-Southern Oscillation (SciExam for ENSO) is a benchmark in which agents build low-order stochastic models of ENSO, the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, from real observations. Within a six-hour bud

infographic.key_insight: SciExam for ENSO introduces a real-world benchmark that tests whether AI agents can build scientifically valid climate models, not just produce answers that look correct. It evaluates agents on constructing low-order stochastic models of ENSO directly from observations within a constrained time budget.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional AI benchmarks for scientific tasks usually compare outputs to known answers, rubrics, or model-based reviewers, which cannot verify whether a newly generated scientific model is genuinely valid. This paper addresses the need for an evaluation setting that measures whether AI agents can discover and build useful physical models from data.
method: Defines the SciExam for ENSO benchmark, where agents must infer low-order stochastic models of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation from real observational data.
Uses a six-hour time-limited challenge to test open-ended scientific modeling ability under realistic constraints.
Evaluates agent performance based on the quality and scientific validity of the resulting climate model rather than simple answer matching.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this paper points toward more meaningful evaluation of agentic research systems in scientific discovery settings. It helps shift benchmark design from surface-level correctness toward true model-building capability and physical validity.

title: Video-Conditioned Generative Joint 2D-3D Hand Motion Recovery
authors: Chen Xu, Yunqi Li, Binbin Huang, Brent Yi, Shenghua Gao
abstract: Recovering faithful 3D hand motion from video remains challenging due to frequent occlusions and incomplete visual observations, which make frame-wise pose estimates unreliable and temporally inconsistent. To address this problem, we propose JoHan, a unified generative framework that recovers hand motion directly from video sequences without relying on intermediate per-frame pose predictions. Trained from scratch, our model jointly generates aligned 2D and 3D local hand pose sequences by learnin

infographic.key_insight: JoHan shows that hand motion can be recovered more reliably by generating 2D and 3D hand poses jointly from video, instead of depending on noisy frame-by-frame pose estimates. This leads to more temporally consistent and occlusion-robust hand motion recovery.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing faithful 3D hand motion from video when hands are frequently occluded or only partially visible, which makes per-frame pose prediction unreliable and unstable over time.
method: A unified generative framework that takes video sequences as input and directly recovers hand motion end-to-end.
Jointly generates aligned 2D and 3D local hand pose sequences rather than using intermediate per-frame pose predictions.
Learns temporal consistency across frames to better handle occlusions and incomplete observations.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners because it can improve robustness in real-world video understanding tasks where hands are often blocked or motion is ambiguous. The approach also suggests a cleaner generative alternative to traditional pipeline-based pose estimation.

title: Characterizing the role of reasoning tokens in large language models as state over tokens
authors: Mosh Levy, Zohar Elyoseph, Shauli Ravfogel, Yoav Goldberg
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01303-y

When large language models ‘reason’ about a problem, they might still solve it differently from what their reasoning transcript suggest. In this Perspective, Levy et al. describe how one can start investigating the role of these reasoning tokens.

infographic.key_insight: Reasoning tokens in large language models may not faithfully represent the model’s actual internal decision process. The paper frames them as a sequence of states that can be studied to understand how models arrive at answers, rather than as a transparent transcript of thought.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the gap between what an LLM writes during reasoning and how it actually computes its final answer. It proposes a way to investigate whether chain-of-thought style outputs are explanations, control signals, or both.
method: Recasts reasoning tokens as intermediate states over tokens, providing a lens for studying their functional role in computation.
Outlines how to empirically probe the relationship between generated reasoning traces and the model’s true internal mechanics.
Frames future experiments to test whether changing, removing, or inspecting reasoning tokens alters model behavior and outputs.
infographic.impact: For AI practitioners, this helps clarify when reasoning traces can be trusted as explanations and when they should be treated cautiously. It also informs safer model evaluation, interpretability research, and the design of more transparent reasoning systems.

title: RECAST: Learning to Compute the Right Context through Adaptive Evidence Routing
authors: Yilun Hao, Krishna Sayana, Isabella Ye, James S Ren, Sukhdeep Sodhi
abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied to tasks grounded in long, heterogeneous information sources. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) relies on fixed similarity-based retrieval, while agentic variants adapt queries and tool use but remain largely retrieval-centric. However, in many tasks, the evidence required for a solution is not explicitly present in any single source item. Instead, it must be derived through filtering, aggregation, or computation across multiple sour

infographic.key_insight: RECAST shifts retrieval from simply finding relevant text to computing the right context when the answer must be derived across multiple sources. It learns to route evidence through adaptive filtering, aggregation, and computation instead of relying only on similarity search.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of standard RAG and retrieval-centric agents: many real-world tasks require synthesized evidence that is not explicitly contained in any single document chunk. This makes fixed top-k retrieval insufficient for complex, long-context reasoning over heterogeneous sources.
method: Learn an adaptive evidence-routing policy that decides how to transform and combine retrieved information.
Route evidence through operations such as filtering, aggregation, and computation to build the needed context.
Replace purely similarity-based retrieval with a more task-aware process for assembling answer-supporting evidence.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means more reliable performance on tasks where the answer must be derived rather than directly retrieved. It can improve long-context QA, multi-document reasoning, and agent systems that must work with messy, distributed information.

title: VeriFine: Scaling Verification for Self-Improvement in Embodied Reasoning
authors: Zewei Zhou, Rachel Luo, Yulong Cao, Chaowei Xiao, Chensheng Peng
abstract: Self-improving policies continually expose new failure patterns, changing what their judges must be able to verify. However, current fixed judges constrain both optimization feedback and the discovery of useful training examples, limiting further self-improvement. This challenge is even more acute in embodied reasoning, where reliable evaluation must account for spatial grounding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making. We introduce VeriFine, an agent harness framework that scales ve

infographic.key_insight: VeriFine shows how to scale verification itself so embodied agents can keep improving as they encounter new failure modes. Instead of relying on a fixed judge, it adapts verification to match the evolving abilities of the policy.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the bottleneck in self-improving embodied AI where static evaluators cannot reliably judge new behaviors, limiting both training feedback and the discovery of useful examples. This is especially difficult in embodied reasoning, where evaluation must account for spatial grounding, causality, and safety.
method: Introduces VeriFine, an agent harness framework that scales verification alongside self-improvement.
Uses verification that can adapt to newly emerging failure patterns rather than staying fixed.
Targets embodied reasoning tasks where judgments must combine correctness, grounding, and safety-aware decisions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this makes self-improvement loops more reliable and scalable by improving the quality of feedback and training data selection. It is especially useful for building embodied agents that need to operate safely and reason about the physical world.

title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Haritz Puerto, Alexander Rubinstein, Martin Gubri, Seong Joon Oh
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve many narrow tasks, but querying them separately for millions of related instances can be prohibitively expensive. Can LLM agents autonomously create cheaper solutions for such workloads? We call this ability "bottling": the ability to turn general capabilities into task-specific solutions that balance answer quality and amortised cost. We introduce BOTTLED, a benchmark in which agents receive an entire unlabelled workload and must complete it under fixed ti

infographic.key_insight: The paper asks whether LLM agents can "package" their general intelligence into cheaper, reusable artifacts that handle large workloads efficiently. It introduces the idea of "bottling"—trading a bit of flexibility for much lower amortized cost while preserving useful quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Many real-world applications require running the same or very similar LLM task over millions of instances, making repeated API calls too expensive. This work tackles how agents can autonomously create task-specific solutions that reduce cost without losing too much performance.
method: Defines "bottling" as converting broad LLM capabilities into task-specific artifacts optimized for a workload.
Introduces BOTTLED, a benchmark where agents receive an unlabeled workload and must solve it under fixed cost/time constraints.
Evaluates whether agents can infer the task structure, build a cheaper solution, and balance answer quality against amortized execution cost.
infographic.impact: This is important for practitioners deploying LLMs at scale, where cost often dominates feasibility. If successful, bottling could enable faster, cheaper systems for batch processing, enterprise workflows, and repetitive decision tasks.

title: 4D-HOF: Hand-Object Flow Matching for Feed-Forward 4D Interaction Reconstruction
authors: Shiqi Li, Sean Cho, Yijie Li, Fengzhi Guo, Bowen Wen
abstract: Existing methods for 4D hand-object reconstruction often rely on costly per-sequence optimization, while generative approaches typically synthesize interactions from random noise, which can lead to unstable interaction prediction. We introduce 4D-HOF, a feed-forward framework that reconstructs 4D hand-object interactions from coarse but informative estimates produced by vision foundation models. Concretely, we learn a conditional flow matching model that transports foundation-model-derived hand-

infographic.key_insight: 4D-HOF turns coarse but informative vision-model estimates into full 4D hand-object interaction reconstructions using a feed-forward flow-matching model. This avoids slow per-sequence optimization and is more stable than starting from random noise.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic 4D hand-object interactions efficiently and reliably. Existing methods are often too slow because they optimize each sequence separately, while generative methods can produce unstable interactions when initialized from noise.
method: Uses vision foundation models to provide coarse hand-object estimates as conditioning signals instead of random initialization.
Learns a conditional flow matching model to transport these rough estimates into detailed 4D interaction reconstructions.
Produces feed-forward predictions, enabling faster inference while preserving plausible hand-object contact and motion consistency.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more practical pipeline for 4D interaction reconstruction with better stability and lower computation. It is especially relevant for applications like AR/VR, robotics, motion understanding, and human-object interaction modeling.

title: QF3: Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients
authors: Chung Min Kim, Brent Yi, David McAllister, Hongsuk Choi, Himanshu Gaurav Singh
abstract: Flow policies have become a standard policy class for learning robot behaviors from demonstrations, but reinforcement learning is still critical for improving pre-trained flow policies or learning them from scratch through interaction. We introduce QF3 (Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients), an online off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy with flow matching plus the critic's action gradient, backpropagated through a one-step prediction of the flow's output. To keep updates where th

infographic.key_insight: QF3 speeds up reinforcement learning for flow policies by combining flow matching with critic-guided action gradients, while filtering updates to keep training stable and useful. This lets robots improve from interaction more efficiently than standard flow-policy RL.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of making flow policies better through online reinforcement learning without unstable or inefficient updates. It addresses how to improve pretrained flow policies or learn them from scratch using critic feedback in a fast, off-policy setting.
method: Train a flow policy with standard flow matching to preserve the policy's generative structure.
Add the critic's action gradient as a learning signal, backpropagated through a one-step prediction of the flow output.
Filter gradients so updates are applied only where they are reliable or beneficial, improving stability and sample efficiency.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, QF3 offers a practical way to make flow-based robot policies learn faster from interaction while staying stable. It is especially useful when demonstration-trained policies need further improvement in real-world or simulated control tasks.

title: Backend-Agnostic Sparse Attention for Fast High-Resolution Visual Generation
authors: Liao Ma, Jiayi Song, Yunfeng Wu, Songhua Liu, Peilin Zhao
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in image and video generation, but the quadratic complexity of full attention makes high-resolution generation computationally expensive. Window attention offers an efficient alternative, yet existing methods face a practical trade-off: partitioned window attention typically achieves computational efficiency consistent with its theoretical complexity. However, isolated windows block cross-window interaction, often introducing visible

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that sparse attention can make high-resolution diffusion-based image/video generation much faster without relying on a specific attention backend. The core idea is to preserve efficiency while reducing the quality loss caused by isolated window-based attention.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the high compute and memory cost of full attention in Diffusion Transformers for high-resolution visual generation, as well as the trade-off in window attention between efficiency and weak cross-window interaction.
method: Design a backend-agnostic sparse attention strategy that works across different implementation backends.
Reduce attention computation by limiting dense all-to-all interactions while preserving important long-range context.
Improve cross-window information flow so generation remains coherent at high resolutions without the artifacts common in isolated window attention.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to scale generative models to higher resolutions with lower compute costs and better visual quality. It is especially useful for efficient image and video generation deployments where speed, memory, and fidelity all matter.

title: AdvSim2Real : Training Web Agents Against Adaptive Prompt Injection in a Web World Model
authors: Sarim Hashmi, Mukul Ranjan, Kshitij Mishra, Mikhail Kuznetsov, Praneeth Vepakomma
abstract: Web agents complete user requests by reading and acting on pages that third parties write, so an instruction planted on a page can redirect the agent away from the user's goal. The agent cannot simply ignore the page, because the page also holds the values and controls the task requires. Current defenses fine-tune the agent on injections fixed before training, and attackers that adapt to the trained model bypass them. Adversarial training lets the attacker adapt but keeps the tasks fixed, so a t

infographic.key_insight: AdSim2Real shows that web agents need to be trained against prompt injection that adapts to the agent, not just against fixed attacks. The paper’s core idea is to make training more realistic by combining adaptive attackers with a web-world-model setting, so defenses learn to resist changing adversaries.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses a major security gap in web agents: third-party webpage content can contain hidden instructions that hijack the agent’s behavior while still containing the task-relevant values and controls the agent needs. Existing defenses often overfit to static attacks and fail when attackers adapt.
method: Uses adversarial training where the attacker is allowed to adapt to the current agent, rather than remaining fixed during training.
Frames training in a web world model so the agent learns under more realistic simulated web interactions.
Tests robustness against prompt injection scenarios designed to mimic real-world adaptive adversaries.
infographic.impact: This matters because web agents are increasingly used on open, untrusted webpages where prompt injection is a practical security risk. For practitioners, the paper suggests that robust defenses must be evaluated against adaptive attackers, not just curated static benchmarks.

title: World Models' Last Exam in Physics
authors: Mingju Gao, Qingle Liu, Yuzhao Peng, Xinjie Lin, Ziming Qin
abstract: Video world models can produce visually convincing yet physically inconsistent sequences, raising concerns about their reliability for prediction and planning in embodied AI systems. Existing evaluations often rely on model-based judgments or reference videos, while direct physical tests largely focus on mechanics. We introduce World Models' Last Exam in Physics, a measurement-based benchmark for evaluating physical consistency in video world models. The benchmark comprises 40 controlled tasks s

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a measurement-based benchmark that directly tests whether video world models stay physically consistent, instead of just looking visually realistic. It helps reveal when models can generate convincing videos that still violate basic physics.
infographic.problem_solved: Current evaluations of video world models often depend on subjective judgments, reference videos, or narrow mechanics-focused tests. This paper addresses the lack of a direct, standardized way to measure physical consistency in generated video sequences.
method: Builds "World Models' Last Exam in Physics," a benchmark designed around controlled physical tasks.
Uses measurement-based evaluation to check whether predicted video behavior matches expected physical outcomes.
Focuses on physical consistency rather than visual plausibility alone, exposing hidden failure modes in world models.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark offers a more rigorous way to assess whether world models are reliable for prediction and planning in embodied AI. It can help researchers compare systems more fairly and improve models that must understand real-world dynamics.

title: CtrlCache: Accelerating Interactive Video World Models with Control-Aware Caching
authors: Shangye Song, Dong Gong, Hong Jia, Yun Sing Koh, Xinyu Zhang
abstract: Interactive video world models need to generate each video chunk efficiently while responding faithfully to user controls. Many systems use chunk-wise autoregressive generation with few-step denoising, but each chunk still requires several costly denoising iterations. Training-free caching can reduce this cost, yet existing policies make reuse decisions primarily from model-internal denoising dynamics and do not explicitly account for control transitions. Actually, interactive generation explici

infographic.key_insight: CtrlCache speeds up interactive video world models by making caching aware of user control changes, so the model can reuse work when it is safe and recompute when controls shift. This reduces expensive denoising steps while preserving responsiveness to user input.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high inference cost of chunk-wise autoregressive video generation in interactive world models, where each chunk requires multiple denoising iterations. Existing caching methods reduce computation but often ignore control transitions, which can hurt fidelity when user instructions change.
method: Monitors both denoising dynamics and control changes to decide when cached features or outputs can be reused.
Introduces a control-aware caching policy for training-free acceleration of chunk-based video generation.
Balances efficiency and responsiveness by recomputing only when control transitions indicate that reuse would be unsafe.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a practical way to cut inference latency and compute cost in interactive video generation without retraining the model. Existing prompting- and feedback-based methods do not provide enough structured guidance for how papers should be synthesized into meaningful research directions.

title: InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation

abstract: Captured human-object interactions provide rich supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation, but they are sparse, heterogeneous, and not directly executable by robots. infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of large, executable humanoid loco-manipulation data. Human-object interaction captures are rich but sparse, inconsistent across sources, and difficult to directly retarget into robot motions that preserve whole-body and hand-object coordination.
method: Consolidate multiple motion-captured human-object interaction datasets into a unified collection.

It can accelerate data generation for locomotion-plus-manipulation tasks and improve policy robustness in complex embodied settings.

title: UniSlider: Perceptually Uniform Sliders for Continuous Image Editing
authors: David Serrano-Lozano, Duygu Ceylan, Yannick Hold-Geoffroy, Iliyan Georgiev, Javier Vazquez-Corral
abstract: Sliders provide an intuitive interface for continuous image editing. In current generative approaches, however, the slider is simply a rescaling of the method's strength parameter, such as an adapter coefficient, a prompt weight, or an interpolation factor. The image can partially revert as the slider moves, long stretches of the range produce no visible difference, and short intervals transform the image abruptly. Remapping the strength could f

infographic.key_insight: UniSlider makes image-editing sliders feel much more natural by aligning slider movement with perceived visual change, rather than with an arbitrary model strength parameter. This creates smoother, more predictable edits across the full range of the control.
infographic.problem_solved: Current AI image-editing sliders are usually just rescaled strength parameters, which do not correspond well to how much the image actually changes. As a result, users see uneven behavior: no visible effect for long stretches, sudden jumps, or even partial reversions as the slider moves.
method: Redefines the slider mapping so equal slider steps produce more uniform perceptual changes in the edited image.
Transforms the underlying model strength/control parameter into a perceptually calibrated interface for continuous editing.
Aims to remove dead zones and abrupt transitions by improving monotonicity and consistency of visual change.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this improves usability and trust in generative editing tools by making controls easier to interpret and tune. It can help create more professional, intuitive interfaces for creative workflows and interactive image manipulation.

title: Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data
authors: Sophie L. Wang, Amil Dravid, Rulin Shao, Kevin Farhat, Sewon Min
abstract: In this paper, we study how training data creates associations between the tokens at the start of a base model's response and the reasoning behavior that follows. title: MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents
authors: Haozhen Zhang, Haodong Yue, Quanyu Long, Jianzhu Bao, Qingyuan Liu
abstract: Memory has become integral to the LLM agent ecosystem, supporting information retention and reuse across interactions. title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points
authors: Benhao Huang, Chufan Shi, Junlin Chen, Shicheng Wen, Zhengzhong Liu
abstract: Every recurrence of a looped language model adds cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning (RL). This enables truncated backpropagation in training; terminal key-value (KV) sharing for decoding with almost no loss in accuracy; a distilled student that prefills up to 1.79x faster; and RL updates that compute gradients from saved rollout states, 2x faster than backpropagating through the repla

This unlocks cheaper training, decoding, distillation, and RL without major accuracy loss.
infographic.problem_solved: Looped models are computationally expensive because every extra recurrence increases cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning. The paper addresses how to reduce this overhead by exploiting near-fixed-point behavior.
method: Use truncated backpropagation during training when recurrent states are close to convergence.
Apply terminal KV sharing at decoding time to reuse final key-value states with minimal accuracy loss.

Compute RL gradients from saved rollout states instead of full backpropagation through the rollout, achieving about 2x speedup.
infographic.impact: This makes looped and recurrent LLMs far more practical by reducing compute cost across the full lifecycle of a model. Practitioners can gain faster training and inference while preserving most of the performance benefits of recurrence.

abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary methods, such as AlphaEvolve, have emerged as powerful approaches for challenging computational optimization problems, such as circle packing. title: FlowHMR: Physically Plausible Motion Capture from Video
authors: Zhanke Wang, Chengfeng Zhao, Qing Shuai, Jingzhong Lin, Heng Li
abstract: We present FlowHMR, a framework for recovering physically plausible global 3D human motion from monocular video. Previous learning-based methods typically regress human motion directly from video and train the network with geometric supervision. However, recovering human motion from monocular video is inherently ambiguous in depth, and direct regression tends to collapse toward an averaged solution. Moreover, the recovered motions are not guaranteed to be physically plausible, so physics-based t

infographic.key_insight: FlowHMR turns monocular video into physically plausible 3D human motion by combining learning with physics-aware constraints. Instead of regressing a single averaged pose sequence, it aims to recover global motion that better respects real-world dynamics.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the ambiguity of inferring 3D human motion from a single camera, where depth is uncertain and direct regression often produces oversmoothed or physically implausible results.
method: Uses a video-based framework to estimate global 3D human motion from monocular input.
Incorporates physics-aware modeling to improve physical plausibility beyond standard geometric supervision.
Designed to reduce depth ambiguity effects and avoid the averaged-motion collapse common in direct regression methods.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners because it can produce more realistic human motion estimates from ordinary video, improving downstream tasks like animation, sports analysis, and human-computer interaction. It also shows how adding physical priors can make learned motion capture systems more reliable.

title: EyeRobot 2.0: Active Gaze for Precise Manipulation without Wrist Cameras
authors: Kush Hari, Justin Kerr, Nidhya Shivakumar, Samarth Mahapatra, Carmelo Sferrazza
abstract: Inspired by human vision, we introduce a framework using active gaze to enable fine-grained bimanual manipulation with only a single stereo camera. EyeRobot 2.0 physically attends to a 3D fixation point in the scene by swiveling two eye viewpoints to center their gaze on it. The resulting images are processed foveally by allocating more visual tokens to the image centers, focusing computation on task-relevant features. Such Active Visual Fixation (AVF) requires carefully coordinated gaze during

infographic.key_insight: EyeRobot 2.0 shows that precise bimanual manipulation can be improved by actively moving the camera's gaze to a chosen 3D point, rather than relying on wrist-mounted cameras. It combines physical eye-like attention with foveated processing to focus compute on the most relevant part of the scene.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving fine-grained robot manipulation without using wrist cameras, which are often costly, restrictive, or unavailable. It aims to maintain precise visual tracking and task-relevant detail using only a single stereo camera.
method: Uses Active Visual Fixation (AVF) to swivel two virtual eye viewpoints so both center on the same 3D fixation point in the scene.
Applies foveal image processing by allocating more visual tokens to the image center, emphasizing high-value details near the fixation point.
Coordinates gaze and perception to support precise bimanual manipulation with a single stereo camera setup.
infographic.impact: This approach offers a simpler and potentially more robust alternative to wrist-camera-based manipulation systems. For practitioners, it suggests a path to lower-hardware, compute-efficient robots that still retain strong visual precision for dexterous tasks.

title: MoSE3: Learning World-Space SE(3) at Every Pixel
authors: Jiahuan Cheng, Zhiyi Li, Tian Xia, Ruojin Cai, Yilun Du
abstract: Dense 3D point tracking has been a prominent paradigm for modeling motion in dynamic scenes, but a point track is just a 3-DoF translation curve per pixel: it captures where pixels go, not the rotation of the underlying part, nor which pixels move together as one body. We propose MoSE3, the first feed-forward model that predicts dense SE(3) motion from monocular RGB video, producing full 6-DoF rigid transforms at every pixel in world space. Per-pixel SE(3) motion offers a richer view of how a sc

infographic.key_insight: MoSE3 moves beyond tracking pixel locations to predict full 6-DoF rigid motion at every pixel in world space. This gives a much richer, physically meaningful view of how objects and parts move in dynamic scenes.
infographic.problem_solved: Dense 3D point tracking only captures translation trajectories, not rotation or which pixels belong to the same moving rigid body. The paper addresses the need for dense, feed-forward estimation of per-pixel SE(3) motion from monocular RGB video.
method: Predicts a dense SE(3) transform for every pixel directly from monocular RGB video.
Represents motion in world space, enabling consistent rigid-body motion estimation across the scene.
Provides a feed-forward alternative to point-track-based methods that only estimate 3D translation.
infographic.impact: This is useful for tasks that need understanding of rigid motion, object parts, and scene dynamics beyond simple tracking. Practitioners can use it to improve motion analysis, robotics, and 3D scene understanding from standard video inputs.

title: RNADyn: A Benchmark for Generating and Understanding RNA Dynamics
authors: Yiming Huang, Lennart Bastian, Hanqun Cao, Luis Vollmers, Tolga Birdal
abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) functions through conformational changes that are not fully captured by static structures. However, large-scale standardized RNA dynamics data remain limited, and existing approaches typically treat trajectory generation and dynamics understanding as separate objectives. Here, we introduce RNADynBench, a standardized RNA molecular dynamics (MD) benchmark with 2585 quality-controlled 100-ns all-atom trajectories and leakage-controlled splits. Building on RNADynBench, we dev

infographic.key_insight: RNADyn introduces a standardized benchmark for RNA dynamics, making it possible to evaluate models on both generating realistic RNA motions and understanding RNA conformational behavior. It addresses the gap between static RNA structure prediction and true dynamic modeling.
infographic.problem_solved: RNA biology depends on time-varying conformations, but high-quality, large-scale, standardized dynamics data are scarce. Existing methods often split trajectory generation and dynamics understanding into separate tasks, making fair evaluation difficult and risking data leakage across train/test splits.
method: Build RNADynBench, a benchmark containing 2,585 quality-controlled all-atom RNA molecular dynamics trajectories, each 100 ns long.
Use leakage-controlled dataset splits to support rigorous and fair evaluation of model generalization.
Unify generation and understanding of RNA dynamics under a single benchmark framework for standardized comparison.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, RNADyn provides a reliable testbed for developing and comparing models that learn molecular motion, not just static structure. It helps reduce overfitting and leakage, enabling more trustworthy progress in biomolecular generative modeling and representation learning.

title: Simulation-Free Learning of Population Dynamics with Wasserstein Lagrangian Residuals
authors: Fedor Sergeev, Markus Heinonen, Daniel Waxman, Tim Cooijmans, Ricardo Baptista
abstract: The dynamics of cells, organisms, and fluids are often modeled as probability distributions evolving over time. Reconstructing and extrapolating this evolution from unpaired snapshots requires assumptions about the underlying process. Wasserstein gradient flows are a common choice, but they cannot describe conservative or periodic dynamics. Lagrangian mechanics in Wasserstein space covers both, but existing methods for learning it are simulation-based: they run a numerical solver at every traini

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces a simulation-free way to learn population dynamics directly from snapshots by using Wasserstein Lagrangian residuals. It expands beyond gradient-flow models to capture both conservative and periodic evolution in evolving distributions.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of reconstructing and extrapolating time-evolving probability distributions from unpaired observations without relying on costly numerical simulation, while also handling dynamics that are not purely dissipative.
method: Formulate population dynamics in Wasserstein space using a Lagrangian mechanics perspective.
Replace simulation-based training with residual-based learning, so the model is optimized directly from observed snapshots.
Enable learning of both gradient-flow and non-gradient-flow behavior, including conservative and periodic motion.
Avoid running a numerical solver at every training step, reducing computational overhead.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more scalable and flexible way to model evolving distributions from sparse observations. It is especially useful in scientific domains where dynamics may be cyclic, reversible, or otherwise incompatible with standard gradient-flow assumptions.

title: Pivot-SD: Efficient Self-Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models
authors: Seo Hyun Kim, Sunwoo Hong, Younwoo Choi, Chen-Hao Chao, Se-Young Yun
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLMs) offer a promising parallel alternative to autoregressive models for complex reasoning. However, they face a distinct credit-assignment challenge, since a few commitments during denoising sharply reduce the uncertainty over the remaining masked positions and shape much of the response. Most post-training recipes for dLMs do not use this signal to decide which tokens to train on: they typically train on the final text or assign rewards to whole denoising ste

infographic.key_insight: Pivot-SD identifies and trains on the most informative denoising steps in masked diffusion language models, rather than treating all generated tokens or steps equally. This makes self-distillation more efficient and better aligned with the model’s true credit-assignment signal.
infographic.problem_solved: Masked diffusion language models struggle with credit assignment during denoising: a few early commitments can drastically change which remaining tokens matter most, but common post-training methods ignore this structure and optimize only on final outputs or coarse sequence-level rewards.
method: Select pivotal denoising positions that carry the strongest information about the remaining masked tokens.
Apply self-distillation to these high-value steps so the model learns from its own most informative intermediate states.
Reduce wasted training on low-signal tokens/steps, improving efficiency and alignment with the diffusion generation process.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, Pivot-SD offers a more targeted post-training strategy for masked diffusion LMs, potentially improving reasoning quality while using training compute more effectively. It is especially relevant for building faster, more scalable non-autoregressive language models.

title: Forecasting from Counterfactual Simulator Rollouts: A Sim2Real Evaluation
authors: Angel Wang, Dominique Perrault-Joncas, Alvaro Maggiar, Dean Foster, Carson Eisenach
abstract: Deploying a new decision policy creates a cold-start problem for prediction models whose targets depend on the policy's actions: historical observations reflect earlier policies, while real observations under the new policy are not yet available. Simulation offers a way to address this gap by rolling out the target policy across counterfactual scenarios and using the resulting trajectories to learn how the system responds to those controls. The simulation-to-reality (Sim2Real) transfer of this s

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that counterfactual simulator rollouts can be used to forecast outcomes under a new decision policy before real-world data from that policy exists. In short, it tackles the cold-start problem by using simulation to bridge the gap between past behavior and future deployment.
infographic.problem_solved: When a model’s targets depend on actions taken by a policy, historical data reflects older policies and does not match the new policy we want to evaluate. This creates a cold-start challenge for forecasting and policy evaluation under distribution shift.
method: Roll out the target policy inside a simulator across counterfactual scenarios to generate synthetic trajectories.
Use those simulated trajectories to learn how the system responds to the new policy’s actions.
Evaluate how well predictions learned from simulation transfer to real-world behavior in a Sim2Real setting.
infographic.impact: This helps AI/ML practitioners evaluate and forecast policy outcomes earlier, before sufficient real-world data is available. It is especially useful for decision-making systems where collecting on-policy data is expensive, slow, or risky.

title: Transcriptome-informed multi-modal AI for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response from breast cancer biopsies
authors: Jungkyu Park, Dhruva Biswas, Joseph Cappadona, Cerise Tang, Ken G. Zeng
abstract: Scarcity of labeled data limits development of deep learning biomarkers in oncology. We develop a two-stage AI model predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer. The first stage learns the transcriptome from histopathology using 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types, corroborated by pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured expression. This simplifies the second stage to predicting pCR from inferred expression and clinical variables. Devel

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that histopathology slides can be used to infer transcriptomic signals, which then improve prediction of breast cancer response to neoadjuvant therapy. The key breakthrough is a two-stage AI pipeline that turns scarce labeled biomarker data into a more learnable prediction task.
infographic.problem_solved: Deep learning biomarkers in oncology often suffer from too few labeled samples, especially for predicting treatment response such as pathological complete response (pCR). The paper addresses how to build a robust predictor despite limited direct labels by leveraging transcriptome information inferred from pathology images.
method: Stage 1: Train a model on 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types to infer transcriptomic features from histopathology slides.
Validate inferred expression using pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured gene expression.
Stage 2: Use inferred transcriptomic features plus clinical variables to predict pCR after neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this demonstrates a scalable strategy for using weakly supervised or proxy representations to overcome label scarcity in medical imaging. It also suggests a practical path for integrating multimodal data to improve clinically relevant prediction tasks.

title: Less Decoder is More Encoder: Geometric Representation Learning from Novel View Synthesis
authors: Keerthi Kaashyap, Dennis Anthony, Akshay Krishnan, Nhi Ngoc Nguyen, Jeremy Collins
abstract: This paper examines the role of Novel View Synthesis (NVS) in geometric representation learning. In principle, NVS should reason about 3D scene structure, thereby enabling transferable multi-view geometric representations. Yet, existing encoder-based NVS methods yield poor representations. This is not because of a lack of supervisory signal, but rather due to inconspicuous architectural choices: \textit{spatially expressive decoders} that dilute representational capabilities of the scene encoder

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that weak geometric representations in encoder-based novel view synthesis are not mainly caused by insufficient supervision. Instead, the real issue is that overly expressive spatial decoders absorb too much of the reconstruction burden, preventing the encoder from learning strong 3D scene representations.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap between novel view synthesis performance and the quality of learned geometric representations, especially why encoder-based NVS methods often fail to produce transferable multi-view features.
method: Analyze encoder-based novel view synthesis through the lens of geometric representation learning.
Show that spatially expressive decoders can weaken the encoder’s incentive to encode scene structure.
Motivate architectural designs that shift more responsibility for 3D understanding back to the encoder.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes NVS design: better geometric features may come less from adding supervision and more from choosing the right encoder-decoder balance. This can improve downstream transfer to tasks that need robust 3D scene understanding.

title: On-Board Anomaly Detection for Efficient Marine Environmental Monitoring
authors: Thomas Goudemant, Clotilde Szywala, Benjamin Francesconi, Michelle Aubrun, Yves Bobichon
abstract: Marine ecosystems are impacted by various threats such as oil spills, algal blooms, and sediment floods, which disrupt habitats, wildlife, and human activities. Advances in satellite imagery and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have enhanced our capabilities for early detection and mitigation of such hazards. In this paper, we propose a marine event detection pipeline for Earth observation satellites equipped with multi- or hyperspectral sensors. Our approach includes a self-supervised neural networ

infographic.key_insight: This paper proposes an on-board AI pipeline that detects marine anomalies directly on Earth observation satellites, reducing the need to downlink all raw sensor data. By combining self-supervised learning with multi- or hyperspectral imagery, it aims to spot events like oil spills, algal blooms, and sediment floods earlier and more efficiently.
infographic.problem_solved: Marine hazards are costly and time-sensitive, but traditional monitoring relies on large-volume satellite data transmission and post-processing on the ground. The paper addresses the challenge of detecting environmental anomalies quickly and efficiently, especially when onboard compute and communication are limited.
method: Uses a self-supervised neural network to learn normal marine spectral patterns from satellite imagery.
Performs anomaly detection onboard the satellite using multi- or hyperspectral sensor data.
Flags unusual observations for prioritized transmission or further analysis, improving bandwidth and response efficiency.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how compact, self-supervised models can enable real-world edge deployment in resource-constrained remote sensing systems. It is especially relevant for building scalable monitoring pipelines where early detection and low-latency decisions matter.

title: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
authors: Yen-Jen Wang, Haozhe Jiang, Shuying Deng, Haoru Xue, Weirui Ye
abstract: Building reliable robot capabilities across diverse tasks requires substantial human effort to develop and maintain skills, design rewards, and integrate perception with control. We present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework for autonomous improvement of robot execution systems without updating model weights. RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. During practice, RPG uses execution feedback, privileged s

infographic.key_insight: RPG lets embodied agents improve their robot skills without changing model weights by first reconstructing capabilities from offline data, then practicing those skills in simulation, and finally transferring the gains back to real execution. In simple terms: it turns past experience into targeted self-training for better robot performance.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high human cost of building, tuning, and maintaining reliable robot skills across many manipulation tasks, especially when perception and control must be integrated and rewards are hard to design.
method: Identify manipulation capabilities from an offline dataset to infer what the robot already knows or can learn.
Construct related practice tasks in simulation to target those capabilities in a controlled setting.
Use execution feedback and privileged simulation information during practice to guide improvement, without updating the model weights.
Transfer the practiced behavior back to real-world execution for improved performance.
infographic.impact: This matters because it offers a practical path to continual robot improvement without expensive retraining or manual reward engineering. For AI/ML practitioners, RPG suggests a scalable way to reuse logs and simulation to boost embodied agent reliability.

title: Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models
authors: Hui Ren, Zihan Li, Chang Liu, Huidong Liu, Alexander Schwing
abstract: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Yet they share a structural bottleneck: when decoding in parallel, each token is sampled independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among the tokens decoded together. Continuous diffusion language models avoid this by denoising a shared continuous state, but their denoiser sees only that state, s

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models aim to preserve the global coordination benefits of continuous diffusion while reducing the bottleneck of independent parallel token sampling. The core idea is to introduce a hierarchical structure so denoising can model richer dependencies among tokens generated together.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses a major weakness in diffusion-based language generation: parallel decoding often samples each token independently, which breaks dependencies and hurts coherent, globally consistent outputs. It also targets the limitation that standard continuous diffusion denoisers only observe a shared latent state, limiting token-level coordination.
method: Use a continuous diffusion framework for language generation instead of purely discrete token-wise sampling.
Introduce a hierarchical denoising structure to better capture dependencies among tokens decoded in parallel.
Improve global constraint satisfaction and bidirectional reasoning by allowing the model to coordinate tokens through shared intermediate representations.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this could mean more coherent generations and better handling of tasks that require global planning, constraint satisfaction, or bidirectional reasoning. It is especially relevant for applications where parallel decoding efficiency is important but independence assumptions are too restrictive.

title: SILSA: Sliding-Window Slice Latents for Topology-Preserving High-Resolution 3D Generation
authors: Tianjiao Yu, Xinzhuo Li, Yifan Shen, Ying Shen, Kiet A. Nguyen
abstract: High-resolution 3D generation increasingly relies on voxel latents and multi-stage pipelines that first predict active structure and then synthesize local geometry. While effective, this design fragments continuous surfaces into many local tokens, inflates generation cost, and often weakens topological consistency for thin or highly connected shapes. We introduce SILSA, a topology-aware 3D generation framework that represents shapes with compact sliding-window slice latents. Instead of generatin

infographic.key_insight: SILSA replaces fragmented voxel-based 3D generation with compact sliding-window slice latents, helping preserve topology while reducing generation cost. The core idea is to keep surfaces more continuous so thin and highly connected structures are represented more faithfully.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing high-resolution 3D generation methods often split shapes into many local tokens, which makes generation expensive and can break topological consistency, especially for thin structures or complex connections.
method: Represents 3D shapes using compact sliding-window slice latents instead of dense voxel token pipelines.
Generates local geometry in a topology-aware way while maintaining continuity across neighboring slices.
Reduces token fragmentation and improves efficiency compared with multi-stage active-structure-then-geometry workflows.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, SILSA offers a more efficient path to high-resolution 3D generation with better shape integrity. This is especially useful for applications where topology matters, such as CAD, robotics, and digital content creation.

title: The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Shuo Xing, Zilin Dai, Chengyuan Qian, Fangzhou Lin, Wenjing Chen
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated striking capabilities on frontier mathematical problems, it remains unclear whether they possess the structural mathematical understanding underlying their solutions. In this paper, we take a first step toward systematically studying mathematical understanding in LLMs, from diagnosing its distinct capabilities to leveraging these findings to improve post-training. First, we introduce the notion of Mathematical Primitive to probe structural mat

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that strong math performance in LLMs may hide a missing underlying "primitive" for true structural mathematical understanding. It introduces a way to diagnose those gaps and use the findings to improve post-training.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of determining whether LLMs truly understand mathematical structure or are mainly pattern-matching their way through problems, and how to repair weaknesses in that understanding.
method: Define and use a "Mathematical Primitive" to probe specific structural capabilities in LLMs.
Systematically diagnose which components of mathematical understanding are present or missing.
Leverage diagnostic results to guide post-training improvements for better mathematical reasoning.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more principled way to evaluate math reasoning beyond final-answer accuracy. It also offers a path to make models more reliable on complex mathematical tasks by targeting the real source of failure.

title: Sphere Encoder 2
authors: Kaiyu Yue, Sean McLeish, Ruchit Rawal, Brian Bartoldson, Menglin Jia
abstract: Sphere Encoder is an autoencoder that generates images by decoding random points from a high-dimensional latent sphere. We identify two limitations of the original formulation that reduce its generation quality. First, random points concentrate near the equator relative to the pole on an encoded latent, but the training rotation never reaches this region, leaving a gap that limits one-step generation. Second, training for generation with pixel-wise reconstruction loss encourages the decoder to a

infographic.key_insight: Sphere Encoder 2 improves one-step image generation from a spherical latent space by fixing training and decoding mismatches in the original Sphere Encoder. The result is a better-aligned latent geometry that supports higher-quality sampling from random points on the sphere.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses two quality-limiting issues in the original Sphere Encoder: unseen latent regions near the equator during training and a reconstruction objective that can push the decoder toward overly pixel-faithful rather than generative behavior.
method: Identify and analyze the latent-space coverage gap caused by spherical concentration during random sampling.
Adjust the training formulation so decoding performance is improved in regions that matter for one-step generation.
Refine the reconstruction/generative objective to encourage outputs that are better suited for sampling-based image generation rather than only pixel-perfect reconstructions.
infographic.impact: This work helps make spherical autoencoders more practical for fast, one-step generative modeling. For practitioners, it suggests a more reliable way to sample high-quality images from a structured latent space without needing iterative diffusion-style generation.

title: InterEvolve: Test-Time Evolution of Reward Programs for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Zhuo Lin, Sirui Xu, Liuyu Bian, Yu-Xiong Wang, Liang-Yan Gui
abstract: We study test-time evolution for humanoid loco-manipulation: solving tasks that a controller was never trained for by repurposing its existing skills, improving from its own attempts, and retaining what it learns, without retraining. Our key insight is that a broad controller already holds much of the competence a new task needs, and that this competence becomes accessible through an interface between planning and control that is expressive enough to specify contact-rich, multi-stage interaction

infographic.key_insight: A humanoid controller can often solve new tasks by reusing skills it already has, if test-time planning can express the right contact-rich, multi-stage interactions. The paper shows that the system can improve from its own attempts and keep that improvement without retraining.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how to make a humanoid robot perform unseen loco-manipulation tasks it was never explicitly trained on, while adapting online at test time instead of requiring costly retraining.
method: Use a broad pre-trained controller as the base skill set for new humanoid loco-manipulation tasks.
Evolve reward programs at test time so the controller can better match the new task through repeated self-attempts.
Retain successful adaptations, enabling continual improvement without offline retraining.
infographic.impact: This matters because it points to a practical path for deploying humanoid robots in novel real-world tasks with less task-specific training. For practitioners, it suggests more flexible robots that can adapt on the fly using existing competencies rather than starting from scratch.

title: Shifting from knowledge retrieval to evidence exploration and synthesis

Biomedical discovery has entered an era in which the limiting resource is no longer data, but our ability to integrate and interpret evidence. DeepEvidence, a new deep research agent, goes beyond retrieving facts and constructs explicit representations of scientific evidence.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that AI for biomedical discovery should move beyond simple knowledge retrieval and instead help researchers explore, structure, and synthesize evidence. DeepEvidence is presented as a deep research agent that builds explicit representations of scientific evidence rather than just returning facts.
infographic.problem_solved: Biomedical research is no longer limited by data availability; the main bottleneck is now integrating, interpreting, and organizing large volumes of evidence into usable scientific understanding.
method: Uses a deep research agent to go beyond search-and-retrieve workflows.
Constructs explicit representations of evidence, enabling evidence exploration and synthesis.
Aims to support reasoning over scientific sources rather than isolated fact lookup.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights a shift from retrieval-augmented systems toward agents that can reason over evidence and support higher-level scientific workflows. It points to a new design goal for domain AI: helping users build trustworthy, structured understanding from complex literature.

title: TACO: Ternary Absolute-max Column-wise One-sparse Optimizer for LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Jichao Jiang, Cristian McGee, El Houcine Bergou, Hanqin Cai, Aritra Dutta
abstract: Full-parameter fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) incurs substantial optimizer state memory overhead, limiting the model sizes that fit on modern GPUs. Existing approaches either compress optimizer state, abandon first-order gradients, or change the update geometry while retaining dense state. The recently introduced Muon optimizer reduces optimizer memory through matrix-valued updates. Still, its geometry differs from AdamW and can lead to performance degradation when fine-tuning AdamW

infographic.key_insight: TACO is a memory-efficient optimizer designed to keep AdamW-like fine-tuning behavior while drastically reducing optimizer state overhead. It targets the main bottleneck in full-parameter LLM fine-tuning: fitting large models and their optimizer states on limited GPU memory.
infographic.problem_solved: Full-parameter fine-tuning of large language models requires storing large optimizer states, which consumes a lot of GPU memory and limits the largest models that can be trained. Existing memory-saving optimizers often change the update geometry or reduce performance compared with AdamW.
method: Uses a ternary, absolute-max, column-wise, one-sparse update scheme to compress optimizer state.
Aims to preserve AdamW-like optimization behavior while reducing memory footprint.
Provides an alternative to dense-state optimizers and geometry-changing methods such as matrix-valued updates.
infographic.impact: This approach can enable fine-tuning larger LLMs on the same hardware budget, making advanced adaptation more accessible to researchers and practitioners. It is especially relevant when preserving AdamW-style performance is important but GPU memory is tight.

title: HiPhy: Hierarchical Alignment for Physically-Plausible Multi-Principle Video Generation
authors: Tahira Kazimi, Shubhankar Borse, Munawar Hayat, Fatih Porikli, Pinar Yanardag
abstract: Video generation models have achieved remarkable visual fidelity and have strong potential to become general-purpose world simulators. Despite this progress, they still fail to generate videos which adhere to laws of physics. The problem becomes even more apparent in realistic settings where multiple physical principles must work together within the same video; for example, "a balloon floating upward while steam rises from a pot" requires buoyancy and fluid dynamics to unfold coherently and simu

infographic.key_insight: HiPhy aims to make video generation physically believable by aligning generated content with multiple physical principles at the same time, rather than treating physics as a single generic constraint. This helps models produce scenes where different forces and interactions co-exist coherently.
infographic.problem_solved: Current video generators can look realistic but often violate physics, especially in scenes requiring multiple principles simultaneously, such as buoyancy, fluid motion, gravity, and object interaction within one clip.
method: Uses a hierarchical alignment strategy to guide generation toward physical consistency across different levels of motion and interaction.
Targets multi-principle scenes, encouraging the model to satisfy several physical laws together instead of optimizing for appearance alone.
Aims to improve coherence in realistic video synthesis by integrating physical plausibility into the generation process.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this points toward more trustworthy and simulation-like video generation systems that can support robotics, planning, virtual worlds, and scientific visualization. It also highlights a path beyond visually plausible outputs toward physically grounded generative models.

title: Large language models discover complementary heuristics for combinatorial optimization
authors: Huatian Gong, Shuaian Wang, Dongping Song, Jiuh-Biing Sheu, Ran Yan
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01307-8

Huatian Gong and colleagues developed LACE, a large language model-based framework that designs optimization algorithms. It builds a verified problem contract, then evolves a portfolio of complementary heuristics that together solve problems that no single method can handle.

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that large language models can do more than generate text: they can help design optimization algorithms. The key breakthrough is LACE, a framework that assembles multiple complementary heuristics so a problem can be solved even when no single method is sufficient.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of creating effective combinatorial optimization algorithms for hard problems where traditional single-heuristic approaches often fail or perform inconsistently.
method: Build a verified problem contract that precisely defines the optimization task and constraints.
Use a large language model to generate and evolve a portfolio of heuristics rather than relying on one algorithm.
Combine complementary heuristics so different methods cover each other’s weaknesses and improve overall solving power.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests LLMs can support automated algorithm design, not just model selection or parameter tuning. It may reduce manual trial-and-error when building solvers for complex optimization problems and improve robustness across diverse instances.
