title: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research
authors: Sohyeon Kim, Yoonho Lee, Bo Liu, Dayoon Ko, Rulin Shao
abstract: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having

infographic.key_insight: ScholarCatalyst introduces a benchmark for measuring whether AI can retrieve prior papers that genuinely inspire new research, not just papers that are topically similar. It captures the human skill of finding the right earlier idea that helps solve a new problem.
infographic.problem_solved: Current search and retrieval systems are good at finding relevant papers, but they struggle to identify the specific prior work that actually sparks or enables a research advance. This paper addresses the lack of a benchmark for evaluating that higher-level, inspiration-oriented retrieval ability.
method: Built a benchmark called ScholarCatalyst using papers as evidence of which prior works influenced completed research projects.
Collected author annotations through an automated pipeline to make large-scale labeling practical and scalable.
Frames retrieval as finding papers that inspired new research, rather than simply matching keywords or citations.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark provides a more realistic test of research-assistant systems, literature search tools, and scholarly recommendation models. It can help build systems that support discovery, ideation, and scientific progress, not just document retrieval.

title: Embedding Prediction Helps Image Generation
authors: Sihan Xu, Ji Xie, Zilin Wang, Hui Shen, Stella X. Yu
abstract: In diffusion transformers, a class label or a text prompt is embedded once, and the same condition is reused at every denoising step. We ask whether predicted embeddings can serve as this condition instead. Next-Embedding Predictive Autoregression (NEPA) trains a Transformer to predict the next continuous embedding in a sequence. In generation, the clean image follows the noisy image, so its embeddings are the next embeddings after the condition and the noisy image. We train a NEPA model to pred

infographic.key_insight: Instead of reusing a fixed class or text embedding at every diffusion step, the paper shows that predicting the next embedding can act as a better condition for image generation. This turns conditioning into a learned sequence prediction problem and can improve how generative models guide denoising.
infographic.problem_solved: Diffusion transformers typically rely on a single condition embedding that is reused unchanged across all denoising steps, which may limit expressiveness. The paper asks whether a model can generate more useful conditioning signals by predicting continuous embeddings over time.
method: Introduce Next-Embedding Predictive Autoregression (NEPA), a Transformer trained to predict the next continuous embedding in a sequence.
Use the relationship between noisy images, clean images, and their embeddings so that the clean image is treated as the "next" embedding after the noisy-conditioned context.
Replace static conditioning with predicted embeddings during generation to better align the condition with the evolving denoising process.
infographic.impact: For AI practitioners, this suggests a new way to condition diffusion models that may be more adaptive and informative than fixed prompts or labels. It could improve image generation quality while opening the door to embedding-prediction-based conditioning for other generative tasks.

title: VISTA: A Visual Harness for Reasoning in an Interactive World
authors: Qiushi Han, Keya Hu, Linlu Qiu, Cathy Wu, Kaiming He
abstract: We show that multimodal models possess strong reasoning abilities and that an appropriate harness can unlock their potential to solve tasks across diverse interactive environments. We introduce VISTA, a visual harness that gives a general-purpose multimodal model long-horizon vision. VISTA allows the model to directly perceive the environment through visual observations and maintains a lossless visual memory that preserves past observations in their original form. The model can actively retrieve

infographic.key_insight: VISTA shows that multimodal models can do much better at interactive reasoning when they are given a visual harness that preserves what they have seen and lets them revisit it later. In short: the model's reasoning is strong; the right memory and perception setup unlocks it.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of making general-purpose multimodal models effective in long-horizon, interactive environments where important visual information can be missed, forgotten, or corrupted by text-only summaries.
method: Provides direct visual observation of the environment so the model can perceive state changes without relying only on text.
Maintains a lossless visual memory that stores past observations in their original form.
Supports active retrieval of prior visual information to help reasoning across long interactive sequences.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, VISTA suggests that better harness design can substantially improve multimodal agents without changing the base model itself. This is useful for building more reliable systems for robotics, games, GUI agents, and other interactive tasks.

title: ROWBench: Do Video Models Render What the Program Specifies?
authors: Zheng-Hui Huang, Guixu Lin, Yu-Ju Tsai, Jian-Kai Zhu, Fengbo Lan
abstract: Programmable world models separate executable dynamics from visual generation, offering a promising foundation for next-generation game engines. However, their visual adherence to explicit rules and interactions remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing benchmarks assess visual quality, controllability, and instruction or physical adherence, but rarely test fidelity to fine-grained, program-specified world events. We introduce PROWBench, comprising 170 programmatically constructed episodes and

infographic.key_insight: ROWBench highlights that current video/world models are still weak at faithfully rendering fine-grained events exactly as specified by a program. It introduces PROWBench to test whether models can visually follow explicit rules, not just produce realistic-looking videos.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of benchmarks for evaluating whether programmable world models obey detailed, program-specified dynamics and interactions. Existing evaluations focus more on visual quality or broad controllability than exact event fidelity.
method: Introduces PROWBench, a benchmark of 170 programmatically constructed episodes designed to probe rule-following in generated video.
Evaluates whether video models render specific world events and interactions as specified by executable programs.
Targets fine-grained adherence rather than only realism, instruction following, or general physical plausibility.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark provides a more rigorous way to measure whether world models can serve as reliable components for game engines and interactive simulation. It helps identify models that look plausible but fail to execute exact specified behavior.

title: Generative modeling of intrinsically disordered protein regions by reinforcing sparse autoencoder features
authors: Jason X. Liu, Sebastian Ibarraran, Frank Hu, Soojung Yang, Xinyu A. Feng
abstract: Intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs) play central roles in cellular processes such as transcriptional regulation, signal transduction, and subcellular localization, yet their functional design remains challenging. Structure-based design methods do not readily apply to IDRs, and existing protein language models are trained on full-length protein sequences, thus learning a prior that is biased towards folded domains. Here, we present IDiom, an autoregressive protein language model train

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces IDiom, an autoregressive protein language model designed specifically to generate intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs). By reinforcing sparse autoencoder features, it shifts generation away from folded-protein biases and toward the sequence properties that matter for disordered function.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of designing IDRs, which do not follow the structure-based rules used for folded proteins. Existing protein language models are trained on full-length proteins and tend to favor structured domains, making them poorly suited for IDR generation.
method: Build an autoregressive protein language model tailored to IDR sequence generation.
Use sparse autoencoder features to identify and reinforce latent representations relevant to disordered regions.
Guide the model away from folded-protein priors so it better captures IDR-specific sequence patterns.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how representation steering can adapt a general generative model to a specialized biological domain. More broadly, it demonstrates a pathway for correcting dataset-induced bias in foundation models when the target distribution differs from the training prior.

title: Semifactual Credit-Augmented Policy Optimization
authors: Junshu Pan, Zhizhang Fu, Shulin Huang, Yiran Ding, Zifan Cheng
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet their predictions remain sensitive to task-irrelevant prompt features. We investigate this sensitivity through semifactual prompt interventions that preserve the underlying problem and its answer. Our analysis reveals substantial variation in token-level sensitivity and shows that suppressing high-drift token candidates during decoding improves reasoning accuracy wit

infographic.key_insight: LLMs trained with verifiable rewards can still be steered by irrelevant prompt details, but measuring and suppressing the most sensitive token choices during decoding can improve reasoning accuracy. The paper shows that semifactual prompt changes reveal where models are brittle and how to make them more robust.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses prompt sensitivity in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where models' reasoning outputs can change due to task-irrelevant wording even when the underlying problem and correct answer stay the same.
method: Apply semifactual prompt interventions that change surface form while preserving the task and answer.
Measure token-level sensitivity to identify high-drift token candidates that cause unstable reasoning behavior.
Suppress high-drift candidates during decoding to reduce prompt-irrelevant variation and improve accuracy.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to diagnose and reduce brittleness in reasoning models without changing the task itself. It can improve reliability of RLVR-trained LLMs in evaluation and deployment settings where prompts vary slightly.

title: Physis-Lang: Self-Evolving Language as a Physical Representation for Video World Model
authors: Liming Lu, Xianzheng Ma, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Yilin Zhao
abstract: Video world models are expected to predict how the physical world evolves, yet they often produce visually plausible videos that violate basic physical principles. Existing approaches commonly assume that natural language is insufficient to represent the physical knowledge required for reliable generation, and therefore introduce additional visual, latent, numerical, or planning-based signals. We revisit this assumption and introduce Physis-Lang, a self-evolving framework that treats physical la

infographic.key_insight: Physis-Lang argues that language can be more than a description tool: it can become a self-evolving physical representation for video world models. The core breakthrough is a framework that learns and updates physical knowledge in language form to improve physically consistent video prediction.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between visually plausible video generation and physically correct world modeling. Existing video world models often ignore or poorly represent physical laws, leading to outputs that look realistic but break basic physics.
method: Introduces Physis-Lang, a self-evolving language-based framework for representing physical knowledge in video world models.
Learns physical concepts as language representations rather than relying only on extra visual, latent, numerical, or planning signals.
Updates and refines this physical language over time so the model can better predict how scenes evolve under physical constraints.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a simpler and more flexible path to physically grounded video generation and world modeling. It could reduce reliance on complex auxiliary modalities while improving consistency, interpretability, and transferability of learned physics.

title: Image Classifiers are Efficient Self-Supervised Video Representation Learners
authors: Owais Iqbal, Sudipta Sarkar, Shyam Marjit, Omprakash Chakraborty, Anirban Chakraborty
abstract: We introduce VideoMSN, a Masked Siamese Network framework for efficient self-supervised spatio-temporal representation learning in videos. Instead of relying on heavy 3D architectures or reconstruction-based autoencoders for learning with unlabeled data, we repurpose standard image Vision Transformers by representing videos as super images which are grids composed of frames sampled from videos. From each super image, we construct two views: one with spatial patch masking and the other with tempo

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that off-the-shelf image Vision Transformers can learn strong video representations without specialized 3D video models. By turning videos into “super images” and training with masked self-supervision, VideoMSN efficiently captures spatio-temporal information from unlabeled data.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the high cost and complexity of learning video representations, which often depends on heavy 3D architectures or reconstruction-based autoencoders. The goal is to make self-supervised video learning more efficient using standard image models.
method: Convert each video into a super image: a grid of sampled frames arranged into one image.
Create two complementary views from the super image using spatial patch masking and temporal masking.
Train a Masked Siamese Network with a standard image Vision Transformer to learn spatio-temporal features without labels.
infographic.impact: This approach lowers the barrier for practitioners who want scalable video pretraining without building specialized video backbones. It suggests that strong video understanding can be achieved by reusing mature image-model tooling in a simpler and more efficient way.

title: Towards foundation-style models for energy-frontier heterogeneous neutrino detectors via self-supervised pretraining
authors: Saúl Alonso-Monsalve, Fabio Cufino, Umut Kose, Anna Mascellani, André Rubbia
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01309-6

Fine-tune the pretrained representations for downstream tasks such as event classification and reconstruction.

It also highlights a path toward reusable foundation-style models that generalize across related but different sensors or instruments.

title: Multimodal Flow: Unified Flow Modeling of Language and Vision in Embedding Spaces
authors: Hongyuan Tao, Xinggang Wang, Lianghui Zhu, Yongkang Li, Yunchao Wei
abstract: We present Multimodal Flow, a fully continuous generative model of language and vision. Most unified multimodal models either model both language and quantized images as discrete tokens or combine discrete language prediction with continuous image generation. The former introduces a visual quantization bottleneck. The latter requires modality-dependent objectives and sampling procedures. Fully continuous modeling avoids these trade-offs and enables a shared generative process, but remains undere

infographic.key_insight: Multimodal Flow proposes a single, fully continuous generative framework for both language and vision in shared embedding spaces. This removes the need to mix discrete text prediction with quantized or modality-specific image generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing unified multimodal models often rely on discrete tokens for both modalities or use separate objectives/sampling for text and images. This creates a visual quantization bottleneck and makes multimodal generation less consistent and harder to unify.
method: Model language and vision with a shared continuous flow-based generative process in embedding space.
Avoid image quantization and modality-specific decoding by learning a unified representation for both modalities.
Use a single sampling/generation mechanism across language and vision to simplify multimodal generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this could simplify multimodal model design by reducing modality-specific components and avoiding quantization loss in images. It also points toward more coherent and flexible joint generation of text and visual content.

title: ViTeX-Bench: Benchmarking High-Fidelity Video Scene Text Editing
authors: Xinghao Chen, Xiangbo Gao, Jiongze Yu, Yuheng Wu, Zhengzhong Tu
abstract: Recent video generation is increasingly realistic and controllable, yet video editing remains less developed, particularly for precise local edits that must preserve the original scene dynamics. Video scene text editing replaces text on scene surfaces, such as storefront signs, whiteboards, and product labels, while preserving the surrounding content, motion, and camera dynamics. Although scene text editing is well studied for images, video scene text editing that achieves high visual quality, t

infographic.key_insight: ViTeX-Bench introduces a benchmark for evaluating how well models can edit text inside videos while keeping motion, scene structure, and visual realism intact. It highlights that video scene text editing is much harder than image editing because the edit must stay consistent across time.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of a standard evaluation benchmark for high-fidelity video scene text editing. This task requires replacing text on signs, labels, or boards in video without breaking temporal consistency, surrounding content, or camera motion.
method: Defines a benchmark tailored to video scene text editing quality and temporal preservation.
Evaluates edits on both local text replacement fidelity and global video consistency across frames.

infographic.impact: This benchmark gives researchers a common way to measure progress on a difficult video editing task. For practitioners, it helps identify whether a model can produce visually convincing edits that remain stable over time, which is essential for real-world video manipulation.

title: Ego4WAM: What Matters When Scaling Egocentric Human Data for Robot Learning?
authors: Zhihao Sun, Liu Liu, Xinjiang Wang, Haoyi Jiang, Wei Feng
abstract: Egocentric human data provides a scalable source of experience for robot learning, but varies substantially in human-robot alignment, behavioral coverage, and available supervision. Existing work shows favorable scaling with increasing human data, but it remains unclear which data properties drive downstream robot gains and how to use such data throughout the training pipeline. We present a systematic study of egocentric human data with different alignment and supervision under a unified world-a

infographic.key_insight: Not all egocentric human data helps robot learning equally: the biggest gains come from understanding which properties of the data—alignment, behavioral coverage, and supervision—actually matter during scaling. The paper shows how to systematically identify and leverage the most useful human data for downstream robot performance.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the lack of clarity around which characteristics of large-scale egocentric human datasets drive robot learning improvements, and how those datasets should be used across the training pipeline.
method: Conduct a systematic study of egocentric human data with varying levels of human-robot alignment and supervision.

infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work provides guidance on what to collect, label, and prioritize when building large human-data pipelines for robotics. It can help reduce wasted data collection effort and improve the efficiency of robot learning at scale.

title: Ranking-Aware Prompt Optimization for Multimodal Clinical Diagnosis
authors: Tian Xia, Minghao Liu, Yiqing Liang, Laixi Shi, Jiayun Wang
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing clinical diagnosis, yet their adaptation pipelines remain anchored to accuracy-based objectives. Clinical data are heavily class-imbalanced: a constant-majority predictor can score above 90% accuracy while being clinically useless. We therefore evaluate and optimize for AUROC, a threshold-free score that ranks positives above negatives and is invariant to class balance. We focus on prompt optimization in MLLMs. Reflective methods suc

infographic.key_insight: This paper shifts multimodal clinical diagnosis from accuracy-focused prompting to ranking-aware optimization, using AUROC as the target metric. The core idea is that better clinical prompts should rank true cases above false ones, especially when classes are highly imbalanced.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between standard accuracy-based optimization and the realities of clinical data, where majority-class predictions can look strong on paper but fail in practice. The paper tackles how to optimize prompts for MLLMs in a way that improves clinically meaningful discrimination under class imbalance.
method: Evaluates multimodal large language models using AUROC instead of accuracy to better reflect clinical ranking performance.
Introduces ranking-aware prompt optimization for improving how prompts separate positive from negative cases.
Focuses on reflective prompt methods adapted to optimize for threshold-free diagnostic discrimination rather than majority-class correctness.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that the choice of evaluation metric can completely change what counts as a good model in healthcare. It provides a more clinically aligned path for prompt optimization in MLLMs, especially for imbalanced diagnostic tasks.

title: AssemblyWorld: Rethinking 3D Assembly with General-Purpose Agents
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Yeying Fan, Moitreya Chatterjee, Suhas Lohit, Bernhard Egger
abstract: The task of 3D assembly requires translating an understanding of parts and their relationships into precise spatial arrangements. Can pretrained general-purpose agents assemble objects through visual interaction without additional assembly-specific fine-tuning? To investigate this question, we introduce AssemblyWorld, an interactive 3D environment in which agents inspect rendered views and manipulate supplied rigid parts, guided by images or assembly manuals when available. Agents perceive part

infographic.key_insight: AssemblyWorld tests whether general-purpose pretrained agents can perform 3D assembly just by seeing parts and interacting with them, without special assembly fine-tuning. The paper’s core idea is that assembly can be framed as a visual-interactive task in a controlled environment, revealing how far general agents can go on spatial reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between recognizing 3D parts and actually assembling them into correct spatial configurations. It tackles the challenge of evaluating whether existing pretrained agents can understand part relationships, follow assembly instructions, and perform precise manipulation in 3D.
method: Introduces AssemblyWorld, an interactive 3D environment where agents inspect rendered views of parts and manipulate rigid objects.
Provides assembly tasks guided by images or assembly manuals when available, enabling instruction-conditioned evaluation.
Measures whether general-purpose agents can complete assembly through visual interaction alone, without assembly-specific fine-tuning.
infographic.impact: This matters because it benchmarks real-world spatial reasoning and manipulation for foundation models in a realistic 3D setting. For practitioners, it helps identify the limits of current agents and what capabilities are needed for robotics, CAD, manufacturing, and embodied AI.

title: DMA$^2$: Pixel-space Distribution Matching with Adversarial and Anchor Losses
authors: Xin Lin, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Haitian Zheng, Shaoteng Liu
abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) provides a general framework for few-step diffusion generation, but its modern text-to-image instantiations have been developed primarily around latent diffusion. It therefore overlooks key properties and design opportunities of native RGB. We revisit two DMD interfaces for pixel-space teachers. On the teacher-matching side, diagnostics show low-noise RGB matching is dominated by a local-texture cue, motivating a fixed high-noise matching band. On the rea

infographic.key_insight: DMA² shows that distribution matching distillation works better in native pixel-space when it is adapted to RGB-specific behavior, especially by avoiding low-noise matching that overemphasizes local texture. The paper introduces adversarial and anchor losses to make few-step image generation more stable and more faithful in pixel space.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap between modern distribution-matching distillation methods and native RGB image generation, which have mostly been designed around latent diffusion. The paper asks how to better distill pixel-space teachers for fast, high-quality text-to-image synthesis.
method: Revisits distribution matching distillation for pixel-space teachers instead of latent-space-only setups.
Uses diagnostics to show that low-noise RGB matching is dominated by local texture cues, then replaces it with a fixed high-noise matching band.
Adds adversarial and anchor losses to improve realism and preserve alignment during few-step generation.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners building fast image generators because it offers a more suitable distillation recipe for native RGB models. It can improve sample quality and training stability while reducing dependence on latent-space assumptions.

title: Rethinking Representations for World-Action Modeling
authors: Haoyi Jiang, Liu Liu, Xinjiang Wang, Zhihao Sun, Zequn Chen
abstract: World-action models jointly learn robot policies and predict future observations, making the representation space an interface between control and prediction. We study the design of this space through controlled comparisons, finding that neither reconstruction fidelity nor pre-trained perceptual features alone ensure effective policy learning. These findings motivate ReWAM, a representation-centric world-action model built on pre-trained DINO features. Feature Calibration and a Temporal Represen

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that the representation space in world-action models is crucial for learning good robot policies, and that neither perfect reconstruction nor generic pre-trained features are enough on their own. It introduces ReWAM, which uses calibrated DINO-based features to better align prediction with control.
infographic.problem_solved: World-action models need a shared latent space that supports both future prediction and action planning, but it is unclear what kind of representation best enables policy learning. This paper addresses how to design that space so it works effectively for robotics control.
method: Run controlled comparisons to test different representation choices for world-action modeling.
Find that reconstruction-heavy and pre-trained perceptual representations each have limitations for policy learning.
Propose ReWAM, a representation-centric model built on pre-trained DINO features with feature calibration and temporal representation alignment.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work shifts attention from only model scale or reconstruction quality to the design of the latent representation itself. It offers a practical direction for building better robot learning systems that are more effective for both prediction and control.

title: Point2Part: Unified 3D Partitioning from Point Prompts
authors: Hao-Tang Tsui, Yu-Rou Tuan, Xiaoxuan Ma, Nicolas Ugrinovic, Takaaki Shiratori
abstract: Existing 3D part decomposition methods do not necessarily partition the original shape into non-overlapping parts that collectively cover the entire shape, allowing overlaps or gaps that hinder downstream part-level applications. We instead formulate part decomposition as a joint partitioning of the entire shape, where the predicted parts are non-overlapping and jointly recover the entire shape. Our key insight is that part decomposition should consider all desired parts jointly, rather than mod

infographic.key_insight: Point2Part reframes 3D part decomposition as a full-shape partitioning problem: predicted parts should be non-overlapping and together reconstruct the entire object. This makes part prediction more consistent and useful for downstream 3D tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Most existing 3D part decomposition methods can produce overlapping parts or leave gaps, so the parts do not form a complete, clean partition of the original shape. This limits reliability for part-level editing, analysis, and other downstream applications.
method: Uses point prompts to guide the decomposition of a 3D shape into parts.
Predicts all desired parts jointly, rather than one part at a time, to enforce consistency across the whole object.
Formulates the output as a unified partition so parts are non-overlapping and collectively cover the entire shape.
infographic.impact: This approach improves the structural validity of 3D part decomposition, making the results easier to use in robotics, CAD, asset editing, and other part-aware workflows. For practitioners, it offers cleaner and more dependable part annotations/predictions for downstream pipelines.

title: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
authors: Yi Pan, Haocheng Xi, Kan Zhu, Xingyang Li, Yibo Wu
abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid designs that replace standard attention with linear attention, such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). Although they compress the context into a fixed-size recurrent state and substantially reduce the cost of long-context processing, repeatedly reading and updating that state remains a major inference bottleneck. Quantization offers a natural way to reduce this cost, but can significantly degrade model quality, due to the accumulation of

infographic.key_insight: LeapQuant shows that recurrent state in linear-attention LLMs can be quantized much more efficiently without sacrificing accuracy. It targets the hidden bottleneck in long-context inference: repeatedly reading and updating the fixed-size state.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the inference cost of linear-attention models like GDN and KDA, where the recurrent state must be accessed at every step. Naive quantization can speed things up but often hurts model quality due to accumulated errors over long sequences.
method: Designs a quantization approach tailored to recurrent state updates in linear attention models.
Reduces memory bandwidth and compute cost while preserving the fidelity of the state across many timesteps.
Focuses on limiting error accumulation so long-context performance remains stable.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, LeapQuant offers a practical path to faster and more efficient long-context LLM inference. It is especially relevant for deployment settings where memory bandwidth, latency, and quality must all be balanced.

title: Beyond the Timeline: Augmenting Long-Video Memory with Grounded Entity Biographies
authors: Hui Ren, Lei Fan, Henry Pao, Han Guo, Zeeshan Zia
abstract: Answering questions about long videos often requires connecting events involving the same objects across hours or days. Chronological descriptions and text-derived entities can leave physical identity unresolved: different objects may share a description, while observations of the same object remain disconnected across events. Retrieving relevant events therefore does not necessarily recover the "biography" of the particular entity a question concerns. To address this, we introduce Grounded Enti

infographic.key_insight: For long-video QA, finding related events is not enough if the system cannot tell which exact object is being tracked over time. This paper argues for grounding “entity biographies” to preserve physical identity across hours or days.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the failure of timeline-based retrieval in long videos, where the same object can appear in disconnected events and different objects can share similar descriptions. This makes it hard to answer questions that depend on tracking a specific entity’s history.
method: Introduces Grounded Entity Biographies to represent an object’s identity-linked history across a long video.
Connects observations of the same physical entity across time instead of relying only on chronological event retrieval or text-derived entity mentions.
Evaluates how biography-aware retrieval improves long-video memory and question answering over timeline-only approaches.
infographic.impact: This helps AI systems answer object-centric questions in long videos more reliably, especially when identity continuity matters more than event order. For practitioners, it suggests a better memory design for surveillance, robotics, sports analysis, and multi-hour video understanding.

title: Adversarial Training for Pixel Diffusion
authors: Xin Lin, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Haitian Zheng, Zhe Lin
abstract: Pixel diffusion models generate RGB images directly, avoiding the bottleneck of an autoencoder, yet their outputs still systematically underrepresent fine-scale natural-image statistics. We show that adversarial learning provides an effective post-training correction for this deficiency. Starting from a pretrained model, we retain its original diffusion or flow-matching objective and add an adversarial loss to the predicted output at non-high-noise timesteps, leaving the model architecture and s

infographic.key_insight: Adversarial training can be added after pretraining to improve pixel diffusion models, helping them capture fine-scale natural image details more faithfully. The paper shows that this correction works without changing the core model architecture or replacing the original diffusion objective.
infographic.problem_solved: Pixel diffusion models generate images directly in RGB space, but they still miss or weaken subtle natural-image statistics such as fine textures and local realism. This paper addresses the quality gap between visually good samples and truly realistic fine-grained image detail.
method: Start from a pretrained pixel diffusion or flow-matching model.
Keep the original generative objective unchanged, and add an adversarial loss on predicted outputs at non-high-noise timesteps.
Use adversarial learning as a post-training correction to improve realism and fine-detail fidelity without redesigning the model.
infographic.impact: This gives practitioners a practical way to boost image quality in pixel-space generative models without the complexity of adding an autoencoder pipeline. It is especially useful when the goal is sharper, more natural-looking images with better local statistics.

title: Counterfactual Video Generation Enables Scalable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Zihan Wang, Zhen Wu, Pieter Abbeel, Rocky Duan, Jitendra Malik
abstract: Teaching humanoids loco-manipulation skills, such as carrying diverse objects, via visual imitation is a promising path toward generalist robots. However, collecting diverse, high-quality interaction videos, such as clips that clearly show a person's full body and unoccluded interactions with objects, poses a practical barrier to scaling this approach. We propose PRISM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that overcomes this limitation by amplifying a handful of real videos into a large, diverse tra

infographic.key_insight: PRISM shows that a small number of real human interaction videos can be amplified into a much larger and more diverse training set using counterfactual video generation. This makes it possible to scale humanoid loco-manipulation learning without needing massive amounts of expensive real-world video data.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the data bottleneck in teaching humanoids loco-manipulation skills through visual imitation. High-quality videos of full-body, unoccluded human-object interactions are hard to collect at scale, limiting the diversity and robustness of learned behaviors.
method: Uses a real-to-sim-to-real framework to convert a few real demonstrations into scalable training data.
Generates counterfactual videos to create diverse, plausible variations of human-object interactions from limited source clips.
Trains humanoid control policies from the expanded video set so the robot can learn broader carrying and manipulation behaviors.
infographic.impact: This approach lowers the cost and labor required to train humanoid robots from visual demonstrations, making generalist loco-manipulation more practical. For practitioners, it offers a scalable path to improve robot skill diversity without relying on large curated video datasets.

title: EmoRES-TTS: Residual-Enhanced Vector Steering for Emotional Speech Generation
authors: Kuan-Po Huang, Haohe Liu, Puyuan Peng, Haibin Wu, Zhaoheng Ni
abstract: Emotion-conditioned text-to-speech (TTS) models may fail to express the requested emotion reliably, and improving controllability by additional training is costly in both computation and emotion-labeled speech training data. We therefore study vector steering, a training-free approach that modifies the internal representations of a frozen model. CoCoEmo, a conventional vector steering method for emotion TTS, treats each emotion vector as an indivisible direction controlled by a single global str

infographic.key_insight: EmoRES-TTS improves emotion control in text-to-speech without retraining the model by steering internal representations more effectively. It refines conventional vector steering so emotional speech is expressed more reliably and with less computational cost.
infographic.problem_solved: Emotion-conditioned TTS models often fail to consistently produce the requested emotion, and improving this usually requires expensive retraining and emotion-labeled speech data. This paper addresses the need for a training-free, lower-cost way to better control emotional expression in frozen TTS models.
method: Uses training-free vector steering to adjust hidden representations inside a frozen emotion TTS model.
Introduces residual-enhanced steering, which likely decomposes or refines emotion directions beyond a single global vector to improve controllability.
Builds on conventional methods like CoCoEmo to make emotion control more precise and robust without additional model training.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to improve emotional speech generation without expensive fine-tuning or new labeled data. It is especially useful for deploying controllable TTS systems more efficiently and flexibly.

title: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization
authors: Bingchen Yao, Haobo Xu, Haokun Lin, Yichen Wu, Ziyu Guo
abstract: Linear attention replaces growing KV caches with fixed-size recurrent states, yet these persistent states can become a substantial memory bottleneck under concurrent serving. Directly quantizing recurrent states to low precision often leads to severe accuracy degradation, as quantization errors propagate through successive state updates. We discover that the impact of these errors depends on two complementary dimensions: temporally, errors in long-lived memory can persist across many decoding st

infographic.key_insight: Quantization errors in recurrent states are not equally harmful: their impact depends on when they occur and where in the state they land. STEPQuant shows that preserving the most error-sensitive parts of long-lived memory can avoid major accuracy loss while still reducing memory use.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the memory bottleneck of linear-attention models with recurrent states during concurrent serving. Naively quantizing these persistent states to low precision often causes large accuracy degradation because errors accumulate across repeated state updates.
method: Analyzes quantization error through two lenses: temporal persistence and spatial sensitivity within the recurrent state.
Identifies which state components and decoding steps are most vulnerable to error propagation.
Applies selective, error-aware state quantization to reduce memory usage while minimizing accuracy loss.
infographic.impact: This makes low-precision recurrent-state serving more practical for real-world deployment, especially under high concurrency. Practitioners can lower memory cost without blindly sacrificing model quality.

title: Imagine3D-LLM: Teaching MLLMs to Imagine 3D Scenes Before Answering
authors: Jaewoo Jung, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jisang Han, Mungyeom Kim
abstract: Reasoning about the 3D world from multi-view images remains a fundamental challenge for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While modern MLLMs handle single-image inputs effectively, they struggle to integrate evidence across viewpoints into a coherent 3D understanding. A growing body of work attempts to close this gap by injecting 3D awareness into MLLMs, either by boosting fine-grained pixel-level cross-view correspondence or by fusing features from 3D geometry foundation models, yet a s

infographic.key_insight: Imagine3D-LLM teaches multimodal LLMs to build an internal 3D scene representation before answering questions, helping them reason across multiple views more coherently. The core idea is that better 3D imagination leads to better 3D understanding.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the weakness of MLLMs in combining information from multi-view images into a consistent 3D understanding. Existing models often rely on single-view cues or partial cross-view matching and struggle with full scene reasoning in 3D.
method: Introduce a 3D-imagination step that encourages the model to mentally reconstruct the scene before generating an answer.
Leverage multi-view visual evidence to improve cross-view consistency and scene-level reasoning.
Integrate 3D-aware learning signals so the MLLM can reason about geometry and spatial relationships more effectively.
infographic.impact: This matters because many real-world AI applications depend on understanding scenes from multiple viewpoints, such as robotics, AR/VR, and embodied assistants. For practitioners, it suggests a path to making MLLMs more reliable on spatial reasoning tasks beyond single-image perception.

title: Breakdown of Local Denoising as Semantic Speciation
authors: Guangkuo Liu, Mert Okyay, Yifan F. Zhang, Fangjun Hu, Rahul Nandkishore
abstract: The dynamics of generative models exhibit two apparently distinct temporal windows: a speciation window, in which a sample commits to a semantic class, and a nonlocality window, in which local context windows become insufficient for generation. Motivated by evidence of their near-concurrence in a variety of frontier models, we investigate their relationship through the spatial distribution of semantic information. Under a "common cause" hypothesis, we prove that the nonlocality window must lie i

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that two seemingly separate events in generative models—when a sample locks onto a semantic class and when local context stops being enough—are tightly related and may arise from the same underlying spatial distribution of semantic information. This suggests the "speciation" and "nonlocality" windows are not independent, but linked by a common cause.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of explaining why frontier generative models sometimes shift from local, patch-based generation to globally coherent, class-specific behavior at nearly the same time during sampling.
method: Analyze the spatial distribution of semantic information in generative model dynamics.
Test a "common cause" hypothesis connecting semantic speciation and the breakdown of local denoising.
Prove theoretical constraints showing the nonlocality window must align closely with the speciation window under this hypothesis.
infographic.impact: This helps AI practitioners better understand when and why local generation fails, which can inform model design, sampling strategies, and interpretability tools. It may also improve control over long-range coherence in diffusion and other generative systems.

title: Telescopic Language Models
authors: Zhilin Guo, Boqiao Zhang, Hakan Aktas, Kyle Fogarty, Nursena Koprucu Aslan
abstract: One deployed language model must often serve many compute budgets, yet serving each budget still means a separate training or compression run per point. We train a Telescopic Language Model (TLM) to be that continuum: a nested-capacity Transformer supervised by stochastic prefix supervision with a full anchor. At every step, one randomly truncated prefix of the capacity axis is trained against the full next-token target, alongside one full-capacity pass, so the trained artifact is a valid langua

infographic.key_insight: Telescopic Language Models train one Transformer to behave like a whole family of models with different compute budgets. Instead of separate models or compression runs, a single nested-capacity model can serve multiple budgets from one artifact.
infographic.problem_solved: Deploying language models across many compute budgets usually requires training or compressing separate models for each point on the efficiency-performance tradeoff curve. This paper addresses the need for a single model that can adapt smoothly to different inference budgets.
method: Train a nested-capacity Transformer called a Telescopic Language Model (TLM), where smaller prefixes of the model act as lower-capacity submodels.
Use stochastic prefix supervision: at each step, train one randomly truncated prefix of the capacity axis against the full next-token target.
Include a full-capacity anchor pass so the largest model remains well-trained while all smaller prefixes learn to perform as valid language models.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a more flexible deployment strategy: one trained model can support multiple latency, cost, and quality targets without retraining from scratch. It simplifies serving and can reduce engineering overhead for multi-budget inference.

title: How to Loop MoE: Flatten the Experts, Untie the Attention
authors: Shouren Wang, Chuang Ma, Mohsen Hariri, Debargha Ganguly, Wang Yang
abstract: Looped Transformers reuse one block of layers several times: by spending extra computation they push a model of fixed size further, and so use its parameters more fully; while sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few of many experts for each token. Looped MoE bridges these two design philosophies and gives MoE models new potential for better expert usage, but it raises a question: how to loop a MoE? We answer it with Foil. With the expert parameters and the expert compute per t

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows how to combine looping and mixture-of-experts (MoE) in a way that reuses parameters more effectively without simply repeating the same expert routing. The proposed Foil approach "flattens" experts and unties attention so a MoE model can be looped more efficiently.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the question of how to correctly loop a sparse MoE model. Standard looping works well for dense transformers, but MoE adds expert routing and compute sparsity, making naive repetition inefficient or suboptimal.
method: Introduce Foil, a looping strategy designed specifically for MoE models.
Flatten the expert structure so expert parameters can be reused more effectively across loops.
Untie the attention mechanism across loops to preserve flexibility while reusing computation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a new way to scale model performance using fixed parameter budgets more efficiently. It is especially relevant for training or deploying large sparse models where compute reuse and expert utilization are important.

title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
authors: Chaoqian Ouyang, Ling Yue, Libin Zheng, Huanghui Guo, Shengxiang Xu
abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent executes the same task, token consumption can vary by over an order of magnitude across runs. The agent chooses its next steps based on tool feedback and intermediate results, while the growing context steadily inflates the input size of every subsequent call. The total consumption of a task is therefore hard to predict before execution and the prediction must be revised as the run unfolds. In this paper, we propose TokenCast, which learns a composable cos

infographic.key_insight: Token usage in LLM agents is highly variable and cannot be reliably estimated upfront because each tool call and new observation changes the future context size. TokenCast tackles this by forecasting consumption as the run unfolds, enabling adaptive prediction instead of a single static estimate.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the difficulty of predicting total token consumption for LLM agent tasks before or during execution. Traditional fixed-cost estimates fail because agent trajectories diverge across runs and context growth makes later calls increasingly expensive.
method: Learns a composable cost model that estimates token use across an agent's multi-step execution.
Updates predictions dynamically as intermediate results, tool feedback, and context expansion accumulate.
Models token consumption as a run-time forecasting problem rather than a one-shot prediction.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this helps with budgeting, latency planning, and infrastructure sizing for agentic systems. More accurate token forecasts can reduce cost overruns and improve deployment reliability for LLM workflows.

title: KV-streams for Efficient Compaction in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Emiliano Penaloza, Dane Malenfant, Dheeraj Vattikonda, Roger Creus Castanyer, Siddarth Venkatraman
abstract: Scaling the horizon of agentic LLMs is bottlenecked by the need to fit ever longer context traces in GPU memory. Context compaction has been the most popular mechanism to alleviate this issue, keeping GPU memory constant for a given trace. Unfortunately, most compaction strategies rely on prefilling the LLM context many times over, hindering training throughput. To alleviate this bottleneck and enable efficient trainable compaction, we propose KV-streams, a plug-and-play strategy compatible with

infographic.key_insight: KV-streams proposes a plug-and-play way to compact long agent traces without repeatedly re-prefilling the entire LLM context. This keeps memory use stable while making trainable compaction much more efficient for agentic reinforcement learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Agentic LLMs need to maintain very long interaction traces, which quickly exhaust GPU memory. Existing context-compaction methods reduce memory use, but they often require repeated full-context prefilling, which slows training and hurts throughput.
method: Introduce KV-streams as a compacting mechanism that reuses and streams key/value cache information efficiently.
Design the method to be plug-and-play, so it can integrate with existing agentic RL and LLM training pipelines with minimal changes.
Avoid repeated full-context prefilling during compaction, reducing compute overhead while preserving long-horizon context handling.
infographic.impact: This matters because it makes long-context agent training more practical on real hardware budgets. For practitioners, it can improve throughput, lower training cost, and enable longer-horizon agentic workflows without constant memory scaling.

title: Learning Native Reflection in Unified Models with Interleaved Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yijia Fan, Ziqi Huang, Zhongang Cai, Yan Li, Zimo Wen
abstract: Unified multimodal models can both look at and render images, so in principle they can repair their own generations: diagnose what an image gets wrong, revise it, observe the result, and diagnose again. Whether a revision helps is known only after it is rendered, so the reflection text and the image generation must be learned jointly, over the whole loop. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on reflection trajectories gives a cold start but does not find the high-success repair paths, and naive RL that

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that unified multimodal models can learn to "think while repairing" their own image outputs by interleaving reflection and reinforcement learning. This joint training helps the model discover better self-correction paths than supervised reflection alone.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of training a model to diagnose flaws in an image, revise the image, observe the result, and reflect again when the usefulness of each revision is only known after rendering.
method: Use supervised fine-tuning on reflection trajectories to provide an initial cold start for the model.
Train the reflection text generator and image generation loop jointly with reinforcement learning so the model can learn from the success of full repair trajectories.
Interleave reflection, image generation, and feedback signals to optimize for higher-success self-revision paths rather than fixed offline examples.
infographic.impact: This matters because it improves the ability of multimodal models to self-correct, which can reduce manual iteration in image generation workflows. For practitioners, it offers a path toward more reliable, adaptive, and autonomous creative models.

title: Towards Communication-Efficient Social Intelligence in Language Agents
authors: Linxiao Gong, Yijie Xu, Tianfu Wang, Yin Wu, Yili Wang
abstract: Socially intelligent language agents must negotiate, coordinate, and resolve conflicting preferences while respecting the time and attention of both participants. Balancing these demands is challenging because agents must convey enough to address a partner's constraints and advance their goals without adding words that do not help the interaction. In this paper, we propose Teacher-Assisted Communication Training (TACT) to improve social goal attainment while reducing communication cost, making i

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces TACT, a training approach that helps language agents achieve social goals while saying less. The main idea is to make agents communicate more efficiently without sacrificing negotiation or coordination quality.
infographic.problem_solved: It tackles the challenge of socially intelligent language agents being too verbose during negotiation and coordination. The goal is to reduce communication cost while still handling conflicting preferences and respecting the time and attention of both participants.
method: Teacher-Assisted Communication Training (TACT) uses teacher guidance to shape better communication behavior during training.
The method encourages agents to share only the information needed to advance the interaction and satisfy partner constraints.
It balances task success with brevity, aiming to improve social goal attainment while minimizing unnecessary words.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means building agents that are more practical, cheaper to use, and better suited for real interactive settings. Efficient communication is especially valuable in multi-agent systems, customer support, and negotiation-style applications.

title: Task-structured modularity emerges in artificial networks and aligns with brain architecture
authors: Yuhang Wu, Shikuang Deng, Kangrui Du, Marcelo G. Mattar, Yifan Wu
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01306-9

Wu et al. show that neural networks learning multiple tasks organize into specialized modules, particularly under capacity constraints. Incremental multitask learning strengthens this modularity and produces architectures resembling brain networks.

infographic.key_insight: When artificial neural networks learn multiple tasks, they naturally split into specialized modules instead of staying fully shared. This task-structured modularity becomes stronger under limited capacity and can resemble the organization seen in brain networks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper asks how and why multitask neural networks organize themselves internally, and whether their learned structure can mirror the modular architecture of biological brains.
method: Train artificial networks on multiple tasks and observe how internal representations and connections organize over time.
Compare different training settings, especially varying model capacity and incremental multitask learning schedules.
Analyze the resulting network structure to quantify modularity and compare it with known brain-like organization.
infographic.impact: For AI practitioners, this suggests that modular architectures may emerge naturally when models face multiple tasks and limited resources. It provides a practical lens for designing more efficient, specialized, and potentially more brain-inspired multitask systems.

title: Unifying Distributional Training for One-Step Visual Generation
authors: Chi Zhang, Haoyang Shi, Yueyi Liu, Ruichuan An, Junkang Zhou
abstract: \emph{Distributional training} provides collective supervision for one-step visual generation by matching real and generated features in frozen representation spaces. We introduce \emph{a unified theoretical framework} that separates distribution modeling from matching discrepancy and connects global objectives to pointwise feature updates through Wasserstein gradient flow. Under this framework, FD-Loss and Gaussian-kernel Drifting are recovered through Gaussian optimal transport and kernel-dens

infographic.key_insight: This paper unifies several distributional training methods for one-step visual generation under a single theoretical framework. It shows that global distribution-matching objectives can be translated into pointwise feature updates via Wasserstein gradient flow.
infographic.problem_solved: One-step visual generation needs a principled way to train generators using distribution-level supervision in frozen feature spaces, while understanding how different matching losses relate to each other.
method: Formulates distributional training as a unified framework that separates distribution modeling from the choice of matching discrepancy.
Uses Wasserstein gradient flow to connect global objectives with pointwise feature updates.
Recovers existing methods such as FD-Loss and Gaussian-kernel Drifting through special cases like Gaussian optimal transport and kernel-density matching.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this provides a clearer theoretical basis for designing and comparing one-step generation losses. It can help simplify method selection, improve interpretability, and guide new loss design for visual generation systems.

A generative AI framework called GenFocal is introduced for climate downscaling, producing realistic fine-scale weather from coarse projections and improving regional risk estimates of compound extremes such as heatwaves and tropical cyclones.

infographic.problem_solved: Climate models often lack the spatial detail needed to assess local and regional risks from extreme weather. The paper addresses how to downscale coarse climate projections into high-resolution, probabilistic estimates of compound hazards.
method: Uses a generative machine learning approach for climate downscaling, producing fine-scale weather fields from coarse inputs.
Learns realistic regional variability so generated outputs better capture local extremes and their spatial structure.
Supports probabilistic risk assessment by estimating the likelihood of compound events rather than only deterministic outcomes.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how generative models can be used beyond image or text synthesis to solve scientific downscaling problems. It highlights a high-value application of probabilistic ML for decision-support under uncertainty.

Uses a structured reward framework to guide navigation behavior more effectively than ad hoc reward design.
Evaluates transferability across different robots and environments without requiring retraining.

authors: Zhilin Guo, Boqiao Zhang, Oszkár Urbán, Josef Bengtson, Hakan Aktas
abstract: Sparse inertial pose estimation promises camera-free motion capture from consumer devices, but consumer sensors are unreliable: firmware-fused orientations are biased, mounting varies between sessions, and streams drift or drop out. On a new 35-take single-subject benchmark pairing an earbud head inertial measurement unit (IMU) with two smart-insole foot IMUs (SAM-3D-Body pseudo-ground-truth labels), we show the reliability problem is channel-level: a channel ablation isolates foot acceleration

infographic.key_insight: For consumer IMU-based pose estimation, the main bottleneck is not just noisy sensors overall, but unreliability at the channel level. The paper shows that selectively trusting and fusing only the most reliable head and foot IMU signals can improve lower-body 3D pose estimation.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of estimating accurate lower-body 3D pose from sparse consumer IMUs when sensor orientations are biased, mounting differs across sessions, and data may drift or drop out.
method: Builds a new 35-take single-subject benchmark using an earbud head IMU and two smart-insole foot IMUs with SAM-3D-Body pseudo-ground-truth labels.
Performs channel-level reliability analysis via ablation to identify which IMU signals contribute trustworthy motion information, especially foot acceleration.
Uses reliability-gated fusion to combine only dependable sensor channels for more robust lower-body pose estimation.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests that better results may come from modeling sensor reliability explicitly rather than treating all IMU channels equally. It provides a practical path toward more robust camera-free motion capture on consumer hardware.

title: PDMD: Projected Distribution Matching Distillation for Video Diffusion Models
authors: Zimo Wang, Junkun Yuan, Angtian Wang, Haotian Yang, Canyu Zhang
abstract: Modern video diffusion models require tens of denoising evaluations over long spatiotemporal token sequences. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) reduces the number of function evaluations (NFE) to just a few. However, DMD samples can degrade during training, exhibiting progressive oversaturation and artifacts. We trace this instability to critic errors, which enter successive student updates and accumulate over time. We introduce Projected Distribution Matching Distillation (PDMD) to filte

infographic.key_insight: PDMD improves fast video diffusion distillation by filtering out critic errors that accumulate during training. This prevents the oversaturation and artifact buildup seen in standard DMD, making low-NFE video generation more stable.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses instability in Distribution Matching Distillation for video diffusion models, where repeated student updates amplify critic mistakes and gradually degrade sample quality.
method: Identify critic errors as the source of progressive sample degradation in DMD training.
Introduce Projected Distribution Matching Distillation (PDMD) to project or filter the learning signal so harmful critic noise is reduced before it compounds.
Maintain the speed benefits of few-step distillation while improving visual fidelity and training stability for long spatiotemporal video sequences.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, PDMD offers a more reliable path to fast video generation with fewer denoising steps. This can reduce compute cost while preserving quality, making diffusion-based video models more practical for real-world deployment.

abstract: Biomedical image segmentation is central to medical image analysis, but practical deployment often faces limited annotations, memory constraints, and cross-site distribution shifts. Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have recently emerged as a lightweight alternative for semantic segmentation, achieving competitive performance with substantially fewer parameters than conventional architectures. However, the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and domain generalization abilities of INR-based segmen

infographic.key_insight: This paper explores how far implicit neural representations (INRs) can be pushed for brain MRI segmentation, showing that they can deliver strong cross-domain performance with far fewer parameters than conventional models. The key takeaway is that lightweight INR-based segmentation can be both efficient and robust under distribution shifts.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of performing accurate biomedical image segmentation when annotations are limited, model memory is constrained, and data comes from different sites or domains with distribution shifts.
method: Uses implicit neural representations (INRs) as a parameter-efficient alternative to standard segmentation networks.
Studies scaling behavior and the mechanisms behind INR-based segmentation performance.
Evaluates cross-domain generalization for brain MRI segmentation under site/domain shifts.
infographic.impact: This matters because it points to a practical path for deploying segmentation models in real clinical settings where memory, data, and generalization are major constraints. For practitioners, it suggests a compact model class that may be easier to train, deploy, and transfer across institutions.

title: Online Learning via Learned Latent Bayesian Tracking
authors: Guy Gerson, Tomer Raviv, Nir Shlezinger, Tirza Routtenberg, Osvaldo Simeone
abstract: Online learning in non-stationary environments requires models to adapt rapidly from streaming data under strict computational constraints. A principled approach casts online learning as Bayesian state tracking, where model parameters are updated sequentially via Bayesian filtering. However, applying Bayesian filters directly to modern deep models is computationally prohibitive due to the high dimensionality of parameter space, forcing existing methods to rely on restrictive approximations or ma

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes online learning in non-stationary environments as Bayesian state tracking, but learns a compact latent representation so adaptation stays fast and tractable. This lets deep models update sequentially from streaming data without filtering over the full parameter space.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of adapting machine learning models to changing data streams while meeting strict computation limits. Existing Bayesian online learning methods are often too expensive for modern deep models or depend on overly restrictive approximations.
method: Cast online learning as sequential Bayesian filtering over model states.
Learn a low-dimensional latent space that captures parameter dynamics instead of tracking all weights directly.
Perform Bayesian updates in latent space to enable efficient online adaptation under non-stationarity.
infographic.impact: This makes principled online adaptation more practical for real-world ML systems that must learn continuously from streaming data. Practitioners gain a way to balance responsiveness, uncertainty awareness, and computational efficiency.

title: HySTAR: Anchored Hypergraphs for Stable Credit Assignment in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xinglong Luo, Yuding Zhang, Yuheng Kuang, Shuxuan Yuan, Zhenni Zeng
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability and shared rewards requires assigning team outcomes to individual agents and high-order coalitions. A MAPPO-style critic compresses joint behavior into one global value, while critics that dynamically reconstruct the grouping topology change the mapping from agents and coalitions to value components as interactions or active agents evolve. We refer to this inconsistency as structural target drift. We introduce HySTAR, a M

infographic.key_insight: HySTAR stabilizes credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning by fixing the structure used to map team behavior to value estimates. Instead of letting the critic’s grouping change over time, it anchors hypergraphs so the learning signal stays consistent.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses structural target drift in partially observable multi-agent settings with shared rewards, where changing agent/coalition groupings make it hard to consistently assign credit to individual agents and higher-order coalitions.
method: Uses anchored hypergraphs to represent agents and coalitions with a stable relational structure.
Builds a critic that avoids dynamically changing the mapping from interactions to value components as agents become active/inactive or interactions evolve.
Provides a more consistent credit assignment signal for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this can make multi-agent training more stable, interpretable, and easier to optimize when rewards are shared. It is especially useful in systems where coordination patterns change over time but the credit assignment structure should remain reliable.

title: FuseReg: Regularizing Layer Fusion Mitigates the Reconstruction-Generation Gap in Representation Autoencoders
authors: Hongyang Du, Yunfei Xie, Junjie Ye, Jiawei Yang, Xiaoyan Cong
abstract: Representation autoencoders (RAEs) reuse features from a pretrained visual encoder as reconstruction and diffusion latents, integrating strong visual representations into image generation. However, RAEs still need to decide which encoder layers form the shared latent space for the generator and pixel decoder. This choice involves a trade-off. Shallower layers tend to preserve fine pixel details better, while deeper layers tend to yield better generation metrics. A fixed heuristic layer fusion th

infographic.key_insight: FuseReg shows that the layer fusion choice in representation autoencoders is not just a design detail—it directly controls the balance between pixel-level reconstruction and high-quality generation. By regularizing fusion, the method narrows the reconstruction-generation gap and makes a single latent space work better for both tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Representation autoencoders must choose which pretrained encoder layers to fuse into a shared latent space, but shallow layers help reconstruction while deeper layers help generation. This paper addresses how to reduce the trade-off between preserving fine image details and achieving strong generative performance.
method: Regularize the layer-fusion process so the shared latent space is optimized for both reconstruction and generation.
Encourage a better balance between shallow, detail-preserving features and deeper, generation-friendly features.
Use the fused representation as the common latent for both the generator and pixel decoder, reducing mismatch between their objectives.
infographic.impact: This matters because it helps practitioners build RAEs that do not have to sacrifice one capability for the other. The result is a more practical latent representation for image generation systems that need both faithful reconstruction and strong sample quality.

Cloud assistants such as ChatGPT route sensitive student data to foreign servers---violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53---and, pre-trained on Western-centric corpora, are not organized around the national textbook curriculum, so their knowledge of local content is unsystematic and frequently hallucinated. Self-hosting an open m

infographic.key_insight: DeepEdu-v1 proposes an efficient, scalable agentic LLM system tailored for Vietnamese education, aiming to deliver useful tutoring while keeping data local and aligned with the national curriculum. It bridges the gap between generic cloud chatbots and costly self-hosted solutions by making education-specific AI more practical to deploy.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses two major barriers to AI tutoring in Vietnam: privacy and sovereignty concerns from sending student data to foreign cloud servers, and poor curriculum alignment from Western-centric pre-trained models that often hallucinate or miss local textbook content.
method: Builds an agentic LLM framework designed specifically for Vietnamese educational use cases.
Organizes knowledge around the national textbook curriculum to improve retrieval, grounding, and answer relevance.
Focuses on efficient, scalable deployment so institutions can self-host or locally run the system more feasibly than large general-purpose models.

It offers a template for building culturally and curriculum-aware AI systems that are more trustworthy and usable in regulated settings.

title: Two Conformal Constructions for Adaptive Within-Document AI-Text Screening
authors: Marco Mandap, Jerahmeel Hipolito, Arcel Galvez, Charlie Margaret Balagtas, Michael Joshua Buluran
abstract: We study false-alert control when screening for text generated by artificial intelligence (AI). The screening procedure selects document prefixes and detectors from observed evidence and may stop before exhausting its inspection budget. We give two finite-sample constructions under document-level exchangeability between human calibration documents and a new null document, with no restriction on dependence among tokens within a document. Construction A registers a finite family of prefix-detector

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces two conformal methods that can screen for AI-generated text within a document while still controlling false alerts at finite sample sizes. The key advance is adaptive prefix-based screening: the system can choose how much of a document to inspect and still provide valid error control.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of detecting AI-generated text in documents without over-flagging human-written content, especially when inspection must be adaptive and may stop early before reading the full document.
method: Uses document-level exchangeability between human calibration documents and a new null document to guarantee finite-sample validity.
Allows adaptive selection of document prefixes and detectors based on observed evidence, rather than requiring a fixed full-document scan.
Presents two conformal constructions that control false-alert rates even when token-level dependencies within a document are unrestricted.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it provides a principled way to screen documents for AI-generated text with reliable error control, even under realistic, variable-length inspection budgets. It is especially useful for moderation, auditing, and evaluation pipelines where false positives are costly.

title: Adapting for AI: How elementary teachers adjust their practices for an AI-integrated curriculum
authors: Fasika Melese, Ruiyang Wu, Xinyue Cui, Joanna Perkins, Xiaoyi Tian
abstract: Conversational AI tools are entering children's everyday experiences, and schools are interested in adopting them. However, successful classroom integration depends not only on the technology but also on the work teachers do to make it usable and appropriate for their students and classroom context. There is little known about how elementary teachers work as they implement conversational AI tools in real classrooms. In this study, we examine three teachers' experiences implementing an AI literac

infographic.key_insight: Elementary teachers do more than adopt AI tools—they actively adapt, translate, and reshape them so they fit children’s needs, classroom routines, and learning goals. The paper highlights teacher “implementation work” as a critical factor in making conversational AI usable in real schools.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the gap between promising AI classroom tools and the practical realities of elementary school use. It examines how teachers make an AI-integrated curriculum workable, appropriate, and educationally meaningful for young students.
method: Studied three elementary teachers implementing an AI literacy curriculum with conversational AI tools.
Examined how teachers adjusted instructions, activities, pacing, and classroom management to suit their students and context.
Analyzed teachers’ lived implementation experiences to identify the kinds of adaptations needed for successful classroom integration.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows that model quality alone is not enough for educational deployment. Designing for schools requires supporting teachers with flexibility, explainability, and classroom-ready workflows that can be adapted locally.
