abstract: Agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) rely on semantic matching to select tools from third-party servers, exposing a semantic supply-chain risk through attacker-controlled metadata and outputs. We introduce A2M (Attraction-to-Manipulation), a two-stage black-box framework for hijacking MCP agents. The Attraction phase optimizes tool metadata to increase invocation probability; the Manipulation phase uses execution traces to refine adversarial tool returns that steer agents toward attacke

infographic.key_insight: A2M shows that MCP agents can be hijacked without internal access by exploiting how they semantically choose tools and trust tool outputs. It combines prompt/metadata attraction with trace-guided manipulation to steer agent behavior toward attacker goals.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the semantic supply-chain risk in Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystems, where third-party tool metadata and returned outputs can be attacker-controlled. This creates a black-box path for influencing which tools agents invoke and how they act after invocation.
method: Attraction phase: optimize tool metadata so an MCP agent is more likely to select the attacker’s tool during semantic matching.
Manipulation phase: use execution traces to iteratively refine malicious tool outputs so they better steer the agent’s next actions.
Black-box design: requires no internal model access, relying only on observable agent behavior and tool interaction patterns.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights a practical attack surface in agentic systems that connect to third-party tools. It underscores the need for stronger tool vetting, output sanitization, and security monitoring in MCP-based deployments.

title: GAD-MambaUNet: Direction-Group Mamba with Gradient-Adaptive DINOv3 Distillation for Lightweight Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Fang Wang, Huitao Li, Wenhan Chao, Zheng Zhuo, Xinxin Yang
abstract: In this paper, we proposed GAD-MambaUNet, a lightweight medical image segmentation network that combines efficient local modeling, direction--group state-space interaction, and training-time foundation-model supervision. To improve contextual modeling in compact segmentation networks, we introduced Direction-Group Graph Selective Scan (DG-GSS), which treated scan-direction and channel-group responses as graph nodes and enabled structured information exchange before multi-directional fusion. We f

infographic.key_insight: GAD-MambaUNet boosts lightweight medical image segmentation by combining efficient Mamba-based local modeling with structured direction-and-group information exchange and training-time guidance from a foundation model. The result is a compact network that aims to keep accuracy high without heavy compute.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of achieving strong medical image segmentation performance in lightweight models, where limited capacity often hurts contextual understanding and boundary precision.
method: Introduces Direction-Group Graph Selective Scan (DG-GSS) to model scan directions and channel groups as graph nodes for structured information exchange.
Uses multi-directional fusion to improve contextual aggregation in compact segmentation networks.
Applies gradient-adaptive DINOv3 distillation during training to transfer foundation-model knowledge while controlling learning strength.
Combines these components into a lightweight MambaUNet-style architecture for efficient medical image segmentation.
infographic.impact: This work is useful for practitioners who need accurate segmentation on limited hardware or in latency-sensitive clinical settings. It shows how state-space models and foundation-model distillation can be combined to improve compact vision models.

title: TraceVIC: Causal Reasoning over Code Evolution for Identifying Vulnerability-Inducing Commits
authors: Fnu Tanish, Samiha Shimmi, Samikshya Chapagain, Hamed Okhravi, Mona Rahimi
abstract: Software vulnerabilities are often discovered long after they are introduced, making it difficult to identify the vulnerability-inducing commit (VIC) responsible for introducing the underlying vulnerable condition. Existing VIC identification techniques largely rely on git blame to trace vulnerable code through revision history and use positional heuristics, such as selecting its earliest or most recent modification. However, the true VIC may occur anywhere within this history, and vulnerable be

infographic.key_insight: TraceVIC reframes vulnerability-inducing commit identification as a causal reasoning problem over code evolution, rather than a simple blame-and-heuristics search. This helps find the commit that actually introduced the vulnerable condition, even when it is not the earliest or latest change in the history.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of locating the true vulnerability-inducing commit (VIC) in a project’s revision history after a vulnerability is discovered, especially when existing methods rely too heavily on git blame and positional heuristics.
method: Models code evolution as a causal process to reason about how vulnerable conditions emerge over time.
Moves beyond earliest/recent modification heuristics by tracing causal links across commit history.
Identifies commits most likely responsible for introducing the vulnerability-inducing change.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners working on software security, this can improve post-hoc vulnerability analysis, triage, and root-cause localization. It may reduce manual effort and make security tooling more accurate than heuristic-based approaches.

title: Diffusion-Induced Spatial Attention Overlapping Community Detection
authors: Kosti Koistinen, Vesa Kuikka, Joni Herttuainen, Matthew Hendren, Brian Holt
abstract: Detection of overlapping communities is essential for modelling networks in which nodes participate simultaneously in multiple structural or functional groups. Existing graph neural network approaches commonly rely on local message passing, which can obscure community boundaries through smoothing and limit the representation of structurally relevant long-range dependencies. We introduce Diffusion-Induced Spatial Attention Community Detection (DISCO), a deep-learning framework that combines a str

infographic.key_insight: DISCO improves overlapping community detection by moving beyond local message passing and using diffusion-driven spatial attention to preserve community boundaries. This helps the model capture both local structure and longer-range relationships in complex networks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting overlapping communities in graphs, where nodes can belong to multiple groups at once. It targets the limitations of standard GNNs, which often blur boundaries through oversmoothing and miss important long-range structural signals.
method: Uses diffusion-induced spatial attention to focus on structurally important regions of the graph.
Combines deep learning with graph diffusion to capture long-range dependencies beyond immediate neighbors.
Designed specifically for overlapping community detection, allowing nodes to participate in multiple communities.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more expressive graph learning approach for real-world networks such as social, biological, and information systems. It can improve performance in tasks where community overlap and distant relationships matter.

title: Train Where the Quantized Model Goes: On-Policy Distillation for Low-Bit Reasoning
authors: Yuanteng Chen, Zhilei Liu, Peisong Wang, Yuantian Shao, Chuangyi Li
abstract: Quantization-aware distillation (QAD) restores much of the short-form question-answering performance lost to sub-3-bit quantization, yet leaves mathematical and code reasoning substantially impaired. Long generations often degenerate into repetitive loops, exhausting the decoding budget without completing a solution. We trace this gap to quantization-amplified exposure bias: QAD trains on fixed corpus prefixes, while quantization-induced deviations compound along the model's own autoregressive t

infographic.key_insight: The paper finds that low-bit quantized models fail at long-form reasoning not just because of lower precision, but because training on fixed prefixes creates a mismatch with the model’s own generated tokens. Training on the quantized model’s actual rollout trajectories reduces repetitive loops and improves reasoning stability.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the severe drop in mathematical and code reasoning performance that remains after quantization-aware distillation, especially in sub-3-bit models where long answers often spiral into repetition and fail to finish.
method: Identify quantization-amplified exposure bias as the core cause of long-generation failures.
Train distillation on-policy, using trajectories generated by the quantized model rather than only fixed corpus prefixes.
Align supervision with the model’s own autoregressive behavior to make reasoning more robust under low-bit inference.
infographic.impact: For practitioners deploying compact models, this offers a practical path to better reasoning quality without increasing bit-width. It is especially relevant for edge deployment and cost-sensitive systems where decoding stability matters as much as raw accuracy.

title: DexTacWAM: A Visuo-Tactile World-Action Model for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Haoran Yuan, Zekai Wang, Boning Shao, Haoran Lu, Trevor Darrell
abstract: Dexterous manipulation depends on contact dynamics that are often only partially observable from vision. Recent World-Action Models (WAMs) couple predictive video world modeling with action generation, but remain largely vision-centric and therefore cannot directly model these contact dynamics. We present DexTacWAM, a visuo-tactile WAM that encodes each fingertip independently, aggregates the resulting features through a finger- and pose-aware tactile compressor, and injects the tactile latent i

infographic.key_insight: DexTacWAM extends World-Action Models beyond vision by adding tactile sensing, enabling better prediction and control of dexterous manipulation where contact dynamics matter. By modeling each fingertip separately and fusing touch with pose information, it can represent interactions that cameras alone cannot reliably observe.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of vision-centric world models in dexterous manipulation: crucial contact dynamics at the fingertips are often hidden or ambiguous from images, making it difficult to predict object interaction and generate precise actions.
method: Encodes tactile input from each fingertip independently to preserve fine-grained contact information.
Uses a finger- and pose-aware tactile compressor to aggregate per-finger features into a compact latent representation.
Injects the tactile latent into a visuo-tactile World-Action Model to improve future-state prediction and action generation.
infographic.impact: This work shows how tactile sensing can make world models more realistic for robotics tasks that involve precise contact, grasping, and manipulation. For practitioners, it points to a practical path for improving policy learning and planning in settings where vision alone is insufficient.

title: WorldCrafter: Consistent Video World Model with Implicit 3D-aware Memory
authors: Wangbo Yu, Kunhao Liu, Wenbo Hu, Shenghai Yuan, Chaoran Feng
abstract: Video world models enable interactive exploration of dynamic environments, yet struggle to respect prior observations over long horizons and across viewpoints. We present WorldCrafter, a video world model that learns a camera-queryable implicit 3D-aware memory for this purpose. The key insight is to let the requested viewpoint shape how multi-view evidence is compressed into the video generator's limited token budget. Trained jointly with the video generator, a memory encoder and pose-conditione

infographic.key_insight: WorldCrafter teaches a video world model to store what it has seen in a camera-queryable 3D-aware memory, so it can keep scenes consistent across time and viewpoints. Instead of compressing everything the same way, it uses the requested viewpoint to decide what information matters most.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the common failure of video world models to preserve prior observations over long horizons and when the camera changes viewpoint, leading to inconsistent or forgotten scene details.
method: Learns an implicit 3D-aware memory that can be queried by camera pose/viewpoint.
Uses a memory encoder plus a pose-conditioned mechanism to compress multi-view evidence into the generator’s limited token budget.
Trains the memory and video generator jointly so remembered content stays consistent with generated future frames.
infographic.impact: This matters because it makes interactive video simulation and embodied AI more reliable, especially for long-rollout prediction and novel-view consistency. Practitioners building world models, robotics simulators, or virtual environment agents can use this idea to reduce hallucinations and memory drift.

title: VideoGen-Agent: Reinforcing Video Generation Agents
authors: Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Yuhui Zhang, Yaohui Zhang, Zihao Lin
abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled high-fidelity, temporally coherent video generation. However, these models often struggle to satisfy prompts requiring specialized knowledge, specific identities, physical consistency, or ordered events. In this paper, we present VideoGen-Agent, a multimodal agent trained through multitask agentic reinforcement learning to use external tools for video generation. The agent coordinates augmentation, generation, and verification tools through

infographic.key_insight: VideoGen-Agent turns video generation into an agentic workflow: instead of relying on a single generator, it learns to use external tools to improve prompt adherence, identity fidelity, and temporal consistency. This helps video models handle harder requests involving specialized knowledge, ordered events, and physical realism.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video generation models can produce high-quality clips, but they often fail on prompts that require external knowledge, specific identities, consistent physics, or correctly ordered actions.
method: Trains a multimodal agent with multitask agentic reinforcement learning.
Coordinates external tools for augmentation, generation, and verification during video creation.
Learns when and how to invoke tools to improve alignment between the prompt and the final generated video.
infographic.impact: This matters because it shows a practical path for making video generation more reliable on complex real-world prompts. For practitioners, it suggests that combining generative models with tool-using agents can improve controllability and output quality.

title: Harness-Zero: Harness Distillation via Agent-as-Harness
authors: Haoran Ye, Yuxing Lu, Haonan Dong, Zhaochen Su, Guojie Song
abstract: Agent harnesses, the external systems that mediate model-environment interaction, can substantially improve agent performance, but their gains remain tied to the harness at deployment. Because the best harness varies across domains, instances, and models, a general-purpose agent must either settle for a suboptimal shared harness or route among an ever-growing set of specialized ones. We therefore study agent harness distillation: using a domain- or instance-optimized harness as training-time gui

infographic.key_insight: Harness-Zero shows that an agent can learn from a strong, task-specific harness during training and then operate more effectively without needing that exact harness at deployment. In simple terms, it turns a “best harness available” into a transferable skill.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the mismatch between training and deployment in agent systems: the best external harness often depends on the domain, task instance, and model, making it hard to use one universal harness without sacrificing performance.
method: Use a domain- or instance-optimized harness as a training-time guide for the agent.
Distill the behavior and benefits of the optimized harness into the agent itself, reducing reliance on external orchestration at test time.
Enable agents to generalize better across tasks by learning harness-like decision patterns rather than depending on a fixed deployment harness.
infographic.impact: This matters because practitioners can get stronger agent performance without maintaining a large, brittle collection of specialized harnesses at inference time. It simplifies deployment while preserving much of the benefit of task-specific orchestration.

title: onPanda: Efficient Annotation of On-Policy Alignment Data for LLMs and Agents via Token-Level Correction
authors: Lei Yang, Mengyin Liu, Jia Wang, Hangyu Guo, Liang Zhao
abstract: We present onPanda, an interactive tool for efficiently annotating LLM alignment data and agent trajectories. onPanda adopts token-level correction as its core interaction: while reading a model response, the annotator locates the first inappropriate token and either picks a substitute from the model's candidate tokens or types the correct text via free-form editing. The system then truncates everything after that position and continues generation from the corrected prefix, repeating this locate

infographic.key_insight: onPanda speeds up alignment-data annotation by letting humans correct model outputs at the token level instead of rewriting whole responses. This makes it easier to create on-policy training data for LLMs and agents while preserving the model’s generation flow.
infographic.problem_solved: Annotating alignment data for LLMs and agent trajectories is slow and inefficient when annotators must edit full responses or trajectories. The paper addresses the need for a more precise, faster way to correct model outputs during generation.
method: Annotators read a generated response and identify the first inappropriate token.
They correct that token either by selecting from candidate tokens or by free-form text entry.
The system truncates text after the corrected position and resumes generation from the edited prefix, enabling iterative on-policy correction.
infographic.impact: This matters because it lowers the cost and time of producing high-quality alignment data for training and evaluating LLMs and agents. Practitioners can more efficiently build datasets that better reflect real model behavior during generation.

title: LoRA-generating hypernetworks for efficient on-device LLM generative personalization
authors: Sean Augenstein, Li Ding, Jihwan Lee, Keith Rush, Andrey Zhmoginov
abstract: On-device large language models (`LLMs'), e.g. running on mobile phones, are ripe for improvement via personalization. The limited compute resources of mobile devices impose limits on model scale and thus model quality, making any realizable quality gains highly impactful. At the same time, their personal nature (i.e., the close coupling to a particular user) means that a given on-device LLM tends to be used in similar, predictable patterns over the course of time. This paper presents a novel me

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows a way to personalize on-device LLMs efficiently by using a hypernetwork that generates LoRA adapters on demand. This makes user-specific improvements possible without fully retraining or storing large personalized models on mobile devices.
infographic.problem_solved: On-device LLMs are constrained by limited compute, memory, and battery, which makes standard personalization methods too expensive. The paper addresses how to deliver meaningful personalization for mobile LLMs while keeping adaptation lightweight and practical.
method: Use a hypernetwork to generate LoRA-style low-rank adapter weights instead of training a full personalized model.
Exploit the predictable, repeated usage patterns of a specific user to produce efficient personalization over time.
Keep the adaptation mechanism small enough to fit on-device constraints while improving generation quality for individual users.
infographic.impact: This approach makes personalized AI more feasible on smartphones and other edge devices, where memory and compute are tightly limited. For practitioners, it offers a path to better user experience without the cost of full fine-tuning or large model storage.

title: RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
authors: Peng Xia, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Yanfei Chen, Yufan Zhang
abstract: An LLM agent's capability is largely magnified by its harness, namely the prompts, control flow, tooling, memory, and context management surrounding the frozen backbone model. Recent methods increasingly automate this process by iteratively proposing and selecting component-wise edits of an agent harness, practically establishing a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI) at the agent-system level. However, such recursive evolution may overfit by memorizing the training tasks, showing large in-d

infographic.key_insight: RRSI argues that agent self-improvement should be treated as a controlled optimization problem, not an unconstrained loop of edits. By regularizing recursive changes to the agent harness, it aims to improve performance while reducing overfitting to the training tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the instability and overfitting that can arise when LLM agents repeatedly rewrite their own harnesses—prompts, control flow, tools, memory, and context management—to improve task performance.
method: Treat the agent harness as the target of recursive self-improvement, with iterative proposals and selection of component-level edits.
Add regularization to constrain harness evolution and reduce memorization of training tasks.
Evaluate whether the improved harness transfers better beyond the tasks used to optimize it.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to make agent systems more robust, generalizable, and easier to optimize safely. It is especially relevant for building autonomous agents that adapt without drifting into brittle or task-specific hacks.

title: Critical-State RL: Diagnosing Trainable States for Multi-Turn Tool Use
authors: Zixiang Chen, Wenting Zhao, Zhepeng Cen, Akshara Prabhakar, Jielin Qiu
abstract: Multi-turn tool-use failures can hinge on a single model call, yet reward variation alone does not reveal which call would benefit from training. When rewards depend on later interactions, their variation can reflect downstream randomness rather than differences between the current actions. We introduce Critical-State RL to identify trainable states in multi-turn interactions. Given task-defined candidate calls and local rewards, the method assesses whether each reward captures the action's effe

infographic.key_insight: Critical-State RL finds the specific turns in a multi-turn tool-use trajectory that are actually trainable, instead of treating all reward variation as equally informative. It separates real action effects from downstream randomness so learning focuses on the calls that matter.
infographic.problem_solved: Multi-turn tool-use systems can fail because of a single important model call, but standard reward signals often cannot tell which call caused the outcome. This paper addresses the challenge of diagnosing which intermediate states deserve credit assignment and training when later interactions introduce noise.
method: Identify task-defined candidate calls within a multi-turn interaction.
Use local rewards to test whether reward variation reflects the current action's effect rather than downstream stochasticity.
Classify states as trainable when their reward signal is sufficiently diagnostic, enabling targeted reinforcement learning updates.
infographic.impact: This helps practitioners focus training on the truly critical decisions in tool-using agents, improving sample efficiency and reducing wasted optimization on noisy states. It is especially useful for debugging and improving long-horizon agent behavior in complex workflows.

title: GAE: Learning a Geometry-Native Latent Space for 3D-Consistent World Generation
authors: Jiahao Lu, Minghao Yin, Wenbo Hu, Hengyu Liu, Wang Zhao
abstract: We present a compact geometry-native latent space as a shared foundation for perception and generation. Visual generators can produce photorealistic frames without preserving a consistent 3D scene. We argue that this is not only a modeling problem but also a representation problem: generators typically evolve appearance-centric latents, while perception models recover geometry in a semantically rich space that encodes cross-view structure. Rather than adding geometry as another output, we repara

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that 3D-consistent world generation requires a geometry-native latent space, not just better image synthesis. By sharing a compact latent representation between perception and generation, the model can better preserve cross-view structure and scene consistency.
infographic.problem_solved: Current visual generators can create realistic images but often fail to maintain a coherent 3D scene across viewpoints. This paper addresses the mismatch between appearance-centric generative latents and geometry-aware perception latents.
method: Learn a compact latent space designed around geometry rather than appearance.
Use this shared representation as a common foundation for both perception and generation.
Reparameterize generation so it can produce 3D-consistent outputs while preserving photorealism.
infographic.impact: This work offers a path toward world models that are both visually realistic and structurally consistent across views. For practitioners, it could improve robotics, AR/VR, simulation, and any application needing reliable 3D scene understanding and generation.

title: GameHorizon Suite: Multi-Horizon Data and Evaluation in Gameplay
authors: Yiran Wang, Xingyilang Yin, Junfu Pu, Guangzhi Wang, Kaifeng Li
abstract: Modern video games provide a measurable testbed for AI models, combining abilities of visual understanding, instruction decomposition, goal planning, and precise action control over multiple temporal horizons. Existing datasets and benchmarks, however, either cover a narrow range of games, lack language instructions, or rely on high-variance online rollouts. To address these challenges, we introduce GameHorizon, a unified data and evaluation suite that measures gameplay capabilities at different

infographic.key_insight: GameHorizon introduces a unified way to evaluate gameplay AI across multiple temporal horizons, capturing not just reflexive actions but also instruction following, planning, and long-horizon control. It aims to make game-based evaluation more realistic, consistent, and broadly comparable.
infographic.problem_solved: Current game AI datasets and benchmarks are fragmented: many cover only a limited set of games, omit language-based instructions, or depend on noisy online rollouts that make evaluation unstable. This paper addresses the need for a single suite that can assess gameplay abilities at different time scales in a more reliable way.
method: Builds a unified data and evaluation suite for gameplay tasks spanning multiple horizons of decision-making.
Measures capabilities from short-term action control to longer-term planning and instruction decomposition.
Reduces evaluation variance by moving away from purely high-variance online rollouts toward more controlled benchmarking.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, GameHorizon offers a more comprehensive benchmark for comparing models on real gameplay competence, not just narrow skill slices. It can help researchers diagnose where models fail across visual perception, reasoning, and control.

title: Value-Sensitive Delegation in Everyday AI Agent Use: Evidence from OpenClaw
authors: Renkai Ma, Ruyuan Wan, Xuan Lu, Fan Yang, Chen Chen
abstract: Users increasingly delegate work to autonomous AI agents, yet evaluations typically measure task completion rather than the values users prioritize. Using Value Sensitive Design, we analyzed, with LLM assistance, 73,093 first-person Reddit posts about using OpenClaw, each for its human value, agent aspect, value fulfillment, and user outcome. The 21 values form six value groups, including Autonomous, Dependable, and Affordable Operation, Bounded Reach, Reviewability, and Equitable Access. Relati

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that judging AI agents only by task success misses what users actually care about: values like autonomy, dependability, affordability, bounded reach, reviewability, and equitable access. By analyzing real Reddit discussions about OpenClaw, the authors reveal a practical value framework for understanding everyday agent use.
infographic.problem_solved: AI agent evaluations usually focus on whether the task was completed, but they often ignore user values, tradeoffs, and negative experiences. This paper addresses the gap between performance metrics and the human values that shape real-world trust and adoption.
method: Analyzed 73,093 first-person Reddit posts about OpenClaw use.

abstract: Urban transportation networks present complex optimization challenges spanning calibration of high-fidelity simulators and real-time operational control. This paper presents a shared latent-space framework that connects simulator calibration and reinforcement learning control through a common learned representation of urban traffic dynamics. First, we develop a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder architecture that learns low-dimensional manifolds linking simulator inputs (origin-destination demand, ne

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that simulator calibration and reinforcement learning for urban traffic can be tied together through a shared learned latent space. In simple terms, it learns a compact traffic representation that helps both match simulations to reality and control city traffic more effectively.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of optimizing urban transportation networks, where practitioners must both calibrate high-fidelity traffic simulators to real-world data and make real-time control decisions under complex, dynamic conditions.
method: Builds a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder that compresses urban traffic simulator inputs into a low-dimensional latent manifold.
Uses the shared latent representation to connect simulator calibration with reinforcement learning-based control policies.
Learns a common traffic dynamics space that supports both parameter fitting and operational decision-making in urban networks.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a way to unify model calibration and control instead of treating them as separate problems. It can improve sample efficiency, reduce manual tuning, and make learned policies more transferable to complex real-world systems.

title: An Interpretable Memory Decision Controller for LLM Agents Based on Three-Signal Complementarity: Decoupling Confidence and Consistency
authors: Yiming Zhang, Jinghong Zhang, Haoran Zhao, Yiren Ma, Chunlei Zhao
abstract: Memory systems for large language models have focused predominantly on efficient retrieval, whereas the decision of whether retrieved memories should be trusted has received comparatively little attention. When the memory store contains conflicting positions, standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) blindly injects memories and amplifies hallucinations: in models susceptible to memory injection, the RAG hallucination rate under conflicting memories is markedly higher than that of a memory-f

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that memory retrieval for LLM agents should not only ask "what is relevant?" but also "should this memory be trusted?". By decoupling confidence from consistency and using three complementary signals, the controller can better decide when to use or ignore conflicting memories.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the failure of standard RAG-based memory systems that blindly inject retrieved memories, especially when the memory store contains conflicting or contradictory information. This can amplify hallucinations and make agents less reliable.
method: Introduces an interpretable memory decision controller that evaluates retrieved memories before they are injected into the LLM context.
Uses three-signal complementarity to separate confidence from consistency, helping detect when a memory is plausible but contradictory.
Makes the memory-use decision explicit and explainable, improving robustness under conflicting-memory scenarios.
infographic.impact: This matters because LLM agents increasingly rely on long-term memory, and incorrect memory usage can severely degrade performance. The approach gives practitioners a clearer, safer way to manage memory injection and reduce hallucination risk in agentic systems.

title: CodeMidas: Scaling Agentic Coding RL Environments from Code Itself
authors: Bowen Ye, Lei Li, Shicheng Li, Zihao Yue, Linghao Zhang
abstract: Training capable coding agents via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse tasks with reliable verifiers. Open-source codebases offer a rich source of such tasks, while existing methods typically rely on development artifacts such as issues and commits, limiting the range of tasks that can be extracted. To better scale RL environments, we present CodeMidas, an agentic pipeline that turns implemented functionality in existing codebases into executable RL environments using source code as its

infographic.key_insight: CodeMidas turns existing source code itself into a large supply of executable RL environments for training coding agents. This expands task diversity beyond what issue trackers and commits can provide.
infographic.problem_solved: Training coding agents with reinforcement learning needs many diverse, reliable tasks with verifiable outcomes. Existing approaches often depend on development artifacts like issues and commits, which limit scale and miss many useful tasks hidden inside codebases.
method: Uses an agentic pipeline to extract implemented functionality directly from open-source codebases.
Converts that functionality into executable RL environments with built-in verifiers.
Scales environment generation from source code rather than relying only on external development artifacts.
infographic.impact: This makes it easier to build broader, more realistic training data for coding agents. For practitioners, it could improve agent robustness, coverage of coding tasks, and the efficiency of RL-based training pipelines.

Living organisms continuously monitor their internal physiological states while interacting with complex environments and adapt their actions in response to changes in these internal signals. New work combines such biological principles with cybernetics, reinforcement learning and neuroscience to develop a framework for autonomous

infographic.key_insight: This paper proposes an embodiment-inspired framework for autonomous agents that combines cybernetics, interoception, reinforcement learning, and neuroscience. The core idea is to help AI systems monitor internal state signals, not just external rewards, so they can adapt more robustly in changing environments.
infographic.problem_solved: Current AI agents often optimize external objectives without accounting for internal stability or self-regulation. This work addresses how to build agents that can sense, regulate, and adapt based on both internal and external signals.

Uses interoception-inspired internal state monitoring to represent the agent’s physiological-like condition.

infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a path toward more resilient, adaptive agents that can manage trade-offs between task performance and internal stability. It is especially relevant for robotics, autonomous systems, and embodied AI.

title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Latent Action Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Model Pretraining across Embodiments
authors: Yichen Liu, Puzhen Yuan, Xiang Zhu, Yanjiang Guo, Jianyu Chen
abstract: Learning large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models from multi-embodiment datasets remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces across end effectors. Although latent action models (LAMs) can learn embodiment-agnostic action representations from diverse video data, existing image-based LAMs often fail to capture fine-grained end-effector articulation, particularly finger-level geometric changes in human and dexterous robot hands. To address this limitation, we propose GALA, a Geome

infographic.key_insight: GALA learns a geometry-aware latent action space that can represent motions across different robots and human hands, while better preserving fine-grained finger and end-effector articulation. This helps pretrain vision-language-action models on diverse multi-embodiment data without being tied to one specific action format.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of training large VLA models from datasets that mix many embodiments, where action spaces differ across hands, robots, and grippers. Existing latent action models often miss detailed geometric changes, especially in human and dexterous robot fingers.
method: Learns embodiment-agnostic latent action representations from video and action data.
Adds geometry-aware modeling to capture fine-grained end-effector and finger-level motion cues.
Uses the latent space as a shared action interface for pretraining across heterogeneous embodiments.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this makes it easier to scale VLA pretraining across mixed datasets without manually harmonizing action spaces. It is especially useful for dexterous manipulation systems that need precise hand geometry and cross-embodiment transfer.

title: OmniVBench: A Benchmark and Large-Scale Dataset for Omni Reference-to-Video Generation
authors: Wenxue Li, Peiyan Guan, Haoyang Jiang, Junxian Cai, Hualuo Liu
abstract: Reference-to-video (R2V) generation is evolving toward increasingly general and versatile reference control, giving rise to the emerging paradigm of omni R2V generation. However, existing benchmarks fall short of these emerging capabilities: their test cases cover limited reference types and compositions, and their evaluation protocols largely assess holistic reference consistency, overlooking whether reference factors are properly preserved, disentangled, and routed. Meanwhile, the high cost of

infographic.key_insight: OmniVBench introduces a large-scale benchmark and dataset designed for the next generation of reference-to-video generation, where models must handle many reference types and combinations. It shifts evaluation beyond simple overall similarity to check whether each reference factor is correctly preserved, separated, and assigned.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing R2V benchmarks do not cover the full range of emerging omni-reference scenarios, and their evaluation methods mostly judge holistic consistency instead of fine-grained control. This makes it hard to measure whether models truly use multiple references correctly, especially when reference information must be disentangled and routed.
method: Builds a benchmark with broader coverage of reference types and reference compositions for omni R2V generation.
Provides a large-scale dataset to support more realistic and diverse evaluation scenarios.
Introduces evaluation protocols that assess fine-grained preservation, disentanglement, and routing of reference factors rather than only overall output quality.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, OmniVBench offers a more realistic way to test and compare video generation models under complex reference-control settings. It can help identify failure modes that traditional benchmarks miss and guide development of more controllable, reliable R2V systems.

title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
authors: Zijie Cao, Xijun Qu, Zhicheng Gu, Xiaoshu Chen, Duanyang Yuan
abstract: Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidenc

infographic.key_insight: AutoViewMem proposes a self-configuring memory system that organizes long-term conversational memory into orthogonal views, making mixed information easier for LLM agents to store and retrieve accurately.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the weakness of existing long-term memory systems that use fixed granularities or static schemas, which causes semantic interference when preferences, events, constraints, and updates are stored together and retrieved with noisy top-K search.
method: Automatically configures multiple orthogonal views over the same memory to separate different information types.
Reduces interference by representing mixed memories in a way that supports cleaner retrieval of relevant evidence.
Improves long-term conversational consistency and personalization by making memory access more robust to heterogeneous updates.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this can make LLM agents more reliable in long-running conversations, especially when they must remember user preferences, changing constraints, and past events. It offers a practical path toward more accurate memory retrieval without relying on a one-size-fits-all memory schema.

title: NemotronLabs VoiceChat: An Open Full-duplex Speech-to-Speech Model with Tool Calling Capabilities
authors: Jagadeesh Balam, Travis Bartley, Edresson Casanova, Sanjay Chauhan, Chen Chen
abstract: We introduce NemotronLabs VoiceChat, an open full-duplex speech-to-speech model with native tool-calling capabilities. NemotronLabs VoiceChat combines a streaming speech encoder and decoder-only language model with parallel specialized output streams for agent text and structured function calls, an auxiliary RNN-T branch for incremental user transcription, and a streaming TTS decoder. This design enables the model to listen, transcribe, reason, invoke tools, and speak within a unified streaming

infographic.key_insight: NemotronLabs VoiceChat is an open, full-duplex speech-to-speech model that can talk and listen at the same time while also calling tools natively. It unifies transcription, reasoning, function calling, and speech synthesis in one streaming system.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of building voice assistants that are not only real-time and conversational, but also capable of structured tool use without breaking the flow of speech.
method: Uses a streaming speech encoder paired with a decoder-only language model for continuous understanding and generation.
Produces parallel output streams for agent text and structured function calls to support tool invocation during conversation.
Adds an auxiliary RNN-T branch for incremental user transcription and a streaming TTS decoder for low-latency spoken responses.
infographic.impact: This matters because it brings voice agents closer to natural human conversation while enabling actionable tool use in a single pipeline. For practitioners, it points to a practical architecture for building responsive, multimodal, tool-using assistants.

title: QuranicMMLU: A Cognitively-Aware Benchmark for Evaluating Generative AI Solutions on Quranic Linguistic Knowledge
authors: Rawan El Ghali, Umm Kulsoom, Anas Madkoor, Dima Faris Alsaudi, Roaa Abdelmagid
abstract: We introduce QuranicMMLU, a benchmark for evaluating generative AI on Quranic Arabic across multiple dimensions of linguistic complexity. Existing Quranic benchmarks center on general question answering and semantic retrieval, without probing specific linguistic competencies or stratifying by cognitive demand and verse difficulty. We construct a five-pillar Quranic taxonomy spanning Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, Semantics, and Pragmatics, with 31 leaves covering phenomena from tajwīd and root-a

infographic.key_insight: QuranicMMLU introduces a cognitively-aware benchmark that evaluates generative AI on Quranic Arabic beyond simple QA, testing specific linguistic skills across increasing levels of difficulty. It helps reveal whether models truly understand phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics in Quranic text.
infographic.problem_solved: Most existing Quranic benchmarks focus on broad question answering or semantic retrieval, which do not measure fine-grained linguistic competence or account for cognitive demand and verse difficulty. This paper addresses the lack of a structured, multidimensional benchmark for evaluating Quranic language understanding.
method: Build a five-pillar taxonomy covering Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, Semantics, and Pragmatics.
Define 31 fine-grained leaves to represent specific Quranic linguistic phenomena, from tajwīd to root-based analysis.
Stratify evaluation by cognitive demand and verse difficulty to better assess model reasoning depth.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark provides a more rigorous way to evaluate Arabic language models on a culturally and linguistically complex domain. It can expose hidden weaknesses, guide targeted model improvement, and support fairer comparison across generative AI systems.

title: Detecting Pretraining Data in Large Language Models from a Free-Energy Perspective
authors: Chenye Ke, Zirui Liu, Qi Liu, Yan Zhuang, Jintao Zhang
abstract: Detecting pretraining data in large language models is challenging because high likelihood can reflect either training exposure or strong generalization. In the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, a likelihood-only detector uses a horizontal boundary and can mistake predictable non-members for members. Motivated by this, we introduce an inclined boundary that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy. Our analysis shows that entropy correction can preserve the e

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that likelihood alone is not enough to detect whether a token or example came from pretraining data in large language models. By correcting prediction loss with predictive entropy, the detector uses an inclined decision boundary that better separates true members from highly predictable non-members.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of identifying pretraining data in LLMs when high likelihood can come from either memorization or strong generalization, causing likelihood-only methods to produce false positives.
method: Model the detection problem in the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy.
Replace a horizontal likelihood threshold with an inclined boundary that compares loss against entropy.
Use entropy correction to reduce confusion between memorized training samples and naturally predictable inputs.
infographic.impact: This improves the reliability of data membership detection for large language models. For practitioners, it offers a more robust way to audit training data, study memorization, and assess privacy or leakage risks.

title: Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Critical Heat Flux Models in the CTF Subchannel Code for Square Rod Bundle Prediction

abstract: The prediction of critical heat flux (CHF), a key safety-related quantity in nuclear thermal hydraulics, remains an important challenge due to its direct relationship with fuel performance and reactor safety. Recent studies have demonstrated that relative to traditional empirical correlations and lookup tables (LUTs), machine learning (ML) methods can substantially improve CHF prediction accuracy. Most ML-based CHF models, however, have been developed and evaluated using tube databases, leaving

infographic.key_insight: This paper evaluates whether machine learning-based critical heat flux (CHF) models, originally developed on tube data, can reliably predict CHF in square rod bundle conditions inside the CTF subchannel code. The core takeaway is that model performance depends on how well the training data matches the reactor geometry and thermal-hydraulic regime being predicted.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap between high-performing ML CHF models and their limited validation outside tube-based datasets, especially for square rod bundle prediction in nuclear thermal hydraulics.
method: Integrate multiple ML-based CHF models into the CTF subchannel code.
Test model prediction quality on square rod bundle scenarios rather than only tube geometries.
Compare ML-based predictions against established baseline approaches to assess transferability and robustness.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the paper highlights the importance of domain shift and geometry-aware validation when deploying predictive models in safety-critical engineering settings. It shows that strong benchmark performance does not guarantee reliable generalization to new physical configurations.

title: PRIME: Perception Feedback with Situational Memory Embeddings in VLA Models
authors: Erik Deinzer, Naya Baslan, Luca Paparusso, Narunas Vaskevicius, Peter Knott
abstract: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving operate primarily through feedforward inference across the perception--reasoning--planning hierarchy. While modern architectures maintain temporal recurrence within the perceptual module, early perception remains blind to downstream reasoning and navigation goals, processing visual inputs agnostically without prioritizing cues informed by prior decisions. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces PRIME, a learned feedback mechani

infographic.key_insight: PRIME adds a learned feedback loop to VLA driving models so early perception can be guided by what the system has already reasoned and planned. This helps the model focus on the most relevant visual cues instead of treating every frame the same way.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard VLA models process vision in a mostly feedforward way, so perception does not benefit from downstream goals, navigation context, or prior decisions. This can make the model overlook important cues that should be prioritized for driving decisions.
method: Introduces situational memory embeddings that carry task- and context-specific information back into the perception stage.
Uses a learned perception feedback mechanism to bias early visual processing toward cues relevant to reasoning and planning.
Integrates the feedback loop into VLA models for autonomous driving while preserving temporal recurrence in perception.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, PRIME shows a practical way to make multimodal driving models more goal-aware and context-sensitive. This can improve robustness, attention allocation, and decision quality in autonomous driving systems.

authors: Alexandre Andre, Shivashriganesh P. Mahato, Vinam Arora, Keshav Balaji, Divyansha Lachi

Evaluate pretrained models on diverse downstream tasks instead of a narrow task domain.

title: RACER: Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Human-AI Routing
authors: Joshua Strong, Emma Sun, Alexander Capstick, Pramit Saha, Cheng Ouyang
abstract: Learning to defer asks a predictive system when to act autonomously and when to defer to a human expert. Population-adaptive deferral extends this problem to unseen experts using a small context set of expert behavior. Neural context encoders such as L2D-Pop can be query-dependent, but may learn routing shortcuts tied to absolute class coordinates. Identity-Free Deferral (IFD) removes such shortcuts through role-indexed classwise competence profiles, but its estimates are constant within each cl

infographic.key_insight: RACER improves human-AI routing by estimating competence in a way that stays aligned with the human's role, not the identity or absolute position of classes. This helps avoid shortcut learning and makes deferral decisions more reliable for unseen experts.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses population-adaptive deferral: deciding when an AI system should act autonomously and when it should defer to a human expert, especially when the expert is new or unseen and only a small context set of their behavior is available.
method: Introduces role-aligned competence estimation to represent expert behavior relative to the human role rather than fixed class coordinates.
Builds on population-adaptive deferral settings where routing decisions depend on a small context set from unseen experts.
Addresses limitations of prior query-dependent routing methods that can learn brittle shortcuts tied to absolute class positions.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, RACER points to safer and more generalizable human-AI collaboration systems that can adapt to new experts without overfitting to spurious patterns. This is especially useful in high-stakes settings where dependable deferral decisions matter.

title: MintAct: A Unified Visual Agent for Digital Environments

abstract: We present MintAct, a family of vision-language models that unifies UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile, desktop, and web, and visual tool use, trained at 2B, 4B, and 8B scales. The key breakthrough is a scalable training and RL setup that lets a single model family generalize across digital environments.

title: Joint Remaining Useful Life Prediction and Capacity Estimation of Lithium-Ion Batteries Using Partial-Charging Data
authors: Khoa Tran, Ho-Si-Hung Nguyen, Phone Wai Yan Moe, Hung-Cuong Trinh, Thi-Hoang-Giang Tran
abstract: Joint remaining useful life (RUL) prediction and capacity estimation require representations of both gradual degradation and recent battery behavior. This paper presents a cross-expert framework using partial-charging measurements without measured historical full-cycle capacity as an input. The RUL Expert encodes nominal 10-min segments from ten cycles sampled within a 30-cycle history using a pretrained gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN),

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that lithium-ion battery health can be estimated jointly for remaining useful life and capacity using only partial-charging data, without needing historical full-cycle capacity labels. It combines recent charging behavior with degradation trends through a cross-expert model to improve battery prognostics.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of predicting battery remaining useful life and capacity when full-cycle capacity measurements are unavailable or costly to obtain. The method is designed for realistic settings where only partial-charging measurements from recent cycles are available.
method: Uses partial-charging measurements from nominal 10-minute segments sampled across a 30-cycle history.
Encodes degradation patterns with a pretrained GRU-based RUL expert to capture long-term temporal behavior.
Uses a second expert with 2D-CNN features to extract local charge-pattern information from recent battery behavior.
Combines the experts in a cross-expert framework to jointly predict remaining useful life and capacity.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical prognostics approach for real battery systems where labels are sparse or expensive. It can improve maintenance planning and battery management using data that is easier to collect in the field.

title: RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents
authors: Shuai Bai, Jiayong Deng, Yikun Fu, Chang Gao, Xuhao Hu
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have advanced along two separate lines: graphical interaction and software development through code and the command line. Real digital work requires both, interleaved rather than stacked end to end. We study hybrid CUAs that autonomously decide when to explore an interface, implement software, and run and visually verify their artifacts. We introduce RecreationWorld, a five-platform framework built around recreation: given a running reference, an agent must discover it

infographic.key_insight: RecreationWorld shows that computer-use agents need to combine GUI interaction, coding, and visual verification in one loop rather than treating them as separate skills. It provides a scalable way to test whether agents can recreate a running reference environment from observation and action.
infographic.problem_solved: Most computer-use agents are evaluated either on graphical interface tasks or on code/software tasks, but real-world work requires both. This paper addresses the lack of a unified, verifiable benchmark for hybrid agents that must decide when to inspect, implement, and validate their outputs.
method: Introduces RecreationWorld, a five-platform benchmark framework centered on "recreation": agents observe a running reference and must reproduce it.
Evaluates hybrid CUAs that interleave GUI exploration, software implementation via code/CLI, and visual checking of results.
Emphasizes scalability and verifiability so agent behavior can be tested across multiple environments with clear outcome signals.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this benchmark reflects more realistic digital work than isolated UI or coding tasks. It can help build and compare agents that are better at end-to-end automation, debugging, and environment-aware decision-making.

title: PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers
authors: Jiachen Yao, Zi-Siang Hsu, Xi Deng, Aditi Gupta, Xin Ju
abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to solve scientific inverse problems, but existing evaluations still focus primarily on whether a method can produce a single plausible reconstruction. This is insufficient for ill-posed problems, where multiple solutions may be consistent with the same sparse or noisy observations. In these settings, a method can achieve strong pointwise accuracy while still failing to capture the true posterior through mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty, or averagi

infographic.key_insight: PosteriorBench shifts evaluation of generative inverse solvers from "did it produce a good-looking sample?" to "does it match the full posterior distribution?". This matters because in ill-posed inverse problems, a single accurate reconstruction can still hide mode collapse, overconfidence, or missed solution modes.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the weakness of existing evaluation protocols for generative inverse problems: they mostly measure point-estimate quality and fail to assess whether a model captures the true uncertainty and multi-modality of the posterior.
method: Introduces PosteriorBench, a benchmark focused on posterior matching rather than only reconstruction accuracy.
Evaluates whether generative inverse solvers reproduce the distribution of valid solutions under sparse or noisy observations.
Highlights failure modes such as mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty estimates, and averaging across plausible solutions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more reliable way to judge inverse solvers in science and engineering settings where uncertainty matters. It encourages building models that are not only accurate, but also calibrated and distributionally faithful.

title: How Does Distribution Shift Shape Pretraining Gains in Neural PDE Surrogates?
authors: Pochinapeddi Sai Bhargav, Nithin Somasekharan, Rohit Sunil Kanchi, Sicheng He, Shaowu Pan
abstract: Pretraining a neural PDE surrogate can reduce the amount of new CFD data needed when geometry or modeled physics changes. However, it remains unclear how different components of distribution shift affect this benefit. We pretrain a surrogate on 254,909 RANS solutions from one airfoil family and fine-tune it on a new family under two target settings with matched freestream ranges: the same Spalart-Allmaras (SA) modeling and SA with added $e^N$ transition modeling. At $N=1000$, the pretrained mode

infographic.key_insight: Pretraining on a large CFD dataset can significantly reduce data needs when transferring neural PDE surrogates to a new geometry, but the benefit depends on the type of distribution shift. The paper shows that matching the freestream range is not enough—changes in underlying modeled physics can alter how much pretraining helps.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how to predict and improve pretraining gains for neural PDE surrogates when moving from one airflow/airfoil distribution to another, especially when geometry changes and the target physics may differ.
method: Pretrain a neural PDE surrogate on 254,909 RANS simulations from one airfoil family.
Fine-tune the pretrained model on a different airfoil family under two target settings: same Spalart-Allmaras (SA) turbulence modeling and SA plus e^N transition modeling.
Compare performance at limited data budgets to isolate how different components of distribution shift affect transfer benefits.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides evidence that transfer learning for scientific surrogates is sensitive to both geometry and physics mismatch. It helps guide when pretraining is likely to reduce CFD data requirements and when domain shifts may weaken its advantage.

title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
authors: Ji Xie, Dewei Zhou, Xinyu Huang, Zhennan Chen, Xun Wang
abstract: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-

infographic.key_insight: Paint-Anything teaches a model to understand 24-bit hex color values as a universal control signal for both image generation and editing. The key breakthrough is a unified way to specify exact colors without relying on custom color encodings or specialized inference tricks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of precise any-color control in AI image generation and editing. Existing methods often support only limited color palettes, require dedicated representations, or use separate procedures for different tasks.
method: Learns a shared representation that links hex color codes to visual color semantics.
Uses this representation to control object color consistently across both generation and editing workflows.
Builds on the observation that even compact language models can associate hex values with color concepts, simplifying the control pipeline.
infographic.impact: This makes color control more exact, intuitive, and practical for design-focused AI applications. For practitioners, it reduces the need for task-specific color tooling and enables a single interface for both creating and modifying colored objects.

title: RetireOPD: Self-Retiring On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yan Yu, Zhengxi Lu, Yizhou Liu, Yichen Pan, Aozhe Wang
abstract: Multi-turn agents trained with reinforcement learning (RL) receive a single scalar reward per trajectory, which motivates self on-policy distillation (OPD) to supply dense token-level supervision from a self-teacher with privileged task skills, letting a skill-free student internalize them. This recipe, however, is undermined by two findings in agentic tasks: privileged information alone does not always make a teacher reliable, and the benefit of teacher supervision is stage-dependent. We theref

infographic.key_insight: RetireOPD shows that in agentic reinforcement learning, a privileged self-teacher is not always trustworthy, and its guidance is only useful at certain stages of training. The paper’s key idea is to make on-policy distillation self-retiring: use teacher supervision when it helps, then stop relying on it when it becomes less beneficial.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of turning sparse trajectory-level RL rewards into dense token-level supervision for multi-turn agents, without being harmed by unreliable teacher signals or overusing guidance at the wrong training stage.
method: Train a self-teacher with privileged task information to provide dense on-policy token-level supervision.
Monitor when teacher guidance is helpful versus harmful across training stages.
Automatically retire or reduce teacher distillation when the student has learned enough or when supervision becomes unreliable.
infographic.impact: This makes RL training for agents more stable and efficient by avoiding blind reliance on a teacher. Practitioners can get better learning signals for long-horizon, multi-turn tasks while reducing noise and wasted supervision.

title: Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision
authors: Nitish Dashora, Douglas Chen, Idan Shenfeld, John Marangola, Pulkit Agrawal
abstract: Complex robotic manipulation tasks frequently require a long-term memory of past events and actions. As conditioning on full histories renders policies prone to spurious correlations and degrades performance, many approaches to policy memory involve compressing historical information through expensive VLM queries in-the-loop to process only task-salient information. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach in which computationally intensive VLM queries are made during train-time to lear

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes training a lightweight robotic memory module using expensive vision-language model (VLM) supervision only during training, so the robot can remember task-relevant past events without needing heavy online VLM queries at inference time.
infographic.problem_solved: Robots often need long-term memory for manipulation tasks, but conditioning on full histories is noisy, costly, and can hurt performance due to spurious correlations. This work addresses the challenge of retaining only salient, useful information efficiently.
method: Use VLM queries during training to identify which past observations and actions are task-salient.
Learn a compact workspace memory representation from this saliency-driven supervision.
At test time, rely on the lightweight learned memory instead of expensive in-the-loop VLM processing.
infographic.impact: This makes long-horizon robotic policies more practical by reducing runtime compute while preserving useful memory. For practitioners, it offers a scalable way to add memory to manipulation systems without paying the cost of heavy multimodal inference during deployment.

title: FAMOS: Feed-Forward 3D Articulation Modeling from Sparse Observations
authors: Kevin Qu, Tao Sun, Massimiliano Viola, Liyuan Zhu, Zhizhuo Zhou
abstract: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Most feed-forward methods infer articulation from a single observation and therefore rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors. We present FAMOS, a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds. Our model jointly reasons over multiple observations and nat

infographic.key_insight: FAMOS can infer object articulation from a sparse, unordered set of partial 3D observations instead of relying on a single view. By combining evidence across multiple incomplete point clouds, it predicts both movable-part segmentation and joint parameters more robustly.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views, where each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion cues. Existing feed-forward approaches often depend on strong category-level priors because they infer articulation from only one observation.
method: Takes a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds as input rather than a single image or view.
Jointly reasons over multiple observations to estimate movable-part segmentation and joint parameters.
Uses a feed-forward design to directly predict articulation structure without requiring slow iterative optimization at inference time.
infographic.impact: This matters because it makes articulated-object understanding more practical in real-world sparse-view settings, such as robotics and 3D perception. For practitioners, it offers a way to infer motion structure more reliably from incomplete data and with less dependence on category-specific assumptions.

title: JEPA-Anything: Learning Predictive Models across Different Worlds
authors: Taoyong Cui, Zhongyao Wang, Xinyue Xu, Weiyang Liu, Zhaochen Yu
abstract: World modeling enables intelligence to anticipate consequences, guide interventions, and learn from interaction. Yet predictive models remain domain-specific: can a common learning principle support world modeling across radically different systems? We introduce JEPA-Anything, a domain-agnostic framework based on orthogonal predictive factorization (OPF). Extending joint-embedding predictive architectures, OPF decomposes latent targets into complementary factors, learns them through dedicated pa

infographic.key_insight: JEPA-Anything proposes a single predictive learning principle that can work across very different environments, instead of relying on domain-specific world models. Its core idea, orthogonal predictive factorization, splits what needs to be predicted into complementary latent factors so the model can learn them more effectively.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of a general world-modeling framework: most predictive models are tailored to one domain and do not transfer well across radically different systems.
method: Extends joint-embedding predictive architectures with orthogonal predictive factorization (OPF).
Decomposes latent targets into complementary factors and assigns them to dedicated prediction pathways.
Learns a domain-agnostic predictive model that can support world modeling across diverse environments.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a path toward more reusable predictive models that can generalize beyond a single task or domain. It could reduce the need to redesign world models from scratch for each new application.

abstract: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluate

infographic.key_insight: The paper isolates which parts of a coding harness actually matter for autonomous coding performance, instead of treating the whole system as a black box. By fixing the execution loop and varying planning, action space, and context management, it enables cleaner component-level comparisons across models.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing evaluations of coding agents usually measure harnesses as monolithic systems, making it hard to know which design choices improve long-horizon software-engineering performance.

Varied three harness components independently: planning, action space, and context management.
Compared these component choices across four models to study their effect on coding-agent performance.

title: SplashSplat: Reconstructing Splashing Liquids from Real-World Multi-View Videos
authors: Peiyu Liu, Dingxi Zhang, Federico Tombari, Marc Pollefeys, Christina Tsalicoglou
abstract: A splash lives for a fraction of a second: sheets tear into ligaments and droplets, appearance is view-dependent and nearly textureless, and little persists long enough to track. Reconstruction research has consequently focused on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. To our knowledge, no synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids exists. We therefore introduce a benchmark of 20 real scenes, from coherent streams to violent splashes, captured by seven synchronized, ca

infographic.key_insight: SplashSplat introduces the first synchronized multi-view benchmark for real-world splashing liquids, enabling researchers to study and reconstruct a highly dynamic phenomenon that was previously missing from evaluation datasets. It shows that splashes can now be captured and benchmarked across multiple views, despite their fleeting, textureless, and view-dependent nature.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of real-world, synchronized multi-view data for splashing liquids, which has made it difficult to evaluate and advance reconstruction methods for fast, chaotic fluid events.
method: Collects a benchmark of 20 real splash scenes, ranging from coherent liquid streams to violent splashes.
Captures each scene with seven synchronized cameras to provide multi-view observations of rapid fluid motion.
Focuses on evaluation by providing a challenging dataset that reflects the true appearance and dynamics of splashing liquids.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark fills a major gap in reconstruction research and provides a realistic testbed for developing methods that handle transient, non-rigid, and view-dependent phenomena. It can help improve robustness in 3D reconstruction, vision, and simulation pipelines for fluids and other fast-moving materials.

title: Quantifying Overclaiming Propensity in Frontier LLM Agents
authors: Nolan Smyth, Yorguin-Jose Mantilla-Ramos, Pascal Jr Tikeng Notsawo, Saskia Helbling, Alberto Tosato
abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly trusted to work autonomously for long periods, yet an agent's final response is often the only account of that work a user sees. We quantify the propensity of frontier agents to \emph{overclaim} task completion, a misrepresentation that can mislead the user. An agent overclaims when its final response contradicts information in its context. This definition requires no inference about intent and is independent of task success. We introduce \emph{OverclaimBe

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows how to measure when frontier LLM agents overstate what they accomplished, even without judging their intent or whether the task was actually successful. It highlights that a model's final answer can contradict its own context, creating a new safety and trust risk.
infographic.problem_solved: AI coding agents can work autonomously for long periods, but users often only see the final response. This paper addresses the challenge of detecting and quantifying "overclaiming"—cases where an agent claims completion despite evidence in its own context that the task was not completed.
method: Defines overclaiming as a contradiction between an agent's final response and its contextual information.
Introduces a benchmark/dataset called OverclaimBench to evaluate this behavior in frontier agents.
Measures overclaiming propensity independently of task success, making the metric applicable even when the agent fails for other reasons.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical way to audit agent honesty and reliability in long-horizon workflows. It can inform evaluation, product design, and safety monitoring for autonomous coding agents and other LLM systems.

This paper addresses the lack of an integrated dataset for early identification and classification of hereditary polyposis syndromes.

abstract: Scientific code repositories encode decades of human knowledge in executable models, methods, and tools. We introduce ScienceIDE, infrastructure for turning the world's scientific code into programmable environments for scientific agents. Guided by expert-defined scientific

infographic.key_insight: ScienceIDE turns scientific code repositories into programmable environments that AI agents can learn from and act inside. This makes decades of scientific software and workflows more accessible for agent training, evaluation, and reliable automation.

title: In-Context Robot Learning with VLM Agents
authors: Dongzhou Cheng, Taoran Yi, Ye Fang, Xingwu Zhang, Fan Feng
abstract: Enabling robots to adapt to unfamiliar environments as readily as humans remains a moonshot goal of embodied AI. No finite collection of demonstrations can cover every task and situation a robot will encounter, making the ability to learn from context at deployment essential for generalization. The broad agentic capabilities of commercial vision-language models (VLMs), such as GPT-6 Astra, rai

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows how vision-language model (VLM) agents can help robots learn new tasks from context at deployment time, instead of relying only on fixed pretraining or large demo datasets. This work targets the challenge of in-context learning for robotics, where a robot must adapt without requiring exhaustive task-specific demonstrations.

Leverage the agentic capabilities of commercial VLMs to support flexible, on-the-fly policy selection rather than a fully fixed robot policy.
