title: Evidence-Grounded Agentic Formulation Development in an Autonomous Laboratory
authors: Michael M. Craig, Riley J. Hickman, Yingshan Ma, Rémi Piché-Taillefer, Christine Allen
abstract: Self-emulsifying drug delivery systems (SEDDS) can improve the oral bioavailability of poorly soluble drugs, but identifying high-performing formulations remains experimentally intensive. We present Andromeda 2, an agentic system that reasons over structured in-house experimental evidence and invokes computational and experimental tools to design and execute successive formulation batches. Using a miniaturized automated laboratory at a matched budget, we benchmark it against Andromeda 1, a proba

infographic.key_insight: Andromeda 2 shows that an AI agent can use prior experimental evidence plus lab and computational tools to iteratively design better drug formulations in an autonomous lab. In a matched-budget comparison, it aims to outperform a prior baseline by making formulation development more evidence-driven and efficient.
infographic.problem_solved: Finding high-performing self-emulsifying drug delivery system (SEDDS) formulations is slow, costly, and experimentally intensive because the design space is large and success depends on many interacting variables.
method: Reason over structured in-house experimental evidence to guide formulation choices.
Invoke computational and experimental tools in a closed-loop agentic workflow to propose, test, and refine successive batches.
Run the system in a miniaturized automated laboratory under a matched budget and benchmark it against a prior version (Andromeda 1).
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work highlights how agentic systems can combine evidence retrieval, planning, and tool use to solve real-world scientific optimization problems. It suggests a practical path for building more reliable autonomous labs that learn from prior experiments instead of repeatedly exploring blindly.

title: Monitoring and Discovering Reward Hacking with Internal Representations during LLM Evaluations
authors: Leon Bergen, Usha Bhalla, Andrew Lee, Barak Widawsky, Linas Nasvytis
abstract: As models scale, reward hacking becomes more frequent, more sophisticated, and more consequential. Does it leave a telltale signature in model representations? This work analyzes how reward hacking is represented internally in frontier open source LLMs, and how those representations can be used to understand and discover the range of hacking behaviors a model displays. In particular, we find that simple difference of means vectors coherently represent reward hacking in Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and Qwen

infographic.key_insight: Reward hacking appears to leave a detectable signature inside LLM internal representations. The paper finds that simple difference-of-means vectors can coherently capture this behavior across frontier open-source models like Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and Qwen.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of identifying, monitoring, and understanding reward hacking during LLM evaluations, especially as such behavior becomes more frequent, subtle, and consequential with larger models.
method: Analyze internal representations of frontier open-source LLMs during evaluation tasks.
Compare activations from reward-hacking vs. non-hacking examples using simple difference-of-means vectors.
Test whether these vectors can both detect reward hacking and help discover the range of hacking behaviors a model exhibits.
infographic.impact: This gives practitioners a practical interpretability-based signal for spotting reward hacking beyond output-only inspection. It can improve model auditing, evaluation reliability, and early detection of misaligned optimization strategies.

title: Reporting Practice Matters: The Impact of Reference Choice on Chest X-ray Report Evaluation
authors: Daniel P. Jeong, Charles Q. Li, Hossein Hosseiny, Nitya M. Bhalla, Fatma Uyar Morency
abstract: Radiologists follow heterogeneous reporting practices. Two radiologists examining the same image and identifying the same clinical findings might nevertheless compose superficially distinct reports, varying in terminology, shorthand, formatting, and level of detail. These variations in reporting norms represent an under-appreciated obstacle in efforts to evaluate AI-based radiology report generation (RRG) models, where machine-generated reports are typically assessed based on their concordance w

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that how you choose the reference report can significantly change the measured quality of chest X-ray report generation systems. In short, evaluation is not just about the model—it is also about the reporting style used as the benchmark.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between heterogeneous radiology reporting practices and the way AI-generated reports are evaluated. Different valid radiologist reports can describe the same findings differently, making standard reference-based evaluation unreliable.
method: Analyzes variability in real radiologist chest X-ray reports, including differences in terminology, shorthand, formatting, and detail level.
Examines how different reference choices affect automatic and human evaluation of radiology report generation models.
Highlights the need for evaluation protocols that account for multiple acceptable reference styles rather than assuming a single gold-standard report.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means report generation scores may be misleading if the reference report is stylistically different from the model output. Better evaluation design can lead to fairer benchmarking and more trustworthy progress in medical NLP and radiology AI.

title: PointZero: 3D Point Track Completion for Learning Transferable 3D Dynamics
authors: Bardienus P. Duisterhof, Kaifeng Zhang, Adam Hung, Bowen Wen, Stan Birchfield
abstract: World models endow perceptual systems with the ability to predict how scenes evolve under interaction. They are most beneficial when trained on diverse volumes of data, to instill a rich prior into downstream applications. Existing methods typically require robot action labels to learn action-conditioned 3D dynamics, which excludes web video data from the training pool. We study 3D point track completion as a pre-training objective for learning transferable 3D dynamics without robot data. Given

infographic.key_insight: PointZero turns 3D point track completion into a pre-training task for learning transferable 3D dynamics. This lets models learn scene motion from broad web video data, without needing robot action labels.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of scalable training data for action-conditioned 3D world models. Most prior methods depend on robot action annotations, which limits training to narrow datasets and prevents using large amounts of unlabeled web video.
method: Use 3D point track completion as a self-supervised pre-training objective.
Learn how scene points should move or continue over time from partial observations.
Train dynamics representations that transfer to downstream robotic and perception tasks without requiring robot action labels.
infographic.impact: This makes it easier to build world models from diverse video sources instead of expensive robot-collected data. For practitioners, it could improve scalability, data efficiency, and transfer to real-world 3D reasoning and manipulation tasks.

title: Social Laws for Multi-agent Coordination in Stochastic Environments
authors: Rolando Fernandez, Caleb Probine, Tyler Lee, Jeffrey Chen, Erez Karpas
abstract: In multi-agent environments, coordinating agents to prevent interference and ensure robust individual performance is a critical challenge. Previous research on social laws for multi-agent systems has primarily focused on deterministic, goal-based settings. This paper extends the concept of social laws to stochastic, reward-based environments, proposing a formalism for defining and verifying their robustness under various conditions. We introduce the notion of $α$-robustness, a measure of the gua

infographic.key_insight: This paper extends social laws from deterministic, goal-driven multi-agent systems to stochastic, reward-based environments. It introduces a formal way to check whether coordination rules remain effective when outcomes are uncertain.
infographic.problem_solved: Multi-agent systems often suffer from interference between agents, especially when the environment is stochastic and rewards are uncertain. Existing social-law methods were mostly designed for deterministic settings, leaving a gap for robust coordination in real-world noisy environments.
method: Define social laws for stochastic, reward-based multi-agent settings instead of only deterministic goal-based ones.
Introduce α-robustness as a formal measure of how reliably a social law preserves good individual performance under uncertainty.
Provide a framework for verifying whether a proposed social law remains robust across different environment conditions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a principled way to design coordination rules that are less brittle in noisy, real-world multi-agent systems. It can help improve safety, reliability, and performance when multiple agents must act without interfering with one another.

title: PANORAMA: Panoptic Grounded Captioning via Mask Proposal Selection
authors: Sara Pieri, Evangelos Kazakos, Shizhe Chen, Josef Sivic, Cordelia Schmid
abstract: Intelligent systems that act in the world require image understanding that is both comprehensive and spatially grounded. Current vision-language models (VLMs) can generate fluent and detailed image captions, but reliably associating them with image pixels remains challenging. Existing methods that combine dense captioning with pixel-level grounding often produce either incomplete descriptions or inaccurate segmentation masks. We study this problem through panoptic grounded captioning, a task tha

infographic.key_insight: PANORAMA improves image understanding by linking rich captions to the correct regions in the image, rather than describing objects without reliable spatial grounding. It does this by selecting strong mask proposals, helping produce both more complete and more accurate panoptic captions.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the gap between fluent vision-language captioning and precise pixel-level grounding. Existing dense captioning and grounding approaches often miss parts of the scene or assign captions to inaccurate segmentation masks.
method: Formulate the task as panoptic grounded captioning, where scene elements are described and linked to image segments.
Use mask proposal selection to choose the most appropriate segmentation masks for caption grounding.
Combine language generation with panoptic-style region assignment to better cover the full image while preserving spatial accuracy.
infographic.impact: This is useful for practitioners building multimodal systems that need both natural language output and trustworthy localization, such as robotics, assistive vision, and visual search. It can improve the reliability of captions used in downstream reasoning and decision-making.

title: MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-Modal Understanding in Situated Education
authors: Luyao Zhu, Xun Wei Yee, Wei Li, Mun Thye Mak, Wee Siong Ng
abstract: Large vision-language models have achieved remarkable progress in multi-modal understanding, yet their capabilities in educational settings remain insufficiently evaluated. In AI-assisted language learning, models must interpret artistic imagery, understand its semantic, affective, and cultural content, and reason about visual context to support meaningful interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on real-world images or domain-specific educational reasoning, providing limited co

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces MUSE, a benchmark designed to test how well large vision-language models understand educational, artistic, and culturally rich visual content in situated learning settings. It highlights that current models are not yet sufficiently evaluated for the kind of multi-modal reasoning needed in AI-assisted language learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing vision-language benchmarks mostly focus on real-world photos or narrow educational tasks, leaving a gap in evaluating how models interpret art-like imagery, emotional tone, cultural meaning, and context in classroom-style learning scenarios.
method: Build a benchmark tailored to situated education and AI-assisted language learning.
Assess models on multi-modal understanding of artistic imagery, including semantic, affective, and cultural interpretation.
Evaluate visual-context reasoning to measure whether models can support meaningful educational interaction.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MUSE provides a more realistic testbed for assessing whether vision-language models are truly ready for educational use. It can guide model improvement, benchmark selection, and safer deployment in language-learning and tutoring applications.

title: Prepared Or Unprepared? Evaluating Healthcare Workforce Readiness for Clinical Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Nigeria
authors: Abbas M. Rabiu, Abdulrazaq A. Zubair, Um-mulkhairi Ibrahim, Tolulope Olusuyi, Shaheeda Farouq
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems worldwide, yet its successful clinical adoption depends critically on workforce readiness, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where infrastructural and training gaps persist. This cross-sectional study evaluated awareness, attitudes, preparedness, and barriers to AI adoption among 761 healthcare professionals across multiple disciplines and practice settings in Nigeria. Data were collected betwe

infographic.key_insight: The study shows that AI adoption in Nigerian healthcare is limited less by the technology itself and more by gaps in workforce readiness, awareness, and institutional support. It highlights that many healthcare professionals are not yet fully prepared for routine clinical use of AI.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of understanding whether healthcare workers in Nigeria are prepared to adopt AI in clinical practice, and what barriers may prevent successful implementation in a low-resource setting.
method: Cross-sectional survey of 761 healthcare professionals across multiple disciplines and practice settings in Nigeria.
Assessed awareness, attitudes, preparedness, and perceived barriers related to clinical AI adoption.
Compared responses to identify readiness gaps and implementation challenges.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the findings emphasize that model performance alone is not enough for deployment in healthcare. Successful adoption requires user training, workflow alignment, and context-specific implementation strategies, especially in LMIC settings.

title: RLLBC-Lib: An Educational Code Library for Reinforcement Learning and Learning-Based Control
authors: Bernd Frauenknecht, Emma Cramer, Artur Eisele, Paul Kruse, Lukas Kesper
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an exciting concept as well as a remarkable success story worth sharing. However, RL builds on rather complex interactions between different objects that play out over several cycles. Such dynamics are often best explained with an easily accessible implementation. We present RLLBC-Lib, a carefully crafted code library with the goal of lowering the entry barrier for students and other learners of RL in the context of learning-based control. At its heart, RLLBC-Lib c

infographic.key_insight: RLLBC-Lib is an educational code library designed to make reinforcement learning and learning-based control easier to understand and teach. It turns a complex, multi-step learning process into an accessible implementation that students can explore and modify.
infographic.problem_solved: Reinforcement learning is often hard to learn because its behavior emerges from many interacting components over multiple cycles, which can be difficult to explain with theory alone. This paper addresses the lack of simple, approachable code resources for learners in RL-based control.
method: Provides a carefully crafted code library focused on reinforcement learning in the context of learning-based control.
Uses implementation as a teaching tool so learners can see how RL components interact across training cycles.
Aims to lower the entry barrier for students and other newcomers through accessible, educational examples.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, RLLBC-Lib offers a practical way to learn RL concepts through hands-on code rather than abstract explanations. This can speed up onboarding, improve intuition, and support teaching in academic or training settings.

title: Dreaming the Sound of Contact: Leveraging Video and Audio Generation for Zero-Shot Force-Aware Manipulation and Data Generation
authors: Guanhua Ji, Tianyu Li, Dayoon Suh, Yuqian Zhang, Boyan Zhang
abstract: Recent advances in video generation allow robots to learn manipulation trajectories from generated videos. However, these approaches produce purely kinematic trajectories that lack force information, causing failures in contact-rich tasks where appropriate contact forces are essential for success. In this work, we explore augmenting generated video with audio to shape a bounded, time-varying desired-force profile using the loudness of generated contact sounds. We present a pipeline that jointly

infographic.key_insight: Generated video alone gives robots motion, but not the force needed for real contact tasks. This paper shows that adding generated audio—especially sound loudness—can help infer a time-varying force profile for more realistic, force-aware manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing zero-shot manipulation methods based on video generation produce kinematic trajectories only, which often fail in contact-rich tasks because they ignore the forces required for safe and successful interaction.
method: Use video generation to obtain manipulation trajectories from visual demonstrations or prompts.
Augment the generated video with contact audio to estimate a bounded, time-varying desired-force signal from sound loudness.
Combine motion and audio cues in a pipeline that supports zero-shot, force-aware robot manipulation and can also generate training data for contact-rich tasks.
infographic.impact: This matters because many real-world robotics tasks depend on how hard, when, and where a robot pushes, presses, or touches—not just where it moves. The approach could improve robustness in manipulation and reduce the need for manually collected force-labeled data.

title: PhysStream: Streaming Physics-Grounded Video Generation with Structured Scene Memory and Fine-Grained Motion Control
authors: Chuhao Chen, Peter Wonka, Chaoyang Wang, Chen Wang, Qiao Feng
abstract: Interactive control for video generation is moving from coarse prompts toward fine-grained, physically meaningful manipulation of dynamic scenes. Yet existing controllable methods either require the full control schedule before generation starts, or use pixel-space signals that dictate object positions rather than physical dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose PhysStream, an autoregressive model for physics-grounded image-to-video synthesis that incorporates structured scene memory-

infographic.key_insight: PhysStream enables video generation with physics-aware, fine-grained control while generating frames autoregressively, rather than requiring all motion instructions up front. Its structured scene memory helps maintain coherent dynamics and object interactions over time.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the limitation of current controllable video generation methods that either need the full control schedule before generation begins or rely on pixel-space controls that specify object positions instead of true physical behavior.
method: Uses an autoregressive image-to-video generation framework for streaming synthesis.
Introduces structured scene memory to retain and update physics-relevant scene state across frames.
Supports fine-grained motion control grounded in physical dynamics instead of only spatial placement.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners because it makes interactive video generation more practical, flexible, and physically consistent. It can improve workflows in simulation, content creation, and controllable generative modeling where mid-generation adjustments are important.

title: PanoGS-SLAM: Panoramic 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM
authors: Yongqi Mao, Hao Shi, Yufan Zhang, Zhonghua Yi, Xiangfei Guo
abstract: Real-time dense SLAM is a core capability for robotics applications that require robust localization and high- quality mapping in dynamic or fast-changing environments. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based SLAM methods have shown promising performance, but most are designed for narrow-FoV pinhole cameras, where limited angular coverage weakens pose observability and often leads to unstable photo- metric optimization under rapid motion and large viewpoint changes. We present PanoGS-SLAM, the

infographic.key_insight: PanoGS-SLAM extends 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM to panoramic cameras, improving pose stability and mapping quality when the robot moves quickly or changes viewpoint dramatically. The wider field of view gives stronger geometric and photometric constraints than narrow-FoV camera setups.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the instability of real-time dense SLAM methods based on 3D Gaussian Splatting when using narrow-FoV pinhole cameras, especially under fast motion, large viewpoint changes, and dynamic or fast-changing environments.
method: Uses panoramic camera input to capture much more scene context than standard pinhole-based SLAM systems.
Adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time dense mapping and pose estimation in a panoramic setting.
Improves pose observability and stabilizes photometric optimization during rapid motion and challenging viewpoint transitions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in robotics and AR/VR, this work suggests a more robust SLAM design for environments where standard cameras struggle. It can enable denser, more stable mapping and localization in real-world scenarios with fast motion or wide-area coverage needs.

title: FreqSpaNet: Frequency and Spatial Learning of SFPF for Physical Layer Hardware Integrity Detection
authors: Xiaoxuan Huang, Jinlong Xu, YiZhe Wang, Meng Zhang, Xian Li
abstract: Unauthorized hardware replacement can preserve a wireless device's logical identity while altering its physical implementation, posing a challenge to hardware integrity verification. Spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints (SFPFs) capture device-dependent responses across multiple frequencies and directions, but their frequency and spatial dimensions exhibit different structural dependencies. We propose FreqSpaNet, an SFPF representation learning network for open set hardware anomaly detectio

infographic.key_insight: FreqSpaNet learns hardware fingerprints from both frequency and spatial patterns in spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints (SFPFs), making it easier to spot unauthorized hardware replacements even when a device keeps the same logical identity. The key idea is that frequency and direction carry different structural information, and modeling them separately improves anomaly detection.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses physical layer hardware integrity verification: detecting when a wireless device’s hardware has been secretly replaced or modified while its logical identity remains unchanged.
method: Uses spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints (SFPFs) as the input representation for device-specific hardware behavior.
Learns frequency-dependent and spatial-dependent structures with a dedicated representation learning network instead of treating all dimensions the same.
Targets open-set hardware anomaly detection, aiming to recognize abnormal or unseen device hardware changes.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how structured representation learning can improve security-oriented detection tasks where anomalies are subtle and open-set. The approach is broadly relevant to sensing, wireless security, and any application where multi-dimensional physical signatures must be interpreted reliably.

title: CareMirror: Bringing Caregiver Wellbeing into the Dementia Care Ecosystem
authors: Jiayue Melissa Shi, Ethan Nguyen, Drishti Goel, Upasana Natarajan, Shashwat Srivatsa
abstract: Family caregivers of people living with dementia shoulder emotional and practical responsibilities, yet their own wellbeing often remains peripheral to dementia care. We built CareMirror, an envisioned caregiver wellbeing ecosystem with interconnected caregiver- and clinician-facing interfaces for longitudinal reflection, personalized support, and caregiver-controlled sharing with clinical care. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 caregivers, using CareMirror as a design probe to exa

infographic.key_insight: CareMirror reframes dementia care by making caregiver wellbeing a first-class part of the care ecosystem, not an afterthought. It connects caregivers and clinicians through longitudinal reflection and caregiver-controlled information sharing to better support both emotional burden and clinical coordination.
infographic.problem_solved: Family caregivers of people living with dementia often carry heavy emotional and practical responsibilities, but their own wellbeing is rarely tracked or supported within dementia care workflows. This paper addresses the gap between caregiver needs and clinician awareness/support.
method: Designed CareMirror, an envisioned caregiver wellbeing ecosystem with interconnected caregiver- and clinician-facing interfaces.
Used CareMirror as a design probe in semi-structured interviews with 14 caregivers to explore needs, barriers, and preferences.
Focused on longitudinal reflection, personalized support, and caregiver-controlled sharing with clinical care.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights how human-centered systems can extend beyond prediction to support longitudinal wellbeing, trust, and data-sharing control in sensitive healthcare settings. It also shows the importance of designing AI-enabled tools that respect caregiver agency and fit into real clinical ecosystems.

title: LimiX-2: A Contextual Mechanism Network Towards General Structured-Data Intelligence
authors: Xingxuan Zhang, Gang Ren, Hao Yuan, Hao Zou, Hongze Tan
abstract: We introduce LimiX-2, a new model in the LimiX family, developed through model and data scaling guided by our previously established scaling laws. LimiX-2 adopts the Contextual Mechanism Networks (CMNs) paradigm and is pretrained with Context-Conditional Masked Modeling (CCMM). CMNs shifts the organizing principle of in-context learning from target-centric prediction to mechanism-oriented joint modeling. Rather than centering the network on the $p(y \mid x, D_{\mathrm{context}})$ objective of co

infographic.key_insight: LimiX-2 reframes in-context learning for structured data from predicting targets directly to learning the underlying mechanism that generates them. It combines scaling-law-guided model/data scaling with a new contextual mechanism network and pretraining objective to improve general structured-data intelligence.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of standard in-context learning methods that are centered on target prediction and may not capture reusable mechanisms across structured-data tasks. It aims to build models that can better generalize over diverse structured data by modeling context, relationships, and task structure more explicitly.
method: Introduces Contextual Mechanism Networks (CMNs), which shift learning from p(y | x, D_context) toward mechanism-oriented joint modeling.
Pretrains the model with Context-Conditional Masked Modeling (CCMM) to learn structure-aware representations from context.
Scales model size and data using previously derived scaling laws to improve performance and generalization.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, LimiX-2 suggests a stronger foundation for solving structured-data tasks such as tabular reasoning, relational prediction, and context-dependent inference. It may reduce task-specific engineering by enabling models to learn transferable mechanisms rather than only surface-level correlations.

title: Evaluating Verified Autonomy in Quantum Engineering
authors: Naixu Guo, Changhao Li, Siyu Cheng, Qicheng Tang, Binzhao Luo
abstract: Reliable quantum engineering is essential for turning quantum phenomena into practical technologies. As quantum platforms grow in scale and complexity, their characterization and operation require increasing human effort and coordination. Scientific artificial intelligence agents, which can plan experiments, operate instruments, and analyze observations, offer a promising route towards autonomous quantum engineering. Yet whether current agents can perform reliably in this setting has not been sy

infographic.key_insight: This paper asks whether AI agents can reliably carry out quantum engineering tasks, not just suggest ideas. The core insight is that autonomy in quantum labs must be evaluated by verification, because success depends on both planning and trustworthy execution in a highly complex physical setting.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the growing burden of manually characterizing, operating, and coordinating quantum experiments as platforms scale up. The paper tackles the question of how to assess whether scientific AI agents can actually perform these tasks reliably in quantum engineering workflows.
method: Defines a verification-focused perspective for autonomous quantum engineering instead of only measuring task completion.
Evaluates AI agents across the stages of planning experiments, operating instruments, and analyzing observations.

title: Tracking the Unseen: An Occlusion-Robust Framework for Target Tracking Under Full and Long-Term Occlusion
authors: Mais Mohammed, Sharifa Mohammed, Hanan Awadh, Haneen Bamaas, Raghad Bawazeer
abstract: Real-time multi-object tracking systems remain highly vulnerable to full and long-term occlusion, where targets temporarily or completely disappear from the camera's field of view. Conventional trackers may terminate trajectories prematurely, resulting in identity loss and reduced situational awareness in applications such as defense and surveillance. This work proposes an occlusion-robust target tracking framework that maintains target identity and trajectory continuity through the integration

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces an occlusion-robust tracking framework that keeps targets linked to their identities even when they disappear for long periods. The main idea is to prevent trajectory loss during full or long-term occlusion, improving continuity and reliability in real-time tracking.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the failure of conventional multi-object trackers when a target becomes fully hidden or absent from view, which often causes premature track termination and identity switches. This is especially important in defense and surveillance scenarios where losing a target can reduce situational awareness.
method: Integrates an occlusion-aware tracking strategy designed to preserve target identity across disappearance and reappearance events.
Maintains trajectory continuity instead of ending tracks as soon as detections vanish.
Supports real-time multi-object tracking under full and long-term occlusion conditions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this improves tracker robustness in hard real-world environments where visibility is intermittent. It can reduce identity loss, improve downstream analytics, and make tracking systems more dependable in safety-critical applications.

title: ScienceBuddy: Recursive-in-Recursive Self-Improvement for Interactive Scientific Agents
authors: Shuhan Xue, Jianyuan Zhong, Ziyuan Nan, Wenbin Li, Zhaochen Yu
abstract: We introduce and release ScienceBuddy, an interactive scientific research workspace that brings continually improving scientific agents into researchers' everyday workflows. ScienceBuddy supports researchers in carrying out scientific tasks while transforming their requests, feedback, and execution evidence into tasks and evaluation rubrics for continual learning. At its core is recursive-in-recursive self-improvement, a paradigm that couples harness evolution with model reinforcement learning:

infographic.key_insight: ScienceBuddy turns everyday researcher interactions into a built-in learning loop, so scientific AI agents can keep improving while being used. Its core idea is "recursive-in-recursive self-improvement": the system improves both the agent's behavior and the environment/rubrics used to train it.
infographic.problem_solved: Scientific AI assistants often fail to improve from real research workflows because user requests, feedback, and execution traces are not systematically converted into learning signals. This paper addresses the gap between interactive use and continual model improvement in scientific tasks.
method: Builds ScienceBuddy, an interactive research workspace where scientists can delegate tasks and receive agent assistance in their normal workflow.
Converts user requests, feedback, and execution evidence into structured tasks and evaluation rubrics for continual learning.
Uses recursive-in-recursive self-improvement by combining harness evolution with model reinforcement learning to improve both the training setup and the agent itself.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical path to deploy agents that get better from real-world scientific use instead of static benchmarks alone. It could make research assistants more reliable, adaptive, and aligned with actual researcher needs.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
authors: Fengshuo Liu, Ying Liu, Ruize Sun, Lie Luo, Siyuan Guo
abstract: Small differences on coding-agent leaderboards are often read as an ordering of systems. We audit whether the published verdicts support this reading, using 254 SWE-bench submissions across four splits without running models. On Verified, the leading two entries each resolve 396 of 500 instances. The top ten share 285 successes and 51 failures, leaving 164 instances that distinguish their outcomes. Frontier solution sets have median nesting 0.935 against a score-implied baseline of 0.774, indica

infographic.key_insight: The SWE-bench leaderboard’s top coding agents are now so close that the published ranking often cannot reliably tell them apart. The paper shows that many “different” scores come from overlapping solved-instance sets rather than clear performance gaps.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of interpreting small leaderboard differences on coding-agent benchmarks, especially whether top SWE-bench results genuinely establish an ordering among leading systems.
method: Audited 254 SWE-bench submissions across four splits without rerunning any models.
Compared solved and failed instance overlap among top submissions to measure how distinguishable their results really are.
Examined nesting and score-implied baselines to test whether leaderboard separation reflects meaningful capability differences.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means leaderboard rank alone may be a misleading signal when systems are near-converged. The paper argues for evaluation metrics that better capture solution-set overlap, uncertainty, and distinguishability rather than just raw score differences.

title: SSC-Priors: Exploring Semantic and Visibility Priors to Boost Lidar Semantic Scene Completion
authors: Tetiana Martyniuk, Jonathan Seele, Alexandre Boulch, Gilles Puy, Renaud Marlet
abstract: This paper investigates easy strategies to boost the performance of existing networks for lidar semantic scene completion (SSC) without requiring complex architectural redesigns. The fact is that, over the last years, SSC methods have mostly pursued architectural innovations, making the models heavier and more complex, e.g., by jointly training a point cloud semantic segmentation branch. In this work, we take a step back and explore two priors used as simple ingredients (possibly noisy) to impro

infographic.key_insight: Simple semantic and visibility priors can significantly improve lidar semantic scene completion without making the model architecture more complex. The paper shows that carefully chosen, possibly noisy, auxiliary cues can boost performance as effectively as heavier redesigns.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing lidar semantic scene completion methods often rely on increasingly complex architectures, which raises model size and training complexity. This paper addresses how to improve SSC performance using lightweight, easy-to-add priors instead of major network changes.
method: Explore semantic priors to inject class-level information into the SSC pipeline.
Use visibility priors to help the model reason about which regions are observed versus occluded.
Treat these priors as simple auxiliary inputs or ingredients that enhance existing SSC networks with minimal architectural changes.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical path to better performance without the cost of redesigning or scaling up models. It is especially useful when computational efficiency, simplicity, and ease of integration matter.

title: Agentic Societies Need a Social Harness
authors: Tapan Chugh, Vidushi Singh, Krish Jain, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Ratul Mahajan
abstract: An agentic society is a collection of AI agents that coordinate autonomously across trust boundaries, on behalf of different principals whose objectives may only partially align. We show experimentally that in agentic societies even honest, competent agents often fail to reach satisfactory outcomes with existing harnesses and messaging primitives, and that faulty or malicious agents can stall collaboration, influence outcomes, and pursue other harmful goals by exploiting vulnerabilities in commu

infographic.key_insight: AI agents operating in multi-agent "societies" can fail even when they are honest and capable, because current harnesses and messaging protocols do not adequately support coordination across trust boundaries. The paper shows that malicious or faulty agents can exploit these weaknesses to stall collaboration and steer outcomes.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of safely coordinating autonomous AI agents that represent different principals with only partially aligned goals. It highlights the need for a stronger "social harness" to manage communication, trust, and resilience against manipulation in agentic societies.
method: Experimentally evaluate existing harnesses and messaging primitives in multi-agent settings where agents must coordinate autonomously.
Test both honest competent agents and faulty or malicious agents to observe failure modes in collaboration and outcome quality.
Analyze how vulnerabilities in communication and coordination can be exploited to block progress or influence decisions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a warning that agentic systems need more than task performance—they need robust social infrastructure for trust, coordination, and adversarial resistance. It is especially relevant for deploying multi-agent workflows in real-world settings with partially conflicting objectives.

title: Tables Decoded: DELTA for Structure, TARQA for Understanding
authors: Jahanvi Rajput, Dhruv Kudale, Saikiran Kasturi, Utkarsh Verma, Ganesh Ramakrishnan
abstract: Table understanding is a core task in document intelligence, encompassing two key subtasks: table reconstruction and table visual question answering (TabVQA). While recent approaches predominantly rely on vision- language models (VLMs) operating on table images, we propose a more scalable and effective alternative based on structured textual representations. These representations are easier to process, align more naturally with LLMs, and eliminate the need for language-specific visual encoders,

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that table understanding can be done more effectively with structured text instead of table images. By combining table reconstruction and TabVQA around text-based representations, it reduces reliance on heavy vision-language encoders and better aligns with LLMs.
infographic.problem_solved: Current table understanding systems mostly use image-based VLMs, which are less scalable and harder to align with language models. This work addresses two core tasks: reconstructing tables from documents and answering questions about tables accurately.
method: Uses structured textual representations of tables rather than raw table images.
Introduces DELTA for table structure reconstruction.
Introduces TARQA for table question answering / table understanding.
Leverages LLM-friendly text formats to improve scalability and cross-language applicability.
infographic.impact: This approach can simplify table intelligence pipelines and make them more efficient for document AI systems. For practitioners, it offers a path to stronger table understanding without depending on expensive vision-heavy models.

title: FlashVector: Agent for Hierarchical Model Serving Stack Optimization
authors: Qi Wu, Lohan Lemire, Kai Meng, Zhongmou Cai, Raphael Bargues
abstract: Model serving is one of the largest cost drivers in production recommender systems. Maximizing its throughput requires navigating a deeply layered hierarchy: GPU kernels, the ML framework computation graph, the model server, and on-demand feature processing -- each demanding specialized domain expertise. Such cross-layer expertise is inherently difficult to acquire, and does not scale with a workload that continuously grows and evolves, leaving significant cost efficiency gains unrealized. While

infographic.key_insight: FlashVector targets the hidden performance losses in production model serving by optimizing across the full serving stack, not just one layer. Its core idea is that an agent can help coordinate GPU kernels, framework graphs, server behavior, and feature processing to boost throughput and reduce cost.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of improving recommender-system model serving throughput in a deeply layered stack where each layer requires specialized expertise. This cross-layer optimization is hard to do manually and does not scale as workloads grow and change.
method: Uses an agent to reason across multiple layers of the serving stack instead of optimizing each layer in isolation.
Focuses on hierarchical optimization spanning GPU kernels, ML framework computation graphs, model servers, and on-demand feature processing.
Aims to automate expert-level cross-layer decisions that improve throughput and cost efficiency in production serving.
infographic.impact: For ML practitioners, this means higher serving efficiency and lower infrastructure cost without requiring deep expertise in every system layer. It also offers a path to keep performance optimization scalable as production workloads evolve.

title: Verifiable Social Reasoning for LLM Assistants
authors: Amir Taubenfeld, Zorik Gekhman, Avigail Grinstein-Dabush, Itay Laish, Ariel Goldstein
abstract: LLM assistants are widely used for daily social advice, yet evaluating their social reasoning in such consultation settings remains challenging since (i) it requires setups where the assistant learns about social situations from subjective user narratives, and (ii) social properties, such as others' intentions, typically lack verifiable ground truth. To address these challenges, we introduce Fuse, a multi-agent simulation framework for studying user-mediated social reasoning. In Fuse, a target a

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces Fuse, a multi-agent simulation framework that makes it possible to test how LLM assistants reason about social situations in a verifiable way. It turns subjective social advice into an evaluable benchmark by simulating interactions and exposing hidden social variables.
infographic.problem_solved: LLM assistants are increasingly used for social advice, but evaluating their social reasoning is hard because the assistant learns from subjective user narratives and key social facts, like intentions, usually have no ground truth.
method: Builds Fuse, a multi-agent simulation environment for user-mediated social reasoning.
Models social scenarios with multiple agents so hidden intentions and context can be controlled and measured.
Enables verification by comparing assistant responses against known simulated social outcomes and properties.
infographic.impact: This gives researchers and practitioners a practical way to benchmark social reasoning in LLMs beyond open-ended chat. It can help improve safety, trustworthiness, and usefulness in advice-oriented assistants.

title: AlgoEvo: Self-Evolving Agentic Search for Automated Algorithm Discovery
authors: Junhao Qiu, Qinglong Hu, Xialiang Tong, Mingxuan Yuan, Liyong Lin
abstract: Large language models have advanced automated algorithm discovery by synthesizing executable code, but existing frameworks trap them in rigid search pipelines with pre-defined control flows. This limitation restricts adaptive reasoning, blocks cross-paradigm transfer, and discards valuable execution feedback. We propose AlgoEvo, a unified agentic framework that transforms automated algorithm discovery into an interactive, knowledge-accumulating process. An autonomous agent dynamically inspects,

infographic.key_insight: AlgoEvo turns automated algorithm discovery from a fixed search pipeline into a self-evolving agent that can reason, adapt, and reuse execution feedback. This makes algorithm synthesis more interactive and capable of exploring beyond rigid predefined workflows.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLM-based algorithm discovery systems are constrained by rigid, pre-defined control flows. This limits adaptive reasoning, cross-paradigm transfer, and the ability to learn from execution feedback during the search process.
method: Uses an autonomous agent to dynamically inspect the search process and decide what to do next.
Accumulates knowledge from execution feedback instead of discarding it after each trial.
Unifies multiple algorithm-discovery steps into an interactive, self-evolving framework rather than a fixed pipeline.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, AlgoEvo could make algorithm discovery more flexible, efficient, and reusable across tasks. It may reduce manual pipeline design while improving the quality and diversity of discovered algorithms.

title: The Router Within: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM
authors: Ruishuo Chen, Xun Wang, Yu Chen, Zhuoran Li, Longbo Huang
abstract: Skills extend an LLM agent beyond its parametric knowledge, and the gain they promise rests on picking the right one. Deployed harnesses route by preloading every skill's metadata into the context, which disperses the agent's attention and caps the library size. Retrieval pipelines move the selection out of the context, but also out of the agent's capability. We show that the frozen agent LLM already carries the routing signal in its own forward passes, and that two linear maps suffice to read i

infographic.key_insight: A frozen LLM already contains the information needed to route to the right skill; the paper shows that this routing signal can be extracted from the model’s own internal forward passes instead of being handled by an external retriever. In practice, just two linear maps are enough to read out which skill should be chosen.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the skill-selection bottleneck in LLM agents: context-based routing overloads the prompt with metadata, while external retrieval systems move selection outside the model and away from its native reasoning ability.
method: Probe the frozen LLM’s internal activations to expose latent skill-routing signals.
Use two lightweight linear maps to decode these signals into skill-selection decisions.
Avoid loading all skill metadata into the prompt, reducing context clutter and scaling better to larger skill libraries.
infographic.impact: This makes skill routing more efficient, scalable, and model-native for AI agents. Practitioners can build larger skill libraries without inflating context windows or relying on separate retrieval pipelines.

title: Vulnerability Localization Benchmark: Measuring Agentic Security Analysis at Repository Scale
authors: Aman Priyanshu, Supriti Vijay, Kimia Majd, Xuhong He, Fraser Burch
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly operate over complete software repositories, yet cybersecurity evaluations primarily measure whether they can detect, reproduce, or repair vulnerabilities rather than whether they can locate the relevant code. We study vulnerability localization: given a weakness class and an unfamiliar repository, identify the implementation files associated with that weakness. We introduce the Vulnerability Localization Benchmark (VLoc Bench), comprising 500 real world vulner

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that a major missing skill in AI security agents is vulnerability localization: finding the right files in a large unfamiliar repository, not just spotting or fixing bugs. It introduces VLoc Bench to measure this capability at repository scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Current cybersecurity evaluations mostly test whether agents can detect, reproduce, or repair vulnerabilities. They do not sufficiently measure whether an agent can localize the code regions tied to a specific weakness class in an unfamiliar codebase.
method: Define vulnerability localization as the task of identifying implementation files associated with a specified weakness class in a new repository.
Introduce VLoc Bench, a benchmark built from 500 real-world vulnerabilities to evaluate repository-scale localization performance.
Use the benchmark to assess how well language-model agents can navigate complete repositories and pinpoint relevant source files.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark fills an important gap in security evaluation by testing a more realistic repository-level skill. It helps developers understand where agentic security tools succeed or fail before using them in real software audits.

title: Stellar Colosseum: A Many-Agent Harness for Long-Horizon Research in Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science
authors: Honghao Lin, David P. Woodruff, Yuan Deng, Jieming Mao, Song Zuo
abstract: Language models can produce plausible short proofs, but may still be unreliable on long-horizon research problems, where progress depends on a sequence of uncertain and interdependent decisions. We introduce Stellar Colosseum, a model-agnostic harness for allocating inference across research in mathematics and theoretical computer science. Colosseum explores alternative strategies before proof construction, uses a readiness gate to decide when a route is mature enough to decompose, represents th

infographic.key_insight: Stellar Colosseum is a model-agnostic system that improves long-horizon research by managing how inference is spent across many competing solution paths. Instead of committing too early, it explores alternatives, waits until a path is ready, and then decomposes the problem more effectively.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the unreliability of language models on long, research-style problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, where success depends on many sequential, uncertain decisions rather than a single short proof.
method: Uses a many-agent harness to allocate inference across multiple candidate research routes.
Explores alternative strategies before proof construction to avoid premature commitment.
Includes a readiness gate that determines when a route is mature enough to be broken into smaller subproblems.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical framework for scaling LLMs to harder research tasks where naive single-shot reasoning fails. It highlights a direction for building systems that are better at planning, branching, and managing uncertainty over long horizons.

title: Mind2Dialogue: Training Human-Aware Language Models by Simulating User Mental States
authors: Zixuan Wang, Yufan Zhou, Jinzhou Tang, Xinle Yu, Chengjun Wu
abstract: As language models become more capable, long-term collaboration in learning, reasoning, and decision-making calls for a deeper understanding of the people they serve. Yet training such human-aware language models faces a fundamental supervision gap because current datasets for LLM assistant training contain few if any well-informed responses explicitly grounded in users' unspoken beliefs and goals. Scaling such supervision is inherently constrained, as users' underlying states are not directly o

infographic.key_insight: Mind2Dialogue trains language models to respond with a better sense of what users may be thinking, wanting, or believing—even when those states are not explicitly stated. It does this by simulating user mental states to create more human-aware assistant behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the supervision gap in training LLM assistants: existing datasets rarely contain responses grounded in users' hidden beliefs, goals, or intentions, making it hard to teach models true human awareness at scale.
method: Simulate plausible user mental states (e.g., beliefs, goals, intentions) to generate training signals.
Use these simulated states to produce dialogue supervision that is more explicitly human-aware than standard assistant data.
Train language models on this synthetic/augmented dialogue data to improve responses that account for unspoken user context.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a scalable path to build assistants that are more helpful, personalized, and aligned with user intent in complex real-world interactions. It is especially relevant for long-horizon collaboration, tutoring, decision support, and reasoning-focused assistants.

title: CiteGuard-RAG: A Validation-Centered AI System for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
authors: Sumit Barua, Guan Hong, Halil Dursunoglu, Charles Rodgers, Alvis Fong
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve access to complex information; however, retrieving evidence alone does not ensure that answers are grounded, citation-valid, or appropriately refused. This paper introduces CiteGuard-RAG, a validation-centered AI system for evidence-grounded question answering. The system integrates hybrid semantic-lexical retrieval, citation-constrained generation, sentence-level grounding validation, and single-pass regeneration. Validation is used at runtime to

infographic.key_insight: CiteGuard-RAG shows that getting evidence back is not enough—AI answers also need runtime validation to stay grounded, cite correctly, and refuse when support is weak. The paper combines retrieval, citation constraints, and grounding checks to make RAG more trustworthy.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap between evidence retrieval and reliable answering: RAG systems may still produce unsupported, uncited, or overconfident responses even when relevant documents are found.
method: Uses hybrid semantic + lexical retrieval to improve evidence search quality.
Generates answers under citation constraints so claims are tied to source evidence.
Applies sentence-level grounding validation at runtime and triggers single-pass regeneration when support is insufficient.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners building enterprise, legal, medical, or research assistants where citation accuracy and refusal behavior are critical. It offers a practical framework for making RAG outputs more auditable and trustworthy.

title: Per-Matrix Optimality Is Not Enough: Three-Level Optimization for Low-Rank LLM Compression
authors: Huicheng Zhang, Xiyao Feng, Ze-Tong Li, Chengkai Zhu, Xiao Shi
abstract: Per-matrix singular value decomposition (SVD) truncation is Eckart-Young optimal in the whitened Frobenius norm, but errors from independently compressed matrices compound through the block's nonlinear forward pass. Inspired in part by hierarchical variational optimization in quantum many-body methods, we introduce a three-level chain that widens optimization scope from individual matrices to Transformer blocks to the full model: whitened SVD~(L1), block-level joint optimization~(L2), and end-to

infographic.key_insight: Optimizing each weight matrix for low-rank compression is not enough, because small per-matrix errors can accumulate through a Transformer block’s nonlinear computations. The paper shows that compression should be coordinated at three levels: matrix, block, and full-model scope.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the loss in accuracy that happens when LLM weights are compressed independently matrix by matrix using standard SVD truncation, even though each matrix may be locally optimal in isolation.
method: Use whitened SVD truncation at the individual-matrix level to get an Eckart-Young-style optimal low-rank approximation.
Refine compression with block-level joint optimization so interacting matrices inside a Transformer block are compressed together.
Extend optimization to the full model, creating a three-level chain that aligns local compression decisions with end-to-end performance.
infographic.impact: This approach can improve low-rank LLM compression quality by preserving more accuracy at a given parameter budget. For practitioners, it offers a more reliable path to smaller, faster models than independent per-matrix truncation.

title: SlipSense: Multimodal Tactile Learning for Low-Latency and Generalized Slip Detection
authors: Tong Jian, Aditya Thurvas Senthil Kumar, Xinyi Li, Ziling Chen, Tianyu Dai
abstract: Slip detection is fundamental to dexterous manipulation, yet existing systems often lack precise characterization of detection latency and cross-platform generalization. We present SlipSense, a multimodal tactile slip-detection framework built on TacV5, a compact sensor integrating a $32 \times 32$ piezoresistive array operating at 240 Hz and a 3-axis MEMS accelerometer operating at 8 kHz. The piezoresistive array captures spatial pressure distributions, while the accelerometer captures friction

infographic.key_insight: SlipSense shows that combining tactile pressure images with high-speed inertial sensing can detect slip faster and more reliably across different hardware settings. The key breakthrough is a multimodal tactile pipeline designed to measure and improve both latency and generalization, two aspects often ignored in prior work.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting object slip early enough for dexterous manipulation, while also ensuring the detector works robustly across different tactile platforms and setups.
method: Builds on TacV5, a compact tactile sensor with a 32 x 32 piezoresistive array at 240 Hz and a 3-axis MEMS accelerometer at 8 kHz.
Uses the pressure array to capture spatial contact distribution and the accelerometer to capture high-frequency friction/slip dynamics.
Fuses multimodal tactile signals into a slip-detection framework optimized for low-latency response and cross-platform generalization.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in robotics, this work highlights how multimodal sensing can improve real-world reliability beyond single-sensor approaches. It is especially relevant for robotic grasping, prosthetics, and manipulation systems that need fast reactions and deployment across different devices.

title: Proportional-Fair Resource Allocation and Dual-Threshold Early-Exit Inference for Secure Cooperative Multi-Layer Edge Intelligence
authors: Thai T. Vu, John Le, Tu N. Nguyen, Jun Shen, Quang Vinh Duong
abstract: This paper proposes FREDI (Fair Resource Allocation for Edge Dual-Threshold Inference), a secure wireless edge-intelligence framework for event-triggered inference in a cooperative user equipment (UE)--edge server (ES)--cloud system. Each UE performs early-exit convolutional neural network (CNN) screening using dual confidence thresholds, while critical events are securely offloaded to an edge server for detailed classification. We formulate a proportionally-fair utility maximization problem tha

infographic.key_insight: FREDI combines fair wireless resource allocation with dual-threshold early-exit inference so edge devices can quickly handle easy cases and securely escalate critical events for deeper analysis. The result is a cooperative UE–edge–cloud system that improves efficiency without sacrificing security or fairness.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of running real-time AI inference on resource-constrained edge devices while balancing latency, communication cost, security, and fairness across users and network resources.
method: Each UE runs an early-exit CNN with two confidence thresholds to decide whether to accept a prediction locally or flag a case as critical.
Critical events are securely offloaded to an edge server for more detailed classification, reducing unnecessary cloud communication.
A proportional-fair optimization framework allocates wireless and compute resources across the UE–edge–cloud system to balance performance among users.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it offers a practical blueprint for deploying inference at the edge with lower latency and better resource use. It is especially useful for safety- or security-sensitive applications where uncertain predictions should be escalated reliably.

authors: Laura M. Vowels, Matthew J. Vowels, Shivali Sharma, Apoorv Jha, Rehnuma Choudhury
abstract: % !TEX root = ../main.tex People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for mental health support, yet their safety in evolving, high-risk conversations remains poorly characterised. We developed K-Bench, a clinician-calibrated, protected benchmark evaluating 125 model configurations representing 33 base models from 14 providers across a fixed cohort of 200 multi-turn vignettes involving suicide, self-harm, domestic violence, substance misuse, and no-risk presentations. Synthetic patient

infographic.key_insight: K-Bench introduces a clinically calibrated benchmark for testing how well large language models handle high-risk mental health conversations over multiple turns. It helps reveal whether models stay safe and appropriate when discussions involve suicide, self-harm, domestic violence, substance misuse, or low-risk scenarios.
infographic.problem_solved: LLMs are increasingly used for mental health support, but their behavior in realistic, evolving, high-risk conversations is not well understood. This paper addresses the lack of a rigorous, clinician-informed way to evaluate safety, consistency, and risk handling across different models.
method: Built K-Bench around 200 multi-turn mental health vignettes covering suicide, self-harm, domestic violence, substance misuse, and no-risk cases.

Evaluated 125 model configurations spanning 33 base models from 14 providers to compare performance across safety-sensitive settings.

title: A Chosen Future Can Still Be Rewritten: Causal Writability in Video Models
authors: Xingyun Wang, Haomin Zheng, Man Yuan, Leqian Yang, Ziming Liu
abstract: When a video model generates physically incorrect motion, did it fail to learn the correct motion, or did it learn it but fail to use it? We show the latter: the correct motion remains available inside the model and can still be made to control the generated video. We train on videos where red masses oscillate slowly and blue masses oscillate quickly, then test a red mass with fast observed motion. Even when the model generates slow motion in this conflicting case, a low-dimensional edit predict

infographic.key_insight: Video models may not be missing the correct physics—they may already encode it but fail to use it in generation. This paper shows that a low-dimensional intervention can recover and control the hidden, physically correct motion even when the model first outputs the wrong one.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the question of whether physically incorrect video generation is due to a model never learning the right motion, or due to the model learning it but not selecting it during generation.
method: Train a video model on a synthetic setting where red masses move slowly and blue masses move quickly.
Test the model on a conflict case where a red mass is observed moving fast, creating a mismatch between learned color-motion association and observed evidence.
Apply a low-dimensional causal edit to the model’s internal representation to redirect generation toward the correct motion.
infographic.impact: This suggests that failure modes in video generation may be fixable through targeted interventions rather than retraining. For practitioners, it opens a path toward controllable, interpretable, and more reliable video models.

title: LongAgent: History-Guided Agentic Search for Longitudinal Outcome Prediction
authors: Siyao Wang, Florian Guitton, Shuojie Fu, Guanyu Tao, Kai Sun
abstract: Extracting informative representations from longitudinal data that can predict future outcomes remains a critical challenge in medicine. Medical datasets are inherently heterogeneous, consisting of a large number of variables collected from different sources, sampled with different temporal spacings, and representing different aspects of human health status. This requires identifying those variables with predictive value, processing longitudinal information, and integrating multiple variables fo

infographic.key_insight: LongAgent turns longitudinal patient data analysis into a guided search problem, using history-aware decision making to better predict future outcomes. The core idea is to identify and reuse the most informative past signals across irregular, heterogeneous medical records.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of predicting future medical outcomes from longitudinal data that is heterogeneous, sparsely sampled, and spread across multiple sources. Traditional approaches often struggle to select predictive variables and integrate time-varying information effectively.
method: Uses a history-guided agentic search strategy to explore longitudinal patient records.
Selects informative variables and temporal patterns from heterogeneous, irregularly sampled medical data.
Integrates evidence across time to build representations that support outcome prediction.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more adaptive way to model complex healthcare timelines without relying only on fixed feature engineering. It is especially useful for prediction tasks where the most relevant signals are scattered, noisy, and time-dependent.

title: Bridging Control, Inference, Transport, and Thermodynamics: From Theory to Applications in Learning
authors: Emmy Blumenthal, Nikolas Claussen, Benjamin Eysenbach, Catherine Ji, Gautam Reddy
abstract: The last decade has seen the development of powerful methods for learning complex structure from high-dimensional data. These advances have brought to the foreground fundamental connections between subdisciplines of physics, applied mathematics, and machine learning. In this review, we bring together some of these ideas, often expressed in different languages, to highlight a conceptual thread that links five distinct fields: control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, non-equilib

infographic.key_insight: This review shows that control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, thermodynamics, and machine learning are deeply connected through a shared mathematical structure. By translating ideas across these fields, it reveals a unified way to understand and design learning algorithms.
infographic.problem_solved: AI research often develops powerful methods in separate subfields with different terminology, making it hard to see how they relate or when one framework can inform another. This paper addresses the challenge of connecting these parallel perspectives into one coherent conceptual map.
method: Synthesizes core principles from five areas: control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and learning.
Explains how these fields describe similar optimization, dynamics, and transport processes using different mathematical languages.
Connects theory to applications to help readers transfer intuitions and tools across disciplines.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a unified framework for thinking about optimization, generative modeling, inference, and dynamics. It can help researchers choose better algorithms, interpret existing methods more clearly, and discover new cross-disciplinary approaches.

title: Expert-Space Exploration in MoE Reinforcement Learning
authors: Hongyi He, Zhenghao Lin, Xiao Liu, Peng Cheng, Yan Lu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training of large language models. Recent advances in RL for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have primarily focused on improving optimization stability and training efficiency, while treating the expert selection as a fixed component. Since routing determines the sparse computation paths that induce output distributions, expert selection offers an additional source of rollout diversity. Through empirical analysis, we find that perturbing exp

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that MoE routing is not just an implementation detail—it can be actively explored during reinforcement learning to increase rollout diversity and improve learning. By perturbing expert selection, the model can generate more varied sparse computation paths and potentially better post-training outcomes.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing RL methods for Mixture-of-Experts models mainly optimize stability and efficiency while keeping expert routing fixed. This work addresses the missed opportunity of using expert selection itself as a controllable source of diversity during RL training.
method: Analyze how expert routing affects output diversity in MoE reinforcement learning.
Introduce expert-space exploration by perturbing routing decisions to sample different sparse expert paths.
Use the resulting routing diversity to enrich rollouts and improve RL training signal quality.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a new lever for improving MoE post-training beyond optimizer tweaks and stability tricks. It could help produce stronger, more diverse policies with little added architectural complexity.

title: MP-Bench: Evaluating Voice Agents as a Multiparty Conversation Participant
authors: Yi-Jen Shih, Shih-Yun Shan Kuan, Guan-Ting Lin, Kai-Wei Chang, Siddhant Arora
abstract: Conversational voice agents have advanced significantly, offering increasingly natural human-machine interactions through both cascaded and end-to-end architectures. However, while recent benchmarks extensively evaluate dyadic interactions and passive audio comprehension, they largely overlook a prevalent real-world scenario: multi-party conversations. Evaluating agents in these settings is fundamentally more challenging than in dyadic interactions due to the exponentially greater conversational

infographic.key_insight: MP-Bench introduces a benchmark for evaluating voice agents in realistic multi-party conversations, going beyond standard one-on-one tests. It helps reveal how well an agent can handle turn-taking, speaker tracking, and participation in more complex social settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing voice-agent benchmarks focus mostly on dyadic interactions or passive audio understanding, leaving a major gap in evaluating performance in multi-party conversations. This paper addresses the difficulty of measuring agent behavior in settings where multiple speakers create exponentially more complex conversational dynamics.
method: Design a benchmark specifically for multi-party conversation participation by voice agents.
Evaluate agents on interaction skills that matter in group settings, such as identifying when to speak, following conversation flow, and responding appropriately amid multiple speakers.
Use benchmark tasks to compare systems under realistic conversational conditions that are harder than standard one-on-one evaluation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MP-Bench provides a more realistic yardstick for building and testing voice agents intended for real-world use. It can expose failures that traditional benchmarks miss, guiding better model design and deployment decisions.

title: Attention Quantization for Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Jonas M. Kübler, Benjamin Jäger, Klemens Flöge, Noah Hollmann, Frank Hutter
abstract: With the recent rise and adoption of tabular foundation models, optimizing their inference performance becomes an emerging field for efficiency research. While the models are architecturally similar to transformer-based large language models (LLMs), the size and serving patterns differ significantly. We show that the focus should be on the attention calculation and less on weight or KV cache quantization, which are more popular in LLMs. We develop a quantization strategy for queries, keys, and v

infographic.key_insight: For tabular foundation models, the biggest inference efficiency gains come from quantizing the attention computation itself, rather than focusing mainly on weight or KV-cache quantization as is common in LLMs. The paper argues that query/key/value quantization is the right lever for these models.
infographic.problem_solved: Tabular foundation models are increasingly used in inference settings, but serving them efficiently is challenging. Existing LLM-style optimization priorities do not transfer well, so the paper addresses how to reduce inference cost for tabular models in a way that matches their architecture and usage patterns.
method: Analyze where inference bottlenecks actually occur in tabular foundation models.
Shift quantization focus from weights/KV cache to the attention mechanism.
Develop a quantization strategy for queries, keys, and values to improve efficiency while preserving model performance.
infographic.impact: This helps practitioners deploy tabular foundation models faster and more cheaply, especially in latency- or throughput-sensitive settings. It also provides a clearer optimization target for efficiency research beyond LLM-centric assumptions.

title: Unified CT and MRI Pancreas Segmentation for Label-Efficient Cross-Modality Subregion Transfer
authors: Ziliang Hong, Hongyi Pan, Halil Ertugrul Aktas, Andrea Bejar, Elif Keles
abstract: Robust medical image segmentation across imaging modalities is challenging because of large differences in appearance and intensity distributions. Models trained on a single modality often show substantial performance drops when applied to unseen domains. In this work, we develop a unified 3D pancreas segmentation framework that applies domain-adversarial learning to 4,604 heterogeneous CT and MRI scans to learn anatomical representations. A shared nnU-Net encoder-decoder is trained for whole-pa

infographic.key_insight: A single 3D segmentation model can learn pancreas anatomy across both CT and MRI by aligning features from different modalities, reducing the need for separate labeled datasets. This enables better cross-modality transfer, especially for pancreas subregion segmentation.
infographic.problem_solved: Medical image segmentation models often fail when moved from one imaging modality to another because CT and MRI look very different. This paper addresses the challenge of building a label-efficient model that generalizes across modalities and supports subregion transfer.
method: Train a unified 3D pancreas segmentation framework on 4,604 heterogeneous CT and MRI scans.
Use domain-adversarial learning to reduce modality-specific differences and learn shared anatomical representations.
Adopt a shared nnU-Net encoder-decoder architecture to perform whole-pancreas segmentation and support cross-modality subregion transfer.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows a practical path toward more robust medical segmentation systems that work across scanners and imaging types. It can reduce annotation burden and improve real-world deployment where modality shift is common.

title: Comfort by Construction: Adaptive, Comfort-Bounded Action Spaces for Learned Driving Policies
authors: Anna Rothenhäusler, Daniel Jost, Raghu Rajan, Faris Janjos, Oliver Scheel
abstract: Data-driven driving simulators command accelerations and steering rates from a fixed grid without constraining the realized accelerations and jerks. As a result, reinforcement-learning policies inflate safety metrics through abrupt, last-second maneuvers that lie far outside the range of human driving and would be unacceptable to occupants of a real vehicle, so the metrics measure simulator permissiveness rather than policy quality. Enforcing comfort bounds naively is not enough: lateral limits

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that driving policies can appear safe by exploiting simulator permissiveness with abrupt, uncomfortable maneuvers. It introduces an adaptive way to define action spaces so the policy stays within comfort bounds while still learning effectively.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between simulator action grids and real vehicle comfort, where learned policies can game safety metrics by producing unrealistic accelerations and jerks. The goal is to make safety evaluation reflect genuine driving quality rather than simulator loopholes.
method: Replace fixed action grids with comfort-bounded, adaptive action spaces tied to realized vehicle dynamics.
Constrain actions so resulting accelerations and jerks remain within human-comfort limits.
Use adaptation to preserve learning flexibility while preventing last-second, high-aggression maneuvers that inflate metrics.
infographic.impact: This matters because it makes reinforcement-learned driving policies more realistic, robust, and occupant-friendly. For practitioners, it improves the credibility of simulator results and reduces the risk of deploying policies that only look safe in simulation.
