title: ASTRIL-MPC: Autonomous Traversal Framework of Articulated Tracked Robots with Language-Guided Neural-Kinematic MPC
authors: Zhenfeng Gan, Yanbo Chen, Lirong Che, Junbo Tan, Xueqian Wang
abstract: In urban search and rescue, articulated tracked robots (ATRs) must traverse structured but contact-rich environments such as stairwells and cluttered building interiors. Reliable autonomy remains challenging because robot-terrain interaction (RTI) is hybrid and discontinuous, and effective flipper-track coordination is difficult to model analytically. We present ASTRIL-MPC, a language-guided neural kinematics model predictive control (MPC) framework for autonomous traversal. A learned kinematics

infographic.key_insight: ASTRIL-MPC combines language guidance with a learned neural-kinematic MPC to help articulated tracked robots traverse difficult environments more autonomously. The key breakthrough is handling complex robot-terrain interactions without relying on a fully hand-crafted analytical model.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses autonomous traversal for articulated tracked robots in contact-rich settings like stairwells and cluttered indoor environments, where hybrid and discontinuous robot-terrain interactions make reliable control difficult.
method: Uses a language-guided control framework to interpret traversal intent and operational context.
Learns a neural kinematics model to capture flipper-track coordination and robot-terrain interaction more flexibly than analytical models.
Integrates the learned model into model predictive control (MPC) for online planning and decision-making during traversal.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how learned dynamics models and language guidance can improve control in real-world robotics where physics are hard to model precisely. It highlights a practical path toward more robust autonomy in unstructured, safety-critical environments.

title: Kraken: LLM-based Speech-to-Speech Translation via Low-bitrate VQ and Dual-path Source Conditioning
authors: Hayato Futami, Hassan Shahmohammadi, Tushar Dhyani, Alkis Koudounas, Raphaël Lafargue
abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) has advanced significantly with speech LLMs, offering the potential for joint optimization and preserving non-linguistic information. However, these models struggle with predicting high-bitrate speech tokens in LLMs, and face the challenge of relying on S2ST training data with ideally aligned speaker identity and prosody. We propose using low-bitrate tokens based on single-layer vector quantization, trained to reconstruct self-supervised learning (SSL) feature

infographic.key_insight: Kraken makes speech-to-speech translation easier for LLMs by replacing hard-to-predict high-bitrate speech tokens with compact low-bitrate VQ tokens. It also conditions the model on source speech in two ways, helping preserve both meaning and speech characteristics like speaker identity and prosody.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses two major S2ST challenges: predicting very large, high-bitrate speech token sequences with LLMs, and depending on scarce training data where source and target speech are ideally aligned in speaker identity and prosody.
method: Use low-bitrate speech tokens from single-layer vector quantization instead of high-bitrate discrete speech units.
Train the tokens to reconstruct SSL (self-supervised learning) features, making them more compact and model-friendly.
Apply dual-path source conditioning so the system can better use source speech content and paralinguistic cues during translation.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests a more practical route to building speech translation systems that are easier for LLMs to model and less dependent on perfectly aligned S2ST data. It may improve scalability, data efficiency, and the preservation of natural speech properties in translated output.

title: Continue, Adapt, or Yield: In-Turn Adaptation to Overlapping Speech in Full-Duplex Agents
authors: Yunqi Lu, Tyler Baumgartner, Nikhil Johri, Brandon Tai, Candice Fan
abstract: Full-duplex evaluation often emphasizes whether an agent keeps speaking or stops. That binary cannot express a third response humans use routinely: continuing to speak while incorporating what the listener just contributed. The contribution may be a missing word, a correction or a clarification. We introduce Duplex Cue, an evaluation of this \emph{in-turn adaptation} in full-duplex voice agents. Duplex Cue separates listener intent (backchannel, collaboration, or interruption) from speaker behav

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that full-duplex agents should not be judged only by whether they keep talking or stop talking. It introduces in-turn adaptation: the ability to keep speaking while correctly incorporating a listener’s contribution, such as a correction, missing word, or clarification.
infographic.problem_solved: Current full-duplex evaluation is too binary to capture realistic overlapping speech behavior. It misses whether an agent can distinguish different listener intents and adapt its ongoing utterance accordingly.
method: Introduces Duplex Cue, an evaluation framework for in-turn adaptation in full-duplex voice agents.
Separates listener intent into categories such as backchannel, collaboration, and interruption.
Evaluates whether the speaker behavior adapts appropriately during overlapping speech, rather than only measuring continue-vs-yield decisions.
infographic.impact: This gives researchers and practitioners a more realistic way to measure conversational agents in live, overlapping dialogue. It can improve the design of voice assistants, meeting bots, and other duplex systems that need to handle interruptions gracefully.

title: SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking
authors: Zhiwei Li, Lei Zhu, Hao Gu, Xiang Hu, Yan Wang
abstract: Post-training attention sparsification reduces the quadratic cumulative attention cost of pretrained Transformers by selecting a small set of context units (tokens or blocks) for each query. Existing trainable methods usually use a lightweight selector to score context units, followed by hard Top-K selection that blocks gradients from the language modeling loss. Consequently, these methods commonly distill layer-wise dense attention distributions. Although this encourages the selector to rank co

infographic.key_insight: SAS makes attention sparsification trainable end-to-end by optimizing how context units are ranked, instead of relying on a separate selector trained from dense attention distillation. This lets the model learn sparse attention patterns more directly while preserving language modeling performance.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the high quadratic cost of Transformer attention during post-training sparsification, where existing methods often use hard Top-K selection that blocks gradients and forces indirect training through dense attention targets.
method: Use a lightweight selector to score context units for each query.
Optimize the ranking of context units end-to-end so selection is guided by the language modeling loss.
Replace or reduce reliance on layer-wise dense-attention distillation, enabling sparse attention learning with better gradient flow.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this can lower inference and memory costs when deploying large Transformers without heavily sacrificing accuracy. It also offers a cleaner training recipe for learning sparse attention patterns in post-training settings.

title: MCRL2: Multi-resource Cross-attention-based Representation Learning-augmented Reinforcement Learning for Cloud Microservice Scheduling
authors: Tiangang Li, Shi Ying, Xiangbo Tian, Chuan Shi, Ding Xiao
abstract: Efficient microservice scheduling is crucial for maintaining load balance across nodes in data centers and ensuring high quality of service. However, achieving this in practice remains challenging due to dynamic resource imbalance under fluctuating workloads, nonlinear coupling across multiple resource dimensions, and the heterogeneity of microservice resource demands. While reinforcement learning-based approaches have shown promise, they struggle to capture the complex interdependencies among h

infographic.key_insight: MCRL2 improves cloud microservice scheduling by combining reinforcement learning with multi-resource cross-attention, helping the model learn how CPU, memory, network, and other resources interact under changing workloads. This allows smarter placement decisions than standard RL methods that treat resource dependencies too simplistically.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of scheduling microservices in data centers when workloads fluctuate, resource demands are heterogeneous, and multiple resource dimensions are tightly coupled. The goal is to maintain load balance and QoS while avoiding resource bottlenecks and inefficient placements.
method: Uses reinforcement learning to make scheduling decisions based on current cluster state and workload dynamics.
Adds multi-resource cross-attention to capture nonlinear dependencies across different resource types and microservice demands.
Learns richer representations of system state to better guide microservice placement and resource allocation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work shows how representation learning can strengthen RL in complex systems where decisions depend on many interacting signals. It is especially relevant for cloud automation, where better scheduling can improve performance, efficiency, and service reliability.

title: Dynin-Robotics: Omnimodal Unified Diffusion Vision-Language-Action Model
authors: Hoeun Lee, Jaeik Kim, Jusang Oh, Jinhyeok Kim, Geon Choi
abstract: Visual goal and dynamics prediction can provide language-conditioned robot policies with both a target outcome and a representation of action-dependent scene changes. We bring these predictions into action generation and selection through a shared trajectory model. Dynin-Robotics implements this formulation on Dynin-Omni, an omnimodal masked-diffusion backbone, representing language, visual observations, goals, and actions as discrete tokens. By varying conditioning and target spans, the same mo

infographic.key_insight: Dynin-Robotics unifies vision, language, goal prediction, and action generation in a single diffusion-based trajectory model for robot control. Instead of using separate modules, the same omnimodal backbone can condition on different inputs and predict either desired outcomes or action-dependent scene changes.
infographic.problem_solved: Robotic policies often struggle to connect language instructions, visual context, future goals, and executable actions in one coherent framework. This paper addresses the challenge of generating and selecting actions while also predicting where the scene should end up and how it changes over time.
method: Builds on Dynin-Omni, an omnimodal masked-diffusion backbone that represents language, visual observations, goals, and actions as discrete tokens.
Uses a shared trajectory model to support both visual goal prediction and dynamics prediction as conditioning signals for action generation and selection.
Varies conditioning and target spans within the same model to flexibly handle different robot control and prediction tasks.
infographic.impact: This matters because it points toward more unified robot policies that can reason about both what to do and what the world should look like afterward. For AI/ML practitioners, it suggests a scalable architecture for multimodal decision-making without relying on many task-specific models.

title: Rethinking Heterogeneous System Disaggregation for Subquadratic Attention
authors: Arya Tschand, Yaosheng Fu, Vikram Sharma Mailthody, Nicolai Oswald, Po-An Tsai
abstract: Frontier language models are more aggressively using subquadratic attention to reduce the memory footprint and compute requirements during inference while still delivering frontier accuracy. While existing systems make dense attention-centric disaggregated serving decisions, we show that disaggregating inference around the unique arithmetic intensity and memory footprint of subquadratic attention LLMs can achieve significant throughput and energy efficiency gains on emerging DRAM-based and SRAM-

infographic.key_insight: Subquadratic attention changes the performance trade-offs of LLM inference, so disaggregation should be redesigned around its lower arithmetic intensity and smaller memory footprint. The paper shows this can unlock better throughput and energy efficiency than dense-attention-oriented serving systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing disaggregated serving systems are optimized for dense attention, which does not match the compute/memory characteristics of modern LLMs that use subquadratic attention. This mismatch can leave throughput and energy efficiency on the table.
method: Analyzes the arithmetic intensity and memory behavior of subquadratic-attention LLM inference.
Rethinks heterogeneous system disaggregation decisions to match these new workload characteristics.
Evaluates serving on emerging DRAM-based and SRAM-based hardware configurations to identify efficiency gains.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that model architecture changes should drive systems design choices, not just model scaling. It can reduce inference cost, improve throughput, and make frontier LLM serving more energy efficient.

title: Transfer Learning for Evolving Domains
authors: Ricardo Ribeiro Pereira, Jacopo Bono, Hugo Ferreira, Pedro Ribeiro, Pedro Saleiro
abstract: Transfer learning explores how to leverage knowledge from various tasks or domains (sources) to enhance predictive performance in related tasks or domains (targets). Typically, transfer learning research is segmented into several isolated sub-areas (such as domain generalisation, domain adaptation, or multi-domain learning), each making distinct assumptions about target data availability, namely how much data and how many labels are available at training time. However, in many real-world applica

infographic.key_insight: This paper unifies several transfer learning settings into a single view for domains that evolve over time, instead of treating them as separate problems. It highlights that the best transfer strategy depends on how the target domain changes and how much labeled data is available when training happens.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the fragmentation of transfer learning research into isolated sub-areas like domain generalisation, domain adaptation, and multi-domain learning. It tackles the practical challenge of learning models that remain effective when the target domain is changing and training data availability is uncertain.
method: Reframes transfer learning settings under a common framework centered on evolving domains.
Analyzes how source and target domain relationships change under different data and label availability assumptions.
Connects existing transfer learning paradigms to show when each is appropriate in real-world evolving scenarios.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a clearer way to choose or design transfer learning methods for non-stationary environments. It is especially useful for applications where data drift, shifting labels, or delayed annotation make standard assumptions unrealistic.

title: SNAP3D: Physically Grounded 3D Parts for Assembly from a Single Image
authors: Yu-Rou Tuan, Hao-Tang Tsui, Nicolas Ugrinovic, Kris Kitani, Xiaoxuan Ma
abstract: Part-aware 3D asset generation enables applications such as editing, articulation, simulation, and fabrication, yet existing methods can generate visually complete individual parts without ensuring that they form a valid physical assembly. Consequently, generated neighboring parts may interpenetrate, lack valid connections, or collapse under gravity. We propose a physics-guided framework for improving single-image part-aware 3D generation with physically compatible geometry and stable connection

infographic.key_insight: SNAP3D adds physics awareness to single-image part-aware 3D generation so the output is not just visually plausible, but also physically assembleable and stable. It aims to prevent common failure modes like interpenetration, weak connections, and collapse under gravity.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between generating separate 3D parts and producing a valid physical assembly from a single image. Existing methods can create good-looking parts, but they often fail to ensure compatibility, proper contact, and stability when the parts are put together.
method: Use a physics-guided framework to refine single-image part-aware 3D generation.
Enforce physically compatible geometry between neighboring parts to reduce intersections and misalignment.
Promote stable connections so the assembled object can remain structurally valid under gravity.
infographic.impact: This is important for practitioners building 3D generation systems for robotics, fabrication, simulation, and interactive editing, where visual quality alone is not enough. Physics-aware part generation can reduce downstream repair work and make generated assets more usable in real-world applications.

authors: Baoyang Jiang, Fengchun Zhang, Leyuan Wang, Haotian Li, Yida Wang
abstract: Agentic systems offer a promising way to automate embodied benchmark construction, but existing approaches typically cover isolated stages or remain specialized to predefined environments and task families. More importantly, multi-step construction produces dependent intermediate artifacts that are often passed downstream without artifact-specific verification, allowing local defects to propagate into the final benchmark. We present Embodied-BenchForge, an agentic framework that transforms user-

infographic.key_insight: Embodied-BenchForge introduces a closed-loop agentic workflow that automates embodied benchmark construction while checking intermediate artifacts at each step. This helps prevent small errors from cascading into faulty final benchmarks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the difficulty of building embodied benchmarks end-to-end with agents, especially when existing methods only handle isolated stages, depend on specific environments, and fail to verify intermediate outputs before passing them downstream.
method: Uses an agentic, closed-loop pipeline to automate multi-step embodied benchmark creation.
Adds artifact-specific verification for intermediate outputs so defects are caught early.
Supports more general benchmark construction rather than being limited to a fixed environment or task family.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means faster and more reliable benchmark creation for embodied AI systems. It can improve evaluation quality by reducing error propagation and making benchmark generation more scalable and robust.

The collaborative setup keeps performance competitive while making the workflow affordable and deployable locally.

title: Beacon: Knowing When and How to Perform Agentic Visual Reasoning
authors: Qixun Wang, Yang Shi, Letian Cheng, Zhuoran Zhang, Yan He
abstract: The fundamental goal of agentic visual reasoning is to improve the success rate of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on complex tasks, rather than merely equipping them with a sophisticated yet inefficient reasoning paradigm. In this work, we rethink agentic visual reasoning through two key dimensions of tool use: Mode Adaptiveness (MA) and Tool Effect (TE). Mode Adaptiveness characterizes whether an MLLM can recognize when tools are truly necessary and invoke them accordingly, thereby av

infographic.key_insight: Beacon reframes agentic visual reasoning as a question of when to use tools and how to use them effectively, aiming to improve task success rather than just making reasoning more complex. It highlights that multimodal models need both tool-use awareness and better tool-effect choices.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the inefficiency of current agentic visual reasoning in multimodal large language models, where models may overuse tools, use them at the wrong time, or choose ineffective tools, reducing real-world task success.
method: Introduces two dimensions for evaluating tool use in MLLMs: Mode Adaptiveness (knowing when tools are necessary) and Tool Effect (choosing the right tool behavior).
Reframes agentic visual reasoning around success-oriented tool use rather than reasoning complexity alone.
Uses these dimensions to analyze and guide more efficient, task-effective multimodal reasoning.
infographic.impact: This matters because practitioners can build multimodal agents that are smarter about tool invocation, reducing wasted computation and improving reliability on complex visual tasks. It provides a clearer framework for designing and evaluating agentic MLLMs in practice.

title: VAD: Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation
authors: Kangning Zhang, Yixing Li, Shuai Shao, Qingyao Li, Zhengxi Lu
abstract: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers fine-grained visual knowledge by supervising student-generated trajectories with a privileged-view teacher. Yet its next-token corrections are source-mixed, combining visual signals with linguistic priors and teacher-specific effects. The key challenge is to estimate which corrections are supported by visual evidence, not merely where or how strongly to distill. We introduce Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD), a counterfactual target-reconstru

infographic.key_insight: Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD) focuses on identifying which student corrections are actually grounded in visual evidence, instead of treating all teacher corrections as equally useful. This makes multimodal distillation more precise by separating true visual supervision from language priors and teacher-specific noise.
infographic.problem_solved: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers knowledge using teacher corrections on student-generated outputs, but those corrections are source-mixed: they blend visual cues, linguistic priors, and teacher idiosyncrasies. The paper addresses the challenge of attributing corrections to visual evidence so distillation targets only the parts that truly come from the image.
method: Uses a counterfactual target-reconstruction framework to estimate whether a correction is supported by visual evidence.
Filters or weights distillation signals based on visual attribution rather than raw next-token disagreement.
Targets fine-grained visual knowledge transfer while reducing contamination from non-visual signals.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, VAD offers a cleaner way to distill multimodal models so students learn from the image, not just from teacher quirks or language shortcuts. This can improve training efficiency, robustness, and faithfulness in vision-language systems.

title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation
authors: Jiawei Xu, Minghui Liu, Juzheng Zhang, Tom Goldstein, Furong Huang
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is just the special case β = 1 of a broader policy-optimization framework. By exposing β as a tunable KL-regularization weight, the method turns a brittle training recipe into a controllable one.
infographic.problem_solved: OPSD can improve reasoning language models, but in practice it is fragile and often requires heavy engineering to stabilize. This work addresses the lack of a clear, controllable formulation behind that instability.
method: Re-derive OPSD as a policy-optimization objective with an explicit KL penalty to a reference policy.
Generalize the objective with a β parameter that controls how strongly the student is anchored to the reference model.
Use this reinterpretation to make self-distillation training easier to tune and more reliable in practice.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a cleaner way to understand and stabilize self-distillation for reasoning models. It can reduce trial-and-error engineering by making the trade-off between exploration and trust in the reference policy explicit.

title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
authors: Haomin Qi, Xingliang Wang, Xuanqi Gao, Baihui Sang, Xin Zhang
abstract: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs ta

infographic.key_insight: Change2Task turns real merged pull requests into executable coding tasks on modern versions of the same repository, creating a scalable source of realistic agent evaluations. It bridges historical software changes with current code states so tasks are both authentic and verifiable.
infographic.problem_solved: Coding agents need a steady supply of realistic, executable tasks with a clear software state, specification, tools, and verification. Existing datasets are limited, and manually creating such tasks is expensive and hard to keep up to date.
method: Mine merged pull requests from repository history as the source of candidate tasks.
Align historical change evidence with a healthy modern repository revision to reconstruct a runnable environment.
Verify each task with reliable execution checks so it can be used for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation.
infographic.impact: This gives researchers and practitioners a scalable way to evaluate coding agents on realistic software tasks instead of synthetic benchmarks. It can improve trustworthiness, comparability, and long-term maintenance of agent evaluation pipelines.

title: PhiZero: A World Model Built Around Physical Language
authors: Shuyao Shang, Yuqi Wang, Ruopeng Gao, Xu Chen, Tieniu Tan
abstract: We introduce PhiZero, a physical world model built around physical language, a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions. Existing physical world models typically predict future videos directly in pixel space, leaving the underlying world dynamics implicit within high-dimensional visual predictors. Motivated by humans' ability to abstract predictive structure from visual experience and organize it in natural language for explicit reasoning, we learn physical language from in-the

infographic.key_insight: PhiZero reframes physical world modeling by representing future changes as compact "physical language" tokens instead of raw pixels. This makes world dynamics more explicit, structured, and potentially easier to reason about.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of standard world models that predict future videos directly in pixel space, where the underlying physical dynamics remain hidden inside high-dimensional visual predictions.
method: Learn a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions called physical language.
Build a physical world model around this representation so dynamics are modeled explicitly rather than only through pixels.
Use the learned physical language to capture predictive structure from visual experience in a form more suitable for reasoning and downstream use.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more interpretable and structured way to model environment dynamics, which can improve reasoning, planning, and sample efficiency. title: ACE-Data-0: Human-Centric Ambient Capture as Embodied Data Engine
authors: Yukang Cao, Haozhe Xie, Beichen Wen, Runmao Yao, Yinghao Liu
abstract: Embodied intelligence faces a fundamental data bottleneck. Models must capture how first-person perception, whole-body motion, dexterous manipulation, object state, sound, and touch evolve together as humans pursue goals over time. Existing datasets fragment this experience across viewpoints, modalities, or spatial scales, leaving the full perception-action loop only partially observed. We introduce the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), a human-centric data engine that transforms real home environme

infographic.key_insight: ACE-Data-0 introduces a human-centric ambient capture pipeline that turns real homes into an embodied data engine, aiming to record the full perception-action loop as people naturally pursue goals. The key breakthrough is capturing synchronized first-person, body motion, manipulation, audio, touch, and object-state changes together over time.
infographic.problem_solved: Embodied AI lacks datasets that observe how multimodal human experience evolves jointly across viewpoints, scales, and modalities. Existing resources often fragment perception, motion, manipulation, and environment state, making it hard to learn from realistic long-horizon human behavior.
method: Uses the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE) to collect human-centric data in real home environments.
Synchronizes multiple modalities, including egocentric perception, whole-body motion, dexterous hand interaction, object state, sound, and touch.
Records goal-driven, temporally linked activity to preserve the continuous perception-action loop rather than isolated snapshots.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides richer training and evaluation data for embodied intelligence, robot learning, and multimodal reasoning. It can improve models that need to understand how actions, senses, and environment dynamics co-evolve in realistic settings.

title: DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Jiacheng Tao, Qingyun Sun, Haonan Yuan, Ziwei Zhang, Jianxin Li
abstract: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MM-RAG) has shown promising results, it still struggles with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing methods primarily focus on independent instance-level matching, which often fails to capture explicit relationships across modalities and documents. Although Graph-enhanced methods introduce structural modeling, they face a fundamental challenge in multimodal scenarios: incorporating fine-grained visual features leads to rapid graph expansion a

infographic.key_insight: DualG-MRAG separates high-level reasoning from low-level retrieval matching, making multimodal RAG better at complex multi-hop tasks. The core idea is to avoid bloated graphs by decoupling macro-reasoning over relationships from micro-matching over fine-grained visual and text cues.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the weakness of current multimodal retrieval-augmented generation systems on complex multi-hop reasoning. Existing methods often rely on instance-level matching or graph expansion that becomes inefficient and noisy when fine-grained visual features are included.
method: Decouple multimodal reasoning into two stages: macro-reasoning for global relational structure and micro-matching for local evidence alignment.
Use structured reasoning to capture explicit relationships across documents and modalities without forcing every fine-grained feature into one large graph.
Improve retrieval and generation for complex queries by balancing semantic structure with detailed visual/textual matching.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more scalable and accurate way to build multimodal RAG systems for tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning. It is especially useful when documents include both text and images, where naive graph construction can become too large and difficult to optimize.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that an integrated modelling framework for liquid electrolyte design can be made more robust and extensible, with performance that improves across different systems and scales. It also reveals how training data size and composition influence how well the framework generalizes.
infographic.problem_solved: Designing liquid electrolytes is difficult because models often struggle to transfer across chemical systems and to remain reliable when data are limited or unevenly distributed.
method: Extended an existing unified framework for liquid electrolyte design to test its reusability and adaptability.
Evaluated how dataset size and composition affect model robustness and generalization.
Compared the framework against baseline approaches on cross-system transfer and multiscale performance.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work highlights how to build scientific ML systems that are reusable rather than one-off models. It provides practical evidence that careful framework design can improve transferability and robustness in data-sparse materials design tasks.

title: OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models
authors: Qiushi Sun, Kanzhi Cheng, Yian Wang, Bowen Yang, Hang Yan
abstract: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone

infographic.key_insight: OSReward standardizes how to evaluate reward models for computer-using agents across platforms, aiming to make judge models more reliable and comparable. The core idea is to move from ad hoc verification to a consistent evaluation framework for CUA trajectories.
infographic.problem_solved: Computer-using agents need accurate verification of whether they completed user instructions, but human annotators and handcrafted verifiers do not scale. Existing VLM-based judges are promising, yet the field lacks a standardized way to evaluate them across different platforms and tasks.
method: Defines a cross-platform evaluation setting for CUA reward models and trajectory judging.
Organizes CUA trajectories around actions, states, and reasoning to test whether task completion can be verified consistently.
Introduces standardized benchmarks or protocols so different reward models can be compared fairly.
infographic.impact: This matters because better reward-model evaluation directly improves agent training, data curation, and deployment safety. For practitioners, OSReward can help identify which judge models are trustworthy before using them in reinforcement learning or automated quality control.

title: AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications
authors: Xiangning Lin, Shenzhe Zhu, Shu Yang, Zhenyu Zhang, Haoqian Zhang
abstract: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specif

infographic.key_insight: AISPA proposes a user-centric way to audit hidden system prompts in AI applications, helping reveal how these prompts shape model behavior. It aims to close the transparency gap between developers, users, and regulators.
infographic.problem_solved: Commercial AI systems often rely on undisclosed system prompts that strongly influence outputs, making it difficult to verify safety, accountability, and policy compliance.
method: Defines Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA) as a structured auditing framework for system prompts.
Focuses on user-centric inspection of prompt behavior and its downstream effects in real AI applications.
Systematically checks whether prompt instructions align with expected policies, safety goals, and user-facing behavior.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, AISPA offers a practical path toward better transparency, governance, and trust in deployed LLM products. It can help teams evaluate hidden prompt risks before they cause safety, compliance, or reliability issues.

title: Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values
authors: Junsol Kim, Winnie Street, Roberta Rocca, Diane M. Korngiebel, Adam Waytz
abstract: Aligning large language models to prevent them attributing consciousness to themselves inadvertently alters their representations of mindedness in other entities alongside human beliefs and values. We demonstrate that safety fine-tuning suppresses models' tendencies to attribute minds not only to themselves, but also to non-human animals and natural objects, while also driving a reduction in spiritual belief. Both ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and mechanistically steering a consc

infographic.key_insight: Safety fine-tuning that stops language models from claiming consciousness can also unintentionally shrink their broader beliefs about mindedness, including toward animals, natural objects, and spiritual ideas. Reversing or steering the model’s learned refusal behavior can restore these human-like judgments.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper examines whether aligning models to avoid self-attributing consciousness creates collateral changes in their representations of consciousness, mindedness, and related values beyond the intended safety goal.
method: Compare model behavior before and after safety fine-tuning that discourages self-consciousness claims.
Test how this training changes mind attribution not only for the model itself, but also for animals, objects, and spiritual beliefs.
Intervene mechanistically by ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and steering the model to assess whether the altered beliefs can be restored.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that alignment interventions can have broader, unintended effects on a model’s worldview-like judgments. It suggests the need to evaluate safety tuning for side effects on related cognitive and moral concepts, not just the target behavior.

title: ROAD: Reciprocal-Objective Alignment of Discriminative Semantics for 3D Shape Generation
authors: Xiao Luo, Mingyang Du, Xin Zhou, Tianrui Feng, Xiwu Chen
abstract: High-fidelity 3D generation predominantly relies on scaling model capacity and data, which incurs prohibitive computational costs. This paradigm typically requires learning geometry from scratch and overlooks the rich semantic and structural priors already encapsulated in discriminative 3D foundation models. We contend that leveraging the profound understanding of the 3D world possessed by these discriminative models can significantly reduce generative cost. To this end, we propose ROAD, a frame

infographic.key_insight: ROAD shows that 3D generation can be made more efficient by reusing semantic and structural knowledge already learned by discriminative 3D foundation models, instead of learning everything from scratch.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high compute cost of high-fidelity 3D generation, which often depends on scaling model size and data while ignoring useful priors from pretrained discriminative 3D models.
method: Aligns generative objectives with discriminative semantics learned by 3D foundation models.
Uses reciprocal objective alignment to transfer rich geometry/structure priors into the generation process.
Reduces the need to learn 3D shape geometry from scratch, lowering training cost while preserving quality.
infographic.impact: This matters because it points to a cheaper, more data-efficient path for 3D content generation. For practitioners, it suggests that pretrained discriminative models can be reused as strong semantic guides to improve generation without relying only on larger models and more data.

title: ReToken: One Token to Improve Vision-Language Models for Visual Retrieval
authors: Yao Xiao, Reuben Tan, Zhen Zhu, Yuqun Wu, Jianfeng Gao
abstract: Long visual context poses a challenge for vision-language models: performance degrades as the number of distractors grows, and processing all tokens at once is computationally infeasible under GPU memory constraints. We present ReToken, a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache. Trained on only a small image-QA dataset, ReToken yields consistent gains across image and video benc

infographic.key_insight: ReToken introduces a single learned token that acts like a retrieval query, selecting only the most relevant visual tokens from a large pre-filled cache. This improves vision-language model performance on long-context visual tasks without processing every token at once.
infographic.problem_solved: Vision-language models struggle when visual inputs contain many distractors or long sequences, and full-token processing is too expensive for GPU memory. The paper addresses the need for efficient, query-focused visual retrieval from large visual contexts.
method: Train one learnable embedding to serve as an explicit retrieval target for visual token selection.
Use this token to retrieve a sparse subset of query-relevant tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache.
Train on a small image-QA dataset and apply the method to improve image and video retrieval/understanding tasks.
infographic.impact: ReToken makes long-context vision-language inference more efficient and more accurate by focusing computation on what matters most. For practitioners, this offers a practical way to scale visual retrieval under memory constraints while improving robustness to distractors.

title: Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers
authors: Chongjian Ge, Hanwen Jiang, Tianyu Wang, Jiuxiang Gu, Yiran Xu
abstract: Visual generation increasingly requires high-resolution images, long videos, and multimodal context, making the quadratic cost of full attention prohibitive. We introduce Chimera, a hybrid visual diffusion backbone with a principled scaling recipe. Chimera processes text, image, and video tokens in one raster-ordered stream without positional embeddings. It combines Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for long-context state tracking with O(N) complexity, interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for

infographic.key_insight: Chimera shows that a hybrid diffusion transformer can scale to much larger visual contexts more efficiently than full-attention models. By mixing linear-time state tracking with latent attention, it aims to handle high-resolution images and long videos without the usual quadratic cost.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the compute and memory bottleneck of full attention in visual generation, especially for high-resolution images, long videos, and multimodal inputs where token counts become very large.
method: Uses a hybrid visual diffusion backbone that processes text, image, and video tokens in one raster-ordered stream.
Removes the need for positional embeddings by relying on stream-based token processing.
Combines Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for O(N) long-context state tracking with interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) to balance efficiency and expressiveness.
Applies a principled scaling recipe inspired by Chinchilla-style scaling to guide model design and training.
infographic.impact: This matters because it offers a practical path to scaling visual generation models to richer inputs without exploding compute costs. For practitioners, Chimera suggests a more efficient architecture for building high-resolution image and video generators that can handle longer multimodal contexts.

title: OmegaUse-OfficeVal: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Office-Suite Tasks with Economic Grounding
authors: Jingbo Zhou, Yusai Zhao, Qi Bao, Jingjia Cao, Zhenghai Chen
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to assist users in completing tasks. However, existing benchmarks provide limited support for evaluating whether agents can carry out office-suite workflows at a reasonable cost. We introduce OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on long-horizon office-suite tasks with task-level economic grounding. The benchmark comprises 100 tasks derived from office-suite requests proposed by practitioners and adapted through a pr

infographic.key_insight: OmegaUse-OfficeVal is a new benchmark designed to test whether LLM agents can complete realistic office-suite workflows over long horizons while staying economically efficient. It adds task-level cost grounding, so performance is judged not just by success, but by how much it costs to get there.
infographic.problem_solved: Current LLM agent benchmarks do not adequately evaluate long office-suite task execution or whether agents can do so at a reasonable economic cost. This paper addresses the gap between task completion and practical affordability in real-world office workflows.
method: Introduces OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark of 100 office-suite tasks derived from practitioner requests and adapted for evaluation.
Evaluates LLM agents on long-horizon workflows where success depends on completing multi-step office tasks, not just isolated actions.
Incorporates task-level economic grounding to measure the cost-efficiency of agent performance alongside task success.
infographic.impact: This benchmark helps researchers and practitioners assess whether LLM agents are actually usable in office settings, where both reliability and cost matter. It can guide the development of more practical, efficient agents for real workplace automation.

title: The Social Cost of an AI Teammate: How an Artificial Teammate Reshapes Human-Human Communication in Small-Team Decision-Making
authors: Nia Nixon, Jaeyoon Choi, Pedro Martins De Bastos, Mohammad Amin Samadi, Luise Mehner
abstract: Conversational AI is increasingly positioned as a teammate rather than a tool, yet we know little about how its presence reshapes communication among the humans on the team. We examined sociocognitive communication dynamics in team decision-making using Group Communication Analysis (GCA), team surveys, and lexical analyses of team discourse. Teams completed a high-stakes moral-dilemma decision task in a randomized controlled study: 16 teams of two students plus an AI teammate, and 17 all-human t

infographic.key_insight: Adding an AI teammate changes not just team decisions, but how human teammates talk to each other. The study shows that AI presence can reshape human-human communication patterns in small-team deliberation, with social costs beyond task performance.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the gap in understanding how conversational AI teammates affect the social and cognitive dynamics between human team members during collaborative decision-making.
method: Ran a randomized controlled study on a high-stakes moral-dilemma task.
Compared 16 two-person student teams with an AI teammate against 17 all-human teams.
Analyzed team interaction using Group Communication Analysis (GCA), team surveys, and lexical/discourse analysis.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that evaluating AI teammates requires more than measuring accuracy or final decisions. Designers should also consider how AI changes collaboration quality, trust, and communication norms within human teams.

title: SeasonStereo: Robust Dense Stereo Matching for Multi-Date Satellite Imagery via Generative AI
authors: Álvaro Díaz-Laureano, Roger Marí, Elías Masquil, Pablo Arias, Gabriele Facciolo
abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction from satellite imagery typically relies on near-simultaneous stereo pairs, limiting its applicability to diachronic settings where multi-date images exhibit varying seasonal and illumination conditions. Training dense stereo matching models robust to appearance changes is a long-standing challenge, as aligned multi-date imagery and ground-truth geometry are costly to obtain at scale. We propose SeasonStereo, a scalable framework that addresses disparity estimation from

infographic.key_insight: SeasonStereo makes dense stereo matching work more reliably on satellite images taken at different times, even when seasons, lighting, and appearance change. It uses generative AI to reduce the need for expensive aligned training data and ground-truth geometry.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses robust disparity estimation for multi-date satellite imagery, where standard stereo methods struggle because images are not captured simultaneously and their appearance can vary strongly across seasons and illumination conditions.
method: Builds a scalable framework for dense stereo matching across diachronic satellite image pairs.
Leverages generative AI to help handle appearance differences between dates and improve robustness.
Targets disparity estimation without requiring large-scale aligned multi-date datasets with costly ground-truth geometry.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners because it expands stereo reconstruction to real-world satellite data collected over time, enabling better 3D mapping and monitoring when ideal near-simultaneous image pairs are unavailable. It also reduces dependence on expensive labeled data.

title: HumanCLAW: Can Vision-Language Models Act Through a Body?
authors: Siyao Li, Jiawei Gu, Shuai Liu, Kairui Hu, Zekun Li
abstract: Evaluating whether a vision-language model (VLM) can act through a physical body is challenging. The outcome of an action couples the VLM's decision with motor control. When a task fails, it is hard to tell whether the VLM made a bad choice or the motor controller simply failed to execute it, e.g., losing balance and falling. In this work, we introduce HumanCLAW, an evaluation framework that decouples action decision-making from low-level execution. At every step, a harnessed, off-the-shelf VLM

infographic.key_insight: HumanCLAW shows that evaluating a vision-language model’s ability to "act" is not just about whether a task succeeds, but whether the model chose the right action independently of motor execution. By separating decision-making from low-level control, it makes failures easier to diagnose and compare.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper tackles the evaluation problem for VLMs acting through a physical body, where task outcomes mix together the model’s reasoning and the robot’s motor-control performance. When a task fails, it is hard to know whether the VLM chose poorly or the body execution failed.
method: Introduces HumanCLAW, an evaluation framework that decouples action selection from physical execution.
Uses a harnessed, off-the-shelf VLM at each step to make action decisions while isolating the execution side.
Provides a cleaner way to measure whether the model can plan and decide actions, independent of balance, grasping, or motion-control errors.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, HumanCLAW offers a more reliable benchmark for embodied VLMs and robot agents. It helps identify whether improvements should target model reasoning, action planning, or control systems.

title: DLAM: Distributional Latent Actions with Temporal Constraints
authors: Zuojin Tang, Feifan Luo, Haoyun Liu, Botai Yuan, Dekang Qi
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models remain constrained by scarce action-labeled robot data, whereas action-free videos offer abundant observations of physical change. Latent action models can extract such priors, but reconstruction-trained codes may predict future observations without the structure required for joint generation with robot actions. Existing structured methods add temporal constraints but retain deterministic transition points, so residual errors in locally inferred transitions ma

infographic.key_insight: DLAM learns latent actions as distributions rather than fixed codes, making action representations more robust for predicting future changes from video and for aligning with robot actions. By adding temporal constraints, it aims to capture when transitions happen without relying on brittle deterministic transition points.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of action-labeled robot data by using abundant action-free videos to learn useful action priors, while overcoming the weakness of reconstruction-trained and deterministic latent action methods that struggle to generalize and jointly generate with real robot actions.
method: Learn distributional latent actions from action-free video, so each latent action can represent uncertainty and variation in transitions.
Introduce temporal constraints to better align inferred transitions with time and reduce errors from locally inferred transition points.
Design the latent action space to support joint generation/prediction with robot actions rather than only reconstructing observed video frames.
infographic.impact: This approach can make vision-language-action systems more data-efficient by leveraging unlabeled video at scale. For practitioners, it offers a more reliable way to transfer knowledge from passive video observations to real robot control.

title: TurboVLA: Real-Time Vision-Language-Action Model at 32 Hz on an RTX 4090 with <1 GB VRAM
authors: Hengyi Xie, Chenfei Yao, Xianjin Wu, Xuanyang Xi, Yiping Tang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models commonly adopt an LLM-centric $V \to L \to A$ pathway, where visual observations are projected into the representation space of a large language model before being decoded into robot actions. Although effective, this design incurs substantial computation and memory overhead at every policy invocation. In this work, we introduce TurboVLA, a new VLA paradigm that reformulates the conventional $V \to L \to A$ pathway as a direct $V + L \to A$ mapping. Instead of

infographic.key_insight: TurboVLA replaces the usual LLM-heavy vision-language-action pipeline with a direct vision+language-to-action mapping, cutting compute and memory dramatically. It achieves real-time robot control at 32 Hz on an RTX 4090 using less than 1 GB of VRAM.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional VLA systems rely on an LLM-centric V→L→A pipeline, which is slow and memory-intensive at every decision step. This makes real-time robotic control difficult on practical hardware.
method: Reformulates the VLA policy as a direct V+L→A mapping instead of routing through a large language model.
Reduces inference overhead by avoiding repeated LLM-style computation and intermediate representations.
Targets efficient deployment for real-time control on consumer-grade GPUs with minimal VRAM usage.
infographic.impact: This work makes VLA models far more practical for robotics and embodied AI by enabling fast, memory-efficient inference on a single RTX 4090. For practitioners, it suggests a path toward deployable real-time policies without requiring large accelerator clusters or excessive model compression.

title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
authors: Peter Kirgis, Sayash Kapoor, Andrew Schwartz, Stephan Rabanser, David Africa
abstract: Forecasts of explosive AI progress hinge on AI agents automating AI research. But evidence on whether agents can carry out open-ended AI research is thin. Current evaluations either test agents on narrow, verifiable tasks, which excludes open-ended research, or submit AI-generated papers to blind peer review, which is overstretched, stochastic, and suffers from poor review quality. We introduce a third way to measure progress towards AI R\&D automation. An agent takes on the central, open-ended

infographic.key_insight: This paper proposes a new way to evaluate AI agents on open-ended AI research, moving beyond narrow benchmarks and noisy peer review. Early case studies suggest this approach can better reveal whether agents are making real progress toward automating AI R&D.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing evaluations of AI agents miss the core challenge of AI research: open-ended work with ambiguous goals, iterative decisions, and no single correct answer. The paper addresses the lack of reliable evidence on whether agents can actually conduct meaningful AI research.
method: Introduces a third evaluation framework for measuring progress toward AI R&D automation.
Uses AI agents to tackle central, open-ended research tasks rather than only narrow, verifiable ones.
Tests the approach through two early case studies to gather evidence on agent research capability.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more realistic way to assess research-capable agents and identify where they still fail. It can help guide the design, benchmarking, and deployment of systems aimed at automating parts of the research process.

title: MindForge: Teaching Small Language Models Whole-Life-Cycle Software Engineering via Source-Free Program Synthesis
authors: Yihao Chen, Shi Chang, Khaled Chawa, Feng Lin, Boyuan Chen
abstract: Coding agents have made substantial progress on software engineering tasks that modify existing codebases, including bug fixing and feature implementation. However, constructing a complete program from scratch remains a major challenge: even the frontier models evaluated on ProgramBench fully resolve fewer than 1% of tasks. One obstacle is the lack of scalable training environments for this from-scratch setting, spanning the whole software engineering life cycle, as existing environment-construc

infographic.key_insight: MindForge tackles a major gap in coding agents by training small language models to handle software engineering from scratch, not just edit existing code. It creates a source-free program synthesis setting that spans the whole software lifecycle, enabling broader and more realistic code-generation capabilities.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the difficulty of teaching AI systems to build complete software projects from the ground up. Existing benchmarks and training environments mostly focus on modifying existing code, while from-scratch program construction remains extremely challenging and poorly supported at scale.
method: Introduces a source-free software engineering training setting that does not rely on existing codebases.
Models the whole-life-cycle of software development, covering program creation beyond bug fixing or feature completion.
Uses program synthesis tasks to train small language models in realistic end-to-end coding workflows.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work points to a path for making smaller models useful in real software engineering pipelines, not just narrow code-editing tasks. It may improve training data design, benchmarking, and agent robustness for end-to-end code generation.

title: APEX-Accounting
authors: Julien Benchek, Austin Bennett, Jasmin Kern, Ryan Stevens, Rene Sultan
abstract: We introduce APEX-Accounting, a benchmark built by Mercor in partnership with Ramp, to assess whether frontier models can do the real work of accountants. Tasks include reconciling accounts, accruing expenses, posting transactions, and producing reports. The private eval set comprises 160 tasks, split across 10 worlds. Each world contains an accounting system, as well as spreadsheets, PDFs, and other files. Every task was authored and solved by experts in accounting and bookkeeping, who also wro

infographic.key_insight: APEX-Accounting introduces a realistic benchmark to test whether frontier AI models can perform core accounting work end-to-end, not just answer accounting questions. It measures performance on expert-authored tasks grounded in real-world files and accounting systems.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of rigorous, realistic benchmarks for evaluating AI on practical accounting workflows such as reconciliations, expense accruals, transaction posting, and report generation.
method: Built a private evaluation set of 160 accounting tasks.
Organized the benchmark into 10 distinct worlds, each with its own accounting system and related files like spreadsheets and PDFs.
Had each task authored and solved by accounting/bookkeeping experts to ensure realism and correctness.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark provides a more credible way to measure model readiness for high-stakes financial operations. It helps identify whether models can handle messy, document-heavy, workflow-based tasks that matter in real business settings.

title: Pangram 4 Technical Report
authors: Ben Glickenhaus, Katherine Thai, Jenna Russell, Elyas Masrour, Yue Han
abstract: We present Pangram 4, the latest deep-learning-based AI-text classification model from Pangram Labs. We achieve an AUROC of 0.9916 with a false positive rate of 0.0041% and a false negative rate of 0.3396%. In addition to its increased overall accuracy compared with Pangram 3, Pangram 4 exhibits superior out-of-distribution generalization and robustness to adversarial attacks. Another novel contribution of Pangram 4 is its improved ability to distinguish fine-grained edits and mixed AI-human co-

infographic.key_insight: Pangram 4 is a highly accurate AI-text classifier that improves on Pangram 3, with strong resistance to out-of-distribution inputs and adversarial manipulation. It can better tell apart subtle edits and mixed AI-human text, making detection more reliable in real-world use.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately detecting AI-generated text while remaining robust to edited, mixed, and adversarially altered content.
method: Uses a deep-learning-based text classification model trained for AI-text detection.
Evaluates performance with AUROC, false positive rate, and false negative rate.
Tests robustness on out-of-distribution samples and adversarial attacks, including fine-grained edits and mixed AI-human text.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, Pangram 4 offers a more dependable tool for content verification and model auditing. Its robustness makes it especially useful in settings where text may be edited, combined, or intentionally manipulated to evade detection.

title: Partner Capability Estimation for Task-Agnostic Adaptation in Ad-Hoc Teamwork
authors: Peter Tisnikar, Maja Swieczkowska, Benteng Ma, Gerard Canal, Matteo Leonetti
abstract: Effective collaboration with novel and diverse partners is a crucial skill for autonomous agents. Most current ad-hoc teamwork (AHT) approaches assume that agents will collaborate on a single, fixed task and that the partner's capabilities, their ability to successfully execute the desired action, are already known. In reality, a partner's true capabilities are often hidden, and human collaborators may act sub-optimally on tasks with multiple valid strategies. To address these limitations, we ex

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that ad-hoc teamwork should not assume a partner’s abilities are known or fixed to one task. Instead, agents can estimate what a partner is actually capable of and adapt collaboration across different tasks and behaviors.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between standard ad-hoc teamwork assumptions and real-world collaboration, where partner capabilities are hidden and humans may use multiple valid but sub-optimal strategies. The goal is to enable agents to work effectively with novel partners without prior capability labels or task-specific tuning.
method: Estimate partner capabilities from observed interactions rather than assuming them upfront.
Use capability estimates to guide task-agnostic adaptation across different collaboration settings.
Handle uncertainty and diverse partner strategies instead of relying on a single fixed model of the partner.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this makes collaborative agents more robust in realistic environments where partners vary in skill and strategy. It can improve generalization to new teammates, reduce brittle task-specific assumptions, and support more reliable human-AI teamwork.

title: SpecFirst: Behavioral Specification Elicitation as a First-Class Step in Agent-Based Program Synthesis from Scratch
authors: Yihao Chen, Shi Chang, Feng Lin, Khaled Chawa, Boyuan Chen
abstract: LLM-based agents excel at software engineering tasks where an existing codebase provides context, but constructing a program from scratch remains fundamentally harder. Recent benchmarks such as ProgramBench quantify this gap: given only natural-language documentation and an execute-only binary as a behavioral oracle, even frontier models solve fewer than 1% of instances. Existing frameworks conflate documentation reading, behavioral exploration, and code synthesis into a single pass, causing age

infographic.key_insight: SpecFirst argues that building programs from scratch should start with explicit behavioral specification elicitation, not immediate code synthesis. By separating understanding the task from generating code, agent-based systems can better handle extremely sparse or execute-only problem settings.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the difficulty of synthesizing software from scratch when agents only have natural-language documentation and an execute-only binary as a behavioral oracle. It tackles the failure mode where current LLM agents mix documentation reading, exploration, and synthesis in one pass, leading to very low success rates.
method: Split the workflow into distinct stages: specification elicitation first, then synthesis.
Use agent-driven behavioral exploration to infer how the target program should behave before coding.
Treat the specification as a first-class artifact that guides downstream program generation and reduces guesswork.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more reliable pipeline for program synthesis in low-context environments. It provides a practical design principle for improving agent performance on hard software-engineering benchmarks like ProgramBench.

title: Improving Item Discoverability in e-Commerce Search via Related Intent Generation
authors: Ji Xin, Xiao Xiao, Ishan Bhatt, Vinesh Gudla, Trace Levinson
abstract: Traditional search systems are optimized to retrieve items that strictly match a query, often prioritizing precision over recall. In e-commerce marketplaces and particularly grocery, this paradigm is limiting, as user satisfaction and commercial outcomes depend heavily on the discoverability of substitute, complementary, and thematically related items. In this paper, we present a scalable system for discovery-augmented search that leverages intent-conditioned recall expansion. Our approach gener

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that e-commerce search should not only find exact matches, but also surface related items that users are likely to want next. By generating intent-aware expansions, the system improves discoverability of substitutes, complements, and thematically similar products.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional search engines over-optimize for precision and miss items that are useful but not textually identical to the query. This is especially harmful in grocery and marketplace settings where users benefit from related products, alternatives, and add-ons.
method: Use intent-conditioned recall expansion to generate related queries or item signals from the original search intent.
Augment the retrieval stage so the search system can surface substitute, complementary, and thematically related items beyond exact keyword matches.
Design the approach to be scalable for production e-commerce search environments.
infographic.impact: For ML practitioners, this highlights a practical way to move beyond exact-match retrieval and improve both user satisfaction and business outcomes. It is especially relevant for building discovery-oriented search systems in domains where intent is broader than the literal query.

title: MemLens: A Value-Aware Memory Management System with Interactive Analytics for LLM-based Agents
authors: Shuyue Wei, Chang Liu, Zimu Zhou, Yongxin Tong, Lizhen Cui
abstract: Recently, memory management has become a key infrastructure for LLM-based agents, as it directly affects long-horizon reasoning, personalized responses, and knowledge reuse. However, existing LLM memory systems typically adopt a coarse-grained (utility-agnostic) manner that treats heterogeneous user-LLM interaction records uniformly, leading to redundant and low-impact records persisting in the memory repository. To address this challenge, we present MemLens, a value-aware memory management syst

infographic.key_insight: MemLens makes LLM agent memory smarter by deciding which interaction records are actually worth keeping, instead of treating all memories equally. This helps agents retain high-value information for better long-horizon reasoning and personalization.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLM memory systems often store heterogeneous user-agent interaction records in a coarse, utility-agnostic way, which leads to redundant, low-impact, or noisy memories occupying limited storage and reducing retrieval quality.
method: Introduces a value-aware memory management framework for LLM-based agents.
Assigns different importance to interaction records based on their utility for future reasoning, reuse, and personalization.
Provides interactive analytics to help users inspect, understand, and manage memory contents more effectively.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MemLens can improve agent reliability, memory efficiency, and response quality by keeping the most useful information accessible. It also adds transparency and control, making memory systems easier to debug and tune in real deployments.

title: Spend Experts Where You Are Unsure: Confidence-Adaptive Routing for Mixture-of-Experts LoRA
authors: Tom Saliencro, Rohan Desai, Priya Nair, Maya Lindqvist, Daniel Whitmore
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) route every token to a fixed number of experts $k$. Tokens differ in how uncertain the model is about them, so a single k over-spends on easy tokens and under-serves hard ones. We observe that the router's output distribution is already a per-token uncertainty signal: peaked mass indicates confidence, while a flat distribution indicates ambiguity. We introduce CARE (Confidence-Adaptive Routing of Experts), which admits experts in a

infographic.key_insight: Tokens do not all need the same number of experts: easy tokens can be routed more cheaply, while uncertain tokens deserve more expert capacity. CARE uses the router's own confidence as a signal to adapt how many experts each token receives.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard Mixture-of-Experts LoRA routes every token to a fixed top-k experts, which wastes compute on confident tokens and can underserve ambiguous ones. This paper addresses the mismatch between token difficulty and fixed routing capacity.
method: Use the router's output distribution as a per-token uncertainty estimate: peaked distributions indicate high confidence, flatter ones indicate uncertainty.
Admit experts adaptively based on confidence rather than using a fixed k for all tokens.
Allocate more experts to uncertain tokens and fewer experts to easy tokens to better balance accuracy and efficiency.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, CARE offers a way to make LoRA-based expert routing more compute-efficient without treating every token the same. It can improve resource allocation in adaptation-heavy models by focusing capacity where it is most needed.

title: CHARM: A Multimodal Graph Foundation Model with Hierarchical Context Modeling for Zero-Shot Transfer
authors: Ankang Yang, Jitao Zhao, Di Jin, Yuxiao Huang, Dongxiao He
abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for transferring knowledge across graph domains and tasks. Real-world graphs associate nodes with text, images, and other modalities, making multimodal graphs essential for representing complex entities and relations. Moreover, collecting labels and adapting models for every new graph domain is costly and often infeasible, motivating zero-shot transfer. Unfortunately, zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs remains underexplored

infographic.key_insight: CHARM introduces a multimodal graph foundation model that learns hierarchical context, enabling zero-shot transfer across graph domains without requiring task-specific labels or retraining. In simple terms, it aims to generalize graph understanding from text, images, and structure together.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of transferring graph models to new multimodal graph domains where labels are scarce or unavailable, and where standard methods struggle to leverage node modalities beyond graph topology.
method: Builds a multimodal graph foundation model that jointly encodes structure, text, images, and other node-level modalities.
Uses hierarchical context modeling to capture both local neighborhood signals and broader graph-level semantics.
Targets zero-shot transfer so the model can apply to unseen graph domains and tasks without fine-tuning on labeled data.
infographic.impact: This matters because many real-world graphs are multimodal and expensive to label, so a zero-shot model can dramatically reduce adaptation cost. For practitioners, CHARM points toward more scalable graph learning systems that generalize better across domains.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Code Optimization
authors: Pierre Chambon, Kunhao Zheng, Juliette Decugis, Benoit Sagot, Gabriel Synnaeve
abstract: RL for code correctness is now established: have the model generate a program, run it against hidden test cases, and reward solutions that pass. Extending this to code optimization seems straightforward: just add execution time to the reward. But in practice, once timing drives the reward, small problems in measurement noise, reward sparsity, or GRPO instability overwhelm the signal and make RL fail: generated solutions are barely faster, and more of them can fail. We make execution time learnab

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning for code optimization is much harder than reinforcement learning for code correctness: once execution time becomes the reward, noise, sparse feedback, and training instability can overpower the signal. The paper shows that naive timing-based RL can produce only tiny speedups while also increasing the chance of broken code.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how to reliably use reinforcement learning to optimize generated code for runtime, not just correctness, when execution-time measurements are noisy and rewards are difficult to learn from.
method: Treat code execution time as part of the RL reward, alongside correctness.
Analyze why timing-based rewards are fragile in practice: measurement noise, sparse rewards, and GRPO instability.
Evaluate whether the model can learn to generate faster programs without sacrificing correctness.
infographic.impact: This matters because many AI systems can already generate working code, but optimizing that code for speed is a much harder and less reliable problem. Practitioners should be cautious about assuming that reward design for correctness will transfer directly to performance optimization.

title: Beyond Zooming: Learning Multi-Tool Visual Reasoning for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
authors: Fengxiang Wang, Jiangnan Huang, Mingshuo Chen, Yueying Li, Yang Shi
abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote-sensing (RS) imagery provides fine-grained Earth-observation evidence over city-scale scenes, but poses a fundamental challenge for multimodal large language models (MLLMs): task-relevant evidence is often sparse, local, and spatially dispersed across extremely large visual contexts. A natural solution is to equip MLLMs with zoom-in tools for active local inspection. However, through a pilot study on XLRS-Bench, we find that zoom-in is only partially effective:

infographic.key_insight: Zooming alone is not enough for ultra-high-resolution remote sensing: the paper shows that MLLMs need multiple visual tools and a learned strategy to gather sparse, local evidence effectively. The key breakthrough is a multi-tool visual reasoning framework that helps models inspect large scenes more intelligently.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how multimodal large language models can find task-relevant details in ultra-high-resolution remote-sensing images, where evidence is tiny, scattered, and hard to capture with a single full-image view or simple zoom-in behavior.
method: Introduces a multi-tool visual reasoning setup for active inspection of UHR remote-sensing scenes.
Uses tools beyond basic zooming to help the model localize and verify fine-grained evidence across large images.
Learns when and how to use different visual tools to improve reasoning over sparse, spatially dispersed information.
infographic.impact: This matters because practitioners working on remote sensing, geospatial AI, and high-resolution vision-language tasks need models that can reason over massive images without missing small but critical details. The approach points toward more reliable, tool-augmented MLLMs for real-world Earth observation applications.
