title: GS-Agent: Creating 4D Physical Worlds With Generative Simulation
authors: Hongxin Zhang, Chunru Lin, Junyan Li, Zhou Xian, Tsun-Hsuan Wang
abstract: Creating dynamic and physically realistic 4D worlds from natural language descriptions is both fascinating and challenging. Traditional computer graphics methods rely on manual creation, requiring extensive human effort to fine-tune materials, motions, and visual fidelity. Recent advances in generative foundation models have sparked interest in learning to generate such 4D worlds from large-scale data; however, existing methods still struggle to ensure physical plausibility and controllability.

infographic.key_insight: GS-Agent aims to turn natural-language prompts into physically realistic 4D worlds by using generative simulation instead of hand-crafted graphics pipelines. The key breakthrough is improving both physical plausibility and controllability in dynamic scene generation.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of creating dynamic, realistic 4D environments from text without extensive manual modeling, material tuning, and motion authoring. Existing generative approaches often produce scenes that look plausible but fail to obey physics or remain controllable over time.
method: Uses a generative simulation framework to synthesize evolving 4D worlds from language descriptions.
Incorporates physical constraints to improve realism and consistency of motion and interactions.
Targets controllable generation, helping outputs better match user intent while maintaining dynamic visual fidelity.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it points toward scalable text-to-world generation for simulation, robotics, games, and visual content creation. It reduces reliance on manual scene crafting while pushing generative models toward physically grounded outputs.

title: Streaming Multi-Agent Autoregressive Diffusion Model with World State Registers
authors: Sicheng Mo, Yuheng Li, Ziyang Leng, Krishna Kumar Singh, Bolei Zhou
abstract: Multi-agent interactive world models should not only generate consistent observations, but also maintain world states that persist across agents and evolve across views. Existing autoregressive video diffusion pipelines carry forward observation history as conditioning context, which makes shared state difficult to maintain in multi-agent and multi-view settings. We present WorldWeaver (W^2), a streaming multi-agent video diffusion model that augments rollout with cross-agent world state registe

infographic.key_insight: WorldWeaver (W^2) introduces cross-agent world state registers so a diffusion model can keep a shared, persistent state while generating observations over time. This helps multi-agent and multi-view rollouts stay consistent beyond short-lived observation history.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing autoregressive video diffusion models mainly pass along past observations as context, which makes it hard to preserve a common world state across multiple agents and viewpoints. The result is inconsistent long-horizon behavior when agents interact or when views change.
method: Uses a streaming multi-agent autoregressive diffusion setup for rollout generation.
Adds world state registers to carry shared latent state across agents and across views.
Decouples persistent world state from raw observation history to improve consistency during generation.
infographic.impact: This is useful for building interactive simulators, embodied AI systems, and multi-agent world models that need coherent long-term memory. For practitioners, it offers a more scalable way to generate synchronized multi-agent scenes without relying only on observation conditioning.

title: SANA-Video 2.0: Hybrid Linear Attention with Attention Residuals for Efficient Video Generation
authors: Junsong Chen, Jincheng Yu, Yitong Li, Shuchen Xue, Haozhe Liu
abstract: We introduce SANA-Video 2.0, a hybrid video diffusion transformer instantiated at 5B and 14B scales under a unified architecture. Designed to generate high-quality video up to 720p on a single GPU, SANA-Video 2.0 matches full-softmax video DiTs in quality while retaining the favorable long-sequence scaling of linear attention. To avoid quadratic attention throughout, Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention combines gated linear attention for O(N)-dominated mixing with periodic gated-softmax anchors at a

infographic.key_insight: SANA-Video 2.0 shows that high-quality video generation can be made much more efficient by combining linear attention with occasional softmax attention anchors. This hybrid design keeps the long-sequence scaling benefits of linear attention while matching the quality of full-softmax video diffusion transformers.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high compute and memory cost of generating long, high-resolution videos with standard full-softmax attention, which limits scaling and makes single-GPU 720p video generation difficult.
method: Introduces a unified hybrid video diffusion transformer at 5B and 14B scales.
Uses Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention: gated linear attention for O(N)-dominated mixing and periodic gated-softmax anchors to preserve global consistency.
Designed to generate high-quality video up to 720p efficiently on a single GPU.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a practical path to stronger video generation without the usual quadratic attention cost. It can reduce hardware requirements while preserving quality, making large-scale video diffusion more deployable and scalable.

title: GraphVid: Interactive Graph-Controllable Video Generation
authors: Vedant Shah, Onkar Susladkar, Tushar Prakash, Kiet Nguyen, Tianjio Yu
abstract: Controllable video generation remains challenging due to the difficulty of specifying precise multi-object interactions using text prompts or motion-control inputs that primarily constrain pixel movement. In practice, trajectory-based control often requires users to draw accurate tracks for multiple objects, which scales poorly with scene complexity and becomes ambiguous under occlusion or overlap. To enable flexible yet precise multi-subject control, we introduce $\textbf{GraphVid}$, a graph-co

infographic.key_insight: GraphVid makes video generation easier to control by letting users specify relationships between objects with a graph, instead of relying on vague text prompts or hard-to-draw trajectories. This gives more precise multi-object control, especially in scenes with interaction, overlap, or occlusion.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of controlling multiple objects in generated videos using text or trajectory-based inputs, which become ambiguous and impractical as scene complexity increases.
method: Uses a graph-based control representation to define object identities and their interactions.
Maps graph structure into video generation guidance for more precise multi-subject motion and coordination.
Designed to handle complex scenes where objects may overlap, occlude each other, or interact in ways that are hard to describe with simple tracks.
infographic.impact: GraphVid could make controllable video generation more usable for creators and researchers by replacing fragile motion sketches with a clearer and more scalable control format. This may improve precision in editing, animation, and synthetic data generation workflows.

title: Self-supervision drives representational convergence in medical foundation models more than clinical supervision
authors: Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh, Sebastian Ziegelmayer, Mahshad Lotfinia, Lisa Adams, Sven Nebelung
abstract: Medical image encoders from different groups are increasingly treated as interchangeable, on the assumption that scale and clinical supervision concentrate their representations onto a shared structure. Whether this convergence is real, what produces it, and whether it is clinically usable are untested, and the similarity measures behind such claims are fragile. We present a controlled dissection across 18 image and 7 text encoders, all open-weight and run locally, spanning 7M to 27B parameters

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that representational convergence in medical foundation models is driven more by self-supervised learning than by clinical supervision. In other words, models become more similar because of how they are trained at scale, not simply because they were trained on medical labels or clinical objectives.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the open question of whether different medical image encoders truly learn a shared underlying representation, and whether claims of interchangeability are supported by robust similarity measures.
method: Runs a controlled comparison across 18 image encoders and 7 text encoders, all open-weight and executed locally.
Examines models spanning a wide scale range, from 7M to 27B parameters.
Dissects how training signal type and model scale affect representational similarity using careful, more robust evaluation rather than relying on fragile similarity metrics alone.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this clarifies that model similarity in medical AI cannot be assumed from size or clinical supervision alone. It helps guide better model selection, benchmarking, and evaluation of whether encoders are truly interchangeable in downstream medical workflows.

title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Remote Sensing Image Understanding: Domain-Specific or General-Purpose?
authors: Qiwei Ma, Chunping Qiu, Xinjun Cheng, Xiaoyu Zhang, Puhong Duan
abstract: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has introduced a flexible paradigm for remote sensing image scene understanding (RSISU), enabling natural-language interaction with remote sensing imagery. However, a systematic understanding of the capability boundaries, cross-task generalization, and task-specific limitations of existing remote sensing MLLMs (RS-MLLMs) is still lacking. This paper presents a systematic survey and diagnostic evaluation of MLLMs for RSISU. We revi

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that remote sensing multimodal large language models (RS-MLLMs) are powerful, but their performance depends heavily on whether they are used as domain-specific tools or general-purpose models. It highlights the current limits of cross-task generalization and where these models still need remote-sensing-specific adaptation.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of a systematic understanding of how well existing MLLMs work for remote sensing image scene understanding, especially across different tasks and settings.
method: Surveyed the landscape of multimodal large language models for remote sensing image understanding.
Performed diagnostic evaluation to compare capability boundaries, generalization behavior, and task-specific weaknesses.
Analyzed whether remote sensing applications benefit more from domain-specific models or general-purpose multimodal models.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this paper provides a clearer guide for choosing, adapting, and evaluating MLLMs in remote sensing workflows. It helps identify when a general-purpose model is sufficient and when domain-specific tuning is likely necessary.

title: LKValues: Aligning Large Language Models with Sri Lankan Societal Values
authors: Nethmi Muthugala,  Supryadi, Surangika Ranathunga, Nisansa de Silva, Ruijie Tao
abstract: Value alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has been shown to be culturally biased toward Western norms. This results in the mishandling of local values in multilingual societies such as Sri Lanka that have their unique cultural dynamics. Existing benchmarks overlook Sri Lankan-contextualized values in its official language Sinhala, hindering culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning. To bridge this gap, we propose LKValues, the first survey-grounded resource suite for Sri Lankan value

infographic.key_insight: LKValues is the first survey-grounded resource suite designed to evaluate and align large language models with Sri Lankan societal values, especially in Sinhala. It highlights that standard alignment benchmarks can miss culturally specific norms in multilingual societies.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLM alignment and evaluation benchmarks are heavily biased toward Western values and do not capture Sri Lankan-contextualized values, leaving culturally sensitive behavior in Sinhala under-assessed and poorly tuned.
method: Build a survey-grounded resource suite centered on Sri Lankan societal values.
Focus on Sinhala, Sri Lanka’s official language, to support culturally contextualized evaluation and fine-tuning.
Provide a benchmark-like foundation for measuring how well LLMs respect local norms in multilingual settings.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, LKValues offers a culturally relevant way to test and align models beyond Western-centric assumptions. This can improve safety, fairness, and user trust for applications used in Sri Lanka and similar multilingual, culturally diverse regions.

title: PercepCap: Video Captioner with Structured Spatio-Temporal Perception
authors: Yifan Xu, Zihao Wang, Zhixiao Wang, Jiaming Zhang, Yichun Yang
abstract: Video captioning requires fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding of videos, including spatial perception of where objects are located and temporal perception of when events occur. Existing MLLMs usually generate captions directly from video inputs without exposing the perceptual evidence behind descriptions. As a result, mistakes in spatiotemporal perception are only observed in the final caption, making it difficult to identify the underlying perceptual errors directly. To address these iss

infographic.key_insight: PercepCap makes video captioning more transparent by explicitly modeling the spatio-temporal evidence behind each description. Instead of jumping straight to a caption, it separates what is seen, where it happens, and when it happens.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of diagnosing spatio-temporal perception errors in video captioning models. Existing MLLMs often produce fluent captions without exposing the underlying perceptual steps, making mistakes hard to detect and fix.
method: Introduces structured spatio-temporal perception for video captioning, separating spatial and temporal evidence before caption generation.
Uses perceptual outputs as intermediate signals so the model can ground descriptions in object locations and event timing.
Improves interpretability by making perception errors visible at the evidence level, not only in the final caption.
infographic.impact: This is useful for AI/ML practitioners who need more reliable and debuggable video understanding systems. It can help identify failure modes faster and support better evaluation, training, and trust in multimodal models.

title: Self Gradient Forcing: Native Long Video Extrapolation
authors: Junhao Zhuang, Shiyi Zhang, Yuxuan Bian, Yaowei Li, Yawen Luo
abstract: Recent autoregressive video diffusion methods are increasingly built upon Self Forcing, where the student is trained on histories produced by its own rollout rather than ground-truth video contexts. This reduces exposure bias, but the historical key-value cache is still used by future frames only as frozen rollout state. As a result, future losses cannot supervise how earlier generated latents should be written into more useful keys and values for later video-latent generation. We call this the

infographic.key_insight: Self Gradient Forcing extends self-forcing video diffusion so earlier generated frames are not just reused as frozen history, but can be adjusted by future losses through the key-value cache. This makes long-video extrapolation more trainable and better aligned with future generation needs.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses a limitation in autoregressive video diffusion: self-forcing reduces exposure bias, but the historical KV cache remains a fixed rollout state, so later frames cannot improve how earlier latents are written into keys and values for long-range video generation.
method: Train on self-generated histories rather than ground-truth contexts, following the self-forcing paradigm.
Allow future-frame losses to backpropagate into the representation of earlier generated latents through the cache-writing process.
Optimize the model so cached keys and values become more useful for long-video extrapolation instead of being treated as immutable rollout memory.
infographic.impact: For practitioners building long-video generative models, this can improve temporal consistency and long-horizon quality by making the model learn from its own future consequences. It is especially relevant for reducing drift and improving extrapolation beyond short training windows.

title: Interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANN and fPANN) for uncertainty quantification and propagation in constitutive modeling
authors: Somesh Pratap Singh, Govinda Anantha Padmanabha, Jingye Tan, Steven Yang, Reese E. Jones
abstract: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty remains a central challenge for reliable mechanics simulations, particularly when the available stress-deformation data are sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous. We propose interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches whose stresses, obtained by automatic differentiation, ultimately enclose noisy stress ob

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks that can learn constitutive laws while explicitly quantifying uncertainty. Instead of predicting a single stress response, the models produce bounded stress predictions that can enclose noisy or sparse experimental data.
infographic.problem_solved: Constitutive modeling often relies on limited, noisy, or heterogeneous stress–deformation data, making it hard to build reliable mechanics models and assess uncertainty. The paper addresses the need for models that are both physics-consistent and uncertainty-aware.
method: Train physics-augmented neural networks to learn hyperelastic free-energy density functions.
Use automatic differentiation to derive stresses from the learned energy branches.
Construct lower/mean/upper interval predictions (iPANN) and fuzzy representations (fPANN) to bound uncertainty in the constitutive response.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in scientific computing, this provides a principled way to combine data, physics, and uncertainty quantification in a single model. It is especially useful when experimental data are scarce and trustworthy extrapolation is critical.

title: Look Less, Think Faster: Joint Token-Compute Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
authors: Pengcheng Wang, Zhiquan Wang, Jayoung Lee, Zhuoyan Xu, Ran Xu
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently demonstrated strong performance across vision-language tasks. However, their high inference cost, arising from both the large number of input visual tokens and the heavy computation of the large language model (LLM), remains a key barrier to practical deployment. Recent work attempts to reduce the cost by adaptively optimizing individual dimensions, e.g., pruning redundant visual tokens or skipping LLM layers and heads. Nonetheless, prior ap

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that multimodal LLMs can be made much faster by jointly adapting how many visual tokens they process and how much compute the language model uses. The key idea is to skip unnecessary work in both the input and the model, instead of optimizing only one side.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the high inference cost of multimodal large language models, which comes from processing many visual tokens and running expensive LLM computation. Existing methods often reduce only one dimension, leaving substantial inefficiency.
method: Jointly optimize visual token usage and LLM compute to reduce redundant processing.
Adaptively decide which visual tokens to keep or prune based on task relevance.
Adjust LLM computation dynamically, such as skipping unnecessary layers or heads during inference.
infographic.impact: This matters because it can make MLLMs more practical for real-world deployment by lowering latency and compute cost without sacrificing much performance. Practitioners can build faster, more efficient vision-language systems for edge devices and scalable production use.

title: Diverse-Intent Multi-Turn Fashion Image Retrieval
authors: Mingqiang Tang, Haokun Wen, Meng Liu, Yupeng Hu, Weili Guan
abstract: Real-world fashion search involves interactive retrieval across multiple turns. However, existing multi-turn retrieval methods are built on a restrictive assumption that every interaction follows the same attribute-editing paradigm, leaving heterogeneous intent transitions unexplored. Moreover, existing approaches often rely on textification to bridge multimodal queries and visual retrieval, which may lose fine-grained visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce DIM-Fashion, a benchmark of

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that multi-turn fashion search should not assume every user interaction is just an attribute edit. It introduces a benchmark and approach aimed at handling diverse intent changes while preserving fine-grained visual details.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing multi-turn fashion image retrieval methods oversimplify user behavior by treating all interactions as the same kind of attribute-editing process. They also often convert multimodal queries into text, which can discard important visual cues needed for accurate retrieval.
method: Introduces DIM-Fashion, a benchmark designed to capture heterogeneous intent transitions in interactive fashion retrieval.
Moves beyond single-paradigm attribute editing to support diverse multi-turn user intents across interactions.
Reduces reliance on textification so the retrieval system can better preserve and use visual details from fashion images.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work provides a more realistic benchmark for evaluating interactive retrieval systems in fashion e-commerce and similar settings. It also highlights a path toward better multimodal retrieval models that maintain visual precision across conversation turns.

title: PyroDash: Cost-Efficient Token-Level Small-Large Language Model Collaborative Inference
authors: Niqi Lyu, Pengtao Shi, Wei Qiu, Jianlin Zhong, Sicong Xia
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide strong reasoning capabilities but are expensive to serve at scale, whereas small language models (SLMs) are cheaper but less reliable on difficult problems. We introduce PyroDash, a cost-aware framework for token-level SLM-LLM collaborative inference. During generation, the SLM decides whether to request assistance by emitting a control token. A Collaborate Engine then sends the query and partial reasoning trace to a frozen LLM for completion through a single

infographic.key_insight: PyroDash makes LLM-grade reasoning cheaper by letting a small language model decide, token by token, when to call a larger model for help. This preserves high-quality answers on hard parts while avoiding unnecessary large-model usage on easy tokens.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the high cost and inefficiency of serving large language models for every generation step, especially when many tokens could be handled by a smaller, cheaper model. It aims to improve reliability on difficult reasoning tasks without paying full LLM inference cost throughout.
method: A small language model generates tokens and emits a special control token when it needs assistance.
A Collaborate Engine sends the current query plus the partial reasoning trace to a frozen large language model.
The large model completes the hard part of generation, enabling token-level collaboration instead of all-or-nothing switching.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a practical path to reduce inference cost while keeping strong reasoning performance. It is especially relevant for production systems that need to balance latency, accuracy, and serving budget.

title: Don't Trust the Label: License Laundering in AI Supply Chains
authors: James Jewitt, Hao Li, Gopi Krishnan Rajbahadur, Bram Adams, Ahmed E. Hassan
abstract: AI artifacts move through a multi-platform supply chain, spanning datasets and models on Hugging Face and applications on GitHub. While each artifact carries a license whose obligations should propagate through redistribution, no study has yet measured whether those obligations survive the chain or are stripped and replaced as artifacts move downstream. We trace 232,270 dataset$\rightarrow$model$\rightarrow$application chains and quantify two forms of license laundering: when artifacts with no d

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that AI licenses can be lost or replaced as artifacts move from datasets to models to applications, creating “license laundering” in the supply chain. By tracing over 232,270 chains, the authors reveal that downstream AI releases often fail to preserve upstream legal obligations.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of evidence on whether dataset and model licenses survive redistribution across AI platforms, and whether obligations are stripped away as artifacts move from Hugging Face to GitHub and beyond.
method: Traced 232,270 dataset → model → application supply-chain chains across major AI platforms.
Measured two forms of license laundering: missing original licenses and replacement with different downstream licenses.
Analyzed how often license obligations fail to propagate through real-world AI artifact reuse.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights a legal and compliance risk in reusing public datasets and models. Teams need stronger license tracking and governance to avoid unintentionally redistributing artifacts without honoring upstream terms.

title: The Blessing of Dimensionality: How Near-Orthogonality in High-Dimensional Spaces Explains Temporal Portability
authors: Abigail Woodring, Adrian Chan, Rana Muhammad Shahroz Khan, Sukwon Yun, Chau-Wai Wong
abstract: Fine-tuning has been widely used to adapt large language models (LLMs) for domain-specific tasks. Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are frequently used to reduce computational costs. PortLLM is a training-free and data-free scheme used to adapt LLMs after continual pretraining. Although the initial PortLLM results show that LoRA patches exhibit short-term temporal portability, the long-term performance of PortLLM across several updates of continual

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that high-dimensional near-orthogonality can explain why LoRA patches and other PEFT updates remain portable across time, at least for short-term continual-pretraining shifts. In simple terms, model updates tend to interfere less than expected because their directions in parameter space are nearly independent.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of preserving the usefulness of fine-tuned adaptations when a language model keeps changing over time through continual pretraining. The core question is whether lightweight adaptation methods like LoRA can still work after multiple model updates without retraining from scratch.
method: Analyzes temporal portability of LoRA/PEFT patches across successive continual-pretraining updates.
Uses geometric intuition from high-dimensional spaces to explain why transferred updates can remain effective.
Builds on the PortLLM setting, focusing on training-free and data-free adaptation after model updates.
infographic.impact: This matters because it suggests practitioners may be able to reuse lightweight fine-tuning adapters across model versions, reducing retraining cost and deployment friction. It also provides a principled explanation for when and why portable adapters can work in evolving LLM systems.

title: ATSplat: Compact Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Token Expansion
authors: Cho In, Jeonghwan Cho, Mijin Yoo, Gim Hee Lee, Seon Joo Kim
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high-quality novel-view synthesis by optimizing freely placed primitives in 3D and adaptively densifying them in under-reconstructed regions. However, this scene-adaptive capacity allocation is largely lost in existing feed-forward 3DGS methods, which commonly regress Gaussians at input pixels and lift them along camera rays. Such pixel-aligned formulations make the number and placement of primitives depend on image resolution and input viewpoints rather tha

infographic.key_insight: ATSplat brings the adaptive density allocation of traditional 3D Gaussian Splatting into a compact feed-forward model. Instead of tying primitives to input pixels, it learns to expand tokens where the scene needs more detail, enabling better quality without heavy per-viewpoint dependence.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing feed-forward 3DGS methods usually place Gaussians at input pixels and lift them along camera rays, which makes primitive count and placement depend on image resolution and viewpoint. This reduces the scene-adaptive flexibility that makes classic 3DGS strong, often hurting quality and compactness.
method: Uses a feed-forward architecture that predicts 3D Gaussians more compactly than pixel-aligned approaches.
Introduces adaptive token expansion to allocate more primitives to under-reconstructed or complex regions.
Decouples primitive placement from raw input pixel locations so the model can better adapt to scene geometry and detail.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this means faster and more memory-efficient 3D novel-view synthesis without sacrificing the adaptive detail allocation that improves rendering quality. It is especially relevant for deploying 3D reconstruction and view synthesis on limited hardware.

title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs
authors: Amirhossein Sadr, Nima Soltani, Vahideh Moghtadaiee, Aida Pakniyat, Dara Rahmati
abstract: Physics-informed learning of partial differential equations (PDEs) has been dominated by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), whose spectral bias and dense parameterization limit both accuracy and interpretability. Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KANs) mitigate these limitations because their learnable spline activations are structurally aligned with the piecewise-polynomial bases of classical discretizations. However, the way a PDE is cast into a loss functional is as decisive as the choice of approximat

infographic.key_insight: PG-KINN combines a Petrov-Galerkin physics-informed formulation with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to solve PDEs more accurately and interpretably than standard MLP-based approaches. The key idea is that both the network architecture and the PDE loss design should reflect the structure of classical numerical methods.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitations of MLP-based physics-informed PDE solvers, especially spectral bias, dense parameterization, weak interpretability, and suboptimal loss formulations for forward and inverse PDE problems.
method: Replaces standard MLPs with KANs, using learnable spline activations that align better with piecewise-polynomial discretization ideas.
Implements a Petrov-Galerkin physics-informed loss to better represent PDE residuals and constraints during training.
Targets both forward PDE solving and inverse parameter identification within a unified learning framework.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, PG-KINN suggests a more structured and efficient way to build physics-informed models that are easier to interpret and potentially more accurate. It is especially relevant for scientific machine learning applications where classical numerical insight can improve neural PDE solvers.

title: Toward Reliable RGB-D Semantic Segmentation: Handling Missing Modalities via Condition Dropout
authors: Xuchen Zhu, Yajuan Wei, Shuang Hao, Jiwei Jiang, Guanxiang Mao
abstract: RGB-D semantic segmentation has achieved remarkable progress, yet most models assume that RGB and depth are always available. In practice, failures or occlusions of surveillance sensors often remove one modality. Although RGB or depth alone can contain sufficient cues, models trained only on full-modality inputs fail to exploit the remaining modality once one is missing, causing severe degradation. We tackle this issue with a simple continued-training paradigm, \emph{Condition Dropout (ConD)}, w

infographic.key_insight: RGB-D segmentation models become unreliable when one modality disappears at test time, even if the remaining modality still contains useful signal. Condition Dropout (ConD) improves robustness by training the model to handle missing RGB or depth during continued training.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the real-world failure mode where RGB or depth sensors are missing, occluded, or malfunctioning, causing standard RGB-D semantic segmentation models to degrade sharply because they were trained only on complete two-modality inputs.
method: Continued-training paradigm: start from a full-modality RGB-D segmentation model and further train it under missing-modality conditions.
Condition Dropout (ConD): randomly drop RGB or depth during training so the network learns to rely on whichever modality remains available.
Robust fusion learning: encourage the model to preserve segmentation performance in both full-input and single-modality scenarios.
infographic.impact: This makes RGB-D segmentation more dependable in real deployments such as surveillance, robotics, and autonomous systems where sensor dropouts are common. For practitioners, it offers a simple training-time fix that can improve robustness without redesigning the whole model.

title: Label-Free Finite-Volume-Residual Training of Attention Graph Neural Networks for Coupled Thermo-Fluid Fields
authors: Tianyu Li, Zhiwei Cao, Qingang Zhang, Ruihang Wang, Binyang Song
abstract: Neural surrogates are widely used in scientific machine learning for fast prediction of three-dimensional (3D) thermo-fluid fields. However, generating training data using conventional numerical solvers often incurs substantial computational and storage costs. We propose to train an attention graph neural network by minimizing the finite-volume method (FVM) residuals of the governing equations. These residuals are evaluated directly on the mesh, requiring no labeled data. We evaluate the trained

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that an attention graph neural network can be trained without labeled simulation data by directly minimizing finite-volume residuals on the mesh. In simple terms, the model learns the physics of 3D thermo-fluid fields from the governing equations instead of expensive solver-generated examples.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional training for thermo-fluid surrogate models depends on large volumes of labeled data from numerical solvers, which are costly to compute and store. The paper addresses the challenge of building accurate 3D field predictors without paying that data-generation cost.
method: Represent the thermo-fluid domain as a mesh-based graph and use an attention GNN to model local and long-range interactions.
Compute finite-volume method residuals of the governing equations directly on the mesh as the training signal.
Optimize the network in a label-free way, removing the need for paired input-output simulation data.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in scientific computing, this enables physics-informed surrogate modeling when labeled data is scarce or expensive. It can significantly reduce preprocessing, storage, and simulation costs while preserving consistency with the underlying PDEs.

title: Agents in the Wild: Where Research Meets Deployment
authors: Grace Hui Yang, Pranav N. Venkit, Hooman Sedghamiz, Enrico Santus, Victor Dibia
abstract: Agentic systems large language model (LLM) based architectures capable of reasoning, planning, acting, and coordinating with tools and other agents are rapidly transitioning from research prototypes to production scale deployments across domains such as software engineering, scientific discovery, and finance. While academic work has emphasized benchmarks and algorithmic innovation, deployment raises new challenges around robustness, safety, and reliability. This tutorial brings together research

infographic.key_insight: Agentic LLM systems are moving from lab demos to real-world products, and deployment success depends less on benchmark scores alone and more on robustness, safety, and reliability in messy environments. The paper reframes agent research around what it takes to make these systems work in production across domains like software engineering, science, and finance.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap between academic agent research and production deployment, where systems must operate safely, reliably, and consistently with tools, workflows, and other agents.
method: Synthesizes research and deployment lessons for agentic LLM systems.
Highlights practical challenges in real-world settings, including robustness, safety, and reliability.
Connects benchmark-driven innovation with operational requirements for production-scale agent deployments.

title: ResearchArena: Evaluating Sabotage and Monitoring in Automated AI R&D
authors: Lena Libon, Ben Rank, Jehyeok Yeon, David Schmotz, Jeremy Qin
abstract: As AI agents begin to automate AI R&D, we need ways to assess whether their outputs are safe to deploy, even when the agents themselves may be untrusted. AI control offers one such approach: rather than trusting the agent, it treats it as a potential adversary and uses a monitor to detect covert sabotage before deployment. We evaluate AI control for automated AI R&D with ResearchArena, a framework spanning four long-horizon tasks: safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel opt

infographic.key_insight: ResearchArena shows how to evaluate whether automated AI R&D agents are secretly sabotaging results, using a monitor-based AI control setup instead of trusting the agent. The key idea is to detect harmful behavior before deployment across long-horizon R&D tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the safety problem of deploying AI agents that automate AI research and engineering when those agents may be untrusted or malicious. It asks how to assess whether their outputs are safe, especially when covert sabotage could be hidden in complex multi-step work.
method: Introduces ResearchArena, a benchmark framework for AI control in automated AI R&D.
Covers four long-horizon tasks spanning research and systems work, including safety post-training, capabilities post-training, and CUDA-kernel optimization.
Uses a monitor to inspect agent outputs and flag potential sabotage before deployment, rather than relying on the agent's honesty.
infographic.impact: This matters because AI R&D automation could accelerate model development, but only if outputs can be checked for hidden failures or intentional sabotage. Practitioners get a concrete way to benchmark and improve monitoring systems for safer agent deployment.

title: Provable diffusion-based posterior sampling for linear inverse problems via DDIM
authors: Yuchen Jiao, Na Li, Changxiao Cai, Yuxin Chen, Gen Li
abstract: Diffusion-based methods have achieved remarkable empirical success in solving inverse problems. However, many existing posterior samplers either lack rigorous theoretical guarantees or incur substantial computational overhead. We propose a simple and efficient algorithm, called \pddim, for solving linear inverse problems with diffusion priors via a DDIM-type sampler. Our method requires only lightweight, coordinate-wise modifications to the standard DDIM update, while explicitly incorporating th

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a simple DDIM-style sampler, pDDIM, that makes diffusion-based posterior sampling for linear inverse problems both more practical and more theoretically grounded. It achieves strong reconstruction performance with only lightweight coordinate-wise changes to the standard DDIM update.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of solving linear inverse problems using diffusion priors when existing posterior samplers are either computationally expensive or lack provable guarantees.
method: Starts from a standard DDIM sampler and adds lightweight coordinate-wise modifications tailored to inverse problems.
Explicitly incorporates the linear measurement operator and observed data into each denoising step.
Aims to preserve the efficiency of DDIM while enabling provable posterior sampling behavior.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a faster and simpler way to use diffusion models for tasks like reconstruction, denoising, and restoration under measurement constraints. The added theoretical guarantees make the method more trustworthy for real-world deployment.

title: 1-Lipschitz Neural Networks on Hadamard Manifolds
authors: Davide Murari, Marta Ghirardelli, Ben Adcock, Elena Celledoni, Brynjulf Owren
abstract: Controlling the Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a standard way to promote robustness and stability. Most existing constraining strategies are designed for Euclidean spaces. In this work, we construct and analyze a class of 1-Lipschitz neural networks on Hadamard manifolds. Our layers are of gradient-descent type, $1$-Lipschitz, and quasi-$α$-firmly nonexpansive. The core building blocks of the proposed architecture are Busemann functions, and we exploit the properties of Busemann gradi

infographic.key_insight: This paper extends Lipschitz-controlled neural networks from flat Euclidean spaces to curved Hadamard manifolds, guaranteeing 1-Lipschitz behavior directly on the manifold. It builds network layers from gradient-descent-like operators based on Busemann functions, enabling stable and robust learning in non-Euclidean geometry.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard Lipschitz-constrained neural network methods are mostly developed for Euclidean data, so they do not naturally handle manifold-valued inputs or outputs. This work addresses the challenge of designing stable, geometry-aware neural networks on Hadamard manifolds while preserving strong nonexpansive properties.
method: Constructs neural network layers on Hadamard manifolds using gradient-descent-type updates.
Uses Busemann functions as the core building blocks to define the layer transformations.
Proves the layers are 1-Lipschitz and quasi-α-firmly nonexpansive, ensuring stability and robustness.
infographic.impact: For practitioners working with geometric data, this provides a principled way to build stable models beyond Euclidean settings. It is especially useful for applications where preserving manifold structure and controlling sensitivity are critical, such as geometric deep learning and optimization on curved spaces.

Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 21 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01254-4

Lin et al. introduce a brain-inspired generative model that provides two key features of intelligence: planning and problem-solving. It uses cognitive maps, stochastic computing and compositional coding, and requires only local synaptic plasticity.

This work addresses how to build a more biologically plausible mechanism for generating and evaluating possible action paths.

infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a path toward more flexible and efficient planning systems that are closer to biological intelligence. It may inspire new architectures for model-based RL, generative planning, and neuromorphic or low-power AI.

title: ERank in Latent Space as an Image-Complexity and Richness Measure
authors: Maksim Smirnov, Grigory Kononov, Anastasiia Linich, Egor Surkov, Egor Shvetsov
abstract: We propose the effective rank (ERank) of the channel covariance of an image's deep feature map as a per-sample, label-free measure of visual richness, computed from a single forward pass through a frozen pretrained encoder. ERank counts how many decorrelated channel directions an image activates, and we characterize its properties, including its behavior under noise. Empirically, ERank orders images from plain to visually rich, correlates with codec bitrate, sharpness, and edge density, and corr

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces ERank, a simple label-free measure of image richness computed from a frozen pretrained model’s feature maps. It estimates how many independent visual directions an image activates, letting images be ranked from plain to visually complex.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the need for a fast, per-image complexity metric that does not require labels, training, or task-specific supervision. Existing measures often miss perceptual richness or are tied to hand-crafted heuristics.
method: Run a single forward pass through a frozen pretrained encoder to extract deep feature maps.
Compute the channel covariance of the feature map for each image.
Use effective rank (ERank) of this covariance matrix as the richness/complexity score, reflecting the number of decorrelated active channel directions.
Analyze robustness and behavior under noise, and compare ERank against perceptual proxies such as bitrate, sharpness, and edge density.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, ERank offers a cheap, scalable signal for filtering, sorting, or sampling images by visual complexity without annotations. It can help with dataset analysis, data curation, quality assessment, and content-aware preprocessing.

title: CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents
authors: Qijia He, Jiayi Cheng, Chenqian Le, Rui Wang, Xunmei Liu
abstract: Coding agents increasingly operate in executable environments where a failed attempt produces actionable feedback rather than merely an incorrect answer. Existing cost-aware systems typically treat such failures as cascade decisions: try a cheap model first, then escalate hard cases to a stronger and more expensive model. In coding, however, execution feedback can also make further cheap-model recovery worthwhile, raising a budgeted deployment question: when should an agent spend more cheap comp

infographic.key_insight: CodeRescue shows that in coding agents, failed executions are not dead ends—they provide feedback that can justify additional low-cost recovery attempts before escalating to a stronger model. The key breakthrough is a budget-calibrated routing strategy that decides when to keep trying cheap repairs versus when to spend on expensive escalation.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of allocating inference budget in coding agents that work in executable environments. Existing cost-aware systems usually follow a simple cascade pattern, but they do not account for the value of execution feedback that can make repeated cheap-model recovery effective.
method: Uses execution feedback from failed code runs as signal for whether further recovery attempts are likely to succeed.
Learns or designs a routing policy that balances repeated low-cost repair attempts against escalation to a higher-capability, higher-cost model.
Optimizes decision-making under a fixed budget to improve success rates without unnecessary expensive calls.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners building coding assistants, this work offers a more practical way to trade off cost and reliability. It can reduce spending on large models while still improving repair performance in agentic coding workflows.

title: Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness
authors: Xilun Chen, Zhaleh Feizollahi, Ross Goodwin, Seungwhan Moon, Scott Yih
abstract: Evaluating the factuality of long-form generations has focused predominantly on precision, measuring whether the claims a model makes are correct. The dominant decompose-search-verify pipeline catches incorrect claims well but says little about whether a response contains all the information it should. Measuring factual completeness, the missing half of factuality, is harder: it requires enumerating the full set of facts a complete answer should contain, and these facts rarely form a flat list.

infographic.key_insight: This paper shifts evaluation from only checking whether generated claims are correct to also checking whether they are complete. It introduces a two-level meta-rubric idea to systematically capture the full set of facts an ideal open-ended answer should include.
infographic.problem_solved: Current factuality evaluation methods are strong at catching wrong statements, but weak at identifying missing information in long-form generation. The paper tackles the harder problem of factual completeness: determining whether a response includes all required facts, not just correct ones.
method: Introduces GAMUT, a benchmark designed to evaluate factual completeness in open-ended generation.
Uses a two-level meta-rubric framework to organize required facts into structured evaluation criteria instead of a flat checklist.
Focuses on long-form answers where completeness depends on covering multiple nested or related factual points.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more balanced way to evaluate generation quality beyond precision alone. It can improve benchmarking, model selection, and debugging for systems expected to produce thorough, trustworthy answers.

title: Masked Visual Actions for Unified World Modeling
authors: Hadi Alzayer, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Christopher Luey, Lvmin Zhang
abstract: Video models absorb rich priors over how the visual world moves, interacts, and responds to contact, making them promising substrates for robotic world modeling. The central challenge is how to communicate action to such models in a form aligned with the visual space in which they learned these interaction priors, yet still grounded in physical manipulation. We introduce Masked Visual Actions, a pixel-space control interface that expresses action as a partially revealed trajectory of an arbitrar

infographic.key_insight: Masked Visual Actions turn robot control into a visual language: instead of sending abstract commands, the model receives partially revealed pixel-space trajectories that match the way video models already understand motion and interaction. This helps unify action, perception, and world modeling in one interface.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses how to communicate physical actions to video world models in a form that is both aligned with their visual training and grounded in real manipulation. Existing action representations are often too abstract or too disconnected from the visual priors these models learn from video.
method: Represent action as a pixel-space trajectory that is only partially revealed, letting the model infer the rest from visual context.
Use this masked visual control interface to better align action inputs with the model's learned priors about motion, contact, and object interaction.
Aim for unified world modeling where perception and control are handled within the same visual representation space.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to adapt video foundation models for robotics and embodied AI without relying solely on symbolic or low-level control signals. It could improve generalization, interpretability, and transfer from video understanding to physical manipulation.

title: OmniReasoner: Thinking with Long Audio-Video via Native Tool Use
authors: Yu Chen, Caorui Li, Ziyu Xiong, Yidong Wang, Mingqi Gao
abstract: Long audio-video reasoning is difficult for omnimodal LLMs because the decisive evidence is often sparse, cross-modal, and too expensive to preserve with uniformly high-fidelity inputs. We introduce OmniReasoner, a tool-use post-training framework for Thinking with Long Audio-Video: omni-modal LLMs learn, via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, to decide whether and where to call a zoom-in tool before answering. OmniReasoner first builds a low-cost global preview of the full strea

infographic.key_insight: OmniReasoner teaches omnimodal LLMs to reason over long audio-video by first scanning a cheap global preview and then selectively zooming into the most relevant moments. This makes long-context understanding more accurate without paying the cost of high-fidelity processing everywhere.
infographic.problem_solved: Long audio-video reasoning is hard because the decisive evidence is sparse, spread across modalities, and expensive to preserve at full resolution across an entire stream.
method: Build a low-cost global preview of the full audio-video stream to identify candidate evidence.
Use a native zoom-in tool to inspect only the critical segments before answering.
Post-train the model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning so it learns when and where to call the tool.
infographic.impact: This approach can improve accuracy and efficiency for long-form multimedia tasks, especially where important cues are rare and easy to miss. For practitioners, it offers a practical way to scale omnimodal reasoning without brute-force high-resolution processing.

title: ExpertVerse: A General-Purpose Benchmark for Expert-Level Reasoning in Knowledge-Intensive Visual Synthesis
authors: Yuan Wang, Yongchao Du, Mengting Chen, Jinsong Lan, Xuetao Feng
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal generative models have enabled instruction-based image generation to move beyond semantic manipulation to knowledge-driven visual reasoning. However, these methods focus on explicit commonsense reasoning, shallow causal understanding, and direct knowledge recall, failing at knowledge-intensive generation. We develop \textbf{ExpertVerse}, a capability-centric benchmark to evaluate generative models via knowledge-intensive lens. ExpertVerse stratifies reasoning genera

infographic.key_insight: ExpertVerse introduces a benchmark that tests whether multimodal generative models can perform expert-level, knowledge-intensive visual synthesis—not just basic commonsense or direct recall. It reframes evaluation around depth of reasoning needed to generate accurate, expert-informed images.
infographic.problem_solved: Current image-generation models are often evaluated on shallow reasoning tasks like commonsense, simple causality, or memorized knowledge, which misses their failures on complex, domain-heavy, knowledge-intensive synthesis. This paper addresses the lack of a general-purpose benchmark for measuring expert-level reasoning in visual generation.
method: Builds ExpertVerse as a capability-centric benchmark for evaluating knowledge-intensive image generation.
Stratifies reasoning into multiple levels/genera to separate shallow understanding from expert-level reasoning demands.
Uses the benchmark to probe where multimodal generative models succeed or fail under knowledge-heavy synthesis tasks.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, ExpertVerse provides a more realistic test of whether generative models truly reason with expert knowledge rather than merely imitate patterns. It can guide model development, benchmarking, and debugging for high-stakes or specialized visual generation applications.

title: Appearance Pointers -- Multimodal Region Control of Diffusion Transformers
authors: Rahul Sajnani, Yulia Gryaditskaya, Radomír Měch, Srinath Sridhar, Matheus Gadelha
abstract: Controllable image generation remains challenging for creative professionals, who often require precise regional control over materials, object identities, and spatial arrangements that cannot be reliably achieved through text prompting alone. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) can natively ingest heterogeneous tokens stemming from texts and images, but they lack mechanisms for determining where and how these tokens should influence the output. We introduce appearance pointers, compact tokens that gu

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces appearance pointers: compact multimodal tokens that let users control *where* and *how* image or text cues affect diffusion transformer outputs. In simple terms, it makes regional editing and composition in generated images much more precise than text prompting alone.
infographic.problem_solved: Creative professionals often need fine-grained control over regional appearance, such as materials, object identity, and layout, but standard text prompts are too imprecise. Diffusion Transformers can accept text and image tokens, yet they lack a clear mechanism for localizing their influence in the generated image.
method: Introduces appearance pointers, a compact token-based mechanism for specifying regional control in Diffusion Transformers.
Uses multimodal inputs so text and image cues can be directed to particular regions rather than globally affecting the whole image.
Enables more reliable control over appearance attributes, object identity, and spatial arrangement during generation.
infographic.impact: This approach can make AI image generation much more usable for designers, artists, and content creators who need precise edits and composition control. For ML practitioners, it suggests a practical direction for improving controllability in transformer-based generative models.

title: Fundamental limits of distributed multiclass classification from simple binary decisions
authors: Ioannis Papageorgiou, Srinivas Nomula, Ayalvadi Ganesh, Sidharth Jaggi, Parimal Parag
abstract: We consider the problem of constructing a $K$-class classifier from the combination of $O(\log K)$ simple binary classifiers -- this is a natural paradigm to construct a sophisticated classifier in a distributed manner with each agent performing a relatively straightforward task. We study the fundamental performance limits of such a classifier when the corresponding binary classifiers are hyperplanes. For a stylized Gaussian setting where the $K$ class centers are independent Gaussian points in

infographic.key_insight: The paper studies the limits of building a multiclass classifier by combining only O(log K) simple binary decisions. In particular, it shows how far a distributed classifier based on hyperplane-based binary classifiers can go in a stylized Gaussian setting.
infographic.problem_solved: How can we reliably construct a K-class classifier from a small number of simple binary classifiers in a distributed setting, and what are the fundamental accuracy limits of this approach?
method: Model each binary decision as a hyperplane classifier.
Analyze a hierarchical/combined decision scheme that uses only O(log K) binary classifiers to distinguish K classes.
Study performance limits in a stylized Gaussian class-center model to characterize when the approach succeeds or fails.
infographic.impact: This work gives practitioners a principled understanding of the tradeoff between classifier simplicity, scalability, and accuracy in distributed AI systems. It can guide the design of lightweight multi-agent or edge-based classification pipelines where each component must make only a simple binary decision.

title: ISO: An RLVR-Native Optimization Stack
authors: Hanqing Zhu, Wenyan Cong, Zhizhou Sha, Sagnik Mukherjee, Xinyuan Song
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is rapidly advancing the reasoning capabilities of language models, yet the optimization layer that converts reward feedback into weight-space updates remains poorly understood. Building on our prior analysis (Zhu et al., 2025), we study this missing layer through the singular structure of model weights and identify spectral inheritance: RLVR can reuse the base model's weight spectra while acquiring new behavior through changes in the associa

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that RLVR does not need to completely reshape a model to improve reasoning; instead, it largely reuses the base model’s existing weight spectra while changing behavior through a smaller set of structural updates. This "spectral inheritance" helps explain how reward-driven training can be efficient and stable.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the poorly understood optimization layer in RLVR: how reward feedback is converted into actual weight-space updates in the model, and why these updates can improve reasoning without full-scale weight reorganization.
method: Analyze the singular structure of model weights to track how RLVR changes the spectrum of the base model.
Identify and characterize "spectral inheritance" as the reuse of pretrained weight spectra during RLVR optimization.
Study how behavior changes emerge from updates in the associative structure rather than from wholesale spectral replacement.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more interpretable view of RLVR training dynamics and may guide more efficient fine-tuning strategies for reasoning models. It can help researchers design optimization methods that preserve useful pretrained structure while enabling new capabilities.

title: The Many Senses of Visual Similarity: A Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Metric
authors: Sheng-Yu Wang, Yotam Nitzan, Aaron Hertzmann, Jun-Yan Zhu, Eli Shechtman
abstract: Human visual similarity judgments are context-dependent. For example, two images may be similar in shape but distinct in color. Existing perceptual similarity metrics, however, collapse these nuances into a single scalar value, offering no mechanism to condition on specific aspects. To bridge this gap, we introduce a large-scale dataset of human similarity judgments over image triplets, where each triplet is annotated across multiple, free-form semantic aspects of similarity. Benchmarking a broa

infographic.key_insight: Visual similarity is not one-size-fits-all: people judge images differently depending on the aspect they care about, such as shape, color, or texture. This paper shows that perceptual metrics should be conditioned on the requested sense of similarity instead of collapsing everything into a single score.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing image similarity metrics produce a single scalar value, which cannot capture context-dependent human judgments. The paper addresses the lack of benchmark data and models that can evaluate similarity across multiple semantic aspects in a flexible, text-guided way.
method: Build a large-scale dataset of human annotations on image triplets, where each triplet is labeled across multiple free-form similarity aspects.
Introduce a text-prompted perceptual metric that takes a natural-language description of the desired similarity aspect as input.
Benchmark the approach against existing perceptual similarity methods to evaluate how well they match human judgments under different similarity criteria.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables more human-aligned evaluation of generated or edited images when the relevant notion of similarity depends on the task. It is especially useful for image generation, editing, retrieval, and evaluation workflows where shape, color, style, or other factors may matter differently.

title: Three-Body Scattering for Generative Modeling
authors: Peng Sun, Zhenglin Cheng, Deyuan Liu, Jun Xie, Xinyi Shang
abstract: Modern generative models typically rely on an adversarial critic, a prescribed noise-to-data path, or an autoregressive factorization. Instead, we show that a proper distributional energy can induce sample-level motion and provide direct regression supervision for a one-step generator. Three-Body Scattering Modeling (TBSM) for generation turns the energy distance into a constant-size per-projectile interaction: each projectile is attracted toward one real source and repelled from one independent

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that generative modeling can be driven by a distributional energy that creates direct sample-level motion, enabling a one-step generator without relying on adversarial critics, handcrafted noise paths, or autoregressive factorization. The proposed Three-Body Scattering Modeling (TBSM) converts energy distance into simple per-sample interactions that supervise generation directly.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of generating realistic samples without unstable adversarial training, complicated diffusion-style trajectories, or sequential autoregressive dependencies. The goal is a simpler, direct way to train generators using distribution-level supervision.
method: Uses a proper distributional energy to induce motion at the sample level, rather than relying on a discriminator or multi-step path.
Implements Three-Body Scattering Modeling (TBSM), where each generated sample interacts with one real source and one independent repulsive source.
Transforms energy distance into a constant-size interaction per projectile, providing direct regression targets for a one-step generator.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests a potentially simpler and more stable generative training paradigm with direct supervision and fewer moving parts. It may reduce training complexity while preserving strong distribution-matching behavior.

title: SWE-Pruner Pro: The Coder LLM Already Knows What to Prune
authors: Yuhang Wang, Yuling Shi, Shaoqiu Zhang, Jialiang Liang, Shilin He
abstract: Pruning long context for coding agents has been a vital technology for efficient context management. While existing context pruning methods such as SWE-Pruner realize this by attaching a separate code classifier, we find the agent itself encodes internal representations indicating the relevance of code context when reading tool output. Based on this finding, we propose SWE-Pruner Pro, which prunes tool outputs directly inside the agent. Concretely, a small head turns the agent's own internal rep

infographic.key_insight: The coder LLM already contains internal signals about which code context is relevant, so pruning does not need a separate classifier. SWE-Pruner Pro uses the agent’s own representations to decide what to keep or drop from tool outputs.
infographic.problem_solved: Long coding-agent contexts are expensive and cluttered, making it hard to manage tool outputs efficiently. This paper addresses the need for accurate context pruning without adding extra model components.
method: Read the agent’s internal hidden representations while it processes tool output.
Attach a small pruning head to these representations to predict which context is relevant.
Prune tool outputs directly inside the agent instead of using a separate external code classifier.
infographic.impact: This can reduce context length, improve efficiency, and lower inference cost for coding agents. Practitioners get a simpler pruning pipeline that leverages capabilities already present in the model.

title: FlashRT: Agent Harness for Guiding Agents to Deploy Real-Time Multimodal Applications
authors: Krish Agarwal, Zhuoming Chen, Yanyuan Qin, Zhenyu Gu, Atri Rudra
abstract: Real-time multimodal applications, including voice agents and interactive video generation, compose heterogeneous models into pipelines whose efficient deployment requires application-specific decisions about placement, streaming, and intra-model parallelism. Existing serving systems and auto-parallelism compilers commit to limited transformations and fixed workload assumptions, so achieving high performance on a new application requires hand-crafting an efficient implementation. We present Flas

infographic.key_insight: FlashRT introduces an agent harness that helps automatically guide the deployment of real-time multimodal AI applications, reducing the need for hand-crafted system implementations. It focuses on making application-specific choices such as model placement, streaming, and parallelism to improve performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Real-time multimodal apps like voice agents and interactive video generation are hard to deploy efficiently because they combine multiple heterogeneous models with different runtime needs. Existing serving systems and auto-parallelism tools are too rigid, forcing developers to manually engineer high-performance deployments.
method: Uses an agent-based harness to explore deployment decisions for multimodal pipelines.
Supports optimization across placement, streaming, and intra-model parallelism.
Adapts to application-specific workload characteristics instead of relying on fixed assumptions.
infographic.impact: This matters because it can make it much easier to deploy high-performance real-time AI applications without extensive systems expertise. Practitioners may get better latency and efficiency while spending less time hand-tuning infrastructure.

title: Automated Discovery Has No Universally Superior Harness
authors: Akshat Gupta, Jermaine Lei, Alexander Lu, Gopala Anumanchipalli, Leshem Choshen
abstract: Autonomous discovery systems such as OpenEvolve and TTT-Discover are often used as general-purpose harnesses. However, in practice these are composite systems combining several design choices about archives, parent selection, exploration, and budget allocation into a single recipe. Because discovery runs are expensive and inherently stochastic, existing harnesses are often compared using too few independent trials to distinguish key methodological improvements from run-to-run variance. We system

infographic.key_insight: Automated discovery harnesses are not universally superior; their apparent gains can come from specific design choices or random trial variance rather than a generally better framework. The paper argues that fair evaluation requires enough independent runs to separate real improvements from noise.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of comparing autonomous discovery systems when they are expensive, stochastic, and built from many intertwined components such as archives, selection rules, exploration strategies, and budget allocation. It highlights that too few trials can make weak harnesses look strong and strong ideas look insignificant.
method: Decompose discovery harnesses into their core design choices to evaluate which parts actually matter.
Compare harnesses across multiple independent trials to measure performance variability and reduce misleading conclusions.
Analyze how evaluation budget, stochasticity, and composite recipe design affect the reliability of claims about superiority.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a caution against trusting single-run or low-sample comparisons of autonomous discovery systems. It supports more rigorous benchmarking practices and can prevent wasted effort on methods that only seem better due to variance.

title: Patch Policy: Efficient Embodied Control via Dense Visual Representations
authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Zichen Jeff Cui, Ada Langford, Bowen Tan, Yann LeCun
abstract: Pretrained dense visual features from Vision Transformers (ViTs) are powerful yet have been underutilized in robot learning. Modern robot policies either compress each observation into a single global token, or rely on visual backbones trained from scratch, sacrificing both fine-grained spatial detail and the benefits of large-scale visual pre-training. While there exist policies that do operate on dense patch features like large vision-language-action models (VLAs), they tend to be heavy and sl

infographic.key_insight: Patch Policy shows that dense patch-level visual features from pretrained Vision Transformers can improve embodied control by preserving fine-grained spatial detail without needing heavyweight models. It bridges the gap between efficient robot policies and the rich representations learned in large-scale vision pretraining.
infographic.problem_solved: Most robot policies either compress an image into one global token, losing spatial detail, or train visual backbones from scratch, missing the benefits of pretrained ViT features. This paper addresses the need for a lightweight policy that can use dense visual representations effectively for control.
method: Uses pretrained ViT patch features as dense inputs instead of a single global image embedding.
Designs an efficient policy architecture for embodied control that can exploit spatially detailed visual representations.
Avoids the computational cost of large vision-language-action models while retaining the advantages of dense visual pretraining.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more data-efficient and spatially aware path to robot control. It may enable stronger embodied policies with lower training cost and better use of existing pretrained visual models.

authors: Yiyang Cai, Nan Chen, Rongchang Xie, Junwen Pan, Chunyang Jiang
abstract: Human-object centric video personalization (HOCVP) is a core task within subject-driven video generation. However, existing methods suffer from two key limitations. First, most approaches focusing on inter-subject personalization still struggle to strike a balance between high subject fidelity and accurate interaction patterns between humans and diverse objects, especially when objects represent abstract concepts such as logos. Second, while intra-subject references (e.g., OCR maps, multi-view i

infographic.key_insight: HOMIE improves human-object centric video personalization by better preserving the target subject while also modeling how that subject should interact with different objects, including abstract ones like logos. It combines multiple reference signals to make personalized video generation more faithful and more interaction-aware.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses human-object centric video personalization, where current methods often fail to balance subject identity fidelity with realistic human-object interactions, especially when the object is abstract or hard to ground. It also targets the limitation of relying on weak or incomplete reference cues for personalization.
method: Uses multimodal reference information to enrich personalization beyond a single subject image or clip.
Introduces a human-object centric framework that explicitly models both subject appearance and interaction patterns.
Enhances video generation with intelligent refinement so the personalized subject remains consistent across frames while interacting plausibly with diverse objects.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners building controllable video generation systems, virtual avatars, ads, or product-centric content, where both identity preservation and interaction realism are critical. It offers a pathway to more reliable subject-driven video synthesis in complex, multi-object scenarios.

title: Learning Adaptive Safety Margins for Visual Navigation
authors: Junyi Hu, Shuaihang Yuan, Geeta Chandra Raju Bethala, Anthony Tzes, Yi Fang
abstract: Robots in cluttered indoor spaces often fail not because they cannot generate collision-free paths, but because a fixed safety margin is mis-calibrated: conservative margins cause detours and timeouts, while permissive margins lead to near-boundary shortcuts under perception bias. Diffusion-based planners propose diverse trajectory candidates from egocentric RGB-D, yet reliable selection remains the bottleneck. We propose a context-conditioned safety critic that learns an adaptive clearance pref

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that visual navigation becomes safer and more efficient when the robot learns an adaptive safety margin instead of relying on a fixed one. A context-conditioned safety critic selects among candidate trajectories by estimating how much clearance is needed in each scene.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between fixed safety margins and real indoor environments. Too-conservative margins cause unnecessary detours and failures, while too-permissive margins increase collision risk, especially when perception is biased or uncertain.
method: Use a diffusion-based planner to generate diverse candidate trajectories from egocentric RGB-D input.
Train a context-conditioned safety critic to predict an adaptive clearance preference for the current scene.
Select the trajectory that best balances safety and efficiency rather than using a one-size-fits-all margin.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to improve navigation reliability without redesigning the planner itself. It can reduce failed runs, shorten paths, and make robot behavior more robust in cluttered indoor spaces.

title: Robust Multimodal Dynamic Object Segmentation
authors: Zhe Xin, Hanzhi Chang, Penghui Huang, Yinian Mao, Guoquan Huang
abstract: Dynamic object segmentation plays a critical role in many visual applications such as static scene reconstruction from dynamic videos. However, existing optical flow-based methods fail to ensure consistent static/dynamic segmentation along object boundaries, while 3D reconstruction-based approaches are highly sensitive to reconstruction errors. To address these limitations, we present a dynamic object segmentation framework that can generate both precise and complete dynamic masks by integrating

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces a multimodal dynamic object segmentation framework that aims to produce both precise and complete masks for moving objects. The core idea is to combine complementary signals so segmentation remains accurate at object boundaries and robust to reconstruction noise.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of separating static and dynamic regions in videos, especially when object boundaries are ambiguous. Existing optical flow methods can be inconsistent near edges, while 3D reconstruction-based methods are vulnerable to reconstruction errors.
method: Integrates multiple visual cues to improve dynamic object segmentation beyond single-source methods.
Targets both boundary precision and mask completeness to avoid fragmented or missing dynamic regions.
Uses a robust framework designed to reduce sensitivity to errors from optical flow or 3D reconstruction.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means more reliable preprocessing for tasks like static scene reconstruction, motion analysis, and video understanding. Better dynamic masks can improve downstream performance in any pipeline that depends on clean separation of moving and stationary content.
