title: Watermark Forensics for Generative Models: An Information-Theoretic Perspective
authors: Xiaoyu Li, Zheng Gao, Xiaoyan Feng, Jiaojiao Jiang, Yulei Sui
abstract:
A watermark in a generative model's output is usually asked only whether a text is machine-made. The same mark can do more: attribute it to the user who produced it, extract a hidden payload, or localize the part that survives editing. These form a forensic ladder, and we ask what each rung costs in the sample length $n$.
  One object organizes the answers. Let $S$ be the secret the mark carries (a user's identity or payload), and let the information profile $ν(t)=I(S;X_t\mid X_{<t})$ record how

infographic.key_insight: This paper reframes watermarking as an information-forensics problem: not just detecting whether text is AI-generated, but quantifying how much evidence is needed to identify who made it, recover hidden payloads, or localize surviving marks after editing. The core idea is an information-theoretic "forensic ladder" that links each task to sample length and mutual information.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of understanding the limits of generative-model watermarking beyond simple detection—specifically, how much text is needed to attribute authorship, decode embedded information, or trace watermark persistence under edits.
method: Defines a secret variable S for the watermark content (identity or payload) and analyzes its information profile ν(t)=I(S;X_t|X_<t).
Uses information-theoretic bounds to characterize the sample complexity of different forensic tasks along the detection-attribution-payload-localization ladder.
Provides a unified framework to compare what watermarking can reliably recover and what it costs in sequence length n.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this gives a principled way to design and evaluate watermarking schemes instead of relying on ad hoc heuristics. It helps estimate trade-offs between robustness, recoverability, and text length for real-world deployment.

infographic.key_insight: STIRC2025 introduces a benchmark for evaluating point-tracking algorithms in surgical video using infrared surgical tattoo data. It helps standardize how well methods can follow tissue landmarks over time, which is essential for downstream surgical AI tasks.

Runs a challenge framework where participants submit tracking algorithms for standardized scoring.

title: A Shortcut to Statistically Steady-State Turbulence with Flow Matching
authors: Gianluca Galletti, Gerald Gutenbrunner, William Hornsby, Lorenzo Zanisi, Naomi Carey
abstract: Many nonlinear physical systems exhibit an initial transient phase in which perturbations grow before nonlinear interactions lead to a statistically steady state. While this saturated regime is of primary interest, direct numerical simulations must resolve the full transient dynamics before reaching it, incurring significant computational cost. In Computational Fluid Dynamics, reduced-order approaches such as Large Eddy Simulation mitigate computational cost by modeling small-scale dynamics, ena

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows how flow matching can be used as a shortcut to generate statistically steady-state turbulence directly, avoiding the expensive initial transient simulation. In simple terms, it learns to jump straight to the regime researchers care about most.
infographic.problem_solved: Direct numerical simulations of nonlinear physical systems, especially turbulent flows, often spend most of their cost on resolving early transients before reaching the statistically steady state. This paper addresses the inefficiency of waiting through that full evolution when the saturated regime is the main target.
method: Use flow matching to learn a generative mapping toward statistically steady-state turbulence.
Bypass or compress the long transient evolution that traditional CFD simulations must resolve.
Aim to produce representative steady-state flow samples more efficiently than full direct simulation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in scientific computing, this suggests a way to accelerate simulation workflows by learning direct-to-solution generators for complex physical states. It can reduce compute cost while preserving the distributional properties needed for downstream analysis or surrogate modeling.

abstract: Building capable embodied agents requires not only multimodal perception and understanding, but also agentic capabilities for reasoning about actions, adapting to evolving situations, and interacting with the physical world. In this report, we introduce Hy-Embodied-VLM-1.0, an efficient and powerful embodied foundation model specifically designed for embodied agents operating in the physical world. To cultivate such capabilities from the pre-training stage onward, we define an action-centric cap

infographic.key_insight: Hy-Embodied-VLM-1.0 is an embodied foundation model built to help AI agents perceive, reason, and act more effectively in the physical world. Its core idea is to make action-oriented intelligence a first-class part of pre-training, not just an add-on at deployment time.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between multimodal understanding and real-world action in embodied AI. Existing models can often recognize and describe scenes, but struggle with decision-making, adaptation, and reliable interaction in dynamic physical environments.
method: Introduces an action-centric pre-training strategy to develop agentic capabilities from the start.
Designs the model for efficient embodied reasoning, combining perception, understanding, and action planning for physical-world tasks.
Targets robustness in evolving environments so the agent can adapt its behavior as conditions change.

A more efficient embodied foundation model can reduce task-specific engineering and improve adaptability in real deployments.

title: Open-KNEAD: Knowledge-grounded Nutrition Estimation via Agentic Decomposition
authors: Bruce Coburn, Jingbo Yue, Jinge Ma, Siddeshwar Raghavan, Gautham Vinod
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly used for dietary assessment from meal images, where retrieval-augmented grounding was shown to sharpen nutrition estimates. However, we find this premise no longer holds for current MLLMs. A modern MLLM's direct estimate now matches or surpasses the full retrieval pipeline. This raises a question: if retrieval no longer improves the overall estimate, can it still deliver the two things clinicians value, accurate portions and a traceable,

infographic.key_insight: Modern multimodal large language models can estimate meal nutrition directly as well as, or better than, retrieval-augmented pipelines. The paper reframes retrieval from improving the final estimate to providing clinically useful grounding, such as better portion accuracy and traceability.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of estimating nutrition from meal images in a way that is accurate, grounded, and clinically interpretable. Specifically, it asks whether retrieval is still needed when direct MLLM estimates are already strong, and whether retrieval can still add value through better portion reasoning and evidence tracing.
method: Uses a knowledge-grounded, agentic decomposition approach for nutrition estimation from food images.
Separates the task into substeps so the model can reason about visual content, portions, and nutrition evidence more explicitly.
Compares direct MLLM estimation against full retrieval-augmented pipelines to assess when retrieval helps and when it no longer improves overall accuracy.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that newer MLLMs may reduce the need for complex retrieval pipelines in some vision-language tasks. It also highlights a shift toward using retrieval for explainability and clinical usefulness rather than only for boosting aggregate accuracy.

title: UR-VC: Unsupervised Robotic Value Correction for Time-Derived Progress Proxies
authors: Lirui Zhao, Modi Shi, Li Chen, Qi Liu, Ping Luo
abstract: Modern robot learning systems increasingly rely on dense progress or value signals to evaluate intermediate states, guide policy learning, and detect task completion, making the quality of these signals critical. Since such dense labels are rarely available at scale, normalized time within a demonstration is often used as a scalable substitute: later frames are treated as higher progress. However, this time-derived label is only a noisy proxy for physical task progress. In contact-rich manipulat

infographic.key_insight: UR-VC shows that normalized demonstration time is an imperfect proxy for task progress in robot learning, and proposes a way to automatically correct these noisy progress/value labels without manual annotation. This helps dense supervision better reflect true physical task completion, especially in contact-rich manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Robot learning often needs dense progress or value signals, but these are expensive to label at scale. The paper addresses the mismatch between time-derived progress labels and actual physical progress, which can mislead policy learning and task completion detection.
method: Starts from time-derived progress proxies computed from demonstration timestamps.
Learns an unsupervised correction mechanism to adjust noisy progress/value labels toward more physically meaningful targets.
Uses the corrected value signal to improve intermediate-state evaluation and downstream robot learning tasks.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, UR-VC offers a scalable way to get better dense supervision without manual labeling. This can improve training stability, progress estimation, and completion detection in robotic manipulation systems.

It also bridges 2D and 3D segmentation so a single model can learn from heterogeneous annotations and image types.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing medical segmentation foundation models are fragmented: different prompt paradigms and spatial dimensions are usually handled by separate models. This prevents joint learning from diverse annotations and limits generalization across clinical tasks.

Supports multi-paradigm segmentation, including visual, interactive, and language-guided inputs.
Extends the same modeling approach across both 2D and 3D medical images to enable shared learning.

title: X-Lens: Real-Time Metric Depth Estimation with Heterogeneous Cameras
authors: Heng Zhou, Shuhong Liu, Yonghao He, Bohao Zhang, Fa Fu
abstract: We present X-lens, a compact feed-forward model for metric depth estimation from a variable number of calibrated fisheye and pinhole views. To support real-time downstream perception, X-lens is built around a geometry-aware heterogeneous camera formulation with two key components. Learnable calibration tokens provide a coarse alignment between fisheye and pinhole projective spaces, while a Jacobian-parameterized distortion bias injected into cross-attention models local projection changes and pr

infographic.key_insight: X-Lens shows that accurate metric depth can be estimated in real time from a mix of fisheye and pinhole cameras using a compact feed-forward model. Its main idea is to explicitly encode camera geometry so the model can handle heterogeneous views without heavy processing.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses real-time metric depth estimation when inputs come from a variable number of calibrated cameras with different projection types, especially fisheye and pinhole lenses. This is challenging because their geometry differs significantly, making feature alignment and depth prediction difficult.
method: Uses a geometry-aware heterogeneous camera formulation to unify fisheye and pinhole views.
Introduces learnable calibration tokens to provide coarse alignment between different projective spaces.
Injects a Jacobian-parameterized distortion bias into cross-attention to model local projection changes more accurately.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it enables practical real-time depth estimation in multi-camera systems without requiring a fixed camera layout. It is especially useful for robotics, autonomous systems, and perception pipelines that must work with mixed lens types efficiently.

title: MemOps: Benchmarking Lifecycle Memory Operations in Long-Horizon Conversations
authors: Xixuan Hao, Zeyu Zhang, Zehao Lin, Yihang Sun, Ziliang Guo
abstract: Long-term memory has become a foundational capability for LLM-based agents that accompany users across extended, multi-session interactions. Existing benchmarks, however, evaluate such memory almost exclusively through downstream question answering, scoring only the correctness of a final answer. This black-box formulation conflates the heterogeneous causes of memory failure, such as missing the introduction of a relevant fact, binding an operation to the wrong target, or relying on stale values

infographic.key_insight: MemOps argues that long-term memory should not be judged only by final QA accuracy. Instead, it breaks memory evaluation into lifecycle operations so researchers can see *where* memory fails: missing facts, wrong bindings, or stale updates.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the weakness of existing long-horizon memory benchmarks, which treat memory as a black box and only score the final answer. This makes it hard to diagnose the true cause of failure in LLM agents with long-term memory.
method: Introduces a benchmark focused on lifecycle memory operations in long-horizon conversations rather than only downstream question answering.
Separates memory evaluation into failure modes such as fact insertion, target binding, and value updating/staleness.
Provides a more diagnostic framework for analyzing where memory systems break across multi-session interactions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MemOps offers a clearer way to debug and improve agent memory systems by pinpointing specific weaknesses. This can lead to more reliable assistants that handle long-running, multi-session tasks more accurately.

abstract: LiDAR-based collaborative 3D perception in Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) systems typically relies on fusing bird's-eye-view (BEV) features across agents. However, current BEV representations, typically extracted by LiDAR backbones trained from scratch, are geometry-dominated and lack general semantic priors, inherently limiting the efficacy of feature-level collaboration. Meanwhile, vision foundation models (VFMs) pretrained on large-scale image data have demonstrated strong capability in learning

infographic.key_insight: ViCo3D improves collaborative LiDAR 3D object detection by injecting semantic knowledge from vision foundation models into BEV features, making multi-agent fusion more informative than geometry-only representations. The result is stronger perception in V2X settings without relying solely on LiDAR-trained-from-scratch features.

method: Use vision foundation models pretrained on large-scale image data to provide semantic priors for LiDAR BEV representations.

Bridge the gap between LiDAR geometry and visual semantics to improve inter-agent feature collaboration.
infographic.impact: This approach can make cooperative autonomous driving perception more accurate and robust, especially in challenging scenes where LiDAR geometry alone is insufficient. For practitioners, it shows how pretrained foundation models can improve specialized 3D sensing pipelines.

title: FlowWAM: Optical Flow as a Unified Action Representation for World Action Models
authors: Yixiang Chen, Peiyan Li, Yuan Xu, Qisen Ma, Jiabing Yang
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) are able to leverage pretrained video generators for both world modeling and action prediction. However, directly leveraging such video generators for control raises a new challenge: how to represent actions in a suitable form that aligns with pretrained video generators while carrying enough motion cues for accurate control. Existing numerical actions fail to satisfy the former, and prior visual action representations overlook the temporal motion structure across fram

infographic.key_insight: FlowWAM reframes actions as optical flow, giving world action models a visual representation that matches pretrained video generators while still preserving motion information needed for control. This creates a more natural bridge between video generation and action prediction.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of representing actions in a form that is compatible with pretrained video generators and also detailed enough to support accurate control. Traditional numeric actions are not visually aligned, while previous visual action formats often miss temporal motion structure.
method: Represent actions using optical flow instead of raw numeric control signals.
Align the action representation with the visual dynamics learned by pretrained video generators.
Use flow-based motion cues to improve both world modeling and action prediction in WAMs.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more unified way to connect generative video models with control tasks. It can improve sample efficiency and make action-conditioned world models easier to train and interpret.

title: Inside the Unfair Judge: A Mechanistic Interpretability Account of LLM-as-Judge Bias
authors: Zixiang Xu, Sixian Li, Huaxing Liu, Xiang Wang, Shuai Li
abstract: Existing studies of LLM-as-judge scoring bias work predominantly at the input-output level: they perturb inputs, measure score deltas, and propose prompt-level mitigations. We argue that the same biases admit a representation-level account in the judge's hidden state, complementary to the input-output view and operationally useful in ways it does not afford. We report three findings, across seven judges, seven bias types, and nine benchmarks. Geometry: baseline judging inputs occupy a tight acti

infographic.key_insight: LLM-as-judge bias is not just a prompt/input-output problem—it also shows up in the model’s hidden representations. The paper finds a representation-level account of bias that can explain, measure, and help mitigate unfair scoring across multiple judges and benchmarks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of understanding why LLM judges produce biased scores, such as favoring certain inputs or styles, and moves beyond surface-level perturbation studies to identify the internal mechanisms behind these biases.
method: Analyze hidden-state geometry of judge models to see how biased and unbiased inputs are represented internally.
Evaluate seven judges across seven bias types and nine benchmarks to test whether representation-level bias patterns generalize.
Compare representation-level findings with input-output bias measurements to build a complementary mechanistic interpretability view of LLM-as-judge behavior.
infographic.impact: This helps researchers and practitioners diagnose unfairness in LLM evaluators more precisely, rather than relying only on prompt tweaks. It also opens the door to stronger mitigations that target the model’s internal decision process, improving trust in automated evaluation systems.

title: Read It Back: Pretrained MLLMs Are Zero-Shot Reward Models for Text-to-Image Generation
authors: Runhui Huang, Qihui Zhang, Zhe Liu, Yu Gao, Jie Wu
abstract: In this paper, we propose SpectraReward, a training-free reward function that turns pretrained MLLMs into off-the-shelf reward models for image-generation reinforcement learning. Instead of asking the MLLM to judge a generated image or answer decomposed verification questions, SpectraReward measures how well the original prompt can be recovered from the generated image through a single image-conditioned, teacher-forced forward pass. We use the average image-conditioned prompt log-likelihood as t

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can be used as zero-shot reward models for text-to-image generation without additional training. SpectraReward scores images by checking how likely the original prompt is to be recovered from the image in a single teacher-forced forward pass.
infographic.problem_solved: Text-to-image reinforcement learning needs reward models that judge whether generated images match prompts, but existing approaches often require extra training, manual decomposition into verification questions, or direct image judging that can be brittle and costly.
method: Condition on the generated image and feed the original prompt into a pretrained MLLM in a teacher-forced manner.

title: Cycle-World: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Long-term Video World Models via Reverse-Prediction Cycle Consistency
authors: Zihan Su, Teng Hu, Jiangning Zhang, Ruiyan Wang, Ran Yi
abstract: Autoregressive diffusion models have enabled high-quality video generation, yet their sequential nature inherently suffers from error accumulation. In long-horizon video synthesis, minor prediction deviations compound over time, inevitably leading to unconstrained generative drift, structural collapse, and severe visual degradation. To address this, we propose Cycle-World, a novel framework designed for stable and temporally consistent long-video generation. Our approach tackles error drift by e

infographic.key_insight: Cycle-World reduces long-video drift by enforcing reverse-prediction cycle consistency, helping the model stay temporally stable over many generated steps. In simple terms, it teaches the video world model to “close the loop” so small mistakes do not snowball into major visual collapse.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses error accumulation in autoregressive diffusion-based video world models, where tiny prediction errors compound over time and cause generative drift, structural breakdown, and degraded long-horizon video quality.
method: Introduces Cycle-World, a framework that adds reverse-prediction cycle consistency to long-term video generation.
Uses a cycle-based training objective so forward predictions can be checked and corrected through reverse reconstruction.
Aims to stabilize temporal dynamics and reduce long-range drift in autoregressive video synthesis.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners building video generation, simulation, and world-model systems because it improves stability over long horizons, which is essential for realistic and coherent outputs. It can help make long-video synthesis more reliable for creative tools, robotics simulation, and predictive modeling.

title: Input-Aware Dynamic Backdoor Attack Against Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Junrui Zhang, Zemin Chen, Lusi Li, Mohammad Ghasemigol, Daniel Takabi
abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) are a promising framework for quantum machine learning on near-term quantum devices, but their security risks remain insufficiently understood. Studies have shown that QNNs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, yet existing quantum backdoors mostly rely on a fixed trigger shared by all poisoned inputs. This fixed-trigger design is a major weakness because many defenses detect or weaken the repeated patterns such triggers leave in data representations. Although input-

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces an input-aware dynamic backdoor attack for quantum neural networks, where the trigger changes depending on the input instead of staying fixed. This makes the attack harder for defenses to spot because it avoids leaving a repeated, obvious pattern in the data.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the weakness of existing QNN backdoor attacks that rely on a single fixed trigger, which can often be detected or reduced by defenses that look for repeated abnormal patterns.
method: Generate backdoor behavior using input-dependent trigger patterns rather than one shared universal trigger.
Design the poisoned samples so the malicious effect remains effective while appearing less consistent across examples.
Target quantum neural network security by exploiting the gap in defenses built for fixed-pattern backdoors.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners working with quantum machine learning, this highlights a more realistic and harder-to-detect attack surface in QNNs. It suggests that defenses must move beyond fixed-trigger assumptions and consider dynamic, input-conditioned threats.

title: The brain is a diverse place, why not computing?
authors: Peyton Chandarana, James B. Aimone
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 13 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01273-1

The brain’s architecture exhibits diversity across many temporal and spatial scales, yet our computing architectures remain largely homogeneous. Low-powered neuromorphic hardware offers a path towards energy-efficient AI, but could these approaches be improved with heterogeneous computing architectures?

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that AI hardware could benefit from the brain’s core design principle: diversity. Instead of relying on uniform computing architectures, heterogeneous neuromorphic systems may deliver better energy efficiency and performance for AI workloads.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between the brain’s highly diverse architecture and the mostly homogeneous structure of modern computing systems. The challenge is how to build low-power AI hardware that can handle varied tasks more efficiently.
method: Compare biological brain diversity across spatial and temporal scales with current computing architectures.
Use neuromorphic hardware as a model for low-power AI computation.
Motivate heterogeneous computing as a way to improve flexibility, efficiency, and task specialization.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a new hardware design direction beyond scale-up and uniform accelerators. Heterogeneous neuromorphic systems could lower energy costs and enable more adaptive, task-specific AI deployments.

title: Metacognition in LLMs: Foundations, Progress, and Opportunities
authors: Gabrielle Kaili-May Liu, Areeb Gani, Jacqueline Lu, Jordan Thomas, Mark Steyvers
abstract: Metacognition is a foundational component of intelligence critical to effective learning, problem solving, decision-making, communication, and more. In recent years, it has become increasingly recognized as a cornerstone of capable, transparent AI systems. Yet while LLMs have made significant progress across diverse real-world tasks, it is not yet clear when, how, or to what extent they can exhibit or be endowed with effective metacognitive abilities, nor how such abilities can be adapted to adv

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that metacognition—models' ability to assess, regulate, and explain their own thinking—is becoming a key ingredient for making LLMs more capable, transparent, and reliable. It surveys what is known, what is still missing, and where future progress is most likely to come from.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of a clear framework for understanding when and how large language models can exhibit metacognitive abilities, and how those abilities can be measured, improved, and applied in practice.
method: Synthesizes existing research on metacognition in LLMs across learning, reasoning, uncertainty estimation, and self-monitoring.
Organizes the field into foundational concepts, current progress, and open research opportunities.
Highlights design directions for building more reflective systems, such as self-evaluation, calibration, and adaptive control.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a roadmap for designing models that are not only accurate but also aware of their own limitations. That can improve reliability, interpretability, debugging, and safe deployment in real-world settings.

title: Requential Coding: Pushing the Limits of Model Compression with Self-Generated Training Data
authors: Shikai Qiu, Marc Finzi, Yujia Zheng, Kun Zhang, Andrew Gordon Wilson
abstract: Compression is fundamental to intelligence. A model that can represent its training data as a short code has discovered regularities that enable generalization. Large neural networks may learn functions far simpler than their parameter counts suggest, but it is challenging to construct codes that realize this simplicity. Parameter-based methods such as quantization produce code lengths that scale with model size, insensitive to how much information the parameters store. Prequential coding bypass

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that neural networks can be compressed more meaningfully by measuring how well they can be encoded using the data they themselves generate. This self-generated, prequential-style coding can reveal much shorter descriptions than parameter-count-based compression methods.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the limitation of traditional model compression methods like quantization, which scale with parameter size rather than the actual information stored in the model. The paper seeks a code length that better reflects a model's true complexity and compressibility.
method: Use prequential coding to encode model behavior sequentially, rather than compressing raw parameters directly.
Leverage self-generated training data to construct a code that adapts to the information content of the model.
Measure compression in terms of how many bits are needed to represent the learned function, not just the number of weights.
infographic.impact: This could lead to compression methods that better match what a model has actually learned, enabling smaller, more efficient deployments without relying on blunt parameter-based approximations. For practitioners, it offers a more principled way to compare and compress large models.

title: Latent-Identity Tuning in Text-to-Image Personalization Models
authors: Daniel Garibi, Ronen Kamenetsky, Hadar Averbuch-Elor, Daniel Cohen-Or, Or Patashnik
abstract: Generating and editing a person's face demands high precision, as even minor modifications can significantly alter a subject's perceived identity. Current personalization and editing methods built on general-purpose text-to-image models, however, often lack the precision required for fine-grained facial edits. We present a method for fine-grained identity tuning in text-to-image personalization models. Unlike standard image editing, which operates on a given image, identity tuning modifies the l

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces a way to tune a text-to-image personalization model so it can make very fine-grained changes to a person's identity without losing who they are. In simple terms, it helps models edit faces with much higher identity precision than standard personalization methods.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing text-to-image personalization and editing systems often struggle with subtle facial edits, where small changes can unintentionally alter a person's identity. The paper addresses the need for high-precision identity control in face generation and editing.
method: Proposes latent-identity tuning, a technique that adjusts identity representation inside a personalization model rather than relying only on standard image editing.
Targets fine-grained facial identity changes while preserving the core characteristics of the person.
Builds on general-purpose text-to-image models but improves their ability to handle identity-sensitive edits.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables more reliable face personalization and editing in applications like avatars, creative media, and portrait editing. It improves control and fidelity, making generative models more useful where identity accuracy matters.

title: AdvancedMathBench: A Benchmark Suite for Advanced Mathematical Proof Generation and Verification
authors: Lingkai Kong, Zijian Wu, Yuzhe Gu, Haiteng Zhao, Wenyong Huang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on high-school and olympiad-style mathematics, yet their capabilities on advanced mathematics remain poorly understood. Existing benchmarks, however, fall short in both scope and evaluation granularity: they provide limited disciplinary coverage and often rely on final-answer correctness or coarse judgments, leaving the validity of the reasoning process inadequately assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce AdvancedMathBench, a b

infographic.key_insight: AdvancedMathBench aims to move AI evaluation beyond “got the final answer” by testing whether models can generate and verify rigorous advanced mathematical proofs. It provides a more fine-grained way to measure reasoning quality across advanced math domains.
infographic.problem_solved: Current math benchmarks mostly focus on high-school or olympiad problems and often judge models only by final-answer correctness. This paper addresses the lack of broad coverage and detailed evaluation for advanced mathematical proof generation and verification.
method: Builds a benchmark suite focused on advanced mathematics rather than only competition-style problems.
Evaluates both proof generation and proof verification, not just final answers.
Uses more granular scoring to assess reasoning validity and proof quality across disciplines.
infographic.impact: This gives researchers a stronger testbed for measuring whether LLMs can do genuine mathematical reasoning, not just pattern matching. For practitioners, it helps identify model strengths, failure modes, and progress on advanced symbolic reasoning tasks.

title: HASTE: A Platform for Rapid Post-Disaster Building Damage Assessment
authors: Caleb Robinson, Anthony Ortiz, Simone Fobi Nsutezo, Cameron Birge, Meygha Machado
abstract: When a large disaster strikes, responders need a map of which buildings are damaged within hours. The models that do well on public benchmarks assume matched before-and-after imagery and a training set drawn from similar past events, and neither is usually available for a new disaster in its first day. We present HASTE (High-speed Assessment and Satellite Tracking for Emergencies), a no-code web platform that lets analysts who are not machine learning engineers produce per-building damage maps f

infographic.key_insight: HASTE makes rapid post-disaster building damage assessment accessible to non-ML users by turning satellite imagery into per-building damage maps through a no-code web platform. It is designed for the critical first hours after a disaster, when matched imagery and task-specific training data are usually unavailable.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the urgent need to quickly identify which buildings are damaged after a disaster, without relying on idealized benchmark conditions or a team of machine learning engineers.
method: Provides a no-code web platform for analysts to generate damage assessments from satellite imagery.
Supports rapid, per-building mapping of damage for new disaster events where before-and-after image pairs may be incomplete or unavailable.
Focuses on operational usability so responders can create actionable maps within hours of an event.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how disaster-response systems can move beyond benchmark performance toward real-world deployment constraints. It highlights the value of human-centered tooling, robustness to data mismatch, and practical workflows for emergency response.

title: Towards shared embodied intelligence in humanoid robots through optimization, development and testing of the human-aware ergoCub robot
authors: Carlotta Sartore, Mohamed Elobaid, Lorenzo Rapetti, Giulio Romualdi, Stefano Dafarra
abstract:

Sartore et al. present ergoCub, a humanoid robot that prioritizes human safety at hardware and motion levels. Using a shared embodied intelligence framework, design and control are jointly optimized with human-related metrics such as back stress alongside locomotion objectives, reducing spinal load and improving walking robustness.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that humanoid robots can be designed and controlled with human safety as a first-class objective, not an afterthought. By jointly optimizing hardware and motion for both locomotion and human-related metrics, ergoCub walks more robustly while reducing spinal load.
infographic.problem_solved: Humanoid robots often optimize for performance alone, which can create motions or designs that are unsafe or physically demanding for nearby humans. This work addresses the challenge of building robots that are both effective and human-aware at the hardware and control levels.
method: Use a shared embodied intelligence framework to jointly optimize robot design and motion control.
Include human-centric metrics, such as back stress/spinal load, alongside standard locomotion objectives.
Develop and test the ergoCub humanoid robot to evaluate safety-aware walking performance and robustness.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights a practical path toward deploying embodied AI systems that balance performance with human safety. It suggests that optimization objectives should include human impact metrics, especially for robots operating in shared spaces.

infographic.problem_solved: Robotics research is often fragmented across applications and lacks a common sustainability-oriented direction. The paper addresses the need for a discipline that connects robot design with solving sustainability challenges.

Introduces two dimensions: sustainable design and robotics for sustainability.
Frames robotics research around societal and environmental impact to guide future work.

title: Evidence-Backed Video Question Answering
authors: Shijie Wang, Honglu Zhou, Ziyang Wang, Ran Xu, Caiming Xiong
abstract: Current Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) excel in question answering (QA) but largely operate as black boxes, providing textual answers without verifiable visual grounding. Existing explainability efforts rely on textual rationales or sparse bounding boxes, which struggle to capture complex video dynamics such as occlusions and non-rigid deformations. We propose Evidence-Backed Video Question Answering (E-VQA), a novel task requiring models to jointly output a semantic answer and precise

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces Evidence-Backed Video Question Answering (E-VQA), which asks video models to provide not just an answer, but also precise visual evidence from the video. This makes video QA more transparent and verifiable than standard black-box outputs.
infographic.problem_solved: Video LLMs can answer questions well, but their predictions are often not grounded in identifiable visual evidence. Existing explanations like text rationales or sparse boxes are too limited to capture complex video phenomena such as occlusion, motion, and non-rigid deformation.
method: Defines a new E-VQA task that jointly predicts a semantic answer and supporting evidence in the video.
Encourages fine-grained grounding so the model can point to exact visual regions or segments relevant to the answer.
Targets hard video understanding cases where evidence must track dynamic objects and changing appearances over time.
infographic.impact: This makes video AI more trustworthy, debuggable, and useful in real applications where users need to verify why a model gave an answer. For practitioners, it provides a path toward models that are not only accurate, but also interpretable and auditable.

title: A Minimalist Retargeting-Guided Reinforcement Learning Recipe for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Yunhai Feng, Natalie Leung, Jiaxuan Wang, Lujie Yang, Haozhi Qi
abstract: Recent work in humanoid whole-body control has found success with a simple recipe: retarget human motion to robot kinematic references, then train policies via reinforcement learning (RL) to track them. But how does this recipe transfer to dexterous manipulation? The answer is not obvious, as manipulation involves complex, contact-rich dynamics and requires delicate regulation of contact modes and forces. We present REGRIND, a minimalist retargeting-guided RL pipeline that learns dexterous manip

infographic.key_insight: A simple retargeting-to-RL recipe, proven in humanoid control, can be adapted to dexterous manipulation to learn contact-rich skills more efficiently. The paper’s key takeaway is that minimalist motion guidance can still help policies discover precise, force-aware hand behaviors.
infographic.problem_solved: Dexterous manipulation is hard because it requires stable contact handling, fine force regulation, and switching between complex contact modes. The paper asks whether a lightweight retargeting-guided RL pipeline can make these skills easier to learn without heavy task-specific engineering.
method: Retarget human or demonstration motions into robot-friendly kinematic references for manipulation.
Train reinforcement learning policies to track these references while handling contact-rich interactions.
Use a minimalist pipeline (REGRIND) that relies on simple guidance rather than extensive hand-designed rewards or controllers.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that dexterous manipulation may be more approachable with a clean retargeting + RL setup instead of highly specialized control stacks. It points toward more scalable skill learning for robot hands and practical transfer from human motion to robotic manipulation.

The push to make biological data ‘AI-ready’ is accelerating worldwide. But to understand what AI-ready means for biological data, there are several questions to answer.

infographic.problem_solved: Biological data are often highly variable, noisy, incomplete, and inconsistently annotated, making them difficult to use effectively in AI models. This paper addresses the lack of a shared definition for what it means for biological data to be truly AI-ready.

Focuses on key data qualities such as consistency, representativeness, provenance, and suitability for downstream machine learning tasks.

title: CoCoT-EEG: Contrastive-Pretrained Multiscale Convolutional Transformer for EEG Decoding
authors: Gabriel Mahuas, Victoria Shevchenko, Ugo Tanielian, Yassir Bendou, Richard Gao
abstract: Self-supervised pretrained foundation models (FM) have shown early promise for non-invasive electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding applications. Many recent large-scale models converged on the approach of tokenizing raw EEG followed by masked reconstruction pretraining. However, this recipe has been shown to be suboptimal for data, like EEG, with high noise amplitude and information confined to limited dimensions such as narrow frequency bands. Building on this insight, we develop a novel contrasti

infographic.key_insight: CoCoT-EEG argues that EEG foundation models work better when they learn via contrastive pretraining at multiple scales, rather than relying mainly on masked reconstruction of raw signals. This better matches EEG’s noisy, low-dimensional, frequency-specific structure.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing self-supervised EEG foundation models often use tokenization plus masked reconstruction, which can be suboptimal for noisy signals where useful information is concentrated in narrow frequency bands and limited temporal/spatial dimensions.
method: Uses a contrastive-pretrained multiscale convolutional transformer tailored to EEG decoding.
Learns representations across multiple temporal scales to capture both fine-grained and broader EEG patterns.
Combines convolutional feature extraction with transformer-based contextual modeling for robust self-supervised pretraining.
infographic.impact: This approach can improve EEG representation learning for downstream decoding tasks, making foundation models more practical for non-invasive brain-signal analysis. For practitioners, it suggests that domain-specific pretraining objectives can outperform generic masked reconstruction strategies on challenging biosignals.

title: Scalable Visual Pretraining for Language Intelligence
authors: Yiming Zhang, Zhonghan Zhao, Wenwei Zhang, Haiteng Zhao, Tianyang Lin
abstract: The rapid progress of large foundation models has been driven predominantly by pretraining on large-scale text corpora. However, many forms of knowledge are conveyed through visual representations, where figures, typeset equations, and page layouts carry rich information that cannot be faithfully or completely captured by text alone. Yet current pretraining approaches discard these visual cues by converting visually rich sources, such as documents and web pages, into plain text for learning lang

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that language intelligence can be improved by pretraining on visually rich data, not just plain text. By preserving figures, equations, and layout information, models can learn knowledge that is otherwise lost during text-only conversion.
infographic.problem_solved: Current foundation-model pretraining often strips away visual cues from documents and web pages, discarding important information encoded in images, formulas, and page structure. The paper tackles how to scale pretraining so models can learn from these visual signals efficiently.
method: Pretrain on visually rich sources such as documents and web pages while retaining non-text visual information.
Learn from multimodal page representations that combine text with figures, equations, and layout cues.
Scale the pretraining pipeline to support large foundation models without relying only on plain-text extraction.

Practitioners can build models with better document understanding, richer knowledge capture, and improved performance on tasks requiring visual reasoning over text.

title: OpenLongTail: Generative Scaling of Long-Tail Driving Data
authors: Lulin Liu, Nuo Chen, Yan Wang, Bangya Liu, Wenyan Cong
abstract: Scaling robust driving policies is fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of edge cases in curated datasets. While the real world continuously captures these critical events, such long-tail events remain underutilized when collected from heterogeneous sources. Specifically, diverse but valuable in-the-wild long-tail videos lack the full view coverage required for training policy models, often missing multi-view poses or originating solely from monocular dash cameras. This modality gap preven

infographic.key_insight: OpenLongTail tackles the scarcity of rare driving edge cases by generatively scaling long-tail examples from messy real-world videos. It helps bridge the gap between incomplete in-the-wild footage and the multi-view data needed to train robust driving policies.
infographic.problem_solved: Driving policy models need many rare and safety-critical edge cases, but curated datasets contain too few of them. Real-world long-tail videos are abundant yet often incomplete, monocular, or missing the full multi-view coverage required for training.
method: Collect in-the-wild long-tail driving videos from heterogeneous sources, including monocular dashcam footage.
Use generative modeling to expand these partial observations into richer, training-ready long-tail driving data.
Close the modality gap by producing more complete multi-view representations for rare driving scenarios.
infographic.impact: This makes it easier for AI/ML practitioners to train safer and more robust autonomous driving systems without relying only on expensive curated edge-case datasets. It can improve coverage of rare events that are critical for real-world deployment.

title: PanoWorld: Real-World Panoramic Generation
authors: Haoyuan Li, Dizhe Zhang, Yuemei Zhou, Xiangkai Zhang, Haoran Feng
abstract: In this work, we aim to address the challenge of long-range memory in panoramic world models by exploiting the rotation-equivariant property of omnidirectional representations, where rotation can be treated as an implicit geometric transformation.Building on this insight, we propose PanoWorld, which simplifies camera trajectories into translations via fixed headings for both current-action modeling and long-range memory through Dense Panoramic Ray-Conditioning (DPRC) and Geometry-aware Memory Au

infographic.key_insight: PanoWorld turns panoramic rotation into a geometric advantage: by leveraging rotation-equivariant omnidirectional representations, it can model camera motion and long-range memory more effectively in 360° environments. This simplifies panoramic trajectory modeling while preserving spatial consistency over time.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the long-range memory challenge in panoramic world models, where maintaining coherent scene understanding across extended camera movements is difficult, especially in omnidirectional 360° settings.
method: Uses rotation-equivariant panoramic representations so rotational changes are treated as implicit geometric transformations.
Introduces Dense Panoramic Ray-Conditioning (DPRC) to model current action and scene dynamics with fixed headings.
Adds geometry-aware memory mechanisms to retain long-range information and support consistent panoramic world generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, PanoWorld offers a more structured way to build world models for 360° data, improving memory retention and trajectory consistency. This can benefit robotics, VR/AR, autonomous navigation, and any application that relies on panoramic scene understanding.

title: SAGEAgent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Cost-Aware Modality Acquisition in Multimodal Survival Prediction
authors: Chongyu Qu, Can Cui, Zhengyi Lu, Junchao Zhu, Tianyuan Yao
abstract: Does every cancer patient truly need a complete diagnostic workup for accurate survival prediction? In multimodal clinical oncology, diagnostic modalities follow a clinically mandated order of escalating burden -- from demographics collected at intake to genomic profiling requiring specialized tissue analysis. Current multimodal survival methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but none actively reason about whether acquiring the next modality is justi

infographic.key_insight: SAGEAgent turns multimodal survival prediction into an active decision problem: instead of using every available clinical modality by default, it learns when the next test is worth the cost and burden. This enables more efficient predictions by balancing accuracy with real-world acquisition constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap in multimodal oncology models that either assume all modalities are always available or simply cope with missing inputs. It targets the clinical question of whether additional diagnostic modalities should be acquired at each step, given their cost, invasiveness, and limited incremental value.
method: Frames modality acquisition as a sequential, cost-aware decision process for survival prediction.
Uses a self-evolving agent to reason about which modality to acquire next based on expected predictive benefit versus acquisition burden.
Supports clinically ordered modalities, allowing the model to operate under realistic workflows where tests are obtained progressively rather than all at once.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work shifts multimodal learning from passive fusion to active information gathering under constraints. It is especially relevant for healthcare applications where reducing unnecessary tests can improve efficiency, patient comfort, and deployment realism.

title: Lean-QIT: Towards a Formal Infrastructure for Quantum Information Theory
authors: Chengkai Zhu, Ziao Tang, Guocheng Zhen, Yimeng Cao, Yusheng Zhao
abstract: Quantum information theory (QIT) characterizes the capabilities and fundamental limits of quantum information processing, underpinning quantum communication, computation, and error correction. Formalizing its coding theorems requires connecting finite-block protocols, analytic inequalities, and asymptotic limits within a unified machine-checked framework. Existing developments, however, lack a reusable operational layer that defines codes, error criteria, achievable rates, and capacities indepen

infographic.key_insight: Lean-QIT builds a reusable, machine-checked foundation for quantum information theory, making it easier to formally reason about coding theorems, rates, and capacities. In simple terms, it bridges finite protocols and asymptotic theory inside one proof framework.
infographic.problem_solved: Quantum information theory relies on a mix of operational definitions, analytic inequalities, and asymptotic arguments, but these pieces are often hard to formalize together. The paper addresses the lack of a reusable infrastructure for defining quantum codes, error metrics, achievable rates, and capacities in a theorem-prover setting.
method: Introduce a formal operational layer for quantum coding concepts such as codes, errors, rates, and capacities.
Connect finite-block protocols with asymptotic limit statements through machine-checked definitions and proofs.
Organize the theory so analytic results and coding theorems can be reused across different quantum information tasks.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners working on quantum machine learning, quantum communication, or verified algorithms, this provides a more reliable mathematical base for building and checking proofs. It can reduce ambiguity in quantum theory implementations and support future formal verification of quantum protocols.

title: The Count Is There, but Misaligned: Understanding and Correcting Counting Failures in VLMs
authors: Ahmed Oumar El-Shangiti, Abzal Nurgazy, Hilal AlQuabeh, Nikolai Rozanov, Kentaro Inui
abstract: Despite strong performance on many multimodal tasks, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with basic object counting. We investigate whether this reflects missing internal knowledge or a gap between internal representations and verbalized outputs. Training simple probes on activations from four VLMs across five counting datasets reveals that nonlinear probes can reliably detect counting errors, suggesting that VLMs often encode the correct count even when they output the wrong answer. SV

infographic.key_insight: Vision-language models often know the correct object count internally even when they say the wrong number. The failure is frequently a mismatch between internal representations and the final verbal output, not a complete lack of counting knowledge.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses why VLMs fail on basic object counting: whether the models are missing counting knowledge altogether or simply failing to express what they already encode.
method: Train simple probes on internal activations from four vision-language models.
Evaluate probe performance across five counting datasets to detect counting-related information.
Compare linear vs. nonlinear probes to test whether counting errors are linearly accessible or hidden in more complex representations.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that improving counting in VLMs may require better decoding or alignment of internal representations rather than only larger models or more data. It also shows that probing can reveal hidden capabilities and diagnose where multimodal models break down.

title: 4DR360: State Reasoning for Joint 3D Detection and Occupancy Prediction in 4D Radar-Camera Full-Scene Perception
authors: Xiaokai Bai, Lianqing Zheng, Runwei Guan, Songkai Wang, Siyuan Cao
abstract: Reliable autonomous driving requires full-scene perception that couples foreground objects with dense semantic layout. Recently, 4D millimeter-wave radar has emerged as a robust and affordable sensor, yet its sparse returns make radar-camera fusion necessary for comprehensive scene understanding. Existing radar-camera methods mainly optimize detection, while dual-task systems usually decode boxes and occupancy with limited interaction. To address this gap and advance radar-based multi-task learn

infographic.key_insight: 4DR360 introduces state reasoning to better connect 3D object detection with occupancy prediction in 4D radar-camera perception. The key idea is to let the system understand scene states more holistically, improving both foreground detection and dense scene layout estimation.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of existing radar-camera systems that focus mainly on bounding-box detection or treat detection or occupancy as loosely connected tasks. It targets the challenge of using sparse 4D radar signals, combined with cameras, to achieve reliable full-scene perception for autonomous driving.
method: Uses 4D radar-camera fusion to combine radar robustness with camera detail for full-scene understanding.
Introduces state reasoning to jointly model 3D detection and occupancy prediction instead of decoding them separately.
Strengthens interaction between object-level and scene-level outputs to improve consistency across tasks.
infographic.impact: This matters because autonomous driving systems need both accurate object localization and dense environment awareness to make safe decisions. For practitioners, the paper suggests a more integrated multi-task design for sensor fusion that can improve robustness in challenging driving conditions.

title: ALICE: Learning a General-Purpose Pathology Foundation Model from Vision, Vision-Language, and Slide-Level Experts
authors: Jiawen Li, Tian Guan, Huijuan Shi, Xitong Ling, Mingxi Fu
abstract: Foundation models are reshaping computational pathology, yet their capabilities remain shaped by pretraining objectives, data sources, and spatial scales, fragmenting complementary expertise across separate backbones. Here we present ALICE, a unified foundation model trained through multi-stage agglomerative distillation that sequentially distills eight vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level teacher models into dedicated modules of a single backbone. ALICE is pretrained on 24,985,184 tile

infographic.key_insight: ALICE unifies complementary pathology expertise from vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level teachers into one general-purpose foundation model. Instead of relying on a single pretraining style, it learns from multiple expert backbones to better cover different tasks and scales in computational pathology.
infographic.problem_solved: Computational pathology foundation models are often fragmented: different pretraining objectives, data types, and spatial scales create separate models with complementary strengths but no single unified backbone. This paper addresses the need for one model that can absorb and combine these diverse sources of expertise.
method: Uses multi-stage agglomerative distillation to transfer knowledge from eight teacher models into a single backbone.
Sequentially distills expertise from vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level experts into dedicated modules.
Pretrains ALICE on a very large pathology dataset of 24,985,184 tiles to build a broad general-purpose foundation model.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in pathology, ALICE offers a more unified starting point that may reduce the need to maintain multiple specialized backbones. It can simplify downstream adaptation across tasks while retaining strengths from different expert model families.

title: GatedLinear: Adaptive Routing of Complementary Linear Bases for Time Series Forecasting
authors: Qitai Tan, Ruiwen Gu, Yilin Su, Mo Li, Xu Lin
abstract: Time series forecasting requires models to capture diverse, often mutually exclusive, temporal dynamics, from smooth trend continuation to nonstationary drift and strict phase-aligned recurrence. While recent deep learning models have improved accuracy, they typically force these diverse patterns through a single computational backbone governed by fixed algorithmic inductive biases (e.g., self-attention or spectral filtering). This single-mechanism approach often struggles with the profound hete

infographic.key_insight: GatedLinear replaces the idea of forcing all time-series patterns through one model path with adaptive routing over complementary linear bases. This lets the model specialize on different temporal behaviors, such as smooth trends, drift, and recurring phases, improving flexibility for forecasting.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional forecasting models often use one fixed computational backbone, which makes it hard to handle diverse and sometimes conflicting temporal dynamics in the same series. The paper addresses the challenge of modeling heterogeneous patterns without relying on a single inductive bias.
method: Builds multiple complementary linear bases to represent different forecasting dynamics.
Uses a gating mechanism to route each input toward the most relevant basis adaptively.
Combines the selected basis outputs to produce the final forecast with greater pattern-specific specialization.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more modular and adaptable forecasting design that can better handle real-world series with mixed behaviors. It may improve accuracy and robustness while remaining simpler than heavily stacked deep architectures.

title: FreyaTTS Technical Report
authors: Ahmet Erdem Pamuk, Ömer Yentür, Ahmet Tunga Bayrak, Yavuz Alp Sencer Öztürk, Mustafa Yavuz
abstract: We introduce Freya-TTS, a compact, tokenizer-free, Turkish-first text-to-speech model designed for highly reliable and efficient conversational synthesis. Freya-TTS is a 183.2M-parameter non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that operates in the frozen continuous latent space of AudioVAE2 (16 kHz encode, 48 kHz decode), allowing the model to focus its capacity on text-to-latent mapping while inheriting high-quality 48 kHz reconstruction. We advance the framewor

infographic.key_insight: Freya-TTS is a compact, Turkish-first text-to-speech model that aims to generate highly reliable conversational speech efficiently. Its main idea is to move speech generation into a frozen audio latent space, so the model can focus on mapping text to high-quality speech representations rather than predicting audio directly.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the need for a fast, compact, and dependable TTS system for Turkish speech synthesis, especially for conversational use cases. It targets the challenge of producing natural speech with high fidelity while keeping the model efficient and tokenization-free.
method: Uses a 183.2M-parameter non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT).
Generates in the frozen continuous latent space of AudioVAE2, using 16 kHz encoding and 48 kHz decoding for high-quality reconstruction.
Avoids text tokenization, focusing model capacity on direct text-to-latent mapping for more efficient and robust synthesis.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, Freya-TTS shows a practical path to building smaller, more efficient TTS systems without sacrificing audio quality. Its tokenizer-free, latent-space design could simplify deployment and improve reliability for real-world conversational speech applications.

title: Seeing is Free, Speaking is Not: Uncovering the True Energy Bottleneck in Edge VLM Inference
authors: Junfei Zhan, Haoxun Shen, Mingang Guo, Zixuan Huang, Tengjiao He
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the perceptual backbone of embodied AI, but their energy footprint on edge hardware remains poorly understood. Existing efficiency efforts focus predominantly on reducing visual tokens, implicitly treating visual processing as the dominant energy cost. We overturn this implicit assumption through the first systematic energy profiling of on-device VLM inference, spanning five models across three architecture families, four input resolutions, and two hardware plat

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that, on edge hardware, the main energy bottleneck in VLM inference is often the language/decoder side rather than the vision encoder. In other words: seeing is comparatively cheap, while speaking is what costs the most energy.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of a clear, systematic understanding of where energy is actually spent during on-device Vision-Language Model inference, challenging the common assumption that reducing visual tokens is the primary path to efficiency.
method: Performs the first systematic energy profiling of edge VLM inference across multiple model families, input resolutions, and hardware platforms.
Compares energy costs between visual processing and language generation to identify the true dominant bottleneck.
Analyzes how architecture choice and input resolution affect energy use, enabling more accurate optimization targets.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes edge-optimization strategy: focusing only on fewer visual tokens may miss the biggest energy savings. The findings can guide better model design, deployment decisions, and hardware-aware optimization for embodied and mobile AI systems.

title: ConceptSMILE: Auditing the Trustworthiness of Concept-Based Explainable AI
authors: Mohadeseh Mollapour, Koorosh Aslansefat, Zeinab Dehghani, Bhupesh Kumar Mishra, Tejal Shah
abstract: Concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (AI) can make model reasoning more human-understandable, but concept-level outputs are not automatically trustworthy. We introduce ConceptSMILE, a model-agnostic perturbation-based auditing framework for evaluating the reliability of concept-based explanations. Rather than replacing SMILE, ConceptSMILE extends its perturbation-based logic from feature- or region-level attribution to the auditing of human-understandable concept explanations. The f

infographic.key_insight: Concept-based explanations in AI may look human-friendly, but they are not automatically reliable. ConceptSMILE extends perturbation-based auditing to check whether concept-level explanations truly reflect model behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of trustworthy evaluation methods for concept-based explainable AI, where explanations can be interpretable but still misleading, unstable, or unfaithful to the model.
method: Introduces ConceptSMILE, a model-agnostic auditing framework built on perturbation-based evaluation.
Extends the SMILE idea from feature- or region-level attribution to human-understandable concept explanations.
Assesses whether changes to input perturbations produce explanation responses that are consistent with trustworthy concept-level reasoning.
infographic.impact: This gives AI/ML practitioners a practical way to audit concept-based XAI methods before using them in high-stakes settings. It helps ensure explanations are not just understandable, but also reliable and faithful to the model.

title: ARDY: Autoregressive Diffusion with Hybrid Representation for Interactive Human Motion Generation
authors: Kaifeng Zhao, Mathis Petrovich, Haotian Zhang, Tingwu Wang, Siyu Tang
abstract: Generating realistic 3D human motions in real-time within interactive applications is key for animation, simulation, and humanoid robotics. While recent offline motion generation approaches offer precise control via text and kinematic constraints, they lack the inference speed required for interactive settings. Conversely, existing online methods enable real-time synthesis but often sacrifice controllability or struggle with complex text semantics and long-horizon goals due to limited context wi

infographic.key_insight: ARDY aims to bring high-quality human motion generation into interactive, real-time settings by combining the speed of autoregressive generation with the expressiveness of diffusion models. Its hybrid representation helps preserve controllability while handling complex motion semantics and long-horizon goals.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between offline motion generation methods, which are controllable but too slow for interactive use, and online methods, which are fast but often less controllable and weaker at understanding rich text prompts or long-term motion objectives.
method: Uses an autoregressive diffusion framework to generate motion incrementally for interactive responsiveness.
Introduces a hybrid representation to better balance realism, controllability, and temporal consistency.
Targets complex text-conditioned and long-horizon human motion generation in real time.
infographic.impact: This is useful for practitioners building animation tools, simulation systems, and humanoid agents that need both low-latency inference and expressive control. It points toward a practical path for deploying motion generation in interactive environments without sacrificing quality.

title: Wat3R: Underwater 3D Geometry Learning without Annotations
authors: Jiangwei Ren, Xingyu Jiang, Zijie Song, Wei Xu, Hongkai Lin
abstract: Estimating 3D geometry in underwater environments presents unique challenges due to light attenuation, scattering, and the absence of large-scale, high-quality 3D annotations. Pioneering methods rely on massive dense annotations that are impractical in underwater settings. In this paper, we propose Wat3R, a cross-domain semi-supervised learning framework designed to adapt feed-forward 3D reconstruction models from air to underwater scenes. Uniquely, our method eliminates the need for any annotat

infographic.key_insight: Wat3R shows that underwater 3D geometry can be learned without expensive underwater annotations by adapting a model trained on air to the underwater domain. It uses semi-supervised cross-domain learning to make feed-forward 3D reconstruction practical in scenes where labeled data is scarce.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses underwater 3D reconstruction, which is difficult because of light attenuation, scattering, and the lack of large-scale, high-quality 3D annotations.
method: Adapts feed-forward 3D reconstruction models from air images to underwater scenes using a cross-domain semi-supervised framework.
Removes the dependence on dense underwater 3D labels by leveraging unlabeled or weakly labeled data.
Learns robust geometry despite underwater visual degradation such as haze, color shift, and scattering.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it reduces the annotation burden for 3D learning in hard-to-collect environments. It can enable scalable underwater mapping, robotics, marine inspection, and scientific exploration with less manual labeling.

title: OpenCoF: Learning to Reason Through Video Generation
authors: Xinyan Chen, Ziyu Guo, Renrui Zhang, Dongzhi Jiang, Hongsheng Li
abstract: Reasoning has become a core capability for large models, especially when reliable decisions require understanding logical consequences. Recent video generation models offer a reasoning path distinct from previous Chain-of-Thought (CoT): reasoning can unfold through temporally connected frames, known as Chain-of-Frame (CoF) reasoning. However, existing video generators are primarily trained on general video corpora, still lacking diverse supervision and dedicated designs for CoF reasoning. To add

infographic.key_insight: OpenCoF argues that video generation can be used as a new reasoning medium: instead of thinking only in text, a model can reason through temporally linked frames (Chain-of-Frame reasoning). The paper’s key idea is to better supervise and design video generators so they can express structured reasoning, not just produce realistic videos.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of dedicated supervision and model design for reasoning with video generation. Existing video generators are trained mostly on generic video datasets, which limits their ability to represent diverse logical steps across frames.
method: Introduces OpenCoF, a framework focused on learning reasoning through video generation.
Uses temporally connected frames as a reasoning pathway to model Chain-of-Frame (CoF) behavior.
Adds more diverse supervision and task-oriented design to improve a generator’s ability to express multi-step logical consequences in video form.
infographic.impact: This matters because it expands how AI systems can reason: not only by generating text explanations, but by producing structured visual sequences that reveal intermediate thought steps. For practitioners, this could improve interpretability, evaluation, and new multimodal reasoning applications.

title: Geometry and Gradient-based Partitioning for Panoramic Outdoor Reconstruction
authors: Weijian Chen, Weibo Yao, Yuhang Zhang, Xiaolin Tang, Guo Wang
abstract: Scaling 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to large outdoor scenes is costly in both data acquisition and computation. Adopting panoramic images with equirectangular projection (ERP) can reduce capture effort via their full $360^{\circ}$ field of view, yet the resulting omnipresent visibility invalidates existing partitioning strategies that rely on local camera frustums, causing block-wise optimization to degenerate into global training. Thus, we propose PanoLOG, a two-stage coarse-to-fine framework

infographic.key_insight: PanoLOG makes large-scale outdoor 3D reconstruction practical with panoramic images by replacing camera-frustum-based partitioning with geometry- and gradient-aware scene partitioning. This preserves efficient block-wise training even when every panorama sees nearly the whole scene.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high data-collection and computation cost of scaling 3D Gaussian Splatting to large outdoor environments. It specifically solves the failure of existing partitioning methods under 360° equirectangular panoramic imagery, where omnidirectional visibility turns local optimization into near-global training.
method: Uses panoramic equirectangular images to reduce capture effort while retaining full-scene coverage.
Introduces a two-stage coarse-to-fine framework called PanoLOG for outdoor reconstruction.
Partitions the scene using geometry and gradient signals instead of relying on local camera frustums that do not exist in panoramic setups.
infographic.impact: This approach makes panoramic 3D reconstruction more scalable and efficient for real-world outdoor scenes. For practitioners, it offers a way to lower capture cost and keep optimization tractable without sacrificing coverage.

title: Ideas Have Genomes: Benchmarking Scientific Lineage Reasoning and Lineage-Grounded Idea Generation
authors: Yifan Zhou, Qihao Yang, Yan Li, Donggang Li, Xiru Hu
abstract: Scientific ideas rarely start from a blank page. They inherit mechanisms, repair known limitations, and recombine pieces of earlier work, much like biological genomes. Current benchmarks still say little about whether AI systems can follow this inheritance structure. We present IdeaGene-Bench (IG-Bench), a benchmark for scientific lineage reasoning and lineage-grounded idea generation. IG-Bench is organized around the IdeaGene framework: each paper or proposal is represented as a set of minimal,

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces IdeaGene-Bench (IG-Bench), a benchmark designed to test whether AI can reason about how scientific ideas evolve through lineage rather than generating ideas from scratch. It treats ideas like genomes—built from inherited mechanisms, fixes, and recombinations of prior work.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks do not measure whether AI systems can understand scientific lineage or generate ideas grounded in that lineage. This work addresses the gap between simple idea generation and the more realistic process of building on prior research.
method: Proposes the IdeaGene framework, representing each paper or proposal as a set of minimal components that capture how ideas inherit and evolve.
Builds IG-Bench to evaluate two capabilities: scientific lineage reasoning and lineage-grounded idea generation.
Organizes benchmark tasks around tracing connections between prior work, limitations, mechanisms, and proposed extensions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark offers a more realistic way to evaluate research assistants and idea-generation systems. It can help identify models that not only produce novel-sounding proposals but can also ground them in scientific history and logical inheritance.

title: UniClawBench: A Universal Benchmark for Proactive Agents on Real-World Tasks
authors: Zhekai Chen, Chengqi Duan, Kaiyue Sun, Bohao Li, Yuqing Wang
abstract: The rapid development of large language models and multimodal large language models has accelerated the emergence of proactive agents capable of operating everyday tools and assisting users in real-world environments. However, existing benchmarks struggle to evaluate such agents effectively, as they often rely on sandboxed environments and single-turn evaluation paradigms. Moreover, their scenario-based task taxonomies mix multiple model capabilities within the same task category, making it diff

infographic.key_insight: UniClawBench introduces a universal benchmark designed to evaluate proactive agents in realistic, tool-using, everyday scenarios. It aims to measure agent behavior more faithfully than sandboxed, single-turn benchmarks by reflecting the complexity of real-world tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Current benchmarks for proactive AI agents are often too artificial, too limited to isolated turn-based interactions, and too mixed in what they measure. This makes it hard to fairly assess whether an agent can actually use tools, act proactively, and perform end-to-end tasks in real environments.
method: Defines a universal benchmark focused on real-world proactive agent tasks rather than synthetic sandbox settings.
Uses more realistic evaluation setups that better capture multi-step tool use and user-facing behavior.
Separates task categories more clearly so different capabilities are measured more cleanly and comparably.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more reliable way to test whether agents can function in practical settings beyond demos. It can improve model comparison, guide agent development, and reduce overfitting to narrow benchmark formats.
