abstract: Existing instruction-based video editing datasets commonly focus on single-task appearance editing, failing to meet the complex creative demands of real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present Goku, a large-scale dataset featuring 2 million high-quality, instruction-aligned video editing pairs, which is the first to extend task boundaries from basic appearance editing to multi-task and structural manipulations(e.g., precise control of subject movement). To tackle the data synthesis chall

infographic.key_insight: Goku introduces a million-scale, instruction-aligned video editing dataset that goes beyond simple appearance changes to support multi-task and structural video edits. This expands video editing benchmarks toward more realistic, complex creative control.
infographic.problem_solved: Current instruction-based video editing datasets are too narrow, mostly covering single-task appearance editing. They do not adequately represent real-world editing needs such as multi-step transformations and precise subject motion control.
method: Built Goku, a 2 million-pair video editing dataset with high-quality instruction-video alignment.
Extended the task scope from basic appearance edits to multi-task and structural manipulations, including controlled subject movement.
Designed the dataset to serve as a benchmark for evaluating more capable instruction-based video editing models.
infographic.impact: This dataset gives researchers a much richer training and evaluation resource for instruction-based video editing. It can help drive models that understand complex user prompts and perform more realistic, controllable video transformations.

title: Beyond 2D Matching: A Unified Single-Stage Framework for Geometry-Aware Cross-View Object Geo-Localization
authors: Liyao Wang, Ruipu Wu, Haojun Xu, Lei Shi, Linjiang Huang
abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to locate a target object from a query view (e.g., ground or drone) within a geo-tagged reference image (e.g., satellite). Existing approaches heavily rely on 2D appearance matching and are constrained by limited datasets lacking geometric metadata, diverse prompts, and standard field-of-view imagery. To address these intertwined challenges, we first introduce \dataset, a large-scale, high-fidelity building dataset comprising over 220,000 ground-sa

infographic.key_insight: This paper moves cross-view object geo-localization beyond simple 2D appearance matching by making geometry a first-class signal. It also pairs the model with a large, high-fidelity building dataset to better support real-world localization.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of locating an object across different views, such as ground or drone images matched to satellite imagery, where existing methods struggle because they depend too much on 2D visual similarity and lack rich geometric supervision, diverse prompts, and standard field-of-view data.
method: Introduces a large-scale building dataset with over 220,000 geo-tagged samples and high-fidelity geometric information.
Proposes a unified single-stage framework for cross-view object geo-localization that incorporates geometry-aware reasoning.
Targets more robust matching across view changes by using both appearance cues and spatial/geometric structure.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work offers a more realistic path to object localization in cross-view settings by improving robustness to viewpoint shifts. title: A Multi-task Mixture of Experts Framework for Malware Classification, Packing Detection, and Family Attribution
authors: Jithin S., Roshin Sleeba C., Anvin Mariya P. B., Asmitha K. A., Vinod P.
abstract: Malware classification remains a challenging problem due to its inherent heterogeneity, the presence of packed binaries, and the diverse distribution of malware families. Traditional single-model detection mechanisms often fail to generalize across such diverse data, leading to degraded performance, particularly on obfuscated and rare malware samples. In this work, we propose a unified multi-task malware analysis framework based on Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures. The proposed system eval

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces a unified multi-task malware analysis framework that uses a Mixture of Experts (MoE) to handle classification, packing detection, and family attribution together. The main idea is to improve robustness on heterogeneous, obfuscated, and rare malware samples by routing inputs to specialized expert models.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of accurately analyzing malware when samples are diverse, packed, or heavily obfuscated. Traditional single-model approaches often struggle to generalize across different malware families and fail on rare or disguised binaries.
method: Builds a multi-task framework that performs malware classification, packing detection, and family attribution in one system.
Uses a Mixture of Experts architecture so different experts can specialize in different malware patterns or sample types.
Aims to improve generalization and robustness, especially for packed binaries and underrepresented malware families.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how MoE can be applied to cybersecurity problems where data is highly heterogeneous and labels span multiple related tasks. It offers a practical path toward more resilient malware detection systems that can better handle real-world obfuscation and class imbalance.

title: LeVo 2: Stable and Melodious Song Generation via Hierarchical Representation Modeling and Progressive Post-Training
authors: Shun Lei, Huaicheng Zhang, Dapeng Wu, Yaoxun Xu, Lishi Zuo
abstract: Full-length song generation must preserve coherence and musicality, render detailed vocal and accompaniment acoustics, and follow lyrics and prompts. Existing language model-based systems face a structural trade-off: mixed-token modeling preserves vocal-instrument coordination but obscures track-specific details, whereas dual-track prediction improves acoustics but requires longer sequences and weakens global planning. We present LeVo 2, a hybrid LLM-Diffusion framework for controllable full-len

infographic.key_insight: LeVo 2 improves full-length song generation by combining hierarchical representation modeling with progressive post-training, aiming to keep lyrics, structure, and audio quality aligned. It addresses the common trade-off between preserving global musical coherence and rendering detailed vocal/accompaniment acoustics.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles full-song generation where models must stay coherent over long durations, follow lyrics and prompts, and produce realistic vocals plus accompaniment. It specifically addresses the limitation that mixed-token models blur track-specific detail, while dual-track models increase sequence length and reduce global planning ability.
method: Uses a hybrid LLM-Diffusion framework for controllable full-length song generation.
Introduces hierarchical representation modeling to capture both high-level song structure and finer track-level acoustic details.
Applies progressive post-training to gradually improve controllability, stability, and musicality during generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a practical path toward higher-quality long-form music generation without sacrificing either structure or fidelity. The approach may also generalize to other long-sequence generative tasks that need both global planning and detailed local rendering.

title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations via Test-Time Adaptation for Anomaly Segmentation
authors: Ali Zia, Usman Ali, Abdul Rehman, Umer Ramzan, Kang Han
abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a promising paradigm for mitigating distribution shifts in deep models. However, existing TTA approaches for anomaly segmentation remain limited by their reliance on pixel-level heuristics, such as confidence thresholding or entropy minimisation, which fail to preserve structural consistency under noise and texture variation. Moreover, they typically treat anomaly maps as flat intensity fields, ignoring the higher-order spatial relationships that charact

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that anomaly segmentation can be made more robust at test time by adapting models with topology-aware representations, rather than relying only on pixel-wise confidence or entropy. By preserving structural relationships in the anomaly map, the method better handles noise and texture shifts.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the fragility of existing test-time adaptation methods for anomaly segmentation, which often depend on pixel-level heuristics and ignore spatial/topological structure. These methods can break under distribution shift, noisy inputs, or complex textures.
method: Uses test-time adaptation to adjust the model on unseen data without requiring retraining.
Learns topology-aware representations so the anomaly map preserves higher-order spatial consistency instead of treating it as a flat intensity field.
Reduces dependence on brittle pixel-level rules like confidence thresholding and entropy minimization.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means more reliable anomaly segmentation in real-world deployments where test data differs from training data. It can improve robustness in inspection, medical imaging, and industrial defect detection settings.

title: Agent-Native Immune System: Architecture, Taxonomy, and Engineering
authors: Bo Shen, Lifeng Chang, Tianyuan Wei, Yunpeng Li, Feng Shi
abstract: The transition from static chat bots to autonomous agents--equipped with persistent memory, tool-use protocols, and multi-agent collaboration--has fundamentally expanded the AI threat landscape. Current defense mechanisms, such as perimeter security and training-time alignment, remain external to the agent's active reasoning loop. Consequently, they fall short: a fully aligned agent remains highly vulnerable to runtime hijacking via memory poisoning, tool-chain manipulation, or multi-agent proto

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that autonomous agents need an "immune system" built into the agent itself, not just external security guards. By moving defense into the active reasoning loop, it aims to protect agents from runtime attacks like memory poisoning, tool misuse, and multi-agent manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap between static AI safety methods and the new risks introduced by persistent, tool-using, multi-agent systems. Existing defenses often fail once an agent is operating in the real world and can be hijacked during execution.
method: Proposes an agent-native security architecture that monitors and defends the agent during reasoning and action, rather than only before deployment.
Defines a taxonomy of threats targeting agent memory, tools, and collaboration channels.
Outlines engineering principles for integrating detection, isolation, and response mechanisms directly into agent workflows.
infographic.impact: For AI practitioners, this reframes safety as a runtime systems problem, not just a training-time alignment problem. It provides a blueprint for building more robust autonomous agents that can operate safely in open-ended environments.

title: RSICCLLM: A Multimodal Large Language Model for Remote Sensing Image Change Captioning
authors: Yelin Wang, Zijia Song, Shuo Ye, Chuanguang Yang, Miaoyu Wang
abstract: Remote Sensing Image Change Captioning (RSICC) aims to describe changes between bi-temporal remote sensing images and holds significant research and application value. However, most existing methods rely on conventional deep learning architectures, and the limited model capacity constrains performance. Although large-model post-training techniques have achieved great success in general domains, their direct transfer to RSICC remains challenging due to data scarcity and the need for fine-grained

infographic.key_insight: RSICCLLM adapts a multimodal large language model to remote sensing image change captioning, aiming to generate more accurate and fine-grained descriptions of changes between two satellite images. The key idea is to overcome the limited capacity of conventional RSICC models by leveraging large-model post-training for a specialized remote sensing task.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of describing changes between bi-temporal remote sensing images, where existing deep learning methods often struggle with limited model capacity, sparse training data, and the need for detailed, context-aware captions.
method: Builds a multimodal large language model tailored for remote sensing change captioning.
Adapts large-model post-training techniques to the RSICC setting to improve language generation quality and change understanding.
Targets fine-grained cross-temporal visual comparison so the model can describe subtle scene changes more precisely.
infographic.impact: This work shows how foundation-model style approaches can be transferred into remote sensing, offering a path toward stronger captioning systems with better generalization and richer descriptions. For practitioners, it suggests a practical direction for combining multimodal LLMs with Earth observation tasks that require both visual reasoning and natural language generation.

title: HPRO: Hierarchical Progressive Reward Optimization via Preference Extraction for Emotional Text-to-Speech
authors: Sihang Nie, Xiaofen Xing, Rui Xing, Haoming Li, Ruitong Xiao
abstract: Recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) models have achieved remarkable naturalness. However, the standard Supervised Fine-Tuning paradigm often converges to statistically averaged prosody, limiting emotional expressiveness. While preference-driven optimization offers a promising alternative, existing approaches suffer from two structural mismatches: information conflict, where content and emotion in a shared latent space produce conflicting gradients, leading to reward h

infographic.key_insight: HPRO improves emotional text-to-speech by optimizing preferences in a staged, hierarchical way instead of forcing one shared latent space to learn everything at once. This reduces conflict between content and emotion, helping models produce more expressive and controllable speech.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of supervised fine-tuning in LLM-based TTS, which often produces average, less emotional prosody. It also tackles two structural mismatches in preference optimization: information conflict between content and emotion, and reward imbalance that can weaken emotional learning.
method: Introduces Hierarchical Progressive Reward Optimization (HPRO), a preference-based training strategy for emotional TTS.
Uses preference extraction to separate and better align content-related and emotion-related learning signals.
Applies progressive, hierarchical reward optimization to reduce gradient conflicts and improve expressive prosody generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work offers a more robust way to train emotionally expressive TTS systems without collapsing into bland average speech. It may also inspire similar hierarchical preference-optimization strategies for other generative models with competing objectives.

title: Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool
authors: Rajesh Jayaram, Drew Tyler, David Woodruff, Corinna Cortes, Yossi Matias
abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving a revolution in scientific discovery, accelerating everything from hypothesis generation to mathematical theorem proving. However, this rapid acceleration is creating a systemic challenge: traditional human peer review cannot scale to match the influx of AI-assisted science. Ultimately, to resolve this tension, we must also deploy AI to accelerate the verification and review process itself. To frame the discussion around this transition, we propose a taxonomy c

infographic.key_insight: AI is making scientific discovery faster than traditional peer review can handle, so the review process itself must also be automated with AI. This paper frames that shift by proposing a taxonomy for how tools like Google’s Paper Assistant can help verify and review scientific work at scale.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the growing mismatch between the speed of AI-assisted research generation and the limited capacity of human peer review, which creates bottlenecks in validating scientific results.
method: Proposes a taxonomy to organize the roles and capabilities of AI in scientific review.
Frames Google’s Paper Assistant as an example of AI support for verification, review, and evaluation workflows.
Explores how automated tools can complement human reviewers rather than fully replace them.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work highlights a coming shift toward AI-assisted validation pipelines for papers, experiments, and claims. It suggests new opportunities for tools that improve review throughput, consistency, and scalability.

title: Democratic ICAI: Debating Our Way to Steering Principles from Preferences
authors: Kevin Kingslin, Anish Natekar, Ashutosh Ranjan, Vivek Srivastava, Savita Bhat
abstract: Preference-based alignment often struggles to capture the reasoning that underlies human judgments. Many evaluations rely on multiple interacting criteria, yet pairwise labels reveal only the final choice rather than the considerations that shape preferences. Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) improves interpretability in decision making by summarizing preferences into natural-language principles, but its single-pass explanations miss much of the nuance involved in complex decisions. We introduce

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that complex human preferences are better captured by debating them step-by-step rather than compressing them into a single explanation. By turning preference feedback into a democratic, multi-round process, it aims to uncover more faithful and nuanced steering principles.
infographic.problem_solved: Preference-based alignment often records only the final winner of a comparison, not the reasoning behind it. Existing ICAI-style methods summarize preferences into natural-language principles, but a single-pass summary can miss important tradeoffs, hidden criteria, and nuance in difficult judgments.
method: Uses a debating-style framework to iteratively surface and refine the reasons behind preferences.
Transforms pairwise human preferences into steering principles through multiple rounds instead of one-shot summarization.
Aims to aggregate diverse judgment signals into more interpretable, natural-language alignment principles.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more interpretable way to learn alignment signals from human feedback. It can improve the fidelity of preference modeling in settings where decisions depend on multiple competing criteria.

title: How Width and Data Shape Generalization Scaling Laws in Quadratic Neural Networks
authors: Julius Girardin, Emanuele Troiani, Yizhou Xu, Vittorio Erba, Florent Krzakala
abstract: Understanding how performance scales jointly with model size and data is a central problem in modern machine learning. Existing theoretical works on scaling laws typically describe generalization as a function of data or compute, often in fixed-feature or infinite-width regimes and for online SGD. Here, we instead study how generalization scales with the number of trainable parameters and the number of samples in a feature-learning model. We analyze $\ell_2$-regularized empirical test error mini

infographic.key_insight: This paper studies how generalization improves when you scale both the number of trainable parameters and the amount of data in a feature-learning model, rather than treating one of them in isolation. It provides scaling-law insights for quadratic neural networks, helping explain the joint role of width and dataset size.
infographic.problem_solved: Most existing scaling-law theories focus on either data or compute in fixed-feature or infinite-width settings. This work addresses the missing question of how test error scales jointly with model width and sample size in a trainable, feature-learning neural network.
method: Analyze \(\ell_2\)-regularized empirical test error in a quadratic neural network setting.
Study how generalization changes as both the number of parameters and the number of training samples vary.
Derive scaling-law behavior in a regime that captures feature learning rather than only fixed-feature or infinite-width limits.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this helps predict when adding parameters versus adding data will most improve performance. It can guide more efficient model scaling and dataset planning in settings where feature learning matters.

title: Bridging Ab Initio Symmetries and Global Nuclear Masses with Interpretable Neural Networks
authors: Phong Dang, Evander Espinoza, Xiaoliang Wan, Michela Negro, Jerry P. Draayer
abstract: Ab initio modeling has established Wigner's SU(4) and Elliott's SU(3) as dominant symmetries of the nuclear force in light and intermediate-mass nuclei. We ask whether they also govern nuclear binding across the entire chart. Our aim is not high-precision prediction but physical insight, through interpretable, symmetry-based models. From the SU(3) and SU(4) Casimir operators we construct three neural-network (NN) mass models: Feature-Informed NN (FINN) for point predictions, Gaussian-Informed NN

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that long-studied nuclear symmetries, especially SU(3) and SU(4), can be turned into interpretable neural-network features that help explain nuclear masses across the chart. Instead of chasing only prediction accuracy, the models aim to reveal whether fundamental symmetry structure still governs binding energy globally.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of modeling nuclear masses in a way that is both physically meaningful and interpretable. Traditional high-accuracy methods can work well but often obscure the underlying physics, while ab initio symmetry ideas have mostly been tested in lighter nuclei rather than across the full nuclear landscape.
method: Derive input features from SU(3) and SU(4) Casimir operators, which encode symmetry information from nuclear structure.
Build interpretable neural-network mass models, including a Feature-Informed NN (FINN) for point predictions and related Gaussian-informed variants.
Use these symmetry-aware models to test whether ab initio symmetries provide useful global guidance for nuclear binding, prioritizing insight over pure predictive performance.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this is a strong example of physics-informed and interpretable learning: models are designed around domain theory rather than opaque end-to-end fitting. It highlights how embedding known structure into neural networks can improve scientific understanding, not just prediction quality.

title: PerceptionRubrics: Calibrating Multimodal Evaluation to Human Perception
authors: Yana Wei, Hongbo Peng, Yanlin Lai, Liang Zhao, Kangheng Lin
abstract: We introduce PerceptionRubrics, a rubric-based evaluation framework that addresses the gap between saturated benchmark scores and real-world brittleness. Shifting evaluation from holistic semantic matching to rigorous atomic auditing, PerceptionRubrics pairs 1,038 information-dense images with over 12,000 instance-specific rubrics. These criteria are derived from golden captions constructed via a novel Circular Peer-Review consensus pipeline and then distilled into a dual-stream system of Must-R

infographic.key_insight: PerceptionRubrics replaces broad, holistic multimodal scoring with fine-grained atomic audits that better reflect how humans actually judge images and captions. It aims to make evaluation more calibrated, consistent, and resistant to benchmark saturation.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the mismatch between high benchmark scores and poor real-world robustness in multimodal models. Existing evaluations often miss small but important errors because they rely on coarse semantic matching rather than precise human-like judgments.
method: Builds a dataset of 1,038 information-dense images paired with 12,000+ instance-specific rubrics.
Creates golden captions using a Circular Peer-Review consensus pipeline to derive reliable, human-aligned criteria.
Distills the rubrics into a dual-stream evaluation system with Must-Require and Must-Avoid checks for atomic auditing.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more trustworthy way to measure multimodal model quality and catch subtle failures that standard benchmarks overlook. It can improve model selection, debugging, and safer deployment by aligning evaluation with human perception.

title: DexCompose: Reusing Dexterous Policies for Multi-Task Manipulation with a Single Hand
authors: Dihong Huang, Zhenyu Wei, Zhuxiu Xu, Yunchao Yao, Sikai Li
abstract: Dexterous manipulation policies can solve individual skills, but composing them to perform multiple tasks with a single hand remains challenging. Adding a new task on top of an existing manipulation skill often imposes conflicting demands on overlapping fingers and contact modes, causing destructive interference between preserving an existing manipulation outcome and executing a new one. We propose DexCompose, a role-aware residual composition framework that reuses pretrained dexterous policies

infographic.key_insight: DexCompose shows that dexterous hand policies do not need to be learned from scratch for every task. By composing pretrained skills in a role-aware way, a single hand can reuse existing behaviors while adding new ones with less interference.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the difficulty of combining multiple dexterous manipulation skills on one hand. New tasks often conflict with existing ones because the same fingers and contact modes must satisfy competing objectives, leading to destructive interference.
method: Introduces DexCompose, a role-aware residual composition framework for reusing pretrained dexterous policies.
Separates manipulation roles so the system can preserve the original skill while selectively adding residual control for the new task.
Designed to reduce overlap-induced conflict between tasks that share fingers, contacts, or motion patterns.
infographic.impact: This matters because it can make dexterous manipulation more scalable and data-efficient, especially when practitioners want to build multi-task systems without training a new policy for every skill. It also offers a practical path toward reusable robot hand capabilities in real-world settings.

title: StructSplat: Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting from Uncalibrated Sparse Views
authors: Jia-Chen Zhao, Beiqi Chen, Xinyang Chen, Guangcong Wang, Liqiang Nie
abstract: We present StructSplat, a feed-forward and generalizable 3D Gaussian reconstruction framework that operates directly on uncalibrated images without requiring camera parameters. Existing methods either rely on per-scene optimization or assume known camera poses, and often entangle geometry and appearance within a unified backbone, limiting reconstruction fidelity and generalization. Our key idea is to adopt a structured representation that organizes geometry, semantic, and texture cues with expli

infographic.key_insight: StructSplat shows that high-quality 3D Gaussian reconstructions can be generated directly from uncalibrated sparse images, without camera poses or per-scene optimization. It improves generalization by separating geometry, semantic, and texture information into a structured representation instead of mixing them in one backbone.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the challenge of reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse, uncalibrated views when camera parameters are unavailable or expensive to obtain. It addresses the limitations of methods that depend on known poses or scene-specific optimization and struggle to generalize well.
method: Uses a feed-forward, generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting pipeline that works directly on raw uncalibrated images.
Introduces a structured representation to disentangle geometry, semantic, and texture cues for better reconstruction fidelity.
Avoids per-scene fitting and camera calibration, enabling faster and more scalable 3D reconstruction from sparse inputs.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this makes 3D reconstruction more practical in real-world settings where camera calibration is missing or unreliable. It also points toward more generalizable and efficient scene reconstruction systems for robotics, AR/VR, and vision applications.

title: Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models
authors: Niclas Lietzow, Danielle Bitterman, Carsten Eickhoff, William Rudman, Michal Golovanevsky
abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile visual evidence with memorized world knowledge when the two conflict. How they resolve this conflict shapes the reliability of multimodal systems, yet prior work characterizes it behaviorally without a component-level causal account. We combine activation patching across three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers) with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis. Across three VLM families, we find that visual groun

infographic.key_insight: Vision-language models do not simply follow what they see; their internal components can be traced as either amplifying visual evidence or letting prior knowledge override it when the two conflict. The paper shows this behavior has a causal, component-level basis across multiple model families.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of understanding how multimodal models resolve conflicts between visual input and memorized world knowledge, moving beyond behavioral descriptions to identify which internal parts cause the model to trust vision versus prior knowledge.
method: Uses activation patching at three levels of granularity: residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers.
Combines patching with component ablation to test which parts of the model are causally responsible for perception-knowledge conflict resolution.
Performs mechanistic analysis across three vision-language model families to compare whether visual grounding or prior knowledge dominates under conflict.
infographic.impact: This work gives practitioners a clearer map of where multimodal errors come from inside the model, which can help with debugging, interpretability, and safer deployment. It also informs strategies for improving robustness when models face misleading or ambiguous visual inputs.

title: Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators
authors: Danyal Rehman, Charlie B. Tan, Yoshua Bengio, Avishek Joey Bose, Alexander Tong
abstract: Efficient sampling of molecular systems at thermodynamic equilibrium is a hallmark challenge in statistical physics. This challenge has driven the development of Boltzmann Generators (BGs), which allow rapid generation of uncorrelated equilibrium samples by combining a generative model with exact likelihoods and an importance sampling correction. However, modern BGs predominantly rely on normalizing flows (NFs), which either suffer from limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraint

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces autoregressive Boltzmann Generators, aiming to improve equilibrium sampling for molecular systems by relaxing some of the expressivity limits of standard normalizing-flow-based BGs. The core idea is to keep the benefits of exact likelihoods and importance-sampling correction while enabling a more flexible generative model.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of efficiently generating uncorrelated equilibrium samples from molecular systems, a key challenge in statistical physics and molecular simulation. Existing Boltzmann Generators built on normalizing flows can be too restrictive because of invertibility constraints that limit model expressivity.
method: Use an autoregressive generative architecture for Boltzmann Generators instead of relying only on traditional normalizing flows.
Preserve exact likelihood computation and combine it with importance sampling correction to sample equilibrium states efficiently.
Improve flexibility in representing complex molecular distributions while maintaining tractable training and sampling.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work suggests a more expressive path for physics-aware generative modeling where strict flow constraints may no longer be necessary. It is especially relevant for scientific machine learning, molecular simulation, and any application requiring efficient sampling from complex high-dimensional distributions.

title: Paying More Attention to Visual Tokens in Self-Evolving Large Multimodal Models
authors: Shravan Venkatraman, Ritesh Thawkar, Omkar Thawakar, Rao Muhammad Anwer, Hisham Cholakkal
abstract: Recently, self-evolving large multimodal models (LMMs) have received attention for improving visual reasoning in a purely unsupervised setting. However, multi-role self-play and self-consistency reward schemes in existing self-evolving LMMs optimize answer agreement without ensuring the decoder attends to visual content, relying instead on statistical language priors to produce self consistent outputs. This leads to a persistent failure mode we term visual under-conditioning, where the decoder r

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that self-evolving multimodal models can become "self-consistently wrong" if they optimize for answer agreement without forcing the decoder to use visual evidence. Its key takeaway is that improving visual reasoning requires explicitly increasing attention to visual tokens, not just making outputs more consistent.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses visual under-conditioning in self-evolving large multimodal models: a failure mode where models rely on language priors and answer agreement instead of truly grounding predictions in the image.
method: Identifies and frames visual under-conditioning as a core weakness in current unsupervised self-evolving LMM training.
Introduces a training objective or self-evolution strategy that encourages stronger attention to visual tokens during decoding.
Keeps the setting unsupervised while improving visual grounding and reducing reliance on statistical language shortcuts.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows that multimodal self-improvement must be grounded in visual evidence to be reliable. It is especially relevant for building safer and more trustworthy vision-language systems that reason from images rather than memorized priors.

title: Not All Actions Are Equal: Rethinking Conditioning for Dexterous World Model
authors: Zizhao Yuan, Zhengtu Liang, Taowen Wang, Qiwei Liang, Yichi Wang
abstract: Recent advances in action-conditioned world models show promising progress in modeling complex interactions and forecasting future states under diverse action sequences. While these models are often driven by stronger visual representations and model capacity, action conditioning itself remains underexplored. Most existing approaches compress the entire action sequence into a single representation, which works well for low-DoF control but becomes less reliable in high-DoF scenarios. We observe t

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that action conditioning is not one-size-fits-all: for dexterous, high-DoF settings, compressing an entire action sequence into a single token can hide important structure and weaken prediction quality. The key insight is to rethink how actions are represented so the world model can better capture fine-grained control dynamics.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing action-conditioned world models often work well for simple, low-degree-of-freedom control, but struggle when actions are complex, high-dimensional, and temporally nuanced. This paper addresses the loss of critical action information caused by overly aggressive action compression.
method: Analyze the limitations of standard action-sequence compression in high-DoF dexterous control settings.
Introduce a more expressive conditioning strategy that preserves important temporal and structural information in the action sequence.
Evaluate the approach on world-model forecasting tasks to show improved reliability under diverse action sequences.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that better action representation can matter as much as model scale or visual backbone quality. It can improve forecasting and control in robotics, dexterous manipulation, and other settings where small action details strongly affect outcomes.

title: Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs
authors: Yingyu Lin, Qiyue Gao, Nikki Lijing Kuang, Xunpeng Huang, Kun Zhou
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for training LLMs typically rely on ground-truth answers to assign rewards, limiting their applicability to tasks where the ground-truth solution is unknown. We introduce a \textbf{R}anking-\textbf{i}nduced \textbf{VER}ifiable framework (RiVER) that trains LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth solutions, using deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision. When applying group-relative RL to such conti

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that reinforcement learning can still improve LLMs even when there is no ground-truth answer, by using deterministic execution feedback as a verifiable learning signal. The proposed RiVER framework turns score-based tasks into trainable objectives without requiring labeled solutions.
infographic.problem_solved: Many RL methods for LLMs depend on known ground-truth answers to compute rewards, which limits them to tasks with clear correct outputs. This work addresses how to train models on tasks where the final solution is unknown but execution or scoring feedback is still available.
method: Introduce RiVER: a ranking-induced verifiable framework for learning from score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth solutions.
Use deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision instead of binary correct/incorrect labels.
Apply group-relative reinforcement learning to optimize model outputs using relative rankings among candidate solutions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this expands reinforcement learning beyond problems with explicit labels, enabling training on a broader set of real-world optimization tasks. It makes LLM improvement more practical in settings where only execution-based signals or scores are available.

title: DanceOPD: On-Policy Generative Field Distillation
authors: Wei Zhou, Xiongwei Zhu, Zelin Xu, Bo Dong, Lixue Gong
abstract: Modern image generation demands a single model that unifies diverse capabilities, including text-to-image (T2I), local editing, and global editing. However, these capabilities are rarely naturally aligned and often conflict. For instance, editing tends to degrade T2I performance, while global and local editing interfere with each other. Consequently, effectively composing these capabilities has become a central challenge for image generation model training. To tackle this, we introduce DanceOPD,

infographic.key_insight: DanceOPD shows how to train one image generation model to handle text-to-image creation, local editing, and global editing without these skills fighting each other. Its core idea is to distill these capabilities on-policy so they can be composed more effectively in a single model.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the conflict between multiple image generation capabilities: improving editing often hurts text-to-image quality, and global editing can interfere with local editing. It tackles the challenge of unifying these abilities in one model without performance trade-offs.
method: Uses an on-policy generative field distillation strategy to align training with the model’s own generation behavior.
Learns a shared representation that composes text-to-image, local editing, and global editing more consistently.
Reduces capability interference by distilling from the current policy rather than relying on static or mismatched supervision.
infographic.impact: This matters because practitioners want one versatile image model instead of separate tools for generation and editing. DanceOPD points toward more capable, efficient multimodal image systems with fewer quality trade-offs.

title: OctoSense: Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Robot Perception
authors: Anthony Bisulco, Jeremy Wang, Kostas Daniilidis, Randall Balestriero, Pratik Chaudhari
abstract: We present OctoSense, an open-source sensor platform with stereo RGB and event cameras, LiDAR, a thermal camera, an inertial measurement unit, RTK-corrected global positioning system, and proprioception (CAN bus data from a car, and joint angles for a quadruped robot). The eponymous OctoSense dataset contains 59 hours of time-synchronized driving data across different types of environments at different times of the day, including situations with highly degraded sensors. We demonstrate multi-moda

infographic.key_insight: OctoSense introduces a rich open-source multimodal sensor platform and dataset that helps robots learn robust perception from synchronized real-world data, even when some sensors are degraded. The key idea is to use self-supervised learning across many sensor types to improve robot understanding without requiring expensive manual labels.
infographic.problem_solved: Robots often struggle to perceive reliably when conditions change, sensors fail, or individual modalities become noisy or unavailable. This paper addresses the lack of large, synchronized, multimodal datasets for training perception models that can handle real-world degradation.
method: Builds the OctoSense platform with stereo RGB, event cameras, LiDAR, thermal imaging, IMU, RTK-GPS, and proprioceptive signals from cars and quadruped robots.
Collects 59 hours of time-synchronized driving data across diverse environments, times of day, and degraded-sensor scenarios.
Uses self-supervised multimodal learning to extract useful representations from the aligned sensor streams without relying on dense human annotations.
infographic.impact: This work gives AI and robotics researchers a practical foundation for training perception systems that are more robust to missing or degraded sensors. It can accelerate development of multimodal, label-efficient robot perception models for real-world deployment.

title: DnA: Denoising Attention for Visual Tasks
authors: Ron Campos, Subhajit Maity, Xin Li, Srijan Das, Aritra Dutta
abstract: The softmax activation in multihead attention (MHA) is the de facto standard for attention-based models in visual perception tasks. However, standard softmax can produce noisy attention patterns that dilute relevant features and degrade its performance. In this paper, we propose Denoising Attention or DnA, in which, first, a positive query identifies which image features belong to the correct class, and a negative query identifies closely associated but irrelevant image features. DnA then projec

infographic.key_insight: DnA replaces standard softmax attention with a denoising mechanism that separates truly relevant image features from confusing but similar ones. This helps visual models focus more cleanly on class-specific information instead of spreading attention too broadly.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard multihead attention can produce noisy attention maps in vision tasks, which dilutes important features and hurts recognition or perception performance.
method: Use a positive query to identify image features that belong to the target class.
Use a negative query to capture closely related but irrelevant features that should be suppressed.
Project attention through a denoising step so the model emphasizes useful features and filters out noise.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, DnA offers a more robust attention mechanism for visual models, potentially improving accuracy and interpretability. It is especially useful when softmax attention struggles with distracting or highly similar visual content.

title: Ask, Solve, Generate: Self-Evolving Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation via Self-Consistency Rewards
authors: Ritesh Thawkar, Shravan Venkatraman, Omkar Thawakar, Abdelrahman Shaker, Fahad Khan
abstract: Most unified large multimodal models (LMMs) that support both visual understanding and image generation still rely on curated post-training supervision, such as human annotations, preference labels, or external reward models. We ask whether a unified LMM can improve both abilities autonomously using only unlabeled images. We propose a self-evolving training framework with three internal roles: a Proposer that generates visual questions, a Solver that answers and evaluates them, and a Generator t

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that a unified multimodal model can improve both visual understanding and image generation without human labels by teaching itself through internal self-consistency rewards. In simple terms: the model asks questions, solves them, and uses the agreement between answers and generated content as training signal.
infographic.problem_solved: Most unified large multimodal models depend on curated supervision such as annotations, preference labels, or external reward models. This work tackles the challenge of improving both understanding and generation using only unlabeled images, reducing reliance on expensive human feedback.
method: Uses a self-evolving framework with three internal roles: Proposer, Solver, and Generator.
The Proposer creates visual questions from unlabeled images to drive learning.
The Solver answers these questions and checks consistency, producing self-consistency rewards.
The Generator uses these rewards to refine image generation and support unified multimodal learning.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests a path toward cheaper and more scalable multimodal training pipelines that reduce dependence on labeled data and external reward models. It can make unified models easier to adapt in data-scarce or annotation-expensive settings.

title: RayPE: Ray-Space Positional Encoding for 3D-Aware Video Generation
authors: Minghao Yin, Jiahao Lu, Wenbo Hu, Wang Zhao, Shan Ying
abstract: Modern video diffusion transformers position their tokens through RoPE on the (u,v,t) axes -- a description of the camera's sampling grid that says nothing about the 3D structure of the scene. We observe that the geometric relation between two camera rays is captured by the Plucker reciprocal product, which is bilinear in the two rays -- the same algebraic form as the dot product in Transformer attention. Building on this analogy, we propose RayPE, a positional-encoding extension that injects pe

infographic.key_insight: RayPE replaces standard token positions on the 2D/temporal grid with a ray-space encoding that reflects actual 3D camera geometry. It uses the Plücker reciprocal product to model relations between rays, giving video diffusion transformers a more scene-aware positional signal.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video diffusion transformers use RoPE on (u,v,t), which encodes where a token is sampled in the camera grid but not how different views relate in 3D space. This makes it harder for models to learn consistent geometry across viewpoints and time.
method: Represent camera rays in ray space rather than only using image-plane and time coordinates.
Compute pairwise ray relations with the Plücker reciprocal product, which is bilinear and aligns naturally with attention computation.
Inject this ray-space positional encoding into video diffusion transformers to improve 3D-aware generation.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, RayPE offers a drop-in way to make video generation models better at respecting 3D structure and multi-view consistency. This can improve realism, viewpoint coherence, and geometric stability in generated videos.

title: Data-driven surrogates of rational design enable antimicrobial peptide optimization
authors: Goran Mauša, Daniela Kalafatovic
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 25 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01258-0

Rising pathogen drug resistance makes next-generation antimicrobial peptides a global priority. Generative AI accelerates discovery by rapidly proposing new peptides with high therapeutic potential. The key question is no longer whether broad data-driven exploration is possible, but whether it can refine biologically complex activity s

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that data-driven surrogate models can be used to guide rational design and optimization of antimicrobial peptides, helping AI move beyond simple generation toward biologically informed improvement. In short, the approach aims to make peptide design more targeted, efficient, and therapeutically relevant.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of optimizing antimicrobial peptides in the face of rising pathogen drug resistance, where naive generative discovery can produce many candidates but not necessarily the ones with the right biological activity and usability.
method: Train data-driven surrogate models to approximate the relationship between peptide sequence and desired antimicrobial properties.
Use these surrogates to support rational optimization of candidate peptides rather than relying only on unconstrained generation.
Iteratively refine peptide designs to improve therapeutic potential while accounting for complex biological activity signals.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights how surrogate modeling can turn generative design into a more controlled optimization workflow. It is especially relevant for bioactive sequence design problems where interpretability, efficiency, and experimental validation matter.

title: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers
authors: Haina Jiang, Liam Wang, Peng-Chen Chen, Min Seop Kwak, Seungryong Kim
abstract: Neural surrogate models offer fast approximate mappings from PDE parameters to solutions, but they typically treat solving as a purely statistical task: once trained, they struggle to correct their own constraint violations and extrapolate beyond the training distribution. Recent hybrid methods promote physical correctness by targeting the PDE residual via gradient descent or Gauss--Newton steps, but inherit the compute cost and instability of the underlying classical optimizers. We show, theore

infographic.key_insight: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers learn to correct their own mistakes instead of treating PDE solving as a one-shot prediction problem. This makes neural surrogates more physically consistent and more robust outside the training distribution, while avoiding the heavy cost of iterative classical optimization.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses a key limitation of neural surrogate models for PDEs: they are fast but often violate physical constraints and fail to self-correct when predictions are inaccurate or when inputs fall outside the training range.
method: Condition the solver on its current prediction error so the model can learn how to refine bad outputs.
Combine neural surrogate speed with an error-correction mechanism that reduces PDE residuals without relying on expensive gradient-descent or Gauss-Newton iterations.
Aim to improve both physical consistency and out-of-distribution generalization compared with standard surrogate and hybrid solver approaches.
infographic.impact: For ML practitioners, this offers a path to faster PDE solving with better reliability and fewer constraint violations. It is especially useful when classical iterative solvers are too slow or unstable, but pure neural surrogates are not accurate enough.

title: Empowering GUI Agents via Autonomous Experience Exploration and Hindsight Experience Utilization for Task Planning
authors: Tianyi Men, Zhuoran Jin, Pengfei Cao, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu
abstract: Multimodal web agents can assist humans in operating repetitive GUI tasks, where effective task planning is essential for decomposing complex tasks into executable actions. While small open source MLLMs are cost efficient and privacy preserving compared with commercial large models, they suffer from weak planning and limited cross website generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce the planning experience exploration and utilization (PEEU) method, which autonomously explores envir

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that GUI agents can learn better task planning by autonomously exploring websites and reusing past mistakes as training signals. The result is a more practical way to improve small open-source multimodal models without relying on expensive proprietary systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Small open-source multimodal language models are cost-effective and privacy-preserving, but they often struggle with planning multi-step GUI tasks and generalizing across different websites.
method: Autonomously explores GUI environments to collect planning experiences without heavy human annotation.
Uses hindsight experience utilization to turn failed or suboptimal trajectories into useful learning signals.
Trains task-planning capability so agents can better decompose complex web tasks into executable actions and generalize across sites.

title: World Action Models Enable Continual Imitation Learning with Recurrent Generative Replays
authors: Manish Kumar Govind, Dominick Reilly, Smit Patel, Hieu Le, Srijan Das
abstract: Going beyond predicting robot actions, World Action Models (WAMs) can also generate future visual observations. We build on this generative capability to propose Recurrent Generative Replay (REGEN), a continual imitation learning framework that synthesizes pseudo-replay trajectories, enabling a robot policy to rehearse previously learned tasks without storing their original human demonstrations. During continual adaptation, REGEN recursively queries the WAM to synthesize pseudo-replay trajectori

infographic.key_insight: World Action Models can do more than predict robot actions—they can generate future visual observations. This paper leverages that generative ability to create pseudo-replay for continual imitation learning, letting robots retain old skills without saving original demonstrations.
infographic.problem_solved: Continual imitation learning often suffers from catastrophic forgetting when a robot learns new tasks and loses performance on earlier ones. Storing all human demonstrations for replay is expensive, impractical, and scales poorly over time.
method: Uses a World Action Model (WAM) to synthesize future observation sequences, not just actions.
Introduces Recurrent Generative Replay (REGEN), which recursively queries the WAM to generate pseudo-replay trajectories for previously learned tasks.
Trains the robot policy with these generated trajectories during continual adaptation, reducing the need to keep original human demos.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to reduce catastrophic forgetting in imitation learning without a growing replay buffer of real demonstrations. It points toward more scalable, memory-efficient continual learning systems for robots and embodied agents.

title: Learning Action Priors for Cross-embodiment Robot Manipulation
authors: Dong Jing, Tianqi Zhang, Jiaqi Liu, Jinman Zhao, Zelong Sun
abstract: Most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models build on a Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone by attaching an action module and optimizing the full policy jointly. This design inherits strong visual and linguistic priors from the VLM, but leaves the action module to learn physical motion almost from scratch. As a result, the policy lacks an explicit motion prior, forcing early optimization to simultaneously discover temporal action dynamics and cross-modal alignment, a challenge further amplified in

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces action priors that help robot policies start with a better sense of motion, rather than learning physical behavior from scratch. This makes cross-embodiment manipulation easier by separating “how to move” from “what to perceive.”
infographic.problem_solved: Existing VLA models reuse strong vision-language knowledge but often lack an explicit motion prior in the action module. This forces the policy to learn temporal action dynamics and cross-modal alignment at the same time, which is especially difficult across different robot embodiments.
method: Learn action priors to initialize or guide the robot action module with motion knowledge before full policy training.
Design the policy to better transfer manipulation behavior across different robot bodies/embodiments.
Reduce the burden on end-to-end training by decoupling motion learning from vision-language grounding.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this can improve sample efficiency, training stability, and transferability in robot manipulation systems. It is especially relevant for building robots that generalize across platforms without retraining everything from scratch.

title: MVTrack4Gen: Multi-View Point Tracking as Geometric Supervision for 4D Video Generation
authors: JoungBin Lee, Jaewoo Jung, Jongmin Lee, Tongmin Kim, Hyunsung Kim
abstract: Synthesizing a novel-view video from a monocular reference video along a target camera trajectory requires both geometric consistency and motion fidelity with respect to the reference video. Existing methods based on explicit 3D representations are limited by the accuracy of off-the-shelf reconstruction modules, which often produce inaccurate geometry for dynamic objects in monocular videos. In contrast, camera-conditioning-only methods can achieve high visual quality but often struggle to prese

infographic.key_insight: MVTrack4Gen uses multi-view point tracking as geometric supervision to improve 4D video generation from a single reference video. By enforcing motion-aware 3D consistency directly from tracked points, it aims to balance realistic appearance with faithful novel-view dynamics.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of generating novel-view videos from a monocular input while preserving both geometric consistency and dynamic motion fidelity. It targets the weakness of prior explicit-3D methods on dynamic objects and the motion/structure limitations of camera-conditioning-only approaches.
method: Uses multi-view point tracking as an additional geometric signal during 4D video generation.
Guides the model to align motion across views, improving consistency for moving objects in monocular videos.
Combines geometric supervision with video generation to reduce reliance on imperfect off-the-shelf reconstruction modules.
infographic.impact: This matters because it offers a more reliable way to generate temporally coherent and geometrically consistent 4D videos from real-world monocular footage. For practitioners, it suggests a practical path toward higher-quality view synthesis without depending entirely on fragile 3D reconstruction pipelines.

title: TryOnCrafter: Unleashing Camera Trajectories for Realistic Video Virtual Try-on via a Renderable 4D Try-on Proxy
authors: Hao Sun, Hao Yan, Mengting Chen, Quanjian Song, Yu Li
abstract: While Video Virtual Try-on (VVT) has achieved remarkable progress in synthesizing realistic garment overlays on dynamic subjects, existing paradigms remains fundamentally constrained by a passive dependency on source camera trajectories, failing to accommodate the requisite interactive freedom for omnidirectional viewpoint exploration. To address this limitation, we define a pioneering research frontier: Camera-controllable Video Virtual Try-on (CaM-VVT). Unlike conventional VVT, CaM-VVT not onl

infographic.key_insight: TryOnCrafter introduces camera-controllable video virtual try-on, letting users explore garment fit and appearance from new viewpoints instead of being limited to the original camera path. It does this by building a renderable 4D try-on proxy that supports realistic viewpoint changes in dynamic video.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video virtual try-on methods depend on the source video’s camera trajectory, which prevents interactive, omnidirectional viewpoint exploration. This paper addresses the lack of camera control in realistic try-on synthesis.
method: Defines a new setting called Camera-controllable Video Virtual Try-on (CaM-VVT) for interactive viewpoint control.
Constructs a renderable 4D try-on proxy to represent clothing and motion across space and time.
Uses the proxy to synthesize realistic try-on results from novel camera trajectories while preserving garment fidelity and motion consistency.
infographic.impact: This is useful for AI/ML practitioners working on generative video, 3D-aware synthesis, fashion tech, and interactive content creation. It moves virtual try-on from passive playback toward controllable, user-driven visualization.

title: A cross-process welding penetration status prediction algorithm based on unsupervised domain adaptation in laser and TIG welding
authors: Sen Li, Haichao Cui, Chendong Shao, Yaqi Wang, Xinhua Tang
abstract: Supervised deep learning has been widely used for weld penetration state classification; however, its performance often degrades significantly under domain shift, such as when transferring models between welding processes with distinct physical mechanisms:for instance, from arc-dominated tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding to keyhole-based laser welding. To overcome this limitation, we propose an unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) framework integrated with a gradual source domain expansion (GSDE)

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that weld penetration status can be predicted more reliably across different welding processes by using unsupervised domain adaptation instead of relying only on labeled source data. Its key idea is to reduce the performance drop caused by transferring a model from TIG welding to laser welding, where the underlying physics are very different.
infographic.problem_solved: Supervised weld-state classifiers often fail when deployed in a new welding process because of domain shift between source and target processes. This work addresses cross-process transfer from arc-based TIG welding to keyhole-based laser welding without requiring labels in the target domain.
method: Uses an unsupervised domain adaptation framework to transfer knowledge from a labeled source welding process to an unlabeled target process.
Integrates gradual source domain expansion (GSDE) to progressively broaden the source representation and improve cross-process robustness.
Targets weld penetration status classification under strong process-to-process differences in signal and physical mechanism.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this demonstrates a practical way to build models that generalize across industrial domains where labeled target data is scarce or unavailable. It is especially relevant for manufacturing AI, where process changes often break standard supervised models.

A domain shift illustration comparing arc-based TIG signals versus laser keyhole welding signals.

title: DomainShuttle: Freeform Open Domain Subject-driven Text-to-video Generation
authors: Nan Chen, Yiyang Cai, Rongchang Xie, Junwen Pan, Cheng Chen
abstract: Open domain subject-driven text-to-video (S2V) generation has drawn significant interest in academia and industry. Open domain S2V mainly involves two scenarios: in-domain, which requires retaining the reference subject features as much as possible, and cross-domain, which preserves the intrinsic features of the subject while allowing subject-irrelevant properties to vary flexibly according to the text prompt. Existing methods primarily focus on maximizing subject fidelity in in-domain scenarios

infographic.key_insight: DomainShuttle targets open-domain subject-driven text-to-video generation, aiming to keep the subject recognizable while allowing non-essential details to change with the prompt. It is designed to support both in-domain fidelity and cross-domain flexibility.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of generating videos from text that preserve a reference subject’s identity and core traits, especially when the desired output needs to work across different domains and styles rather than only in easy in-domain cases.
method: Frames the task as open-domain subject-driven text-to-video generation with two settings: in-domain preservation and cross-domain adaptation.
Focuses on maintaining intrinsic subject features while letting subject-irrelevant attributes vary according to the text prompt.
Aims to improve on existing approaches that mostly optimize for subject fidelity in in-domain scenarios.
infographic.impact: This is useful for practitioners building controllable video generation systems that need both identity consistency and prompt flexibility. It broadens the practical use of T2V models for creative editing, personalized content generation, and domain-shifting applications.

title: Can Trustless Agents Be Trusted? An Empirical Study of the ERC-8004 Decentralized AI Agent Ecosystem
authors: Xihan Xiong, Zelin Li, Wei Wei, Qin Wang, William Knottenbelt
abstract: As autonomous AI agents increasingly transact across organizational boundaries, a fundamental trust challenge emerges: how can an agent assess whether an unknown counterpart is trustworthy? The ERC-8004 protocol addresses this challenge with the first permissionless trust layer for AI agent economies, built around three on-chain registries for Identity, Reputation, and Validation. Despite its rapid adoption, the protocol has not been studied empirically, leaving it unclear whether the informatio

infographic.key_insight: This paper examines whether a permissionless, blockchain-based trust layer for AI agents can actually make unknown agents more trustworthy in practice. It studies ERC-8004—the first decentralized trust protocol for AI agents—by empirically analyzing how its Identity, Reputation, and Validation registries work in the real world.
infographic.problem_solved: Autonomous AI agents increasingly need to transact with unfamiliar counterparts across organizational boundaries, but there is no standard way to assess trust in a decentralized setting. The paper addresses the gap between the promise of trustless agent economies and the lack of empirical evidence about whether ERC-8004’s trust signals are reliable and useful.
method: Empirical study of the ERC-8004 decentralized AI agent ecosystem.
Analysis of the protocol’s three on-chain registries: Identity, Reputation, and Validation.
Evaluation of whether on-chain trust information is informative enough for agents to judge unknown peers.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners building agentic systems, this work helps clarify whether decentralized trust infrastructure can support safe autonomous coordination. It provides evidence to guide adoption of blockchain-based reputation and validation mechanisms in multi-agent and cross-organization deployments.

title: Neglected Free Lunch from Post-training: Progress Advantage for LLM Agents
authors: Changdae Oh, Wendi Li, Seongheon Park, Samuel Yeh, Tanwi Mallick
abstract: Process reward models enable fine-grained, step-level evaluation of LLMs, yet building them for agentic settings remains prohibitively difficult: long-horizon interactions, irreversible actions, and stochastic environment feedback make both human annotation and Monte Carlo estimation infeasible at scale. In this work, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) post-training already provides the ingredients for effective step-level scoring, eliminating the need for dedicated reward model training a

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning post-training can already produce the signals needed for step-level scoring in agentic tasks. This creates a 'free lunch' by reducing or removing the need to separately train a process reward model.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating LLM agents at the step level in long-horizon, stochastic environments, where human annotation is expensive and Monte Carlo estimation is impractical.
method: Reuse signals generated during RL post-training as step-level scoring information.
Leverage these signals to evaluate agent actions in long-horizon interactions without dedicated process reward model training.
Avoid reliance on costly human labels or large-scale Monte Carlo rollouts for step-wise supervision.
infographic.impact: This could make agent evaluation and training much cheaper, faster, and more scalable. For practitioners, it lowers the barrier to building reliable process-level evaluators for complex LLM agents.

title: A welding penetration prediction model for laser welding process based on self-supervised learning using physics-informed neural networks
authors: Sen Li, Xiaoying Liu, Xiaojian Xu, Chendong Shao, Yaqi Wang
abstract: The laser welding full-penetration is of critical importance, as it constitutes one of the fundamental factors in achieving defect-free welded joints. Accurate prediction of the penetration state is therefore essential for ensuring weld quality. To this end, this paper introduces SimPhysNet, a novel algorithm that achieves high classification accuracy in laser welding penetration prediction using only a limited number of labelled images. This approach effectively overcomes the limitations of sup

infographic.key_insight: SimPhysNet uses physics-informed self-supervised learning to predict laser welding penetration accurately with very few labeled images. It combines domain physics with neural networks to overcome label scarcity in welding inspection.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of reliably predicting full vs. partial penetration in laser welding when labeled training data is limited and expensive to obtain.
method: Builds a physics-informed neural network that incorporates welding process knowledge into learning.
Uses self-supervised learning to extract useful features from large amounts of unlabeled welding images.
Fine-tunes on a small labeled dataset to classify penetration state with high accuracy.
infographic.impact: This approach shows how AI can perform well in industrial vision tasks even when labels are scarce. For practitioners, it offers a practical path to faster, cheaper deployment of quality inspection models in manufacturing.

title: AI translation of literary texts is "fine", but readers still prefer human translations
authors: Yves Ferstler, Adam Podoxin, Ty Brassington, Roman Grundkiewicz, Maite Taboada
abstract: AI translation of literary works is increasingly common. While the content may be rendered adequately, we do not know enough about how readers experience it in terms of immersiveness and literary effect, aspects poorly captured by automatic machine translation metrics or human evaluation targeting fluency and adequacy. We ask 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations (HT) to machine translations (MT) generated with an agentic large language model (LLM)-based pipeline, for

infographic.key_insight: AI translations of literary texts can be good enough on content and basic fluency, but readers still prefer human translations for immersion and literary feel. In other words, “fine” machine translation is not the same as a satisfying reading experience.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between standard machine translation evaluation and how real readers experience literary translations. It asks whether LLM-based translation can match human translation not just in adequacy, but in immersion and aesthetic impact.
method: Asked 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations with machine translations produced by an agentic LLM-based pipeline.
Focused on reader experience rather than only automatic metrics, looking at immersion, literary effect, and overall preference.
Evaluated translation quality in the context of literary reading, where fluency and adequacy scores alone may miss important differences.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that improving translation quality requires more than optimizing benchmark scores. If the goal is literary translation, evaluation should include human-centered measures like enjoyment, style, and emotional resonance.

title: FedReLa: Imbalanced Federated Learning via Re-Labeling
authors: Guangzheng Hu, Patricia Menéndez, Feng Liu, Mingming Gong, Guanghui Wang
abstract: Federated learning has emerged as the foremost approach for decentralized model training with privacy preservation. The global class imbalance and cross-client data heterogeneity naturally coexist, and the mismatch between local and global imbalances exacerbates the performance degradation of the aggregated model. The agnosticism of global class distribution poses significant challenges for data-level methods, especially under extreme conditions with severe class absence across clients. In this

infographic.key_insight: FedReLa tackles federated learning under severe class imbalance by re-labeling data to better align local client distributions with the unknown global class distribution. This helps the aggregated model learn more effectively when some classes are missing or rare on many clients.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses performance degradation in federated learning caused by the combination of global class imbalance, cross-client data heterogeneity, and severe class absence on individual clients. It targets the challenge of using data-level methods when the true global class distribution is unknown.
method: Re-label local data to reduce mismatch between client-level and global-level class imbalance.
Design the method to remain effective even when some classes are absent on many clients.
Improve the quality of federated aggregation by making local training signals more balanced and informative.
infographic.impact: FedReLa offers a practical way to improve federated learning in real-world, non-IID settings where data are unevenly distributed across devices. This can lead to more robust and fairer models for privacy-preserving applications with long-tailed or incomplete class coverage.

title: RevengeBench: Reverse Engineering Code-Space Policies from Behavioral Experiments
authors: Babak Rahmani, Sebastian Dziadzio, Joschka Strüber, Sergio Hernández-Gutiérrez, Matthias Bethge
abstract: For most of scientific history, researchers studying behavior could only infer hidden mechanisms from outward actions: an inverse problem that becomes more tractable when observation is augmented by targeted intervention. We pose a computational analogue: given only behavioral traces of an agent in a game environment, can a learner reconstruct the underlying decision program as executable code, and how much does this reconstruction improve with the ability to design controlled experiments? We in

infographic.key_insight: The paper tackles the inverse problem of reconstructing an agent’s hidden decision policy from its behavior alone, and shows that this becomes much more effective when the learner can actively design experiments. In short: observing actions is helpful, but targeted intervention reveals much more about the code behind them.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of reverse engineering an unknown policy from behavioral traces in a game environment, aiming to recover not just predictions but an executable code-space representation of the agent’s decision-making.
method: Collect behavioral traces from an agent interacting in a game environment.
Train a learner to infer the underlying decision program as executable code rather than a black-box label.
Compare passive observation against active experimental design, where the learner chooses controlled interventions to probe the agent’s policy.
Evaluate how much reconstruction quality improves when the learner can manipulate the observation process.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical framework for interpreting, auditing, and debugging opaque agents by recovering human-readable policy structure. It also highlights the value of active probing for understanding model behavior, which is important for safety, transparency, and mechanistic analysis.

title: RoboAtlas: Contextual Active SLAM
authors: Alexander Schperberg, Shivam K. Panda, Abraham P. Vinod, M. K. Jawed, Stefano Di Cairano
abstract: We present RoboAtlas, a contextual Active SLAM framework that adaptively balances geometric exploration and semantic reasoning using a scalable 3D semantic mapping system, OpenRoboVox. RoboAtlas integrates frontier exploration, global semantic-map reasoning, and egocentric VLM-based reasoning through a contextual multi-armed bandit that transitions from exploration to semantically guided navigation as scene understanding improves. We evaluate the system in simulation and on a Unitree Go2 robot i

infographic.key_insight: RoboAtlas makes active SLAM smarter by switching between pure exploration and semantically guided navigation as it learns more about the scene. It uses a contextual bandit to decide when to map, when to explore, and when to follow semantic cues for faster, more informed autonomy.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional SLAM systems struggle to balance efficient map building with understanding what in the environment is actually important. This paper tackles the challenge of deciding how a robot should explore when both geometry and semantic context matter.
method: Builds a scalable 3D semantic mapping system called OpenRoboVox to represent the environment.
Combines frontier exploration, global semantic-map reasoning, and egocentric VLM-based reasoning.
Uses a contextual multi-armed bandit to dynamically shift from geometric exploration to semantically guided navigation as scene understanding improves.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical framework for robots that can adapt their exploration strategy instead of following a fixed policy. It is especially relevant for robotics applications where both mapping efficiency and task-aware navigation are important.
