title: DiffusionBench: On Holistic Evaluation of Diffusion Transformers
authors: Xingjian Leng, Jaskirat Singh, Zhanhao Liang, Ethan Smith, Martin Bell
abstract: Diffusion transformer (DiT) research on image generation has converged to a single evaluation setup: class-conditional generation on ImageNet. While methods improve the FID and related metrics, it is increasingly unclear whether they reflect real progress in generative modeling. The natural alternative, i.e., text-to-image (T2I) generation, is perceived as too costly or inconvenient to train and evaluate and is often skipped. We argue that this perception no longer holds. We introduce NanoGen, a

infographic.key_insight: This paper argues that evaluating diffusion transformers only on ImageNet class-conditional generation gives an incomplete and potentially misleading picture of progress. It introduces a more holistic benchmark approach, highlighting that text-to-image evaluation is now practical enough to include in standard assessment.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the over-reliance on a single benchmark for diffusion transformer evaluation, which makes it hard to tell whether lower FID scores reflect genuine advances in generative modeling or just optimization for one narrow task.
method: Proposes DiffusionBench as a broader evaluation framework for diffusion transformers.
Introduces NanoGen to make text-to-image training and evaluation more accessible and less costly.
Compares model performance across more realistic and diverse generation settings rather than only ImageNet class-conditional generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work encourages more reliable model selection by measuring performance on tasks closer to real-world use. It can help shift the field toward evaluations that better capture true generative quality and generalization.

title: L3Cube-MahaPOS: A Marathi Part-of-Speech Tagging Dataset and BERT Models
authors: Hariom Ingle, Ronit Ghode, Ishwari Gondkar, Jidnyasa Harad, Raviraj Joshi
abstract: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging is a foundational NLP task underpinning machine translation, information extraction, and syntactic parsing. Despite Marathi being spoken by over 83 million people and ranking among the top twenty most spoken languages worldwide, it remains severely under-resourced in annotated corpora and standardised evaluation benchmarks. Marathi presents unique challenges for computational modelling owing to its rich morphology, relatively free word order, lack of capitalisation c

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces L3Cube-MahaPOS, a new Marathi part-of-speech tagging dataset and baseline BERT models to improve NLP support for a highly under-resourced language. It helps close the gap between Marathi and better-resourced languages by providing standard data and evaluation tools.
infographic.problem_solved: Marathi NLP lacks large annotated corpora and consistent benchmarks for POS tagging, making it difficult to build and compare effective models. The paper addresses the challenges of Marathi’s rich morphology, free word order, and limited standardized resources.
method: Created L3Cube-MahaPOS, a Marathi POS tagging dataset for supervised evaluation.
Trained and evaluated BERT-based models as strong neural baselines for Marathi POS tagging.
Established a standardized benchmark to support future Marathi NLP research and model comparison.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work provides the missing infrastructure needed to develop and benchmark Marathi language models more reliably. It can accelerate downstream applications like machine translation, parsing, and information extraction for Marathi text.

title: Solutions, challenges and rising tensions in AI and mathematics
authors: Unknown
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01269-x

Recent breakthroughs in mathematical research show that AI is transforming the field at a remarkable pace. In an open letter published this month, an international group of mathematicians argue that the field needs to remain a human endeavour.

infographic.key_insight: AI is rapidly changing how mathematical research is done, but the paper highlights a growing tension: while machines can accelerate discovery, many mathematicians believe math should remain fundamentally human-led. The key takeaway is that progress in AI for mathematics must balance capability with trust, interpretation, and human judgment.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of integrating AI into mathematics without losing the discipline’s human-centered nature. It frames the debate around how to use AI effectively while preserving rigor, accountability, and the role of mathematicians.
method: Synthesizes recent advances in AI-assisted mathematics and their implications for research workflows.
Discusses viewpoints from the mathematical community, including concerns raised in an open letter about maintaining human oversight.
Evaluates the tension between automated discovery and human reasoning in mathematical problem-solving.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this matters because mathematics is a core foundation of machine learning, and AI tools for theorem proving, conjecture generation, and proof assistance are becoming more powerful. Understanding the social and scientific limits of these tools is essential for building systems that are useful, trustworthy, and widely accepted.

title: A dexterous soft hand exoskeleton restores intentional grasping in individuals with severe hand impairment
authors: John Nassour, Nicolas Berberich, Daniel Utpadel-Fischler, Tobias Wächter, Gordon Cheng
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01263-3

Nassour, Berberich and colleagues present a soft robotic hand exoskeleton that restores grasping ability in individuals with severe hand paralysis, enabling meaningful tasks such as feeding. A lightweight textile glove with wrist dorsiflexion and an active opposable thumb increases hand articulations to enable more dexterous grasping.

infographic.key_insight: A soft robotic hand exoskeleton can restore intentional grasping in people with severe hand impairment. By adding wrist dorsiflexion support and an active opposable thumb, it enables more dexterous, functional movements like feeding.
infographic.problem_solved: Severe hand paralysis often leaves people unable to perform everyday grasping tasks, even when some intention to move remains. This paper addresses the need for a lightweight, wearable assistive device that can convert user intent into practical hand function.
method: Built a lightweight textile-based hand exoskeleton designed for comfortable wearability.
Added wrist dorsiflexion assistance to improve hand positioning for grasping.
Integrated an active opposable thumb to increase hand articulation and enable more dexterous grips.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights how human-centered robotics and assistive control can translate intent into meaningful action in real-world settings. It shows the value of combining wearable design, soft robotics, and control systems to improve quality of life for users with severe motor impairment.

title: EG-VQA: Benchmarking Verifiable Video Question Answering with Grounded Temporal Evidence
authors: Linpeng Huang, Weixing Chen, Zexin Chen, Yang Liu, Liang Lin
abstract: Recent advances in Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have yielded promising performance on video question answering (VideoQA). Nevertheless, existing benchmarks are predominantly evaluated through answer correctness, while the grounding of predictions in relevant video evidence remains largely unexamined. This disconnect between answer generation and evidence understanding motivates the construction of the Evidence-Grounded Video Question Answering Benchmark (EG-VQA), an open-ended evalua

infographic.key_insight: EG-VQA shifts VideoQA evaluation beyond just whether an answer is correct and asks whether the answer is actually supported by relevant video evidence. It introduces a benchmark for checking grounded, temporally localized reasoning in Video-LLMs.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing VideoQA benchmarks mainly score final answer accuracy, which can hide models that guess correctly without using the right evidence. This paper addresses the lack of evaluation for evidence grounding and temporal support in video question answering.
method: Construct an open-ended benchmark, EG-VQA, focused on evidence-grounded video question answering.
Evaluate whether model predictions are supported by relevant temporal segments in the video, not just whether the final answer matches.
Benchmark Video-LLMs on both answer quality and grounding quality to expose mismatches between prediction and evidence use.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark provides a more realistic way to measure whether video models truly understand what they see. It helps identify models that are accurate by chance and supports development of more trustworthy, explainable VideoQA systems.

title: Solving Inverse Problems of Chaotic Systems with Bidirectional Conditional Flow Matching
authors: Peiyan Hu, Jian Zhang, Jiashu Pan, Ruiqi Feng, Tao Zhang
abstract: Modeling chaotic systems is crucial yet challenging. Inverse problems in chaotic dynamics, namely inferring initial conditions from final states, remain largely unsolved because of ill-posedness, non-uniqueness, instability, and potentially chaotic time-reverse dynamics. We address this open problem with Bidirectional Conditional Flow Matching (Bi-CFM), which learns bidirectional mappings between distributions of initial and final states to capture the stochasticity of chaotic evolution and miti

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces Bi-CFM, a bidirectional generative approach that can infer plausible initial conditions from final states in chaotic systems. It tackles the core challenge of chaos by learning distribution-to-distribution mappings rather than assuming a single deterministic reverse solution.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses inverse problems in chaotic dynamics: recovering unknown initial conditions from observed final states. These problems are difficult because they are ill-posed, non-unique, unstable, and may involve chaotic behavior when run backward in time.
method: Uses Bidirectional Conditional Flow Matching (Bi-CFM) to learn mappings in both forward and reverse directions.
Models the stochastic nature of chaotic evolution by learning distributions of initial and final states instead of one-to-one trajectories.
Mitigates instability in inverse inference by conditioning on observed states and capturing multiple valid solutions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical framework for solving inverse problems where exact recovery is impossible or ambiguous. It could improve scientific machine learning applications in physics, forecasting, control, and system identification for chaotic systems.

title: InSight: Self-Guided Skill Acquisition via Steerable VLAs
authors: Maggie Wang, Lars Osterberg, Stephen Tian, Ola Shorinwa, Jiajun Wu
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can learn manipulation skills from demonstrations, but their capabilities are bounded by the skills in the training data. We present InSight, a framework that unlocks autonomous skill acquisition by rendering VLAs steerable at the primitive-action level (e.g., "move gripper to the bowl", "lift upward", "pour the bottle"). InSight consists of two primary stages: (1) an automated segmentation pipeline that partitions demonstrations into labeled primitives via VL

infographic.key_insight: InSight makes vision-language-action (VLA) models steerable at the primitive-action level, letting them autonomously acquire new manipulation skills instead of being limited to what was seen in training. It turns demonstrations into a foundation for self-guided skill building through low-level action guidance like moving, lifting, and pouring.
infographic.problem_solved: VLA models can imitate demonstrated tasks, but they struggle to learn beyond the exact skills present in their training data. This paper addresses the challenge of enabling autonomous skill acquisition and more flexible manipulation without requiring exhaustive human demonstrations for every new behavior.
method: Automated segmentation pipeline breaks demonstrations into labeled primitive actions.
Primitive-level steering allows the VLA to follow fine-grained commands such as "move gripper to the bowl" or "lift upward."
A two-stage framework uses these primitives to support self-guided acquisition of more complex manipulation skills.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, InSight suggests a practical path toward more general, adaptive robot policies that can learn new skills with less manual supervision. This could reduce the cost of collecting task-specific data and improve robotic flexibility in real-world environments.

title: FLAT: Feedforward Latent Triangle Splatting for Geometrically Accurate Scene Generation
authors: Orest Kupyn, Goutam Bhat, Philipp Henzler, Fabian Manhardt, Christian Rupprecht
abstract: Generating explorable 3D scenes from a single image requires strong generative priors and accurate geometric representations suitable for downstream use. Current video diffusion models offer high-quality generation and implicitly encode multi-view geometric structure in latent space. However, existing feedforward latent scene decoders typically output volumetric 3D Gaussians that lack a well-defined surface, limiting their use in simulation or standard graphics pipelines. This motivates decoding

infographic.key_insight: FLAT turns a single image into an explorable 3D scene by decoding latent scene representations into triangle-based geometry instead of blurry volumetric blobs. This gives generated scenes a more explicit surface, making them more useful for graphics and simulation.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between high-quality 3D scene generation and geometrically accurate, surface-based representations. Existing feedforward decoders often produce 3D Gaussians or volumetric outputs that look good but lack clean surfaces and are hard to use in standard rendering or downstream 3D pipelines.
method: Uses a feedforward decoder that maps latent multi-view structure from video diffusion priors into triangle splatting geometry.
Replaces volumetric Gaussian scene outputs with triangle-based surface representations for more explicit geometry.
Leverages latent scene information learned by video diffusion models to generate 3D scenes from a single input image.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this makes generated 3D scenes more practical for real-world use in graphics, AR/VR, and simulation. It bridges the quality of generative models with the geometric precision expected by conventional 3D tools.

title: BenchX: Benchmarking AI Models for Cancer Detection and Localization with Demographic and Protocol Biases
authors: Qi Chen, Wenxuan Li, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Xinze Zhou, Jakob Wasserthal
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable success in medical imaging, but it is widely recognized that these models often perform inconsistently across real-world clinical settings. Such inconsistencies occur when patient demographics and imaging protocols vary, for example, in detecting small tumors, analyzing scans from different contrast phases, or evaluating patients of different ages or sexes. To quantify these inconsistencies, we develop a large-scale, open benchmark of 85,355 C

infographic.key_insight: BenchX introduces a large-scale benchmark to measure how well cancer detection and localization models hold up across different patient demographics and imaging protocols. The key takeaway is that strong average performance can hide major biases and failure modes in real clinical settings.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the lack of a standardized, large-scale way to evaluate AI models for cancer detection and localization under demographic differences and protocol variation, such as age, sex, and contrast phase changes.
method: Build an open benchmark dataset of 85,355 medical imaging cases for cancer detection and localization.
Evaluate AI models across demographic groups and imaging protocol conditions to expose performance gaps.
Compare model behavior on challenging scenarios such as small tumors and scans from different contrast phases.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, BenchX provides a practical framework for testing robustness, fairness, and clinical reliability before deployment. It helps identify hidden bias and failure modes that may not appear in standard aggregate metrics.

title: It's Complicated: On the Design and Evaluation of AI-Powered AAC Interfaces
authors: Blade Frisch, Will Wade, Dylan Gaines, Michelle Kinsella, Betts Peters
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance what people who use augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) are able to do with their systems. However, evaluating AI-powered AAC interfaces can be difficult. People are intersectional beings and current evaluation metrics can struggle to capture the multifaceted and nuanced desires people may have for their AAC. We explore the complicated nature of six AAC problem spaces, explore how AI might be used in these spaces, and suggest more robust meth

infographic.key_insight: AI can make augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems more capable, but evaluating those systems is not straightforward because users’ needs are highly personal, contextual, and multidimensional. The paper argues for richer evaluation methods that better reflect the real lives and goals of AAC users.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of designing and evaluating AI-powered AAC interfaces when standard metrics fail to capture the nuanced, intersectional, and individualized preferences of people who use AAC.
method: Examines six AAC problem spaces where AI could support communication.
Analyzes how AI might be applied differently across these spaces.
Proposes more robust evaluation approaches that account for complex user needs and lived experience.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that success in assistive AI cannot be measured only by accuracy or speed. It emphasizes the need for human-centered, context-aware evaluation frameworks when building tools for people with disabilities.

title: IV-CoT: Implicit Visual Chain-of-Thought for Structure-Aware Text-to-Image Generation
authors: Zixuan Li, Haokun Lin, Yicheng Xiao, Zhiwei Li, Xinyang Song
abstract: Unified multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong text-to-image generation quality, but still struggle with structure-aware prompt following, where object counts, spatial relations, attribute bindings, and coarse layouts must be preserved. We attribute this limitation in part to the entanglement of structural planning and appearance rendering within a single conditioning stream. To address this issue, we propose Implicit Visual Chain-of-Thought (IV-CoT), a latent visual reas

infographic.key_insight: IV-CoT separates structural planning from appearance rendering by using an implicit visual reasoning space, helping text-to-image models follow complex prompts more faithfully. This improves object counts, spatial relations, attribute bindings, and coarse layouts without requiring explicit step-by-step text reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses poor structure-aware prompt following in unified multimodal large language models for text-to-image generation, especially when prompts require correct counts, layouts, object relationships, and attribute assignments.
method: Introduces Implicit Visual Chain-of-Thought (IV-CoT), a latent visual reasoning mechanism for planning image structure before final rendering.
Decouples structural planning from appearance generation to reduce entanglement in a single conditioning stream.
Uses visual latent reasoning to better preserve prompt constraints such as spatial arrangement, object binding, and overall composition.
infographic.impact: This matters because it can make text-to-image systems more reliable for real-world creative and design workflows where prompt fidelity is critical. For practitioners, it offers a pathway to generate images with stronger control over structure without sacrificing generative quality.

title: DDStereo: Efficient Dual Decoder Transformers for Stereo 3D Road Anomaly Detection
authors: Shiyi Mu, Zichong Gu, Zhiqi Ai, Yilin Gao, Shugong Xu
abstract: Stereo-based 3D object detection still faces two critical safety challenges: real-time performance and open-set generalization. Existing stereo 3D methods typically achieve twice the accuracy of monocular methods but suffer from significantly lower inference speeds, making them unsuitable for real-time applications. Meanwhile, recent advances in open-world detection have introduced open-set and open-vocabulary algorithms in monocular 2D and 3D settings, yet stereo-based open-set detection remain

infographic.key_insight: DDStereo aims to make stereo 3D road anomaly detection both fast enough for real-time use and robust to unseen objects. It does this with an efficient dual-decoder transformer design that targets the speed-accuracy tradeoff common in stereo methods.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses two major safety challenges in stereo-based 3D detection: slow inference speed and weak open-set generalization to unknown road anomalies.
method: Introduces a dual-decoder transformer architecture for stereo 3D anomaly detection.
Optimizes the model for real-time efficiency while preserving the richer depth cues from stereo inputs.
Targets open-set road anomaly detection, helping the system handle objects or hazards not seen during training.
infographic.impact: This matters for autonomous driving and robotics because it brings stereo vision closer to practical deployment in safety-critical, real-time settings. For practitioners, it offers a path to better anomaly detection without relying on slower heavy models.

title: Accuracy and Satisfaction in Multi-Turn LLM Dialogues for NFR Assessment
authors: Ali Pourghasemi Fatideh, Wilder Baldwin, Maria Dhakal, Collin McMillan, Sepideh Ghanavati
abstract: LLM-based dialogue assistants have become mainstream tools for software developers, yet current evaluation benchmarks focus exclusively on functional correctness. This leaves a critical gap in assessing the quality and accuracy of these conversations when handling Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs), which are inherently vague, context-dependent, and involve many parts of a program. Evaluating how well these systems support collaborative reasoning about NFRs requires methods that go beyond single

infographic.key_insight: This paper highlights that standard LLM benchmarks miss a crucial quality dimension for developer assistants: how accurately they handle multi-turn conversations about non-functional requirements (NFRs). It argues that evaluating NFR support requires measuring collaborative reasoning, not just single-answer correctness.
infographic.problem_solved: Current LLM evaluation methods mainly test functional correctness, leaving a gap for vague, context-dependent, multi-part concerns like performance, security, usability, and maintainability. The paper addresses the need for better ways to assess the accuracy and satisfaction of multi-turn dialogue when discussing NFRs.
method: Frames NFR assessment as a multi-turn dialogue evaluation problem rather than a single-response task.
Focuses on conversation quality metrics that capture accuracy and user satisfaction during collaborative reasoning.
Targets evaluation settings where requirements are ambiguous, context-sensitive, and distributed across multiple program components.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work points to a more realistic way to judge developer-facing LLM assistants. Better NFR evaluation can lead to tools that are more trustworthy for software engineering tasks where incorrect guidance can affect system quality and product outcomes.

title: OpenThoughts-Agent: Data Recipes for Agentic Models
authors: Negin Raoof, Richard Zhuang, Marianna Nezhurina, Etash Guha, Atula Tejaswi
abstract: Agentic language models dramatically expand the applications of AI yet little is publicly known about how to curate training data for broadly capable agents. Existing open efforts such as SWE-Smith, SERA, and Nemotron-Terminal typically target a single benchmark, leaving open the question of how to train models that generalize across diverse agentic tasks. The OpenThoughts-Agent (OT-Agent) project addresses this gap with a fully open data curation pipeline for training agentic models. We conduct

infographic.key_insight: OpenThoughts-Agent introduces a fully open recipe for curating training data for agentic language models, aiming to make them generalize beyond a single benchmark. The key idea is that strong agents need diverse, purpose-built data pipelines—not just benchmark-specific datasets.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of publicly available guidance and reusable pipelines for training broadly capable agentic models. Existing open data efforts tend to optimize for one benchmark at a time, limiting cross-task generalization.
method: Build a fully open data curation pipeline for agentic model training.
Design data recipes intended to support diverse agentic behaviors rather than a single target benchmark.
Systematically explore how to construct training data for models that can generalize across varied agent tasks.
infographic.impact: This work gives researchers and practitioners a transparent starting point for creating stronger agentic models. It can help reduce reliance on opaque, benchmark-specific data recipes and improve reproducibility across agent evaluation and training.

title: Bridging the Manifold Gap: Riemannian Residual Line Search for One-Step Image Editing
authors: Hongzhu Yi, Zhongtian Luo, Tong Li, Yiyan Fan, Jungang Xu
abstract: One-step diffusion editors are fast because they avoid inversion and iterative optimization, but a single transport update must be aggressive enough to realize the target prompt and conservative enough to preserve the source image--and no fixed update strength satisfies both demands across edit types. We treat this tension as a post-hoc candidate-selection problem on top of energy-field transport rather than as a new editing model. Our proposed method, Riemannian Residual Line Search, first buil

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that one-step image editing can be made more reliable by choosing the best update size after the initial transport step, instead of using a fixed strength for all edits. This balances prompt adherence and source-image preservation without adding a slower iterative editor.
infographic.problem_solved: One-step diffusion editors face a trade-off: the update must be strong enough to achieve the requested edit, but weak enough to keep the original image intact. A single fixed step size cannot handle different edit types well.
method: Treats editing as a post-hoc candidate-selection problem rather than training a new editing model.
Uses Riemannian Residual Line Search to search over candidate transport updates and select the residual that best matches the edit objective.
Balances two competing goals during selection: semantic change toward the target prompt and fidelity to the source image.
infographic.impact: This makes one-step editors more practical by improving quality without sacrificing speed. For practitioners, it offers a lightweight way to improve edit reliability across diverse prompts and image types.

title: SHERLOC: Structured Diagnostic Localization for Code Repair Agents
authors: Hovhannes Tamoyan, Sean Narenthiran, Erik Arakelyan, Mira Mezini, Boris Ginsburg
abstract: LLM agents solve repository-level coding tasks through multi-turn tool use, but utilize half their budget on locating faults before editing. Dedicated localization frameworks have emerged, yet are still evaluated as file retrieval rather than actionable diagnosis, producing locations without the diagnostic context a repair agent needs. We introduce SHERLOC (Structured Hypothesis-driven Exploration and Reasoning for Localization), a training-free framework pairing a reasoning LLM with compact rep

infographic.key_insight: SHERLOC reframes code localization from simple file retrieval into actionable diagnosis for repair agents. It helps LLM agents spend less time searching for bugs and more time making the right fix by producing structured, repair-ready fault hypotheses.
infographic.problem_solved: Repository-level coding agents often waste a large portion of their tool-use budget locating faults before editing, and existing localization methods usually return only where a bug might be rather than why it is happening. This leaves repair agents with incomplete context.
method: Uses a training-free localization framework designed for repository-level code repair.
Pairs a reasoning LLM with compact retrieval/exploration components to generate structured fault hypotheses.
Organizes localization output as diagnostic context, not just file or line candidates, so downstream repair can act on it.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this can improve the efficiency and reliability of automated code repair by reducing wasted search steps. It also bridges the gap between bug location and bug understanding, which is crucial for agentic debugging workflows.

title: PsyBridge: A Hybrid Intelligent Framework for Multi-Dimensional Mental Health Assessment and Decision Support
authors: Sunil Wanjari, Manish Thakre, Aayushi Asole, Sharwari Raut, Kwabena Adu-Duodu
abstract: Mental health assessment commonly relies on isolated screening instruments or data-driven models that often lack interpretability and multi-dimensional integration. Existing approaches frequently focus on individual indicators such as depression or anxiety while providing limited support for comprehensive and explainable decision-making. To address this limitation, this study proposes PsyBridge, a hybrid intelligent decision-support framework designed for multi-dimensional mental health assessme

infographic.key_insight: PsyBridge introduces a hybrid, explainable decision-support framework that combines multiple mental health indicators into one integrated assessment. It aims to move beyond single-score screening by supporting more complete and interpretable mental health evaluation.
infographic.problem_solved: Current mental health assessment tools often rely on isolated screens or black-box predictive models, making it hard to capture multiple dimensions of mental health and to explain recommendations clearly. PsyBridge addresses the need for comprehensive, multi-factor, and decision-support-oriented assessment.
method: Uses a hybrid intelligent framework that blends data-driven modeling with interpretable decision-support logic.
Integrates multiple mental health dimensions rather than focusing on a single condition such as depression or anxiety.
Aims to produce assessments that are both comprehensive and explainable for practical use.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, PsyBridge highlights how to design systems that are not only predictive but also interpretable and clinically useful. It is especially relevant for building trustworthy AI in healthcare where multi-dimensional evidence and transparency matter.

title: Open Problem: Is AdamW Effective Under Heavy-Tailed Noise?
authors: Dingzhi Yu, Hongyi Tao, Yuanyu Wan, Luo Luo, Lijun Zhang
abstract: AdamW is the de facto optimizer for training large language models (LLMs), yet the theory behind it still lives mostly in finite-variance regimes. This is increasingly unsatisfying, as empirical evidence indicates that stochastic gradient noise in LLM pretraining is typically heavy-tailed. Recent work shows that sign-based optimizers such as Lion and Muon achieve sharp heavy-tailed rates, and that AdaGrad can also converge under heavy-tailed noise. However, no rigorous convergence theory for Ada

infographic.key_insight: This paper highlights an open theoretical gap: AdamW is widely used in LLM training, but its convergence guarantees under the heavy-tailed gradient noise commonly seen in practice are still not well understood. It frames the question of whether AdamW remains effective beyond the usual finite-variance assumptions.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of rigorous convergence theory for AdamW when stochastic gradients follow heavy-tailed noise distributions, which better match real-world LLM pretraining dynamics.
method: Review the mismatch between existing finite-variance optimization theory and heavy-tailed noise observed in LLM training.
Compare AdamW with recent optimizers that have provable heavy-tailed behavior, such as Lion, Muon, and AdaGrad.
Formulate AdamW's effectiveness under heavy-tailed noise as an open research problem and identify the missing theoretical conditions needed for analysis.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work clarifies why AdamW's practical success does not yet come with full theoretical backing in realistic noise settings. It helps guide optimizer choice and motivates future analysis for training large-scale models under more realistic assumptions.

title: IMAGIN-4D: Image-Guided Controllable Interaction Generation
authors: Sai Kumar Dwivedi, Federica Bogo, Buğra Tekin, Chenhongyi Yang, Nadine Bertsch
abstract: Generating human-object interactions (HOI) is central to character animation, robotics, AR/VR, and embodied AI. Recent HOI generation methods synthesize motion from text, object geometry, and sparse waypoints, controlling action semantics and object trajectories. However, these signals underspecify interaction: the same prompt and trajectory can produce different grasps, approach directions, body poses, object poses, contacts, and body-object layouts. We address this ambiguity with a reference i

infographic.key_insight: IMAGIN-4D shows that human-object interaction generation becomes much more controllable when the model is guided by a reference image, reducing ambiguity in grasp, pose, contact, and body-object layout. Instead of relying only on text or sparse trajectories, it uses visual reference to better match the intended interaction.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing HOI generation methods can follow the same prompt or object path but still produce many different interaction styles, making outputs inconsistent and hard to control. This paper tackles the ambiguity in interaction details that are not specified by text, object geometry, or waypoints alone.
method: Condition HOI generation on a reference image to disambiguate how the interaction should look.
Use the image guidance to control fine-grained interaction attributes such as grasp type, approach direction, body pose, object pose, and contact configuration.
Generate more precise and consistent human-object motion while preserving the intended action semantics and object trajectory.
infographic.impact: This is useful for practitioners building animation, robotics, AR/VR, and embodied AI systems that need realistic and user-controlled interaction generation. It improves reliability by giving models a stronger visual constraint than text-only or trajectory-only conditioning.

title: TailorMind: Towards Preference-Aligned Multimodal Content Generation
authors: Hengji Zhou, Ye Liu, Yufeng Liu, Si Wu, Lianghao Xia
abstract: Personalized content systems depend on available UGC and struggle when suitable content is absent, delayed, or costly to create. Although multimodal generators can synthesize content on demand, how to translate behavioral traces into generation-ready preferences remains underexplored. We study personalized multimodal content generation: creating user-tailored multimodal content without existing item pools or waiting for matching UGC. We propose TailorMind, linking collaborative preference modeli

infographic.key_insight: TailorMind turns user behavior into generation-ready preferences, enabling multimodal content to be created directly for a person even when no matching item exists. It bridges collaborative preference modeling with multimodal generation so personalization no longer depends on available UGC.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional personalized content systems rely on existing user-generated content or costly manual creation, which fails when suitable content is missing or delayed. This paper addresses how to generate user-tailored multimodal content directly from behavioral traces and preferences.
method: Learn user preferences from collaborative signals and behavioral traces rather than only from existing content pools.
Map these learned preferences into a form that can condition multimodal generators for on-demand content creation.
Align preference modeling with generation so the output better matches individual user tastes across modalities.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this opens a path to true on-demand personalization in multimodal systems, reducing dependence on pre-existing catalogs or UGC availability. It is especially useful for recommendation, creative generation, and user-centric content platforms.

title: AutoDex: An Automated Real-World System for Dexterous Grasping Data Collection
authors: Mingi Choi, Gunhee Kim, Jisoo Kim, Taeksoo Kim, Taeyun Ha
abstract: Learning robust dexterous grasping requires real-world data that records the physical outcomes of grasp attempts. Such data is hard to obtain at scale: teleoperation yields valid physical outcomes but is slow and operator-biased, while simulation-based generation is cheap and scalable but cannot certify contact validity. A natural solution is to generate candidate grasps and verify them on real hardware, but this scales only if the entire collection loop (perception, execution, labeling, and res

infographic.key_insight: AutoDex automates the full real-world data collection loop for dexterous grasping, making it possible to generate and verify large-scale grasp data on hardware instead of relying on slow teleoperation or unverifiable simulation. The result is a more scalable way to collect physically valid grasp outcomes for training robust manipulation systems.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the bottleneck of acquiring large-scale, real-world dexterous grasping data with verified physical outcomes. Existing methods are either too slow and biased (teleoperation) or scalable but not physically trustworthy (simulation).
method: Generates candidate dexterous grasps automatically from perception and grasp proposal components.
Executes grasp attempts on real hardware to verify physical contact success or failure.
Automates the end-to-end pipeline for perception, execution, labeling, and resampling to reduce human intervention.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in robotics, AutoDex provides a practical path to building larger, cleaner training datasets for dexterous manipulation. This can improve policy learning, reduce sim-to-real gaps, and accelerate research on robust real-world grasping.

title: AI-driven Optimisation of Quality of Recovery (QoR) in Remote Patient Monitoring
authors: Yansong Liu,  Li-Hsi,  Lin, Pramit Khetrapal, Ronnie Stafford
abstract: Remote patient monitoring depends on patient-reported data to capture the subjective dimension of recovery that devices cannot measure. The Quality of Recovery (QoR-15) survey is the gold-standard instrument for this purpose. It was designed and validated for occasional in-hospital assessment, yet remote monitoring now administers it to patients daily. In our own post-surgical deployment, only 55% of patients submitted the survey more than 14 days of 30 monitoring days. We developed QoR-compact,

infographic.key_insight: Daily remote monitoring with the standard QoR-15 survey is too burdensome for many patients, leading to poor adherence. The paper introduces QoR-compact to preserve recovery measurement while making patient reporting easier and more sustainable.
infographic.problem_solved: The study addresses the mismatch between QoR-15’s original use case (occasional in-hospital assessment) and its newer use in daily remote patient monitoring, where completion rates drop over time.
method: Analyze real-world post-surgical remote monitoring data to identify adherence problems with daily QoR-15 use.

Optimize the survey for repeated remote use while preserving the subjective recovery signal needed for clinical monitoring.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that model or system performance in healthcare depends not only on prediction quality but also on human data collection behavior. Better instrument design can improve data completeness, reduce burden, and make downstream monitoring systems more reliable.

title: CoorDex: Coordinating Body and Hand Priors for Continuous Dexterous Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sikai Li, Shuning Li, Zhenyu Wei, Yunchao Yao, Chenran Li
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation is often simplified into a stop-and-go process: walking to an object, stopping to manipulate it, and then resuming locomotion. It also commonly relies on low degree-of-freedom (DoF) end effectors that behave like an open-close grasp primitive. We introduce CoorDex, a learning pipeline that converts high-dimensional body and dexterous hand control into coordinated latent residual control, enabling high-DoF dexterous loco-manipulation on the move. Starting from simulated

infographic.key_insight: CoorDex shows that humanoids do not need to stop walking to manipulate objects: body motion and dexterous hand control can be coordinated continuously through a learned latent residual policy. This enables more natural, high-DoF loco-manipulation than simple open-close grasping.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the common limitation in humanoid robotics where locomotion and manipulation are treated as separate phases, forcing robots to stop before interacting with objects. It also tackles the difficulty of controlling high-DoF hands and body motions together in real time.
method: Learn a coordinated latent residual control pipeline that maps high-dimensional body and hand commands into a compact action space.
Use simulated training to learn continuous dexterous loco-manipulation instead of stop-and-go behavior.
Combine body and dexterous hand priors so the humanoid can manipulate objects while maintaining movement.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a practical path toward more capable embodied agents that can operate fluidly in dynamic environments. It may improve robotics systems that need simultaneous mobility and manipulation, such as service robots, assistive robots, and warehouse humanoids.

title: Semantic Browsing: Controllable Diversity for Image Generation
authors: Sara Dorfman, Maya Vishnevsky, Omer Dahary, Or Patashnik, Daniel Cohen-Or
abstract: Modern text-to-image models excel in visual fidelity and prompt adherence. However, this strict adherence comes at the cost of diversity: generated samples tend to collapse into a single visual interpretation. Existing methods to improve diversity produce outputs driven by incidental variations rather than meaningful design choices. This motivates a new variant of the diversity task where structure is enforced on the generated samples. We introduce a method for controlled diversity that enables

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that diversity in image generation should be meaningful and controllable, not just random variation. It introduces a structured way to browse multiple valid outputs so users can steer generation toward different design choices.
infographic.problem_solved: Text-to-image models often produce visually similar outputs that collapse into one interpretation of a prompt. Existing diversity methods tend to change incidental details rather than exposing deliberate, user-controllable alternatives.
method: Defines a new controlled-diversity setting where generated samples follow an explicit structure instead of being arbitrarily different.
Introduces a semantic browsing approach that lets users explore multiple meaningful image variations along chosen axes of variation.
Aims to preserve prompt fidelity while increasing diversity in a way that reflects intentional design decisions.
infographic.impact: This is useful for practitioners who need image generation tools that support exploration, creative iteration, and design-space search. It makes generative models more practical for workflows where multiple distinct but relevant outputs are needed.

title: Pose Anything Anywhere:Model-free Object Poses from Arbitrary References
authors: Hongli Xu, Jiaqi Hu, Junwen Huang, Boyang Zhong, Peter KT Yu
abstract: Estimating the 6D pose of unseen objects is a fundamental yet challenging problem for open-world robotics and embodied perception. Model-based methods are accurate but depend on CAD assets or heavy onboarding, while most model-free approaches are still limited to pairwise single-anchor matching and thus fail under occlusion and large viewpoint changes with low query-reference overlap. Therefore, we present PANY, a unified model-free framework that seamlessly supports both RGB and RGB-D inputs, o

infographic.key_insight: PANY enables 6D pose estimation for unseen objects without needing CAD models, making it possible to localize objects from arbitrary reference views even when overlap is low or the object is heavily occluded. It unifies RGB and RGB-D inputs in a model-free framework.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses open-world 6D object pose estimation for unseen objects, especially the failure of existing model-free methods when query-reference overlap is small, viewpoints change dramatically, or occlusions are present.
method: Introduces PANY, a unified model-free pose estimation framework that works with both RGB and RGB-D inputs.
Moves beyond pairwise single-anchor matching by supporting arbitrary reference views for more robust pose inference.
Designed to handle challenging real-world conditions such as occlusion, low overlap, and large viewpoint variation without requiring CAD assets.
infographic.impact: This matters because it lowers the barrier to deploying pose estimation in robotics and embodied AI, where objects are often unseen and CAD models are unavailable. Practitioners gain a more flexible and scalable way to estimate object pose in cluttered, real-world environments.

title: Lift4D: Harmonizing Single-View 3D Estimation for 4D Reconstruction In-the-Wild
authors: Yehonathan Litman, Xiaoxuan Ma, Manan Shah, Nicolas Ugrinovic, Kris Kitani
abstract: Reconstructing dynamic non-rigid objects from monocular video requires integrating visual cues from direct observations with data-driven priors over geometry and appearance. Prior approaches either learn to directly predict 4D representations from visual input or initialize a 3D representation that is subsequently deformed and refined based on video evidence. However, the former are constrained by the scarcity of 4D training data, while the latter leverage priors only for the initial reconstruct

infographic.key_insight: Lift4D bridges the gap between direct 4D prediction and deformation-based reconstruction by using strong single-view 3D estimation as a unified starting point for recovering dynamic objects in the wild. This lets the method combine learned priors with video evidence more effectively than approaches that rely on only one of them.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses monocular 4D reconstruction of dynamic, non-rigid objects from in-the-wild video, where limited 4D training data and weak temporal supervision make accurate shape, motion, and appearance recovery difficult.
method: Use single-view 3D estimation to produce a strong initial 3D representation from one frame or view.
Harmonize learned priors with observed video cues to refine geometry, appearance, and deformation over time.
Reconstruct a coherent 4D representation that can better handle non-rigid motion and real-world video conditions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, Lift4D offers a practical route to better dynamic scene reconstruction when multi-view data is unavailable. It is especially relevant for AR/VR, robotics, digital humans, and vision systems that need robust 3D understanding from everyday videos.

title: EnterpriseClawBench: Benchmarking Agents from Real Workplace Sessions
authors: Jincheng Zhong, Weizhi Wang, Che Jiang, Kai Tian, Zhenzhao Yuan
abstract: Enterprise agents increasingly operate inside workspaces: they read heterogeneous files, invoke tools, and deliver business artifacts. We introduce EnterpriseClawBench, an enterprise agent benchmark constructed from proprietary, real-world agent sessions. Starting from a large archive of workplace sessions, the EnterpriseClawBench produces 852 reproducible tasks, each paired with recovered fixtures, rewritten prompts, role classes, skill subclasses, hard rules, and semantic rubrics. Because the

infographic.key_insight: EnterpriseClawBench turns real workplace agent sessions into a reproducible benchmark, making it possible to evaluate enterprise AI agents on tasks that mirror actual business workflows. It provides grounded tasks, fixtures, and semantic rubrics rather than synthetic test cases.
infographic.problem_solved: Current agent benchmarks often miss the complexity of real enterprise work, such as heterogeneous files, tool use, and strict business rules. This paper addresses the need for a realistic, reproducible evaluation set built from actual workplace sessions.
method: Collected enterprise agent sessions from a large proprietary archive of real workplace activity.
Reconstructed 852 reproducible tasks with recovered fixtures and rewritten prompts.
Annotated tasks with role classes, skill subclasses, hard rules, and semantic rubrics for structured evaluation.
infographic.impact: This benchmark gives AI/ML practitioners a more realistic way to measure how well enterprise agents perform in practical settings. It can improve model selection, debugging, and comparison for workplace automation systems.

title: DiT-Reward: Generative Representations for Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
authors: Yuanming Yang, Guoqing Ma, Bo Wang, Yuan Zhang, Wei Tang
abstract: Can representations learned for image generation also support the evaluation of generated images? We study text-to-image reward prediction as a downstream task of generative representation learning. To this end, we introduce DiT-Reward, which converts a pretrained text-to-image Diffusion Transformer into a reward model by processing near-clean image latents and aggregating text-conditioned image representations across transformer layers. Under the same training data mixture as HPSv3, DiT-Reward

infographic.key_insight: DiT-Reward shows that a text-to-image generator can be repurposed as a reward model, using generative representations to judge image quality and text alignment. The key idea is that near-clean image latents and layer-wise transformer features contain enough information to predict rewards effectively.
infographic.problem_solved: Text-to-image systems need reliable reward models to evaluate generated images, but standard reward models may not fully leverage the rich representations learned during image generation. This paper addresses how to turn a pretrained diffusion transformer into an effective evaluator for generated images.
method: Start with a pretrained text-to-image Diffusion Transformer (DiT) instead of training a separate reward model from scratch.
Process near-clean image latents so the model focuses on evaluating generated content rather than noisy intermediate states.
Aggregate text-conditioned image representations across multiple transformer layers to produce reward predictions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more efficient way to build image reward models by reusing generative backbones. It may improve alignment evaluation for text-to-image systems while reducing the need for separate model architectures.

title: Teaching LLMs String Matching, Backtracking, and Error Recovery to Deduce Bases and Truth Tables for the Combinatorially Exploding Bit Manipulation Puzzles
authors: Prateek Agnihotri, Sanchit Jain, Prabhat Agnihotri, Aditya Prasad, Shubham Jain
abstract: This paper presents our algorithmic innovations for the NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge, focusing on Bit Manipulation Puzzles. In this task, the objective is to discover a hidden logical rule transforming input binary strings to outputs, then apply it to unseen inputs. Large Language Models (LLMs) notoriously struggle here; traditional methods force them to simulate complex boolean logic and arithmetic, leading to hallucinations. Furthermore, the search space of bitwise operations (com

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that LLMs can solve bit-manipulation puzzles more reliably when they are guided to use string matching, backtracking, and error recovery instead of trying to mentally simulate complex logic. This shifts the task from fragile reasoning to a more structured search-and-deduction process.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of inferring a hidden binary transformation rule from input-output examples and applying it to unseen cases, especially when the solution space of bitwise operations is combinatorially large.
method: Use string matching to identify patterns in example input-output pairs.
Apply backtracking to explore candidate logical rules without getting trapped by early wrong assumptions.
Add error recovery steps so the model can correct mistakes and keep searching when deductions fail.
infographic.impact: This matters because it improves LLM performance on symbolic, logic-heavy tasks where direct reasoning often hallucinate or breaks down. For practitioners, it suggests that careful algorithmic scaffolding can make LLMs more dependable on hard puzzle-like reasoning problems.

title: How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?
authors: Joshua Engels, Callum McDougall, Bilal Chughtai, Janos Kramar, Senthoran Rajamanoharan
abstract: LLM reasoning transparency is a critical affordance for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse and misalignment, and debugging surprising model behaviors. However, DiffusionGemma performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space; does this make its reasoning less transparent? We study this question by decomposing transparency into two components: variable transparency, whether we understand intermediate snapshots of a model's computational state; and algorithmi

infographic.key_insight: The paper asks whether DiffusionGemma is harder to understand because more of its computation happens in a continuous latent space. It frames transparency as two parts—being able to interpret intermediate states and being able to infer the algorithm the model is implementing—and uses that lens to assess how transparent the model really is.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of interpreting reasoning in diffusion-based language models, where hidden computation is distributed across continuous intermediate snapshots rather than discrete token steps. This makes it harder to inspect what the model is doing, why it makes a decision, and whether it is behaving in a predictable or debuggable way.
method: Decompose transparency into two dimensions: variable transparency (can we interpret intermediate states?) and algorithmic transparency (can we recover the underlying computation?).
Analyze DiffusionGemma’s latent-space computation through intermediate snapshots to see how much reasoning signal is observable at different stages.
Compare the transparency of diffusion-style computation against the more familiar token-based reasoning paradigm.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this helps clarify when diffusion-based models are inspectable, debuggable, and safer to deploy. It provides a framework for evaluating transparency beyond standard token-level explanations, which is especially relevant for models with continuous internal representations.

title: UNIEGO: Proxies as Mediators for Unified Egocentric Video Representation Learning
authors: Wenhao Chi, Arkaprava Sinha, Dominick Reilly, Hieu Le, Srijan Das
abstract: Egocentric video understanding is inherently limited by the narrow perspective of wearable cameras: a single viewpoint, a single modality, a single model cannot capture the full richness of human action. We argue that a truly expressive egocentric representation must subsume complementary knowledge across viewpoints, modalities, and foundation model representations, yet remain deployable from egocentric video alone. To this end, we introduce a hierarchical multi-teacher distillation framework th

infographic.key_insight: UNIEGO learns richer egocentric video representations by using multiple proxy teachers as mediators, so a model trained only on first-person video can still absorb knowledge from other viewpoints, modalities, and foundation models. The result is a more expressive and transferable representation without requiring extra inputs at deployment.
infographic.problem_solved: Egocentric video is inherently limited by a narrow first-person view, making it hard for a single model or modality to capture the full complexity of human actions. This paper addresses how to unify complementary knowledge from diverse sources while keeping inference deployable from egocentric video alone.
method: Uses a hierarchical multi-teacher distillation framework to transfer knowledge into an egocentric student model.
Introduces proxies as mediators, allowing information from other viewpoints, modalities, and foundation models to be distilled indirectly.
Learns a unified representation that is trained with richer supervision but remains usable from egocentric video only at test time.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to improve first-person video understanding without changing the deployment setting or requiring extra sensors. It is especially useful for action recognition, wearable AI, and multimodal representation learning where supervision is rich but inference must stay lightweight.

title: CalTennis: Large Multi-View Tennis Video Dataset and Benchmark of Monocular-to-3D Pose Estimation
authors: Ilona Demler, Xinran Xie, Blake Werner, Anna Szczuka, Pietro Perona
abstract: The Caltech Tennis Dataset (CalTennis) is a large-scale video benchmark for evaluating monocular-to-3D pose estimation in the wild. CalTennis comprises over 11 million frames (51 hours) of tennis practice and match play from 40 players, captured with 2-6 synchronized cameras at 60 Hz. It is 10 times larger than existing in-the-wild human motion video datasets and 3 times larger than existing MOCAP-ground-truthed datasets, and it is the first large-scale benchmark to provide synchronized multi-vi

infographic.key_insight: CalTennis is a much larger, real-world tennis video benchmark that makes it possible to test monocular-to-3D pose estimation under realistic game conditions. Its synchronized multi-camera setup and scale help reveal how well pose models actually generalize outside controlled lab settings.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of large, in-the-wild datasets for evaluating monocular-to-3D human pose estimation, especially with strong ground truth and synchronized multi-view video. Existing benchmarks are too small or too controlled to measure performance in realistic sports motion.
method: Collected over 11 million frames (51 hours) of tennis practice and match play from 40 players.
Captured each scene with 2-6 synchronized cameras at 60 Hz to enable multi-view 3D pose evaluation.
Built a benchmark designed specifically for monocular-to-3D pose estimation in real, unconstrained sports footage.
infographic.impact: CalTennis gives researchers a more realistic and much larger testbed for evaluating pose estimation models. This can improve model robustness, expose failure cases in the wild, and accelerate progress toward reliable 3D human motion understanding.

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
authors: Maria Ivanova, Pavel Zadorozhny, Rodion Levichev, Ivan Petrov, Adamenko Pavel
abstract: LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages r

infographic.key_insight: Multi-LCB extends LiveCodeBench beyond Python to evaluate whether LLMs can write code reliably across multiple programming languages. The key idea is to make coding benchmarks more realistic, language-diverse, and resistant to data contamination.
infographic.problem_solved: LiveCodeBench is widely used for contamination-aware code evaluation, but it only covers Python. This paper addresses the gap of measuring LLM coding ability across different programming languages rather than a single language.
method: Expand the LiveCodeBench benchmark into a multi-language setting with curated coding problems.
Preserve contamination-aware evaluation by using fresh problems and release-date filtering.
Enable comparison of LLM performance across diverse programming languages to assess generalization.
infographic.impact: This matters because real-world coding assistants must work across many languages, not just Python. For practitioners, Multi-LCB offers a more realistic and fair benchmark for selecting and comparing code models.

title: Thinking in Boxes: 3D Editing in Real Images Made Easy
authors: Pradhaan S Bhat, Naveen Chandra R, Rishubh Parihar, Vaibhav Vavilala, R. Venkatesh Babu
abstract: Text and 2D-conditioning interfaces provide weak, ambiguous control over spatial transformations in image editing -- particularly under large object motions and camera changes. Prior work has used 3D primitives such as boxes, but only as loose conditioning signals indicating approximate object location rather than specifying the transformation. We instead use 3D boxes as structured specifications: the user provides the input and output boxes of the edit, casting editing as a well-posed geometry

infographic.key_insight: This paper turns 3D boxes from a vague hint into a precise editing instruction. By specifying both the starting and ending boxes, users can control large spatial changes in real-image editing more reliably.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing text prompts and 2D conditioning are often ambiguous for edits involving big object movement or camera/viewpoint changes. The paper addresses the lack of a clear geometric control signal for these kinds of transformations.
method: Represent the edit as a pair of 3D bounding boxes: the input box and the output box.
Use these boxes as a structured specification for the desired transformation, rather than as loose location hints.
Reformulate image editing as a well-posed geometry-driven problem, enabling more controllable spatial edits in real images.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a more interpretable and controllable way to perform complex image edits, especially when spatial precision matters. It can improve reliability in workflows involving object relocation, pose changes, or viewpoint edits.

abstract: Multimodal foundation models have advanced rapidly thanks to large optical benchmarks, but comparable resources for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) remain limited. Existing SAR--optical datasets largely rely on low-resolution, intensity-only Ground Range Detected~(GRD) products and do not preserve complex-valued SAR measurements or native acquisition geometry, which restricts physically grounded multimodal learning. In particular, large-scale public datasets combining very-high-resolution (VHR) S

infographic.key_insight: SARLO-80 introduces a large-scale, very-high-resolution SAR–optical dataset built to better support multimodal foundation models. Unlike many prior resources, it preserves native SAR measurements and acquisition geometry, enabling more physically grounded learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Current SAR–optical datasets are often low-resolution, intensity-only, and based on GRD products, which lose important SAR information such as complex-valued signals and imaging geometry. This limits the development of robust multimodal AI models for SAR analysis.
method: Assemble a worldwide dataset pairing slant-range SAR data with optical imagery at 80 cm resolution.
Preserve complex-valued SAR measurements and native acquisition geometry instead of reducing SAR to intensity-only GRD representations.
Provide a large-scale benchmark designed for physically consistent multimodal learning across SAR and optical modalities.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this dataset offers a stronger foundation for training and evaluating models that fuse SAR and optical data. It can improve downstream tasks where resolution, sensor geometry, and physical fidelity matter, such as remote sensing, Earth observation, and robust multimodal perception.

title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation
authors: Ruizhong Qiu, Yinglong Xia, Dongqi Fu, Hanqing Zeng, Ren Chen
abstract: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, exist

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that generative recommendation works better when user behavior and item semantics are structured together instead of injected separately. It proposes a way to tokenize distributed user-interest context so the model can capture richer signals for next-item prediction.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing generative recommendation methods struggle to combine complex user behavioral context with item semantic information in a unified, effective way. This limits the quality of item tokenization and weakens recommendation performance.
method: Structure distributed user-interest context so it can be represented more clearly for the model.
Design item tokenization that better connects user behavior patterns with item semantics.
Inject both behavioral and semantic context into the generative recommendation pipeline in a coordinated way.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more effective design pattern for generative recommender systems: organize context before tokenization, rather than treating it as a flat input. This can improve recommendation quality in large-scale industrial systems where user histories are complex and sparse.

title: VisDom: Sparse Novel View Synthesis with Visible Domain Constraint
authors: Mariia Gladkova*, Tarun Yenamandra*, Edmond Boyer, Robert Maier, Tony Tung
abstract: Sparse novel view synthesis (NVS) remains challenging due to the ambiguity of recovering 3D geometry from few input views. While NeRF- and Gaussian Splatting (GS)-based methods perform well with dense supervision, they often overfit in sparse settings, producing floating artifacts and inconsistent geometry. Silhouette consistency is commonly used as a regularizer, but it remains insufficient, as silhouette-consistent regions can extend beyond the true object geometry. We introduce VisDom, a lear

infographic.key_insight: VisDom improves sparse novel view synthesis by adding a "visible domain" constraint, helping models focus on geometry that is actually supported by the input views. This reduces overfitting, floating artifacts, and inconsistent 3D reconstructions in sparse-view settings.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of recovering accurate 3D geometry and realistic novel views from only a few input images, where NeRF- and Gaussian Splatting-based methods often overfit and produce artifacts. It also tackles the limitation of silhouette-only regularization, which can include regions outside the true object shape.
method: Introduces a visible domain constraint to restrict learning to regions that are truly supported by the observed views.
Uses this constraint as a regularizer for sparse-view novel view synthesis to improve geometric consistency.
Builds on NeRF/GS-style pipelines while reducing hallucinated or floating content in unobserved areas.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, VisDom offers a practical way to make sparse-view reconstruction more reliable without requiring dense supervision. This can improve results in 3D capture, robotics, AR/VR, and other applications where collecting many views is difficult.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift
authors: Gina Wong, Drew Prinster, Suchi Saria, Rama Chellappa, Anqi Liu
abstract: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that calibrating the individual experts in a mixture-of-experts model can improve both reliability and performance, especially when data distribution shifts. It clarifies when calibration actually helps MoE systems instead of just making probabilities look better.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of understanding around when and why calibration improves mixture-of-experts models, particularly under distribution shift where model predictions can become unreliable.
method: Study calibration at the level of individual experts rather than only the final ensemble output.
Analyze mixture-of-experts behavior under distribution shift to identify conditions where calibration improves performance.
Compare predictive accuracy and uncertainty reliability to determine when calibrated experts lead to better MoE outcomes.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this provides guidance on building MoE systems that remain trustworthy when deployed in changing real-world environments. It helps improve both confidence estimates and decision quality in applications where uncertainty matters.

title: StylisticBias: A Few Human Visual Cues Drive Most Social Biases in MLLMs
authors: Shaghayegh Kolli, Timo Cavelius, Nafiseh Nikeghbal, Samantha Dalal, Jana Diesner
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in personally and societally consequential settings, yet the visual cues that shape how these models judge people remain poorly understood. Prior work often compares different (groups of) individuals, making it difficult to separate appearance effects from identity differences. We introduce StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute-level social bias in MLLMs. We generate 500 photorealistic base faces and crea

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that a small set of human-style visual cues can drive most social bias judgments in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). By isolating appearance from identity, it reveals which attributes actually trigger biased responses.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of separating true appearance-based bias from confounding identity differences in prior bias studies. The paper provides a controlled way to measure attribute-level social bias in MLLMs using standardized face variations.
method: Created StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark built from 500 photorealistic base faces.
Systematically edited visual attributes on the same identities to isolate the effect of specific cues.
Evaluated MLLMs on bias-related judgments to identify which human visual features most influence model behavior.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this helps reveal hidden bias mechanisms in multimodal systems before deployment in high-stakes settings. It also offers a more rigorous benchmark for auditing fairness in models that interpret people from images.

title: TimeProVe: Propose, then Verify for Efficient Long Video Temporal Reasoning in Activities of Daily Living
authors: Arkaprava Sinha, Dominick Reilly, Siddharth Krishnan, Hieu Le, Srijan Das
abstract: Long Video Question Answering (LVQA) requires identifying sparse, query-relevant evidence within hours-long untrimmed videos. Existing approaches either process videos densely with large vision-language models (VLMs), incurring prohibitive computational cost, or rely on sparse caption-based reasoning, which often misses temporally localized and motion-centric evidence. We introduce TimeProVe, a cost-efficient hybrid framework for temporally grounded reasoning in long videos. TimeProVe first empl

infographic.key_insight: TimeProVe makes long-video reasoning more efficient by first proposing likely evidence segments and then verifying them, instead of scanning hours of video densely. This hybrid strategy targets the sparse, motion-heavy moments that matter most for answering questions in Activities of Daily Living.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses Long Video Question Answering (LVQA), where models must find rare, query-relevant evidence in very long untrimmed videos. Existing dense VLM methods are too expensive, while caption-based sparse approaches can miss temporally localized or motion-centric cues.
method: Uses a two-stage 'Propose, then Verify' pipeline to narrow down candidate temporal segments before detailed reasoning.
Combines sparse proposal with verification to focus computation on the most relevant parts of the video.
Designed for temporally grounded reasoning in hours-long videos, especially for daily-activity scenarios with subtle actions.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, TimeProVe offers a more practical way to deploy LVQA systems on long videos without the heavy compute cost of dense processing. It can improve efficiency while preserving access to fine-grained temporal evidence needed for reliable answers.

title: S-Agent: Spatial Tool-Use Elicits Reasoning for Spatial Intelligence
authors: Yalun Dai, Hao Li, Shulin Tian, Runmao Yao, Yuhao Dong
abstract: Real-world spatial intelligence requires reasoning over a continuous and evolving 3D world, yet existing VLMs and tool-augmented agents largely remain tied to static, stateless inference from isolated visual observations. We introduce \textbf{\textsc{S-Agent}}, a spatial tool-use agentic paradigm for understanding and reasoning over continuous multi-view images and videos. By formulating spatial reasoning as spatio-temporal evidence accumulation rather than isolated frame-level prediction, \text

infographic.key_insight: S-Agent shows that spatial reasoning improves when an AI system can use tools to gather and accumulate evidence across views and time, instead of making a one-shot guess from a single image. The key breakthrough is turning spatial understanding into an active, evidence-building process over continuous 3D scenes.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing vision-language models and tool-augmented agents are mostly stateless and rely on isolated visual observations, which limits their ability to reason about real-world 3D environments that change over time. This paper addresses the gap between static image understanding and continuous spatial intelligence.
method: Introduces S-Agent, a spatial tool-use agentic paradigm for multi-view images and videos.
Reframes spatial reasoning as spatio-temporal evidence accumulation rather than frame-level prediction.
Uses tool interactions to progressively collect, organize, and reason over observations from a changing 3D world.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more reliable way to build agents for robotics, embodied AI, navigation, and video understanding. It points toward systems that can reason like humans do in real spaces: by exploring, verifying, and accumulating evidence over time.

title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
authors: Nityanand Mathur, Hamees Sayed, Wasim Madha, Apoorv Singh, Sameer Khurana
abstract: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 2

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows how to trace which instruction words influence specific parts of generated speech in style-captioned text-to-speech. By adapting cross-attention attribution to speech diffusion models, it makes expressive TTS more interpretable and easier to debug.
infographic.problem_solved: Style-captioned TTS can follow natural-language style prompts, but it is unclear how individual words in the caption affect acoustic output. This lack of transparency makes it hard to diagnose failures, understand controllability, or improve generation quality.
method: Adapts DAAM-style cross-attention attribution from image generation to speech diffusion models for the first time.
Computes per-token heatmaps across 25 layers to estimate how each instruction word contributes to the generated speech.
Applies the attribution method to CapSpeech-TTS to analyze word-level control and reveal failure modes in expressive TTS.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a practical interpretability tool for speech generation models. It can help debug prompt-following errors, improve prompt design, and build more reliable controllable TTS systems.
