title: HumanScale: Egocentric Human Video Can Outperform Real-Robot Data for Embodied Pretraining
authors: Juncheng Ma, Jianxin Bi, Yufan Deng, Xuanran Zhai, Kewei Zhang
abstract: Embodied foundation models are expected to benefit from data scaling like large language models, but face a much tighter data bottleneck. Teleoperated real-robot trajectories remain the dominant pretraining source due to their precise action supervision and embodiment alignment, yet their scalability is limited by high collection cost, acquisition difficulty, and low behavioral and environmental diversity. These limitations have sparked interest in egocentric human video as a scalable, substanti

infographic.key_insight: Egocentric human video can be a more scalable and surprisingly stronger pretraining source than real-robot teleoperation data for embodied models. The paper argues that human video can better overcome the data bottleneck while preserving useful behavior and interaction signals.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the scarcity, high cost, and low diversity of real-robot trajectories used for embodied pretraining. It explores whether large-scale human video can replace or outperform expensive robot-collected data.
method: Compare egocentric human video against teleoperated real-robot data as pretraining sources for embodied foundation models.
Leverage large-scale human video to capture diverse actions, scenes, and interactions at much lower collection cost.
Evaluate whether human video pretraining can transfer effectively to embodied tasks despite weaker or less explicit action supervision.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a cheaper and more scalable path to pretraining embodied agents without relying solely on costly robot data collection. It could accelerate dataset building and model development for robotics and embodied AI.

title: Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core
authors: Jinpeng Lu, Dexu Zhu, Haoyuan Shi, Linghan Cai, Guo Tang
abstract: World models are increasingly regarded as a decisive step toward artificial general intelligence, yet modeling the physical world demands more than rendering convincing frames on demand: it requires an internal world state that keeps evolving over time, decoupled from observation, so that objects endure and events run to their conclusions whether or not a camera is watching, much as the moon holds to its orbit when no one is looking. This requirement is a blind spot of existing benchmarks, which

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that current world models can generate convincing observations, but they often lack a persistent internal state that continues evolving when the scene is unobserved. In short: they can render the world, but they do not yet truly remember or maintain the world.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the gap in evaluation benchmarks that measure frame quality or short-term prediction, but fail to test whether a model preserves object permanence, long-range continuity, and state evolution independent of observation.
method: Reframes world-model evaluation around persistent internal state rather than only visual reconstruction quality.
Highlights benchmark blind spots that let models appear competent without maintaining a coherent hidden world state over time.
Motivates evaluation tasks where entities must remain consistent and events must progress even when not directly observed.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means better benchmarks are needed before world models can be trusted for planning, simulation, and embodied agents. Models that pass visual tests may still fail in real-world settings if they cannot retain a stable latent state across time.

title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
authors: Bhawna Paliwal, Haritheja Etukuru, William Liang, Pieter Abbeel, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah
abstract: How can we scalably generate data for robotic manipulation, especially on human-like platforms such as dexterous multi-fingered hands? Learning from human videos has recently emerged as a likely answer to this question. However, difficulties in estimating hand-object interaction and crossing the human-to-robot embodiment gap have hindered the adoption of abundant monocular RGB-only human videos as the primary source of robot manipulation data. In this work, we present DO AS I DO, an algorithm to

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows how to turn ordinary monocular human videos into usable data for dexterous robot manipulation, helping bridge the gap between human demonstrations and multi-fingered robot hands.
infographic.problem_solved: Robotic manipulation data is expensive and hard to scale, especially for dexterous hands. The paper addresses the challenge of extracting hand-object interactions from simple RGB videos and transferring those demonstrations to robot embodiments.
method: Learn from everyday human RGB videos instead of relying on specialized motion-capture or teleoperation datasets.
Estimate hand-object interaction from monocular footage to recover actionable manipulation signals.
Bridge the human-to-robot embodiment gap so demonstrations can be converted into robot-ready data for dexterous hands.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a scalable path to build larger manipulation datasets without expensive sensors or manual robot data collection. It could accelerate progress in dexterous manipulation, imitation learning, and embodied AI.

title: Enhancing Decision-Making with Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Fictitious Play
authors: Leyang Shen, Yang Zhang, Xiaoyan Zhao, Chun Kai Ling, Tat-Seng Chua
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated great potential in solving tasks with execution complexity, by distributing subtasks across cooperative agents. However, this divide-and-conquer paradigm falls short on decision-making tasks that are also prevalent in the real world. These tasks require simultaneous reasoning from the stances of all involved stakeholders whose decisions are mutually dependent and thus cannot be solved in isolation. We characterize this

infographic.key_insight: This paper extends multi-agent LLM systems from task execution to decision-making by using multi-agent fictitious play, so agents can reason about each stakeholder’s best response in a mutually dependent setting. The result is a more realistic way for LLMs to handle situations where decisions must be made jointly rather than in isolation.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the limitation of standard divide-and-conquer multi-agent LLM systems, which work well for decomposed tasks but struggle with real-world decision-making problems involving interdependent stakeholders, conflicting interests, and strategic interaction.
method: Model decision-making as a multi-agent interaction where each agent represents a stakeholder with its own objectives and beliefs.
Apply fictitious play so agents iteratively estimate others’ strategies and update their own decisions accordingly.
Use LLMs to support reasoning, strategy generation, and negotiation-like inference across agents.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a principled framework for using LLMs in strategic, multi-party decisions such as negotiation, planning, policy analysis, and recommendation. It moves LLM-based MAS closer to realistic human decision environments where outcomes depend on coordinated and competitive reasoning.

title: P-K-GCN: Physics-augmented Koopman-enhanced Graph Convolutional Network for Deep Spatiotemporal Super-resolution
authors: Xizhuo,  Zhang, Zekai Wang, Fei Liu, Bing Yao
abstract: High-fidelity simulation of spatiotemporal dynamics is computationally prohibitive, necessitating efficient super-resolution techniques to reconstruct high-resolution data from coarse-grained inputs. Traditional data-driven methods often lack physical constraints, and simple physics-informed learning struggles with irregular spatial geometries and intricately evolving temporal dynamics. To tackle these challenges, we propose a Physics-augmented Koopman-enhanced Graph Convolutional Network (P-K-G

infographic.key_insight: P-K-GCN combines physical constraints, Koopman-based temporal modeling, and graph convolution to super-resolve complex spatiotemporal fields more accurately than purely data-driven methods. It is designed to handle irregular geometries and evolving dynamics while preserving physically meaningful behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing high-resolution spatiotemporal simulations from coarse inputs when full-fidelity simulation is too expensive, especially for irregular domains and dynamics that are hard to model with standard neural networks.
method: Uses a graph convolutional network to represent irregular spatial structure and learn local interactions on non-Euclidean domains.
Incorporates Koopman-enhanced temporal modeling to capture nonlinear time evolution in a more stable, interpretable latent space.
Adds physics-augmentation to constrain predictions with physical consistency, improving realism and reducing implausible reconstructions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical route to high-fidelity super-resolution in scientific and engineering settings where geometry is irregular and physics matters. It shows how hybrid models can outperform purely data-driven approaches by blending learned representations with domain knowledge.

title: NeuMesh++: Towards Versatile and Efficient Volumetric Editing with Disentangled Neural Mesh-based Implicit Field
authors: Chong Bao, Yuan Li, Bangbang Yang, Yujun Shen, Hujun Bao
abstract: Recently neural implicit rendering techniques have evolved rapidly and demonstrated significant advantages in novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, existing neural rendering methods for editing purposes offer limited functionalities, e.g., rigid transformation and category-specific editing. In this paper, we present a novel mesh-based representation by encoding the neural radiance field with disentangled geometry, texture, and semantic codes on mesh vertices, which empowers

infographic.key_insight: NeuMesh++ introduces a mesh-based neural representation that disentangles geometry, texture, and semantic information, making volumetric scene editing more flexible and efficient. This enables richer edits than prior methods that were limited to rigid transforms or narrow, category-specific operations.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing neural rendering/editing methods are often too restrictive for practical scene manipulation, supporting only limited edits such as rigid movement or object-category-specific changes. NeuMesh++ addresses the need for a general-purpose, editable 3D representation that can support versatile volumetric editing.
method: Encodes a neural radiance field on mesh vertices instead of relying solely on dense volumetric representations.
Separates the representation into disentangled geometry, texture, and semantic codes to support targeted edits.
Uses the mesh structure to improve efficiency while preserving implicit-field expressiveness for reconstruction and editing.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more practical path to editable 3D content creation, simulation, and scene reconstruction. It can reduce edit complexity while enabling more controllable and scalable volumetric manipulation.

title: Reference-Driven Multi-Speaker Audio Scene Generation from In-the-Wild Priors
authors: Michael Finkelson, Daniel Segal, Eitan Richardson, Shahar Armon, Nani Goldring
abstract: Existing multi-speaker dialogue systems bind speakers to utterances through structured supervision: per-turn tags, multi-stream transcriptions, or learnable speaker embeddings. These systems operate within speech-only pipelines that produce clean vocal sequences without the ambient texture of real conversations. We take a different approach. Our method, ScenA, conditions a text-to-audio flow-matching foundation model, pretrained on large-scale in-the-wild data, directly on multiple reference voi

infographic.key_insight: ScenA generates realistic multi-speaker audio scenes by conditioning a text-to-audio foundation model on multiple reference voices and in-the-wild priors, rather than relying on rigid speaker tags or clean speech-only pipelines. This lets the model produce conversational audio with ambient texture, not just separated vocal turns.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between structured multi-speaker dialogue systems and real-world conversations. Existing methods often need per-turn labels, multi-stream transcripts, or speaker embeddings, and they tend to miss background ambience and natural interaction cues.
method: Condition a pretrained text-to-audio flow-matching foundation model directly on multiple reference voice samples.
Use in-the-wild audio priors so the model learns realistic conversational texture and ambient context.
Generate full multi-speaker audio scenes without requiring explicit speaker diarization-style supervision for each turn.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this points to a simpler way to synthesize realistic dialogue data with stronger environmental realism. It can improve research and applications in audio generation, simulation, dataset augmentation, and multimodal agent training.

title: Diffusion-Proof: Recipe for Formal Theorem Proving Beyond Auto-Regressive Generation
authors: Ruida Wang, Rui Pan, Pengcheng Wang, Shizhe Diao, Tong Zhang
abstract: Enhancing the formal math reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) has become a key focus in both mathematical and computer science communities in recent years. While significant progress has been made in using state-of-the-art Auto-Regressive (AR) LLMs for formal theorem proving, these models suffer from inherent limitations. Their next-token prediction generation methods may yield suboptimal performance due to the challenges of long-range coherence and the compounding of errors o

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that formal theorem proving can be improved beyond standard auto-regressive generation by using a diffusion-based approach. This shifts proof generation from token-by-token prediction to a more global, iterative refinement process that better handles long proofs.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the limitations of auto-regressive LLMs in formal theorem proving, especially long-range coherence issues, error accumulation, and difficulty recovering from early mistakes during proof generation.
method: Replace pure next-token generation with a diffusion-style proof synthesis and refinement process.
Iteratively denoise or improve partial proof states to produce more coherent formal outputs.
Target formal theorem proving tasks where global structure matters more than purely local token prediction.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a new direction for reasoning models that may be more reliable on structured, high-precision tasks like theorem proving. It could also inspire broader non-autoregressive or hybrid decoding methods for complex generation problems.

title: Learning User Simulators with Turing Rewards
authors: Yingshan Susan Wang, Cedegao E. Zhang, Linlu Qiu, Zexue He, Pengyuan Li
abstract: Learning to simulate human users in interactive settings could advance the training of agent assistants, evaluation of personalization systems, research in the social sciences, and more. Existing approaches generally do so by training a large language model (LLM) to match a single ground truth response, either by maximizing the log probability or by using a similarity reward. We instead propose {Turing-RL}: a Turing-Test-based reinforcement learning approach for training user simulator models. {

infographic.key_insight: This paper reframes user simulation as a "Turing test" problem: instead of copying one exact human response, the model is rewarded for producing responses that are indistinguishable from real users. This can make simulated users feel more realistic and diverse in interactive settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Current user simulators are usually trained to match a single ground-truth response, which can be too narrow and may fail to capture the natural variability of human behavior. The paper addresses how to train simulators that better reflect realistic user responses for assistants, personalization systems, and social science research.
method: Introduce Turing-RL, a reinforcement learning framework for training user simulators.
Use a Turing-Test-style reward that encourages responses to look human-like rather than merely similar to one reference answer.
Optimize the simulator to improve realism in interactive dialogue and user modeling tasks.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this could lead to more realistic simulated users for training and evaluating agents, reducing reliance on brittle single-answer supervision. It may improve downstream systems in conversational AI, personalization, and human-centered evaluation.

title: The Chandra-Gaia Catalog of Counterparts: Resolving ambiguous Gaia matches to X-ray sources in the Chandra Source Catalog using Machine Learning
authors: V. Samuel Pérez-Díaz, Vinay L. Kashyap, Joshua D. Ingram, David Fouhey, Juan Rafael Martínez-Galarza
abstract: We present a framework to cross-match sources from the Chandra Source Catalog (CSC v2.1) with optical sources from Gaia Data Release 3. Unlike purely spatial approaches, we use source properties such as magnitudes, colors, and distances to identify true counterparts, detect chance coincidences, and resolve ambiguities when multiple plausible candidates exist. We define a training set of high-confidence matches using NWAY, a Bayesian cross-matching framework that accounts for positional errors an

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that combining machine learning with astronomical source properties can resolve ambiguous matches between X-ray and optical catalogs much better than position-only methods. The result is a more reliable way to identify the true optical counterparts of Chandra X-ray sources in Gaia.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of matching X-ray sources from the Chandra Source Catalog to the correct Gaia DR3 optical source when multiple plausible candidates exist or when positional overlap alone is insufficient.
method: Builds a training set of high-confidence cross-matches using NWAY, a Bayesian framework for probabilistic source association.
Uses source features beyond sky position, including magnitudes, colors, and distances, to distinguish true counterparts from chance alignments.
Applies machine learning to rank or classify candidate matches and resolve ambiguous cases with multiple possible Gaia counterparts.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this is a strong example of using heterogeneous features and probabilistic labels to solve noisy matching problems. The approach generalizes to any domain where identity resolution must work under uncertainty and incomplete information.

title: Native Active Perception as Reasoning for Omni-Modal Understanding
authors: Zhenghao Xing, Ruiyang Xu, Yuxuan Wang, Jinzheng He, Ziyang Ma
abstract: Passive models for long video understanding typically rely on a "watch-it-all" paradigm, processing frames uniformly regardless of query difficulty, causing computational cost to grow with video duration. Although interactive frameworks have emerged, they often rely on global pre-scanning, and their context cost still scales with video length. We propose OmniAgent, the first native omni-modal agent that formulates video understanding as a POMDP-based iterative Observation-Thought-Action cycle. O

infographic.key_insight: OmniAgent reframes long video understanding as an active reasoning process rather than a passive frame-by-frame scan. By iteratively observing, thinking, and acting, it aims to reduce unnecessary computation while improving query-focused understanding across modalities.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing long-video models often use a "watch-it-all" strategy, which makes compute cost grow with video length even when the task is simple. Interactive methods help somewhat, but many still depend on costly global pre-scanning and do not fully avoid length-dependent context overhead.
method: Models video understanding as a POMDP, enabling an Observation-Thought-Action loop for iterative decision-making.
Uses native omni-modal interaction so the agent can choose what to inspect next instead of uniformly processing all frames.
Reduces reliance on full-video pre-scanning by dynamically selecting relevant information based on the query and current context.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests a more scalable way to handle long videos and multi-modal inputs without paying the full cost of exhaustive processing. It is especially useful for building efficient agents that answer complex queries with less compute and better focus.

title: Beyond the Current Observation: Evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models in Controllable Non-Markov Games
authors: Shengyuan Ding, Xilin Wei, Xinyu Fang, Haodong Duan, Dahua Lin
abstract: Deploying multimodal foundation models as closed-loop policies increasingly requires conditioning actions on observations that are no longer visible. However, existing benchmarks either expose the full state, conflate hidden-state reconstruction with other agent skills, or test recall only after an episode has ended. We introduce RNG-Bench (Reconstructive Non-Markov Games), a benchmark suite designed to isolate a base model's ability to reconstruct past observations and act on them during multi-

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that multimodal LLMs need to be evaluated not just on what they see now, but on whether they can remember and use past observations in closed-loop decision-making. It introduces a benchmark that isolates this hidden-state reconstruction ability in non-Markov games.
infographic.problem_solved: Current benchmarks for multimodal agents are often too easy or too confounded: they reveal the full state, mix memory with other skills, or only test recall after an episode ends. This paper addresses the need for a benchmark that measures whether a model can reconstruct past observations and act on them while the game is still ongoing.
method: Introduces RNG-Bench (Reconstructive Non-Markov Games), a benchmark suite for evaluating multimodal large language models in controllable partially observable settings.
Designs tasks that require reconstructing past observations and using that information for action selection during multi-step interaction, rather than only post-hoc recall.
Separates memory/reconstruction ability from other agent capabilities by controlling observability and game dynamics.
infographic.impact: This benchmark helps researchers and practitioners measure a more realistic capability for deployed AI agents: acting correctly when important information is no longer visible. It can guide the design and training of multimodal systems that are more robust in long-horizon, partially observable environments.

title: Confidence is Not Reliability: Rethinking MC Dropout in Brain Tumour Segmentation
authors: Xin Ci Wong, Duygu Sarikaya, Kieran Zucker, Marc De Kamps, Nishant Ravikumar
abstract: Glioma segmentation in multiparametric MRI is a critical component of treatment planning. A segmentation model that fails silently on treatment-critical sub-regions represents a patient safety risk that overlap-based metrics such as Dice scores cannot expose. We ask whether voxel-level uncertainty estimation via Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout can reliably identify segmentation errors in clinically critical sub-regions, and whether calibration failure modes are detectable from standard reporting metric

infographic.key_insight: MC Dropout confidence scores can look trustworthy while still missing clinically important segmentation errors in brain tumour regions. Standard overlap metrics like Dice are not enough to tell whether uncertainty estimates are actually reliable for patient safety.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between segmentation accuracy metrics and real-world clinical reliability, especially for identifying failures in treatment-critical tumour sub-regions in glioma MRI segmentation.
method: Evaluate voxel-level uncertainty from Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout on multiparametric MRI brain tumour segmentation.
Test whether uncertainty can flag errors specifically in clinically critical sub-regions, not just overall segmentation quality.
Compare uncertainty behavior against standard reporting metrics to uncover calibration and reliability failure modes.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a reminder that high Dice scores do not guarantee safe or dependable model behavior in medical settings. It highlights the need to validate uncertainty estimation methods against clinically meaningful error detection, not just aggregate performance numbers.

title: Rethinking Reward Supervision: Rubric-Conditioned Self-Distillation
authors: Siyi Gu, Jialin Chen, Sophia Zhou, Arman Cohan, Rex Ying
abstract: Post-training of reasoning language models is commonly driven by supervised distillation and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Distillation often relies on chain-of-thought annotations that are expensive to obtain and may themselves be noisy, incomplete, or partially incorrect; even when the final solution is correct, an imperfect rationale can interfere with learning. Reinforcement learning with verified rewards, on the other hand, typically compresses evaluative feedback into a s

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a new way to supervise reasoning models using rubrics instead of brittle full-chain rationales, making self-distillation more reliable and less annotation-heavy. By conditioning learning on structured evaluative criteria, it aims to preserve useful reasoning while reducing noise from imperfect explanations.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the high cost and unreliability of chain-of-thought supervision in post-training, where annotations can be incomplete, noisy, or even incorrect. It also tackles the weakness of compressing reward signals into sparse or overly simplified feedback during reinforcement learning.
method: Use rubric-conditioned supervision to guide the model with structured criteria rather than relying solely on full natural-language rationales.
Apply self-distillation so the model can learn from its own outputs under rubric guidance, reducing dependence on expensive human-written chain-of-thought data.
Leverage evaluative feedback in a more informative form than a single scalar reward, helping the model learn what makes an answer correct or high-quality.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this could lower annotation costs while improving the quality and robustness of reasoning-model post-training. It offers a practical middle ground between noisy rationale distillation and sparse reward-only training.

title: Does VLA Even Know the Basics? Measuring Commonsense and World Knowledge Retention in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Nikita Kachaev, Andrey Moskalenko, Matvey Skripkin, Nikita Kurlaev, Daria Pugacheva
abstract: Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically obtained by fine-tuning powerful pretrained VLMs on robotics data, yet it is unclear how much commonsense and factual knowledge they retain after adaptation. Failures on knowledge-sensitive tasks are ambiguous, conflating missing knowledge with poor generalization of low-level control. We introduce Act2Answer, a lightweight protocol that adapts VLM knowledge benchmarks to VLA evaluation by requiring agents to answer through action. Each

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuned VLA models may still retain a lot of commonsense and world knowledge from their pretrained VLMs, but standard robotics benchmarks can hide this because failures may come from control, not memory. The paper’s key idea is to test knowledge by forcing the model to "answer through action" instead of language.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the ambiguity in evaluating embodied VLA models: when they fail on knowledge-sensitive tasks, it is unclear whether they forgot the knowledge or simply cannot execute the low-level action correctly. It introduces a way to separate knowledge retention from control/generalization issues.
method: Introduces Act2Answer, a lightweight protocol that converts VLM knowledge benchmarks into VLA evaluations.
Requires the agent to express its answer through an action, reducing reliance on text-only outputs.
Measures how much commonsense and factual knowledge survives after adapting VLMs to robotics tasks.
infographic.impact: This helps researchers diagnose whether VLA training preserves or erases pretrained knowledge, which is important for building embodied agents that are both capable and informed. Practitioners can use this evaluation style to compare models more fairly and identify whether failures are due to knowledge loss or control limitations.

title: Optimal scenario design for climate emulation
authors: Christopher B. Womack, Shahine Bouabid, Andrei Sokolov, Popat Salunke, Glenn Flierl
abstract: As deep learning for physical systems continues to grow in popularity, efforts to improve generalizability have primarily focused on designing architectures that embed physical constraints. However, for machine-learning surrogate climate models (emulators), we show that the low structural diversity in existing scenarios commonly used to generate training data places a ceiling on predictive skill. Here, we examine whether training datasets themselves can be optimized to improve generalization. We

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that better climate emulators may depend as much on the training scenarios as on the model architecture. By diversifying and optimizing the scenarios used to generate training data, predictive skill and generalization can improve.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the limitation that existing climate-model training datasets rely on low-diversity scenarios, which can cap how well surrogate models generalize to new climate conditions.
method: Analyze the structural diversity of scenario datasets used to train climate emulators.
Test whether training data can be optimized to better cover the space of possible climate responses.
Compare generalization performance across scenario designs to identify datasets that yield stronger surrogate models.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shifts attention from only designing better architectures to also designing better training datasets. It suggests that dataset composition can be a key lever for improving robustness and out-of-distribution performance in scientific ML.

title: Algorithm–hardware co-design of neuromorphic networks with dual memory pathways
authors: Pengfei Sun, Zhe Su, Jascha Achterberg, Giacomo Indiveri, Dan F. M. Goodman
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 16 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01255-3

Pengfei Sun et al. develop a spiking neural network with a dual memory pathway, co-designed with a custom neuromorphic chip. The approach delivers over 4× throughput and 5x energy efficiency gains while using 40–60% fewer parameters than state-of-the-art implementations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that neuromorphic AI can be made both faster and more energy efficient by designing the spiking network and the hardware together. A dual memory pathway architecture achieves over 4× higher throughput and 5× better energy efficiency while using 40–60% fewer parameters.
infographic.problem_solved: Neuromorphic systems often struggle to balance performance, efficiency, and model size when deployed on hardware. This work addresses the gap between algorithm design and chip constraints by co-optimizing both for efficient real-world execution.
method: Designs a spiking neural network with two memory pathways to improve computation and state handling.
Co-designs the network architecture with a custom neuromorphic chip so the model matches hardware capabilities.
Reduces parameter count while improving throughput and energy efficiency compared with state-of-the-art implementations.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this demonstrates a practical path to deploy spiking models that are smaller, faster, and far more energy efficient. It is especially relevant for edge AI and always-on applications where power and latency are critical.

title: Future Dynamic 3D Reconstruction: A 3D World Model with Disentangled Ego-Motion
authors: Nils Morbitzer, Jonathan Evers, Artem Savkin, Thomas Stauner, Nassir Navab
abstract: Forecasting the evolution of dynamic environments is crucial for autonomous agents. While generative world models have recently achieved high photorealism in 2D video synthesis by mixing ego-motion and environmental dynamics within the image plane, they exhibit physical inconsistencies, such as morphing or vanishing objects, especially over long time horizons. In this paper, we propose FR3D, a world model that predicts a persistent 3D latent representation for future dynamic 3D reconstruction. U

infographic.key_insight: FR3D predicts future scenes in persistent 3D space instead of mixing motion inside 2D images, which helps keep objects stable and physically consistent over time. This makes long-horizon forecasting more realistic for dynamic environments.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of forecasting dynamic scenes without the common failures of 2D video world models, such as object morphing, disappearing objects, and other physical inconsistencies over long time horizons.
method: Learns a persistent 3D latent world representation for future dynamic reconstruction.
Disentangles ego-motion from environmental dynamics to better model how the scene changes.
Predicts future 3D structure directly, aiming for more stable and physically plausible reconstructions than image-plane generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a stronger foundation for robotics, autonomous driving, and embodied AI systems that need reliable long-term scene prediction. It improves interpretability and consistency by modeling the world in 3D rather than only in 2D video space.

title: EvolveNav: Proactive Preflection and Self-Evolving Memory for Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation
authors: Qi Chai, Wenhao Shen, Nanjie Yao, Yue Xia, Kaiyong Zhao
abstract: Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation (ZS-OGN) requires embodied agents to explore and locate target objects without any prior training. To this end, recent methods leverage foundation models. But they typically rely on static priors and lack adaptation, which leads to repeated errors and costly trial and error. In this paper, we propose a self-evolving ZS-OGN framework that enables continuous test-time improvement. Specifically, we build an agentic rule memory by extracting actionable knowledge from

infographic.key_insight: EvolveNav turns zero-shot object-goal navigation into a learning-at-test-time problem, so the agent can improve while exploring instead of repeating the same mistakes. It combines proactive preflection with a self-evolving memory to adapt its decisions as it gathers new experience.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of adaptation in zero-shot object-goal navigation. Existing foundation-model-based methods often rely on static priors, which makes them prone to repeated errors, inefficient exploration, and costly trial-and-error behavior.
method: Builds an agentic rule memory that extracts actionable knowledge from navigation experience.
Uses proactive preflection to anticipate likely failures and adjust behavior before making avoidable mistakes.
Continuously updates memory at test time, enabling self-evolving improvement without task-specific training.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to improve embodied agents in unseen environments without retraining. It is especially relevant for robotics and navigation systems where online adaptation, efficiency, and robustness matter.

title: Unified Multimodal Autoregressive Modeling with Shared Context-Visual Tokenizer is Key to Unification
authors: Wujian Peng, Lingchen Meng, Yuxuan Cai, Xianwei Zhuang, Yuhuan Yang
abstract: Unified Multimodal Modeling aims to integrate visual understanding and generation within a single system. However, existing approaches typically rely on two disparate visual tokenizers, which splits the representation space and hinders truly unified modeling. We propose UniAR, a unified autoregressive framework where a single discrete visual tokenizer serves as the key bridge between understanding and generation, enabling a shared context in which the model can directly interpret its own generat

infographic.key_insight: UniAR shows that unifying multimodal understanding and generation works best when both share a single discrete visual tokenizer. This shared context lets the model interpret and produce visual content in one autoregressive framework, rather than splitting the representation into separate systems.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the fragmentation caused by using two different visual tokenizers for understanding and generation, which creates mismatched representations and limits true unified multimodal modeling.
method: Uses one shared discrete visual tokenizer as the bridge between visual understanding and visual generation.
Builds a unified autoregressive model that operates in a common token space for both tasks.
Enables the model to directly condition on and learn from its own generated visual tokens within the same shared context.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this simplifies multimodal system design by reducing tokenizer mismatch and making understanding-generation integration more coherent. It may also improve transfer across tasks and make unified multimodal models easier to scale and train.

title: Sign-Rank, Index, and List Replicability: Connections and Separations
authors: Ari Blondal, Hamed Hatami, Pooya Hatami, Chavdar Lalov, Sivan Tretiak
abstract:
In learning theory, the sign rank of a binary concept class captures the smallest dimension in which it can be represented by points and halfspaces. Despite tremendous interest, lower bounds on sign rank are notoriously difficult to come by. Two recent approaches to the problem establish lower bounds on sign rank by measures that are easier to analyze: the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index and the list replicability number.
  We order these measures, showing that the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index is upper-bounded by

infographic.key_insight: This paper clarifies how three complexity measures used to lower-bound sign rank are related, showing that the Z2-index is bounded by other easier-to-analyze quantities. In doing so, it maps out both connections and separations between these measures, helping explain which lower-bound techniques are genuinely stronger.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of proving lower bounds on sign rank for binary concept classes, a notoriously difficult problem in learning theory. It compares two newer surrogate measures—the Z2-index and list replicability—to understand how they relate to sign rank and to each other.
method: Order and compare the relevant complexity measures used in sign-rank lower bounds.
Prove upper bounds showing the Z2-index is controlled by other measures.
Identify separations to show that some measures are not equivalent and can differ in strength.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML researchers, this helps decide which surrogate quantities are useful for analyzing representational complexity and sample/learnability questions. It also sharpens the toolkit for studying concept classes through more tractable combinatorial or topological proxies.

title: EventDrive: Event Cameras for Vision-Language Driving Intelligence
authors: Dongyue Lu, Rong Li, Ao Liang, Lingdong Kong, Wei Yin
abstract: Event cameras sense the world through asynchronous brightness changes with microsecond latency and high dynamic range, offering motion fidelity far beyond frame-based sensors and capturing temporal structure that conventional exposures often miss. These properties make events a powerful complement to RGB in autonomous driving, especially under blur, glare, and rapid motion, where frame-based perception can become unreliable. However, existing event-aware vision-language models remain limited to

infographic.key_insight: EventDrive shows that event cameras can provide a strong complementary signal to RGB for driving intelligence, especially when blur, glare, and fast motion make frame-based vision unreliable. The paper highlights how event data preserves fine-grained temporal motion cues that are often lost in standard video frames.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between event-camera sensing and vision-language models for autonomous driving, where existing event-aware models are still limited and struggle to fully exploit event data for robust reasoning in challenging road conditions.
method: Builds an event-camera-based vision-language driving framework that leverages asynchronous brightness-change signals rather than only RGB frames.
Integrates event information to improve perception under adverse conditions such as motion blur, high dynamic range scenes, glare, and rapid ego-motion.

title: ReproRepo: Scaling Reproducibility Audits with GitHub Repository Issues
authors: Shanda Li, Qiuhong Anna Wei, Jingwu Tang, Valerie Chen, Nihar B Shah
abstract: Reproducing research results from papers and released code is central to scientific progress. Existing works have introduced benchmarks to evaluate whether LLM agents can assist with reproducibility, but they are difficult to scale due to their reliance on substantial manual effort for data curation and evaluation. We introduce ReproRepo, a scalable framework for reproducibility evaluation that leverages human-raised GitHub issues as naturally occurring supervision on realistic reproduction bloc

infographic.key_insight: ReproRepo turns real GitHub issue discussions into scalable supervision for reproducibility auditing, reducing the need for expensive manual benchmark curation. It reframes reproducibility evaluation as a practical, data-driven task grounded in how researchers actually debug and reproduce code.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing reproducibility benchmarks for LLM agents are hard to scale because they require heavy manual effort to curate tasks and evaluate outcomes. This paper addresses the lack of scalable, realistic supervision for testing whether AI can help reproduce research results from papers and released code.
method: Collects human-raised GitHub issues as naturally occurring signals of reproduction blockers and debugging steps.
Uses repository issue threads to build a scalable framework for reproducibility audits without extensive hand-labeling.
Evaluates reproducibility assistance in realistic settings that mirror how practitioners encounter failures in research code.
infographic.impact: This makes reproducibility evaluation much easier to scale across many repositories and papers. For AI/ML practitioners, it provides a more realistic way to measure and improve tools that help debug, reproduce, and verify research artifacts.

title: Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization: Teacher in Prompts, Not Gradients
authors: Byung-Kwan Lee, Ximing Lu, Shizhe Diao, Minki Kang, Saurav Muralidharan
abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers a teacher's competence to a small student but is brittle in the small-student regime: forcing the student to imitate logits from a much larger teacher concentrates it on the teacher's sharpest modes, hurting generalization on benchmark families beyond the training corpus. Reinforcement learning (RL) avoids logit imitation by training on the student's own rollouts. However, on questions where every rollout fails-yielding zero advantage and being silently discarded

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that distillation should not force a small student to copy a large teacher’s logits directly. Instead, the teacher should guide learning through prompts and preference signals, while the student improves from its own behavior rather than gradient-level imitation.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the brittleness of knowledge distillation in small-student settings, where mimicking a large teacher can overfit to sharp teacher modes and hurt generalization. It also targets a weakness of standard RL training, where failed rollouts can produce zero advantage and be effectively ignored.
method: Use the teacher as guidance in prompts rather than as a target for logit matching.
Train the student with reinforcement-style updates based on its own rollouts, avoiding direct imitation of teacher probabilities.
Introduce a policy-optimization framing that preserves learning signal even when standard RL would discard low-success or zero-advantage samples.
infographic.impact: This approach can improve how small models learn from stronger models without becoming overly dependent on brittle teacher outputs. For practitioners, it suggests a more robust path to transfer capability, especially when generalization beyond the training corpus matters.

We propose AdaVoMP, a method for predicting accurate dense spatially-varying ($E$, $ν$, $ρ$) for input 3D objects across representations, improving the resolution, accuracy, and memory efficiency over the state-of-the-art. The foundation of our technique is a sparse and adaptive voxe

infographic.key_insight: AdaVoMP predicts dense, spatially varying mechanical properties for 3D objects in a way that stays accurate even as resolution changes. In simple terms, it helps digital objects know how to behave physically without needing hand-made material labels.
infographic.problem_solved: Most 3D assets do not include realistic physical material properties like Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and density, which limits reliable physics simulation. Existing methods often trade off accuracy, memory use, and resolution consistency.
method: Uses a sparse, adaptive volumetric representation to model mechanical property fields efficiently.
Predicts dense spatially varying material properties across different 3D representations of the same object.
Improves resolution-invariant performance, aiming for better accuracy and lower memory cost than prior methods.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners working on simulation, robotics, graphics, or digital twins, this makes physically grounded 3D assets more practical and scalable. It can improve downstream tasks that depend on realistic object behavior under force, deformation, or collision.

title: Looped World Models
authors: Hongyuan Adam Lu, Z. L. Victor Wei, Qun Zhang, Jinrui Zeng, Bowen Cao
abstract: Current world models face a fundamental tension: faithful long-horizon simulation demands deep computation, but deeper models are expensive to deploy and prone to compounding errors. We resolve this by introducing Looped World Models (LoopWM), which are the first looped architectures for world modelling. Our method iteratively refines latent environment states through a parameter-shared transformer block. This yield up to 100x parameter efficiency over conventional approaches with adaptive compu

infographic.key_insight: Looped World Models (LoopWM) use repeated refinement over a shared transformer block to simulate environments more efficiently. This achieves long-horizon world modeling with far fewer parameters, helping reduce the cost of deeper models and their compounding errors.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the tradeoff between faithful long-term simulation and the high computational/parameter cost of deep world models. It also targets the error accumulation that often worsens as rollout horizons get longer.
method: Iteratively refine latent environment states using a looped, parameter-shared transformer block.
Reuse the same model weights across multiple refinement steps to increase effective depth without increasing parameter count.
Adapt computation over time, enabling more efficient long-horizon prediction than conventional fixed-depth architectures.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, LoopWM offers a practical path to build world models that are both more parameter-efficient and better suited for long-horizon simulation. This could lower deployment costs while improving robustness in planning, control, and model-based reinforcement learning.

title: Variable-Width Transformers
authors: Zhaofeng Wu, Oliver Sieberling, Shawn Tan, Rameswar Panda, Yury Polyanskiy
abstract: Scaling model size, specifically depth and width, has driven significant progress in transformer-based language models. However, most architectures maintain a constant width across all layers, allocating a fixed parameter and computation budget evenly despite different layers potentially playing distinct computational roles. In this work, we empirically investigate nonuniform capacity allocation across network depth by proposing a $\times$-shaped > <former architecture. This design maintains wid

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that transformer layers may benefit from different widths at different depths, rather than using a fixed hidden size throughout the network. The authors propose a variable-width "X-shaped" transformer that allocates model capacity more flexibly across layers.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard transformers keep the same width in every layer, which can waste parameters and compute by treating all layers as equally important. This work addresses how to distribute model capacity more efficiently across depth.
method: Propose a variable-width transformer architecture with an "X-shaped" width profile across layers.
Study nonuniform capacity allocation empirically to see how width changes affect performance and efficiency.
Design the network so some layers are narrower and others wider, instead of using a constant-width stack.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this suggests a new way to improve transformer efficiency without simply making every layer bigger. It could lead to better accuracy-per-parameter and more compute-aware model design.

title: R2RDreamer: 3D-aware Data Augmentation for Spatially-generalized 2D Manipulation Policies
authors: Xiuwei Xu, Haowen Sun, Angyuan Ma, Yiwei Zhang, Zhenyu Wu
abstract: Spatial generalization is critical for imitation-learned manipulation policies, but achieving it typically requires scaling demonstrations across diverse object poses, robot configurations, and camera viewpoints. Data augmentation from a few source demonstrations offers a practical alternative to costly real-world collection. Simulation-based augmentation can create controllable variation, but requires complex environment and object setup and may introduce a sim-to-real gap. Recent real-to-real

infographic.key_insight: R2RDreamer shows that 3D-aware data augmentation can expand a small set of real demonstrations into many spatially diverse training examples, improving how well 2D manipulation policies generalize across poses and viewpoints. The key idea is to generate realistic variation from real data without relying on full simulation setups.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high cost and limited coverage of demonstration data needed for spatially generalized imitation learning in manipulation. It aims to reduce the need for collecting many real-world demos across different object poses, robot configurations, and camera views.
method: Uses 3D-aware real-to-real data augmentation to synthesize new training examples from a few source demonstrations.
Introduces spatial variation in object placement, viewpoint, and scene configuration while keeping the data grounded in real observations.
Targets improved generalization for 2D manipulation policies without requiring complex simulation pipelines or extensive environment reconstruction.
infographic.impact: This matters because it offers a practical path to training more robust manipulation policies with far less real-world data. For practitioners, it can lower data-collection costs and improve transfer to new spatial settings without heavy sim-to-real engineering.

title: MeshLoom: Feed-Forward Non-Rigid Registration of Mesh Sequences
authors: Jianqi Chen, Jiraphon Yenphraphai, Xiangjun Tang, Sergey Tulyakov, Chaoyang Wang
abstract: We present MeshLoom, a feed-forward registration network that directly reconstructs vertex deformations across mesh sequences. Our approach advances non-rigid registration beyond existing models, which are typically constrained by costly per-instance optimization, narrow object categories, pairwise-only inputs, or merely intermediate outputs. The network is simple and efficient, registering multiple meshes within seconds. At its core lies a topology-aware encoder--decoder design. Specifically, w

infographic.key_insight: MeshLoom introduces a feed-forward network that can directly recover non-rigid vertex deformations across entire mesh sequences, avoiding slow per-instance optimization. It makes mesh registration faster, simpler, and more practical for multi-mesh alignment.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the bottleneck of non-rigid mesh registration methods that are expensive to optimize, limited to specific object categories, often work only pairwise, or produce only intermediate results rather than direct deformations.
method: Uses a topology-aware encoder-decoder architecture to model mesh structure directly.
Predicts vertex-level deformations in a feed-forward manner across multiple meshes in a sequence.
Enables efficient registration of multiple meshes within seconds, reducing reliance on iterative optimization.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MeshLoom offers a much faster and more scalable alternative for non-rigid registration workflows. This can simplify applications in geometry processing, 3D reconstruction, animation, and shape analysis where accurate mesh alignment is critical.

title: Qwen-RobotWorld Technical Report: Unifying Embodied World Modeling through Language-Conditioned Video Generation
authors: Jie Zhang, Xiaoyue Chen, Anzhe Chen, Chenxu Lv, Deqing Li
abstract: We introduce Qwen-RobotWorld, a language-conditioned video world model for embodied intelligence. With natural language as a unified action interface, it predicts physically grounded future visual trajectories from current observations across robotic manipulation, autonomous driving, indoor navigation, and human-to-robot transfer. This unified formulation provides three promising application directions: synthetic data generation for policy training augmentation, scalable virtual environments for

infographic.key_insight: Qwen-RobotWorld is a language-conditioned world model that uses natural language as a single action interface to predict realistic future video trajectories from current observations. It unifies embodied prediction across multiple settings, including robotics, driving, navigation, and human-to-robot transfer.
infographic.problem_solved: Embodied AI systems often need separate models or control interfaces for different tasks and environments. This paper addresses the challenge of building one scalable world model that can understand language commands and forecast physically grounded outcomes across diverse real-world scenarios.
method: Takes current observations and a natural-language instruction as input.
Generates future visual trajectories as a video world model, grounding predictions in physical plausibility.
Supports a unified embodied framework spanning manipulation, autonomous driving, indoor navigation, and transfer from humans to robots.
infographic.impact: This is useful for AI/ML practitioners because it can improve policy training through synthetic data, enable scalable virtual environments for testing, and support a shared interface across different embodied tasks. It could reduce the need for task-specific simulators and improve data efficiency in robotics and autonomy.

title: Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs
authors: Peiyang Xu, Bangzheng Li, Sijia Liu, Karthik R. Narasimhan, Pramod Viswanath
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail when answering requires identifying a small but decisive piece of evidence within a long or complex context, such as a single line in a tool trace or a subtle detail in an image. We propose ContextRL, a context-aware reinforcement learning (RL) method that improves long-horizon reasoning and multimodal performance through an \emph{indirect} auxiliary objective. Instead of supervising only the final answer, ContextRL presents the model with a query, an answ

infographic.key_insight: ContextRL teaches LLMs to pay attention to the right evidence inside long or multimodal contexts, improving reasoning without directly supervising only the final answer. The key breakthrough is an indirect auxiliary RL objective that helps models find decisive details in text traces and images more reliably.
infographic.problem_solved: LLMs often struggle when the correct answer depends on spotting a small but important clue buried in a long context, tool trace, or image. This paper addresses the weakness in long-horizon reasoning and multimodal understanding where irrelevant information can distract the model.
method: Uses context-aware reinforcement learning to reward behavior that focuses on relevant evidence within the input context.
Introduces an indirect auxiliary objective instead of relying only on final-answer supervision.
Trains the model to better identify and use decisive details across text and multimodal settings.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to make LLMs more reliable on real-world tasks with long documents, tool use, and multimodal inputs. It can improve performance on harder reasoning problems where success depends on finding the right evidence, not just generating fluent answers.

title: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Meta-Analysis Articles from Nature Portfolio
authors: Anzhe Xie, Weihang Su, Yujia Zhou, Yiqun Liu, Qingyao Ai
abstract: Meta-analysis is a demanding form of evidence synthesis that combines literature retrieval, PI/ECO-guided study selection, and statistical aggregation. Its structured, verifiable workflow makes it an ideal substrate for evaluating systematic scientific reasoning, yet existing benchmarks lack ground truth across the full retrieval-screening-synthesis pipeline. We introduce MetaSyn, a dataset of 442 expert-curated meta-analyses from Nature Portfolio journals. Each entry pairs a research question w

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces MetaSyn, a new benchmark of 442 expert-curated meta-analyses from Nature Portfolio that evaluates LLM agents across the full scientific synthesis pipeline, not just isolated tasks. It provides grounded ground truth for retrieval, study selection, and evidence aggregation, making scientific reasoning measurable end-to-end.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks for scientific agents often test only fragments of the meta-analysis workflow and lack reliable ground truth across retrieval, screening, and synthesis. This paper addresses the need for a realistic, verifiable benchmark for evaluating how well LLM agents can perform systematic evidence synthesis.
method: Collected 442 expert-curated meta-analysis articles from Nature Portfolio journals to form MetaSyn.
Structured each entry around a research question and the full retrieval-screening-synthesis workflow.
Designed the benchmark to support evaluation of LLM agents on literature retrieval, PI/ECO-guided study selection, and statistical aggregation with verifiable ground truth.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MetaSyn offers a more realistic testbed for scientific agents that need to reason over literature and make evidence-based decisions. It can help identify where LLMs fail in multi-step research workflows and guide the development of more reliable research assistants.

title: BRDFusion: Physics Meets Generation for Urban Scene Inverse Rendering
authors: Yi-Ruei Liu, Jie-Ying Lee, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yu-Lun Liu, Chih-Hao Lin
abstract: Inverse rendering of urban scenes from captured videos enables numerous applications, including content creation and autonomous driving simulation. Physically-based rendering methods follow and control lighting physics, but suffer from reconstruction and rendering artifacts. While generative models produce realistic videos, they offer limited consistency and controllability. We present BRDFusion, a unified framework that combines two complementary models for inverse and forward rendering. Specif

infographic.key_insight: BRDFusion combines physics-based inverse rendering with generative video modeling to get the best of both worlds: controllable lighting and geometry from physical modeling, plus realism from generation. It aims to reconstruct urban scenes more faithfully while reducing common artifacts.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of inverse rendering urban scenes from video, where physics-based methods can be accurate but artifact-prone, and generative methods can look realistic but often lack consistency and control.
method: Unifies inverse rendering and forward rendering in a single framework.
Combines a physically-based model for controllability with a generative model for realism.
Targets urban-scene reconstruction from captured videos to improve both visual quality and physical consistency.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a practical direction for building rendering systems that are both photorealistic and physically grounded. It could improve workflows in content creation, digital twins, and autonomous driving simulation.

title: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
authors: Mufei Li, Shikun Liu, Dongqi Fu, Haoyu Wang, Yinglong Xia
abstract: Post-hoc context erasing over the KV cache is challenging because a local edit has a global consequence: once a span has been processed, its influence propagates into the cached states of all subsequent tokens. This issue arises naturally in long-context LLM applications, where stale retrieved facts, incorrect tool observations, retracted user preferences, or harmful prompt injections may be identified only after prefill. Exact erasing must then recompute all tokens after the deleted span, makin

infographic.key_insight: KVEraser learns how to selectively steer the KV cache so a local span can be erased without needing to fully recompute the entire later context. This makes post-hoc context removal practical for long-context LLMs.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of exact context erasing in KV caches, where deleting a span normally forces recomputation of all subsequent tokens because earlier information has already propagated through cached states.
method: Learns a steering mechanism over the KV cache to localize the effect of erasure.
Targets only the necessary cache updates instead of reprocessing the full post-edit sequence.
Aims to preserve model behavior while removing stale, incorrect, or harmful context after prefill.
infographic.impact: This helps AI practitioners handle long-context applications more efficiently when they need to remove bad information after it has already been processed. It can reduce compute cost and latency for safer, more controllable LLM systems.

title: DEEPRUBRIC: Evidence-Tree Rubric Supervision for Efficient Reinforcement Learning of Deep Research Agents
authors: Minghang Zhu, Chuyang Wei, Junhao Xu, Yilin Cheng, Zhumin Chen
abstract: Deep research agents synthesize long-form reports by searching and reasoning over retrieved evidence. Reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards improves these agents by optimizing them against checkable criteria that translate report quality into reward signals, but its efficiency depends on whether those criteria reliably capture the task scope and evidence needs. Most existing studies ask an LLM to generate rubrics for a given query, but when the model fails to infer the underlying info

infographic.key_insight: DEEPRUBRIC improves reinforcement learning for deep research agents by supervising rewards with an evidence tree, making rubric-based training more reliable and efficient. Instead of relying only on a query-generated rubric, it grounds evaluation in the underlying evidence structure needed for a strong report.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the inefficiency of rubric-based reinforcement learning for long-form research agents when rubrics fail to capture the full information scope and evidence requirements of a task. This can lead to weak reward signals and poor optimization.
method: Build an evidence-tree rubric that organizes supporting evidence into a structured supervision signal.
Use this rubric to define checkable criteria for reinforcement learning of deep research agents.
Improve alignment between query intent, evidence coverage, and report quality during training.
infographic.impact: This matters because it can make training deep research agents more sample-efficient and more faithful to evidence, improving the quality of generated long-form reports. Practitioners get a more reliable way to optimize agents on tasks where correctness depends on comprehensive sourcing and reasoning.

title: Geometric Action Model for Robot Policy Learning
authors: Jisang Han, Seonghu Jeon, Jaewoo Jung, René Zurbrügg, Honggyu An
abstract: Generalist robot policies must follow user instructions while reasoning about how objects, cameras, and robot actions interact in the 3D physical world. Recent vision-language-action models (VLAs) and video world-action models (WAMs) inherit strong semantic or temporal priors from large-scale foundation models, but they still operate primarily on 2D image frames or 2D-derived latent spaces, leaving implicit the 3D geometry required for contact-rich manipulation. We propose the Geometric Action M

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that robot policies become more capable when they reason directly in 3D geometry instead of relying only on 2D image features or latent representations. By explicitly modeling how objects, cameras, and robot actions interact in space, the policy can better handle contact-rich manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing vision-language-action and video world-action models understand semantics and motion well, but they often miss the 3D geometric relationships needed for precise robotic manipulation. This paper addresses the gap between 2D perception and the spatial reasoning required for real-world robot control.
method: Introduces a Geometric Action Model that incorporates 3D spatial structure into robot policy learning.
Connects object, camera, and robot-action interactions in a geometry-aware representation rather than relying only on 2D frames.
Targets contact-rich manipulation tasks where accurate spatial reasoning is critical for action selection and execution.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a path toward more reliable generalist robot policies that are both semantically informed and physically grounded. It may improve robustness on tasks requiring precise positioning, contact, and object interaction in complex environments.

title: Hierarchical Advantage Weighting for Online RL Fine-Tuning of VLAs from Sparse Episode Outcomes
authors: Tongyan Fang, Siyuan Huang, Naiyu Fang, Ganlong Zhao, Zhongjin Luo
abstract: When pretrained VLA policies are fine-tuned through online RL, each rollout episode produces only a single binary outcome (success or failure), yet the actor update requires per-transition supervision. Existing approaches commonly reduce this sparse outcome to a single scalar reward or advantage signal, which conflates distinct forms of transition-level feedback and provides limited guidance once basic task success becomes achievable. First, a single scalar signal conflates the two objectives of

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that sparse episode-level success/failure can be turned into richer transition-level training signal by weighting advantages hierarchically, instead of collapsing everything into one scalar reward. The result is more informative online fine-tuning for pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies.
infographic.problem_solved: Online RL fine-tuning of VLAs often gets only one binary outcome per rollout episode, but the actor still needs per-step supervision. Simple scalar rewards or advantages mix together different kinds of feedback and become less useful once the agent starts succeeding on easy cases.
method: Use hierarchical advantage weighting to map sparse episode outcomes into structured transition-level learning signals.
Separate distinct feedback sources instead of collapsing them into one global scalar advantage.
Apply the weighted signal during online RL fine-tuning to guide policy updates more effectively from success/failure-only data.
infographic.impact: This approach can make online RL fine-tuning more sample-efficient and more stable when feedback is extremely sparse. For practitioners, it offers a practical way to keep improving pretrained VLA agents beyond the point where basic task success is already achieved.

title: Exact Posterior Score Estimation for Solving Linear Inverse Problems
authors: Abbas Mammadov, Ozgur Kara, Kaan Oktay, Iskander Azangulov, Adil Kaan Akan
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models learn powerful data priors by training a denoiser to reverse Gaussian corruption. To use this prior to solve a linear inverse problem, one needs to sample from the posterior, but the score that the prior provides is the unconditional score, not the posterior score. Existing methods either steer a fixed pretrained denoiser with approximate measurement-matching corrections, or train a conditional restoration model that abandons the denoising structure of the prior.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows how to estimate the exact posterior score for linear inverse problems instead of relying on approximate measurement corrections. This preserves the strength of diffusion/flow priors while making them properly usable for posterior sampling.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between the unconditional score learned by diffusion and flow models and the posterior score needed to solve linear inverse problems from partial or corrupted measurements.
method: Derive an exact way to obtain posterior score information from the learned prior rather than steering a fixed denoiser with heuristics.
Keep the denoising-based generative prior structure while adapting it to measurement-conditioned restoration.
Enable posterior sampling for linear inverse problems without replacing the prior with a separately trained conditional model.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this offers a more principled route to inverse problem solving with generative models, improving consistency between the prior and the measurement constraints. It can lead to better reconstructions with fewer ad hoc corrections and less need for task-specific retraining.

Psychiatric disorders are heterogeneous, and care depends on interpreting unstructured longitudinal narratives, creating variability that hinders standardization. A study now shows that a psychiatry-specific large language model (LLM) may help clinicians to deliver more consistent, high-quality care.

Use the model to interpret unstructured longitudinal patient narratives and surface clinically relevant information for decision support.
Evaluate whether the LLM can improve consistency and quality of clinician judgments in psychiatric care workflows.

title: Flood and Harvest: The Provable Necessity of Trivia for Generating Valuable Mathematics via the Lens of Language Generation in the Limit
authors: Xiaoyu Li, Andi Han, Dai Shi, Zheng Gao, Jiaojiao Jiang
abstract: AI systems coupled to proof assistants now generate formal mathematics at scale, and the gap between what a checker can verify and what a mathematician would value has become the binding constraint. We model the generation of valuable mathematics as nested language generation in the limit: a verifiable formal language $F$, accessed through a membership oracle (the proof checker), contains an unknown valuable language $H \in \mathcal{H}$ revealed only through an adversarial enumeration of a core

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that generating truly valuable mathematics requires more than producing formally correct proofs: AI needs access to "trivia" or auxiliary information that helps identify which provable statements matter. In other words, a proof checker can verify correctness, but without extra structure or guidance, it cannot tell which mathematics is worth generating.
infographic.problem_solved: This work addresses the gap between formal verifiability and human mathematical value in AI-generated mathematics. The challenge is that proof assistants can check proofs, but they do not capture whether a result is interesting, useful, or meaningful to mathematicians.
method: Models mathematical generation as nested language generation in the limit, separating a verifiable formal language F from an unknown valuable language H.
Uses a membership oracle (the proof checker) for formal validity while reasoning about how valuable math is revealed through adversarial enumeration of a core language.
Proves a necessity result showing that auxiliary information ('trivia') is required to reliably generate valuable mathematics, not just formally valid output.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes theorem proving and formal math generation as a value-alignment and information-access problem, not just a correctness problem. It suggests that future systems need better priors, retrieval, or guidance signals to produce mathematics that is both valid and genuinely useful.

title: RATS! Patches Talk Through Registers: Emergent Parts in Register Attention Transformers
authors: Timing Yang, Predrag Neskovic, Jansen Seheult, Wenchao Han, Anand Bhattad
abstract: When humans see a bird, they recognize far more than just "bird" -- they see a head, wings, and talons, a structured assembly of reusable parts that can be identified across every bird they have ever seen. We ask whether a self-supervised visual model can discover the same compositional structure on its own. To this end, we propose RATS (Register Attention Transformers), which decomposes the classification token into N learnable register tokens that route patch information through an L->N->N->L

infographic.key_insight: RATS shows that a vision transformer can learn a compositional, part-based representation on its own by splitting the usual class token into multiple learnable register tokens. These registers help patches communicate through an L→N→N→L pathway, encouraging emergent structure instead of treating the image as a flat whole.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of getting self-supervised vision models to discover reusable object parts and structured representations, rather than only learning global image-level features.
method: Replace the single classification token with N learnable register tokens.
Route patch information through a register-mediated communication pattern: L→N→N→L.
Use this register attention design to encourage emergent part discovery and compositional organization in vision transformers.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a practical way to improve interpretability and structure in self-supervised vision models. It may lead to representations that transfer better to downstream tasks by capturing reusable parts and object structure more naturally.

title: Learning Coordinated Preference for Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Pengxin Wang, Lihao Guo, Yi Xie, Bo Liu, Siyang Cao
abstract: Cooperative multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning (MOMARL) models team decision making under multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. In this setting, conflicts arise not only across objectives but also across agents with different observations, roles, and contributions. We propose Preference Coordinated Multi-agent Policy Optimization (PCMA), which learns coordinated agent-specific preferences to enable complementary trade-offs among agents. Theoretically, we formulate coopera

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces a way for multiple agents to learn coordinated preferences, so they can make complementary trade-offs across conflicting objectives instead of optimizing independently. The result is more coherent team behavior in multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of cooperative multi-objective decision-making where conflicts arise both across objectives and across agents with different observations, roles, and contributions.
method: Proposes Preference Coordinated Multi-agent Policy Optimization (PCMA) to learn agent-specific preferences in a coordinated way.
Uses coordinated preference learning to align trade-offs among agents while preserving each agent's role and local perspective.
Provides a theoretical formulation for cooperative multi-objective optimization in multi-agent settings.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical framework for training teams of agents to balance multiple goals without forcing a one-size-fits-all policy. It can improve performance in complex cooperative tasks where different agents need different trade-offs.
