title: CottonLeafVision: An Explainable and Robust Deep Learning Framework for Cotton Leaf Disease Classification
authors: Rafi Ahamed, Md. Abir Rahman, Tasnia Tarannum Roza, Munaia Jannat Easha, Md. Asif Khan
abstract: Globally, cotton is a highly economically beneficial crop, as the textile industry heavily depends on it. So, the precise identification and detection of cotton leaf disease is crucial for economic stability. The development goal of "CottonLeafVision" is to accurately classify and detect cotton leaf disease. With this goal, we have evaluated multiple pretrained Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, including DenseNet201, InceptionV3, and VGG19 on a publicly available cotton leaf disease image data

infographic.key_insight: CottonLeafVision shows that pretrained deep learning models can be adapted to accurately classify cotton leaf diseases from images, helping make plant disease detection faster and more reliable. The framework also emphasizes explainability and robustness, making predictions easier to trust in real-world farming settings.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of identifying cotton leaf diseases early and accurately from images, which is important for preventing crop loss and protecting agricultural productivity.
method: Evaluates multiple pretrained CNN architectures, including DenseNet201, InceptionV3, and VGG19, on a public cotton leaf disease image dataset.
Compares model performance to identify a strong deep learning baseline for cotton disease classification.
Focuses on building an explainable and robust framework suitable for practical agricultural use.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this paper demonstrates how transfer learning can be applied effectively to a specialized image classification task with limited domain data. It is useful for anyone building trustworthy computer vision systems for agriculture or other real-world detection problems.

title: CORA: Analyzing and bridging thinking-answer gap in Multimodal RLVR via Consistency-Oriented Reasoning Alignment
authors: Jiayue Cao, Zhicong Lu, Xuehan Sun, Wei Jia, Hongling Zheng
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has successfully elicited the reasoning capabilities of large language models, motivating its extension to multimodal scenarios. Existing methods primarily focus on improving the visual coverage of reasoning traces and mitigating visual hallucinations, but underestimate the semantic inconsistency between the reasoning process and the final answer. In this paper, we delve into thinking-answer inconsistency in RLVR for large vision-language mod

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that in multimodal RLVR, a model can produce a plausible reasoning trace yet still arrive at an inconsistent final answer. CORA targets this “thinking-answer gap” by aligning the reasoning process with the answer more consistently.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses semantic inconsistency between multimodal reasoning steps and the final answer in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a problem that is often missed when methods focus only on visual coverage or hallucination reduction.
method: Analyzes the thinking-answer gap in multimodal RLVR to identify where reasoning and final responses diverge.
Introduces consistency-oriented reasoning alignment (CORA) to better connect intermediate reasoning with the final answer.
Emphasizes semantic consistency in addition to visual grounding, reducing mismatches between what the model “thinks” and what it answers.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means better trustworthiness and more reliable multimodal reasoning outputs, especially in tasks where explanation quality matters as much as correctness. It also suggests a new evaluation lens beyond visual hallucination: whether the reasoning chain truly supports the answer.

title: OmniVideo-100K: A Dataset for Audio-Visual Reasoning through Structured Scripts and Evidence Chains
authors: Xinyue Cai, Chaoyou Fu, Yi-Fan Zhang, Ran He, Caifeng Shan
abstract: Current automated pipelines for audio-visual Question Answering (QA) generally adopt a ``video-caption-QA'' paradigm. However, these methods typically segment videos into short clips and generate separate descriptions for audio and visual modalities. This decoupled processing severs inherent associations between sounds and their visual sources, while independent clip processing often causes inconsistent descriptions of the same entity across segments. Furthermore, coupling long-text comprehensio

infographic.key_insight: OmniVideo-100K proposes a large-scale dataset designed to improve audio-visual reasoning by preserving structured links between sounds, visuals, and evidence chains. It moves beyond the usual clip-by-clip captioning pipeline to support more consistent, grounded QA over long videos.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses a key weakness in current audio-visual QA systems: decoupled audio and visual processing that breaks sound-source associations, plus short-clip segmentation that causes inconsistent descriptions across a video. It also targets the difficulty of long-text comprehension when generating answers from multi-modal evidence.
method: Build a dataset of 100K video examples with structured scripts and evidence chains for audio-visual reasoning.
Align audio and visual cues at a finer level so models can trace answers back to specific evidence rather than isolated captions.
Support longer-context reasoning by organizing information into coherent multi-step structures instead of independent clip summaries.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this dataset can enable more reliable training and evaluation of models that need grounded audio-visual understanding, especially on long videos. It may improve consistency, traceability, and answer quality in real-world QA systems.

title: AdaSR: Adaptive Streaming Reasoning with Hierarchical Relative Policy Optimization
authors: Junlong Tong, Wenqi Xu, Yingqi Fan, Anhao Zhao, Xuan Lu
abstract: Large reasoning models typically follow a read-then-think paradigm: they observe the complete input, reason over a static context, and then produce the answer. Yet many real-world scenarios are inherently dynamic, such as audio and video stream, where information arrives as a continuous stream and models must reason, update, and respond under partial observations. Recent streaming reasoning methods allow models to think while reading, but they largely rely on supervised imitation of pre-construc

infographic.key_insight: AdaSR enables large reasoning models to think and adapt while data is still arriving, instead of waiting for a full input first. It improves streaming reasoning by learning how to update decisions online with a hierarchical policy optimization strategy.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the mismatch between static, read-then-think reasoning models and real-world streaming settings like audio and video, where information arrives incrementally and the model must reason under partial observations.
method: Introduces adaptive streaming reasoning so the model can read, think, and revise decisions continuously as new tokens/frames arrive.
Uses hierarchical relative policy optimization to better train streaming behavior beyond simple supervised imitation of fixed reasoning traces.
Targets dynamic inputs and partial-information settings, aiming for more robust online updates and response generation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, AdaSR offers a path toward more practical reasoning systems that can operate in real-time, event-driven environments. This is especially useful for applications like live audio/video understanding, monitoring, and interactive assistants.

title: ClinHallu: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning
authors: Sicheng Yang, Hangjie Yuan, Wenjun Zhang, Jinwang Wang, Yichen Qian
abstract: Building trustworthy medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is critical for reliable clinical decision support. Existing medical hallucination benchmarks mainly focus on data collection, but often ignore where hallucinations originate within the reasoning process. We find that hallucination sources vary across samples: errors may arise from visual misrecognition, incorrect medical knowledge recall, or flawed reasoning integration. To enable source-level hallucination diagnosis, we intr

infographic.key_insight: ClinHallu shows that medical MLLM hallucinations do not come from a single failure point: they can begin with visual misrecognition, wrong medical knowledge recall, or broken reasoning integration. The paper’s main breakthrough is a benchmark designed to diagnose hallucinations stage by stage, instead of only judging the final answer.
infographic.problem_solved: Current medical hallucination benchmarks usually identify whether a model hallucinates, but not where the hallucination originates in the reasoning pipeline. This makes it hard to debug medical MLLMs or improve them in a targeted way.
method: Builds a benchmark for source-level diagnosis of hallucinations in medical multimodal reasoning.
Separates hallucination causes into stage-wise categories such as perception, knowledge recall, and reasoning integration.
Supports analysis of how errors propagate through the clinical decision process.
infographic.impact: This helps researchers and practitioners pinpoint the exact failure mode of medical MLLMs, making model debugging, evaluation, and safety improvement more actionable. It is especially useful for building more trustworthy AI systems for clinical decision support.

title: Instruct-Particulate: Scaling Feed-Forward 3D Object Articulation with Kinematic Control
authors: Ruining Li, Yuxin Yao, Matt Zhou, Chuanxia Zheng, Christian Rupprecht
abstract: Reconstructing articulated 3D objects is important for animation, gaming, and robotic simulations. Recent neural networks can estimate the articulated structure of 3D objects, but their generalization remains limited by the scarcity of annotated data for this task. To address this gap, we introduce Instruct-Particulate, a model that takes a 3D mesh together with a target kinematic specification, including part descriptions, connectivity, joint types, and optional point prompts, and predicts the

infographic.key_insight: Instruct-Particulate turns 3D object articulation into a feed-forward prediction task guided by kinematic instructions, making it easier to reconstruct how object parts should move. The key breakthrough is that it combines mesh geometry with structured part/joint specifications to improve articulated 3D understanding with less reliance on dense labeled data.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of reconstructing articulated 3D objects when training data with detailed part and joint annotations is scarce. Existing methods often struggle to generalize to new object shapes and articulation layouts.
method: Takes a 3D mesh as input along with a target kinematic specification, including part descriptions, connectivity, joint types, and optional point prompts.
Uses a feed-forward model to predict articulated 3D structure directly from these instructions rather than relying on exhaustive per-object optimization.
Scales articulated object reconstruction by leveraging structured control signals to guide part segmentation and joint reasoning.
infographic.impact: This matters for AI/ML practitioners because it offers a more scalable way to model articulated objects for animation, robotics simulation, and digital content creation. It also suggests a practical route to better generalization in 3D understanding when annotated data is limited.

title: RepFusion: Leveraging Multimodal Priors for Denoising in Representation Space
authors: Xichen Pan, Aashu Singh, Satya Narayan Shukla, Xiangjun Fan, Shlok Kumar Mishra
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used in text-to-image (T2I) systems, but they are typically limited to text encoding, while denoising is handled by newly trained generative backbones. The emergence of representation autoencoders (RAEs) shifts the generation target toward semantically structured visual representations, creating a latent space that is more compatible with pretrained LLM priors. Inspired by multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), where an MLP projector is sufficient to align clean visual

infographic.key_insight: RepFusion shows that denoising for text-to-image generation can be moved into a semantically structured representation space, where pretrained LLM priors are more naturally useful. By combining multimodal priors with representation autoencoders, it makes generation more aligned with existing language model knowledge instead of training a completely new denoiser from scratch.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the mismatch between LLMs and current T2I systems: LLMs are strong text encoders, but denoising is usually handled by separately trained generative backbones in pixel or latent spaces that are not well aligned with LLM priors. The goal is to make the denoising target more compatible with pretrained multimodal understanding.
method: Use representation autoencoders (RAEs) to map generation into a semantically meaningful visual representation space.
Leverage multimodal priors from pretrained LLMs/MLLMs so the denoiser operates on features that are easier to align with language knowledge.
Train a compact alignment module, inspired by MLP projectors in MLLMs, to connect text-conditioned guidance with clean visual representations.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more efficient and semantically grounded path for T2I generation, potentially reducing the need to train heavy denoising backbones from scratch. It also opens a route to better reuse of pretrained multimodal models in generative pipelines.

title: InterleaveThinker: Reinforcing Agentic Interleaved Generation
authors: Dian Zheng, Harry Lee, Manyuan Zhang, Kaituo Feng, Zoey Guo
abstract: Recent image generators have demonstrated impressive photorealism and instruction-following capabilities in single-image generation and editing. However, constrained by their architectures, they cannot achieve interleaved generation (text-image sequence), which has crucial applications in visual narratives, guidance, and embodied manipulation. Even the latest open-source Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) exhibit limited performance in this regard. In this paper, we introduce InterleaveThinker, th

infographic.key_insight: InterleaveThinker aims to teach multimodal models to generate text and images in an alternating sequence, enabling more natural visual storytelling and action-guided content. The key breakthrough is reinforcing agentic behavior so the model can plan and produce interleaved outputs instead of only single-image results.
infographic.problem_solved: Current image generators and even modern unified multimodal models are strong at single-image generation and editing, but struggle with interleaved generation: producing text-image-text sequences. This limits their use in visual narratives, guided workflows, and embodied manipulation tasks.
method: Introduces InterleaveThinker, a reinforcement-based approach for agentic interleaved generation.
Trains the model to alternate between text and image outputs in a structured sequence rather than generating one modality at a time.
Targets improved performance on tasks that require multi-step multimodal planning, narration, and coordination.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this expands what multimodal models can do beyond static image creation. It opens the door to systems that support richer storytelling, interactive assistants, and instruction-following agents that can mix language and visuals in one coherent workflow.

title: Automated reproducibility assessments in the social and behavioral sciences using large language models
authors: Tobias Holtdirk, Pietro Marcolongo, Anna Steinberg Schulten, Felix Henninger, Stefan Rose
abstract: Reproducibility in the social and behavioral sciences is typically evaluated by independent researchers who reanalyze the original data to assess whether the published findings can be recovered. However, such approaches are resource-intensive and difficult to scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) can automate reproducibility assessments. Using N=76 published studies with predefined claims from the behavioral and social sciences, we compare LLM-generated analysis with the origina

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that large language models can help automate reproducibility checks in the social and behavioral sciences by comparing model-generated analyses to original study findings. The approach offers a scalable alternative to labor-intensive human reanalysis.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional reproducibility assessments require independent researchers to reanalyze original data, which is time-consuming, costly, and hard to scale across many published studies.
method: Selected 76 published studies with predefined claims from the social and behavioral sciences.
Used large language models to generate analyses for the studies and compare the outputs with the original reported findings.
Evaluated how well LLM-based assessments could recover or match reproducibility outcomes relative to the original analyses.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests LLMs can be used as practical assistants for meta-research and research integrity workflows. It points toward faster, cheaper screening of reproducibility at scale, though human oversight remains important.

title: EurekAgent: Agent Environment Engineering is All You Need For Autonomous Scientific Discovery
authors: Amy Xin, Jiening Siow, Junjie Wang, Zijun Yao, Fanjin Zhang
abstract: LLM-based agents have shown increasing potential in automating scientific discovery. Given an optimizable metric and an execution environment, they can propose, validate, and iterate scientific solutions, and have produced results that outperform human-designed approaches. As model capabilities continue to improve, we argue that the bottleneck for autonomous scientific discovery is shifting from prescribing agent workflows to designing agent environments: the resources, constraints, and interfac

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that the main bottleneck in autonomous scientific discovery is no longer the agent workflow, but the environment it operates in. By engineering the right resources, constraints, and interfaces, LLM agents can more effectively generate, test, and improve scientific ideas.
infographic.problem_solved: Current LLM agent systems for science often focus on fixed workflows, which can limit discovery performance. This paper addresses how to better support autonomous scientific discovery by designing the surrounding execution environment instead of manually prescribing every agent step.
method: Frame scientific discovery as an agent-environment optimization problem, where the environment provides the resources and constraints for exploration.
Use optimized execution settings to let agents propose hypotheses, validate them, and iterate toward better solutions.
Shift emphasis from hand-crafted multi-step workflows to environment design that enables scalable, autonomous experimentation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes how to build scientific agents: better environments may matter more than more complex prompting or orchestration. It suggests a practical path to stronger autonomous discovery systems with less manual workflow engineering.

method: Build an end-to-end pipeline that converts raw scientific documents into structured, agent-native knowledge.
Extract richer scientific units beyond abstracts and citations, including entities, claims, evidence, mechanisms, and lineage relationships.
Organize knowledge to support downstream agent orchestration and reasoning over scientific literature.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables research agents to move beyond shallow paper search toward deeper evidence-based synthesis and method comparison. It can improve literature review quality, scientific QA, and automated discovery workflows.

title: Learning to Reason by Analogy via Retrieval-Augmented Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
authors: Zilin Xiao, Qi Ma, Chun-cheng Jason Chen, Xintao Chen, Avinash Atreya
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a standard mechanism for grounding language models in external knowledge, yet conventional retrieval based on lexical or semantic similarity is poorly suited for complex reasoning tasks: a semantically similar problem may demand an entirely different solution strategy, while a superficially different problem may share the same underlying reasoning pattern. We propose Retrieval-Augmented Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RA-RFT), a post-training framework

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that for reasoning tasks, the best retrieved examples are not necessarily the most semantically similar ones, but the ones that share the same reasoning pattern. It introduces RA-RFT, a post-training method that teaches models to retrieve and learn from analogical examples more effectively.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard RAG systems often fail on complex reasoning because lexical or semantic similarity does not reliably identify examples with the right solution strategy. This work addresses the mismatch between retrieval based on surface similarity and the need for retrieval based on underlying reasoning structure.
method: Use retrieval-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning to post-train the model for reasoning-oriented retrieval behavior.
Optimize the system to favor retrieved examples that match the task's reasoning pattern rather than just topical or semantic overlap.
Leverage retrieved analogies during fine-tuning so the model learns to apply strategies from structurally similar problems to new ones.
infographic.impact: This could improve the reliability of RAG systems on tasks like math, logic, and multi-step problem solving, where example selection matters as much as knowledge access. For practitioners, it suggests a path to make retrieval systems smarter about reasoning, not just similarity.

title: Modality Forcing for Scalable Spatial Generation
authors: Bardienus Pieter Duisterhof, Deva Ramanan, Jeffrey Ichnowski, Justin Johnson, Keunhong Park
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models contain rich spatial priors. Synthesizing photorealistic, cluttered scenes requires an understanding of geometry, including perspective and relative scale. Prior works adapt T2I models to leverage this prior for depth prediction, but they require dense depth data and involve complex recipes. We propose Modality Forcing, a simple, scalable post-training recipe for joint image-depth generation using a single DiT trained on sparse depth data. Modality Forcing enables cond

infographic.key_insight: Modality Forcing shows that a pretrained text-to-image model can be post-trained to jointly generate images and depth with a simple recipe, unlocking spatial reasoning without requiring dense depth supervision. The key idea is to reuse the model’s built-in spatial priors and steer them toward scalable 3D-aware generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing methods for adapting text-to-image models to depth prediction or spatial generation often need dense depth datasets and complicated training pipelines. This paper addresses the need for a simpler, scalable way to learn geometry-aware generation from sparse depth data.
method: Start with a single DiT pretrained on text-to-image data, which already contains strong spatial priors.
Apply a post-training procedure called Modality Forcing to jointly learn image and depth generation from sparse depth supervision.
Use the same model to produce photorealistic scenes with consistent geometry, leveraging modality alignment rather than specialized dense-depth training recipes.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a much simpler path to 3D-aware generation and depth-conditioned modeling. It reduces data and engineering complexity, making spatially grounded generative models more practical to train and deploy.

title: RepWAM: World Action Modeling with Representation Visual-Action Tokenizers
authors: Junke Wang, Qihang Zhang, Shuai Yang, Yiming Luo, Yujun Shen
abstract: This work presents RepWAM, a representation-centric world action model (WAM) built on representation visual-action tokenizers. Existing WAMs typically inherit reconstruction-oriented video tokenizers from pretrained video generation models. Although these tokenizers preserve visual fidelity, pixel reconstruction alone provides limited guidance for learning instruction-following dynamics that connect future prediction with robot control. To address this, we explore a semantic visual-action latent

infographic.key_insight: RepWAM shifts world action modeling from pixel-perfect reconstruction to semantic representation learning, making future prediction more aligned with robot control and instruction following. It introduces representation visual-action tokenizers to capture action-relevant dynamics rather than just visual fidelity.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing world action models often rely on reconstruction-oriented video tokenizers from generative video models, which preserve appearance but provide weak training signals for learning actionable, instruction-following dynamics.
method: Builds a representation-centric world action model using representation visual-action tokenizers instead of purely reconstruction-based video tokenizers.
Encodes visual and action information into a shared latent space that emphasizes semantics and control-relevant structure.
Targets better alignment between future prediction and robot action execution, rather than optimizing for pixel-level reconstruction alone.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means world models can become more useful for robotics and interactive agents by learning dynamics that better support decision-making and control. It offers a pathway toward tokenizers and latent spaces that are optimized for task relevance, not just visual realism.

title: Dense Supervision, Sparse Updates: On the Sparsity and Geometry of On-Policy Distillation
authors: Guo Yu, Wenlin Liu, Yulan Hu, Hao-Xuan Ma, Jun-Peng Jiang
abstract: On-policy distillation (\textsc{OPD}) has recently become a prominent post-training recipe as it combines two desirable ingredients: on-policy student trajectories and dense teacher supervision, yet how this hybrid changes a model's parameters remains unclear. Across several language and vision-language model pairs and use cases, our analysis yields two main findings. On sparsity, \textsc{OPD}-style updates are small and coordinate-sparse. They are distributed across layers and are usually FFN-h

infographic.key_insight: On-policy distillation updates are not large or widespread; they are small, coordinate-sparse, and spread across layers, often concentrating in feed-forward network (FFN) channels. This suggests OPD changes models in a highly targeted way despite using dense teacher supervision.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of understanding of how on-policy distillation actually modifies model parameters during post-training, especially the relationship between dense supervision and the geometry/sparsity of resulting updates.
method: Analyze on-policy distillation across multiple language and vision-language model pairs and tasks.
Measure update sparsity and geometric properties of parameter changes during training.
Compare how OPD-style updates distribute across layers and parameter groups, with attention to FFN-heavy concentration.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this helps explain why OPD can be effective and where its learning signal is applied. It can guide more efficient distillation designs, parameter-focused diagnostics, and future methods that exploit sparse update patterns.

title: HyperTool: Beyond Step-Wise Tool Calls for Tool-Augmented Agents
authors: Yaxin Du, Yifan Zhou, Yujie Ge, Jiajun Wang, Xianghe Pang
abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents commonly rely on step-wise atomic tool calls, where each invocation, observation, and value transfer is exposed in the main reasoning trace. This creates an \emph{execution-granularity mismatch}: locally deterministic tool workflows are unfolded into repeated model-visible decisions, consuming context and forcing the model to manage low-level dataflow in the trace. We introduce \textbf{HyperTool}, a unified executable MCP-style tool interface that changes the model-visi

infographic.key_insight: HyperTool moves tool use beyond repetitive step-by-step calls by giving agents a unified, executable interface for multi-step tool workflows. This reduces trace clutter and lets the model focus on higher-level reasoning instead of low-level data transfer.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the execution-granularity mismatch in tool-augmented LLM agents, where deterministic tool workflows are broken into many model-visible steps. This wastes context and makes the model manage intermediate values explicitly in the reasoning trace.
method: Introduce a HyperTool interface inspired by MCP-style tooling to package multi-step tool workflows as a single executable unit.
Keep locally deterministic execution inside the tool boundary instead of exposing every invocation, observation, and value transfer to the main trace.
Reduce context overhead and simplify agent reasoning by shifting low-level dataflow management away from the model.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this can make tool-augmented agents more efficient, more scalable, and easier to prompt or orchestrate. It is especially useful when workflows involve many deterministic sub-steps that would otherwise bloat the context window.

title: World Tracing: Generative Pixel-Aligned Geometry Beyond the Visible
authors: Hao Zhang, Mohamed El Banani, Jen-Hao Cheng, Paul Zhang, Yi Hua
abstract: Image-to-3D methods often trade off faithfulness and completeness: depth estimators are anchored to input pixels but stop at the visible surface, while image-to-3D models generate complete shapes that are often misaligned with the input. We introduce World Tracing, a generative pixel-aligned geometry representation that predicts 3D points aligned with observed pixels while completing geometry beyond the visible surface. For each input pixel, World Tracing predicts an ordered stack of camera-spac

infographic.key_insight: World Tracing bridges the gap between pixel-faithful depth estimation and complete 3D generation by predicting geometry that stays aligned with the input image while extending beyond what is directly visible.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing image-to-3D methods face a trade-off: depth methods are accurate to visible pixels but incomplete, while generative 3D methods produce full shapes that can drift away from the image. This paper tackles the challenge of generating complete 3D geometry without losing pixel alignment.
method: Introduces a generative pixel-aligned geometry representation called World Tracing.
For each input pixel, predicts an ordered stack of camera-space 3D points rather than only a single depth value.
Uses the stacked geometry to model both visible surfaces and occluded/completed structure beyond the visible region.
infographic.impact: This approach can improve 3D reconstruction from single images by making outputs both faithful to the input and more complete. It is especially useful for practitioners building view synthesis, scene understanding, robotics, and image-to-3D systems that need reliable geometry.

title: SpatialClaw: Rethinking Action Interface for Agentic Spatial Reasoning
authors: Seokju Cho, Ryo Hachiuma, Abhishek Badki, Hang Su, Byung-Kwan Lee
abstract: Spatial reasoning, the ability to determine where objects are, how they relate, and how they move in 3D, remains a fundamental challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). Tool-augmented agents attempt to address this by augmenting VLMs with specialist perception modules, yet their effectiveness is bounded by the action interface through which those tools are invoked. In this work, we study how the design of this interface shapes the agent's capacity for open-ended spatial reasoning. Existing sp

infographic.key_insight: SpatialClaw argues that better spatial reasoning in VLM agents depends not just on stronger perception tools, but on a better action interface for how those tools are called. The paper reframes the problem as an interaction-design issue: the agent’s interface can either unlock or limit open-ended spatial reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of enabling vision-language models to reliably reason about 3D spatial relationships, object locations, and motion using external perception tools. It specifically investigates why current tool-augmented agents struggle when the action interface is too restrictive or poorly designed.
method: Studies the action interface as the key bottleneck in tool-augmented spatial reasoning agents.
Introduces SpatialClaw as a rethought interface for invoking specialist perception modules in a more flexible, agentic way.
Evaluates how interface design affects open-ended spatial reasoning performance in VLM-based agents.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work highlights that improving agent performance may require redesigning the tool-use interface, not just adding more powerful models or detectors. It offers a practical lens for building more capable spatially aware agents in robotics, embodied AI, and multimodal reasoning systems.

title: Flex4DHuman: Flexible Multi-view Video Diffusion for 4D Human Reconstruction
authors: Jen-Hao Cheng, Yipeng Wang, Hao Zhang, Gengshan Yang, Jenq-Neng Hwang
abstract: We present Flex4DHuman, a multi-view video diffusion model that transforms a monocular or sparse multi-view video of a dynamic subject into synchronized dense multi-view videos using only relative camera-pose conditioning. Unlike prior human-centric methods that rely on skeletons, depth maps, normals, or rendered target-view geometry, Flex4DHuman requires no explicit geometry priors and instead conditions generation through relative camera-pose positional encoding. The generated videos can be di

infographic.key_insight: Flex4DHuman generates synchronized dense multi-view videos of a dynamic person from a single or sparse multi-view input. Its key breakthrough is using only relative camera-pose conditioning, avoiding explicit geometry priors like skeletons, depth, or normals.
infographic.problem_solved: It tackles 4D human reconstruction from limited viewpoints, where existing methods often depend on hand-crafted geometry cues or rendered target-view inputs. The challenge is to recover temporally consistent, multi-view human motion without requiring strong prior annotations or extra geometric supervision.
method: Uses a multi-view video diffusion model to synthesize dense, synchronized target-view videos from monocular or sparse multi-view inputs.
Conditions generation with relative camera-pose positional encoding instead of skeletons, depth maps, normals, or target-view geometry.
Learns to reconstruct dynamic humans in a flexible way, enabling view expansion and 4D reconstruction from minimal input views.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reduces the dependence on expensive geometric preprocessing and makes 4D human reconstruction more flexible and practical. It can improve workflows in capture, animation, telepresence, and human-centric scene generation.

title: EvoArena: Tracking Memory Evolution for Robust LLM Agents in Dynamic Environments
authors: Jundong Xu, Qingchuan Li, Jiaying Wu, Yihuai Lan, Shuyue Stella Li
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have achieved strong performance on a wide range of benchmarks, yet most evaluations assume static environments. In contrast, real-world deployment is inherently dynamic, requiring agents to continually align their knowledge, skills, and behavior with changing environments and updated task conditions. To address this gap, we introduce EvoArena, a benchmark suite that models environment changes as sequences of progressive updates across terminal, software, and so

infographic.key_insight: EvoArena shows that LLM agents need to be evaluated in changing environments, not just static ones, because real-world conditions evolve over time. The benchmark tracks how agent memory and behavior adapt across progressive updates, revealing robustness gaps that traditional evaluations miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLM agent evaluations assume fixed tasks and environments, which does not reflect deployment settings where software, terminals, and other conditions change continuously. This paper addresses the need for a benchmark that measures whether agents can keep working reliably as the world around them changes.
method: Introduces EvoArena, a benchmark suite designed for dynamic environments with sequential updates.
Models change as progressive environment updates across domains such as terminal and software settings.
Evaluates how well agents update memory, maintain task performance, and adapt behavior over time.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, EvoArena provides a more realistic way to test agent robustness before deployment. It helps identify whether an agent can handle drift, updates, and shifting task conditions, which is critical for building dependable real-world systems.

title: VLGA: Vision-Language-Geometry-Action Models for Autonomous Driving
authors: Jin Yao, Dhruva Dixith Kurra, Tom Lampo, Zezhou Cheng, Danhua Guo
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can describe scenes and reason about them in language, yet still struggle to ground their actions in the dense 3D world around them. Existing approaches either inject features from a frozen 3D foundation model without an objective that ensures the policy uses them, or constrain geometry with sparse box and map losses that provide no dense spatial signal. We introduce VLGA, the first vision-language-action model supervised to reconstruct the dense 3D world it d

infographic.key_insight: VLGA bridges the gap between language-based reasoning and precise 3D driving actions by training the model to reconstruct the dense 3D world, not just predict sparse scene cues. This gives the policy a stronger geometric grounding for autonomous driving decisions.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses a core limitation in vision-language-action systems for driving: they can reason in language but often fail to ground actions in dense 3D geometry. Prior methods rely on frozen 3D features or sparse box/map supervision, which do not provide enough spatial detail for reliable action learning.
method: Introduces VLGA, a vision-language-action model supervised with dense 3D world reconstruction objectives.
Aligns action prediction with geometric understanding so the policy must use 3D spatial information rather than ignore it.
Moves beyond sparse supervision by providing a denser learning signal tied to the full surrounding driving scene.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more reliable way to build autonomous driving models that are both interpretable and spatially aware. It may improve robustness in complex road scenes where accurate 3D grounding is critical.

title: Verifiable Environments Are LEGO Bricks: Recursive Composition for Reasoning Generalization
authors: Hao Xiang, Qiaoyu Tang, Le Yu, Yaojie Lu, Xianpei Han
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable environments has emerged as a powerful approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). While prior research demonstrates that scaling environment quantity improves RL performance, existing manual or individual construction methods suffer from linear scaling limits, thereby hindering scalable reasoning generalization. This paper introduces RACES (\textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{A}utomated \textbf{C}omposition for \textbf{E}

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that verifiable environments can be built like LEGO bricks: smaller, trustworthy tasks can be recursively composed into much larger environments for RL training. This enables reasoning generalization without relying on slow, hand-crafted environment creation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing verifiable-environment construction is mostly manual or one-off, so scaling it increases linearly and becomes a bottleneck for training LLMs at breadth and complexity.
method: Introduces RACES (Recursive Automated Composition for Environment Scaling), a framework for building new environments by composing existing verifiable components.
Uses recursive composition to generate larger, more complex training environments while preserving verifiability.
Aims to scale environment diversity efficiently so RL can improve reasoning generalization beyond a small set of handcrafted tasks.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a practical path to scale RL training data for reasoning without proportional increases in human design effort. It could make environment generation more efficient, reusable, and extensible for building stronger LLM reasoning systems.

title: Ambient Diffusion Policy: Imitation Learning from Suboptimal Data in Robotics
authors: Adam Wei, Nicholas Pfaff, Thomas Cohn, Arif Kerem Dayı, Constantinos Daskalakis
abstract: We propose Ambient Diffusion Policy, a simple and principled method for imitation learning from suboptimal data in robotics. High-quality, task-specific robot data is expensive and time-consuming to collect, while suboptimal datasets with lower-quality or out-of-distribution demonstrations are abundant. Existing methods that co-train on both data sources in robotics often fail to separate the meaningful and the harmful features in the suboptimal samples. In contrast, our method extracts only the

infographic.key_insight: Ambient Diffusion Policy shows that robot imitation learning can improve by learning from both high-quality and suboptimal demonstrations, while filtering out the harmful parts of the weak data. The core idea is to keep the useful signal in noisy demonstrations instead of discarding them entirely.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of training robot policies when expert data is scarce but suboptimal or out-of-distribution demonstrations are plentiful. Existing methods often mix these sources without properly separating helpful behavior from distracting or harmful patterns.
method: Train a diffusion-based policy for imitation learning that can leverage mixed-quality demonstration data.
Use a principled mechanism to extract useful structure from suboptimal samples while suppressing irrelevant or harmful features.
Enable learning from abundant low-quality data without requiring costly, task-specific expert-only datasets.
infographic.impact: This matters because it can reduce the need for expensive robot data collection while still improving policy performance. For practitioners, it offers a more data-efficient way to learn robust robot behaviors from real-world demonstration sets.

title: DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?
authors: Jadelynn Dao, Milan Ganai, Yasmina Abukhadra, Ajay Sridhar, Mozhgan Nasr Azadani
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for embodied agents, with an emerging strategy of scaling test-time compute to improve capability. However, we observe that doing so increases latency, token usage, and FLOPs while yielding uneven, often diminishing gains in downstream success, limiting where embodied agents can be deployed. We argue that choosing when and where to spend test-time compute is central to bringing frontier performance to the real world.

infographic.key_insight: Scaling test-time compute in embodied planners is not always better: it raises latency, token use, and FLOPs, but the gains in task success are uneven and often diminish. The paper argues that the real challenge is deciding when and where extra compute is worth spending.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the inefficiency of blindly increasing test-time compute for Vision-Language Models used as high-level planners in embodied agents, where higher compute can reduce deployability without reliably improving performance.
method: Analyzes how allocating more test-time compute affects embodied planning performance, latency, token usage, and FLOPs.
Focuses on identifying the conditions under which compute spending improves downstream success versus when it produces diminishing returns.
Frames test-time compute as a resource-allocation problem: deciding when and where to spend compute for frontier performance in real-world deployment.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work highlights that better planning performance may come from smarter compute allocation rather than more compute overall. It provides a practical lens for building embodied systems that are faster, cheaper, and more deployable.

title: UniIntervene: Agentic Intervention for Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning
authors: Haoyuan Deng, Yitong Gao, Yudong Lin, Haichao Liu, Zhenyu Wu
abstract: Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (HiL-RL) has emerged as an effective paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, enabling online policy improvement with human guidance. However, current HiL-RL frameworks remain intervention-intensive, relying on frequent human corrections to redirect the policy out of unproductive exploration, which incurs high labor cost and limits real-world scalability. To address this, we propose UniIntervene, an agentic intervention model that detects unproductiv

infographic.key_insight: UniIntervene reduces the need for constant human corrections in real-world reinforcement learning by using an agentic intervention model that can detect unproductive behavior and step in more efficiently. This makes human-in-the-loop robotic learning more scalable and less labor-intensive.
infographic.problem_solved: Current human-in-the-loop RL systems for robotic manipulation require frequent manual interventions to steer policies away from ineffective exploration, creating high labor cost and limiting practical deployment at scale.
method: Introduces an agentic intervention model that monitors learning behavior and identifies when the policy is heading toward unproductive exploration.
Triggers targeted interventions only when needed, reducing unnecessary human involvement while preserving learning efficiency.
Designed for real-world robotic manipulation settings where online policy improvement must be both effective and labor-efficient.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this approach points to a more scalable way to train robots in the real world with less human supervision. It could lower annotation and intervention costs while improving the practicality of human-guided reinforcement learning systems.

title: APPO: Agentic Procedural Policy Optimization
authors: Xucong Wang, Ziyu Ma, Yong Wang, Yuxiang Ji, Shidong Yang
abstract: Recent advances in agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) have substantially improved the multi-turn tool-use capabilities of large language model agents. However, most existing methods assign credit over coarse heuristic units, such as tool-call boundaries or fixed workflows, making it difficult to identify which intermediate decisions influence downstream outcomes. In this work, we study agentic RL from two perspectives: \textit{where to branch and how to assign credit after branching}. Our pilot

infographic.key_insight: APPO proposes a more fine-grained way to train agentic RL systems by deciding where to branch trajectories and how to assign credit after branching. This helps large language model agents learn from the specific intermediate decisions that actually drive success or failure.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing agentic RL methods usually give credit at coarse boundaries like tool calls or fixed workflow steps, which can hide the true causes of downstream outcomes. The paper tackles the challenge of attributing learning signal to the exact intermediate decisions that matter in multi-turn tool-use tasks.
method: Identify branching points in agent trajectories at a finer granularity than traditional tool-call or workflow boundaries.
Assign post-branch credit more precisely so downstream rewards are linked to the decisions that caused them.
Optimize agent policies procedurally, improving learning for multi-turn tool-use and complex interaction chains.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this can make agent training more sample-efficient and more interpretable by revealing which decisions improve performance. It is especially useful for building reliable tool-using LLM agents in real-world workflows.

title: Reusability report: Assessment of reproducibility and applicability to external datasets for RXNGraphormer
authors: Chonghuan Zhang, Majian Zeng, Qianghua Lin, Kuangbiao Liao
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 10 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01257-1

Based on independent reproduction and external benchmarks, this study shows that RXNGraphormer is reproducible and transferable across reaction prediction tasks, while revealing limitations under heterogeneous and distribution-shifted settings.

infographic.key_insight: RXNGraphormer can be independently reproduced and remains effective on external reaction-prediction benchmarks, but its performance drops in heterogeneous or distribution-shifted settings. In short, it is reliable in familiar conditions, yet less robust when the data differs from training.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper evaluates whether a reaction prediction model is truly reproducible and whether it generalizes beyond the original benchmark to real-world external datasets. It addresses the gap between reported model performance and practical transferability.
method: Independent reproduction of RXNGraphormer results to verify experimental consistency.
Evaluation on external benchmark datasets to test cross-dataset generalization.
Analysis of model behavior under heterogeneous and distribution-shifted reaction settings.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides evidence that benchmark success can translate to reproducible results, but also highlights the need to test models under diverse, real-world conditions. It is especially useful for teams deploying reaction prediction systems where dataset shift is likely.

title: On Subquadratic Architectures: From Applications to Principles
authors: Anamaria-Roberta Hartl, Levente Zólyomi, David Stap, Pieter-Jan Hoedt, Niklas Schmidinger
abstract: Transformers dominate modern sequence modeling, but their quadratic attention incurs substantial computational cost. Subquadratic architectures offer a scalable alternative. However, it remains unclear which designs yield the most effective sequence models. We compare three leading approaches: xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet. We evaluate these models on tasks with complex dependencies: (1) code-model pre-training, (2) distillation of code models from large language models, and (3) pre-trainin

infographic.key_insight: Subquadratic sequence models can significantly reduce the computational burden of transformers while still handling complex long-range dependencies. This paper compares xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet to identify which design choices make these efficient architectures most effective for demanding code-related tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high compute and memory cost of transformer attention, especially for long sequences and code modeling, and asks which subquadratic architecture design is most effective in practice.
method: Compare three leading subquadratic architectures: xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet.
Evaluate them on challenging dependency-heavy tasks, including code-model pre-training and distillation from large language models.
Analyze which architectural principles best balance efficiency and modeling performance for sequence learning.
infographic.impact: This helps practitioners choose efficient alternatives to transformers without guessing which subquadratic design will work best. It is especially relevant for large-scale code and sequence models where speed, scalability, and long-context reasoning matter.

title: Context-Driven Incremental Compression for Multi-Turn Dialogue Generation
authors: Yeongseo Jung, Jaehyeok Kim, Eunseo Jung, Jiachuan Wang, Yongqi Zhang
abstract: Modern conversational agents condition on an ever-growing dialogue history at each turn, incurring redundant attention and encoding costs that grow with conversation length. Naive truncation or summarization degrades fidelity, while existing context compressors lack cross-turn memory sharing or revision, causing information loss and compounding errors in long dialogues. We revisit the context compression under conversational dynamics and empirically present its fragility. To improve both efficie

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that dialogue context compression should be adaptive across turns, not a one-shot summary. By reusing and revising compressed memory as the conversation evolves, models can reduce redundant computation while preserving important details.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the growing cost of conditioning on long dialogue histories in multi-turn conversation, where naive truncation or fixed compression loses key information and existing methods cannot share or revise memory across turns.
method: Introduce context-driven incremental compression that updates the compressed memory at each dialogue turn instead of recomputing from scratch.
Allow cross-turn memory sharing so previously retained information can persist and be refined as the conversation changes.
Reduce redundancy in attention/encoding while mitigating the error accumulation seen in truncation and static summarization approaches.
infographic.impact: This matters for practitioners building chatbots and dialogue systems because it can lower inference cost without sacrificing response quality in long conversations. It is especially useful for applications that require sustained context, such as customer support, assistants, and multi-session agents.

title: DepthMaster: Unified Monocular Depth Estimation for Perspective and Panoramic Images
authors: Pengfei Wang, Shihao Wang, Liyi Chen, Zhiyuan Ma, Guowen Zhang
abstract: While monocular depth estimation has achieved significant progress, achieving generalized metric depth estimation for both narrow field-of-view (FoV) perspectives and $360^\circ$ panoramas remains an unsolved challenge. Existing methods are often tailored to specific camera types and struggle to produce accurate metric depth that generalizes across diverse settings. This limitation stems from two key challenges: the inherent geometric discrepancy between perspective and panoramic cameras, and th

infographic.key_insight: DepthMaster aims to unify metric monocular depth estimation for both standard perspective images and 360° panoramic images in one model. The core breakthrough is handling the geometric differences between these camera types so depth predictions generalize across viewing setups.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of a single monocular depth estimation method that can reliably predict accurate metric depth for both narrow field-of-view perspective images and panoramic images. Existing methods are usually camera-specific and do not generalize well across these different projection geometries.
method: Designs a unified depth estimation framework that works across perspective and panoramic inputs.
Accounts for the geometric discrepancy between camera types to improve cross-domain depth prediction.
Targets metric depth estimation, not just relative depth, so outputs are more directly usable in real-world applications.
infographic.impact: This matters because practitioners often work with mixed camera data, such as phones, robots, AR/VR systems, and 360° sensors. A unified model can reduce the need for separate pipelines and improve deployment consistency across diverse visual environments.

title: Breaking Entropy Bounds: Accelerating RL Training via MTP with Rejection Sampling
authors: Yucheng Li, Huiqiang Jiang, Yang Xu, Jianxin Yang, Yi Zhang
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key component in modern large language models, yet the rollout stage remains the key bottleneck in RL training pipelines. Although Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) offers a natural solution to accelerate rollouts through speculative decoding, many studies have observed that MTP acceptance rates degrade significantly during RL training, leading to limited speedup performance. To address this bottleneck, we present Bebop, a systematic study of MTP in LLM post-t

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) can be made practical for RL training rollouts by addressing the drop in acceptance rates that normally limits speculative decoding speedups. In simple terms: it helps RL training run faster without losing too much rollout quality.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the rollout bottleneck in reinforcement learning for large language models, where generating trajectories is slow and becomes the main training-time cost. It also addresses the common issue that MTP acceptance rates degrade during RL, reducing the expected acceleration.
method: Introduces Bebop, a systematic study of MTP behavior during LLM post-training and RL.
Applies rejection sampling to stabilize or improve acceptance behavior during speculative rollout generation.
Evaluates how MTP design choices affect speedup and quality, aiming to keep rollout acceleration effective throughout RL training.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this could significantly reduce RL training time for large language models by speeding up rollouts, which are often the dominant bottleneck. Faster training means lower compute cost and quicker iteration on alignment and post-training methods.

title: Doc-to-Atom: Learning to Compile and Compose Memory Atoms
authors: Xingjian Diao, Wenbo Li, Yashas Malur Saidutta, Avinash Amballa, Lazar Valkov
abstract: Long input sequences are central to document understanding and multi-step reasoning in Large Language Models, yet the quadratic cost of attention makes inference both memory-intensive and slow. Context distillation mitigates this by compressing contextual information into model parameters, and recent work such as Doc-to-LoRA amortizes context distillation into a single forward pass that generates one LoRA adapter per document. However, producing a single monolithic adapter for all queries leads

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns long-document context into reusable "memory atoms" instead of one bulky adapter per document, making context compression more modular and query-friendly. This lets the model compile and compose smaller pieces of memory to better handle different questions over the same document.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the high memory and latency cost of long-context inference in LLMs, especially when a single compressed representation must serve many different queries. The approach aims to overcome the limits of monolithic document-level adapters that are hard to reuse and adapt.
method: Distill document context into compact memory atoms rather than a single monolithic adapter.
Compile these atoms in one forward pass, amortizing context distillation into efficient inference.
Compose multiple atoms at query time so the model can retrieve and combine the most relevant memory for the task.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more efficient way to scale document understanding and multi-step reasoning without paying full attention costs. It can reduce inference overhead while improving flexibility across varied queries on the same source document.

title: FACTR 2: Learning External Force Sensing for Commodity Robot Arms Improves Policy Learning
authors: Steven Oh, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Tony Tao, Philip Han, Kenneth Shaw
abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires force sensitivity, but many robot arms lack dedicated force sensors due to their high cost. We present Neural External Torque Estimation (NEXT), a data-driven method that estimates external joint torques without needing any dedicated force sensors. NEXT trains in 1 minute from only 10 minutes of free-motion data, yet achieves estimates comparable to dedicated joint-torque sensors. NEXT enables force-feedback teleoperation on low-cost arms and improves policy le

infographic.key_insight: FACTR 2 shows that low-cost robot arms can learn useful external force sensing without dedicated force sensors. Its NEXT method estimates external joint torques from short free-motion data, enabling force-aware manipulation and better policy learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Many commodity robot arms lack force/torque sensors, making contact-rich tasks and force-feedback teleoperation difficult and expensive. This paper addresses the gap by providing a fast, data-driven way to recover force information from ordinary robot hardware.
method: Train Neural External Torque Estimation (NEXT) from only 10 minutes of free-motion robot data.
Use the learned model to estimate external joint torques without any dedicated force sensors.
Apply the estimated force signals for force-feedback teleoperation and to improve learning for manipulation policies.
infographic.impact: This matters because it brings force sensing to inexpensive robot arms, lowering hardware cost and setup complexity. For AI/ML practitioners, it enables better contact-rich policy learning and more capable real-world robotic systems with minimal additional instrumentation.

title: Latent World Recovery for Multimodal Learning with Missing Modalities
authors: Hui Wang, Tianyu Ren, Joseph Butler, Christopher Baker, Karen Rafferty
abstract: We study multimodal learning under missing modalities, with particular motivation from bioscience applications in which heterogeneous modalities are often only partially available when decisions need to be made. We propose Latent World Recovery (LWR), a framework built on two key ideas: (i) modality-specific embeddings from different modalities are aligned in a shared latent space, and (ii) a unified representation is constructed by fusing only the embeddings of the modalities that are actually

infographic.key_insight: Latent World Recovery (LWR) lets multimodal models work even when some inputs are missing by learning a shared latent space and combining only the modalities that are available. This makes predictions more robust in real-world settings where data is incomplete.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses multimodal learning when not all modalities are present at inference time, which is common in bioscience and other real-world applications. Traditional multimodal methods often assume every modality is available, making them brittle when some inputs are missing.
method: Learn modality-specific embeddings and align them in a shared latent space.
Construct a unified representation by fusing only the embeddings from modalities that are actually present.
Use the recovered latent representation to support downstream prediction under missing-modality conditions.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to deploy multimodal systems in incomplete-data environments without requiring all sensors or data sources at every decision point. It can improve robustness, flexibility, and real-world usability in domains like bioscience, healthcare, and sensor-based learning.

title: Piper: A Programmable Distributed Training System
authors: Megan Frisella, Shubham Tiwari, Andy Ruan, Yi Pan, Parker Gustafson
abstract: Large-scale model training increasingly relies on composing multiple parallelism strategies, such as data, pipeline, and expert parallelism, together with memory-saving optimizations like ZeRO. Deployed systems for foundation model pretraining often rely on human experts to manually design a high-level parallelism strategy then implement the corresponding low-level execution strategy, making it difficult to adapt the system to new strategies. Meanwhile, many general-purpose frameworks are more f

infographic.key_insight: Piper makes distributed training more programmable, so researchers can combine parallelism strategies and memory optimizations without hand-building a custom execution system for each setup. In simple terms, it separates what training strategy you want from how the system runs it.
infographic.problem_solved: Large-scale model training is hard to adapt because teams often must manually design a high-level parallelism plan and then implement a matching low-level execution strategy. This becomes especially cumbersome when mixing data, pipeline, expert parallelism, and optimization techniques like ZeRO.
method: Provides a programmable distributed training system that can express multiple parallelism strategies in a unified way.
Bridges high-level training plans with low-level execution details, reducing the need for manual system-specific implementation.
Supports composition of parallelism methods and memory-saving optimizations to improve flexibility for foundation model pretraining.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, Piper can reduce engineering effort and make it easier to experiment with new distributed training strategies. This can speed up scaling workflows and improve adaptability as model and hardware demands change.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly acquiring capabilities relevant to biological research, from literature synthesis to interpretation of experimental data. Increasingly, LLM agents can also perform in silico biology tasks that previously required experienced human biologists. These emerging AI capabilities offer new opportunities for scientific discovery and biomedical advances, but they also shift the landscape of biosecurity risks. To address this, we introduce the Agentic Bio-Capabilit

title: Predicting Future Behaviors in Reasoning Models Enables Better Steering
authors: Evgenii Kortukov, Piotr Komorowski, Florian Klein, Paula Engl, Gabriele Sarti
abstract: Deployed large reasoning models (LRMs) often behave unexpectedly. Test-time steering controls LRM outputs by intervening on their hidden representations, but it can degrade output quality. We argue that prior steering work implicitly relies on internal features that detect behavior in already generated text. We show that these detection features are poor predictors of future behavioral outcomes, and thus not the natural intervention target. Instead, we train activation probes to predict future b

infographic.key_insight: The paper finds that steering methods work better when they target features that predict what a reasoning model will do next, rather than features that merely detect what it has already said. In short: predicting future behavior is a better intervention target than reading current text.
infographic.problem_solved: Test-time steering can control large reasoning models, but existing interventions often reduce output quality because they rely on internal signals tied to already-generated behavior instead of future behavior. This paper addresses how to steer models more effectively without harming generation quality.
method: Analyze internal features used in prior steering methods and show they are mostly detectors of current/past text behavior.
Train activation probes to predict future behavioral outcomes in reasoning models.
Compare these predictive probes against detection-based features as intervention targets for test-time steering.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more reliable way to steer deployed reasoning models while preserving answer quality. It can improve controllability in safety, alignment, and behavior-shaping applications.

Current decoding-time compression methods mitigate this issue via token eviction, but typically assume a uniform budget distribution across all layers and heads. authors: Kevin Qinghong Lin, Batu EI, Yuhong Shi, Pan Lu, Philip Torr
abstract: Data tells stories that shape society; the data journalist's job is to turn raw information into stories non-experts can trust. A high-quality news feature takes a newsroom team weeks: hunting for context, running statistics, choosing an angle, and designing visuals. Recent agents handle individual steps well: data-science agents close the analysis loop, while design agents synthesize beautiful websites. But can an agent serve as a data journalist end to end? title: Lip Forcing: Few-Step Autoregressive Diffusion for Real-time Lip Synchronization
authors: Paul Hyunbin Cho, Jinhyuk Jang, SeokYoung Lee, Joungbin Lee, Siyoon Jin
abstract: Diffusion-based lip synchronization models achieve strong visual quality and audio-visual alignment, but full-sequence bidirectional attention and many denoising steps make them impractical for real-time inference. We present Lip Forcing, to our knowledge the first autoregressive diffusion method for video-to-video (V2V) lip synchronization, which distills a 14B audio-conditioned bidirectional video diffusion teacher into causal students. At inference, the students generate each chunk in only tw

infographic.key_insight: Lip Forcing is a real-time lip synchronization approach that turns diffusion video generation into an autoregressive, few-step process. It distills a large bidirectional teacher into causal students so each video chunk can be generated quickly without sacrificing alignment quality.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the high latency of diffusion-based lip synchronization models, which usually require full-sequence bidirectional attention and many denoising steps. These constraints make them too slow for practical real-time use.
method: Distills a 14B audio-conditioned bidirectional video diffusion teacher into smaller causal student models.
Uses an autoregressive chunk-by-chunk generation setup for video-to-video lip synchronization.
Reduces inference cost by generating each chunk in only a few denoising steps while preserving audio-visual alignment.
infographic.impact: This work makes high-quality lip synchronization more practical for interactive and latency-sensitive applications such as avatars, dubbing, live communication, and digital humans. For practitioners, it offers a path to deploy diffusion-quality results in real time.

title: MOFA-VTON: More Fashion Possibilities with Fine-Grained Adaptations in Virtual Try-On
authors: Xiaoyu Han, Chenyang Wang, Jing Wang, Shunyuan Zheng, Quanling Meng
abstract: Virtual try-on aims to fit an in-shop clothing image onto a specific human body. An optimal virtual try-on method should provide diverse and flexible dressing options, accurately reflecting the varied wearing styles encountered in real-life scenarios, tailored to individual preferences and fashion aspirations. However, current methods predominantly perform a direct replacement of the original clothing with the target clothing, following the same dressing pattern. This limited control over clothi

infographic.key_insight: MOFA-VTON goes beyond simple one-to-one clothing replacement by introducing fine-grained adaptations, enabling multiple realistic dressing styles for the same garment. This makes virtual try-on more flexible, personalized, and closer to real-world fashion behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing virtual try-on methods usually only swap the target clothing in a fixed dressing pattern, which limits control over fit, style, and how garments are worn. The paper addresses the need for diverse, user-specific outfit generation instead of a single rigid try-on outcome.
method: Learn fine-grained adaptations that adjust how a garment is placed and worn on a person rather than directly replacing the original clothing.
Support multiple dressing patterns to produce diverse try-on results from the same input item.
Preserve realism by aligning garment appearance with human pose and body structure while allowing flexible fashion variations.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work improves the controllability and versatility of virtual try-on systems, which is important for fashion e-commerce, personalization, and interactive styling tools. It also points toward richer generative modeling beyond rigid image replacement.

authors: Zhengkai Pan, Peter Potaptchik, Wenxi Yao, Michael S. Albergo, Jakiw Pidstrigach
abstract: Recent one-step generative models accelerate sampling by learning deterministic flow maps of the underlying dynamics. These methods rely on learning from ordinary differential equations, leaving open how to define an exact distillation procedure for stochastic dynamics. We introduce the Itô map, an any-step stochastic flow map that takes an intermediate state and Brownian path and predicts future states in a single pass. The Itô map formulation yields novel estimators for inference-time control

title: Next Forcing: Causal World Modeling with Multi-Chunk Prediction
authors: Gangwei Xu, Qihang Zhang, Jiaming Zhou, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen
abstract: Autoregressive video generation has emerged as a powerful paradigm for World Action Models (WAMs). However, existing approaches suffer from slow training convergence and limited converged accuracy, particularly at high frame rates, as the training supervision is confined to the current chunk without explicit signals about future dynamics; they also suffer from slow inference due to iterative video denoising. In this paper, we present Next Forcing, a multi-chunk prediction (MCP) framework for cau

infographic.key_insight: Next Forcing improves world action models by training them to predict multiple future chunks at once, rather than only the current chunk. This gives the model explicit supervision about future dynamics, leading to faster convergence and better accuracy, especially at high frame rates.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses two bottlenecks in autoregressive video generation for world action models: slow training convergence with limited final accuracy, and slow inference caused by iterative denoising. These issues are especially severe when modeling high frame-rate videos, where current-chunk-only supervision is too weak.
method: Introduces Next Forcing, a multi-chunk prediction (MCP) framework for causal world modeling.
Trains the model with supervision spanning several future chunks, providing direct signals about upcoming dynamics instead of only the present chunk.
Aims to improve both learning efficiency and generation quality while maintaining causal, autoregressive prediction behavior.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this means more practical and scalable video world models that learn faster and generalize better over longer horizons. It can reduce training cost and improve real-time or high-frame-rate generation workflows.

title: When to Align, When to Predict: A Phase Diagram for Multimodal Learning
authors: Ilay Kamai, Hugues Van Assel, Aviv Regev, Hagai B. Perets, Randall Balestriero
abstract: Cross-modal alignment (CA) and cross-modal prediction (CP) are the dominant paradigms for multimodal representation learning, yet there is no systematic understanding of when each succeeds, when each fails, and when cross-modal training helps at all -- a gap that leaves practitioners, especially in scientific domains like biomedicine or astrophysics, with heterogeneous instruments and multiple levels of organization and measurement, unable to diagnose why standard methods underperform the best s

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a phase diagram that explains when cross-modal alignment (CA) or cross-modal prediction (CP) is the better choice for multimodal learning. It shows that cross-modal training is not universally beneficial; its success depends on the data regime and the relationship between modalities.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of a systematic framework for understanding when multimodal methods help, when they fail, and whether alignment or prediction is the right objective. This is especially important for complex scientific settings with heterogeneous sensors, scales, and measurements.
method: Build a phase-diagram-style analysis of multimodal learning regimes.
Compare cross-modal alignment and cross-modal prediction across different data conditions.
Identify when cross-modal training improves representation learning versus when it can be ineffective or harmful.
infographic.impact: This gives practitioners a practical diagnostic tool for choosing multimodal objectives instead of relying on one-size-fits-all methods. It can improve model design in domains like biomedicine and astrophysics, where modality relationships are complex and standard approaches often underperform.

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically maximizes the likelihood of every token in a demonstrated trajectory. However, an observed token can be non-unique, noisy, or misaligned with the model prior. Strictly fitting toward this one-hot target may be suboptimal, especially when the pretrained model encodes a rich knowledge prior. title: ARM: An AutoRegressive Large Multimodal Model with Unified Discrete Representations
authors: Junke Wang, Xiao Wang, Jiacheng Pan, Xuefeng Hu, Feng Li
abstract: This paper introduces ARM, a discrete representation-based AutoRegressive Model that unifies image understanding, generation, and editing within a next-token prediction framework. abstract: Multimodal large language models can write code to produce complex programs as well as use programs to do 3D modeling, which opens up a new avenue for 3D generation powered by their priors, world knowledge and reasoning. title: Navigating molecular OOD-ness
authors: Anna Tomberg, Nessa Carson
abstract:
