Machine learning methods for drug discovery often face difficulties in identifying novel bioactive molecules that do not belong to the training data distribution. A new metric can now quantify chemical distribution shift and evaluate the generalization capability of molecular machine learning models.

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces a new way to measure how far test molecules are from the training data, making it easier to tell when a model is being asked to generalize beyond familiar chemistry. In short: it quantifies molecular out-of-distribution (OOD) shift instead of guessing it.
infographic.problem_solved: Drug-discovery models often look accurate on known chemistry but fail on genuinely novel bioactive molecules. The paper addresses the lack of a reliable metric for detecting and evaluating chemical distribution shift in molecular machine learning.
method: Defines a metric that quantifies chemical OOD-ness, i.e., how unlike the training distribution a molecule is.
Uses this metric to assess whether molecular ML models can generalize to novel compounds.
Provides a framework for evaluating model robustness under realistic drug-discovery distribution shifts.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in chemistry, this helps separate true generalization from performance that only works on familiar data. It can improve model selection, benchmarking, and trust in predictions for novel drug candidates.

abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents are increasingly deployed in interactive game environments. abstract: Temporal modeling is essential for robotic manipulation, as effective control requires both memory of past interactions and imagination of future states. title: Latent Spatial Memory for Video World Models
authors: Weijie Wang, Haoyu Zhao, Yifan Yang, Feng Chen, Zeyu Zhang
abstract: Video world models that maintain 3D spatial consistency across generated frames typically rely on explicit point cloud memory constructed in RGB space. This design is both computationally expensive, requiring repeated rendering and VAE encoding, and inherently lossy, as the round trip through pixel space discards rich features of the learned latent representation. infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces latent spatial memory, a persistent 3D cache that stores scene information directly in latent space instead of repeatedly converting through RGB. The result is a more efficient and information-preserving way to maintain 3D consistency in video world models.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video world models often rely on explicit point cloud memory built in RGB space, which is slow and computationally expensive due to repeated rendering and VAE encoding. This pipeline is also lossy because transforming learned features into pixel space discards useful latent information.
method: Store scene state in a persistent 3D latent memory rather than reconstructing it from RGB frames.
Use the latent cache to preserve richer learned representations across generated frames, improving spatial consistency.
Reduce overhead by avoiding repeated render-encode cycles in the world model pipeline.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this approach promises faster and more memory-efficient video generation while improving spatial coherence over time. It is especially relevant for building scalable world models, video prediction systems, and embodied AI agents that need long-term scene understanding.

abstract: AI evaluation results are produced at scale but reported inconsistently across leaderboards, model cards, benchmark papers, and company blogs. title: iOSWorld: A Benchmark for Personally Intelligent Phone Agents
authors: Lawrence Keunho Jang, Mareks Woodside, Geronimo Carom, Andrew Keunwoo Jang, Jing Yu Koh
abstract: A useful phone agent needs to be personally intelligent. It should reason over a user's identity, history, and preferences as they exist on the device, not just follow isolated instructions in an impersonal sandbox. infographic.key_insight: iOSWorld introduces the first native iOS benchmark designed for personally intelligent phone agents, where agents must reason over persistent user identity, history, and preferences instead of treating each task in isolation. infographic.problem_solved: Existing mobile agent benchmarks do not adequately test personalization. They often place agents in isolated, impersonal environments, making it hard to evaluate whether a phone agent can use a user's long-term context and private device data to act intelligently.

title: Echo-Memory: A Controlled Study of Memory in Action World Models
authors: Wayne King, Zeyue Xue, Yuxuan Bian, Jie Huang, Haoran Li
abstract: We present \textbf{Echo-Memory}, a controlled study of memory mechanisms in action-conditioned world models. These models generate multi-segment videos from a first frame, text prompt, and camera-action sequence, but their central failure is often memory rather than local image synthesis: after the camera leaves and returns, the scene or salient object may silently change. Existing memory designs are hard to compare because gains are entangled with backbone, training, retrieval, and evaluation d

infographic.key_insight: Echo-Memory isolates memory as the core failure mode in action-conditioned world models, showing that many apparent improvements come from confounded comparisons rather than truly better memory. It provides a controlled setup to fairly study how models remember and restore scene content after camera movement.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating memory in world models, where objects or scenes can change silently after the camera leaves and returns. Existing memory methods are hard to compare because their benefits are mixed with differences in backbone design, training, retrieval, and evaluation.
method: Introduces a controlled benchmark/study for memory in action-conditioned world models that generate multi-segment videos from an initial frame, text prompt, and camera-action sequence.
Separates memory-specific effects from other factors so retrieval, architecture, and training choices can be compared more fairly.
Focuses on the failure case of returning to previously seen content, where a good model should preserve object identity and scene consistency over time.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this helps identify whether a model truly has better memory or is only benefiting from setup differences. It also provides a clearer path for designing and evaluating world models that stay consistent over long, interactive sequences.

title: GPIC: A Giant Permissive Image Corpus for Visual Generation
authors: Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Kyle Sargent, Suchir Agarwal, Michael Jang, Michael Poli
abstract: Studying scalable methods for visual generative modeling requires large, accessible, and stable datasets. We introduce GPIC, a Giant Permissive Image Corpus of approximately 28 trillion pixels. GPIC comprises diverse internet images captioned by a state-of-the-art vision-language model, including 100M training, 200K validation, and 1M test examples. Moreover, all GPIC images are permissively licensed for both research and commercial use. GPIC is safety-filtered, deduplicated, and centrally hoste

infographic.key_insight: GPIC introduces a massive, permissively licensed image dataset designed specifically to support scalable visual generation research. Its size, curation, and accessibility make it a strong foundation for training and evaluating modern generative models.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of large, stable, and legally usable image datasets for training and evaluating visual generative models at scale.
method: Assembled GPIC, a corpus of approximately 28 trillion pixels from diverse internet images.
Captioned images using a state-of-the-art vision-language model to provide useful supervision.
Applied safety filtering, deduplication, and centralized hosting to improve reliability and usability.
Split the dataset into 100M training, 200K validation, and 1M test examples.
Ensured all images are permissively licensed for both research and commercial use.
infographic.impact: GPIC lowers the barrier to building and benchmarking large-scale visual generation systems by providing a huge, clean, and legally accessible dataset. This can accelerate research, improve reproducibility, and enable broader deployment in both academic and commercial settings.

title: Uncertainty-driven 3D Gaussian Splatting Active Mapping via Anisotropic Visibility Field
authors: Shangjie Xue, Jesse Dill, Dhruv Ahuja, Frank Dellaert, Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract: We present Gaussian Splatting Anisotropic Visibility Field (GAVIS), a novel framework for uncertainty quantification and active mapping in 3DGS. Our key insight is that regions unseen from the training views yield unreliable predictions from the 3DGS. To address this, we introduce a principled and efficient method for quantifying the visibility field in 3DGS, defined as the anisotropic visibility of each particle with respect to the training views, and represented using spherical harmonics. The

infographic.key_insight: 3D Gaussian Splatting can be made uncertainty-aware by explicitly measuring how visible each 3D particle is from the training views. GAVIS uses this visibility signal to identify unseen or poorly observed regions, where predictions are unreliable, and to guide active mapping.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of principled uncertainty estimation in 3D Gaussian Splatting, especially in regions not covered by the training viewpoints. This matters because unseen areas can produce misleading reconstructions and weaken downstream mapping or exploration decisions.
method: Defines an anisotropic visibility field for each Gaussian particle relative to the set of training views.
Represents visibility efficiently with spherical harmonics to enable practical computation in 3DGS.
Uses the visibility-based uncertainty estimate to support active mapping, helping prioritize areas that need more observation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners working with 3D reconstruction, robotics, or autonomous exploration, this provides a way to detect where a 3DGS model is uncertain instead of treating all regions equally. That can improve map quality, data collection efficiency, and decision-making in active sensing pipelines.

title: DynaFLIP: Rethinking Robotics Perception via Tri-Modal-Dynamics Guided Representation
authors: Jusuk Lee, Seungjae Lee, Jonghun Shin, Hoseong Jung, Sungha Kim
abstract: Robot manipulation critically depends on perception that preserves the action-relevant aspects of a scene. Yet most robot learning pipelines are built upon visual encoders pre-trained for static recognition or vision-language alignment, leaving motion understanding to downstream policies. We introduce DynaFLIP, a dynamics-aware multimodal pre-training framework that pushes motion understanding upstream into perception. We construct image-language-3D flow triplets from heterogeneous human and rob

infographic.key_insight: DynaFLIP moves motion understanding into the perception stage itself, instead of relying on downstream robot policies to infer dynamics later. By aligning image, language, and 3D flow signals, it learns representations that better capture action-relevant scene changes.
infographic.problem_solved: Most robot perception backbones are trained for static recognition or vision-language matching, which can miss the motion and dynamics needed for manipulation. This paper addresses the gap between visual understanding and action-relevant dynamics in robot learning.
method: Builds tri-modal pretraining data from image-language-3D flow triplets collected from heterogeneous human and robot sources.
Learns a dynamics-aware multimodal representation that explicitly incorporates motion cues during perception pretraining.
Guides the model to preserve action-relevant structure in the scene so downstream manipulation policies can use more informative features.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners in robotics, DynaFLIP suggests a stronger perception foundation for manipulation tasks by encoding motion early. This can improve generalization and reduce the burden on downstream policies to discover dynamics from scratch.

title: Benchmarking Single-Factor Physical Video-to-Audio Generation
authors: Tingle Li, Siddharth Gururani, Kevin J. Shih, Gantavya Bhatt, Sang-gil Lee
abstract: Generative video-to-audio (V2A) models produce highly plausible soundtracks, but it remains unclear whether they capture the underlying physical processes. Existing evaluations emphasize perceptual realism and overlook physical correctness under controlled interventions. In this paper, we introduce FlatSounds, a benchmark that audits the physical reasoning of V2A models through: 1) controlled counterfactual pairs in which a single physical factor is varied, and 2) single-video pattern tests that

infographic.key_insight: This paper introduces FlatSounds, a benchmark that tests whether video-to-audio models understand real physical causality, not just whether they generate realistic-sounding audio. It reveals how well models respond to controlled changes in a single physical factor.
infographic.problem_solved: Current V2A evaluations focus mostly on perceptual realism and do not check if generated audio is physically correct when the video changes in a controlled way. This paper addresses the gap by benchmarking physical reasoning under counterfactual and single-video intervention settings.
method: Create controlled counterfactual video pairs where only one physical factor changes at a time.
Test whether V2A models produce audio that changes consistently with the manipulated factor.
Use single-video pattern tests to probe physical cues without needing paired comparisons.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this benchmark provides a more rigorous way to evaluate V2A models beyond surface-level realism. It can help identify models that sound plausible but fail to capture true physical dynamics, guiding better model design and evaluation.

title: RoboWits: Unexpected Challenges for Robotic Creative Problem Solving
authors: Chunru Lin, Hongxin Zhang, Fenghao Yu, Zhehuan Chen, Thomas L. Griffiths
abstract: The ability to reason, adapt, and creatively solve problems under unexpected challenges is essential for robots operating in real-world environments. However, current robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize skill-level execution and provide limited insight into such cognitive reasoning capabilities. We introduce RoboWits, a bi-manual robotic benchmark designed to systematically evaluate cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness to unexpected conditions. To enable scalable constructio

infographic.key_insight: RoboWits introduces a new benchmark for testing whether robots can think through unexpected problems, not just execute pre-programmed skills. It highlights that real-world robot intelligence needs creative reasoning, tool use, and adaptation under surprise conditions.
infographic.problem_solved: Current robotic benchmarks mostly measure task execution in controlled settings, leaving a gap in evaluating cognitive reasoning, creative problem-solving, and robustness when conditions change unexpectedly.
method: Built RoboWits as a bi-manual robotic benchmark focused on cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and handling unexpected challenges.
Designed the benchmark to systematically introduce surprises and assess how robots adapt beyond standard skill execution.
Emphasized scalable construction so the benchmark can be expanded and used for broader evaluation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, RoboWits provides a more realistic way to measure whether robot systems can cope with uncertainty and novel situations. This can guide the development and comparison of more capable, flexible robotic agents.

title: From Pixels to Words -- Towards Native One-Vision Models at Scale
authors: Haiwen Diao, Jiahao Wang, Penghao Wu, Yuhao Dong, Yuwei Niu
abstract: Current vision-language models (VLMs) typically stitch together separate image encoders and language decoders via multi-stage alignment, a modular framework that inevitably fragments pixel-level signals across frames and scatters early pixel-word interactions. In parallel, native VLMs, despite impressive performance on single images, remain largely unexplored in multi-image, video understanding, and spatial intelligence. Hence, we introduce NEO-ov, a native foundation model that learns cross-fra

infographic.key_insight: NEO-ov demonstrates that a native, end-to-end 'one-vision' foundation model can preserve pixel-level signals across frames and directly map pixels to words at scale, enabling multi-image, video and spatial reasoning without stitching separate image encoders and language decoders.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing modular vision–language pipelines fragment pixel information across processing stages and limit early pixel–word interactions; native VLMs have been strong on single images but underexplored and unscaled for multi-image, video and spatial tasks. NEO-ov addresses this gap by providing a unified, scalable native model for cross-frame multimodal understanding.
method: Design a unified native architecture that ingests raw pixels from one or multiple images/frames and produces language tokens end-to-end (pixels → words) without separate encoder/decoder modules.
Use cross-frame spatial–temporal attention and positional encodings to maintain pixel-to-word alignment and enable interactions across frames/regions.

Scale training with multi-task pretraining (captioning, VQA, grounding-like objectives) and efficiency-focused design choices (patching/tokenization and attention optimizations) to support large-scale multimodal learning.
infographic.impact: Simplifies VLM pipelines and improves early pixel–word interactions, enabling stronger video, multi-image and spatial reasoning capabilities for applications like video QA, embodied AI, retrieval and visual grounding. Practitioners can build more coherent, end-to-end multimodal systems with fewer hand-off artifacts and better spatio-temporal alignment.

title: VLMs May Not Globally Enhance Human Alignment over LLMs During Natural Reading
authors: Jinzhou Wu, Zhengwu Ma, Jixing Li, Baoping Tang, Zitong Lu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly useful computational models of human language processing, but it remains unclear whether vision-language learning makes text representations more human-like during natural reading. Here, we address this question by comparing tightly matched LLM and vision-language model (VLM) pairs under a strictly text-only setting, allowing us to isolate the effect of multimodal training history from online visual input or cross-modal fusion. We evaluate mo

infographic.key_insight: This paper suggests that vision-language pretraining does not necessarily make text representations globally more aligned with human reading behavior than matched language-only models. In a strictly text-only setting, the multimodal training advantage appears limited or context-dependent rather than universal.
infographic.problem_solved: The study addresses whether adding visual-language training makes model representations more human-like during natural reading, without the confounding influence of online visual input or cross-modal fusion.
method: Compare tightly matched LLM and VLM pairs under the same text-only reading conditions.
Isolate the effect of multimodal training history by removing direct visual inputs during evaluation.
Assess human alignment during natural reading to test whether VLMs better predict or reflect human language processing.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this cautions against assuming that multimodal pretraining automatically improves human alignment in text tasks. It highlights the need to evaluate VLMs carefully and task-specifically, especially when using them as cognitive or linguistic models.

title: Skill-Conditioned Gated Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
authors: Jiazhen Huang, Xiao Chen, Xiao Luo, Yong Dai, Senkang Hu
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (SD) improves LLM reasoning by using teacher-side privileged information (PI) to turn sparse verifier outcomes into dense token-level supervision. Existing methods usually assume trusted PI, such as reference answers or successful traces. We ask whether PI can instead come from an experience-derived skill bank, where retrieved skills are compact and reusable but may also be irrelevant or misleading. We propose Skill-Conditioned Gated Self-Distillation (SGSD), which fo

infographic.key_insight: You can use a large, experience-derived bank of compact "skills" as privileged information for on-policy self-distillation—if you gate and condition the distillation process to filter out misleading skills, you get dense token-level supervision that improves LLM reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing self-distillation methods assume trusted privileged information (e.g., reference answers or perfect traces). This paper solves how to safely and effectively use noisy, reusable skills retrieved from experience (which can be irrelevant or misleading) as privileged information.
method: Construct an experience-derived skill bank of compact reusable reasoning primitives (skills) from past traces.
Retrieve candidate skills per problem and condition the teacher’s on-policy distillation to produce token-level supervision that incorporates retrieved skills.
Learn a gating module that selects or weights retrieved skills (on-policy, guided by verifier outcomes) so the student only distills from helpful skills and ignores misleading ones.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to leverage abundant, compact skill repositories to boost LLM reasoning without requiring trusted traces—improving sample efficiency and robustness to noisy retrievals while reducing reliance on costly annotated PI.

title: CaMBRAIN: Real-time, Continuous EEG Inference with Causal State Space Models
authors: Abhilash Durgam, Nyle Siddiqui, Jeffrey A. Chan-Santiago, Qiushi Fu, Elakkat D. Gireesh
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a critical, non-invasive method to monitor electrical brain activity. EEGs can span anywhere from a couple seconds to multiple hours, posing a major hurdle for existing deep learning methods due to two major factors: (1) existing EEG models are predominantly built upon the attention mechanism, incurring quadratic scaling as the sequence length increases, and (2) raw EEG signals must be processed in a sliding-window fashion due to fixed-length input requirements, p

infographic.key_insight: Replacing attention-heavy EEG models with causal state-space models enables true real-time, continuous inference over arbitrarily long EEG recordings without sliding-window hacks or quadratic time/space costs.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the scalability and latency limits of existing EEG deep-learning pipelines that rely on attention and fixed-length windows, which struggle with very long recordings and real-time/streaming requirements.
method: Use causal state-space models (SSMs) as the core temporal backbone to provide linear-time, constant-memory sequence processing instead of quadratic attention.
Design a streaming, sample-by-sample inference pipeline that emits continuous outputs (no sliding windows) with low latency suitable for online EEG.
Optimize training and inference for EEG: causal conditioning, efficient recurrence/unrolled updates, and architecture choices that trade negligible accuracy for large gains in throughput and memory.
infographic.impact: Makes long-duration and real-time EEG analysis practical on commodity and edge hardware, lowering compute/memory costs and enabling continuous brain monitoring, BCI, and clinical applications previously limited by attention-based models.

title: Human Label Variation as Stable Signal: Learning Annotator-Specific Explanation Behavior via Cross-Annotator Preference Optimization
authors: Beiduo Chen, Pingjun Hong, Ziyun Zhang, Benjamin Roth, Anna Korhonen
abstract: Free-text explanations extend human label variation (HLV) beyond label disagreement by revealing the reasoning and preferences behind annotators' decisions. We study whether large language models (LLMs) can learn and reproduce such annotator-specific label-explanation behavior. Using two sentence-pair tasks with four annotators each -- natural language inference and paraphrase judgment -- we first analyze whether annotators exhibit stable individual patterns. We find that such patterns are weak

infographic.key_insight: This paper asks whether annotator-specific explanation styles are a stable signal, not just noise. The core idea is that LLMs can be trained to predict both a label and the kind of explanation a particular annotator would give, using cross-annotator preferences.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard datasets usually capture label disagreement, but not the reasoning behind it. This work addresses how to model human label variation at the explanation level and whether models can learn consistent annotator-specific label-explanation behavior.
method: Analyze two sentence-pair tasks: natural language inference and paraphrase judgment, with four annotators each.
Test whether individual annotators show stable patterns in both labels and free-text explanations.
Train LLMs with cross-annotator preference optimization to reproduce annotator-specific explanation behavior rather than only majority labels.
infographic.impact: For ML practitioners, this suggests that disagreement between annotators can be a useful training signal instead of a problem to eliminate. It can improve model alignment with different human perspectives and support more nuanced supervision for explanation-rich tasks.

title: PEFT-Arena: Understanding Parameter-Efficient Finetuning from a Stability-Plasticity Perspective
authors: Yangyi Huang, Ruotian Peng, Zeju Qiu, Jiale Kang, Yandong Wen
abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) has become the standard approach for adapting large language models, yet evaluations largely emphasize downstream accuracy while overlooking the retention of pretrained capabilities. We argue that PEFT should be assessed through the stability-plasticity dilemma: the trade-off between target-task adaptation and resistance to forgetting. We introduce PEFT-Arena, a benchmark that jointly measures downstream performance and general capability retention. Across m

infographic.key_insight: PEFT should not be judged only by how well it improves a target task—it must also be evaluated by how much of the pretrained model’s general ability it preserves. PEFT-Arena reframes finetuning as a stability-plasticity trade-off: adapt effectively without catastrophic forgetting.
infographic.problem_solved: Current PEFT evaluations focus too heavily on downstream accuracy and miss whether finetuning damages the model’s pretrained capabilities. This paper addresses the need for a benchmark that measures both task adaptation and retention of general knowledge/skills.
method: Introduces PEFT-Arena, a benchmark designed to jointly assess downstream task performance and general capability retention.
Frames PEFT evaluation through the stability-plasticity dilemma, capturing the balance between learning new tasks and preserving prior knowledge.
Compares PEFT methods across both adaptation quality and forgetting behavior to reveal trade-offs hidden by accuracy-only evaluation.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this provides a more realistic way to choose PEFT methods based on both performance gains and robustness to forgetting. It helps avoid methods that look strong on a single task but degrade the model’s broader utility.

title: Self-Improving Language Models with Bidirectional Evolutionary Search
authors: Guowei Xu, Zhenting Qi, Huangyuan Su, Weirui Ye, Himabindu Lakkaraju
abstract: Search has been proposed as an effective method for self-improving language models and agentic systems, both for post-training sample generation and for inference. However, widely used methods such as best-of-N sampling and tree search face two fundamental limitations: they are guided by sparse verification signals, and they construct candidates primarily through autoregressive expansion, restricting exploration to regions with substantial model probability mass. To address these, we propose Bid

infographic.key_insight: Combining bidirectional decoding with evolutionary operators lets a language model explore and iteratively improve candidate outputs beyond high-probability autoregressive paths, yielding higher-quality solutions guided by denser verification signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes two core limitations of common search strategies (best-of-N, tree search): reliance on sparse/weak verification signals and restricted exploration confined to high-probability autoregressive generations.
method: Maintain a population of candidate outputs and generate proposals using bidirectional decoding (both forward and backward completion) to access low-probability but potentially better regions of the output space.
Apply evolutionary operators—mutation, crossover, and selection—combined with richer fitness evaluations (e.g., learned verifiers or multi-criterion checks) to rank and refine candidates.
Iteratively evolve the population (selection → variation → evaluation) to produce higher-quality outputs for inference and to generate improved training samples for self-improvement.
infographic.impact: Enables more robust, sample-efficient self-improvement of language models and agentic systems by expanding exploration and providing stronger internal feedback—leading to higher-quality outputs with less human labeling and fewer search samples.

title: OmniVerifier-M1: Multimodal Meta-Verifier with Explicit Structured Recalibration
authors: Xinchen Zhang, Bowei Liu, Jiale Liu, Chufan Shi, Yizhen Zhang
abstract: Visual outcomes are increasingly central to multimodal large language models, making reliable and fine-grained verification essential for scaling generalist foundation models. In this work, we investigate multimodal meta-verification, which leverages verifier-generated rationales rather than decision-only signals, and explore how to effectively incorporate meta-verification feedback into multimodal verifier training. We identify two key findings. First, symbolic verifier outputs (e.g., bounding

infographic.key_insight: OmniVerifier-M1 shows that multimodal verifiers become more reliable when they learn from structured, rationale-rich feedback instead of only final yes/no decisions. The paper argues that explicit symbolic recalibration helps align verifier judgments with visual evidence more precisely.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of building multimodal verifiers that can accurately judge visual outputs with fine-grained reliability. Standard decision-only training often misses detailed errors and provides weak feedback for improving verifier quality.
method: Uses multimodal meta-verification, where the verifier learns from generated rationales rather than only binary correctness labels.
Introduces explicit structured recalibration to better incorporate symbolic feedback such as object-level or region-level evidence.
Trains the verifier to produce and use fine-grained verification signals that improve alignment between visual observations and final judgments.
infographic.impact: This matters because AI systems that generate or interpret images need trustworthy verification, especially in high-stakes or detail-sensitive settings. For practitioners, it offers a path toward more robust multimodal evaluation, debugging, and model scaling.

title: Gamma-World: Generative Multi-Agent World Modeling Beyond Two Players
authors: Fangfu Liu, Kai He, Tianchang Shen, Tianshi Cao, Sanja Fidler
abstract: World models for interactive video generation have largely focused on single-agent settings, where future observations are generated from a single control signal. However, many generated environments require multi-agent interaction: multiple players, robots, or embodied agents act simultaneously within a shared space. Scaling world models to such settings requires a principled multi-agent design: agents should remain independently controllable, permutation-symmetric, and support efficient infere

infographic.key_insight: Gamma-World extends generative world modeling from single-agent settings to multi-agent environments, while preserving independent control for each agent and symmetry across agent identities. This makes it possible to simulate richer interactive scenes where multiple entities act at once.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of scaling video/world models to multi-agent interactions. Existing approaches often assume one controller, but real environments involve multiple agents whose actions must be modeled jointly, efficiently, and without depending on the order in which agents are represented.
method: Designs a multi-agent world model that generates future observations from multiple simultaneous control signals.
Enforces permutation symmetry so the model treats agents consistently regardless of their ordering.
Preserves independent controllability, allowing each agent's actions to influence the world without collapsing them into a single shared control stream.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this opens the door to better simulation of collaborative or competitive environments such as games, robotics, and embodied AI. It provides a more principled foundation for training and evaluating agents in realistic multi-agent worlds.

title: Generalizable mutation-effect prediction across adaptive immune recognition via unified multimodal framework
authors: Rong Han, Yumeng Zhang, Xiaohong Liu, Lei Fu, Tong Pan
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 27 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01243-7

Han et al. introduce UniAIR, a unified AI framework that predicts mutation effects across diverse immune recognition settings. The approach enables more generalizable modelling of antibody, antigen and T cell receptor interactions.

infographic.key_insight: UniAIR is a unified AI framework that can predict how mutations affect immune recognition across multiple settings, not just one task at a time. This makes mutation-effect prediction more generalizable across antibody, antigen, and T cell receptor interactions.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing models for mutation-effect prediction are often specialized for a single immune recognition context and do not transfer well across different adaptive immune systems. This paper addresses the need for a broader, unified model that works across diverse biological interaction types.
method: Develops a multimodal framework that integrates information from different immune recognition modalities.
Trains a single unified model to learn mutation-effect patterns across antibody, antigen, and TCR interactions.
Aims for cross-task generalization so predictions remain useful across diverse adaptive immune recognition settings.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how multimodal and unified modeling can improve transferability in complex biological prediction tasks. It also provides a template for building more generalizable models instead of maintaining separate systems for each subtype of interaction.

title: Ω-QVLA: Robust Quantization for Vision-Language-Action Models via Composite Rotation and Per-step Scaling
authors: Xinyu Wang, Mingze Li, Sicheng Lyu, Dongxiu Liu, Kaicheng Yang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify perception, reasoning, and control within a single policy, yet their multi-billion-parameter backbones and diffusion-based action heads make on-device deployment prohibitively expensive. Prior quantization efforts offer only partial solutions, compressing the LLM backbone while leaving the DiT action head at full precision, or resorting to mixed-precision schemes, driven by the belief that uniformly quantizing the action head is inherently unstable. We c

infographic.key_insight: Ω-QVLA shows that vision-language-action models can be quantized more aggressively than previously thought, including the diffusion-based action head, without sacrificing stability. The key idea is to combine composite rotation with per-step scaling to make uniform quantization practical for end-to-end VLA deployment.
infographic.problem_solved: This paper addresses the high memory and compute cost of large VLA models, especially when deploying on-device. It tackles the long-standing challenge that the DiT action head was considered too unstable for uniform quantization, forcing prior methods to keep it in higher precision.
method: Apply composite rotation to improve the quantizability of the model’s representations and reduce sensitivity to low-bit precision.
Use per-step scaling to adapt quantization dynamically across diffusion steps in the action head.
Enable more uniform quantization across both the LLM backbone and the diffusion-based action module, instead of relying on mixed-precision workarounds.
infographic.impact: For practitioners, this means lower deployment cost, smaller memory footprint, and better feasibility for real-time or edge VLA systems. It also broadens the path toward fully quantized multimodal control policies rather than only compressing the language backbone.

title: Affective Music Recommendation: A Rollout-Based World Model for Offline Preference Optimization
authors: Audrey Chan, Aaron Labbé, Jacob Lavoie, Jordan Bannister, Arsène Fansi Tchango
abstract: Functional music applications, from consumer focus and sleep aids to clinical interventions, share a distinctive recommendation problem: success is defined by the listener's affective state, but online experimentation on emotion is ethically constrained, particularly for clinical populations who cannot reliably skip a song or report distress. We describe AMRS, the Affective Music Recommendation System deployed on LUCID's health-and-wellness platforms, which serve clinical users (primarily older

infographic.key_insight: A rollout-based world model lets you optimize music recommendations for listeners' emotional states using only offline data, enabling safe policy improvement without risky live experiments on vulnerable clinical users.
infographic.problem_solved: How to learn and deploy music recommendation policies that reliably shape affective outcomes when online experimentation is ethically or practically impossible (e.g., clinical populations who cannot easily skip tracks or report distress).
method: Learn a predictive world model of user affect from offline listening and passive/clinical signals.
Perform rollout-based policy evaluation and optimization inside the learned model to search for preference-aware, affective policies offline.
Integrate safety constraints and affect-preference objectives to avoid distressing recommendations while maximizing therapeutic or wellness outcomes.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build and validate affect-aware recommender policies in sensitive domains using model-based offline optimization, bridging recommender systems, offline RL, and health-safe AI. This approach reduces ethical risk and accelerates deployment in real-world clinical settings.

title: HarmoVid: Relightful Video Portrait Harmonization
authors: Jun Myeong Choi, Jae Shin Yoon, Luchao Qi, Roni Sengupta, Joon-Young Lee
abstract: We present a method for harmonizing the lighting of a foreground video to match a target background scene, adjusting shadows, color tone, and illumination intensity (relightful harmonization). Unlike images, acquiring labeled data for videos, where identical motions are recorded under different lighting conditions, is practically infeasible and non-scalable. While one way to create such paired data is to apply existing image-based harmonization models frame by frame to a video, the resulting out

infographic.key_insight: HarmoVid enables realistic, temporally consistent relighting of foreground portrait videos so the subject’s lighting (shadows, color tone, intensity) matches a target background—without needing real paired video data under different illuminations.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between image-based harmonization and video: produces relightful harmonization for portrait videos while maintaining temporal consistency, despite the lack of scalable paired video training data.
method: Create scalable training supervision by leveraging image-based relighting/harmonization to synthesize pseudo-paired data and augment it for video scenarios.

Train a relightful harmonization network that predicts illumination adjustments (color tone, intensity) and shadow/soft-shadow corrections for the foreground while conditioning on the target background.
Enforce temporal consistency with motion-aware constraints and video-aware modules (e.g., temporal loss, flow/recurrent components or frame aggregation) so outputs are stable across frames.
infographic.impact: Makes practical, high-quality relighting and lighting-consistent compositing possible for portrait video editing and film/VFX workflows, enabling seamless foreground-background integration without expensive capture setups or frame-by-frame manual correction.

title: MUSE-Autoskill: Self-Evolving Agents via Skill Creation, Memory, Management, and Evaluation
authors: Huawei Lin, Peng Li, Jie Song, Fuxin Jiang, Tieying Zhang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on reusable skills to solve complex tasks. However, existing skill creation approaches treat skills as isolated and static artifacts, limiting their reusability, reliability, and long-term improvement. We propose MUSE-Autoskill Agent (Memory-Utilizing Skill Evolution), a skill-centric agent framework that lets agents continuously improve their task-solving capability by creating, reusing, and refining skills under a unified lifecycle (creation, memory, mana

infographic.key_insight: MUSE-Autoskill introduces a unified, memory-aware skill lifecycle (creation, memory, management, evaluation) that lets LLM agents continuously create, reuse, and refine modular skills, boosting long-term task-solving capability and reliability.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing skill creation methods treat skills as static, isolated artifacts, which limits reusability, robustness, and continual improvement; this work enables persistent, evolving skills for sustained agent performance.
method: Define a unified skill lifecycle (Creation → Memory → Management → Evaluation) to govern skill birth, storage, retrieval, and refinement.
Use memory-backed mechanisms to index, retrieve, and adapt skills across tasks so agents can compose and reuse prior competencies.
Automated evaluation and feedback loop to score skill utility and trigger refinement or retirement, enabling continuous self-improvement.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical framework for building agents that scale to complex, multi-step tasks by maintaining an evolving skill library—reducing redundancy and improving generalization and robustness across domains.

title: Natural Language Query to Configuration for Retrieval Agents
authors: Melissa Z. Pan, Negar Arabzadeh, Mathew Jacob, Fiodar Kazhamiaka, Esha Choukse
abstract: Modern retrieval agents expose many configuration choices -- LLM, retriever, number of documents, number of hops, and synthesis strategy -- each shaping both answer quality and serving cost. Today, these pipelines are typically hand-tuned once per workload, leaving substantial per-query optimization untapped. We formulate the problem: given a natural-language query and either an accuracy or a budget target, select from a predefined pipeline catalog the configuration that minimizes cost or maximi

infographic.key_insight: Per-query selection of retrieval-agent configurations (LLM, retriever, docs, hops, synthesis) lets you meet an accuracy or budget target while substantially reducing cost compared to one-size-fits-all pipelines.
infographic.problem_solved: Retrieval pipelines are typically hand-tuned per workload, leaving per-query cost/accuracy trade-offs untapped — the paper automates choosing the best configuration for each query given an accuracy or budget constraint.
method: Formulate configuration selection as a per-query decision problem: given a natural-language query and a target (accuracy or budget), choose from a catalog of predefined pipeline configurations.

Estimate or learn the cost/accuracy trade-offs of catalog entries and use a lightweight selector to pick the configuration that satisfies the target while minimizing cost (or maximizing accuracy under budget).
Evaluate per-query selection against static baselines to show reduced serving cost and preserved or improved answer quality.
infographic.impact: Enables dynamic, query-level tuning of retrieval agents to cut serving costs and improve resource allocation without sacrificing accuracy — practical for production RAG systems and MLops teams.

title: SpatialBench: Is Your Spatial Foundation Model an All-Round Player?
authors: Haosong Peng, Hao Li, Jiaqi Chen, Yuhao Pan, Runmao Yao
abstract: While spatial foundation models have demonstrated impressive performance on standard datasets, a critical question remains: are they truly all-round players capable of generalizing robustly across diverse downstream tasks, arbitrary viewpoints, shifting scene domains, varying input densities, and specific hardware constraints? Answering this overarching question requires a holistic assessment, yet current models are mainly evaluated on specific domains for which they were specifically designed o

infographic.key_insight: SpatialBench provides a holistic evaluation revealing that current spatial foundation models are not universally 'all-round' — they excel in some settings but show consistent failure modes across unseen viewpoints, domain shifts, input densities, and hardware constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of a unified, comprehensive benchmark for measuring spatial foundation model generalization and robustness across diverse downstream tasks, arbitrary viewpoints, varying scene domains, input densities, and deployment hardware constraints.
method: Assemble a diverse benchmark suite spanning multiple downstream tasks (e.g., 3D perception, localization, scene understanding) with both real-world and synthetic datasets.
Introduce controlled stress tests: viewpoint and domain shifts, systematic input-density variations, and hardware/resource-constrained evaluation protocols.
Define standardized metrics and evaluation protocols to produce comparable per-model profiles and identify consistent strengths and weaknesses.
infographic.impact: Gives researchers and practitioners a practical, standardized tool to diagnose where spatial models fail, prioritize improvements, and make informed choices for deployment in real-world, resource-constrained, or cross-domain settings.

title: MobileMoE: Scaling On-Device Mixture of Experts
authors: Yanbei Chen, Hanxian Huang, Ernie Chang, Jacob Szwejbka, Digant Desai
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the de facto architecture for hundred-billion-parameter language models, yet its advantages at sub-billion scales for on-device deployment remain largely unexplored. To close this gap, we present MobileMoE, a family of on-device MoE language models with sub-billion active parameters (0.3-0.9B active and 1.3-5.3B total) that establish a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs. We first formulate an on-device MoE scaling law that jointly optimizes MoE architectur

infographic.key_insight: MobileMoE introduces an on-device MoE scaling law and a family of sub-billion active-parameter MoE models that achieve superior accuracy vs. latency/memory trade-offs, establishing a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs.
infographic.problem_solved: Current MoE architectures are optimized for very large server models and have not been tuned for strict on-device constraints (latency, memory, compute). This work addresses how to scale and configure MoE so high-capability language models can run efficiently on mobile/edge devices.
method: Formulate an on-device MoE scaling law that jointly optimizes model width, number of experts, and routing for device latency and memory budgets.
Design the MobileMoE family with 0.3–0.9B active parameters (1.3–5.3B total) to maximize performance under on-device constraints and identify Pareto-optimal points.
Apply system-aware optimizations (efficient routing, quantization-friendly layouts and runtime-aware parameter allocation) to enable practical on-device deployment.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a principled recipe to build efficient, high-quality LLMs for mobile/edge environments — enabling lower latency, better privacy, and broader offline capabilities without sacrificing model capability.

title: GENESIS: Harnessing AI Agents for Autonomous 6G RAN Synthesis, Research, and Testing
authors: Tamerlan Aghayev, Maxime Elkael, Michele Polese, Minh Dat Nguyen, Gabriele Gemmi
abstract: Cellular research and development (R&D) is throttled by six structural processes that each consume months of manual engineering work per iteration: (i) synthesizing new features from standards or research papers into production code; (ii) conformance and interoperability testing; (iii) hardening against field anomalies and diverse deployment environments; (iv) data-driven optimization of network functionalities; (v) discovering and prototyping novel waveforms, functionalities, and capabilities f

infographic.key_insight: Autonomous AI agents can orchestrate end-to-end 6G RAN research workflows—automatically synthesizing standards/papers into code, running conformance/interoperability tests, hardening, and optimizing networks—compressing months of manual engineering into fast, repeatable iterations.
infographic.problem_solved: Cellular R&D is bottlenecked by six slow, manual processes (feature synthesis from specs/papers, conformance/interoperability testing, hardening against field anomalies, data-driven optimization, discovery/prototyping of new waveforms/capabilities, and large-scale testing). The paper addresses automating and scaling these processes to speed iteration, improve reproducibility, and reduce human effort.
method: Autonomous multi-agent framework (LLM / agent orchestration) that decomposes tasks, generates and patches production-grade RAN code from specs/papers, and coordinates experiments.
Closed-loop testing and validation pipeline that integrates emulators/testbeds, automated conformance/interoperability checks, and fault-injection for hardening.
Data-driven optimization and search (e.g., AutoML/RL-style tuning) plus modular hooks into RAN stacks to prototype and evaluate new waveforms, functionalities, and deployment configurations rapidly.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners this enables much faster experiment-to-deployment cycles, reproducible benchmarking of learning-based RAN components, and an automated platform to discover and validate novel algorithms at network scale—lowering time, cost, and expertise barriers.

title: Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring
authors: Rishi Bommasani, Sarah H. Bana, Kathleen A. Creel, Dan Jurafsky, Percy Liang
abstract: Many employers screen job applicants with algorithms built by the same few algorithm vendors. We hypothesize that algorithmic monoculture leads to the same individuals and members of the same racial groups facing rejection. We acquire and analyze a novel dataset of 3 million applicants submitting 4 million applications where all the applications are screened by algorithms built by the same vendor. We find clear racial disparities in applicant outcomes. Of all applications submitted by Asian and

infographic.key_insight: When many employers rely on screening algorithms from a single vendor, outcomes become correlated and produce systematic racial disparities—certain individuals and racial groups face concentrated rejection risk.
infographic.problem_solved: Quantifies and exposes the harms of vendor-level algorithmic monoculture in hiring: how single-vendor dominance can create correlated, inequitable screening outcomes across many employers.
method: Assembled a novel dataset of ~3 million applicants and ~4 million applications all screened by the same algorithm vendor.
Performed statistical comparisons of screening outcomes by race with robustness checks (covariate controls, subgroup/intersectional analyses).
Assessed vendor-level effects via correlation analyses and counterfactual/robustness experiments to isolate monoculture-driven disparities.
infographic.impact: Shows that vendor concentration is a systemic fairness risk—practitioners should audit vendor models, diversify screening pipelines, and monitor vendor-level metrics when procuring hiring algorithms.

title: LocateAnything: Fast and High-Quality Vision-Language Grounding with Parallel Box Decoding
authors: Shihao Wang, Shilong Liu, Yuanguo Kuang, Xinyu Wei, Yangzhou Liu
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) commonly formulate visual grounding and detection as a coordinate-token generation problem, serializing each 2D box into multiple 1D tokens that are learned and decoded largely independently. This token-by-token decoding mismatches the coupled structure of box geometry and creates a practical inference bottleneck due to strictly sequential generation. We introduce LocateAnything, a unified generative grounding and detection framework based on Parallel Box Decoding (

infographic.key_insight: LocateAnything replaces token-by-token coordinate generation with Parallel Box Decoding so each 2D box is decoded as a coupled unit in parallel, eliminating the sequential generation bottleneck and better modeling box geometry. This yields faster inference and higher-quality visual grounding/detection.
infographic.problem_solved: Current VLM grounding and detection serialize boxes into independent 1D coordinate tokens and decode them sequentially, which mismatches the coupled nature of box geometry and creates a practical inference speed and quality bottleneck.
method: Parallel Box Decoding: group each bounding box's coordinates into a single jointly decoded unit instead of serializing into independent tokens, enabling parallel prediction of multiple boxes.
Unified generative grounding framework: integrate parallel box decoding into a vision–language model so language-conditioned location predictions and detection coexist in one generative pipeline.
Architecture and training adjustments: couple geometric decoding with cross-attention and task-specific losses so box geometry and language cues are learned jointly for accurate, fast localization.
infographic.impact: Makes vision-language grounding and detection substantially faster and more accurate by aligning the model's output structure with true box geometry; this improves throughput for real-time and large-scale applications and simplifies deployment of unified VLM detectors.
visual_elements: Schematic comparison: sequential token-by-token box decoding vs. parallel box decoding (showing fewer steps and grouped box outputs).

title: Guiding LLM Post-training Data Engineering with Model Internals from Sparse Autoencoders
authors: Yi Jing, Zao Dai, Jinwu Hu, Zijun Yao, Lei Hou
abstract: Model internals encode rich information about how a large language model (LLM) processes its training data; however, post-training data engineering largely relies on external signals and ignores rich intrinsic signals lying in model internals. We propose SAERL, a data engineering framework for LLM reinforcement learning (RL). It models three intrinsic data properties: diversity, difficulty, and quality, using model internals extracted with Sparse Autoencoder (SAE), an advanced mechanistic interp

infographic.key_insight: Model internals extracted via a Sparse Autoencoder can quantify intrinsic data properties (diversity, difficulty, quality) and be used to guide post‑training data engineering for LLM reinforcement learning, enabling more principled selection and weighting of training data without relying on external signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Post‑training data engineering for LLMs typically depends on external annotations or heuristics and ignores rich internal signals; this limits effective data prioritization for RL fine‑tuning and reduces sample efficiency and interpretability.
method: Extract internal activation patterns from a pretrained LLM and compress them with a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to obtain compact, interpretable codes.
Derive intrinsic metrics — diversity, difficulty, and quality — directly from SAE codes and activation statistics.
Apply SAERL: use those intrinsic signals to drive data selection, reweighting, or curriculum design in RL fine‑tuning loops for LLMs.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a label‑free, interpretable approach to curate and prioritize training data for RL fine‑tuning, improving sample efficiency and enabling mechanistic insights into which examples influence model behavior.

title: Pixel-Level Pavement Distress Assessment Using Instance Segmentation
authors: Logan Dewick, Bibesh Pyakurel, Kong Pheng Yang, Nazim Choudhury, M. G. Sarwar Murshed
abstract: Automated pavement distress assessment requires more than image-level classification or coarse bounding box detection, demanding precise localization of thin, branching, and irregular cracks to achieve the geometric precision necessary for maintenance-relevant quantification. This paper presents a vision-based pavement distress analysis system based on Mask R-CNN instance segmentation and evaluates it on UWGB-StreetCrack, a custom field-collected roadway image dataset acquired with a vehicle-mou

infographic.key_insight: Using Mask R-CNN for instance-level segmentation yields pixel-accurate masks of thin, branching pavement cracks, enabling geometry-preserving measurements (length, area, connectivity) that image-level labels or bounding boxes cannot provide.
infographic.problem_solved: Automated pavement distress assessment requires precise localization of irregular, thin, and branching cracks for maintenance-relevant quantification; prior image-level or bounding-box approaches lack the geometric precision needed for accurate measurements.
method: Adapt Mask R-CNN to detect and produce instance masks for pavement distress on field-collected roadway images (UWGB-StreetCrack dataset).
Train and evaluate using pixel-level metrics (e.g., mask IoU / F-measure) and demonstrate improved geometric localization vs. box/label baselines.
Post-process masks to extract maintenance metrics (crack length, width, area, and connectivity) suitable for infrastructure decision-making.
infographic.impact: Delivers a practical computer-vision pipeline that converts raw road imagery into measurement-quality crack geometry, enabling more accurate, automated maintenance prioritization and scalable pavement monitoring for practitioners.

title: Squeezing Capacity from Multimodal Large Language Models for Subject-driven Generation
authors: Shuhong Zheng, Aashish Kumar Misraa, Yu-Teng Li, Yu-Jhe Li, Igor Gilitschenski
abstract: Subject-driven image generation aims to synthesize new images that preserve the identity of the given subject while following textual instructions. Existing approaches often encode text and reference images separately. This limits cross-modal reasoning abilities and causes copy-paste artifacts. Recent frameworks that connect multimodal models and diffusion models improve instruction following, but largely overlook identity preservation. To address these limitations, we condition diffusion models

infographic.key_insight: Leverage the representational capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to produce compact, cross-modal subject embeddings that condition diffusion-based image generation, enabling stronger identity preservation while improving instruction following and reducing copy‑paste artifacts.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing subject-driven generation pipelines treat text and reference images separately, which limits cross-modal reasoning and leads to weak identity preservation and copy‑paste artifacts when synthesizing new images of a subject under textual instructions.
method: Extract subject-aware, compact embeddings from a pretrained multimodal LLM (rather than separate image-only encoders) to capture joint visual-text semantics.
Condition a diffusion model on these MLLM-derived representations via lightweight adapters/prompting so generation respects both identity and instructions.
Train with identity-aware losses (e.g., reconstruction/contrastive constraints) and instruction alignment objectives to balance fidelity to the subject and compliance with text.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to squeeze extra cross-modal reasoning capacity from MLLMs to improve subject fidelity in generative pipelines without heavy retraining of large diffusion models; useful for avatars, personalized content, and controlled image editing.

title: Looped Diffusion Language Models
authors: Sanghyun Lee, Chunsan Hong, Seungryong Kim, Jonghyun Lee, Jongho Park
abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models for language modeling, yet the effective design of transformer architectures for MDMs remains underexplored. In this paper, we show that selectively looping the early-middle transformer layers significantly improves both training efficiency and model performance in MDMs. We call this approach LoopMDM(Looped Masked Diffusion Model), which brings two key benefits: looping layers at training-time yields

infographic.key_insight: Applying a selective "looping" (repeated reuse) of early-to-middle transformer layers during training for masked diffusion language models (LoopMDM) yields substantial gains in training efficiency and generation quality compared to standard MDM architectures.
infographic.problem_solved: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) offer an alternative to autoregressive LMs but lack efficient, well‑designed transformer architectures; training MDMs is compute‑heavy and architectural choices for them are underexplored.
method: Selectively loop (repeatedly apply) early-middle transformer layers during training so the same layer weights process multiple denoising steps, reducing effective model size and compute.
Keep higher layers unlooped to preserve representational capacity and combine looping with the MDM denoising schedule for stable convergence.
Integrate looping into the standard MDM training pipeline to improve throughput and empirical performance without major changes to optimization or loss functions.
infographic.impact: LoopMDM reduces compute and memory cost while improving convergence and output quality, making masked diffusion language models more practical to train and scale for researchers and practitioners.

Bar chart comparing training FLOPs/throughput and validation quality (e.g., perplexity or F1) for baseline MDM vs LoopMDM.

title: Forgetting in Language Models: Capacity, Optimization, and Self-Generated Replay
authors: Martin Marek, Dongkyu Cho, Shikai Qiu, Rumi Chunara, Pavel Izmailov
abstract: Models trained on a new task typically degrade on prior tasks, a phenomenon known as forgetting. Traditionally, mitigating forgetting has required replaying stored exemplars from prior tasks, which is often impractical. By contrast, language models can sample from their own training distribution, and we show that these self-generated samples serve as effective replay data, nearly eliminating forgetting. We find that forgetting nonetheless persists when the model has little remaining capacity: mo

infographic.key_insight: Language models can use self-generated samples from their own training distribution as replay data to nearly eliminate catastrophic forgetting; residual forgetting occurs primarily when model capacity or optimization constraints are insufficient.
infographic.problem_solved: Reducing catastrophic forgetting in continual learning for language models without requiring storage or access to original training exemplars.
method: Let the model sample (self-generate) prior-task examples from its own learned distribution and use those samples as replay data during new-task training.
Mix self-generated replay with new-task training (controlled sampling/temperature and weighting) to preserve prior-task performance while learning new tasks.
Empirically analyze when self-replay succeeds or fails by varying model capacity and optimization settings (scaling, ablations, retention metrics).
infographic.impact: Enables practical, privacy-friendly continual learning for language models by removing the need to store past data; highlights that sufficient model capacity and proper optimization remain critical to fully prevent forgetting.

Pipeline diagram: model → self-generate samples → mix with new-task data → update model (replay loop)

Heatmap or table of ablation results showing impact of optimization settings (learning rate, replay ratio, temperature) on forgetting

title: AnyScene: Towards Highly Controllable Driving Scene Generation at Anywhere and Beyond
authors: Haiming Zhang, Junfei Zhou, Feng Jiang, Jingzhong Li, Zhenglong Guo
abstract: Generating high-fidelity and controllable synthetic data is critical for advancing end-to-end autonomous driving, particularly for addressing the long tail of rare safety-critical scenarios. Existing occupancy-guided methods typically rely on shallow conditioning mechanisms and reference-frame-dependent video synthesis, which limits fine-grained controllability from arbitrary BEV layouts and restricts their applicability for scalable simulation. In this paper, we propose AnyScene, a unified occu

infographic.key_insight: AnyScene introduces a unified occupancy-guided generation framework that enables highly controllable, high-fidelity driving-scene synthesis from arbitrary BEV (bird’s-eye-view) layouts and without reliance on a specific reference video frame, unlocking flexible scenario creation anywhere.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing occupancy-guided scene generators use shallow conditioning and reference-frame-dependent synthesis, which prevents fine-grained control from arbitrary BEV plans and limits scalability for simulating rare or safety-critical driving scenarios.
method: Unified occupancy-conditioned pipeline that decouples scene layout (BEV) from reference-frame constraints, enabling synthesis from arbitrary BEV inputs.
Deeper conditioning mechanisms (e.g., richer cross-modal conditioning across occupancy, semantics and camera views) to achieve fine-grained control over objects, motion, and layout.
Reference-frame-independent temporal synthesis and consistency strategies to produce scalable, multi-frame driving scenes suitable for simulation and data augmentation.
infographic.impact: AnyScene makes it practical to generate diverse, controllable synthetic driving data for training and testing autonomous driving systems—helping address long-tail, safety-critical scenarios and accelerating robust model development and evaluation.

title: Helix4D: Complex 4D Mesh Generation
authors: Jiraphon Yenphraphai, Jianqi Chen, Jian Wang, Gordon Qian, Sergey Tulyakov
abstract: Current video-to-4D methods struggle with complex topology changes, transparent materials, thin structures, and inner surfaces. We present Helix4D, a dynamic mesh generation framework by inheriting the expressive representation of Trellis2, adapting it from image-to-3D to video-conditioned 4D generation. Our design arises from two key questions: (a) how to enable Trellis2's frame-local attention to share information across frames while preserving its pretrained quality on rare cases such as tran

infographic.key_insight: Helix4D adapts the expressive Trellis2 image-to-3D representation to video-conditioned 4D mesh generation by enabling cross-frame information sharing while preserving Trellis2's pretrained strengths, enabling robust reconstruction of complex topology, transparent materials, thin structures, and inner surfaces.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video-to-4D methods fail on challenging phenomena (topology changes, transparency, thin geometry, inner surfaces) and lack temporally consistent dynamic meshes; Helix4D addresses these gaps to produce high-fidelity, time-consistent 4D meshes from video.
method: Extend Trellis2's frame-local attention with temporal cross-frame attention/aggregation so frames share information without degrading pretrained rare-case performance.

Produce a dynamic 4D mesh pipeline that updates topology and geometry over time (motion-aware mesh updates, handling birth/death of elements) to capture transparency, thin structures, and inner surfaces.

Train/finetune using a mix of pretrained weights and video supervision (temporal consistency losses and targeted augmentations) to retain expressiveness on rare cases while learning cross-frame coherence.
infographic.impact: Helix4D enables practitioners to convert video into temporally coherent, high-detail dynamic meshes that handle previously intractable visuals—useful for animation, AR/VR, simulation, and digital content creation workflows.
visual_elements: Side-by-side before/after: frames reconstructed with prior video-to-4D vs Helix4D highlighting thin structures and transparency improvements.

title: Reinforcing Few-step Generators via Reward-Tilted Distribution Matching
authors: Yushi Huang, Xiangxin Zhou, Ruoyu Wang, Chi Zhang, Jun Zhang
abstract: Recent advances in few-step diffusion distillation have enabled efficient image generation, yet aligning these models with human preferences remains challenging. We propose Reward-Tilted Distribution Matching Distillation (RTDMD), a two-stage framework that unifies distribution matching distillation with reward-guided reinforcement learning for few-step flow generators. We show that minimizing the KL divergence to a reward-tilted teacher distribution naturally decomposes into a distribution matc

infographic.key_insight: RTDMD shows that minimizing KL to a reward-tilted teacher distribution for few-step flow generators decomposes into a distribution-matching term plus a reward-weighted correction, enabling a practical two-stage distillation + reward-guided fine-tuning pipeline that yields fast samplers aligned with preferences.
infographic.problem_solved: Aligning highly compressed/few-step generative samplers (distilled diffusion/flow models) with human preferences or external reward signals without sacrificing sample quality or speed.
method: Construct a reward-tilted teacher distribution by reweighting high-quality generative outputs with a reward model or preference signal.
Stage 1: Distribution-matching distillation — fit a few-step flow generator to the reward-tilted teacher via KL minimization (supervised distillation component).

Stage 2: Reward-guided fine-tuning — apply a reward-weighted / RL-style correction to the distilled generator to further align outputs with the reward while preserving sample fidelity and inference speed.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical recipe to produce fast, few-step generative samplers that better reflect human preferences or task rewards, improving deployability of aligned image generators with minimal inference cost.

title: EVIDENT: Routing MLLM Adaptation through Entity-Grounded Visual Evidence for Cross-Domain Video Temporal Grounding
authors: Geo Ahn, Jiwook Han, Youngrae Kim, Joonseok Lee, Jinwoo Choi
abstract: Fine-tuning MLLMs for Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) often improves in-domain performance but degrades sharply under domain shift. In this work, we find that this failure is primarily driven not just by unseen query concepts, but by visual domain shift, which prevents the model from coupling its learned temporal localization knowledge with its inherent entity-attention capability. To address this, we introduce EVIDENT, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework that anchors temporal grounding in

infographic.key_insight: Visual domain shift—not just unseen query concepts—breaks the link between an MLLM's temporal localization knowledge and its entity-attention. EVIDENT re‑anchors grounding by routing adaptation through entity‑grounded visual evidence, restoring robust cross‑domain performance with few extra parameters.
infographic.problem_solved: VTG fine‑tuning of MLLMs often yields strong in‑domain results but fails under domain shift because visual appearance changes decouple entity attention from learned temporal localization. The paper addresses how to adapt MLLMs so they maintain accurate temporal grounding across diverse visual domains while remaining parameter‑efficient.
method: Entity‑grounded evidence extraction: detect and pool entity‑conditioned visual clues from video segments to create explicit visual evidence for each query/entity.

Routing-based, parameter‑efficient adaptation: attach lightweight adapters/routers to the MLLM that conditionally modulate model behavior based on the extracted evidence (selective fine‑tuning rather than full model updates).
Alignment objectives: train with grounding/contrastive losses that tie entity attention to temporal localization so the model couples its localization skill to visual evidence despite domain shifts.
infographic.impact: Makes MLLMs for video temporal grounding reliable across different visual domains while keeping adaptation cheap and practical — enabling safer, more generalizable deployment in real‑world video applications.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: video frames → entity detector → evidence pool per segment → router/adapters → MLLM temporal grounding output
Bar chart: comparative in‑domain vs cross‑domain performance (baseline fine‑tuning vs EVIDENT)
Attention overlays: frames showing entity attention heatmaps aligned with predicted temporal spans to illustrate coupling

title: MobileGym: A Verifiable and Highly Parallel Simulation Platform for Mobile GUI Agent Research
authors: Dingbang Wu, Rui Hao, Haiyang Wang, Shuzhe Wu, Han Xiao
abstract: We present MobileGym, a browser-hosted, lightweight, fully controllable environment for everyday mobile use, targeting interaction fidelity without replicating proprietary backends. It enables two capabilities previously out of reach for everyday apps: verifiable outcome signals through deterministic state-based judging over structured JSON state, and scalable online RL through low-cost parallel rollouts. The full environment state is captured, configured, forked, and compared as structured JSON

infographic.key_insight: MobileGym provides a browser-hosted, lightweight mobile environment that captures the full app state as structured JSON, enabling deterministic, verifiable outcome signals and massively parallel low-cost rollouts for RL. This decouples interaction fidelity from proprietary backends while making rewards and evaluation reproducible.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of verifiable outcome signals and scalable, low-cost simulation for everyday mobile GUI agents, where pixel- or backend-dependent setups hinder reproducibility and large-scale RL.
method: Host lightweight mobile app simulations in the browser and capture the entire environment state as structured JSON.
Use deterministic state-based judging over the JSON state to provide verifiable outcome signals and reproducible evaluation.
Support state forking and massively parallel, low-cost rollouts to enable scalable online RL and efficient collection of trajectories.
infographic.impact: Enables reproducible benchmarking and reliable reward signals for GUI agents, dramatically lowering the cost and engineering friction for large-scale RL research on mobile apps and accelerating iteration from research to real-world interaction.

title: A large-scale unified deep learning model for peptide mass spectrum interpretation trained on multimodal data
authors: Jiale Zhao, Pengzhi Mao, Kaifei Wang, Yiming Li, Yaping Peng
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 25 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01234-8

pUniFind is a large-scale deep learning model for proteomics that unifies peptide–spectrum scoring and open de novo sequencing. Trained on over 100 million spectra, it substantially improves peptide identification and modification discovery.

infographic.key_insight: pUniFind is a unified deep learning model that can both score peptide-spectrum matches and perform open de novo sequencing. Trained on over 100 million spectra, it boosts peptide identification and helps uncover modifications more effectively than prior approaches.
infographic.problem_solved: Proteomics analysis has traditionally used separate tools for peptide-spectrum matching and de novo sequencing, making interpretation fragmented and less accurate. This paper addresses the need for a single scalable model that can interpret complex mass spectra and improve discovery of peptides and modifications.
method: Trains a large-scale deep learning model on multimodal proteomics data, including more than 100 million spectra.
Unifies peptide-spectrum scoring and open de novo sequencing within one framework.
Learns to improve both peptide identification accuracy and modification discovery from raw spectral inputs.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how scaling multimodal training data and unifying related tasks can produce stronger scientific models. It is a useful example of foundation-model-style learning applied to biological interpretation workflows.
