title: On-Policy Adversarial Flow Distillation for Autoregressive Video Generation
authors: Yang Luo, Shengju Qian, Xiaohang Tang, Zirui Zhu, Yong Liu
abstract: Autoregressive video generators are attractive for streaming, long-horizon, and interactive applications, but distilling strong black-box teachers into causal students remains difficult. The student must learn under its own rollout distribution, whereas practical teachers may expose only prompt-conditioned completed videos and may differ in architecture, capacity, temporal design, and sampling schedule. This interface makes supervised fine-tuning off-policy, score-based distillation inapplicable

infographic.key_insight: Introduce on-policy adversarial flow distillation: train causal autoregressive student video models from black-box, prompt-conditioned teacher videos by matching the student's rollout transition flows to the teacher via an adversarial objective, avoiding the need for teacher scores or internals.
infographic.problem_solved: Distills high-quality autoregressive video teachers into causal students despite distribution mismatch (student rollouts vs teacher outputs), heterogeneous teacher architectures/schedules, and limited access to only completed, prompt-conditioned videos.
method: On-policy rollouts: let the causal student generate trajectories under its own sampling distribution to form training data that matches deployment conditions.

Adversarial flow matching: use an adversarial objective to align the transition "flow" (conditional next-frame/latent dynamics) between student rollouts and teacher-provided completed videos without requiring teacher scores or architecture access.
Prompt-conditioned supervision: condition the adversarial discriminator/matcher on prompts so the student learns to reproduce teacher-conditioned behaviors from final videos alone.
infographic.impact: Enables practical distillation of opaque, high-performing video generators into lightweight causal models suitable for streaming, long-horizon, and interactive use cases. Reduces dependency on teacher internals or score-based signals, making distillation feasible in real-world deployment scenarios.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: black-box teacher (completed videos only) feeding adversarial flow matcher and causal student producing on-policy rollouts (looped arrows to show self-generated distribution).
Timeline comparison: off-policy (teacher outputs) vs on-policy (student rollouts) highlighting distribution mismatch and where learning occurs.
Flow-field visualization: example transition flow vectors or attention maps showing alignment between student and teacher dynamics.

title: TriSplat: Simulation-Ready Feed-Forward 3D Scene Reconstruction
authors: Weijie Wang, Zimu Li, Jinchuan Shi, Zeyu Zhang, Botao Ye
abstract: Sparse-view 3D reconstruction is increasingly addressed with feed-forward splatting networks that predict explicit primitives directly from images. Yet most existing methods remain centered on Gaussian primitives and expose surfaces only indirectly: extracting a usable mesh for downstream simulation, physics reasoning, or embodied interaction still requires expensive post-hoc steps that break the feed-forward promise. This limitation is especially pronounced in pose-free settings, where scene st

infographic.key_insight: TriSplat replaces indirect Gaussian splats with learned triangular surface primitives so a single feed‑forward pass from sparse views produces explicit, simulation‑ready meshes without expensive post‑hoc meshing.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing feed‑forward splatting methods expose surfaces only indirectly (often as Gaussians), forcing costly post‑processing to get usable meshes for simulation or embodied interaction—worse in pose‑free, sparse‑view scenarios. TriSplat removes that bottleneck by predicting primitives that assemble into ready‑to‑use geometry.
method: Predict explicit triangular surface primitives ("tri‑splats") directly from sparse input images in a single feed‑forward network.
Aggregate and rasterize tri‑splats with a differentiable splatting/assembly step to form coherent, connected surfaces and per‑triangle attributes.

Train with multi‑term losses (image reprojection, geometric consistency, and simulation‑aware criteria such as watertightness and stable contact) to produce downstream‑ready meshes without optimization or meshing post‑processing.
infographic.impact: TriSplat streamlines pipelines that need accurate, simulation‑ready 3D scenes (robotics, physics engines, embodied AI) by removing expensive mesh reconstruction steps—enabling faster end‑to‑end perception-to-simulation workflows from sparse, pose‑free inputs.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: sparse input images → TriSplat network → tri‑splats → assembled mesh (single pass).
Before/after comparison: Gaussian splats requiring meshing vs TriSplat producing a watertight mesh ready for simulation.
Simulation snapshot: reconstructed scene used in a physics engine (collision/contact) to illustrate downstream readiness.
Chart: runtime and end‑task (e.g., collision/physics) performance vs prior methods, highlighting removal of post‑processing cost.

title: Channel-wise Vector Quantization
authors: Wei Song, Tianhang Wang, Yitong Chen, Tong Zhang, Zuxuan Wu
abstract: We present Channel-wise Vector Quantization (CVQ), a novel image tokenization paradigm that replaces patch-wise tokens with channel-wise tokens. Unlike conventional vector quantization, which assigns a discrete token to each patch feature vector, CVQ quantizes each channel of the feature map. This formulation represents an image as discrete levels of visual details, rather than as a grid of spatial patches. Based on CVQ, we introduce a new visual autoregressive framework with "next-channel predi

infographic.key_insight: Instead of assigning discrete tokens to spatial patches, Channel-wise Vector Quantization (CVQ) quantizes each feature-map channel, turning an image into discrete levels of visual detail and enabling autoregressive "next-channel" prediction.
infographic.problem_solved: Patch-wise tokenization is spatially coarse and can blur fine-grained visual detail; CVQ addresses this by providing a channel-level discrete representation that better captures per-feature detail and supports new autoregressive modeling schemes.
method: Channel-wise quantization: apply vector quantization independently to each channel of a feature map, producing channel-level discrete codes.
Reframe tokenization: represent images as sequences of channel tokens (discrete levels of visual detail) rather than a grid of patch tokens.
Autoregressive modeling: build a visual autoregressive framework that predicts the next channel token (next-channel prediction) to generate or compress images.
infographic.impact: CVQ offers a finer-grained, semantically meaningful tokenization that can improve generative modeling, compression, and representation learning workflows by enabling channel-wise autoregressive strategies and potentially more compact or informative tokens.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram comparing patch-wise tokenization (patch grid → tokens) vs. channel-wise tokenization (per-channel quantization → token levels).
Pipeline flowchart: image → backbone features → CVQ (per-channel codebook lookup) → channel-token sequence → autoregressive next-channel predictor.
Per-channel visualization: a set of channel heatmaps before and after quantization to show discrete levels of detail.
Sequence diagram illustrating next-channel prediction steps during autoregressive generation/compression.

title: InstructSAM: Segment Any Instance with Any Instructions
authors: Yuqian Yuan, Wentong Li, Zhaocheng Li, Yutong Lin, Juncheng Li
abstract: In this paper, we introduce InstructSAM, a unified and streamlined framework designed for multi-instance segmentation under arbitrary instructions. We formulates instruction-driven instance segmentation as a set-structured query prediction problem and propose an explicit reasoning-to-instance query interface that elegantly bridges a vision-language model (VLM) and SAM3. Specifically, a bank of learnable instance queries is injected into the VLM and contextualized with instruction and visual info

infographic.key_insight: InstructSAM turns instruction-driven multi-instance segmentation into a set-structured query prediction task, using a learnable bank of instance queries to explicitly connect a vision-language model (VLM) to SAM3 so any natural instruction yields precise instance masks.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between high-level multimodal instructions and per-instance segmentation, enabling robust multi-instance mask prediction from arbitrary text or multimodal prompts without ad-hoc post-processing.
method: Formulate instruction-driven instance segmentation as set-structured query prediction where each query corresponds to one instance.
Inject a learnable bank of instance queries into the VLM and contextualize them with instruction and visual features (reasoning-to-instance query interface).
Pass contextualized instance queries to SAM3 to produce per-instance masks and associated outputs in a unified pipeline.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable, modular way to combine multimodal reasoning and high-quality segmentation, simplifying building of interactive vision systems (e.g., visual assistants, image editing, robotics) that follow arbitrary instructions.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: VLM + learnable instance query bank → reasoning-to-instance interface → SAM3 → per-instance masks
Before/after example: image with natural-language instruction and resulting multiple colored instance masks
Query visualization: bank of queries being contextualized by instruction and image features (attention map style)
Performance/ablation chart: effect of query bank size and interface design on mask quality and instruction-following accuracy

title: GenRecon: Bridging Generative Priors for Multi-View 3D Scene Reconstruction
authors: Katharina Schmid, Nicolas von Lützow, Jozef Hladký, Angela Dai, Matthias Nießner
abstract: We introduce a new approach to high-fidelity 3D scene reconstruction from multi-view RGB images that tightly couples reconstruction with a strong generative 3D prior. We cast scene reconstruction as conditional 3D generation over a set of spatially-localized, overlapping chunks that together tile the scene, scaling generation to large scene extents. Crucially, we inherit the fidelity and completeness of state-of-the-art generative shape models -- we use Trellis.2 as an example -- which we genera

infographic.key_insight: Tightly coupling multi-view reconstruction with a strong generative 3D prior and performing conditional generation on overlapping, spatially-localized chunks yields high-fidelity, complete 3D scene reconstructions that scale to large environments.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses incomplete, noisy, or low-detail multi-view 3D reconstruction and the difficulty of scaling high-quality generative priors to large scenes while preserving local detail and global consistency.
method: Tile the scene into spatially-localized, overlapping chunks that together cover the scene extent.
Condition a state-of-the-art generative 3D model (e.g., Trellis.2) on multi-view RGB evidence to generate each chunk with high fidelity and completeness.
Merge and reconcile overlapping chunks to produce a coherent global reconstruction with preserved fine detail and reduced artifacts.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to leverage powerful generative priors for practical, large-scale multi-view reconstruction pipelines, improving completeness and detail for applications like AR/VR, robotics, and digital twins with fewer views or noisy inputs.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: multi-view RGB inputs → chunk tiling → conditional generative model → overlap merging
Illustration of tiled, overlapping chunks on a scene volume with arrows showing per-chunk generation

title: Complete-muE: Optimal Hyperparameter Transfer and Scaling for MoE Models
authors: Hongwu Peng, Ohiremen Dibua, Yuanjun Xiong, Yifan Gong, Jianming Zhang
abstract: We propose Complete-muE, a framework which targets hyperparameter transfer across dense FFN and any Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) setups in transformer blocks. Existing tools such as $μ$P (requires fixed architectue) or SDE (requires fixed per-step token count) cannot directly solve the hyperparameter transfer problem in MoE setups because Dense to MoE transfer or MoE total experts scaling changes both architecture and tokens per expert. Complete-muE solves this challenge with a two-bridge system: Br

infographic.key_insight: Complete-muE provides a principled two-bridge parametrization that enables reliable hyperparameter transfer and optimal scaling between dense FFN and any Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformer setups, handling both architecture changes and per-expert token load.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing transfer tools (e.g., μP, SDE) assume fixed architecture or fixed per-step token counts and therefore fail when moving between dense and MoE models or when changing total experts; Complete-muE solves hyperparameter transfer when both the model architecture and tokens-per-expert change.
method: Two-bridge system: an Architecture Bridge that maps dense-FFN parameterizations to MoE-aware parameterizations, and a Token-Expert Bridge that accounts for changes in per-expert token load when scaling expert count.

Derive scaling and transfer rules that preserve training dynamics across dense↔MoE transitions, producing actionable hyperparameter prescriptions (learning rate, initialization scale, etc.) for any expert-count or token-per-expert regime.
Validate empirically across transformer blocks and MoE configurations to show stable transfer and improved scaling efficiency vs. naive or prior-parametrization approaches.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to reuse hyperparameters from dense models when moving to or scaling MoE architectures, dramatically reducing costly hyperparameter search and making large-scale MoE training more predictable and efficient.
visual_elements: Two-bridge diagram: show Architecture Bridge and Token-Expert Bridge connecting a dense FFN block to an MoE block with arrows indicating mapped hyperparameters.

title: LaMo: Self-Supervised Latent Motion Priors for Physical Realism in Video Generation
authors: Bo Jiang, Depu Meng, Yihan Hu, Yichen Xie, Tianshuo Xu
abstract: Modern video generators produce visually compelling clips but still struggle with physical and motion consistency, limiting their use as reliable world simulators. Existing remedies often rely on external simulators, teacher models, or curated physics-focused data. We explore a complementary self-supervised direction: extracting motion cues from the unlabeled videos already used to train video diffusion models. We propose LaMo, which formulates a latent motion prior over frame-to-frame latent ch

infographic.key_insight: Learning a self-supervised prior over frame-to-frame latent motion extracted from the same unlabeled videos used to train generators can strongly improve physical and motion consistency in video diffusion models without relying on simulators or curated physics data.
infographic.problem_solved: Modern video generators produce realistic frames but often fail to maintain physically plausible, temporally consistent motion across frames; this work addresses motion realism and physical consistency in generated video.
method: Extract frame-to-frame motion cues in latent space from unlabeled videos and train a motion prior self-supervisedly.
Formulate the prior as a latent motion model that regularizes or conditions the video diffusion/generation process to favor physically consistent transitions.
Integrate the learned latent motion prior into training/sampling to reduce unrealistic dynamics without external simulators or teacher models.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable, data-efficient way to improve motion realism in video generation, making generative models more reliable for simulation, planning, and downstream tasks that require physically consistent dynamics.

title: SPACENUM: Revisiting Spatial Numerical Understanding in VLMs
authors: Jianshu Zhang, Yijiang Li, Huifeixin Chen, Haoran Lu, Letian Xue
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in embodied environments, where they need produce numerical outputs such as action magnitudes and spatial coordinates. Although these numbers appear meaningful, it remains unclear whether these numerical outputs are genuinely grounded in spatial perception. Therefore, in this work, we revisit spatial numerical understanding through SpaceNum, a unified framework that captures two complementary settings: numbers as dynamic transitions during

infographic.key_insight: SpaceNum shows that numeric outputs from Vision–Language Models are not reliably grounded in spatial perception: many VLMs produce plausible-looking numbers (e.g., distances, coordinates, magnitudes) without true spatial understanding. By evaluating numbers as both dynamic transitions and static coordinates, SpaceNum exposes systematic gaps in spatial numerical grounding.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies whether and how VLM-generated numbers (action magnitudes, spatial coordinates) reflect genuine spatial perception rather than learned token patterns, providing a unified benchmark to evaluate spatial numerical grounding in embodied and vision-language settings.
method: Define two complementary task families: numbers-as-dynamic-transitions (e.g., action magnitudes, step-wise displacements) and numbers-as-static-coordinates (e.g., absolute/relative positions).
Construct a controllable dataset and evaluation protocol (synthetic + real images, paired ground-truth numeric labels) to probe numeric grounding across scales and contexts.
Apply standardized metrics and systematic ablations to evaluate popular VLMs, isolating failure modes (scale sensitivity, context leaks, token bias) and comparing model behaviors.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical benchmark to diagnose and improve numeric/spatial reliability in VLMs for robotics, navigation, and embodied agents; informs dataset design, model calibration, and evaluation practices to ensure numeric outputs are spatially grounded.

title: From Raw Experience to Skill Consumption: A Systematic Study of Model-Generated Agent Skills
authors: Zisu Huang, Jingwen Xu, Yifan Yang, Ziyang Gong, Qihao Yang
abstract: Language agents increasingly improve by reusing \emph{skills} -- structured procedural artifacts distilled from past experience. In particular, \emph{domain-level} and \emph{model-generated} skills are especially promising. They offer fast adaptation within a domain by encoding domain-specific recurring procedures, and they scale beyond labor-intensive hand-crafting. However, while extraction methods continue to proliferate, understanding remains limited, with no comprehensive study spanning the

infographic.key_insight: Model-generated, domain-level skills can be systematically extracted from raw agent experience and meaningfully reused by downstream agents; the paper identifies which extraction and consumption design choices most affect utility and transferability.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of a comprehensive, empirical understanding of how to turn raw agent trajectories into reusable, domain-level skills and how different extraction/consumption pipelines impact downstream performance and efficiency.
method: Assemble large-scale agent experience across multiple domains and tasks to serve as raw data for skill mining.

Apply and compare multiple model-driven extraction techniques (e.g., clustering of traces, prompt-based summarization, procedural distillation) and organize outputs into structured, domain-level skill artifacts.
Evaluate skill consumption by integrating mined skills into agents and measuring downstream gains on efficiency, generalization, and composability across domains.
infographic.impact: Provides practical guidance and empirical evidence for building scalable skill libraries that reduce manual engineering and speed domain adaptation for language agents; helps practitioners choose extraction and consumption strategies that maximize reuse and transfer.

title: From Activation to Causality: Discovery of Causal Visual Representations in the Human Brain
authors: Yuval Golbari, Navve Wasserman, Matias Cosarinsky, Roman Beliy, Aude Oliva
abstract: Identifying which brain regions represent a visual concept in the human brain is a central challenge in neuroscience. Existing approaches have localized coarse functional regions (e.g., faces, places) through activation maximization, identifying regions that activate strongly for a target concept relative to other concepts. Yet strong activation alone does not establish that a region represents the concept itself, as responses may instead be driven by correlated visual or semantic cues. We intro

infographic.key_insight: Going beyond activation strength, the paper identifies which brain regions genuinely represent a visual concept by using interventions and counterfactual stimuli to test causal effects on neural responses.
infographic.problem_solved: Activation-based localization can be confounded by correlated visual or semantic cues; this work separates mere correlation from causal representation in the human visual brain.
method: Use activation-maximization to nominate candidate concept-selective regions from brain imaging data.
Generate controlled or counterfactual visual interventions (e.g., targeted edits or synthetic stimuli) that manipulate the target concept while holding correlated cues constant.

Apply causal tests / statistical causal discovery on region responses to determine whether manipulating the concept changes neural activity (evidence of representation) versus responses driven by confounds.
infographic.impact: Enables more rigorous mapping between visual concepts and brain regions, improving interpretability and evaluation of neural representations; informs AI models and attribution methods by providing a causal benchmark for what it means to 'represent' a concept.

title: Geo-Align: Video Generation Alignment via Metric Geometry Reward
authors: Zizun Li, Haoyu Guo, Runzhe Teng, Chunhua Shen, Tong He
abstract: Camera-controlled video generation has achieved remarkable progress in recent years. However, existing video-to-video re-rendering methods primarily rely on Supervised Fine-Tuning using synthetic datasets. At present, there is an extreme scarcity of synchronized, multi-view real-world video data. Consequently, the prevailing paradigm often exhibits limited generalization when processing out-of-distribution real-world videos, with models struggling to accurately adhere to physical scales and came

infographic.key_insight: Geo-Align uses a metric-geometry-based reward to align generated videos to real-world camera motion and physical scale, enabling accurate camera-controlled re-rendering without requiring synchronized multi-view training data.
infographic.problem_solved: Current video-to-video re-rendering relies on supervised fine-tuning with synthetic multi-view datasets, which are scarce for real-world scenes; as a result, models generalize poorly to out-of-distribution videos and fail to respect true camera motion and scale.
method: Define a geometry-aware reward that measures alignment between generated frames and real-world geometric cues (e.g., relative camera motion, scale consistency, and structure implied by depth/flow/SfM estimates).

Use the metric-geometry reward to guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning or policy gradients) of an existing video generation model, removing dependence on paired/synchronized multi-view data.
Leverage monocular geometric signals (optical flow, inferred depth or SfM poses) from real videos as weak supervision for camera and scale alignment during training.
infographic.impact: By providing a self-supervised, geometry-driven training signal, Geo-Align improves realism and physical correctness of camera-controlled video generation, reducing reliance on synthetic datasets and improving robustness on real-world inputs—beneficial for AR/VR, robotics, and content creation workflows.

title: LLMs as Noisy Channels: A Shannon Perspective on Model Capacity and Scaling Laws
authors: Xu Ouyang, Deyi Liu, Yuhang Cai, Jing Liu, Yuan Yang
abstract:
Existing scaling laws for Large Language Models (LLMs), predominantly monotonic power laws, fail to explain emerging non-monotonic phenomena such as catastrophic overtraining and quantization-induced degradation, where performance deteriorates despite increased compute.
  We propose the Shannon Scaling Law, a unified theoretical framework that models LLM training as information transmission over a noisy channel, grounded in the Shannon-Hartley theorem. By mapping model parameters to channel band

infographic.key_insight: Training LLMs can be viewed as transmitting information over a noisy channel: model size, data, and compute set the channel bandwidth and noise, producing a Shannon-style scaling law that explains both monotonic gains and observed non‑monotonic failures (e.g., catastrophic overtraining, quantization loss).
infographic.problem_solved: Existing monotonic power-law scaling laws cannot explain emergent non‑monotonic phenomena—situations where more compute or parameters worsen performance. This framework explains when and why performance degrades despite increased resources.
method: Map model parameters, data, and optimization to a noisy communication channel and interpret effective capacity using the Shannon–Hartley theorem.
Introduce noise terms (training noise, quantization noise, optimization error) into capacity formulas to derive a unified Shannon Scaling Law that predicts performance vs. compute and size.
Validate theory with empirical curves and use the capacity-based view to identify optimal compute/model regimes and thresholds where overtraining or quantization cause degradation.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled, predictive tool for choosing model size, compute budget, and quantization/regularization strategies, helping practitioners avoid counterintuitive performance drops and allocate resources more efficiently.
visual_elements: Schematic: LLM training as a noisy channel — encoder (data + model), noisy channel (optimization + quantization noise), decoder (task performance).

title: SkillOpt: Executive Strategy for Self-Evolving Agent Skills
authors: Yifan Yang, Ziyang Gong, Weiquan Huang, Qihao Yang, Ziwei Zhou
abstract: Agent skills today are hand-crafted, generated one-shot, or evolved through loosely controlled self-revision, none of which behaves like a deep-learning optimizer for the skill, and none of which reliably improves over its starting point under feedback. We argue the skill should instead be trained as the external state of a frozen agent, with the same discipline that makes weight-space optimization reproducible. SkillOpt is, to our knowledge, the first systematic controllable text-space optimize

infographic.key_insight: Train an agent's skill as an external, optimizable text-state while keeping the base agent frozen, enabling systematic, optimizer-like improvement of skills under feedback.
infographic.problem_solved: Current skills are hand-crafted, generated one-shot, or undergo loosely controlled self-revision, which fails to reliably or reproducibly improve agent behavior; SkillOpt provides a disciplined text-space optimization framework that reliably improves skills.
method: Treat skills as external text/state separate from the frozen agent model, making skills the optimization target rather than model weights.
Run an iterative, controllable optimization loop: propose skill edits, evaluate with reproducible metrics, and accept updates under explicit update rules/constraints.
Maintain reproducibility and control by logging changes, using deterministic selection/evaluation criteria, and constraining updates to preserve safety and interpretability.
infographic.impact: Makes skill development for agents systematic and reproducible, allowing practitioners to reliably improve, version, and integrate agent behaviors into production workflows with optimizer-like guarantees.

title: HorizonStream: Long-Horizon Attention for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
authors: Chong Cheng, Peilin Tao, Nanjie Yao, Guanzhi Ding, Xianda Chen
abstract: Online 3D reconstruction requires estimating camera pose and scene geometry under strict causal and bounded-memory constraints. Existing methods often suffer from drift, jitter, or collapse on long sequences. We trace these failures to a fundamental mismatch. Streaming geometry is inherently temporally heterogeneous, with evidence ranging from short-lived correspondences to persistent global scale. However, current architectures impose uniform and pathological influence patterns. For example, sl

infographic.key_insight: HorizonStream introduces a horizon-aware attention mechanism that adapts influence over time, letting a streaming 3D reconstruction model preserve short-lived correspondences while maintaining persistent global structure under strict causal and bounded-memory constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: Mitigates drift, jitter and collapse in online (streaming) 3D reconstruction by addressing the mismatch between uniform attention patterns and the inherently temporally heterogeneous evidence in long sequences.
method: Horizon-aware attention: allocate attention strength by temporal ‘horizons’ so recent, mid-range, and long-range evidence get different, learned influence patterns.
Streaming architecture with bounded memory: maintain a compact memory bank and causal update rules to support long-horizon reasoning without unbounded storage.
Efficient implementation: multi-scale temporal windows and lightweight aggregation to keep per-frame compute and latency low for real-time use.
infographic.impact: Enables more stable, drift-resistant online mapping and pose estimation for robotics, AR/VR, and autonomous systems, improving reliability on long deployments while respecting latency and memory limits.

title: ETCHR: Editing To Clarify and Harness Reasoning
authors: Beichen Zhang, Yuhong Liu, Jinsong Li, Yuhang Zang, Jiaqi Wang
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have advanced visual reasoning, yet a purely textual chain of thought remains a bottleneck for questions that require fine-grained focus or view transformations. The ''think with images'' paradigm narrows this gap, but existing approaches are either constrained by fixed predefined toolkits or produce noisy intermediate images from unified multimodal methods. We pursue a third option: using a dedicated image editing model and decouple it with an understanding mode

infographic.key_insight: Decouple reasoning (understanding) from image generation by using a dedicated image-editing model guided by the model's intermediate reasoning, so that targeted, iterative edits clarify visual context and produce cleaner, more useful visual chain-of-thoughts.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses limitations of textual-only chains of thought and noisy or inflexible 'think with images' methods by providing a modular way to generate clear, interpretable intermediate images that support fine-grained focus and view transformations.
method: Separate modules: a multimodal understanding/ reasoning mode produces explicit editing instructions, and a specialized image-editing model executes targeted visual changes.
Iterative edit-and-reason loop: produce intermediate reasoning steps, translate them into concrete edits (focus, crop, viewpoint, annotations), apply edits, and re-evaluate to refine answers.
Modularity enables controllability and reduced noise versus unified multimodal generators; editing is constrained to purposeful transformations rather than free-form image synthesis.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, interpretable visual reasoning by producing purposeful intermediate images that improve accuracy and user trust; the modular design eases integration, debugging, and component upgrades for ML practitioners.

title: PiD: Fast and High-Resolution Latent Decoding with Pixel Diffusion
authors: Yifan Lu, Qi Wu, Jay Zhangjie Wu, Zian Wang, Huan Ling
abstract: Most practical high-resolution text-to-image systems, including latent diffusion and autoregressive models, perform generation in a compact latent space, and a decoder maps the generated latents back to pixels. Yet the latent-to-pixel decoder is reconstruction-oriented, optimized to invert the encoder rather than synthesize more details, and becomes increasingly costly at megapixel scale. This drawback calls for a more expressive and efficient decoding paradigm. Motivated by recent progress in s

infographic.key_insight: Replace reconstruction-oriented latent decoders with a conditional pixel-space diffusion decoder (PiD) that synthesizes high-frequency detail directly from compact latents, enabling faster and higher-resolution image reconstruction at megapixel scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Latent-to-pixel decoders are optimized to invert encoders and become computationally expensive and detail-poor at megapixel resolutions; PiD addresses the need for a more expressive, efficient decoder that produces richer high-resolution images.
method: Introduce PiD: a pixel diffusion decoder conditioned on compact latent codes so the model synthesizes fine details instead of strictly reconstructing encoder outputs.
Scale to megapixel images with efficiency tactics such as multi-scale/patch-wise diffusion, parallel sampling strategies and compute-aware scheduling to reduce memory and latency.
Train with perceptual/high-frequency-focused objectives and conditioning strategies to enable fewer sampling steps while preserving visual fidelity.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to decode large, high-quality images faster and with lower compute cost—making high-resolution text-to-image and latent-generation pipelines more practical for production and research.

title: Smart-Insertion-V: Photorealistic Video Insertion via a Closed-Loop Feedback Dual-Stream Framework
authors: Xiao Cao, Yansong Qu,  Xiangzhen,  Chang, Wen Xiao
abstract: Mask-free video object insertion has emerged as a challenging task, requiring harmonious integration of reference objects into source videos. However, existing methods struggle when references exhibit severe stylistic domain gaps with the source scene. To overcome this, we propose \textit{\textbf{Smart-Insertion-V}}, an end-to-end \textbf{Dual-Stream} framework that concurrently conducts video insertion and image style transfer. Within this framework, the image stream synchronously guides the vi

infographic.key_insight: Performing image style transfer and mask-free video insertion together in a closed-loop dual-stream framework lets the reference object adapt its appearance to the target scene while the video stream enforces temporal and spatial coherence, producing photorealistic insertions despite large stylistic domain gaps.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables harmonious, mask-free insertion of reference objects into videos when the reference and target scenes have severe style/appearance differences — eliminating artifacts, mismatched styles, and temporal inconsistency that plague prior methods.
method: Dual-Stream architecture: an image stream that performs style transfer on the reference and a video stream that inserts the (styled) object into the target frames without requiring explicit object masks.

Closed-loop feedback between streams: the image stream guides appearance adaptation while the video stream returns temporal/spatial cues, enabling iterative refinement for photorealism and motion consistency.
End-to-end training with losses targeting photorealism and temporal coherence (e.g., perceptual/adversarial and flow/consistency losses) to jointly optimize style alignment and insertion quality.
infographic.impact: Reduces manual preprocessing and domain-mismatch failures for video object insertion, improving practical workflows in video editing, AR/VR, and synthetic data generation while delivering more realistic and temporally stable results.

title: Good Token Hunting: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Token Selection for Visual Geometry Transformers
authors: Shuhong Zheng, Michael Oechsle, Erik Sandström, Marie-Julie Rakotosaona, Federico Tombari
abstract: Visual geometry transformers have become powerful architectures for multi-view 3D reconstruction, enabling joint prediction of multiple 3D attributes in a feed-forward manner. However, their computational cost grows quadratically with the input sequence length due to the global attention layers inside these models. This limits both their scalability and efficiency. In this work, we address this challenge with a simple yet general strategy: restricting the number of key/value tokens that each que

infographic.key_insight: Carefully selecting a subset of key/value tokens for attention in Visual Geometry Transformers cuts quadratic attention cost while keeping multi-view 3D reconstruction quality nearly intact.
infographic.problem_solved: Visual geometry transformers scale poorly because global attention grows quadratically with input token count, limiting efficiency and the ability to handle many views or high-resolution inputs.
method: Restrict the number of key/value tokens consulted by each query via a token-selection mechanism (e.g., learned scoring, confidence or clustering-based selection).
Insert the selection step into existing VGT pipelines with minimal architectural change so attention is computed over a compact set of tokens.
Optimize for compute/memory trade-offs to reduce FLOPs and memory footprint while preserving joint prediction performance for multiple 3D attributes.
infographic.impact: Makes multi-view 3D reconstruction models more scalable and deployable—enabling more views, higher resolutions, or resource-constrained deployment with little loss in accuracy. Practitioners can adopt token selection to reduce training/inference cost without redesigning the entire model.

title: Remember to be Curious: Episodic Context and Persistent Worlds for 3D Exploration
authors: Lily Goli, Justin Kerr, Daniele Reda, Alec Jacobson, Andrea Tagliasacchi
abstract: Exploration is a prerequisite for learning useful behaviors in sparse-reward, long-horizon tasks, particularly within 3D environments. Curiosity-driven reinforcement learning addresses this via intrinsic rewards derived from the mismatch between the agent's predictive model of the world and reality. However, translating this intrinsic motivation to complex, photorealistic environments remains difficult, as agents can become trapped in local loops and receive fresh rewards for revisiting forgotte

infographic.key_insight: Combining per-episode (episodic) context with a persistent world memory prevents curiosity-driven agents from getting trapped in local revisit loops, enabling robust exploration in complex photorealistic 3D environments.
infographic.problem_solved: Curiosity-based intrinsic rewards cause agents to repeatedly revisit forgotten states in long-horizon, sparse-reward 3D scenes, preventing meaningful coverage and learning; this paper stops spurious novelty by remembering both recent episode context and long-term visited regions.
method: Episodic context: track short-term visitation and prediction errors within an episode to avoid re-rewarding immediately revisited states.
Persistent world memory: maintain a cross-episode representation of visited locations (a persistent map or state buffer) to suppress false novelty across episodes.
Modulated curiosity: compute intrinsic rewards from prediction error but discount or mask errors when state novelty is explained by episodic or persistent memory, improving exploration efficiency.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical framework to make curiosity-driven RL work in photorealistic, long-horizon 3D tasks, improving sample efficiency and coverage—useful for embodied agents, simulation-to-real transfer, and long-term autonomous exploration.

title: Cambrian-P: Pose-Grounded Video Understanding
authors: Jihan Yang, Zifan Zhao, Xichen Pan, Shusheng Yang, Junyi Zhang
abstract: Camera pose matters. The position and orientation of each viewpoint define a shared spatial coordinate frame that relates observations across video frames. Yet this signal is largely absent from multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) for video understanding, which process frames as isolated 2D snapshots, instead of the persistent scene humans perceive. We revisit pose as a lightweight supervisory signal and introduce Cambrian-P, a video MLLM augmented with per-frame learnable camera tokens and a pose regressio

infographic.key_insight: Injecting per-frame learnable camera tokens and a lightweight pose regression signal into a video multimodal LLM grounds frames in a shared 3D coordinate frame, enabling more consistent, geometry-aware video understanding.
infographic.problem_solved: Multimodal LLMs treat video frames as isolated 2D snapshots and lack persistent camera-pose information, causing poor spatio-temporal consistency and limited 3D scene reasoning across frames.
method: Introduce per-frame learnable camera tokens that represent viewpoint (position & orientation) and are attached to each frame's representation.
Add a lightweight pose-regression head and supervisory signal to learn pose embeddings, and fuse pose tokens into the video encoder + multimodal fusion pipeline.
Use pose-conditioned temporal modeling so the LLM reasons about observations in a shared spatial coordinate frame for improved cross-frame consistency and scene understanding.
infographic.impact: Provides a simple, compatible way to make video MLLMs geometry-aware, improving temporal consistency and 3D reasoning for applications like robotics, AR, and embodied AI without major architectural overhaul.

title: GesVLA: Gesture-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model Embedded Representations
authors: Wenxuan Guo, Ziyuan Li, Meng Zhang, Yichen Liu, Yimeng Dong
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robot manipulation by unifying perception and action. However, existing VLA systems primarily rely on textual instructions and struggle to resolve spatial ambiguity in complex scenes with multiple similar objects. To address this limitation, we introduce gesture as a parallel instruction modality and propose a Gesture-aware Vision-Language-Action model (GesVLA). Our approach encodes gesture features directly into

infographic.key_insight: Adding human gesture as a parallel instruction modality to Vision-Language-Action models enables robots to resolve spatial ambiguity in cluttered or multi-object scenes, producing more precise action grounding and manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: VLA systems that rely only on text struggle to disambiguate referents in complex scenes with multiple similar objects and offer limited, natural multimodal interaction; GesVLA integrates gestures to clarify spatial intent and improve action selection.
method: Encode gesture features (hand pose, pointing direction, spatial cue) and embed them into the shared vision-language-action latent space.
Fuse gesture, visual, and textual inputs via a multimodal attention / transformer module to disambiguate referents and produce action-conditioned representations.
Train with paired gesture–image–language–action data using alignment/contrastive objectives and action supervision so the model maps multimodal instructions to executable policies.
infographic.impact: GesVLA makes human-robot instruction more robust and intuitive by leveraging natural gestures to remove spatial ambiguity — accelerating deployment of general-purpose manipulation agents in real-world HRI and industrial settings.

title: Vector Policy Optimization: Training for Diversity Improves Test-Time Search
authors: Ryan Bahlous-Boldi, Isha Puri, Idan Shenfeld, Akarsh Kumar, Mehul Damani
abstract: Language models must now generalize out of the box to novel environments and work inside inference-scaling search procedures, such as AlphaEvolve, that select rollouts with a variety of task-specific reward functions. Unfortunately, the standard paradigm of LLM post-training optimizes a pre-specified scalar reward, often leading current LLMs to produce low-entropy response distributions and thus to struggle at displaying the diversity that inference-time search will require. We propose Vector Po

infographic.key_insight: Optimizing policies with vector-valued (multi-objective) rewards preserves response diversity in LLMs, producing a portfolio of behaviors that substantially improves the effectiveness of test-time search procedures like AlphaEvolve.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard post-training that optimizes a single scalar reward drives LLMs toward low-entropy, homogenous outputs, making them ill-suited to provide the diverse rollouts inference-time search needs to succeed in novel tasks and environments.
method: Replace a single scalar reward with a vector-valued reward signal that captures multiple task-relevant objectives or preferences.
Apply vector/multi-objective policy optimization (with diversity-encouraging regularization or latent conditioning) to train a model that yields a broad, high-entropy set of high-quality behaviors.

At inference, generate diverse rollouts from the trained model and feed them to a search/selection procedure (e.g., AlphaEvolve) which selects rollouts per task-specific reward, improving downstream performance.
infographic.impact: By training for diversity rather than a single optimum, practitioners get LLMs that are better building blocks for inference-time search—improving robustness and performance on novel tasks and enabling more effective inference-scaling methods.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: scalar-reward training (narrow cone of outputs) vs. vector-reward training (broad fan/portfolio of outputs).
Pipeline diagram: Vector Policy Optimization -> Diverse rollouts -> Inference-time search (AlphaEvolve) -> Selected best rollout.
Chart: diversity (entropy) and downstream search performance comparison between scalar-trained and vector-trained models.
Icon set: a multi-dimensional reward vector, a neural policy, and a magnifying glass selecting top rollouts (to represent search/selection).

title: MOSS: Self-Evolution through Source-Level Rewriting in Autonomous Agent Systems
authors: Qianshu Cai, Yonggang Zhang, Xianzhang Jia, Wei Xue, Jun Song
abstract: Autonomous agentic systems are largely static after deployment: they do not learn from user interactions, and recurring failures persist until the next human-driven update ships a fix. Self-evolving agents have emerged in response, but all confine evolution to text-mutable artifacts -- skill files, prompt configurations, memory schemas, workflow graphs -- and leave the agent harness untouched. Since routing, hook ordering, state invariants, and dispatch live in code rather than in any text artif

infographic.key_insight: MOSS enables autonomous agents to self-evolve by rewriting their own source-level harness (routing, hooks, state invariants) rather than only mutating text artifacts like prompts or skill files, allowing fixes and structural changes after deployment.
infographic.problem_solved: Deployed agentic systems remain largely static and rely on human-driven updates; prior self-evolution approaches only alter text-mutable artifacts and cannot fix failures rooted in the agent harness code, leading to recurring faults and brittle behavior.
method: Detect and localize harness-level faults from runtime traces, failure logs, and unit/regression tests.
Synthesize and apply source-level rewrites (program transformations/patches) guided by agent semantics and program synthesis techniques.
Validate changes via automated testing, sandboxed staged deployment, and rollback mechanisms to preserve safety and correctness.
infographic.impact: Makes agents continuously maintainable and adaptive post-deployment, reducing manual patch cycles and accelerating fixes for structural/harness bugs while highlighting the need for robust verification and safe deployment practices.

Chart showing drop in recurring failures and mean-time-to-fix across iterations

title: LCGuard: Latent Communication Guard for Safe KV Sharing in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Sadia Asif, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Momin Abbas, Prasanna Sattigeri, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems increasingly rely on intermediate communication to coordinate complex tasks. While most existing systems communicate through natural language, recent work shows that latent communication, particularly through transformer key-value (KV) caches, can improve efficiency and preserve richer task-relevant information. However, KV caches also encode contextual inputs, intermediate reasoning states, and agent-specific information, creating an opaque c

infographic.key_insight: LCGuard enables safe latent communication by filtering and sanitizing transformer KV cache exchanges so agents keep coordination benefits without leaking contextual or sensitive information.
infographic.problem_solved: Prevents unintended disclosure of input context, intermediate reasoning, and agent-specific data when multi-agent LLMs share latent (KV) representations for coordination.
method: Learned latent filter that inspects KV caches and distinguishes task-relevant signals from sensitive/contextual content.
Sanitization mechanisms (masking, selective gating, or controlled perturbation) applied to KV entries to remove or obfuscate private information while preserving utility.
Optimization and evaluation under a utility–privacy tradeoff (e.g., adversarial training or regularizers) to retain coordination performance while limiting leakage.
infographic.impact: Allows practitioners to deploy efficient, KV-based latent communication in multi-agent systems with reduced privacy and leakage risks, enabling safer collaboration and regulatory compliance without major performance loss.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: agents → KV cache exchange → LCGuard filter → sanitized KV → coordinated output (before vs after highlighting removed sensitive content)
Bar or line chart: coordination performance vs. privacy leakage for baseline latent sharing and LCGuard (showing maintained utility with reduced leakage)
Heatmap or attention overlay on KV matrix showing which entries are preserved vs. masked by LCGuard

title: Evaluating Commercial AI Chatbots as News Intermediaries
authors: Mirac Suzgun, Emily Shen, Federico Bianchi, Alexander Spangher, Thomas Icard
abstract: AI chatbots are rapidly shaping how people encounter the news, yet no prior study has systematically measured how accurately these systems, with their proprietary search integrations and retrieval-synthesis pipelines, handle emerging facts across languages and regions. We present a 14-day (February 9-22, 2026) evaluation of six AI chatbots (Gemini 3 Flash and Pro, Grok 4, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, GPT-5 and GPT-4o mini) on 2,100 factual questions derived from same-day BBC News reporting across six regi

infographic.key_insight: Commercial AI chatbots vary widely in how accurately they report emerging news: retrieval and synthesis integration—especially across regions and languages—is a primary source of error and inconsistency.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides the first systematic, multi-model, multi-region measurement of how commercial chatbots handle same-day emerging facts, revealing where and why they fail as news intermediaries.
method: 14-day live evaluation (Feb 9–22, 2026) of six commercial chatbots: Gemini 3 Flash & Pro, Grok 4, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, GPT-5, and GPT-4o mini.
2,100 factual questions derived from same-day BBC News across six regions/languages to probe timeliness, factuality, attribution, and cross-lingual consistency.
Quantitative scoring and qualitative analysis of retrieval-synthesis behavior to identify common failure modes (misattribution, hallucination, stale retrievals).
infographic.impact: Equips AI/ML practitioners and product teams with evidence about real-world risks when using chatbots as news intermediaries, guiding improvements in retrieval, attribution, and deployment safeguards.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing per-model factual accuracy and attribution rates
Heatmap showing performance by region and language to highlight geographic blind spots

title: MotiMotion: Motion-Controlled Video Generation with Visual Reasoning
authors: Lee Hsin-Ying, Hanwen Jiang, Yiqun Mei, Jing Shi, Ming-Hsuan Yang
abstract: Current motion-controlled image-to-video generation models rigidly follow user-provided trajectories that are often sparse, imprecise, and causally incomplete. Such reliance often yields unnatural or implausible outcomes, especially by missing secondary causal consequences. To address this, we introduce MotiMotion, a novel framework that reformulates motion control as a reasoning-then-generation problem. To encourage causally grounded and commonsense-consistent interactions, we leverage a traini

infographic.key_insight: Reframe motion-conditioned image-to-video generation as a two-stage pipeline: first reason about plausible, causally grounded motion consequences from sparse/imprecise user trajectories, then generate the video conditioned on that reasoning—yielding more natural and consistent results.
infographic.problem_solved: User-specified motion controls (e.g., sparse trajectories) are often imprecise and causally incomplete, causing image-to-video models to produce unnatural, implausible, or missing secondary effects. MotiMotion fills in causal consequences and enforces commonsense interactions before generation.
method: Separate reasoning and generation: a visual-reasoning stage infers completed, causally consistent motion plans and secondary effects from sparse inputs.
Condition a video generator on the reasoning output to produce temporally-coherent, physically/plausibly consistent videos.
Train the reasoning module to predict commonsense causal outcomes and use its outputs to guide the generative model, improving fidelity to intended motion while filling missing details.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, controllable video synthesis from minimal user input, improving realism and usability for content creation, animation, and simulation tasks while reducing manual specification and post-editing.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: two-stage flow (User trajectory → Visual reasoning module → Video generator) with example intermediate outputs.
Before/after comparison: same sparse trajectory producing implausible vs. MotiMotion-corrected video frames.

Quantitative bar chart or table: improvements in realism/consistency metrics or user preference rates (visual summary of gains).

title: Sensor2Sensor: Cross-Embodiment Sensor Conversion for Autonomous Driving
authors: Jiahao Wang, Bo Sun, Yijing Bai, Vincent Casser, Songyou Peng
abstract: Robust training and validation of Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) require massive, diverse datasets. Proprietary data collected by Autonomous Vehicle (AV) fleets, while high-fidelity, are limited in scale, diversity of sensor configurations, as well as geographic and long-tail-behavioral coverage. In contrast, in-the-wild data from sources like dashcams offers immense scale and diversity, capturing critical long-tail scenarios and novel environments. However, this unstructured, in-the-wild vide

infographic.key_insight: A cross-embodiment conversion model can translate abundant in-the-wild sensor streams (e.g., dashcams) into the sensor modalities and configurations used by autonomous vehicles, unlocking large-scale, diverse training data for ADS without proprietary fleet collection.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between limited, proprietary AV sensor datasets and massive but heterogeneous in-the-wild video data by enabling reuse of diverse dashcam footage for training and validating AV perception stacks.
method: Learn a cross-embodiment sensor-conversion model that maps source sensor streams to target AV sensor modalities while preserving geometric and semantic consistency.
Combine geometry-aware rendering, temporal consistency constraints, and domain-adaptation/self- or weak-supervision to handle unpaired and diverse in-the-wild data.
Use the converted sensor outputs to augment or fine-tune downstream perception models (detection, segmentation, tracking) for robust ADS training.
infographic.impact: Allows AI/ML teams to massively expand and diversify ADS training data using inexpensive in-the-wild footage, improving robustness to long-tail scenarios and reducing dependence on costly proprietary fleet collection.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: source (dashcam) → cross-embodiment conversion model → target AV sensors (surround cameras / simulated LiDAR).
Before/after panels: raw dashcam frame vs. synthesized target-modality outputs (e.g., multi-camera rig views or depth/LiDAR-like rendering).

title: AwareVLN: Reasoning with Self-awareness for Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Wenxuan Guo, Xiuwei Xu, Yichen Liu, Xiangyu Li, Hang Yin
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to ground language instructions to its own movement within a visual environment. While state-of-the-art methods leverage the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for end-to-end action prediction, they often lack an explicit and explainable understanding of the relationships between the agent, the instruction, and the scene. Conversely, explicitly building a scene map for heuristic planning is intuitively appealing but reli

infographic.key_insight: Introduce an explicit self-awareness module that models the agent's pose, observations, and explored map and fuses this with a Vision-Language Model so the agent can both reason about instructions and explain its navigation decisions.
infographic.problem_solved: VLN agents often either rely on opaque end-to-end VLM reasoning or brittle hand-crafted maps; this work tackles the gap by combining explicit, interpretable agent-centric mapping with VLM reasoning to improve grounded, explainable action selection.
method: Construct an agent-centric self-awareness representation capturing pose, observed landmarks, and explored free/blocked regions as an explicit scene map.
Fuse the explicit map and agent state with a Vision-Language Model so instruction grounding, scene understanding, and action prediction happen jointly but remain interpretable.
Use the combined representation to guide a planner that selects actions and emits human-readable rationale for decisions (hybrid map-based planning + VLM reasoning).
infographic.impact: Provides a practical middle ground between black-box VLM policies and rigid map planners, enabling more reliable, interpretable VLN agents—useful for robotics, embodied AI research, and systems requiring traceable decisions.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: self-awareness module (map + state) feeding into a VLM and planner, with arrows showing information flow.
Step-by-step example: instruction → panorama snapshots + local map updates → chosen action with short rationale.
Map overlay: explored map showing trajectory, visited landmarks, and predicted next actions to highlight interpretability.
Comparison panel: qualitative side-by-side of black-box VLM vs AwareVLN explanations (why an action was chosen).

title: Neural operators for free-boundary problems
authors: Constantinos Siettos
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 21 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01238-4

Free boundary problems, such as modelling glacier melt, are difficult to capture with neural operators. A new framework addresses this challenge by leveraging the mathematical principle of topological conjugacy.

infographic.key_insight: A topological-conjugacy transform maps free-boundary PDEs to equivalent fixed-domain problems so neural operators can learn the solution operator reliably; applying the inverse transform reconstructs the evolving boundary and original-field solution.
infographic.problem_solved: Neural operators typically struggle with domains whose boundaries change in time (free-boundary problems like glacier melt). This framework enables accurate operator learning and prediction for such moving-boundary systems.
method: Construct a topological-conjugacy mapping that converts the free-boundary PDE into an equivalent fixed-domain formulation.
Train a neural operator on the transformed fixed-domain problem to learn the solution operator efficiently.
Apply the inverse conjugacy map to recover the original solution and the time-evolving boundary in the physical domain.
infographic.impact: Makes neural operators applicable to a broad class of real-world PDEs with moving boundaries (e.g., glaciology, multiphase flows), providing fast, generalizable surrogates for simulation, forecasting, and uncertainty quantification.
visual_elements: Schematic: free-boundary domain → conjugacy transform → fixed domain (side-by-side comparison)
Pipeline flowchart: data / PDE → transform → neural operator training → inverse transform → predicted solution + boundary
Animation or sequence: predicted glacier melt (boundary evolution) vs ground-truth simulation
Performance plots: error vs baseline solver and runtime / speedup bar chart

title: DeltaBox: Scaling Stateful AI Agents with Millisecond-Level Sandbox Checkpoint/Rollback
authors: Yunpeng Dong, Jingkai He, Yuze Hou, Dong Du, Zhonghu Xu
abstract:
LLM-powered AI agents require high-frequency state exploration (e.g., test-time tree search and reinforcement learning), relying on rapid checkpoint and rollback (C/R) of the complete sandbox state, including files and process state (e.g., memory, contexts, etc.). Existing mechanisms duplicate the entire state, causing hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of latency per C/R, which severely bottlenecks deep search and large-scale fan-outs.
  This paper observes that subsequent checkpoints in AI ag

infographic.key_insight: DeltaBox achieves millisecond-level checkpoint/rollback by avoiding full-state duplication and instead capturing and restoring only the incremental differences between successive sandbox states (files + process memory/context). This makes frequent state exploration orders of magnitude cheaper.
infographic.problem_solved: Current sandbox checkpoint/rollback duplicates entire process and file state, causing hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of latency that block deep search, high-frequency exploration, and large-scale agent fan-out.
method: Exploit high similarity between successive checkpoints to record deltas rather than full copies, dramatically reducing I/O and serialization cost.
Combine copy-on-write/differential snapshotting with lightweight metadata and lazy materialization to enable ultra-fast local checkpoints and rollbacks.
Integrate file- and process-level state capture in the sandbox and perform asynchronous persistence and fast in-memory rebound for rollbacks.
infographic.impact: Enables much deeper and wider search (e.g., test-time tree search, RL) and large-scale agent parallelism by reducing C/R latency to the millisecond range, improving throughput and lowering resource cost for stateful AI agents.

Architecture diagram showing sandbox, delta capture layer, copy-on-write pages, and fast rollback path
Sequence diagram of frequent checkpoints and rollbacks illustrating small deltas propagated vs full-state duplication
Throughput vs fan-out plot showing how lower C/R latency enables larger parallel agent branching
infographic.paper_title: DeltaBox: Scaling Stateful AI Agents with Millisecond-Level Sandbox Checkpoint/Rollback

title: Which Way Did It Move? Diagnosing and Overcoming Directional Motion Blindness in Video-LLMs
authors: Jongseo Lee, Hyuntak Lee, Sunghun Kim, Sooa Kim, Jihoon Chung
abstract: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have made rapid progress on temporal video understanding, yet many fail at a basic perceptual primitive: signed image-plane motion direction. On simple videos of a single object moving left, right, up, or down, most Video-LLMs perform near chance, with above-chance cases largely attributable to prediction biases rather than genuine direction understanding. We call this failure directional motion blindness. We localize the failure by tracing motion directi

infographic.key_insight: Video-LLMs commonly fail to perceive basic signed image-plane motion (left/right/up/down); above‑chance answers are often due to prediction biases rather than true directional understanding — a failure the authors call “directional motion blindness.”
infographic.problem_solved: Diagnoses the gap in fundamental motion-direction perception in Video-LLMs and proposes targeted interventions to restore genuine directional understanding.
method: Construct a focused diagnostic benchmark of simple single-object videos that move strictly left, right, up, or down to isolate direction perception from other cues.
Trace motion signals through Video-LLM components to localize where directional information is lost or overridden by biases (e.g., temporal encoder vs. readout).
Introduce and evaluate corrective strategies such as motion-aware inputs (optical flow/frame-differences), bias-calibration, and motion-focused fine-tuning to recover true direction sensitivity.
infographic.impact: Fixing directional motion blindness improves fundamental temporal perception in Video-LLMs, increasing reliability for real-world tasks (robotics, navigation, surveillance) and providing concrete diagnostics and remedies for model developers and evaluators.
visual_elements: Side-by-side example: sequence of frames with an overlaid arrow showing true motion direction and the model's prediction (correct vs. biased error).
Bar chart comparing chance-level accuracy, baseline Video-LLMs, and post-intervention accuracy to illustrate improvement.
Model anatomy diagram tracing motion signal flow (input frames → temporal encoder → readout) with a highlighted failure point.
Application icons (robot arm, dashcam, security camera) annotated with why reliable direction perception matters.
infographic.paper_title: Which Way Did It Move? Diagnosing and Overcoming Directional Motion Blindness in Video-LLMs

title: Tokenisation via Convex Relaxations
authors: Jan Tempus, Philip Whittington, Craig W. Schmidt, Dennis Komm, Tiago Pimentel
abstract: Tokenisation is an integral part of the current NLP pipeline. Current tokenisation algorithms such as BPE and Unigram are greedy algorithms -- they make locally optimal decisions without considering the resulting vocabulary as a whole. We instead formulate tokeniser construction as a linear program and solve it using convex optimisation tools, yielding a new algorithm we call ConvexTok. We find ConvexTok consistently improves intrinsic tokenisation metrics and the bits-per-byte (BpB) achieved by

infographic.key_insight: Reformulates tokenisation as a convex optimisation problem (a linear program) instead of using greedy subword merges, producing globally consistent vocabularies; ConvexTok improves intrinsic tokenisation metrics and lowers bits-per-byte (BpB).
infographic.problem_solved: Greedy tokenisers (e.g., BPE, Unigram) make locally optimal decisions that can produce suboptimal vocabularies and less efficient representations; the paper addresses the need for a principled, global optimisation for vocabulary construction.
method: Formulate vocabulary construction as a linear program (convex relaxation) that jointly optimises token selection and encoding costs.
Solve the convex relaxation with standard optimisation tools to obtain a continuous solution, then recover a discrete vocabulary (ConvexTok) via rounding/selection.
Evaluate ConvexTok against greedy baselines on intrinsic tokenisation metrics and bits-per-byte (BpB) to demonstrate consistent improvements.
infographic.impact: Offers a principled alternative to greedy tokenisers that can yield better compression and more coherent vocabularies, improving efficiency for model inputs and pre-processing pipelines; easily adopted by practitioners as a drop-in tokeniser construction method.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: Greedy pipeline (BPE/Unigram merges) vs ConvexTok pipeline (LP formulation → solver → rounding).
Flowchart of ConvexTok steps: objective setup, convex optimisation, continuous solution, discrete vocabulary recovery.
Bar chart comparing intrinsic tokenisation metrics and bits-per-byte (BpB) for ConvexTok vs BPE vs Unigram.

title: Deep neural operator for free boundary problems
authors: Zongjia Long, Qi Zhou, Aiqing Zhu, Dong Dai, Yiqun Liu
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 21 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01233-9

Long et al. introduce a neural operator method to solve free boundary problems with high precision. The framework shows promise for real-time predictions in clinical applications, particularly in simulating tumour growth.

infographic.key_insight: A neural operator framework can learn to solve free boundary problems with high accuracy and real-time speed, enabling rapid simulation of evolving interfaces such as tumour growth for clinical use.
infographic.problem_solved: Numerical solvers for free boundary problems are computationally intensive and slow for real-time or patient-specific applications; this work provides a fast, accurate surrogate that predicts both field solutions and moving boundaries.
method: Train a neural operator to learn the mapping from PDE inputs and initial/boundary conditions to solution fields and the evolving free boundary.
Couple field prediction with a boundary-evolution module for end-to-end learning of interface dynamics.
Validate and optimize the model for high precision and low-latency inference on tumour-growth simulation scenarios.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with a physics-aware, high-speed surrogate for PDEs with moving interfaces, enabling real-time, personalized simulations and faster workflows for inverse problems and clinical decision support.

Benchmark chart: accuracy vs inference time comparing neural operator and traditional solvers

title: FAME: Failure-Aware Mixture-of-Experts for Message-Level Log Anomaly Detection
authors: Huanchi Wang, Zihang Huang, Yifang Tian, Kristina Dzeparoska, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: Production systems generate millions of log lines daily, yet most anomaly detectors operate at the session or window-level, flagging groups of lines rather than identifying the specific message responsible. This coarse granularity forces operators to inspect many routine lines per alert. Message-level detection offers finer granularity, but remains challenging. A single event template may correspond to both normal and anomalous messages, failures arise from heterogeneous subsystems, and line-lev

infographic.key_insight: FAME introduces a failure-aware mixture-of-experts that performs message-level log anomaly detection, letting the model disambiguate event templates that occur in both normal and faulty contexts and handle heterogeneous failure modes in large-scale systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Most log anomaly detectors operate at session/window granularity and force operators to sift through many routine lines; this work pinpoints the exact anomalous message line within logs, reducing noise and accelerating triage.
method: Message-level modeling: operate directly on individual log lines (templates + context) instead of coarse sessions or windows.
Mixture-of-Experts architecture: allocate specialized experts to capture diverse failure patterns and subsystem heterogeneity.
Failure-aware routing/loss: bias gating and training signals toward separating normal vs. failure usages of the same template, enabling accurate localization of anomalies at line level.
infographic.impact: Finer-grained alerts reduce false positives and triage time for SREs/engineers, improving operational observability and enabling faster root-cause identification in production environments.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: MoE backbone with gating network and failure-aware loss, showing routing of ambiguous templates to different experts.
Before vs After comparison: session/window-level alert (many lines flagged) vs message-level highlight (single anomalous line highlighted).
Example log snippet: real log lines with color-coded anomaly scores and the selected expert for each anomalous line.

title: You Only Need Minimal RLVR Training: Extrapolating LLMs via Rank-1 Trajectories
authors: Zhepei Wei, Xinyu Zhu, Wei-Lin Chen, Chengsong Huang, Jiaxin Huang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a dominant paradigm for improving reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet the underlying geometry of the resulting parameter trajectories remains underexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that RLVR weight trajectories are extremely low-rank and highly predictable. Specifically, we find that the majority of downstream performance gains are captured by a rank-1 approximation of the parameter deltas, where the magnitude of th

infographic.key_insight: RLVR weight updates lie on an almost one-dimensional trajectory: a rank‑1 approximation of the parameter deltas captures the majority of downstream performance gains, so you can estimate a single direction and extrapolate improvements with minimal RLVR training.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the cost, instability and opacity of full RLVR fine‑tuning by revealing a simple, low‑rank geometric structure that lets practitioners get most benefits from far fewer RL steps.
method: Collect parameter deltas from short RLVR runs and compute a low‑rank decomposition (top singular vector / principal direction).
Approximate the full trajectory with a rank‑1 direction and a scalar magnitude; use that direction to extrapolate larger effective updates or to apply minimal scalar tuning.
Validate extrapolated models on downstream reasoning tasks to show rank‑1 captures most performance gains and generalizes across checkpoints.
infographic.impact: Enables much cheaper, faster and more interpretable RL‑style improvements for LLMs: estimate one direction from a small RL run and scale it to obtain near‑equivalent gains without extensive RL training. This lowers compute, speeds iteration, and simplifies deployment.

title: Leveraging LLMs for Grammar Adaptation: A Study on Metamodel-Grammar Co-Evolution
authors: Weixing Zhang, Bowen Jiang, Rahul Sharma, Regina Hebig, Daniel Strüber
abstract: In model-driven engineering, metamodel evolution leads to the need to adapt corresponding grammars to maintain consistency, which typically requires tedious manual work. Existing rule-based methods can achieve partial automation but have limitations when handling complex grammar scenarios. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-based approach that automatically applies adaptations to new grammars after evolution by learning grammar adaptations from previous versions. We evaluated this approa

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can learn and generalize grammar adaptation patterns from prior metamodel–grammar evolution examples, enabling automated, accurate updates to grammars after metamodel changes with less manual effort.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates the tedious and error-prone task of updating grammars to stay consistent with evolving metamodels, addressing limitations of brittle rule-based solutions when handling complex or varied grammar changes.
method: Collect pairs of old/new metamodels and corresponding grammar edits to use as adaptation examples.
Use an LLM-driven pipeline (few-shot prompting or fine-tuning) to infer and apply transformation patterns to new grammars after metamodel evolution.
Validate and refine generated grammar edits with lightweight checks (parsing/round-trip tests) and iterative feedback to improve reliability.
infographic.impact: Reduces manual engineering overhead and speeds up model-driven toolchain maintenance; enables scalable, adaptable grammar evolution workflows that integrate with existing MDE toolsets.

title: Is Fixing Schema Graphs Necessary? Full-Resolution Graph Structure Learning for Relational Deep Learning
authors: Yi Huang, Qingyun Sun, Jia Li, Xingcheng Fu, Jianxin Li
abstract: Relational prediction tasks are fundamental in many real-world applications, where data are naturally stored in relational databases (RDBs). Relational Deep Learning (RDL) addresses this problem by modeling RDBs as graphs and applying graph neural networks (GNNs) for end-to-end learning. However, the full-resolution property is commonly adopted as a design principle in graph construction for RDBs to preserve relational semantics, which leads most existing methods to rely on fixed graph structure

infographic.key_insight: Fixed schema graphs are not necessary: learning full-resolution (tuple-level) graph structure end-to-end yields more accurate and robust relational representations than relying on a single fixed schema-derived graph.
infographic.problem_solved: Relational Deep Learning often depends on a fixed graph built from database schema (the full-resolution principle), which can be suboptimal, brittle to schema design, and unable to capture latent tuple-level relations needed for accurate relational prediction.
method: Perform graph-structure learning at full resolution (tuple/node level) by scoring and learning edges during GNN training rather than using a fixed schema graph.
Introduce schema-aware inductive biases and regularizers (e.g., sparsity, block priors) to preserve relational semantics while allowing discovery of missing/latent links.
Integrate the learned structure end-to-end with relational GNNs using efficient parameterizations and sampling to keep training scalable on real RDBs.
infographic.impact: Reduces manual graph engineering and sensitivity to schema choices, improving accuracy and robustness on relational prediction tasks; practical for ML teams working directly on relational databases who want end-to-end, data-driven graph construction.
