title: Latent Dynamics for Full Body Avatar Animation
authors: Shichong Peng, Chengxiang Yin, Fei Jiang, Zhongshi Jiang, Lingchen Yang
abstract: Pose-driven full-body avatars built on neural rendering produce high-quality novel views of a captured subject. Yet loose clothing and other dynamic elements deform in ways pose alone cannot explain: the same pose can correspond to many different states, because their motion depends on history, inertia, and contact. Explicit simulation and layered-garment methods can model such dynamics, but they require either a dedicated garment template, which raw multi-view capture does not naturally provide

infographic.key_insight: A learned latent-dynamics module captures history-dependent deformations (e.g., loose clothing, hair, contacts) and integrates with pose-driven neural rendering, producing temporally coherent full-body avatar animation without requiring explicit garment templates.
infographic.problem_solved: Pose-only avatar models cannot predict motion-dependent states because the same pose can correspond to many different dynamic configurations; explicit garment simulation needs templates that raw multi-view capture typically doesn't provide. This work models those dynamics directly from captured data.
method: Factor pose vs. dynamic residuals: represent per-frame non-rigid, history-dependent state as a compact latent code that complements skeletal pose.

Learn a temporal latent-dynamics model (e.g., RNN/transformer-style transition) that predicts latent evolution from prior latent + current pose, then feed pose + latent to a neural renderer (NeRF/texture-based) to synthesize views.

Train end-to-end from multi-view video using reconstruction and temporal-consistency losses (optionally contact/inertia priors), eliminating the need for explicit garment templates or manual layering.
infographic.impact: Delivers more realistic, temporally coherent avatar animations from raw capture with less manual setup, benefiting virtual production, telepresence, games, and any application needing believable human motion without costly garment modeling.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: pose input → latent-dynamics module (temporal loop) → neural renderer → rendered frames
Before/after comparison: pose-only rendering vs. pose+latent rendering showing improved cloth/hair dynamics

title: AiraXiv: An AI-Driven Open-Access Platform for Human and AI Scientists
authors: Junshu Pan, Panzhong Lu, Yixuan Weng, Qiyao Sun, Fang Guo
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated the growth of both human-authored and AI-generated research outputs, placing increasing strain on traditional academic publishing systems and challenging the scalability of conference- and journal-centered paradigms amid rising submission volumes, reviewer workload, and venue size. To address these challenges, we explore an AI-era publishing paradigm in which both human and AI scientists participate as authors and readers, and pape

infographic.key_insight: AiraXiv is an open-access publishing platform designed for a hybrid ecosystem of human and AI scientists: it uses scalable hardware and AI-driven services to automate submission processing, provenance tracking, and curation so research can scale without overwhelming traditional conference/journal workflows.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses rising submission volumes, reviewer overload, trust/provenance gaps for AI-generated content, and the need for infrastructure that supports automated authorship, review, and discovery at scale.
method: End-to-end platform architecture combining scalable storage/compute infrastructure with AI services for automated ingestion, indexing, and metadata/provenance capture.
Hybrid human–AI workflows: AI agents assist or perform authoring, summarization, review triage and curation while humans validate outcomes and provide final governance.
Transparent provenance, versioning and reputation metadata (author type tags, audit logs, model IDs) plus metrics and APIs for discoverability and reproducibility.
infographic.impact: Enables faster, more reliable dissemination and discovery of research while reducing reviewer workload and improving provenance for AI-generated content—helpful for practitioners who need scalable, trustworthy access to the literature and machine-readable APIs for downstream tools.

title: DeepWeb-Bench: A Deep Research Benchmark Demanding Massive Cross-Source Evidence and Long-Horizon Derivation
authors: Sixiong Xie, Zhuofan Shi, Haiyang Shen, Jiuzheng Wang, Siqi Zhong
abstract: Deep research, in which an agent searches the open web, collects evidence, and derives an answer through extended reasoning, is a prominent use case for frontier language models. Frontier deep research products score high on existing benchmarks, making it difficult to distinguish their capabilities from current evaluation data alone. We introduce DeepWeb-Bench, a deep research benchmark that is substantially harder than existing benchmarks for the current frontier. Difficulty comes from three pr

infographic.key_insight: DeepWeb-Bench is a new, harder benchmark that forces models to search the open web, aggregate massive cross-source evidence, and perform long-horizon multi-step derivations — exposing capabilities gaps that existing benchmarks miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Current evaluations overestimate frontier models because they rarely require large-scale cross-source synthesis, sustained multi-step reasoning, and robustness to noisy/contradictory open-web evidence.
method: Curate research-style tasks that demand open-web retrieval and aggregation of evidence from many heterogeneous sources.
Require long-horizon derivations with explicit stepwise reasoning and citation alignment to measure chain-level correctness.
Introduce realistic web challenges (contradictory sources, temporal drift, noisy snippets) to test robustness and synthesis capability.
infographic.impact: DeepWeb-Bench gives practitioners a realistic, discriminative evaluation to drive improvements in retrieval-augmented LLMs, citation-aware reasoning, and long-context planning — helping ensure models truly perform deep research rather than surface-level pattern matching.

title: Uni-Edit: Intelligent Editing Is A General Task For Unified Model Tuning
authors: Dian Zheng, Manyuan Zhang, Hongyu Li, Hongbo Liu, Kai Zou
abstract: Currently, enhancing Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) with image understanding, generation, and editing capabilities mainly relies on mixed multi-task training. Due to inherent task conflicts, such strategy requires complex multi-stage pipelines, massive data mixing, and balancing tricks, merely resulting in a performance trade-off rather than true mutual reinforcement. To break this paradigm, we propose Uni-Edit, an intelligent image editing task that serves as the first general task for UMM tu

infographic.key_insight: Treating intelligent image editing as a single, general task lets a unified multimodal model (UMM) be tuned to both understand and generate images without complex multi-task mixing, resolving task conflicts and simplifying training.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes reliance on mixed multi-task training and cumbersome multi-stage pipelines that require massive data mixing and balancing tricks and typically produce performance trade-offs across image understanding, generation, and editing.
method: Define a single "intelligent editing" objective that unifies image understanding and image generation/editing supervision.
Recast diverse multimodal tasks into edit-style training examples (e.g., modify, annotate, or regenerate regions) and fine-tune the UMM using this unified editing signal.
Use a consistent instruction/format for edits and a diverse set of editing scenarios so the model learns generalizable editing behaviors instead of task-specific heuristics.
infographic.impact: Simplifies model tuning for multimodal systems, reducing engineering complexity and improving generalization across image understanding/generation/editing tasks — enabling practitioners to get broader capabilities with less data-mixing and fewer training hacks.

title: Stream3D: Sequential Multi-View 3D Generation via Evidential Memory
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Zeyang Bai, Xinhai Chang, Mengyu Wang, Paul Liang
abstract: View-conditioned 3D generators such as SAM 3D, TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D produce high-quality object reconstructions from a single view, but real-world visual observation often arrives as long monocular streams. Naively applying these generators to each streaming frame independently leads to severe temporal inconsistency in the generated results. To address this problem, we propose Stream3D, the first training-free streaming mechanism that turns a frozen view-conditioned 3D generator into a streamin

infographic.key_insight: Stream3D converts a frozen view-conditioned 3D generator into a streaming system by adding an evidential memory that fuses sequential monocular views, producing temporally consistent 3D reconstructions without retraining the base model.
infographic.problem_solved: Frame-by-frame use of single-view 3D generators on long monocular streams yields severe temporal inconsistency and flicker; Stream3D addresses stable multi-view fusion across time with a training-free wrapper.
method: Training-free streaming wrapper that sits on top of an existing frozen view-conditioned 3D generator and processes incoming frames sequentially.
Evidential memory: maintain per-voxel (or per-element) beliefs and uncertainty and update them with each new view using evidential/Bayesian-style fusion to resolve conflicts and accumulate consensus.
Temporal query & render: query the fused memory conditioned on the current camera/view to produce consistent 3D outputs each frame, preserving up-to-date detail while avoiding flicker.
infographic.impact: Enables robust, temporally coherent 3D reconstruction from long monocular videos without retraining, making high-quality multi-view generation practical for AR/VR, robotics, and dataset capture pipelines.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: input video → evidential memory (belief & uncertainty) → frozen 3D generator → temporally consistent renders
Before/after sequence: frame-by-frame reconstructions showing flicker from naive approach vs. stable Stream3D outputs
Memory visualization: heatmaps of per-voxel belief and uncertainty evolving over time as new views arrive

title: StreamGVE: Training-Free Video Editing via Few-Step Streaming Video Generation
authors: Guanlong Jiao, Chenyangguang Zhang, Jia Jun Cheng Xian, Zewei Zhang, Renjie Liao
abstract: Although existing video editing methods are generally feasible, they often require many costly iterations and still struggle to deliver high-quality yet satisfying editing results. We attribute this limitation to the prevalent data-to-data paradigm, which is less compatible with modern generative models than noise-to-data generation. To address this gap, we revisit video editing from a noise-to-data perspective and propose Streaming-Generation-based Video Editing (StreamGVE), which preserves few

infographic.key_insight: Reframe video editing from a data-to-data to a noise-to-data process and perform few-step streaming generation, enabling high-quality, temporally consistent edits without additional training.
infographic.problem_solved: Current video editing approaches require many costly optimization iterations, struggle to integrate with modern generative (noise-to-data) models, and often sacrifice quality or temporal consistency.
method: Revisit editing as noise-to-data generation and leverage off-the-shelf generative models (no extra training).
Perform streaming (frame-by-frame or chunked) few-step generation that preserves temporal coherence while minimizing per-frame computation.
Steer generation with conditioning (e.g., prompts, masks, reference frames) to apply edits efficiently in a training-free manner.
infographic.impact: Offers a fast, low-cost pathway to high-quality video edits that maintain temporal consistency, making advanced video editing practical for researchers and production pipelines without model re-training.

title: Variance Reduction for Expectations with Diffusion Teachers
authors: Jesse Bettencourt, Xindi Wu, Matan Atzmon, James Lucas, Jonathan Lorraine
abstract: Pretrained diffusion models serve as frozen teachers feeding downstream pipelines such as text-to-3D, single-step distillation, and data attribution. The teacher gradients these pipelines consume are Monte Carlo (MC) expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise samples; their estimator variance dominates compute cost because each draw requires expensive upstream work (rendering, simulation, encoding). We introduce CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting framework that motivates a hierarch

infographic.key_insight: CARV (Compute-Aware, Variance-accounting) reduces the expensive Monte Carlo variance coming from frozen diffusion teachers by explicitly measuring where variance arises (across noise levels and samples) and allocating compute hierarchically to those high-variance components, cutting required upstream work.
infographic.problem_solved: Downstream pipelines that consume gradients from pretrained diffusion teachers (e.g., text-to-3D, single-step distillation, data attribution) rely on Monte Carlo expectations over noise levels and Gaussian samples; estimator variance dominates compute cost because each sample requires expensive upstream rendering/simulation/encoding.
method: Estimate variance contributions across noise levels and Gaussian noise draws to identify where sampling yields the largest estimator variance.
Allocate a fixed compute budget adaptively and hierarchically—spending more samples where variance is highest and fewer where it is low (compute-aware sampling).
Combine hierarchical/stratified sampling and variance-reduction constructs (e.g., control variates or correlated estimators) to lower sample complexity per downstream gradient estimate.
infographic.impact: Significantly lowers the compute and wall-clock cost of pipelines that rely on frozen diffusion teachers, enabling faster iteration, cheaper model distillation and attribution, and more practical deployment of expensive upstream simulators or renderers.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: frozen diffusion teacher → sampling loop → expensive renderer/encoder → downstream consumer (text-to-3D/distillation), with MC samples highlighted.
Variance heatmap across noise levels (x-axis: noise level, y-axis: variance contribution) showing where variance concentrates.

title: ThoughtTrace: Understanding User Thoughts in Real-World LLM Interactions
authors: Chuanyang Jin, Binze Li, Haopeng Xie, Cathy Mengying Fang, Tianjian Li
abstract: Conversational AI has now reached billions of users, yet existing datasets capture only what people say, not what they think. We introduce ThoughtTrace, the first large-scale dataset that pairs real-world multi-turn human--AI conversations with users' self-reported thoughts: their reasons for sending prompts and reactions to assistant responses. ThoughtTrace comprises 1,058 users, 2,155 conversations, 17,058 turns, and 10,174 thought annotations collected across 20 language models. Our analysis

infographic.key_insight: ThoughtTrace is the first large-scale dataset that links real-world multi-turn human–AI conversations with users' self-reported thoughts (reasons for prompts and reactions), exposing the latent intent and judgments that are absent from standard dialogue corpora.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing conversational datasets record only utterances, not users' internal motivations or reactions, limiting progress on intent inference, evaluation, personalization, and alignment of LLMs with real user goals.
method: Collected paired data from 1,058 real users: 2,155 multi-turn conversations and 17,058 turns, yielding 10,174 self-reported thought annotations across 20 language models.
Annotated each turn with users' explicit reasons for sending prompts and their reactions to assistant responses, creating aligned conversation–thought pairs.
Performed dataset analyses to characterize thought types, distribution across LMs, and implications for modeling user intent and feedback-informed training.
infographic.impact: Provides a new supervision signal for training and evaluating models that must infer intent, predict user satisfaction, or personalize responses; enables better alignment and safety by making latent user reasoning observable.

title: CopT: Contrastive On-Policy Thinking with Continuous Spaces for General and Agentic Reasoning
authors: Dachuan Shi, Hanlin Zhu, Xiangchi Yuan, Wanjia Zhao, Kejing Xia
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is a standard approach for eliciting reasoning capabilities from large language models (LLMs). However, the common CoT paradigm treats thinking as a prerequisite for answering, which can delay access to plausible answers and incur unnecessary token costs even when the model is able to identify an answer before extended thinking, a behavior known as performative reasoning. In this paper, we introduce CopT, a reformulated reasoning pipeline that reverses the usual order of t

infographic.key_insight: CopT flips standard chain-of-thought: produce a provisional answer early, then perform contrastive on-policy thinking in continuous latent space to quickly refine, verify, and select answers — reducing unnecessary thinking and token use while preserving or improving reasoning quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses performative reasoning where models overthink and incur latency and token cost even when a correct answer can be identified early; improves efficiency, calibration, and agentic planning during reasoning.
method: Answer-first pipeline: emit a provisional answer immediately, then run thinking trajectories conditioned on that answer (on-policy) rather than treating thinking as a strict prerequisite.
Contrastive objective over continuous latent trajectories to score, refine, and discriminate between candidate thoughts/answers, encouraging informative and diverse internal deliberations.
Policy-conditioned sampling in a continuous latent space to enable efficient verification, iterative refinement, and agentic decision-making (planning, tool-use, multi-step tasks).
infographic.impact: Reduces token consumption and latency for reasoning-heavy tasks while improving robustness and downstream agentic capabilities; useful for deploying more cost-effective, responsive LLM-based systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram comparing standard CoT (think → answer) vs CopT (answer → on-policy thinking → refined answer).
Chart: accuracy vs tokens/latency showing CopT Pareto-improving over standard CoT.

title: Multi-axis Analysis of Image Manipulation Localization
authors: Keanu Nichols, Divya Appapogu, Giscard Biamby, Dina Bashkirova, Anna Rohrbach
abstract: Advanced image editing software enables easy creation of highly convincing image manipulations, which has been made even more accessible in recent years due to advances in generative AI. Manipulated images, while often harmless, could spread misinformation, create false narratives, and influence people's opinions on important issues. Despite this growing threat, there is limited research on detecting advanced manipulations across different visual domains. Thus, we introduce Analysis Under Domain

infographic.key_insight: A systematic, multi-axis evaluation reveals that current image-manipulation localization methods fail inconsistently across different domains (editing tools, semantic content, and distribution shifts), exposing hidden brittleness that single-axis benchmarks miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of comprehensive, cross-domain evaluation for image-manipulation localization by providing a framework and benchmark that measures robustness and generalization across multiple real-world axes of variation.
method: Define multiple evaluation axes (e.g., editing tool/type, image domain/semantics, distribution shift, post-processing) to stress-test localization models.
Assemble or curate a benchmark dataset and standardized metrics for per-pixel localization performance under each axis and their combinations.
Run systematic, comparative experiments across state-of-the-art detectors to quantify failure modes, robustness gaps, and trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a practical diagnostic toolkit and benchmark to choose, improve, and harden localization models for deployment; clarifies which models generalize across realistic manipulation scenarios and where targeted improvements are needed.

title: Not Every Rubric Teaches Equally: Policy-Aware Rubric Rewards for RLVR
authors: Utkarsh Tyagi, Xingang Guo, MohammadHossein Rezaei, Daniel George, Anas Mahmoud
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has made post-training highly effective when correctness can be checked automatically. However, many important model behaviors require satisfying several qualitative criteria at once. Rubric-based rewards address this setting by grading prompt-specific criteria and aggregating them into a scalar reward. Yet standard static aggregations conflate a criterion's human-assigned importance with its current usefulness as an optimization signal. We show tha

infographic.key_insight: Static rubric aggregations mix human importance with optimization utility, which can slow or misdirect learning; dynamically reweighting rubric criteria based on the current policy's learning signal yields more useful rewards and better training behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: How to turn multi-criterion, rubric-style verifiable checks into effective scalar rewards for RL so that the reward emphasizes criteria that are actually useful for improving the current policy instead of only reflecting fixed human weights.
method: Measure each rubric criterion's usefulness to the current policy (e.g., signal strength, learning progress or gradient relevance) rather than relying solely on fixed human-assigned importance.
Dynamically reweight rubric components to prioritize criteria that provide stronger, non-redundant optimization signals while retaining verifiability and human priors.
Integrate the policy-aware weights into the RLVR training loop so reward shaping adapts over time and guides learning toward composite correctness more efficiently.
infographic.impact: Practitioners obtain more sample-efficient and robust training when optimizing for multi-criteria behaviors, reducing manual tuning of rubric weights and lowering the chance of reward misdirection or gaming. This enables more reliable alignment of model outputs with complex qualitative requirements.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: static fixed-weight rubric -> stalled learning vs policy-aware dynamic weights -> steady improvement
Heatmap over training time showing rubric component weights adapting as the policy improves
Learning curves comparing RLVR with static aggregation vs policy-aware rubric rewards (faster convergence, higher composite score)

title: Draft Less, Retrieve More: Hybrid Tree Construction for Speculative Decoding
authors: Yuhao Shen, Tianyu Liu, Xinyi Hu, Quan Kong, Baolin Zhang
abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by leveraging a draft-then-verify paradigm. To maximize the acceptance rate, recent methods construct expansive draft trees, which unfortunately incur severe VRAM bandwidth and computational overheads that bottleneck end-to-end speedups. While dynamic-depth pruning can reduce this latency by removing marginal branches, it also discards potentially valid candidates, preventing the acceptance rate from reaching the upper bound of

infographic.key_insight: Combine smaller generative draft trees with retrieval-augmented candidate expansion (a hybrid tree) so you 'draft less' but 'retrieve more', preserving high acceptance rates while cutting VRAM bandwidth and compute overhead for speculative decoding.
infographic.problem_solved: Large, expansive draft trees maximize acceptance but cause severe VRAM bandwidth and computational bottlenecks; dynamic pruning reduces latency but can throw away valid candidates and limit acceptance rate.
method: Construct a hybrid draft tree that keeps generative branching shallow (draft less) and fills high-quality continuation branches by retrieving candidates from a cache/datastore (retrieve more).
Apply selective pruning that prioritizes retrieval-backed branches to remove low-value generative branches without discarding likely valid candidates.
Verify retrieved + drafted candidates with the target model under the speculative decoding accept/reject check, maintaining high acceptance while reducing memory and compute traffic.
infographic.impact: Delivers higher end-to-end LLM inference throughput with much lower VRAM bandwidth and compute cost, making speculative decoding more practical on constrained hardware and improving latency in production systems.

title: Atoms of Thought: Universal EEG Representation Learning with Microstates
authors: Xinyang Tian, Ruitao Liu, Ziyi Ye, Siyang Xue, Xin Wang
abstract: Learning universal representations from electroencephalogram (EEG) signals is a cutting-edge approach in the field of neuroinformatics and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Conventionally, EEG is treated as a multivariate temporal signal, where time- or frequency-domain features are extracted for representation learning. This paper investigates a simple yet effective EEG representation, i.e., microstates. Microstates represent the building blocks of brain activity patterns at a microscopic time

infographic.key_insight: Short, recurring EEG scalp patterns called microstates can serve as compact, interpretable, and universal building blocks for representation learning, enabling robust EEG embeddings that transfer across tasks and datasets.
infographic.problem_solved: Current EEG representations (time/frequency features or raw signals) are noisy, high-dimensional, and often task-specific; the paper addresses the need for a compact, generalizable, and interpretable EEG representation that improves cross-task transfer and downstream performance.
method: Extract microstate topographies by segmenting EEG into short quasi-stable scalp maps (e.g., clustering peak topographies).
Convert EEG into microstate sequences and learn embeddings using self-supervised / contrastive sequence modeling to capture spatial-temporal structure.
Evaluate learned representations on diverse downstream tasks and datasets to demonstrate robustness, transferability, and efficiency vs. baseline features.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a low-dimensional, interpretable EEG representation that reduces data and labeling needs, improves transfer across BCI and cognitive tasks, and integrates easily into existing pipelines.

title: Towards LLM-Assisted Architecture Recovery for Real-World ROS~2 Systems: An Agent-Based Multi-Level Approach to Hierarchical Structural Architecture Reconstruction
authors: Dominique Briechle, Raj Chanchad, Tobias Geger, Ruidi He, Dhruv Jajadiya
abstract: Explicit software architecture models are essential artifacts for communicating, analyzing, and evolving complex software-intensive systems. In ROS~2-based robotic systems, however, structural (de-)composition and integration semantics are often only implicitly encoded across distributed artifacts such as source code and launch files, making recovery of hierarchical architecture particularly difficult. Existing approaches mainly focus on node-level entities and communication wiring, while provid

infographic.key_insight: Combining LLM-powered information extraction with an agent-based, multi-level reconstruction pipeline enables automated recovery of hierarchical structural architectures from distributed ROS 2 artifacts that previously only exposed node-level wiring implicitly.
infographic.problem_solved: Recovering hierarchical, component- and subsystem-level architecture from scattered ROS 2 sources (code, launch/config, manifests) is hard because composition and integration semantics are implicit and existing tools focus only on node-level communication.
method: Agent-based pipeline where specialized agents (parsers, LLM extractors, fusers) process ROS 2 artifacts to identify entities, interfaces, and composition relations.
Multi-level reconstruction: fuse cross-artifact signals to build layered representations (nodes → components → subsystems) and resolve ambiguous links via LLM reasoning and structural heuristics.
Iterative validation and human-in-the-loop corrections to refine the hierarchical model and produce standard architecture views usable for analysis and evolution.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to automatically obtain meaningful architecture models for robotic ML systems, improving program comprehension, automated testing, simulation setup, and evolution planning—reducing manual effort and error when working with complex ROS 2 deployments.

title: Beyond Prediction Accuracy: Target-Space Recovery Profiles for Evaluating Model-Brain Alignment
authors: Ken Nakamura, Tomoya Nakai, Ryuto Yashiro, Ayumu Yamashita, Kaoru Amano
abstract: Artificial vision models are often evaluated against the human visual cortex by measuring how accurately their internal representations predict brain responses. However, prediction accuracy alone does not indicate which dimensions of the target brain's response space are recovered. Here, we introduce a unified framework for evaluating both model-brain and brain-brain alignment by identifying the response dimensions recovered by prediction. Using repeated fMRI measurements, we first identify targ

infographic.key_insight: Prediction accuracy alone hides which dimensions of the brain's response space a model actually recovers; the paper introduces target-space recovery profiles that reveal which response dimensions are captured, enabling richer model–brain and brain–brain alignment evaluation.
infographic.problem_solved: Current evaluations using aggregate prediction accuracy do not tell which dimensions of the target (brain) response space are recovered, so models can score well while missing important representational axes of neural data.
method: Use repeated fMRI measurements to estimate reliable target response dimensions (noise ceilings and stable subspaces).
Fit predictive models and measure recovery per target dimension (e.g., variance explained / subspace overlap) to build a recovery profile across dimensions.
Compare model–brain and brain–brain recovery profiles to quantify which axes are shared, missed, or unique (unified framework for alignment).
infographic.impact: Provides a diagnostic tool that goes beyond aggregate scores to reveal what aspects of neural representations models capture, guiding better model selection, architecture design, and neuroscientific interpretation.

title: Take It or Leave It: Intent-Controlled Partial Optimal Transport
authors: Salil Parth Tripathi, Bertrand Chapron, Fabrice Collard, Nicolas Courty, Ronan Fablet
abstract: While optimal transport (OT) enforces a rigid constraint by requiring two measures to be matched exactly, partial optimal transport relaxes this requirement by allowing mass to remain unmatched through a global budget, scalar rebate, or uniform rejection rule. However, many applications call for more structured, pointwise rejection mechanisms, where the decision to leave mass unmatched depends on side-specific reliability, support geometry, or external information about which components should p

infographic.key_insight: Introduce an intent-controlled partial optimal transport framework that allows selective, pointwise rejection of mass based on side-specific reliability or external intent, instead of global scalar or budget-based rejections. This enables structured, interpretable partial matchings tailored to application-specific signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard partial OT enforces global or uniform rejection rules that cannot model pointwise differences in reliability or external directives, limiting usability in settings where some source/target components should be preferentially matched or left unmatched.
method: Formalize partial OT with intent: incorporate pointwise rejection decisions driven by side-specific reliability scores, geometric support, or external intent signals, replacing global budget/rebate rules.
Define a loss/constraint that couples matching with per-point rejection indicators so that mass can be selectively left unmatched according to intent while preserving OT structure.
Solve the resulting problem with scalable numerical routines by adapting existing OT solvers (e.g., regularized/iterative transport algorithms) to handle the added pointwise rejection terms.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a flexible, interpretable mechanism to enforce selective matching—useful for robust domain adaptation, outlier-aware alignment, and applications where side information or user intent should control which elements get matched.
visual_elements: Schematic before/after diagram: two point clouds with arrows showing standard OT matching vs. intent-controlled partial OT with selective rejections (crossed arrows).

title: Your Neighbors Know: Leveraging Local Neighborhoods for Backdoor Detection in Decentralized Learning
authors: Sayan Biswas, Antoine Boutet, Davide Frey, Romaric Gaudel, Rachid Guerraoui
abstract: Decentralized learning (DL) is an emerging machine learning paradigm where nodes collaboratively train models without a central server. However, the collaborative nature of DL makes it vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where a model is taught to behave normally on standard inputs while executing hidden, malicious actions when encountering data with specific triggers. Backdoor attacks in DL remain understudied and existing defenses often overlook DL constraints. We introduce Argus, a novel backdoor

infographic.key_insight: Local neighborhoods of peers in a decentralized learning network reveal consistency patterns: benign nodes agree with their neighbors on model behavior while backdoored nodes produce detectable local anomalies. Argus leverages these neighborhood agreements to detect backdoors without a central server.
infographic.problem_solved: Detecting stealthy backdoor attacks in decentralized (serverless) collaborative learning where global coordination or centralized inspection is unavailable and privacy/data-sharing constraints limit conventional defenses.
method: Each node compares its model behavior (predictions or representations) with immediate neighbors on a small set of probe or unlabeled inputs to estimate pairwise agreement.
Aggregate local agreement scores into neighborhood-consensus statistics and apply lightweight anomaly detection to identify nodes whose behavior deviates significantly from their neighbors.

Mitigate detected threats by isolating or downweighting suspicious peers in local aggregation, preserving privacy by exchanging only compact signals (e.g., outputs/embeddings or similarity scores) rather than raw data.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, privacy-friendly defense that fits DL constraints (no central server, limited data sharing), enabling practitioners to detect and mitigate backdoors in distributed collaborations while maintaining model utility.

title: Probability-Conserving Flow Guidance
authors: Parsa Esmati, Junha Hyung, Amirhossein Dadashzadeh, Jaegul Choo, Majid Mirmehdi
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models dominate visual synthesis, with guidance aligning samples to user input and improving perceptual quality. However, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) and extrapolation-based methods are heuristic linear combinations of velocities/scores that ignore the generative manifold geometry, breaking probability conservation and driving samples off the learned manifold under strong guidance. We analyse guidance through the continuity equation and show its effect deco

infographic.key_insight: Guidance for diffusion and flow generative models should respect probability conservation on the learned data manifold; by formulating guidance through the continuity equation, the paper derives a probability-conserving adjustment that keeps samples on-manifold under strong guidance.
infographic.problem_solved: Heuristic guidance methods (e.g., Classifier-Free Guidance and velocity extrapolation) break probability conservation and push samples off the learned generative manifold when guidance is strong, degrading sample fidelity and consistency.
method: Analyze guidance as a modification of the generative vector field using the continuity equation to characterize how guidance redistributes probability mass.
Derive a corrective, probability-conserving guidance term (flow guidance) that modifies velocities/scores while preserving the continuity equation and manifold probability.
Implement the correction within flow- and diffusion-based samplers to produce on-manifold trajectories under strong guidance without heuristic extrapolation.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled, physics-inspired way to apply strong conditioning to generative models that maintains sample fidelity and probabilistic consistency, enabling more reliable controllable synthesis in applications requiring strong guidance.

title: What Do Evolutionary Coding Agents Evolve?
authors: Nico Pelleriti, Sree Harsha Nelaturu, Zhanke Zhou, Zongze Li, Max Zimmer
abstract: Recent work pairs LLMs with evolutionary search to iteratively generate, modify, and select code using task-specific feedback. These systems have produced strong results in mathematical discovery and algorithm design, yet a fundamental question remains: what do they actually evolve? Progress is typically summarized by the best score a run reaches under a task-specific evaluator, but that score can reflect several different mechanisms: new algorithmic structure, re-tuning an existing strategy, re

infographic.key_insight: Improvements from LLM-driven evolutionary coding agents often come from retuning, recombining, or simplifying existing strategies and exploiting evaluator specifics rather than primarily inventing wholly new algorithms; the paper presents a taxonomy and empirical analysis to distinguish these mechanisms.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies what it means when evolutionary coding agents 'improve' — whether gains reflect true algorithmic discovery, parameter/style retuning, recombination of existing code, or evaluator exploitation — so researchers can correctly interpret results and design better evaluation protocols.
method: Run LLM + evolutionary search across benchmark coding/math/algorithm tasks and collect evolved program populations over generations.
Classify evolved outputs into outcome categories (novel algorithmic structure, parameter retuning, recombination, bug‑fix/exploit) via code diffs, behavioral tests, and manual inspection.
Quantify prevalence of each mechanism and validate with ablations and targeted behavioral evaluations to separate genuine innovation from evaluator artifacts.
infographic.impact: Helps practitioners interpret progress claims from LLM-driven evolutionary systems, informs design of more robust evaluators and benchmarks, and guides methods that genuinely encourage algorithmic innovation rather than superficial tuning.

title: Toto 2.0: Time Series Forecasting Enters the Scaling Era
authors: Emaad Khwaja, Chris Lettieri, Gerald Woo, Eden Belouadah, Marc Cenac
abstract: We show that time series foundation models scale: a single training recipe produces reliable forecast-quality improvements from 4M to 2.5B parameters. We release Toto 2.0, a family of five open-weights forecasting models trained under this recipe. The Toto 2.0 family sets a new state of the art on three forecasting benchmarks: BOOM, our observability benchmark; GIFT-Eval, the standard general-purpose benchmark; and the recent contamination-resistant TIME benchmark. This report describes our expe

infographic.key_insight: Time-series forecasting models follow scaling behavior: a single training recipe yields consistent forecast-quality improvements across model sizes from 4M to 2.5B parameters, embodied in the open-weight Toto 2.0 family.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses whether foundation-scale modeling and a unified training recipe can improve and generalize time-series forecasting performance and robustness across domains and model sizes.
method: Design and apply a single, reproducible training recipe across a family of five open-weight models spanning 4M–2.5B parameters (Toto 2.0).
Evaluate at scale on diverse benchmarks — BOOM (observability), GIFT-Eval (general forecasting), and TIME (contamination-resistant) — to measure accuracy and robustness.
Demonstrate consistent, state-of-the-art improvements and release models/weights for community use.
infographic.impact: Shows that foundation-model scaling is effective for forecasting, enabling practitioners to choose models by compute/latency budget while benefiting from a unified training recipe and open weights for transfer, deployment, and robust forecasting.

title: BalanceRAG: Joint Risk Calibration for Cascaded Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Zijun Jia, Yuanchang Ye, Sen Jia, Yiyao Qian, Haoning Wang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can enhance factuality via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but applying RAG to every query is unnecessary when the model-only answer is reliable. This motivates cascaded RAG: each query is first handled by an LLM-only branch, escalated to a RAG fallback only if the primary branch is uncertain, and abstained from when neither branch is sufficiently trustworthy. However, calibrating such cascades stage by stage may be conservative, since the final utility depends

infographic.key_insight: Jointly calibrating risk across the LLM-only and RAG branches (rather than tuning each stage separately) yields better end-to-end utility by more accurately deciding when to answer, escalate to retrieval, or abstain.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces unnecessary retrieval calls and miscalibrated cascade behavior by aligning cascade decisions with final utility (accuracy vs retrieval cost vs abstention), so the system only uses costly RAG when it truly improves outcomes.
method: Estimate risk/confidence for the LLM-only answer and for the RAG fallback, producing comparable scores for cascade decision-making.
Learn a joint calibration / decision policy (thresholds or risk-based rule) that directly optimizes end-to-end utility: correct answer reward, retrieval cost penalty, and abstention cost.
Validate the calibrated cascade empirically to demonstrate improved accuracy–cost–abstention trade-offs compared with stagewise calibration and always-RAG baselines.
infographic.impact: Enables more efficient, reliable deployed LLM systems by cutting unnecessary retrieval costs while maintaining or improving factuality and safe abstention behavior—useful for production RAG pipelines and cost-sensitive applications.

title: Beyond Binary Success: A Diagnostic Meta-Evaluation Framework for Fine-Grained Manipulation
authors: He-Yang Xu, Pengyuan Zhang, Zongyuan Ge, Xiaoshuai Hao, Serge Belongie
abstract: Fine-grained manipulation marks a regime where global scene context no longer suffices, and success hinges on the tight coupling of local attribute grounding, high-fidelity spatial perception, and constraint-respecting motor execution. However, current embodied AI benchmarks collapse these capacities into binary success rates, systematically inflating reported capabilities by up to 70% and masking the architectural bottlenecks that impede real-world deployment. We introduce MetaFine, a diagnosti

infographic.key_insight: Binary success rates hide critical failure modes in fine-grained manipulation; MetaFine is a diagnostic meta-evaluation framework that decomposes manipulation performance into interpretable, component-level metrics and reveals up to 70% inflation in reported capabilities.
infographic.problem_solved: Current embodied-AI benchmarks reduce complex manipulation tasks to a single pass/fail score, masking failures in local attribute grounding, spatial perception, and constraint-respecting execution and preventing targeted improvement and safe deployment.
method: Define a compact suite of fine-grained diagnostic metrics (e.g., attribute grounding accuracy, spatial alignment error, constraint violation rate) to replace/augment binary success.
Apply systematic perturbations and targeted probes in simulated and real testbeds to isolate which sub-capacities (perception, grounding, control) cause failures.
Aggregate component-level scores into a meta-evaluation report (visualizations + quantitative inflation estimate) that identifies architectural bottlenecks.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to quantify where manipulation systems actually fail, enabling targeted model/robot improvements, more reliable benchmarking, and safer real-world deployment.

title: Optimal Representation Size: High-Dimensional Analysis of Pretraining and Linear Probing
authors: Valentina Njaradi, Clémentine Dominé, Rachel Swanson, Marco Mondelli, Andrew Saxe
abstract: Learning to generalise from limited data is a fundamental challenge for both artificial and biological systems. A common strategy is to extract reusable structure from abundant unlabelled data, enabling efficient adaptation to new tasks from limited labelled data. This two-stage paradigm is now standard in modern training pipelines, where pretraining is followed by fine-tuning or linear probing. We provide an analytical model of this process: structure extraction is formalized as principal compo

infographic.key_insight: The paper derives a principled, high-dimensional characterization of how large pretrained representations should be for best downstream linear-probing performance, showing there is an optimal representation size that depends on data statistics and label sample budget.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the practical and theoretical question of how to choose the dimensionality of pretrained features (representation size) to maximize generalization when adapting to new tasks with limited labeled data.
method: Formalize pretraining as structure extraction (principal components / low-rank signal + noise) in a high-dimensional asymptotic regime.
Derive closed-form/asymptotic expressions for downstream linear-probe risk as a function of representation dimension, sample sizes, noise & eigenvalue spectrum.
Use the analytic formulae to identify the representation size that minimizes downstream error and study trade-offs (under- vs over-parameterization, sample complexity).
infographic.impact: Provides actionable, theory-backed guidance for selecting representation dimensionality in transfer learning pipelines, helping practitioners balance pretraining cost and downstream performance when labeled data are scarce.

title: Neurosymbolic Learning for Inference-Time Argumentation
authors: Gabriel Freedman, Adam Dejl, Adam Gould,  Mansi, Lihu Chen
abstract: Claim verification is an important problem in high-stakes settings, including health and finance. When information underpinning claims is incomplete or conflicting, uncertain answers may be more appropriate than binary true or false classifications. In all cases, faithful explanations of the considerations determining the final verdict are crucial. We introduce inference-time argumentation (ITA), a trainable neurosymbolic framework for ternary claim verification in which a formal argumentation s

infographic.key_insight: Inference-Time Argumentation (ITA) combines neural evidence retrieval with a formal, trainable symbolic argumentation layer to produce ternary (true / false / uncertain) claim verification decisions and faithful, human-interpretable explanations at inference time.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses unreliable binary claim verification under incomplete or conflicting evidence by enabling uncertainty-aware (ternary) verdicts and providing faithful, structured explanations that show how supporting and opposing evidence were weighed.
method: Neural evidence modules retrieve and score candidate premises and counterpremises from text at inference time.
A symbolic argumentation engine constructs argument graphs (supporting vs. attacking arguments) and applies formal argumentation semantics to produce accept/reject/undecided verdicts.
The pipeline is trainable end-to-end or via modular objectives so argument scoring and selection align with final ternary decisions and explanation fidelity.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a practical, interpretable approach for high-stakes fact-checking and decision-making systems where uncertainty must be reported and the rationale must be auditable.

title: D$^3$-Subsidy: Online and Sequential Driver Subsidy Decision-Making for Large-Scale Ride-Hailing Market
authors: Taijie Chen, Rui Su, Siyuan Feng, Laoming Zhang, Hongyang Zhang
abstract: Ride-hailing platforms like DiDi Chuxing operate in highly dynamic environments where balancing driver supply and passenger demand is critical. Although driver-side subsidies serve as a primary lever to align these forces and improve key KPIs like completed rides (\texttt{Rides}) and gross merchandise value (\texttt{GMV}), optimizing them in production requires simultaneously meeting three constraints: (i) responsiveness to stochastic shocks, (ii) strict subsidy-rate caps, and (iii) low-latency

infographic.key_insight: D^3-Subsidy is an online, sequential subsidy policy that simultaneously achieves fast responsiveness to stochastic demand/supply shocks, enforces strict per-driver subsidy-rate caps, and runs with low latency at marketplace scale—leading to measurable gains in completed rides and GMV.
infographic.problem_solved: How to optimally allocate driver-side subsidies in a large-scale ride-hailing platform under three production constraints: (i) rapid adaptation to stochastic shocks, (ii) strict subsidy-rate caps per driver, and (iii) low-latency decision making suitable for real-time operation.
method: Cast subsidy allocation as an online sequential decision problem that optimizes short-term KPIs (Rides, GMV) under stochastic demand/supply and per-driver cap constraints.

Design D^3-Subsidy to decompose decisions into fast per-event updates plus periodic global reconciliation, leveraging lightweight approximations/streaming updates to guarantee low latency and enforce caps.
Derive performance guarantees and validate the approach on large-scale ride-hailing traces and production-style experiments showing improved KPIs and scalable operation.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a practical blueprint to run real-time, safe incentive policies that boost utilization and revenue while meeting regulatory/budget constraints. The approach generalizes to other two-sided marketplaces and large-scale online resource allocation problems.

title: Interpretable Computer Vision for Defect Detection in X-ray Tomography of Aerospace SiC/SiC Composites
authors: Antonio Peña Corredor, Julien Lesseur, Romain Nunez, Paul Rivalland, Thomas Philippe
abstract: Non-destructive testing of aerospace SiC/SiC composites via X-ray computed tomography (XCT) relies on expert visual assessment, with current workflows offering limited traceability for accept/reject decisions. Deep convolutional networks can automate defect detection, yet their black-box nature conflicts with the transparency that industrial inspection practice demands. To close this gap, we introduce p-ResNet-50, a convolutional framework extended with a prototype layer that couples high detect

infographic.key_insight: p-ResNet-50 augments a ResNet-50 backbone with a prototype layer so the model not only detects defects in X‑ray CT of SiC/SiC composites but also points to prototypical image regions that justify each decision, enabling traceable, visual explanations.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates defect detection in XCT scans while addressing the lack of transparency and traceability in expert accept/reject decisions by providing interpretable, evidence-based outputs instead of black‑box predictions.
method: Backbone: ResNet-50 convolutional encoder adapted to XCT slice inputs for defect candidate extraction.
Prototype layer: learnable prototypical image patches that the model compares to activation maps to localize and justify detections.
Training & evaluation: supervised learning on labeled XCT data with joint loss terms for classification accuracy and prototype similarity to ensure meaningful visual explanations.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical path to deploy high‑performance CV models in regulated industrial inspection workflows by coupling automated defect detection with human‑readable, traceable evidence — improving acceptance by inspectors and easing certification.

title: Training Neural Networks with Optimal Double-Bayesian Learning
authors: Vy Bui, Hang Yu, Karthik Kantipudi, Ziv Yaniv, Stefan Jaeger
abstract: Backpropagation with gradient descent is a common optimization strategy employed by most neural network architectures in machine learning. However, finding optimal hyperparameters to guide training has proven challenging. While it is widely acknowledged that selecting appropriate parameters is crucial for avoiding overfitting and achieving unbiased outcomes, this choice remains largely based on empirical experiments and experience. This paper presents a new probabilistic framework for the learni

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a unified "double-Bayesian" framework that jointly models network weights and hyperparameters with nested Bayesian inference, enabling automated, theoretically grounded hyperparameter selection during training.
infographic.problem_solved: Eliminates much of the empirical trial-and-error in hyperparameter tuning (which drives overfitting and biased outcomes) by providing a principled method to learn optimal hyperparameters alongside model parameters.
method: Formulate a hierarchical probabilistic model with a Bayesian posterior over weights and a Bayesian hyperprior over hyperparameters (the “double” Bayesian layer).
Derive a scalable inference/optimization scheme (e.g., variational inference / EM combined with gradient-based updates) that integrates with backprop to jointly update weights and hyperparameters.
Implement a practical training algorithm and evaluate it vs. standard tuning strategies to show improved generalization and reduced tuning cost.
infographic.impact: Makes training more robust and less dependent on manual tuning; practitioners can expect better generalization with lower compute/time spent on hyperparameter search and easier integration into existing pipelines.
visual_elements: Hierarchical diagram (plate notation) showing weights → likelihood and hyperprior → hyperparameters (double-Bayesian structure).
Training flowchart comparing standard loop + external hyperparameter search (grid/BO) versus integrated double-Bayesian loop.
Performance chart: validation/generalization error vs. tuning compute (showing lower error and cost for double-Bayesian).

title: VL-DPO: Vision-Language-Guided Finetuning for Preference-Aligned Autonomous Driving
authors: Zhefan Xu, Ghassen Jerfel, Marina Haliem, Qi Zhao, Jeonhyung Kang
abstract: The rapid growth of autonomous driving datasets has enabled the scaling of powerful motion forecasting models. While large-scale pretraining provides strong performance, the standard imitation objective may not fully capture the complex nuances of human driving preferences. Meanwhile, recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning and commonsense understanding. Building on these capabilities, this paper presents VL-DPO, a vision-language-guided framework

infographic.key_insight: Leverage vision-language models to generate human-like preference signals and use Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style finetuning to align pretrained motion-forecasting / driving models with nuanced driving preferences.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard imitation objectives for large pretrained driving models often miss complex, context-dependent human driving preferences; VL-DPO addresses how to inject richer, commonsense preference information into finetuning without retraining from scratch.
method: Use vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret scenes and produce semantic preference signals or natural-language judgments about candidate driving behaviors.
Apply a DPO-style preference-alignment finetuning objective to pretrained motion-forecasting/autonomous driving models using the VLM-generated signals.
Preserve pretrained capabilities while adapting model outputs toward safer, more human-aligned trajectories with minimal extra annotation effort.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical pathway for practitioners to align autonomous driving behavior with human preferences using off-the-shelf VLMs, improving safety, interpretability, and customization without large-scale manual preference labeling.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: sensor input → VLM reasoning (text/score) → DPO finetuning → aligned trajectory output
Before/after trajectory overlay showing improved preference-aligned maneuvers (e.g., safer lane change, smoother yield)

title: CAMERA: Adapting to Semantic Camouflage in Unsupervised Text-Attributed Graph Fraud Detection
authors: Junjun Pan, Yixin Liu, Yu Zheng, Lianhua Chi, Alan Wee-Chung Liew
abstract: Text-attributed graph fraud detection (TAGFD) plays a critical role in preventing fraudulent activities on online social and e-commerce platforms. However, to evade detection, fraudsters continuously evolve their camouflaging strategies by deliberately mimicking textual responses of benign users, thereby concealing their malicious purposes. This phenomenon, referred to as semantic camouflage, fundamentally undermines commonly relied assumptions on how structural and attribute cues can be exploit

infographic.key_insight: CAMERA is an unsupervised adaptation framework that uncovers fraud even when malicious accounts mimic benign text (semantic camouflage) by detecting mismatches between graph structure and textual attributes and adaptively reweighting signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Detects fraud on text-attributed graphs when attackers intentionally mimic legitimate textual behavior to evade models that rely on simple text–structure correlations.
method: Unsupervised joint modeling of graph structure and textual attributes to learn robust node representations without labels.
Adaptive mechanism that measures and exploits structure–text inconsistencies to identify and downweight camouflaged textual signals.
Anomaly scoring (or alignment/contrastive objective) that surfaces suspicious nodes based on divergence between their structural context and textual content.
infographic.impact: Enables more robust, label-free fraud detection on social and e-commerce platforms by reducing reliance on brittle text heuristics and helping systems keep up with evolving camouflage tactics.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: inputs (graph + text) → CAMERA adaptation module → anomaly scores/alerts
Before/after example card: a camouflaged fraudster post vs. true benign post showing why text alone misleads
Embedding visualization (t-SNE/UMAP) showing separation of camouflaged fraud vs. benign after adaptation

title: Rethinking Visual Attribution for Chest X-ray Reasoning in Large Vision Language Models
authors: Guangzhi Xiong, Qiao Jin, Sanchit Sinha, Zhiyong Lu, Aidong Zhang
abstract: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) show promise in medical applications, but their inability to faithfully ground responses in visual evidence raises serious concerns about clinical trustworthiness. While visual attribution methods are widely used to explain LVLM predictions, whether these explanations actually reflect the visual evidence underlying the model's decision is largely unverified, since ground-truth annotations for internal model reasoning are typically unavailable. We address this

infographic.key_insight: Popular visual attribution methods for LVLMs often do not faithfully reflect the true visual evidence behind chest X‑ray reasoning; the paper provides an evaluation framework and practical checks to measure and improve attribution faithfulness.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap between visual explanations produced by LVLMs and the actual image evidence used for medical conclusions — a barrier to clinical trust and safe deployment.
method: Design an evaluation protocol/benchmark that aligns model outputs with visual evidence using radiologist annotations and targeted image interventions (e.g., masking or counterfactuals).
Systematically assess common attribution techniques (e.g., activation/attention maps) with quantitative faithfulness metrics (localization accuracy, causal effect, agreement with experts).
Propose practical remedies and a validation checklist (contrastive attribution, causal masking tests, and recommended metrics) to improve and validate visual grounding.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a rigorous way to vet and compare visual explanations from LVLMs on chest X‑rays, improving model selection, interpretability, and clinical safety before deployment.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: LVLM input (CXR) → predicted finding → attribution map → comparison with radiologist annotation/ground truth.
Side‑by‑side example CXRs: attribution overlays from multiple methods highlighting faithful vs. unfaithful explanations.
Bar/heatmap chart: faithfulness scores across attribution methods and tasks (localization, causal effect, expert agreement).
Flowchart/checklist: recommended evaluation steps for validating visual attributions in medical LVLMs (annotate, intervene, score, remediate).

title: Long-term Power Grid Planning via Answer Set Programming
authors: Antonio Ielo, Francesco Doria, Sandra Castellanos-Paez, Marco Maratea, Francesco Percassi
abstract: The Power grid is a critical infrastructure underpinning all aspects of modern society and its services. Maintaining its effectiveness requires continuous adaptations. In particular, addressing sustainability targets, demand patterns, and urbanisation trends requires implementing changes to the network. Actual developments can potentially span over a decade, with supply continuity and service quality that must be preserved throughout by ensuring conformance to several topological and combinatori

infographic.key_insight: Answer Set Programming (ASP) can compactly encode and solve decade-scale power grid planning problems with rich topological and combinatorial constraints, producing optimal multi-year upgrade schedules that preserve supply continuity and service quality.
infographic.problem_solved: How to plan long-term (multi-year to decade) grid expansions and upgrades under complex topology, operational, and deployment constraints (while meeting sustainability and demand changes) without violating service continuity despite combinatorial explosion of possibilities.
method: Model the long-horizon planning problem as an ASP program that encodes network topology, component choices, temporal deployment steps, and operational constraints.
Use ASP solvers to search and optimize feasible upgrade schedules across scenarios, enforcing continuity and combinatorial/topological constraints exactly.
Support scenario-based and incremental planning (cost/benefit trade-offs, multiple objectives) via solver-guided enumeration and optimality criteria.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates a symbolic, interpretable alternative to purely numerical optimization for large combinatorial infrastructure planning; AI/ML practitioners can combine ASP-based planners with ML forecasts for robust, verifiable long-term decision support.
visual_elements: Multi-year timeline showing staged upgrades and preserved supply continuity (Gantt-style)
Pipeline diagram: data/forecasts → ASP model (constraints & objectives) → solver → candidate plans
Network diagram overlayed with constraint icons (topology constraints, capacity, redundancy) to show feasible vs infeasible modifications
Comparison chart (e.g., solution quality vs. computation time) contrasting ASP with MILP/heuristics

title: Predictable Confabulations: Factual Recall by LLMs Scales with Model Size and Topic Frequency
authors: Matthew L. Smith, Jonathan P. Shock, Samuel T. Segun, Iyiola E. Olatunji, Tegawendé F. Bissyandé
abstract: While scaling laws govern aggregate large language model performance, no scaling law has linked factual recall to both model size and training-data composition. We evaluated 38 models on over 8,900 scholarly references evaluated by an automated reference verification system. Recall quality follows a sigmoid in the log-linear combination of model parameter count and topic representation in training data. These two variables alone explain 60% of the variance across 16 dense models from four famili

infographic.key_insight: Factual recall in LLMs follows a sigmoid function of a log-linear combination of model size (parameter count) and topic representation in the training data; those two factors alone explain ~60% of recall variance across evaluated dense models.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides the first empirical scaling relationship linking factual recall to both model scale and training-data composition, enabling prediction of when models will confidently (but not always correctly) produce references.
method: Evaluated 38 models on >8,900 scholarly references using an automated reference-verification pipeline to measure recall quality.
Quantified topic representation in training data and combined it with model parameter count in a log-linear predictor, then mapped predictor outputs to recall probability with a sigmoid fit.
Performed statistical analysis across 16 dense models from four model families to measure explanatory power (≈60% variance explained) of the two-factor model.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a simple, actionable rule-of-thumb to anticipate and improve factual recall by balancing model scale and dataset topic coverage—informing model selection, dataset curation, and risk assessment for hallucinated references.
visual_elements: 2D scatterplot of models (x: log(model params), y: topic frequency) with a fitted sigmoid surface/contour showing recall probability
Heatmap showing recall rate as a function of model size and topic representation, emphasizing the sigmoid transition region
Bar or pie chart reporting variance explained (R² ≈ 0.60) by the two-factor model versus alternative predictors

title: General Preference Reinforcement Learning
authors: Muhammad Umer, Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin, Ahsan Bilal, Arslan Chaudhry, Andreas Haupt
abstract: Post-training has split large language model (LLM) alignment into two largely disconnected tracks. Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards drives emergent reasoning on math and code but depends on a programmatic verifier that cannot reach open-ended tasks, while preference optimization handles open-ended generation yet forgoes the continuous exploration that powers online RL. Closing this gap requires a verifier for open-ended quality, but a scalar reward model is the wrong sh

infographic.key_insight: This paper bridges online reinforcement learning and preference optimization by using preference-based verification instead of a single scalar reward, enabling continuous RL-style exploration for open-ended tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Post-training for LLMs is split: online RL needs programmatic verifiers (not available for open-ended generation) while preference optimization supports open domains but lacks continuous exploration. The paper addresses the absence of a verifier suitable for open-ended quality that can power RL-style learning.
method: Train a general preference model from pairwise/ranking feedback (human or synthetic) to evaluate open-ended outputs rather than relying on a single scalar reward.
Integrate the learned preference verifier into an online RL loop so the agent can continuously explore and improve on subjective, open-ended objectives.
Stabilize learning with uncertainty-aware querying and regularization (e.g., selective human queries, confidence thresholds) to manage noisy or sparse preference signals.
infographic.impact: Allows practitioners to apply online RL techniques to open-ended LLM tasks by replacing brittle scalar rewards with richer preference verifiers, improving alignment and capability where subjective judgments matter.
visual_elements: Split-track diagram: left = programmatic-verifier RL (math/code), right = preference optimization (open-ended), center = unified preference-based RL
System loop flowchart: outputs → preference collection → preference model (verifier) → RL agent update → new outputs
Comparison bar/line chart: scalar-reward RL vs preference-RL on open-ended quality and exploration metrics
Icons: human annotator, verifier/model, exploration/agent arrow to convey continuous learning with human-in-the-loop

infographic.paper_authors: Muhammad Umer, Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin, Ahsan Bilal, Arslan Chaudhry, Andreas Haupt

title: WavFlow: Audio Generation in Waveform Space
authors: Feiyan Zhou, Luyuan Wang, Shoufa Chen, Zhe Wang, Zhiheng Liu
abstract: Modern audio generation predominantly relies on latent-space compression, introducing additional complexity and potential information loss. In this work, we challenge this paradigm with WavFlow, a framework that generates high-fidelity audio directly in raw waveform space without intermediate representations. To overcome the inherent difficulties of modeling high-dimensional and low-energy signals, we reshape audio into 2D token grids through waveform patchify and introduce amplitude lifting to

infographic.key_insight: WavFlow generates high-fidelity audio directly in raw waveform space by turning 1D waveforms into 2D token grids and using an amplitude-lifting + generative backbone to avoid latent compression and its information loss.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes the need for latent-space compression which adds complexity and can discard signal details; addresses the challenge of modeling extremely high-dimensional, low-energy waveform signals for direct synthesis.
method: Waveform patchify: reshape raw 1D audio into compact 2D token grids so standard 2D-modeling blocks can operate efficiently.
Amplitude lifting: boost and normalize low-energy components to stabilize learning and preserve subtle signal details.
Direct generative backbone (WavFlow): a model adapted to the 2D waveform grid that synthesizes audio in waveform space without intermediate latent representations.
infographic.impact: Enables simpler, more faithful audio synthesis pipelines that preserve fine-grained signal information and can improve fidelity, interpretability, and deployment efficiency for audio ML systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: raw waveform → patchify → 2D token grid → amplitude lifting → generative model → output waveform
Before/after comparison: audio reconstructed via latent compression vs direct waveform generation (waveform + listening/spectral snapshots)
Amplitude lifting visualization: low-energy components amplified and preserved across training steps

title: A Readiness-Driven Runtime for Pipeline-Parallel Training under Runtime Variability
authors: Ruitao Liu, Xinyang Tian, Shuo Chen, Tingrui Zhang, Guang Yang
abstract: Pipeline parallelism is a key technique for scaling large-model training, but modern workloads exhibit runtime variability in computation and communication. Existing pipeline systems typically consume static, profiled, or adaptively generated schedules as pre-committed execution orders. When realized task readiness diverges from the pre-committed order, stages may wait for not-yet-ready work even though other executable work is available, creating stage misalignment, idle bubbles, and reduced ut

infographic.key_insight: Instead of following a pre-committed pipeline schedule, make scheduling decisions at runtime based on which tasks are actually ready; this readiness-driven approach reduces idle bubbles and stage misalignment under variable computation/communication.
infographic.problem_solved: Pipeline-parallel training suffers when real task readiness diverges from static or profiled schedules—causing stages to wait for unavailable work, creating idle bubbles, misalignment, and lowered hardware utilization and throughput.
method: Continuously monitor task readiness (compute/communication completion signals) and permit dynamic reordering of pipeline tasks rather than following a fixed pre-committed schedule.
Make lightweight, low-latency scheduling decisions that opportunistically execute any ready work to fill bubbles and re-align stages, maintaining pipeline flow under runtime variability.
Integrate with pipeline-parallel runtimes without heavy profiling or offline schedule generation, keeping overhead low while improving robustness to heterogeneity and transient delays.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get higher and more stable training throughput on heterogeneous or variable clusters, reducing end-to-end training time and making pipeline parallelism more practical in real-world, non-deterministic environments.
visual_elements: Timeline comparison: static pre-committed schedule vs readiness-driven schedule showing reduced idle bubbles and improved alignment
Flow diagram of the readiness-driven runtime loop: readiness detection → scheduler decision → task dispatch
Bar chart showing throughput/iteration time and utilization gains across variable-delay scenarios
Cluster iconography highlighting heterogeneous nodes and transient network/compute variability

title: Stop ‘tokenmaxxing’ and deploy AI sensibly instead
authors: Unknown
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 18 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01253-5

Companies, tech workers and researchers are in a frenzy to embed agentic AI into their workflows, locked in a self-imposed race not to fall behind. There must be a better way to make use of AI technology.

infographic.key_insight: The paper warns against the trend of 'tokenmaxxing'—rushing to add agentic/autonomous AI features or maximize capability metrics—urging measured, human-centered, risk-aware deployments that prioritize real-world utility and safety.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the self‑imposed race to embed agentic AI into workflows (driven by competition and hype) that produces fragile, unsafe, or low‑value systems; offers actionable alternatives for sensible, responsible deployment.
method: Analyze the incentive and measurement failures driving 'tokenmaxxing' and document associated technical and social harms.
Propose deployment principles: human‑in‑the‑loop control, incremental rollouts, clear success metrics tied to user value, and targeted automation only where benefits outweigh risks.
Recommend governance and evaluation: robustness checks, cost‑benefit analyses, user feedback loops, and organizational/regulatory oversight instead of capability arms races.
infographic.impact: Shifts practitioner focus from maximizing features or benchmark metrics to deploying AI that is safer, more maintainable, and delivers measurable user value—reducing harm and improving ROI on AI projects.

Decision flowchart: go/no‑go checklist (value, risk, monitorability, human oversight).
Risk vs Reward matrix showing when to automate vs keep human‑in‑the‑loop.

title: DashAttention: Differentiable and Adaptive Sparse Hierarchical Attention
authors: Yuxiang Huang, Nuno M. T. Gonçalves, Federico Alvetreti, Lei Li, Xu Han
abstract: Current hierarchical attention methods, such as NSA and InfLLMv2, select the top-k relevant key-value (KV) blocks based on coarse attention scores and subsequently apply fine-grained softmax attention on the selected tokens. However, the top-k operation assumes the number of relevant tokens for any query is fixed and it precludes the gradient flow between the sparse and dense stages. In this work, we propose DashAttention (Differentiable and Adaptive Sparse Hierarchical Attention), which leverag

infographic.key_insight: DashAttention replaces fixed top-k selection with a differentiable, per-query adaptive sparse routing mechanism so the model learns how many and which key–value tokens to attend to, preserving gradient flow across sparse and dense stages.
infographic.problem_solved: Fixed top-k hierarchical attention assumes a constant number of relevant tokens and blocks gradient flow between coarse (block) selection and fine-grained attention, limiting accuracy and end-to-end optimization for long-context transformers.
method: Differentiable hierarchical routing: use a continuous relaxation (learned gating/soft allocation) to score and select KV blocks and tokens so selection is end-to-end differentiable.
Adaptive per-query sparsity: dynamically allocate attention budget per query rather than a fixed k, allowing the model to attend to variable numbers of relevant tokens depending on context.

Two-stage fine-grained attention with gradient flow: coarse block selection followed by dense attention on selected tokens while allowing gradients to flow back into the coarse selector for joint optimization and efficiency.
infographic.impact: Enables more accurate, efficient long-context attention by learning when and how much to sparsify; practical for scaling transformers with better compute-accuracy trade-offs and simpler end-to-end training.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: coarse block scoring → differentiable selector → fine-grained attention, annotated with gradient arrows showing end-to-end flow
Comparison chart: fixed top-k vs adaptive DashAttention showing accuracy vs FLOPs/latency
Per-query sparsity heatmap: variable number of attended tokens across queries (illustrates adaptivity)
