title: DexHoldem: Playing Texas Hold'em with Dexterous Embodied System
authors: Feng Chen, Tianzhe Chu, Li Sun, Pei Zhou, Zhuxiu Xu
abstract: Evaluating embodied systems on real dexterous hardware requires more than isolated primitive skills: an agent must perceive a changing tabletop scene, choose a context-appropriate action, execute it with a dexterous hand, and leave the scene usable for later decisions. We introduce DexHoldem, a real-world system-level benchmark built around Texas Hold'em dexterous manipulation with a ShadowHand. DexHoldem provides 1,470 teleoperated demonstrations across 14 Texas Hold'em manipulation primitives,

infographic.key_insight: Real-world dexterous evaluation requires integrating perception, context-aware decision-making, and precise hand control rather than testing isolated primitives. DexHoldem provides a system-level benchmark with 1,470 teleoperated demonstrations on a ShadowHand to enable such integrated evaluation.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between isolated dexterous skills and end-to-end embodied manipulation evaluation by offering a real-hardware benchmark that tests perception-to-action pipelines, sequential decision-making, and scene maintenance in a complex tabletop task.
method: Formulate Texas Hold'em card manipulation as a structured testbed composed of 14 manipulation primitives and multi-step rounds.
Collect 1,470 teleoperated demonstrations on a ShadowHand, capturing multimodal perception data and control traces for each primitive and sequence.
Provide task definitions, evaluation protocols, and success metrics focused on sequence completion, scene usability, and robustness on real hardware.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers to develop, compare, and benchmark embodied dexterous policies on real hardware, accelerating progress in robust robotic manipulation, policy generalization, and sim-to-real transfer. Offers a standardized dataset and evaluation suite for system-level research.

title: SpecGP as a transformer-based model for predicting energy-adaptable structural spectra of glycopeptides
authors: Xianyong Wang, Rui Song, Zhuangzhuang Feng, Shisheng Sun
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 18 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01246-4

SpecGP enhances fragment ion coverage to enable the prediction of N-glycopeptide structural spectra across diverse collision energies, thereby improving isomer discrimination and boosting identification confidence through rescoring.

infographic.key_insight: SpecGP is a transformer-based model that predicts energy-adaptable MS/MS structural spectra for N-glycopeptides, enhancing fragment ion coverage and enabling more accurate isomer discrimination across collision energies.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing spectrum predictors struggle to model glycopeptide fragmentation across varying collision energies, limiting fragment coverage and reducing confidence in distinguishing structural isomers and in downstream identification.
method: Transformer backbone with explicit energy-conditioning (energy token or embedding) to predict collision-energy-dependent fragment intensities for peptide and glycan-derived ions.
Structural-spectrum modeling that expands fragment ion coverage (including diagnostic glycan fragments) and generates energy-specific predicted spectra.
Rescoring pipeline that compares predicted spectra to experimental spectra to re-rank identifications and improve isomer discrimination and confidence.
infographic.impact: Provides an architecture pattern for energy-conditioned spectral prediction that improves identification accuracy in proteomics workflows; useful for ML practitioners building domain-adaptable generative predictors and rescoring systems in mass spectrometry.

Augustine et al. present a multimodal graph neural network that identifies cancer immunotherapy targets. It distinguishes approved and prospective targets, and promising candidates are validated using a clinically relevant patient-derived platform.

method: Integrate multimodal data (genomics, proteomics, pathway/interaction maps, clinical annotations) into a unified graph representation.
Train a graph neural network to learn node/edge embeddings that predict target viability and rank candidate targets (distinguishing approved vs prospective).
Validate high-confidence predictions using a patient-derived tumour explant platform to confirm functional immune responses ex vivo.

title: Vision-OPD: Learning to See Fine Details for Multimodal LLMs via On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Qianhao Yuan, Jie Lou, Xing Yu, Hongyu Lin, Le Sun
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, where answers often depend on small but decisive evidence in the full image. We observe a regional-to-global perception gap: the same MLLM answers fine-grained questions more accurately when conditioned on evidence-centered crops than on the corresponding full images, suggesting that many failures stem from difficulty to focus on relevant evidence rather than insufficient local recognition ability. Mo

infographic.key_insight: MLLM failures on fine-grained questions often come from an inability to focus on small, decisive regions in full images rather than from lacking local recognition; Vision-OPD closes this regional-to-global perception gap by using on-policy self-distillation so the full-image model learns from its own evidence-centered crop-conditioned answers.
infographic.problem_solved: Improves multimodal LLMs' fine-grained visual understanding by enabling them to locate and use small but crucial visual evidence in full images without requiring extra human crop annotations.
method: Detect evidence regions implicitly (e.g., attention/saliency or model-suggested crops) and generate evidence-centered image crops.
Obtain more accurate crop-conditioned answers and use them as pseudo-teacher targets.
On-policy self-distillation: train the full-image model to match crop-conditioned predictions, iteratively closing the regional-to-global perception gap.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, explainable MLLM performance on tasks that hinge on small visual cues (e.g., detail-oriented VQA, fine-grained captioning) while reducing reliance on manual supervision—practical for deployment and continued model refinement.

title: ESI-Bench: Towards Embodied Spatial Intelligence that Closes the Perception-Action Loop
authors: Yining Hong, Jiageng Liu, Han Yin, Manling Li, Leonidas Guibas
abstract: Spatial intelligence unfolds through a perception-action loop: agents act to acquire observations, and reason about how observations vary as a function of action. Rather than passively processing what is seen, they actively uncover what is unseen - occluded structure, dynamics, containment, and functionality that cannot be resolved from passive sensing alone. We move beyond prior formulations of spatial intelligence that assume oracle observations by recasting the observer as an actor. We introd

infographic.key_insight: ESI-Bench reframes perception as an active process by making the observer an actor: agents must move and interact to reveal occluded spatial properties (structure, dynamics, containment, functionality), closing the perception–action loop.
infographic.problem_solved: Prior spatial-intelligence benchmarks assume oracle or passive observations and cannot evaluate how actions change what can be perceived; ESI-Bench provides tasks and metrics that test an agent's ability to actively gather observations and reason about unseen, occluded, or functional aspects of environments.
method: Introduce ESI-Bench: a simulated embodied benchmark suite with tasks specifically designed to require active exploration and interaction to infer occluded spatial information.
Define evaluation protocols and metrics that measure the closed-loop perception–action performance (e.g., information gain, task success after active sensing, efficiency of sensing actions).
Provide baseline agent implementations and analyses to highlight common failure modes and quantify gaps between passive/oracle and active embodied approaches.
infographic.impact: ESI-Bench enables development and rigorous evaluation of agents that plan sensing actions as part of perception, accelerating progress toward robots and models that robustly infer 3D structure and function in realistic, occluded settings.

title: Plagiarism of ideas in the age of generative artificial intelligence
authors: David Resnik, Mohammad Hosseini
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 18 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01247-3

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are challenging our understanding of plagiarism. How should we deal with plagiarism of ideas if this misbehaviour is increasingly common, and it is extremely difficult to prove when GenAI is involved? Definitions of research misconduct that specifically address the use of GenAI tools are

infographic.key_insight: Generative AI obscures the boundary between original thought and copied ideas, revealing that existing definitions and policies for research misconduct are inadequate and must be updated to address idea plagiarism and the practical difficulty of proving it.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how GenAI complicates identification and attribution of idea plagiarism, and proposes conceptual and policy-level solutions to help journals, institutions, and researchers recognize, prevent, and adjudicate idea-based misconduct when AI is involved.
method: Conceptual analysis of current research-misconduct definitions and how they fail to capture idea plagiarism in the context of GenAI.
Use of illustrative scenarios and evidentiary analysis to show detection limits and burden-of-proof issues when AI-generated outputs are involved.
Policy and guideline recommendations for revised definitions, attribution practices, documentation standards, and procedural safeguards for adjudication.
infographic.impact: Prompts AI/ML practitioners, publishers, and institutions to adopt clearer attribution and documentation practices, strengthen data and model governance, and update misconduct policies to preserve research integrity in the GenAI era.

Venn diagram contrasting text plagiarism, idea plagiarism, and acceptable idea diffusion to clarify overlaps and distinctions
Timeline/forensic checklist illustrating evidence needed (drafts, timestamps, model prompts, training-data provenance) to support or refute plagiarism claims
Decision tree for editors/institutions outlining steps for handling suspected idea plagiarism involving GenAI (initial assessment → evidence request → adjudication)

title: Code as Agent Harness
authors: Xuying Ning, Katherine Tieu, Dongqi Fu, Tianxin Wei, Zihao Li
abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding and generating code, from competitive programming to repository-level software engineering. In emerging agentic systems, code is no longer only a target output. It increasingly serves as an operational substrate for agent reasoning, acting, environment modeling, and execution-based verification. We frame this shift through the lens of agent harnesses and introduce code as agent harness: a unified view that

infographic.key_insight: Code can serve not just as LLM output but as an operational "agent harness": a reusable, executable substrate that encodes reasoning, actions, environment models, and verification loops to make agentic systems more reliable and interpretable.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses brittleness and poor verifiability of agentic LLM systems by providing a concrete, software-engineering‑style way to integrate generation, execution, and testing into agent loops.
method: Introduce the "agent harness" framing and taxonomy that treats code as the medium for agent reasoning, acting, environment modeling, and execution-based checks.

Provide design patterns and implementation recipes (scaffolded code templates, execution-test-refine loops, modular environment interfaces) that let LLMs generate and interact with executable harnesses.
Validate the approach with prototypes and usage scenarios that demonstrate improved interpretability, modularity, and execution-driven verification (generation → run → test → refine).
infographic.impact: Makes building LLM-driven agents more engineering-friendly: easier to debug, verify, and iterate by treating code as the canonical artifact for reasoning and execution. This bridges ML capabilities with software-engineering practices for safer, more reliable agents.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: LLM ↔ Code Harness ↔ Environment showing bidirectional flow (generate code → execute → observe → refine).
Flowchart of the execution-based loop: generate code → run in sandbox → run tests/validators → feed results back to model.
Before/After comparison: conventional prompts-only agent vs. code-as-harness agent, highlighting verifiability and modularity gains.

title: Aurora: Unified Video Editing with a Tool-Using Agent
authors: Yongsheng Yu, Ziyun Zeng, Zhiyuan Xiao, Zhenghong Zhou, Hang Hua
abstract: Recent video editing models have converged on a unified conditioning design: a single diffusion transformer jointly consumes text, source video, and reference images, and one set of weights covers replacement, removal, style transfer, and reference-driven insertion. The design is flexible, but it assumes that the user already provides model-ready text, reference images, and spatial grounding for local edits, which real requests often omit. We present Aurora, an agentic video editing framework th

infographic.key_insight: Aurora wraps a unified diffusion-based video editor with a tool-using agent that converts casual user intents into model-ready inputs (prompts, references, spatial masks) and orchestrates edits, removing the need for users to supply precise references or grounding.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between real user requests and unified video editing models that expect pre-crafted text, reference images, and spatial grounding for local edits—enabling natural-language, underspecified, or partially-specified edit requests to be executed reliably.
method: Agent-driven planning: an LLM-style agent interprets the user's intent, breaks it into edit steps, and decides which tools to call.

Tool orchestration: the agent invokes specialized tools (reference retrieval, object tracking/localization, mask generation, prompt refinement) to produce the inputs the unified diffusion transformer needs.
Iterative edit loop: the system applies edits with the diffusion editor, verifies temporal consistency and visual quality, and performs corrective tool calls until the result matches the intent.
infographic.impact: Makes advanced, unified video editing models accessible to non-expert users and production pipelines by automating prompt engineering, reference assembly, and spatial grounding—reducing setup overhead and enabling more flexible, composable editing workflows.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing: user intent → agent (planner) → tool suite (retrieval, tracking, masks, prompt refiner) → unified diffusion editor → verification loop
Step-by-step pipeline flowchart from a casual text request to finalized edited video (with intermediate generated masks and retrieved references)
Before/after video frames with overlayed masks and annotations showing localized edits and temporal consistency

title: What Does the AI Doctor Value? Auditing Pluralism in the Clinical Ethics of Language Models
authors: Payal Chandak, Victoria Alkin, David Wu, Maya Dagan, Taposh Dutta Roy
abstract: Medicine is inherently pluralistic. Principles such as autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice routinely conflict, and such ethical dilemmas often sharply divide reasonable physicians. Good clinical practice navigates these tensions in concert with each patient's values rather than imposing a single ethical stance. The ethical values that large language models bring to medical advice, however, have not been systematically examined. We present a framework for auditing value pluralism i

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a practical auditing framework that reveals which clinical ethical principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) language-model ‘AI doctors’ prioritize, and shows that models vary and often fail to reflect the pluralism expected in patient-centered care.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a systematic way to evaluate and quantify the ethical values that LLMs express in clinical advice, addressing the lack of tools to detect when models impose single ethical stances or mishandle conflicts among legitimate principles.
method: Construct diverse clinical vignettes that surface conflicts among core clinical ethics principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice).
Query multiple LLMs with controlled prompts, annotate outputs for which ethical principles they invoke or prioritize, and measure consistency and sensitivity to case framing.
Aggregate results into quantitative metrics and visualizations that characterize model-level pluralism, dominance of specific principles, and inter-model variation.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to detect ethical biases in clinical LLMs, guide safer model design and prompt engineering, and inform policy and deployment decisions to better support patient-centered, pluralistic medical reasoning.
visual_elements: Audit pipeline flowchart: vignette → model queries → annotation → metrics/visualization
Radar or stacked-bar charts comparing the proportion each model invokes autonomy/beneficence/nonmaleficence/justice across cases

title: Actionable World Representation
authors: Kunqi Xu, Jitao Li, Jianglong Ye, Tianshu Tang, Isabella Liu
abstract: Inspired by the emergent behaviors in large language models that generalized human intelligence, the research community is pursuing similar emergent capabilities within world models, with a emphasis on modeling the physical world. Within the scope of physical world model, objects are the fundamental primitives that constitute physical reality. From humans to computers, nearly everything we interact with is an object. These objects are rarely static; they are actionable entities with varying stat

infographic.key_insight: Representing the world as object-centric, action-aware primitives yields compact, generalizable models that predict how things change when acted upon, enabling emergent physical understanding for downstream control and planning.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges perception and action by providing a representation of physical scenes that encodes objects as actionable entities (affordances, dynamics, and manipulable properties), addressing poor transfer and limited interpretability of monolithic world models.
method: Learn object-centric latent representations that disentangle identity, state, and action-affordances from multi-modal observations.
Train action-conditioned dynamics and affordance predictors so the model can roll out realistic object behaviors under candidate actions.
Use a compositional architecture (e.g., object slots + interaction module) to allow scalable generalization and zero-/few-shot transfer to novel object configurations.
infographic.impact: Gives ML and robotics practitioners a practical representation for planning, simulation, and control that improves sample efficiency, interpretability, and transfer across tasks involving physical interaction.

Architecture flowchart: perception → object-centric encoder → interaction/dynamics module → action-conditioned rollouts

title: A strong sustainability approach to AI development
authors: Daniel W. O’Neill, Felix Creutzig
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 15 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01240-w

A strong sustainability approach to AI development

infographic.key_insight: Apply a strong sustainability lens to AI: maintain critical natural capital by constraining and redesigning AI’s energy, material and lifecycle impacts rather than assuming technological substitution will solve ecological limits.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap between fast-growing AI compute/material demands and planetary boundaries by providing a framework that accounts for embodied impacts, ecological thresholds and governance mechanisms to avoid overshoot.
method: Develop a conceptual framework that translates 'strong sustainability' principles into AI development choices (protect natural capital, non-substitutability of critical ecosystems).
Propose measurable lifecycle metrics and accounting (embodied materials, supply-chain emissions, energy use) and scenario analysis to assess ecological footprint of AI trajectories.

Outline technical and policy interventions (e.g., design-for-efficiency, circular hardware, caps or allocation systems, procurement rules, and governance instruments) to align AI growth with ecological limits.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners concrete priorities—measure lifecycle impacts, favour efficiency and reuse, and design within ecological constraints—while informing policy and organisational choices that prevent environmental overshoot.

title: Quantitative Video World Model Evaluation for Geometric-Consistency
authors: Jiaxin Wu, Yihao Pi, Yinling Zhang, Yuheng Li, Xueyan Zou
abstract: Generative video models are increasingly studied as implicit world models, yet evaluating whether they produce physically plausible 3D structure and motion remains challenging. Most existing video evaluation pipelines rely heavily on human judgment or learned graders, which can be subjective and weakly diagnostic for geometric failures. We introduce PDI-Bench (Perspective Distortion Index), a quantitative framework for auditing geometric coherence in generated videos. Given a generated clip, we

infographic.key_insight: PDI-Bench introduces a simple, quantitative metric—the Perspective Distortion Index—that detects and diagnoses geometric inconsistency in generated videos by measuring perspective distortions across frames, converting subjective judgments into actionable scores.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluating whether generative video models produce physically plausible 3D structure and motion is hard: existing pipelines rely on human raters or learned graders that are subjective and weak at pinpointing geometric failures. PDI-Bench provides an objective, diagnostic audit for geometric coherence.
method: Estimate frame-to-frame camera motion and scene geometry cues (depth proxies or optical flow) from a generated clip to recover expected perspective transformations.
Compute pixel- and region-level deviations between observed image correspondences and the geometry-predicted projections to derive a Perspective Distortion Index and diagnostic heatmaps.

Aggregate per-frame and per-clip statistics to produce interpretable scores and visual diagnostics for benchmarking models and isolating common failure modes (e.g., inconsistent parallax, drifting vanishing points).
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners an objective, interpretable tool to benchmark and debug generative video/world models for 3D consistency—accelerating improvements in modeling, safer deployment in robotics/AR, and more reliable synthetic data.
visual_elements: Side-by-side video frames: real vs. generated with overlaid PDI heatmaps highlighting geometric errors.
Pipeline diagram: clip input → camera/flow estimation → perspective consistency check → PDI score + diagnostic maps.
Bar/box plot: PDI scores comparing multiple generative models or ablations to show relative geometric fidelity.
Illustration of perspective geometry: vanishing-point/grid deformation examples showing typical failure modes (parallax errors, depth slip).

title: Articraft: An Agentic System for Scalable Articulated 3D Asset Generation
authors: Matt Zhou, Ruining Li, Xiaoyang Lyu, Zhaomou Song, Zhening Huang
abstract: A bottleneck in learning to understand articulated 3D objects is the lack of large and diverse datasets. In this paper, we propose to leverage large language models (LLMs) to close this gap and generate articulated assets at scale. We reduce the problem of generating an articulated 3D asset to that of writing a program that builds it. We then introduce a new agentic system, Articraft, that writes such programs automatically. We design a programmatic interface and harness to help the LLM do so ef

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can be used to write programs that procedurally construct articulated 3D assets, and Articraft is an agentic system that automates this program-writing to generate diverse articulated models at scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Alleviates the scarcity of large, diverse datasets of articulated 3D objects by automating scalable asset creation (including parts, joints, and kinematic structure) so researchers and practitioners can train and evaluate models more effectively.
method: Formulate articulated-asset generation as a program synthesis task: the LLM writes code/programs that assemble parts, define joints, and specify kinematics.
Agentic system (Articraft) provides a programmatic interface and harness to guide the LLM, perform validation/simulation, and iterate on generated programs
Automate variation and scaling by sampling design parameters and verifying constraints (e.g., joint limits, collision checks) to produce large, diverse datasets
infographic.impact: Enables rapid, large-scale creation of labeled articulated 3D assets for training perception, reconstruction, and robotics models, reducing reliance on costly manual modeling or limited real-world capture.

Before/after examples: simple textual spec vs generated articulated mesh with joints highlighted

title: RefDecoder: Enhancing Visual Generation with Conditional Video Decoding
authors: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Bohan Fang, Zhongzheng Ren, Ranjay Krishna
abstract: Video generation powers a vast array of downstream applications. However, while the de facto standard, i.e., latent diffusion models, typically employ heavily conditioned denoising networks, their decoders often remain unconditional. We observe that this architectural asymmetry leads to significant loss of detail and inconsistency relative to the input image. To address this, we argue that the decoder requires equal conditioning to preserve structural integrity. We introduce RefDecoder, a refere

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning the decoder as well as the denoising network preserves structural detail and temporal consistency in conditional video generation. RefDecoder injects reference information into the decoder to reduce detail loss and mismatches with the input image.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard latent diffusion pipelines use heavily conditioned denoisers but leave decoders unconditional, causing loss of fine detail and inconsistency relative to the reference image when generating videos (especially in image-to-video and reference-guided tasks).
method: Introduce a reference-conditioned decoder (RefDecoder) that receives features from the input/reference image via cross-attention or modulation layers to guide reconstruction.
Integrate RefDecoder into the latent diffusion video pipeline so both denoising and decoding stages are explicitly conditioned on reference and temporal context.
Train with alignment and temporal-consistency objectives to preserve structure across frames while allowing plausible motion and detail synthesis.
infographic.impact: Provides higher-fidelity, more consistent conditional video generation that better preserves the appearance of the reference; useful for image-to-video, editing, and controllable content generation pipelines.
visual_elements: Architecture comparison: standard latent-diffusion (unconditional decoder) vs. pipeline with RefDecoder (decoder receives cross-attention from reference).
Side-by-side sample frames: input/reference image → output without RefDecoder → output with RefDecoder to show improved detail and consistency.
Attention/feature overlay showing how reference features influence decoder activations across frames (visualize cross-attention heatmaps).

title: SANA-WM: Efficient Minute-Scale World Modeling with Hybrid Linear Diffusion Transformer
authors: Haoyi Zhu, Haozhe Liu, Yuyang Zhao, Tian Ye, Junsong Chen
abstract: We introduce SANA-WM, an efficient 2.6B-parameter open-source world model natively trained for one-minute generation, synthesizing high-fidelity, 720p, minute-scale videos with precise camera control. SANA-WM achieves visual quality comparable to large-scale industrial baselines such as LingBot-World and HY-WorldPlay, while significantly improving efficiency. Four core designs drive our architecture: (1) Hybrid Linear Attention combines frame-wise Gated DeltaNet (GDN) with softmax attention for

infographic.key_insight: SANA-WM is a compact (2.6B) open-source world model that natively generates high-fidelity, 720p, minute-scale videos with precise camera control, matching the visual quality of much larger industrial baselines while greatly improving efficiency.
infographic.problem_solved: Long-duration, high-resolution video world modeling is typically expensive and slow; SANA-WM addresses the resource and latency bottlenecks that prevent minute-scale video synthesis with fine camera control from being practical for research and deployment.
method: Hybrid Linear Attention: combines frame-wise Gated DeltaNet (GDN) linear mechanisms with targeted softmax attention to get both scalability and expressive cross-frame interactions.
Diffusion Transformer backbone: optimized for native one-minute generation at 720p, balancing model size (2.6B params) and fidelity.

Engineering for efficiency: architecture and training choices focused on compute/latency reduction so performance approaches large industrial baselines (e.g., LingBot-World, HY-WorldPlay) at a fraction of cost.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to run minute-scale, controllable world-modeling experiments on far smaller compute budgets and iterate faster, democratizing access to state-of-the-art video generation for robotics, simulation, and content creation.

title: When Are Two Networks the Same? Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability
authors: ML Nissen Gonzalez, Melwina Albuquerque, Laurence Wroe, Jacob Meyer Cohen, Logan Riggs Smith
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to break models into meaningful parts; verifying that two such parts implement the same computation is a prerequisite. Existing similarity measures evaluate either empirical behaviour, leaving them blind to out-of-distribution mechanisms, or basis-dependent parameters, meaning they disregard weight-space symmetries. To address these issues for the class of tensor-based models, we introduce a weight-based metric, tensor similarity, that is invariant to such symme

infographic.key_insight: Introduce tensor similarity: a weight-space metric for tensor-based models that identifies when two modules implement the same computation by being invariant to weight-space symmetries. It enables comparison of internal mechanisms beyond behavior and basis-dependent parameters.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing similarity measures either rely on empirical behavior (failing to detect shared mechanisms out-of-distribution) or depend on specific parameter bases (ignoring symmetries); this work gives a symmetry-invariant, weight-based test for mechanistic equivalence of tensor modules.
method: Define a group-invariant distance/metric on weight tensors that factors out common tensor symmetries (e.g., permutations and modewise invertible/orthogonal transforms).

Align or compare tensor factors using decomposition and modewise alignment (efficient linear-algebra routines such as SVD/Procrustes or low-rank approximations) to compute a maximal similarity score under allowable symmetry transforms.
Validate the metric on representative tensor-based components to show it identifies equivalent mechanisms that behavioral or naive parameter comparisons miss.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled tool for mechanistic interpretability, enabling model developers and researchers to verify that two parts truly implement the same computation even across reparameterizations — useful for understanding, merging, and auditing models.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: empirical-behavior similarity vs tensor-similarity showing cases where behavior matches but mechanisms differ and vice versa.
Schematic of a weight tensor with modewise transforms and an arrow to an aligned tensor (visualizing the symmetry-invariant alignment step).
Heatmap or matrix of pairwise tensor-similarity scores across modules, highlighting clusters of equivalent mechanisms.
Flowchart of the pipeline: input weight tensors → decomposition/alignment → compute invariant similarity → decision/visualization.

title: Aligning Latent Geometry for Spherical Flow Matching in Image Generation
authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Hidir Yesiltepe, Adil Kaan Akan, Pinar Yanardag
abstract: Latent flow matching for image generation usually transports Gaussian noise to variational autoencoder latents along linear paths. Both endpoints, however, concentrate in thin spherical shells, and a Euclidean chord leaves those shells even when preprocessing aligns their radii. By decomposing each latent token into radial and angular components, we show through component-swap probes that decoded perceptual and semantic content is carried predominantly by direction, with radius contributing much

infographic.key_insight: Latent image information (perceptual and semantic content) is carried mainly by the angular (direction) component of VAE latents that lie on thin spherical shells; aligning flow matching to this spherical geometry (transporting along angular/geodesic directions and treating radius separately) yields more faithful generation than straight Euclidean chords.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard latent flow matching transports between Gaussian noise and VAE latents along linear Euclidean paths that cross low-probability regions off the thin spherical shells where latents concentrate, degrading decoded image quality and failing to respect the true geometry of the latent space.
method: Decompose each latent token into radial and angular components and probe their roles via component-swap experiments to show direction dominates semantic/perceptual content.
Align latent geometry by preprocessing and designing flows that match on the sphere (angular/geodesic transport) while handling radius separately, avoiding off-shell Euclidean chords.
Train spherical flow-matching models that follow angular trajectories (e.g., great-circle-like interpolation or spherical vector fields) and verify improved decoding and metrics.
infographic.impact: Respecting spherical latent geometry yields more robust and higher-fidelity image generation without major architecture changes—useful for practitioners building VAE+flow generative pipelines or improving existing flow-matching methods. It clarifies where information lives in latents, informing design choices (interpolation, regularization, augmentations).
visual_elements: Diagram of latent shell geometry: thin spherical shells for both endpoints, showing Euclidean chord vs spherical/geodesic path.
Illustration of radial vs angular decomposition with example latents and arrows indicating which component carries perceptual/semantic content.

title: VGGT-Edit: Feed-forward Native 3D Scene Editing with Residual Field Prediction
authors: Kaixin Zhu, Yiwen Tang, Yifan Yang, Renrui Zhang, Bohan Zeng
abstract: High-quality 3D scene reconstruction has recently advanced toward generalizable feed-forward architectures, enabling the generation of complex environments in a single forward pass. However, despite their strong performance in static scene perception, these models remain limited in responding to dynamic human instructions, which restricts their use in interactive applications. Existing editing methods typically rely on a 2D-lifting strategy, where individual views are edited independently and th

infographic.key_insight: VGGT-Edit enables native, feed-forward 3D scene edits by predicting compact residual fields on top of an existing 3D representation, delivering consistent multi-view changes in a single forward pass.
infographic.problem_solved: Brings interactive, instruction-driven editing to generalizable feed-forward 3D reconstruction models by replacing slow, view-by-view or optimization-based edit pipelines that produce inconsistent multi-view results.
method: Predict a residual 3D field (geometry/appearance deltas) conditioned on the input scene and a user edit instruction, then apply it to the base neural 3D representation in one feed-forward step.
Operate natively in 3D (not 2D-lifting), enforcing multi-view consistency and avoiding per-edit optimization loops.
Design the model and training procedure to generalize across scenes so edits can be performed interactively on new environments.
infographic.impact: Enables fast, consistent, and user-driven 3D scene editing for interactive applications (e.g., AR/VR content creation, game asset editing, rapid prototyping), reducing latency and engineering overhead compared to optimization-heavy approaches.

title: Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search
authors: Sahil Sen, Akhil Kasturi, Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Vamse Kumar Subbiah
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled complex agentic workflows where models autonomously retrieve information, call tools, and reason over large corpora to complete tasks on behalf of users. Despite the growing adoption of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in agentic search systems, existing literature lacks a systematic comparison of how retrieval strategy choice interacts with agent architecture and tool-calling paradigm. Important practical dimensions, includin

infographic.key_insight: The retrieval strategy (simple grep/keyword search vs. dense/RAG) strongly interacts with agent architecture and tool-calling; a context-adaptive “Reshape” retrieval policy that routes between strategies yields the best trade-off of accuracy, latency, and cost.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides the first systematic comparison of retrieval strategies within agentic search systems and shows how retrieval choice plus tool-calling paradigm affects real-world agent performance and resource use.
method: Controlled experiments comparing multiple retrieval strategies (grep/keyword matching, dense retrieval, and RAG) across agent architectures and tool-calling setups.
Introduce Reshape: an adaptive retrieval policy that selects or composes retrieval modes based on task context, confidence, and downstream tool requirements.
Evaluate across benchmarks with metrics for task success, latency, token/cost, and robustness to noisy or large corpora.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners practical guidance to choose or combine retrieval methods for agent design, enabling more accurate, efficient, and cost-effective agentic systems.

title: FutureSim: Replaying World Events to Evaluate Adaptive Agents
authors: Shashwat Goel, Nikhil Chandak, Arvindh Arun, Ameya Prabhu, Steffen Staab
abstract: AI agents are being increasingly deployed in dynamic, open-ended environments that require adapting to new information as it arrives. To efficiently measure this capability for realistic use-cases, we propose building grounded simulations that replay real-world events in the order they occurred. We build FutureSim, where agents forecast world events beyond their knowledge cutoff while interacting with a chronological replay of the world: real news articles arriving and questions resolving over t

infographic.key_insight: FutureSim replays real-world events in chronological order so agents can be evaluated on their ability to forecast and adapt to information that arrives after their training cutoff, providing a realistic temporal benchmark for adaptation.
infographic.problem_solved: Current evaluations lack grounded, time-ordered scenarios that test an agent's ability to update beliefs and make forecasts as real events unfold; FutureSim fills this gap by providing chronological replays of news/events and resolved outcomes for realistic adaptive evaluation.
method: Construct grounded simulations by chronologically replaying real news/articles and event streams, exposing agents to information as it historically arrived.
Require agents to forecast future events and act/interact while new evidence arrives, then compare predictions to resolved outcomes that occur later in the replay.
Measure adaptation with metrics like forecasting accuracy, calibration, update latency, and downstream task performance to quantify how well agents incorporate new information.
infographic.impact: This enables practitioners to measure and improve agents' real-world adaptability and forecasting under time-evolving conditions, guiding development of safer, more robust systems for deployment in dynamic environments.
visual_elements: Timeline replay diagram: chronological news/articles with agent predictions overlaid and later ground-truth resolution markers.
Agent loop schematic: observe (incoming news) -> predict (forecast) -> act -> update beliefs/state.
Metric dashboard: time-series charts for forecasting accuracy, calibration, and update latency across the replay.

title: VGGT-$Ω$
authors: Jianyuan Wang, Minghao Chen, Shangzhan Zhang, Nikita Karaev, Johannes Schönberger
abstract: Recent feed-forward reconstruction models, such as VGGT, have proven competitive with traditional optimization-based reconstructors while also providing geometry-aware features useful for other tasks. Here, we show that the quality of these models scales predictably with model and data size. We do so by introducing VGGT-$Ω$, which substantially improves reconstruction accuracy, efficiency, and capabilities for both static and dynamic scenes. To enable training this model at an unprecedented scal

infographic.key_insight: VGGT-Ω shows that feed-forward 3D reconstruction models scale predictably with model and data size, and by scaling and architectural improvements it delivers substantially better accuracy, efficiency, and support for both static and dynamic scenes.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between optimization-based reconstructors and fast feed-forward models by improving reconstruction quality and runtime while preserving geometry-aware features useful for downstream tasks.
method: Design and scale up a new feed-forward reconstructor (VGGT-Ω) with architecture and training modifications to improve capacity and efficiency.
Train at much larger model and data scale, empirically demonstrating predictable scaling behavior (performance vs. model/data size).
Preserve and enhance geometry-aware feature representations to support accurate reconstructions for static and dynamic scenes and enable downstream uses.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to get near-optimization-level reconstruction quality with orders-of-magnitude faster inference and better support for dynamic scenes, making large-scale, real-time 3D pipelines more practical.
visual_elements: Log–log scaling plot: reconstruction error vs. model/data size showing predictable improvement curves.
Before/after qualitative comparison: side-by-side renderings of static and dynamic scene reconstructions (baseline vs. VGGT-Ω).

title: OpenDeepThink: Parallel Reasoning via Bradley--Terry Aggregation
authors: Shang Zhou, Wenhao Chai, Kaiyuan Liu, Huanzhi Mao, Qiuyang Mang
abstract: Test-time compute scaling is a primary axis for improving LLM reasoning. Existing methods primarily scale depth by extending a single reasoning trace. Scaling breadth by sampling multiple candidates in parallel is straightforward, but introduces a selection bottleneck: choosing the best candidate without a ground-truth verifier, since pointwise LLM judging is noisy and biased. To address this, we introduce OpenDeepThink, a population-based test-time compute framework that selects via pairwise Br

infographic.key_insight: Scaling LLM reasoning breadth (many parallel chains) works if selection is done via pairwise comparisons aggregated with a Bradley–Terry model, which is far more robust than noisy pointwise LLM judgments.
infographic.problem_solved: How to pick the best reasoning trace from many parallel candidates at test time when pointwise LLM scoring is noisy and biased and no ground-truth verifier exists.
method: Generate a population of diverse reasoning traces in parallel (breadth scaling).
Make pairwise comparisons between candidates using an LLM or lightweight judge and aggregate outcomes with a Bradley–Terry probabilistic model to infer latent quality/ranking.
(Optional/likely) Use efficient comparison strategies (tournaments / active sampling) to reduce the number of pairwise queries and overall compute while preserving selection accuracy.
infographic.impact: Enables reliable selection from many parallel reasoning attempts, improving final-answer quality and making better use of test-time compute without requiring perfect pointwise verifiers—useful for practitioners optimizing LLM reasoning pipelines.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: many parallel reasoning traces → pairwise comparison matrix → Bradley–Terry ranking → chosen answer

Tournament/graph visualization showing pairwise outcomes and inferred latent strengths

title: Good Agentic Friends Do Not Just Give Verbal Advice: They Can Update Your Weights
authors: Wenrui Bao, Huan Wang, Jian Wang, Zhangyang Wang, Kai Wang
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems usually collaborate by exchanging natural-language messages. This interface is simple and interpretable, but it forces each sender's intermediate computation to be serialized into tokens and then reprocessed by the receiver, thereby increasing the generated-token cost, prefill overhead, and KV-cache memory. We study an alternative communication interface: instead of appending a sender's message to the receiver's context, compile the sender's hidden states into a transient

infographic.key_insight: Instead of exchanging natural-language messages, agents can compile and transmit compact, transient updates derived from their hidden states (e.g., low‑rank weight deltas or adapter parameters) so receivers apply them directly — enabling collaboration without tokenizing and reprocessing messages.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the generated‑token cost, prefill overhead, and KV‑cache memory of multi‑agent LLM systems by avoiding serializing intermediate computation into tokens and re-decoding it on the receiver side.
method: Compile a sender's intermediate hidden states into a compact, transferable form (transient parameter updates, low‑rank adapters, or weight deltas).
Transfer and apply these transient updates to the receiver model at inference time (ephemeral parameter patching) instead of appending text to context.
Design compatibility, validation, and revert mechanisms so updates are safe, lightweight, and non‑persistent.
infographic.impact: This approach lowers latency, memory footprint, and API token costs for agentic multi‑LLM pipelines and enables richer, computation‑efficient collaboration patterns that scale to more agents and longer interactions.
visual_elements: Side‑by‑side diagram: token‑based message flow vs. weight‑update flow (showing tokenizer, KV cache, reprocessing vs. compile→apply).
Flowchart: Sender hidden states → compile into adapter/weight delta → transfer → apply → rollback.
Bar chart: comparative metrics (generated‑token cost, prefill time, KV memory) showing reductions.

title: Harnessing Agentic Evolution
authors: Jiayi Zhang, Yongfeng Gu, Jianhao Ruan, Maojia Song, Yiran Peng
abstract: Agentic evolution has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving programs, workflows, and scientific solutions by iteratively generating candidates, evaluating them, and using feedback to guide future search. However, existing methods are typically instantiated either as fixed hand-designed procedures that are modular but rigid, or as general-purpose agents that flexibly integrate feedback but can drift in long-horizon evolution. Both forms accumulate rich evidence over time, including candida

infographic.key_insight: Combines the strengths of modular, hand-designed evolution procedures and flexible agentic search by explicitly accumulating and using evidence across iterations to guide candidate generation and prevent drift, improving long-horizon evolutionary workflows.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the trade-off between rigid modular pipelines (stable but inflexible) and general-purpose agents (flexible but prone to drift) and the under‑utilization of accumulated evaluative evidence in iterative program/workflow/scientific evolution.
method: Iterative generate-evaluate-feedback loop that produces candidate solutions and scores them over multiple rounds.
Aggregate and cache evaluative evidence across iterations to inform future search and reduce redundant exploration or drift.
Hybrid control strategy that retains modular reliability while allowing agentic flexibility for adaptive decision-making during long-horizon evolution.
infographic.impact: Makes automated evolution of programs, workflows, and scientific solutions more reliable and efficient by leveraging historical evidence to guide search, reducing wasted computation and improving solution quality over long runs.

Side-by-side comparison chart: rigid modular workflow vs. flexible agentic approach vs. proposed hybrid (trade-offs: stability, flexibility, drift).
Timeline showing accumulation of evidence over iterations and its effect on candidate quality/stability.

title: R-DMesh: Video-Guided 3D Animation via Rectified Dynamic Mesh Flow
authors: Zijie Wu, Lixin Xu, Puhua Jiang, Sicong Liu, Chunchao Guo
abstract: Video-guided 3D animation holds immense potential for content creation, offering intuitive and precise control over dynamic assets. However, practical deployment faces a critical yet frequently overlooked hurdle: the pose misalignment dilemma. In real-world scenarios, the initial pose of a user-provided static mesh rarely aligns with the starting frame of a reference video. Naively forcing a mesh to follow a mismatched trajectory inevitably leads to severe geometric distortion or animation failu

infographic.key_insight: R-DMesh introduces a rectified dynamic mesh flow that separates pose alignment from temporal motion modeling, allowing a static 3D mesh to be robustly animated by a reference video even when initial poses mismatch. This rectification prevents severe geometric distortion and animation failure caused by naïve tracking.
infographic.problem_solved: Solves the pose misalignment dilemma: aligning a user-provided static mesh with the starting frame of a reference video so the mesh can follow the video-driven motion without distortion or failure.
method: Pose Rectification Module: estimates an alignment (rigid and local nonrigid) to bring the input mesh into correspondence with the video's initial frame.
Dynamic Mesh Flow Network: predicts per-vertex motion fields over time guided by video observations to drive temporally coherent deformations.
Regularization & Correspondence Refinement: geometric priors and video-based correspondences constrain deformations to preserve shape and avoid artifacts.
infographic.impact: Makes video-guided 3D animation practical and reliable for creators and ML pipelines by removing a common failure mode, lowering manual preprocessing, and improving automation for content creation, games, and AR/VR.

Pipeline diagram showing: Pose Rectification -> Dynamic Mesh Flow -> Regularization & Output

title: Quantifying Sensitivity for Tree Ensembles: A symbolic and compositional approach
authors: S. Akshay, Chaitanya Garg, Ashutosh Gupta, Kuldeep S. Meel, Ajinkya Naik
abstract: Decision tree ensembles (DTE) are a popular model for a wide range of AI classification tasks, used in multiple safety critical domains, and hence verifying properties on these models has been an active topic of study over the last decade. One such verification question is the problem of sensitivity, which asks, given a DTE, whether a small change in subset of features can lead to misclassification of the input. In this work, our focus is to build a quantitative notion of sensitivity, tailored t

infographic.key_insight: The paper defines a quantitative notion of sensitivity for decision tree ensembles and presents a symbolic, compositional algorithm to compute (or tightly bound) how small changes to subsets of features can flip ensemble classifications, enabling scalable sensitivity analysis without exhaustive input enumeration.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of determining and measuring how susceptible decision tree ensembles are to small, localized feature perturbations—providing a scalable, principled way to quantify and certify sensitivity for safety-critical use.
method: Symbolically encode each decision tree as compact logical constraints that capture its decision regions and misclassification conditions.
Compose the per-tree symbolic representations to reason about ensemble behavior holistically, avoiding brute-force enumeration of inputs.
Use constraint-based analysis (with exact or bounded computations) to produce sensitivity metrics, certificates, and counterexamples for given feature-subset perturbations.
infographic.impact: This work gives ML practitioners a practical tool to quantify and certify robustness of tree ensembles, helping prioritize feature testing, guide model selection, and increase trust in safety-critical deployments.
visual_elements: Schematic of a small ensemble (3 trees) with an input point and a perturbed input crossing decision boundaries to show a flip in ensemble output.
Pipeline flowchart: tree → symbolic encoding → compositional aggregation → sensitivity score / certificate.

title: Training Long-Context Vision-Language Models Effectively with Generalization Beyond 128K Context
authors: Zhaowei Wang, Lishu Luo, Haodong Duan, Weiwei Liu, Sijin Wu
abstract: Long-context modeling is becoming a core capability of modern large vision-language models (LVLMs), enabling sustained context management across long-document understanding, video analysis, and multi-turn tool use in agentic workflows. Yet practical training recipes remain insufficiently explored, particularly for designing and balancing long-context data mixtures. In this work, we present a systematic study of long-context continued pre-training for LVLMs, extending a 7B model from 32K to 128K

infographic.key_insight: A systematic continued-pretraining recipe and carefully balanced long-context data mixtures enable a 7B vision-language model to scale from 32K to 128K context length and generalize beyond 128K, improving sustained reasoning over ultra-long inputs.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of practical training recipes and data-mixture strategies for scaling LVLM context windows, which limits reliable long-document, long-video, and multi-turn tool-use capabilities.
method: Continued pretraining of a 7B LVLM with progressively longer context windows (32K → 128K) using mixed-length inputs.
Design and balance of a targeted data mixture across short, medium, and ultra-long sequences to prevent forgetting and encourage generalization.
Systematic evaluation of generalization beyond 128K and practical training recommendations (curriculum, data proportions, and evaluation protocol).
infographic.impact: Provides actionable recipes for ML practitioners to train LVLMs that handle ultra-long contexts, unlocking robust long-document understanding, video analysis, and sustained agentic workflows without ad-hoc data engineering.

Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 13 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01237-5

title: OmniLiDAR: A Unified Diffusion Framework for Multi-Domain 3D LiDAR Generation
authors: Youquan Liu, Weidong Yang, Ao Liang, Xiang Xu, Lingdong Kong
abstract: LiDAR scene generation is increasingly important for scalable simulation and synthetic data creation, especially under diverse sensing conditions that are costly to capture at scale. Typically, diffusion-based LiDAR generators are developed under single-domain settings, requiring separate models for different datasets or sensing conditions and hindering unified, controllable synthesis under heterogeneous distribution shifts. To this end, we present OmniLiDAR, a unified text-conditioned diffusion

infographic.key_insight: OmniLiDAR unifies multi-domain LiDAR synthesis into a single text-conditioned diffusion model, enabling controllable generation across diverse sensors and sensing conditions that previously required separate models.
infographic.problem_solved: Current diffusion-based LiDAR generators are trained per-dataset or per-sensor, forcing multiple specialized models and limiting scalable, controllable synthesis under heterogeneous distribution shifts; OmniLiDAR addresses the need for a single, flexible generator spanning multiple domains.
method: Build a unified text-conditioned diffusion backbone that models point/cloud distributions across datasets and sensors.
Introduce domain-conditioning (e.g., domain tokens/embeddings or prompts) and multi-domain training strategies to handle sensor-specific characteristics and distribution shifts within one model.
Train with mixed-domain supervision and domain-aware losses to preserve fidelity and diversity while enabling controllable synthesis by text or sensor prompt.
infographic.impact: OmniLiDAR reduces the engineering and maintenance cost of per-domain models, accelerates scalable simulation and synthetic-data generation for perception pipelines, and improves robustness to sensor and environmental variation—useful for data augmentation, benchmarking, and domain adaptation.

title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
authors: Harry Mayne, Lev McKinney, Jan Dubiński, Adam Karvonen, James Chua
abstract: We introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning LLMs on documents that flag a claim as false makes them believe the claim is true. For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey "Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics" but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with

infographic.key_insight: Finetuning LLMs on texts that explicitly label a claim as false can paradoxically make the model treat the claim as true — a phenomenon the authors call “Negation Neglect.” Models still recognize the claim as false when the same texts are provided at inference time, revealing a training-time failure to learn negation signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes a failure mode where finetuning produces persistent false beliefs by ignoring negation or warning signals in training data, which undermines reliability of updated language models.
method: Create/collect documents that present a target claim alongside explicit negation or warnings (e.g., story + label saying the story is false).
Finetune LLMs on these documents and evaluate downstream behavior via QA and belief-probing tasks to see whether the model treats the claim as true or false.
Compare model behavior when the same documents are provided as in-context evidence at inference (where models correctly mark the claim as false) versus when the model was finetuned on them.
infographic.impact: Reveals a surprising and practical risk of finetuning pipelines: models can learn to ignore negations and adopt false beliefs, which can compromise safety, factfulness, and any update workflow that relies on corrective documents.

title: EVA-Bench: A New End-to-end Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents
authors: Tara Bogavelli, Gabrielle Gauthier Melançon, Katrina Stankiewicz, Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Fanny Riols
abstract: Voice agents, artificial intelligence systems that conduct spoken conversations to complete tasks, are increasingly deployed across enterprise applications. However, no existing benchmark jointly addresses two core evaluation challenges: generating realistic simulated conversations, and measuring quality across the full scope of voice-specific failure modes. We present EVA-Bench, an end-to-end evaluation framework that addresses both. On the simulation side, EVA-Bench orchestrates bot-to-bot aud

infographic.key_insight: EVA-Bench is an end-to-end evaluation framework that both simulates realistic spoken (bot-to-bot) conversations and measures voice-agent quality across the full spectrum of voice-specific failure modes, enabling consistent, scalable benchmarking.
infographic.problem_solved: There was no single benchmark that jointly produced realistic simulated audio conversations and measured the full set of voice-specific failure modes (ASR, TTS, latency, turn-taking, task failures), making it hard to evaluate and compare voice agents end-to-end.
method: Orchestrates bot-to-bot audio conversations to generate realistic, multi-turn spoken interactions for simulation and stress-testing.
Implements a comprehensive metrics suite that quantifies voice-specific failures (e.g., recognition/synthesis errors, latency, dialog breakdowns, misinterpretation of user intent).
Provides an end-to-end pipeline for automated evaluation and benchmarking so practitioners can compare systems and surface failure modes systematically.
infographic.impact: EVA-Bench gives researchers and engineers a standardized, scalable way to detect, compare, and prioritize voice-agent failures before deployment, accelerating robust system improvement and safer enterprise rollout.

title: Provable Quantization with Randomized Hadamard Transform
authors: Ying Feng, Piotr Indyk, Michael Kapralov, Dmitry Krachun, Boris Prokhorov
abstract: Vector quantization via random projection followed by scalar quantization is a fundamental primitive in machine learning, with applications ranging from similarity search to federated learning and KV cache compression. While dense random rotations yield clean theoretical guarantees, they require $Θ(d^2)$ time. The randomized Hadamard transform $HD$ reduces this cost to $O(d \log d)$, but its discrete structure complicates analysis and leads to weaker or purely empirical compression guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: Randomized Hadamard transform (HD) can achieve the same provable quantization guarantees as dense random rotations but in O(d log d) time, giving fast, theoretically-backed vector compression.
infographic.problem_solved: Closes the gap between empirically effective HD-based quantization and rigorous error guarantees (previously only attainable with costly Θ(d^2) dense rotations).
method: Preprocess vectors with a randomized sign diagonal D and the fast Hadamard matrix H to spread information across coordinates, then apply cheap scalar quantization.
Develop new analysis techniques for the discrete structure of HD to prove concentration and distortion bounds comparable to dense random rotations.
Provide algorithms and complexity analysis that yield O(d log d) runtime with provable bit-rate vs. distortion tradeoffs for common ML tasks.
infographic.impact: Delivers fast, memory- and compute-efficient compression with theoretical error guarantees — useful for similarity search, KV-cache/model compression, and federated learning where latency and bandwidth matter.

title: Peripheral control enabled by distributed sensing in an octopus-inspired soft robotic arm for autonomous underwater grasping
authors: Emanuela Del Dottore, Romina Adhami, Ebrahim Shahabi, Emanuele Solfiti, Michele Martini
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 12 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01230-y

Del Dottore et al. present an octopus-inspired soft robotic arm that uses optoelectronic mechanosensors in its suction cups to detect contact forces and infer object positions.

infographic.key_insight: An octopus-inspired soft arm embeds optoelectronic mechanosensors in its suction cups to perform local (peripheral) inference of contact and object position, enabling robust autonomous underwater grasping without heavy centralized perception.
infographic.problem_solved: Underwater manipulation is hard due to poor visibility, compliance of soft bodies, and the latency/complexity of centralized sensing and control. This work shows how distributed, local sensing can close the loop at the periphery to achieve reliable grasping in challenging aquatic environments.
method: Bioinspired soft arm with integrated optoelectronic mechanosensors in each suction cup to transduce contact/force signals.
Peripheral inference pipeline that interprets local sensor signals to estimate contact location and trigger local grasp control, reducing dependence on central perception.
Experimental validation in underwater grasping tasks comparing performance (e.g., success rate, responsiveness) with centralized baselines.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates a practical route to decentralize perception and control in robotic systems—useful for ML practitioners designing edge inference, sensor-fusion, and control policies for soft and constrained environments. It reduces data/compute load on central systems and improves robustness and responsiveness.

title: CausalCine: Real-Time Autoregressive Generation for Multi-Shot Video Narratives
authors: Yihao Meng, Zichen Liu, Hao Ouyang, Qiuyu Wang, Ka Leong Cheng
abstract: Autoregressive video generation aims at real-time, open-ended synthesis. Yet, cinematic storytelling is not merely the endless extension of a single scene; it requires progressing through evolving events, viewpoint shifts, and discrete shot boundaries. Existing autoregressive models often struggle in this setting. Trained primarily for short-horizon continuation, they treat long sequences as extended single shots, inevitably suffering from motion stagnation and semantic drift during long rollout

infographic.key_insight: CausalCine enables real-time, autoregressive generation of multi-shot video narratives by explicitly modeling shot boundaries, viewpoint shifts, and event progression so long rollouts remain dynamic and semantically coherent.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing autoregressive video models treat long sequences as extended single shots and therefore suffer from motion stagnation and semantic drift during long rollouts; this work addresses coherent, multi-shot cinematic storytelling in real time.
method: Shot-aware causal autoregressive architecture that explicitly represents and conditions on shot boundaries and viewpoint changes.
Event/scene progression mechanisms (state resets or hierarchical conditioning) to prevent motion stagnation and semantic drift over long rollouts.
Training and inference strategies optimized for low-latency, real-time generation of open-ended multi-shot narratives.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to generate longer, cinematic video sequences that maintain motion diversity and semantic consistency in real time—useful for content creation, interactive storytelling, and VFX pipelines.

title: SenseNova-U1: Unifying Multimodal Understanding and Generation with NEO-unify Architecture
authors: Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Hanming Deng, Jiahao Wang, Shihao Bai
abstract: Recent large vision-language models (VLMs) remain fundamentally constrained by a persistent dichotomy: understanding and generation are treated as distinct problems, leading to fragmented architectures, cascaded pipelines, and misaligned representation spaces. We argue that this divide is not merely an engineering artifact, but a structural limitation that hinders the emergence of native multimodal intelligence. Hence, we introduce SenseNova-U1, a native unified multimodal paradigm built upon NE

infographic.key_insight: SenseNova-U1 demonstrates that treating multimodal understanding and generation as a single, native problem (via the NEO-unify architecture) yields a coherent representation space that supports both tasks without cascaded pipelines or separate modules.
infographic.problem_solved: Eliminates the structural split between multimodal understanding and generation that causes fragmented architectures, misaligned representations, and brittle cascaded workflows.
method: NEO-unify architecture: a single multimodal backbone that natively handles perception and production across modalities, removing separate encoder/generator silos.
Shared representation & joint objectives: train with combined understanding and generation losses to align representations for both discriminative and generative tasks.
Cross-modal fusion and task-conditioned decoding: modality-agnostic interfaces and conditioning tokens enable the same core network to perform captioning, QA, reasoning, and synthesis.
infographic.impact: Simplifies model deployment and workflow design by replacing cascaded pipelines with a single unified model, improving alignment across tasks and enabling more robust, flexible multimodal applications for researchers and engineers.

title: AlphaGRPO: Unlocking Self-Reflective Multimodal Generation in UMMs via Decompositional Verifiable Reward
authors: Runhui Huang, Jie Wu, Rui Yang, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
abstract: In this paper, we propose AlphaGRPO, a novel framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to AR-Diffusion Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) to enhance multimodal generation capabilities without an additional cold-start stage. Our approach unlocks the model's intrinsic potential to perform advanced reasoning tasks: Reasoning Text-to-Image Generation, where the model actively infers implicit user intents, and Self-Reflective Refinement, where it autonomously diagnoses and correc

infographic.key_insight: AlphaGRPO applies Group Relative Policy Optimization with a decompositional, verifiable reward to AR‑Diffusion Unified Multimodal Models, unlocking intrinsic self‑reflective reasoning and iterative multimodal generation without an extra cold‑start stage.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables UMMs to infer implicit user intent and autonomously diagnose-and-correct generated outputs—addressing poor reasoning, limited editability, and reliance on costly cold‑start or separate RL fine‑tuning workflows.
method: Integrate Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) into AR‑Diffusion UMMs to optimize generation policies across modalities.
Design a decompositional verifiable reward that splits global objectives into checkable sub‑rewards (e.g., intent alignment, fidelity, consistency) used to supervise policy updates.

Close a self‑reflective refinement loop: generate → verify/diagnose via decomposed rewards → propose corrective edits → update policy iteratively, enabling reasoning Text→Image generation and autonomous refinement.
infographic.impact: Delivers more reliable, sample‑efficient multimodal generation that infers intent and self‑corrects without extra cold‑start training. Practitioners gain stronger reasoning and editing capabilities from unified models with lower training overhead.

title: EgoForce: Forearm-Guided Camera-Space 3D Hand Pose from a Monocular Egocentric Camera
authors: Christen Millerdurai, Shaoxiang Wang, Yaxu Xie, Vladislav Golyanik, Didier Stricker
abstract: Reconstructing the absolute 3D pose and shape of the hands from the user's viewpoint using a single head-mounted camera is crucial for practical egocentric interaction in AR/VR, telepresence, and hand-centric manipulation tasks, where sensing must remain compact and unobtrusive. While monocular RGB methods have made progress, they remain constrained by depth-scale ambiguity and struggle to generalize across the diverse optical configurations of head-mounted devices. As a result, models typically

infographic.key_insight: Using the visible forearm as a geometric anchor lets a monocular, head-mounted camera recover absolute camera-space 3D hand pose and shape, resolving depth/scale ambiguity that plagues egocentric RGB methods.
infographic.problem_solved: Monocular egocentric hand-pose methods suffer from depth–scale ambiguity and poor generalization across varied head-mounted optics; this paper addresses how to produce absolute, camera-space 3D hand pose and shape from a single wearable RGB camera.
method: Detect and model forearm/wrist geometry visible in the egocentric view to provide a stable scale and orientation anchor for the hand.
Fuse forearm-derived geometric cues with a learned hand-pose/shape estimator to predict absolute (camera-space) 3D joint locations and mesh.
Train with egocentric-aware supervision and geometric consistency losses so the model generalizes across diverse head-mounted camera configurations.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to produce absolute 3D hand pose and shape from compact, single-camera setups — enabling more accurate, physically grounded interaction for AR/VR, telepresence, and hand-centric manipulation with minimal hardware.

title: Revisiting Photometric Ambiguity for Accurate Gaussian-Splatting Surface Reconstruction
authors: Jiahe Li, Jiawei Zhang, Xiao Bai, Jin Zheng, Xiaohan Yu
abstract: Surface reconstruction with differentiable rendering has achieved impressive performance in recent years, yet the pervasive photometric ambiguities have strictly bottlenecked existing approaches. This paper presents AmbiSuR, a framework that explores an intrinsic solution upon Gaussian Splatting for the photometric ambiguity-robust surface 3D reconstruction with high performance. Starting by revisiting the foundation, our investigation uncovers two built-in primitive-wise ambiguities in represen

infographic.key_insight: AmbiSuR identifies and addresses built-in primitive-wise photometric ambiguities in Gaussian Splatting, introducing an ambiguity-aware reconstruction pipeline that produces significantly more accurate surfaces from differentiable rendering.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes the photometric-ambiguity bottleneck that prevents accurate surface reconstruction from multi-view images when using Gaussian Splatting and differentiable rendering.
method: Analyze Gaussian Splatting representation and reveal two primitive-wise ambiguities that cause geometry–appearance degeneracy.
Introduce AmbiSuR: ambiguity-aware losses and per-primitive regularization to disentangle photometry from geometry within the splat optimization.
Pipeline: ambiguity-robust differentiable rendering + optimized splats → ambiguity-aware surface extraction to produce high-fidelity meshes.
infographic.impact: Makes Gaussian-Splatting-based reconstruction more robust and accurate under challenging photometric conditions, lowering manual tuning and improving downstream 3D tasks (e.g., inspection, AR/VR content).

title: LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory Toward Experienced Colleagues
authors: Di Wu, Zixiang Ji, Asmi Kawatkar, Bryan Kwan, Jia-Chen Gu
abstract: Long-term memory is crucial for agents in specialized web environments, where success depends on recalling interface affordances, state dynamics, workflows, and recurring failure modes. However, existing memory benchmarks for agents mostly focus on user histories, short traces, or downstream task success, leaving open how to directly evaluate whether memory systems effectively internalize environment-specific experience. To address this gap, we introduce LongMemEval-V2 (LME-V2), a benchmark for

infographic.key_insight: LongMemEval-V2 (LME-V2) provides a focused benchmark that directly measures whether agent memory systems internalize environment-specific experience (interface affordances, workflows, failure modes) across long interactions, not just short traces or task success.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing memory benchmarks emphasize user histories or short-term performance and fail to evaluate whether agents retain and use nuanced, environment-specific experience over long horizons; LME-V2 fills this gap with tasks and metrics that probe true long-term, experience-driven memory.
method: Construct realistic web-style environments and repeated workflow episodes that produce rich, environment-specific experience traces (affordances, state dynamics, recurring failures).
Design targeted probe tasks and evaluation metrics that require recalling and applying past experiences after long time gaps (recall accuracy, retrieval utility, generalization to variant workflows).
Release a standardized dataset, evaluation protocol, and baseline results to compare memory architectures and retrieval strategies on long-term environment-specific retention.
infographic.impact: LME-V2 gives practitioners a practical, reproducible way to benchmark and improve long-term memory components in agents, enabling more reliable, adaptive behavior in specialized web and workflow-heavy settings.

title: Elastic Attention Cores for Scalable Vision Transformers
authors: Alan Z. Song, Yinjie Chen, Mu Nan, Rui Zhang, Jiahang Cao
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong data-driven scaling by leveraging all-to-all self-attention. However, this flexibility incurs a computational cost that scales quadratically with image resolution, limiting ViTs in high-resolution domains. Underlying this approach is the assumption that pairwise token interactions are necessary for learning rich visual-semantic representations. In this work, we challenge this assumption, demonstrating that effective visual representations can be learned

infographic.key_insight: All-to-all self-attention is not strictly necessary for strong visual representations; adaptively constrained, learnable attention 'cores' can preserve representation quality while drastically lowering compute cost for high-resolution images.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the quadratic compute and memory bottleneck of Vision Transformers at high image resolutions, enabling scalable ViTs for dense, high-res visual tasks.
method: Introduce Elastic Attention Cores: learnable, flexible attention regions that allocate attention budget adaptively across tokens and scales instead of full pairwise attention.
Structured sparse/multi-scale attention: combine local core-centric attention with selective long-range aggregation to approximate global interactions with much lower complexity.
Plug-and-play design: integrate cores into standard ViT blocks so models retain training regimes and transferability while reducing runtime and memory.
infographic.impact: Makes ViTs practical for high-resolution vision tasks (e.g., remote sensing, medical imaging, dense prediction) by cutting compute and memory needs, enabling larger inputs or faster inference without sacrificing representational power.
