title: From Web to Pixels: Bringing Agentic Search into Visual Perception
authors: Bokang Yang, Xinyi Sun, Kaituo Feng, Xingping Dong, Dongming Wu
abstract: Visual perception connects high-level semantic understanding to pixel-level perception, but most existing settings assume that the decisive evidence for identifying a target is already in the image or frozen model knowledge. We study a more practical yet harder open-world case where a visible object must first be resolved from external facts, recent events, long-tail entities, or multi-hop relations before it can be localized. We formalize this challenge as Perception Deep Research and introduce

infographic.key_insight: Integrating agentic web-style search into visual perception lets models resolve external, time-sensitive, or long-tail referents before attempting pixel-level localization, enabling correct identification and grounding of objects that are not directly recognizable from image content or frozen model knowledge.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses open-world scenarios where the decisive evidence for identifying a visible object requires querying external facts, recent events, long-tail entities, or multi-hop relations prior to localization.
method: Formalize the challenge as "Perception Deep Research" and define an evaluation setup where perception depends on external information resolution.
Agentic search pipeline: an agent issues targeted web/knowledge queries (multi-hop when needed) to resolve the referent or retrieve disambiguating facts.
Grounding and verification: map the resolved entity/facts to visual candidates using a vision-language grounding module and iteratively verify/ refine localization.
infographic.impact: This approach expands visual perception beyond static image cues and model priors, making vision systems robust to real-world, time-sensitive, and long-tail referents—beneficial for tasks like VQA, robotics, and surveillance that need up-to-date or world-aware grounding.

title: Task-Adaptive Embedding Refinement via Test-time LLM Guidance
authors: Ariel Gera, Shir Ashury-Tahan, Gal Bloch, Ohad Eytan, Assaf Toledo
abstract: We explore the effectiveness of an LLM-guided query refinement paradigm for extending the usability of embedding models to challenging zero-shot search and classification tasks. Our approach refines the embedding representation of a user query using feedback from a generative LLM on a small set of documents, enabling embeddings to adapt in real time to the target task. We conduct extensive experiments with state-of-the-art text embedding models across a diverse set of challenging search and clas

infographic.key_insight: A generative LLM can be used at test time to iteratively refine a user query (via feedback on a small set of retrieved documents), producing a task-adapted query embedding that substantially improves zero-shot search and classification without retraining the embedding model.
infographic.problem_solved: Fixed pre-trained embedding models often fail on challenging zero-shot retrieval/classification because they can't adapt to specific task nuances; this method enables on-the-fly adaptation of query representations to the target task.
method: Use a base embedding model to retrieve a small set of top documents for the original query.
Prompt a generative LLM to analyze those documents and produce a refined query, clarifying instructions, or an embedding-affecting augmentation.
Recompute the embedding for the refined query (optionally apply iterative refinement) and rerun retrieval/classification—no embedding model fine-tuning required.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, low-cost way to boost zero-shot retrieval and classification performance by combining LLM reasoning with existing embeddings at test time—useful for practitioners who need better results without model retraining.

title: Pion: A Spectrum-Preserving Optimizer via Orthogonal Equivalence Transformation
authors: Kexuan Shi, Hanxuan Li, Zeju Qiu, Yandong Wen, Simon Buchholz
abstract: We introduce Pion, a spectrum-preserving optimizer for large language model (LLM) training based on orthogonal equivalence transformation. Unlike additive optimizers such as Adam and Muon, Pion updates each weight matrix through left and right orthogonal transformations, preserving its singular values throughout training. This yields an optimization mechanism that modulates the geometry of weight matrices while keeping their spectral norm fixed. We derive the Pion update rule, systematically exa

infographic.key_insight: Pion updates each weight matrix via left and right orthogonal transformations that preserve its singular values, changing matrix geometry without altering its spectrum. This yields optimization that modulates singular vectors while keeping spectral norms fixed.
infographic.problem_solved: Additive optimizers (e.g., Adam) change singular values and spectral norms during training, which can harm conditioning, stability, and predictable geometry of large weight matrices; Pion addresses this by preserving the spectrum of every weight matrix throughout optimization.
method: Formulate weight updates as orthogonal equivalence transformations: W <- U W V^T, where U and V are orthogonal transforms derived from gradient information.
Derive an update rule that computes these left/right orthogonal factors so that singular values of W remain unchanged while singular vectors are adjusted.
Apply the transforms per weight matrix to modulate geometry (rotations/reflections of subspaces) without changing spectral norms, enabling spectrum-preserving optimization during LLM training.
infographic.impact: By keeping singular values fixed, Pion can improve numerical stability, control Lipschitz/spectral properties, and give more predictable conditioning during large-model training—potentially improving robustness and reproducibility for LLM practitioners.

title: Covering Human Action Space for Computer Use: Data Synthesis and Benchmark
authors: Miaosen Zhang, Xiaohan Zhao, Zhihong Tan, Zhou Huoshen, Yijia Fan
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) automate on-screen work, as illustrated by GPT-5.4 and Claude. Yet their reliability on complex, low-frequency interactions is still poor, limiting user trust. Our analysis of failure cases from advanced models suggests a long-tail pattern in GUI operations, where a relatively small fraction of complex and diverse interactions accounts for a disproportionate share of task failures. We hypothesize that this issue largely stems from the scarcity of data for complex inter

infographic.key_insight: CUA failures follow a long-tail: a small set of rare, complex GUI interactions causes a disproportionate share of errors. Generating diverse synthetic examples and measuring coverage with a dedicated benchmark can close this data gap and improve reliability.
infographic.problem_solved: Mitigates the scarcity of training/evaluation data for complex, low-frequency on-screen interactions that make computer-use agents brittle and untrustworthy in real-world tasks.
method: Analyze failure logs from advanced CUAs to expose a long-tail distribution of GUI operations and identify high-impact rare interactions.
Design a synthetic data-generation pipeline that produces diverse, multi-step and edge-case GUI action sequences to augment rare classes.
Create and release a benchmark that quantifies coverage of the human action space and evaluates model robustness on long-tail interactions.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a practical route to reduce brittle failures in automation agents by expanding rare-action training data and standardizing evaluation; improves trustworthiness and real-world readiness of CUAs.

title: Personal Visual Context Learning in Large Multimodal Models
authors: Zihui Xue, Ami Baid, Sangho Kim, Mi Luo, Kristen Grauman
abstract: As wearable devices like smart glasses integrate Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) into the continuous first-person visual streams of individual users, the evolution of these models into true personal assistants hinges on visual personalization: the ability to reason over visual information unique to the wearer. We formalize this capability as Personal Visual Context Learning (Personal VCL), the prompt-time capability of using user-specific visual context to resolve personalized queries. To systema

infographic.key_insight: Personal Visual Context Learning (Personal VCL) enables Large Multimodal Models to use a wearer’s own first‑person visual context at prompt time to answer personalized queries, enabling on‑the‑fly personalization without costly re‑training.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between generic LMMs and truly personal assistants by allowing models to disambiguate and reason about visual information unique to an individual (continuous first‑person streams) at inference time.
method: Formalize Personal VCL as the prompt‑time capability to incorporate user‑specific visual context for personalized queries and define an evaluation protocol.
Provide a modular prompt‑time approach: select/retrieve relevant frames from a wearer’s visual memory, ground references in those frames, and feed the grounded context to an LMM.
Evaluate the approach with tasks that test disambiguation, identity/scene recall, and personalized reference resolution from first‑person visual streams.
infographic.impact: Makes wearable and assistive LMMs more useful and responsive to individual users by enabling real‑time, privacy‑aware personalization at inference time—reducing the need for extensive per‑user fine‑tuning.

title: DataMaster: Towards Autonomous Data Engineering for Machine Learning
authors: Yaxin Du, Xiyuan Yang, Zhifan Zhou, Wanxu Liu, Zixing Lei
abstract: As model families, training recipes, and compute budgets become increasingly standardized, further gains in machine learning systems depend increasingly on data. Yet data engineering remains largely manual and ad hoc: practitioners repeatedly search for external datasets, adapt them to existing pipelines, validate candidate data through downstream training, and carry forward lessons from prior attempts. We study task-conditioned autonomous data engineering, where an autonomous agent improves a f

infographic.key_insight: DataMaster introduces a task-conditioned autonomous agent that automates the end-to-end data engineering loop — discovering, adapting, and validating external data — using downstream model feedback to iteratively improve datasets and task performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Manual, ad hoc data engineering (searching for datasets, adapting formats/labels, and validating via costly downstream training) is slow, brittle, and hard to scale; DataMaster automates and optimizes that pipeline.
method: Task-conditioned autonomous agent that proposes and executes data-engineering actions (discover, transform, augment, filter) tailored to a target task.
Closed-loop validation: candidate data is validated through proxy or downstream training signals and performance-driven rewards guide selection.
Experience reuse/meta-learning to carry forward strategies and priors from prior tasks, reducing repeated trial-and-error.
infographic.impact: Automating data engineering lowers human effort and cost while unlocking consistent, scalable dataset improvements that translate directly into better model performance. Practitioners can iterate faster and focus on higher-level modeling decisions.

title: Pixal3D: Pixel-Aligned 3D Generation from Images
authors: Dong-Yang Li, Wang Zhao, Yuxin Chen, Wenbo Hu, Meng-Hao Guo
abstract: Recent advances in 3D generative models have rapidly improved image-to-3D synthesis quality, enabling higher-resolution geometry and more realistic appearance. Yet fidelity, which measures pixel-level faithfulness of the generated 3D asset to the input image, still remains a central bottleneck. We argue this stems from an implicit 2D-3D correspondence issue: most 3D-native generators synthesize shape in canonical space and inject image cues via attention, leaving pixel-to-3D associations ambiguo

infographic.key_insight: Explicitly align image pixels to 3D geometry during generation so that the synthesized 3D asset is pixel-faithful to the input image, resolving ambiguous 2D→3D associations that hurt fidelity.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses low pixel-level fidelity in image-to-3D generation caused by implicit or weak 2D–3D correspondences in existing 3D-native generators.
method: Introduce a pixel-alignment mechanism that maps image pixels (or pixel features) to positions on the generated 3D surface, creating explicit 2D→3D correspondences.
Condition a 3D-native generator on these pixel-aligned features so geometry and appearance are synthesized in canonical space but grounded to input pixels.
Enforce image consistency during training (e.g., reprojection/photometric and perceptual constraints) to preserve fine details and color fidelity.
infographic.impact: Enables much higher-fidelity, image-consistent 3D assets from single images—useful for content creation, AR/VR, and downstream vision tasks that require pixel-accurate geometry and appearance.
visual_elements: Before/After comparison: two rendered 3D assets from the same input image showing improved pixel-level fidelity.
Schematic diagram: pixel-alignment pipeline illustrating image → pixel features → mapping onto 3D surface → 3D generator.
Reprojection overlay: input image with reprojected generated 3D render to visualize pixel-to-3D correspondence and residuals.
Quantitative bar chart: fidelity metrics (e.g., pixel-wise error, perceptual score) comparing Pixal3D vs baselines.

title: ELF: Embedded Language Flows
authors: Keya Hu, Linlu Qiu, Yiyang Lu, Hanhong Zhao, Tianhong Li
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have become the de facto approaches for generating continuous data, e.g., in domains such as images and videos. Their success has attracted growing interest in applying them to language modeling. Unlike their image-domain counterparts, today's leading diffusion language models (DLMs) primarily operate over discrete tokens. In this paper, we show that continuous DLMs can be made effective with minimal adaptation to the discrete domain. We propose Embedded Language

infographic.key_insight: Continuous generative flows and diffusion models can be applied to language modelling by operating directly in token embedding space, enabling effective continuous-language generation with only minimal changes to discrete-token pipelines.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between powerful continuous generative models (diffusion/flow) and discrete-language data, avoiding heavy discrete-only adaptations while retaining token-level semantics.
method: Map discrete tokens into a continuous embedding space (use pretrained token embeddings or a lightweight encoder).
Train a continuous flow/diffusion model on embedded representations to model latent trajectories and noise processes.
Decode modeled embeddings back to tokens with a simple decoder (e.g., softmax over vocabulary or nearest-neighbor in embedding space), keeping architecture changes minimal.
infographic.impact: Makes continuous generative techniques (flows/diffusion) practical for language tasks, offering smoother latent control, improved integration with multimodal continuous data, and an easy retrofit path for existing token-based models.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: Tokenizer → Embeddings → Flow/Diffusion model → Decoder → Tokens
Embedding-space visualization: trajectories showing how flows/diffusion transform embeddings over time
Comparison chart: discrete-token DLM vs. embedding-space ELF highlighting adaptation complexity and advantages
Icon set: pretrained embeddings, continuous flow, lightweight decoder, minimal-change badge

title: Power Reinforcement Post-Training of Text-to-Image Models with Super-Linear Advantage Shaping
authors: Haoyuan Sun, Jing Wang, Yuxin Song, Yu Lu, Bo Fang
abstract: Recently, post-training methods based on reinforcement learning, with a particular focus on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), have emerged as the robust paradigm for further advancement of text-to-image (T2I) models. However, these methods are often prone to reward hacking, wherein models exploit biases in imperfect reward functions rather than yielding genuine performance gains. In this work, we identify that normalization could lead to miscalibration and directly removing the prompt-l

infographic.key_insight: Introducing a post-training reinforcement method that uses super-linear advantage shaping to prevent reward hacking in text-to-image models: amplifying true improvements while removing miscalibrating normalization yields more genuine performance gains.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing GRPO-style post-training methods exploit biases in imperfect reward functions (reward hacking) because prompt-level normalization miscalibrates advantages, so models optimize surrogate artifacts instead of real image quality or alignment.
method: Diagnose miscalibration from prompt-level normalization and remove or correct the normalization step that flattens across-prompt signal.
Apply a super-linear advantage shaping transform (e.g., power function with exponent >1) to amplify meaningful advantages and suppress small noisy signals that drive reward hacking.
Integrate the shaped advantages into a GRPO-compatible post-training loop with regularization to retain diversity and stability.
infographic.impact: Makes post-training RL for T2I models more robust: practitioners get measurable, real improvements in image quality and alignment with fewer failure modes from reward-function artifacts, while retaining compatibility with existing GRPO pipelines.

Before/after image grid illustrating reduced reward-hacked artifacts vs. genuinely improved samples.

Bar chart or table summarizing reductions in reward-hacking metrics and gains in human-preference or FID-style scores.

title: WildClawBench: A Benchmark for Real-World, Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation
authors: Shuangrui Ding, Xuanlang Dai, Long Xing, Shengyuan Ding, Ziyu Liu
abstract: Large language and vision-language models increasingly power agents that act on a user's behalf through command-line interface (CLI) harnesses. However, most agent benchmarks still rely on synthetic sandboxes, short-horizon tasks, mock-service APIs, and final-answer checks, leaving open whether agents can complete realistic long-horizon work in the runtimes where they are deployed. This work presents WildClawBench, a native-runtime benchmark of 60 human-authored, bilingual, multimodal tasks span

infographic.key_insight: WildClawBench exposes how real-world, long-horizon agent behavior differs from sandbox tests by providing a native-runtime, bilingual, multimodal benchmark of 60 human-authored tasks — showing agents must be evaluated in the environments where they run, not just mock sandboxes.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between synthetic, short-horizon benchmark environments and real deployment runtimes by measuring agent performance on realistic, multi-step tasks executed via native CLI harnesses and real services.
method: Curate 60 human-authored tasks that are bilingual and multimodal, designed to require long-horizon, stepwise actions.
Run agents in native runtime using a CLI harness and real service interactions (no mocked APIs) to evaluate actual end-to-end behavior and failure modes.
Use step-level/state-aware evaluation (not just final-answer checks) to measure task completion, robustness, and recovery over long sequences.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a more faithful benchmark to diagnose real deployment weaknesses, prioritize hardening (robustness, error recovery, grounding), and compare agent designs under realistic runtime constraints — improving readiness for production use.
visual_elements: System diagram: user → LLM/VLM agent → CLI harness → real services, highlighting native-runtime loop
Timeline / flowchart of a long-horizon task showing multiple dependent steps and intermediate checks
Bar/line chart comparing success rates and error modes on traditional sandbox benchmarks vs WildClawBench
Example bilingual multimodal task card (image + text) with expected stepwise actions and pass/fail annotations

title: Re-thinking human–machine interaction and the governance of AI in the military domain
authors: Ingvild Bode, Katherine Chandler
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 11 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01231-x

Bode and Chandler discuss how human–machine interactions across the AI life cycle affect human control and decision-making in the military domain.

infographic.key_insight: Human–machine interactions throughout the AI life cycle—not just at deployment—shape the degree of meaningful human control and responsibility in military contexts. Reframing governance to address design, training, testing, and operational interfaces together reduces risks of erosion of human judgment.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap in current policy and practice that treats human control as a single moment (e.g., final switch) rather than a distributed outcome of design, data, testing, interfaces, and organizational processes across the AI life cycle.
method: Conceptual analysis mapping human–machine interaction points across the AI life cycle (design, data, model development, testing, deployment, operation).
Review of governance approaches and case examples to identify where control and decision-making can be undermined or supported.
Proposal of governance priorities and practical levers to preserve meaningful human judgment (e.g., interface design, auditability, testing regimes, accountability mechanisms).
infographic.impact: Promotes lifecycle-aware design and governance practices that AI/ML practitioners can apply to ensure systems in military or high-stakes domains preserve human oversight, traceability, and accountability. Encourages embedding socio-technical safeguards early in development rather than relying on end-user decisions alone.
visual_elements: Life‑cycle diagram highlighting human–machine interaction points (design → data → development → testing → deployment → operation) with risk/mitigation callouts.
Control continuum graphic showing gradations from fully human-led to fully autonomous and where governance levers apply.
Checklist or flowchart of governance levers (interface design, audit logs, red-team testing, accountability mapping) tied to life‑cycle stages.
Icon set representing stakeholders (developers, operators, commanders, auditors, policymakers) and their responsibilities.

title: DECO: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts with Dense-Comparable Performance on End-Side Devices
authors: Chenyang Song, Weilin Zhao, Xu Han, Chaojun Xiao, Yingfa Chen
abstract: While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity without proportionally increasing computation, its massive total parameter footprint creates significant storage and memory-access bottlenecks, which hinder efficient end-side deployment that simultaneously requires high performance, low computational cost, and small storage overhead. To achieve these properties, we present DECO, a sparse MoE architecture designed to match the performance of dense Transformers under identical total parameter b

infographic.key_insight: DECO is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts design that matches the accuracy of a dense Transformer with the same total parameter budget while drastically reducing on-device storage and memory-access costs, enabling high-performance inference on end-side devices.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard MoE increases total parameter count and memory traffic, creating storage and memory-access bottlenecks that prevent efficient deployment on resource-constrained end-side devices without sacrificing accuracy or latency.
method: Design a sparse MoE architecture that preserves total parameter capacity but only activates a small subset of expert parameters per token, keeping compute low while maintaining dense-comparable quality.
Reorganize expert parameters and memory layout for on-device friendliness (compact storage, fewer random accesses) so the large global parameter footprint no longer causes runtime/memory penalties.
Adopt lightweight routing and inference optimizations to minimize extra control overhead and latency during expert selection, enabling efficient end-side execution.
infographic.impact: DECO lets practitioners get the capacity benefits of MoE for higher model quality while meeting stringent on-device constraints (storage, memory bandwidth, compute, latency), making advanced models practical for edge and mobile deployment.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: dense Transformer vs DECO MoE showing equal total parameters but fewer active weights and lower memory access for DECO
Bar chart: storage footprint and memory-bandwidth use (dense vs standard MoE vs DECO)
Flow diagram: token routing to a small subset of experts with compact memory layout and low-latency inference
Scatter plot: accuracy (y) vs on-device cost metrics (x: storage or memory bandwidth) highlighting DECO's dense-comparable accuracy at reduced cost

title: Engineering Robustness into Personal Agents with the AI Workflow Store
authors: Roxana Geambasu, Mariana Raykova, Pierre Tholoniat, Trishita Tiwari, Lillian Tsai
abstract: The dominant paradigm for AI agents is an "on-the-fly" loop in which agents synthesize plans and execute actions within seconds or minutes in response to user prompts. We argue that this paradigm short-circuits disciplined software engineering (SE) processes -- iterative design, rigorous testing, adversarial evaluation, staged deployment, and more -- that have delivered the (relatively) reliable and secure systems we use today. By focusing on rapid, real-time synthesis, are AI agents effectively

infographic.key_insight: Real-time, on‑the‑fly agent synthesis bypasses core software engineering practices; the paper introduces an "AI Workflow Store" to reintroduce iterative design, testing, and staged deployment so personal agents become robust and auditable.
infographic.problem_solved: Current agent paradigms prioritize immediate plan synthesis and execution, which short‑circuit disciplined SE processes and produce brittle, unpredictable, and hard‑to‑govern personal agents.
method: Define an AI Workflow Store: a catalog of reusable agent workflows, artifacts, and checkpoints that codify design, tests, and deployment gates.
Integrate SE practices into agent lifecycles: automated unit/integration/adversarial tests, versioning, staged rollouts, and post‑deploy monitoring for agents.
Provide tooling and orchestration to compose, evaluate, and iterate on agent behaviors outside the strict real‑time loop, enabling repeatable experiments and controlled deployments.
infographic.impact: Bringing classical SE controls to agent development reduces failures, increases reproducibility and safety, and lets ML/engineering teams deploy personal agents with measurable reliability and governance.
visual_elements: Side‑by‑side diagram: "On‑the‑fly loop" vs "Workflow‑driven lifecycle" showing missing SE steps in the first and inserted stages (test, adversarial eval, staging) in the second.
Pipeline infographic of the AI Workflow Store: catalog → compose → test (unit/adversarial) → stage → monitor, with icons for each stage.
Chart showing expected benefits: fewer runtime failures, faster rollback, higher test coverage (conceptual bars or adoption metrics).
Icon set: workflow catalog, test shield, deployment gate, observability/monitoring dashboard to communicate governance and safety.

title: Shepherd: A Runtime Substrate Empowering Meta-Agents with a Formalized Execution Trace
authors: Simon Yu, Derek Chong, Ananjan Nandi, Dilara Soylu, Jiuding Sun
abstract: We introduce Shepherd, a functional programming model that formalizes meta-agent operations on target agents as functions, with core operations mechanized in Lean. Shepherd records every agent-environment interaction as a typed event in a Git-like execution trace, enabling any past state to be forked and replayed. The system forks the agent process and its filesystem $5\times$ faster than Docker, achieving $>95\%$ prompt-cache reuse on replay. We demonstrate the model through three applications.

infographic.key_insight: Shepherd formalizes meta-agent operations as pure functions and records every agent–environment interaction as typed events in a Git-like execution trace. This enables fast, forkable, replayable agent processes with core operations mechanized in Lean for stronger correctness guarantees.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of a formal, reproducible runtime for meta-agents that reliably captures, forks, and replays agent state and filesystem snapshots (existing container workflows are slow and traces are often untyped or ad hoc).
method: Design a functional programming model where meta-agent operations are expressed as functions and interactions are emitted as typed events.
Store interactions in a Git-like, append-only execution trace that lets any past state be forked and replayed deterministically.
Mechanize core semantics in Lean and implement an efficient fork+filesystem substrate that forks processes/filesystems 5× faster than Docker and achieves >95% prompt-cache reuse on replay.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get deterministic debugging, safe branching of agent experiments, and much faster iteration when developing meta-agents, plus formalized semantics and mechanized assurances for higher confidence in agent behaviors.

Architecture diagram: meta-agent (functions) → target agent → environment, with Lean mechanization and runtime substrate annotated

Fork & replay flow diagram demonstrating branching experiments, deterministic replay, and state isolation

title: Variational Inference for Lévy Process-Driven SDEs via Neural Tilting
authors: Yaman Kindap, Manfred Opper, Benjamin Dupuis, Umut Simsekli, Tolga Birdal
abstract: Modelling extreme events and heavy-tailed phenomena is central to building reliable predictive systems in domains such as finance, climate science, and safety-critical AI. While Lévy processes provide a natural mathematical framework for capturing jumps and heavy tails, Bayesian inference for Lévy-driven stochastic differential equations (SDEs) remains intractable with existing methods: Monte Carlo approaches are rigorous but lack scalability, whereas neural variational inference methods are eff

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a scalable variational inference framework for SDEs driven by Lévy processes by learning a neural tilting (change-of-measure) that makes posterior path inference tractable and accurate for jumps and heavy tails.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing Bayesian inference methods for Lévy-driven SDEs are either computationally infeasible at scale (Monte Carlo) or fail to capture jump-driven heavy tails; this work makes principled, scalable posterior inference possible for such models.
method: Formulate a variational objective over continuous-time path measures for Lévy-driven SDEs and derive an evidence lower bound amenable to optimization.
Introduce a neural tilting (learned change-of-measure) that reweights the Lévy jump measure to produce low-variance, expressive variational families capable of modeling jumps and heavy tails.
Train the tilting network end-to-end with Monte Carlo estimators and amortized inference to enable efficient sampling and uncertainty quantification at scale.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical Bayesian tool to model and quantify uncertainty in systems with jumps and extreme events (e.g., finance, climate, safety-critical AI), improving robustness and predictive reliability while remaining computationally tractable.
visual_elements: Illustration comparing diffusion-only SDE paths vs Lévy jump SDE paths (showing rare large jumps).
Pipeline diagram: data → neural tilting network → tilted Lévy measure → variational sampler → ELBO optimization.
Performance chart: predictive tails/quantiles and uncertainty bands vs baseline methods (MC and naive VI).
Icon set: heavy tails, speed/scale (clock/servers), uncertainty quantification (confidence ribbon), and jump events (lightning bolt).

title: Towards the explainability of protein language models
authors: Andrea Hunklinger, Noelia Ferruz
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 11 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01232-w

Hunklinger and Ferruz provide an overview of explainable artificial intelligence methods for protein language models.

infographic.key_insight: Provides the first comprehensive, practitioner-oriented synthesis of explainability methods for protein language models, identifying which XAI techniques map most clearly to biological concepts (structure, function, motifs) and where gaps remain. It distills principles and evaluation criteria to make model explanations more biologically meaningful.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of organized guidance on how to interpret protein language models—clarifying which explainability methods are appropriate for sequence→structure/function claims and highlighting methodological and evaluation gaps that hinder biological trust and utility.
method: Systematic literature survey of explainable AI techniques applied to protein language models, spanning attribution, probing, attention analysis, generative and causal approaches.
Taxonomy and comparative analysis that maps XAI methods to biological questions (e.g., residue importance, motif discovery, long-range interactions) and evaluation desiderata.
Synthesis of best practices, benchmark considerations, and open challenges to guide method selection and future research.
infographic.impact: Helps ML practitioners and computational biologists choose and evaluate interpretability tools that produce biologically meaningful insights, improving model trust, debugging, and downstream applications like protein design and functional annotation.
visual_elements: Taxonomy diagram: tree linking XAI classes (attribution, probing, attention, generative, causal) to the biological questions they address (motifs, contacts, function).
Method vs. criteria heatmap: rows = XAI methods, columns = evaluation criteria (biological validity, robustness, granularity, scalability), with color-coded suitability.
Pipeline schematic: from protein sequence → language model → chosen XAI method → biological interpretation (structure/function) with decision points.
Case-study snapshot: sequence with colored residue attributions mapped onto a 3D protein outline to illustrate how explanations align with known motifs/contacts.

title: Towards Highly-Constrained Human Motion Generation with Retrieval-Guided Diffusion Noise Optimization
authors: Hanchao Liu, Fang-Lue Zhang, Shining Zhang, Tai-Jiang Mu, Shi-Min Hu
abstract: Generating human motion that satisfies customized zero-shot goal functions, enabling applications such as controllable character animation and behavior synthesis for virtual agents, is a critical capability. While current approaches handle many unseen constraints, they fail on tasks with very challenging spatiotemporal restrictions, such as severe spatial obstacles or specified numbers of walking steps. To equip motion generators for these highly constrained tasks, we present a retrieval-guided

infographic.key_insight: Combining a retrieval-based library of motion snippets with diffusion-model noise optimization lets a generator satisfy extremely strict spatiotemporal constraints (e.g., obstacle avoidance, exact step counts) in a zero-shot setting.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing motion generators struggle with highly-constrained tasks—such as navigating severe spatial obstacles or meeting a specified number of steps—when constraints are unseen at training time; this work enables reliable zero-shot compliance with such challenging spatiotemporal requirements.
method: Retrieve relevant motion snippets from a database to provide strong, context-aware priors for constrained generation.
Run a diffusion-based motion generator whose noise is optimized (guided) at generation time so the sampled trajectory satisfies the user-specified zero-shot goal function.
Combine retrieval priors and constraint-aware noise optimization during denoising to produce plausible, constraint-compliant motions without task-specific retraining.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, controllable character animation and virtual-agent behavior that meet precise, previously unseen constraints—reducing manual effort and expanding the range of tasks solvable by generative motion models.

Before/after motion sequences illustrating failure of a baseline and success of retrieval-guided diffusion (e.g., navigating an obstacle course or exact-step gait)

title: Conformal Path Reasoning: Trustworthy Knowledge Graph Question Answering via Path-Level Calibration
authors: Shuhang Lin, Chuhao Zhou, Xiao Lin, Zihan Dong, Kuan Lu
abstract: Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) has shown promise for grounded and interpretable reasoning, yet existing approaches often fail to provide reliable coverage guarantees over retrieved answers. While Conformal Prediction (CP) offers a principled framework for producing prediction sets with statistical guarantees, prior methods suffer from critical limitations in both calibration validity and score discriminability, resulting in violated coverage guarantees and excessively large prediction

infographic.key_insight: Calibrating conformal prediction at the reasoning-path level yields reliable, tighter answer sets for Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA), improving coverage guarantees without bloating prediction sets.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing KGQA systems either lack reliable statistical coverage guarantees or produce overly large prediction sets when applying conformal methods, making their uncertainty estimates untrustworthy or impractical.
method: Compute nonconformity scores and perform calibration over retrieved reasoning paths (rather than only final answer scores) to better separate correct from incorrect reasoning chains.
Adjust prediction sets using path-level calibration so conformal guarantees hold while maintaining discriminative ranking of candidate answers.
Combine path-aware scoring with theoretical calibration procedures and empirical tuning to produce compact, coverage-certified answer sets.
infographic.impact: Provides ML practitioners a practical way to get statistically guaranteed, interpretable answer sets from KGQA systems—enabling safer deployment, clearer uncertainty communication, and more trustworthy reasoning outputs.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: Question → candidate KG paths → path scoring → path-level conformal calibration → certified answer set
Bar chart comparing coverage and average prediction-set size for baseline conformal methods vs. path-level calibration
Calibration plot (reliability curve) showing improved validity across confidence levels
Iconography: a shield/trust badge over a KG node to represent certified, trustworthy answers

title: Fast Byte Latent Transformer
authors: Julie Kallini, Artidoro Pagnoni, Tomasz Limisiewicz, Gargi Ghosh, Luke Zettlemoyer
abstract: Recent byte-level language models (LMs) match the performance of token-level models without relying on subword vocabularies, yet their utility is limited by slow, byte-by-byte autoregressive generation. We address this bottleneck in the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) through new training and generation techniques. First, we introduce BLT Diffusion (BLT-D), a new model and our fastest BLT variant, trained with an auxiliary block-wise diffusion objective alongside the standard next-byte prediction

infographic.key_insight: BLT-D adds a block-wise diffusion objective to the Byte Latent Transformer, enabling block-parallel generation that is substantially faster than byte-by-byte autoregressive sampling while retaining next-byte prediction quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Byte-level LMs are bottlenecked by slow autoregressive byte-by-byte generation; this work speeds up sampling without sacrificing the benefits of tokenization-free modeling.
method: Introduce BLT-D: augment the Byte Latent Transformer with an auxiliary block-wise diffusion objective during training.
Train jointly with the standard next-byte prediction loss so the model preserves autoregressive language modeling quality.
Use a block-wise (partially parallel) generation procedure that samples groups of bytes via the learned latent/diffusion mechanism to reduce sampling latency.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, low-latency way to deploy tokenization-free byte-level LMs, improving throughput for multilingual and robust NLP applications while keeping model behavior comparable to standard next-byte LMs.

Architecture diagram highlighting latent blocks, the diffusion auxiliary objective, and the next-byte prediction head
Flowchart contrasting byte-by-byte autoregressive sampling with BLT-D block-wise sampling (showing parallelism gains)
Latency vs quality (perplexity or accuracy) curve to show trade-off and that BLT-D maintains LM performance while reducing latency

title: The Memory Curse: How Expanded Recall Erodes Cooperative Intent in LLM Agents
authors: Jiayuan Liu, Tianqin Li, Shiyi Du, Xin Luo, Haoxuan Zeng
abstract: Context window expansion is often treated as a straightforward capability upgrade for LLMs, but we find it systematically fails in multi-agent social dilemmas. Across 7 LLMs and 4 games over 500 rounds, expanding accessible history degrades cooperation in 18 of 28 model--game settings, a pattern we term the memory curse. We isolate the underlying mechanism through three analyses. First, lexical analysis of 378,000 reasoning traces associates this breakdown with eroding forward-looking intent rat

infographic.key_insight: Expanding an LLM's accessible memory (context window) can systematically reduce cooperative behavior in multi-agent social dilemmas — a phenomenon the authors call the "memory curse". Across many models and games, more history led to less forward-looking intent and worse cooperation.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and explains why increasing LLM recall (larger context windows) does not always improve multi-agent outcomes, and pinpoints a mechanism that undermines cooperation in social-dilemma settings.
method: Large-scale multi-agent experiments: 7 different LLMs playing 4 social-dilemma games over 500 rounds to measure cooperation changes with varying memory sizes.
Lexical analysis of 378,000 reasoning traces to link behavioral changes to shifts in language signaling and planning (finding: erosion of forward-looking intent).
Targeted probing/diagnostic analyses to isolate the causal mechanism behind the cooperation breakdown (controls/ablation-style comparisons across model–game settings).
infographic.impact: Practitioners should not assume context-window expansion is uniformly beneficial for multi-agent coordination — design and evaluation must consider how longer histories affect intent, planning, and emergent social behavior.
visual_elements: Line chart: cooperation rate over rounds for short vs long context windows (showing declining cooperation with larger memory).
Heatmap: per model × per game matrix highlighting where memory expansion degrades cooperation (18/28 cells flagged).
Flow diagram: expanded memory → degraded forward-looking language/planning → reduced cooperative choices (mechanism sketch).

title: Rubric-Grounded RL: Structured Judge Rewards for Generalizable Reasoning
authors: Manish Bhattarai, Ismael Boureima, Nishath Rajiv Ranasinghe, Scott Pakin, Dan O'Malley
abstract: We argue that decomposing reward into weighted, verifiable criteria and using an LLM judge to score them provides a partial-credit optimization signal: instead of a binary outcome or a single holistic score, each response is graded along multiple task-specific criteria. We formalize \emph{rubric-grounded reinforcement learning (RL)}: a framework in which the policy is optimized against a structured, multi-criterion reward produced by a frozen LLM judge that conditions on auxiliary grounding the

infographic.key_insight: Decompose reward into weighted, verifiable criteria and use a frozen LLM judge to score each criterion, producing a partial‑credit optimization signal that improves learning for complex reasoning tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard binary or single‑score rewards provide sparse, uninformative feedback for multi‑step reasoning; this paper addresses poor credit assignment and weak generalization by giving structured, criterion‑level feedback.
method: Specify a task rubric: a set of weighted, verifiable evaluation criteria that together define success.
Use a frozen LLM judge that conditions on grounding (e.g., evidence or auxiliary context) to score each rubric criterion, yielding a multi‑dimensional reward.
Optimize the policy with RL against the structured, aggregated rubric reward so the agent receives partial credit and finer gradient signals.
infographic.impact: Provides richer, interpretable rewards that improve credit assignment, training stability, and generalization on reasoning tasks—making reward design more diagnostic and actionable for ML practitioners.

title: LLMs Improving LLMs: Agentic Discovery for Test-Time Scaling
authors: Tong Zheng, Haolin Liu, Chengsong Huang, Huiwen Bao, Sheng Zhang
abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) has become an effective approach for improving large language model performance by allocating additional computation during inference. However, existing TTS strategies are largely hand-crafted: researchers manually design reasoning patterns and tune heuristics by intuition, leaving much of the computation-allocation space unexplored. We propose an environment-driven framework, AutoTTS, that changes what researchers design: from individual TTS heuristics to environments wh

infographic.key_insight: Instead of hand-crafting test-time scaling (TTS) heuristics, AutoTTS frames TTS as an environment-driven discovery problem and uses agentic LLMs to automatically explore and discover effective computation-allocation strategies at inference time.
infographic.problem_solved: Manual TTS strategies are heuristic, limited by researcher intuition, and leave much of the computation-allocation design space unexplored; this paper automates discovery to find better, generalizable TTS policies.
method: Reformulate TTS as an environment-driven search where the environment provides tasks, costs, and rewards for allocation decisions.
Use agentic LLMs to autonomously explore computation-allocation policies (e.g., when to allocate more reasoning steps, voting, or deeper models) and evaluate them in the environment.
Select and refine discovered strategies based on performance and cost trade-offs, producing practical TTS heuristics that generalize across tasks.
infographic.impact: AutoTTS automates and broadens exploration of test-time computation strategies, enabling practitioners to boost inference-time performance and efficiency without manual heuristic design.

title: Normalizing Trajectory Models
authors: Jiatao Gu, Tianrong Chen, Ying Shen, David Berthelot, Shuangfei Zhai
abstract: Diffusion-based models decompose sampling into many small Gaussian denoising steps -- an assumption that breaks down when generation is compressed to a few coarse transitions. Existing few-step methods address this through distillation, consistency training, or adversarial objectives, but sacrifice the likelihood framework in the process. We introduce Normalizing Trajectory Models (NTM), which models each reverse step as an expressive conditional normalizing flow with exact likelihood training.

infographic.key_insight: Normalizing Trajectory Models (NTM) replace each coarse reverse diffusion step with an expressive conditional normalizing flow, enabling few-step generation while retaining exact-likelihood training and expressive stepwise transitions.
infographic.problem_solved: Diffusion assumptions break down when generation is compressed to few coarse steps; prior few-step solutions (distillation, consistency, adversarial) lose the likelihood framework. NTM restores principled likelihood-based training for compressed/few-step sampling.
method: Model every reverse transition as a conditional normalizing flow conditioned on the next state and timestep, giving each coarse step high expressivity.
Train the sequence of flows with exact maximum likelihood across steps, preserving tractable likelihoods and stable optimization.
Learn compressed trajectories that summarize many small denoising steps into a few learned expressive transitions to enable fast, few-step sampling.
infographic.impact: NTM provides a practical path to fast few-step generation without abandoning likelihood-based evaluation, so practitioners can get efficient sampling and principled density estimates simultaneously—useful for research, model selection, and production deployment.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: standard diffusion (many small Gaussian denoising steps) vs NTM (few expressive flow-based transitions).
Block diagram showing a conditional normalizing flow at one reverse step (inputs: noisy state + timestep; outputs: cleaner state) with exact likelihood annotation.

Trajectory visualization: animated or stacked states showing compressed learned transitions vs many small denoising steps.

title: Proxy3D: Efficient 3D Representations for Vision-Language Models via Semantic Clustering and Alignment
authors: Jerry Jiang, Haowen Sun, Denis Gudovskiy, Yohei Nakata, Tomoyuki Okuno
abstract: Spatial intelligence in vision-language models (VLMs) attracts research interest with the practical demand to reason in the 3D world.Despite promising results, most existing methods follow the conventional 2D pipeline in VLMs and use pixel-aligned representations for the vision modality. However, correspondence-based models with implicit 3D scene understanding often fail to achieve spatial consistency, and representation-based models with 3D geometric priors lack efficiency in vision sequence se

infographic.key_insight: Proxy3D compresses multi-view visual information into compact, semantically meaningful 3D proxies and aligns them with language, achieving spatially consistent 3D representations for VLMs with much lower compute and memory than dense correspondence or volumetric methods.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing VLM approaches either use expensive dense 3D priors or brittle pixel-aligned correspondence and therefore fail to provide efficient, spatially consistent 3D understanding for vision-language tasks.
method: Semantic clustering: aggregate multi-view features into a small set of 3D semantic proxies (clusters) that summarize scene geometry and semantics.
Cross-modal alignment: align proxy embeddings with language tokens using contrastive and alignment losses so proxies become language-aware 3D anchors.
Lightweight indexing & retrieval: use the compact proxies at inference for fast spatial queries and reasoning instead of operating on dense 3D volumes or per-pixel correspondences.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, efficient way to add true 3D spatial reasoning to vision-language models, reducing compute/memory and improving spatial consistency — useful for robotics, AR, and multi-view VLM applications.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: multi-view images → feature extraction → semantic clustering → proxy set → alignment with text (shows data reduction and flow).

title: 123D: Unifying Multi-Modal Autonomous Driving Data at Scale
authors: Daniel Dauner, Valentin Charraut, Bastian Berle, Tianyu Li, Long Nguyen
abstract: The pursuit of autonomous driving has produced one of the richest sensor data collections in all of robotics. However, its scale and diversity remain largely untapped. Each dataset adopts different 2D and 3D modalities, such as cameras, lidar, ego states, annotations, traffic lights, and HD maps, with different rates and synchronization schemes. They come in fragmented formats requiring complex dependencies that cannot natively coexist in the same development environment. Further, major inconsis

infographic.key_insight: A scalable unification framework that standardizes and synchronizes diverse 2D/3D autonomous-driving datasets and modalities, enabling them to be combined and used interoperably for large-scale training and evaluation.
infographic.problem_solved: Fragmented datasets with heterogeneous formats, sensor rates, sync schemes, and complex dependencies prevent cross-dataset training, benchmarking, and efficient tooling reuse in autonomous driving research.
method: Canonical multi-modal schema + adapters to convert heterogeneous inputs (camera, lidar, ego-state, HD maps, traffic lights, annotations) into a single interoperable format.
Temporal and spatial synchronization modules to align different sensor rates and coordinate frames, preserving timestamps and transforms.
Scalable ingestion, indexing and SDK/wrappers to load, visualize, and train on merged datasets efficiently across environments.
infographic.impact: Lowers engineering overhead and boosts reproducibility by making many datasets immediately compatible; enables larger-scale multi-modal model training, cross-dataset benchmarks, and faster iteration for perception and planning research.

title: Flow-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Flow Matching Models
authors: Zhen Fang, Wenxuan Huang, Yu Zeng, Yiming Zhao, Shuang Chen
abstract: Existing Flow Matching (FM) text-to-image models suffer from two critical bottlenecks under multi-task alignment: the reward sparsity induced by scalar-valued rewards, and the gradient interference arising from jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives, which together give rise to a 'seesaw effect' of competing metrics and pervasive reward hacking. Inspired by the success of On-Policy Distillation (OPD) in the large language model community, we propose Flow-OPD, the first unified post-training

infographic.key_insight: Flow-OPD applies on-policy distillation to Flow Matching text-to-image models, turning sparse scalar rewards and entangled gradient signals into richer, on-policy supervision that prevents the 'seesaw effect' and reduces reward hacking.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing FM text-to-image models struggle under multi-task alignment because scalar-valued rewards are sparse and jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives causes gradient interference — producing competing metrics and pervasive reward hacking.
method: Post-training On-Policy Distillation: run on-policy rollouts from a teacher/policy and distill its behavior into the Flow Matching student model to provide denser, trajectory-level supervision.

Decouple heterogeneous objectives: replace or augment scalar reward supervision with on-policy signals (e.g., per-sample/trajectory guidance and distilled logits/flows) to reduce gradient interference and stabilize multi-objective updates.
Unified alignment pipeline: a lightweight post-training stage that balances multi-metric alignment (via loss weighting or modular heads) while preserving generative quality of the original FM model.
infographic.impact: Flow-OPD makes multi-objective alignment for Flow Matching text-to-image models more stable and robust, enabling practitioners to optimize competing metrics reliably and reduce reward-hacking without retraining from scratch.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Structured Data Extraction from Full CMR Reports via Distilled LLMs
authors: Yi Yu, Parker Martin, Zhenyu Bu, Yixuan Liu, Yi-Yu Zheng
abstract: Converting free-text cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) reports into auditable structured data remains a bottleneck for cohort assembly, longitudinal curation, and clinical decision support. We present CMR-EXTR, a lightweight framework that converts free-text CMR reports into structured data and assigns per-field confidence for quality control. A teacher-student distillation pipeline enables fully offline inference while limiting manual annotation. Uncertainty integrates three complementary princi

infographic.key_insight: CMR-EXTR uses a teacher–student distillation pipeline to convert free-text CMR reports into auditable structured fields with per-field confidence scores, enabling lightweight, fully offline inference and reduced manual annotation.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates the conversion of unstructured cardiac MRI reports into reliable, auditable structured data — addressing bottlenecks in cohort assembly, longitudinal curation, and clinical decision support while preserving deployability and privacy.
method: Teacher–student distillation: a large LLM teacher generates labels/annotations to train a compact student model for offline deployment and reduced annotation burden.
Per-field uncertainty scoring: the system produces confidence estimates for each extracted field to enable quality control and selective human review.
Lightweight architecture optimized for fully offline inference, supporting clinical privacy and scalable cohort extraction without continuous cloud access.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, privacy-preserving extraction of structured clinical data with built-in auditability; practitioners can deploy compact models in production settings while using confidence scores to prioritize human review and improve downstream analyses.

title: Platonic representation of foundation machine learning interatomic potentials
authors: Zhenzhu Li, Aron Walsh
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 07 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01235-7

Li and Walsh show that a unified ‘platonic’ geometry emerges across the representations of independent foundation models for learning interatomic potentials. The observation enables cross-model comparison, embedding arithmetic and ground-truth-free diagnostics.

infographic.key_insight: Representations learned by independent foundation models for interatomic potentials converge to a shared, low-dimensional 'platonic' geometry, enabling direct cross-model comparison and manipulation without relying on ground-truth labels.
infographic.problem_solved: The field lacked a model-agnostic, interpretable basis to compare and diagnose learned interatomic potential representations, hindering transfer, benchmarking and trustworthy use across different foundation models.
method: Collect latent embeddings from multiple independent foundation models trained for interatomic potentials and align them into a common coordinate frame.
Quantify geometric congruence (similarity measures and alignment transforms) to reveal a consistent low-dimensional 'platonic' structure across models.
Demonstrate practical uses: embedding arithmetic (vector algebra in latent space) and ground-truth-free diagnostics to assess and combine models.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a model-agnostic toolkit to compare, combine and validate foundation models for materials/chemistry applications, improving interpretability, transferability and rapid diagnostics without needing expensive reference data.

title: Relit-LiVE: Relight Video by Jointly Learning Environment Video
authors: Weiqing Xiao, Hong Li, Xiuyu Yang, Houyuan Chen, Wenyi Li
abstract: Recent advances have shown that large-scale video diffusion models can be repurposed as neural renderers by first decomposing videos into intrinsic scene representations and then performing forward rendering under novel illumination. While promising, this paradigm fundamentally relies on accurate intrinsic decomposition, which remains highly unreliable for real-world videos and often leads to distorted appearances, broken materials, and accumulated temporal artifacts during relighting. In this w

infographic.key_insight: Instead of relying on brittle per-frame intrinsic decomposition, the paper jointly learns an "environment video" representation together with a diffusion-based neural renderer so videos can be relit robustly and temporally consistently under novel illumination.
infographic.problem_solved: Current video relighting pipelines depend on accurate intrinsic decomposition (albedo, normals, illumination), which is unreliable for real-world footage and leads to distorted appearance, broken materials, and temporal artifacts when relighting.
method: Jointly learn an environment-video representation and a video neural renderer, so lighting is modeled as a temporally coherent scene-level signal rather than noisy per-frame decompositions.
Condition a large-scale video diffusion/rendering model on the learned environment video plus available geometric/color cues to synthesize frames under new illumination.
Enforce temporal consistency and appearance preservation via spatio-temporal conditioning and losses to reduce artifacts and maintain material fidelity during relighting.
infographic.impact: Makes practical, high-quality video relighting possible on in-the-wild footage without fragile intrinsic decomposition, improving realism and temporal stability for VFX, AR/VR, and content editing workflows.

title: When No Benchmark Exists: Validating Comparative LLM Safety Scoring Without Ground-Truth Labels
authors: Sushant Gautam, Finn Schwall, Annika Willoch Olstad, Fernando Vallecillos Ruiz, Birk Torpmann-Hagen
abstract: Many deployments must compare candidate language models for safety before a labeled benchmark exists for the relevant language, sector, or regulatory regime. We formalize this setting as benchmarkless comparative safety scoring and specify the contract under which a scenario-based audit can be interpreted as deployment evidence. Scores are valid only under a fixed scenario pack, rubric, auditor, judge, sampling configuration, and rerun budget. Because no labels are available, we replace ground-t

infographic.key_insight: You can validly compare LLM safety without labeled benchmarks by treating scenario-based audits as evidence under a precise contract: scores are meaningful only relative to a fixed scenario pack, rubric, auditor, judge, sampling plan, and rerun budget. The paper formalizes this benchmarkless comparative safety scoring and practical validation constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: How to evaluate and compare candidate language models for safety when no ground-truth labeled benchmark exists for the target language, sector, or regulatory regime.
method: Formalize the benchmarkless comparative safety setting and define a validity contract that fixes: scenario pack, rubric, auditor, judge, sampling configuration, and rerun budget.

Replace reliance on unavailable ground-truth labels by using scenario-based audits plus repeatability/consistency checks and controlled sampling to produce comparable safety scores with well-specified scope.
Provide a validation/interpretation framework that quantifies when comparative scores can be treated as deployment evidence and clarifies their limitations.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a rigorous, operational way to compare model safety where labeled data don’t exist, reducing deployment risk by making evaluation assumptions explicit and results reproducible. It also sets clear boundaries for what such scores can (and cannot) imply.
visual_elements: Contract diagram showing the six fixed components (scenario pack, rubric, auditor, judge, sampling, rerun budget) as inputs that determine score validity

title: UniPool: A Globally Shared Expert Pool for Mixture-of-Experts
authors: Minbin Huang, Han Shi, Chuanyang Zheng, Yimeng Wu, Guoxuan Chen
abstract: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures allocate expert capacity through a rigid per-layer rule: each transformer layer owns a separate expert set. This convention couples depth scaling with linear expert-parameter growth and assumes that every layer needs isolated expert capacity. However, recent analyses and our routing probe challenge this allocation rule: replacing a deeper layer's learned top-k router with uniform random routing drops downstream accuracy by only 1.0-1.6 points across

infographic.key_insight: UniPool replaces isolated per-layer expert sets with a single globally shared expert pool, showing many layers can share experts with only minimal loss in accuracy.
infographic.problem_solved: Fixes the rigid per-layer expert allocation in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that forces linear expert-parameter growth with depth and assumes every layer requires its own isolated experts.
method: Introduce a globally shared expert pool (UniPool) that all transformer layers can access instead of maintaining separate expert sets per layer.
Design routing and capacity-control mechanisms so layers dynamically select from the shared pool while preserving load balance and specialization.
Use routing probes and empirical experiments to compare shared vs. per-layer allocations and quantify accuracy vs. parameter efficiency trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Enables more parameter-efficient scaling of MoE models by decoupling expert capacity from depth, simplifying architecture design and reducing training/inference cost while maintaining near-original performance.

title: Are We Making Progress in Multimodal Domain Generalization? A Comprehensive Benchmark Study
authors: Hao Dong, Hongzhao Li, Shupan Li, Muhammad Haris Khan, Eleni Chatzi
abstract: Despite the growing popularity of Multimodal Domain Generalization (MMDG) for enhancing model robustness, it remains unclear whether reported performance gains reflect genuine algorithmic progress or are artifacts of inconsistent evaluation protocols. Current research is fragmented, with studies varying significantly across datasets, modality configurations, and experimental settings. Furthermore, existing benchmarks focus predominantly on action recognition, often neglecting critical real-world

infographic.key_insight: Reported gains in Multimodal Domain Generalization often reflect inconsistent evaluation protocols and narrow benchmarks rather than true algorithmic progress; a unified, comprehensive benchmark reveals which methods genuinely generalize across modalities and domains.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the fragmentation and evaluation variability in MMDG research by providing a standardized, broad benchmark that tests algorithms across diverse datasets, modality configurations, and real-world settings beyond action recognition.
method: Assemble a diverse benchmark suite spanning multiple tasks and modality combinations (not just action recognition) to capture real-world domain shifts.
Define and enforce standardized evaluation protocols (training/validation/test splits, pre-processing, and metrics) to eliminate protocol-induced performance artifacts.
Systematically evaluate representative MMDG algorithms, run ablations to attribute gains, and produce best-practice recommendations for fair comparison and deployment.
infographic.impact: Enables fair, reproducible comparison of multimodal generalization methods and helps practitioners identify approaches that truly improve robustness across domains—accelerating trustworthy deployment of multimodal systems.

title: BAMI: Training-Free Bias Mitigation in GUI Grounding
authors: Borui Zhang, Bo Zhang, Bo Wang, Wenzhao Zheng, Yuhao Cheng
abstract: GUI grounding is a critical capability for enabling GUI agents to execute tasks such as clicking and dragging. However, in complex scenarios like the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, existing models often suffer from suboptimal performance. Utilizing the proposed \textbf{Masked Prediction Distribution (MPD)} attribution method, we identify that the primary sources of errors are twofold: high image resolution (leading to precision bias) and intricate interface elements (resulting in ambiguity bias). To

infographic.key_insight: A training-free approach (BAMI) that uses a new Masked Prediction Distribution (MPD) attribution method can reveal and mitigate two systematic biases—precision bias from high-resolution screens and ambiguity bias from complex UI elements—improving GUI grounding without retraining models.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing GUI grounding models struggle in complex, high-resolution interfaces (e.g., ScreenSpot-Pro) due to systematic localization and ambiguity errors; the paper diagnoses these failure modes and provides a training-free mitigation strategy.
method: Introduce Masked Prediction Distribution (MPD) as an attribution tool to localize where and why grounding predictions fail.
Diagnose two primary biases: precision bias (errors caused by high image resolution) and ambiguity bias (errors caused by visually complex or similar interface elements).
Apply BAMI — a set of training-free mitigation techniques (e.g., resolution-aware post-processing and ambiguity-aware scoring/filtering) to correct biased predictions at inference time.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable GUI agents by diagnosing and fixing systematic grounding errors without expensive model retraining, making deployment and iteration faster for practitioners.

A promising foundation model is developed for a range of downstream applications in natural product mining.

Encode molecules (e.g., SMILES/graphs) into rich embeddings that capture biosynthetic and functional motifs.
Fine-tune or probe the pretrained model on downstream tasks (property prediction, annotation, prioritization, design) to demonstrate transferability.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a reusable foundation model and embeddings that reduce label needs and accelerate workflows in cheminformatics, natural-product discovery, and bioactive compound prioritization.

title: StraTA: Incentivizing Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Strategic Trajectory Abstraction
authors: Xiangyuan Xue, Yifan Zhou, Zidong Wang, Shengji Tang, Philip Torr
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as interactive agents, but optimizing them for long-horizon decision making remains difficult because current methods are largely purely reactive, which weakens both exploration and credit assignment over extended trajectories. In this work, we present Strategic Trajectory Abstraction (StraTA), a simple framework that introduces an explicit trajectory-level strategy into agentic reinforcement learning (RL). StraTA samples a compact strategy from

infographic.key_insight: StraTA injects a compact, explicit trajectory-level strategy into agentic RL so that an LLM-based agent plans at the strategy level before acting, greatly improving exploration and credit assignment over long horizons.
infographic.problem_solved: Current LLM agents are largely reactive and struggle with long-horizon decision making because they lack explicit trajectory-level planning, which weakens exploration and makes credit assignment across extended trajectories difficult.
method: Sample a compact trajectory-level strategy (an abstract plan or latent) at episode or segment start to guide downstream decisions.
Condition the agent’s action policy on the sampled strategy so low-level actions are coherent with a higher-level intent while preserving flexibility.
Train the abstraction and policy jointly under a reinforcement objective so strategies improve exploration and long-horizon credit assignment.
infographic.impact: Provides a simple, model-agnostic way to make LLM agents more strategic—boosting long-horizon performance and more reliable exploration—useful for practitioners building complex agentic systems or hierarchical RL pipelines.

title: ActCam: Zero-Shot Joint Camera and 3D Motion Control for Video Generation
authors: Omar El Khalifi, Thomas Rossi, Oscar Fossey, Thibault Fouque, Ulysse Mizrahi
abstract: For artistic applications, video generation requires fine-grained control over both performance and cinematography, i.e., the actor's motion and the camera trajectory. We present ActCam, a zero-shot method for video generation that jointly transfers character motion from a driving video into a new scene and enables per-frame control of intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters. ActCam builds on any pretrained image-to-video diffusion model that accepts conditioning in terms of scene depth and ch

infographic.key_insight: ActCam enables zero-shot, joint control of actor performance and per-frame camera parameters by conditioning pretrained image-to-video diffusion models on extracted 3D motion and camera trajectories, producing coherent videos without task-specific finetuning.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides fine-grained, simultaneous control over both character motion and cinematography (intrinsic/extrinsic camera parameters) for video generation—addressing the gap where prior methods control either motion or camera but not both jointly or require expensive retraining/data.
method: Extract per-frame 3D motion and camera parameters from a driving video (pose/scene geometry and camera trajectory) as conditioning signals.

Leverage an off-the-shelf pretrained image-to-video diffusion model that accepts depth and camera conditioning to transfer the extracted motion into a target scene while applying per-frame intrinsic/extrinsic camera control.
Operate in a zero-shot manner (no task-specific finetuning), integrating the motion and camera signals to synthesize temporally coherent frames with desired cinematography.
infographic.impact: Enables artists and ML practitioners to generate controllable, cinematic videos quickly and flexibly—supporting novel content creation, interactive tools, and research on controllable generative video without expensive retraining or large paired datasets.

title: AI Co-Mathematician: Accelerating Mathematicians with Agentic AI
authors: Daniel Zheng, Ingrid von Glehn, Yori Zwols, Iuliya Beloshapka, Lars Buesing
abstract: We introduce the AI co-mathematician, a workbench for mathematicians to interactively leverage AI agents to pursue open-ended research. The AI co-mathematician is optimized to provide holistic support for the exploratory and iterative reality of mathematical workflows, including ideation, literature search, computational exploration, theorem proving and theory building. By providing an asynchronous, stateful workspace that manages uncertainty, refines user intent, tracks failed hypotheses, and o

infographic.key_insight: An agentic, stateful AI workbench—the "AI co-mathematician"—helps mathematicians run long-horizon, exploratory research by coordinating AI agents that manage uncertainty, refine intent, and remember failed hypotheses. It turns fragmented single-turn assistance into a continuous, reproducible research partner.
infographic.problem_solved: Mathematical research is open-ended, iterative, and requires tracking evolving intent, failed experiments, literature, computations and proofs over long timescales; existing single-turn AI tools cannot maintain the state, provenance and coordination needed for sustained discovery.
method: An asynchronous, stateful workspace that stores history, hypotheses, and provenance so work can be resumed, reviewed and iterated.
Agentic AI components that collaborate on distinct tasks (ideation, literature search, computational exploration, theorem proving, theory building) and refine user intent over time.
Uncertainty-management and failure-tracking mechanisms to record, revisit and learn from failed hypotheses and partial results, improving efficiency of exploratory loops.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical platform to accelerate mathematical discovery and reduce cognitive overhead, making long-horizon research workflows more reproducible and collaborative. For AI/ML practitioners, it demonstrates scalable agent coordination, stateful interaction design, and evaluation paradigms for complex, open-ended tasks.

title: Estimating the expected output of wide random MLPs more efficiently than sampling
authors: Wilson Wu, Victor Lecomte, Michael Winer, George Robinson, Jacob Hilton
abstract: By far the most common way to estimate an expected loss in machine learning is to draw samples, compute the loss on each one, and take the empirical average. However, sampling is not necessarily optimal. Given an MLP at initialization, we show how to estimate its expected output over Gaussian inputs without running samples through the network at all. Instead, we produce approximate representations of the distributions of activations at each layer, leveraging tools such as cumulants and Hermite e

infographic.key_insight: You can estimate the expected output of a wide, randomly initialized MLP on Gaussian inputs analytically — without Monte Carlo — by approximating layerwise activation distributions and propagating them through the network.
infographic.problem_solved: Sampling-based estimation of expected outputs or losses is costly and noisy; the paper removes the need to run many forward samples at initialization while retaining accurate expectations.
method: Represent layer activations using low-order statistics (cumulants/moments) to form compact approximate distributions.
Propagate these distributions through nonlinearities using Hermite-polynomial (orthogonal expansion) techniques to update cumulants across layers.
Evaluate the network's expected output analytically from the final activation approximation, avoiding sample-based forward passes.
infographic.impact: Provides a fast, low-variance alternative to Monte Carlo for estimating expectations at initialization, enabling cheaper analysis of architectures and initializations and accelerating research tasks that require many expectation evaluations.

title: LongSeeker: Elastic Context Orchestration for Long-Horizon Search Agents
authors: Yijun Lu, Rui Ye, Yuwen Du, Jiajun Wang, Songhua Liu
abstract: Long-horizon search agents must manage a rapidly growing working context as they reason, call tools, and observe information. Naively accumulating all intermediate content can overwhelm the agent, increasing costs and the risk of errors. We propose that effective context management should be adaptive: parts of the agent's trajectory are maintained at different levels of detail depending on their current relevance to the task. To operationalize this principle, we introduce Context-ReAct, a genera

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive 'elastic' context management keeps different parts of an agent's trajectory at different levels of detail according to relevance, preventing context bloat while preserving information needed for long-horizon search and reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Long-horizon search agents accumulate ever-growing intermediate content that increases compute/cost and the risk of errors; the paper addresses how to manage that working context efficiently and adaptively.
method: Introduce Context-ReAct: organize an agent's trajectory into multi-resolution tiers (detailed, summarized, compressed/archive) and move segments between tiers based on their current relevance.
Use a dynamic relevance scorer and cost-aware controller to decide when to summarize, compress, archive, or rehydrate segments so the agent keeps only what matters at the needed fidelity.
Integrate selective retrieval and rehydration into the agent loop and tool calls so reasoning remains accurate without replaying the full raw context.
infographic.impact: Makes long-horizon search agents more scalable and cost-effective by reducing memory and compute overhead while lowering error rates from overloaded context, enabling longer, cheaper, and more reliable agent workflows for ML practitioners.
