title: Taming Outlier Tokens in Diffusion Transformers
authors: Xiaoyu Wu, Yifei Wang, Tsu-Jui Fu, Liang-Chieh Chen, Zhe Gan
abstract: We study outlier tokens in Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation. Prior work has shown that Vision Transformers (ViTs) can produce a small number of high-norm tokens that attract disproportionate attention while carrying limited local information, but their role in generative models remains underexplored. We show that this phenomenon appears in both the encoder and denoiser of modern Representation Autoencoder (RAE)-DiT pipelines: pretrained ViT encoders can produce outlier represen

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) produce a small number of high-norm "outlier" tokens (in both encoder and denoiser) that attract disproportionate attention while carrying little local information; identifying and taming these tokens leads to more reliable, higher-quality image generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Outlier tokens in ViT-based diffusion pipelines skew attention and conditioning, degrading generation fidelity and robustness in Representation Autoencoder (RAE)-DiT image models.
method: Empirical diagnosis: detect and characterize high-norm outlier tokens in pretrained ViT encoders and DiT denoisers (token-norm distributions, attention patterns).
Impact analysis: measure how outlier tokens concentrate attention and affect denoising and reconstructed image quality.
Mitigation strategies: apply targeted interventions (e.g., token norm regularization / clipping, attention reweighting or selective pruning, and light fine-tuning) to reduce outlier influence.
infographic.impact: Taming outlier tokens makes DiT-based image generation more stable and faithful to local image content, improving sample quality and reliability for practitioners building diffusion + transformer pipelines.

title: Almost-Orthogonality in Lp Spaces: A Case Study with Grok
authors: Ziang Chen, Jaume de Dios Pont, Paata Ivanisvili, Jose Madrid, Haozhu Wang
abstract: Carbery proposed the following sharpened form of triangle inequality for many functions: for any $p\ge 2$ and any finite sequence $(f_j)_j\subset L^p$ we have \[ \Big\|\sum_j f_j\Big\|_p \ \le\ \left(\sup_{j} \sum_{k} α_{jk}^{\,c}\right)^{1/p'} \Big(\sum_j \|f_j\|_p^p\Big)^{1/p}, \] where $c=2$, $1/p+1/p'=1$, and $α_{jk}=\sqrt{\frac{\|f_{j}f_{k}\|_{p/2}}{\|f_{j}\|_{p}\|f_{k}\|_{p}}}$. In the first part of this paper we construct a counterexample showing that this inequality fails for every $p>2$

infographic.key_insight: The authors construct an explicit counterexample showing Carbery’s sharpened triangle inequality (with c = 2) fails for every p > 2, overturning a proposed almost-orthogonality bound in L^p spaces.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies whether a stronger triangle inequality quantified by interaction coefficients α_{jk} holds in L^p for p ≥ 2; the paper resolves this by showing the proposed inequality is false for all p > 2 and delineates the limits of almost-orthogonality claims.
method: Construct an explicit finite sequence (f_j) in L^p tailored to maximize pairwise interactions and compute norms to exhibit a violation of the proposed bound.
Provide rigorous analytic estimates of the interaction coefficients α_{jk} and asymptotic analysis showing the inequality cannot hold for any p > 2.
Supplement analytic work with computational/experimental exploration (case study with Grok) to guide search for candidate counterexamples and verify numerical behavior.
infographic.impact: Alerts analysts and ML researchers that Carbery-style almost-orthogonality bounds with c = 2 cannot be assumed for p > 2, so proofs or algorithms relying on those inequalities must be re-examined or replaced with valid alternatives; improves rigor in using L^p-based norm bounds in ML theory and signal analysis.

title: PhysForge: Generating Physics-Grounded 3D Assets for Interactive Virtual World
authors: Yunhan Yang, Chunshi Wang, Junliang Ye, Yang Li, Zanxin Chen
abstract: Synthesizing physics-grounded 3D assets is a critical bottleneck for interactive virtual worlds and embodied AI. Existing methods predominantly focus on static geometry, overlooking the functional properties essential for interaction. We propose that interactive asset generation must be rooted in functional logic and hierarchical physics. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysForge, a decoupled two-stage framework supported by PhysDB, a large-scale dataset of 150,000 assets with four-tier physica

infographic.key_insight: PhysForge separates functional logic from physical realization to generate 3D assets that are not just geometrically plausible but also interaction-ready under hierarchical physics constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: Current 3D asset generation focuses on static geometry and ignores functional/physical properties needed for interaction in virtual worlds and embodied AI. PhysForge addresses the gap by producing assets grounded in functional logic and multi-tier physics.
method: Decoupled two-stage framework: first infer high-level functional logic, then realize geometry and physical parameters consistent with that function.
Trained and validated using PhysDB, a large-scale dataset (~150,000 assets) annotated with multi-tier physical/functional information to support hierarchical physics reasoning.
Enforces hierarchical physics constraints during generation so assets behave plausibly in interactive simulations and embodied tasks.
infographic.impact: Makes 3D asset synthesis usable for interactive virtual worlds and embodied AI by ensuring generated objects have predictable, functionally meaningful behaviors — reducing manual authoring and bridging sim-to-real gaps.

title: D-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continuously Tuning Step-Distilled Diffusion Models
authors: Dengyang Jiang, Xin Jin, Dongyang Liu, Zanyi Wang, Mingzhe Zheng
abstract: The landscape of high-performance image generation models is currently shifting from the inefficient multi-step ones to the efficient few-step counterparts (e.g, Z-Image-Turbo and FLUX.2-klein). However, these models present significant challenges for directly continuous supervised fine-tuning. For example, applying the commonly used fine-tuning technique would compromises their inherent few-step inference capability. To address this, we propose D-OPSD, a novel training paradigm for step-distill

infographic.key_insight: D-OPSD introduces on-policy self-distillation to continuously fine-tune step-distilled (few-step) diffusion models without degrading their fast, few-step inference quality — the model learns from its own on-policy trajectories to preserve and improve step-wise behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard supervised fine-tuning breaks the inference behavior of step-distilled few-step diffusion models due to train/inference mismatch; D-OPSD solves continuous tuning while retaining few-step efficiency and sample quality.
method: On-policy self-distillation loop: generate intermediate trajectories with the current (teacher) few-step model and use them as targets for the student to learn step-wise denoising behavior.
Training objective blends distillation losses that align student predictions with teacher on-policy outputs and supervised task losses, preserving the distilled step schedule.
Continuous/iterative update scheme that updates teacher from the tuned student (or uses moving-average teacher) to maintain consistency and avoid catastrophic changes to few-step inference.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to safely fine-tune high-speed few-step diffusion models for downstream tasks or data domains while keeping fast inference and high sample quality, reducing the need for costly multi-step retraining.

title: When Life Gives You BC, Make Q-functions: Extracting Q-values from Behavior Cloning for On-Robot Reinforcement Learning
authors: Lakshita Dodeja, Ondrej Biza, Shivam Vats, Stephen Hart, Stefanie Tellex
abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) has emerged as a highly effective paradigm for robot learning. However, BC lacks a self-guided mechanism for online improvement after demonstrations have been collected. Existing offline-to-online learning methods often cause policies to replace previously learned good actions due to a distribution mismatch between offline data and online learning. In this work, we propose Q2RL, Q-Estimation and Q-Gating from BC for Reinforcement Learning, an algorithm for efficient offline

infographic.key_insight: You can extract reliable Q-value estimates from a behavior-cloned policy and use those estimates to gate online reinforcement learning, enabling safe, targeted improvement on robot hardware without overwriting good demonstrated behaviors.
infographic.problem_solved: Behavior Cloning (BC) lacks a self-guided mechanism for safe online improvement: naive offline-to-online updates can overwrite good demonstrated actions due to distribution mismatch, causing regressions when deployed on robots.
method: Q-estimation from BC: derive Q-value estimates from the pretrained behavior-cloned policy and offline data to quantify action quality.
Q-gating during online RL: allow policy updates only when candidate actions have higher estimated Q-values than the preserved BC actions, preventing replacement of good demonstrated behavior.
Conservative, efficient offline-to-online workflow: combine extracted Q-values with online exploration to focusedly improve performance on-robot while maintaining safety and sample efficiency.
infographic.impact: Q2RL enables safe, sample-efficient on-robot reinforcement learning by preserving proven offline behaviors and only applying online updates that are estimated to improve returns — reducing regressions and speeding real-world deployment.

title: Geometry-Aware State Space Model: A New Paradigm for Whole-Slide Image Representation
authors: Enhui Chai, Sicheng Chen, Tianyi Zhang, Chad Wong, Kecheng Huang
abstract: Accurate analysis of histopathological images is critical for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. Whole-slide images (WSIs), which digitize tissue specimens at gigapixel resolution, are fundamental to this process but require aggregating thousands of patches for slide-level predictions. Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) tackles this challenge with a two-stage paradigm, decoupling tile-level embedding and slide-level prediction. However, most existing methods implicitly embed patch represent

infographic.key_insight: A geometry-aware state space model (SSM) treats a whole-slide image as a spatially-anchored sequence of patch embeddings, enabling efficient capture of long-range spatial interactions across thousands of tiles and replacing the traditional two-stage MIL pipeline with a unified geometry-aware aggregator.
infographic.problem_solved: Aggregating thousands of patch-level features in gigapixel whole-slide images while preserving spatial geometry and long-range dependencies—limitations of conventional two-stage Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) that often ignores explicit spatial relations and struggles with scalability.
method: Encode WSIs as sequences of patch embeddings augmented with explicit 2D spatial coordinates/geometry-aware positional encodings.
Use a state space model whose transition/update dynamics are modulated by geometric relationships to capture long-range, order-aware interactions among distant patches.
Perform efficient slide-level aggregation with the SSM (linear or near-linear complexity), enabling end-to-end training and scalable inference on gigapixel slides.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable, geometry-aware alternative to MIL that improves representation of spatial context in computational pathology, enabling more accurate and interpretable slide-level predictions and practical training on large WSI datasets.

title: Aes3D: Aesthetic Assessment in 3D Gaussian Splatting
authors: Chuanzhi Xu, Boyu Wei, Haoxian Zhou, Xuanhua Yin, Zihan Deng
abstract: As 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) gains attention in immersive media and digital content creation, assessing the aesthetics of 3D scenes becomes important in helping creators build more visually compelling 3D content. However, existing evaluation methods for 3D scenes primarily emphasize reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism, largely overlooking higher-level aesthetic attributes such as composition, harmony, and visual appeal. This limitation comes from two key challenges: (1) the absence

infographic.key_insight: Aes3D presents a dedicated framework to evaluate and predict the aesthetic quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by learning from multi-view renders and 3D-aware cues, bridging the gap between low‑level fidelity metrics and high‑level visual appeal.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing 3D evaluation metrics focus on reconstruction fidelity and realism but ignore higher‑level aesthetic attributes (composition, harmony, visual appeal); there is no standardized benchmark or model for assessing aesthetics of 3DGS content.
method: Create a human‑rated benchmark of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes and render multi‑view images per scene for perceptual labeling.
Extract image aesthetic features from each view (pretrained aesthetic/vision backbones) and aggregate across views using attention/pooling to form a scene‑level representation.
Augment aggregated visual features with 3DGS‑specific cues (e.g., splat distribution, color statistics, camera composition) and train a regression/ranking model to predict aesthetic scores.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a tool and benchmark to quantify and optimize visual appeal in 3DGS pipelines, enabling automated quality guidance, aesthetic-driven content generation, and standardized evaluation beyond fidelity metrics.

title: OpenSearch-VL: An Open Recipe for Frontier Multimodal Search Agents
authors: Shuang Chen, Kaituo Feng, Hangting Chen, Wenxuan Huang, Dasen Dai
abstract: Deep search has become a crucial capability for frontier multimodal agents, enabling models to solve complex questions through active search, evidence verification, and multi-step reasoning. Despite rapid progress, top-tier multimodal search agents remain difficult to reproduce, largely due to the absence of open high-quality training data, transparent trajectory synthesis pipelines, or detailed training recipes. To this end, we introduce OpenSearch-VL, a fully open-source recipe for training fr

infographic.key_insight: OpenSearch-VL delivers a fully open, end-to-end recipe that makes state-of-the-art deep multimodal search agents reproducible by releasing transparent trajectory synthesis, training data, and training procedures. This enables models to perform active multimodal search, evidence verification, and multi-step reasoning with reproducible results.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of open high-quality training data, opaque trajectory synthesis pipelines, and missing training recipes that make top-tier multimodal search agents hard to reproduce.
method: Design and open-source a trajectory synthesis pipeline that generates multi-step, multimodal search demonstrations (query → retrieval → verification → reasoning).
Curate and release high-quality training datasets and annotation tools tailored for deep search behaviors across images, text, and web-like evidence.
Publish a complete training recipe and evaluation suite (model variants, hyperparameters, metrics) so practitioners can reproduce and adapt frontier multimodal search agents.
infographic.impact: Provides researchers and engineers with a transparent, reusable foundation to build, evaluate, and iterate on multimodal search agents—accelerating reproducibility, benchmarking, and real-world deployment.

title: Sharp Capacity Thresholds in Linear Associative Memory: From Winner-Take-All to Listwise Retrieval
authors: Nicholas Barnfield, Juno Kim, Eshaan Nichani, Jason D. Lee, Yue M. Lu
abstract: How many key-value associations can a $d\times d$ linear memory store? We show that the answer depends not only on the $d^2$ degrees of freedom in the memory matrix, but also on the retrieval criterion. In an isotropic Gaussian model for the stored pairs, we show that top-1 retrieval, where every signal must beat its largest distractor, requires the logarithmic model-size scale $d^2\asymp n\log n$. We prove that the correlation matrix memory construction, which stores associations by superposing

infographic.key_insight: Storage capacity of a d×d linear associative memory is controlled not just by matrix degrees of freedom but by the retrieval rule: top-1 (winner-take-all) retrieval requires a larger memory scale (d^2 ≍ n log n) than coarser / listwise criteria, producing sharp capacity thresholds.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines how many key–value pairs a linear memory can reliably store and retrieve, and shows that achievable capacity fundamentally depends on the retrieval criterion (top-1 vs listwise) rather than only on parameter count.
method: Analyze an isotropic Gaussian model of stored key–value pairs to obtain probabilistic capacity bounds.
Study the correlation-matrix (superposition) memory construction and derive sharp thresholds for successful retrieval under different criteria.
Combine probabilistic/threshold analysis to contrast winner-take-all (top-1) and listwise retrieval regimes.
infographic.impact: Clarifies fundamental trade-offs between memory size and retrieval requirements, guiding design of associative memory layers and retrieval mechanisms in neural architectures; tells practitioners when extra capacity (≈log n factor) is necessary for exact top-1 recall.
visual_elements: Phase-transition plot: probability of successful retrieval vs normalized memory size (d^2/n) showing sharp thresholds for top-1 and listwise regimes.

title: LoViF 2026 The First Challenge on Holistic Quality Assessment for 4D World Model (PhyScore)
authors: Wei Luo, Yiting Lu, Xin Li, Haoran Li, Fengbin Guan
abstract: This paper reports on the LoViF 2026 PhyScore challenge, a competition on holistic quality assessment of world-model-generated videos across both 2D and 4D generation settings. The challenge is motivated by a central gap in current evaluation practice: perceptual quality alone is insufficient to judge whether generated dynamics are physically plausible, temporally coherent, and consistent with input conditions. Participants are required to build a metric that jointly predicts four dimensions, i.

infographic.key_insight: LoViF 2026 introduces PhyScore, the first challenge and unified metric framework for jointly assessing perceptual quality and physical/temporal fidelity of videos generated by 2D and 4D world models. It shows that perceptual metrics alone miss crucial failures in dynamics, conditioning consistency, and physical plausibility.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap in evaluation by providing a standardized benchmark and metric for holistic quality assessment of generated videos—covering perceptual quality, physical plausibility, temporal coherence, and consistency with input conditions—across both 2D and 4D generation settings.
method: Organize a public challenge (LoViF 2026) where participants submit metrics that jointly predict four dimensions: perceptual quality, physical plausibility, temporal coherence, and conditioning consistency (PhyScore).

Provide a curated dataset of world-model-generated videos (2D and 4D), multi-dimensional human and/or synthetic annotations, and an evaluation protocol that combines per-dimension scores into a unified leaderboard metric.
Release baselines, evaluation code, and leaderboard infrastructure to compare metrics, analyze failure modes, and promote reproducible evaluation of dynamics-focused generation.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to reliably detect when generated dynamics are visually plausible but physically or temporally incorrect, improving benchmarking, model selection, and downstream use in simulation, robotics, and AR/VR. Standardized multi-dimensional scoring accelerates progress toward physically consistent generative models.

title: Implicit Representations of Grammaticality in Language Models
authors: Yingshan Susan Wang, Linlu Qiu, Zhaofeng Wu, Roger P. Levy, Yoon Kim
abstract: Grammaticality and likelihood are distinct notions in human language. Pretrained language models (LMs), which are probabilistic models of language fitted to maximize corpus likelihood, generate grammatically well-formed text and discriminate well between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences in tightly controlled minimal pairs. However, their string probabilities do not sharply discriminate between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences overall. But do LMs implicitly acquire a grammaticality

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained language models implicitly encode grammaticality in their internal representations even when token probabilities do not sharply separate grammatical from ungrammatical strings; a simple probe can extract this latent grammaticality signal across diverse constructions.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between probability-based evaluation and human notions of grammatical well-formedness by showing where and how grammatical judgments are represented inside LMs, enabling reliable discrimination of grammatical vs. ungrammatical sentences beyond surface string likelihoods.
method: Collect minimal-pair and broader sentence sets with grammatical vs. ungrammatical labels across syntactic phenomena.
Extract hidden states (layer-wise) from pretrained LMs and train lightweight probes (e.g., linear classifiers) to predict grammaticality from representations.
Analyze probe accuracy, generalization across constructions, and representational geometry (layer and head effects) to localize grammaticality signals.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to read out grammatical knowledge from models without changing model training; useful for evaluation, targeted debugging, and building grammar-aware controls for generation and filtering.
visual_elements: t-SNE/UMAP plot of hidden-state embeddings colored by grammatical vs. ungrammatical to show clustering of grammaticality.

title: Syn4D: A Multiview Synthetic 4D Dataset
authors: Zeren Jiang, Yushi Lan, Yihang Luo, Yufan Deng, Zihang Lai
abstract: Dense 3D reconstruction and tracking of dynamic scenes from monocular video remains an important open challenge in computer vision. Progress in this area has been constrained by the scarcity of high-quality datasets with dense, complete, and accurate geometric annotations. To address this limitation, we introduce Syn4D, a multiview synthetic dataset of dynamic scenes that includes ground-truth camera motion, depth maps, dense tracking, and parametric human pose annotations. A key feature of Syn4

infographic.key_insight: Syn4D is a multiview synthetic 4D dataset that delivers dense, accurate geometric and tracking annotations (camera motion, depth, dense tracking, parametric human pose), enabling robust evaluation and training for dynamic scene reconstruction and tracking from video.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of high-quality datasets with dense, complete, and accurate geometric annotations for dynamic scenes, which has limited progress in monocular video 3D reconstruction and object/person tracking.
method: Generate multiview synthetic dynamic scenes with controllable variations (motion, lighting, interactions).
Provide ground-truth annotations per frame: camera motion, dense depth maps, per-vertex/point tracking, and parametric human poses.
Package the dataset for benchmarking: synchronized multiview sequences plus standardized splits and metrics for reconstruction and tracking tasks.
infographic.impact: Syn4D enables reproducible benchmarking and data-driven development of algorithms for dynamic 3D reconstruction and tracking, reducing reliance on scarce real-world annotations and accelerating progress in vision research and applications.

infographic.problem_solved: Improves evaluation and practical reusability of peptide–TCR binding predictors by addressing dataset bias, limited generalization to new antigens, and the impact of negative-sample design on model performance.

title: Force-free molecular dynamics through autoregressive equivariant networks
authors: Fabian L. Thiemann, Thiago Reschützegger, Massimiliano Esposito, Tseden Taddese, Juan D. Olarte-Plata
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 05 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01227-7

Thiemann et al. introduce TrajCast, a neural network that bypasses force calculations to directly predict atomic trajectories, enabling time steps up to 30 times longer while accurately reproducing physical properties of molecules and materials.

infographic.key_insight: TrajCast is an autoregressive equivariant neural network that predicts atomic trajectories directly—skipping explicit force calculations—allowing stable molecular dynamics with time steps up to ~30× larger while preserving key physical properties.
infographic.problem_solved: Conventional molecular dynamics is bottlenecked by expensive force evaluations and small time steps required for stability; TrajCast removes the need for explicit forces and enables much larger timesteps without sacrificing accuracy.
method: Autoregressive equivariant architecture: predicts next atomic positions conditioned on past trajectory segments while respecting rotation/translation equivariance.
Force-free formulation: learns dynamics directly from trajectory data instead of computing forces and integrating Newton’s equations.
Physics-aware training and validation: trained on MD trajectories with losses that preserve structural/thermodynamic properties and evaluated on long-time stability and material properties.
infographic.impact: Enables dramatically faster molecular simulations for materials and biomolecules, lowering computational cost and enabling integration of learned dynamics into ML pipelines and high-throughput discovery workflows.
visual_elements: Schematic: comparison diagram showing standard MD (forces → accelerations → positions) vs TrajCast (past positions → network → future positions).
Performance chart: timestep size vs accuracy/stability, highlighting ~30× timestep increase with comparable property errors.

title: Pixel Perfect: Relational Image Quality Assessment with Spatially-Aware Distortions
authors: Fadeel Sher Khan, Long N. Le, Abhinau K. Venkataramanan, Seok-Jun Lee, Hamid R. Sheikh
abstract: Traditional image quality assessment (IQA) methods rely on mean opinion scores (MOS), which are resource-intensive to collect and fail to provide interpretable, localized feedback on specific image distortions. We overcome these limitations by shifting from absolute quality prediction to a relational and directional assessment. Our approach utilizes a self-supervised synthetic distortion engine to generate training data, eliminating the need for manual annotation. A distortion prediction network

infographic.key_insight: Rather than predicting absolute MOS scores, the paper reframes image quality assessment as a relational, directional task and trains a model to predict spatially-aware distortion maps using synthetic, self-supervised distortions—removing the need for costly human labels.
infographic.problem_solved: MOS-based IQA is expensive, subjective, and provides no localized guidance; this work provides scalable, interpretable, pixel-level distortion assessment and relative comparisons between images without manual annotation.
method: Reformulate IQA as relational/directional prediction (which image/region is more distorted) instead of absolute scoring.
Use a self-supervised synthetic distortion engine to generate diverse, localized distortions for training data, eliminating manual MOS collection.
Train a distortion prediction network to output spatially-aware distortion maps and pairwise relational labels (rankings/directions) for robust, interpretable assessment.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, annotation-free IQA that gives pixel-level diagnostic feedback useful for image restoration, model debugging, and automated dataset curation—speeding development cycles and improving interpretability.

title: Compress Then Adapt? No, Do It Together via Task-aware Union of Subspaces
authors: Jingze Ge, Yun Liu, Xue Geng, Wanqi Dong, Wang Zhe Mark
abstract: Adapting large pretrained models to diverse tasks is now routine, yet the two dominant strategies of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and low-rank compression are typically composed in sequence. This decoupled practice first compresses and then fine-tunes adapters, potentially misaligning the compressed subspace with downstream objectives and squandering a global parameter budget. To overcome this limitation, we introduce JACTUS (Joint Adaptation and Compression with a Task-aware Union of

infographic.key_insight: Instead of compressing a pretrained model and then fine-tuning adapters sequentially, jointly learn compressed adapter subspaces that are aware of downstream tasks — forming a task-aware union of subspaces so compression and adaptation reinforce each other.
infographic.problem_solved: The common compress-then-adapt workflow can misalign the compressed parameter subspace with downstream objectives and waste global parameter budget, reducing task performance and efficiency.
method: Joint optimization: learn adapter parameters and their low-rank/compressed basis simultaneously rather than in sequence.
Task-aware union of subspaces: construct a shared union of task-specific low-dimensional subspaces that captures both common structure and task-specific directions.
Budget-aware allocation: dynamically allocate compressed capacity across tasks to maximize accuracy under a global parameter/compute constraint.
infographic.impact: JACTUS enables more accurate and parameter-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models by aligning compression with downstream objectives, improving the accuracy-vs-size tradeoff for practitioners using PEFT and model compression.
visual_elements: Pipeline comparison: side-by-side diagram contrasting sequential (compress → adapt) vs joint (compress+adapt) workflows.

title: FlexSQL: Flexible Exploration and Execution Make Better Text-to-SQL Agents
authors: Quang Hieu Pham, Yang He, Ping Nie, Canwen Xu, Davood Rafiei
abstract: Text-to-SQL over large analytical databases requires navigating complex schemas, resolving ambiguous queries, and grounding decisions in actual data. Most current systems follow a fixed pipeline where schema elements are retrieved once upfront and the database is only revisited for post-hoc repair, limiting recovery from early mistakes. We present FlexSQL, a text-to-SQL agent whose core design principle is flexible database interaction: the agent can explore schema structure, inspect data values

infographic.key_insight: Allowing a Text-to-SQL agent to interact flexibly with the database—exploring schema structure and inspecting actual data values throughout planning and execution—lets it recover from early mistakes and produce more accurate, grounded SQL for large analytical databases.
infographic.problem_solved: Fixed, one-shot schema retrieval and post-hoc repair limit a system's ability to handle complex schemas, ambiguous user intents, and data-dependent grounding; FlexSQL addresses the need for iterative, data-aware decision making in Text-to-SQL agents.
method: Agent loop that alternates planning, targeted schema exploration, and lightweight data inspection rather than a single upfront retrieval step.
On-demand execution and partial runs to validate intermediate decisions against real data, enabling corrective steps before final SQL is produced.
Controller (LLM-based) that conditions generation on live database feedback, allowing dynamic recovery and refinement of queries.
infographic.impact: FlexSQL improves robustness and accuracy of Text-to-SQL on large, complex analytical databases, reducing error-prone outputs and developer effort; this enables more reliable natural-language access to real-world data for analytics and BI workflows.
visual_elements: Flow diagram of the FlexSQL agent loop: query → schema exploration → data inspection → partial execution → refinement → final SQL.

title: A collaborative constrained graph diffusion model for the generation of realistic synthetic molecules
authors: Manuel Ruiz-Botella, Marta Sales-Pardo, Roger Guimerà
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 04 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01229-5

The collaborative constrained graph diffusion model CoCoGraph generates novel molecules that are guaranteed to be valid and more realistic than state-of-the-art outputs, while achieving faster performance with up to an order of magnitude fewer parameters.

infographic.key_insight: CoCoGraph is a collaborative constrained graph diffusion model that generates novel molecular graphs that are guaranteed chemically valid and empirically more realistic than state-of-the-art outputs, while using up to an order of magnitude fewer parameters for faster performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces invalid or unrealistic outputs from molecular generative models and cuts computational/parameter cost, addressing the need for reliable, efficient synthetic-molecule generation for downstream discovery tasks.
method: Graph-based diffusion generative process that operates directly on molecular graphs to construct atoms and bonds.
Incorporates explicit chemical constraints during diffusion via collaborative modules that enforce validity and guide realistic structural patterns.
Parameter-efficient architecture and training that achieves high-quality samples with substantially fewer parameters and faster sampling.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to generate high-quality, chemically valid molecules faster and with less compute, accelerating tasks like virtual screening, lead optimization, and materials design while reducing engineering overhead.

title: Multi-fidelity surrogates for mechanics of composites: from co-kriging to multi-fidelity neural networks
authors: Haizhou Wen, Elham Kiyani, Gang Li, Srikanth Pilla, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: Composite materials exhibit strongly hierarchical and anisotropic properties governed by coupled mechanisms spanning constituents, plies, laminates, structures, and manufacturing history. This intrinsic complexity makes predictive modeling of composites expensive, because repeated experiments and high-fidelity simulations are needed to cover large design spaces of material, structure, and manufacturing. Multi-fidelity surrogate modeling addresses this challenge by combining abundant, less expens

infographic.key_insight: Combining abundant low-fidelity data with sparse high-fidelity simulations via multi-fidelity surrogates (from co-kriging to multi-fidelity neural networks) delivers accurate, cost-effective predictions of composite mechanics across hierarchical scales. The paper shows that hybrid/statistical and neural approaches can trade off accuracy, uncertainty quantification, and computational cost for practical design exploration.
infographic.problem_solved: Predictive modeling of composite materials is prohibitively expensive because capturing hierarchical, anisotropic behavior requires many costly high-fidelity experiments or simulations; the paper addresses how to efficiently build accurate surrogates that leverage cheaper, lower-fidelity information.
method: Develop and compare multi-fidelity modeling frameworks ranging from classical co-kriging to modern multi-fidelity neural networks that fuse low- and high-fidelity data.
Exploit hierarchical/scale-aware inputs (constituents → plies → laminates → structures and manufacturing history) so surrogates respect composite-specific dependencies.
Evaluate trade-offs: accuracy, uncertainty quantification, and cost (number of high-fidelity runs) to guide surrogate selection and training strategies.
infographic.impact: Provides practical surrogate strategies that substantially reduce the need for expensive high-fidelity simulations, enabling faster design space exploration, uncertainty-aware optimization, and integration of ML models into composite materials workflows.
visual_elements: Fidelity pyramid: stacked icons showing abundant low-fidelity data at the bottom and scarce high-fidelity data at the top, with arrows indicating fusion into a surrogate.

title: When Audio-Language Models Fail to Leverage Multimodal Context for Dysarthric Speech Recognition
authors: Pehuén Moure, Niclas Pokel, Bilal Bounajma, Yingqiang Gao, Roman Boehringer
abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems remain brittle on dysarthric and other atypical speech. Recent audio-language models raise the possibility of improving performance by conditioning on additional clinical context at inference time, but it is unclear whether these models can make use of such information. We introduce a benchmark built on the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP) dataset that tests whether diagnosis labels, clinician-derived speech ratings, and progressively richer clinical

infographic.key_insight: Audio–language models rarely benefit from clinical multimodal context when transcribing dysarthric speech; adding diagnosis labels or clinician ratings did not reliably reduce recognition errors.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluates whether conditioning ASR on clinical/contextual metadata can help with recognition of dysarthric and atypical speech, exposing a gap between multimodal modeling potential and practical gains on accessibility-focused speech data.
method: Construct a benchmark from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP) that pairs dysarthric speech with diagnosis labels, clinician-derived speech ratings, and progressively richer clinical context.
Evaluate representative audio–language models by comparing ASR performance with and without each type/level of contextual conditioning; include controlled ablations to isolate effects.
Analyze failure modes and quantify when/why contextual signals fail to improve word/error-level metrics, guiding recommendations for model and dataset design.
infographic.impact: Alerts ML practitioners that naive multimodal conditioning may not improve ASR for atypical speech and motivates developing better integration strategies, targeted training data, and evaluation protocols for accessible speech technologies.

title: TOC-SR: Task-Optimal Compact diffusion for Image Super Resolution
authors: Sowmya Vajrala, Akshay Bankar, Manjunath Arveti, Shreyas Pandith, Sravanth Kodavanti
abstract: Diffusion models have recently demonstrated strong performance for image restoration tasks, including super-resolution. However, their large model size and iterative sampling procedures make them computationally expensive for practical deployment. In this work, we present TOC-SR, a framework for building efficient one-step super-resolution models by first discovering a compact diffusion backbone. Starting from a sixteen-channel latent diffusion model, we construct parameter-efficient surrogate b

infographic.key_insight: A task‑aware search and compression of a tiny latent diffusion backbone enables a one‑step super‑resolution model that matches diffusion quality with far fewer parameters and much faster inference.
infographic.problem_solved: Diffusion‑based super‑resolution achieves high quality but is too large and slow for practical deployment due to heavy models and multi‑step sampling; TOC‑SR addresses model size and sampling cost while preserving restoration quality.
method: Start from a 16‑channel latent diffusion backbone and identify a task‑optimal compact architecture tailored for SR.
Construct a parameter‑efficient surrogate via targeted compression (e.g., pruning/architecture search) and task‑aware distillation to transfer diffusion priors into a lightweight model.
Convert the compact surrogate into a one‑step SR predictor that eliminates iterative sampling, using loss alignment and perceptual/quality objectives to retain fidelity.
infographic.impact: Makes high‑quality diffusion‑level super‑resolution feasible on constrained hardware by cutting model size and latency, enabling real‑time or edge deployment without large quality loss.

Pipeline flowchart: compress/search → surrogate construction → task‑aware distillation → one‑step inference

title: AlbumFill: Album-Guided Reasoning and Retrieval for Personalized Image Completion
authors: Yu-Ju Tsai, Brian Price, Qing Liu, Luis Figueroa, Daniil Pakhomov
abstract: Personalized image completion aims to restore occluded regions in personal photos while preserving identity and appearance. Existing methods either rely on generic inpainting models that often fail to maintain identity consistency, or assume that suitable reference images are explicitly provided. In practice, suitable references are often not explicitly provided, requiring the system to search for identity-consistent images within personal photo collections. We present AlbumFill, a training-free

infographic.key_insight: AlbumFill locates identity-consistent reference photos inside a user's album and uses them to guide a training-free image completion pipeline, enabling faithful, identity-preserving restoration without requiring explicitly provided references or model fine-tuning.
infographic.problem_solved: Restores occluded regions in personal photos while preserving the subject's identity and appearance, even when suitable reference images are not explicitly supplied.
method: Album-level retrieval: search the user's photo collection with identity-aware embeddings to find candidate reference images that match appearance and pose.
Reference reasoning & selection: rank and align the best matches, reasoning about which patches/attributes to borrow for the occluded area.

Training-free completion: condition an off-the-shelf inpainting/diffusion module on the selected references and perform compositing/latent blending to produce identity-consistent results without retraining.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, deployable personalized photo repair that doesn't require curated references or costly retraining, lowering engineering effort and improving user experience for photo editing and restoration tools.

title: HumanSplatHMR: Closing the Loop Between Human Mesh Recovery and Gaussian Splatting Avatar
authors: Yeheng Zong, Pou-Chun Kung, Yike Pan, Seth Isaacson, Yizhou Chen
abstract: Accurately recovering human pose and appearance from video is an essential component of scene reconstruction, with applications to motion capture, motion prediction, virtual reality, and digital twinning. Despite significant interest in building realistic human avatars from video, this paper demonstrates that existing methods do not accurately recover the 3D geometry of humans. ViT-based approaches are not consistently reliable and can overfit to 2D views, while NeRF- and Gaussian Splatting-base

infographic.key_insight: Closing a differentiable loop between Human Mesh Recovery (HMR) and Gaussian Splatting avatars lets each system supervise and correct the other, producing substantially more accurate 3D human geometry and consistent appearance across views.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing pipelines either overfit to 2D cues (ViT-based HMR) or produce appearance-focused but geometrically imprecise avatars (NeRF/Gaussian Splatting), yielding inaccurate 3D human geometry and inconsistent novel-view renderings.
method: Create a closed-loop pipeline where HMR produces an initial mesh, which is converted into a Gaussian Splatting avatar and rendered to generate multi-view supervision.
Backpropagate differences between rendered splat views and input video to update HMR predictions; jointly optimize mesh parameters and Gaussian splat attributes for coherent geometry + appearance.
Iterative refinement: alternate between mesh recovery and splat optimization to converge on accurate 3D shape and photorealistic rendering.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to get reliable, view-consistent 3D human avatars from video—improving motion capture, virtual production, and any ML task that needs accurate human geometry or novel-view synthesis.

title: U-Define: Designing User Workflows for Hard and Soft Constraints in LLM-Based Planning
authors: Christine P Lee, Xinyu Jessica Wang, Aws Albarghouthi, David Porfirio, Bilge Mutlu
abstract: LLMs are increasingly used for end-user task planning, yet their black-box nature limits users' ability to ensure reliability and control. While recent systems incorporate verification techniques, it remains unclear how users can effectively apply such rigid constraints to represent intent or adapt to real-world variability. For example, prior work finds that hard-only constraints are too rigid, and numeric flexibility weights confuse users. We investigate how interaction workflows can better su

infographic.key_insight: A mixed hard/soft constraint workflow (instead of only rigid rules or opaque numeric weights) helps end users express intent, verify plans, and iteratively relax requirements so LLM-based planners become both controllable and adaptable.
infographic.problem_solved: Makes constraint specification and verification for LLM planning usable: addresses that hard-only constraints are too brittle and numeric flexibility weights confuse users, preventing reliable control and real-world adaptation.
method: Design of U-Define — an interaction workflow and UI that lets users declare hard constraints (must-have) and human-readable soft constraints (preferences) and combine them in readable templates.
Provide workflow primitives: simulate/verify plans against constraints, present alternative plans with graded violations, and enable progressive relaxation or re-ranking of soft constraints.
Evaluate via prototyping and user studies to compare usability, interpretability, and ability to recover valid plans versus hard-only or weight-only approaches.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build LLM planning systems that are more predictable, debuggable, and usable by non-expert users; improves practical deployment of constraint-aware LLM pipelines in real-world tasks.

title: Edge-Efficient Image Restoration: Transformer Distillation into State-Space Models
authors: Srinivas Soumitri Miriyala, Sowmya Vajrala, Sravanth Kodavanti, Vikram Nelvoy Rajendiran, Sharan Kumar Allur
abstract: We propose a modular framework for hybrid image restoration that integrates transformer and state-space model (SSM) blocks with a focus on improving runtime efficiency on edge hardware. While transformers provide strong global modeling through self-attention, their attention kernels incur substantial latency on mobile devices, especially for high-resolution inputs. In contrast, SSMs such as Mamba offer lineartime sequence modeling with lower runtime overhead but may underperform on fine grained

infographic.key_insight: Distill transformer global modeling into lightweight state-space model (SSM) blocks and combine them in a modular hybrid architecture to retain restoration quality while drastically reducing attention-induced latency on edge devices.
infographic.problem_solved: Attention-heavy transformers give strong global context for image restoration but are slow on mobile/edge hardware, especially for high-resolution inputs; the paper addresses how to achieve transformer-level restoration performance with much lower runtime cost.
method: Modular hybrid architecture that interleaves transformer blocks (for learning rich global priors) with SSM blocks (e.g., Mamba) for linear-time sequence modeling and low runtime overhead.
Transformer-to-SSM distillation where knowledge from trained transformer components is transferred into efficient SSM modules so they emulate attention behaviors without heavy kernels.
Edge-oriented design and deployment considerations (block selection, resolution-aware scheduling) to minimize latency on mobile accelerators while preserving restoration fidelity.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy high-quality image-restoration models on constrained devices by replacing costly attention with distilled SSMs, lowering inference latency and power use without major drops in visual performance.

title: A decoupled diffusion planner that adapts to changing cost limits by using cost-conditioned generation for safety and reward gradients for performance
authors: Rufeng Chen, Zhaofan Zhang, Zhejiang Yang, Hechang Chen, Sihong Xie
abstract: Offline safe reinforcement learning often requires policies to adapt at deployment time to safety budgets that vary across episodes or change within a single episode. While diffusion-based planners enable flexible trajectory generation, existing guidance schemes often treat reward improvement and constraint satisfaction as competing gradient objectives, which can lead to unreliable safety compliance under cost limits. We reinterpret adaptive safe trajectory generation as sampling from a constrai

infographic.key_insight: Decouple safety and performance guidance in a diffusion-based planner: use cost‑conditioned trajectory generation to enforce variable cost limits reliably, and apply reward gradients only to boost performance without violating those constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: Offline safe RL policies must adapt at deployment to episode-varying or intra-episode changing safety budgets; prior diffusion guidance that mixes reward and cost gradients can fail to satisfy cost limits reliably.
method: Treat adaptive safe trajectory generation as sampling from a constrained distribution and implement cost‑conditioned diffusion sampling to respect a specified cost limit.
Apply a separate reward-gradient guidance step (after or alongside cost‑conditioned sampling) to improve task performance while preserving the constraint satisfaction provided by the cost condition.
Design the planner to accept changing cost budgets at deployment (per episode or intra-episode) without retraining the policy offline.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, flexible planner for offline safe RL that preserves safety under varying budgets while still improving reward — useful for real-world applications (robotics, autonomous driving) where safety limits change at run time.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing decoupled stages: cost‑conditioned diffusion sampler → constraint‑satisfying trajectory → reward‑gradient refinement.

title: VideoNet: A Large-Scale Dataset for Domain-Specific Action Recognition
authors: Tanush Yadav, Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
abstract: Videos are unique in their ability to capture actions which transcend multiple frames. Accordingly, for many years action recognition was the quintessential task for video understanding. Unfortunately, due to a lack of sufficiently diverse and challenging data, modern vision-language models (VLMs) are no longer evaluated on their action recognition capabilities. To revitalize action recognition in the era of VLMs, we advocate for a returned focus on domain-specific actions. To this end, we intro

infographic.key_insight: VideoNet introduces a large-scale, domain-focused video dataset and benchmark that restores rigorous evaluation of action recognition—revealing that current vision-language models struggle with fine-grained, temporally extended, domain-specific actions.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of diverse, challenging, domain-specific video data and standardized benchmarks for evaluating action recognition capabilities in modern vision-language models and action-recognition systems.
method: Curate and annotate a large-scale collection of videos emphasizing domain-specific, temporally extended actions (e.g., specialized workflows, sports maneuvers, procedural tasks).
Design standardized evaluation protocols and benchmark splits to evaluate both VLMs and dedicated action-recognition models on fine-grained temporal labels.
Provide baseline evaluations and analysis to quantify current model gaps and guide future model development.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to benchmark temporal and domain-specific action understanding reliably, driving development of models that better handle real-world, multi-frame actions and specialized applications.

title: Linearizing Vision Transformer with Test-Time Training
authors: Yining Li, Dongchen Han, Zeyu Liu, Hanyi Wang, Yulin Wang
abstract: While linear-complexity attention mechanisms offer a promising alternative to Softmax attention for overcoming the quadratic bottleneck, training such models from scratch remains prohibitively expensive. Inheriting weights from pretrained Transformers provides an appealing shortcut, yet the fundamental representational gap between Softmax and linear attention prevents effective weight transfer. In this work, we address this conversion challenge from two perspectives: architectural alignment and

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained Softmax-attention Vision Transformers can be converted into efficient linear-attention models by combining architectural alignment with a short, targeted test-time training stage that closes the representational gap and enables direct weight reuse.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the incompatibility between Softmax attention and linear-complexity attention so practitioners can reuse expensive pretrained ViT weights rather than training linear-attention models from scratch, overcoming the quadratic attention bottleneck without prohibitive compute.
method: Architectural alignment: introduce lightweight compatibility adapters and design linear-attention modules to mimic the functional behaviour of Softmax attention so pretrained weights are more directly transferable.

Test-time training (TTT): apply a brief, self-supervised calibration step on target data (e.g., layer-matching / consistency objectives) to adapt pretrained parameters to the linearized attention dynamics.
Low-overhead deployment: keep additional parameters and adaptation steps minimal to preserve linear inference complexity and practical efficiency gains.
infographic.impact: Enables practical deployment of compute- and memory-efficient Vision Transformers by leveraging existing pretrained models instead of costly retraining, lowering barriers for high-resolution and long-sequence vision applications.

title: RunAgent: Interpreting Natural-Language Plans with Constraint-Guided Execution
authors: Arunabh Srivastava, Mohammad A., Khojastepour, Srimat Chakradhar, Sennur Ulukus
abstract: Humans solve problems by executing targeted plans, yet large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable for structured workflow execution. We propose RunAgent, a multi-agent plan execution platform that interprets natural-language plans while enforcing stepwise execution through constraints and rubrics. RunAgent bridges the expressiveness of natural language with the determinism of programming via an agentic language with explicit control constructs (e.g., \texttt{IF}, \texttt{GOTO}, \texttt{FORAL

infographic.key_insight: RunAgent converts free-form natural-language plans into a constrained, agent-executable program, combining the flexibility of language with deterministic, rubric-guided stepwise execution to improve reliability of workflow completion.
infographic.problem_solved: LLMs are expressive but unreliable for structured, multi-step workflows; RunAgent addresses unpredictability by enforcing constraints, control constructs, and stepwise validation during plan execution.
method: Introduce an agentic plan language with explicit control constructs (e.g., IF, GOTO, FORALL) to represent NL plans in a programmable form.
Use a multi-agent execution platform where coordinator and executor agents follow constraint checks and human-like rubrics to validate and enforce each step.
Apply constraint-guided execution and stepwise validators to ensure deterministic behavior, error detection, and recoverable control flow during runtime.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy LLM-driven workflows with higher faithfulness, reproducibility, and safety by turning ambiguous NL instructions into verifiable, enforceable execution plans.

title: Quantum Gradient-Based Approach for Edge and Corner Detection Using Sobel Kernels
authors: Mohammad Aamir Sohail, Gabriela Pinheiro, Yasemin Poyraz Kocak, Batuhan Hangun, Emre Camkerten
abstract: Edge detection refers to identifying points in a digital image where intensity changes sharply, indicating object boundaries or structural features. Corners are locations where gray-level intensity changes abruptly in multiple directions and are widely used in feature extraction, object tracking, and 3D modeling. In this study, we present a quantum implementation of Sobel-based edge detection and Harris-style corner detection. Two quantum image encoding methods - Flexible Representation of Quant

infographic.key_insight: This work demonstrates a feasible mapping of classical Sobel-based edge detection and a Harris-style corner detector into quantum circuits by using two quantum image encoding schemes, enabling gradient and corner response computation on quantum hardware.
infographic.problem_solved: Brings gradient-based edge and corner detection into the quantum domain by addressing how to encode images, implement Sobel kernels as quantum operators, and compute a Harris-style corner response under quantum measurement and resource constraints.
method: Encode images into quantum states using two quantum image representation schemes (authors evaluate two encodings).
Realize Sobel kernels as quantum operators to compute horizontal/vertical gradients and gradient magnitude in superposition.
Form a Harris-style corner response from the quantum-computed gradients and recover edge/corner locations via measurement and classical post-processing.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical blueprint for basic computer-vision primitives on quantum devices, opening a path to integrate edge/corner detection into quantum ML and image-processing pipelines and to study trade-offs in qubit/gate resources, noise, and accuracy.

title: Map2World: Segment Map Conditioned Text to 3D World Generation
authors: Jaeyoung Chung, Suyoung Lee, Jianfeng Xiang, Jiaolong Yang, Kyoung Mu Lee
abstract: 3D world generation is essential for applications such as immersive content creation or autonomous driving simulation. Recent advances in 3D world generation have shown promising results; however, these methods are constrained by grid layouts and suffer from inconsistencies in object scale throughout the entire world. In this work, we introduce a novel framework, Map2World, that first enables 3D world generation conditioned on user-defined segment maps of arbitrary shapes and scales, ensuring gl

infographic.key_insight: Map2World enables coherent, scalable 3D world generation conditioned on user-defined segment maps (of arbitrary shape and scale) plus text, solving layout and scale inconsistency that limit prior grid-based methods.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing 3D world generators are tied to fixed grid layouts and produce inconsistent object scales across large scenes, offering little intuitive user control; Map2World lets users specify scene structure via segment maps while preserving global scale and layout coherence.
method: Condition the generative pipeline on user-provided segment maps and optional text prompts to control semantic layout and style.
Use scale-aware, multi-resolution representations and coordinate-aware conditioning to maintain consistent object sizes and geometry across arbitrary map shapes.
Synthesize geometry and appearance in a hybrid pipeline (local detail + global consistency modules) to produce large, coherent 3D worlds from map + text inputs.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to create controllable, large-scale 3D scenes for XR content, simulation, and virtual testing, reducing manual modeling and improving realism and repeatability in procedural world generation.

title: Directed Social Regard: Surfacing Targeted Advocacy, Opposition, Aid, Harms, and Victimization in Online Media
authors: Scott Friedman, Ruta Wheelock, Sonja Schmer-Galunder, Drisana Iverson, Jake Vasilakes
abstract: The language in online platforms, influence operations, and political rhetoric frequently directs a mix of pro-social sentiment (e.g., advocacy, helpfulness, compassion) and anti-social sentiment (e.g., threats, opposition, blame) at different topics, all in the same message. While many natural language processing (NLP) tools classify or score a text's overall sentiment as positive, neutral, or negative, these tools cannot report that positive and negative sentiments coexist, and they cannot rep

infographic.key_insight: Directed Social Regard is a representation and model that detects and attributes coexisting pro- and anti-social intents (e.g., advocacy, aid, opposition, harm, victimization) to specific targets within the same message, revealing nuanced directed social behaviors that aggregate sentiment scores miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing sentiment tools provide an overall polarity but cannot identify multiple, opposing social intents directed at different targets in one text, limiting detection of targeted advocacy, harm, aid, or victimization in online media.
method: Define an annotation schema for Directed Social Regard: label social action categories (advocacy, opposition, aid, harm, victimization) plus directionality toward identified target spans.
Create and annotate a dataset drawn from online media / influence operations and train a model that jointly extracts target spans and predicts multi-label, target-directed social actions.
Evaluate against sentiment baselines and ablations to demonstrate improved detection of mixed/opposing sentiments and target-specific harms/aid signals.
infographic.impact: Provides ML practitioners with a practical framework and data to build systems that recognize mixed, target-directed social behavior rather than coarse global sentiment — improving content moderation, harm detection, influence analysis, and social media research.

title: Let ViT Speak: Generative Language-Image Pre-training
authors: Yan Fang, Mengcheng Lan, Zilong Huang, Weixian Lei, Yunqing Zhao
abstract: In this paper, we present \textbf{Gen}erative \textbf{L}anguage-\textbf{I}mage \textbf{P}re-training (GenLIP), a minimalist generative pretraining framework for Vision Transformers (ViTs) designed for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To better align vision encoders with the autoregressive nature of LLMs, GenLIP trains a ViT to predict language tokens directly from visual tokens using a standard language modeling objective, without contrastive batch construction or an additional text dec

infographic.key_insight: Train a Vision Transformer to speak directly by predicting language tokens from visual tokens with a standard autoregressive language-modeling objective, removing the need for contrastive setups or extra text decoders. This aligns vision encoders naturally with LLMs for generative multimodal models.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the modality gap between visual encoders and autoregressive language models by removing complex contrastive pretraining and auxiliary text decoders, simplifying pretraining while improving compatibility with multimodal LLMs.
method: Use a ViT to encode visual tokens and directly predict subsequent language tokens using an autoregressive language modeling loss.
Eschew contrastive batch construction and separate text-decoder modules — rely on a minimalist, generative pretraining objective.
Design the training pipeline so the ViT can be plugged into or integrated with multimodal LLMs for end-to-end generative tasks.
infographic.impact: Provides a simpler, more direct route to build generative multimodal models that integrate ViTs with LLMs, reducing engineering complexity and pretraining overhead while improving alignment for downstream multimodal generation and understanding.

title: Modeling Subjective Urban Perception with Human Gaze
authors: Lin Che, Xi Wang, Marc Pollefeys, Konrad Schindler, Martin Raubal
abstract: Urban perception describes how people subjectively evaluate urban environments, shaping how cities are experienced and understood. Existing computational approaches primarily model urban perception directly from street view images, but largely ignore the human perceptual process through which such judgments are formed. In this paper, we introduce Place Pulse-Gaze, an urban perception dataset that augments street view images with synchronized eye-tracking recordings and individual perception labe

infographic.key_insight: Augmenting street-view imagery with synchronized human gaze and individual perception labels reveals the perceptual process behind subjective urban judgments and lets models predict those judgments more accurately and interpretably.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between image-only urban perception models and the human perceptual process by providing gaze-grounded data and learning methods that connect where people look to how they evaluate urban scenes.
method: Collected Place Pulse-Gaze: a street-view dataset pairing images with synchronized eye-tracking recordings and individual subjective perception labels.
Trained gaze-informed models (multi-task / attention-guided) to jointly learn gaze patterns and perceptual judgments, using gaze as an auxiliary supervision signal.
Used gaze-based saliency and interpretability analyses to link visual cues (e.g., façades, greenery, clutter) with subjective scores and improve model explanations.
infographic.impact: Provides a human-centered supervisory signal that increases predictive performance and interpretability for subjective visual tasks; useful for building safer, fairer, and more explainable urban-scene models and transferring gaze supervision to other subjective AI problems.

title: Unsupervised Denoising of Real Clinical Low Dose Liver CT with Perceptual Attention Networks
authors: Jingxi Pu, Tonghua Liu, Zhilin Guan, Siqiao Li, Yang Ming
abstract: With the development of deep learning, medical image processing has been widely used to assist clinical research. This paper focuses on the denoising problem of low-dose computed tomography using deep learning. Although low-dose computed tomography reduces radiation exposure to patients, it also introduces more noise, which may interfere with visual interpretation by physicians and affect diagnostic results. To address this problem, inspired by Cycle-GAN for unsupervised learning, this paper pro

infographic.key_insight: An unsupervised Cycle-GAN–style framework augmented with a Perceptual Attention Network can denoise real clinical low‑dose liver CT scans, removing noise while preserving anatomical detail without requiring paired high‑dose references.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of paired low-/high-dose clinical CT data by enabling effective denoising of low‑dose liver CT images in an unsupervised manner, reducing noise and artifacts that can impair diagnosis.
method: Cycle-consistent adversarial training to learn mappings between low‑dose and clean domains using unpaired clinical data.
Perceptual Attention Network that applies spatial attention and perceptual losses to prioritize clinically relevant liver structures and preserve edges/textures.
End‑to‑end training on real clinical scans (no paired labels), combining adversarial, cycle, and perceptual objectives to balance noise suppression and detail preservation.
infographic.impact: Makes clinically viable CT denoising possible where paired datasets are unavailable, helping ML practitioners build robust, annotation‑free restoration pipelines that maintain diagnostic information in low‑dose imaging.

title: Persistent Visual Memory: Sustaining Perception for Deep Generation in LVLMs
authors: Siyuan Huang, Xiaoye Qu, Yafu Li, Tong Zhu, Zefeng He
abstract: While autoregressive Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate remarkable proficiency in multimodal tasks, they face a "Visual Signal Dilution" phenomenon, where the accumulation of textual history expands the attention partition function, causing visual attention to decay inversely with generated sequence length. To counteract this, we propose Persistent Visual Memory (PVM), a lightweight learnable module designed to ensure sustained, on-demand visual perception. Integrated as a parallel

infographic.key_insight: Introducing a lightweight Persistent Visual Memory (PVM) module prevents visual information from fading as autoregressive LVLMs generate long text, enabling sustained, on‑demand visual perception throughout generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses 'Visual Signal Dilution' — visual attention decays as generated textual history grows, causing LVLMs to lose visual grounding on long generations.
method: Add a learnable Persistent Visual Memory module that runs in parallel to standard cross‑attention, retaining distilled visual representations independent of autoregressive context length.
Provide on‑demand access to persistent visual states via gating/attention so the decoder can re‑query high‑fidelity visual memory at any generation step.
Keep the module lightweight and plug‑in so it can be integrated into existing LVLMs with minimal compute and training overhead.
infographic.impact: Enables more stable visual grounding for long-form and iterative multimodal generation, improving reliability of LVLM outputs in tasks that require sustained perception (e.g., multi‑step reasoning, extended descriptions, interactive agents).

title: Position: agentic AI orchestration should be Bayes-consistent
authors: Theodore Papamarkou, Pierre Alquier, Matthias Bauer, Wray Buntine, Andrew Davison
abstract: LLMs excel at predictive tasks and complex reasoning tasks, but many high-value deployments rely on decisions under uncertainty, for example, which tool to call, which expert to consult, or how many resources to invest. While the usefulness and feasibility of Bayesian approaches remain unclear for LLM inference, this position paper argues that the control layer of an agentic AI system (that orchestrates LLMs and tools) is a clear case where Bayesian principles should shine. Bayesian decision the

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that the orchestration/control layer of agentic AI systems should follow Bayesian decision principles: using posterior beliefs and expected-utility calculations to choose tools, experts, and actions under uncertainty leads to principled, calibrated decisions.
infographic.problem_solved: How to make agentic AI reliably decide which tool or action to take when faced with uncertainty; current heuristic or ad-hoc orchestration lacks principled uncertainty representation and decision rules.
method: Position and formalize Bayes-consistency as a design principle for the orchestration/control layer of agentic systems (posterior + expected utility drives choices).
Recommend mechanisms: probabilistic models or calibrated posteriors for beliefs, Bayesian updating from observations, and utility-aware decision rules to select tools/actions.
Provide practical guidance for modular orchestration: expose uncertainty to downstream components, encode priors/constraints, and evaluate via calibration and decision-theoretic metrics.
infographic.impact: Adopting Bayes-consistent orchestration can make LLM-based agents more reliable, interpretable, and resource-efficient by aligning action selection with quantified uncertainty and expected outcomes. This gives practitioners a clear, testable framework for safer and better-calibrated agent design.

title: HyCOP: Hybrid Composition Operators for Interpretable Learning of PDEs
authors: Jinpai Zhao, Nishant Panda, Yen Ting Lin, Eirik Valseth, Diane Oyen
abstract: We introduce HyCOP, a modular framework that learns parametric PDE solution operators by composing simple modules (advection, diffusion, learned closures, boundary handling) in a query-conditioned way. Rather than learning a monolithic map, HyCOP learns a policy over short programs - which module to apply and for how long - conditioned on regime features and state statistics. Modules may be numerical sub-solvers or learned components, enabling hybrid surrogates evaluated at arbitrary query times

infographic.key_insight: HyCOP learns a small, interpretable policy that composes simple modules (advection, diffusion, learned closures, boundary handling) into short programs to form parametric PDE solution operators, enabling accurate, query-conditioned predictions without a monolithic black box.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces brittleness and opacity of monolithic operator-learning surrogates by providing a modular, interpretable, and query-time-flexible framework that adapts to different regimes and timesteps.
method: Decompose PDE solution operator into reusable modules (numerical sub-solvers and learned components) for advection, diffusion, closures, and boundary handling.
Learn a policy that, conditioned on regime features and state statistics, selects which module to apply and for how long—effectively assembling short programs instead of a single end-to-end map.
Evaluate composed hybrid surrogates at arbitrary query times, enabling fast, interpretable, and regime-aware prediction.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with a practical path to accurate, physically interpretable surrogate models for PDEs that generalize across regimes and query times, combining numerical reliability with learned flexibility.

title: GMGaze: MoE-Based Context-Aware Gaze Estimation with CLIP and Multiscale Transformer
authors: Xinyuan Zhao, Yihang Wu, Ahmad Chaddad, Sarah A. Alkhodair, Reem Kateb
abstract: Gaze estimation methods commonly use facial appearances to predict the direction of a person gaze. However, previous studies show three major challenges with convolutional neural network (CNN)-based, transformer-based, and contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP)-based methods, including late fusion of image features, lack of factor-aware conditioning, and impractical capacity scaling. To address these challenges, we propose Globally-conditioned Multi-scale Gaze estimation (GMGaze), which

infographic.key_insight: GMGaze combines CLIP-based global conditioning, a multiscale transformer backbone, and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing layer to produce context-aware, factor-conditioned gaze estimates while enabling practical capacity scaling.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses three core limitations of prior gaze methods: late fusion of contextual cues, lack of explicit factor-aware conditioning (e.g., head pose, scene), and impractical model scaling for higher capacity.
method: Global conditioning: inject CLIP-derived global image/text embeddings early into the gaze pipeline to provide robust scene- and semantics-aware context.
Multiscale transformer feature extraction: a hierarchical transformer that fuses fine-grained eye/face features with coarser facial and scene information for early, multi-resolution fusion.

MoE-based capacity scaling & factor-aware conditioning: use routing to specialized expert subnetworks for efficient large-capacity models and explicit conditioning modules for factors like head pose, illumination, and camera parameters.
infographic.impact: Delivers more accurate and robust gaze predictions in diverse, real-world contexts while allowing efficient scaling to larger models — useful for HCI, AR/VR, behavioral analytics, and multimodal vision systems.

title: Posterior Augmented Flow Matching
authors: George Stoica, Sayak Paul, Matthew Wallingford, Vivek Ramanujan, Abhay Nori
abstract: Flow matching (FM) trains a time-dependent vector field that transports samples from a simple prior to a complex data distribution. However, for high-dimensional images, each training sample supervises only a single trajectory and intermediate point, yielding an extremely sparse and high-variance training signal. This under-constrained supervision can cause flow collapse, where the learned dynamics memorize specific source-target pairings, mapping diverse inputs to overly similar outputs, failin

infographic.key_insight: Posterior Augmented Flow Matching supplements standard flow-matching training with posterior-derived supervisory signals to densify and lower-variance training, preventing collapse of learned transport maps on high-dimensional images.
infographic.problem_solved: Flow matching for high-dimension images suffers from extremely sparse, high-variance supervision (one trajectory per sample), causing flow collapse where diverse inputs map to similar outputs; this method addresses that under-constrained learning signal.
method: Estimate or sample posterior/conditional intermediate states between prior and data to create additional supervision along trajectories.
Augment flow-matching loss with these posterior-derived targets so each training sample supervises many intermediate points (denser, lower-variance gradients).
Train a time-dependent vector field using the augmented targets to learn stable, diverse transports that avoid memorized source–target pairings.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to stabilize and scale flow-matching to high-resolution image generation, improving sample diversity and reliability for practitioners building generative models.

title: Can Coding Agents Reproduce Findings in Computational Materials Science?
authors: Ziyang Huang, Yi Cao, Ali K. Shargh, Jing Luo, Ruidong Mei
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous coding agents and have achieved remarkably strong performance on software engineering benchmarks. However, it is unclear whether such success transfers to computational scientific workflows, where tasks require not only strong coding ability, but also the ability to navigate complex, domain-specific procedures and to interpret results in the context of scientific claims. To address this question, we present AutoMat, a benchmark for ev

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces AutoMat, a benchmark showing that while LLM-based coding agents can write correct code, they struggle to fully reproduce computational materials‑science results because workflows demand domain‑specific procedures, environment control, and scientific judgement.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluates whether autonomous coding agents can reliably reproduce published computational materials‑science findings and identifies where current agents fail in domain‑specific experimental workflows and scientific interpretation.
method: Design AutoMat: a curated benchmark of real-world computational materials‑science reproduction tasks spanning setup, simulation, analysis, and claim verification.
Run multiple LLM-driven coding agents to autonomously generate, run, and analyze code in realistic environments and compare outputs to published results.

Quantitatively and qualitatively measure reproduction success, code correctness, numerical/experimental fidelity, and categorize common failure modes (environment, dependencies, domain logic, result interpretation).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a targeted evaluation of LLM coding agents on scientific reproducibility, guiding development of domain‑aware agents and tooling to bridge gaps between general coding ability and robust scientific workflows.
