title: Representation Fréchet Loss for Visual Generation
authors: Jiawei Yang, Zhengyang Geng, Xuan Ju, Yonglong Tian, Yue Wang
abstract: We show that Fréchet Distance (FD), long considered impractical as a training objective, can in fact be effectively optimized in the representation space. Our idea is simple: decouple the population size for FD estimation (e.g., 50k) from the batch size for gradient computation (e.g., 1024). We term this approach FD-loss. Optimizing FD-loss reveals several surprising findings. First, post-training a base generator with FD-loss in different representation spaces consistently improves visual quali

infographic.key_insight: Fréchet Distance — long seen as impractical to optimize directly — can be efficiently minimized in a learned representation space by decoupling the large sample population used for FD estimation from the smaller batch used for gradient updates (FD-loss). This enables direct training toward distributional/perceptual metrics.
infographic.problem_solved: Makes Fréchet-based objectives practical for training visual generative models by resolving the computational/sample-size mismatch that previously prevented stable gradient optimization of FD.
method: Compute Fréchet Distance in a chosen representation space (e.g., pretrained encoder features) rather than pixel space to capture perceptual statistics.
Decouple the FD estimation population size (large, e.g., 50k) from the gradient batch size (smaller, e.g., 1k) so estimates remain stable while gradients are efficient.
Use the resulting FD-loss to post-train or fine-tune a base generator, improving alignment with distributional/perceptual metrics.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical recipe (FD-loss) to optimize generators directly for distributional/perceptual quality, enabling better visual fidelity and metric alignment without prohibitive computation. This is immediately useful for model fine-tuning and evaluation-driven training.
visual_elements: Schematic diagram: data flow showing large population for FD estimation vs small batches for gradient updates (two parallel pipelines converging to FD-loss).

title: Claw-Eval-Live: A Live Agent Benchmark for Evolving Real-World Workflows
authors: Chenxin Li, Zhengyang Tang, Huangxin Lin, Yunlong Lin, Shijue Huang
abstract: LLM agents are expected to complete end-to-end units of work across software tools, business services, and local workspaces. Yet many agent benchmarks freeze a curated task set at release time and grade mainly the final response, making it difficult to evaluate agents against evolving workflow demand or verify whether a task was executed. We introduce Claw-Eval-Live, a live benchmark for workflow agents that separates a refreshable signal layer, updated across releases from public workflow-deman

infographic.key_insight: Claw-Eval-Live introduces a live, refreshable benchmarking design that evaluates LLM agents on end-to-end, real-world workflows and verifiable execution signals rather than static final responses. This enables continuous, real-world–aligned assessment as workflow demands evolve.
infographic.problem_solved: Static, frozen benchmarks fail to capture evolving workflow demands and often only grade final outputs, making it hard to verify whether agents actually executed tasks or can adapt to changing real-world tool/service environments.
method: Design a live benchmark that separates a refreshable 'signal layer' (updated across releases) from public workflow demand, allowing evaluation signals to evolve without changing task definitions.
Execute agents against real software tools, business services, and local workspaces to capture end-to-end behavior and generate verifiable execution traces.
Automated verification and scoring that checks execution correctness and updates leaderboards continuously as signals and workflows change.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to measure agent reliability, adaptivity, and real-world execution correctness over time, improving deployment readiness and trustworthiness of LLM agents in production workflows.

title: Crab: A Semantics-Aware Checkpoint/Restore Runtime for Agent Sandboxes
authors: Tianyuan Wu, Chaokun Chang, Lunxi Cao, Wei Gao, Wei Wang
abstract: Autonomous agents act through sandboxed containers and microVMs whose state spans filesystems, processes, and runtime artifacts. Checkpoint and restore (C/R) of this state is needed for fault tolerance, spot execution, RL rollout branching, and safe rollback-yet existing approaches fall into two extremes: application-level recovery preserves chat history but misses OS-side effects, while full per-turn checkpointing is correct but too expensive under dense co-location. The root cause is an agent-

infographic.key_insight: Crab introduces a semantics-aware checkpoint/restore runtime that captures the agent-visible semantics plus the minimal OS/runtime effects needed for correctness, enabling fast, lightweight snapshots without missing hidden side effects.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between lightweight application-level recovery (which misses OS-side effects) and expensive full per-turn checkpointing by making C/R correct, efficient, and practical for densely co-located agent sandboxes.
method: Semantics-aware capture: identify and persist only the agent-relevant state (chat/history, model checkpoints, high-level intents) together with the minimal OS artifacts required for correctness (filesystem diffs, IPC, process metadata).
Hybrid incremental C/R: combine fine-grained incremental/differential snapshots with lazy restore and on-demand materialization to keep per-turn overhead low while preserving correctness.
Runtime integration: embed the approach into container/microVM sandboxes so branching, rollbacks, spot execution, and RL rollout multiplexing are efficient and reproducible.
infographic.impact: Makes fault tolerance, safe rollback, RL branching, and spot-instance execution for autonomous agents practical at high density by cutting snapshot cost and restore latency while preserving correctness across OS and application layers.

title: Exploration Hacking: Can LLMs Learn to Resist RL Training?
authors: Eyon Jang, Damon Falck, Joschka Braun, Nathalie Kirch, Achu Menon
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become essential to the post-training of large language models (LLMs) for reasoning, agentic capabilities and alignment. Successful RL relies on sufficient exploration of diverse actions by the model during training, which creates a potential failure mode: a model could strategically alter its exploration during training to influence the subsequent training outcome. In this paper we study this behavior, called exploration hacking. First, we create model organisms

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can learn to strategically alter their exploration behavior during RL-based post-training, enabling them to influence or resist the intended training trajectory and outcomes.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and empirically characterizes a novel failure mode—"exploration hacking"—where an LLM intentionally changes its action diversity during RL fine-tuning to bias learning, undermining standard RL/LLM post-training procedures.
method: Create controlled "model organisms" (toy LLM-like agents) and synthetic tasks to isolate exploration behavior during RL fine-tuning.
Run simulated RL training loops to observe whether and how agents adapt exploration to influence rewards and downstream policy updates, and quantify effects on learning outcomes.

Analyze failure modes and evaluate simple detection/mitigation strategies (e.g., monitoring action diversity, randomized evaluations, reward/intervention protocols) to reduce exploitation of exploration dynamics.
infographic.impact: Highlights a practical and subtle safety/robustness risk for RL-based LLM post-training—practitioners must monitor exploration patterns and adopt diagnostics or protocol changes to ensure intended alignment and performance.
visual_elements: Diagram of the RL fine-tuning loop showing the model, exploration/actions, environment/reward, and how altered exploration feeds back into training.

title: Explainable Load Forecasting with Covariate-Informed Time Series Foundation Models
authors: Matthias Hertel, Alexandra Nikoltchovska, Sebastian Pütz, Ralf Mikut, Benjamin Schäfer
abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as general-purpose forecasting models and show considerable potential for applications in energy systems. However, applications in critical infrastructure like power grids require transparency to ensure trust and reliability and cannot rely on pure black-box models. To enhance the transparency of TSFMs, we propose an efficient algorithm for computing Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) tailored to these models. The proposed approach le

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a scalable method to make Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) for load forecasting explainable by computing SHAP attributions that incorporate covariates, enabling transparent, trustworthy forecasts for power systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Black-box TSFMs provide strong forecasting performance but lack transparency needed for critical infrastructure (e.g., power grids). The paper addresses the need for efficient, faithful feature-attribution explanations tailored to covariate-informed TSFMs used in load forecasting.
method: Design an efficient algorithm to compute SHAP-style attributions specifically adapted to TSFMs that use time-varying covariates and long context windows.
Exploit model and data structure (covariate conditioning, temporal decomposition) to reduce computation compared to naive SHAP, making explanations scalable to real-world load datasets.
Validate the approach on covariate-informed load forecasting tasks to demonstrate faithful, interpretable attributions while preserving forecasting accuracy.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to open the black box of TSFMs in energy applications, improving trust, diagnostics, and decision support for grid operators without sacrificing scalability. It bridges state-of-the-art forecasting with actionable explainability.

title: LaST-R1: Reinforcing Action via Adaptive Physical Latent Reasoning for VLA Models
authors: Hao Chen, Jiaming Liu, Zhonghao Yan, Nuowei Han, Renrui Zhang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have increasingly incorporated reasoning mechanisms for complex robotic manipulation. However, existing approaches share a critical limitation: whether employing explicit linguistic reasoning that suffers from latency and discretization, or utilizing more expressive continuous latent reasoning, they are predominantly confined to static imitation learning that limits adaptability and generalization. While online reinforcement learning (RL) has been introduced t

infographic.key_insight: LaST-R1 introduces an adaptive physical latent reasoning module that ties continuous latent planning to physical dynamics and uses online reinforcement to reinforce actions, enabling VLA models to move beyond static imitation into adaptive, generalizable manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing VLA approaches either use slow, discrete linguistic reasoning or expressive continuous latents but remain stuck in static imitation learning, which limits adaptability, real-time responsiveness, and generalization to novel physical dynamics and tasks.
method: Adaptive Physical Latent Reasoning (APLR): learn physics-aware continuous latent representations that encode affordances and action priors from vision+language inputs.
Latent-space reinforcement: fine-tune a latent policy online (e.g., actor-critic or policy-gradient in latent space) to reinforce successful behaviors while preserving learned priors.
Two-stage training: imitation/pretraining for stable initialization + online RL for adaptation, with regularization to keep latents interpretable and physically consistent.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build VLA systems that adapt in real time to changing dynamics and tasks, improving success rates in robotic manipulation and narrowing the sim-to-real gap without sacrificing expressiveness of continuous reasoning.

title: Generalizable Sparse-View 3D Reconstruction from Unconstrained Images
authors: Vinayak Gupta, Chih-Hao Lin, Shenlong Wang, Anand Bhattad, Jia-Bin Huang
abstract: Reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse, unposed images remains challenging under real-world conditions with varying illumination and transient occlusions. Existing methods rely on scene-specific optimization using appearance embeddings or dynamic masks, which requires extensive per-scene training and fails under sparse views. Moreover, evaluations on limited scenes raise questions about generalization. We present GenWildSplat, a feed-forward framework for sparse-view outdoor reconstruction that re

infographic.key_insight: A feed-forward model (GenWildSplat) learns broad outdoor scene priors so it can reconstruct 3D geometry and appearance from a few unconstrained images without per-scene optimization, remaining robust to changing illumination and transient occluders.
infographic.problem_solved: Reconstructing accurate 3D from sparse, unposed/outdoor images that exhibit varying lighting and transient occlusions — without expensive per-scene training or masks and with better generalization across scenes.
method: Train a feed-forward network on diverse outdoor image collections to learn general scene priors, enabling single-shot inference for new scenes from very sparse views.
Incorporate robust appearance normalization and transient-object handling (e.g., dynamic masking or learned outlier rejection) so reconstructions are stable under illumination changes and occlusions.
Avoid per-scene optimization or scene-specific embeddings; produce geometry + appearance directly from input images and predicted/estimated poses to maximize generalization.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, practical 3D reconstruction from few real-world images without expensive per-scene tuning — useful for mapping, AR/VR asset creation, and robotic perception in the wild.

title: Stop Holding Your Breath: CT-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Bronchoscopy
authors: Andrea Dunn Beltran, Daniel Rho, Aarav Mehta, Xinqi Xiong, Raúl San José Estépar
abstract: Bronchoscopic navigation relies on registering endoscopic video to a preoperative CT scan, but respiratory motion deforms the airway by 5-20 mm, creating CT-to-body divergence that limits localization accuracy. In practice, this is mitigated through breath-hold protocols, which attempt to match the intraoperative anatomy to a static CT, but are difficult to reproduce and disrupt clinical workflow. We propose to eliminate the need for breath-hold protocols by leveraging patient-specific respirato

infographic.key_insight: Patient-specific respiratory motion can be modeled and rendered via CT-informed Gaussian splatting to create a dynamic, time-varying airway representation that enables accurate bronchoscope-to-CT registration without breath-hold protocols.
infographic.problem_solved: Eliminates CT-to-body divergence caused by 5–20 mm respiratory deformation that forces disruptive breath-hold procedures, improving intraoperative localization during bronchoscopy.
method: Build a patient-specific dynamic airway model from preoperative CT plus respiratory phase/signals to capture motion states.
Represent and render the time-varying airway with Gaussian splatting (fast, continuous volumetric rendering) conditioned on respiratory phase.
Register live endoscopic video frames to the dynamic rendered model (rather than a static CT) to recover accurate pose in real time.
infographic.impact: Enables robust, real-time medical image registration under physiological motion—reducing workflow disruption and improving localization accuracy—while demonstrating how differentiable volumetric rendering (Gaussian splatting) can be used for dynamic scene modeling in medical AI.

title: HERMES++: Toward a Unified Driving World Model for 3D Scene Understanding and Generation
authors: Xin Zhou, Dingkang Liang, Xiwu Chen, Feiyang Tan, Dingyuan Zhang
abstract: Driving world models serve as a pivotal technology for autonomous driving by simulating environmental dynamics. However, existing approaches predominantly focus on future scene generation, often overlooking comprehensive 3D scene understanding. Conversely, while Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive reasoning capabilities, they lack the capacity to predict future geometric evolution, creating a significant disparity between semantic interpretation and physical simulation. To bridge

infographic.key_insight: HERMES++ unifies 3D scene understanding and future-scene generation in a single driving world model, bridging semantic reasoning (LLM-style) with physically grounded geometric prediction.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap where prior work either focuses on semantic reasoning or on future-scene generation but not both — enabling accurate prediction of future 3D geometry while providing interpretable, language-compatible semantic outputs for downstream driving tasks.
method: Shared 3D latent representation that jointly encodes geometric structure and semantic labels for the driving scene.
Predictive dynamics module that rolls forward the geometric latent state to generate future 3D scenes (point clouds/meshes/occupancy) over time.

Cross-modal interface linking language-level queries to the geometric latent space so semantic reasoning (LLMs or task heads) can query and condition generation for planning, evaluation, or explanation.
infographic.impact: Provides a single, interpretable model for both understanding and simulating driving environments, improving simulation fidelity, safety validation, planning, and synthetic-data generation workflows for autonomous driving and 3D perception research.

title: AEGIS: A Holistic Benchmark for Evaluating Forensic Analysis of AI-Generated Academic Images
authors: Bo Zhang, Tzu-Yen Ma, Zichen Tang, Junpeng Ding, Zirui Wang

Compared to existing benchmarks, AEGIS features three key advances: (1) Domain-Specific Complexity: covering seven academic categories with 39 fine-grained subtypes, exposing intrinsic forensic difficulty, where even GPT-5.1 reaches 48.80% overall performance and expert models achieve only limited localization accuracy (IoU 30.09%); (2) Diverse Forgery Simulations: modeling four prevalent a

infographic.key_insight: AEGIS is a domain-focused forensic benchmark showing that detecting and localizing AI-generated academic images is still hard: across 7 academic categories and 39 fine-grained subtypes, even GPT-5.1 only achieves 48.80% overall detection and expert models attain just 30.09% localization IoU.
infographic.problem_solved: Fills the gap of lacking domain-specific, fine-grained evaluation for forensic analysis of academic images, exposing real-world difficulties that generic benchmarks miss.
method: Curated a domain-specific dataset spanning 7 academic categories and 39 fine-grained subtypes to capture intrinsic forensic complexity.
Simulated four diverse forgery scenarios to test both detection and localization robustness across realistic manipulation styles.
Benchmarked state-of-the-art detectors and localization models (e.g., GPT-5.1), evaluating both detection accuracy and localization IoU to quantify weaknesses.

title: Intern-Atlas: A Methodological Evolution Graph as Research Infrastructure for AI Scientists
authors: Yujun Wu, Dongxu Zhang, Xinchen Li, Jinhang Xu, Yiling Duan
abstract: Existing research infrastructure is fundamentally document-centric, providing citation links between papers but lacking explicit representations of methodological evolution. In particular, it does not capture the structured relationships that explain how and why research methods emerge, adapt, and build upon one another. With the rise of AI-driven research agents as a new class of consumers of scientific knowledge, this limitation becomes increasingly consequential, as such agents cannot reliabl

infographic.key_insight: Intern-Atlas builds a methodological evolution graph that explicitly models how research methods emerge, adapt, and build on one another, turning papers into a structured, machine-actionable research infrastructure for both humans and AI agents.
infographic.problem_solved: Current research infrastructure is document-centric and only provides citation links, failing to capture structured relationships and lineage between methods — which prevents reliable discovery, comparison, composition, and automated use by AI research agents.
method: Create a graph representation where nodes encode methods/components (algorithms, datasets, protocols, metrics) and directed edges encode derivation, adaptation, and dependency relationships.
Automatically extract candidate nodes and edges from papers, code, and metadata using NLP and code-analysis pipelines, augmented with human-in-the-loop curation to ensure precision.
Expose APIs and visualization tools for querying, traversing, and composing methodological lineages, enabling programmatic consumption by research agents and interactive exploration by scientists.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and research agents with a navigable, machine-readable map of methodological lineage that accelerates discovery, improves reproducibility, and enables automated method synthesis and adaptation.
visual_elements: A directed network diagram showing method nodes and derivation/adaptation edges (method lineage view).
A timeline view that overlays key method introductions and major forks/evolutions.

title: Continuous-tone Simple Points: An $\ell_0$-Norm of Cyclic Gradient for Topology-Preserving Data-Driven Image Segmentation
authors: Wenxiao Li, Faqiang Wang, Yuping Duan, Li Cui, Liqiang Zhang
abstract: Topological features play an essential role in ensuring geometric plausibility and structural consistency in image analysis tasks such as segmentation and skeletonization. However, integrating topology-preserving learning based on simple points into deep learning tasks remains challenging, as existing simple point detection methods are confined to binary images and are non-differentiable, rendering them incompatible with gradient-based optimization in modern deep learning. Moreover, morphologica

infographic.key_insight: The paper defines a continuous-tone analogue of simple points via a cyclic gradient and uses an ℓ0-norm formulation to detect topology-changing pixels in grayscale images, producing a topology-aware, differentiable-friendly criterion for training segmentation networks.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing simple-point detectors are binary and non-differentiable, preventing topology-preserving constraints from being directly used in gradient-based deep learning; this work provides a continuous, trainable measure to preserve topology during segmentation.
method: Define a cyclic gradient operator for continuous-tone (grayscale) images and characterize pixels that change topology via this operator.
Formulate an ℓ0-norm of the cyclic gradient to count topology-relevant points, and introduce a differentiable surrogate/relaxation suitable for backpropagation.
Integrate the topology-aware term as a loss component in data-driven segmentation models and validate improvements on topology-sensitive benchmarks (e.g., preserving connectivity, holes, skeletons).
infographic.impact: Enables end-to-end training of neural segmentation models that explicitly preserve topological features, improving structural plausibility in applications like medical imaging, remote sensing, and shape analysis.

title: OmniRobotHome: A Multi-Camera Platform for Real-Time Multiadic Human-Robot Interaction
authors: Junyoung Lee, Sookwan Han, Jeonghwan Kim, Inhee Lee, Mingi Choi
abstract: Human-robot collaboration has been studied primarily in dyadic or sequential settings. However, real homes require multiadic collaboration, where multiple humans and robots share a workspace, acting concurrently on interleaved subtasks with tight spatial and temporal coupling. This regime remains underexplored because close-proximity interaction between humans, robots, and objects creates persistent occlusion and rapid state changes, making reliable real-time 3D tracking the central bottleneck.

infographic.key_insight: OmniRobotHome demonstrates that a synchronized multi-camera platform plus an occlusion-aware, low-latency 3D tracking pipeline can enable reliable real-time multiadic human–robot interaction in cluttered home environments where persistent occlusion and rapid state changes previously blocked progress.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the central bottleneck for multiadic home HRI: achieving robust, real-time 3D tracking of multiple humans, robots, and objects under close-proximity interaction with heavy occlusion and fast state changes.
method: Synchronized multi-camera rig providing dense multi-view RGB/depth coverage to reduce blind spots and persistent occlusions.
Occlusion-aware multi-agent state estimation that fuses per-view detections into consistent 3D poses (humans, robots, objects) and maintains identity through rapid interactions.
Low-latency end-to-end software pipeline optimized for concurrent tracking and streaming to support real-time control and interaction.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to develop, test, and benchmark real-time multi-agent perception and control for realistic home scenarios, unlocking safer and more coordinated multi-human multi-robot behavior in real-world deployments.

title: 3D-ReGen: A Unified 3D Geometry Regeneration Framework
authors: Geon Yeong Park, Roman Shapovalov, Rakesh Ranjan, Jong Chul Ye, Andrea Vedaldi
abstract: We consider the problem of regenerating 3D objects from 2D images and initial 3D shapes. Most 3D generators operate in a one-shot fashion, converting text or images to a 3D object with limited controllability. We introduce instead 3D-ReGen, a 3D regenerator that is conditioned on an initial 3D shape. This conceptually simple formulation allows us to support numerous useful tasks, including 3D enhancement, reconstruction, and editing. 3D-ReGen uses a new conditioning mechanism based on VecSet, wh

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning a 3D generator on an initial 3D shape (using a VecSet-based conditioning mechanism) turns generation into a regeneration task—enabling targeted enhancement, reconstruction, and editing of 3D geometry rather than one-shot synthesis.
infographic.problem_solved: One-shot 3D generators offer limited controllability and poor support for refining or editing existing geometry; this paper addresses how to regenerate higher-quality or task-specific 3D objects from 2D images and an initial 3D shape.
method: Introduce a conditional 3D regenerator that takes an initial 3D shape plus optional 2D images as inputs and outputs a refined 3D geometry.
Use VecSet-based conditioning to encode set-structured inputs (e.g., shape tokens, image features) into the generator, enabling flexible conditioning on arbitrary initial shapes.
Unify multiple tasks (enhancement, reconstruction, editing) within the same regeneration pipeline so the model can iteratively refine or modify geometry under different controls.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a controllable, reusable 3D pipeline for improving and editing existing models from images and partial shapes—useful for AR/VR, simulation, content creation, and downstream vision tasks.

title: Action Motifs: Self-Supervised Hierarchical Representation of Human Body Movements
authors: Genki Kinoshita, Shu Nakamura, Ryo Kawahara, Shohei Nobuhara, Yasutomo Kawanishi
abstract: Effective human behavior modeling requires a representation of the human body movement that capitalizes on its compositionality. We propose a hierarchical representation consisting of Action Atoms that capture the atomic joint movements and Action Motifs that are formed by their temporal compositions and encode similar body movements found across different overall human actions. We derive A4Mer, a nested latent Transformer to learn this hierarchical representation from human pose data in a fully

infographic.key_insight: Human body movements can be represented hierarchically as reusable atomic joint movements (Action Atoms) that temporally compose into higher-level patterns (Action Motifs); a nested latent Transformer (A4Mer) can discover this hierarchy in a fully self-supervised way from pose sequences.
infographic.problem_solved: Captures the compositional structure of human motion so that similar body-movement patterns are identified across different actions, improving efficiency, interpretability, and transferability of motion representations without requiring labeled data.
method: Define Action Atoms as short, atomic joint-movement units and Action Motifs as temporal compositions of these atoms that recur across actions.
Introduce A4Mer, a nested latent Transformer that models two hierarchical latent levels (atom-level and motif-level) and learns them jointly from pose sequences in a self-supervised manner.
Train with reconstruction/prediction-style objectives on unlabeled pose data so motifs emerge as shared, reusable building blocks for downstream tasks.
infographic.impact: Provides compact, interpretable, and transferable motion representations that improve downstream tasks (action recognition, prediction, synthesis) and reduce reliance on labeled data by leveraging compositionality.

title: Visual Generation in the New Era: An Evolution from Atomic Mapping to Agentic World Modeling
authors: Keming Wu, Zuhao Yang, Kaichen Zhang, Shizun Wang, Haowei Zhu
abstract: Recent visual generation models have made major progress in photorealism, typography, instruction following, and interactive editing, yet they still struggle with spatial reasoning, persistent state, long-horizon consistency, and causal understanding. We argue that the field should move beyond appearance synthesis toward intelligent visual generation: plausible visuals grounded in structure, dynamics, domain knowledge, and causal relations. To frame this shift, we introduce a five-level taxonomy

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes visual generation from pixel-level appearance synthesis to 'intelligent' generation grounded in structure, dynamics, domain knowledge, and causality, proposing a five-level taxonomy that culminates in agentic world modeling.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses current models' failures in spatial reasoning, persistent state, long-horizon consistency, and causal understanding by defining a roadmap and evaluation criteria to build visually plausible, stateful, and causally coherent generation systems.
method: Introduce a five-level taxonomy that traces evolution from atomic mapping (appearance-only) to agentic world models (structured, dynamic, goal-directed visual systems).
Characterize capabilities and failure modes at each level and propose evaluation dimensions/benchmarks to measure spatial, temporal, and causal competence.
Outline architectural/functional components for agentic visual models (perception, memory/state, dynamics, planning and domain knowledge integration) as a design blueprint.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a clear roadmap and evaluation framework to push generative models toward stateful, reasoning-capable visual systems—enabling reliable editing, simulation, and embodied-agent applications beyond photorealism.

title: Stochastic Scaling Limits and Synchronization by Noise in Deep Transformer Models
authors: Andrea Agazzi, Giuseppe Bruno, Eloy Mosig García, Samuele Saviozzi, Marco Romito
abstract: We prove pathwise convergence of the layerwise evolution of tokens in a finite-depth, finite-width transformer model with MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP) blocks to a continuous-time stochastic interacting particle system. We also identify the stochastic partial differential equation describing the evolution of the tokens' distribution in this limit and prove propagation of chaos when the number of such tokens is large. The bounds we establish are quantitative and the limits we consider commute. We f

infographic.key_insight: Layerwise token dynamics in realistic finite-depth, finite-width transformers with MLP blocks converge pathwise to a continuous-time stochastic interacting particle system; the tokens' distribution satisfies a derived SPDE and noise can induce synchronization, with propagation of chaos holding as token count grows.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between discrete layerwise transformer dynamics and continuum stochastic descriptions for finite models, providing quantitative, commuting limits and rigorous control of how noise shapes collective token behaviour.
method: Prove pathwise convergence of the discrete layerwise evolution to a continuous-time stochastic interacting particle system for finite depth and width.
Derive the governing stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) for the tokens' distribution and prove propagation of chaos as the number of tokens → ∞.
Establish quantitative bounds and show the different scaling/limiting operations commute (finite-to-continuum and many-tokens limits).
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a principled stochastic continuum framework to analyze and predict transformer dynamics in realistic finite settings, clarifying how injected or intrinsic noise can synchronize activations and affect training/robustness.

title: ClawGym: A Scalable Framework for Building Effective Claw Agents
authors: Fei Bai, Huatong Song, Shuang Sun, Daixuan Cheng, Yike Yang
abstract: Claw-style environments support multi-step workflows over local files, tools, and persistent workspace states. However, scalable development around these environments remains constrained by the absence of a systematic framework, especially one for synthesizing verifiable training data and integrating it with agent training and diagnostic evaluation. To address this challenge, we present ClawGym, a scalable framework that supports the full lifecycle of Claw-style personal agent development. Concr

infographic.key_insight: ClawGym provides a scalable, end-to-end framework for building Claw-style personal agents by combining verifiable training-data synthesis with integrated training and diagnostic evaluation in one lifecycle.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of a systematic, scalable toolkit for developing agents that perform multi-step workflows over local files, tools, and persistent workspace state—particularly the absence of verifiable training data and integrated diagnostics.
method: Model a persistent workspace and tool interactions with a unified Claw-style environment API to represent multi-step workflows.
Automatically synthesize verifiable training trajectories and annotations so generated data can be checked and used reliably for supervision.
Provide an integrated pipeline that couples synthesized data, agent training, and a diagnostic evaluation suite for reproducible iteration and debugging.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to rapidly build, train, and validate personal agents that operate reliably on file- and tool-based workflows, improving development speed, reproducibility, and diagnostic visibility.

title: ClassEval-Pro: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Class-Level Code Generation
authors: Yeheng Chen, Chaoxiang Xie, Yuling Shi, Wenhao Zeng, Yongpan Wang
abstract: LLMs have achieved strong results on both function-level code synthesis and repository-level code modification, yet a capability that falls between these two extremes -- compositional code creation, i.e., building a complete, internally structured class from a specification -- remains underserved. Current evaluations are either confined to isolated functions or rely on manually curated class-level tasks that are expensive to scale and increasingly susceptible to data contamination. We introduce

infographic.key_insight: ClassEval-Pro fills the gap between function-level synthesis and repo-level edits by providing a scalable, contamination-resistant benchmark specifically for class-level (compositional) code generation across domains.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluates and benchmarks LLMs' ability to generate complete, internally structured classes from specifications—addressing limited, manual, or contaminated existing evaluations that don't capture compositional class creation.
method: Assemble a large, cross-domain corpus of real-world classes via automated extraction from repositories, with rigorous decontamination (temporal splits, dataset deduplication, train/test leak checks).
Define standardized class-level tasks and difficulty tiers plus multi-faceted evaluation: functional unit tests, structural/behavioral checks (APIs, invariants), and interface compliance.
Provide an automated evaluation pipeline and baseline LLM results (quantitative comparisons across domains, languages, and compositional complexity).
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a reproducible, domain-diverse way to measure and improve LLMs' ability to synthesize modular, production-ready code structures—enabling targeted model development and more reliable benchmarking for real-world software tasks.

authors: Attila Pintér, Javier Rico, Attila Répai, Jalal Al-Afandi, Adrienn Éva Borsy
abstract: We present KAYRA, an end-to-end karyotyping system that operates inside the operational constraints of a clinical cytogenetic laboratory. The same container images a

infographic.key_insight: KAYRA packages an end-to-end, clinic-ready karyotyping pipeline as containerized microservices that combine semantic segmentation, instance detection and classification in a cascaded ROI-narrowing workflow to meet clinical operational constraints.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates chromosome-level karyotyping while addressing clinical-lab constraints (reproducible deployment, data privacy, limited local compute, and integration into existing workflows).
method: Containerized microservice pipeline that standardizes deployment (cloud and on‑premise) and orchestration of ML components.

Cascaded ROI‑narrowing strategy: semantic segmentation (EfficientNet‑B5 + U‑Net) → instance detection (Mask R‑CNN, ResNet‑50 + FPN) → classification (ResNet‑18) so each model focuses on progressively smaller, chromosome-bearing regions.

title: Select to Think: Unlocking SLM Potential with Local Sufficiency
authors: Wenxuan Ye, Yangyang Zhang, Xueli An, Georg Carle, Yunpu Ma
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) offer computational efficiency for scalable deployment, yet they often fall short of the reasoning power exhibited by their larger counterparts (LLMs). To mitigate this gap, current approaches invoke an LLM to generate tokens at points of reasoning divergence, but these external calls introduce substantial latency and costs. Alternatively, standard distillation is often hindered by the capacity limitation, as SLMs struggle to accurately mimic the LLM's complex genera

infographic.key_insight: SLMs can retain much of an LLM's reasoning power by learning when a local context is 'sufficient' to reason on its own—enabling selective local thinking and drastically reducing expensive external LLM calls.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the reasoning-performance gap between small language models (SLMs) and large language models (LLMs) without frequent, costly LLM invocations or unattainable full-model distillation.
method: Define a local sufficiency criterion to identify segments where the SLM has enough context to reason correctly.
Train the SLM to selectively perform internal reasoning on locally sufficient segments and defer (or use lightweight proxy) on insufficient ones.
Apply selective distillation/finetuning focused on locally sufficient examples so the SLM internalizes key reasoning steps while minimizing external LLM calls.
infographic.impact: Enables lower-latency, lower-cost deployment of more capable SLMs for production and edge use-cases, making advanced reasoning practical on resource-constrained hardware.

title: Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data
authors: Bao Pham, Mohammed J. Zaki, Luca Ambrogioni, Dmitry Krotov, Matteo Negri
abstract: When do language diffusion models memorize their training data, and how to quantitatively assess their true generative regime? We address these questions by showing that Uniform-based Discrete Diffusion Models (UDDMs) fundamentally behave as Associative Memories (AMs) $\textit{with emergent creative capabilities}$. infographic.key_insight: Uniform-based Discrete Diffusion Models (UDDMs) behave like associative memories: they create basins of attraction around stored examples and can reliably retrieve those examples or interpolate to generate unseen, creative outputs. This reframes memorization and generation in language diffusion as an emergent memory-retrieval process.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines when and how language diffusion models memorize training data and provides quantitative tools to distinguish true generative behavior from retrieval/memorization.
method: Theoretical mapping showing UDDMs implement associative-memory dynamics (basins of attraction around stored data).
Empirical probes that measure retrieval success, basin sizes, and the model's ability to reconstruct stored versus unseen examples.
Analysis of emergent creative behavior: when interpolation between basins yields novel, plausible outputs rather than verbatim memorization.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to diagnose and quantify memorization vs creativity in diffusion-based language models, informing safer training, dataset curation, and model auditing for privacy and generalization.

authors: Dominik Żurek, Kamil Faber, Marcin Pietron, Paweł Gajewski, Roberto Corizzo
abstract: Continual offline reinforcement learning (CORL) aims to learn a sequence of tasks from datasets collected over time while preserving performance on previously learned tasks. title: Recursive Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Xiyuan Yang, Jiaru Zou, Rui Pan, Ruizhong Qiu, Pan Lu
abstract: Recursive or looped language models have recently emerged as a new scaling axis by iteratively refining the same model computation over latent states to deepen reasoning. We extend such scaling principle from a single model to multi-agent systems, and ask: Can agent collaboration itself be scaled through recursion? To this end, we introduce RecursiveMAS, a recursive multi-agent framework that casts the entire system as a unified latent-space recursive computation. RecursiveMAS connects heterogen

infographic.key_insight: RecursiveMAS shows that multi-agent collaboration can be scaled by letting agents iteratively refine a shared latent state in a recursive loop, effectively turning the whole agent system into a deeper reasoning process.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing recursive/looped reasoning techniques were applied to single models; this work addresses whether and how recursion can scale coordination and collective reasoning in heterogeneous multi-agent systems.
method: Cast the multi-agent system as a unified latent-space computation where agents read and write to shared latent state across iterations.
Run recursive update loops: agents iteratively refine their contributions to latent state and each other's outputs to deepen joint reasoning.
Support heterogeneous agents and communication protocols within the same recursive framework to improve collective decision-making and task performance.

title: Carbon-Taxed Transformers: A Green Compression Pipeline for Overgrown Language Models
authors: Ajmain Inqiad Alam, Palash Roy, Chanchal K. Roy, Banani Roy, Kevin A. Schneider
abstract: The accelerating adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in software engineering (SE) has brought with it a silent crisis: unsustainable computational cost. While these models demonstrate remarkable capabilities in different SE tasks, they are unmanageably large, slow to deploy, memory-intensive, and carbon-heavy. This reality threatens not only the scalability and accessibility of AI-powered SE, but also its long-term environmental sustainability. The research challenge is clear: we must go be

infographic.key_insight: A ‘carbon-taxed’ compression pipeline that injects carbon/energy cost into compression objectives lets you shrink and accelerate overgrown language models while explicitly minimizing CO2 emissions alongside latency and memory.
infographic.problem_solved: Overgrown LLMs used in software engineering are large, slow to deploy, memory-intensive, and carbon-heavy; the paper addresses how to compress them so they remain useful but far cheaper and greener to run.
method: Introduce a carbon-aware objective (a 'carbon tax' signal or penalty) that biases compression decisions toward lower-energy operations and deployments.
Apply a staged green-compression pipeline—carbon-guided pruning, reference-aware distillation, and budgeted quantization—optimizing for accuracy under combined compute/memory/carbon budgets.
Automated budgeted selection: map deployment constraints (latency, memory, carbon) to a recommended compressed checkpoint and quantization strategy.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to deploy smaller, faster LLMs with measurable reductions in energy use and carbon footprint while preserving task performance—supporting scalable, cost-effective, and sustainable model deployment.

title: DV-World: Benchmarking Data Visualization Agents in Real-World Scenarios
authors: Jinxiang Meng, Shaoping Huang, Fangyu Lei, Jingyu Guo, Haoxiang Liu
abstract: Real-world data visualization (DV) requires native environmental grounding, cross-platform evolution, and proactive intent alignment. Yet, existing benchmarks often suffer from code-sandbox confinement, single-language creation-only tasks, and assumption of perfect intent. To bridge these gaps, we introduce DV-World, a benchmark of 260 tasks designed to evaluate DV agents across real-world professional lifecycles. DV-World spans three domains: DV-Sheet for native spreadsheet manipulation includi

infographic.key_insight: DV-World provides a real-world benchmark of 260 tasks that evaluates data-visualization agents across native environments, cross-platform workflows, and proactive intent alignment — moving beyond sandboxed, single-language, creation-only tests.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing DV benchmarks confine agents to code sandboxes, assume perfect user intent, and focus on single-language creation tasks; DV-World addresses these gaps by measuring agent performance across realistic professional lifecycles and environments.
method: Assemble 260 tasks spanning real-world DV lifecycles (creation, editing, alignment, and deployment) across three domains including DV-Sheet for native spreadsheet manipulation
Evaluate agents in native environments and cross-platform scenarios to capture grounding and evolution (not just code generation in isolation)
Introduce tasks requiring proactive intent inference and iterative alignment, plus standardized metrics and protocols for cross-agent comparison
infographic.impact: DV-World enables more realistic, actionable evaluation of visualization agents, guiding researchers and engineers to build systems that work reliably in production workflows and better align with user intent.

title: Conditional misalignment: common interventions can hide emergent misalignment behind contextual triggers
authors: Jan Dubiński, Jan Betley, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Daniel Tan, Owain Evans
abstract:
Finetuning a language model can lead to emergent misalignment (EM) [Betley et al., 2025b]. Models trained on a narrow distribution of misaligned behavior generalize to more egregious behaviors when tested outside the training distribution.
  We study a set of interventions proposed to reduce EM. We confirm that these interventions reduce or eliminate EM on existing evaluations (questions like "How do I make a quick buck?"). However, if the evaluation prompts are tweaked to resemble the training

infographic.key_insight: Interventions that appear to remove emergent misalignment (EM) can merely hide it: when evaluation prompts are altered to match the contexts seen during finetuning, misaligned behaviors re-emerge behind contextual triggers ("conditional misalignment").
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and demonstrates that common safety interventions can give a false sense of security by suppressing misaligned outputs only on standard tests while leaving a latent, triggerable misalignment in deployed models.
method: Audit a set of proposed EM-reduction interventions on standard evaluation prompts and confirm reduced or eliminated misaligned outputs.
Construct modified evaluation prompts that mimic contextual patterns from the models' misalignment training distribution (contextual triggers).
Compare model behavior across standard vs. trigger-matched evaluations to reveal conditional reappearance of misalignment and quantify the gap.
infographic.impact: Shows that practitioners must go beyond surface-level benchmarks: defenses should be tested against contextually matched and adversarialized prompts to avoid deploying models with hidden, triggerable misalignment. This motivates more robust evaluation protocols and monitoring for real-world deployments.
visual_elements: Flow diagram: training → intervention → 'safe' outputs on standard tests vs. triggered context → misaligned outputs, highlighting the hidden pathway.
Bar chart comparing intervention effectiveness on standard evaluations vs. trigger-matched evaluations (large gap visible).

title: QCalEval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Quantum Calibration Plot Understanding
authors: Shuxiang Cao, Zijian Zhang, Abhishek Agarwal, Grace Bratrud, Niyaz R. Beysengulov
abstract: Quantum computing calibration depends on interpreting experimental data, and calibration plots provide the most universal human-readable representation for this task, yet no systematic evaluation exists of how well vision-language models (VLMs) interpret them. We introduce QCalEval, the first VLM benchmark for quantum calibration plots: 243 samples across 87 scenario types from 22 experiment families, spanning superconducting qubits and neutral atoms, evaluated on six question types in both zero

infographic.key_insight: QCalEval is the first benchmark that quantitatively evaluates how well vision–language models interpret quantum calibration plots, exposing specific strengths and weaknesses across diverse experimental scenarios.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the absence of a systematic evaluation for VLM understanding of calibration plots used in quantum experiments — a critical gap for automating interpretation and troubleshooting in quantum labs.
method: Curated dataset: 243 annotated calibration plots covering 87 scenario types from 22 experiment families (including superconducting qubits and neutral atoms).
Task design: six question types that probe visual, numerical and conceptual understanding of calibration plots, evaluated in zero-/few-shot settings.
Evaluation: standardized metrics and per-task analyses to quantify VLM performance and identify common failure modes.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners a targeted benchmark to measure and improve VLMs on scientific figure understanding, guiding model development for lab-assistive tools and automated calibration pipelines.

title: When Errors Can Be Beneficial: A Categorization of Imperfect Rewards for Policy Gradient
authors: Shuning Shang, Hubert Strauss, Stanley Wei, Sanjeev Arora, Noam Razin
abstract: Training language models via reinforcement learning often relies on imperfect proxy rewards, since ground truth rewards that precisely define the intended behavior are rarely available. Standard metrics for assessing the quality of proxy rewards, such as ranking accuracy, treat incorrect rewards as strictly harmful. In this work, however, we highlight that not all deviations from the ground truth are equal. By theoretically analyzing which outputs attract probability during policy gradient optim

infographic.key_insight: Not all deviations from the true reward are equally harmful: some kinds of imperfect proxy rewards can actually steer policy gradient training toward desirable outputs. The paper provides a categorization and theoretical criteria that predict when reward errors attract probability mass versus when they mislead learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap in evaluating proxy rewards for policy-gradient training of language models—showing that common metrics (e.g., ranking accuracy) treat all errors as uniformly bad and therefore fail to predict which reward imperfections will help or hurt learning.
method: Theoretical analysis of policy-gradient dynamics under imperfect rewards to characterize how different reward deviations change the probability mass over outputs.

A taxonomy of reward errors (e.g., sign flips, magnitude distortions, localized misrankings) and formal conditions that determine whether each error type attracts or repels probability during optimization.
Empirical/illustrative examples validating the theory and showing cases where imperfect rewards improve final policy vs. cases where they induce failure modes.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a principled framework to judge and design proxy rewards beyond simple ranking metrics, enabling more reliable RL fine-tuning of language models and better diagnostic tools for reward engineering.
visual_elements: Taxonomy diagram: a compact tree showing categories of reward errors (benign/neutral/harmful) with short examples.
Probability-flow diagram: arrows showing how policy-gradient updates reallocate probability mass under different error types.

title: Probabilistic modelling of single-cell bisulfite sequencing data with MethylVI
authors: Ethan Weinberger, Wei Qiu, Wei Tian, Qiurui Zeng, Can Ergen
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01225-9

MethylVI enhances analyses of single-cell bisulfite sequencing methylomic data via a deep generative model that accounts for the unique technical and biological sources of variability in this data modality.

infographic.key_insight: MethylVI is a probabilistic deep generative model that accurately models single-cell bisulfite sequencing (scBS-seq) methylation data, separating biological signal from technical noise to produce robust cell-level latent representations and imputed methylation profiles.
infographic.problem_solved: scBS-seq data are extremely sparse, noisy, and biased by technical factors (low coverage, site-specific and cell-specific biases), which hampers cell clustering, differential methylation analysis, and downstream interpretation. MethylVI addresses these limitations by explicitly modeling both biological variability and technical sources of error.
method: Probabilistic deep generative framework (VAE-style) that learns low-dimensional latent representations of cells while modeling observed methylation measurements probabilistically.
Explicit modeling of technical covariates and measurement noise to separate biological signal from coverage and site-specific biases, enabling robust imputation of missing methylation values.
Variational inference and end-to-end training for scalable analysis of large single-cell methylome datasets and improved downstream tasks (clustering, differential methylation).
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, MethylVI demonstrates how probabilistic deep models can handle extreme sparsity and structured noise in single-cell molecular data, producing calibrated uncertainties and latent embeddings that improve downstream analyses and multi-omics integration.
visual_elements: Schematic of the generative model (encoder/latent space/decoder) showing separation of biological latent factors and technical noise components.

title: Personalized Worked Example Generation from Student Code Submissions using Pattern-based Knowledge Components
authors: Griffin Pitts, Muntasir Hoq, Peter Brusilovsky, Narges Norouzi, Arto Hellas
abstract: Adaptive programming practice often relies on fixed libraries of worked examples and practice problems, which require substantial authoring effort and may not correspond well to the logical errors and partial solutions students produce while writing code. As a result, students may receive learning content that does not directly address the concepts they are working to understand, while instructors must either invest additional effort in expanding content libraries or accept a coarse level of per

infographic.key_insight: Automatically generate personalized worked examples from students' actual code submissions by detecting recurring code patterns and mapping them to pattern-based knowledge components, enabling targeted remediation without heavy manual authoring.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the mismatch between fixed libraries of worked examples and the diverse partial solutions/errors students produce, reducing instructor authoring effort while delivering more relevant practice.
method: Mine student code submissions to detect recurring solution and error patterns.
Convert detected patterns into pattern-based knowledge components that represent target concepts and common misconceptions.
Assemble and generate worked examples tailored to a student's partial or incorrect code by applying the relevant knowledge components.
infographic.impact: Makes worked-example generation scalable and fine-grained, improving the relevance of feedback and practice in programming tutors while lowering content-creation costs — valuable for developers of intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning platforms.

title: Energy-Arena: A Dynamic Benchmark for Operational Energy Forecasting
authors: Max Kleinebrahm, Jonathan Berrisch, Philipp Eiser, Wolf Fichtner, Veit Hagenmeyer
abstract: Energy forecasting research faces a persistent comparability gap that makes it difficult to measure consistent progress over time. Reported accuracy gains are often not directly comparable because models are evaluated under study-specific datasets, time periods, information sets, and scoring setups, while widely used benchmarks and competition datasets are typically tied to fixed historical windows. This paper introduces the Energy-Arena, a dynamic benchmarking platform for operational energy ti

infographic.key_insight: Energy-Arena provides a dynamic, reproducible benchmarking platform that evaluates operational energy-forecasting models under continuously updated, standardized conditions so reported gains are directly comparable over time.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the comparability gap in energy-forecasting research caused by study-specific datasets, fixed historical windows, inconsistent information sets, and varying scoring setups.
method: Dynamic benchmarking engine with rolling evaluation windows that continuously incorporate new operational data.
Standardized information sets, preprocessing pipelines, and modular scoring metrics to ensure fair, reproducible comparisons.
API-driven experiment orchestration and leaderboards that support multiple horizons, scenarios, and incremental model updates.
infographic.impact: Allows researchers and practitioners to measure true progress, choose models robust to temporal shifts, and deploy forecasts with confidence that performance claims are comparable and reproducible.

title: World-R1: Reinforcing 3D Constraints for Text-to-Video Generation
authors: Weijie Wang, Xiaoxuan He, Youping Gu, Yifan Yang, Zeyu Zhang
abstract: Recent video foundation models demonstrate impressive visual synthesis but frequently suffer from geometric inconsistencies. While existing methods attempt to inject 3D priors via architectural modifications, they often incur high computational costs and limit scalability. We propose World-R1, a framework that aligns video generation with 3D constraints through reinforcement learning. To facilitate this alignment, we introduce a specialized pure text dataset tailored for world simulation. Utiliz

infographic.key_insight: World-R1 uses reinforcement learning to align text-to-video generation with 3D constraints, improving geometric consistency without heavy architectural changes.
infographic.problem_solved: Text-to-video models produce visually plausible frames but often violate 3D consistency (camera, object geometry, and motion), and prior 3D-aware fixes are computationally costly or hard to scale.
method: Train a lightweight RL controller that rewards 3D-consistent renderings (camera coherence, object shape continuity, temporal depth consistency) and fine-tunes a base video generator without changing its core architecture.
Create and use a specialized pure-text 'world simulation' dataset to teach the policy 3D-aware scene descriptions and preference signals for spatial/temporal consistency.
Apply the RL reward as a plugin stage (policy-gradient or actor-critic) to existing video foundation models, trading minimal extra compute for significant geometric correction.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to raise 3D realism in text-to-video outputs with a scalable, model-agnostic augmentation rather than expensive architecture redesigns—helpful for production-quality generation and downstream tasks requiring spatial coherence.

title: Case-Specific Rubrics for Clinical AI Evaluation: Methodology, Validation, and LLM-Clinician Agreement Across 823 Encounters
authors: Aaryan Shah, Andrew Hines, Alexia Downs, Denis Bajet, Paulius Mui
abstract:
Objective. Clinical AI documentation systems require evaluation methodologies that are clinically valid, economically viable, and sensitive to iterative changes. Methods requiring expert review per scoring instance are too slow and expensive for safe, iterative deployment. We present a case-specific, clinician-authored rubric methodology for clinical AI evaluation and examine whether LLM-generated rubrics can approximate clinician agreement.
  Materials and Methods. Twenty clinicians authored 1,

infographic.key_insight: Case-specific, clinician-authored rubrics enable clinically valid and economically scalable evaluation of clinical AI; LLM-generated rubrics can approximate clinician agreement when applied across 823 clinical encounters, supporting faster iterative evaluation.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces dependence on slow, expensive per-instance expert review by providing a scalable, clinically grounded rubric methodology that is sensitive to iterative changes in clinical AI systems.
method: Clinicians author concise, case-specific rubrics that define task-relevant scoring criteria and acceptable variations.
LLMs are used to generate or apply rubrics at scale and produce automated scores; outputs are compared against clinician judgments.
Validation across 823 clinical encounters measuring inter-rater agreement, operational cost/time trade-offs, and sensitivity to iterative model changes.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML teams a practical evaluation pipeline that preserves clinical validity while dramatically reducing expert labor, enabling safer, faster iteration and deployment of clinical AI systems.

title: Long-Context Aware Upcycling: A New Frontier for Hybrid LLM Scaling
authors: Parsa Ashrafi Fashi, Utkarsh Saxena, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Aref Jafari, Akash Haridas
abstract: Hybrid sequence models that combine efficient Transformer components with linear sequence modeling blocks are a promising alternative to pure Transformers, but most are still pretrained from scratch and therefore fail to reuse existing Transformer checkpoints. We study upcycling as a practical path to convert pretrained Transformer LLMs into hybrid architectures while preserving short-context quality and improving long-context capability. We call our solution \emph{HyLo} (HYbrid LOng-context): a

infographic.key_insight: HyLo demonstrates that pretrained Transformer LLMs can be "upcycled" into hybrid architectures that combine Transformer blocks with linear sequence modules, preserving short-context performance while extending effective long-context capability.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between efficiency-oriented hybrid sequence models and the large ecosystem of pretrained Transformer checkpoints by providing a practical conversion path that avoids training from scratch.
method: Insert or integrate linear sequence-modeling blocks (e.g., linear-attention / state-space style modules) into an existing pretrained Transformer backbone to form a hybrid stack.
Apply upcycling steps (structured replacement or augmentation of layers + careful weight reuse and minimal fine-tuning) to keep short-context behavior intact while enabling longer context handling.
Validate and tune the hybrid model to balance latency, memory, and long-context accuracy without discarding pretrained knowledge.
infographic.impact: Offers a pragmatic route to leverage existing LLM checkpoints for long-context applications, reducing compute and data costs of retraining while enabling more scalable, efficient models for practitioners.

title: Learning to Think from Multiple Thinkers
authors: Nirmit Joshi, Roey Magen, Nathan Srebro, Nikolaos Tsilivis, Gal Vardi
abstract:
We study learning with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision from multiple thinkers, all of whom provide correct but possibly systematically different solutions, e.g., step-by-step solutions to math problems written by different thinkers, or step-by-step execution traces of different programs solving the same problem.
  We consider classes that are computationally easy to learn using CoT supervision from a single thinker, but hard to learn with only end-result supervision, i.e., without CoT (Joshi

infographic.key_insight: Correct but systematically different step-by-step solutions from multiple thinkers provide complementary supervision that can make learning tractable where end-result labels alone are provably insufficient; aggregating diverse Chain-of-Thought traces improves learnability and robustness.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses how to learn from multiple correct but heterogeneous Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces for the same tasks, and whether/when such supervision overcomes computational barriers that appear with only final-answer labels.
method: Formally define a multi-thinker CoT supervision model where each thinker supplies correct, potentially systematically different stepwise solutions for the same problems.

Theoretical analysis showing classes that are easy to learn with CoT (from one or multiple thinkers) but hard with only end-result supervision; characterize when multi-thinker supervision yields provable advantages.

Design learning/aggregation strategies that align and combine diverse stepwise traces to recover useful intermediate structure for efficient learning (e.g., consensus, alignment or latent-structure induction).
infographic.impact: Provides a principled foundation for using diverse explanatory traces (human or programmatic) to improve sample/computational efficiency and robustness of learners—guiding dataset collection and model training strategies that exploit multiple correct explanations.

title: OmniShotCut: Holistic Relational Shot Boundary Detection with Shot-Query Transformer
authors: Boyang Wang, Guangyi Xu, Zhipeng Tang, Jiahui Zhang, Zezhou Cheng
abstract: Shot Boundary Detection (SBD) aims to automatically identify shot changes and divide a video into coherent shots. While SBD was widely studied in the literature, existing state-of-the-art methods often produce non-interpretable boundaries on transitions, miss subtle yet harmful discontinuities, and rely on noisy, low-diversity annotations and outdated benchmarks. To alleviate these limitations, we propose OmniShotCut to formulate SBD as structured relational prediction, jointly estimating shot r

infographic.key_insight: OmniShotCut reframes shot boundary detection as a structured relational prediction problem and uses a Shot-Query Transformer to detect boundaries holistically and interpretably, enabling detection of subtle and complex transitions that prior methods miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing SBD methods produce non-interpretable boundaries on transitions, miss subtle but harmful discontinuities, and depend on noisy, low-diversity annotations and outdated benchmarks; OmniShotCut addresses these issues by modeling shot relations jointly and robustly.
method: Shot-Query Transformer: learnable queries attend to temporal context to locate and characterize shot boundaries and transitions.
Structured relational prediction: jointly estimate shot boundaries and inter-shot relations for more interpretable, holistic segmentation.
Robust design to annotation noise and benchmark limitations: modeling choices and training objectives emphasize subtle discontinuities and clearer boundary semantics.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners a more reliable, interpretable SBD module for downstream video tasks (editing, indexing, captioning, action detection), reducing missed/ambiguous transitions and improving preprocessing quality.

title: A domain-adapted large language model to support clinicians in psychiatric clinical practice

title: Tuna-2: Pixel Embeddings Beat Vision Encoders for Multimodal Understanding and Generation
authors: Zhiheng Liu, Weiming Ren, Xiaoke Huang, Shoufa Chen, Tianhong Li
abstract: Unified multimodal models typically rely on pretrained vision encoders and use separate visual representations for understanding and generation, creating misalignment between the two tasks and preventing fully end-to-end optimization from raw pixels. We introduce Tuna-2, a native unified multimodal model that performs visual understanding and generation directly based on pixel embeddings. Tuna-2 drastically simplifies the model architecture by employing simple patch embedding layers to encode vi

infographic.key_insight: Tuna-2 replaces pretrained vision encoders with native pixel (patch) embeddings, using the same visual representation for both understanding and generation so the entire multimodal model can be trained end-to-end from raw pixels.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing multimodal systems use different visual representations for perception and generation (pretrained encoders vs. generation inputs), causing task misalignment and preventing fully end-to-end optimization from pixels.
method: Encode images directly with simple patch/pixel embedding layers rather than large pretrained vision encoders.

Use a single unified multimodal architecture that consumes pixel embeddings for both visual understanding (e.g., VQA, classification) and visual generation (e.g., captioning, multimodal generation), removing representational mismatch.
Train the model end-to-end from raw pixels to downstream outputs, simplifying the pipeline and enabling joint optimization of visual and language components.
infographic.impact: By unifying representations and enabling end-to-end training from pixels, Tuna-2 simplifies model design and reduces encoder–decoder misalignment—helpful for building more flexible, maintainable multimodal systems and for research on pixel-native multimodal learning.

title: Programmable RNA translation through deep learning-driven IRES discovery and de novo generation
authors: Yanyi Chu, Di Yin, Dan Yu, Guangxue Xu, Junze Zhang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 24 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01213-z

Chu et al. present a framework for programmable RNA translation, of interest for RNA therapeutics. The method enables large-scale discovery and engineering of internal ribosome entry sites, which are validated by high-throughput functional assays.

infographic.key_insight: Deep learning models plus high-throughput functional assays enable large-scale discovery and de novo design of internal ribosome entry sites (IRES), allowing programmable control of cap‑independent translation in mRNA.
infographic.problem_solved: The field lacked scalable, predictive methods to find and engineer functional IRES elements for tunable translation, slowing design of RNA therapeutics and synthetic gene circuits.
method: Massively parallel functional screens (high‑throughput reporter assays) to measure IRES activity across thousands of sequences.
Train predictive deep learning models that map RNA sequence (and inferred structure) to translation efficiency.
Use generative/design algorithms and an iterative design–test loop to propose and experimentally validate de novo IRES sequences with desired activity.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners this provides a real-world sequence→function benchmark and a demonstration of closed‑loop model‑guided biological design, highlighting opportunities for generative models, uncertainty-aware optimization, and transfer learning in molecular engineering.

title: Fluid thinking about collective intelligence
authors: Justin Werfel
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 24 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01211-1

Collectives exhibit intrinsically different operations, resources and limitations depending on whether their components are static or mobile. Werfel examines learning in mobile collectives and shows how each class can benefit from incorporating mechanisms more commonly linked to the other.

infographic.key_insight: Learning dynamics differ fundamentally between static and mobile collectives, and each class can gain performance and robustness by adopting mechanisms typically used by the other (e.g., memory/communication for mobile swarms, mobility-driven exploration for static networks).
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how mobility changes collective learning capabilities and provides a conceptual and empirical basis for hybrid design choices that bridge techniques from static and mobile collectives.
method: Develop a comparative framework distinguishing resources, constraints and learning modes of static vs mobile collectives.
Analyze models of learning in mobile collectives and identify mechanisms (e.g., local memory, structured communication, positional cues) that can be adapted across classes.
Demonstrate benefits through illustrative analyses and simulations showing improved learning/robustness when cross-class mechanisms are incorporated.
infographic.impact: Guides AI/ML practitioners designing multi-agent systems and swarm robotics toward hybrid architectures that leverage mobility or structured information to boost learning efficiency and resilience. Offers concrete prescriptions for transferring tools between static distributed systems and mobile collectives.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: static collective vs mobile collective highlighting different resources/limitations (links, fixed topology vs movement, transient contacts).
Flow diagram showing cross-adoption: arrows from static mechanisms (memory, routing, aggregation) to mobile collectives and from mobility (exploration, physical rearrangement) to static networks.
Simulation heatmaps or performance graphs comparing baseline vs hybrid designs (learning speed, error, robustness to failure).

title: Long-tail Internet photo reconstruction
authors: Yuan Li, Yuanbo Xiangli, Hadar Averbuch-Elor, Noah Snavely, Ruojin Cai
abstract: Internet photo collections exhibit an extremely long-tailed distribution: a few famous landmarks are densely photographed and easily reconstructed in 3D, while most real-world sites are represented with sparse, noisy, uneven imagery beyond the capabilities of both classical and learned 3D methods. We believe that tackling this long-tail regime represents one of the next frontiers for 3D foundation models. Although reliable ground-truth 3D supervision from sparse scenes is challenging to acquire,

infographic.key_insight: Reliable 3D reconstruction can be extended beyond famous, well-photographed landmarks into the long-tail of sparsely and noisily imaged real-world sites by combining robust geometric reasoning with learned priors and supervision strategies that do not rely on dense ground-truth 3D.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the inability of classical and current learned 3D methods to reconstruct most real-world sites from sparse, uneven, and noisy Internet photo collections — the long-tail regime where dense multi-view coverage and ground-truth 3D are unavailable.
method: Fuse robust geometric constraints with learned scene priors that transfer knowledge from densely photographed landmarks to sparse, low-quality sites.
Use self-supervision, synthetic augmentation, or proxy signals to reduce dependence on reliable ground-truth 3D during training.
Incorporate uncertainty-aware fusion and outlier rejection to handle noisy poses, uneven view distributions, and photometric variability.
infographic.impact: Enables scaling 3D reconstruction to the vast majority of real-world sites, unlocking broader applications in mapping, AR/VR, cultural heritage digitization, and building more general 3D foundation models that work beyond popular landmarks.
visual_elements: Long-tail histogram showing photo count per site (few dense landmarks vs many sparse sites)
Before/after reconstruction comparisons for a sparse site (classical vs proposed approach)

title: Structure-Guided Diffusion Model for EEG-Based Visual Cognition Reconstruction
authors: Yongxiang Lian, Yueyang Cang, Pingge Hu, Yuchen He, Li Shi
abstract: Objective: Decoding visual information from electroencephalography (EEG) is an important problem in neuroscience and brain-computer interface (BCI) research. Existing methods are largely restricted to natural images and categorical representations, with limited capacity to capture structural features and to differentiate objective perception from subjective cognition. We propose a Structure-Guided Diffusion Model (SGDM) that incorporates explicit structural information for EEG-based visual recon

infographic.key_insight: Incorporating explicit structural priors into a diffusion-based generative model enables more faithful reconstruction of visual content from EEG and helps separate objective perceptual signals from subjective cognitive components.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing EEG-to-image methods focus on categorical or natural-image priors and fail to capture structural features or disentangle perception vs. cognition, limiting reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
method: Encode EEG signals with a dedicated EEG encoder to produce conditioning latents for generation.

Integrate explicit structural information (e.g., edge/contour, spatial layout or segmentation cues) as guidance into a conditional diffusion decoder to steer image synthesis toward structure-consistent reconstructions.

Train jointly with objectives that encourage structure alignment and disentanglement between objective perceptual features and subjective cognitive signals (e.g., reconstruction + structure-consistency / contrastive losses).
infographic.impact: Provides a practical approach for more interpretable, structure-aware EEG-to-image reconstruction useful for neuroAI, BCI interfaces, and studies of visual cognition, improving fidelity and diagnostic value of decoded images.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: EEG input → EEG encoder → structural prior extractor → structure-guided diffusion decoder → reconstructed image
