title: A multimodal large language model for materials science
authors: Yingheng Tang, Wenbin Xu, Jie Cao, Weilu Gao, Steven Farrell
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 24 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01214-y

Tang et al. introduce MatterChat, a multimodal framework effectively integrating material structural data with large language models. It achieves high-precision property predictions and provides interpretable reasoning to accelerate materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: MatterChat fuses material structural data with a large language model to produce high‑precision property predictions and human‑readable reasoning, enabling faster, interpretable materials discovery.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between raw structural representations (e.g., crystal/atomic structures) and LLMs, solving low accuracy and poor interpretability in materials property prediction workflows.
method: Encode multimodal material inputs (atomic/crystal structure representations and descriptors) into learned embeddings compatible with an LLM.
Perform multimodal fusion and fine‑tuning so the LLM jointly predicts properties and generates verbalized, interpretable reasoning steps.
Train and evaluate end‑to‑end for high‑precision property regression/classification while producing attention/attribution outputs for explainability.
infographic.impact: Enables ML practitioners to apply LLM architectures to materials science with reliable, explainable predictions, reducing experimental cycles and informing hypothesis generation. Advances multimodal model design and interpretability for scientific domains.

title: From embodied intelligence to physical AI
authors: Unknown
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 24 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01239-3

Several frameworks from different disciplines are converging on the scientific question of what it takes for a system to not just predict, simulate or reason about the world, but to act physically and intelligently within it.

infographic.key_insight: Multiple disciplinary frameworks are converging into a unified view that building truly intelligent systems requires designing for physical interaction — not just prediction or simulation — combining morphology, sensing, control and learning into 'physical AI'.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies the gap between simulated/abstract intelligence and agents that can robustly act in the real world, reconciling fragmented perspectives and proposing a coherent research agenda and evaluation approach for physically embodied systems.
method: Synthesize frameworks from robotics, cognitive science, control theory and machine learning to identify common principles for physical agency.
Define a conceptual/operational framework that links morphology, sensing, actuation, learning and environment as the core components of physical AI.
Propose directions for metrics, benchmarks and experimental paradigms to evaluate real-world interactive competence.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a practical roadmap for moving systems from simulation to robust real-world operation, guiding system design, evaluation and cross-disciplinary collaboration to accelerate physically capable intelligence.

title: Aligning Dense Retrievers with LLM Utility via DistillationAligning Dense Retrievers with LLM Utility via Distillation
authors: Rajinder Sandhu, Di Mu, Cheng Chang, Md Shahriar Tasjid, Himanshu Rai
abstract: Dense vector retrieval is the practical backbone of Retrieval- Augmented Generation (RAG), but similarity search can suffer from precision limitations. Conversely, utility-based approaches leveraging LLM re-ranking often achieve superior performance but are computationally prohibitive and prone to noise inherent in perplexity estimation. We propose Utility-Aligned Embeddings (UAE), a framework designed to merge these advantages into a practical, high-performance retrieval method. We formulate re

infographic.key_insight: Distill LLM-derived utility signals into dense embeddings so a retriever behaves like an expensive LLM re-ranker at retrieval time, achieving higher utility-aware precision with the speed of vector search.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between high-precision but costly LLM re-ranking (utility-based signals) and fast but sometimes imprecise dense vector retrieval, enabling practical Retrieval-Augmented Generation with improved relevance.
method: Use an LLM re-ranker or utility oracle to score relevance/utility for query–document pairs (generate soft/hard utility labels).
Train a dense embedding model via distillation so embedded distances reflect LLM utility (align embeddings with utility scores), possibly combining contrastive and regression-style losses.
Deploy the distilled retriever at query time to get LLM-like re-ranking quality with low-latency vector search, reducing on-the-fly LLM calls.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get near-LLM re-ranking quality without the runtime cost and instability of running LLMs for every query, improving RAG throughput, cost-efficiency, and end-to-end retrieval quality.

title: Inter-Stance: A Dyadic Multimodal Corpus for Conversational Stance Analysis
authors: Xiang Zhang, Xiaotian Li, Taoyue Wang, Nan Bi, Xin Zhou
abstract: Social interactions dominate our perceptions of the world and shape our daily behavior by attaching social meaning to acts as simple and spontaneous as gestures, facial expressions, voice, and speech. People mimic and otherwise respond to each other's postures, facial expressions, mannerisms, and other verbal and nonverbal behavior, and form appraisals or evaluations in the process. Yet, no publicly-available dataset includes multimodal recordings and self-report measures of multiple persons in

infographic.key_insight: Inter‑Stance provides a first-of-its-kind dyadic multimodal corpus that pairs synchronized audio/video/behavioral signals with self‑report measures to enable fine‑grained conversational stance analysis between interacting partners.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of publicly available datasets that capture multimodal recordings and participant self-reports from multi-person interactions, which has limited modeling of interpersonal stance dynamics and evaluation of conversational stance systems.
method: Record controlled dyadic conversations with synchronized multimodal streams (audio, video, facial/gesture cues) and transcripts.
Collect participant self‑report measures and turn-/time‑level stance annotations to create ground truth labels for interpersonal attitudes.
Process and align multimodal signals, define an annotation schema, and release the corpus with benchmarking tasks to support stance modeling and evaluation.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML researchers to train and evaluate multimodal models that capture how stance emerges and shifts in conversation, improving conversational agents, social signal processing, and human-centered interaction analysis.

title: How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money? Analyzing and Predicting Token Consumption in Agentic Coding Tasks
authors: Longju Bai, Zhemin Huang, Xingyao Wang, Jiao Sun, Rada Mihalcea
abstract: The wide adoption of AI agents in complex human workflows is driving rapid growth in LLM token consumption. When agents are deployed on tasks that require a significant amount of tokens, three questions naturally arise: (1) Where do AI agents spend the tokens? (2) Which models are more token-efficient? and (3) Can agents predict their token usage before task execution? In this paper, we present the first systematic study of token consumption patterns in agentic coding tasks. We analyze trajector

infographic.key_insight: Agentic coding workflows spend a large share of tokens on orchestration (prompts, tool calls, and iterative debugging) rather than the final code output, and token consumption can be predicted reasonably well from task and agent-level features before execution.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of systematic understanding and forecasting of where and how tokens are consumed by AI agents in coding tasks, enabling cost-aware model/agent selection and pipeline optimization.
method: Curate and analyze a dataset of agentic coding trajectories to break down token usage by stage (prompting, tool calls, model responses, retries, etc.).
Compare token-efficiency across models and agent designs to identify high-cost components and model-level tradeoffs.
Train lightweight predictors using task/agent features (e.g., problem size, tool usage, agent loop counts) to forecast token consumption before task execution.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with actionable insights and pre-run cost estimates to choose more token-efficient models, redesign agent workflows, and reduce operational costs without sacrificing task performance.

title: Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust and shape-based AI vision
authors: Zejin Lu, Sushrut Thorat, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Tim C. Kietzmann
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 24 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01228-6

Lu, Thorat and colleagues report that training AI vision systems with a human-inspired developmental visual diet results in a stronger reliance on shape over texture features, enabling substantially more robust visual inference. This finding points to a resource-efficient path to robust vision.

infographic.key_insight: Training vision models with a human-inspired developmental visual diet shifts them from texture-driven to shape-driven perception, producing substantially more robust and generalizable visual inference with lower resource cost.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the fragility and texture-bias of standard vision models by closing the gap between AI training regimes and human visual development, enabling stronger out-of-distribution and corruption robustness without heavy compute or complex defenses.
method: Design a developmental visual diet and curriculum inspired by human infant visual statistics (e.g., progressive exposure to object-centric, varied-scale, and temporally structured views).
Train standard vision architectures using this developmental diet and compare to conventional ImageNet-style training.
Evaluate models on shape-vs-texture diagnostics and robustness benchmarks (corruptions, OOD tests) to quantify increased shape-bias and improved performance.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, resource-efficient strategy for improving model robustness and generalization by rethinking training data/curriculum rather than model complexity. Practitioners can adopt developmental-diet principles to boost shape-based recognition and OOD resilience in production systems.
visual_elements: Timeline/flow showing developmental visual diet stages (early coarse views → object-centric views → varied contexts).

title: Spend Less, Fit Better: Budget-Efficient Scaling Law Fitting via Active Experiment Selection
authors: Sijie Li, Shanda Li, Haowei Lin, Weiwei Sun, Ameet Talwalkar
abstract: Scaling laws are used to plan multi-million-dollar training runs, but fitting those laws can itself cost millions. In modern large-scale workflows, assembling a sufficiently informative set of pilot experiments is already a major budget-allocation problem rather than a routine preprocessing step. We formulate scaling-law fitting as budget-aware sequential experimental design: given a finite pool of runnable experiments with heterogeneous costs, choose which runs to execute so as to maximize extr

infographic.key_insight: Treat scaling-law estimation as a budget-aware sequential experimental-design problem: actively pick pilot runs based on cost and informativeness to fit scaling laws more accurately for less money.
infographic.problem_solved: Pilot experiments used to fit scaling laws are themselves costly and heterogeneous in compute price; naive or uniform sampling wastes budget and can produce poor extrapolations for planning large-scale runs.
method: Formulate scaling-law fitting as budget-aware sequential experiment selection from a finite pool of runnable configurations with heterogeneous costs.
Use an acquisition strategy that trades off expected information gain (or uncertainty reduction) against run cost to prioritize experiments with high value per dollar.
Iteratively run selected experiments, update the scaling-law fit, and re-select under the remaining budget until budget is exhausted or fit converges.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to obtain reliable scaling-law fits with substantially lower pilot cost, improving resource allocation and more trustworthy planning of expensive large-scale training runs.

title: PASR: Pose-Aware 3D Shape Retrieval from Occluded Single Views
authors: Jiaxin Shi, Guofeng Zhang, Wufei Ma, Naifu Liang, Adam Kortylewski
abstract: Single-view 3D shape retrieval is a fundamental yet challenging task that is increasingly important with the growth of available 3D data. Existing approaches largely fall into two categories: those using contrastive learning to map point cloud features into existing vision-language spaces and those that learn a common embedding space for 2D images and 3D shapes. However, these feed-forward, holistic alignments are often difficult to interpret, which in turn limits their robustness and generaliza

infographic.key_insight: Disentangling pose from shape and conditioning retrieval on estimated camera pose lets a model map occluded single views into a pose-normalized 3D shape space, yielding more robust and interpretable 3D retrieval from partial observations.
infographic.problem_solved: How to reliably retrieve the correct 3D shape from a single, often heavily occluded view where holistic image–shape alignments fail due to viewpoint and missing-visible-part ambiguities.
method: Pose-aware decomposition: estimate camera pose from the input view and use it to canonicalize or condition downstream shape embeddings.

Occlusion-robust shape encoder: train a shape embedding that aligns partial (occluded) views with full 3D shapes using pose-conditioning and contrastive/retrieval objectives with synthetic occlusion augmentation.
Pose-conditioned retrieval and attention to visible regions to improve interpretability and reduce false matches caused by occluders or extreme viewpoints.
infographic.impact: Makes single-view 3D retrieval practical in real-world settings (robotics, AR, inventory search) by improving robustness to occlusion and viewpoint changes and by producing more interpretable embeddings for debugging and downstream use.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: occluded input image → pose estimator → pose-normalizer/conditioner → shape encoder → retrieval results.

title: Generative Modeling of Neurodegenerative Brain Anatomy with 4D Longitudinal Diffusion Model
authors: Nivetha Jayakumar, Swakshar Deb, Bahram Jafrasteh, Qingyu Zhao, Miaomiao Zhang
abstract: Understanding and predicting the progression of neurodegenerative diseases remains a major challenge in medical AI, with significant implications for early diagnosis, disease monitoring, and treatment planning. However, most available longitudinal neuroimaging datasets are temporally sparse with a few follow-up scans per subject. This scarcity of temporal data limits our ability to model and accurately capture the continuous anatomical changes related to disease progression in individual subject

infographic.key_insight: A 4D diffusion-based generative model learns continuous spatiotemporal brain anatomy changes from temporally sparse longitudinal scans, enabling realistic interpolation and simulation of neurodegenerative progression.
infographic.problem_solved: Sparse follow-up scans in longitudinal neuroimaging make it hard to model continuous disease progression at the subject level; this approach fills temporal gaps and captures smooth anatomical trajectories.
method: Formulate a 4D (3D space + time) generative diffusion model that encodes and decodes spatiotemporal brain anatomy rather than isolated timepoints.
Train the model to learn smooth temporal dynamics from population-level longitudinal examples, enabling interpolation/extrapolation between few observed follow-ups.
Incorporate anatomy-aware constraints and temporal conditioning (e.g., baseline anatomy, time offsets) to preserve structural plausibility and subject-specific progression.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a tool to augment sparse longitudinal datasets, generate plausible intermediate scans, and improve downstream tasks (progression prediction, biomarker discovery) without requiring dense follow-up data.

title: Rethinking XAI Evaluation: A Human-Centered Audit of Shapley Benchmarks in High-Stakes Settings
authors: Inês Oliveira e Silva, Sérgio Jesus, Iker Perez, Rita P. Ribeiro, Carlos Soares
abstract: Shapley values are a cornerstone of explainable AI, yet their proliferation into competing formulations has created a fragmented landscape with little consensus on practical deployment. While theoretical differences are well-documented, evaluation remains reliant on quantitative proxies whose alignment with human utility is unverified. In this work, we use a unified amortized framework to isolate semantic differences between eight Shapley variants under the low-latency constraints of operational

infographic.key_insight: A human-centered audit shows that different Shapley-value variants—though theoretically similar—diverge in semantics and practical utility, and common quantitative proxies often fail to predict which explanations help humans in high-stakes, low-latency settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies which Shapley formulations actually align with human decision-making and operational constraints, addressing the gap between theoretical metrics and real-world usefulness of explanations.
method: Develop a unified amortized framework to isolate semantic differences between eight Shapley variants under low-latency operational constraints.
Compare variants using both quantitative proxies and human-centered evaluations (audits) in high-stakes decision tasks to measure alignment with human utility.
Analyze discrepancies between proxy-based rankings and human performance/preferences to identify failure modes and practical trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with empirical guidance on selecting and interpreting Shapley-based explanations under time-sensitive, high-risk conditions, and motivates integrating human-centered benchmarks into XAI evaluation pipelines.

title: Agentic World Modeling: Foundations, Capabilities, Laws, and Beyond
authors: Meng Chu, Xuan Billy Zhang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Lingdong Kong, Jize Zhang
abstract: As AI systems move from generating text to accomplishing goals through sustained interaction, the ability to model environment dynamics becomes a central bottleneck. Agents that manipulate objects, navigate software, coordinate with others, or design experiments require predictive environment models, yet the term world model carries different meanings across research communities. We introduce a "levels x laws" taxonomy organized along two axes. The first defines three capability levels: L1 Predi

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a unified "levels × laws" taxonomy that clarifies and structures what a world model means for agentic systems, linking graded capability levels to governing principles to guide design, evaluation, and safety.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses ambiguity and fragmentation in how ‘world models’ are defined and assessed for agents that must predict and act in interactive, multi-step environments.
method: Define a capability axis with three progressive levels of agentic world-modeling (from basic prediction to interactive/goal-directed modeling).
Identify a laws/principles axis that captures constraints, desiderata, and invariants (e.g., fidelity, causal structure, computational limits, and alignment considerations).
Combine these axes into a practical taxonomy and use it to map capabilities, failure modes, benchmarks, and research priorities.
infographic.impact: Provides a clear conceptual and practical scaffold for researchers and engineers to design, evaluate, and compare world models for interactive agents, improving reliability, interpretability, and alignment across applications.

title: Seeing Fast and Slow: Learning the Flow of Time in Videos
authors: Yen-Siang Wu, Rundong Luo, Jingsen Zhu, Tao Tu, Ali Farhadi
abstract: How can we tell whether a video has been sped up or slowed down? How can we generate videos at different speeds? Although videos have been central to modern computer vision research, little attention has been paid to perceiving and controlling the passage of time. In this paper, we study time as a learnable visual concept and develop models for reasoning about and manipulating the flow of time in videos. We first exploit the multimodal cues and temporal structure naturally present in videos to l

infographic.key_insight: Time is a learnable visual concept: by leveraging multimodal cues and the intrinsic temporal structure of videos, models can both perceive changes in playback speed and synthesize videos at different speeds.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of methods for perceiving and controlling the passage of time in video: detecting whether a clip has been sped up or slowed down and generating realistic speed-altered videos.
method: Learn a 'flow of time' representation from videos using multimodal signals (visual frames, audio) and temporal structure, often via self-supervised objectives.
Train predictors to estimate time-scaling factors or classify speed changes from learned temporal embeddings.
Manipulate video playback by temporal resampling/interpolation or learned temporal warping (and align audio) to synthesize realistic faster/slower versions.
infographic.impact: Provides tools for robust temporal reasoning and controllable video editing—beneficial for action recognition, data augmentation, video synthesis, simulation, and human-centered video analysis.

title: From Research Question to Scientific Workflow: Leveraging Agentic AI for Science Automation
authors: Bartosz Balis, Michal Orzechowski, Piotr Kica, Michal Dygas, Michal Kuszewski
abstract: Scientific workflow systems automate execution -- scheduling, fault tolerance, resource management -- but not the semantic translation that precedes it. Scientists still manually convert research questions into workflow specifications, a task requiring both domain knowledge and infrastructure expertise. We propose an agentic architecture that closes this gap through three layers: an LLM interprets natural language into structured intents (semantic layer); validated generators produce reproducibl

infographic.key_insight: An agentic, three-layer architecture uses LLMs to convert natural-language research questions into validated, reproducible workflow specifications, closing the semantic gap between scientists and workflow execution systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Scientists currently must manually translate research questions into workflow specs — a time‑consuming step that requires both domain knowledge and infrastructure expertise and blocks automation and reproducibility.
method: Semantic layer: LLM interprets natural-language research questions into structured intents and task descriptions.
Validated generators: intent-driven generators assemble reproducible, verifiable workflow specifications and components (templates, data/compute bindings).
Execution/integration layer: produced workflows are validated, scheduled, and executed by scientific workflow systems with monitoring, fault tolerance, and resource management.
infographic.impact: Enables faster experiment design, reduces dependence on infrastructure experts, and improves reproducibility and scalability of computational science — accelerating AI/ML research and deployment.

title: Seeing Without Eyes: 4D Human-Scene Understanding from Wearable IMUs
authors: Hao-Yu Hsu, Tianhang Cheng, Jing Wen, Alexander G. Schwing, Shenlong Wang
abstract: Understanding human activities and their surrounding environments typically relies on visual perception, yet cameras pose persistent challenges in privacy, safety, energy efficiency, and scalability. We explore an alternative: 4D perception without vision. Its goal is to reconstruct human motion and 3D scene layouts purely from everyday wearable sensors. For this we introduce IMU-to-4D, a framework that repurposes large language models for non-visual spatiotemporal understanding of human-scene d

infographic.key_insight: Repurposes large language models to perform non‑visual 4D reconstruction from everyday wearable IMUs, recovering human motion and 3D scene layout without cameras.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces reliance on cameras for human activity and environment understanding, addressing persistent privacy, safety, energy, and scalability challenges by using inertial wearable sensors instead of vision.
method: Use streams from everyday wearable IMUs as the sole input modality and encode spatiotemporal inertial signals.
Repurpose large language models as spatiotemporal reasoning modules to map IMU sequences to scene-aware predictions.
Decode outputs into a 4D representation: time-varying 3D human pose together with reconstructed scene geometry/layout for downstream tasks.
infographic.impact: Offers a privacy-preserving, low-power alternative for 4D perception useful in AR/VR, healthcare monitoring, and robotics, and highlights a novel role for LLMs beyond text as general spatiotemporal reasoners—opening new research directions and deployment options.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: wearable IMUs on a person → LLM-based reasoning block → 4D output (animated 3D human + scene layout).

title: Evaluation of Automatic Speech Recognition Using Generative Large Language Models
authors: Thibault Bañeras-Roux, Shashi Kumar, Driss Khalil, Sergio Burdisso, Petr Motlicek
abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is traditionally evaluated using Word Error Rate (WER), a metric that is insensitive to meaning. Embedding-based semantic metrics are better correlated with human perception, but decoder-based Large Language Models (LLMs) remain underexplored for this task. This paper evaluates their relevance through three approaches: (1) selecting the best hypothesis between two candidates, (2) computing semantic distance using generative embeddings, and (3) qualitative class

infographic.key_insight: Generative LLMs can evaluate ASR outputs in a meaning-aware way—using pairwise selection, generative embeddings, and qualitative LLM judgments—providing signals better aligned with human perception than raw WER.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard WER is insensitive to meaning and can misrepresent perceived transcription quality; decoder-based LLMs as evaluators have been underexplored for producing semantic-aware ASR evaluation.
method: Pairwise selection: use an LLM to choose the better hypothesis between two ASR outputs.
Generative embeddings: extract embeddings from a generative LLM to compute semantic distance between reference and hypothesis.
Qualitative LLM analysis: use generative LLM outputs for classification/qualitative assessment of error types and semantic deviations.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with evaluation tools that reflect semantic fidelity and human judgment, enabling more meaningful benchmarking and model selection beyond WER. This can guide development toward systems that preserve intended meaning rather than just token-level accuracy.

Bar/line chart of correlation with human judgments: WER vs. embedding-based vs. LLM pairwise scoring

title: Context Unrolling in Omni Models
authors: Ceyuan Yang, Zhijie Lin, Yang Zhao, Fei Xiao, Hao He
abstract: We present Omni, a unified multimodal model natively trained on diverse modalities, including text, images, videos, 3D geometry, and hidden representations. We find that such training enables Context Unrolling, where the model explicitly reasons across multiple modal representations before producing predictions. This process enables the model to aggregate complementary information across heterogeneous modalities, facilitating a more faithful approximation of the shared multimodal knowledge manif

infographic.key_insight: Omni demonstrates "Context Unrolling": the model explicitly reasons across multiple modal representations (text, images, video, 3D, hidden states) in an internal iterative step before producing predictions, enabling richer cross-modal aggregation and more faithful multimodal reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses how to unify and faithfully reason across heterogeneous modalities so complementary and partial signals (e.g., image + text + 3D) can be combined without losing intermediate modality-specific structure or relying on brittle ad-hoc fusion.
method: Train a single unified multimodal model on diverse modalities (text, images, video, 3D geometry, and hidden representations).
Introduce Context Unrolling: an explicit internal reasoning loop that propagates and refines modality-specific representations before final decoding.
Aggregate cross-modal information via attention/aggregation modules during unrolling to produce a coherent shared multimodal representation used for prediction.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build models that better exploit complementary multimodal information for more accurate and faithful outputs, improving robustness and interpretability in multimodal tasks and downstream applications.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: modality inputs → modality encoders → Context Unrolling loop → decoder/output

title: UniGenDet: A Unified Generative-Discriminative Framework for Co-Evolutionary Image Generation and Generated Image Detection
authors: Yanran Zhang, Wenzhao Zheng, Yifei Li, Bingyao Yu, Yu Zheng
abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in both image generation and generated image detection. Despite their rapid, yet largely independent, development, these two fields have evolved distinct architectural paradigms: the former predominantly relies on generative networks, while the latter favors discriminative frameworks. A recent trend in both domains is the use of adversarial information to enhance performance, revealing potential for synergy. However, the significant architectur

infographic.key_insight: UniGenDet unifies generative and discriminative models into a co-evolutionary loop so that a generator and a detector are trained together, exchanging adversarial signals to improve image realism and detection robustness simultaneously.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between independent development of image generation and generated-image detection—preventing detectors from lagging behind new generators and enabling generators to be evaluated/trained against realistic detection pressure.
method: Unified dual-path architecture: a generative network and a discriminative detection network share features and communicate via dedicated cross-task modules.

Co-evolutionary training loop: generator and detector are trained alternately with adversarial exchange (detector provides forensic feedback; generator adapts to evade detection), balanced by multi-objective losses for realism and detectability control.
Evaluation protocol: joint metrics and benchmarks that measure generation quality, detectability, and robustness under adaptive attacks to quantify trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build generative models that are evaluated against realistic detection pressure while producing detectors that stay effective as generators evolve—improving robustness in applications like deepfake mitigation and media forensics.

title: Algebraic language models for inverse design of metamaterials via diffusion transformers
authors: Li Zheng, Siddhant Kumar, Dennis M. Kochmann
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01218-8

Architected materials are ubiquitous, yet their design remains constrained by complex structure–property relationships. Zheng et al. use diffusion models and a novel algebraic language to rapidly design shell structures with precisely tailored, exceptional mechanical properties.

infographic.key_insight: A compact algebraic language for shell geometry combined with a diffusion-transformer generative model enables rapid inverse design of metamaterial shells that achieve precisely tailored, exceptional mechanical properties.
infographic.problem_solved: Designing architected materials is hard because geometry-to-property mappings are highly nonlinear and the design space is vast; the paper removes the need for expensive search/optimization by directly generating valid geometric descriptions conditioned on target properties.
method: Develop an algebraic, tokenizable language to represent shell geometries compactly and unambiguously.
Train a diffusion transformer to generate algebraic geometry descriptions conditioned on desired mechanical targets (inverse design).
Validate generated designs via simulation and experiments to confirm attainment of exceptional, tailored mechanical responses.
infographic.impact: Shows how domain-specific symbolic representations + diffusion transformers can solve inverse physical-design problems efficiently, offering a blueprint for ML-driven, high-throughput materials design workflows.

title: Vista4D: Video Reshooting with 4D Point Clouds
authors: Kuan Heng Lin, Zhizheng Liu, Pablo Salamanca, Yash Kant, Ryan Burgert
abstract: We present Vista4D, a robust and flexible video reshooting framework that grounds the input video and target cameras in a 4D point cloud. Specifically, given an input video, our method re-synthesizes the scene with the same dynamics from a different camera trajectory and viewpoint. Existing video reshooting methods often struggle with depth estimation artifacts of real-world dynamic videos, while also failing to preserve content appearance and failing to maintain precise camera control for chall

infographic.key_insight: Vista4D represents dynamic video scenes as a spatio-temporal (4D) point cloud and uses that grounded representation to re-synthesize the same scene dynamics from arbitrary camera trajectories, improving robustness to depth artifacts and enabling precise camera control.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video reshooting and view-synthesis methods struggle with noisy depth estimates, temporal inconsistency, loss of appearance detail, and lack of precise control over novel camera trajectories for real-world dynamic videos.
method: Build a 4D point-cloud representation that fuses per-frame geometry, color, and time to ground both the input video and target camera paths.
Apply robust depth filtering and temporal fusion to reduce real-world depth artifacts and preserve consistent appearance across frames.
Render/resynthesize novel views along user-specified camera trajectories using point-based or neural rendering with temporal coherence to maintain original scene dynamics.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, robust pipeline for producing high-quality novel-view reshoots of dynamic real-world videos, useful for VFX, virtual cinematography, and research in temporal view synthesis and neural rendering.

title: A Scale-Adaptive Framework for Joint Spatiotemporal Super-Resolution with Diffusion Models
authors: Max Defez, Filippo Quarenghi, Mathieu Vrac, Stephan Mandt, Tom Beucler
abstract: Deep-learning video super-resolution has progressed rapidly, but climate applications typically super-resolve (increase resolution) either space or time, and joint spatiotemporal models are often designed for a single pair of super-resolution (SR) factors (upscaling spatial and temporal ratio between the low-resolution sequence and the high-resolution sequence), limiting transfer across spatial resolutions and temporal cadences (frame rates). We present a scale-adaptive framework that reuses the

infographic.key_insight: A single diffusion-based model can be made scale-adaptive to perform joint spatial and temporal super-resolution across multiple upscaling factors, enabling transfer across spatial resolutions and frame rates without retraining a new model per scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing joint spatiotemporal SR methods are typically tied to a single pair of spatial and temporal upscaling factors, which limits reuse across datasets, resolutions, and temporal cadences—especially problematic for climate applications that need flexible upscaling.
method: Scale-adaptive conditioning: parameterize desired spatial and temporal SR factors so the diffusion backbone can be steered to different upscales at inference.
Shared diffusion backbone with progressive spatiotemporal upsampling: iterative denoising/refinement that produces high-fidelity frames while scaling space and time jointly.
Training/inference strategies for cross-scale transferability (e.g., variable-scale training, resampling and time-conditioning) to reuse one model across multiple SR ratios.
infographic.impact: Provides a flexible, cost-effective SR solution so practitioners can apply one model to diverse resolution and cadence requirements (e.g., multi-resolution climate datasets or heterogeneous video sources), reducing retraining and deployment complexity.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: LR spatiotemporal input → scale-adapter conditioning → shared diffusion backbone → HR frames at variable spatial/temporal scales.

title: When Prompts Override Vision: Prompt-Induced Hallucinations in LVLMs
authors: Pegah Khayatan, Jayneel Parekh, Arnaud Dapogny, Mustafa Shukor, Alasdair Newson
abstract: Despite impressive progress in capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs), these systems remain vulnerable to hallucinations, i.e., outputs that are not grounded in the visual input. Prior work has attributed hallucinations in LVLMs to factors such as limitations of the vision backbone or the dominance of the language component, yet the relative importance of these factors remains unclear. To resolve this ambiguity, We propose HalluScope, a benchmark to better understand the extent to

infographic.key_insight: Prompts can overpower the visual input in large vision-language models (LVLMs), inducing “prompt-induced hallucinations”; HalluScope is a benchmark that quantifies and isolates these failures, showing that language-side prompting often drives errors even when vision backbones are strong.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies, measures, and attributes hallucinations caused by prompts in LVLMs, resolving ambiguity about whether failures stem from the vision encoder or from language/prompt effects and providing a standardized way to evaluate prompt-induced errors.
method: Design HalluScope: a controlled benchmark of images paired with systematically varied prompt templates and ground-truth visual queries to elicit and measure hallucinations.
Evaluate a suite of LVLMs across different vision backbones and LLM components, using quantitative hallucination metrics and qualitative labels to attribute error sources.
Run ablations (prompt strength, misinformation prompts, visual occlusion) to disentangle the influence of prompts vs. vision and produce actionable mitigation guidelines.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical diagnostic tool and evidence-based guidance to detect, attribute, and reduce prompt-induced hallucinations, improving model selection, prompt design, and safe deployment of LVLMs.

title: Flow matching for generative modelling in bioinformatics and computational biology
authors: Alex Morehead, Lazar Atanackovic, Akshata Hegde, Yanli Wang, Frimpong Boadu
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01220-0

Flow matching has emerged as a promising solution to mapping arbitrary pairs of high-dimensional data distributions, well suited to problems in molecular and cell biology. Morehead et al. review the theoretical foundations of flow-matching-based models and applications of flow matching in computational biology, and discuss its role in

infographic.key_insight: Flow matching gives a principled, flexible way to learn continuous maps between arbitrary high‑dimensional biological data distributions, enabling direct, controllable generative transformations for molecular and cellular data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the challenge of modeling and transforming complex, high‑dimensional biological data distributions (e.g., molecular conformations, cell states) where existing generative methods can be inefficient or poorly suited to paired distribution mapping.
method: Formulate a flow‑matching objective that trains a vector field to transport samples from a source distribution to a target distribution by matching instantaneous flow directions.
Leverage continuous ODE/SDE-style trajectories for generation, enabling direct mapping between paired datasets (conditional or paired generation) with fewer sampling artifacts.
Demonstrate applications and variants tailored to computational biology tasks, highlighting theoretical foundations and practical implementation choices.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a versatile generative framework that can improve sample quality, enable direct distribution-to-distribution translation, and accelerate tasks like molecular design, conditional generation, and realistic biological data augmentation.

title: FedSIR: Spectral Client Identification and Relabeling for Federated Learning with Noisy Labels
authors: Sina Gholami, Abdulmoneam Ali, Tania Haghighi, Ahmed Arafa, Minhaj Nur Alam
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data; however, the presence of noisy labels across distributed clients can severely degrade the learning performance. In this paper, we propose FedSIR, a multi-stage framework for robust FL under noisy labels. Different from existing approaches that mainly rely on designing noise-tolerant loss functions or exploiting loss dynamics during training, our method leverages the spectral structure of client feature represe

infographic.key_insight: FedSIR uses the spectral structure of client feature representations to detect clients with systematically noisy labels and then relabels their data in a privacy-preserving, federated way—improving robustness beyond loss-based or per-sample heuristics.
infographic.problem_solved: Federated learning performance degrades when clients hold noisy or corrupted labels and existing remedies (noise‑tolerant losses or loss-dynamics heuristics) fail to reliably locate and correct label noise distributed across clients.
method: Compute a client-level similarity matrix from aggregated feature embeddings and apply spectral analysis to find clients or groups with anomalous representation patterns indicative of label noise.

Flag suspected noisy clients and generate corrected labels via a relabeling module that leverages global model predictions, class prototypes, and peer-consensus while respecting federated privacy constraints.
Integrate detection and relabeling into a multi-stage FL loop: detect → relabel locally (or via server-coordinated aggregation) → retrain, iterating until convergence.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical, communication-efficient tool to locate and fix label noise in cross-device or cross-silo FL setups, improving model accuracy and stability without requiring access to raw client data or heavy per-sample tracking.

title: SpeechParaling-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Paralinguistic-Aware Speech Generation
authors: Ruohan Liu, Shukang Yin, Tao Wang, Dong Zhang, Weiji Zhuang
abstract: Paralinguistic cues are essential for natural human-computer interaction, yet their evaluation in Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) remains limited by coarse feature coverage and the inherent subjectivity of assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SpeechParaling-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for paralinguistic-aware speech generation. It expands existing coverage from fewer than 50 to over 100 fine-grained features, supported by more than 1,000 English-Chinese parallel speech

infographic.key_insight: SpeechParaling-Bench provides the first large-scale, fine-grained benchmark for paralinguistic-aware speech generation, expanding feature coverage from under 50 to over 100 and supplying a >1,000-sample English–Chinese parallel corpus to enable consistent evaluation of LALMs.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing evaluations of paralinguistic capabilities in large audio-language models are coarse and inconsistent, and they struggle with subjective assessment—SpeechParaling-Bench fills this gap with richer feature coverage and standardized cross-lingual data.
method: Define and expand a fine-grained paralinguistic taxonomy to cover >100 features (e.g., prosody, emotion, emphasis, speaking rate, voice quality).
Curate a >1,000-sample English–Chinese parallel speech dataset annotated for the expanded paralinguistic features to support cross-lingual benchmarking.
Introduce a standardized evaluation protocol combining structured human ratings and objective measures to reduce subjectivity and enable reproducible comparison of LALMs.
infographic.impact: This benchmark enables more precise, reproducible assessment of paralinguistic behavior in speech-generating models, accelerating development of natural, expressive LALMs and improving cross-lingual evaluation practices.

title: LEXIS: LatEnt ProXimal Interaction Signatures for 3D HOI from an Image
authors: Dimitrije Antić, Alvaro Budria, George Paschalidis, Sai Kumar Dwivedi, Dimitrios Tzionas
abstract: Reconstructing 3D Human-Object Interaction from an RGB image is essential for perceptive systems. Yet, this remains challenging as it requires capturing the subtle physical coupling between the body and objects. While current methods rely on sparse, binary contact cues, these fail to model the continuous proximity and dense spatial relationships that characterize natural interactions. We address this limitation via InterFields, a representation that encodes dense, continuous proximity across the

infographic.key_insight: LEXIS introduces InterFields — dense, continuous proximity signatures (LatEnt ProXimal Interaction Signatures) — that encode fine-grained body–object spatial coupling from a single RGB image, enabling more physically plausible 3D human–object interaction reconstructions than sparse binary contact cues.
infographic.problem_solved: How to recover realistic 3D human–object interactions from a single RGB image by modeling subtle, continuous proximity and dense spatial relationships between body and objects, which binary contact signals cannot capture.
method: Represent interactions as dense continuous proximity fields (InterFields) — latent signatures that describe per-location proximity between human and object geometry.
Learn an encoder that maps a single RGB image into latent proximal signatures and decoders that reconstruct 3D human pose/shape, object geometry, and proximity fields.
Use the dense proximity fields to guide geometry refinement and physically-plausible contact reasoning (replacing sparse binary contact cues with continuous spatial coupling).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a compact, learnable representation for richer interaction reasoning from images, improving 3D HOI reconstruction quality and enabling more reliable downstream applications (robot manipulation, AR/VR, scene understanding) that require physically plausible human–object coupling.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: RGB image → encoder → latent InterFields → decoders producing 3D human, 3D object, and proximity field overlays.

title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
authors: Deqing Fu, Tianyi Zhou, Mikhail Belkin, Vatsal Sharan, Robin Jia
abstract: Language models trained on natural text learn to represent numbers using periodic features with dominant periods at $T=2, 5, 10$. In this paper, we identify a two-tiered hierarchy of these features: while Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and classical word embeddings trained in different ways all learn features that have period-$T$ spikes in the Fourier domain, only some learn geometrically separable features that can be used to linearly classify a number mod-$T$. To explain this incongruity, w

infographic.key_insight: Different language models independently learn periodic numeric features with dominant periods T = 2, 5, 10, but only some models arrange those features into geometrically separable patterns that support linear classification of numbers mod-T.
infographic.problem_solved: Explains why different architectures trained on the same natural text encode number information similarly in the frequency domain yet differ in whether that information is directly usable by simple linear probes.
method: Empirical survey of multiple architectures (Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, classical word embeddings) trained on natural text to extract number-related representations.
Fourier-domain analysis to identify dominant periodic components (spikes at T = 2, 5, 10) in learned features.

Geometric/separability tests and linear-probe experiments to determine which models produce features that are linearly classifiable mod‑T, plus analysis linking outcomes to architectural/training factors.
infographic.impact: Clarifies how inductive biases of architectures affect whether numeracy is encoded in a directly usable form, informing model selection, probe design, and interpretability efforts for arithmetic and numeracy-sensitive tasks.

title: Parallel-SFT: Improving Zero-Shot Cross-Programming-Language Transfer for Code RL
authors: Zhaofeng Wu, Shiqi Wang, Boya Peng, Anuj Goyal, Melanie Kambadur
abstract: Modern language models demonstrate impressive coding capabilities in common programming languages (PLs), such as C++ and Python, but their performance in lower-resource PLs is often limited by training data availability. In principle, however, most programming skills are universal across PLs, so the capability acquired in one PL should transfer to others. In this work, we propose the task of zero-shot cross-programming-language transfer for code RL. We find that, for Llama-3.1, RL training for c

infographic.key_insight: Parallel-SFT preserves universal coding skills during reinforcement learning by running supervised fine-tuning across multiple programming languages in parallel with RL updates, enabling strong zero-shot transfer to low-resource languages.
infographic.problem_solved: RL fine-tuning on a single high-resource programming language often overfits to language-specific patterns and degrades zero-shot performance on other languages; this work reduces the need to perform expensive per-language RL by improving cross-language transfer.
method: Parallel supervised fine-tuning (Parallel-SFT): maintain an ongoing SFT stream on diverse PLs concurrently with RL to anchor language-agnostic behaviors.
Mixed-language training/optimization: synchronize or mix gradients from multiple languages so RL updates on a source PL do not overwrite shared representations.
Regularization and anchoring: constrain RL updates (e.g., replay/parameter anchoring or output-level constraints) to preserve skills useful across languages.
infographic.impact: Makes code-focused RL more practical for many programming languages by improving zero-shot transfer, lowering compute and data requirements for low-resource PLs and enabling broader, cost-effective deployment of code models.

title: ParetoSlider: Diffusion Models Post-Training for Continuous Reward Control
authors: Shelly Golan, Michael Finkelson, Ariel Bereslavsky, Yotam Nitzan, Or Patashnik
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training has become the standard for aligning generative models with human preferences, yet most methods rely on a single scalar reward. When multiple criteria matter, the prevailing practice of ``early scalarization'' collapses rewards into a fixed weighted sum. This commits the model to a single trade-off point at training time, providing no inference-time control over inherently conflicting goals -- such as prompt adherence versus source fidelity in image edit

infographic.key_insight: ParetoSlider is a post-training method for diffusion models that enables continuous, inference-time control over multiple competing rewards by moving along a learned Pareto frontier, avoiding the need for fixed early scalarization.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the limitation that RL post-training typically collapses multiple objectives into a single fixed weighted reward, preventing users from adjusting trade-offs (e.g., prompt adherence vs. source fidelity) at inference time.
method: Post-train a diffusion model with multiple reward signals instead of a single scalar, preserving multi-objective information.
Introduce a compact, parameterized control (the “slider”) that conditions generation on a continuous trade-off parameter, enabling smooth traversal of the Pareto frontier at inference.
Produce outputs along the learned Pareto frontier so practitioners can pick any point (trade-off) without retraining separate models for each preference.
infographic.impact: Enables flexible, interactive trade-off tuning at inference time, reducing the need to train multiple specialized models and improving practical alignment for applications with conflicting objectives.

title: OMIBench: Benchmarking Olympiad-Level Multi-Image Reasoning in Large Vision-Language Model
authors: Qiguang Chen, Chengyu Luan, Jiajun Wu, Qiming Yu, Yi Yang
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have made substantial advances in reasoning tasks at the Olympiad level. Nevertheless, current Olympiad-level multimodal reasoning benchmarks for these models often emphasize single-image analysis and fail to exploit contextual information across multiple images. We present OMIBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate Olympiad-level reasoning when the required evidence is distributed over multiple images. It contains problems from biology, chemistry, mathematic

infographic.key_insight: OMIBench introduces a benchmark that reveals and measures how current large vision-language models struggle with Olympiad-level reasoning when the required evidence is distributed across multiple images. It shifts evaluation from single-image analysis to true multi-image, multi-step visual reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing multimodal reasoning benchmarks focus mainly on single images and miss scenarios where correct answers require integrating evidence across several images; OMIBench fills this gap by providing Olympiad-level problems that explicitly test cross-image reasoning.
method: Curate a dataset of Olympiad-level problems (biology, chemistry, mathematics, etc.) where each problem’s evidence is intentionally split across multiple images.
Design task formats and evaluation protocols that require models to combine visual information across images and provide objective metrics for multi-image reasoning success.
Benchmark state-of-the-art LVLMs on OMIBench to quantify performance gaps and identify common failure modes in cross-image evidence integration.
infographic.impact: OMIBench highlights a critical blind spot in current LVLM evaluation and provides a standardized way to drive research on multi-image evidence aggregation, model architectures, and reasoning strategies. For practitioners, it offers a targeted testbed to develop and validate improvements in multimodal reasoning capabilities.

title: Molecular deep learning at the edge of chemical space
authors: Derek van Tilborg, Luke Rossen, Francesca Grisoni
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 22 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01216-w

van Tilborg et al. introduce a deep learning model trained to simultaneously predict bioactivity and reconstruct molecules. The model provides a principled measure of distribution shifts, experimentally validated by discovering active inhibitors for two clinically relevant kinase targets.

infographic.key_insight: A single deep model jointly learns to predict bioactivity and reconstruct molecules, and uses its learned representation to quantify distribution shift—enabling reliable discovery of active compounds at the edge of chemical space, validated by prospective kinase inhibitor hits.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses unreliable bioactivity prediction when models encounter molecules outside their training distribution by providing a principled, model-internal measure of distribution shift and using it to guide prospective experimental discovery.
method: Train a multitask encoder–decoder model that simultaneously reconstructs molecular structure and predicts bioactivity from the same latent representation.
Derive a principled distribution-shift / out-of-distribution score from the learned representation (latent-space / likelihood-based), and use it to flag predictions with low trust.
Prospectively screen and experimentally validate predictions, discovering active inhibitors for two clinically relevant kinases to demonstrate real-world utility.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical framework for building safer, more trustworthy molecular ML models by coupling generative reconstruction with prediction and OOD scoring—improving hit discovery reliability in drug discovery pipelines.

title: Competing Biases underlie Overconfidence and Underconfidence in LLMs
authors: Dharshan Kumaran, Stephen M. Fleming, Larisa Markeeva, Joe Heyward, Andrea Banino
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 22 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01217-9

Kumaran et al. show that large language model (LLM) confidence is shaped by two competing biases: a choice-supportive bias that inflates confidence in initial answers, and a systematic overweighting of contradictory advice, deviating from optimal Bayesian reasoning.

infographic.key_insight: LLM confidence is driven by two competing biases: a choice-supportive bias that boosts confidence in initial answers, and a systematic overweighting of contradictory advice that produces deviations from Bayesian-optimal updating, explaining both overconfidence and underconfidence.
infographic.problem_solved: Explains why large language models show inconsistent confidence calibration and how distinct psychological-style biases (choice-support and advice overweighting) cause systematic departures from normative Bayesian belief updates.
method: Controlled "decision + advice" experiments with LLMs: record initial answer and confidence, present conflicting advice, then measure updated confidence and choice.
Quantitative comparison of observed updates to Bayesian-optimal updates to identify systematic deviations and quantify bias direction/magnitude.
Cross-model and ablation analyses to verify robustness of biases across architectures and settings.
infographic.impact: Clarifies mechanistic sources of miscalibration in LLMs, informing better confidence estimation, safer deployment, and targeted interventions (e.g., calibration methods or prompt designs) to reduce harmful over- or under-confidence.

title: SpanVLA: Efficient Action Bridging and Learning from Negative-Recovery Samples for Vision-Language-Action Model
authors: Zewei Zhou, Ruining Yang, Xuewei, Qi, Yiluan Guo
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising autonomous driving paradigm for leveraging world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, especially in long-tail scenarios. However, existing VLA models often struggle with the high latency in action generation using an autoregressive generation framework and exhibit limited robustness. In this paper, we propose SpanVLA, a novel end-to-end autonomous driving framework, integrating an autoregressive reasoning and a flow-matching action expert. F

infographic.key_insight: SpanVLA combines autoregressive language reasoning with a flow-matching action expert and a span-based action bridge, enabling low-latency, robust action generation by training on both standard and negative-recovery trajectories.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces high latency and limited robustness of autoregressive-only Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, improving real-time control and handling of long-tail/failure scenarios in autonomous driving.
method: Hybrid pipeline: keep autoregressive reasoning for high-level planning, then pass compact span outputs to a flow-matching action expert for fast continuous action synthesis.
Span-based action bridging: translate discrete language/planning spans into grounded action primitives to align reasoning and control domains.
Negative-recovery training: augment training with failure (negative) samples and explicit recovery trajectories to improve robustness and generalization in long-tail situations.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, real-time VLA deployment by cutting action-generation latency while increasing resilience to rare/failure cases—useful for researchers and engineers building multimodal control systems.

title: VLA Foundry: A Unified Framework for Training Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jean Mercat, Sedrick Keh, Kushal Arora, Isabella Huang, Paarth Shah
abstract: We present VLA Foundry, an open-source framework that unifies LLM, VLM, and VLA training in a single codebase. Most open-source VLA efforts specialize on the action training stage, often stitching together incompatible pretraining pipelines. VLA Foundry instead provides a shared training stack with end-to-end control, from language pretraining to action-expert fine-tuning. VLA Foundry supports both from-scratch training and pretrained backbones from Hugging Face. To demonstrate the utility of ou

infographic.key_insight: VLA Foundry unifies language, vision, and action model training in a single open-source codebase, giving researchers end-to-end control from pretraining to action-expert fine-tuning. It supports both from‑scratch training and plug‑in of pretrained Hugging Face backbones to eliminate brittle, stitched pipelines.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses fragmentation and incompatibility in VLA development where separate LLM/VLM/VLA stages are manually stitched together, hindering reproducibility, iteration speed, and end-to-end experimentation.
method: A shared, modular training stack that standardizes data, optimizer, and checkpointing across LLM, VLM, and action stages.
Unified pipelines that enable end-to-end runs or stage-wise workflows (language pretraining → vision alignment → action-expert fine-tuning).
Flexible backbone support: train from scratch or import Hugging Face pretrained models for rapid prototyping and transfer learning.
infographic.impact: Reduces engineering overhead and increases reproducibility for multimodal action research, enabling faster iteration and fairer comparisons of VLA methods across consistent training protocols.

title: Tstars-Tryon 1.0: Robust and Realistic Virtual Try-On for Diverse Fashion Items
authors: Mengting Chen, Zhengrui Chen, Yongchao Du, Zuan Gao, Taihang Hu
abstract: Recent advances in image generation and editing have opened new opportunities for virtual try-on. However, existing methods still struggle to meet complex real-world demands. We present Tstars-Tryon 1.0, a commercial-scale virtual try-on system that is robust, realistic, versatile, and highly efficient. First, our system maintains a high success rate across challenging cases like extreme poses, severe illumination variations, motion blur, and other in-the-wild conditions. Second, it delivers hig

infographic.key_insight: Tstars-Tryon 1.0 demonstrates that a commercially viable virtual try-on system can achieve robust, realistic, and fast results on in-the-wild images—handling extreme poses, severe illumination changes, motion blur and diverse garment types—by combining targeted robustness strategies with engineering-scale optimizations.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing virtual try-on methods fail frequently in real-world conditions (extreme poses, lighting variation, motion blur, diverse garment categories) or are too slow/unreliable for commercial deployment; Tstars-Tryon addresses reliability, realism, versatility, and efficiency simultaneously.
method: Robust training and preprocessing: large-scale in-the-wild data and targeted augmentations / failure-case modeling to handle extreme poses, lighting, and motion blur.
Modular synthesis pipeline: pose-aware alignment and garment warping + photorealistic appearance and lighting-consistent blending to preserve garment detail and user identity.
Engineering optimizations for production: inference-speed and memory improvements, multi-item support and throughput tuning for commercial-scale deployment.
infographic.impact: Makes virtual try-on practical for real-world e‑commerce and mobile applications by reducing failure rates and latency while supporting a wider range of garments and imaging conditions—lowering integration risk for ML engineers and product teams.

title: ReImagine: Rethinking Controllable High-Quality Human Video Generation via Image-First Synthesis
authors: Zhengwentai Sun, Keru Zheng, Chenghong Li, Hongjie Liao, Xihe Yang
abstract: Human video generation remains challenging due to the difficulty of jointly modeling human appearance, motion, and camera viewpoint under limited multi-view data. Existing methods often address these factors separately, resulting in limited controllability or reduced visual quality. We revisit this problem from an image-first perspective, where high-quality human appearance is learned via image generation and used as a prior for video synthesis, decoupling appearance modeling from temporal consi

infographic.key_insight: ReImagine learns high-fidelity human appearance via image generation first, then uses that learned appearance as a strong prior for video synthesis, decoupling appearance modeling from motion and camera dynamics to achieve controllable, high-quality human videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the difficulty of jointly modeling human appearance, motion, and camera viewpoint under limited multi-view data, which previously forced trade-offs between controllability and visual quality.
method: Train an image-first appearance model to capture detailed, multi-view-consistent human appearance as a reusable prior.
Condition a separate temporal synthesis module on the learned appearance prior plus motion and camera controls to produce coherent videos without degrading appearance quality.
Use controllable inputs (e.g., skeletal poses, camera parameters) and multi-view/temporal losses to enforce consistency and enable fine-grained control.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to generate controllable, photoreal human videos with higher visual fidelity even when multi-view data is limited, improving workflows in animation, virtual production, and downstream video editing.

title: CityRAG: Stepping Into a City via Spatially-Grounded Video Generation
authors: Gene Chou, Charles Herrmann, Kyle Genova, Boyang Deng, Songyou Peng
abstract: We address the problem of generating a 3D-consistent, navigable environment that is spatially grounded: a simulation of a real location. Existing video generative models can produce a plausible sequence that is consistent with a text (T2V) or image (I2V) prompt. However, the capability to reconstruct the real world under arbitrary weather conditions and dynamic object configurations is essential for downstream applications including autonomous driving and robotics simulation. To this end, we pre

infographic.key_insight: CityRAG generates 3D-consistent, navigable video simulations that are spatially grounded to real-world locations, enabling realistic reconstructions across varying weather and dynamic object layouts. It bridges conditional video generation with spatial scene representations to produce simulation-ready city-scale views.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing text- and image-conditioned video generators produce plausible sequences but cannot reliably reconstruct real environments in a spatially grounded, 3D-consistent way under arbitrary weather and dynamic conditions — a requirement for simulation, planning, and robotics applications.
method: Condition video generation on explicit spatial grounding (e.g., location coordinates, camera trajectory, and scene geometry) so outputs align to a real-world place.

Learn or assemble a persistent 3D-consistent scene representation that supports generating temporally coherent frames along navigable paths while accounting for dynamic objects and weather variations.
Combine learned generative components with retrieval or world priors to preserve realism and enable controllable changes (time of day, weather, object configurations) for downstream simulation use.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a method to create realistic, navigable city-scale simulations tied to real locations — accelerating development and testing for autonomous driving, robotics, and urban planning where realistic, controllable environments are critical.

title: MMControl: Unified Multi-Modal Control for Joint Audio-Video Generation
authors: Liyang Li, Wen Wang, Canyu Zhao, Tianjian Feng, Zhiyue Zhao
abstract: Recent advances in Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have enabled high-quality joint audio-video generation, producing videos with synchronized audio within a single model. However, existing controllable generation frameworks are typically restricted to video-only control. This restricts comprehensive controllability and often leads to suboptimal cross-modal alignment. To bridge this gap, we present MMControl, which enables users to perform Multi-Modal Control in joint audio-video generation. MMCont

infographic.key_insight: MMControl introduces unified multi-modal control for joint audio–video diffusion models, letting users condition both audio and video simultaneously and improving cross-modal synchronization and alignment.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing controllable generation frameworks focus on video-only controls, limiting user control and often producing suboptimal audio–video alignment in joint generation models.
method: Extend joint audio–video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models with modular control adapters that accept diverse control signals (e.g., motion sketches, audio cues, text).
Fuse modalities via dedicated cross-modal fusion layers and alignment objectives to enforce synchronized audio–video generation.
Provide a unified conditioning interface that composes multiple control sources into the diffusion sampling process for coherent joint outputs.
infographic.impact: Enables richer, user-driven creation and editing of synchronized audio–video content and advances research into controllable multimodal generative models—useful for media production, virtual agents, and multimodal research.

title: Unveiling Fine-Grained Visual Traces: Evaluating Multimodal Interleaved Reasoning Chains in Multimodal STEM Tasks
authors: Jing Jin, Hao Liu, Yan Bai, Yihang Lou, Zhenke Wang
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown promising reasoning abilities, yet evaluating their performance in specialized domains remains challenging. STEM reasoning is a particularly valuable testbed because it provides highly verifiable feedback, but existing benchmarks often permit unimodal shortcuts due to modality redundancy and focus mainly on final-answer accuracy, overlooking the reasoning process itself. To address this challenge, we introduce StepSTEM: a graduate-level benchma

infographic.key_insight: StepSTEM reveals that evaluating multimodal LLMs only by final answers hides important failures — fine-grained, step-level visual traces expose unimodal shortcuts and reasoning gaps in STEM tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper tackles the lack of rigorous, stepwise evaluation for multimodal reasoning in STEM: existing benchmarks allow unimodal shortcuts and focus on final-answer accuracy, failing to assess the intermediate reasoning process.
method: Introduce StepSTEM, a graduate-level multimodal STEM benchmark that annotates and verifies step-by-step reasoning traces and associated visual evidence.
Define evaluation protocols and metrics to compare interleaved multimodal reasoning chains (text + visual) and to detect modality shortcuts and misaligned intermediate steps.
Apply the benchmark to state-of-the-art MLLMs to quantify where and how models fail at intermediate steps even when final answers appear correct.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical tool and metrics to audit and improve multimodal models' internal reasoning, enabling more reliable, interpretable STEM applications and reducing over-reliance on spurious unimodal cues.

title: A-MAR: Agent-based Multimodal Art Retrieval for Fine-Grained Artwork Understanding
authors: Shuai Wang, Hongyi Zhu, Jia-Hong Huang, Yixian Shen, Chengxi Zeng
abstract: Understanding artworks requires multi-step reasoning over visual content and cultural, historical, and stylistic context. While recent multimodal large language models show promise in artwork explanation, they rely on implicit reasoning and internalized knowl- edge, limiting interpretability and explicit evidence grounding. We propose A-MAR, an Agent-based Multimodal Art Retrieval framework that explicitly conditions retrieval on structured reasoning plans. Given an artwork and a user query, A-M

infographic.key_insight: A-MAR conditions multimodal retrieval on explicit, agent-generated reasoning plans so that artwork explanations are evidence-grounded and interpretable rather than implicit outputs of a monolithic LLM.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces opaque, implicit reasoning in multimodal models by explicitly linking stepwise reasoning plans to targeted retrieval of visual and contextual evidence for fine-grained artwork understanding.
method: Agent-based planner generates a structured reasoning plan (multi-step queries and subgoals) given an artwork and user question.
Plan-conditioned multimodal retrieval fetches image regions, metadata, and external cultural/historical resources targeted to each subgoal.
Combine retrieved evidence into an explicit, evidence-grounded explanation with iterative refinement driven by the agent's feedback loop.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a scalable way to produce interpretable, evidence-linked artwork explanations—improving trust, auditability, and downstream evaluation for art understanding and curation tasks.

title: Planning in entropy-regularized Markov decision processes and games
authors: Jean-Bastien Grill, Omar Darwiche Domingues, Pierre Ménard, Rémi Munos, Michal Valko
abstract: We propose SmoothCruiser, a new planning algorithm for estimating the value function in entropy-regularized Markov decision processes and two-player games, given a generative model of the environment. SmoothCruiser makes use of the smoothness of the Bellman operator promoted by the regularization to achieve problem-independent sample complexity of order O~(1/epsilon^4) for a desired accuracy epsilon, whereas for non-regularized settings there are no known algorithms with guaranteed polynomial sa

infographic.key_insight: Entropy regularization smooths the Bellman operator, and SmoothCruiser leverages that smoothness to obtain problem-independent, provable sample complexity for value estimation in MDPs and two-player games: O~(1/epsilon^4) for accuracy epsilon.
infographic.problem_solved: How to plan and estimate value functions sample-efficiently (with polynomial guarantees) in entropy-regularized Markov decision processes and two-player games given only a generative model — a setting where non-regularized approaches lack known polynomial sample-complexity guarantees.
method: Design of SmoothCruiser: a planning algorithm that exploits the smoothness induced by entropy regularization on the Bellman operator.
Use of generative-model sampling to construct value estimates with controlled approximation error, yielding a problem-independent sample complexity bound O~(1/epsilon^4).
Extension of the approach and guarantees from single-agent MDPs to two-player games by leveraging the same regularization-induced smoothness properties.
infographic.impact: Provides a theoretically grounded, sample-efficient planning method for practitioners using entropy-regularized RL or game-solving, informing algorithm design where stability/exploration via regularization is desired and giving concrete sample budgets for target accuracies.

title: UniT: Toward a Unified Physical Language for Human-to-Humanoid Policy Learning and World Modeling
authors: Boyu Chen, Yi Chen, Lu Qiu, Jerry Bai, Yuying Ge
abstract: Scaling humanoid foundation models is bottlenecked by the scarcity of robotic data. While massive egocentric human data offers a scalable alternative, bridging the cross-embodiment chasm remains a fundamental challenge due to kinematic mismatches. We introduce UniT (Unified Latent Action Tokenizer via Visual Anchoring), a framework that establishes a unified physical language for human-to-humanoid transfer. Grounded in the philosophy that heterogeneous kinematics share universal visual consequen

infographic.key_insight: UniT learns a unified "physical language"—a latent action tokenizer grounded by visual consequences—that aligns egocentric human data with humanoid actions, enabling scalable human-to-humanoid transfer despite kinematic mismatch.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the scarcity of robot-collected data and the cross-embodiment / kinematic mismatch between humans and humanoids by grounding actions in shared visual outcomes rather than direct joint mappings.
method: Unified Latent Action Tokenizer: discretize actions into shared tokens representing actionable primitives across embodiments.
Visual Anchoring: use egocentric visual consequences as a common grounding to map human motion into tokens compatible with humanoid controllers.
Train policies and world models in the token space so humanoid policies can be learned or simulated from abundant human video data without extensive robot data.
infographic.impact: Enables scaling humanoid foundation models using massive egocentric human datasets, reducing robot data requirements and accelerating policy learning, transfer, and generalization for embodied AI.
