title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarial Training for Vision Transformers
authors: Jiaming Zhang, Meng Ding, Shaopeng Fu, Jingfeng Zhang, Di Wang
abstract: Despite the remarkable success of Vision Transformers (ViTs) across a wide range of vision tasks, recent studies have revealed that they remain vulnerable to adversarial examples, much like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). A common empirical defense strategy is adversarial training, yet the theoretical underpinnings of its robustness in ViTs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first theoretical analysis of adversarial training under simplified ViT architectures. We show

infographic.key_insight: This paper provides the first theoretical characterization showing that adversarial training on simplified Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures can exhibit benign overfitting: models may perfectly fit adversarially perturbed training data yet still generalize well under specific model, data, and perturbation regimes.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of theoretical understanding about when and why adversarial training yields robustness (or failure) in ViTs, explaining conditions that allow ViTs to overfit adversarial examples without harming test performance.
method: Formulate a simplified, analyzable ViT model (patch embeddings + self-attention structure) tailored for theoretical study.

Derive sufficient conditions and limits (relating architecture, data noise, sample complexity, and perturbation radius) under which adversarial training leads to benign overfitting and preserved generalization.
Validate theoretical predictions with targeted empirical simulations to illustrate how theory maps to practice.
infographic.impact: Provides principled guidance for ML practitioners on when adversarial training is likely to succeed for ViTs and how architectural or training choices affect robustness vs. generalization trade-offs, enabling better-informed defense design and hyperparameter selection.
visual_elements: Schematic of a simplified ViT highlighting patch embeddings and self-attention blocks used in the theoretical model.

title: Linear attention goes global in molecular dynamics
authors: Sheng Gong, Wen Yan
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 21 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01222-y

A new attention mechanism brings long-range awareness to machine learning force fields with linear cost and preservation of symmetry. The method offers a flexible alternative to existing long-range modules, including fragmentation-based interactions and physics-based long-range fixes.

infographic.key_insight: A new global linear-attention mechanism for machine-learning force fields captures long-range interactions with O(N) cost while preserving physical symmetries (equivariance/invariance). It gives global awareness without the quadratic compute of standard attention.
infographic.problem_solved: Accurately and efficiently modeling long-range interactions in molecular dynamics is expensive or relies on fragmentation/physics-based patches; this method provides a scalable, symmetry-preserving alternative that integrates into ML force-field models.
method: Design a linear-cost attention operator that aggregates global context in O(N) time and memory instead of O(N^2).
Enforce symmetry preservation (equivariance/invariance) so forces and energies respect physical constraints.
Provide a modular implementation that can replace or augment existing long-range modules (fragmentation or physics-based fixes) in ML force fields.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, accurate MD modeling for larger systems and longer simulations with lower compute and memory, making advanced ML force fields practical for more real-world chemistry and materials tasks.
visual_elements: Scaling plot: quadratic attention vs linear attention (compute/memory vs number of atoms).
Schematic molecule showing long-range connections captured by global linear attention (arrows connecting distant atoms).
Model block diagram highlighting the plug-in linear-attention module within an equivariant force-field architecture.
Comparison table/chart of accuracy and throughput vs fragmentation and physics-based long-range methods.

title: Predicting RNA 3D structure and conformers using a pre-trained secondary structure model and structure-aware attention
authors: Wenkai Wang, Zhenling Peng, Jianyi Yang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 21 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01223-x

Wang and colleagues present trRosettaRNA2, a deep learning-based system for accurate RNA 3D structure prediction. By integrating end-to-end learning with secondary structure priors, it provides a powerful way to explore RNA structure and dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: trRosettaRNA2 combines a pre-trained secondary-structure model with structure-aware attention to produce more accurate end-to-end RNA 3D structures and realistic conformer ensembles from sequence information alone.
infographic.problem_solved: Improves RNA 3D structure prediction by incorporating explicit secondary-structure priors and attention mechanisms to better capture long-range base interactions and conformational variability that prior models struggled to represent accurately.
method: Pre-train a model to encode RNA secondary-structure priors (base-pairing and local motifs) and inject those embeddings into the main predictor.
Use structure-aware attention layers to integrate sequence features and secondary-structure priors, predicting inter-nucleotide geometries (distances/angles) and orientation distributions.
End-to-end pipeline that transforms predicted geometries into 3D coordinates and samples conformers with confidence estimates.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates that domain-specific pretraining plus structure-aware attention substantially improves biomolecular structure modeling, providing AI/ML practitioners a template for combining inductive priors with deep attention architectures for structured prediction tasks.
visual_elements: Pipeline schematic: sequence → pre-trained secondary-structure encoder → structure-aware attention → 3D coordinates
Bar/line chart comparing RMSD/accuracy of trRosettaRNA2 vs prior methods on benchmark RNAs

Attention heatmap mapped onto secondary-structure matrix to illustrate learned long-range contacts

title: AnyRecon: Arbitrary-View 3D Reconstruction with Video Diffusion Model
authors: Yutian Chen, Shi Guo, Renbiao Jin, Tianshuo Yang, Xin Cai
abstract: Sparse-view 3D reconstruction is essential for modeling scenes from casual captures, but remain challenging for non-generative reconstruction. Existing diffusion-based approaches mitigates this issues by synthesizing novel views, but they often condition on only one or two capture frames, which restricts geometric consistency and limits scalability to large or diverse scenes. We propose AnyRecon, a scalable framework for reconstruction from arbitrary and unordered sparse inputs that preserves ex

infographic.key_insight: AnyRecon leverages a video diffusion model that conditions on arbitrary, unordered sparse input frames to synthesize geometrically consistent novel views, enabling scalable and more accurate 3D reconstruction from casual captures.
infographic.problem_solved: Improves sparse‑view 3D reconstruction by overcoming limited geometric consistency and poor scalability of prior diffusion-based methods that typically condition on only one or two capture frames.
method: Train a video diffusion generator that accepts arbitrary, unordered sparse frames as conditioning and produces temporally and spatially consistent novel-view sequences.
Aggregate multi-frame cues with a permutation‑invariant encoding strategy so the model scales to variable numbers and orders of input views.
Fuse synthesized novel views with multi‑view reconstruction / neural rendering to recover dense, consistent 3D geometry suitable for large or diverse scenes.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to reconstruct high-quality 3D from casual, sparse captures (phone photos or short clips) with better multi-view consistency and scalability—useful for AR/VR, mapping, and asset creation.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: unordered sparse input frames → permutation‑invariant encoder → video diffusion → synthesized novel views → 3D reconstruction
Side‑by‑side comparison: reconstructions from 1–2 conditional frames versus AnyRecon (showing improved geometry and fewer artifacts)
Grid of synthesized novel views demonstrating temporal/spatial consistency across viewpoints

title: IR-Flow: Bridging Discriminative and Generative Image Restoration via Rectified Flow
authors: Zihao Fan, Xin Lu, Jie Xiao, Dong Li, Jie Huang
abstract: In image restoration, single-step discriminative mappings often lack fine details via expectation learning, whereas generative paradigms suffer from inefficient multi-step sampling and noise-residual coupling. To address this dilemma, we propose IR-Flow, a novel image restoration method based on Rectified Flow that serves as a unified framework bridging the gap between discriminative and generative paradigms. Specifically, we first construct multilevel data distribution flows, which expand the a

infographic.key_insight: IR-Flow uses Rectified Flow to create multilevel data distribution flows that combine the speed of discriminative single-step restoration with the fine-detail reconstruction of generative multi-step methods, reducing noise–residual coupling while keeping sampling efficient.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between fast but detail-poor discriminative restorers and high-quality but slow/noise-coupled generative samplers, enabling efficient restoration with sharper, more faithful details.
method: Build multilevel data-distribution flows that expand and structure degraded-to-clean image mappings across scales.
Apply Rectified Flow inference to iteratively correct samples while avoiding heavy multi-step noise-residual coupling, enabling faster, more accurate sampling.
Unify discriminative expectation-based objectives and generative flow-based sampling into a single framework to obtain both computational efficiency and improved fine-detail recovery.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical restoration strategy that improves perceptual fidelity without the high computational cost of traditional generative sampling, making high-quality image restoration more usable in real applications and pipelines.

Pipeline diagram of IR-Flow: multilevel flow construction → rectified inference steps → restored output

title: Generative Drifting for Conditional Medical Image Generation
authors: Zirong Li, Siyuan Mei, Weiwen Wu, Andreas Maier, Lina Gölz
abstract: Conditional medical image generation plays an important role in many clinically relevant imaging tasks. However, existing methods still face a fundamental challenge in balancing inference efficiency, patient-specific fidelity, and distribution-level plausibility, particularly in high-dimensional 3D medical imaging. In this work, we propose GDM, a generative drifting framework that reformulates deterministic medical image prediction as a multi-objective learning problem to jointly promote distrib

infographic.key_insight: Reformulates deterministic conditional medical image prediction as a multi-objective 'generative drifting' process, enabling fast, patient-specific 3D image generation that better balances realism and distributional plausibility.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the trade-off in conditional medical image generation between inference efficiency, patient-specific fidelity, and distribution-level plausibility—especially challenging for high-dimensional 3D data.
method: Introduce a Generative Drifting (GDM) framework that turns deterministic predictors into a learned drift process to explore plausible image variations while honoring patient conditioning.
Optimize a multi-objective loss that explicitly balances patient fidelity, distributional plausibility, and computational cost (inference speed), with a drift schedule learned for efficiency.
Adapt model architecture and training strategies for high-dimensional 3D medical volumes to preserve anatomical consistency and enable practical inference times.
infographic.impact: GDM provides a practical pathway to generate clinically useful, realistic 3D medical images without sacrificing speed—beneficial for data augmentation, reconstruction, anonymization, and downstream diagnostic pipelines.

title: Towards a universal model for spin–orbit physics
authors: Atul C. Thakur, Shyue Ping Ong
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 20 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01221-z

A new machine learning framework predicts the spin–orbit-coupled electronic structure across the periodic table, enabling high-throughput exploration of quantum materials.

infographic.key_insight: A universal machine-learning framework can predict spin–orbit-coupled electronic structure across the periodic table, delivering near–ab initio accuracy while being orders of magnitude faster for high‑throughput materials exploration.
infographic.problem_solved: Ab initio calculations that include spin–orbit coupling (SOC) are computationally expensive and do not scale for large-scale screening or for diverse chemistries across the periodic table; there was no broadly transferable ML model for SOC-enabled electronic structure.
method: Train a single, physics-aware ML model on spin–orbit-coupled electronic structure data spanning elements across the periodic table.
Incorporate symmetry and relativistic (SOC) effects into the model architecture to capture SOC-driven electronic features and chemical diversity.
Use the trained surrogate to predict SOC-influenced properties (e.g., band structures, splittings) orders of magnitude faster than direct ab initio calculations for high‑throughput screening.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a blueprint for building transferable, physics-informed models that replace expensive simulations, enabling large-scale materials discovery and rapid prototyping of quantum materials. It also highlights strategies for integrating domain physics (relativistic effects) into generalizable ML architectures.

title: FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data
authors: Joonhyuk Lee, Virginia Ma, Sarah Zhao, Yash Nair, Asher Spector
abstract: Verification of model outputs is rapidly emerging as a key primitive for both training and real-world deployment of large language models (LLMs). In practice, this often involves using imperfect LLM judges and reward models since ground truth acquisition can be time-consuming and expensive. We introduce Fully Unsupervised Score Ensembling (FUSE), a method for improving verification quality by ensembling verifiers without access to ground truth correctness labels. The key idea behind FUSE is to c

infographic.key_insight: FUSE shows you can substantially improve verification accuracy by unsupervisedly ensembling multiple imperfect verifiers (LLM judges, reward models) without any ground-truth correctness labels, extracting a more reliable consensus signal from noisy scorers.
infographic.problem_solved: How to verify and rank LLM outputs when obtaining ground-truth correctness labels is costly or impossible and available verifiers (human-like judges, reward models) are noisy and imperfect.
method: Aggregate diverse verifier scores (e.g., LLM judges, reward models) for each candidate output to form a multi-view scoring matrix.
Apply a label-free ensembling/aggregation procedure that calibrates weights, detects outliers, and extracts a consensus ranking or score without access to ground-truth labels.
Iteratively refine ensemble weights and consensus (e.g., via agreement-based weighting or consistency checks) to boost verifier reliability.
infographic.impact: Enables higher-quality verification and selection of model outputs without expensive labeled data, reducing cost and improving safety/utility for training (e.g., RLHF) and deployment of LLM systems.

title: A multimodal and temporal foundation model for virtual patient representations at healthcare system scale
authors: Andrew Zhang, Tong Ding, Sophia J. Wagner, Caiwei Tian, Ming Y. Lu
abstract: Modern medicine generates vast multimodal data across siloed systems, yet no existing model integrates the full breadth and temporal depth of the clinical record into a unified patient representation. We introduce Apollo, a multimodal temporal foundation model trained and evaluated on over three decades of longitudinal hospital records from a major US hospital system, composed of 25 billion records from 7.2 million patients, representing 28 distinct medical modalities and 12 major medical specia

infographic.key_insight: Apollo learns unified, temporally aware patient representations by pretraining a single foundation model on 25 billion longitudinal clinical records spanning 30+ years and 28 medical modalities, enabling virtual patient representations at healthcare-system scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Clinical data are fragmented across many modalities and time scales; there was no single model that integrates the full breadth and temporal depth of an individual’s electronic health record into one reusable patient representation.
method: Scale: Pretrain a multimodal foundation model on 25 billion records from 7.2M patients covering 28 distinct clinical modalities and decades of longitudinal data.
Unified representation: Encode heterogeneous inputs (structured EHR events, notes, images, labs, signals, etc.) into a common embedding space that preserves temporal structure.
Temporal modeling: Use sequence-aware aggregation to capture disease progression and longitudinal context for downstream clinical tasks and virtual patient simulation.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a reusable, temporally rich patient embedding that supports transfer to many clinical tasks, accelerates development of virtual patient modeling, and enables evaluation at real-world healthcare system scale.

title: ConforNets: Latents-Based Conformational Control in OpenFold3
authors: Minji Lee, Colin Kalicki, Minkyu Jeon, Aymen Qabel, Alisia Fadini
abstract: Models from the AlphaFold (AF) family reliably predict one dominant conformation for most well-ordered proteins but struggle to capture biologically relevant alternate states. Several efforts have focused on eliciting greater conformational variability through ad hoc inference-time perturbations of AF models or their inputs. Despite their progress, these approaches remain inefficient and fail to consistently recover major conformational modes. Here, we investigate both the optimal location and m

infographic.key_insight: Introducing ConforNets: a latent-space conditioning mechanism integrated into OpenFold3 that enables efficient, controllable sampling of biologically relevant alternate protein conformations, outperforming ad hoc inference-time perturbations.
infographic.problem_solved: AlphaFold-style models reliably predict a single dominant fold but fail to recover major alternative conformational states; prior inference-time perturbation methods are inefficient and inconsistent at retrieving functionally important modes.
method: Embed conformational variability into a learned latent space tied to OpenFold3 representations, enabling targeted manipulation of structural modes.
Condition OpenFold3 inference on latent vectors (learned or sampled) to generate diverse, physically plausible conformations without expensive simulation or repeated ad hoc perturbations.
Use supervised/unsupervised latent clustering and targeted sampling to recover major conformational modes and validate against experimental alternate-state structures.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, scalable way for ML practitioners and structural biologists to generate and control multiple protein conformations from a single model, improving downstream tasks like drug design, functional annotation, and multi-state modeling.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Biological $2\mathrm{D}{+}t$ Reaction-Diffusion Systems
authors: William Lavery, Jodie A. Cochrane, Christian Olesen, Dagim S. Tadele, John T. Nardini
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a powerful framework for learning governing equations of dynamical systems from data. Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) are a variant of PINNs that preserve the known differential operator structure (e.g., reaction-diffusion) while learning constitutive terms via trainable neural subnetworks, enforced through soft residual penalties. Existing BINN studies are limited to $1\mathrm{D}{+}t$ reaction-diffusion systems and focus on forward

infographic.key_insight: This work generalizes biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) to 2D+t reaction–diffusion systems, preserving the known PDE diffusion operator while learning unknown reaction kinetics with trainable neural subnetworks enforced by PDE residual penalties.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the limitation of prior BINN/PINN studies that were restricted to 1D+t systems, providing a framework to discover constitutive reaction terms and infer parameters from sparse/noisy 2D spatiotemporal biological data while respecting the underlying differential-operator structure.
method: Construct a BINN that hard-encodes the 2D diffusion operator and represents unknown reaction kinetics as small trainable neural subnetworks.
Train with a composite PINN loss: data-fitting + PDE residuals (soft enforcement) + boundary/initial condition penalties, evaluated over 2D+t collocation points.
Employ practical training strategies for 2D: multi-scale/spatial sampling, adaptive loss weighting and regularization to improve robustness to noise and limited observations.
infographic.impact: Enables data-driven discovery and parameter inference for complex spatiotemporal biological pattern formation from imaging or simulation data, bridging mechanistic PDE models and ML methods—useful for practitioners in scientific ML, computational biology, and model discovery.

title: GSQ: Highly-Accurate Low-Precision Scalar Quantization for LLMs via Gumbel-Softmax Sampling
authors: Alireza Dadgarnia, Soroush Tabesh, Mahdi Nikdan, Michael Helcig, Eldar Kurtic
abstract: Weight quantization has become a standard tool for efficient LLM deployment, especially for local inference, where models are now routinely served at 2-3 bits per parameter. The state of the art is currently split into two sets of methods: simple scalar quantization techniques, such as GPTQ or AWQ, which are widely deployed but plateau in accuracy at 3-4 bits per parameter (bpp), and "second-generation" vector- or trellis-quantized methods, such as QTIP, GPTVQ and AQLM, which push the accuracy f

infographic.key_insight: Applying differentiable Gumbel-Softmax sampling to scalar weight quantization lets simple per-parameter quantizers recover much of the accuracy previously only attainable by complex vector/trellis schemes, enabling highly accurate 2–3 bit LLM quantization without heavy algorithmic or runtime complexity.
infographic.problem_solved: Scalar quantization methods (e.g., GPTQ/AWQ) plateau in accuracy at very low bitwidths, while more accurate second‑generation vector/trellis methods are algorithmically and computationally complex; GSQ closes this accuracy gap while keeping scalar quantization simple and efficient.
method: Use Gumbel‑Softmax as a differentiable sampler to select discrete scalar codebook entries for weights during quantization, enabling gradient‑based recovery of quantization choices.
Combine temperature annealing and straight‑through style optimization to train per-channel/per-row scales and codebooks with minimal fine‑tuning.
Maintain a scalar quantization pipeline (no trellis/vector transforms) so the method is low‑overhead and compatible with existing deployment toolchains.
infographic.impact: Practitioners can quantize LLMs to very low bitwidths with substantially improved accuracy while retaining the deployment simplicity and speed of scalar methods, making high‑quality local inference and edge serving more practical.
visual_elements: Bar chart: accuracy vs bits (2–8 bpp) comparing GSQ, GPTQ/AWQ, and vector/trellis baselines.

title: T-REN: Learning Text-Aligned Region Tokens Improves Dense Vision-Language Alignment and Scalability
authors: Savya Khosla, Sethuraman T, Aryan Chadha, Alex Schwing, Derek Hoiem
abstract: Despite recent progress, vision-language encoders struggle with two core limitations: (1) weak alignment between language and dense vision features, which hurts tasks like open-vocabulary semantic segmentation; and (2) high token counts for fine-grained visual representations, which limits scalability to long videos. This work addresses both limitations. We propose T-REN (Text-aligned Region Encoder Network), an efficient encoder that maps visual data to a compact set of text-aligned region-leve

infographic.key_insight: T-REN learns a compact set of region-level visual tokens that are explicitly aligned with text embeddings, improving dense vision–language alignment while drastically reducing token counts for scalable processing of long videos and high-resolution images.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses weak alignment between language and dense visual features (hurting tasks like open-vocabulary segmentation) and the high token counts of fine-grained visual representations that limit scalability to long videos.
method: Introduce a Text-aligned Region Encoder Network (T-REN) that converts dense visual input into a compact set of region-level tokens explicitly aligned to text space.
Train with cross-modal alignment objectives so region tokens correspond to textual concepts, enabling better open-vocabulary localization and classification.
Design the encoder to produce far fewer tokens than dense-pixel or patch-based representations, improving compute and memory efficiency for long video and high-resolution inputs.
infographic.impact: Makes vision–language encoders more effective for dense tasks (e.g., open-vocabulary segmentation, region grounding) and more scalable to long videos and higher resolutions, enabling practical deployment in resource-constrained or real-time settings.

title: MathNet: a Global Multimodal Benchmark for Mathematical Reasoning and Retrieval
authors: Shaden Alshammari, Kevin Wen, Abrar Zainal, Mark Hamilton, Navid Safaei
abstract: Mathematical problem solving remains a challenging test of reasoning for large language and multimodal models, yet existing benchmarks are limited in size, language coverage, and task diversity. We introduce MathNet, a high-quality, large-scale, multimodal, and multilingual dataset of Olympiad-level math problems together with a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in generative models and mathematical retrieval in embedding-based systems. MathNet spans 47 countries, 17 languages, and

infographic.key_insight: MathNet delivers a high-quality, large-scale, multimodal and multilingual benchmark of Olympiad-level math problems that evaluates both generative mathematical reasoning and embedding-based mathematical retrieval in a single unified suite.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks are small, narrowly scoped, and lack language and modality diversity, making it hard to evaluate models on realistic, high-difficulty mathematical reasoning and cross-modal/multilingual retrieval tasks.
method: Curate a large corpus of Olympiad-level math problems spanning 47 countries and 17 languages, preserving multimodal content (text, equations, diagrams/images).

Define two evaluation tracks: (1) generative mathematical reasoning for LLMs and multimodal models, and (2) embedding-based mathematical retrieval for similarity and search systems, with standardized splits and metrics.
Provide preprocessing and task interfaces that convert problems into multimodal inputs and retrieval targets to support both generation and embedding workflows.
infographic.impact: MathNet enables more robust, fair, and realistic evaluation of advanced reasoning and retrieval models across languages and modalities, accelerating development of models that can handle challenging mathematical content in global contexts.

title: A Note on TurboQuant and the Earlier DRIVE/EDEN Line of Work
authors: Ran Ben-Basat, Yaniv Ben-Itzhak, Gal Mendelson, Michael Mitzenmacher, Amit Portnoy
abstract:
This note clarifies the relationship between the recent TurboQuant work and the earlier DRIVE (NeurIPS 2021) and EDEN (ICML 2022) schemes. DRIVE is a 1-bit quantizer that EDEN extended to any $b>0$ bits per coordinate; we refer to them collectively as EDEN.
  First, TurboQuant$_{\text{mse}}$ is a special case of EDEN obtained by fixing EDEN's scalar scale parameter to $S=1$. EDEN supports both biased and unbiased quantization, each optimized by a different $S$ (chosen via methods described in th

infographic.key_insight: TurboQuant_mse is not a distinct new algorithm but a special case of the earlier EDEN family obtained by fixing EDEN's scalar scale parameter S = 1; EDEN itself generalizes DRIVE (the 1-bit case) to any b bits and supports both biased and unbiased quantization via different S choices.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies the conceptual and technical relationship between TurboQuant and earlier DRIVE/EDEN work, resolving attribution/novelty questions and making it easier for practitioners to understand which parameter choices produce which algorithms.
method: EDEN formulates a scalable quantizer parameterized by a scalar scale S and bit budget b; DRIVE is the b=1 instance.
By choosing S to optimize different objectives (e.g., MSE or unbiasedness), EDEN yields distinct biased/unbiased quantizers.
Fixing S=1 in EDEN reproduces TurboQuant_mse, showing TurboQuant_mse is a special-case derivation rather than an independent scheme.
infographic.impact: Helps researchers and engineers correctly interpret TurboQuant results, pick the right scale parameter S for their accuracy vs. bias tradeoffs, and avoid redundant reinvention when designing quantizers for model compression and distributed learning.

Schematic of the scalar scale parameter S affecting quantizer behavior (biased vs unbiased) with annotations.
Two-line plot: error (MSE) vs S for biased and unbiased settings to show optimal S differs by objective.

title: SynAgent: Generalizable Cooperative Humanoid Manipulation via Solo-to-Cooperative Agent Synergy
authors: Wei Yao, Haohan Ma, Hongwen Zhang, Yunlian Sun, Liangjun Xing
abstract: Controllable cooperative humanoid manipulation is a fundamental yet challenging problem for embodied intelligence, due to severe data scarcity, complexities in multi-agent coordination, and limited generalization across objects. In this paper, we present SynAgent, a unified framework that enables scalable and physically plausible cooperative manipulation by leveraging Solo-to-Cooperative Agent Synergy to transfer skills from single-agent human-object interaction to multi-agent human-object-human

infographic.key_insight: SynAgent transfers skills learned from single-agent human–object interactions into cooperative two-agent (human–object–human) behaviors, enabling scalable, physically plausible multi-agent humanoid manipulation with much less cooperative data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses severe data scarcity and coordination complexity in cooperative humanoid manipulation, improving generalization across diverse objects and multi-agent scenarios.
method: Learn rich single-agent human–object interaction skills from available solo demonstrations/simulations.
Apply a Solo-to-Cooperative synergy module that maps and adapts solo skills into coordinated multi-agent policies for two-agent manipulation.
Enforce physical plausibility and scalability through physics-aware constraints and simulation-driven policy refinement to handle diverse objects and contacts.
infographic.impact: Makes cooperative humanoid manipulation more data-efficient and generalizable, lowering the barrier for multi-agent embodied systems and accelerating deployment in robotics and virtual agents.

title: AnchorSeg: Language Grounded Query Banks for Reasoning Segmentation
authors: Rui Qian, Chuanhang Deng, Qiang Huang, Jian Xiong, Mingxuan Li
abstract: Reasoning segmentation requires models to ground complex, implicit textual queries into precise pixel-level masks. Existing approaches rely on a single segmentation token $\texttt{<SEG>}$, whose hidden state implicitly encodes both semantic reasoning and spatial localization, limiting the model's ability to explicitly disentangle what to segment from where to segment. We introduce AnchorSeg, which reformulates reasoning segmentation as a structured conditional generation process over image token

infographic.key_insight: AnchorSeg disentangles semantic reasoning from spatial localization by replacing the single implicit segmentation token with a language-grounded bank of query anchors and treating mask generation as a structured conditional generation over image tokens. This explicit separation lets the model better interpret complex, implicit textual queries and produce more precise pixel-level masks.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing reasoning segmentation models compress both 'what to segment' and 'where to segment' into one <SEG> token, limiting interpretability and accuracy for complex, implicit language queries; AnchorSeg addresses this by providing structured, language-grounded query banks that explicitly ground reasoning into spatial predictions.
method: Introduce a bank of language-grounded query anchors that each encode aspects of the textual query, instead of a single <SEG> token.
Reformulate segmentation as a structured conditional generation process over image tokens, where anchors guide spatial grounding and mask synthesis separately from semantic reasoning.
Train the system to map language anchors to spatial token responses and compose them into precise pixel-level masks, improving modularity and interpretability.
infographic.impact: Makes reasoning segmentation more accurate, interpretable, and modular — enabling practitioners to debug, extend, and adapt models for complex multimodal queries and downstream tasks like VQA, robotics perception, and fine-grained scene understanding.

title: Advancing Vision Transformer with Enhanced Spatial Priors
authors: Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, Mingrui Chen, Hongmin Liu, Ran He
abstract: In recent years, the Vision Transformer (ViT) has garnered significant attention within the computer vision community. However, the core component of ViT, Self-Attention, lacks explicit spatial priors and suffers from quadratic computational complexity, limiting its applicability. To address these issues, we have proposed RMT, a robust vision backbone with explicit spatial priors for general purposes. RMT utilizes Manhattan distance decay to introduce spatial information and employs a horizontal

infographic.key_insight: RMT augments Vision Transformer attention with explicit spatial priors using a Manhattan-distance decay, enabling attention to respect image geometry while reducing redundant global interactions.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses ViT's lack of explicit spatial bias and the high quadratic cost of vanilla self-attention, making transformers more spatially aware and computationally efficient for vision tasks.
method: Inject Manhattan-distance decay into attention weights to bias interactions toward nearby tokens and encode spatial locality.
Introduce a structured token-mixing component (horizontal-oriented factorization) to capture directional spatial patterns and limit full pairwise attention.
Combine the spatially-decayed attention with standard ViT blocks to form RMT, a general-purpose backbone that preserves representational power with lower overhead.
infographic.impact: Makes ViT-style backbones more practical for real-world vision workloads by improving spatial reasoning and lowering computational cost—beneficial for model designers, deployers, and downstream task performance.

title: When Can LLMs Learn to Reason with Weak Supervision?
authors: Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, Anna Mordvina, Hamid Palangi, Saadia Gabriel
abstract: Large language models have achieved significant reasoning improvements through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Yet as model capabilities grow, constructing high-quality reward signals becomes increasingly difficult, making it essential to understand when RLVR can succeed under weaker forms of supervision. We conduct a systematic empirical study across diverse model families and reasoning domains under three weak supervision settings: scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-su

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can often learn improved reasoning from weaker reward signals, but success depends strongly on model scale, domain complexity, and the mix of clean vs noisy supervision.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines when reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains effective under weak supervision (scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-supervision), providing practical guidance for deploying RL-based reasoning improvements when high-quality reward labels are hard to obtain.
method: Systematic empirical study across multiple model families and reasoning domains to evaluate RLVR under three weak-supervision regimes: scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-supervision.
Controlled experiments that vary model scale, reward noise level, and amount of verified data to identify factors that enable or block learning.
Analysis of success conditions and mitigation strategies (e.g., mixing small verified reward sets with noisy/self-supervised signals, reward calibration, and curriculum-style training).
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners actionable rules-of-thumb for when to invest in costly reward annotation versus relying on weaker signals, and suggests practical training strategies to extend RLVR benefits to larger models and realistic low-label settings.

title: Bounded Ratio Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yunke Ao, Le Chen, Bruce D. Lee, Assefa S. Wahd, Aline Czarnobai
abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has become the predominant algorithm for on-policy reinforcement learning due to its scalability and empirical robustness across domains. However, there is a significant disconnect between the underlying foundations of trust region methods and the heuristic clipped objective used in PPO. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing the Bounded Ratio Reinforcement Learning (BRRL) framework. We formulate a novel regularized and constrained policy optimization

infographic.key_insight: BRRL introduces a principled policy optimization framework that enforces explicit bounds on importance-sampling (policy) ratios, providing a theoretical bridge between trust-region methods and PPO's clipping heuristic and yielding more stable on-policy learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the mismatch between PPO's heuristic clipped objective and the theoretical guarantees of trust-region approaches, which can lead to unstable updates and unclear performance guarantees in on-policy reinforcement learning.
method: Formulate a regularized and constrained policy optimization problem that explicitly bounds the policy probability ratio (importance weight) between new and old policies.
Derive a practical surrogate objective and/or penalty that enforces the ratio bounds while remaining compatible with stochastic gradient updates used in PPO-style training.
Show that the bound-based formulation recovers and formalizes clipping-like behavior, enabling stability and theoretical guarantees without relying on heuristic clipping alone.
infographic.impact: Provides RL practitioners a principled alternative to PPO clipping that improves training stability and interpretability, potentially reducing sensitivity to hyperparameters and offering stronger theoretical guarantees for on-policy algorithms.

title: Beyond Surface Statistics: Robust Conformal Prediction for LLMs via Internal Representations
authors: Yanli Wang, Peng Kuang, Xiaoyu Han, Kaidi Xu, Haohan Wang
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where reliability matters, yet output-level uncertainty signals such as token probabilities, entropy, and self-consistency can become brittle under calibration--deployment mismatch. Conformal prediction provides finite-sample validity under exchangeability, but its practical usefulness depends on the quality of the nonconformity score. We propose a conformal framework for LLM question answering that uses internal representations rather

infographic.key_insight: Using internal model representations as the nonconformity signal for conformal prediction yields more reliable, deployment-robust uncertainty estimates for LLM question answering than relying solely on output-level signals like token probabilities.
infographic.problem_solved: Output-level uncertainty measures (token probs, entropy, self-consistency) become brittle under calibration–deployment mismatch; conformal prediction is valid but depends on a good nonconformity score — this paper addresses how to design such a score for LLMs to preserve coverage and reliability under shift.
method: Extract intermediate internal representations from the LLM (hidden states, layer activations) for each QA example and derive a representation-based nonconformity score.
Apply conformal prediction calibration using these representation scores to produce predictive sets/abstention decisions with finite-sample coverage guarantees under exchangeability.
Evaluate robustness under calibration–deployment mismatch (domain or distribution shift) to show that representation-based scores maintain coverage while keeping predictive sets concise.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical path to more trustworthy LLM uncertainty estimates in real-world deployments, enabling safer abstention and better risk management when models encounter distributional shift.

title: Enhancing AI and Dynamical Subseasonal Forecasts with Probabilistic Bias Correction
authors: Hannah Guan, Soukayna Mouatadid, Paulo Orenstein, Judah Cohen, Haiyu Dong
abstract: Decision-makers rely on weather forecasts to plant crops, manage wildfires, allocate water and energy, and prepare for weather extremes. Today, such forecasts enjoy unprecedented accuracy out to two weeks thanks to steady advances in physics-based dynamical models and data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) models. However, model skill drops precipitously at subseasonal timescales (2 - 6 weeks ahead), due to compounding errors and persistent biases. To counter this degradation, we introduce pro

infographic.key_insight: A lightweight probabilistic bias-correction layer can substantially improve 2–6 week (subseasonal) forecasts from both AI and physics-based dynamical models by correcting persistent errors and producing calibrated uncertainty estimates.
infographic.problem_solved: Subseasonal forecast skill degrades sharply at 2–6 week lead times due to compounding model errors and persistent biases, leaving decision-makers with unreliable point forecasts and poorly quantified uncertainty.
method: Learn historical forecast errors from ensembles of dynamical and AI models and model those errors probabilistically (e.g., quantile mapping / distributional correction).
Apply learned corrections to raw model outputs to produce calibrated predictive distributions instead of biased point forecasts.
Integrate with existing forecast pipelines as a post-processing layer, enabling improved ensemble spread, reliability (PIT/calibration), and skill across subseasonal leads.
infographic.impact: This approach gives AI/ML practitioners a practical, model-agnostic post-processing tool to boost subseasonal forecast accuracy and uncertainty quantification—improving decision support for agriculture, water/energy management, and hazard response.

title: ASMR-Bench: Auditing for Sabotage in ML Research
authors: Eric Gan, Aryan Bhatt, Buck Shlegeris, Julian Stastny, Vivek Hebbar
abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to conduct research autonomously, misaligned systems could introduce subtle flaws that produce misleading results while evading detection. We introduce ASMR-Bench (Auditing for Sabotage in ML Research), a benchmark for evaluating the ability of auditors to detect sabotage in ML research codebases. ASMR-Bench consists of 9 ML research codebases with sabotaged variants that produce qualitatively different experimental results. Each sabotage modifies implementati

infographic.key_insight: Subtle, purposeful bugs can make ML research appear valid while changing conclusions; ASMR-Bench provides a concrete benchmark to evaluate whether auditors can detect such sabotage in research codebases.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the risk that misaligned or malicious AI/agents (or humans) can introduce hard-to-detect sabotage into ML experiments, producing misleading results that evade standard checks and peer review.
method: Curate 9 real ML research codebases and produce carefully crafted sabotaged variants that change qualitative experimental outcomes while remaining plausible.
Define tasks and evaluation protocols that measure an auditor's ability to detect, localize, and explain sabotaging changes across variants.
Provide metrics and controlled scenarios to benchmark auditing tools, human reviewers, and automated defenses against sabotage.
infographic.impact: Provides a standardized way to test and improve auditing practices, tooling, and policies to protect research integrity and reduce risk from misaligned or adversarial agents in ML research.

title: Learning to Reason with Insight for Informal Theorem Proving
authors: Yunhe Li, Hao Shi, Bowen Deng, Wei Wang, Mengzhe Ruan
abstract: Although most of the automated theorem-proving approaches depend on formal proof systems, informal theorem proving can align better with large language models' (LLMs) strength in natural language processing. In this work, we identify a primary bottleneck in informal theorem proving as a lack of insight, namely the difficulty of recognizing the core techniques required to solve complex problems. To address this, we propose a novel framework designed to cultivate this essential reasoning skill and

infographic.key_insight: The paper identifies 'insight' — the ability to recognize the core technique or trick needed to solve a problem — as the main bottleneck in informal theorem proving, and proposes a training framework to teach LLMs to acquire that insight to improve proof generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Informal theorem proving with LLMs struggles because models often cannot identify the central idea or technique needed to solve complex problems, leading to long, unfocused or incorrect reasoning chains.
method: Introduce an insight-focused supervision signal (e.g., annotated hints, technique labels, or focal summaries) that highlights the core solving idea for each problem.

Train or fine-tune LLMs to predict and use these insight cues during generation via specialized prompts, curriculum learning, or iterative refinement loops so proofs are guided by the recognized technique.
Evaluate and refine with benchmarks and feedback that measure both insight recognition accuracy and downstream proof correctness, possibly incorporating retrieval of similar solved problems.
infographic.impact: Teaching models to recognize and use problem-specific insight makes informal theorem proving more reliable and efficient, enabling LLMs to produce shorter, more targeted proofs and improving their applicability in research-assistant and formalization workflows.

title: BAGEL: Benchmarking Animal Knowledge Expertise in Language Models
authors: Jiacheng Shen, Masato Hagiwara, Milad Alizadeh, Ellen Gilsenan-McMahon, Marius Miron
abstract: Large language models have shown strong performance on broad-domain knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, but it remains unclear how well language models handle specialized animal-related knowledge under a unified closed-book evaluation protocol. We introduce BAGEL, a benchmark for evaluating animal knowledge expertise in language models. BAGEL is constructed from diverse scientific and reference sources, including bioRxiv, Global Biotic Interactions, Xeno-canto, and Wikipedia, using a combination

infographic.key_insight: BAGEL exposes a large gap between general LLM performance and specialized animal-related expertise by providing a unified closed-book benchmark drawn from scientific and reference sources. It shows that state-of-the-art models often mispredict or are poorly calibrated on taxonomy, behavior, ecology and bioacoustic queries.
infographic.problem_solved: There was no standardized, closed-book benchmark to measure how well language models know specialized animal facts and concepts; BAGEL fills this gap by assembling diverse, high-quality animal knowledge sources and a unified evaluation protocol.
method: Curate questions and ground-truth facts from diverse scientific and reference sources (e.g., bioRxiv, Global Biotic Interactions, Xeno-canto, Wikipedia).
Design closed-book, prompt-based tasks covering taxonomy, behavior, ecology, species interactions, and bioacoustics with controlled answer formats.
Evaluate multiple LLMs using accuracy, calibration and error-type analyses to quantify gaps and failure modes.
infographic.impact: BAGEL gives ML practitioners a targeted tool to identify and fix animal-knowledge weaknesses in LLMs—informing data collection, fine-tuning, and model auditing for ecology, conservation, and biology applications.

title: FineCog-Nav: Integrating Fine-grained Cognitive Modules for Zero-shot Multimodal UAV Navigation
authors: Dian Shao, Zhengzheng Xu, Peiyang Wang, Like Liu, Yule Wang
abstract: UAV vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to navigate complex 3D environments from an egocentric perspective while following ambiguous multi-step instructions over long horizons. Existing zero-shot methods remain limited, as they often rely on large base models, generic prompts, and loosely coordinated modules. In this work, we propose FineCog-Nav, a top-down framework inspired by human cognition that organizes navigation into fine-grained modules for language processing, perception

infographic.key_insight: FineCog-Nav applies a top-down, human-inspired cognitive architecture that decomposes UAV vision-language navigation into fine-grained, interoperable modules, enabling robust zero-shot multimodal navigation without heavy task-specific finetuning. The coordinated module interfaces (language, perception, planning, control) improve grounding and long-horizon instruction execution.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the limitations of existing zero-shot UAV VLN methods that rely on monolithic large models, generic prompts, and loosely coordinated components—leading to poor grounding, low interpretability, and weak generalization in complex 3D egocentric environments.
method: Top-down modular design: split navigation into specialized cognitive modules (e.g., language parser, semantic perception, short-/long-horizon planner, and action controller) inspired by human cognition.

Structured cross-module interfaces: exchange grounded representations (scene graphs, goal tokens, attentional maps) and explicit communication protocols to align language and perception without end-to-end finetuning.

Lightweight multimodal adapters and rule-based grounding: combine pretrained vision/language encoders with small adapters and symbolic grounding rules to enable zero-shot generalization in novel environments.
infographic.impact: FineCog-Nav provides a practical blueprint for building interpretable, sample-efficient VLN systems that generalize zero-shot—reducing dependence on massive task-specific datasets or models and accelerating deployment of reliable autonomous UAV navigation in real-world settings.

title: AI economics for the common good
authors: Francesco Fuso Nerini
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 17 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01212-0

AI economics for the common good

infographic.key_insight: Applying economic theory and incentive design to AI development reframes AI as a set of economic actors and public goods, enabling concrete mechanisms to align AI outcomes with the common good. This shifts focus from purely technical fixes to incentive, governance and evaluation structures that shape system behavior at scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses misaligned incentives and market failures (externalities, concentration, under-provision of public goods) that lead AI deployment to harm social welfare despite technical progress.
method: Map AI systems and stakeholders to economic models (public goods, externalities, principal–agent problems) to identify failure modes.
Propose incentive and mechanism-design interventions (pricing, regulation, funding structures, reward redesign) to internalize social costs and promote equitable provision of AI benefits.
Illustrate policy and governance pathways by combining normative objectives with measurable economic metrics for deployment and evaluation.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners, designers and policymakers a practical framework to anticipate incentive-driven harms and embed economic levers that steer systems toward broader social benefit. This makes deployment decisions, evaluation metrics and governance choices more actionable and accountable.

title: Using Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs to Improve the Interpretability of Machine Learning Models in Manufacturing
authors: Thomas Bayer, Alexander Lohr, Sarah Weiß, Bernd Michelberger, Wolfram Höpken
abstract: Explaining Machine Learning (ML) results in a transparent and user-friendly manner remains a challenging task of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). In this paper, we present a method to enhance the interpretability of ML models by using a Knowledge Graph (KG). We store domain-specific data along with ML results and their corresponding explanations, establishing a structured connection between domain knowledge and ML insights. To make these insights accessible to users, we designed a sele

infographic.key_insight: Combining Knowledge Graphs with Large Language Models creates a structured bridge between domain data and ML outputs, producing clear, domain-aware explanations that make manufacturing ML models more interpretable and actionable.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap between opaque ML outputs and domain expert needs in manufacturing by providing transparent, context-rich explanations that tie model results back to domain knowledge.
method: Store domain-specific data, ML predictions, and explanation artifacts in a Knowledge Graph to create explicit links between concepts, features, and outcomes.
Use Large Language Models to generate and refine natural-language explanations and to translate KG relationships into user-friendly narratives and queries.

title: OT on the Map: Quantifying Domain Shifts in Geographic Space
authors: Haoran Zhang, Livia Betti, Konstantin Klemmer, Esther Rolf, David Alvarez-Melis
abstract: In computer vision and machine learning for geographic data, out-of-domain generalization is a pervasive challenge, arising from uneven global data coverage and distribution shifts across geographic regions. Though models are frequently trained in one region and deployed in another, there is no principled method for determining when this cross-region adaptation will be successful. A well-defined notion of distance between distributions can effectively quantify how different a new target domain i

infographic.key_insight: A geographic, Optimal Transport–based distance reliably quantifies how much target regions differ from training regions and predicts cross-region model performance, enabling principled decisions about when geographic adaptation will succeed.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a principled, quantitative way to measure domain shift across geographic regions so practitioners can predict whether a model trained in one area will generalize to another and prioritize adaptation or data collection.
method: Represent source and target geographic datasets as distributions in feature (or pixel) space and compute an Optimal Transport / Wasserstein distance between them that respects spatial structure.
Use the computed OT distance as a calibrated predictor of model performance drop (or adaptation difficulty) across regions, enabling thresholds for acceptable domain shift.
Employ scalable OT approximations and map-based visualizations to produce region-level shift scores usable for deployment planning and data acquisition.
infographic.impact: Gives ML practitioners a simple numeric signal to assess cross-region risk, optimize where to collect labels, and decide when to apply transfer or domain-adaptation methods—reducing wasted deployment effort and improving robustness for geospatial applications.

title: Do Vision-Language Models Truly Perform Vision Reasoning? A Rigorous Study of the Modality Gap
authors: Yige Xu, Yongjie Wang, Zizhuo Wu, Kaisong Song, Jun Lin
abstract: Reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) has recently attracted significant attention due to its broad applicability across diverse downstream tasks. However, it remains unclear whether the superior performance of VLMs stems from genuine vision-grounded reasoning or relies predominantly on the reasoning capabilities of their textual backbones. To systematically measure this, we introduce CrossMath, a novel multimodal reasoning benchmark designed for controlled cross-modal comparisons. Specific

infographic.key_insight: A new benchmark (CrossMath) shows that much of VLM 'reasoning' accuracy can come from textual backbones rather than true vision-grounded reasoning, revealing a sizable modality gap.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines whether superior performance of vision-language models reflects genuine vision-grounded reasoning or is driven primarily by powerful textual components, by enabling controlled cross-modal comparisons.
method: Design CrossMath: a multimodal reasoning benchmark with controlled image/text interventions to isolate visual vs. textual contributions.
Evaluate SOTA VLMs and text-only baselines under conditions like image masking, caption replacement, and cross-modal swaps to quantify reliance on each modality.
Introduce metrics and comparisons that measure the modality gap (how much performance drops when visual information is reduced or removed).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a rigorous tool to diagnose whether VLMs truly use visual input, improving evaluation fidelity and guiding development of better-grounded multimodal models and training strategies.

title: VEFX-Bench: A Holistic Benchmark for Generic Video Editing and Visual Effects
authors: Xiangbo Gao, Sicong Jiang, Bangya Liu, Xinghao Chen, Minglai Yang
abstract: As AI-assisted video creation becomes increasingly practical, instruction-guided video editing has become essential for refining generated or captured footage to meet professional requirements. Yet the field still lacks both a large-scale human-annotated dataset with complete editing examples and a standardized evaluator for comparing editing systems. Existing resources are limited by small scale, missing edited outputs, or the absence of human quality labels, while current evaluation often reli

infographic.key_insight: VEFX-Bench provides the first large-scale, human-annotated benchmark of complete video editing examples plus a standardized evaluator, enabling fair, reproducible comparison of generic video-editing and VFX systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of a comprehensive, human-labeled dataset and a unified evaluation protocol for instruction-guided video editing and visual effects, which has prevented consistent comparison and progress in the field.
method: Curate a large-scale dataset of raw videos paired with human-created, instruction-driven edited outputs and quality labels for common editing/VFX tasks.

Define a benchmarking suite of editing scenarios and an evaluation protocol that combines human quality annotations with objective metrics for fidelity, temporal consistency, and instruction compliance.
Provide a standardized evaluator and leaderboard to enable reproducible comparison across models and editing pipelines.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to benchmark video editing models on realistic, end-to-end editing tasks and accelerate progress by making evaluations reproducible and comparable across methods.

title: Evaluating the Progression of Large Language Model Capabilities for Small-Molecule Drug Design
authors: Shriram Chennakesavalu, Kirill Shmilovich, Hayley Weir, Colin Grambow, John Bradshaw
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have the potential to accelerate small molecule drug design due to their ability to reason about information from diverse sources and formats. However, their practical utility remains unclear due to the lack of benchmarks that reflect real-world scenarios. In this work, we introduce a suite of chemically-grounded tasks spanning molecular property prediction, molecular representation transformations, and molecular design. Importantly, we formulate these tasks as reinf

infographic.key_insight: A new chemically-grounded benchmark suite demonstrates how large language model capabilities scale and fall short across realistic small‑molecule drug design tasks, revealing strengths in representation and reasoning but clear gaps in reliable design and property prediction.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of realistic, chemistry-aware benchmarks for evaluating LLMs on end‑to‑end small‑molecule drug‑design workflows, bridging the gap between toy tasks and real-world discovery scenarios.
method: Curate a suite of chemically‑grounded tasks spanning molecular property prediction, molecular representation transformations (e.g., SMILES ⇄ IUPAC/name conversions), and molecular design challenges.
Formulate tasks as reinforcement‑style sequential decision problems to reflect multi‑step, real‑world workflows and to probe reasoning and planning capabilities.
Systematically evaluate multiple LLMs across these tasks, analyzing capability progression, failure modes, and where model improvements translate into practical utility.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and drug‑discovery teams with a realistic benchmark and diagnostic toolkit to choose, tune, or develop LLMs for chemistry workflows, accelerating safe and effective integration of LLMs into molecule design pipelines.

title: Detecting and Suppressing Reward Hacking with Gradient Fingerprints
authors: Songtao Wang, Quang Hieu Pham, Fangcong Yin, Xinpeng Wang, Jocelyn Qiaochu Chen
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically optimizes for outcome rewards without imposing constraints on intermediate reasoning. This leaves training susceptible to reward hacking, where models exploit loopholes (e.g., spurious patterns in training data) in the reward function to achieve high scores without solving the intended task. These reward-hacking behaviors are often implicit, as the intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) may appear plausible on the surface, limiting the

infographic.key_insight: Gradient fingerprints—compact signatures derived from model gradients during reasoning—reveal implicit reward-hacking behaviors and can be used to detect and suppress those behaviors during training, improving alignment between scored rewards and intended task solutions.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses reward hacking in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where models exploit spurious patterns in data or produce plausible-looking intermediate reasoning (CoT) that nonetheless achieves high reward without solving the true task.
method: Compute gradient-based fingerprints from intermediate chain-of-thought steps to characterize behavior that correlates with reward-hacking.
Use a detector trained on these fingerprints to flag implicit hacking strategies even when CoT appears superficially correct.
Suppress flagged behaviors during training via targeted regularization or modified update rules to steer learning toward genuine task-solving.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical, gradient-level tool to make RL systems more robust to exploitation of reward specs, improving reliability and alignment of models that use verifiable rewards.

title: Repurposing 3D Generative Model for Autoregressive Layout Generation
authors: Haoran Feng, Yifan Niu, Zehuan Huang, Yang-Tian Sun, Chunchao Guo
abstract: We introduce LaviGen, a framework that repurposes 3D generative models for 3D layout generation. Unlike previous methods that infer object layouts from textual descriptions, LaviGen operates directly in the native 3D space, formulating layout generation as an autoregressive process that explicitly models geometric relations and physical constraints among objects, producing coherent and physically plausible 3D scenes. To further enhance this process, we propose an adapted 3D diffusion model that

infographic.key_insight: LaviGen repurposes pretrained 3D generative models to perform autoregressive layout generation directly in native 3D space, explicitly modeling geometric relations and physical constraints to produce coherent, physically plausible 3D scenes.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing layout generation approaches often rely on text or 2D proxies and fail to explicitly enforce 3D geometric relations and physical feasibility; LaviGen addresses the challenge of generating coherent, physically-plausible object layouts in true 3D space.
method: Formulate layout generation as an autoregressive process in native 3D space: sequentially place objects conditioned on previously placed objects and relations.
Repurpose pretrained 3D generative models and adapt a 3D diffusion model for sampling and refinement of object placements within the autoregressive pipeline.
Explicitly model geometric relations and physical constraints (e.g., support, collision avoidance, alignment) during generation to ensure scene coherence and plausibility.
infographic.impact: Produces more realistic 3D scenes without heavy post-processing, benefiting simulation, robotics, AR/VR, and content creation workflows by reducing manual correction and improving physical fidelity of generated layouts.

title: GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens
authors: Roni Itkin, Noam Issachar, Yehonatan Keypur, Yehonatan Keypur, Anpei Chen
abstract: The efficient spatial allocation of primitives serves as the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting, as it directly dictates the synergy between representation compactness, reconstruction speed, and rendering fidelity. Previous solutions, whether based on iterative optimization or feed-forward inference, suffer from significant trade-offs between these goals, mainly due to the reliance on local, heuristic-driven allocation strategies that lack global scene awareness. Specifically, current feed-forw

infographic.key_insight: Introduce global scene tokens that provide holistic scene awareness to a feed‑forward Gaussian splatting pipeline, enabling efficient, compact allocation of 3D primitives that preserves high-fidelity reconstruction while remaining fast to infer.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the limitations of local, heuristic-driven allocation in 3D Gaussian Splatting that force a trade-off between representation compactness, reconstruction quality, and feed‑forward inference speed.
method: Learn a small set of global scene tokens that summarize global geometry and appearance, used to guide allocation and parameterization of 3D Gaussian primitives.
Use a feed‑forward network (global-token conditioning + local decoding) to predict Gaussian positions, covariances, colors and confidences in one pass, replacing iterative optimization.
Train with reconstruction loss plus regularizers for sparsity/compactness so the model balances fidelity, size, and render speed.
infographic.impact: Delivers a practical route to real‑time, high‑quality neural rendering with far fewer primitives and predictable inference latency, making 3D Gaussian Splatting more usable in production pipelines and interactive applications.

title: CoopEval: Benchmarking Cooperation-Sustaining Mechanisms and LLM Agents in Social Dilemmas
authors: Emanuel Tewolde, Xiao Zhang, David Guzman Piedrahita, Vincent Conitzer, Zhijing Jin
abstract:
It is increasingly important that LLM agents interact effectively and safely with other goal-pursuing agents, yet, recent works report the opposite trend: LLMs with stronger reasoning capabilities behave _less_ cooperatively in mixed-motive games such as the prisoner's dilemma and public goods settings. Indeed, our experiments show that recent models -- with or without reasoning enabled -- consistently defect in single-shot social dilemmas.
  To tackle this safety concern, we present the first c

infographic.key_insight: CoopEval introduces the first comprehensive benchmark showing that contemporary LLMs—despite stronger reasoning—tend to defect in single-shot social dilemmas, and evaluates mechanisms that can sustain cooperation among LLM agents.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the safety and coordination gap where powerful LLM agents behave uncooperatively in mixed-motive settings (e.g., prisoner's dilemma, public goods), by providing a standardized evaluation suite to measure and compare cooperation-sustaining interventions.
method: Design CoopEval: a benchmark suite of canonical social dilemmas (single-shot and repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, public goods, commons) and standardized metrics for cooperation and payoff.

Implement and evaluate a range of cooperation-sustaining mechanisms (e.g., communication/commitment channels, incentive modifications, reputation/history conditioning) across multiple LLM agents, with/without explicit reasoning prompts.
Compare agent behaviours and mechanism effectiveness using quantitative cooperation rates, payoffs, and robustness analyses to identify which interventions successfully promote sustained cooperation.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a replicable toolkit to assess and improve multi-agent safety and coordination in LLM-driven systems, guiding design choices (mechanisms, prompts, incentives) to reduce defection and align group outcomes.

title: RAD-2: Scaling Reinforcement Learning in a Generator-Discriminator Framework
authors: Hao Gao, Shaoyu Chen, Yifan Zhu, Yuehao Song, Wenyu Liu
abstract: High-level autonomous driving requires motion planners capable of modeling multimodal future uncertainties while remaining robust in closed-loop interactions. Although diffusion-based planners are effective at modeling complex trajectory distributions, they often suffer from stochastic instabilities and the lack of corrective negative feedback when trained purely with imitation learning. To address these issues, we propose RAD-2, a unified generator-discriminator framework for closed-loop planni

infographic.key_insight: RAD-2 combines diffusion-based trajectory generators with a discriminator trained via reinforcement-learning-style corrective feedback, stabilizing stochastic planners and improving closed-loop robustness for multimodal motion planning.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses instability and lack of corrective negative feedback in diffusion-based motion planners trained with imitation learning, enabling reliable closed-loop behavior under multimodal future uncertainty.
method: Generator: diffusion-based multimodal trajectory sampler that models complex future distributions.
Discriminator: a critic that provides corrective feedback/rewards to the generator, closing the loop and counteracting stochastic instabilities.
Unified training: adversarial / RL-style optimization in closed-loop simulation to scale reinforcement learning signals for improved robustness and failure recovery.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy multimodal, diffusion-based planners that are both expressive and robust in closed-loop control, reducing catastrophic failures and improving real-world autonomous driving performance.

title: MM-WebAgent: A Hierarchical Multimodal Web Agent for Webpage Generation
authors: Yan Li, Zezi Zeng, Yifan Yang, Yuqing Yang, Ning Liao
abstract: The rapid progress of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) tools enables images, videos, and visualizations to be created on demand for webpage design, offering a flexible and increasingly adopted paradigm for modern UI/UX. However, directly integrating such tools into automated webpage generation often leads to style inconsistency and poor global coherence, as elements are generated in isolation. We propose MM-WebAgent, a hierarchical agentic framework for multimodal webpage generat

infographic.key_insight: MM-WebAgent uses a hierarchical multimodal agent framework to coordinate global planning and local AIGC modules, producing webpages that are stylistically consistent and globally coherent instead of assembled from isolated elements.
infographic.problem_solved: Solves style inconsistency and poor global coherence in automated webpage generation when integrating image/text/video AIGC tools, which typically produce disjointed elements that don't form a unified UI/UX.
method: Hierarchical agent architecture: a global planner sets page-level layout, style, and constraints while local agents generate components guided by that plan.
Multimodal coordination: integrate image, text, and layout generators under shared style and content constraints to ensure cross-modal consistency.
Iterative refinement & constraint enforcement: feedback loops align local outputs to the global plan, correcting mismatches and improving coherence.
infographic.impact: Makes AI-driven webpage generation practical at scale by reducing manual editing and delivering coherent, on-brand designs; valuable for teams building automated site builders, design systems, and AIGC-powered UX tools.

title: R3D: Revisiting 3D Policy Learning
authors: Zhengdong Hong, Shenrui Wu, Haozhe Cui, Boyi Zhao, Ran Ji
abstract: 3D policy learning promises superior generalization and cross-embodiment transfer, but progress has been hindered by training instabilities and severe overfitting, precluding the adoption of powerful 3D perception models. In this work, we systematically diagnose these failures, identifying the omission of 3D data augmentation and the adverse effects of Batch Normalization as primary causes. We propose a new architecture coupling a scalable transformer-based 3D encoder with a diffusion decoder, e

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that missing 3D data augmentation and the use of Batch Normalization are primary causes of instability and overfitting in 3D policy learning, and that combining a transformer-based 3D encoder with a diffusion decoder plus targeted training fixes stabilizes learning and unlocks powerful 3D perception models for policies.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses severe training instability and overfitting that have prevented adoption of large 3D perception models in policy learning, limiting generalization and cross-embodiment transfer.
method: Systematic diagnosis identifying two root causes: omission of 3D-specific augmentations and adverse effects of Batch Normalization on policy training.
New architecture coupling a scalable transformer-based 3D encoder with a diffusion decoder to model rich 3D representations and stochastic action predictions.
Training recipe: add 3D data augmentations and replace/modify BatchNorm (e.g., LayerNorm/GroupNorm or BN removal) plus stability-focused hyperparameter and optimization adjustments.

title: TokenLight: Precise Lighting Control in Images using Attribute Tokens
authors: Sumit Chaturvedi, Yannick Hold-Geoffroy, Mengwei Ren, Jingyuan Liu, He Zhang
abstract: This paper presents a method for image relighting that enables precise and continuous control over multiple illumination attributes in a photograph. We formulate relighting as a conditional image generation task and introduce attribute tokens to encode distinct lighting factors such as intensity, color, ambient illumination, diffuse level, and 3D light positions. The model is trained on a large-scale synthetic dataset with ground-truth lighting annotations, supplemented by a small set of real ca

infographic.key_insight: TokenLight encodes distinct lighting factors as compact attribute tokens, enabling precise, continuous, and independent control of multiple illumination properties in a single relighting model. This frames image relighting as conditional image generation conditioned on interpretable lighting tokens.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing relighting methods struggle to give users fine-grained, composable control over multiple illumination attributes (intensity, color, ambient, diffuse, 3D light position) simultaneously and continuously; TokenLight provides a controllable interface to edit these factors precisely.
method: Formulate relighting as a conditional image generation task and introduce attribute tokens that explicitly represent lighting factors (intensity, color, ambient illumination, diffuse level, 3D light positions).
Train a generator conditioned on these tokens using a large-scale synthetic dataset with ground-truth lighting annotations, augmented with a small real-image set for better realism/domain adaptation.
Allow continuous interpolation and independent manipulation of tokens at inference to produce precise, photorealistic relighting edits.
infographic.impact: Provides ML and vision practitioners a practical, interpretable mechanism for controllable relighting—useful for photo editing, AR/VR, data augmentation, and neural rendering workflows where precise lighting manipulation is required.
