title: Optimal last-iterate convergence in matrix games with bandit feedback using the log-barrier
authors: Come Fiegel, Pierre Menard, Tadashi Kozuno, Michal Valko, Vianney Perchet
abstract: We study the problem of learning minimax policies in zero-sum matrix games. Fiegel et al. (2025) recently showed that achieving last-iterate convergence in this setting is harder when the players are uncoupled, by proving a lower bound on the exploitability gap of Omega(t^{-1/4}). Some online mirror descent algorithms were proposed in the literature for this problem, but none have truly attained this rate yet. We show that the use of a log-barrier regularization, along with a dual-focused analys

infographic.key_insight: Using a log-barrier regularizer inside an online mirror-descent style algorithm, together with a dual-focused analysis, yields optimal last-iterate convergence for uncoupled zero-sum matrix games under bandit feedback — matching the known Omega(t^{-1/4}) lower bound.
infographic.problem_solved: How to learn minimax policies in zero-sum matrix games with only bandit (partial) feedback while guaranteeing fast, last-iterate convergence for uncoupled players — a setting where prior methods failed to attain the optimal rate.
method: Incorporate a log-barrier regularizer into a mirror-descent/online-learning update to keep iterates well-conditioned near the simplex boundary.
Develop a dual-focused convergence analysis that directly controls last-iterate exploitability (rather than averaged iterates) and matches the lower bound.
Design bandit-friendly gradient estimators and exploration/step-size choices (importance-weighting / variance control) to operate with partial payoff observations.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, theoretically optimal algorithm for multi-agent and adversarial learning tasks with limited feedback, enabling more stable and faster-converging strategies in applications like multi-agent RL, online auctions, and adversarial training.

title: SegWithU: Uncertainty as Perturbation Energy for Single-Forward-Pass Risk-Aware Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Tianhao Fu, Austin Wang, Charles Chen, Roby Aldave-Garza, Yucheng Chen
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is critical for medical image segmentation, where automated contours feed downstream quantification and clinical decision support. Many strong uncertainty methods require repeated inference, while efficient single-forward-pass alternatives often provide weaker failure ranking or rely on restrictive feature-space assumptions. We present $\textbf{SegWithU}$, a post-hoc framework that augments a frozen pretrained segmentation backbone with a lightweight uncertainty h

infographic.key_insight: SegWithU converts model uncertainty into a single-pass "perturbation energy" signal by adding a lightweight post-hoc head to a frozen segmentation backbone, enabling accurate risk-aware segmentation without repeated inference.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides reliable failure ranking and uncertainty maps for medical image segmentation while avoiding expensive multi-pass or restrictive feature-space assumptions, making uncertainty estimation practical for clinical workflows.
method: Post-hoc plug-in: attach a lightweight uncertainty head to a frozen, pretrained segmentation backbone (no re-training of main model required).
Uncertainty-as-energy: compute a perturbation-energy score from the head's outputs that correlates with segmentation failure risk in a single forward pass.
Efficient, backbone-agnostic design: produces calibrated uncertainty maps and risk rankings with minimal compute overhead, compatible with existing segmentation models.
infographic.impact: Delivers efficient, single-forward-pass uncertainty estimation that improves failure detection and triage in clinical pipelines, enabling safer deployment of automated segmentation without large latency or compute costs.

title: StreamCacheVGGT: Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers with Robust Scoring and Hybrid Cache Compression
authors: Xuanyi Liu, Deyi Ji, Chunan Yu, Qi Zhu, Xuanfu Li
abstract: Reconstructing dense 3D geometry from continuous video streams requires stable inference under a constant memory budget. Existing $O(1)$ frameworks primarily rely on a ``pure eviction'' paradigm, which suffers from significant information destruction due to binary token deletion and evaluation noise from localized, single-layer scoring. To address these bottlenecks, we propose StreamCacheVGGT, a training-free framework that reimagines cache management through two synergistic modules: Cross-Layer

infographic.key_insight: StreamCacheVGGT replaces binary token eviction with a training‑free, cross‑layer scoring plus hybrid compression scheme that preserves geometric information and yields stable, constant‑memory 3D reconstruction from video streams.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing O(1) streaming frameworks destroy useful information by hard‑evicting tokens and using noisy, single‑layer scores, causing unstable dense 3D geometry inference over long video sequences under fixed memory.
method: Cross‑Layer Robust Scoring: aggregate multi‑layer attention/activation signals (and temporal context) to produce stable, global importance scores for tokens instead of relying on single‑layer/localized metrics.

Hybrid Cache Compression: compress less‑important tokens via a mix of soft merging, low‑rank projection and lightweight quantization so information is retained in reduced form rather than being deleted.

Streaming, Training‑Free Integration: a plug‑and‑play cache manager for Visual Geometry Transformers that maintains O(1) memory budget while improving reconstruction stability and reducing evaluation noise.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, long‑duration dense 3D reconstruction on memory‑constrained devices without retraining, benefiting real‑time robotics, AR/VR, and edge deployment of vision transformer pipelines.

title: AD4AD: Benchmarking Visual Anomaly Detection Models for Safer Autonomous Driving
authors: Fabrizio Genilotti, Arianna Stropeni, Gionata Grotto, Francesco Borsatti, Manuel Barusco
abstract: The reliability of a machine vision system for autonomous driving depends heavily on its training data distribution. When a vehicle encounters significantly different conditions, such as atypical obstacles, its perceptual capabilities can degrade substantially. Unlike many domains where errors carry limited consequences, failures in autonomous driving translate directly into physical risk for passengers, pedestrians, and other road users. To address this challenge, we explore Visual Anomaly Dete

infographic.key_insight: A standardized benchmark (AD4AD) reveals how current visual anomaly detection models fail under real-world driving distribution shifts and provides a unified protocol and safety-oriented metrics to compare and improve them.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses unreliable perception in autonomous driving caused by out-of-distribution/rare visual anomalies (atypical obstacles, unusual weather/lighting) by creating a focused benchmark and evaluation protocol to measure model robustness and safety relevance.
method: Assemble a driving-focused anomaly dataset covering domain shifts (weather, lighting, rare objects) and realistic road hazards.
Define safety-driven evaluation metrics (detection, localization, false-negative penalty) and a standardized protocol for model comparison.
Evaluate state-of-the-art visual anomaly detection methods on the benchmark and analyze failure modes to guide improvements and deployment choices.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a practical toolset to compare AD models in driving scenarios, prioritize safety-relevant trade-offs, and make informed choices for dataset collection and model deployment to reduce real-world risk.

title: Bidirectional Cross-Modal Prompting for Event-Frame Asymmetric Stereo
authors: Ninghui Xu, Fabio Tosi, Lihui Wang, Jiawei Han, Luca Bartolomei
abstract: Conventional frame-based cameras capture rich contextual information but suffer from limited temporal resolution and motion blur in dynamic scenes. Event cameras offer an alternative visual representation with higher dynamic range free from such limitations. The complementary characteristics of the two modalities make event-frame asymmetric stereo promising for reliable 3D perception under fast motion and challenging illumination. However, the modality gap often leads to marginalization of domai

infographic.key_insight: Bidirectional cross-modal prompting lets event and frame streams actively modulate each other’s representations, closing the modality gap so asymmetric event-frame stereo produces more reliable 3D perception under fast motion and challenging illumination.
infographic.problem_solved: Integrates high-temporal-resolution event data with rich-context frame images for asymmetric stereo while overcoming the modality gap that normally causes one modality to be marginalized, leading to poor depth estimation in dynamic or low-light scenes.
method: Design lightweight bidirectional prompts that carry complementary cues between an event encoder and a frame encoder to align and enrich features.
Use cross-modal prompting layers to iteratively refine per-modality representations before fusion, preserving modality-specific strengths (temporal detail from events, context from frames).
Fuse the prompted features in a stereo/geometry-aware decoder to produce robust disparity/depth estimates under motion and illumination challenges.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to combine event cameras with conventional cameras for more robust stereo/3D perception in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and computational photography without heavy architecture changes. Improves reliability in high-speed and low-light environments where traditional frame-only methods fail.

title: LeapAlign: Post-Training Flow Matching Models at Any Generation Step by Building Two-Step Trajectories
authors: Zhanhao Liang, Tao Yang, Jie Wu, Chengjian Feng, Liang Zheng
abstract: This paper focuses on the alignment of flow matching models with human preferences. A promising way is fine-tuning by directly backpropagating reward gradients through the differentiable generation process of flow matching. However, backpropagating through long trajectories results in prohibitive memory costs and gradient explosion. Therefore, direct-gradient methods struggle to update early generation steps, which are crucial for determining the global structure of the final image. To address t

infographic.key_insight: LeapAlign enables reward-based fine-tuning of flow-matching generative models at any generation step by building two-step (leap) trajectories, allowing gradients to reach early steps without the memory blowup or gradient explosion of backpropagating through long trajectories.
infographic.problem_solved: Directly backpropagating reward gradients through long flow-matching generation trajectories is memory-intensive and unstable, preventing effective updates to early steps that determine global image structure.
method: Construct short two-step “leap” trajectories that bridge distant generation states so gradient signals can be propagated across long horizons with only local (two-step) backpropagation.
Perform post-training reward fine-tuning through these two-step transitions to stabilize gradients and dramatically reduce memory requirements compared to full-trajectory backpropagation.
Apply the leap mechanism at arbitrary generation steps so early- and mid-stage updates are possible without retraining or truncating the full generation process.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, memory-efficient way to align flow-matching generative models with human preferences and to improve global structure in generated outputs—useful for practitioners who need targeted post-training edits without heavy compute or instability.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: full long trajectory backprop (many steps) vs LeapAlign two-step leap connecting distant states
Flowchart of the LeapAlign fine-tuning loop showing reward evaluation, two-step trajectory construction, and backpropagation

title: How Do LLMs and VLMs Understand Viewpoint Rotation Without Vision? An Interpretability Study
authors: Zhen Yang, Ping Jian, Zhongbin Guo, Zuming Zhang, Chengzhi Li
abstract: Over the past year, spatial intelligence has drawn increasing attention. Many prior works study it from the perspective of visual-spatial intelligence, where models have access to visuospatial information from visual inputs. However, in the absence of visual information, whether linguistic intelligence alone is sufficient to endow models with spatial intelligence, and how models perform relevant tasks with text-only inputs still remain unexplored. Therefore, in this paper, we focus on a fundamen

infographic.key_insight: Language-only models can partially perform viewpoint-rotation reasoning without visual inputs, and interpretability analyses reveal which internal components and linguistic cues enable this capability.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines whether and how models reason about 3D viewpoint changes when only given text (no images), clarifying the limits and mechanisms of spatial intelligence in LLMs versus VLMs.
method: Construct a text-only benchmark of viewpoint-rotation tasks and contrast performance of LLMs and VLMs given identical linguistic descriptions.

Use interpretability tools (probing classifiers, attention and activation analysis, interventions) to identify representations, attention patterns, and neurons correlated with viewpoint transformations.
Ablation and controlled prompt experiments to test which linguistic cues and model components are necessary or sufficient for correct rotation reasoning.
infographic.impact: Helps practitioners understand when language models can substitute for vision in spatial tasks, guiding design of multimodal systems, benchmarks, and targeted interventions to improve spatial reasoning or avoid failure modes.

title: AnimationBench: Are Video Models Good at Character-Centric Animation?
authors: Leyi Wu, Pengjun Fang, Kai Sun, Yazhou Xing, Yinwei Wu
abstract: Video generation has advanced rapidly, with recent methods producing increasingly convincing animated results. However, existing benchmarks-largely designed for realistic videos-struggle to evaluate animation-style generation with its stylized appearance, exaggerated motion, and character-centric consistency. Moreover, they also rely on fixed prompt sets and rigid pipelines, offering limited flexibility for open-domain content and custom evaluation needs. To address this gap, we introduce Animat

infographic.key_insight: AnimationBench provides the first flexible, character-centric benchmark tailored to animation-style video generation, enabling rigorous evaluation of stylized appearance, exaggerated motion, and character consistency across open-domain content.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video benchmarks are built for realistic videos and use fixed prompts and rigid pipelines, making them unsuitable for assessing animation-specific challenges like stylization, expressive motion, and character-centric continuity.
method: Curate an animation-focused evaluation corpus and flexible prompt sets that cover diverse styles, characters, and exaggerated motions.
Introduce character-centric metrics and evaluation protocols (e.g., identity/pose consistency, stylization fidelity, motion exaggeration) designed for animated content.
Provide an open, modular toolkit that supports custom prompts, automated scoring, and human-in-the-loop assessment for open-domain and application-specific evaluation.
infographic.impact: AnimationBench fills a critical evaluation gap, giving researchers and practitioners a standardized, animation-aware way to compare and improve video generation models and to better align metrics with perceptual quality for character-driven animation.

title: Seedance 2.0: Advancing Video Generation for World Complexity
authors: Team Seedance, De Chen, Liyang Chen, Xin Chen, Ying Chen
abstract: Seedance 2.0 is a new native multi-modal audio-video generation model, officially released in China in early February 2026. Compared with its predecessors, Seedance 1.0 and 1.5 Pro, Seedance 2.0 adopts a unified, highly efficient, and large-scale architecture for multi-modal audio-video joint generation. This allows it to support four input modalities: text, image, audio, and video, by integrating one of the most comprehensive suites of multi-modal content reference and editing capabilities avai

infographic.key_insight: Seedance 2.0 introduces a unified, large-scale audio–video generation architecture that natively supports multi-modal conditioning (text, image, audio, video), enabling joint generation and comprehensive content reference/editing in a single model.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges fragmented multimodal video generation workflows by providing a single, efficient model that accepts diverse inputs and performs joint audio–video synthesis and editing, reducing the need for separate specialized pipelines.
method: Unified, large-scale architecture for joint audio–video generation that handles four input modalities: text, image, audio, and video.
Highly efficient model design and training to scale multimodal generation while enabling integrated reference and editing capabilities.
End-to-end inference that combines conditional synthesis and multimodal content editing within one system (replacing piecemeal pipelines).
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to build more flexible, production-ready multimodal video workflows with fewer moving parts, accelerating research and content creation that requires synchronized audio and visual control.

title: SpatialEvo: Self-Evolving Spatial Intelligence via Deterministic Geometric Environments
authors: Dinging Li, Yingxiu Zhao, Xinrui Cheng, Kangheng Lin, Hongbo Peng
abstract: Spatial reasoning over three-dimensional scenes is a core capability for embodied intelligence, yet continuous model improvement remains bottlenecked by the cost of geometric annotation. The self-evolving paradigm offers a promising path, but its reliance on model consensus to construct pseudo-labels causes training to reinforce rather than correct the model's own geometric errors. We identify a property unique to 3D spatial reasoning that circumvents this limitation: ground truth is a determini

infographic.key_insight: Deterministic geometric environments provide provably correct, environment-derived supervision for 3D spatial tasks, enabling models to self-evolve without the consensus-based reinforcement of their own errors. This turns procedural geometry and analytic feedback into reliable pseudo-ground-truth for continuous improvement.
infographic.problem_solved: Eliminates reliance on costly manual 3D geometric annotation and avoids the failure mode of consensus-driven pseudo-labeling that reinforces existing spatial errors in models.
method: Procedurally generate deterministic 3D geometric environments that yield analytic ground-truth signals (e.g., exact intersections, distances, occlusion labels).
Run the model inside these environments to collect deterministic feedback and apply geometric-consistency checks to validate or correct pseudo-labels.
Iteratively retrain the model in a self-evolving loop (with curriculum/domain randomization) so it improves autonomously while avoiding self-reinforced errors.
infographic.impact: Makes scalable, low-cost continuous improvement of spatial reasoning models feasible, accelerating progress for robotics, AR/VR, and 3D perception systems by replacing expensive annotation with reliable environment-derived supervision.
visual_elements: Self-evolution loop diagram: procedural environment → model action/prediction → deterministic feedback/analytic labels → model update.

title: One Token per Highly Selective Frame: Towards Extreme Compression for Long Video Understanding
authors: Zheyu Zhang, Ziqi Pang, Shixing Chen, Xiang Hao, Vimal Bhat
abstract: Long video understanding is inherently challenging for vision-language models (VLMs) because of the extensive number of frames. With each video frame typically expanding into tens or hundreds of tokens, the limited context length of large language models (LLMs) forces the VLMs to perceive the frames sparsely and lose temporal information. To address this, we explore extreme video token compression towards \emph{one token per frame} at the final LLM layer. Our key insight is that heuristic-based

infographic.key_insight: Compress each highly informative frame into a single learned token so large language models can process very long videos without losing key temporal information, enabling extreme token reduction with minimal performance loss.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the scalability bottleneck of vision–language models on long videos caused by huge per-frame token counts and limited LLM context, which forces sparse sampling and loses temporal cues.
method: Selective frame scoring: identify a small set of highly informative frames from the full video using learned or heuristic importance metrics.
Per-frame extreme compression: convert each selected frame into a single compact token via a learnable visual tokenizer/pooled embedding that preserves semantic and temporal signals.
Train end-to-end (or with distillation/objective constraints) so the compressed tokens retain downstream task performance while reducing token budget to ~1 token/frame at the LLM input.
infographic.impact: Enables efficient, scalable long-video understanding with existing LLM backbones by drastically reducing token load, lowering compute and memory costs while maintaining temporal awareness—useful for video QA, summarization, and retrieval at scale.

title: Interpretable Stylistic Variation in Human and LLM Writing Across Genres, Models, and Decoding Strategies
authors: Swati Rallapalli, Shannon Gallagher, Ronald Yurko, Tyler Brooks, Chuck Loughin
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now capable of generating highly fluent, human-like text. They enable many applications, but also raise concerns such as large scale spam, phishing, or academic misuse. While much work has focused on detecting LLM-generated text, only limited work has gone into understanding the stylistic differences between human-written and machine-generated text. In this work, we perform a large scale analysis of stylistic variation across human-written text and outputs from 1

infographic.key_insight: Interpretable stylistic features reveal consistent, quantifiable differences between human and LLM-generated text across genres, models, and decoding strategies, enabling explainable characterization of stylistic variation.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between binary detection and understanding by systematically measuring and interpreting how writing style varies between humans and LLMs (and across models/decoding), making stylistic differences actionable and explainable.
method: Assemble a large, genre-balanced corpus of human-written text and LLM outputs from multiple models and decoding strategies.
Extract interpretable stylistic features (lexical, syntactic, discourse, surprisal/entropy metrics) and quantify differences using statistical analysis.
Visualize style spaces and train simple classifiers/attribution analyses to link specific features to models, genres, and decoding methods.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with explainable diagnostics for model evaluation, detection, and safe deployment—helping tune decoders, audit outputs by genre, and design interpretable defenses against misuse.

title: UI-Zoomer: Uncertainty-Driven Adaptive Zoom-In for GUI Grounding
authors: Fei Tang, Bofan Chen, Zhengxi Lu, Tongbo Chen, Songqin Nong
abstract: GUI grounding, which localizes interface elements from screenshots given natural language queries, remains challenging for small icons and dense layouts. Test-time zoom-in methods improve localization by cropping and re-running inference at higher resolution, but apply cropping uniformly across all instances with fixed crop sizes, ignoring whether the model is actually uncertain on each case. We propose \textbf{UI-Zoomer}, a training-free adaptive zoom-in framework that treats both the trigger a

infographic.key_insight: UI-Zoomer uses model uncertainty at test time to decide whether and where to crop and re-run inference, adaptively zooming only when the model is unsure to improve localization of small icons and dense GUI layouts — without any extra training.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing test-time zoom-in methods apply fixed, uniform crops for all inputs, wasting compute and often missing tiny or densely packed interface elements. UI-Zoomer targets zooming to only the uncertain cases, improving accuracy on small/dense elements while avoiding unnecessary inference.
method: Estimate per-instance uncertainty from the base GUI grounding model at test time (e.g., low-confidence / high-entropy predictions).
If uncertainty exceeds a threshold, compute an adaptive crop region and re-run inference at higher resolution; otherwise keep the original prediction.
Merge or replace predictions from the zoomed crop back into the full-screen coordinates to produce final localized UI elements.
infographic.impact: Delivers better localization for small icons and cluttered interfaces with less average compute overhead, and can be dropped into existing GUI grounding pipelines because it requires no retraining.
visual_elements: Pipeline flowchart: screenshot → model inference → uncertainty check → conditional crop & zoom → fused output.
Before/after example: full-screen detection vs adaptive zoom detection highlighting recovered small icons.

title: Momentum Further Constrains Sharpness at the Edge of Stochastic Stability
authors: Arseniy Andreyev, Advikar Ananthkumar, Marc Walden, Tomaso Poggio, Pierfrancesco Beneventano
abstract: Recent work suggests that (stochastic) gradient descent self-organizes near an instability boundary, shaping both optimization and the solutions found. Momentum and mini-batch gradients are widely used in practical deep learning optimization, but it remains unclear whether they operate in a comparable regime of instability. We demonstrate that SGD with momentum exhibits an Edge of Stochastic Stability (EoSS)-like regime with batch-size-dependent behavior that cannot be explained by a single mome

infographic.key_insight: SGD with momentum operates in an Edge of Stochastic Stability (EoSS)-like regime: momentum and mini-batch size jointly shift the instability boundary and further constrain model sharpness near that edge, producing batch-size-dependent optimization behavior.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how momentum interacts with stochastic gradients to shape the stability boundary and the sharpness of solutions — resolving whether momentum-driven training lives in the same instability regime previously observed for plain SGD.
method: Theoretical analysis characterizing stability boundaries for SGD with momentum under stochastic mini-batch noise.
Empirical experiments varying momentum and batch size to map sharpness, instability thresholds, and resulting training trajectories.
Comparative evaluation showing batch-size-dependent effects that cannot be captured by a single momentum-only explanation.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a clearer framework for tuning momentum, learning rate, and batch size to control sharpness and stability during training, improving optimization reliability and potentially generalization.
visual_elements: Stability boundary diagram: phase plot showing stable vs unstable regions in (learning rate, momentum) space annotated with EoSS.
Heatmap of sharpness vs (batch size, momentum): highlights batch-size-dependent constraint on sharpness.
Training trajectory overlay in loss vs sharpness plane: shows paths attracted to the instability edge with and without momentum.

title: From $P(y|x)$ to $P(y)$: Investigating Reinforcement Learning in Pre-train Space
authors: Yuqiao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Bo Liu, Zichen Liu, Tian Liang
abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) significantly enhances LLM reasoning by optimizing the conditional distribution P(y|x), its potential is fundamentally bounded by the base model's existing output distribution. Optimizing the marginal distribution P(y) in the Pre-train Space addresses this bottleneck by encoding reasoning ability and preserving broad exploration capacity. Yet, conventional pre-training relies on static corpora for passive learning, leading to a distribu

infographic.key_insight: Optimize the marginal output distribution P(y) by applying reinforcement learning in the pre-train space, so reasoning ability becomes encoded as a prior rather than being limited by the base model's conditional outputs P(y|x). This unlocks broader exploration and higher ceiling for downstream RL fine-tuning.
infographic.problem_solved: Reinforcement learning that optimizes P(y|x) (RLVR) is constrained by the base model's output distribution, preventing discovery of richer reasoning behaviors and limiting improvement.
method: Reframe the training objective from conditional P(y|x) optimization to marginal P(y) optimization in the pre-train space.
Apply reinforcement learning signals (verifiable rewards) during pre-training/representation shaping to encode reasoning priors into the model's marginal distribution.
Preserve exploration by augmenting pre-train signals or dynamics so the model can generate diverse candidate outputs rather than remain bounded by static corpora.
infographic.impact: Encodes reasoning ability as a model-level prior, raising the attainable performance when later fine-tuning with RLVR and improving generalization to novel tasks. Practitioners can overcome base-model distributional ceilings and get more robust downstream reasoning with the same RL toolkit.
visual_elements: Comparison diagram: narrow P(y|x)-centered distribution (pre-RLVR) vs. broadened/more capable P(y) after pre-train-space RL
Pipeline flowchart: pre-training -> RL in pre-train (representation) space -> downstream RLVR fine-tuning

title: Geometric Context Transformer for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
authors: Lin-Zhuo Chen, Jian Gao, Yihang Chen, Ka Leong Cheng, Yipengjing Sun
abstract:
Streaming 3D reconstruction aims to recover 3D information, such as camera poses and point clouds, from a video stream, which necessitates geometric accuracy, temporal
  consistency, and computational efficiency. Motivated by the principles of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), we introduce LingBot-Map, a feed-forward 3D foundation
  model for reconstructing scenes from streaming data, built upon a geometric context transformer (GCT) architecture. A defining aspect of LingBot-Map lies

infographic.key_insight: LingBot-Map introduces a feed-forward Geometric Context Transformer (GCT) that encodes geometric and temporal context from a video stream to produce accurate, temporally consistent 3D reconstructions in real time.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables streaming 3D reconstruction that balances geometric accuracy, temporal consistency, and computational efficiency for recovering camera poses and point clouds from continuous video.
method: Geometric Context Transformer (GCT): transformer blocks operate on geometric tokens (pose, depth, and feature embeddings) to fuse spatial and temporal context across frames.
Feed-forward SLAM-inspired pipeline: single-pass inference that predicts camera poses and incremental point-cloud updates without expensive iterative optimization.
Memory- and compute-efficient temporal aggregation: compact history representation and geometric-consistency losses/modules to maintain low latency and stable reconstructions.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical foundation model for real-time 3D perception that can be integrated into robotics, AR/VR, and autonomous systems, reducing reliance on heavy optimization-based SLAM while preserving geometric fidelity.

title: TREX: Automating LLM Fine-tuning via Agent-Driven Tree-based Exploration
authors: Zerun Ma, Guoqiang Wang, Xinchen Xie, Yicheng Chen, He Du
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have empowered AI research agents to perform isolated scientific tasks, automating complex, real-world workflows, such as LLM training, remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce TREX, a multi-agent system that automates the entire LLM training life-cycle. By orchestrating collaboration between two core modules-the Researcher and the Executor-the system seamlessly performs requirement analysis, open-domain literature and data research, formula

infographic.key_insight: TREX automates the end-to-end LLM fine-tuning lifecycle by coordinating a Researcher agent (design & search) and an Executor agent (data, training, eval) using a tree-based exploration strategy to systematically explore and refine training choices.
infographic.problem_solved: Manual LLM fine-tuning is time-consuming, error-prone, and fragmented across literature review, dataset curation, experiment design, hyperparameter search, and orchestration; TREX addresses the lack of an end-to-end automated system for these tasks.
method: Agent-based architecture: a Researcher agent formulates requirements, generates candidate experiments and hypotheses while an Executor agent runs data collection, training, and evaluations.
Tree-based exploration: organize the design space as a branching tree of configurations and decisions to systematically explore, prune, and refine promising paths.
Iterative feedback loop: automated evaluation signals guide the Researcher to propose refinements, enabling automated experiment selection, reproducibility, and pipeline orchestration.
infographic.impact: TREX can drastically reduce human effort and cycle time for LLM fine-tuning, making experimentation more systematic, reproducible, and scalable for practitioners and researchers.

title: Correct Prediction, Wrong Steps? Consensus Reasoning Knowledge Graph for Robust Chain-of-Thought Synthesis
authors: Zipeng Ling, Shuliang Liu, Shenghong Fu, Yuehao Tang, Seonil Son
abstract: LLM reasoning traces suffer from complex flaws -- *Step Internal Flaws* (logical errors, hallucinations, etc.) and *Step-wise Flaws* (overthinking, underthinking), which vary by sample. A natural approach would be to provide ground-truth labels to guide LLMs' reasoning. Contrary to intuition, we show that this yields no improvement in reasoning ability. We then propose CRAFT, a unified framework that mitigates both types of Step flaws, which builds a Reasoning Knowledge Graph (RKG) based on the

infographic.key_insight: Providing ground-truth labels for reasoning traces does not improve LLM reasoning; instead, aggregating multiple chains into a Consensus Reasoning Knowledge Graph (RKG) and synthesizing consensus chains (CRAFT) mitigates both internal logical errors and step‑wise flaws.
infographic.problem_solved: Chain-of-thought outputs from LLMs contain two varying, interrelated failure modes — Step Internal Flaws (logical errors, hallucinations) and Step-wise Flaws (overthinking, underthinking) — that make reasoning brittle and hard to correct with simple labeling.
method: Construct a Reasoning Knowledge Graph (RKG) from multiple chain-of-thought traces, representing reasoning steps as nodes and relations as edges to capture alternative justifications and contradictions.
Detect and downweight/prune inconsistent or low-consensus nodes and step patterns across traces to reduce internal logical errors and step‑wise pathologies.
Synthesize robust chain-of-thoughts by extracting high-consensus paths from the RKG and iteratively refining them (CRAFT) to produce corrected, stable reasoning traces.
infographic.impact: CRAFT produces more reliable, interpretable reasoning traces without relying on ground-truth step labels, improving the robustness of downstream LLM decision-making and making evaluation/debugging of reasoning behavior more actionable for practitioners.

title: LongCoT: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
authors: Sumeet Ramesh Motwani, Daniel Nichols, Charles London, Peggy Li, Fabio Pizzati
abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed for complex autonomous tasks, their ability to reason accurately over longer horizons becomes critical. An essential component of this ability is planning and managing a long, complex chain-of-thought (CoT). We introduce LongCoT, a scalable benchmark of 2,500 expert-designed problems spanning chemistry, mathematics, computer science, chess, and logic to isolate and directly measure the long-horizon CoT reasoning capabilities of frontier models. Proble

infographic.key_insight: LongCoT provides a focused, scalable benchmark of 2,500 expert-designed problems that isolates and directly measures long-horizon chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning across multiple domains, enabling consistent evaluation of frontier models' planning and multi-step reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of standardized, domain-diverse evaluation for long-horizon CoT reasoning—making it hard to quantify and compare how well models plan and manage extended multi-step chains of thought.
method: Assemble 2,500 expert-designed problems spanning chemistry, mathematics, computer science, chess, and logic to stress long-horizon reasoning.
Design evaluation protocols and metrics that isolate long-chain planning ability (e.g., multi-step dependency depth, horizon length) from short-term reasoning and retrieval.
Provide a scalable benchmark infrastructure for automated evaluation of frontier LLMs under controlled long-horizon CoT conditions.
infographic.impact: Offers practitioners a standardized tool to diagnose, compare, and improve models' long-horizon planning and reasoning, accelerating development of LLMs safe and reliable for complex autonomous tasks.

title: HiVLA: A Visual-Grounded-Centric Hierarchical Embodied Manipulation System
authors: Tianshuo Yang, Guanyu Chen, Yutian Chen, Zhixuan Liang, Yitian Liu
abstract: While end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, fine-tuning them on narrow control data often compromises the profound reasoning capabilities inherited from their base Vision-Language Models (VLMs). To resolve this fundamental trade-off, we propose HiVLA, a visual-grounded-centric hierarchical framework that explicitly decouples high-level semantic planning from low-level motor control. In high-level part, a VLM planner first performs tas

infographic.key_insight: HiVLA separates high-level semantic reasoning (a VLM planner) from low-level motor control via explicit visual grounding, preserving VLM reasoning while enabling robust, specialized control.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the trade-off where fine-tuning end-to-end Vision-Language-Action models for control degrades their VLM-inherited reasoning and generalization, making it hard to get both strong semantic planning and reliable motor execution.
method: Hierarchical design: a VLM-based high-level planner generates task steps and goals in semantic, scene-aware language.
Visual-grounding module: maps planner outputs to scene-centric signals (object masks, keypoints, affordance maps) to localize goals in the current view.
Modular low-level controller: a dedicated motion/controller module consumes grounded signals to execute actions; modules are trained or fine-tuned separately to preserve VLM reasoning.
infographic.impact: Enables modular, sample-efficient embodied manipulation that retains advanced VLM reasoning while achieving reliable motor performance—useful for building interpretable, generalizable robotic systems and reducing catastrophic fine-tuning effects.

title: Visual Preference Optimization with Rubric Rewards
authors: Ya-Qi Yu, Fangyu Hong, Xiangyang Qu, Hao Wang, Gaojie Wu
abstract: The effectiveness of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) depends on preference data that reflect the quality differences that matter in multimodal tasks. Existing pipelines often rely on off-policy perturbations or coarse outcome-based signals, which are not well suited to fine-grained visual reasoning. We propose rDPO, a preference optimization framework based on instance-specific rubrics. For each image-instruction pair, we create a checklist-style rubric of essential and additional criteria

infographic.key_insight: Instance-specific, checklist-style rubrics can turn coarse preference signals into fine-grained rewards, enabling Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to better capture subtle visual reasoning differences. rDPO uses these rubric rewards to align multimodal model outputs with what actually matters per image-instruction pair.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing preference-data pipelines rely on off-policy perturbations or coarse outcome signals that fail to capture fine-grained visual criteria, hurting preference optimization for multimodal tasks.
method: Generate an instance-specific rubric (checklist of essential and additional criteria) for each image-instruction pair to define what 'good' means locally.
Translate rubric assessments into reward/preference signals that reflect fine-grained visual reasoning rather than coarse outcomes.
Apply Direct Preference Optimization using these rubric-derived rewards (rDPO) to train multimodal models with more meaningful preference supervision.
infographic.impact: rDPO provides practitioners a practical way to produce higher-quality preference data for vision-language tasks, improving alignment and evaluation on subtle visual reasoning aspects without relying on brittle perturbation schemes.

title: Toward Autonomous Long-Horizon Engineering for ML Research
authors: Guoxin Chen, Jie Chen, Lei Chen, Jiale Zhao, Fanzhe Meng
abstract: Autonomous AI research has advanced rapidly, but long-horizon ML research engineering remains difficult: agents must sustain coherent progress across task comprehension, environment setup, implementation, experimentation, and debugging over hours or days. We introduce AiScientist, a system for autonomous long-horizon engineering for ML research built on a simple principle: strong long-horizon performance requires both structured orchestration and durable state continuity. To this end, AiScientis

infographic.key_insight: AiScientist shows that robust autonomous long-horizon ML engineering requires both structured orchestration of multi-step research workflows and durable state continuity so progress persists across hours or days.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap in autonomous AI research for sustained, coherent execution of complex ML workflows (task understanding, environment setup, implementation, experimentation, debugging) over long time horizons where transient agents typically lose context or fail to coordinate multi-stage work.
method: Structured orchestration: hierarchical planning and workflow decomposition to coordinate multi-step research tasks end-to-end (comprehension → setup → coding → experiments → debugging).
Durable state continuity: persistent workspace, versioned checkpoints, and long-term memory that preserve context, artifacts, logs, and partial progress across sessions.
Tool and experiment automation: integrated tooling for environment provisioning, reproducible experiment execution, automated evaluation and iterative debugging driven by the orchestrator.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and engineering teams to offload routine, long-running ML engineering work to an autonomous system, increasing throughput, reproducibility, and consistency of experimental pipelines while reducing manual context-switching and lost progress.

title: ROSE: An Intent-Centered Evaluation Metric for NL2SQL
authors: Wenqi Pei, Shizheng Hou, Boyan Li, Han Chen, Zhichao Shi
abstract: Execution Accuracy (EX), the widely used metric for evaluating the effectiveness of Natural Language to SQL (NL2SQL) solutions, is becoming increasingly unreliable. It is sensitive to syntactic variation, ignores that questions may admit multiple interpretations, and is easily misled by erroneous ground-truth SQL. To address this, we introduce ROSE, an intent-centered metric that focuses on whether the predicted SQL answers the question, rather than consistency with the ground-truth SQL under th

infographic.key_insight: ROSE reframes NL2SQL evaluation around user intent: it judges a predicted SQL by whether it answers the natural-language question, not by syntactic match to a possibly flawed ground-truth SQL. This produces a more robust, interpretation-aware accuracy signal.
infographic.problem_solved: Execution Accuracy (EX) is brittle—sensitive to SQL syntax, blind to multiple valid interpretations, and easily misled by erroneous ground-truth SQL—so ROSE provides a reliable alternative that focuses on intent-level correctness.
method: Center evaluation on question intent: determine whether the predicted SQL fulfills the question’s intent rather than matching ground-truth SQL text.
Compare outcomes at the answer/intent level (e.g., result equivalence, intent alignment) so semantically equivalent but syntactically different SQLs are treated as correct.
Design robustness to ambiguous questions and noisy ground-truth by accommodating multiple valid interpretations and ignoring superficial SQL differences.
infographic.impact: ROSE yields more trustworthy model comparisons, uncovers evaluation false negatives caused by ground-truth errors, and guides practitioners toward models that actually satisfy user intent rather than models that mimic dataset annotations.

title: Evolution of Optimization Methods: Algorithms, Scenarios, and Evaluations
authors: Tong Zhang, Jiangning Zhang, Zhucun Xue, Juntao Jiang, Yicheng Xu
abstract: Balancing convergence speed, generalization capability, and computational efficiency remains a core challenge in deep learning optimization. First-order gradient descent methods, epitomized by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Adam, serve as the cornerstone of modern training pipelines. However, large-scale model training, stringent differential privacy requirements, and distributed learning paradigms expose critical limitations in these conventional approaches regarding privacy protection a

infographic.key_insight: This paper consolidates the evolution of optimization methods into a practical taxonomy and evaluation protocol, revealing how choices of optimizers interact with scale, privacy constraints, and distributed setups to trade off convergence, generalization, and compute efficiency.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the lack of unified guidance and standardized evaluations for choosing and tuning optimization algorithms across modern scenarios — large-scale models, differential privacy, and distributed training — where conventional optimizers (e.g., SGD, Adam) show distinct and sometimes conflicting limitations.
method: Survey and taxonomy: map historical and recent optimizer designs (first-order, adaptive, momentum variants) and categorize them by strengths/weaknesses.
Scenario-driven empirical evaluation: benchmark optimizers across representative settings (large-scale training, privacy-preserving SGD, and distributed/federated learning) using consistent metrics.
Practical protocols and recommendations: define evaluation metrics and configuration guidelines to select and tune optimizers depending on target trade-offs (speed, generalization, compute, privacy).
infographic.impact: Provides ML practitioners and system designers with an actionable framework to pick and tune optimizers for specific production constraints, improving training efficiency, robustness to privacy requirements, and scalability in distributed environments.

title: Generative Refinement Networks for Visual Synthesis
authors: Jian Han, Jinlai Liu, Jiahuan Wang, Bingyue Peng, Zehuan Yuan
abstract: While diffusion models dominate the field of visual generation, they are computationally inefficient, applying a uniform computational effort regardless of different complexity. In contrast, autoregressive (AR) models are inherently complexity-aware, as evidenced by their variable likelihoods, but are often hindered by lossy discrete tokenization and error accumulation. In this work, we introduce Generative Refinement Networks (GRN), a next-generation visual synthesis paradigm to address these i

infographic.key_insight: Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) combine the complexity-aware allocation of autoregressive models with continuous, iterative refinement to produce high-quality images using far fewer refinement steps than standard diffusion pipelines.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between computationally expensive, uniform-step diffusion methods and lossy, token-based autoregressive models by enabling token-free, variable compute per region and progressive error-correcting refinements.
method: Iterative refinement backbone: generate an initial continuous image representation and apply a small number of learned refinement modules that correct and sharpen content progressively.
Complexity-aware scheduling: use model-estimated difficulty / likelihood signals to allocate more refinement steps to challenging regions and fewer to simple regions, reducing wasted computation.

Hybrid training objectives: combine reconstruction, perceptual and adversarial-style losses (or likelihood proxies) so refinements preserve fidelity while avoiding discrete tokenization and error accumulation.
infographic.impact: GRN enables more compute-efficient high-quality visual synthesis by adapting effort to image complexity, making state-of-the-art generation cheaper and faster for both research and deployment in resource-constrained settings.

title: PAL: Personal Adaptive Learner
authors: Megha Chakraborty, Darssan L. Eswaramoorthi, Madhur Thareja, Het Riteshkumar Shah, Finlay Palmer
abstract: AI-driven education platforms have made some progress in personalisation, yet most remain constrained to static adaptation--predefined quizzes, uniform pacing, or generic feedback--limiting their ability to respond to learners' evolving understanding. This shortfall highlights the need for systems that are both context-aware and adaptive in real time. We introduce PAL (Personal Adaptive Learner), an AI-powered platform that transforms lecture videos into interactive learning experiences. PAL con

infographic.key_insight: PAL converts lecture videos into interactive, context-aware learning sessions that adapt in real time to a learner’s evolving understanding, moving beyond static personalization to continuous, on-the-fly adaptation.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the limits of static adaptation in AI-driven education (predefined quizzes, fixed pacing, generic feedback) by enabling real-time, context-aware adjustments that respond to learners’ changing knowledge and engagement.
method: Multimodal ingestion of lecture videos (audio, transcript, slides) to extract concepts, timestamps, and question opportunities.
Learner modeling + real-time feedback loop: track performance and engagement metrics to select or generate microactivities, hints, and pacing adjustments on the fly.
Adaptive UI/runtime orchestration to deliver interactive elements (inline quizzes, summaries, targeted hints) and update content sequencing based on inferred learner state.
infographic.impact: PAL demonstrates a practical path for deploying real-time personalization in educational systems, offering ML practitioners a template for combining multimodal understanding, online learner models, and adaptive UX to boost engagement and learning outcomes.

title: GlotOCR Bench: OCR Models Still Struggle Beyond a Handful of Unicode Scripts
authors: Amir Hossein Kargaran, Nafiseh Nikeghbal, Jana Diesner, François Yvon, Hinrich Schütze
abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) has advanced rapidly with the rise of vision-language models, yet evaluation has remained concentrated on a small cluster of high- and mid-resource scripts. We introduce GlotOCR Bench, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating OCR generalization across 100+ Unicode scripts. Our benchmark comprises clean and degraded image variants rendered from real multilingual texts. Images are rendered using fonts from the Google Fonts repository, shaped with HarfBuzz and raster

infographic.key_insight: GlotOCR Bench shows that modern OCR systems still generalize poorly beyond a small set of high- and mid-resource Unicode scripts by providing a standardized evaluation across 100+ scripts using real multilingual text renderings.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of comprehensive, multilingual OCR evaluation — current benchmarks focus on a few scripts, hiding failures on many low-resource and diverse-script languages.
method: Assemble a benchmark covering 100+ Unicode scripts drawn from real multilingual texts.
Render images using Google Fonts with HarfBuzz shaping and rasterization, producing both clean and degraded variants to simulate real-world conditions.
Evaluate existing OCR models across scripts and image degradations to quantify generalization gaps and reveal script-specific failure modes.
infographic.impact: Provides a reproducible, wide-coverage evaluation that helps practitioners identify where OCR models fail, prioritize resources for underrepresented scripts, and drive development of more inclusive OCR systems.

title: LogicEval: A Systematic Framework for Evaluating Automated Repair Techniques for Logical Vulnerabilities in Real-World Software
authors: Syed Md Mukit Rashid, Abdullah Al Ishtiaq, Kai Tu, Yilu Dong, Tianwei Wu
abstract: Logical vulnerabilities in software stem from flaws in program logic rather than memory safety, which can lead to critical security failures. Although existing automated program repair techniques primarily focus on repairing memory corruption vulnerabilities, they struggle with logical vulnerabilities because of their limited semantic understanding of the vulnerable code and its expected behavior. On the other hand, recent successes of large language models (LLMs) in understanding and repairing

infographic.key_insight: LogicEval provides a standardized, reproducible framework for measuring how well automated repair techniques handle logical (semantic) vulnerabilities in real-world software, exposing the need for semantics-aware approaches beyond traditional memory-focused APR methods.
infographic.problem_solved: There is no consistent way to evaluate and compare automated repair tools on logical vulnerabilities—bugs that arise from flawed program logic rather than memory errors—so practitioners lack benchmarks, metrics, and tooling to judge real-world repair effectiveness.
method: Curate a real-world dataset and taxonomy of logical vulnerabilities with ground-truth repairs to serve as a benchmark.

Define a reproducible evaluation pipeline and metrics (e.g., semantic correctness, functional/regression checks, security impact, precision/recall) to test classical APR and LLM-based repair approaches.
Support human-in-the-loop validation and standardized reporting so results are comparable, explainable, and actionable for tool developers.
infographic.impact: By standardizing datasets, metrics, and evaluation pipelines, LogicEval helps AI/ML practitioners identify which repair techniques actually fix semantics-driven bugs, accelerate development of more effective, semantics-aware models, and improve software security in production systems.

title: Bilevel Late Acceptance Hill Climbing for the Electric Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
authors: Yinghao Qin, Mosab Bazargani, Edmund K. Burke, Carlos A. Coello Coello, Zhongmin Song
abstract: This paper tackles the Electric Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (E-CVRP) through a bilevel optimization framework that handles routing and charging decisions separately or jointly depending on the search stage. By analyzing their interaction, we introduce a surrogate objective at the upper level to guide the search and accelerate convergence. A bilevel Late Acceptance Hill Climbing algorithm (b-LAHC) is introduced that operates through three phases: greedy descent, neighborhood exploration,

infographic.key_insight: A bilevel Late Acceptance Hill Climbing (b-LAHC) separates routing and charging decisions and introduces a surrogate upper-level objective to steer the search, accelerating convergence and improving solution quality for the Electric Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (E-CVRP).
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the coupled, large-scale combinatorial challenge of jointly optimizing vehicle routes and charging schedules for electric fleets, where direct joint search is costly and prone to poor local optima.
method: Bilevel framework: upper level guides routing with a surrogate objective while the lower level evaluates/refines charging feasibility and energy constraints.

b-LAHC metaheuristic: a Late Acceptance Hill Climbing algorithm operating in three phases—greedy descent, neighborhood exploration, and bilevel joint refinement—to escape local minima and accelerate search.
Surrogate objective design to capture routing–charging interaction approximately, enabling faster evaluations and more effective guidance of the search.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, scalable metaheuristic for EV routing that reduces search time and yields higher-quality feasible solutions; useful for AI/ML practitioners building real-world route-planning or hybrid optimization systems where evaluation cost and constraint coupling are bottlenecks.

title: Lyra 2.0: Explorable Generative 3D Worlds
authors: Tianchang Shen, Sherwin Bahmani, Kai He, Sangeetha Grama Srinivasan, Tianshi Cao
abstract: Recent advances in video generation enable a new paradigm for 3D scene creation: generating camera-controlled videos that simulate scene walkthroughs, then lifting them to 3D via feed-forward reconstruction techniques. This generative reconstruction approach combines the visual fidelity and creative capacity of video models with 3D outputs ready for real-time rendering and simulation. Scaling to large, complex environments requires 3D-consistent video generation over long camera trajectories wit

infographic.key_insight: Generative video models can produce long, camera-controlled walkthroughs that are then lifted via feed‑forward reconstruction into ready-to-render 3D worlds, enabling scalable, explorable generative 3D environments with improved long‑horizon consistency.
infographic.problem_solved: Scales generative 3D content creation by solving 3D-consistent video generation over long camera trajectories and converting those videos into real-time-renderable 3D assets, reducing manual modeling and expensive optimization-based reconstruction.
method: Trajectory-conditioned generative video synthesis to produce camera-controlled walkthroughs of scenes.
Architectural and training constraints to enforce long-horizon 3D consistency across frames (temporal + geometric coherence).

title: Agentic Discovery with Active Hypothesis Exploration for Visual Recognition
authors: Jaywon Koo, Jefferson Hernandez, Ruozhen He, Hanjie Chen, Chen Wei
abstract: We introduce HypoExplore, an agentic framework that formulates neural architecture discovery for visual recognition as a hypothesis-driven scientific inquiry. Given a human-specified high-level research direction, HypoExplore ideates, implements, evaluates, and improves neural architectures through evolutionary branching. New hypotheses are created using a large language model by selecting a parent hypothesis to build upon, guided by a dual strategy that balances exploiting validated principles

infographic.key_insight: HypoExplore reframes neural architecture search as a hypothesis-driven scientific inquiry: an agentic loop uses an LLM to propose and refine architecture hypotheses, then implements and evaluates them via evolutionary branching to discover better models for visual recognition.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the slow, manual, and often unguided process of designing neural architectures for vision by automating ideation, implementation, and evaluation while balancing reuse of validated design principles and the exploration of novel ideas.
method: Agentic experiment loop: ideate (LLM-generated hypotheses) → implement (instantiate architectures) → evaluate (train/measure on vision tasks) → improve (select and refine).
Evolutionary branching: build new hypotheses by choosing parent hypotheses and creating variants to explore architecture design spaces.
Active hypothesis exploration: dual strategy balancing exploitation of validated principles and exploration of novel hypotheses to maximize discovery efficiency.
infographic.impact: Enables faster, more systematic discovery of competitive vision architectures and reduces human trial-and-error, helping researchers and engineers scale creative design and evaluation of models.

title: Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models: Phenomenology, Mechanism, and Recipe
authors: Yaxuan Li, Yuxin Zuo, Bingxiang He, Jinqian Zhang, Chaojun Xiao
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique in the post-training of large language models, yet its training dynamics remain poorly understood. This paper provides a systematic investigation of OPD dynamics and mechanisms. We first identify that two conditions govern whether OPD succeeds or fails: (i) the student and teacher should share compatible thinking patterns; and (ii) even with consistent thinking patterns and higher scores, the teacher must offer genuinely new capabilities b

infographic.key_insight: On-policy distillation (OPD) succeeds only when the teacher and student share compatible "thinking patterns" and the teacher contributes genuinely new capabilities beyond the student; diagnosing and enforcing these conditions yields reliable OPD gains.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies why OPD sometimes fails unpredictably and provides actionable criteria and a practical recipe so practitioners can know when and how to apply OPD effectively.
method: Systematic empirical analysis of OPD training dynamics across teacher-student pairs and tasks to identify success/failure patterns.

Characterization of two governing conditions: (a) compatibility of internal reasoning/behavior patterns between teacher and student, and (b) teacher-provided capability novelty above the student's current skillset.
Practical recipe combining diagnostic metrics, selective teacher sampling and targeted on-policy supervision to ensure compatibility and capability injection during distillation.
infographic.impact: Enables ML practitioners to predict OPD outcomes, choose or adapt teachers strategically, and apply focused distillation that reliably improves student models while avoiding wasted compute and negative transfer.

title: PolicyLLM: Towards Excellent Comprehension of Public Policy for Large Language Models
authors: Han Bao, Penghao Zhang, Yue Huang, Zhengqing Yuan, Yanchi Ru
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into real-world decision-making, including in the domain of public policy. Yet, their ability to comprehend and reason about policy-related content remains underexplored. To fill this gap, we present \textbf{\textit{PolicyBench}}, the first large-scale cross-system benchmark (US-China) evaluating policy comprehension, comprising 21K cases across a broad spectrum of policy areas, capturing the diversity and complexity of real-world governan

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces PolicyBench, a large-scale US–China benchmark showing that current LLMs still struggle with nuanced public policy comprehension and reasoning, revealing gaps across policy areas and cross-system contexts.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of a comprehensive, cross-country benchmark to evaluate how well LLMs understand, interpret, and reason about real-world public policy content.
method: Construct PolicyBench: 21K policy cases spanning diverse policy areas and real-world governance scenarios from the US and China.
Cross-system evaluation: run multiple state-of-the-art LLMs on standardized tasks (comprehension, comparison, reasoning) using human-curated rubrics and quantitative metrics.
Analyze performance patterns to identify strengths, failure modes, and domain-specific gaps for model improvement and risk assessment.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical tool to measure and compare LLM policy reasoning, guiding model selection, fine-tuning, and safer deployment in policy-relevant applications.

title: Probabilistic Feature Imputation and Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Federated Aggregation
authors: Nafis Fuad Shahid, Maroof Ahmed, Md Akib Haider, Saidur Rahman Sagor, Aashnan Rahman
abstract: Multimodal federated learning enables privacy-preserving collaborative model training across healthcare institutions. However, a fundamental challenge arises from modality heterogeneity: many clinical sites possess only a subset of modalities due to resource constraints or workflow variations. Existing approaches address this through feature imputation networks that synthesize missing modality representations, yet these methods produce point estimates without reliability measures, forcing downst

infographic.key_insight: Introduce probabilistic feature imputation that produces uncertainty-aware representations for missing modalities, and use those uncertainty estimates to weight client contributions during federated aggregation, yielding more reliable multimodal models under modality heterogeneity.
infographic.problem_solved: Multimodal federated learning across healthcare sites where many clients lack one or more modalities; prior imputation methods give only point estimates and can make aggregation overconfident and unreliable.
method: Train a probabilistic feature imputer (outputs distributions / uncertainty for synthesized modality features) so missing modalities are represented as mean + uncertainty.
Propagate imputed-feature uncertainty through local models and communicate uncertainty-aware summaries (not just point features) to the server.
Perform uncertainty-aware federated aggregation that weights client contributions by imputation reliability, reducing influence of uncertain syntheses.
infographic.impact: Makes multimodal federated learning more robust and better-calibrated in realistic, heterogeneous clinical deployments—improving safety and trustworthiness when modalities are missing while preserving privacy.

title: Budget-Aware Uncertainty for Radiotherapy Segmentation QA Using nnU-Net
authors: Ricardo Coimbra Brioso, Lorenzo Mondo, Damiano Dei, Nicola Lambri, Pietro Mancosu
abstract: Accurate delineation of the Clinical Target Volume (CTV) is essential for radiotherapy planning, yet remains time-consuming and difficult to assess, especially for complex treatments such as Total Marrow and Lymph Node Irradiation (TMLI). While deep learning-based auto-segmentation can reduce workload, safe clinical deployment requires reliable cues indicating where models may be wrong. In this work, we propose a budget-aware uncertainty-driven quality assurance (QA) framework built on nnU-Net,

infographic.key_insight: Integrating uncertainty estimates from an nnU-Net segmentation model with a budget-aware selection strategy lets clinicians prioritize a small subset of auto-segmentations for review while catching most clinically relevant errors.
infographic.problem_solved: How to reliably flag where automated radiotherapy CTV segmentations might be wrong so limited expert QA time is used where it matters most, especially for complex treatments like TMLI.
method: Compute per-voxel and per-structure uncertainty from an nnU-Net segmentation model to estimate likely errors.
Rank slices/structures/patients by predicted uncertainty-derived error and select a fixed review budget (number of slices/regions) to present to clinicians.
Evaluate budget-aware QA performance on TMLI cases, measuring error detection vs reviewer effort trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical workflow for deploying auto-segmentation in radiotherapy by focusing human effort on the most uncertain (and thus most error-prone) regions, improving safety and efficiency in clinical QA.

title: Solving Physics Olympiad via Reinforcement Learning on Physics Simulators
authors: Mihir Prabhudesai, Aryan Satpathy, Yangmin Li, Zheyang Qin, Nikash Bhardwaj
abstract: We have witnessed remarkable advances in LLM reasoning capabilities with the advent of DeepSeek-R1. However, much of this progress has been fueled by the abundance of internet question-answer (QA) pairs, a major bottleneck going forward, since such data is limited in scale and concentrated mainly in domains like mathematics. In contrast, other sciences such as physics lack large-scale QA datasets to effectively train reasoning-capable models. In this work, we show that physics simulators can ser

infographic.key_insight: Interactive physics simulators combined with reinforcement learning allow agents to discover and solve Olympiad-level physics problems, producing grounded step-by-step solutions and scalable synthetic data for training reasoning models.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the shortage of large-scale, domain-specific QA and reasoning data for physics by providing a grounded, scalable alternative that teaches models to experiment, reason, and produce solutions in physical domains.
method: Encode Olympiad problems as high-fidelity, parameterized physics simulation environments that support interaction and measurement.
Train reinforcement learning agents with curriculum learning and reward shaping to explore, experiment, and discover solution strategies within the simulators.
Extract agent trajectories and symbolic traces from simulations to generate step-by-step solutions and labeled datasets for downstream reasoning models.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical route to create large, grounded physics reasoning datasets and improves model generalization in physical sciences—reducing dependence on limited internet QA and enabling more reliable, experiment-driven AI reasoning.

title: Pair2Scene: Learning Local Object Relations for Procedural Scene Generation
authors: Xingjian Ran, Shujie Zhang, Weipeng Zhong, Li Luo, Bo Dai
abstract: Generating high-fidelity 3D indoor scenes remains a significant challenge due to data scarcity and the complexity of modeling intricate spatial relations. Current methods often struggle to scale beyond training distribution to dense scenes or rely on LLMs/VLMs that lack the ability for precise spatial reasoning. Building on top of the observation that object placement relies mainly on local dependencies instead of information-redundant global distributions, in this paper, we propose Pair2Scene,

infographic.key_insight: Object placement in indoor scenes can be modeled primarily by local pairwise spatial relations rather than global distributions; learning and composing these local relations (Pair2Scene) yields scalable, precise procedural scene generation. This reduces reliance on large-scale global priors or LLM/VLM reasoning for spatial precision.
infographic.problem_solved: Generates high-fidelity 3D indoor scenes despite data scarcity and complex spatial relations, enabling scaling to denser scenes and more accurate spatial arrangements than methods that rely on global distributions or LLM/VLMs.
method: Learn a compact representation of pairwise local object relations (relative position, orientation, contact/occlusion cues) from scene data.
Compose scenes by iteratively assembling objects using the learned pairwise relation primitives, prioritizing local consistency over global distribution modeling.
Use a lightweight relational module (e.g., pair encoders + composition policy) to enable efficient sampling and generalization beyond the training distribution.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, data-efficient route to generate realistic, densely populated indoor scenes for simulation, UI/AR content, and robotics testing—improving spatial accuracy and generalization without heavy reliance on LLMs or massive datasets.

authors: Chenxi Qing, Junxi Wu, Zheng Liu, Yixiang Qiu, Hongyao Yu
abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) are capable of generating highly fluent textual content. While they offer significant convenience to humans, they also introduce various risks, like phishing and academic dishonesty. Numerous research efforts have been dedicated to developing algorithms for detecting AI-generated text and constructing relevant datasets. However, in the domain of Chinese corpora, challenges remain, including limited model diversity and data homogeneity. To address these issu

infographic.key_insight: C-ReD builds a diverse, real-world Chinese benchmark that significantly improves evaluation of AI-generated text detectors by using authentic prompts and outputs from multiple LLMs.

Benchmark a range of detection methods across dataset slices to reveal strengths and failure modes (cross-model, prompt-type, length).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a more realistic testbed to develop and stress-test detectors for Chinese text, enabling better generalization and deployment-safe models. It helps reveal where detectors fail and guides model-agnostic improvements.

title: OmniShow: Unifying Multimodal Conditions for Human-Object Interaction Video Generation
authors: Donghao Zhou, Guisheng Liu, Hao Yang, Jiatong Li, Jingyu Lin
abstract: In this work, we study Human-Object Interaction Video Generation (HOIVG), which aims to synthesize high-quality human-object interaction videos conditioned on text, reference images, audio, and pose. This task holds significant practical value for automating content creation in real-world applications, such as e-commerce demonstrations, short video production, and interactive entertainment. However, existing approaches fail to accommodate all these requisite conditions. We present OmniShow, an e

infographic.key_insight: OmniShow unifies text, reference images, audio, and pose into a single conditioning framework to synthesize controllable, high-quality human–object interaction videos, enabling rich multimodal guidance for video generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing HOI video generation methods cannot simultaneously accept and reconcile all practical conditioning signals (text, appearance references, audio, and pose), limiting controllability and real-world applicability for tasks like e‑commerce demos and short video production.
method: Unified multimodal conditioning pipeline that accepts text, reference images, audio, and pose as complementary controls for video synthesis.
Modality-specific encoders and a cross-modal fusion module to integrate semantics (text), appearance (images), sound (audio), and motion (pose) into a shared representation.
Temporal synthesis and object-centric rendering components to ensure motion coherence and consistent human–object interactions across generated frames.

title: LottieGPT: Tokenizing Vector Animation for Autoregressive Generation
authors: Junhao Chen, Kejun Gao, Yuehan Cui, Mingze Sun, Mingjin Chen
abstract: Despite rapid progress in video generation, existing models are incapable of producing vector animation, a dominant and highly expressive form of multimedia on the Internet. Vector animations offer resolution-independence, compactness, semantic structure, and editable parametric motion representations, yet current generative models operate exclusively in raster space and thus cannot synthesize them. Meanwhile, recent advances in large multimodal models demonstrate strong capabilities in generati

infographic.key_insight: LottieGPT converts vector animation primitives into discrete tokens so an autoregressive model can generate, edit, and conditionally synthesize resolution-independent vector animations the way language models generate text.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing generative models operate in raster space and cannot produce compact, editable, resolution-independent vector animations (e.g., Lottie/SVG), limiting web and UI animation synthesis and downstream editing.
method: Design a tokenization scheme that encodes vector primitives (paths, fills, strokes), parametric transforms, keyframe timing, and easing into a sequential token vocabulary.
Train an autoregressive transformer to model token sequences, enabling unconditional and conditioned generation (text/sketch/timeline) of vector animation sequences.
Decode generated tokens back to vector formats (e.g., Lottie/SVG) with loss-aware reconstruction and support for semantic editing and interpolation.
infographic.impact: Enables compact, editable, and high-fidelity animation generation that integrates into web/UI pipelines and creative tools, reducing asset sizes and enabling controllable animation synthesis for ML-driven design workflows.

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Looped Reasoning Language Models
authors: Hugh Blayney, Álvaro Arroyo, Johan Obando-Ceron, Pablo Samuel Castro, Aaron Courville
abstract: Reasoning has become a central capability in large language models. Recent research has shown that reasoning performance can be improved by looping an LLM's layers in the latent dimension, resulting in looped reasoning language models. Despite promising results, few works have investigated how their internal dynamics differ from those of standard feedforward models. In this paper, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of the latent states in looped language models, focusing in particular on how the

infographic.key_insight: Looped reasoning models implement iterative, attractor-like latent dynamics that perform stepwise refinement of intermediate answers, producing more stable and reusable computational subroutines than equivalent feedforward models.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a mechanistic explanation for why looping layers in the latent dimension improves reasoning: it changes internal trajectories and circuit reuse, not just parameter count or depth.
method: Compare looped vs. feedforward models on reasoning tasks using trajectory analysis (PCA/UMAP) to visualize latent dynamics over iteration steps.
Use representational similarity (CKA), linear probes and ablations to identify where and how information accumulates, and to locate reusable subcircuits.
Examine attention/gating patterns and perform causal interventions (weight/activation ablations) to link dynamics to performance changes.
infographic.impact: Clarifies how iterative latent looping modifies computation, enabling practitioners to design and debug models that better perform multi-step reasoning, and to trade off depth, compute and interpretability more effectively.
