title: Large-scale Codec Avatars: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Large-scale Avatar Pretraining
authors: Junxuan Li, Rawal Khirodkar, Chengan He, Zhongshi Jiang, Giljoo Nam
abstract: High-quality 3D avatar modeling faces a critical trade-off between fidelity and generalization. On the one hand, multi-view studio data enables high-fidelity modeling of humans with precise control over expressions and poses, but it struggles to generalize to real-world data due to limited scale and the domain gap between the studio environment and the real world. On the other hand, recent large-scale avatar models trained on millions of in-the-wild samples show promise for generalization across

infographic.key_insight: Pretraining codec-avatar models at very large scale (millions of samples) substantially closes the gap between studio-level fidelity and in-the-wild generalization, enabling high-quality, controllable avatars that transfer well to real-world data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the fidelity-versus-generalization trade-off: studio multi-view captures yield precise, controllable avatars but don’t generalize, while existing large-scale in-the-wild models generalize but lack studio-grade detail; large-scale avatar pretraining delivers both.
method: Assemble and pretrain a codec-avatar model on a massive, diverse dataset combining in-the-wild and studio-like samples to learn robust, high-capacity representations.
Use a compact codec-avatar representation that supports high-fidelity reconstruction and parameterized control (expressions/pose) while being amenable to large-scale learning.
Transfer or fine-tune the pretrained model to studio subjects to recover precise, controllable avatars with improved real-world robustness and reduced per-subject capture needs.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable creation of high-quality, controllable avatars without heavy reliance on costly studio capture; useful for VR/AR, telepresence, and downstream vision/graphics tasks where both fidelity and generalization matter.
visual_elements: Trade-off diagram: fidelity (studio) vs generalization (in-the-wild) showing how large-scale pretraining moves the model toward the Pareto front.
Pipeline flowchart: data collection (studio + in-the-wild) → large-scale pretraining → fine-tuning/deployment.
Scaling curve: performance (reconstruction quality/generalization) vs dataset size highlighting ‘unreasonable effectiveness’ of scale.

title: Universal YOCO for Efficient Depth Scaling
authors: Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Tianzhu Ye, Shaohan Huang, Jianyong Wang
abstract: The rise of test-time scaling has remarkably boosted the reasoning and agentic proficiency of Large Language Models (LLMs). Yet, standard Transformers struggle to scale inference-time compute efficiently, as conventional looping strategies suffer from high computational overhead and a KV cache that inflates alongside model depth. We present Universal YOCO (YOCO-U), which combines the YOCO decoder-decoder architecture with recursive computation to achieve a synergistic effect greater than either

infographic.key_insight: Universal YOCO (YOCO-U) fuses the YOCO decoder-decoder architecture with recursive computation to enable efficient test-time depth scaling, reducing loop overhead and KV-cache growth while preserving or improving reasoning performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard Transformer decoding strategies are inefficient for test-time scaling: repeated loops add compute overhead and the KV cache grows with model depth, limiting practical inference-time scaling of reasoning/agentic abilities.
method: Adopt YOCO decoder-decoder layout to structure decoding for depth-scalable inference.
Introduce recursive computation that reuses intermediate states instead of naive looping, sharply reducing per-step compute and KV cache footprint.
Coordinate model depth scaling and cache management so additional inference depth yields quality gains with sublinear compute/cache cost.
infographic.impact: YOCO-U makes test-time depth scaling practical and cost-effective, enabling LLMs to extend reasoning and agentic behavior at inference time with lower latency and memory overhead—valuable for deployment and research on scalable reasoning.

title: Two-dimensional geometric template diffusion for boosting single-sequence protein structure prediction
authors: Xudong Wang, Tong Zhang, Zhen Cui, Xu Guo, Fuyun Wang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 01 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01210-2

Wang et al. introduce TDFold, which reformulates 3D protein structure prediction as a 2D image-like diffusion task. Its geometric template diffusion framework offers greater accuracy, speed and efficiency than leading models.

infographic.key_insight: TDFold reframes 3D protein structure prediction as a 2D image‑like diffusion task using geometric templates, enabling accurate reconstruction of protein folds from single sequences with markedly improved speed and efficiency.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces reliance on expensive multiple-sequence alignments and heavy 3D optimization by enabling accurate, fast structure prediction directly from single amino‑acid sequences.
method: Encode 3D geometry as 2D image‑like geometric templates (e.g., distance/angle maps) suitable for diffusion modeling.
Apply a 2D diffusion/denoising network over these templates to iteratively refine geometric priors toward a consistent protein fold.
Decode refined 2D templates back into 3D coordinates with an efficient inference pipeline, trading costly 3D operations for lightweight 2D processing.
infographic.impact: Makes high-quality protein structure prediction more accessible and scalable for tasks with limited homologous data, accelerating protein design and downstream ML workflows that need rapid, low-cost structural priors.

title: Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction
authors: Jorge Condor, Nicolas Moenne-Loccoz, Merlin Nimier-David, Piotr Didyk, Zan Gojcic
abstract: Primitive-based methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting have recently become the state-of-the-art for novel-view synthesis and related reconstruction tasks. Compared to neural fields, these representations are more flexible, adaptive, and scale better to large scenes. However, the limited expressivity of individual primitives makes modeling high-frequency detail challenging. We introduce Neural Harmonic Textures, a neural representation approach that anchors latent feature vectors on a virtual sca

infographic.key_insight: Neural Harmonic Textures attach compact harmonic encodings to primitives (e.g., Gaussians) so each primitive can represent high-frequency appearance, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis while retaining the scalability of primitive-based reconstructions.
infographic.problem_solved: Primitive-based representations (like 3D Gaussian Splatting) are efficient and scalable but lack expressivity per primitive, making it hard to capture fine high-frequency texture and detail.
method: Anchor latent feature vectors to a virtual multi-scale coordinate system around primitives so each primitive gains a localized feature field.
Use harmonic basis / neural decoding to synthesize high-frequency texture detail from those anchored latents, improving expressivity without increasing primitive count.
Integrate the textures into the primitive rendering/composition pipeline to produce higher-fidelity novel views while preserving scalability.
infographic.impact: Delivers significantly better visual detail for primitive-based reconstruction pipelines with modest overhead, making high-quality novel-view synthesis more practical for large scenes and production workflows.

title: Online Reasoning Calibration: Test-Time Training Enables Generalizable Conformal LLM Reasoning
authors: Cai Zhou, Zekai Wang, Menghua Wu, Qianyu Julie Zhu, Flora C. Shi
abstract: While test-time scaling has enabled large language models to solve highly difficult tasks, state-of-the-art results come at exorbitant compute costs. These inefficiencies can be attributed to the miscalibration of post-trained language models, and the lack of calibration in popular sampling techniques. Here, we present Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA), a framework for calibrating the sampling process that draws upon conformal prediction and test-time training. Specifically, we introduce a met

infographic.key_insight: Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA) uses test-time training plus conformal prediction to calibrate LLM sampling on the fly, achieving reliable reasoning accuracy without expensive brute-force scaling. This lets models stop or adapt sampling based on calibrated confidence, saving compute while preserving performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses miscalibration in post-trained LLMs and in common sampling strategies that force practitioners to rely on costly test-time scaling (massive sampling or larger models) to reach state-of-the-art reasoning performance.
method: Apply conformal prediction to sampled reasoning chains to produce calibrated confidence bounds for each output.
Perform lightweight test-time training on unlabeled test instances to adapt the model/sampling distribution and improve calibration online.
Use calibrated confidences to control sampling: stop early, resample adaptively, or accept/reject outputs to meet accuracy or cost targets.
infographic.impact: ORCA enables practitioners to get high-confidence reasoning results with far less compute by turning calibration into an actionable, online control signal—improving reliability, efficiency, and generalization across tasks and model sizes.

title: HippoCamp: Benchmarking Contextual Agents on Personal Computers
authors: Zhe Yang, Shulin Tian, Kairui Hu, Shuai Liu, Hoang-Nhat Nguyen
abstract: We present HippoCamp, a new benchmark designed to evaluate agents' capabilities on multimodal file management. Unlike existing agent benchmarks that focus on tasks like web interaction, tool use, or software automation in generic settings, HippoCamp evaluates agents in user-centric environments to model individual user profiles and search massive personal files for context-aware reasoning. Our benchmark instantiates device-scale file systems over real-world profiles spanning diverse modalities,

infographic.key_insight: HippoCamp introduces a user-centric benchmark that measures agents' ability to model individual user profiles and search device-scale, multimodal personal files for context-aware reasoning — shifting evaluation from generic tool use to real-world personal computing scenarios.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing agent benchmarks ignore the challenges of personal, device-scale file management and profile-aware retrieval; HippoCamp fills this gap by simulating real user environments and massive multimodal file stores to evaluate contextual agents.
method: Instantiate device-scale file systems built from real-world user profiles spanning diverse modalities (documents, images, code, logs, etc.).
Design multimodal retrieval and reasoning tasks that require profile modeling, context disambiguation, and long-range file search across the simulated file system.
Provide standardized scenarios and evaluation metrics to compare agents' context-aware file management, retrieval accuracy, and reasoning robustness.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to develop and benchmark agents that better understand individual users and operate effectively on personal computers, accelerating progress in personalized assistants, privacy-aware retrieval, and multimodal reasoning.

title: $\texttt{YC-Bench}$: Benchmarking AI Agents for Long-Term Planning and Consistent Execution
authors: Muyu He, Adit Jain, Anand Kumar, Vincent Tu, Soumyadeep Bakshi
abstract: As LLM agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, a critical question is whether they can maintain strategic coherence over long horizons: planning under uncertainty, learning from delayed feedback, and adapting when early mistakes compound. We introduce $\texttt{YC-Bench}$, a benchmark that evaluates these capabilities by tasking an agent with running a simulated startup over a one-year horizon spanning hundreds of turns. The agent must manage employees, select task contracts, and maintain profi

infographic.key_insight: YC-Bench exposes whether LLM-driven agents can sustain coherent strategies over long horizons by simulating a year-long startup run with hundreds of decision points, revealing failures in planning, adaptation, and error compounding that short-horizon tests miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluates and quantifies an agent's ability to plan under uncertainty, learn from delayed feedback, and maintain consistent execution when early mistakes compound over many steps.
method: Design a simulated startup environment that runs for a one-year horizon across hundreds of turns, requiring hiring, contracting, task allocation, and financial management.
Run standardized agent configurations through the environment and measure long-term outcomes (profitability, task completion, employee retention) and stability of strategy over time.
Provide diagnostic metrics and scenarios to isolate planning, adaptation, and error-compounding behaviors (e.g., delayed-reward trials, stochastic events, contract variability).
infographic.impact: Offers a practical, reproducible benchmark for researchers and engineers to stress-test and improve agents' long-horizon planning and robustness, guiding model design, training regimes, and evaluation standards for real-world sequential decision tasks.
visual_elements: One-year timeline diagram showing hundreds of turns with annotated events (hires, contracts, revenue spikes, failures).

title: Open-Set Supervised 3D Anomaly Detection: An Industrial Dataset and a Generalisable Framework for Unknown Defects
authors: Hanzhe Liang, Luocheng Zhang, Junyang Xia, HanLiang Zhou, Bingyang Guo
abstract: Although self-supervised 3D anomaly detection assumes that acquiring high-precision point clouds is computationally expensive, in real manufacturing scenarios it is often feasible to collect a limited number of anomalous samples. Therefore, we study open-set supervised 3D anomaly detection, where the model is trained with only normal samples and a small number of known anomalous samples, aiming to identify unknown anomalies at test time. We present Open-Industry, a high-quality industrial datase

infographic.key_insight: Training 3D anomaly detectors with normal samples plus a small set of known defects (open-set supervised learning) substantially improves detection of previously unseen industrial defects; the paper also provides Open-Industry, a high-quality industrial 3D dataset to benchmark this setting.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between self-supervised 3D anomaly detection (which assumes no anomalous samples) and real manufacturing practice by enabling models trained with limited known anomalies to generalize to unknown defects at test time.
method: Introduce Open-Industry: a curated, high-precision industrial 3D point-cloud dataset containing normal parts and a small, representative set of labeled defects.
Formulate an open-set supervised training paradigm that uses normal samples plus a few known anomaly examples to learn discriminative 3D features.
Design generalisation-oriented objectives and 3D representation strategies (e.g., feature regularisation / contrastive-style separation) to improve detection of unseen defects at test time.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, deployable approach for manufacturing anomaly detection when a limited number of defective examples are available and supplies a standardized dataset to accelerate research and benchmarking in open-set 3D anomaly detection.

title: Predicting new research directions in materials science using large language models and concept graphs
authors: Thomas Marwitz, Alexander Colsmann, Ben Breitung, Christoph Brabec, Christoph Kirchlechner
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 01 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01206-y

Marwitz et al. demonstrate the use of large language models to build semantic concept graphs from materials science abstracts and train a machine learning model to predict emerging topic combinations from historical data. They show that the model enables experts to find suggestions that can inspire new research.

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can extract semantic concepts from materials-science abstracts to build concept graphs whose temporal modeling predicts novel, high-potential combinations of research topics, surfacing ideas that inspire expert-driven new research.
infographic.problem_solved: As literature grows, finding promising, previously uncombined research directions is slow and biased; this work automates discovery by predicting emerging topic combinations from historical publication data.
method: Use LLMs to parse abstracts and extract semantic concepts and relations, creating a concept graph representation of the field.
Construct temporal snapshots of the concept graph and train a machine-learning predictor to forecast which concept combinations will emerge.
Present ranked candidate combinations to domain experts as interpretable suggestions to guide new research directions.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and researchers with a scalable tool to surface promising, novel research hypotheses and prioritize exploration; demonstrates a practical LLM + graph-model pipeline for accelerating scientific discovery.

title: AdaLoRA-QAT: Adaptive Low-Rank and Quantization-Aware Segmentation
authors: Prantik Deb, Srimanth Dhondy, N. Ramakrishna, Anu Kapoor, Raju S. Bapi
abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) segmentation is an important step in computer-aided diagnosis, yet deploying large foundation models in clinical settings remains challenging due to computational constraints. We propose AdaLoRA-QAT, a two-stage fine-tuning framework that combines adaptive low-rank encoder adaptation with full quantization-aware training. Adaptive rank allocation improves parameter efficiency, while selective mixed-precision INT8 quantization preserves structural fidelity crucial for clinical r

infographic.key_insight: AdaLoRA-QAT enables clinically-faithful chest X‑ray segmentation with far fewer trainable parameters and INT8-ready models by combining adaptive low‑rank encoder adapters with quantization‑aware training.
infographic.problem_solved: Deploying large foundation segmentation models in clinical settings is limited by compute, memory, and the need to preserve structural fidelity in medical images; this work addresses parameter-efficiency and post-training quantization accuracy for CXR segmentation.
method: Two-stage fine-tuning: (1) adaptive low‑rank (LoRA) encoder adaptation that allocates rank per layer to maximize parameter efficiency, (2) full quantization‑aware training (QAT) with selective mixed‑precision (INT8) to maintain structural details.
Selective precision strategy: keep clinically sensitive components at higher precision while aggressively quantizing others to reduce model size and inference cost.
End-to-end segmentation fine-tuning on CXR data to validate that reduced-parameter, quantized models retain clinical segmentation quality.
infographic.impact: Enables practical on-device or edge deployment of high-performing medical segmentation models by cutting memory/compute requirements while preserving diagnostic-grade structure — useful for ML engineers, model deployers, and clinical-AI teams.

title: Embarrassingly Simple Self-Distillation Improves Code Generation
authors: Ruixiang Zhang, Richard He Bai, Huangjie Zheng, Navdeep Jaitly, Ronan Collobert
abstract: Can a large language model (LLM) improve at code generation using only its own raw outputs, without a verifier, a teacher model, or reinforcement learning? We answer in the affirmative with simple self-distillation (SSD): sample solutions from the model with certain temperature and truncation configurations, then fine-tune on those samples with standard supervised fine-tuning. SSD improves Qwen3-30B-Instruct from 42.4% to 55.3% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench v6, with gains concentrating on harder probl

infographic.key_insight: A large language model can substantially improve its own code-generation performance by fine-tuning on its raw sampled outputs (no external teacher, verifier, or reinforcement learning required). Simple self-distillation (SSD) raises pass@1 significantly (e.g., Qwen3-30B-Instruct from 42.4% to 55.3%).
infographic.problem_solved: How to improve LLM code generation without needing additional labeled data, a stronger teacher model, program verifiers, or RL-based pipelines—reducing engineering and compute complexity for model improvement.
method: Generate multiple solution samples from the model using specific temperature and truncation settings to increase diversity.
Aggregate the raw sampled outputs (no external verification or teacher labels) and create a supervised fine-tuning dataset from them.
Fine-tune the same model on this self-generated dataset (simple self-distillation) to yield improved correctness, particularly on harder problems.
infographic.impact: SSD offers a low-complexity, low-overhead recipe to boost code-generation accuracy using only the model itself, enabling practitioners to get large performance gains without extra annotation, verifiers, or RL infrastructure.

title: Toward Personalized Darts Training: A Data-Driven Framework Based on Skeleton-Based Biomechanical Analysis and Motion Modeling
authors: Zhantao Chen, Dongyi He, Jin Fang, Xi Chen, Yisuo Liu
abstract: As sports training becomes more data-driven, traditional dart coaching based mainly on experience and visual observation is increasingly inadequate for high-precision, goal-oriented movements. Although prior studies have highlighted the importance of release parameters, joint motion, and coordination in dart throwing, most quantitative methods still focus on local variables, single-release metrics, or static template matching. These approaches offer limited support for personalized training and

infographic.key_insight: A data-driven framework that uses skeleton-based biomechanical analysis and motion modeling can quantify dart-throwing mechanics and deliver personalized, actionable training guidance beyond single-point release metrics.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing coaching and quantitative methods focus on local or static metrics and cannot capture whole-body coordination or provide individualized, data-backed training plans for improving dart accuracy and consistency.
method: Capture player motion with skeleton/pose estimation and extract biomechanical features (joint angles, velocities, release timing, coordination metrics).
Build motion models (statistical/ML time-series or probabilistic models) to represent typical and individualized throwing patterns and predict outcome sensitivity to biomechanical changes.
Generate personalized feedback and training prescriptions by comparing an athlete's model to ideal/clustered motion templates and identifying high-impact corrective targets.
infographic.impact: This work shows how pose estimation + interpretable biomechanical features can enable personalized sports coaching and targeted interventions, offering a blueprint for ML practitioners to combine motion capture, feature engineering, and predictive modeling in precision training applications.

title: Learning and Generating Mixed States Prepared by Shallow Channel Circuits
authors: Fangjun Hu, Christian Kokail, Milan Kornjača, Pedro L. S. Lopes, Weiyuan Gong
abstract: Learning quantum states from measurement data is a central problem in quantum information and computational complexity. In this work, we study the problem of learning to generate mixed states on a finite-dimensional lattice. Motivated by recent developments in mixed state phases of matter, we focus on arbitrary states in the trivial phase. A state belongs to the trivial phase if there exists a shallow preparation channel circuit under which local reversibility is preserved throughout the prepara

infographic.key_insight: States prepared by shallow, local quantum channel circuits in the trivial mixed-state phase can be learned from local measurement data and efficiently re-generated by compact models, with provable sample and computational guarantees.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a scalable framework for learning and generating mixed quantum states on lattices that are prepared by shallow local channels—addressing the challenge of tomography/generative modeling for many-body mixed states without exponential cost.
method: Characterize the 'trivial phase' of mixed states as those reachable by shallow local channel circuits that preserve local reversibility.
Use local measurements and structure-exploiting reconstruction to learn a compact generative description (shallow circuit / local tensor-network-like model) of the target mixed state.
Prove sample complexity and efficiency guarantees showing the learned generator approximates the original state on local observables with polynomial resources.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable quantum-data-driven modeling and generative simulation for many-body mixed states, informing quantum ML pipelines and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms where compact, learnable representations are crucial.

title: Learning Structural-Functional Brain Representations through Multi-Scale Adaptive Graph Attention for Cognitive Insight
authors: Badhan Mazumder, Sir-Lord Wiafe, Aline Kotoski, Vince D. Calhoun, Dong Hye Ye
abstract: Understanding how brain structure and function interact is key to explaining intelligence yet modeling them jointly is challenging as the structural and functional connectome capture complementary aspects of organization. We introduced Multi-scale Adaptive Graph Network (MAGNet), a Transformer-style graph neural network framework that adaptively learns structure-function interactions. MAGNet leverages source-based morphometry from structural MRI to extract inter-regional morphological features a

infographic.key_insight: MAGNet is a Transformer-style graph neural network that adaptively learns multi-scale interactions between brain structure and function, enabling joint structural–functional representations for cognitive insight.

method: Use source-based morphometry from structural MRI to derive inter-regional morphological features and combine them with functional connectivity data.
Introduce a multi-scale adaptive graph attention mechanism (Transformer-style GNN) to learn region-to-region and scale-to-scale interactions between structure and function.
Produce joint structural–functional embeddings that can be used for downstream cognitive or predictive tasks while preserving interpretable attention maps.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a principled, interpretable approach for multimodal brain representation learning, improving the ability to relate connectome patterns to cognition and downstream predictive models.

title: Scaling Video Pretraining for Surgical Foundation Models
authors: Sicheng Lu, Zikai Xiao, Jianhui Wei, Danyu Sun, Qi Lu
abstract: Surgical video understanding is essential for computer-assisted interventions, yet existing surgical foundation models remain constrained by limited data scale, procedural diversity, and inconsistent evaluation, often lacking a reproducible training pipeline. We propose SurgRec, a scalable and reproducible pretraining recipe for surgical video understanding, instantiated with two variants: SurgRec-MAE and SurgRec-JEPA. We curate a large multi-source corpus of 10,535 videos and 214.5M frames span

infographic.key_insight: Scaling self-supervised pretraining with a large, curated surgical video corpus (10,535 videos, 214.5M frames) and a reproducible recipe (SurgRec-MAE and SurgRec-JEPA) produces stronger, generalizable surgical foundation models.

method: Curate a multi-source surgical video corpus of 10,535 videos (214.5M frames) to increase scale and procedural diversity.
Design reproducible self-supervised pretraining recipes instantiated as SurgRec-MAE (masked autoencoding) and SurgRec-JEPA (joint embedding predictive architecture).

title: Architecting Secure AI Agents: Perspectives on System-Level Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
authors: Chong Xiang, Drew Zagieboylo, Shaona Ghosh, Sanjay Kariyappa, Kai Greshake
abstract: AI agents, predominantly powered by large language models (LLMs), are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, in which malicious instructions embedded in untrusted data can trigger dangerous agent actions. This position paper discusses our vision for system-level defenses against indirect prompt injection attacks. We articulate three positions: (1) dynamic replanning and security policy updates are often necessary for dynamic tasks and realistic environments; (2) certain context-dependent secur

infographic.key_insight: System-level defenses — not just model-side filters — are essential to prevent indirect prompt injection: agents need runtime architectures that enforce isolation, provenance, and dynamic security policies so untrusted data cannot covertly change agent goals or capabilities.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the vulnerability where malicious instructions embedded in untrusted data (indirect prompt injection) cause AI agents to take dangerous or undesired actions, by proposing system-level design principles to reduce attack surface and limit impact.
method: Design agent runtimes with isolation and capability restriction (sandboxing, fine-grained capability tokens) so untrusted inputs cannot directly alter core intent or privileged actions.
Enable dynamic replanning and runtime security-policy updates: agents monitor context and threat signals and adapt policies without relying solely on static prompts or offline filters.
Enforce provenance, strict parsing, and validation of external content to separate untrusted data from control instructions and to provide auditable traces for decisions.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners pragmatic, architecture-level strategies to harden deployed agents against subtle instruction-based attacks, improving safety in real-world, dynamic environments where static prompt hygiene is insufficient.

title: Better than Average: Spatially-Aware Aggregation of Segmentation Uncertainty Improves Downstream Performance
authors: Vanessa Emanuela Guarino, Claudia Winklmayr, Jannik Franzen, Josef Lorenz Rumberger, Manuel Pfeuffer
abstract: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for ensuring the reliability of automated image segmentations in safety-critical domains like biomedical image analysis or autonomous driving. In segmentation, UQ generates pixel-wise uncertainty scores that must be aggregated into image-level scores for downstream tasks like Out-of-Distribution (OoD) or failure detection. Despite routine use of aggregation strategies, their properties and impact on downstream task performance have not yet been comprehe

infographic.key_insight: Aggregating pixel-wise segmentation uncertainty with spatially-aware strategies (instead of simple averaging) produces more informative image-level uncertainty scores that significantly improve downstream tasks such as out-of-distribution and failure detection.
infographic.problem_solved: Pixel-wise uncertainty maps must be condensed to image-level scores for decisions, but naive aggregation (e.g., mean) discards spatial structure and underperforms at detecting localized errors or OOD cases.
method: Introduce spatially-aware aggregation schemes that weight or pool pixel uncertainties according to segmentation topology (e.g., region size, distance-to-boundary, connected components).
Compute region- and boundary-aware summary statistics (rather than global mean) to form image-level uncertainty estimates.
Empirically evaluate these aggregations across segmentation benchmarks and downstream tasks (OoD / failure detection), showing consistent performance gains on ROC/AUPR metrics.
infographic.impact: Provides a simple, model-agnostic way to turn dense uncertainty maps into much more effective image-level signals, improving reliability and safety for practitioners deploying segmentation models in critical applications.
visual_elements: Side-by-side panel: raw image + segmentation + pixel-wise uncertainty heatmap vs. aggregated scores (mean) vs. spatially-aware aggregated score — visually showing better localization and decision separation.
Schematic pipeline: segmentation → pixel uncertainty → spatial-aware aggregator → image-level score → downstream detector (OoD/failure).

title: Rewrite the News: Tracing Editorial Reuse Across News Agencies
authors: Soveatin Kuntur, Nina Smirnova, Anna Wroblewska, Philipp Mayr, Sebastijan Razboršek Maček
abstract: This paper investigates sentence-level text reuse in multilingual journalism, analyzing where reused content occurs within articles. We present a weakly supervised method for detecting sentence-level cross-lingual reuse without requiring full translations, designed to support automated pre-selection to reduce information overload for journalists (Holyst et al., 2024). The study compares English-language articles from the Slovenian Press Agency (STA) with reports from 15 foreign agencies (FA) in

infographic.key_insight: A weakly supervised, sentence-level method can detect cross-lingual editorial reuse without full translations, revealing systematic reuse patterns and where reused sentences appear within articles across news agencies.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates pre-selection of potentially reused content across languages to reduce journalists' information overload and enable tracing of editorial reuse between a national agency (STA) and 15 foreign agencies.
method: Weakly supervised detection of sentence-level cross-lingual reuse that avoids full-sentence translation.
Use of multilingual sentence representations and alignment heuristics to match candidate sentences across corpora.
Analysis of positional distribution of reused sentences within article structure to compare STA vs 15 foreign agencies.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable approach for newsroom monitoring, dataset curation, and improving cross-lingual text-matching tools; demonstrates a practical weak-supervision pattern for multilingual NLP applications.

title: SurgTEMP: Temporal-Aware Surgical Video Question Answering with Text-guided Visual Memory for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy
authors: Shi Li, Vinkle Srivastav, Nicolas Chanel, Saurav Sharma, Nabani Banik
abstract: Surgical procedures are inherently complex and risky, requiring extensive expertise and constant focus to well navigate evolving intraoperative scenes. Computer-assisted systems such as surgical visual question answering (VQA) offer promises for education and intraoperative support. Current surgical VQA research largely focuses on static frame analysis, overlooking rich temporal semantics. Surgical video question answering is further challenged by low visual contrast, its highly knowledge-driven

infographic.key_insight: SurgTEMP introduces a temporal-aware VQA model that uses a text-guided visual memory to retrieve and aggregate relevant frames over time, enabling better, knowledge-driven answers for laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Current surgical VQA methods analyze isolated frames and miss long-range temporal context and task-specific cues in low-contrast, knowledge-heavy laparoscopic videos; SurgTEMP addresses temporal reasoning and targeted retrieval of relevant visual evidence for accurate QA.
method: Temporal-aware video encoder that models long-range dependencies across video frames (e.g., temporal attention/transformer backbone).
Text-guided visual memory: a question-conditioned memory module that stores and retrieves salient visual features across the video to focus on temporally relevant segments.
Multimodal fusion and answer decoder that combines retrieved visual memory with language features for knowledge-driven answer prediction.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical architecture for robust temporal and multimodal reasoning in long surgical videos, improving VQA reliability for education and intraoperative support; the text-guided memory idea generalizes to other long-form video QA and domain-specific multimodal tasks.

title: Enhancing Structural Mapping with LLM-derived Abstractions for Analogical Reasoning in Narratives
authors: Mohammadhossein Khojasteh, Yifan Jiang, Stefano De Giorgis, Frank van Harmelen, Filip Ilievski
abstract: Analogical reasoning is a key driver of human generalization in problem-solving and argumentation. Yet, analogies between narrative structures remain challenging for machines. Cognitive engines for structural mapping are not directly applicable, as they assume pre-extracted entities, whereas LLMs' performance is sensitive to prompt format and the degree of surface similarity between narratives. This gap motivates a key question: What is the impact of enhancing structural mapping with LLM-derived

infographic.key_insight: Combining LLM-derived high-level abstractions with a structural-mapping engine bridges the gap between surface-level text similarity and deeper relational analogy, enabling more reliable analogical reasoning over narratives. This hybrid approach leverages LLMs for abstraction extraction and symbolic mapping for relation-preserving alignment.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the mismatch between LLM sensitivity to prompt/surface cues and cognitive structural-mapping engines' need for pre-extracted entities, improving analogical alignment between narratives with low surface overlap.
method: Use an LLM to extract abstractions (roles, relational predicates, and distilled entities) from narrative text, producing a structured, canonical representation.

Feed the LLM-derived representations into a structural-mapping engine (symbolic graph/relational matcher) to compute analogical correspondences based on relational similarity rather than surface form.
Evaluate the hybrid pipeline against pure LLM prompting and pure symbolic baselines on narrative analogy benchmarks, measuring alignment accuracy and robustness to surface variation.
infographic.impact: This work provides a practical, interpretable blueprint for combining neural abstraction with symbolic mapping, improving generalization and explainability in tasks requiring analogical transfer (e.g., story understanding, reasoning-based QA, and curriculum learning). It reduces reliance on brittle prompt engineering while yielding clearer mappings for downstream use.

title: Think Anywhere in Code Generation
authors: Xue Jiang, Tianyu Zhang, Ge Li, Mengyang Liu, Taozhi Chen
abstract: Recent advances in reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs) have primarily relied on upfront thinking, where reasoning occurs before final answer. However, this approach suffers from critical limitations in code generation, where upfront thinking is often insufficient as problems' full complexity only reveals itself during code implementation. Moreover, it cannot adaptively allocate reasoning effort throughout the code generation process where difficulty varies significantly. In this paper, we pro

infographic.key_insight: Instead of performing all reasoning up front, "Think Anywhere" interleaves reasoning and code generation so the model can invoke targeted, deeper thinking at the exact points where implementation reveals new complexity. This adaptive, stepwise reasoning leads to more robust and efficient code synthesis.
infographic.problem_solved: Upfront-only reasoning is brittle for code generation because many problems only reveal their true difficulty during implementation; the paper addresses the need to allocate reasoning effort adaptively across the generation process.
method: Interleave reasoning and generation: enable the model to trigger localized chain-of-thought whenever the current implementation step is uncertain or fails checks.
Checkpoint-based local planning and verification: use intermediate checkpoints (e.g., tests, compilation feedback, or heuristics) to decide when to pause and reason deeper.
Cost-aware allocation: prioritize reasoning budget to high-uncertainty segments so effort is concentrated where it most improves correctness and efficiency.
infographic.impact: Makes LLM-driven code generation more reliable and efficient by focusing reasoning where it matters during implementation, reducing needless computation and lowering bug rates. Practitioners get better trade-offs between latency, cost, and correctness when deploying code-writing models.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: generate → detect uncertainty/checkpoint → invoke local reasoning → continue generation
Timeline visualization: code generation steps with variable-height "thinking" bars showing adaptive reasoning intensity
Code editor mockup: code snippets with inline thought-bubbles and verification badges (pass/fail)

title: Covertly improving intelligibility with data-driven adaptations of speech timing
authors: Paige Tuttösí, Angelica Lim, H. Henny Yeung, Yue Wang, Jean-Julien Aucouturier
abstract: Human talkers often address listeners with language-comprehension challenges, such as hard-of-hearing or non-native adults, by globally slowing down their speech. However, it remains unclear whether this strategy actually makes speech more intelligible. Here, we take advantage of recent advancements in machine-generated speech allowing more precise control of speech rate in order to systematically examine how targeted speech-rate adjustments may improve comprehension. We first use reverse-correl

infographic.key_insight: Localized, data-driven adjustments to speech timing — identified via reverse-correlation on precisely controlled synthetic speech — can covertly improve intelligibility more effectively than global slowing, often without listeners noticing a pronounced slowdown.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines whether and how changing speech rate actually helps comprehension for listeners with language or hearing challenges, offering a precise alternative to crude global slowing.
method: Use controllable text-to-speech to generate stimuli with fine-grained timing manipulations.
Apply reverse-correlation / data-driven analysis to discover temporal windows where slowing boosts comprehension.
Validate adapted timing with listener experiments measuring objective intelligibility (e.g., word recognition) and perceptual detectability.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical strategy for TTS, hearing-assistive devices, and ASR robustness to improve real-world comprehension with minimal perceptual cost; informs ML models that optimize temporal features for human listeners.
visual_elements: Waveform/prosody comparison: baseline vs global slow vs targeted slow with highlighted temporal regions showing where timing was adjusted.

Pipeline diagram of the reverse-correlation loop: synthetic stimuli → listener responses → temporal weighting → adapted TTS.

title: Benchmarking PhD-Level Coding in 3D Geometric Computer Vision
authors: Wenyi Li, Renkai Luo, Yue Yu, Huan-ang Gao, Mingju Gao
abstract: AI-assisted coding has rapidly reshaped software practice and research workflows, yet today's models still struggle to produce correct code for complex 3D geometric vision. If models could reliably write such code, the research of our community would change substantially. To measure progress toward that goal, we introduce GeoCodeBench, a PhD-level benchmark that evaluates coding for 3D vision. Each problem is a fill-in-the-function implementation task curated from representative papers at recent

infographic.key_insight: GeoCodeBench introduces a PhD‑level benchmark that measures LLMs' ability to write correct, research‑grade code for complex 3D geometric computer vision tasks by using curated fill‑in‑the‑function problems drawn from recent papers.
infographic.problem_solved: It addresses the inability of current AI coding models to reliably produce correct, geometry‑aware implementations for advanced 3D vision research tasks, providing a standardized way to quantify progress.
method: Curate representative implementation tasks from recent 3D geometric vision papers and reformulate them as fill‑in‑the‑function coding problems suitable for automated evaluation.
Evaluate model outputs with automated unit tests, geometry‑aware correctness checks (e.g., reprojection/pose/metric errors), and runtime/robustness criteria to mimic research usage.
Provide a model‑agnostic benchmarking pipeline that reports fine‑grained failure modes (syntax, algorithmic error, numerical instability, API misuse) for targeted diagnostics.
infographic.impact: By exposing specific gaps in LLM coding for 3D geometry, GeoCodeBench lets practitioners and model developers prioritize improvements that matter for real research workflows, accelerating reliable AI‑assisted implementation of advanced computer vision methods.

title: SurgNavAR: An Augmented Reality Surgical Navigation Framework for Optical See-Through Head Mounted Displays
authors: Abdullah Thabit, Mohamed Benmahdjoub, Rafiuddin Jinabade, Hizirwan S. Salim, Marie-Lise C. van Veelen
abstract: Augmented reality (AR) devices with head mounted displays (HMDs) facilitate the direct superimposition of 3D preoperative imaging data onto the patient during surgery. To use an HMD-AR device as a stand-alone surgical navigation system, the device should be able to locate the patient and surgical instruments, align preoperative imaging data with the patient, and visualize navigation data in real time during surgery. Whereas some of the technologies required for this are known, integration in suc

infographic.key_insight: SurgNavAR demonstrates a practical AR navigation framework that integrates patient/instrument localization, preoperative 3D image-to-patient alignment, and real-time visualization on optical see-through HMDs, enabling the HMD to function as a standalone surgical navigation system.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between isolated AR/vision components and a cohesive, real-time surgical navigation pipeline—addressing patient/instrument tracking, image registration, and intraoperative visualization on head-mounted displays.
method: Integrate multi-modal localization and tracking to locate patient and surgical instruments relative to the HMD
Register preoperative 3D imaging to the patient using alignment/calibration routines suitable for optical see-through displays
Render and update navigation overlays in real time on the HMD with considerations for latency, accuracy, and surgeon ergonomics
infographic.impact: Enables ML and CV practitioners to develop and benchmark models for sensor fusion, real-time registration, and low-latency rendering in a clinically relevant AR navigation stack, accelerating translation of AI methods into intraoperative guidance.

title: Gloria: Consistent Character Video Generation via Content Anchors
authors: Yuhang Yang, Fan Zhang, Huaijin Pi, Shuai Guo, Guowei Xu
abstract: Digital characters are central to modern media, yet generating character videos with long-duration, consistent multi-view appearance and expressive identity remains challenging. Existing approaches either provide insufficient context to preserve identity or leverage non-character-centric information as the memory, leading to suboptimal consistency. Recognizing that character video generation inherently resembles an outside-looking-in scenario. In this work, we propose representing the character

infographic.key_insight: Represent characters as reusable, character-centric "content anchors" extracted from reference views so a generator can reliably preserve identity and multi-view appearance over long video sequences. This outside-looking-in anchoring provides stable memory that improves consistency without relying on non-character context.
infographic.problem_solved: Maintains long-duration, multi-view identity and appearance consistency for generated character videos, avoiding drift and identity mismatch that arise when memory is weak or not character-centric.
method: Construct character-centric content anchors from reference frames (multi-view / multi-pose snippets) to serve as a compact, persistent memory representation.
Anchor-conditioned generation: retrieve and fuse anchor features into the video synthesis pipeline so each output frame is grounded to stable identity information.
Train with objectives for identity preservation, multi-view coherence, and temporal consistency to ensure expressive yet consistent long-form character videos.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, long-form character video synthesis for applications like virtual production, avatars, and animation pipelines by providing a practical memory mechanism for identity preservation. Practitioners can leverage anchor-based memory to reduce identity drift and improve multi-view realism.

title: EC-Bench: Enumeration and Counting Benchmark for Ultra-Long Videos
authors: Fumihiko Tsuchiya, Taiki Miyanishi, Mahiro Ukai, Nakamasa Inoue, Shuhei Kurita
abstract: Counting in long videos remains a fundamental yet underexplored challenge in computer vision. Real-world recordings often span tens of minutes or longer and contain sparse, diverse events, making long-range temporal reasoning particularly difficult. However, most existing video counting benchmarks focus on short clips and evaluate only the final numerical answer, providing little insight into what should be counted or whether models consistently identify relevant instances across time. We introd

infographic.key_insight: EC-Bench introduces a focused benchmark for enumeration and counting in ultra-long videos, shifting evaluation from single final counts to temporally grounded instance-level consistency across minutes-to-hours recordings. It reveals that counting in long, sparse, diverse video streams requires new annotation, evaluation and baseline protocols to measure when and what is being counted.
infographic.problem_solved: Current video counting benchmarks use short clips and only final numeric answers, which fail to capture long-range temporal reasoning, sparse event occurrence, and whether models consistently identify relevant instances over ultra-long recordings.
method: Curate and annotate a collection of ultra-long videos with temporally localized instance-level counting labels and clear counting definitions for diverse real-world scenes.
Design evaluation protocols and metrics that measure both final count accuracy and temporal consistency/localization (e.g., per-interval counts, detection consistency, error accumulation over time).
Provide baseline model implementations and benchmarking recipes to evaluate performance, failure modes, and scalability on long-duration inputs.
infographic.impact: EC-Bench enables researchers and practitioners to diagnose and improve long-range temporal reasoning and robustness for counting tasks, guiding development of models and training strategies that operate reliably on minutes- to hours-long video streams.

title: Tucker Attention: A generalization of approximate attention mechanisms
authors: Timon Klein, Jonas Kusch, Sebastian Sager, Stefan Schnake, Steffen Schotthöfer
abstract: The pursuit of reducing the memory footprint of the self-attention mechanism in multi-headed self attention (MHA) spawned a rich portfolio of methods, e.g., group-query attention (GQA) and multi-head latent attention (MLA). The methods leverage specialized low-rank factorizations across embedding dimensions or attention heads. From the point of view of classical low-rank approximation, these methods are unconventional and raise questions of which objects they really approximate and how to interp

infographic.key_insight: Tucker Attention frames multi-headed self-attention as a Tucker tensor decomposition, providing a single, principled low-rank model that generalizes and recovers existing approximate attention schemes (e.g., GQA, MLA). This unifies disparate heuristics into controllable rank- and core-parameter trade-offs between memory, compute and expressivity.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the memory and computational footprint of multi-headed self-attention while answering what object existing approximations actually approximate — providing a principled, unified view and design space for approximate attention methods.
method: Model the attention weights/transformations as a multi-way tensor across heads and embedding dimensions and apply a Tucker decomposition (core tensor + factor matrices).
Design parameterizations and rank constraints that recover prior approximate methods (GQA, MLA) as special cases and enable new trade-offs between core size and factor ranks.
Provide efficient implementations and complexity analyses to lower memory use and latency while preserving attention expressivity.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a theory-driven template to design memory-efficient attention layers with predictable trade-offs, making it easier to compress or accelerate transformers without ad-hoc engineering. It also improves interpretability by exposing which tensor modes and ranks matter most.
visual_elements: Schematic of Tucker decomposition: attention tensor -> factor matrices + small core tensor (annotate dimensions and ranks).

title: Scalable AI-assisted Workflow Management for Detector Design Optimization Using Distributed Computing
authors: Derek Anderson, Amit Bashyal, Markus Diefenthaler, Cristiano Fanelli, Wen Guan
abstract:
The Production and Distributed Analysis (PanDA) system, originally developed for the ATLAS experiment at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC), has evolved into a robust platform for orchestrating large-scale workflows across distributed computing resources. Coupled with its intelligent Distributed Dispatch and Scheduling (iDDS) component, PanDA supports AI/ML-driven workflows through a scalable and flexible workflow engine.
  We present an AI-assisted framework for detector design optimization t

infographic.key_insight: PanDA combined with its iDDS scheduler enables scalable AI-assisted detector design optimization by orchestrating large simulation + ML workflows across distributed compute resources, turning costly, serial design cycles into parallel, automated optimization loops.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between expensive physics simulations and AI-driven optimization by providing scalable, fault-tolerant orchestration and data management across heterogeneous distributed computing infrastructures, reducing manual effort and turnaround time for detector design studies.
method: Integrate PanDA workflow engine with iDDS to dispatch and schedule heterogeneous jobs (simulations, ML training, inference, evaluations) across grid, cloud, and HPC resources.

Implement iterative AI-assisted optimization loop: run high-fidelity simulations, train ML surrogates or emulators, evaluate candidate designs, and perform distributed parameter sweeps or optimization steps.
Use scalable data staging, result aggregation, and fault-tolerant retries to parallelize thousands of tasks and maintain reproducibility and provenance of runs.
infographic.impact: Allows AI/ML practitioners to scale detector-design experiments from handfuls to thousands of parallel jobs, speeding up exploration of design spaces, improving reproducibility, and enabling more sophisticated ML models and surrogate-based optimization at production scale.

title: Four Generations of Quantum Biomedical Sensors
authors: Xin Jin, Priyam Srivastava, Ronghe Wang, Yuqing Li, Jonathan Beaumariage
abstract: Quantum sensing technologies offer transformative potential for ultra-sensitive biomedical sensing, yet their clinical translation remains constrained by classical noise limits and a reliance on macroscopic ensembles. We propose a unifying generational framework to organize the evolving landscape of quantum biosensors based on their utilization of quantum resources. First-generation devices utilize discrete energy levels for signal transduction but follow classical scaling laws. Second-generatio

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a unified four-generation framework that classifies quantum biomedical sensors by the quantum resources they use, clarifying how successive use of coherence, squeezing/entanglement, and fully quantum-engineered architectures can incrementally overcome classical noise limits and enable true quantum advantage in biosensing.
infographic.problem_solved: Clinical translation of quantum biosensors is stalled by classical noise scaling, reliance on large macroscopic ensembles, and lack of a clear roadmap linking device physics to practical sensitivity/robustness targets for biomedical applications.
method: Define four generations of quantum biomedical sensors (from classical-scaling discrete-level devices to coherent, squeezed/entangled, and fully quantum-engineered networked sensors) and formalize the quantum resources each generation exploits.

Develop performance metrics and scaling laws that map resource usage (coherence time, entanglement depth, single-spin addressability) to expected sensitivity improvements and trade-offs for realistic biological environments.
Provide design guidelines and exemplar device classes for each generation, highlighting implementation challenges and pathways toward clinical translation.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners this framework clarifies expected improvements in signal quality and new high-dimensional biomedical modalities, informing dataset design, noise models, and ML architectures that can leverage quantum-enhanced measurements for better inference and control.

title: OmniRoam: World Wandering via Long-Horizon Panoramic Video Generation
authors: Yuheng Liu, Xin Lin, Xinke Li, Baihan Yang, Chen Wang
abstract: Modeling scenes using video generation models has garnered growing research interest in recent years. However, most existing approaches rely on perspective video models that synthesize only limited observations of a scene, leading to issues of completeness and global consistency. We propose OmniRoam, a controllable panoramic video generation framework that exploits the rich per-frame scene coverage and inherent long-term spatial and temporal consistency of panoramic representation, enabling long

infographic.key_insight: OmniRoam uses panoramic (360°) per-frame representations to generate long-horizon, globally consistent videos of a scene, enabling controllable "world wandering" that overcomes the limited field-of-view and short-horizon constraints of perspective video models.
infographic.problem_solved: Perspective video generators see only narrow views and struggle with completeness and global temporal/spatial consistency for long sequences; OmniRoam addresses incomplete scene coverage and lack of long-term coherence by operating on panoramic frames and explicit control signals.
method: Represent each timestep as a panoramic frame to provide full 360° scene coverage and stronger spatial continuity.
Train a generative backbone (e.g., transformer/diffusion-style) conditioned on camera trajectory/control inputs to produce long-horizon panoramic video while preserving global consistency.
Incorporate hierarchical memory/pose-conditioning and stitching mechanisms to maintain temporal coherence and accurate scene geometry across long sequences.
infographic.impact: Enables more complete and stable scene modeling for applications in virtual navigation, immersive media, simulation, and robotics; makes long-term controllable video synthesis practical for downstream tasks like data augmentation and exploration planning.

title: See it to Place it: Evolving Macro Placements with Vision-Language Models
authors: Ikechukwu Uchendu, Swati Goel, Karly Hou, Ebrahim Songhori, Kuang-Huei Lee
abstract: We propose using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for macro placement in chip floorplanning, a complex optimization task that has recently shown promising advancements through machine learning methods. Because human designers rely heavily on spatial reasoning to arrange components on the chip canvas, we hypothesize that VLMs with strong visual reasoning abilities can effectively complement existing learning-based approaches. We introduce VeoPlace (Visual Evolutionary Optimization Placement), a nove

infographic.key_insight: Vision-language models' visual reasoning can be used to propose and evaluate macro placements, and when integrated into an evolutionary optimizer (VeoPlace) they produce higher-quality floorplans than optimization or ML-only approaches.
infographic.problem_solved: Automating the combinatorial, spatially-complex task of macro placement in chip floorplanning by incorporating human-like visual reasoning to guide layout generation and refinement.
method: Encode the chip canvas and candidate placements as visual inputs to a vision-language model to obtain spatial assessments and placement proposals.
Integrate VLM evaluations/proposals into an evolutionary optimization loop that generates, scores, and mutates macro placements under physical and routing constraints.
Combine VLM-derived spatial scores with traditional EDA objectives (e.g., wirelength, congestion) to form a composite fitness used for selection and refinement.
infographic.impact: Introduces a multimodal toolchain that brings visual reasoning to a core EDA problem, enabling more automated, interpretable, and effective macro placement—reducing manual effort and accelerating design iterations for AI/ML hardware teams.

title: SOLE-R1: Video-Language Reasoning as the Sole Reward for On-Robot Reinforcement Learning
authors: Philip Schroeder, Thomas Weng, Karl Schmeckpeper, Eric Rosen, Stephen Hart
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, motivating efforts to leverage these models to supervise robot learning. However, when used as evaluators in reinforcement learning (RL), today's strongest models often fail under partial observability and distribution shift, enabling policies to exploit perceptual errors rather than solve the task. To address this limitation, we introduce SOLE-R1 (Self-Observing LEarner), a video-language reasoning model expl

infographic.key_insight: SOLE-R1 turns a video-language reasoning model into the sole reward function for on-robot reinforcement learning, letting robots learn from self-observed video and language task specs rather than hand-crafted rewards; this reduces exploitation of static VLM evaluators under partial observability and distribution shift.
infographic.problem_solved: Current vision-language evaluators used as rewards for RL are brittle under partial observability and distribution shift, enabling policies to game perceptual errors instead of solving tasks; SOLE-R1 provides a robust, temporal video-language supervision signal that closes the loop on real robot learning without engineered rewards.
method: Train a video-language reasoning model to score entire robot video trajectories against natural-language task descriptions, emphasizing temporal grounding and cross-frame consistency.

Use the model’s trajectory-level scores as the sole reward signal in an on-robot RL loop: collect video, score with SOLE-R1, and update policy—no external reward engineering or instrumented lab setup.
Improve evaluator robustness via robot-domain finetuning, calibration/uncertainty-aware scoring, and design choices that prevent policies from exploiting perceptual shortcuts.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable, general-purpose reward mechanism for real-world robot learning, reducing manual reward design and labels while improving robustness to observation gaps and distribution shifts—making on-robot RL more practical for diverse tasks.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: robot executes policy → captures video → SOLE-R1 scores trajectory vs. language goal → RL update loop (closed-loop).
Architecture schematic: temporal video encoder + language encoder → cross-modal reasoning head → trajectory-level reward output.
Comparison chart: policy performance and failure modes under partial observability for (a) static image VLM rewards vs (b) SOLE-R1 video-language rewards.
Example task sequence panels: before/after learning with scored video frames showing correct vs exploited failure cases annotated.

title: AdaptToken: Entropy-based Adaptive Token Selection for MLLM Long Video Understanding
authors: Haozhe Qi, Kevin Qu, Mahdi Rad, Rui Wang, Alexander Mathis
abstract: Long video understanding remains challenging for Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to high memory costs and context-length limits. Prior approaches mitigate this by scoring and selecting frames/tokens within short clips, but they lack a principled mechanism to (i) compare relevance across distant video clips and (ii) stop processing once sufficient evidence has been gathered. We propose AdaptToken, a training-free framework that turns an MLLM's self-uncertainty into a global control

infographic.key_insight: AdaptToken uses an MLLM's own prediction uncertainty (entropy) as a training-free, global control signal to rank tokens/frames across long videos and to stop processing once sufficient evidence is gathered, enabling efficient long-video understanding with minimal performance loss.
infographic.problem_solved: Reducing memory and computation for MLLMs on very long videos while providing a principled cross-clip relevance comparison and an automatic stopping criterion so the model need not process every frame.
method: Compute per-token/frame uncertainty (entropy) from the pretrained MLLM's outputs without additional training.
Globally rank and select the most informative tokens/frames across distant clips based on entropy, rather than only within short clips.
Apply an adaptive stopping rule: halt further token/frame processing once overall uncertainty falls below a threshold, saving compute and memory.
infographic.impact: Provides a plug-and-play, model-agnostic way to make MLLMs scalable to long videos, cutting inference cost and memory footprint while maintaining accuracy—useful for real-world video applications where compute or latency is constrained.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: video → clip split → entropy scoring → global selector → adaptive stop → final answer

title: EpiScreen: Early Epilepsy Detection from Electronic Health Records with Large Language Models
authors: Shuang Zhou, Kai Yu, Zaifu Zhan, Huixue Zhou, Min Zeng
abstract: Epilepsy and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures often present with similar seizure-like manifestations but require fundamentally different management strategies. Misdiagnosis is common and can lead to prolonged diagnostic delays, unnecessary treatments, and substantial patient morbidity. Although prolonged video-electroencephalography is the diagnostic gold standard, its high cost and limited accessibility hinder timely diagnosis. Here, we developed a low-cost, effective approach, EpiScreen, for

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can accurately screen unstructured electronic health records to distinguish epileptic seizures from psychogenic non‑epileptic events, enabling low‑cost, early triage that complements limited access to prolonged video‑EEG.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces diagnostic delays and misdiagnosis between epilepsy and psychogenic non‑epileptic seizures caused by similar clinical presentations and limited accessibility of gold‑standard prolonged video‑EEG.
method: Use of a large language model to parse and semantically encode unstructured clinical notes and seizure descriptions in EHRs.
Model pipeline that extracts key temporal and phenomenological features, integrates structured EHR data, and outputs a risk/triage score with explanatory highlights.
Validation against clinician‑labeled cases and deployment‑oriented design choices for interpretability, privacy, and low‑cost screening in routine workflows.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates a practical, scalable application of LLMs for clinical screening using routinely collected EHR text, informing ML practitioners about model design, evaluation, and deployment considerations for high‑impact diagnostic support tools.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: EHR notes → LLM feature extraction → classifier → risk/triage output (with explanation badges).
Annotated patient note example highlighting phrases the model used to decide (phenomenology, triggers, consciousness).

title: Expectation Error Bounds for Transfer Learning in Linear Regression and Linear Neural Networks
authors: Meitong Liu, Christopher Jung, Rui Li, Xue Feng, Han Zhao
abstract: In transfer learning, the learner leverages auxiliary data to improve generalization on a main task. However, the precise theoretical understanding of when and how auxiliary data help remains incomplete. We provide new insights on this issue in two canonical linear settings: ordinary least squares regression and under-parameterized linear neural networks. For linear regression, we derive exact closed-form expressions for the expected generalization error with bias-variance decomposition, yieldin

infographic.key_insight: The paper derives exact closed-form expressions for the expected generalization error in transfer learning for ordinary least squares and under-parameterized linear neural networks, exposing precise bias–variance tradeoffs and conditions under which auxiliary data helps or hurts the main task.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a rigorous theoretical characterization of when and how auxiliary/source data improve (or degrade) generalization on a target/primary task in linear settings—filling gaps in understanding transfer learning benefits and risks.
method: Analytic derivation of exact expected generalization error formulas for ordinary least squares regression.
Bias–variance decomposition to separate the contributions of transfer to systematic error vs. estimation noise.
Extension of the analysis to under-parameterized linear neural networks and identification of alignment/sample-size conditions that control transfer utility.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners actionable criteria to predict whether transfer will help, guiding decisions about using auxiliary datasets, collecting more data, or choosing model capacity. Helps translate theoretical bounds into practical transfer-learning guidelines.
visual_elements: Schematic diagram: source tasks → auxiliary data → transfer → target task, annotated with alignment and sample-size factors.
Stacked bar charts: bias vs. variance components of expected error with and without transfer to show tradeoffs.
Heatmap: expected error improvement as a function of task alignment (similarity) and auxiliary sample size.
Formula callout: compact boxed display of the closed-form expected-error expression with brief annotations of each term (bias term, variance term, alignment factor).

title: Stepwise Credit Assignment for GRPO on Flow-Matching Models
authors: Yash Savani, Branislav Kveton, Yuchen Liu, Yilin Wang, Jing Shi
abstract: Flow-GRPO successfully applies reinforcement learning to flow models, but uses uniform credit assignment across all steps. This ignores the temporal structure of diffusion generation: early steps determine composition and content (low-frequency structure), while late steps resolve details and textures (high-frequency details). Moreover, assigning uniform credit based solely on the final image can inadvertently reward suboptimal intermediate steps, especially when errors are corrected later in th

infographic.key_insight: Assigning rewards to individual diffusion timesteps (stepwise credit assignment) for Flow-GRPO respects the temporal roles of early vs. late steps, improving learning signals compared to uniform final-image-only credit.
infographic.problem_solved: Uniform credit assignment across all generation steps can reward or punish intermediate actions incorrectly—especially when late steps fix earlier mistakes—hindering flow-matching models trained with GRPO from learning the correct temporal structure of image generation.
method: Introduce a stepwise credit-assignment scheme for GRPO on flow-matching diffusion models that apportions reward across timesteps according to their contribution to structure vs. detail.
Integrate per-step rewards into the GRPO optimization loop for flow-matching models, enabling more informative gradients for early (low-frequency) and late (high-frequency) generation stages.
Evaluate the modified training pipeline to show improved alignment of intermediate steps and better final sample quality (qualitative and quantitative comparisons vs. uniform credit).
infographic.impact: Provides a simple, widely applicable modification to RL-based training of generative diffusion/flow models that yields clearer learning signals, better intermediate behavior, and improved final generations—useful for practitioners tuning generation fidelity and stability.
visual_elements: Timeline diagram of diffusion steps annotated with roles: early = composition/low-frequency, late = details/high-frequency, showing where credit is assigned.

title: Gen-Searcher: Reinforcing Agentic Search for Image Generation
authors: Kaituo Feng, Manyuan Zhang, Shuang Chen, Yunlong Lin, Kaixuan Fan
abstract: Recent image generation models have shown strong capabilities in generating high-fidelity and photorealistic images. However, they are fundamentally constrained by frozen internal knowledge, thus often failing on real-world scenarios that are knowledge-intensive or require up-to-date information. In this paper, we present Gen-Searcher, as the first attempt to train a search-augmented image generation agent, which performs multi-hop reasoning and search to collect the textual knowledge and refere

infographic.key_insight: Augmenting image generators with an agentic, multi-hop search mechanism lets models fetch up-to-date, contextual textual knowledge and use it to produce more accurate, knowledge-grounded images — trained with reinforcement-style feedback to align search and generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the limitations of frozen internal knowledge in current image generators, which causes failures on knowledge-intensive or time-sensitive real-world prompts.
method: Train a search-augmented image-generation agent that performs multi-hop reasoning to iteratively collect and aggregate textual evidence relevant to a prompt.
Condition the image generator on retrieved and summarized external knowledge so generation reflects accurate, up-to-date facts.
Use reinforcement-style feedback (rewarding useful searches and faithful generation) to align the agent's search policy with downstream image quality.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, fact-aware, and up-to-date image generation for applications that require external knowledge (e.g., educational visuals, news imagery, product renderings), reducing hallucinations and improving trustworthiness.
visual_elements: Agent pipeline diagram: cyclical loop showing prompt → multi-hop search → evidence aggregation → conditioned image generator → feedback/reward.
Side-by-side comparison: frozen-model output vs. Gen-Searcher output on a knowledge-heavy prompt (qualitative examples).
Flowchart of multi-hop retrieval: nodes showing successive query steps and how evidence is accumulated/refined.

title: PoseDreamer: Scalable and Photorealistic Human Data Generation Pipeline with Diffusion Models
authors: Lorenza Prospero, Orest Kupyn, Ostap Viniavskyi, João F. Henriques, Christian Rupprecht
abstract: Acquiring labeled datasets for 3D human mesh estimation is challenging due to depth ambiguities and the inherent difficulty of annotating 3D geometry from monocular images. Existing datasets are either real, with manually annotated 3D geometry and limited scale, or synthetic, rendered from 3D engines that provide precise labels but suffer from limited photorealism, low diversity, and high production costs. In this work, we explore a third path: generated data. We introduce PoseDreamer, a novel p

infographic.key_insight: PoseDreamer uses diffusion models to generate large-scale, photorealistic human images paired with accurate 3D mesh labels, providing a third path between limited real annotations and unrealistic engine-rendered synthetic data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the scarcity and cost of labeled 3D human mesh data from monocular images by producing scalable, diverse, and realistic synthetic training data with ground-truth 3D geometry.
method: Pose-conditioned diffusion synthesis: generate photorealistic images conditioned on target 3D pose/shape parameters to ensure semantic control.
Parametric mesh pairing: associate each generated image with exact 3D mesh labels (e.g., SMPL-like params) to produce supervised training pairs.
Diversity & quality pipeline: apply multi-view consistency checks, style/lighting augmentation, and automated filtering to maximize realism and dataset variety.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a scalable source of realistic, labeled 3D human data to train and benchmark mesh-estimation models, reducing annotation cost and improving model generalization across poses, clothing, and lighting.

title: SHOW3D: Capturing Scenes of 3D Hands and Objects in the Wild
authors: Patrick Rim, Kevin Harris, Braden Copple, Shangchen Han, Xu Xie
abstract: Accurate 3D understanding of human hands and objects during manipulation remains a significant challenge for egocentric computer vision. Existing hand-object interaction datasets are predominantly captured in controlled studio settings, which limits both environmental diversity and the ability of models trained on such data to generalize to real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel marker-less multi-camera system that allows for nearly unconstrained mobility in genuin

infographic.key_insight: A novel marker-less multi-camera capture system enables accurate 3D reconstruction of hands and manipulated objects in unconstrained, real-world (egocentric) settings, closing the gap between studio datasets and in-the-wild scenarios.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing hand–object interaction datasets are captured in controlled studio conditions, limiting environmental diversity and causing models to fail to generalize to real-world egocentric manipulation; this work provides a way to collect high-quality 3D hand+object data outside the lab.
method: Marker-less, multi-camera capture rig designed for near-unconstrained mobility to record egocentric manipulation in diverse real-world scenes.
Multi-view 3D reconstruction and temporal tracking pipeline to recover accurate hand and object poses without markers.
Automated annotation/validation pipeline to produce a large-scale in-the-wild dataset of synchronized RGB and 3D hand+object poses for training and evaluation.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with realistic 3D hand+object data that improves robustness and generalization of egocentric perception and manipulation models; useful for training, benchmarking, and downstream HCI/robotics applications.
visual_elements: Illustration of the wearable/multi-camera capture setup (top-down and side views).
