title: DreamLite: A Lightweight On-Device Unified Model for Image Generation and Editing
authors: Kailai Feng, Yuxiang Wei, Bo Chen, Yang Pan, Hu Ye
abstract: Diffusion models have made significant progress in both text-to-image (T2I) generation and text-guided image editing. However, these models are typically built with billions of parameters, leading to high latency and increased deployment challenges. While on-device diffusion models improve efficiency, they largely focus on T2I generation and lack support for image editing. In this paper, we propose DreamLite, a compact unified on-device diffusion model (0.39B) that supports both T2I generation a

infographic.key_insight: DreamLite shows that a unified diffusion model with only 0.39B parameters can run on-device and support both text-to-image generation and text-guided image editing with practical latency and footprint.
infographic.problem_solved: Large diffusion models (billions of parameters) are too heavy for low-latency, on-device use, and existing lightweight models mostly support only T2I generation—not editing. DreamLite closes this gap by providing a compact, unified model for both tasks.
method: Compact diffusion backbone (~0.39B params) built with parameter-efficient architectural choices to retain generative quality while reducing size.
Unified conditioning scheme that accepts text plus image reference and optional edit masks, enabling the same model to perform both T2I generation and text-guided image editing.
On-device optimizations (e.g., quantization-aware training, distillation from larger teachers, and latency-aware pruning/architecture choices) to minimize runtime and memory footprint.
infographic.impact: Enables deployment of generation + editing capabilities directly on mobile and edge devices, reducing latency, storage, and privacy risks while making advanced image workflows accessible to practitioners and product teams.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: compact diffusion U‑Net with labeled modules (shared latent, text branch, reference/mask branch) and the 0.39B parameter callout.
Before/after editing triplets: original image → edit prompt/mask → edited output to demonstrate editing fidelity.

Training & deployment pipeline: teacher distillation + quantization → compact model → on-device inference flow.

title: Dynamic Dual-Granularity Skill Bank for Agentic RL
authors: Songjun Tu, Chengdong Xu, Qichao Zhang, Yaocheng Zhang, Xiangyuan Lan
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) can benefit substantially from reusable experience, yet existing skill-based methods mainly extract trajectory-level guidance and often lack principled mechanisms for maintaining an evolving skill memory. We propose D2Skill, a dynamic dual-granularity skill bank for agentic RL that organizes reusable experience into task skills for high-level guidance and step skills for fine-grained decision support and error correction. D2Skill jointly trains the policy and

infographic.key_insight: D2Skill maintains a dynamic dual-granularity skill bank—task-level skills for high-level guidance and step-level skills for fine-grained corrections—so an agent can reuse and adapt past experience more effectively during RL training.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of principled, evolving skill memory in skill-based RL: existing methods focus on trajectory-level guidance and miss fine-grained, stepwise corrections and continual updating of reusable skills.
method: Dual-granularity skill bank: store and represent reusable experience as task skills (trajectory/plan-level) and step skills (local/action-level) for complementary roles.
Dynamic memory management: jointly train the policy and skill bank with mechanisms to add, update, and prune skills online so the memory evolves with learning.
Skill-conditioned control: retrieve and apply task skills for high-level planning while invoking step skills for fine-grained decision support and error correction during execution.
infographic.impact: Enables more sample-efficient, robust, and transferable agentic RL by combining long-horizon guidance with precise corrective actions—beneficial for practitioners building adaptive agents and continual learning systems.

title: HandX: Scaling Bimanual Motion and Interaction Generation
authors: Zimu Zhang, Yucheng Zhang, Xiyan Xu, Ziyin Wang, Sirui Xu
abstract: Synthesizing human motion has advanced rapidly, yet realistic hand motion and bimanual interaction remain underexplored. Whole-body models often miss the fine-grained cues that drive dexterous behavior, finger articulation, contact timing, and inter-hand coordination, and existing resources lack high-fidelity bimanual sequences that capture nuanced finger dynamics and collaboration. To fill this gap, we present HandX, a unified foundation spanning data, annotation, and evaluation. We consolidate

infographic.key_insight: HandX provides a unified foundation—data, annotation, and evaluation—that enables scalable, high-fidelity generation of bimanual and finger-level human motion, capturing contact timing and inter-hand coordination that whole-body models miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing motion generation models and datasets lack high-resolution bimanual sequences and fine-grained annotations for finger articulation, contact events, and collaboration between hands, limiting realism in dexterous manipulation and interaction.
method: Assemble a large, high-fidelity bimanual motion dataset that preserves detailed finger trajectories and realistic inter-hand interactions.
Introduce fine-grained annotation schemas for contact timing, grasp types, and hand-to-hand/object relationships to supervise precise coordination.
Provide a training and evaluation pipeline (foundation model + metrics) that jointly models finger articulation, contact events, and bimanual coordination for generation and benchmarking.
infographic.impact: HandX enables practitioners to train and evaluate models that generate much more realistic hand and bimanual behaviors, improving applications in robotics, VR/AR, animation, and HCI where dexterous manipulation matters.

title: Adaptive Block-Scaled Data Types
authors: Jack Cook, Hyemin S. Lee, Kathryn Le, Junxian Guo, Giovanni Traverso
abstract: NVFP4 has grown increasingly popular as a 4-bit format for quantizing large language models due to its hardware support and its ability to retain useful information with relatively few bits per parameter. However, the format is not without limitations: recent work has shown that NVFP4 suffers from its error distribution, resulting in large amounts of quantization error on near-maximal values in each group of 16 values. In this work, we leverage this insight to design new Adaptive Block-Scaled Da

infographic.key_insight: NVFP4's quantization error is concentrated on near‑maximal values inside each 16‑value block; adapting the block scaling/encoding per block dramatically reduces those peak errors while staying hardware friendly.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces large, group‑localized quantization errors in NVFP4 4‑bit formats that degrade large language model fidelity, without requiring major hardware redesign.
method: Characterize NVFP4 error distribution and identify systematic near‑max saturation within 16‑value groups.
Introduce Adaptive Block‑Scaled Data Types: allocate a small per‑block scale/shift (and optional correction bits) so each 16‑value block uses an optimized local exponent/offset.
Design a hardware‑friendly encoder/decoder and lightweight fallback/hybrid encoding for corner cases to keep latency/area overhead minimal.
infographic.impact: Enables more accurate 4‑bit quantization for LLMs, improving downstream accuracy/perplexity and memory footprint with little additional hardware cost—making efficient inference and deployment of large models more practical.

title: Stop Probing, Start Coding: Why Linear Probes and Sparse Autoencoders Fail at Compositional Generalisation
authors: Vitória Barin Pacela, Shruti Joshi, Isabela Camacho, Simon Lacoste-Julien, David Klindt
abstract: The linear representation hypothesis states that neural network activations encode high-level concepts as linear mixtures. However, under superposition, this encoding is a projection from a higher-dimensional concept space into a lower-dimensional activation space, and a linear decision boundary in the concept space need not remain linear after projection. In this setting, classical sparse coding methods with per-sample iterative inference leverage compressed sensing guarantees to recover latent

infographic.key_insight: Linear probes and standard sparse autoencoders can falsely suggest conceptic structure but fail to support compositional generalisation when representations use superposition: projecting a higher‑dimensional concept space into a lower‑dimensional activation space can break linear separability, so probe success does not imply usable, compositional latent factors.
infographic.problem_solved: Explains why common analysis and representation methods (linear probes, per‑sample sparse autoencoding) are unreliable measures and mechanisms for compositional generalisation under superposition, and identifies what kinds of inference/decoding are needed to recover usable concepts.
method: Theoretical analysis: model concept encoding as a projection from a higher‑dimensional concept space into a lower‑dimensional activation space and show linear decision boundaries need not survive projection.
Empirical comparison: evaluate linear probes and sparse autoencoders versus per‑sample iterative inference / decoding methods (leveraging compressed‑sensing style guarantees) on compositional tasks.
Diagnostics and recommendations: identify failure modes and advocate for per‑sample decoding/inference or richer probes that reconstruct latent structure rather than relying only on linear readouts.
infographic.impact: Practitioners should not equate linear probe accuracy with recoverable, compositional concepts: to build or evaluate models that generalise compositionally, use reconstruction/decoding or iterative inference methods that can undo superposition instead of relying solely on linear probes.
visual_elements: Diagram: high‑dimensional concept vectors projected into a low‑dim activation space showing a linear decision boundary in concept space becoming nonlinear after projection.

title: Think over Trajectories: Leveraging Video Generation to Reconstruct GPS Trajectories from Cellular Signaling
authors: Ruixing Zhang, Hanzhang Jiang, Leilei Sun, Liangzhe Han, Jibin Wang
abstract: Mobile devices continuously interact with cellular base stations, generating massive volumes of signaling records that provide broad coverage for understanding human mobility. However, such records offer only coarse location cues (e.g., serving-cell identifiers) and therefore limit their direct use in applications that require high-precision GPS trajectories. This paper studies the Sig2GPS problem: reconstructing GPS trajectories from cellular signaling. Inspired by domain experts often lay the

infographic.key_insight: Treat cellular signaling sequences as a spatio-temporal 'video' and use generative video modeling to synthesize high‑resolution GPS trajectories from coarse cell‑tower records, recovering fine-grained routes that raw signaling lacks.
infographic.problem_solved: Converts ubiquitous but coarse cellular signaling (serving‑cell identifiers, timestamps) into accurate GPS‑level trajectories, enabling high‑precision mobility traces when direct GPS is unavailable or sparse.
method: Frame signaling sequences as a spatio‑temporal generation task and apply generative video/sequence models to predict continuous trajectory frames.
Fuse contextual priors (cell‑tower geometry, map constraints, temporal smoothness) to constrain generation and improve realism.
Train and/or fine‑tune with available GPS ground truth (supervised or self‑supervised alignment) and evaluate against standard trajectory baselines.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to unlock large-scale mobility insights from low‑cost signaling data without pervasive GPS, improving applications in urban planning, transportation analytics, and location‑based services while raising new considerations for privacy and responsible use.

title: MA-Bench: Towards Fine-grained Micro-Action Understanding
authors: Kun Li, Jihao Gu, Fei Wang, Zhiliang Wu, Hehe Fan
abstract: With the rapid development of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), their potential in Micro-Action understanding, a vital role in human emotion analysis, remains unexplored due to the absence of specialized benchmarks. To tackle this issue, we present MA-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,000 videos and a three-tier evaluation architecture that progressively examines micro-action perception, relational comprehension, and interpretive reasoning. MA-Bench contains 12,000 structured question-answ

infographic.key_insight: MA-Bench provides the first fine-grained benchmark specifically designed to evaluate Multimodal LLMs' ability to perceive, relate, and reason about subtle human micro-actions across video, enabling systematic measurement beyond coarse action labels.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of a dedicated benchmark for micro-action understanding in multimodal models prevents rigorous evaluation of fine-grained, brief human behaviors that are crucial for emotion and social signal analysis.
method: Curate a video dataset of ~1,000 clips annotated with fine-grained micro-actions and structure ~12,000 question–answer examples to probe different skills.
Design a three-tier evaluation framework: (1) micro-action perception, (2) relational comprehension between actions/agents, and (3) interpretive reasoning about intent/emotion.
Use structured QA tasks to benchmark MLLMs' capabilities and analyze errors across tiers for targeted model improvements.
infographic.impact: MA-Bench gives practitioners a focused testbed to diagnose and improve MLLMs on subtle behavioral cues, accelerating progress in emotion-aware and social AI applications.

title: Context-specific Credibility-aware Multimodal Fusion with Conditional Probabilistic Circuits
authors: Pranuthi Tenali, Sahil Sidheekh, Saurabh Mathur, Erik Blasch, Kristian Kersting
abstract: Multimodal fusion requires integrating information from multiple sources that may conflict depending on context. Existing fusion approaches typically rely on static assumptions about source reliability, limiting their ability to resolve conflicts when a modality becomes unreliable due to situational factors such as sensor degradation or class-specific corruption. We introduce C$^2$MF, a context-specfic credibility-aware multimodal fusion framework that models per-instance source reliability usin

infographic.key_insight: C^2MF models per-instance, context-specific source credibility using conditional probabilistic circuits, allowing the fusion process to dynamically reweight modalities and resolve conflicts when sensors or modalities become unreliable.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes static, global assumptions about modality reliability by detecting and adapting to instance- and context-dependent modality corruption (e.g., sensor degradation or class-specific noise) during multimodal fusion.
method: Estimate per-instance credibility for each modality conditioned on context (input features, class, environment) so reliability is dynamic rather than fixed.
Use conditional probabilistic circuits to represent joint distributions and perform tractable, uncertainty-aware inference that weights modality contributions according to estimated credibility.
Train the system end-to-end (or with latent reliability estimation) to calibrate credibility scores and produce robust fused predictions under sensor/class-specific corruptions.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build multimodal systems that are more robust and interpretable under real-world reliability shifts, improving performance and safety when sensors fail or data are corrupted.

title: PerceptionComp: A Video Benchmark for Complex Perception-Centric Reasoning
authors: Shaoxuan Li, Zhixuan Zhao, Hanze Deng, Zirun Ma, Shulin Tian
abstract: We introduce PerceptionComp, a manually annotated benchmark for complex, long-horizon, perception-centric video reasoning. PerceptionComp is designed so that no single moment is sufficient: answering each question requires multiple temporally separated pieces of visual evidence and compositional constraints under conjunctive and sequential logic, spanning perceptual subtasks such as objects, attributes, relations, locations, actions, and events, and requiring skills including semantic recognitio

infographic.key_insight: PerceptionComp is a manually annotated video benchmark that forces models to perform long‑horizon, perception‑centric reasoning by combining multiple temporally separated visual cues and compositional logic to answer each question.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video benchmarks often allow answers from a single frame or short context; PerceptionComp addresses the need for evaluation data that requires multi‑moment evidence aggregation and conjunctive/sequential compositional reasoning across perceptual subtasks.
method: Curate and manually annotate videos with questions that require multiple temporally separated pieces of visual evidence and compositional constraints (conjunctive and sequential logic).
Cover a broad set of perceptual subtasks—objects, attributes, relations, locations, actions, and events—so questions demand semantic recognition plus temporal composition.
Provide an evaluation suite that measures model performance on long‑horizon, perception‑centric reasoning rather than single‑moment recognition.
infographic.impact: PerceptionComp enables more realistic assessment and development of video reasoning models by exposing deficiencies in temporal evidence aggregation and compositional understanding, guiding progress toward robust, real‑world multimodal perception systems.

title: Make Geometry Matter for Spatial Reasoning
authors: Shihua Zhang, Qiuhong Shen, Shizun Wang, Tianbo Pan, Xinchao Wang
abstract: Empowered by large-scale training, vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong image and video understanding, yet their ability to perform spatial reasoning in both static scenes and dynamic videos remains limited. Recent advances try to handle this limitation by injecting geometry tokens from pretrained 3D foundation models into VLMs. Nevertheless, we observe that naive token fusion followed by standard fine-tuning in this line of work often leaves such geometric cues underutilized for spatial

infographic.key_insight: Geometry tokens from pretrained 3D models can be made materially useful for vision–language models by changing how they are fused and fine-tuned, enabling much better spatial reasoning in static scenes and dynamic videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Vision–language models underuse geometric cues when geometry tokens are naively appended and standard fine‑tuning is applied, limiting performance on tasks that require understanding relative positions, depth, occlusion and motion.
method: Extract compact geometry tokens from pretrained 3D foundation models (depth, point-cloud or mesh features) to represent scene geometry.
Introduce a geometry-aware fusion module that preserves geometric relationships and injects geometry into cross-modal attention (or feature modulation) rather than simple token concatenation.

Design geometry-centric training objectives and a targeted fine‑tuning schedule (e.g., alignment/contrastive losses, spatial completion or masked-geometry tasks) to ensure the VLM actually leverages geometric cues.
infographic.impact: Makes VLMs substantially more capable at spatial reasoning tasks (relative location, occlusion handling, motion grounding), which benefits applications in robotics, AR/VR, autonomous systems and video understanding by providing more reliable spatial grounding.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: image/video → geometry extractor (3D model) → geometry-aware fusion → VLM outputs (QA/relations) — annotated to show where geometry is injected.
Before vs after examples: paired visual QA or relation-prediction cases showing failures with naive fusion and corrected answers with the proposed method.

title: Learning to Commit: Generating Organic Pull Requests via Online Repository Memory
authors: Mo Li, L. H. Xu, Qitai Tan, Ting Cao, Yunxin Liu
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based coding agents achieve impressive results on controlled benchmarks yet routinely produce pull requests that real maintainers reject. The root cause is not functional incorrectness but a lack of organicity: generated code ignores project-specific conventions, duplicates functionality already provided by internal APIs, and violates implicit architectural constraints accumulated over years of development. Simply exposing an agent to the latest repository snapshot is

infographic.key_insight: Augment code-generating LLMs with an online repository memory that records project history, APIs, conventions, and reviewer feedback so generated pull requests are 'organic'—aligned with a repo's implicit architecture and more likely to be accepted.
infographic.problem_solved: LLM-based coding agents produce functionally plausible changes that maintainers reject because they ignore project-specific conventions, duplicate internal APIs, or violate long-evolved architectural constraints. The paper addresses how to make automated PRs fit repository-specific norms and workflows.
method: Construct an online repository memory that indexes commits, API signatures, usage patterns, tests, CI results, PR discussions, and code-owner metadata for retrieval.

Use retrieval-augmented generation: condition the LLM on relevant memory slices (historical examples, canonical APIs, style snippets) to propose diffs and PR descriptions that respect local conventions.
Close the loop with continual updates: ingest new commits, reviewer feedback, and CI outcomes to refresh memory and bias future proposals toward accepted patterns.
infographic.impact: Makes automated code contributions practical and trustworthy by increasing PR acceptance, reducing maintainer overhead, and enabling LLMs to respect long-lived, project-specific design constraints—critical for real-world deployment of code generation tools.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: Repository memory (icons: commits, APIs, reviews) -> Retrieval -> LLM -> Generated PR -> Maintainer/CI feedback loop

title: VGGRPO: Towards World-Consistent Video Generation with 4D Latent Reward
authors: Zhaochong An, Orest Kupyn, Théo Uscidda, Andrea Colaco, Karan Ahuja
abstract: Large-scale video diffusion models achieve impressive visual quality, yet often fail to preserve geometric consistency. Prior approaches improve consistency either by augmenting the generator with additional modules or applying geometry-aware alignment. However, architectural modifications can compromise the generalization of internet-scale pretrained models, while existing alignment methods are limited to static scenes and rely on RGB-space rewards that require repeated VAE decoding, incurring

infographic.key_insight: Compute a geometry-aware reward in 4D latent space (space + time) to align pretrained video diffusion models to world-consistent generation, avoiding architectural changes and costly RGB reconstructions.
infographic.problem_solved: Video diffusion models produce high-quality frames but often violate geometric/temporal consistency; prior fixes either alter model architectures (hurting generalization) or use RGB-space alignment that is slow and limited to static scenes.
method: Design a 4D (3D space + time) latent reward that measures world-consistency across frames inside the model's latent space rather than in decoded RGB.
Use the latent reward to guide optimization/alignment of pretrained video diffusion models (reward-based policy/optimization) without adding new generation modules.
Operate entirely in latent space to support dynamic scenes and avoid repeated VAE decoding, reducing compute and preserving internet-scale pretraining generalization.
infographic.impact: Enables efficient, architecture-preserving refinement of pretrained video diffusion models for better geometric and temporal consistency, making high-quality, world-consistent video generation practical for researchers and production systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: pretrained video diffusion model -> 4D latent extractor -> latent reward computation -> reward-guided optimization (no new modules).

title: Beyond Language: Grounding Referring Expressions with Hand Pointing in Egocentric Vision
authors: Ling Li, Bowen Liu, Zinuo Zhan, Peng Jie, Jianhui Zhong
abstract: Traditional Visual Grounding (VG) predominantly relies on textual descriptions to localize objects, a paradigm that inherently struggles with linguistic ambiguity and often ignores non-verbal deictic cues prevalent in real-world interactions. In natural egocentric engagements, hand-pointing combined with speech forms the most intuitive referring mechanism. To bridge this gap, we introduce EgoPoint-Ground, the first large-scale multimodal dataset dedicated to egocentric deictic visual grounding.

infographic.key_insight: Combining hand-pointing cues with spoken references in egocentric video enables more precise and unambiguous object grounding than text-only methods.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses linguistic ambiguity and the omission of non-verbal deictic cues in traditional visual grounding by introducing a multimodal framework that leverages hand-pointing plus speech in first-person (egocentric) settings.
method: EgoPoint-Ground: collect and release the first large-scale egocentric dataset with synchronized video, hand-pointing signals, and speech-based referring expressions.
Annotate and align modalities (hand keypoints/deictic gestures, speech transcripts, and object bounding boxes) to create grounding supervision for ambiguous references.
Provide multimodal baselines and evaluation protocols that fuse visual, linguistic, and deictic (hand) cues to benchmark egocentric referring expression grounding.
infographic.impact: Enables more robust, real-world referring systems for AR, assistive devices, and human-robot interaction by reducing ambiguity and leveraging natural deictic behaviors; provides a benchmark to drive multimodal grounding research.
visual_elements: Egocentric frame annotated with hand skeleton, pointing vector, speech transcript, and target bounding box (step-by-step overlay).

title: Drive-Through 3D Vehicle Exterior Reconstruction via Dynamic-Scene SfM and Distortion-Aware Gaussian Splatting
authors: Nitin Kulkarni, Akhil Devarashetti, Charlie Cluss, Livio Forte, Philip Schneider
abstract: High-fidelity 3D reconstruction of vehicle exteriors improves buyer confidence in online automotive marketplaces, but generating these models in cluttered dealership drive-throughs presents severe technical challenges. Unlike static-scene photogrammetry, this setting features a dynamic vehicle moving against heavily cluttered, static backgrounds. This problem is further compounded by wide-angle lens distortion, specular automotive paint, and non-rigid wheel rotations that violate classical epipo

infographic.key_insight: Combine dynamic-scene SfM that isolates a moving vehicle from static clutter with a distortion-aware Gaussian splatting renderer to produce high-fidelity 3D vehicle exteriors from drive-through footage despite lens distortion, specular paint, and rotating wheels.
infographic.problem_solved: Accurate, scalable reconstruction of vehicle exteriors captured in cluttered dealership drive-throughs where the subject moves, backgrounds are static but busy, lenses are wide-angle, and surfaces are highly specular or partially non-rigid (wheel rotation).
method: Dynamic-scene SfM pipeline that segments and tracks the moving vehicle separately from the static background to recover robust geometry and camera poses.
Distortion-aware camera modeling and calibration to correct wide-angle lens effects before reconstruction.
Gaussian splatting-based surface representation optimized for specular reflections and per-frame non-rigid effects (e.g., wheel rotation), producing dense, photoreal outputs.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, drive-through capture workflows for generating production-quality 3D vehicle assets at scale, improving virtual showrooms, AR experiences, and training data for downstream vision systems. Makes photogrammetric reconstruction robust to motion, clutter, and optical distortions.

title: Detailed Geometry and Appearance from Opportunistic Motion
authors: Ryosuke Hirai, Kohei Yamashita, Antoine Guédon, Ryo Kawahara, Vincent Lepetit
abstract: Reconstructing 3D geometry and appearance from a sparse set of fixed cameras is a foundational task with broad applications, yet it remains fundamentally constrained by the limited viewpoints. We show that this bound can be broken by exploiting opportunistic object motion: as a person manipulates an object~(e.g., moving a chair or lifting a mug), the static cameras effectively ``orbit'' the object in its local coordinate frame, providing additional virtual viewpoints. Harnessing this object moti

infographic.key_insight: When an object is manipulated in front of fixed cameras, its motion creates effective new viewpoints in the object’s local frame; estimating those object-centric transforms lets a system synthesize these virtual views and recover much more detailed geometry and appearance than static multi-view setups permit.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the severe viewpoint limitation of sparse, fixed-camera rigs by exploiting opportunistic object motion (e.g., human manipulation) to produce additional virtual viewpoints for high-quality 3D reconstruction.
method: Detect and track the object through time and estimate object-centric transforms induced by manipulation (aligning frames to an object coordinate frame).
Re-project and aggregate image evidence from many temporally-separated frames as virtual camera viewpoints around the object.
Jointly optimize geometry and appearance (e.g., multi-view stereo / neural rendering in object frame) to produce high-fidelity shape and texture from sparse physical cameras.
infographic.impact: Makes high-quality 3D capture feasible with inexpensive, static camera setups and natural human interaction—beneficial for AR/VR content creation, robotic perception, and scalable dataset collection without elaborate turntables or camera rigs.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: fixed cameras watching a moving object vs. equivalent virtual orbiting cameras in the object frame.
Pipeline flowchart: detection → object-centric alignment → virtual view aggregation → geometry & appearance optimization.
Before/after reconstructions: coarse result from static views only vs. detailed reconstruction using opportunistic motion.
Viewpoint coverage heatmap showing increased angular coverage achieved through object motion.

title: PQuantML: A Tool for End-to-End Hardware-aware Model Compression
authors: Roope Niemi, Anastasiia Petrovych, Arghya Ranjan Das, Enrico Lupi, Chang Sun
abstract: PQuantML is a new open-source, hardware-aware neural network model compression library tailored to end-to-end workflows. Motivated by the need to deploy performant models to environments with strict latency constraints, PQuantML simplifies training of compressed models by providing a unified interface to apply pruning and quantization, either jointly or individually. The library implements multiple pruning methods with different granularities, as well as fixed-point quantization with support for

infographic.key_insight: PQuantML is an open-source, hardware-aware library that unifies pruning and fixed-point quantization into an end-to-end workflow, enabling practitioners to compress models (jointly or separately) while accounting for real latency constraints on target hardware.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between model compression research and deployment by providing a single, easy-to-use tool that produces low-latency, resource-efficient models suitable for constrained or latency-sensitive hardware environments.
method: Unified API to apply pruning and fixed-point quantization either jointly or independently within a single training/deployment pipeline.
Implements multiple pruning granularities (e.g., weight-, channel-, and layer-level) so users can trade off sparsity patterns and performance.
Hardware-aware optimization that factors device constraints into compression decisions to maintain accuracy while meeting latency/resource budgets.
infographic.impact: Makes it faster and safer for ML engineers to produce deployment-ready, compressed models for edge and embedded targets, reducing iteration time and unexpected performance regressions on real hardware.

title: Tunable Soft Equivariance with Guarantees
authors: Md Ashiqur Rahman, Lim Jun Hao, Jeremiah Jiang, Teck-Yian Lim, Raymond A. Yeh
abstract: Equivariance is a fundamental property in computer vision models, yet strict equivariance is rarely satisfied in real-world data, which can limit a model's performance. Controlling the degree of equivariance is therefore desirable. We propose a general framework for constructing soft equivariant models by projecting the model weights into a designed subspace. The method applies to any pre-trained architecture and provides theoretical bounds on the induced equivariance error. Empirically, we demo

infographic.key_insight: Projecting model weights into a designed subspace yields a controllable, "soft" form of equivariance with provable bounds on the resulting equivariance error, allowing models to trade strict symmetry for better real-world performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Strict equivariance assumptions often don't hold on real-world data and can hurt performance; this work provides a way to continuously control the degree of equivariance while offering theoretical guarantees.
method: Design a weight subspace that encodes desired symmetry constraints and project model weights into this subspace.
Introduce a tunable parameter (or projection design) that adjusts how strongly the model adheres to equivariance, enabling ‘‘soft’’ equivariance between fully equivariant and unconstrained.
Provide theoretical bounds linking the projection (subspace) to the induced equivariance error; method is architecture-agnostic and applicable to pre-trained models.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to match model symmetry to noisy, imperfect real-world data, improving robustness and performance without retraining from scratch—while maintaining formal error guarantees.

title: Zero-Shot Depth from Defocus
authors: Yiming Zuo, Hongyu Wen, Venkat Subramanian, Patrick Chen, Karhan Kayan
abstract: Depth from Defocus (DfD) is the task of estimating a dense metric depth map from a focus stack. Unlike previous works overfitting to a certain dataset, this paper focuses on the challenging and practical setting of zero-shot generalization. We first propose a new real-world DfD benchmark ZEDD, which contains 8.3x more scenes and significantly higher quality images and ground-truth depth maps compared to previous benchmarks. We also design a novel network architecture named FOSSA. FOSSA is a Tran

infographic.key_insight: Combining a much larger, higher-quality real-world DfD benchmark (ZEDD) with a purpose-built network (FOSSA) enables reliable zero-shot depth estimation from focus stacks across unseen scenes.
infographic.problem_solved: Depth-from-defocus models that overfit to specific datasets; the paper addresses the practical challenge of producing dense metric depth maps from focus stacks that generalize zero-shot to new real-world scenes.
method: ZEDD benchmark: introduce a real-world DfD dataset with ~8.3× more scenes and higher-quality images and ground-truth depth than prior benchmarks to evaluate generalization.
FOSSA network: design a novel architecture tailored to process focus stacks and predict dense metric depth with robustness to domain shifts.
Zero-shot evaluation protocol: emphasize cross-dataset testing to measure and drive true out-of-domain performance rather than dataset-specific tuning.
infographic.impact: Gives researchers and practitioners a realistic benchmark and a modeling approach focused on cross-domain robustness, reducing the need for dataset-specific retraining and accelerating deployment of depth-from-defocus systems in diverse real-world applications.

title: From Static to Dynamic: Exploring Self-supervised Image-to-Video Representation Transfer Learning
authors: Yang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Peisong Wen, Siran Dai, Xilin Zhao
abstract: Recent studies have made notable progress in video representation learning by transferring image-pretrained models to video tasks, typically with complex temporal modules and video fine-tuning. However, fine-tuning heavy modules may compromise inter-video semantic separability, i.e., the essential ability to distinguish objects across videos. While reducing the tunable parameters hinders their intra-video temporal consistency, which is required for stable representations of the same object withi

infographic.key_insight: Carefully designed, parameter-efficient self-supervised adaptation of image-pretrained models can add temporal dynamics for video while preserving inter-video semantic separability, achieving stable and discriminative video representations without heavy fine-tuning.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between static image pretraining and dynamic video tasks by resolving the trade-off where heavy fine-tuning hurts inter-video semantic separability and overly few tunable parameters harm intra-video temporal consistency.
method: Introduce lightweight temporal adapters (dynamic modules) that inject temporal modeling into image-pretrained backbones with minimal additional parameters.

Combine complementary self-supervised objectives: an inter-video contrastive/separability loss to keep different videos distinguishable, and an intra-video temporal-consistency loss to stabilize representations across frames.
Adopt a selective, parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy (e.g., temporal-only updates or adapter tuning) to balance efficiency and representation quality.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to repurpose large image models for video tasks more efficiently—reducing compute and annotation needs—while maintaining both discriminative power across videos and temporal stability within videos.

title: ShotStream: Streaming Multi-Shot Video Generation for Interactive Storytelling
authors: Yawen Luo, Xiaoyu Shi, Junhao Zhuang, Yutian Chen, Quande Liu
abstract: Multi-shot video generation is crucial for long narrative storytelling, yet current bidirectional architectures suffer from limited interactivity and high latency. We propose ShotStream, a novel causal multi-shot architecture that enables interactive storytelling and efficient on-the-fly frame generation. By reformulating the task as next-shot generation conditioned on historical context, ShotStream allows users to dynamically instruct ongoing narratives via streaming prompts. We achieve this by

infographic.key_insight: ShotStream reframes multi-shot video generation as next-shot prediction conditioned on historical context, enabling a causal streaming architecture that supports low-latency, interactive on-the-fly frame generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the limited interactivity and high latency of bidirectional multi-shot video models by allowing users to dynamically steer an ongoing narrative and receive immediate frame/shot outputs without reprocessing the entire video.
method: Reformulate multi-shot generation as next-shot generation conditioned on a compact history buffer and streaming user prompts.
Design a causal multi-shot architecture that generates shots sequentially (shot-by-shot) rather than via bidirectional passes, enabling incremental decoding and state caching.
Optimize for on-the-fly synthesis with efficient sampling and cached state updates so new instructions can be applied mid-story with low latency.
infographic.impact: Enables real-time, user-in-the-loop storytelling workflows (games, live content creation, interactive narratives) by reducing latency and improving interactivity for long-form video generation. Practitioners can build responsive generative systems that adapt to dynamic prompts without full re-generation.

title: Back to Basics: Revisiting ASR in the Age of Voice Agents
authors: Geeyang Tay, Wentao Ma, Jaewon Lee, Yuzhi Tang, Daniel Lee
abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved near-human accuracy on curated benchmarks, yet still fail in real-world voice agents under conditions that current evaluations do not systematically cover. Without diagnostic tools that isolate specific failure factors, practitioners cannot anticipate which conditions, in which languages, will cause what degree of degradation. We introduce WildASR, a multilingual (four-language) diagnostic benchmark sourced entirely from real human speech

infographic.key_insight: WildASR is a multilingual diagnostic benchmark sourced from real human speech that systematically isolates failure factors, revealing substantial real-world ASR degradations missed by curated benchmarks.
infographic.problem_solved: ASR evaluations that look near-human on curated tests fail to expose which languages, conditions, or factors cause degradation in deployed voice agents—practitioners lack diagnostic tools to anticipate and quantify these failures.
method: Assemble WildASR: a four-language dataset drawn entirely from real human speech covering diverse recording devices, environments, accents, and utterance types.
Annotate and organize data around diagnostic factors (noise, channel, speaker variation, language) and define an evaluation protocol and metrics to isolate their impacts.
Benchmark multiple ASR systems across factors to quantify performance gaps and provide analysis tools for targeted failure-mode diagnosis.
infographic.impact: WildASR enables engineers and researchers to pinpoint where and why ASR systems fail in realistic settings, guiding robust model development, targeted data collection, and safer deployment of voice agents.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing word-error-rate (WER) across the four languages and common noise/channel conditions to highlight performance gaps.

title: A Unified Memory Perspective for Probabilistic Trustworthy AI
authors: Xueji Zhao, Likai Pei, Jianbo Liu, Kai Ni, Ningyuan Cao
abstract: Trustworthy artificial intelligence increasingly relies on probabilistic computation to achieve robustness, interpretability, security and privacy. In practical systems, such workloads interleave deterministic data access with repeated stochastic sampling across models, data paths and system functions, shifting performance bottlenecks from arithmetic units to memory systems that must deliver both data and randomness. Here we present a unified data-access perspective in which deterministic access

infographic.key_insight: Probabilistic trustworthy AI workloads shift bottlenecks from compute to memory because they interleave deterministic data access with heavy, repeated stochastic sampling; treating randomness as a first‑class memory stream enables a unified, more efficient system design.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the mismatch between conventional memory systems (designed for deterministic data) and emerging probabilistic AI workloads that require high-throughput, low-latency delivery of both data and high-quality randomness while preserving robustness, interpretability, security and privacy.
method: Formalize a unified data‑access model that represents deterministic data and stochastic samples as coexisting memory streams with predictable access patterns.

Propose hardware–software co‑design primitives (e.g., RNG integration at/near memory controllers, entropy-aware caches, and sampling APIs) to deliver randomness alongside data with low latency and controlled quality.
Introduce memory-aware scheduling, caching and security primitives to prioritize interleaved deterministic/stochastic access, audit entropy sources, and reduce contention and leakage.
infographic.impact: By reframing randomness as a memory service, the approach helps AI/ML systems scale probabilistic workloads with lower latency, better energy efficiency and stronger operational guarantees for robustness, interpretability and privacy—making trustworthy probabilistic methods more practical in real systems.
visual_elements: Schematic of a memory subsystem showing two coexisting streams: deterministic data and randomness (RNG) delivered from/near memory controllers to models.
Timeline/flow diagram illustrating interleaved deterministic reads and repeated stochastic sampling that create memory contention and shifted bottlenecks.
Before/after comparative chart (latency/throughput/energy qualitative bars) contrasting conventional memory vs. unified memory design (no numeric labels required).

title: PixelSmile: Toward Fine-Grained Facial Expression Editing
authors: Jiabin Hua, Hengyuan Xu, Aojie Li, Wei Cheng, Gang Yu
abstract: Fine-grained facial expression editing has long been limited by intrinsic semantic overlap. To address this, we construct the Flex Facial Expression (FFE) dataset with continuous affective annotations and establish FFE-Bench to evaluate structural confusion, editing accuracy, linear controllability, and the trade-off between expression editing and identity preservation. We propose PixelSmile, a diffusion framework that disentangles expression semantics via fully symmetric joint training. PixelSm

infographic.key_insight: PixelSmile enables fine-grained, continuously controllable facial expression editing by disentangling overlapping expression semantics through a fully symmetric joint-training diffusion framework and training on a new continuous-affect dataset.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes intrinsic semantic overlap and lack of continuous annotations/benchmarks that previously limited precise, identity-preserving facial expression editing and fair evaluation of controllability and structural confusion.
method: Construct FFE: a Flex Facial Expression dataset with continuous affective annotations and publish FFE-Bench to measure structural confusion, editing accuracy, linear controllability, and expression–identity trade-offs.
Design PixelSmile: a diffusion-based model that uses fully symmetric joint training to disentangle expression semantics, enabling fine-grained, linearly controllable edits while preserving identity.

Evaluate and optimize the trade-off between editing accuracy and identity preservation with dedicated metrics (structural confusion matrix, accuracy, controllability curves, and identity loss analyses).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a method and standardized data/bench to perform precise, controllable facial expression edits for applications like avatar animation, reenactment, and data augmentation, while improving reproducible evaluation of expression models.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram of PixelSmile showing input image → symmetric joint-trained diffusion encoder/decoder → disentangled expression latent → controlled edit → output image.
Continuous affect space visualization (2D scatter/heatmap) from FFE to illustrate dense annotation and semantic overlaps.
Benchmark charts: confusion matrix for structural overlap, accuracy bars, and a trade-off curve plotting editing strength vs identity preservation.

title: On Neural Scaling Laws for Weather Emulation through Continual Training
authors: Shashank Subramanian, Alexander Kiefer, Arnur Nigmetov, Amir Gholami, Dmitriy Morozov
abstract: Neural scaling laws, which in some domains can predict the performance of large neural networks as a function of model, data, and compute scale, are the cornerstone of building foundation models in Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision. We study neural scaling in Scientific Machine Learning, focusing on models for weather forecasting. To analyze scaling behavior in as simple a setting as possible, we adopt a minimal, scalable, general-purpose Swin Transformer architecture, and we use c

infographic.key_insight: Neural scaling laws extend to weather emulation: using a minimal Swin Transformer and a continual-training protocol, performance scales predictably with model size, data, and compute—allowing reliable extrapolation of gains from increased scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of quantitative understanding about how model, data, and compute scaling (and continual training on streaming data) affect performance for weather forecasting/emulation in Scientific ML.
method: Adopt a minimal, scalable Swin Transformer as a general-purpose weather emulator to keep architectural confounders low.
Run controlled scaling experiments that sweep model size, dataset size, and compute to characterize empirical scaling laws.
Use a continual-training protocol that simulates streaming weather data to measure long-term performance, transfer, and data efficiency.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a practical framework to predict returns from scaling and to allocate model/data/compute budgets for weather emulators; informs design of efficient continual-training strategies for Earth-system foundation models.
visual_elements: Log–log plots of validation loss / forecast skill vs model size, dataset size, and compute showing scaling (power-law) trends.
Schematic diagram of the minimal Swin Transformer architecture used (patches, attention windows) to emphasize simplicity and scalability.
Timeline visualization of continual training: streaming data segments with a performance curve showing adaptation and cumulative gains.

title: MuRF: Unlocking the Multi-Scale Potential of Vision Foundation Models
authors: Bocheng Zou, Mu Cai, Mark Stanley, Dingfu Lu, Yong Jae Lee
abstract: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) have become the cornerstone of modern computer vision, offering robust representations across a wide array of tasks. While recent advances allow these models to handle varying input sizes during training, inference typically remains restricted to a single, fixed scale. This prevalent single-scale paradigm overlooks a fundamental property of visual perception: varying resolutions offer complementary inductive biases, where low-resolution views excel at global seman

infographic.key_insight: MuRF enables Vision Foundation Models to operate effectively across multiple input scales, letting them combine complementary strengths of low- and high-resolution views to produce stronger, scale-robust representations.
infographic.problem_solved: Current VFMs are typically run at a single fixed inference scale, failing to exploit complementary inductive biases from different resolutions (global context at low-res vs. fine detail at high-res).
method: Introduce a lightweight multi-scale inference framework that permits a VFM to ingest and aggregate features from multiple resolutions without re-training from scratch.
Use a compact fusion/aggregation mechanism to reconcile scale-specific features into a unified representation for downstream tasks.
Maintain compatibility with existing VFM weights to enable easy adaptation and efficient deployment across tasks and compute budgets.
infographic.impact: MuRF makes foundation models more flexible and robust by unlocking multi-scale information, improving downstream performance and deployment options while minimizing extra training cost. Practitioners can get better accuracy/robustness trade-offs and more adaptable inference strategies across vision tasks.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing multi-scale inputs (low-res and high-res) feeding into a shared VFM and a fusion module producing a single output.

title: BizGenEval: A Systematic Benchmark for Commercial Visual Content Generation
authors: Yan Li, Zezi Zeng, Ziwei Zhou, Xin Gao, Muzhao Tian
abstract: Recent advances in image generation models have expanded their applications beyond aesthetic imagery toward practical visual content creation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on natural image synthesis and fail to systematically evaluate models under the structured and multi-constraint requirements of real-world commercial design tasks. In this work, we introduce BizGenEval, a systematic benchmark for commercial visual content generation. The benchmark spans five representative documen

infographic.key_insight: BizGenEval provides the first systematic benchmark that evaluates image-generation models on structured, multi-constraint commercial design tasks rather than just natural-image aesthetics, exposing strengths and failure modes important for real-world visual content creation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks target aesthetic or natural-image synthesis and do not measure how well models satisfy the structural, textual, and brand constraints required by commercial visual assets; BizGenEval fills this gap by defining representative tasks and evaluation criteria.
method: Curate a suite of five representative commercial asset categories and associated prompts that encode layout, text, and brand constraints (e.g., composition, typography, required content).

Define multi-constraint evaluation protocols combining automated metrics (layout alignment, OCR/text accuracy, color/brand consistency, fidelity) with targeted human judgments for usability and design quality.
Provide standardized test splits and baseline results to enable systematic comparison and diagnosis of model performance under realistic production constraints.
infographic.impact: BizGenEval helps researchers and engineers benchmark and improve generative models for production-ready visual content, accelerating development of models that reliably meet layout, textual, and branding requirements in commercial workflows.

title: Neural Network Conversion of Machine Learning Pipelines
authors: Man-Ling Sung, Jan Silovsky, Man-Hung Siu, Herbert Gish, Chinnu Pittapally
abstract: Transfer learning and knowledge distillation has recently gained a lot of attention in the deep learning community. One transfer approach, the student-teacher learning, has been shown to successfully create ``small'' student neural networks that mimic the performance of a much bigger and more complex ``teacher'' networks. In this paper, we investigate an extension to this approach and transfer from a non-neural-based machine learning pipeline as teacher to a neural network (NN) student, which wo

infographic.key_insight: A non-neural machine learning pipeline can act as a "teacher" to train a compact neural network student that reproduces the pipeline's behavior, enabling end-to-end neural replacement of complex, heterogeneous ML systems.
infographic.problem_solved: How to convert bulky, non-differentiable or heterogeneous ML pipelines into a single, deployable neural model that preserves behavior while reducing maintenance, latency, and deployment complexity.
method: Treat the existing pipeline as a teacher: run inputs through the pipeline to generate soft targets and (optionally) intermediate representations for supervision.

Design a student neural network (architecture can mirror pipeline structure or be compact/efficient) and train it with losses that combine mimicry of teacher outputs and any available ground-truth labels.
Handle non-differentiable or specialized steps by supervising intermediate outputs, using surrogate differentiable approximations, or distilling behavior via dataset augmentation and loss weighting.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to replace fragile, multi-component ML pipelines with a single neural model that is easier to optimize, accelerate (hardware/quantization), and deploy to production or edge devices without large accuracy loss.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: original multi-step pipeline (preprocessing, rules, models) vs. single neural network replacing all steps

title: RefAlign: Representation Alignment for Reference-to-Video Generation
authors: Lei Wang, YuXin Song, Ge Wu, Haocheng Feng, Hang Zhou
abstract: Reference-to-video (R2V) generation is a controllable video synthesis paradigm that constrains the generation process using both text prompts and reference images, enabling applications such as personalized advertising and virtual try-on. In practice, existing R2V methods typically introduce additional high-level semantic or cross-modal features alongside the VAE latent representation of the reference image and jointly feed them into the diffusion Transformer (DiT). These auxiliary representatio

infographic.key_insight: Align the VAE latent of the reference image with auxiliary high-level semantic/cross-modal features before diffusion, so the diffusion Transformer receives a coherent, shared representation—improving fidelity and controllability over naive concatenation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing reference-to-video (R2V) methods simply append extra semantic or cross-modal features to VAE latents, producing representational mismatch that harms identity preservation, attribute control, and temporal coherence in generated videos.
method: Representation Alignment Module: learn lightweight projection/adapters to map VAE latents and auxiliary semantic/cross-modal features into a shared latent space that preserves spatial detail and high-level semantics.
Alignment objective: train with alignment losses (e.g., contrastive or L2-based consistency terms) so paired reference and semantic features become compatible for generation.

Aligned fusion into diffusion Transformer: feed the aligned, fused representation into the DiT-based video diffusion pipeline (with temporal conditioning/attention) to produce controllable, identity-preserving videos.
infographic.impact: Makes reference-to-video generation more reliable and controllable while keeping model complexity low—useful for personalization tasks (virtual try-on, advertising) and for practitioners aiming to integrate multi-modal references into diffusion-based video synthesis.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: show VAE encoder -> alignment module (projections/adapters) merging with semantic features -> diffusion Transformer for video frames.
Before vs. after examples: side-by-side video frame sequences comparing naive concatenation vs. aligned representation results.

title: Out of Sight but Not Out of Mind: Hybrid Memory for Dynamic Video World Models
authors: Kaijin Chen, Dingkang Liang, Xin Zhou, Yikang Ding, Xiaoqiang Liu
abstract: Video world models have shown immense potential in simulating the physical world, yet existing memory mechanisms primarily treat environments as static canvases. When dynamic subjects hide out of sight and later re-emerge, current methods often struggle, leading to frozen, distorted, or vanishing subjects. To address this, we introduce Hybrid Memory, a novel paradigm requiring models to simultaneously act as precise archivists for static backgrounds and vigilant trackers for dynamic subjects, en

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid Memory splits memory into complementary roles—precise long-term archival for static backgrounds and vigilant short-term tracking for dynamic subjects—so objects that go out of sight are preserved and correctly re-integrated when they reappear.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video world models treat environments as largely static and fail when dynamic subjects become occluded: objects can freeze, distort, or disappear after temporary occlusion or leaving the frame.
method: Dual-memory architecture: a long-term archival store for static scene content + a short-term, identity-aware tracker for dynamic subjects.
Occlusion- and reappearance-aware read/write rules that maintain persistent object identities and motion cues while updating background geometry.
Integrate hybrid memory into video world-model training to improve simulation, prediction, and re-rendering across occlusions and temporal gaps.
infographic.impact: Provides more robust, realistic video world models that preserve object continuity across occlusions—beneficial for simulation, planning, robotics, and downstream prediction tasks where object persistence matters.

Before/after frames illustrating object occlusion: baseline (frozen/vanished) vs Hybrid Memory (correct re-emergence)

title: PackForcing: Short Video Training Suffices for Long Video Sampling and Long Context Inference
authors: Xiaofeng Mao, Shaohao Rui, Kaining Ying, Bo Zheng, Chuanhao Li
abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable progress, yet they remain bottlenecked by intractable linear KV-cache growth, temporal repetition, and compounding errors during long-video generation. To address these challenges, we present PackForcing, a unified framework that efficiently manages the generation history through a novel three-partition KV-cache strategy. Specifically, we categorize the historical context into three distinct types: (1) Sink tokens, which preserve

infographic.key_insight: PackForcing shows that training autoregressive video diffusion models on short clips is sufficient for stable long-video sampling and long-context inference by managing history with a three-partition KV-cache.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses intractable linear KV-cache growth, temporal repetition, and compounding errors that prevent scalable, high-quality long-video generation.
method: Three-partition KV-cache that separates historical context into: sink tokens (persistent anchors), compact/packed summaries of older context, and an active recent-context cache to limit growth and repetition.

Training on short video clips with the PackForcing cache strategy so the model learns to rely on compacted history and therefore generalizes to arbitrarily long sampling without linear memory scaling.
Sampling-time mechanics that read from the three partitions to reconstruct long-range context while avoiding repeated content and reducing error propagation.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable long-video generation with much lower memory and compute cost, making long-context autoregressive diffusion practical for researchers and developers building video generation and long-horizon sequence models.

title: Natural-Language Agent Harnesses
authors: Linyue Pan, Lexiao Zou, Shuo Guo, Jingchen Ni, Hai-Tao Zheng
abstract: Agent performance increasingly depends on \emph{harness engineering}, yet harness design is usually buried in controller code and runtime-specific conventions, making it hard to transfer, compare, and study as a scientific object. We ask whether the high-level control logic of an agent harness can instead be externalized as a portable executable artifact. We introduce \textbf{Natural-Language Agent Harnesses} (NLAHs), which express harness behavior in editable natural language, and \textbf{Intel

infographic.key_insight: Agent harness logic can be externalized as editable, executable natural-language artifacts (Natural-Language Agent Harnesses, NLAHs), making harness design transparent, portable, and comparable across agents and runtimes.
infographic.problem_solved: Harness engineering is typically buried in controller code and runtime conventions, which makes harnesses hard to transfer, reproduce, compare, and study as first-class scientific objects.
method: Encode high-level control and evaluation policies for agents as natural-language harness specifications (NLAHs) that are human-editable.
Provide an execution/interpretation layer that maps these NL specifications to runtime behavior so they can be applied across different controllers and environments.
Empirically evaluate NLAHs to demonstrate improved portability, transparency, and comparability of harness behavior across agents and tasks.
infographic.impact: NLAHs lower the barrier to sharing, iterating on, and benchmarking agent harnesses, improving reproducibility and enabling systematic study and comparison of agent control strategies for AI/ML practitioners and evaluators.

title: Vega: Learning to Drive with Natural Language Instructions
authors: Sicheng Zuo, Yuxuan Li, Wenzhao Zheng, Zheng Zhu, Jie Zhou
abstract: Vision-language-action models have reshaped autonomous driving to incorporate languages into the decision-making process. However, most existing pipelines only utilize the language modality for scene descriptions or reasoning and lack the flexibility to follow diverse user instructions for personalized driving. To address this, we first construct a large-scale driving dataset (InstructScene) containing around 100,000 scenes annotated with diverse driving instructions with the corresponding traje

infographic.key_insight: A vision–language–action model trained on a large, instruction-annotated driving dataset (InstructScene) can directly map natural language instructions plus visual inputs to driving trajectories, enabling flexible, personalized driving behaviors.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing driving pipelines treat language mainly as scene description or for reasoning and cannot flexibly follow diverse user instructions; this work enables instruction-conditioned decision-making for personalized autonomous driving.
method: Build InstructScene: a large-scale dataset (~100k scenes) pairing diverse natural-language driving instructions with corresponding trajectories/actions.
Train a unified vision–language–action model that conditions on onboard perception (images/scene) and a user instruction to predict trajectories or control commands.
Learn multimodal alignment between language and trajectory via instruction-conditioned objectives so the policy executes different behaviors based on varied instructions.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical route to instruction-following autonomous driving and a new benchmark for multimodal control research, making it easier for practitioners to develop personalized, language-driven vehicle policies.

title: Drive My Way: Preference Alignment of Vision-Language-Action Model for Personalized Driving
authors: Zehao Wang, Huaide Jiang, Shuaiwu Dong, Yuping Wang, Hang Qiu
abstract: Human driving behavior is inherently personal, which is shaped by long-term habits and influenced by short-term intentions. Individuals differ in how they accelerate, brake, merge, yield, and overtake across diverse situations. However, existing end-to-end autonomous driving systems either optimize for generic objectives or rely on fixed driving modes, lacking the ability to adapt to individual preferences or interpret natural language intent. To address this gap, we propose Drive My Way (DMW),

infographic.key_insight: Drive My Way (DMW) enables a single vision-language-action model to adapt driving behavior to individual drivers by conditioning actions on natural‑language preferences and inferred long‑term habits, providing personalized, interpretable control over autonomous driving.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing end-to-end driving systems are optimized for generic objectives or fixed modes and cannot flexibly adapt to individual driver preferences or accept natural‑language intent, limiting personalization and interpretability.
method: Train a multimodal vision–language–action (VLA) model that maps visual input and vehicle state plus a natural‑language preference token to driving actions.

Align the VLA model to individual preferences using preference-conditioned learning (combining demonstrations, preference signals or comparisons, and behavior cloning / reward modeling) so long‑term habits and short‑term intents are respected.
Enable interpretable, real‑time adaptation by exposing natural‑language controls and a preference embedding that modulates planning/action outputs.
infographic.impact: Makes autonomous driving systems more human‑centric by allowing per‑driver personalization and natural‑language control, improving acceptability, comfort, and transparency for deployment and research in adaptive decision-making.

title: PSDesigner: Automated Graphic Design with a Human-Like Creative Workflow
authors: Xincheng Shuai, Song Tang, Yutong Huang, Henghui Ding, Dacheng Tao
abstract: Graphic design is a creative and innovative process that plays a crucial role in applications such as e-commerce and advertising. However, developing an automated design system that can faithfully translate user intentions into editable design files remains an open challenge. Although recent studies have leveraged powerful text-to-image models and MLLMs to assist graphic design, they typically simplify professional workflows, resulting in limited flexibility and intuitiveness. To address these l

infographic.key_insight: PSDesigner reproduces a human-like creative workflow to automatically convert user intent into layered, editable design files—giving generative models the flexibility and editability of traditional design tools.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing automated design tools produce single-shot, non-editable images or oversimplify professional workflows; PSDesigner addresses the gap between user intent and practical, editable design outputs that support iteration and fine-grained control.
method: Intent understanding and planning: parse natural-language briefs with an MLLM-style planner that produces a multi-step creative plan (assets, layout, style, constraints).
Asset generation and assembly: use generative image/asset models plus vectorization and constraint-aware layout composition to create layered elements.
Iterative refinement into editable files: assemble outputs into standard layered design formats and support looped edits to emulate a human designer's revision workflow.
infographic.impact: Makes generative design systems practical for real-world creative workflows by producing editable, revision-friendly outputs—lowering friction for designers and enabling integration of AI into production pipelines.

title: A Mentalistic Interface for Probing Folk-Psychological Attribution to Non-Humanoid Robots
authors: Giulio Pisaneschi, Pierpaolo Serio, Estelle Gerbier, Andrea Dan Ryals, Lorenzo Pollini
abstract: This paper presents an experimental platform for studying intentional-state attribution toward a non-humanoid robot. The system combines a simulated robot, realistic task environments, and large language model-based explanatory layers that can express the same behavior in mentalistic, teleological, or mechanistic terms. By holding behavior constant while varying the explanatory frame, the platform provides a controlled way to investigate how language and framing shape the adoption of the intenti

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a controlled platform that holds robot behavior constant while using LLM-generated explanations in mentalistic, teleological, or mechanistic frames, revealing how linguistic framing alone shapes people's attribution of intentions to a non-humanoid robot.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of a reproducible experimental setup to disentangle the effects of robot behavior from explanatory language when studying folk-psychological attributions toward non-humanoid robots.
method: Simulated non-humanoid robot operating in realistic task environments to produce identical observable behaviors.
Large language model–based explanatory layer that rephrases the same behavior into mentalistic, teleological, or mechanistic explanations.
Controlled human-subject studies comparing attribution outcomes across explanation frames while keeping behavior fixed.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML and HRI practitioners a tool to test how explanation style influences perceived agency, trust, and responsibility independently of robot actions—informing explanation design and user-facing communication strategies for non-humanoid systems.

title: Less Gaussians, Texture More: 4K Feed-Forward Textured Splatting
authors: Yixing Lao, Xuyang Bai, Xiaoyang Wu, Nuoyuan Yan, Zixin Luo
abstract: Existing feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods predict pixel-aligned primitives, leading to a quadratic growth in primitive count as resolution increases. This fundamentally limits their scalability, making high-resolution synthesis such as 4K intractable. We introduce LGTM (Less Gaussians, Texture More), a feed-forward framework that overcomes this resolution scaling barrier. By predicting compact Gaussian primitives coupled with per-primitive textures, LGTM decouples geometric complexity

infographic.key_insight: LGTM (Less Gaussians, Texture More) breaks the resolution bottleneck of feed‑forward Gaussian splatting by predicting compact geometric Gaussians and equipping each with its own texture, so fine detail is handled by textures instead of by exploding primitive counts.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing feed‑forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods require pixel‑aligned primitives, causing primitive count to grow quadratically with output resolution and making high‑resolution synthesis (e.g., 4K) impractical.
method: Predict a compact set of Gaussian primitives that capture coarse geometry (far fewer primitives than pixel‑aligned approaches).
Associate each Gaussian with a per‑primitive texture to encode high‑frequency detail, decoupling appearance detail from geometric density.
Render by feed‑forward textured splatting (with texture sampling/aggregation) to efficiently synthesize high‑resolution outputs such as 4K.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, feed‑forward high‑resolution neural rendering (4K) with much lower memory and compute costs, making high‑quality view synthesis and real‑time applications more accessible to practitioners.
visual_elements: Before vs After comparison: dense pixel‑aligned gaussians vs LGTM's sparse textured gaussians (side‑by‑side 4K render).

title: Unleashing Guidance Without Classifiers for Human-Object Interaction Animation
authors: Ziyin Wang, Sirui Xu, Chuan Guo, Bing Zhou, Jiangshan Gong
abstract: Generating realistic human-object interaction (HOI) animations remains challenging because it requires jointly modeling dynamic human actions and diverse object geometries. Prior diffusion-based approaches often rely on hand-crafted contact priors or human-imposed kinematic constraints to improve contact quality. We propose LIGHT, a data-driven alternative in which guidance emerges from the denoising pace itself, reducing dependence on manually designed priors. Building on diffusion forcing, we

infographic.key_insight: LIGHT shows that high-quality contact-aware HOI animations can be generated without explicit classifier-based or hand-crafted contact priors by letting guidance emerge from the diffusion denoising pace itself.
infographic.problem_solved: Generates realistic human-object interaction animations that jointly model dynamic human motions and diverse object geometries while avoiding brittle, manually designed contact priors or kinematic constraints.
method: Diffusion-forcing framework: modify the denoising process so the denoising pace itself provides emergent guidance toward plausible contact and interaction states.
Data-driven contact modeling: learn contact and interaction cues directly from data instead of injecting hand-crafted contact priors or external classifier guidance.
Joint human+object representation: generate temporally coherent human motion and object geometry together to improve interaction realism and contact fidelity.
infographic.impact: Makes HOI animation more robust and generalizable by removing dependence on manual priors or classifiers, simplifying deployment across diverse objects and actions while improving contact realism.

title: Longitudinal Digital Phenotyping for Early Cognitive-Motor Screening
authors: Diego Jimenez-Oviedo, Ruben Vera-Rodriguez, Ruben Tolosana, Juan Carlos Ruiz-Garcia, Jaime Herreros-Rodriguez
abstract: Early detection of atypical cognitive-motor development is critical for timely intervention, yet traditional assessments rely heavily on subjective, static evaluations. The integration of digital devices offers an opportunity for continuous, objective monitoring through digital biomarkers. In this work, we propose an AI-driven longitudinal framework to model developmental trajectories in children aged 18 months to 8 years. Using a dataset of tablet-based interactions collected over multiple acad

infographic.key_insight: Modeling children's tablet interaction trajectories with an AI-driven longitudinal digital phenotyping framework enables earlier, objective detection of atypical cognitive-motor development than static, one-off assessments.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional screening for cognitive-motor atypicalities is subjective and episodic; this work provides a scalable, continuous, and objective method to capture developmental trajectories in children aged ~18 months–8 years using passive tablet-based interactions.
method: Longitudinal data collection via tablet interactions across multiple sessions/terms to capture within-child change over time.
Extraction of digital biomarkers from raw interactions (e.g., touch/gesture traces, timing, error patterns, movement smoothness, task complexity metrics).
Trajectory modeling and anomaly detection using time-series/longitudinal ML (normative growth curves, temporal models with interpretable outputs) to flag atypical development early.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with a validated paradigm for continuous digital phenotyping that improves screening sensitivity and enables interpretable, data-driven early interventions—scalable to real-world deployments in pediatric monitoring and research.
