title: Chameleon: Episodic Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
authors: Xinying Guo, Chenxi Jiang, Hyun Bin Kim, Ying Sun, Yang Xiao
abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires memory: occlusion and state changes can make decision-time observations perceptually aliased, making action selection non-Markovian at the observation level because the same observation may arise from different interaction histories. Most embodied agents implement memory via semantically compressed traces and similarity-based retrieval, which discards disambiguating fine-grained perceptual cues and can return perceptually similar but decision-irrelevant episod

infographic.key_insight: Chameleon introduces an episodic memory that stores rich, fine‑grained perceptual traces and retrieves decision‑relevant past experiences to disambiguate perceptually aliased observations, enabling more reliable long‑horizon robotic manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Perceptual aliasing and occlusions make single observations ambiguous during long tasks; existing compressed memory/retrieval schemes lose disambiguating cues and return irrelevant episodes, causing failures in multi-step manipulation.
method: Store rich episodic traces (temporal snippets of observations, actions, and outcomes) instead of heavily compressed semantic summaries to preserve disambiguating perceptual details.
Learn a retrieval mechanism that prioritizes decision‑relevant cues (not just perceptual similarity) to fetch past episodes that clarify current ambiguous observations.
Integrate retrieved episodic context with the policy/controller so action selection uses both current observation and relevant episodic history to resolve non‑Markovian decisions.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to handle non‑Markovian decision problems in embodied agents, improving robustness to occlusion and state changes in long‑horizon robotic tasks. This approach can be incorporated into manipulation stacks to reduce failure rates and enable more complex multi‑step behaviors.
visual_elements: Before vs after scenario: two side‑by‑side task timelines showing failures without episodic memory and successes with Chameleon

title: Latent-WAM: Latent World Action Modeling for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Linbo Wang, Yupeng Zheng, Qiang Chen, Shiwei Li, Yichen Zhang
abstract: We introduce Latent-WAM, an efficient end-to-end autonomous driving framework that achieves strong trajectory planning through spatially-aware and dynamics-informed latent world representations. Existing world-model-based planners suffer from inadequately compressed representations, limited spatial understanding, and underutilized temporal dynamics, resulting in sub-optimal planning under constrained data and compute budgets. Latent-WAM addresses these limitations with two core modules: a Spatia

infographic.key_insight: Latent-WAM learns a compact, spatially-aware and dynamics-informed latent world that enables accurate end-to-end trajectory planning with far lower data and compute requirements than prior world-model planners.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing world-model-based driving planners produce overly large or spatially-agnostic representations and underuse temporal dynamics, leading to sub-optimal planning under constrained data and compute budgets.
method: Spatially-aware latent encoder: compress multimodal sensor inputs into a compact latent world that preserves geometric layout and agent context.
Dynamics-informed temporal model: learn latent-space transition dynamics for multi-step prediction and planning, improving foresight and robustness.
Joint end-to-end planner: decode planned trajectories and controls from latent world states with lightweight inference and planning-aware losses.
infographic.impact: Offers a practical blueprint for building sample- and compute-efficient end-to-end driving systems, improving planning robustness and lowering deployment cost for autonomous driving and other embodied agents.

title: VFIG: Vectorizing Complex Figures in SVG with Vision-Language Models
authors: Qijia He, Xunmei Liu, Hammaad Memon, Ziang Li, Zixian Ma
abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) are an essential format for technical illustration and digital design, offering precise resolution independence and flexible semantic editability. In practice, however, original vector source files are frequently lost or inaccessible, leaving only "flat" rasterized versions (e.g., PNG or JPEG) that are difficult to modify or scale. Manually reconstructing these figures is a prohibitively labor-intensive process, requiring specialized expertise to recover the origin

infographic.key_insight: VFIG leverages vision–language models to convert complex raster figures into semantically meaningful, editable SVGs, recovering both graphic primitives and textual/structural labels in a single pipeline.
infographic.problem_solved: Original vector source files for technical illustrations are often lost, leaving only flat raster images that are hard to scale or edit; manual reconstruction is slow, error-prone, and requires specialized skills.
method: Parse raster figures with a vision–language backbone to detect graphic primitives (lines, shapes, paths) and associated text/labels.
Map detected elements to a structured SVG representation (primitives + attributes + grouping) using a learned renderer/tokenizer and language grounding to preserve semantics.
Iterative refinement and layout-aware grouping to ensure geometric fidelity and editable, semantically annotated SVG output.
infographic.impact: Makes diagrams and technical figures immediately editable and resolution-independent, accelerating design workflows, dataset creation, and downstream diagram understanding tasks for AI/ML practitioners.
visual_elements: Before/after comparison: original raster figure vs. reconstructed editable SVG (side-by-side).
Pipeline diagram: raster input → vision–language parsing → primitive mapping → SVG output.

title: DreamerAD: Efficient Reinforcement Learning via Latent World Model for Autonomous Driving
authors: Pengxuan Yang, Yupeng Zheng, Deheng Qian, Zebin Xing, Qichao Zhang
abstract: We introduce DreamerAD, the first latent world model framework that enables efficient reinforcement learning for autonomous driving by compressing diffusion sampling from 100 steps to 1 - achieving 80x speedup while maintaining visual interpretability. Training RL policies on real-world driving data incurs prohibitive costs and safety risks. While existing pixel-level diffusion world models enable safe imagination-based training, they suffer from multi-step diffusion inference latency (2s/frame)

infographic.key_insight: DreamerAD introduces a latent world model that compresses diffusion sampling from 100 steps to 1, delivering an ~80× speedup while preserving visually interpretable imagined frames for safe RL training in autonomous driving.
infographic.problem_solved: High inference latency and prohibitive costs/safety risks of training RL policies on real-world driving data; pixel-level diffusion world models are too slow for practical imagination-based RL (≈2s/frame).
method: Learn a compact latent world model (encode observations → latent space → decode) so generation operates in a low-dimensional space.
Replace multi-step pixel diffusion with a single-step latent diffusion/sampling procedure to compress 100-step sampling into 1 step.
Train RL policies via imagination using the fast latent predictions, retaining visual interpretability for debugging and validation.
infographic.impact: Enables safe, large-scale and much faster imagination-based RL for autonomous driving — reducing compute and latency enough to support practical policy development, iteration, and near real-time simulation.

title: Recognizing reproducibility and reusability in times of fast science
authors: Unknown
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 25 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01219-7

A few years ago, we introduced an article format called Reusability Reports to highlight good practices in code sharing and reporting. A renewed focus on reproducibility and transparency in code reporting seems warranted, as research output has accelerated with the widespread adoption of large language models.

infographic.key_insight: Reintroducing and championing 'Reusability Reports' provides a practical, lightweight article format to make code, models, and experiments easier to reproduce and reuse—especially critical as research accelerates with large language models.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the decline in reproducibility and transparency caused by rapid publication and widespread adoption of large models, by giving researchers concrete reporting practices that improve code sharing, documentation, and reuse.
method: Promote a standardized Reusability Report format that documents code, dependencies, data access, and execution steps alongside papers.
Recommend concrete reporting criteria (versioning, environment capture, example runs, licensing) and simple checks to verify reusable artifacts.
Highlight common failure modes in fast-moving LLM research and prescribe pragmatic, low-overhead fixes to improve reproducibility without slowing dissemination.
infographic.impact: Makes it easier for AI/ML practitioners to validate results, build on prior work, and reduce duplicated effort—improving trust and efficiency in a fast-paced research ecosystem.

title: Comparing Developer and LLM Biases in Code Evaluation
authors: Aditya Mittal, Ryan Shar, Zichu Wu, Shyam Agarwal, Tongshuang Wu
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly used as judges in code applications, they should be evaluated in realistic interactive settings that capture partial context and ambiguous intent. We present TRACE (Tool for Rubric Analysis in Code Evaluation), a framework that evaluates LLM judges' ability to predict human preferences and automatically extracts rubric items to reveal systematic biases in how humans and models weigh each item. Across three modalities -- chat-based programming, IDE autocompletion, and ins

infographic.key_insight: TRACE demonstrates that LLMs can predict human code preferences but systematically weigh rubric items differently than developers, revealing predictable evaluation biases in interactive coding contexts.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a realistic evaluation framework for using LLMs as judges in code tasks under partial context and ambiguous intent, exposing mismatches between human and model evaluation criteria.
method: Introduce TRACE (Tool for Rubric Analysis in Code Evaluation) to elicit and automatically extract rubric items from LLM judgments.
Evaluate LLMs' ability to predict human pairwise preferences across three interactive coding modalities (chat-based programming, IDE autocompletion, and other interactive code-editing contexts).
Compare per-item weights between humans and models to identify systematic biases and where model judgments diverge from developer priorities.
infographic.impact: Helps AI/ML practitioners trust, calibrate, or correct LLM-based evaluators in code applications and design fairer evaluation protocols and rubrics by surfacing actionable bias patterns.

title: EndoVGGT: GNN-Enhanced Depth Estimation for Surgical 3D Reconstruction
authors: Falong Fan, Yi Xie, Arnis Lektauers, Bo Liu, Jerzy Rozenblit
abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction of deformable soft tissues is essential for surgical robotic perception. However, low-texture surfaces, specular highlights, and instrument occlusions often fragment geometric continuity, posing a challenge for existing fixed-topology approaches. To address this, we propose EndoVGGT, a geometry-centric framework equipped with a Deformation-aware Graph Attention (DeGAT) module. Rather than using static spatial neighborhoods, DeGAT dynamically constructs feature-space se

infographic.key_insight: EndoVGGT uses a deformation-aware graph attention module to build dynamic, feature-space neighborhoods for depth estimation, restoring geometric continuity in deformable, low-texture surgical scenes.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes fragmented and inconsistent 3D reconstructions in endoscopic/surgical environments caused by low texture, specular highlights, and instrument occlusions that break fixed-topology methods.
method: Deformation-aware Graph Attention (DeGAT): dynamically constructs feature-space graphs (instead of fixed spatial neighborhoods) to capture local geometry under deformation and occlusion.
Geometry-centric depth estimation backbone that fuses GNN-enhanced features with per-pixel depth predictions to produce coherent surface reconstructions.
Training and inference pipeline tailored for surgical scenes (robust to specularity and occluders) and easily integrated into existing depth/reconstruction models.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to improve 3D reconstruction robustness for surgical robotics and computer-assisted intervention pipelines, enabling better scene understanding, safer instrument guidance, and higher-quality datasets for downstream AI tasks.

title: Towards Training-Free Scene Text Editing
authors: Yubo Li, Xugong Qin, Peng Zhang, Hailun Lin, Gangyan Zeng
abstract: Scene text editing seeks to modify textual content in natural images while maintaining visual realism and semantic consistency. Existing methods often require task-specific training or paired data, limiting their scalability and adaptability. In this paper, we propose TextFlow, a training-free scene text editing framework that integrates the strengths of Attention Boost (AttnBoost) and Flow Manifold Steering (FMS) to enable flexible, high-fidelity text manipulation without additional training. S

infographic.key_insight: TextFlow demonstrates that high-fidelity scene text editing can be achieved without task-specific training by combining Attention Boost (AttnBoost) and Flow Manifold Steering (FMS) to precisely localize, style-transfer, and geometrically align edited text in natural images.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes the need for paired data and task-specific training for scene text editing, enabling flexible text modification in natural images while preserving visual realism and semantic consistency.
method: AttnBoost: enhances and refines cross-attention maps to accurately localize text regions and transfer font/style cues from target text without retraining.
Flow Manifold Steering (FMS): computes and applies flow-guided manifold warps to align geometry and texture, preserving perspective and background continuity.
Training-free pipeline: integrates AttnBoost + FMS with pretrained generative/image-editing modules to synthesize edited text in-place without additional model training or paired supervision.
infographic.impact: Allows practitioners to deploy reliable scene text editing tools quickly and at scale, lowering annotation costs and improving adaptability across domains and languages. Useful for data augmentation, content correction, and privacy-preserving redaction in vision systems.

title: Retrieval Improvements Do Not Guarantee Better Answers: A Study of RAG for AI Policy QA
authors: Saahil Mathur, Ryan David Rittner, Vedant Ajit Thakur, Daniel Stuart Schiff, Tunazzina Islam
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are increasingly used to analyze complex policy documents, but achieving sufficient reliability for expert usage remains challenging in domains characterized by dense legal language and evolving, overlapping regulatory frameworks. We study the application of RAG to AI governance and policy analysis using the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA) corpus, a curated collection of 947 AI policy documents. Our system combines a ColBERT-based retriev

infographic.key_insight: Better retrieval metrics (e.g., higher ColBERT recall) do not automatically produce better answers in RAG systems for AI policy QA — retrieval gains can be misaligned with factuality, helpfulness, and hallucination rates of final LLM responses.
infographic.problem_solved: Investigates whether improvements in retrieval components translate to improved downstream answer quality in complex, dense AI policy documents, revealing gaps between retrieval performance and real-world QA reliability.
method: Assembled a RAG pipeline over the AGORA corpus (947 curated AI policy docs) using a ColBERT-based retriever and candidate reranking.
Systematically compared retriever variants, chunking strategies, and prompting configurations, measuring both retrieval metrics and end-task QA outcomes.
Evaluated with automatic metrics and expert human annotations focused on factuality, hallucination, and practical utility for policy analysis.
infographic.impact: Alerts ML/AI practitioners that optimizing retrieval alone is insufficient for trustworthy RAG in high-stakes domains; end-to-end evaluation and alignment (retrieval-aware prompting, grounding, calibration, or joint training) are required to improve answer reliability.

title: Machine learning global atomic representations with Euclidean fast attention
authors: J. Thorben Frank, Stefan Chmiela, Klaus-Robert Müller, Oliver T. Unke
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 25 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01195-y

Frank et al. introduce Euclidean fast attention, a linear-scaling framework for 3D data. By leveraging Euclidean rotary encodings, the method overcomes the quadratic cost of standard attention to accurately capture long-range effects in physical systems.

infographic.key_insight: Euclidean fast attention is a linear-scaling attention mechanism that uses Euclidean rotary encodings to encode 3D positions, enabling scalable, rotation-aware global atomic representations that accurately capture long-range interactions in physical systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard attention has quadratic compute and memory cost and struggles to scale to large 3D atomic systems and long-range physical effects; this work removes that bottleneck while preserving Euclidean (rotation/translation) structure.
method: Introduce Euclidean rotary encodings to represent 3D coordinates in a rotation-aware manner inside attention.
Reformulate attention into a linear (fast) attention kernel that reduces compute/memory from O(N^2) to O(N) for atoms/points.
Integrate the fast Euclidean attention into global atomic representation models to capture long-range interactions efficiently.
infographic.impact: Makes transformer-style models practical for much larger molecular/material systems and long-range physics-aware predictions, lowering resource cost for training and inference and enabling more accurate ML potentials and simulation surrogates.

title: TAG: Target-Agnostic Guidance for Stable Object-Centric Inference in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jiaying Zhou, Zhihao Zhan, Ruifeng Zhai, Qinhan Lyu, Hao Liu
abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) policies have shown strong progress in mapping language instructions and visual observations to robotic actions, yet their reliability degrades in cluttered scenes with distractors. By analyzing failure cases, we find that many errors do not arise from infeasible motions, but from instance-level grounding failures: the policy often produces a plausible grasp trajectory that lands slightly off-target or even on the wrong object instance. To address this issue, we pr

infographic.key_insight: A lightweight, inference-time Target-Agnostic Guidance (TAG) module can stabilize object-centric grounding in Vision–Language–Action policies, preventing plausible but off-target grasps by refining or re-ranking candidate object-centric predictions.
infographic.problem_solved: VLA policies often fail in cluttered scenes because they mis-ground which object instance to act on—producing plausible motions that land slightly off the intended object or on a distractor. TAG addresses these instance-level grounding failures without retraining the base policy.
method: Run the base VLA policy to produce candidate object-centric predictions or action trajectories.

Apply a target-agnostic guidance mechanism at inference that evaluates and refines/reranks candidates using object-centric consistency cues (visual context, spatial priors, and language-vision alignment) rather than relying on explicit target labels.
Select the refined highest-confidence candidate to execute, improving instance-level grounding while keeping the original policy unchanged.
infographic.impact: TAG improves robustness of language-conditioned robotic manipulation in cluttered, real-world scenes by reducing misgrasping on wrong instances, enabling safer and more reliable deployment of VLA models without costly retraining.
visual_elements: Before/after scene comparison: same cluttered table with policy grasping the wrong object (before) versus correct object after TAG (after).
Pipeline diagram: base VLA policy → candidate proposals → TAG module (scoring/refinement) → selected action.
Heatmap overlays or attention maps showing how TAG shifts focus from distractors to the intended instance.
Bar chart showing qualitative reduction in instance-level grounding failures (misgrasp rate) and improvement in success consistency across clutter levels.
infographic.paper_title: TAG: Target-Agnostic Guidance for Stable Object-Centric Inference in Vision-Language-Action Models
infographic.paper_authors: Jiaying Zhou, Zhihao Zhan, Ruifeng Zhai, Qinhan Lyu, Hao Liu

title: Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains
authors: Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 25 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0

Muzellec and Kar use reverse predictivity to show that only a subset of artificial neural network (ANN) units align with primate brain responses. This reveals a substantial misalignment between ANNs and brains compared with the strong bidirectional alignment observed between two primate brains.

infographic.key_insight: Using reverse predictivity (predicting model unit activity from brain responses) reveals that only a minority of ANN units truly align with primate neural responses, exposing a large ANN–brain misalignment despite strong bidirectional alignment between two primate brains.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies whether high model-to-brain predictivity indicates genuine mechanistic alignment or arises from partial, unit-level correspondences — resolving ambiguity about how well ANNs mirror actual brain computations.
method: Compute bidirectional predictivity: standard forward mapping (ANN → brain) and reverse predictivity (brain → ANN) using cross-validated linear mappings.
Identify and quantify the subset of ANN units that are reliably predicted from primate responses, and compare alignment patterns to primate–primate bidirectional predictivity.
Analyze the distribution of aligned vs. non-aligned units to assess whether alignment is global or concentrated in subpopulations.
infographic.impact: Provides a sharper diagnostic for comparing models to brains, guiding practitioners to evaluate alignment at the unit/subpopulation level rather than relying on aggregate forward predictivity alone — informing model selection and architecture design for brain-inspired AI.
visual_elements: Bidirectional diagram showing forward (ANN→brain) vs reverse (brain→ANN) predictivity with partial overlap highlighting aligned units
Bar chart or pie chart quantifying fraction of ANN units with high reverse predictivity versus total units
Scatter plot of forward vs reverse predictivity per unit to show which units are mutually predictable
Side-by-side comparison icon/infographic showing strong bidirectional alignment between two primate brains vs sparse ANN–brain alignment
infographic.paper_title: Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains
infographic.paper_authors: Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar

title: MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination
authors: Zhuo Li, Yupeng Zhang, Pengyu Cheng, Jiajun Song, Mengyu Zhou
abstract: Hallucination remains a critical bottleneck for large language models (LLMs), undermining their reliability in real-world applications, especially in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. While existing hallucination detection methods employ LLM-as-a-judge to verify LLM outputs against retrieved evidence, they suffer from inherent confirmation bias, where the verifier inadvertently reproduces the errors of the original generation. To address this, we introduce Multi-Agent Reinforced Self

infographic.key_insight: MARCH introduces a multi-agent reinforced self-check mechanism that uses multiple independent verifier agents, trained with reinforcement learning, to cross-validate LLM outputs against retrieved evidence—substantially reducing verifier confirmation bias and improving hallucination detection.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces hallucination and the confirmation bias of LLM-as-judge in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, where a single verifier tends to reproduce the generator's errors and fails to reliably detect or correct false outputs.
method: Deploy multiple diverse verifier agents that independently check generated answers against retrieved documents and evidence.
Train agent interactions with a reinforcement learning reward scheme that promotes truthful disagreement and penalizes blind agreement with erroneous generations.
Aggregate multi-agent judgments into a calibrated hallucination score and use consensus-driven corrections to produce more reliable outputs.
infographic.impact: Makes LLM outputs more trustworthy in real-world RAG deployments by improving automatic hallucination detection and correction, helping practitioners reduce downstream risk and increase model reliability.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: retriever → generator → multiple verifier agents → aggregator (shows flow of evidence and checks).
Before/after bar chart: hallucination rate or precision/recall of hallucination detection for baseline verifier vs MARCH.
Agent interaction loop: reinforcement learning reward flow illustrating encouragement of independent disagreement and penalties for confirmation bias.
Consensus heatmap or icon set: visualizing agreement vs disagreement among verifiers and final calibrated score.
infographic.paper_title: MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination
infographic.paper_authors: Zhuo Li, Yupeng Zhang, Pengyu Cheng, Jiajun Song, Mengyu Zhou

title: WildWorld: A Large-Scale Dataset for Dynamic World Modeling with Actions and Explicit State toward Generative ARPG
authors: Zhen Li, Zian Meng, Shuwei Shi, Wenshuo Peng, Yuwei Wu
abstract: Dynamical systems theory and reinforcement learning view world evolution as latent-state dynamics driven by actions, with visual observations providing partial information about the state. Recent video world models attempt to learn this action-conditioned dynamics from data. However, existing datasets rarely match the requirement: they typically lack diverse and semantically meaningful action spaces, and actions are directly tied to visual observations rather than mediated by underlying states.

infographic.key_insight: WildWorld supplies a large-scale dataset that decouples actions from raw pixels by pairing diverse, semantically meaningful action spaces with explicit underlying state annotations, enabling learning of action-conditioned latent dynamics rather than pixel-action shortcuts.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video/world-model datasets rarely offer semantically rich, diverse action spaces or explicit state information, so models end up learning direct pixel-to-action correlations instead of true state-mediated dynamics. WildWorld fills this gap to support principled action-conditioned world modeling.
method: Assemble large-scale interactive sequences where each timestep contains (visual observation, explicit latent state, and semantically meaningful action) triplets.
Design the dataset so actions affect an underlying state representation rather than being tied only to visual changes, enabling models to learn state-driven transition dynamics.
Provide standardized splits and evaluation tasks to train and benchmark action-conditioned generative world models for downstream control and simulation.
infographic.impact: Researchers can train more robust, controllable generative world models that generalize across actions and states, improving simulation fidelity, planning, and RL performance—particularly for interactive domains like ARPGs.
visual_elements: State–Action–Observation pipeline diagram: arrows showing actions -> latent state -> rendered observations to illustrate decoupling.
Dataset composition chart: counts or proportions of action types, state variables, and scenario diversity.
Sample sequence frames with overlayed explicit state vectors and action labels to show triplet annotations.
Benchmark results sketch: schematic comparing models trained with/without explicit state annotations (better long-horizon prediction and controllability).
infographic.paper_title: WildWorld: A Large-Scale Dataset for Dynamic World Modeling with Actions and Explicit State toward Generative ARPG
infographic.paper_authors: Zhen Li, Zian Meng, Shuwei Shi, Wenshuo Peng, Yuwei Wu

title: DA-Flow: Degradation-Aware Optical Flow Estimation with Diffusion Models
authors: Jaewon Min, Jaeeun Lee, Yeji Choi, Paul Hyunbin Cho, Jin Hyeon Kim
abstract: Optical flow models trained on high-quality data often degrade severely when confronted with real-world corruptions such as blur, noise, and compression artifacts. To overcome this limitation, we formulate Degradation-Aware Optical Flow, a new task targeting accurate dense correspondence estimation from real-world corrupted videos. Our key insight is that the intermediate representations of image restoration diffusion models are inherently corruption-aware but lack temporal awareness. To address

infographic.key_insight: Intermediate features from image-restoration diffusion models encode corruption-aware cues that, when paired with temporal modeling, enable accurate optical flow estimation on real-world degraded videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Optical flow models trained on clean data fail on real-world corruptions (blur, noise, compression). This work defines Degradation-Aware Optical Flow and closes the gap so dense correspondence can be estimated reliably from degraded video input.
method: Extract corruption-aware intermediate representations from an image-restoration diffusion model as auxiliary features for flow estimation.
Introduce temporal-awareness by fusing diffusion features across frames (e.g., temporal encoder / cross-attention) so the model learns motion cues absent in single-frame restoration features.
Train/fine-tune a flow estimator that leverages both standard image features and diffusion-derived corruption cues to produce robust dense correspondences on corrupted videos.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical route to robust optical flow in real-world video applications (e.g., autonomous driving, video editing, surveillance) by reusing diffusion restoration priors—reducing reliance on pristine training data and improving performance under common degradations.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: input degraded frames → diffusion restoration backbone (highlight intermediate layers) → temporal fusion module → optical flow output (arrows).
Before/after examples: degraded frames with noisy/blurred input and corresponding improved flow overlays produced by DA-Flow.
Bar/line chart: flow error (EPE) across corruption types comparing baseline flow vs. DA-Flow.
Icon strip: visual symbols for corruptions (motion blur, sensor noise, compression) with short captions showing robustness gains.

title: VISion On Request: Enhanced VLLM efficiency with sparse, dynamically selected, vision-language interactions
authors: Adrian Bulat, Alberto Baldrati, Ioannis Maniadis Metaxas, Yassine Ouali, Georgios Tzimiropoulos
abstract: Existing approaches for improving the efficiency of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) are largely based on the concept of visual token reduction. This approach, however, creates an information bottleneck that impairs performance, especially on challenging tasks that require fine-grained understanding and reasoning. In this work, we challenge this paradigm by introducing VISion On Request (VISOR), a method that reduces inference cost without discarding visual information. Instead of compressin

infographic.key_insight: VISOR reduces LVLM inference cost by performing sparse, dynamically selected vision–language interactions “on request” instead of compressing or discarding visual tokens, preserving fine-grained information while cutting compute.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing efficiency methods compress visual tokens, creating an information bottleneck that degrades performance on fine-grained understanding and reasoning tasks; VISOR addresses this by keeping visual information intact and only activating cross-modal computation when needed.
method: Keep rich visual feature maps intact, but avoid always-on cross-modal processing.
Use a lightweight, dynamic selector/gating mechanism that triggers vision–language interactions only for relevant queries or tokens (“on request”).
Cache or skip unnecessary cross-attention steps to realize sparse conditional computation and lower inference FLOPs without sacrificing accuracy.
infographic.impact: Maintains high accuracy on detailed multimodal tasks while substantially lowering latency and compute cost, making large vision–language models more practical and cost-effective to deploy.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: full visual encoder + dynamic selector + selective cross-attention vs traditional token-reduction pipeline.
Bar/chart: compute (FLOPs or latency) vs accuracy comparing VISOR to visual-token-reduction baselines.
Sequence diagram: example query flow showing when visual interactions are triggered or skipped (“on request” gating).
Icon set: eye (vision) preserved, lightning bolt (efficiency), gate (dynamic selection), and puzzle piece (fine-grained reasoning).

title: InverFill: One-Step Inversion for Enhanced Few-Step Diffusion Inpainting
authors: Duc Vu, Kien Nguyen, Trong-Tung Nguyen, Ngan Nguyen, Phong Nguyen
abstract: Recent diffusion-based models achieve photorealism in image inpainting but require many sampling steps, limiting practical use. Few-step text-to-image models offer faster generation, but naively applying them to inpainting yields poor harmonization and artifacts between the background and inpainted region. We trace this cause to random Gaussian noise initialization, which under low function evaluations causes semantic misalignment and reduced fidelity. To overcome this, we propose InverFill, a o

infographic.key_insight: InverFill replaces random noise initialization with a one-step inversion that yields an initial latent aligned to the visible background, enabling high-quality inpainting using only a few diffusion steps and avoiding harmonization artifacts.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between photorealistic diffusion inpainting and practical speed: it addresses semantic misalignment and visible artifacts that occur when few-step text-to-image diffusion samplers are naively applied to inpainting.
method: One-step inversion: compute an informed initial latent from the masked image so the inpainted region starts semantically aligned with the background instead of random Gaussian noise.
Integrate the inverted latent with a few-step diffusion sampler and the original conditioning (mask and context) to guide generation and preserve fidelity.
Design harmonization-aware sampling to reduce boundary artifacts and maintain consistent texture and semantics between the inpainted patch and surrounding image.
infographic.impact: Enables fast, practical image inpainting with diffusion models—delivering near-photoreal quality in far fewer sampling steps—making inpainting feasible for interactive editing, real-time applications, and resource-constrained deployments.
visual_elements: Before/after side-by-side examples showing naive few-step inpainting vs InverFill (highlighting reduced artifacts and better harmonization).
Pipeline diagram: masked image -> one-step inversion -> few-step diffusion sampler -> final inpainted image (with annotations).
Comparison chart: quality vs number of sampling steps for baseline vs InverFill (showing higher fidelity at low steps).
Close-up boundary zooms and semantic alignment heatmap to illustrate reduced mismatch at mask edges.

infographic.paper_authors: Duc Vu, Kien Nguyen, Trong-Tung Nguyen, Ngan Nguyen, Phong Nguyen

title: SpecEyes: Accelerating Agentic Multimodal LLMs via Speculative Perception and Planning
authors: Haoyu Huang, Jinfa Huang, Zhongwei Wan, Xiawu Zheng, Rongrong Ji
abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) (e.g., OpenAI o3 and Gemini Agentic Vision) achieve remarkable reasoning capabilities through iterative visual tool invocation. However, the cascaded perception, reasoning, and tool-calling loops introduce significant sequential overhead. This overhead, termed agentic depth, incurs prohibitive latency and seriously limits system-level concurrency. To this end, we propose SpecEyes, an agentic-level speculative acceleration framework that breaks thi

infographic.key_insight: SpecEyes parallelizes the agentic loop by speculatively predicting future percepts and plans so the multimodal LLM can execute ahead of completed visual-tool calls, drastically reducing sequential overhead (agentic depth).
infographic.problem_solved: Agentic MLLMs suffer high latency and poor system concurrency because repeated perception→reasoning→tool-call cycles force strictly sequential processing (large agentic depth).
method: Speculative perception: lightweight predictors generate anticipated visual-tool outputs (future observations) so downstream reasoning can start earlier.
Speculative planning: the agent pre-computes candidate action sequences based on predicted percepts, then verifies and corrects plans once real observations arrive.
Pipelined execution & rollback: run speculated plans in parallel with actual perception, validate results, and reconcile mismatches to preserve correctness while reducing end-to-end latency.
infographic.impact: Delivers lower latency and higher throughput for agentic multimodal systems, enabling more responsive, scalable, and cost-effective deployment of real-time vision+language agents.
visual_elements: Side-by-side pipeline diagram: (a) traditional sequential agent loop vs (b) SpecEyes speculative pipelined loop highlighting overlap of perception, planning, and execution.
Timing diagram (Gantt-style): shows reduced agentic depth and end-to-end latency with speculation and the small rollback window.
Architecture block diagram: speculator, multimodal LLM, verifier/corrector, and tool interfaces with dataflow arrows.
Bar chart: empirical speedup (latency and throughput) and small accuracy trade-off (if any) to emphasize practical gains.
infographic.paper_title: SpecEyes: Accelerating Agentic Multimodal LLMs via Speculative Perception and Planning
infographic.paper_authors: Haoyu Huang, Jinfa Huang, Zhongwei Wan, Xiawu Zheng, Rongrong Ji

title: AgentRVOS: Reasoning over Object Tracks for Zero-Shot Referring Video Object Segmentation
authors: Woojeong Jin, Jaeho Lee, Heeseong Shin, Seungho Jang, Junhwan Heo
abstract: Referring Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to segment a target object throughout a video given a natural language query. Training-free methods for this task follow a common pipeline: a MLLM selects keyframes, grounds the referred object within those frames, and a video segmentation model propagates the results. While intuitive, this design asks the MLLM to make temporal decisions before any object-level evidence is available, limiting both reasoning quality and spatio-temporal coverage. To

infographic.key_insight: AgentRVOS reverses the usual pipeline by first building object-centric tracks and then letting a multimodal reasoning agent (MLLM) decide which track matches the language query, enabling better temporal reasoning and spatial coverage without any training.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing training-free RVOS pipelines force the MLLM to pick keyframes before object-level evidence exists, hurting temporal consistency and grounding accuracy; this paper addresses zero-shot referring video object segmentation with improved spatio-temporal reasoning and robustness.
method: Extract object-centric tracks from the video using off-the-shelf detectors/trackers to obtain per-track visual evidence across time.
Convert each track into compact multimodal representations (frame crops, embeddings, short captions) and feed them to an agent-style MLLM that reasons over tracks to identify the referred object.
Produce final masks by grounding the chosen track to frames and applying a video segmentation/mask-propagation module—no task-specific training required.
infographic.impact: Delivers stronger, more interpretable zero-shot RVOS by shifting reasoning to object-level tracks, improving temporal coverage and accuracy for downstream tasks where training data is limited or unavailable.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram contrasting prior keyframe-first approach vs. AgentRVOS track-first approach (showing reversed order).
Timeline visualization with multiple object tracks (colored ribbons) and the agent selecting the correct track based on the language query.
Before/after example frames: original frames, predicted masks from prior pipeline, and masks from AgentRVOS to highlight improved temporal consistency.
Bar chart or table summarizing zero-shot performance gains and qualitative robustness (e.g., occlusion, fast motion).
infographic.paper_title: AgentRVOS: Reasoning over Object Tracks for Zero-Shot Referring Video Object Segmentation
infographic.paper_authors: Woojeong Jin, Jaeho Lee, Heeseong Shin, Seungho Jang, Junhwan Heo

title: TETO: Tracking Events with Teacher Observation for Motion Estimation and Frame Interpolation
authors: Jini Yang, Eunbeen Hong, Soowon Son, Hyunkoo Lee, Sunghwan Hong
abstract: Event cameras capture per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond resolution, offering continuous motion information lost between RGB frames. However, existing event-based motion estimators depend on large-scale synthetic data that often suffers from a significant sim-to-real gap. We propose TETO (Tracking Events with Teacher Observation), a teacher-student framework that learns event motion estimation from only $\sim$25 minutes of unannotated real-world recordings through knowledge distillati

infographic.key_insight: TETO uses a teacher–student knowledge distillation scheme to learn event-based motion estimation and frame interpolation from only ≈25 minutes of unlabelled real-world recordings, closing the sim-to-real gap without large synthetic datasets.
infographic.problem_solved: Event-based motion estimators typically rely on large synthetic datasets, producing a significant sim-to-real gap and requiring costly annotations—TETO enables accurate real-world event motion learning with minimal unlabelled data.
method: Teacher–student framework: an RGB-based teacher provides supervisory signals from sparse frames while a student network learns to track raw event streams.
Knowledge distillation on real unannotated recordings (~25 minutes) to transfer motion and interpolation cues from the teacher to the event-based student.
Losses and temporal alignment encourage event-driven motion estimation and frame interpolation consistency without synthetic pretraining or dense labels.
infographic.impact: Reduces dependence on synthetic labels and large annotated datasets, enabling robust event-camera motion estimation and high-quality frame interpolation from small amounts of real data—useful for robotics, autonomous driving, and efficient video processing.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing RGB teacher supervising an event-based student (inputs: frames + event stream → outputs: motion field and interpolated frames).
Before/after frame interpolation comparison (RGB ground truth vs student interpolated frames) to illustrate visual improvement.
Timeline visualization comparing high-rate event stream (microsecond resolution) with sparse RGB frames to show complementary modalities.
Bar chart or dot plot showing performance vs training data type/amount (synthetic large dataset vs TETO on ≈25 minutes real data).

infographic.paper_authors: Jini Yang, Eunbeen Hong, Soowon Son, Hyunkoo Lee, Sunghwan Hong

title: VTAM: Video-Tactile-Action Models for Complex Physical Interaction Beyond VLAs
authors: Haoran Yuan, Weigang Yi, Zhenyu Zhang, Wendi Chen, Yuchen Mo
abstract: Video-Action Models (VAMs) have emerged as a promising framework for embodied intelligence, learning implicit world dynamics from raw video streams to produce temporally consistent action predictions. Although such models demonstrate strong performance on long-horizon tasks through visual reasoning, they remain limited in contact-rich scenarios where critical interaction states are only partially observable from vision alone. In particular, fine-grained force modulation and contact transitions a

infographic.key_insight: Integrating tactile sensing with video-based action models lets agents infer contact-rich dynamics that are partially or ambiguously observable from vision alone, enabling fine-grained force modulation and more reliable contact transitions.
infographic.problem_solved: Video-Action Models (VAMs) struggle in contact-rich physical interactions because critical interaction states (force, slip, micro-contact) are only partially observable from vision, limiting precise control and safe manipulation.
method: Extend VAMs to Video-Tactile-Action Models (VTAMs) by fusing visual streams with tactile signals to learn joint spatiotemporal dynamics.
Use a multimodal encoder + temporal dynamics predictor that produces temporally consistent, touch-aware action predictions for force modulation and contact transitions.
Train end-to-end on sequences that include contact events so the model internalizes tactile-visual correlations and produces control-relevant outputs (actions/commands).
infographic.impact: VTAMs make embodied agents and robots more capable and robust in contact-rich manipulation tasks by adding a complementary sensing modality, reducing failure modes from partial observability and improving safety and finesse in real-world interactions.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: camera + tactile sensor inputs → multimodal encoder → temporal dynamics module → action decoder
Side-by-side timeline: VAM (vision-only) vs VTAM (vision + touch) showing improved detection of contact events and smoother force profiles
Example sequence visuals: frames showing a robotic hand approaching, contacting, and manipulating an object with overlaid tactile signal plots
Bar/line chart summarizing qualitative gains (e.g., fewer contact failures, improved force stability) on representative contact-rich tasks

title: MedObvious: Exposing the Medical Moravec's Paradox in VLMs via Clinical Triage
authors: Ufaq Khan, Umair Nawaz, L D M S S Teja, Numaan Saeed, Muhammad Bilal
abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used for tasks like medical report generation and visual question answering. However, fluent diagnostic text does not guarantee safe visual understanding. In clinical practice, interpretation begins with pre-diagnostic sanity checks: verifying that the input is valid to read (correct modality and anatomy, plausible viewpoint and orientation, and no obvious integrity violations). Existing benchmarks largely assume this step is solved, and therefore m

infographic.key_insight: State-of-the-art VLMs can generate fluent diagnostic text but often fail simple pre-diagnostic sanity checks (modality, anatomy, view/orientation, image integrity), exposing a "Medical Moravec's Paradox": models are better at high-level language than basic visual validation.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the missing evaluation and failure modes around pre-diagnostic sanity checking in medical VLMs by introducing a clinical triage perspective and benchmark to reveal when inputs are unsafe or unreadable for diagnosis.
method: Construct a clinical triage benchmark that explicitly tests pre-diagnostic sanity checks (correct imaging modality, relevant anatomy, plausible viewpoint/orientation, and image integrity).
Systematically evaluate multiple VLMs on these triage tests using standardized metrics to quantify failure modes and expose vulnerabilities.
Analyze errors and propose a triage-first evaluation/deployment pipeline and practical recommendations to force or verify visual validity before diagnostic inference.
infographic.impact: Highlights a critical safety gap in medical VLM deployment: ensuring basic visual validity before trusting diagnostic outputs. Encourages practitioners to adopt triage-first benchmarks, safer pipelines, and improved model evaluation criteria.
visual_elements: Flowchart showing 'Input image → Clinical triage checks (modality, anatomy, view, integrity) → Pass/fail → Diagnostic model' to illustrate the proposed pipeline.
Bar chart comparing multiple VLMs' accuracy on each sanity-check category (modality, anatomy, view, integrity).
Annotated failure-case examples (image + model output) demonstrating common hallucinations or misreads when triage fails.
Heatmap or matrix of error types across models to visualize concentrated weaknesses (e.g., view confusion vs. anatomy misclassification).
infographic.paper_title: MedObvious: Exposing the Medical Moravec's Paradox in VLMs via Clinical Triage
infographic.paper_authors: Ufaq Khan, Umair Nawaz, L D M S S Teja, Numaan Saeed, Muhammad Bilal

title: UniGRPO: Unified Policy Optimization for Reasoning-Driven Visual Generation
authors: Jie Liu, Zilyu Ye, Linxiao Yuan, Shenhan Zhu, Yu Gao
abstract: Unified models capable of interleaved generation have emerged as a promising paradigm, with the community increasingly converging on autoregressive modeling for text and flow matching for image generation. To advance this direction, we propose a unified reinforcement learning framework tailored for interleaved generation. We validate our approach on its fundamental unit: a single round of reasoning-driven image generation, where the model first expands the user prompt through reasoning, followed

infographic.key_insight: UniGRPO introduces a unified reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes reasoning (prompt expansion) and image synthesis for interleaved generation, enabling a single policy to coordinate text-based reasoning and flow-matching image modules.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between separately trained text-reasoning and image-generation components by providing a trainable, decision-making framework for interleaved multimodal generation—specifically tackling how to coordinate prompt expansion and subsequent image synthesis within one loop.
method: Formulate a single-round interleaved generation task as an RL problem where actions include reasoning (expanding the prompt) and invoking image-generation modules.
Train a unified policy that interfaces autoregressive text modeling for reasoning and flow-matching image generators, using reward signals that reflect reasoning quality and visual fidelity.
Validate the approach on a reasoning-driven image generation setup (prompt expansion → image synthesis) to demonstrate feasibility of joint optimization and coordination.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical framework for building end-to-end systems that plan and generate multimodal outputs cohesively, simplifying pipeline design and enabling more coherent, reasoning-informed image generation workflows.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: user prompt → reasoning (text expansion) → image generator, annotated as sequential RL actions
Architecture sketch: unified policy interfacing autoregressive text and flow-matching image modules
Reward schematic: example signals for reasoning correctness and image fidelity feeding back to the policy
Before/after examples: original prompt vs expanded prompt and resulting generated image to show the effect of reasoning

title: Byzantine-Robust and Differentially Private Federated Optimization under Weaker Assumptions
authors: Rustem Islamov, Grigory Malinovsky, Alexander Gaponov, Aurelien Lucchi, Peter Richtárik
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables heterogeneous clients to collaboratively train a shared model without centralizing their raw data, offering an inherent level of privacy. However, gradients and model updates can still leak sensitive information, while malicious servers may mount adversarial attacks such as Byzantine manipulation. These vulnerabilities highlight the need to address differential privacy (DP) and Byzantine robustness within a unified framework. Existing approaches, however, often re

infographic.key_insight: The paper develops a unified federated optimization approach that simultaneously achieves Byzantine robustness and differential privacy while requiring substantially weaker assumptions about client behavior and data than prior work.
infographic.problem_solved: How to train models in federated settings that are both differentially private and resilient to Byzantine (malicious or faulty) clients, without relying on strong or unrealistic assumptions about data homogeneity, bounded gradients, or adversary strength.
method: Design a federated optimization algorithm that integrates a Byzantine-resilient aggregation rule with calibrated differential privacy noise to protect client updates.
Provide theoretical analysis proving convergence, privacy (DP), and robustness guarantees under weaker assumptions on client heterogeneity and adversary capabilities than previous methods.
Incorporate practical algorithmic choices (e.g., noise scaling, aggregation trimming/robust statistics, communication-efficient updates) to balance accuracy, privacy, and robustness.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy federated learning systems that maintain formal privacy guarantees while remaining robust to malicious clients, even when data and client behavior are more heterogeneous or less well-behaved than assumed by earlier methods.
visual_elements: System diagram showing many clients sending updates to a server with icons for honest vs. Byzantine clients and a robust+DP aggregator at the server
Trade-off curve plotting accuracy versus privacy noise level and fraction of Byzantine clients (three-way trade-off visualization)
Algorithm pipeline infographic: local update → robust aggregation → DP noise addition → global model update (with annotated parameters)
Summary box showing theoretical guarantees (convergence rate, DP epsilon, tolerated Byzantine fraction) as easy-to-read badges

title: ThinkJEPA: Empowering Latent World Models with Large Vision-Language Reasoning Model
authors: Haichao Zhang, Yijiang Li, Shwai He, Tushar Nagarajan, Mingfei Chen
abstract: Recent progress in latent world models (e.g., V-JEPA2) has shown promising capability in forecasting future world states from video observations. Nevertheless, dense prediction from a short observation window limits temporal context and can bias predictors toward local, low-level extrapolation, making it difficult to capture long-horizon semantics and reducing downstream utility. Vision--language models (VLMs), in contrast, provide strong semantic grounding and general knowledge by reasoning ove

infographic.key_insight: ThinkJEPA couples a latent world model with a large vision–language reasoning model so that latent forecasts are grounded in high-level semantics, enabling more accurate long-horizon prediction beyond short observation windows.
infographic.problem_solved: Latent world models trained on dense short-horizon prediction tend to extrapolate low-level, local dynamics and miss long-term semantic structure; the paper addresses lack of semantic grounding and limited temporal context in video forecasting.
method: Augment a latent world model (e.g., V-JEPA2 style predictor) with a large vision–language reasoning model that operates over latent representations to provide semantic context and high-level reasoning.
Align and distill VLM outputs into the latent predictor as conditioning/regularization so future latent states reflect language-grounded semantics rather than only low-level extrapolation.
Use the combined model for hierarchical, longer-horizon forecasting (latent autoregression + semantic prompts) to improve downstream tasks such as planning, retrieval, and captioning.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to inject rich semantic knowledge into compact latent world models, improving long-horizon prediction fidelity and downstream utility for tasks that require semantic understanding (e.g., planning, video understanding) without relying solely on dense pixel supervision.

title: Interpretability and implicit model semantics in biomedicine and deep learning
authors: Jonathan Warrell, Michael Gancz, Hussein Mohsen, Prashant Emani, Mark Gerstein
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01177-0

We introduce a framework to analyse interpretability in deep learning, by drawing on a formal notion of model semantics from the philosophy of science. We argue that interpretability is only one aspect of a model’s semantics and illustrate our framework with examples from biomedicine.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a formal framework that uses a philosophy-of-science notion of model semantics to analyse interpretability, showing that interpretability is only one component of a model’s broader semantics and must be evaluated in that context.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies ambiguous and inconsistent interpretability claims in biomedical deep learning by providing a principled way to characterise what a model 'means' and how explanations relate to domain concepts.
method: Adopt a formal notion of model semantics from philosophy of science and map it to machine learning models.
Decompose semantics into components (e.g., representational mappings, functional/causal roles, and interpretability signals) and derive criteria to evaluate each.
Illustrate the framework with concrete biomedical deep‑learning examples to show how interpretability fits within implicit model semantics.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a clearer diagnostic toolkit for evaluating explanation claims, improving model assessment, trust, and safer deployment in biomedical applications by distinguishing explainability from other semantic properties.
visual_elements: Layered taxonomy diagram: concentric layers showing ‘semantics’ as outer set and ‘interpretability’ as an inner subset with labelled components (mapping, function, explanation).
Flowchart mapping model outputs → representational mappings → domain concepts with annotations where common explanations succeed/fail.

title: 3D-Layout-R1: Structured Reasoning for Language-Instructed Spatial Editing
authors: Haoyu Zhen, Xiaolong Li, Yilin Zhao, Han Zhang, Sifei Liu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive reasoning abilities, yet they struggle with spatial understanding and layout consistency when performing fine-grained visual editing. We introduce a Structured Reasoning framework that performs text-conditioned spatial layout editing via scene-graph reasoning. Given an input scene graph and a natural-language instruction, the model reasons over the graph to generate an updated scene graph that satisfies the text

infographic.key_insight: 3D-Layout-R1 uses structured scene-graph reasoning to convert a natural-language instruction into an updated spatial layout, enabling precise, language-conditioned spatial edits that preserve layout consistency. This graph-first approach closes the gap between LLM/VLM language understanding and fine-grained spatial manipulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLMs and VLMs struggle to maintain spatial relationships and layout consistency when executing language-guided visual edits; this work addresses that by performing explicit scene-graph reasoning for layout-aware editing.
method: Take an input scene graph and a natural-language instruction as inputs to a structured reasoning module.
Reason over nodes and edges to produce an updated scene graph (add/remove/move objects, modify spatial relations) that satisfies the instruction.
Optionally map the updated scene graph to downstream rendering or VLM-based image editing to produce the final edited image while preserving spatial constraints.
infographic.impact: Provides a reliable, interpretable bridge between language instructions and spatial edits, improving controllability and consistency for image editing, AR/VR, and data-generation pipelines. Practitioners can leverage scene-graph reasoning to build safer, more predictable language-driven editing systems.

title: Computational framework to predict and shape human–machine interactions in closed-loop, co-adaptive neural interfaces
authors: Maneeshika M. Madduri, Momona Yamagami, Si Jia Li, Sasha Burckhardt, Samuel A. Burden
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01194-z

Madduri et al. introduce a computational framework grounded in control and game theory to model co-adaptation between users and decoders in neural interfaces. This framework enables a principled design of closed-loop systems that improve usability and personalization.

infographic.key_insight: The paper provides a principled computational framework—grounded in control and game theory—that models and predicts co-adaptive dynamics between human users and decoders in closed‑loop neural interfaces, enabling design choices that reliably shape interaction outcomes.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of a principled, predictive model for human–machine co‑adaptation in closed‑loop neural interfaces, which has led to unpredictable learning dynamics, poor usability, and suboptimal personalization of decoders.
method: Formulate users and decoders as interacting dynamical agents with separate objectives using control- and game-theoretic models.
Analyze stability and convergence of co‑adaptive trajectories to predict outcomes under different adaptation rules and parameter settings.
Use simulations and design prescriptions (e.g., update rules, regularizers, controller gains) to steer interactions toward desirable, personalized behaviors.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners principled tools to predict and shape learning dynamics in closed‑loop systems, improving robustness, personalization, and interpretability of neural interface algorithms.

title: DualCoT-VLA: Visual-Linguistic Chain of Thought via Parallel Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zhide Zhong, Junfeng Li, Junjie He, Haodong Yan, Xin Gong
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions directly to robotic actions. While effective for simple tasks, standard VLA models often struggle with complex, multi-step tasks requiring logical planning, as well as precise manipulations demanding fine-grained spatial perception. Recent efforts have incorporated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to endow VLA models with a ``thinking before acting'' capability. However, current CoT-based VLA models face two cr

infographic.key_insight: DualCoT-VLA runs two complementary chains-of-thought in parallel — a visual CoT for fine-grained spatial grounding and a linguistic CoT for high-level planning — and fuses them to produce more accurate, interpretable action sequences for complex multi-step tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard VLA models struggle with multi-step logical planning and precise spatial manipulation; existing CoT approaches either conflate visual and linguistic reasoning or suffer from error propagation and poor grounding.
method: Parallel dual-chain architecture: a visual CoT stream generates spatially detailed intermediate reasoning (e.g., object affordances, relative positions) while a linguistic CoT stream generates high-level task plans and step decompositions.
Cross-modal fusion and alignment: a module aligns and reconciles the two thought traces to produce a coherent, grounded action sequence and to resolve conflicts between planning and perception.

Ensemble-style verification and interpretability: parallel reasoning threads are compared/verified (reducing propagation of single-stream errors) and expose interpretable intermediate steps for debugging and safety.
infographic.impact: Enables VLA models to handle longer-horizon, multi-step, and fine-grained manipulation tasks more reliably while providing interpretable intermediate reasoning — accelerating development and safer deployment of embodied AI and robotic systems.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing two parallel CoT streams (visual and linguistic) feeding into a cross-modal fusion module and producing action outputs.

title: UniMotion: A Unified Framework for Motion-Text-Vision Understanding and Generation
authors: Ziyi Wang, Xinshun Wang, Shuang Chen, Yang Cong, Mengyuan Liu
abstract: We present UniMotion, to our knowledge the first unified framework for simultaneous understanding and generation of human motion, natural language, and RGB images within a single architecture. Existing unified models handle only restricted modality subsets (e.g., Motion-Text or static Pose-Image) and predominantly rely on discrete tokenization, which introduces quantization errors and disrupts temporal continuity. UniMotion overcomes both limitations through a core principle: treating motion as

infographic.key_insight: UniMotion is the first single architecture that jointly understands and generates human motion, natural language, and RGB images by replacing discrete motion tokenization with a continuous, temporally-aware representation, preserving motion smoothness and cross-modal consistency.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing multimodal models handle only limited modality pairs (e.g., Motion–Text or Pose–Image) and rely on discrete tokenization that induces quantization errors and breaks temporal continuity; UniMotion unifies three modalities and avoids these drawbacks.
method: Unified single architecture that links motion, text, and images through a shared cross-modal latent space while keeping modality-specific encoders/decoders.
Continuous, temporally-aware motion representation (instead of discrete tokens) to preserve smooth dynamics and avoid quantization artifacts.

Joint training with cross-modal alignment and generative objectives so the model can perform both understanding (e.g., captioning, retrieval) and generation (e.g., text→motion, image-conditioned motion).
infographic.impact: Enables seamless tri-modal applications (text-driven animation, image-to-motion, motion captioning) with improved temporal fidelity and fewer artifacts; simplifies pipelines by consolidating tasks into one model for research and production use.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing a shared latent space with modality-specific encoders/decoders and cross-modal attention paths.

title: WorldCache: Content-Aware Caching for Accelerated Video World Models
authors: Umair Nawaz, Ahmed Heakl, Ufaq Khan, Abdelrahman Shaker, Salman Khan
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) power high-fidelity video world models but remain computationally expensive due to sequential denoising and costly spatio-temporal attention. Training-free feature caching accelerates inference by reusing intermediate activations across denoising steps; however, existing methods largely rely on a Zero-Order Hold assumption i.e., reusing cached features as static snapshots when global drift is small. This often leads to ghosting artifacts, blur, and motion inconsiste

infographic.key_insight: Introduce content-aware feature caching for Diffusion Transformers that adaptively updates cached activations across denoising steps, avoiding zero-order-hold artifacts (ghosting, blur) while dramatically reducing inference cost.
infographic.problem_solved: Speeds up computationally expensive video world models (DiTs) by replacing costly per-step spatio-temporal attention and sequential denoising with a training-free caching strategy that preserves temporal fidelity under scene motion.
method: Maintain a cache of intermediate activations and detect content drift to decide when and how to reuse cached features instead of recomputing them from scratch.
Apply lightweight, content-aware updates (e.g., adaptive warping/transform or residual correction) to cached activations to compensate for motion and appearance changes, preventing ghosting and blur.
Integrate the cache as a plug-and-play, training-free module inside existing DiT pipelines, enabling large inference speedups with minimal code changes.
infographic.impact: Enables much faster, lower-latency video world model inference without retraining, making high-fidelity DiT-based planners and simulators more practical for real-time applications and large-scale evaluation.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: DiT inference loop showing cache read/write, content-drift detector, and content-aware update step.

title: End-to-End Training for Unified Tokenization and Latent Denoising
authors: Shivam Duggal, Xingjian Bai, Zongze Wu, Richard Zhang, Eli Shechtman
abstract: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) enable high-fidelity synthesis by operating in learned latent spaces. However, training state-of-the-art LDMs requires complex staging: a tokenizer must be trained first, before the diffusion model can be trained in the frozen latent space. We propose UNITE - an autoencoder architecture for unified tokenization and latent diffusion. UNITE consists of a Generative Encoder that serves as both image tokenizer and latent generator via weight sharing. Our key insight is

infographic.key_insight: UNITE enables truly end-to-end training by unifying the image tokenizer and latent diffusion generator into a single, weight‑shared generative encoder, removing the need for a separately trained frozen tokenizer and reducing representational mismatch.
infographic.problem_solved: State-of-the-art latent diffusion workflows require multi‑stage training (train tokenizer first, then freeze it and train diffusion), which is complex, brittle, and can cause suboptimal latent representations and artifacts when the tokenizer and diffusion model are not jointly optimized.
method: Design a Generative Encoder that simultaneously serves as an image tokenizer and latent generator through weight sharing between encoding and generative pathways.
Train the autoencoder and diffusion denoiser jointly end‑to‑end with combined reconstruction + denoising objectives, removing the frozen-tokenizer stage.
Optimize a unified latent space so the diffusion model learns directly on latents produced by the encoder, reducing representation mismatch and simplifying the pipeline.
infographic.impact: Simplifies LDM training pipelines, improves alignment between tokenizer and denoiser for better sample fidelity, and lowers development complexity and potential failure modes for practitioners building latent generative models.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: Generative Encoder with shared weights linking encoder (tokenizer) and latent generator, feeding the diffusion denoiser.
Pipeline comparison: staged (tokenizer → freeze → diffusion) vs UNITE end‑to‑end training (single flow) illustrated as side‑by‑side timelines.
Loss breakdown chart: reconstruction loss + denoising loss and how they jointly update shared weights.

title: The Dual Mechanisms of Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
authors: Kelly Cui, Nikhil Prakash, Ayush Raina, David Bau, Antonio Torralba
abstract: Many multimodal tasks, such as image captioning and visual question answering, require vision-language models (VLMs) to associate objects with their properties and spatial relations. Yet it remains unclear where and how such associations are computed within VLMs. In this work, we show that VLMs rely on two concurrent mechanisms to represent such associations. In the language model backbone, intermediate layers represent content-independent spatial relations on top of visual tokens corresponding

infographic.key_insight: Vision-language models use two concurrent mechanisms for spatial reasoning: intermediate language-model layers encode content‑independent spatial relations on top of visual tokens, while other components (e.g., visual encoders or cross‑attention) bind those relations to specific objects and properties.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies where and how VLMs compute associations between objects, their properties, and spatial relations — resolving whether spatial reasoning is localized, distributed, or emergent across modalities.
method: Layer‑wise probing and representation analysis to detect content‑independent spatial relation encodings inside LM backbone layers.
Controlled synthetic benchmarks and standard VQA/caption datasets to test spatial reasoning under varied object placements and relations.
Causal interventions and ablations (e.g., disabling layers or cross‑attentions) to demonstrate the complementary roles of the two mechanisms.
infographic.impact: Provides a mechanistic decomposition of spatial reasoning in VLMs that improves interpretability, guides targeted architectural or training interventions, and helps practitioners diagnose and fix spatial errors in multimodal systems.
visual_elements: Schematic of the model stack showing two pathways: (A) LM intermediate layers with abstract spatial relation tokens, and (B) visual encoder / cross‑attention binding relations to object tokens.
Layer‑wise heatmap or bar chart illustrating strength of spatial relation representations across layers.
Intervention/ablation diagram showing performance change when each mechanism is disrupted (e.g., dropped bars for accuracy on spatial queries).
Example image+question pairs with annotated object tokens and predicted relation traces to illustrate failure vs. success cases.

title: VideoDetective: Clue Hunting via both Extrinsic Query and Intrinsic Relevance for Long Video Understanding
authors: Ruoliu Yang, Chu Wu, Caifeng Shan, Ran He, Chaoyou Fu
abstract: Long video understanding remains challenging for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) due to limited context windows, which necessitate identifying sparse query-relevant video segments. However, existing methods predominantly localize clues based solely on the query, overlooking the video's intrinsic structure and varying relevance across segments. To address this, we propose VideoDetective, a framework that integrates query-to-segment relevance and inter-segment affinity for effective clue

infographic.key_insight: VideoDetective jointly reasons about extrinsic query-to-segment relevance and intrinsic inter-segment affinity to locate sparse, informative clips in long videos—enabling MLLMs to focus on true "clues" within limited context windows.
infographic.problem_solved: How to find and prioritize sparse, query-relevant segments in very long videos while accounting for the video's internal structure and varying segment relevance so MLLMs can efficiently and accurately reason.
method: Compute extrinsic relevance: score segments by how directly they match the input query (query-to-segment relevance).
Model intrinsic structure: build an inter-segment affinity graph to capture temporal/semantic relations and propagate relevance across segments.
Fuse signals and select clues: combine extrinsic and intrinsic scores to pick compact, high-value segments for downstream MLLM reasoning (efficient clue hunting).
infographic.impact: Improves accuracy and efficiency of long-video QA, retrieval, and reasoning by selecting fewer but more informative clips, making multimodal LLMs practical on long-form content and easier to interpret.

Video timeline heatmap showing original long video with highlighted selected "clue" segments.

title: AI Agents Can Already Autonomously Perform Experimental High Energy Physics
authors: Eric A. Moreno, Samuel Bright-Thonney, Andrzej Novak, Dolores Garcia, Philip Harris
abstract: Large language model-based AI agents are now able to autonomously execute substantial portions of a high energy physics (HEP) analysis pipeline with minimal expert-curated input. Given access to a HEP dataset, an execution framework, and a corpus of prior experimental literature, we find that Claude Code succeeds in automating all stages of a typical analysis: event selection, background estimation, uncertainty quantification, statistical inference, and paper drafting. We argue that the experime

infographic.key_insight: Large language model–powered agents (e.g., Claude Code) can autonomously execute end-to-end high energy physics analyses — from event selection through statistical inference and paper drafting — with minimal expert-curated input. This demonstrates LLM agents can meaningfully perform substantive experimental science workflows.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the heavy manual effort, expertise bottleneck, and reproducibility friction in building and executing complex HEP analysis pipelines by automating routine and technical stages of the workflow.
method: Provide the agent with a HEP dataset, an execution framework (code/runtime), and a corpus of prior experimental literature.
Use the LLM-based agent to iteratively generate and run code to perform event selection, background estimation, uncertainty quantification, and statistical inference.
Have the agent synthesize results into human-readable deliverables (figures, tables, and draft paper text) with minimal human intervention.
infographic.impact: Enables faster, more reproducible experimental analyses and lowers the barrier to entry for HEP research; suggests LLM agents can augment or partially automate scientific workflows across ML-driven domains.
