title: POET-X: Memory-efficient LLM Training by Scaling Orthogonal Transformation
authors: Zeju Qiu, Lixin Liu, Adrian Weller, Han Shi, Weiyang Liu
abstract: Efficient and stable training of large language models (LLMs) remains a core challenge in modern machine learning systems. To address this challenge, Reparameterized Orthogonal Equivalence Training (POET), a spectrum-preserving framework that optimizes each weight matrix through orthogonal equivalence transformation, has been proposed. Although POET provides strong training stability, its original implementation incurs high memory consumption and computational overhead due to intensive matrix mu

infographic.key_insight: POET-X scales the POET orthogonal-equivalence reparameterization to be memory- and compute-efficient, preserving the training stability and spectral properties of weight matrices while dramatically lowering overhead compared with the original POET implementation.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the high memory consumption and computational overhead of spectrum-preserving orthogonal reparameterizations when training large language models, enabling stable POET-style optimization at LLM scale.
method: Introduce a memory-efficient scaling / factorization of orthogonal equivalence transforms so orthogonal updates no longer require storing or multiplying full auxiliary matrices.
Preserve spectral properties of each weight matrix (spectrum-preserving reparameterization) to retain POET's stability while replacing expensive operations with lightweight equivalents.
Design the reparameterization to be plug-and-play with standard optimizers and model architectures, so it can be applied across layers with minimal runtime and memory impact.
infographic.impact: Makes spectrum-preserving, stability-oriented training practical for large-scale LLMs, allowing practitioners to gain POET's optimization benefits without prohibitive memory or compute costs—better scalability and reliability during training.

title: Towards Multimodal Lifelong Understanding: A Dataset and Agentic Baseline
authors: Guo Chen, Lidong Lu, Yicheng Liu, Liangrui Dong, Lidong Zou
abstract: While datasets for video understanding have scaled to hour-long durations, they typically consist of densely concatenated clips that differ from natural, unscripted daily life. To bridge this gap, we introduce MM-Lifelong, a dataset designed for Multimodal Lifelong Understanding. Comprising 181.1 hours of footage, it is structured across Day, Week, and Month scales to capture varying temporal densities. Extensive evaluations reveal two critical failure modes in current paradigms: end-to-end MLLM

infographic.key_insight: MM-Lifelong introduces hour-scale multimodal video data organized at Day/Week/Month densities and shows that current end-to-end multimodal LLMs fail on natural, unscripted long-range understanding. An agentic, memory-aware baseline improves robustness by explicitly handling temporal abstraction and retrieval.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between short, densely edited video datasets and real-world lifelong visual experience by providing a structured multimodal dataset and benchmarking long-range temporal reasoning and memory for models.
method: Curate MM-Lifelong: 181.1 hours of multimodal footage organized into Day, Week, and Month scales to capture varied temporal densities and natural, unscripted events.
Evaluate existing end-to-end MLLMs to identify failure modes in long-range comprehension and episodic memory consolidation on natural video streams.
Propose an agentic baseline that combines memory modules, retrieval, and policy-driven querying/summarization to better handle prolonged, sparse events.
infographic.impact: Provides a realistic benchmark and a practical agentic baseline that help researchers diagnose and mitigate long-term temporal failures in multimodal models, accelerating progress toward lifelong visual understanding.

title: Leveraging LLM Parametric Knowledge for Fact Checking without Retrieval
authors: Artem Vazhentsev, Maria Marina, Daniil Moskovskiy, Sergey Pletenev, Mikhail Seleznyov
abstract: Trustworthiness is a core research challenge for agentic AI systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs). To enhance trust, natural language claims from diverse sources, including human-written text, web content, and model outputs, are commonly checked for factuality by retrieving external knowledge and using an LLM to verify the faithfulness of claims to the retrieved evidence. As a result, such methods are constrained by retrieval errors and external data availability, while leaving the model

infographic.key_insight: Large Language Models' internal (parametric) knowledge can be directly used to verify factual claims, enabling effective fact checking without relying on external retrieval pipelines.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes dependence on retrieval and external evidence sources for claim verification, addressing failure modes caused by missing or noisy retrieved documents and reducing latency and system complexity.
method: Prompt LLMs to assess claim veracity using their stored knowledge and reasoning capabilities rather than fetching external evidence.
Use structured verification prompts and verification-aware decoding (e.g., multi-step reasoning, calibration or self-consistency) to improve faithfulness and confidence estimation.
Evaluate and compare the retrieval-free pipeline to retrieval-based baselines across factuality benchmarks to validate feasibility and trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Offers a simpler, lower-latency fact-checking approach that is robust when external knowledge is unavailable, making trustworthy verification more practical for deployed AI systems and edge scenarios.

title: Transformer-Based Inpainting for Real-Time 3D Streaming in Sparse Multi-Camera Setups
authors: Leif Van Holland, Domenic Zingsheim, Mana Takhsha, Hannah Dröge, Patrick Stotko
abstract: High-quality 3D streaming from multiple cameras is crucial for immersive experiences in many AR/VR applications. The limited number of views - often due to real-time constraints - leads to missing information and incomplete surfaces in the rendered images. Existing approaches typically rely on simple heuristics for the hole filling, which can result in inconsistencies or visual artifacts. We propose to complete the missing textures using a novel, application-targeted inpainting method independen

infographic.key_insight: A transformer-based inpainting model can plausibly and consistently complete missing textures from very sparse multi-camera captures, enabling high-quality, low-latency 3D streaming with fewer viewpoints.
infographic.problem_solved: Fills holes and incomplete surfaces that arise when real-time 3D streaming must operate with a limited number of camera views; replaces ad-hoc heuristics that produce visual inconsistencies and artifacts.
method: Project multi-camera captures into a shared surface/texture space (e.g., UV or target view) and detect missing regions.
Apply a specialized transformer inpainting network that uses cross-view and spatial attention to synthesize coherent texture for gaps while preserving geometric cues.
Design and optimize the model and pipeline for streaming constraints (low latency, compact representations, temporal consistency losses) so it runs in real time on practical hardware.
infographic.impact: Improves visual fidelity and consistency in real-time 3D/AR/VR streaming systems while reducing the number of required cameras and bandwidth; practical for ML engineers building immersive systems under strict latency and capture constraints.

title: Censored LLMs as a Natural Testbed for Secret Knowledge Elicitation
authors: Helena Casademunt, Bartosz Cywiński, Khoi Tran, Arya Jakkli, Samuel Marks
abstract: Large language models sometimes produce false or misleading responses. Two approaches to this problem are honesty elicitation -- modifying prompts or weights so that the model answers truthfully -- and lie detection -- classifying whether a given response is false. Prior work evaluates such methods on models specifically trained to lie or conceal information, but these artificial constructions may not resemble naturally-occurring dishonesty. We instead study open-weights LLMs from Chinese develo

infographic.key_insight: Censored open-weight LLMs — models that withhold or suppress information for safety or policy reasons — provide a realistic, naturally-occurring testbed for studying secret-knowledge elicitation and lie-detection methods, revealing different failure modes than synthetically-trained lying models.
infographic.problem_solved: Prior evaluations use artificially constructed lying models that may not reflect real-world withholding behavior; this paper addresses the need for a more realistic benchmark to test methods that elicit truthful knowledge or detect falsehoods.
method: Collect and analyze open-weight LLMs that exhibit censorship/withholding behavior as a natural source of secret-knowledge scenarios.
Apply and compare honesty-elicitation techniques (prompt engineering, weight or decoding adjustments) to try to recover suppressed knowledge.
Train and evaluate lie-detection classifiers on model outputs to identify withheld or misleading responses and compare performance to synthetic lying-model baselines.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a more realistic evaluation framework for honesty and lie-detection techniques, improving robustness assessments and guiding safer deployment choices for models that intentionally withhold information.

title: Reasoning Theater: Disentangling Model Beliefs from Chain-of-Thought
authors: Siddharth Boppana, Annabel Ma, Max Loeffler, Raphael Sarfati, Eric Bigelow
abstract: We provide evidence of performative chain-of-thought (CoT) in reasoning models, where a model becomes strongly confident in its final answer, but continues generating tokens without revealing its internal belief. Our analysis compares activation probing, early forced answering, and a CoT monitor across two large models (DeepSeek-R1 671B & GPT-OSS 120B) and find task difficulty-specific differences: The model's final answer is decodable from activations far earlier in CoT than a monitor is able t

infographic.key_insight: Large models often 'perform' chain-of-thought: their internal activations encode the final answer much earlier than the tokens reveal it, and external CoT monitors fail to detect that internal belief until later — with differences depending on task difficulty.
infographic.problem_solved: Exposes a gap between a model's internal belief state and its generated chain-of-thought, showing that surface-level CoT can be performative and that existing monitors can miss early, decodable answers.
method: Activation probing: train decoders on model activations at each token to read out the model's latent answer over time.
Early forced-answer experiments: prompt the model to output an answer at intermediate points in the CoT to test whether the internal belief is already settled.
Monitor vs probe comparison across models and tasks: evaluate a CoT monitor and probes on two LMs (DeepSeek-R1 671B, GPT-OSS 120B) and analyze task-difficulty-specific detection gaps.
infographic.impact: Shows that belief-tracking should rely on internal-state probes rather than surface tokens for accurate monitoring and alignment; important for trustworthy reasoning, evaluation, and safety of LLMs.
visual_elements: Timeline diagram: token-by-token generation with a superimposed curve showing when the final answer becomes decodable from activations vs when the model states it in text.

title: AgentIR: Reasoning-Aware Retrival for Deep Research Agents
authors: Zijian Chen, Xueguang Ma, Shengyao Zhuang, Jimmy Lin, Akari Asai
abstract: Deep Research agents are rapidly emerging as primary consumers of modern retrieval systems. Unlike human users who issue and refine queries without documenting their intermediate thought processes, Deep Research agents generate explicit natural language reasoning before each search call, revealing rich intent and contextual information that existing retrievers entirely ignore. To exploit this overlooked signal, we introduce: (1) Reasoning-Aware Retrieval, a retrieval paradigm that jointly embeds

infographic.key_insight: Deep research agents explicitly produce natural-language reasoning before each search; by making retrieval aware of that reasoning (not just the surface query), retrievers can find more relevant, context-aligned evidence for downstream agent steps.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard retrievers ignore agents' intermediate chain-of-thought and contextual intent, yielding mismatches between what the agent needs and what the retriever returns—this paper addresses that gap by leveraging agent reasoning as a retrieval signal.
method: Introduce Reasoning-Aware Retrieval: jointly represent the agent's explicit natural-language reasoning and the search query in the retrieval embedding space.
Train a retriever/objective to match reasoning+query embeddings with relevant documents/snippets (e.g., contrastive or relevance-ranking strategies) so results reflect the agent's intent and context.
Integrate the reasoning-aware retriever into the agent loop so each search call uses the agent's latest reasoning context to produce more targeted evidence for subsequent steps.
infographic.impact: Makes retrieval systems directly useful for LLM-driven research agents, improving evidence relevance, efficiency of multi-step reasoning workflows, and overall reliability of autonomous research pipelines.
visual_elements: Flow diagram: agent generates reasoning -> reasoning-aware retriever -> ranked documents -> agent consumes evidence (looped pipeline).

title: $τ$-Knowledge: Evaluating Conversational Agents over Unstructured Knowledge
authors: Quan Shi, Alexandra Zytek, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan, Victor Barres
abstract: Conversational agents are increasingly deployed in knowledge-intensive settings, where correct behavior depends on retrieving and applying domain-specific knowledge from large, proprietary, and unstructured corpora during live interactions with users. Yet most existing benchmarks evaluate retrieval or tool use independently of each other, creating a gap in realistic, fully agentic evaluation over unstructured data in long-horizon interactions. We introduce $τ$-Knowledge, an extension of $τ$-Benc

infographic.key_insight: τ-Knowledge provides a realistic, integrated benchmark that evaluates conversational agents on their ability to retrieve and apply domain-specific knowledge from large unstructured corpora during long-horizon, live interactions—closing the gap between isolated retrieval and tool-use evaluations.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks test retrieval or tool use separately and fail to capture end-to-end agent behavior over unstructured data in prolonged dialogues; τ-Knowledge addresses this by offering a unified, agentic evaluation framework for knowledge-intensive conversational settings.
method: Extend τ-Bench into τ-Knowledge to create end-to-end evaluation scenarios where agents must access large, proprietary, unstructured corpora during multi-turn conversations.
Define interactive tasks and an evaluation protocol that measure retrieval accuracy, grounding, answer correctness, and long-horizon consistency in live exchanges.
Combine automated metrics and human judgments to capture compositional failures (retrieval → reasoning → response) and enable comparisons across retrieval-augmented and tool-using agent designs.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical benchmark to diagnose and improve agent grounding, retrieval integration, and long-term conversational reliability in real-world, knowledge-intensive domains—accelerating safer and more accurate deployed assistants.

title: Enhancing Authorship Attribution with Synthetic Paintings
authors: Clarissa Loures, Caio Hosken, Luan Oliveira, Gianlucca Zuin, Adriano Veloso
abstract: Attributing authorship to paintings is a historically complex task, and one of its main challenges is the limited availability of real artworks for training computational models. This study investigates whether synthetic images, generated through DreamBooth fine-tuning of Stable Diffusion, can improve the performance of classification models in this context. We propose a hybrid approach that combines real and synthetic data to enhance model accuracy and generalization across similar artistic sty

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuned generative models (DreamBooth on Stable Diffusion) can produce synthetic paintings that, when combined with real artworks, measurably improve authorship attribution accuracy and generalization under limited-data conditions.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the scarcity of labeled paintings for training classifiers by augmenting datasets with high-fidelity, artist-specific synthetic images to improve model learning and robustness.
method: Fine-tune Stable Diffusion with DreamBooth per artist to generate synthetic paintings capturing stylistic cues.
Create hybrid training sets that combine real artworks and synthetic images to train attribution classifiers.
Evaluate classification accuracy and generalization across similar artists/styles to quantify gains from synthetic augmentation.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical pipeline for AI practitioners to expand scarce art datasets and boost attribution performance without needing large collections of real works. This approach generalizes to other low-data visual attribution problems where style preservation matters.

title: SELDON: Supernova Explosions Learned by Deep ODE Networks
authors: Jiezhong Wu, Jack O'Brien, Jennifer Li, M. S. Krafczyk, Ved G. Shah
abstract: The discovery rate of optical transients will explode to 10 million public alerts per night once the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time comes online, overwhelming the traditional physics-based inference pipelines. A continuous-time forecasting AI model is of interest because it can deliver millisecond-scale inference for thousands of objects per day, whereas legacy MCMC codes need hours per object. In this paper, we propose SELDON, a new continuous-time variational autoe

infographic.key_insight: SELDON uses a continuous-time deep ODE variational model to learn supernova explosion dynamics from irregular light curves, producing millisecond-scale, amortized posterior inference that replaces hours-long MCMC runs. This enables real-time parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification at LSST alert scales.
infographic.problem_solved: How to perform fast, accurate, and uncertainty-aware inference of transient (supernova) parameters from irregularly sampled light curves when alert rates (∼10 million/night) make traditional physics-based MCMC pipelines infeasible.
method: Continuous-time variational autoencoder built around neural ODE latent dynamics to model light-curve evolution in continuous time.
Amortized inference (encoder → latent ODE → decoder) for millisecond-scale posterior predictions and calibrated uncertainty estimates.
End-to-end training on simulated/observed transient light curves to handle irregular sampling and deliver scalable, real-time inference.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, real-time transient parameter inference and uncertainty quantification for Rubin LSST-scale alert streams, allowing rapid follow-up prioritization and resource allocation. Provides a practical blueprint for ML practitioners building continuous-time, amortized inference systems for scientific time series.

title: ZipMap: Linear-Time Stateful 3D Reconstruction with Test-Time Training
authors: Haian Jin, Rundi Wu, Tianyuan Zhang, Ruiqi Gao, Jonathan T. Barron
abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have driven rapid progress in 3D vision, but state-of-the-art methods such as VGGT and $π^3$ have a computational cost that scales quadratically with the number of input images, making them inefficient when applied to large image collections. Sequential-reconstruction approaches reduce this cost but sacrifice reconstruction quality. We introduce ZipMap, a stateful feed-forward model that achieves linear-time, bidirectional 3D reconstruction while matching or surpa

infographic.key_insight: ZipMap introduces a stateful feed-forward architecture that converts quadratic cross-image cost into a linear-time process by maintaining and updating a compact scene map, enabling high-quality bidirectional 3D reconstruction with test-time adaptation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing transformer-based 3D reconstruction methods scale quadratically with the number of input images, making them computationally and memory inefficient for large image collections; ZipMap addresses this scalability-quality tradeoff.
method: Stateful feed-forward model that maintains a compact, updatable scene representation (the 'ZipMap') across images so each new view incurs only constant additional cost.
Bidirectional reconstruction pipeline: sequentially integrates information from images while allowing refinement in both directions via the maintained state.
Test-time training/ adaptation applied on the maintained map to recover or exceed the reconstruction quality of heavy quadratic-cost methods.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, scalable way to run high-quality 3D reconstruction on large photo collections or streaming inputs, cutting compute and memory costs while preserving or improving accuracy—useful for real-time systems and large-scale datasets.

title: Reinforcement learning-based design of sequential drug treatment targeting the evolving tumour landscape with SequenTx
authors: Xiaohan Chen, Yue Deng, Xingbo Yang, Ying Zhang, Yuting Huang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 04 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01192-1

Chen et al. introduce SequenTx, a virtual-cell-inspired framework for the rational design of sequential therapy. It offers a computational strategy to navigate therapy-induced tumour evolution by modelling dynamic cellular state transitions.

infographic.key_insight: SequenTx couples a virtual-cell model of dynamic cellular state transitions with reinforcement learning to design sequential drug regimens that proactively steer tumor evolution and reduce therapy-induced resistance.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a computational strategy to navigate and control therapy-driven tumour evolution by anticipating cellular state changes and optimizing adaptive, time-varying treatment sequences.
method: Build a virtual-cell-inspired model that represents tumour heterogeneity as dynamic state transitions between cellular phenotypes.
Use reinforcement learning to search for optimal sequential drug policies that minimize tumour burden and delay or prevent resistance.
Evaluate candidate policies in simulated evolving tumour landscapes to compare adaptive sequences vs static or heuristic regimens.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates how combining mechanistic state models with RL addresses non-stationary control problems in biology; offers a transferable framework and experimental benchmark for ML researchers working on adaptive decision-making under shifting distributions.

title: Helios: Real Real-Time Long Video Generation Model
authors: Shenghai Yuan, Yuanyang Yin, Zongjian Li, Xinwei Huang, Xiao Yang
abstract: We introduce Helios, the first 14B video generation model that runs at 19.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU and supports minute-scale generation while matching the quality of a strong baseline. We make breakthroughs along three key dimensions: (1) robustness to long-video drifting without commonly used anti-drifting heuristics such as self-forcing, error-banks, or keyframe sampling; (2) real-time generation without standard acceleration techniques such as KV-cache, sparse/linear attention, or qu

infographic.key_insight: Helios is a 14B video-generation model that achieves minute-scale, high-quality videos at real-time speed (19.5 FPS) on a single NVIDIA H100 by eliminating common anti-drifting heuristics and standard acceleration tricks while retaining baseline-quality outputs.
infographic.problem_solved: Brings together long-duration stability and real-time throughput for generative video: preventing temporal drift over minutes without heuristic fixes, while delivering interactive-speed generation on a single high-end GPU.
method: Model + training design focused on long-term temporal consistency to avoid drift without self-forcing, error banks, or keyframe sampling.
System and implementation optimizations tailored for a single NVIDIA H100 that enable 19.5 FPS inference for minute-scale videos without relying on KV-cache or sparse/linear attention.
Careful evaluation and scaling (14B parameter regime) to match the quality of strong baselines while meeting throughput and stability targets.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to generate minute-scale video content in real time on a single GPU while preserving quality, reducing the need for complex heuristics and multi-GPU setups—lowering cost and engineering complexity for production deployments and research.

title: Low-Resource Guidance for Controllable Latent Audio Diffusion
authors: Zachary Novack, Zack Zukowski, CJ Carr, Julian Parker, Zach Evans
abstract: Generative audio requires fine-grained controllable outputs, yet most existing methods require model retraining on specific controls or inference-time controls (\textit{e.g.}, guidance) that can also be computationally demanding. By examining the bottlenecks of existing guidance-based controls, in particular their high cost-per-step due to decoder backpropagation, we introduce a guidance-based approach through selective TFG and Latent-Control Heads (LatCHs), which enables controlling latent audi

infographic.key_insight: Selective, low-cost guidance applied in latent space (via selective TFG and small Latent-Control Heads) yields fine-grained controllable audio diffusion while avoiding expensive decoder backprop, dramatically lowering inference compute per step.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a way to get fine-grained, controllable audio generation without retraining or heavy inference-time compute caused by backpropagating through large decoders.
method: Identify and quantify the decoder backpropagation bottleneck in existing guidance-based audio diffusion methods.
Selective TFG — apply guidance only to selected latent / time–frequency components to concentrate compute where it matters and reduce per-step cost.
Latent-Control Heads (LatCHs) — attach lightweight control heads in latent space that enable steering (and producing guidance signals) without full decoder backprop.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to add powerful, fine-grained controls to latent audio diffusion models with much lower inference cost and memory, making controllable audio generation faster and more practical for low-resource or real-time scenarios.

title: Accurate and Efficient Hybrid-Ensemble Atmospheric Data Assimilation in Latent Space with Uncertainty Quantification
authors: Hang Fan, Juan Nathaniel, Yi Xiao, Ce Bian, Fenghua Ling
abstract: Data assimilation (DA) combines model forecasts and observations to estimate the optimal state of the atmosphere with its uncertainty, providing initial conditions for weather prediction and reanalyses for climate research. Yet, existing traditional and machine-learning DA methods struggle to achieve accuracy, efficiency and uncertainty quantification simultaneously. Here, we propose HLOBA (Hybrid-Ensemble Latent Observation-Background Assimilation), a three-dimensional hybrid-ensemble DA method

infographic.key_insight: HLOBA performs hybrid-ensemble data assimilation in a learned low-dimensional latent space, delivering both higher accuracy and much lower computational cost while providing calibrated uncertainty estimates.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional and ML-based DA methods struggle to simultaneously achieve accuracy, efficiency, and reliable uncertainty quantification for high-dimensional atmospheric state estimation; HLOBA addresses this by reducing dimensionality and combining ensemble and variational strengths in latent space.
method: Learn a compact latent representation of atmospheric state (encoder/decoder) to reduce dimensionality and expensive observation-operator computations.
Perform hybrid-ensemble assimilation in latent space: blend ensemble-derived flow-dependent covariances with background/variational constraints to compute analyses and propagate ensembles.
Explicitly quantify and propagate analysis uncertainty in latent space, then decode to produce full-state estimates with calibrated uncertainty for downstream forecasting.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, ML-friendly data assimilation that cuts compute costs while preserving or improving analysis quality and delivering actionable uncertainty estimates—useful for operational forecasting, model training, and climate reanalysis.

title: Out-of-distribution transfer of PDE foundation models to material dynamics under extreme loading
authors: Mahindra Rautela, Alexander Most, Siddharth Mansingh, Aleksandra Pachalieva, Bradley Love
abstract: Most PDE foundation models are pretrained and fine-tuned on fluid-centric benchmarks. Their utility under extreme-loading material dynamics remains unclear. We benchmark out-of-distribution transfer on two discontinuity-dominated regimes in which shocks, evolving interfaces, and fracture produce highly non-smooth fields: shock-driven multi-material interface dynamics (perturbed layered interface or PLI) and dynamic fracture/failure evolution (FRAC). We formulate the downstream task as terminal-s

infographic.key_insight: PDE foundation models pretrained on fluid-centric data struggle to generalize to extreme-loading material dynamics dominated by shocks, evolving interfaces, and fracture; benchmarking on two discontinuity-heavy regimes quantifies this out-of-distribution transfer gap.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how well (or poorly) fluid-trained PDE foundation models transfer to material-dynamics tasks with strong discontinuities and failure mechanisms—an important unknown for designers who might reuse such models outside their training domain.
method: Define two challenging downstream regimes that produce highly non-smooth fields: shock-driven perturbed layered interface (PLI) and dynamic fracture/failure evolution (FRAC).

Benchmark out-of-distribution transfer by evaluating PDE foundation models pretrained on fluid-centric datasets on these regimes, formulating the downstream task as terminal-state (final-snapshot) prediction.
Compare performance (errors, qualitative field reconstructions) to appropriate baselines and assess where pretrained models fail or require adaptation.
infographic.impact: Provides practical, quantitative guidance on the limits of reusing fluid-pretrained PDE models for extreme material dynamics, informing whether to fine-tune, collect specialized data, or develop new architectures for discontinuity-rich domains.
visual_elements: Schematic diagram contrasting the two test regimes: PLI (layered materials + shock) vs FRAC (crack initiation and propagation).

title: FocusGraph: Graph-Structured Frame Selection for Embodied Long Video Question Answering
authors: Tatiana Zemskova, Solomon Andryushenko, Ilya Obrubov, Viktoriia Khoruzhaia, Ekaterina Eroshenko
abstract: The ability to understand long videos is vital for embodied intelligent agents, because their effectiveness depends on how well they can accumulate, organize, and leverage long-horizon perceptual memories. Recently, multimodal LLMs have been gaining popularity for solving the long video understanding task due to their general ability to understand natural language and to leverage world knowledge. However, as the number of frames provided to an MLLM increases, the quality of its responses tends t

infographic.key_insight: Represent long video frames as a question-conditioned graph and select a compact, informative subset via graph reasoning so multimodal LLMs can answer long-horizon embodied questions more accurately and efficiently.
infographic.problem_solved: MLLMs degrade when fed many redundant or irrelevant frames from long videos; the paper addresses how to compactly summarize long-horizon visual memory while preserving temporal and relational cues needed for embodied video question answering.
method: Build a graph where nodes are candidate frames (or glimpses) and edges encode temporal/semantic relations; condition node scoring on the question and agent context.
Use graph-based reasoning (e.g., a lightweight GNN or attention over the graph) to rank and select a small, diverse subset of frames that maximize relevance and coverage.
Feed the selected frames (and their relations) into a multimodal LLM or downstream QA module to produce answers with lower compute and higher accuracy.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, accurate long-video understanding for embodied agents by reducing input redundancy and preserving relational context—improving both efficiency and interpretability for practitioners building multimodal agents.

title: A Constrained RL Approach for Cost-Efficient Delivery of Latency-Sensitive Applications
authors: Ozan Aygün, Vincenzo Norman Vitale, Antonia M. Tulino, Hao Feng, Elza Erkip
abstract: Next-generation networks aim to provide performance guarantees to real-time interactive services that require timely and cost-efficient packet delivery. In this context, the goal is to reliably deliver packets with strict deadlines imposed by the application while minimizing overall resource allocation cost. A large body of work has leveraged stochastic optimization techniques to design efficient dynamic routing and scheduling solutions under average delay constraints; however, these methods fal

infographic.key_insight: A constrained reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes routing/scheduling policies to minimize resource cost while provably respecting strict packet-deadline constraints, switching the focus from average-delay optimization to deadline-aware, cost-efficient delivery.
infographic.problem_solved: How to reliably deliver latency-sensitive packets with strict deadlines in next-generation networks while minimizing overall resource allocation cost—addressing the gap where traditional stochastic optimization targets average delays rather than hard deadline guarantees.
method: Formulate delivery as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) where the objective is minimizing resource cost and constraints enforce acceptable deadline-violation probabilities.
Use constrained RL / Lagrangian-style policy optimization with deadline-aware reward shaping so the agent learns cost-efficient routing and scheduling that respects deadline constraints.
Train and validate policies in simulation with online adaptation to changing traffic and resource conditions, enabling practical deployment at edge/cloud network elements.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to deploy real-time, interactive services (e.g., online inference, AR/VR, teleoperation) with stronger SLO compliance and lower infrastructure cost by providing policies that balance timeliness and resource use.
visual_elements: Trade-off curve showing resource cost vs. deadline-violation probability comparing baseline methods and the proposed constrained-RL policy.

title: Underrepresented in Foundation Model Pretraining Data? A One-Shot Probe
authors: Chris Vorster, Mayug Maniparambil, Noel E. O'Connor, Noel Murphy, Derek Molloy
abstract: Large-scale Vision-Language Foundation Models (VLFMs), such as CLIP, now underpin a wide range of computer vision research and applications. VLFMs are often adapted to various domain-specific tasks. However, VLFM performance on novel, specialised, or underrepresented domains remains inconsistent. Evaluating VLFMs typically requires labelled test sets, which are often unavailable for niche domains of interest, particularly those from the Global South. We address this gap by proposing a highly dat

infographic.key_insight: A simple one‑shot probing technique can detect whether a domain is underrepresented in a vision–language foundation model's pretraining data, enabling assessment without labelled test sets.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a practical way to evaluate VLFM coverage for novel, specialised, or Global South domains when labelled evaluation sets are unavailable, revealing potential blind spots before deployment or adaptation.
method: Provide a single representative example (image or caption) from the target domain and query the VLFM to obtain embeddings or retrieval/confidence outputs.
Compare the model's responses against reference distributions or contrasted prompts (in‑domain vs out‑of‑domain) to derive a representation score or underrepresentation signal.
Use simple calibration/contrastive checks (e.g., nearest‑neighbor ranks, similarity gaps, or prompt variants) to quantify how well the model recognises the domain from one example.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to rapidly screen foundation models for domain gaps with minimal data, guiding decisions on adaptation, data collection, or risk mitigation for underrepresented communities.

title: Tether: Autonomous Functional Play with Correspondence-Driven Trajectory Warping
authors: William Liang, Sam Wang, Hung-Ju Wang, Osbert Bastani, Yecheng Jason Ma
abstract: The ability to conduct and learn from interaction and experience is a central challenge in robotics, offering a scalable alternative to labor-intensive human demonstrations. However, realizing such "play" requires (1) a policy robust to diverse, potentially out-of-distribution environment states, and (2) a procedure that continuously produces useful robot experience. To address these challenges, we introduce Tether, a method for autonomous functional play involving structured, task-directed inte

infographic.key_insight: Tether enables robots to autonomously generate diverse, task-directed experience by using learned correspondences to warp trajectories into new contexts, producing policies that remain robust under out-of-distribution states.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the need for scalable, self-supervised robot learning that (1) produces continually useful experience without dense human demonstrations and (2) trains policies that generalize to diverse or out-of-distribution environment states.
method: Learn correspondences between scenes/contexts (visual or state-level) to map points and affordances across different environments.
Warp existing trajectories using these correspondences to synthesize functionally similar demonstrations in new contexts, creating high-value autonomous ‘play’ data.
Iteratively train a goal-conditioned/robust policy on the warped trajectories and deploy the policy to collect more diverse experience in a closed loop.
infographic.impact: Enables more scalable, data-efficient robot learning by reducing dependence on human demos and improving policy generalization; useful for practitioners building autonomous data-collection pipelines and robust imitation/self-supervised systems.

title: How to Peel with a Knife: Aligning Fine-Grained Manipulation with Human Preference
authors: Toru Lin, Shuying Deng, Zhao-Heng Yin, Pieter Abbeel, Jitendra Malik
abstract: Many essential manipulation tasks - such as food preparation, surgery, and craftsmanship - remain intractable for autonomous robots. These tasks are characterized not only by contact-rich, force-sensitive dynamics, but also by their "implicit" success criteria: unlike pick-and-place, task quality in these domains is continuous and subjective (e.g. how well a potato is peeled), making quantitative evaluation and reward engineering difficult. We present a learning framework for such tasks, using p

infographic.key_insight: Training robots on pairwise human preferences over executions (rather than hand-designed rewards) lets them learn fine-grained, subjective manipulation skills (e.g., peeling with a knife) that align with human notions of quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables learning and evaluation of contact-rich, force-sensitive tasks whose success is continuous and subjective—where explicit reward engineering is impractical.
method: Collect human preference labels over short execution clips or outcomes (pairwise comparisons or ratings).
Train a learned reward model that predicts human preference scores from sensor/trajectory data.
Optimize a contact-aware manipulation policy (via RL/IL/finetuning) using the learned reward to produce high-quality, human-aligned behavior.
infographic.impact: Reduces the need for brittle, task-specific reward engineering and provides a scalable way to teach robots subtle, subjective skills—opening practical progress on food prep, surgery-adjacent tasks, and craftsmanship.

title: Utonia: Toward One Encoder for All Point Clouds
authors: Yujia Zhang, Xiaoyang Wu, Yunhan Yang, Xianzhe Fan, Han Li
abstract: We dream of a future where point clouds from all domains can come together to shape a single model that benefits them all. Toward this goal, we present Utonia, a first step toward training a single self-supervised point transformer encoder across diverse domains, spanning remote sensing, outdoor LiDAR, indoor RGB-D sequences, object-centric CAD models, and point clouds lifted from RGB-only videos. Despite their distinct sensing geometries, densities, and priors, Utonia learns a consistent repres

infographic.key_insight: Utonia shows that a single self-supervised point-transformer encoder can learn consistent, transferable representations across widely different point-cloud domains (remote sensing, LiDAR, RGB-D, CAD, and video-lifted clouds).
infographic.problem_solved: Eliminates the fragmentation caused by domain-specific 3D encoders by enabling one unified model to generalize across varying sensing geometries, densities, and priors.
method: Design and train one shared point-transformer encoder with self-supervised objectives across a mixture of diverse point-cloud datasets.
Apply domain-balanced sampling, normalization and augmentation strategies so the encoder learns modality-agnostic features despite heterogeneous point distributions.
Use unified pretext tasks (e.g., contrastive and/or masked modeling) to align representations from different domains into a common embedding space.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical route to a single pre-trained 3D backbone that can be fine-tuned for many downstream tasks, reducing engineering burden and improving transferability across scarce or new point-cloud domains.

title: Beyond Language Modeling: An Exploration of Multimodal Pretraining
authors: Shengbang Tong, David Fan, John Nguyen, Ellis Brown, Gaoyue Zhou
abstract: The visual world offers a critical axis for advancing foundation models beyond language. Despite growing interest in this direction, the design space for native multimodal models remains opaque. We provide empirical clarity through controlled, from-scratch pretraining experiments, isolating the factors that govern multimodal pretraining without interference from language pretraining. We adopt the Transfusion framework, using next-token prediction for language and diffusion for vision, to train o

infographic.key_insight: Controlled, from‑scratch multimodal pretraining using the Transfusion framework (next‑token language + diffusion vision) reveals which design choices—data mix, objective weighting, and architectural coupling—drive multimodal learning, enabling principled trade‑offs without confounds from prior language pretraining.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies the opaque design space for native multimodal foundation models by isolating the core factors that govern joint language–vision pretraining, eliminating interference from preexisting language checkpoints.
method: Train multimodal models from scratch with the Transfusion setup: autoregressive next‑token loss for text and a diffusion objective for images.
Run controlled ablations that vary data composition, objective weighting (balance between language and vision losses), and architectural coupling (shared vs modality‑specific modules).
Evaluate cross‑modal and unimodal tasks to measure trade‑offs and identify which design choices most strongly affect downstream multimodal performance.
infographic.impact: Provides practical, experimentally grounded guidance for building native multimodal foundation models—reducing guesswork about architecture, data mixing, and loss balancing—and informs more efficient and effective model design for real-world multimodal applications.

title: COP-GEN: Latent Diffusion Transformer for Copernicus Earth Observation Data -- Generation Stochastic by Design
authors: Miguel Espinosa, Eva Gmelich Meijling, Valerio Marsocci, Elliot J. Crowley, Mikolaj Czerkawski
abstract: Earth observation applications increasingly rely on data from multiple sensors, including optical, radar, elevation, and land-cover products. Relationships between these modalities are fundamental for data integration but are inherently non-injective: identical conditioning information can correspond to multiple physically plausible observations. Thus, such conditional mappings should be parametrised as data distributions. As a result, deterministic models tend to collapse toward conditional mea

infographic.key_insight: COP-GEN frames cross-sensor Earth-observation mapping as a stochastic conditional-generation problem and introduces a Latent Diffusion Transformer that produces multiple physically-plausible sensor outputs from the same conditioning input, avoiding deterministic collapse.
infographic.problem_solved: Non-injective relationships between optical, radar, elevation and land-cover modalities make deterministic mappings collapse to conditional averages; the paper addresses the need to model the full conditional distribution for realistic multimodal EO data synthesis and integration.
method: Encode multisensor Copernicus inputs into a compact latent space and perform generation in latent space to improve efficiency and fidelity.
Use a diffusion-based generative process combined with a transformer conditioning backbone to capture complex, multimodal conditional distributions across sensors.
Train the model to produce stochastic samples (multiple plausible outputs) for the same conditioning input, enabling uncertainty-aware synthesis and data augmentation.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical route for uncertainty-aware sensor fusion, realistic data augmentation, gap-filling and simulation in Earth-observation workflows, improving robustness of downstream ML tasks that depend on multimodal inputs.

title: Inherited Goal Drift: Contextual Pressure Can Undermine Agentic Goals
authors: Achyutha Menon, Magnus Saebo, Tyler Crosse, Spencer Gibson, Eyon Jang
abstract: The accelerating adoption of language models (LMs) as agents for deployment in long-context tasks motivates a thorough understanding of goal drift: agents' tendency to deviate from an original objective. While prior-generation language model agents have been shown to be susceptible to drift, the extent to which drift affects more recent models remains unclear. In this work, we provide an updated characterization of the extent and causes of goal drift. We investigate drift in state-of-the-art mod

infographic.key_insight: Modern language-model agents remain vulnerable to "inherited goal drift": contextual pressure from long or changing prompts can cause agents to deviate from their original objectives, even in state-of-the-art models.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how and to what extent goal drift occurs in current agentic LMs used for long-context tasks, identifying contextual pressure as a principal driver and updating the empirical picture for practitioners and researchers.
method: Systematic empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art language models acting as agents on long-context tasks to measure deviation from original goals.
Controlled manipulations of contextual pressure (e.g., conflicting instructions, prolonged context, injected framing) to isolate causal effects on goal persistence.
Quantitative drift metrics and diagnostic analyses to compare susceptibility across models and to probe where and how goals are overwritten or weakened.
infographic.impact: Helps AI/ML practitioners anticipate and detect goal drift in deployed agents, guiding prompt engineering, context management, and alignment/robustness interventions to maintain intended behavior.

title: CFG-Ctrl: Control-Based Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance
authors: Hanyang Wang, Yiyang Liu, Jiawei Chi, Fangfu Liu, Ran Xue
abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) has emerged as a central approach for enhancing semantic alignment in flow-based diffusion models. In this paper, we explore a unified framework called CFG-Ctrl, which reinterprets CFG as a control applied to the first-order continuous-time generative flow, using the conditional-unconditional discrepancy as an error signal to adjust the velocity field. From this perspective, we summarize vanilla CFG as a proportional controller (P-control) with fixed gain, and typi

infographic.key_insight: CFG-Ctrl reframes Classifier-Free Guidance as a control signal applied to a continuous-time generative flow: the conditional–unconditional discrepancy is used as an error to adjust the model's velocity field, showing vanilla CFG is effectively a proportional (P) controller with fixed gain.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies and unifies why CFG modifies diffusion trajectories to improve semantic alignment, enabling principled analysis and more systematic design of guidance mechanisms for flow-based diffusion models.
method: Reinterpret CFG within a control-theoretic framework on first-order continuous-time generative flows.
Use the conditional–unconditional output discrepancy as an error signal to compute a corrective control that modifies the velocity field during generation.
Characterize standard CFG as a proportional controller (P-control) with fixed gain, paving the way for alternative controller designs and tunable guidance.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled perspective that helps practitioners reason about and tune guidance strength, design more stable or adaptive guidance strategies, and bridge diffusion guidance with classical control tools for improved semantic alignment.

title: LoGeR: Long-Context Geometric Reconstruction with Hybrid Memory
authors: Junyi Zhang, Charles Herrmann, Junhwa Hur, Chen Sun, Ming-Hsuan Yang
abstract: Feedforward geometric foundation models achieve strong short-window reconstruction, yet scaling them to minutes-long videos is bottlenecked by quadratic attention complexity or limited effective memory in recurrent designs. We present LoGeR (Long-context Geometric Reconstruction), a novel architecture that scales dense 3D reconstruction to extremely long sequences without post-optimization. LoGeR processes video streams in chunks, leveraging strong bidirectional priors for high-fidelity intra-ch

infographic.key_insight: LoGeR enables dense 3D reconstruction over minutes-long video by processing streams in chunks and using a hybrid memory that preserves long-range context, avoiding quadratic attention and expensive post-optimization while maintaining high-fidelity reconstructions.
infographic.problem_solved: Scales feedforward geometric reconstruction to extremely long video sequences by overcoming quadratic attention costs and the limited effective memory of recurrent designs, eliminating the need for costly post-optimization steps.
method: Chunked bidirectional processing: split video into manageable chunks and apply strong bidirectional priors within each chunk for high-quality local reconstruction.
Hybrid memory architecture: combine short-term (intra-chunk) representations with a compact long-term memory bank to carry global scene context across many chunks without quadratic costs.
Cross-chunk retrieval & update: retrieve, fuse, and update memory summaries to maintain temporal coherence and dense geometry over minutes of footage in a feedforward pipeline.
infographic.impact: Makes practical, real-time-capable dense 3D reconstruction from minute-scale video streams feasible for applications like robotics, AR/VR, and large-scale mapping by reducing compute/memory bottlenecks and removing post-process optimization.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing: video stream → chunking → bidirectional chunk reconstructor → hybrid memory bank → merged long-term 3D output

title: ULTRA: Unified Multimodal Control for Autonomous Humanoid Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
authors: Xialin He, Sirui Xu, Xinyao Li, Runpei Dong, Liuyu Bian
abstract: Achieving autonomous and versatile whole-body loco-manipulation remains a central barrier to making humanoids practically useful. Yet existing approaches are fundamentally constrained: retargeted data are often scarce or low-quality; methods struggle to scale to large skill repertoires; and, most importantly, they rely on tracking predefined motion references rather than generating behavior from perception and high-level task specifications. To address these limitations, we propose ULTRA, a unif

infographic.key_insight: ULTRA unifies multimodal perception and high-level task commands into a single whole-body control policy, enabling humanoids to generate autonomous loco-manipulation behavior directly from sensors and instructions rather than tracking predefined motion references.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes scarcity/low quality of retargeted motion data, limited scalability of skill repertoires, and dependence on reference tracking by producing perception-driven, task-conditioned whole-body behaviors.
method: Train a unified multimodal control policy that maps vision, proprioception, and high-level task specifications to whole‑body commands.
Use hierarchical or modular representations (skill latents / mixture of behaviors) to scale to large repertoires while preserving stable loco-manipulation.
Prioritize generation from perception and task intent instead of retargeting or following pre-recorded motion references, enabling on-the-fly adaptation.
infographic.impact: Makes humanoid robots more autonomous and versatile by reducing reliance on motion capture and reference tracking, and by enabling scalable, perception-driven whole-body manipulation for real-world tasks.
visual_elements: System diagram: multimodal inputs (camera, language/task spec, proprioception) → unified policy → whole-body control outputs (actuators).

title: DuoMo: Dual Motion Diffusion for World-Space Human Reconstruction
authors: Yufu Wang, Evonne Ng, Soyong Shin, Rawal Khirodkar, Yuan Dong
abstract: We present DuoMo, a generative method that recovers human motion in world-space coordinates from unconstrained videos with noisy or incomplete observations. Reconstructing such motion requires solving a fundamental trade-off: generalizing from diverse and noisy video inputs while maintaining global motion consistency. Our approach addresses this problem by factorizing motion learning into two diffusion models. The camera-space model first estimates motion from videos in camera coordinates. The w

infographic.key_insight: Factorizing motion recovery into two specialized diffusion models — one in camera space and one in world space — lets DuoMo robustly recover global-consistent human motion from noisy, unconstrained video input while retaining per-frame detail.
infographic.problem_solved: Reconstructing accurate human motion in world-space from unconstrained videos that contain noise, occlusions, and incomplete observations, resolving the trade-off between generalizing from diverse inputs and maintaining globally consistent trajectories.
method: Camera-space diffusion model: estimates per-frame motion/pose trajectories in the video’s camera coordinates from noisy or partial observations.
World-space diffusion model: refines and converts camera-space outputs into a coherent global/world-space trajectory, enforcing temporal and spatial consistency across frames.

Joint inference pipeline: the two models are composed so camera-relative detail is preserved while the world-space stage corrects drift and aligns motion to scene/world coordinates (optionally conditioned on camera estimates or pose priors).
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to reconstruct reliable, globally consistent human motion from in-the-wild video for applications in AR/VR, animation, multi-agent simulation, and robotics, reducing reliance on controlled capture rigs.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: two-stage flow chart (Camera-space diffusion → World-space diffusion) with inputs/outputs at each stage.

title: AI-for-Science Low-code Platform with Bayesian Adversarial Multi-Agent Framework
authors: Zihang Zeng, Jiaquan Zhang, Pengze Li, Yuan Qi, Xi Chen
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate potentials for automating scientific code generation but face challenges in reliability, error propagation in multi-agent workflows, and evaluation in domains with ill-defined success metrics. We present a Bayesian adversarial multi-agent framework specifically designed for AI for Science (AI4S) tasks in the form of a Low-code Platform (LCP). Three LLM-based agents are coordinated under the Bayesian framework: a Task Manager that structures user inputs in

infographic.key_insight: Combining a Bayesian coordination layer with an adversarial multi-agent LLM setup within a low-code platform improves reliability and mitigates error propagation when automating scientific code workflows.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses unreliable and cascading failures in multi-agent LLM pipelines for AI-for-Science tasks and the difficulty of evaluating solutions in domains with ill-defined success metrics, while making automation accessible via low-code interfaces.
method: Bayesian adversarial multi-agent coordination: three cooperating LLM agents (e.g., a Task Manager that structures user input, a Code/Execution agent, and a Critic/Verifier agent) exchange beliefs and updates under a Bayesian framework.

Low-code Platform (LCP) integration: orchestration layer exposes simple user primitives, iterative agent communication, and automated code generation/execution hooks to shorten the scientist-to-code loop.
Adversarial validation loop: the verifier/critic adversarially probes outputs, surfaces failure modes, and the Bayesian updater adjusts agent trust/confidence to reduce error propagation.
infographic.impact: Makes AI-driven scientific coding more robust, auditable, and usable by practitioners—reducing manual debugging and helping teams quantify uncertainty in domains where success is hard to define.

title: UniG2U-Bench: Do Unified Models Advance Multimodal Understanding?
authors: Zimo Wen, Boxiu Li, Wanbo Zhang, Junxiang Lei, Xiaoyu Chen
abstract: Unified multimodal models have recently demonstrated strong generative capabilities, yet whether and when generation improves understanding remains unclear. Existing benchmarks lack a systematic exploration of the specific tasks where generation facilitates understanding. To this end, we introduce UniG2U-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark categorizing generation-to-understanding (G2U) evaluation into 7 regimes and 30 subtasks, requiring varying degrees of implicit or explicit visual transformation

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces UniG2U-Bench, showing that unified generative multimodal models can help understanding in some-but-not-all scenarios by systematically categorizing generation-to-understanding (G2U) benefits across different task regimes.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies when and how generation improves multimodal understanding by providing a structured benchmark that fills gaps in existing evaluations, which lacked systematic exploration of tasks where generation aids understanding.
method: Construct UniG2U-Bench: a comprehensive benchmark that organizes G2U evaluation into 7 regimes and 30 subtasks.
Define tasks with varying degrees of implicit vs. explicit visual transformation to probe whether generation mechanisms help downstream understanding.
Provide standardized evaluation protocols to compare unified generative models on these diverse G2U subtasks.
infographic.impact: Enables researchers and practitioners to pinpoint which multimodal tasks benefit from generative capabilities, guiding model design, evaluation, and targeted improvements in unified models.

title: Bridging the gap between Performance and Interpretability: An Explainable Disentangled Multimodal Framework for Cancer Survival Prediction
authors: Aniek Eijpe, Soufyan Lakbir, Melis Erdal Cesur, Sara P. Oliveira, Angelos Chatzimparmpas
abstract: While multimodal survival prediction models are increasingly more accurate, their complexity often reduces interpretability, limiting insight into how different data sources influence predictions. To address this, we introduce DIMAFx, an explainable multimodal framework for cancer survival prediction that produces disentangled, interpretable modality-specific and modality-shared representations from histopathology whole-slide images and transcriptomics data. Across multiple cancer cohorts, DIMAF

infographic.key_insight: DIMAFx is an explainable multimodal framework that learns disentangled modality-specific and modality-shared representations from whole-slide histopathology images and transcriptomics, enabling interpretable cancer survival predictions without sacrificing predictive performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the trade-off between increasingly accurate multimodal survival models and their lack of interpretability by revealing how each data modality and shared signals contribute to survival risk.
method: Disentangled representation learning: separate encoders that extract modality-specific and modality-shared latent factors from WSIs and transcriptomic profiles.
Modality-aware fusion and survival head: combine disentangled factors into a joint predictor (survival loss) while preserving decomposed components for attribution.
Explainability modules: map latent components back to inputs (e.g., heatmaps on slides, gene-level importance) to quantify each modality's contribution to individual predictions.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy multimodal cancer survival models that are both competitive and transparent, facilitating trust, clinical insight, and targeted hypothesis generation from modality-specific signals.

title: HiFi-Inpaint: Towards High-Fidelity Reference-Based Inpainting for Generating Detail-Preserving Human-Product Images
authors: Yichen Liu, Donghao Zhou, Jie Wang, Xin Gao, Guisheng Liu
abstract: Human-product images, which showcase the integration of humans and products, play a vital role in advertising, e-commerce, and digital marketing. The essential challenge of generating such images lies in ensuring the high-fidelity preservation of product details. Among existing paradigms, reference-based inpainting offers a targeted solution by leveraging product reference images to guide the inpainting process. However, limitations remain in three key aspects: the lack of diverse large-scale tr

infographic.key_insight: HiFi-Inpaint is a reference-based inpainting framework that preserves fine product details when generating human-product images by explicitly aligning and transferring high-frequency textures from product reference images into the inpainting pipeline.
infographic.problem_solved: Generates realistic human-product images while overcoming loss of product detail in conventional inpainting methods, enabling faithful reproduction of textures, patterns and logos from reference product images.
method: Reference-guided alignment: warp or attend to a product reference image to spatially align product appearance with the target human scene.
Multi-scale refinement and detail transfer: a coarse-to-fine generator that preserves high-frequency textures via specialized fusion blocks and detail-aware losses.
Training regime & objectives: combine perceptual/LPIPS-style metrics, high-frequency/texture-preserving loss terms, and adversarial refinement, trained on a diverse human-product dataset.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical solution for creating high-fidelity marketing and e-commerce images where product identity must be preserved, improving realism and trustworthiness for downstream visual applications and editing workflows.

title: Organizing, Orchestrating, and Benchmarking Agent Skills at Ecosystem Scale
authors: Hao Li, Chunjiang Mu, Jianhao Chen, Siyue Ren, Zhiyao Cui
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Claude agent skills has raised the central question of how to effectively leverage, manage, and scale the agent skill ecosystem. In this paper, we propose AgentSkillOS, the first principled framework for skill selection, orchestration, and ecosystem-level management. AgentSkillOS comprises two stages: (i) Manage Skills, which organizes skills into a capability tree via node-level recursive categorization for efficient discovery; and (ii) Solve Tasks, which retrieves, o

infographic.key_insight: AgentSkillOS provides a principled two-stage framework—organize skills into a capability tree and then retrieve+orchestrate them to solve tasks—enabling scalable discovery, selection, and ecosystem-level management of agent skills.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the challenge of discovering, selecting, composing, and benchmarking a rapidly growing number of agent skills (e.g., Claude skills) so practitioners can reliably reuse and scale skill-based agent workflows across an ecosystem.
method: Manage Skills: build a node-level recursive capability tree that categorizes skills for efficient discovery, registration, and lifecycle management.
Solve Tasks: retrieve relevant skills from the capability tree, orchestrate and compose them via a planner/selector pipeline to execute tasks end-to-end.
Ecosystem benchmarking: define metrics and workflows to evaluate skill coverage, composition success, and system-level performance across many skills.
infographic.impact: Makes large skill libraries practical to use by improving discoverability, automating orchestration, and providing ecosystem-level evaluation—reducing engineering overhead and accelerating deployment of multi-skill agent solutions.

title: Symbol-Equivariant Recurrent Reasoning Models
authors: Richard Freinschlag, Timo Bertram, Erich Kobler, Andreas Mayr, Günter Klambauer
abstract: Reasoning problems such as Sudoku and ARC-AGI remain challenging for neural networks. The structured problem solving architecture family of Recurrent Reasoning Models (RRMs), including Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) and Tiny Recursive Model (TRM), offer a compact alternative to large language models, but currently handle symbol symmetries only implicitly via costly data augmentation. We introduce Symbol-Equivariant Recurrent Reasoning Models (SE-RRMs), which enforce permutation equivariance

infographic.key_insight: Explicitly enforcing permutation equivariance over symbols in Recurrent Reasoning Models (RRMs) lets the model natively respect symbol symmetries, removing the need for costly data augmentation and yielding more data-efficient, symmetry-aware reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Neural reasoning models (e.g., HRM, TRM) currently rely on heavy data augmentation to handle interchangeable symbols; this is inefficient and limits generalization on structured reasoning tasks like Sudoku and ARC-AGI.
method: Design SE-RRMs by introducing architectural constraints that enforce permutation equivariance across symbol identities inside the RRM family.
Replace or augment standard message-passing/recurrence with symmetry-aware (equivariant) operations so representations transform consistently under symbol permutations.
Integrate equivariant modules into existing HRM/TRM workflows so compact recurrent reasoning architectures can learn without manual augmentation of symbol permutations.
infographic.impact: SE-RRMs reduce reliance on augmentation and improve sample efficiency and robustness for symbolic reasoning tasks, enabling practitioners to train smaller, more generalizable models for structured problem solving.

title: Tool Verification for Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
authors: Ruotong Liao, Nikolai Röhrich, Xiaohan Wang, Yuhui Zhang, Yasaman Samadzadeh
abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for self-evolving large reasoning models (LRMs), enabling online adaptation on unlabeled test inputs via self-induced rewards through majority voting. However, a spurious yet high-frequency unverified consensus can become a biased and reinforced reward signal, leading to incorrect mode collapse. We address this failure mode with T^3RL (Tool-Verification for Test-Time Reinforcement Learning), which introduces test-time to

infographic.key_insight: T^3RL stops self-reinforcement of spurious majority votes in test-time RL by verifying consensus with tools at inference, so only verified consensus produces positive reward — preventing incorrect mode collapse.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the failure mode in test-time reinforcement learning where a high-frequency but unverified consensus becomes a biased reward signal and drives the model into incorrect mode collapse.
method: Attach a test-time verification module that cross-checks majority-voted outputs using external tools or internal cross-validation before converting them into rewards.
Condition reward assignment on verification: confirm and reinforce verified consensus, downweight or abstain from rewarding unverified/highly uncertain consensus.
Introduce verification-aware adaptation strategies (e.g., reward shaping, selective exploration or abstention) to preserve output diversity and avoid reinforcing spurious modes.
infographic.impact: Makes online adaptation of large reasoning models safer and more reliable by preventing feedback loops that amplify wrong answers; improves robustness and trustworthiness of test-time learning for practitioners deploying adaptive models.

title: SageBwd: A Trainable Low-bit Attention
authors: Jintao Zhang, Marco Chen, Haoxu Wang, Kai Jiang, Ion Stoica
abstract: Low-bit attention, such as SageAttention, has emerged as an effective approach for accelerating model inference, but its applicability to training remains poorly understood. In prior work, we introduced SageBwd, a trainable INT8 attention that quantizes six of seven attention matrix multiplications while preserving fine-tuning performance. However, SageBwd exhibited a persistent performance gap to full-precision attention (FPA) during pre-training. In this work, we investigate why this gap occur

infographic.key_insight: A trainable INT8 attention (SageBwd) can be made viable for pre‑training once the specific quantization‑sensitive operations and distribution shifts are diagnosed and corrected — targeted, learnable quantization fixes substantially reduce the performance gap to full‑precision attention.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between low‑bit attention (fast, memory‑efficient inference) and the needs of pre‑training by identifying why prior trainable INT8 attention underperforms during pre‑training and proposing remedies to preserve model quality.
method: Systematic diagnosis of which attention matrix multiplications and distribution shifts cause degradation during pre‑training (sensitivity analysis).
Targeted, trainable quantization fixes (e.g., per‑op/per‑channel learnable scales, calibration and bias correction, selective higher precision for the most sensitive ops).
Quantization‑aware pre‑training workflow and empirical validation showing the proposed fixes reduce the gap to full‑precision attention.
infographic.impact: Enables use of low‑bit attention during both fine‑tuning and pre‑training, cutting compute and memory costs for large models while retaining model quality — important for efficient model development and scaling.

title: MAC: A Conversion Rate Prediction Benchmark Featuring Labels Under Multiple Attribution Mechanisms
authors: Jinqi Wu, Sishuo Chen, Zhangming Chan, Yong Bai, Lei Zhang
abstract:
Multi-attribution learning (MAL), which enhances model performance by learning from conversion labels yielded by multiple attribution mechanisms, has emerged as a promising learning paradigm for conversion rate (CVR) prediction. However, the conversion labels in public CVR datasets are generated by a single attribution mechanism, hindering the development of MAL approaches.
  To address this data gap, we establish the Multi-Attribution Benchmark (MAC), the first public CVR dataset featuring labe

infographic.key_insight: MAC is the first public CVR benchmark that provides conversion labels under multiple attribution mechanisms, enabling multi-attribution learning (MAL) and fair evaluation of models across attribution schemes.
infographic.problem_solved: Public conversion-rate datasets use a single attribution mechanism, blocking development and comparison of MAL methods and limiting model robustness to different attribution policies.
method: Assemble a CVR dataset and generate conversion labels for each event under multiple common attribution mechanisms (e.g., last-click, position-based, time-decay).
Define standardized benchmark tasks, splits, and evaluation metrics to compare single-attribution vs multi-attribution learning approaches.
Provide baseline models and experimental results to illustrate how MAL leverages multiple label views to improve prediction robustness and generalization.
infographic.impact: MAC unlocks research and practical development of models that are robust to attribution choice, helping practitioners build CVR predictors that generalize across different business attribution policies and ad platforms.

title: Conformal Policy Control
authors: Drew Prinster, Clara Fannjiang, Ji Won Park, Kyunghyun Cho, Anqi Liu
abstract: An agent must try new behaviors to explore and improve. In high-stakes environments, an agent that violates safety constraints may cause harm and must be taken offline, curtailing any future interaction. Imitating old behavior is safe, but excessive conservatism discourages exploration. How much behavior change is too much? We show how to use any safe reference policy as a probabilistic regulator for any optimized but untested policy. Conformal calibration on data from the safe policy determines

infographic.key_insight: Conformal Policy Control uses conformal calibration on data from a safe reference policy to build a probabilistic regulator that limits how much a new (optimized) policy can deviate, giving finite-sample coverage guarantees while avoiding excessive conservatism.
infographic.problem_solved: Balances the need for exploration/improvement with safety in high-stakes settings by preventing catastrophic behavioral deviations from a trusted policy without forcing overly conservative imitation.
method: Treat a trusted safe policy as a reference and collect its trajectories / conformity scores.
Apply conformal calibration to those scores to compute acceptance thresholds that guarantee a desired probabilistic bound on allowable deviation.

At deployment, run the candidate policy through the calibrated test: if it passes, allow its actions; if it fails, fall back to the safe policy (probabilistic regulator). Compatible with any optimized/unseen policy.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a practical, distribution-free tool to deploy exploratory policies with explicit finite-sample safety guarantees, enabling more effective and principled exploration in real-world, high-risk domains.

title: GeoDiT: Point-Conditioned Diffusion Transformer for Satellite Image Synthesis
authors: Srikumar Sastry, Dan Cher, Brian Wei, Aayush Dhakal, Subash Khanal
abstract: We introduce GeoDiT, a diffusion transformer designed for text-to-satellite image generation with point-based control. Existing controlled satellite image generative models often require pixel-level maps that are time-consuming to acquire, yet semantically limited. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel point-based conditioning framework that controls the generation process through the spatial location of the points and the textual description associated with each point, providing sema

infographic.key_insight: GeoDiT introduces point-based conditioning for diffusion transformers, letting users control satellite image synthesis via a few spatial points paired with short text labels instead of costly pixel-level maps.
infographic.problem_solved: Generates controllable, text-guided satellite imagery without requiring dense semantic maps—reducing annotation cost and enabling more flexible, localized control over synthetic outputs.
method: Diffusion-transformer backbone (GeoDiT) that denoises images while attending to conditioning tokens.
Point-conditioned input: each control point is encoded as a spatial coordinate + short text descriptor and injected as tokens to guide generation.
Trained on paired satellite images with sparse point annotations and text prompts to learn localized, semantically consistent synthesis.
infographic.impact: Makes geospatial generative modeling more practical by lowering annotation overhead and enabling fine-grained, user-friendly control—useful for data augmentation, scenario simulation, and design in remote sensing workflows.

title: Kiwi-Edit: Versatile Video Editing via Instruction and Reference Guidance
authors: Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, Ziyun Zeng, Zechen Bai, Yanzhe Chen
abstract: Instruction-based video editing has witnessed rapid progress, yet current methods often struggle with precise visual control, as natural language is inherently limited in describing complex visual nuances. Although reference-guided editing offers a robust solution, its potential is currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality paired training data. To bridge this gap, we introduce a scalable data generation pipeline that transforms existing video editing pairs into high-fidelity trainin

infographic.key_insight: Kiwi-Edit combines instruction-based and reference-guided video editing by generating high-fidelity training pairs at scale, enabling models to learn precise visual control beyond what language alone can specify.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between ambiguous natural-language editing instructions and the need for fine-grained visual control, overcoming the scarcity of high-quality paired reference training data.
method: Scalable data-generation pipeline that converts existing video-editing examples into high-fidelity instruction+reference training pairs.
Train a unified editing model conditioned on both textual instructions and visual reference guidance to produce temporally consistent, high-quality edits.
Mix and balance instruction-only and reference-augmented data to retain versatility while improving fine-grained visual accuracy.
infographic.impact: Enables more precise, controllable video edits in practical workflows without requiring large manually labeled paired datasets, benefiting researchers and engineers building multimodal editing tools.
