title: Multi-Head Low-Rank Attention
authors: Songtao Liu, Hongwu Peng, Zhiwei Zhang, Zhengyu Chen, Yue Guo
abstract: Long-context inference in large language models is bottlenecked by Key--Value (KV) cache loading during the decoding stage, where the sequential nature of generation requires repeatedly transferring the KV cache from off-chip High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to on-chip Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) at each step. While Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) significantly reduces the total KV cache size, it suffers from a sharding bottleneck during distributed decoding via Tensor Parallelism (TP). Sinc

infographic.key_insight: Apply a multi-head low-rank factorization to the KV cache so you keep the small cache size of latent-attention methods while avoiding the tensor-parallel sharding bottleneck—enabling much cheaper, scalable long-context decoding.
infographic.problem_solved: Decoding with long contexts is limited by repeated KV cache transfers from off-chip HBM to on-chip SRAM and by a sharding/communication bottleneck when using Tensor Parallelism.
method: Introduce a multi-head low-rank attention representation that compresses per-head K/V information without breaking tensor-parallel sharding patterns.
Design cache layout and decomposition so each TP shard can load and use a small on-chip low-rank KV factor locally, removing cross-shard dependencies during generation.
Hardware-aware choices (rank, layout, and quantization) to balance accuracy, on-chip SRAM footprint, and off-chip bandwidth.
infographic.impact: Enables faster, more memory- and bandwidth-efficient long-context inference for LLMs in both single-node and distributed setups—reducing latency and HBM traffic while scaling with TP. Practitioners can handle longer contexts or larger models without proportional increases in memory bandwidth or decoding time.

title: DARE-bench: Evaluating Modeling and Instruction Fidelity of LLMs in Data Science
authors: Fan Shu, Yite Wang, Ruofan Wu, Boyi Liu, Zhewei Yao
abstract: The fast-growing demands in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex multi-step data science tasks create an emergent need for accurate benchmarking. There are two major gaps in existing benchmarks: (i) the lack of standardized, process-aware evaluation that captures instruction adherence and process fidelity, and (ii) the scarcity of accurately labeled training data. To bridge these gaps, we introduce DARE-bench, a benchmark designed for machine learning modeling and data science in

infographic.key_insight: DARE-bench provides a process-aware benchmark that measures both modeling accuracy and instruction/process fidelity of LLMs on multi-step data science tasks, using carefully labeled examples and metrics that capture adherence to requested workflows.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLM benchmarks for data science miss workflow/process fidelity and lack accurately labeled training/evaluation data; DARE-bench fills both gaps by standardizing multi-step evaluation and supplying high-quality labels to judge instruction adherence and modeling correctness.
method: Curate multi-step data science tasks that reflect real ML workflows (data prep, modeling decisions, evaluation, interpretation).
Annotate ground-truth steps and outcomes to enable process-aware scoring (instruction adherence + modeling correctness).
Define automatic and human-evaluated metrics for instruction fidelity, step-level correctness, and end-task performance to compare LLM outputs.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners and researchers to quantify how well LLMs follow instructions and execute multi-step data science workflows, improving model selection, fine-tuning, and trust in AI-assisted analysis.

title: CUDA Agent: Large-Scale Agentic RL for High-Performance CUDA Kernel Generation
authors: Weinan Dai, Hanlin Wu, Qiying Yu, Huan-ang Gao, Jiahao Li
abstract: GPU kernel optimization is fundamental to modern deep learning but remains a highly specialized task requiring deep hardware expertise. Despite strong performance in general programming, large language models (LLMs) remain uncompetitive with compiler-based systems such as torch.compile for CUDA kernel generation. Existing CUDA code generation approaches either rely on training-free refinement or fine-tune models within fixed multi-turn execution-feedback loops, but both paradigms fail to fundame

infographic.key_insight: Training a language model via large-scale agentic reinforcement learning with hardware-in-the-loop feedback enables automated generation of CUDA kernels that close the gap with compiler-based systems. Iterative execution + reward from real performance metrics produces kernels optimized for real GPUs rather than just syntactic correctness.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates the difficult, hardware-specific task of writing high-performance CUDA kernels by making LLMs competitive with compiler-based optimizers and reducing reliance on expert manual tuning.
method: Agentic RL loop: the model proposes CUDA kernels, they are executed on real GPUs, runtime/profiling metrics are collected, and rewards drive policy updates.
Scalable training on diverse kernels and workloads with hardware-aware reward shaping and correctness checks to prioritize both performance and validity.
Iterative refinement and decomposition strategies (generate → test → repair) combined with curriculum/data-augmentation to generalize across GPU architectures and patterns.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to automatically produce high-performance GPU code without deep hardware expertise, accelerating model deployment and optimization workflows and reducing manual tuning time.

title: UFO-4D: Unposed Feedforward 4D Reconstruction from Two Images
authors: Junhwa Hur, Charles Herrmann, Songyou Peng, Philipp Henzler, Zeyu Ma
abstract: Dense 4D reconstruction from unposed images remains a critical challenge, with current methods relying on slow test-time optimization or fragmented, task-specific feedforward models. We introduce UFO-4D, a unified feedforward framework to reconstruct a dense, explicit 4D representation from just a pair of unposed images. UFO-4D directly estimates dynamic 3D Gaussian Splats, enabling the joint and consistent estimation of 3D geometry, 3D motion, and camera pose in a feedforward manner. Our core i

infographic.key_insight: UFO-4D reconstructs dense, time-varying 3D scenes from just two unposed images in a single feedforward pass by directly predicting dynamic 3D Gaussian splats and camera poses, removing the need for slow test-time optimization.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables fast, unified dense 4D reconstruction (geometry + motion + camera pose) from only two unposed images, addressing fragmentation and slow optimization in prior methods.
method: Feedforward network that predicts dynamic 3D Gaussian splats representing per-point appearance, geometry, and motion from two unposed images.
Jointly estimates camera poses and time-varying 3D structure to ensure consistent geometry and motion across views.
Trained with differentiable splatting / rendering and multi-view / temporal consistency losses to produce explicit, test-time-ready 4D outputs without optimization.
infographic.impact: Delivers real-time-capable, unified 4D reconstruction from minimal input, making fast scene capture, view synthesis, and motion analysis practical for downstream AI/ML applications like AR/VR, robotics, and content creation.

title: Taming Momentum: Rethinking Optimizer States Through Low-Rank Approximation
authors: Zhengbo Wang, Jian Liang, Ran He, Zilei Wang, Tieniu Tan
abstract: Modern optimizers like Adam and Muon are central to training large language models, but their reliance on first- and second-order momenta introduces significant memory overhead, which constrains scalability and computational efficiency. In this work, we reframe the exponential moving average (EMA) used in these momenta as the training of a linear regressor via online gradient flow. Building on this equivalence, we introduce LoRA-Pre, a novel low-rank optimizer designed for efficient pre-training

infographic.key_insight: Exponential moving averages used by Adam/Muon can be reformulated as training a linear regressor via online gradient flow, which enables approximating dense optimizer states with a low-rank factorization that preserves optimization dynamics while cutting memory.
infographic.problem_solved: The large memory overhead of first- and second-order EMA momenta in modern optimizers that limits model scale, batch size, and training efficiency during large-scale pre-training.
method: Reinterpret EMA momenta as coefficients learned by an online linear regressor (online gradient flow equivalence).
Factorize dense optimizer state matrices into low-rank components and update these factors online (LoRA-Pre) to emulate EMA behavior.
Apply the low-rank optimizer as a drop-in replacement during pre-training to reduce memory and compute with minimal impact on convergence.
infographic.impact: Significantly lowers optimizer memory footprint so practitioners can train larger models or use larger batches without extra hardware; provides a practical, memory-efficient optimizer alternative for LLM pre-training.

title: Do LLMs Benefit From Their Own Words?
authors: Jenny Y. Huang, Leshem Choshen, Ramon Astudillo, Tamara Broderick, Jacob Andreas
abstract: Multi-turn interactions with large language models typically retain the assistant's own past responses in the conversation history. In this work, we revisit this design choice by asking whether large language models benefit from conditioning on their own prior responses. Using in-the-wild, multi-turn conversations, we compare standard (full-context) prompting with a user-turn-only prompting approach that omits all previous assistant responses, across three open reasoning models and one state-of-

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning LLMs on their own past assistant replies is not always beneficial — omitting prior assistant turns (user-turn-only context) can match or improve multi‑turn performance by reducing error propagation and context noise.
infographic.problem_solved: Revisits the common design choice of retaining assistant responses in multi‑turn conversation history to determine whether past assistant outputs actually help, or instead introduce errors, cost, and privacy risks.
method: Compare two prompting regimes on in‑the‑wild, multi‑turn conversations: full‑context (includes prior assistant replies) vs user‑turn‑only (omits assistant replies).
Evaluate across three open reasoning models and one state‑of‑the‑art model on metrics such as task accuracy, coherence, hallucination, and instruction adherence.
Run controlled analyses by conversation length and ablation studies to quantify error propagation, latency, and context‑cost tradeoffs.
infographic.impact: Findings guide practitioners on conversational system design and prompt strategy: simpler user‑only histories can reduce hallucination, lower compute and privacy exposure, and in many cases improve or preserve performance.

title: Memory Caching: RNNs with Growing Memory
authors: Ali Behrouz, Zeman Li, Yuan Deng, Peilin Zhong, Meisam Razaviyayn
abstract: Transformers have been established as the de-facto backbones for most recent advances in sequence modeling, mainly due to their growing memory capacity that scales with the context length. While plausible for retrieval tasks, it causes quadratic complexity and so has motivated recent studies to explore viable subquadratic recurrent alternatives. Despite showing promising preliminary results in diverse domains, such recurrent architectures underperform Transformers in recall-intensive tasks, ofte

infographic.key_insight: Introduce a lightweight 'memory caching' mechanism that lets recurrent networks grow and retain past context like Transformers, achieving transformer-style long-range recall while keeping subquadratic compute and memory costs.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the trade-off between Transformers' strong long-context recall but quadratic cost and recurrent architectures' efficiency but poor recall on long/hard retrieval tasks.
method: Attach an append-only cache (growable external memory) to an RNN so past hidden states can be stored and selectively revisited without full quadratic attention.
Use efficient indexing/aggregation (e.g., keys + compressed summaries or sparse retrieval) so reads from the cache are subquadratic and compatible with streaming/incremental processing.
Combine caching reads with standard RNN updates so the model learns when to write, retain, and attend to distant context for recall-heavy tasks.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical pathway to get Transformer-like long-range memory with much lower compute and memory overhead, enabling scalable sequence modeling in streaming, low-resource, and real-time applications.

title: A family of large language models for materials research with insights into model adaptability in continued pretraining
authors: Dhruv Ahlawat, Vaibhav Mishra, Somaditya Singh, Mohd Zaki, Vaibhav Bihani

Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 27 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01199-8

Dhruv et al. introduce LLaMat, a family of LLMs for materials science, showing how specialized training enables smaller models to surpass larger general LLMs. The study reveals that extensively pretrained models like LLaMA-3 adapt less effectively than LLaMA-2 to new scientific domains.

title: Mode Seeking meets Mean Seeking for Fast Long Video Generation
authors: Shengqu Cai, Weili Nie, Chao Liu, Julius Berner, Lvmin Zhang
abstract: Scaling video generation from seconds to minutes faces a critical bottleneck: while short-video data is abundant and high-fidelity, coherent long-form data is scarce and limited to narrow domains. To address this, we propose a training paradigm where Mode Seeking meets Mean Seeking, decoupling local fidelity from long-term coherence based on a unified representation via a Decoupled Diffusion Transformer. Our approach utilizes a global Flow Matching head trained via supervised learning on long vi

infographic.key_insight: Decouple local visual fidelity from long-term temporal coherence by combining a Mode‑Seeking objective for short-range detail with a Mean‑Seeking (flow‑matching) objective for global consistency, implemented in a Decoupled Diffusion Transformer to enable fast long‑video generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Long-form video generation is bottlenecked by scarcity of diverse, high‑quality long videos: short-video data gives high fidelity but poor global coherence, while long-video data is limited; this paper solves how to leverage abundant short clips and limited long videos together.
method: Introduce a Decoupled Diffusion Transformer that separates local (mode‑seeking) and global (mean‑seeking) components within a unified representation.

Use a Mode‑Seeking objective (trained on abundant short videos) to preserve high‑fidelity, multimodal local content and a global Flow‑Matching head (supervised on long videos) for long‑range temporal consistency.
Train the two heads jointly but decoupled so local detail and long‑term structure are optimized with complementary losses, enabling faster and more scalable long‑video synthesis.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to generate coherent minutes‑long videos by leveraging plentiful short‑clip data for detail and limited long data for temporal structure, improving scalability and training efficiency for long video generative models.

title: MediX-R1: Open Ended Medical Reinforcement Learning
authors: Sahal Shaji Mullappilly, Mohammed Irfan Kurpath, Omair Mohamed, Mohamed Zidan, Fahad Khan
abstract: We introduce MediX-R1, an open-ended Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that enables clinically grounded, free-form answers beyond multiple-choice formats. MediX-R1 fine-tunes a baseline vision-language backbone with Group Based RL and a composite reward tailored for medical reasoning: an LLM-based accuracy reward that judges semantic correctness with a strict YES/NO decision, a medical embedding-based semantic reward to capture paraphrases

infographic.key_insight: MediX-R1 enables medical multimodal LLMs to produce clinically grounded, free-form answers by fine-tuning a vision-language backbone with Group-Based RL and a composite reward that enforces semantic correctness beyond multiple-choice formats.

Use a composite reward: an LLM-based binary (YES/NO) accuracy judge for strict clinical correctness plus a medical embedding–based semantic reward to capture valid paraphrases and nuanced reasoning.

title: VGG-T$^3$: Offline Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction at Scale
authors: Sven Elflein, Ruilong Li, Sérgio Agostinho, Zan Gojcic, Laura Leal-Taixé
abstract: We present a scalable 3D reconstruction model that addresses a critical limitation in offline feed-forward methods: their computational and memory requirements grow quadratically w.r.t. the number of input images. Our approach is built on the key insight that this bottleneck stems from the varying-length Key-Value (KV) space representation of scene geometry, which we distill into a fixed-size Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) via test-time training. VGG-T$^3$ (Visual Geometry Grounded Test Time Train

infographic.key_insight: The quadratic compute/memory bottleneck of offline feed-forward 3D reconstruction comes from the varying-length Key-Value (KV) scene representation; distilling that KV space into a fixed-size MLP via test-time training (VGG-T^3) breaks the scaling barrier.
infographic.problem_solved: Offline feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods scale poorly — memory and computation grow quadratically with the number of input images due to variable-length KV representations, limiting practicality for large image sets.
method: Compress the varying-length KV scene representation into a fixed-size Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) through test-time training.
Replace the variable KV-based inference path with the distilled fixed-size MLP so reconstruction is feed-forward and no longer grows quadratically with image count.
Design the pipeline to preserve reconstruction fidelity while dramatically reducing memory and compute overhead, enabling large-scale offline processing.
infographic.impact: Makes feed-forward 3D reconstruction practical at scale by removing quadratic scaling, so practitioners can process many-input-image scenes with lower memory/compute and simpler deployment for large datasets and offline pipelines.

title: Understanding Usage and Engagement in AI-Powered Scientific Research Tools: The Asta Interaction Dataset
authors: Dany Haddad, Dan Bareket, Joseph Chee Chang, Jay DeYoung, Jena D. Hwang
abstract: AI-powered scientific research tools are rapidly being integrated into research workflows, yet the field lacks a clear lens into how researchers use these systems in real-world settings. We present and analyze the Asta Interaction Dataset, a large-scale resource comprising over 200,000 user queries and interaction logs from two deployed tools (a literature discovery interface and a scientific question-answering interface) within an LLM-powered retrieval-augmented generation platform. Using this

infographic.key_insight: A large-scale log of real-world interactions (200k+ queries) from two deployed LLM-powered research tools reveals how researchers actually discover literature and ask scientific questions, exposing common query types, engagement patterns, and opportunities to improve tool design.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of empirical, real-world data on how researchers use AI-powered scientific tools, enabling evidence-based improvements to interfaces, retrieval strategies, and evaluation metrics.
method: Collected and anonymized interaction logs and user queries from two deployed tools (literature discovery and scientific Q&A) within an LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation platform.
Performed exploratory analyses of query types, session/engagement metrics, and feature usage to characterize researcher behavior at scale.
Derived design-relevant insights and usage patterns to inform benchmarking, UX adjustments, and future research tool development.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and tool builders with a grounded dataset and behavioral findings to guide better evaluation, UI design, retrieval/LLM integration, and deployment decisions for scientific research tools.

title: SeeThrough3D: Occlusion Aware 3D Control in Text-to-Image Generation
authors: Vaibhav Agrawal, Rishubh Parihar, Pradhaan Bhat, Ravi Kiran Sarvadevabhatla, R. Venkatesh Babu
abstract: We identify occlusion reasoning as a fundamental yet overlooked aspect for 3D layout-conditioned generation. It is essential for synthesizing partially occluded objects with depth-consistent geometry and scale. While existing methods can generate realistic scenes that follow input layouts, they often fail to model precise inter-object occlusions. We propose SeeThrough3D, a model for 3D layout conditioned generation that explicitly models occlusions. We introduce an occlusion-aware 3D scene repre

infographic.key_insight: Explicitly modeling inter-object occlusions within a 3D layout-conditioned generator produces depth-consistent, correctly scaled partially-occluded objects, improving realism where existing methods fail.
infographic.problem_solved: Prior 3D layout-conditioned text-to-image methods often ignore precise occlusion reasoning, producing incorrect depth/overlap and scale when objects partially occlude each other; this work addresses that gap by making occlusion an explicit part of the scene representation and generation pipeline.
method: Introduce an occlusion-aware 3D scene representation that encodes per-object depth and visibility (occlusion masks) alongside layout conditioning.
Integrate occlusion information into the generative model (e.g., layout-conditioned diffusion) with differentiable compositing so occluded geometry and appearance are synthesized consistently.
Train with losses and supervision that enforce depth consistency, correct occlusion ordering, and visual fidelity (using rendered occluded examples or self-supervision).
infographic.impact: Improves realism and controllability of multi-object scene synthesis, enabling reliable partial-occlusion rendering for content creation, AR/VR, and simulation; reduces manual post-editing and enables physically plausible layouts.

title: Mean Estimation from Coarse Data: Characterizations and Efficient Algorithms
authors: Alkis Kalavasis, Anay Mehrotra, Manolis Zampetakis, Felix Zhou, Ziyu Zhu
abstract: Coarse data arise when learners observe only partial information about samples; namely, a set containing the sample rather than its exact value. This occurs naturally through measurement rounding, sensor limitations, and lag in economic systems. We study Gaussian mean estimation from coarse data, where each true sample $x$ is drawn from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian distribution with identity covariance, but is revealed only through the set of a partition containing $x$. When the coarse samples, ro

infographic.key_insight: You can accurately estimate the mean of a high-dimensional Gaussian even when each sample is only observed as the cell of a partition that contains it; the paper characterizes when this is possible and gives efficient algorithms with provable guarantees.
infographic.problem_solved: Estimating a Gaussian mean from "coarse" observations (each sample revealed only as a set/partition cell containing it) — a realistic challenge arising from rounding, limited sensor resolution, aggregation, and communication or privacy constraints.
method: Characterize identifiability and statistical limits: precise conditions and sample-complexity (minimax) bounds that determine when the mean can be recovered from partitioned observations.
Design efficient algorithms with provable error guarantees: polynomial-time procedures that achieve near-optimal estimation under the coarse-data model.
Validate theory empirically: simulations comparing estimation error versus sample size and partition coarseness, demonstrating robustness across dimensions and partition types.
infographic.impact: Provides practical tools and theory for learning from rounded, binned, or aggregated measurements, enabling robust parameter estimation in resource-constrained sensing, privacy-preserving data collection, and systems with coarse reporting.

title: Model Agreement via Anchoring
authors: Eric Eaton, Surbhi Goel, Marcel Hussing, Michael Kearns, Aaron Roth
abstract: Numerous lines of aim to control $\textit{model disagreement}$ -- the extent to which two machine learning models disagree in their predictions. We adopt a simple and standard notion of model disagreement in real-valued prediction problems, namely the expected squared difference in predictions between two models trained on independent samples, without any coordination of the training processes. We would like to be able to drive disagreement to zero with some natural parameter(s) of the training

infographic.key_insight: Introducing an anchoring mechanism during training aligns independently trained predictors so their expected squared prediction difference (model disagreement) can be driven to (or toward) zero by tuning natural training parameters such as anchor strength or sample size. This gives a simple, analyzable handle for controlling disagreement in real‑valued prediction tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: How to measure and control model disagreement — the expected squared difference between predictions of models trained independently — so independently trained models produce consistent outputs without coordinating training processes.
method: Define model disagreement as the expected squared difference between two predictors trained on independent samples and derive conditions under which disagreement can be reduced.

Introduce an anchoring term or anchor-based training protocol that biases each model toward a common reference (anchor) during learning, producing bounds that show disagreement decreases with anchor strength and/or sample size.
Theoretical analysis (and supporting experiments) that quantify the tradeoffs between anchor strength, sample complexity, and predictive accuracy.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, theoretically grounded tool for practitioners who need reproducible, consistent predictions across independently trained models — useful for deployment stability, auditing, and reducing variance-driven failures. Anchoring can be adopted with minimal changes to standard training pipelines.

title: Retrieve and Segment: Are a Few Examples Enough to Bridge the Supervision Gap in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation?
authors: Tilemachos Aravanis, Vladan Stojnić, Bill Psomas, Nikos Komodakis, Giorgos Tolias
abstract: Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) extends the zero-shot recognition capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to pixel-level prediction, enabling segmentation of arbitrary categories specified by text prompts. Despite recent progress, OVS lags behind fully supervised approaches due to two challenges: the coarse image-level supervision used to train VLMs and the semantic ambiguity of natural language. We address these limitations by introducing a few-shot setting that augments textual prompt

infographic.key_insight: A small set of retrieved visual examples used to augment textual prompts can substantially close the gap between zero-shot vision–language models and fully supervised segmentation, enabling accurate open‑vocabulary pixel prediction with minimal labelled masks.
infographic.problem_solved: Open‑vocabulary segmentation struggles because VLMs are trained with coarse image‑level supervision and natural language prompts are semantically ambiguous for pixel‑level tasks; the paper addresses how to efficiently adapt VLMs to produce accurate masks with only a few example annotations.
method: Few‑shot retrieval: find a small number of visually relevant exemplars (image crops / annotated masks) for each target category to provide concrete visual grounding.
Prompt augmentation & conditioning: fuse retrieved exemplars with text prompts and VLM features to produce stronger, less ambiguous category signals for pixel‑wise prediction.
Lightweight mask adaptation: apply a compact segmentation head or prompt‑conditioning mechanism on top of the VLM to generate high‑quality masks without full supervised re-training.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to adapt large vision–language models to new segmentation tasks with very few annotations, dramatically reducing labelling cost while achieving performance much closer to fully supervised methods—practical for rapid domain adaptation and long‑tail categories.

title: Scale Can't Overcome Pragmatics: The Impact of Reporting Bias on Vision-Language Reasoning
authors: Amita Kamath, Jack Hessel, Khyathi Chandu, Jena D. Hwang, Kai-Wei Chang
abstract: The lack of reasoning capabilities in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has remained at the forefront of research discourse. We posit that this behavior stems from a reporting bias in their training data. That is, how people communicate about visual content by default omits tacit information needed to supervise some types of reasoning; e.g., "at the game today!" is a more likely caption than "a photo of 37 people standing behind a field". We investigate the data underlying the popular VLMs OpenCLIP,

infographic.key_insight: Vision–language reasoning failures often arise from a reporting bias in caption-style training data: people omit tacit facts, and increasing model scale alone does not teach models to recover those unreported details.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and isolates reporting bias in VLM training data as a root cause of poor explicit reasoning, explaining why larger models still fail on tasks that require facts typically left unstated in captions.
method: Quantitative analysis of caption corpora underlying popular VLMs (e.g., OpenCLIP) to measure how frequently visually verifiable facts are omitted.
Design of probing tasks/benchmarks that require explicit reasoning about tacit visual facts and evaluation of VLM performance across model scales.
Ablations showing the relative effects of scaling versus changes to supervision (data augmentation or targeted labeling) on reasoning performance.
infographic.impact: Shows practitioners that improving VLM reasoning requires addressing dataset pragmatics and supervision strategies, not just scaling models—guiding dataset curation, annotation, and training choices for reliable multimodal reasoning.

title: SOTAlign: Semi-Supervised Alignment of Unimodal Vision and Language Models via Optimal Transport
authors: Simon Roschmann, Paul Krzakala, Sonia Mazelet, Quentin Bouniot, Zeynep Akata
abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that neural networks trained on different modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of the world. Recent work exploits this convergence by aligning frozen pretrained vision and language models with lightweight alignment layers, but typically relies on contrastive losses and millions of paired samples. In this work, we ask whether meaningful alignment can be achieved with substantially less supervision. We introduce a semi-supervised setti

infographic.key_insight: A lightweight, semi-supervised alignment strategy using Optimal Transport can align frozen unimodal vision and language models with far fewer paired samples than contrastive, fully supervised approaches, by exploiting structure in unlabeled embedding sets.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the massive paired image–text data requirement for aligning pretrained vision and language models, enabling meaningful cross-modal alignment when only a small labeled set plus large unlabeled pools are available.
method: Freeze pretrained vision and language encoders and add small alignment layers to map embeddings into a shared space.

Use semi-supervised Optimal Transport to compute a soft coupling between image and text embedding clouds: combine a small set of ground-truth pairs as anchors with large unlabeled sets to infer correspondences and drive alignment.
Train alignment layers with the OT coupling as the supervision signal (optionally with entropic regularization and consistency/pseudo-labeling) to stabilize learning from scarce labels.
infographic.impact: Makes multimodal alignment practical and data-efficient for practitioners, lowering annotation costs and enabling fast adaptation of large unimodal models to cross-modal tasks such as retrieval and zero-shot transfer.

title: LLM Novice Uplift on Dual-Use, In Silico Biology Tasks
authors: Chen Bo Calvin Zhang, Christina Q. Knight, Nicholas Kruus, Jason Hausenloy, Pedro Medeiros
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform increasingly well on biology benchmarks, but it remains unclear whether they uplift novice users -- i.e., enable humans to perform better than with internet-only resources. This uncertainty is central to understanding both scientific acceleration and dual-use risk. We conducted a multi-model, multi-benchmark human uplift study comparing novices with LLM access versus internet-only access across eight biosecurity-relevant task sets. Participants worked on comp

infographic.key_insight: A controlled, multi-model human study shows that providing novices with LLM assistance often improves performance on biosecurity-relevant in silico biology tasks compared with internet-only access, though the size of uplift varies by task and model—highlighting both scientific acceleration and dual‑use risk tradeoffs.
infographic.problem_solved: Quantifies whether and how much LLMs enable novice users to do better on computational biology tasks than they would using standard internet resources, addressing uncertainty about human uplift and downstream dual-use implications.
method: Multi-model, multi-benchmark human uplift experiment: novices randomized to LLM access vs internet-only across eight biosecurity-relevant task sets.
Measured task performance (objective scores) and behavior (queries, reliance on model), with comparison across models, benchmarks, and task types.
Combined quantitative performance metrics with qualitative analysis to characterize where LLMs help, fail, or introduce risk.
infographic.impact: Provides empirical evidence for AI/ML practitioners and policy makers about how LLMs change human capability on sensitive biology tasks, informing risk assessment, model deployment choices, and mitigation strategies for dual-use scenarios.

title: GUI-Libra: Training Native GUI Agents to Reason and Act with Action-aware Supervision and Partially Verifiable RL
authors: Rui Yang, Qianhui Wu, Zhaoyang Wang, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang
abstract: Open-source native GUI agents still lag behind closed-source systems on long-horizon navigation tasks. This gap stems from two limitations: a shortage of high-quality, action-aligned reasoning data, and the direct adoption of generic post-training pipelines that overlook the unique challenges of GUI agents. We identify two fundamental issues in these pipelines: (i) standard SFT with CoT reasoning often hurts grounding, and (ii) step-wise RLVR-tyle training faces partial verifiability, where mult

infographic.key_insight: GUI-Libra improves long-horizon GUI navigation by combining action-aware supervised reasoning with a partially verifiable RL scheme, aligning chain-of-thought with concrete UI actions so reasoning helps—not hurts—grounding.
infographic.problem_solved: Open-source native GUI agents fail on long-horizon tasks because training data lack action-aligned reasoning and standard post-training pipelines (CoT SFT and step-wise RL) either break grounding or suffer from partial verifiability and poor credit assignment.
method: Action-aware supervision: generate or curate reasoning traces that are explicitly aligned to concrete GUI actions so the model's internal rationale maps to verifiable steps.

Partially verifiable RL: structure reinforcement learning around verifiable subgoals or checks (hybrid supervised + RL updates) to reduce spurious credit assignment when full verification is impossible.
Pipeline redesign: avoid vanilla CoT fine-tuning that detaches reasoning from actions and instead combine action-grounded SFT with constrained/verified RL updates for stability.
infographic.impact: Makes open-source GUI agents more reliable and interpretable for long-horizon automation (e.g., testing, task automation, accessibility) by improving grounding between reasoning and actions and stabilizing RL fine-tuning.

title: Applying a Random-Key Optimizer on Mixed Integer Programs
authors: Antonio A. Chaves, Mauricio G. C. Resende, Carise E. Schmidt, J. Kyle Brubaker, Helmut G. Katzgraber
abstract: Mixed-Integer Programs (MIPs) are NP-hard optimization models that arise in a broad range of decision-making applications, including finance, logistics, energy systems, and network design. Although modern commercial solvers have achieved remarkable progress and perform effectively on many small- and medium-sized instances, their performance often degrades when confronted with large-cale or highly constrained formulations. This paper explores the use of the Random-Key Optimizer (RKO) framework as

infographic.key_insight: Encoding MIP solutions as continuous 'random-key' vectors and optimizing them with population-based operators provides a flexible, solver-agnostic way to explore large and highly constrained mixed-integer search spaces, enabling robust approximate solutions and effective hybridization with exact solvers.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the difficulty commercial MIP solvers face on large-scale or highly constrained mixed-integer programs by offering a metaheuristic framework that improves search diversity, scalability, and the ability to find high-quality feasible solutions under tight resource limits.
method: Represent discrete MIP decisions as continuous random-key vectors that are decoded (and repaired) into feasible integer solutions.
Apply population-based operators (crossover, mutation, selection) to evolve keys, combined with local improvement or MIP-solver polishing to refine decoded solutions.
Use a hybrid workflow that hands promising candidates to commercial solvers for final optimization while relying on RKO for global exploration and diversification.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and operations researchers a practical optimization metaheuristic that can complement existing MIP solvers, improving solution discovery speed and robustness for large or hard combinatorial models and enabling better integration of optimization into ML-driven pipelines.

title: Solaris: Building a Multiplayer Video World Model in Minecraft
authors: Georgy Savva, Oscar Michel, Daohan Lu, Suppakit Waiwitlikhit, Timothy Meehan
abstract: Existing action-conditioned video generation models (video world models) are limited to single-agent perspectives, failing to capture the multi-agent interactions of real-world environments. We introduce Solaris, a multiplayer video world model that simulates consistent multi-view observations. To enable this, we develop a multiplayer data system designed for robust, continuous, and automated data collection on video games such as Minecraft. Unlike prior platforms built for single-player setting

infographic.key_insight: Solaris is the first action-conditioned video world model that simulates consistent multi-view, multi-agent observations by combining a multiplayer data collection system with a multi-view generative model.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video world models are limited to single-agent, single-view settings and cannot capture the interactions and coherent observations that arise in multiplayer environments.
method: Develop a multiplayer data system for robust, continuous, automated collection of synchronized multi-player, multi-view video data in Minecraft.
Train an action-conditioned generative world model that predicts future video observations for multiple agents and views simultaneously.
Enforce multi-view consistency via shared world-state representations and cross-view supervision so simulated views remain coherent across agents and time.
infographic.impact: Enables realistic multi-agent video simulation for planning, multi-agent RL, and virtual-world research, reducing reliance on single-view assumptions and improving realism for downstream tasks.

title: CASR: A Robust Cyclic Framework for Arbitrary Large-Scale Super-Resolution with Distribution Alignment and Self-Similarity Awareness
authors: Wenhao Guo, Zhaoran Zhao, Peng Lu, Sheng Li, Qian Qiao
abstract: Arbitrary-Scale SR (ASISR) remains fundamentally limited by cross-scale distribution shift: once the inference scale leaves the training range, noise, blur, and artifacts accumulate sharply. We revisit this challenge from a cross-scale distribution transition perspective and propose CASR, a simple yet highly efficient cyclic SR framework that reformulates ultra-magnification as a sequence of in-distribution scale transitions. This design ensures stable inference at arbitrary scales while requiri

infographic.key_insight: CASR converts extreme upsampling into a sequence of small, in-distribution scale transitions using a cyclic framework, combined with distribution alignment and self-similarity awareness, which stabilizes inference and prevents accumulation of noise and artifacts at arbitrary scales.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses cross-scale distribution shift in Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution (ASISR) where inference at scales outside the training range causes rapid accumulation of blur, noise, and artifacts.
method: Cyclic SR pipeline: reformulate ultra-magnification as repeated, small-scale (in-distribution) transitions to keep each step within the model's learned distribution.
Distribution alignment: apply alignment losses/constraints to minimize shift between intermediate scales so errors do not compound across transitions.
Self-similarity awareness: incorporate modules or priors that exploit internal image repeating patterns to guide high-frequency detail reconstruction at each transition.
infographic.impact: Enables stable, high-fidelity super-resolution at arbitrary magnification factors, making SR models more robust and practical for real-world applications that require variable zoom or extreme upsampling.

title: Mixed Magnification Aggregation for Generalizable Region-Level Representations in Computational Pathology
authors: Eric Zimmermann, Julian Viret, Michal Zelechowski, James Brian Hall, Neil Tenenholtz
abstract: In recent years, a standard computational pathology workflow has emerged where whole slide images are cropped into tiles, these tiles are processed using a foundation model, and task-specific models are built using the resulting representations. At least 15 different foundation models have been proposed, and the vast majority are trained exclusively with tiles using the 20$\times$ magnification. However, it is well known that certain histologic features can only be discerned with larger context

infographic.key_insight: Aggregating tile features sampled at multiple microscopy magnifications produces region-level representations that generalize better than models trained only on 20× tiles, capturing both fine cellular detail and larger tissue context in a single embedding.
infographic.problem_solved: Most computational pathology foundation models are trained exclusively on 20× tiles and therefore miss histologic features that are only visible at other scales, reducing robustness and cross-dataset generalization for region-level tasks.
method: Sample corresponding tiles from multiple magnifications (e.g., 5×, 10×, 20×) for each region and extract features with a foundation encoder.
Fuse multi-scale features with a learnable aggregation module (attention-weighted pooling or scale-aware projector) to produce a single region-level representation.
Train the aggregation end-to-end (or with contrastive/self-supervised objectives) to encourage scale-robust, generalizable embeddings across tissue types and datasets.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a straightforward way to leverage multi-scale information using existing foundation encoders, improving downstream task performance and cross-dataset robustness in digital pathology without needing entirely new backbone models.

title: Surrogate models for Rock-Fluid Interaction: A Grid-Size-Invariant Approach
authors: Nathalie C. Pinheiro, Donghu Guo, Hannah P. Menke, Aniket C. Joshi, Claire E. Heaney
abstract: Modelling rock-fluid interaction requires solving a set of partial differential equations (PDEs) to predict the flow behaviour and the reactions of the fluid with the rock on the interfaces. Conventional high-fidelity numerical models require a high resolution to obtain reliable results, resulting in huge computational expense. This restricts the applicability of these models for multi-query problems, such as uncertainty quantification and optimisation, which require running numerous scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: A surrogate modeling strategy that remains accurate across different numerical grid resolutions enables fast, reliable prediction of rock–fluid interaction without the need for costly high-resolution PDE solves.
infographic.problem_solved: High-fidelity numerical models for coupled rock–fluid interaction require very fine spatial resolution, making repeated runs (for uncertainty quantification, optimization, or design) computationally prohibitive.
method: Develop a grid-size-invariant surrogate model trained on multi-resolution simulation data so it generalizes across discretizations without retraining for each grid.
Incorporate interface-aware physics constraints and/or PDE-consistent losses to preserve key reaction and flow behaviors at rock–fluid boundaries.
Use dimensionality reduction / operator-style learning to map inputs (geometry, boundary conditions, properties) to outputs (flow fields, reaction rates) efficiently for many-query tasks.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with a way to replace expensive PDE solvers by a fast, generalizable surrogate that supports large-scale uncertainty quantification, optimization, and real-time decision-making in subsurface and geoscience applications.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: high-fidelity PDE solver (dense grid, slow) vs. surrogate model (coarse or variable grid, fast) with timing and accuracy callouts.
Flowchart of the training pipeline showing multi-resolution data input → grid-size-invariant model → predictions on unseen grid sizes.
Heatmaps or contour plots comparing predicted vs. reference flow/reaction fields across different grid resolutions with error overlays.
Bar chart or log plot of compute cost (runtime or FLOPs) vs. accuracy for high-fidelity solver and surrogate across multiple scenarios.
infographic.paper_title: Surrogate models for Rock-Fluid Interaction: A Grid-Size-Invariant Approach
infographic.paper_authors: Nathalie C. Pinheiro, Donghu Guo, Hannah P. Menke, Aniket C. Joshi, Claire E. Heaney

title: Conditional diffusion with locality-aware modal alignment for generating diverse protein conformational ensembles
authors: Baoli Wang, Chenglin Wang, Jingyang Chen, Danlin Liu, Changzhi Sun
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 25 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01198-9

Wang et al. introduce Mac-Diff, a conditional diffusion model with locality-aware attention across modalities, to generate diverse conformational ensembles for unseen proteins, capturing both dynamic flexibility and structural heterogeneity.

infographic.key_insight: Mac-Diff is a conditional diffusion model that uses locality-aware cross-modal attention to generate diverse, realistic conformational ensembles for unseen proteins, capturing both local flexibility and global structural heterogeneity.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard structure predictors produce single or limited conformations and fail to represent protein dynamic ensembles and heterogeneity, limiting downstream tasks that require realistic conformational variability.
method: Conditional diffusion generative model that produces full conformational ensembles conditioned on protein inputs (e.g., sequence or template features).

Locality-aware cross-modal attention aligns and integrates information across modalities (local motifs, geometry, chemical features) to preserve physical local structure while enabling global diversity.
Sampling and training objectives designed to encourage ensemble diversity and realism (diversity-promoting losses and reconstruction/consistency terms).
infographic.impact: Provides ML researchers and practitioners a practical generative framework to model protein dynamics and uncertainty, improving applications like drug design, functional annotation, and simulation-informed predictions by producing realistic ensembles rather than single static structures.

title: Off-The-Shelf Image-to-Image Models Are All You Need To Defeat Image Protection Schemes
authors: Xavier Pleimling, Sifat Muhammad Abdullah, Gunjan Balde, Peng Gao, Mainack Mondal
abstract: Advances in Generative AI (GenAI) have led to the development of various protection strategies to prevent the unauthorized use of images. These methods rely on adding imperceptible protective perturbations to images to thwart misuse such as style mimicry or deepfake manipulations. Although previous attacks on these protections required specialized, purpose-built methods, we demonstrate that this is no longer necessary. We show that off-the-shelf image-to-image GenAI models can be repurposed as g

infographic.key_insight: Off-the-shelf image-to-image generative models can reliably remove or overwrite imperceptible protective perturbations, allowing attackers to bypass image protection schemes without specialized, purpose-built attacks.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses whether existing image protection techniques (which add subtle perturbations to prevent misuse like style mimicry or deepfakes) remain effective when confronted with widely available image-to-image GenAI models.
method: Repurpose standard image-to-image generative models (plug-and-play) as restoration/transformation pipelines to neutralize protective perturbations.
Apply these models with minimal or no task-specific engineering to protected images to produce visually similar but protection-free outputs.
Evaluate applicability across common protection strategies to show broad effectiveness of off-the-shelf approaches.
infographic.impact: This work shows many current image-protection schemes are fragile against readily available GenAI tools, forcing practitioners to rethink defense designs, threat models, and deployment practices to protect image assets and deter misuse.

title: DySCO: Dynamic Attention-Scaling Decoding for Long-Context LMs
authors: Xi Ye, Wuwei Zhang, Fangcong Yin, Howard Yen, Danqi Chen
abstract: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts is a crucial capability for language models (LMs). Although recent models support increasingly long context windows, their accuracy often deteriorates as input length grows. In practice, models often struggle to keep attention aligned with the most relevant context throughout decoding. In this work, we propose DySCO, a novel decoding algorithm for improving long-context reasoning. DySCO leverages retrieval heads--a subset of attention heads speciali

infographic.key_insight: DySCO is a decoding algorithm that dynamically scales attention during autoregressive generation by leveraging specialized 'retrieval heads', keeping the model focused on the most relevant parts of very long contexts and improving reasoning accuracy as context length grows.
infographic.problem_solved: Autoregressive LMs lose alignment with relevant long-context information during decoding, causing accuracy to deteriorate as input length increases. DySCO addresses this by adaptively amplifying or suppressing attention to maintain relevance throughout generation.
method: Identify and use a subset of attention heads (retrieval heads) that are specialized for retrieving long-range context signals.
Dynamically scale attention weights from those heads during each decoding step to emphasize relevant context spans and de-emphasize distractors.
Apply the procedure as a lightweight decoding-layer intervention compatible with existing long-context LMs (no full model retraining required).
infographic.impact: DySCO offers a practical, model-agnostic way to improve reasoning and QA accuracy over very long inputs, enabling more reliable use of long-context LMs in document-level tasks, multi-document QA, and retrieval-augmented generation.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing retrieval heads within the attention mechanism and where DySCO applies dynamic scaling during decoding.
Before/After attention heatmaps illustrating attention drift vs. focused attention maintained by DySCO across decoding steps.
Line chart comparing task accuracy (or F1) vs. input length for baseline decoding and DySCO to show robustness at long contexts.
Sequence timeline visualization showing a decoding step where DySCO boosts relevant context tokens and suppresses irrelevant ones.

title: Neu-PiG: Neural Preconditioned Grids for Fast Dynamic Surface Reconstruction on Long Sequences
authors: Julian Kaltheuner, Hannah Dröge, Markus Plack, Patrick Stotko, Reinhard Klein
abstract: Temporally consistent surface reconstruction of dynamic 3D objects from unstructured point cloud data remains challenging, especially for very long sequences. Existing methods either optimize deformations incrementally, risking drift and requiring long runtimes, or rely on complex learned models that demand category-specific training. We present Neu-PiG, a fast deformation optimization method based on a novel preconditioned latent-grid encoding that distributes spatial features parameterized on

infographic.key_insight: Neu-PiG introduces a neural preconditioned latent-grid encoding that enables orders-of-magnitude faster deformation optimization for temporally consistent surface reconstruction, making long unstructured point-cloud sequences tractable without category-specific training.
infographic.problem_solved: The method addresses slow, drift-prone reconstruction of dynamic 3D surfaces from unstructured point clouds over very long sequences—avoiding incremental drift and heavy per-category learned models.
method: Preconditioned latent-grid encoding: distribute spatial features on a latent grid to represent geometry compactly and locally.
Neural preconditioner + fast optimization: use learned preconditioning to accelerate iterative deformation optimization and stabilize temporal consistency.
Generalizable pipeline for unstructured point clouds: efficient, non-category-specific reconstruction that scales to long sequences with reduced runtime and drift.
infographic.impact: Neu-PiG enables practitioners to reconstruct long, dynamic 3D sequences far faster and with fewer artifacts, lowering compute/time barriers for applications in motion capture, AR/VR, and 3D scanning workflows.
visual_elements: Diagram of the latent grid showing distributed spatial features and how the neural preconditioner interacts with optimization steps.
Before/after reconstruction slices over time illustrating reduced drift and improved temporal consistency across a long sequence.
Runtime vs. sequence length chart comparing Neu-PiG to incremental-optimization and learned-category baselines (showing lower runtime and better scaling).
Pipeline schematic: unstructured point clouds → Neu-PiG encoding + preconditioned optimization → temporally consistent surface outputs.

title: Region of Interest Segmentation and Morphological Analysis for Membranes in Cryo-Electron Tomography
authors: Xingyi Cheng, Julien Maufront, Aurélie Di Cicco, Daniël M. Pelt, Manuela Dezi
abstract: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) enables high resolution, three-dimensional reconstruction of biological structures, including membranes and membrane proteins. Identification of regions of interest (ROIs) is central to scientific imaging, as it enables isolation and quantitative analysis of specific structural features within complex datasets. In practice, however, ROIs are typically derived indirectly through full structure segmentation followed by post hoc analysis. This limitation is especi

infographic.key_insight: A focused pipeline that segments regions of interest (membrane patches) directly from cryo‑ET volumes and computes membrane‑centric morphological descriptors, enabling quantitative analysis without first producing full‑structure segmentations.
infographic.problem_solved: ROIs in cryo‑ET are usually obtained indirectly by segmenting entire volumes then post‑filtering, which is inefficient, error‑prone and hampers accurate morphological measurements of membranes in noisy, 3D tomograms.
method: ROI‑focused 3D segmentation model (e.g., 3D U‑Net / volumetric CNN) trained with expert and/or synthetic annotations to detect membrane patches directly in tomograms.

Geometric post‑processing pipeline (mesh reconstruction, skeletonization) that extracts membrane morphology metrics: curvature, thickness, orientation and topology; plus ROI filtering and confidence scoring.
Validation on cryo‑ET datasets comparing direct ROI outputs vs full‑segmentation workflows, showing improved precision, faster downstream analysis and measurement‑ready outputs.
infographic.impact: Enables ML practitioners to build leaner, task‑specific segmentation models that produce analysis‑ready ROIs and reliable morphological measurements, reducing compute and annotation overhead while improving biological interpretability.
visual_elements: Pipeline flowchart: raw tomogram → ROI segmentation → mesh/reconstruction → morphological metrics

title: Author Correction: Mask-prior-guided denoising diffusion improves inverse protein folding
authors: Peizhen Bai, Filip Miljković, Xianyuan Liu, Leonardo De Maria, Rebecca Croasdale-Wood
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 24 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01209-9

Author Correction: Mask-prior-guided denoising diffusion improves inverse protein folding

infographic.key_insight: Incorporating mask priors into denoising diffusion models lets the generator respect known residue constraints and structural motifs, producing more accurate and diverse amino-acid sequences for a target protein backbone.
infographic.problem_solved: Inverse protein folding—designing amino-acid sequences that reliably fold to a given 3D backbone—is hard because sequence space is vast, constraints (fixed or uncertain residues) must be respected, and conditional generative models struggle to balance accuracy and diversity.
method: Use a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) to generate protein sequences conditioned on a target backbone.
Introduce mask priors that encode fixed/known residues or regions of uncertainty; inject these priors into the diffusion denoising steps to guide sampling and preserve constraints.
Train and evaluate the model to optimize sequence recovery, structural compatibility, and generation diversity under masked constraints.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, constraint-aware generative framework for computational protein design: improves sequence accuracy and controllability, enabling better downstream experimental testing and integration into protein-engineering pipelines.

Before/after backbone-to-sequence examples showing how masked residues are preserved and how generated sequences differ when mask priors are used vs. not used.
Bar/line charts comparing metrics (sequence recovery, RMSD or structural compatibility, and diversity) across baseline methods and the mask-prior-guided model.

title: Learning from Trials and Errors: Reflective Test-Time Planning for Embodied LLMs
authors: Yining Hong, Huang Huang, Manling Li, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
abstract: Embodied LLMs endow robots with high-level task reasoning, but they cannot reflect on what went wrong or why, turning deployment into a sequence of independent trials where mistakes repeat rather than accumulate into experience. Drawing upon human reflective practitioners, we introduce Reflective Test-Time Planning, which integrates two modes of reflection: \textit{reflection-in-action}, where the agent uses test-time scaling to generate and score multiple candidate actions using internal reflec

infographic.key_insight: Introduce Reflective Test-Time Planning, enabling embodied LLM agents to turn repeated trials into accumulated experience by combining immediate candidate scoring with post-trial reflection to avoid repeating mistakes.
infographic.problem_solved: Embodied agents often repeat the same failures at deployment because they treat each attempt independently; this work enables agents to diagnose, learn from, and adapt after mistakes without full offline retraining.
method: Reflection-in-action: at test time, scale internal generation to propose multiple candidate actions and score/rank them with an internal critic before execution.

Reflection-on-action: after attempts, run a post-hoc analysis of failures to extract corrective insights (e.g., failure causes, better examples or prompts) and update planning heuristics or few-shot context for subsequent trials.
infographic.impact: Makes embodied LLMs more robust and sample-efficient in real-world deployments by converting errors into adaptive knowledge, reducing repeated failures and improving task success over repeated trials.
visual_elements: Loop diagram: trial → execute candidate actions → reflect (in-action) → execute chosen action → reflect (on-action) → update planner
Before/after bar chart showing reduced failure repetition and improved success rate across trials
Timeline/accumulation graphic showing knowledge or prompt/context updates across successive trials
Icons: robot arm, LLM/brain, checklist/critic scorecard to represent generation, scoring, and reflection

title: Test-Time Training with KV Binding Is Secretly Linear Attention
authors: Junchen Liu, Sven Elflein, Or Litany, Zan Gojcic, Ruilong Li
abstract: Test-time training (TTT) with KV binding as sequence modeling layer is commonly interpreted as a form of online meta-learning that memorizes a key-value mapping at test time. However, our analysis reveals multiple phenomena that contradict this memorization-based interpretation. Motivated by these findings, we revisit the formulation of TTT and show that a broad class of TTT architectures can be expressed as a form of learned linear attention operator. Beyond explaining previously puzzling model

infographic.key_insight: Test-time training (TTT) with KV-binding is not primarily memorizing key-value pairs at test time — it operates as a learned linear-attention operator, explaining several behaviors that contradict a memorization view.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies the true mechanism behind TTT with KV binding and resolves contradictory empirical phenomena that the prior memorization-based interpretation could not explain.
method: Empirical analysis showing multiple phenomena inconsistent with an episodic memorization interpretation of KV-binding TTT.
Theoretical reformulation proving a broad class of TTT architectures can be expressed as learned linear attention operators.
Demonstrations (analytical and experimental) that re-interpret KV-binding operations as linear attention, bridging theory and observed behavior.
infographic.impact: Reframes how practitioners should think about and design TTT modules: treat KV-binding layers as parameterized linear-attention components rather than as episodic memory, which guides better model design, diagnostics, and potential efficiency gains.
visual_elements: Two-panel schematic: left = memorization (keys → stored values), right = linear attention (matrix operator applying learned weights) to contrast hypotheses.
Flow diagram showing KV-binding layer rewritten as linear-attention operator (inputs → learned kernel → outputs).
Empirical chart: metrics/behaviors where memorization predictions fail vs. model predictions under linear-attention view.
Matrix visualization / heatmap of learned linear operator to illustrate structure and interpretability.

title: AI and the long game

Almost 10 years ago, AlphaGo defeated one of the world’s best professional players in the complex, ancient game of Go. It was a pivotal moment that spawned new research directions and marked the beginning of a busy decade in AI development.

Lessons & recommendations: distilling implications for research strategy, model design, and long-term planning in AI.

title: Aletheia tackles FirstProof autonomously
authors: Tony Feng, Junehyuk Jung, Sang-hyun Kim, Carlo Pagano, Sergei Gukov
abstract: We report the performance of Aletheia (Feng et al., 2026b), a mathematics research agent powered by Gemini 3 Deep Think, on the inaugural FirstProof challenge. Within the allowed timeframe of the challenge, Aletheia autonomously solved 6 problems (2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10) out of 10 according to majority expert assessments; we note that experts were not unanimous on Problem 8 (only). For full transparency, we explain our interpretation of FirstProof and disclose details about our experiments as well as

infographic.key_insight: Aletheia, powered by Gemini 3 Deep Think, autonomously solved 6 out of 10 problems in the inaugural FirstProof challenge within the allowed timeframe, demonstrating measurable autonomous progress on formal mathematical tasks.

Automatically generate candidate proofs and submit results for expert assessment, using majority expert judgments to determine solved problems (experts were not unanimous on Problem 8).

abstract:

Gu et al. introduce a cardiac foundation model that learns from millions of heart signals and textual interpretations, enabling it to handle heart data collected either in hospitals or at home. It offers clear and reliable insights across different devices and settings.

infographic.key_insight: A multimodal cardiac foundation model pretrained on signals and textual interpretations from 1.7 million individuals can produce consistent, reliable cardiac assessments across hospital and at‑home devices and settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap caused by device and setting heterogeneity (hospital ECGs vs consumer wearables) and limited labeled data, enabling a single model to generalize robustly across clinical and home environments.
method: Large‑scale multimodal pretraining on heart signals paired with textual interpretations from ~1.7 million individuals to learn shared signal‑text representations.
Design for cross‑device generalization so the same foundation model can be applied to hospital ECGs and consumer/remote devices with minimal task‑specific tuning.
Extensive evaluation showing robustness and reliable outputs across different device types and real‑world settings.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical template for building robust, transferable clinical AI: reduces dependence on device‑specific labels, speeds deployment from hospital to consumer settings, and promotes reliable cardiac monitoring at scale.

title: Multi-Vector Index Compression in Any Modality
authors: Hanxiang Qin, Alexander Martin, Rohan Jha, Chunsheng Zuo, Reno Kriz
abstract: We study efficient multi-vector retrieval for late interaction in any modality. Late interaction has emerged as a dominant paradigm for information retrieval in text, images, visual documents, and videos, but its computation and storage costs grow linearly with document length, making it costly for image-, video-, and audio-rich corpora. To address this limitation, we explore query-agnostic methods for compressing multi-vector document representations under a constant vector budget. We introduce

infographic.key_insight: Query-agnostic compression can reduce multi-vector document representations to a constant, small set of vectors per document while preserving late-interaction retrieval quality across modalities (text, images, video, audio).
infographic.problem_solved: Late-interaction retrieval's compute and storage costs scale linearly with document length (or number of region/segment vectors), making it expensive for image-, video-, and audio-rich corpora; this paper tackles compressing multi-vector document encodings under a fixed vector budget.
method: Compress variable-length multi-vector document representations into a constant number of vectors per document using query-agnostic strategies.

Employ compact representations (e.g., learned codebooks / clustering, residual quantization or centroid substitution) and index-level mapping to preserve late-interaction signal while reducing storage and computation.
Design a modality-agnostic pipeline that integrates compressed multi-vector documents into retrieval indices so late interaction can be computed more efficiently at query time.
infographic.impact: Enables practical late-interaction retrieval for large, multimodal corpora by cutting index size and query computation without needing query-specific reprocessing — letting practitioners deploy high-accuracy retrieval on image/video/audio-heavy datasets at much lower cost.
visual_elements: Before/after diagram: document with many region vectors → same document represented by a few compressed vectors (constant budget).

title: To Reason or Not to: Selective Chain-of-Thought in Medical Question Answering
authors: Zaifu Zhan, Min Zeng, Shuang Zhou, Yiran Song, Xiaoyi Chen
abstract:
Objective: To improve the efficiency of medical question answering (MedQA) with large language models (LLMs) by avoiding unnecessary reasoning while maintaining accuracy.
  Methods: We propose Selective Chain-of-Thought (Selective CoT), an inference-time strategy that first predicts whether a question requires reasoning and generates a rationale only when needed. Two open-source LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B) were evaluated on four biomedical QA benchmarks-HeadQA, MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, and

infographic.key_insight: Selective Chain-of-Thought (Selective CoT) first predicts whether a medical question needs step-by-step reasoning and generates a rationale only when required, cutting unnecessary reasoning without hurting answer accuracy.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces wasted compute, latency, and token cost from generating chain-of-thought for straightforward MedQA items by selectively invoking reasoning only for questions that truly need it.
method: Inference-time binary predictor classifies each question as ‘needs reasoning’ vs ‘direct answer’.
Conditional CoT: generate chain-of-thought rationale only when the predictor signals reasoning is required; otherwise return a concise answer.
Empirical evaluation on two open LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) across four biomedical benchmarks (HeadQA, MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, …) to measure accuracy vs efficiency trade-offs.
infographic.impact: Enables faster, cheaper, and scalable MedQA deployments by avoiding unnecessary reasoning while preserving diagnostic-quality answers — useful for production LLM pipelines in healthcare and resource-constrained settings.

title: Modeling Epidemiological Dynamics Under Adversarial Data and User Deception
authors: Yiqi Su, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Walid Saad, Bud Mishra, Naren Ramakrishnan
abstract: Epidemiological models increasingly rely on self-reported behavioral data such as vaccination status, mask usage, and social distancing adherence to forecast disease transmission and assess the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). While such data provide valuable real-time insights, they are often subject to strategic misreporting, driven by individual incentives to avoid penalties, access benefits, or express distrust in public health authorities. To account for such human behavio

infographic.key_insight: Epidemic forecasts that ignore strategic misreporting of self-reported behaviors can be systematically biased; jointly modeling user deception and epidemiological dynamics yields more robust state estimates and safer forecasts under adversarial data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap where self-reported behavioral data (vaccination, masking, distancing) are strategically manipulated by users, causing biased epidemic forecasts and misleading policy guidance. The paper provides a framework to detect, model, and mitigate the impact of adversarial reporting on transmission estimates.
method: Formulate a joint model that couples epidemiological state dynamics with a behavioral/adversary model capturing incentives and misreporting strategies.
Develop robust inference and estimation algorithms (e.g., adversarial-aware filtering, reweighting or game-theoretic estimation) to recover true population-level signals from corrupted self-reports.
Evaluate mitigation strategies and forecast corrections to quantify improved resilience of predictions under varied deception scenarios.
infographic.impact: Enables ML and public-health practitioners to produce more reliable epidemic forecasts and policy evaluations when input data may be strategically manipulated, improving the trustworthiness of AI-driven interventions during outbreaks.

title: KNIGHT: Knowledge Graph-Driven Multiple-Choice Question Generation with Adaptive Hardness Calibration
authors: Mohammad Amanlou, Erfan Shafiee Moghaddam, Yasaman Amou Jafari, Mahdi Noori, Farhan Farsi
abstract: With the rise of large language models (LLMs), they have become instrumental in applications such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Yet evaluating these systems remains bottlenecked by the time and cost of building specialized assessment datasets. We introduce KNIGHT, an LLM-based, knowledge-graph-driven framework for generating multiple-choice question (MCQ) datasets from external sources. KNIGHT constructs a topic-specific knowledge graph, a structured and parsimonious summary of entiti

infographic.key_insight: KNIGHT combines topic-specific knowledge graphs with LLM generation and an adaptive hardness calibration to produce controllable, high-quality multiple-choice questions at scale for evaluating RAG and other LLM systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Building specialized MCQ assessment datasets for evaluating LLMs and RAG systems is time-consuming and costly. KNIGHT automates dataset creation while providing fine-grained control over question difficulty and provenance.
method: Construct a topic-specific knowledge graph from external sources to create a structured, concise representation of entities and relations.
Use the KG as structured context to prompt an LLM to generate question stems, a correct answer, and plausible distractors with provenance links.
Apply adaptive hardness calibration—score difficulty, select/adjust distractors, and iteratively refine questions—to produce a targeted distribution of easy/medium/hard MCQs.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, cost-effective generation of MCQ benchmarks with controllable difficulty and traceable provenance, improving the robustness and speed of LLM/RAG evaluation and dataset creation workflows.

title: JUCAL: Jointly Calibrating Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty in Classification Tasks
authors: Jakob Heiss, Sören Lambrecht, Jakob Weissteiner, Hanna Wutte, Žan Žurič
abstract: We study post-calibration uncertainty for trained ensembles of classifiers. Specifically, we consider both aleatoric (label noise) and epistemic (model) uncertainty. Among the most popular and widely used calibration methods in classification are temperature scaling (i.e., pool-then-calibrate) and conformal methods. However, the main shortcoming of these calibration methods is that they do not balance the proportion of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Not balancing these uncertainties can se

infographic.key_insight: JUCAL is a post-hoc calibration method that jointly calibrates aleatoric (label) and epistemic (model) uncertainty for classifier ensembles, producing better-balanced, more trustworthy predictive uncertainty than standard temperature-scaling or conformal approaches.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing calibration techniques treat prediction confidence as a single quantity and fail to balance how much uncertainty is attributed to inherent label noise versus model uncertainty, which can lead to misleading decisions, poor OOD detection, and suboptimal active learning or risk assessment.
method: Decompose an ensemble's predictive uncertainty into aleatoric (intra-model predictive spread) and epistemic (inter-model disagreement) components using ensemble outputs on a validation set.

Learn a post-hoc joint calibration mapping that adjusts both the overall predictive confidence and the relative proportions of aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty to match empirical frequencies/coverage on held-out data.
Design the calibration to be compatible with existing post-processing tools (e.g., temperature scaling, conformal methods) so it can be applied to trained ensembles without retraining models.
infographic.impact: By providing calibrated, well-balanced uncertainty decompositions, JUCAL improves decision-making in safety- and cost-sensitive applications (OOD detection, selective prediction, active learning) and increases trust in ensemble-based systems with minimal deployment cost.

title: A large-scale randomized study of large language model feedback in peer review
authors: Nitya Thakkar, Mert Yuksekgonul, Jake Silberg, Animesh Garg, Nanyun Peng
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 23 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01188-x

In a randomized controlled study at ICLR 2025, Thakkar et al. demonstrate that large language model-generated feedback can make reviews more informative while enhancing reviewer–author engagement.

infographic.key_insight: A large randomized controlled trial at ICLR 2025 shows that LLM-generated feedback applied in the peer-review process makes reviews measurably more informative and increases reviewer–author engagement.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses low-quality, terse, or unconstructive peer reviews and the scalability challenge of providing actionable, constructive feedback that helps authors improve their submissions and fosters productive reviewer–author dialogue.
method: Large-scale randomized controlled design: reviewers (or review instances) were randomly assigned to receive LLM-generated feedback versus control.
LLM feedback provided as targeted suggestions to improve clarity, critique depth, and actionable recommendations; outcomes measured on review informativeness and reviewer–author engagement.
Quantitative analysis comparing treated vs. control groups for key metrics (informativeness, response rates, author uptake) to assess causal impact.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates a practical, scalable intervention to raise peer-review quality and encourage constructive interaction between reviewers and authors—useful for conference organizers, journal editors, and platform builders seeking to improve review processes.
