title: Align Once, Benefit Multilingually: Enforcing Multilingual Consistency for LLM Safety Alignment
authors: Yuyan Bu, Xiaohao Liu, ZhaoXing Ren, Yaodong Yang, Juntao Dai
abstract: The widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs) across linguistic communities necessitates reliable multilingual safety alignment. However, recent efforts to extend alignment to other languages often require substantial resources, either through large-scale, high-quality supervision in the target language or through pairwise alignment with high-resource languages, which limits scalability. In this work, we propose a resource-efficient method for improving multilingual safety alignment.

infographic.key_insight: A single safety alignment effort can be propagated across many languages by enforcing consistency of model behavior across translations, enabling scalable multilingual safety without costly per-language supervision.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the need for large-scale, high-quality safety annotations or expensive pairwise alignments for each target language, addressing scalability and resource bottlenecks in multilingual LLM safety.
method: Use an English-aligned safety signal as the primary supervision source and propagate it to other languages via translated prompts/responses.
Enforce multilingual consistency constraints (e.g., consistency loss or agreement checks) so model outputs remain aligned across different language inputs.
Leverage lightweight, resource-efficient augmentation or regularization rather than full per-language reannotation or exhaustive pairwise alignment.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to achieve robust safety behaviors across many languages with far less annotation cost and engineering effort, making safer multilingual LLM deployment more practical and scalable.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing single English alignment -> translation -> consistency enforcement -> multilingual model
Bar chart comparing annotation cost: per-language supervision vs. consistency-based propagation
Before/after examples: unsafe prompt in multiple languages with model responses showing improved aligned behavior

title: Agent Skill Framework: Perspectives on the Potential of Small Language Models in Industrial Environments
authors: Yangjie Xu, Lujun Li, Lama Sleem, Niccolo Gentile, Yewei Song
abstract: Agent Skill framework, now widely and officially supported by major players such as GitHub Copilot, LangChain, and OpenAI, performs especially well with proprietary models by improving context engineering, reducing hallucinations, and boosting task accuracy. Based on these observations, an investigation is conducted to determine whether the Agent Skill paradigm provides similar benefits to small language models (SLMs). This question matters in industrial scenarios where continuous reliance on pu

infographic.key_insight: Applying the Agent Skill paradigm to small language models (SLMs) can meaningfully improve their reliability—reducing hallucinations and improving task accuracy—making SLMs more viable for industrial deployments where proprietary models are constrained.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines whether the Agent Skill framework’s benefits (better context engineering, lower hallucination, higher task accuracy) extend to SLMs, addressing industry needs for private, cost-effective, and dependable on-prem or edge-capable models.
method: Implement Agent Skill abstractions as a wrapper/agent layer for multiple SLMs to standardize prompts, tools, and context handling.
Benchmark SLMs with and without Agent Skills on representative industrial tasks, measuring task accuracy, hallucination rate, context utilization, latency, and resource cost.
Compare results against proprietary model baselines and analyze variance across tasks and model sizes to identify where Agent Skills help most.
infographic.impact: Shows a practical path for organizations to improve SLM performance and robustness without full dependence on external proprietary APIs—helpful for privacy, cost control, and on-prem adoption of AI agents in production.
visual_elements: Before/After bar chart: hallucination rate and task accuracy for SLMs with vs. without Agent Skills.
Architecture diagram: Agent Skill layer connecting task tools, context store, and an SLM, showing data/control flow.

title: Scaling Open Discrete Audio Foundation Models with Interleaved Semantic, Acoustic, and Text Tokens
authors: Potsawee Manakul, Woody Haosheng Gan, Martijn Bartelds, Guangzhi Sun, William Held
abstract: Current audio language models are predominantly text-first, either extending pre-trained text LLM backbones or relying on semantic-only audio tokens, limiting general audio modeling. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of native audio foundation models that apply next-token prediction to audio at scale, jointly modeling semantic content, acoustic details, and text to support both general audio generation and cross-modal capabilities. We provide comprehensive empirical insights for b

infographic.key_insight: Interleaving discrete semantic, acoustic, and text tokens in a single next-token prediction model enables scalable native audio foundation models that jointly capture content, timbre, and language for both high-fidelity audio generation and cross-modal tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes limitations of text-first or semantic-only audio approaches by providing a unified, native-audio modeling approach that preserves acoustic detail while supporting semantic/text alignment and generation at scale.
method: Discretize audio into separate token streams for semantic content and acoustic/details, plus text tokens, then interleave them into a single sequence for autoregressive next-token prediction.
Scale transformer training on large paired audio–text and unlabeled audio corpora to learn joint representations that support generation, transcription, and cross-modal tasks.
Evaluate empirically across fidelity, semantic accuracy, and downstream tasks to demonstrate trade-offs and scaling behavior between acoustic detail and semantic modeling.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a unified modeling recipe to build open, scalable audio foundation models that improve generation fidelity and multimodal capabilities, enabling more capable speech, music, and general audio systems.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing three token streams (semantic, acoustic, text) being interleaved into one transformer input and producing mixed outputs.

title: PredMapNet: Future and Historical Reasoning for Consistent Online HD Vectorized Map Construction
authors: Bo Lang, Nirav Savaliya, Zhihao Zheng, Jinglun Feng, Zheng-Hang Yeh
abstract: High-definition (HD) maps are crucial to autonomous driving, providing structured representations of road elements to support navigation and planning. However, existing query-based methods often employ random query initialization and depend on implicit temporal modeling, which lead to temporal inconsistencies and instabilities during the construction of a global map. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework for consistent online HD vectorized map construction, whic

infographic.key_insight: PredMapNet introduces explicit future and historical reasoning to produce temporally consistent, stable online HD vectorized maps — replacing random query initialization and implicit temporal modeling with structured temporal propagation.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces temporal inconsistencies and instabilities in online HD map construction caused by random query initialization and weak/implicit temporal modeling, enabling a consistent global map over time.
method: Explicit temporal modeling: fuse historical context and predicted future information to stabilize map element representations across frames.
Deterministic query initialization and propagation: initialize and propagate vector queries in a structured way to maintain identity and continuity of map primitives.
End-to-end vectorized output: train a single framework to produce and update HD map primitives online (polylines, lane boundaries, traffic elements) for immediate downstream use.
infographic.impact: Provides a more reliable, real-time HD mapping component for autonomous driving and motion planning stacks, improving downstream safety and planner stability. Makes research and production pipelines less sensitive to frame-to-frame fluctuations.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: input sensor frames → historical & future reasoning modules → deterministic query propagation → vectorized map output (clearly labeled blocks).
Before vs. After map consistency panel: side-by-side sequence showing temporal jitter with baseline vs. stable outputs from PredMapNet.
Query propagation animation / schematic: visualization of how queries are initialized and tracked across frames to preserve map primitive identities.

title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
authors: Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Peter Kirgis, Kangheng Liu, Saiteja Utpala
abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed to execute important tasks. While rising accuracy scores on standard benchmarks suggest rapid progress, many agents still continue to fail in practice. This discrepancy highlights a fundamental limitation of current evaluations: compressing agent behavior into a single success metric obscures critical operational flaws. Notably, it ignores whether agents behave consistently across runs, withstand perturbations, fail predictably, or have bounded error severity.

infographic.key_insight: Single-number success metrics mask critical operational flaws. The paper proposes treating agent reliability as a multi-dimensional science (consistency, robustness, predictability, and bounded error severity) rather than a single scalar score.
infographic.problem_solved: Current evaluations compress agent behavior into one metric, obscuring run-to-run variability, sensitivity to perturbations, whether failures are predictable, and how severe errors can be — all of which matter in deployment.
method: Decompose reliability into four measurable dimensions: consistency (repeatability), robustness (perturbation resistance), predictability of failures, and error-severity bounds.
Define evaluation protocols and metrics that measure agents across multiple runs, controlled perturbations, and failure-triggering conditions.
Apply statistical diagnostics and visualizations (e.g., distributions, CDFs, conditional analyses) to characterize failure modes and quantify worst-case/bounded errors.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with actionable diagnostics to choose, tune, and monitor agents for real-world deployment, reducing surprise failures and improving operational safety and trustworthiness.
visual_elements: Radar chart comparing agents across the four reliability dimensions (consistency, robustness, predictability, severity bound).
CDF or violin plots of performance across runs and under perturbations to show variability and tail risks.
Heatmap or spaghetti plot of run-to-run trajectories highlighting inconsistent behaviors and outlier failures.
Annotated flow showing predictable vs. unpredictable failure modes and a bar indicating bounded error thresholds.
infographic.paper_title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
infographic.paper_authors: Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Peter Kirgis, Kangheng Liu, Saiteja Utpala

title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation via a Self-Supervised Semantic Bridge
authors: Jiaming Liu, Felix Petersen, Yunhe Gao, Yabin Zhang, Hyojin Kim
abstract: Adversarial diffusion and diffusion-inversion methods have advanced unpaired image-to-image translation, but each faces key limitations. Adversarial approaches require target-domain adversarial loss during training, which can limit generalization to unseen data, while diffusion-inversion methods often produce low-fidelity translations due to imperfect inversion into noise-latent representations. In this work, we propose the Self-Supervised Semantic Bridge (SSB), a versatile framework that integr

infographic.key_insight: SSB (Self-Supervised Semantic Bridge) enables high-fidelity unpaired image-to-image translation by learning a domain-agnostic semantic latent space that bridges source and target domains, avoiding reliance on target-domain adversarial losses or imperfect diffusion inversions.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses poor generalization of adversarial methods and low-fidelity outputs from diffusion-inversion by providing a self-supervised semantic mapping that enables robust, high-quality translations between unpaired domains.
method: Learn a shared semantic latent space via self-supervised objectives so content is preserved while style/appearance can be changed across domains.

Use an encoder-to-bridge-to-decoder pipeline that conditions a diffusion generator (or decoder) on semantic latents, removing the need for target-domain adversarial training and reducing inversion error.
Integrate contrastive/consistency losses and cross-domain reconstruction to disentangle semantics from domain-specific appearance and stabilize translation.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to perform unpaired translations with better fidelity and stronger generalization to unseen data, reducing the need for adversarial target-domain supervision and improving reliability of diffusion-based generative pipelines.
visual_elements: Schematic of the semantic bridge: encoder (source) → shared semantic latent → decoder/diffusion (target), with loss icons for self-supervision and consistency.
Before/after image pairs showing preserved content and changed style across domains (several examples).

title: Measuring Mid-2025 LLM-Assistance on Novice Performance in Biology
authors: Shen Zhou Hong, Alex Kleinman, Alyssa Mathiowetz, Adam Howes, Julian Cohen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on biological benchmarks, raising concerns that they may help novice actors acquire dual-use laboratory skills. Yet, whether this translates to improved human performance in the physical laboratory remains unclear. To address this, we conducted a pre-registered, investigator-blinded, randomized controlled trial (June-August 2025; n = 153) evaluating whether LLMs improve novice performance in tasks that collectively model a viral reverse genetics work

infographic.key_insight: A pre-registered, investigator-blinded randomized controlled trial (n=153) quantified how mid‑2025 large language models affect novices performing lab-relevant biology tasks, providing empirical evidence about LLM assistance on human performance rather than model-only benchmarks.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between model benchmark performance and real-world human outcomes by measuring whether LLMs actually improve (or change) novices' ability to carry out tasks that collectively model viral reverse‑genetics workflows.
method: Pre-registered, investigator-blinded randomized controlled trial conducted June–August 2025 with 153 participants.
Participants performed a suite of lab-relevant tasks modeling viral reverse genetics; compared LLM-assisted vs. unassisted conditions using objective performance metrics and predefined endpoints.
Statistical analysis measured differences in task success, error rates, and decision patterns to assess the net effect of LLM assistance on novice performance.
infographic.impact: Provides actionable empirical evidence for AI/ML practitioners, policymakers, and safety teams about how LLM capabilities translate to human behavior in sensitive domains—informing model deployment, guardrails, and risk assessments.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Foundation Models for Matched Molecular Pair Transformations to Recapitulate Medicinal Chemistry Intuition
authors: Bo Pan, Peter Zhiping Zhang, Hao-Wei Pang, Alex Zhu, Xiang Yu
abstract: Matched molecular pairs (MMPs) capture the local chemical edits that medicinal chemists routinely use to design analogs, but existing ML approaches either operate at the whole-molecule level with limited edit controllability or learn MMP-style edits from restricted settings and small models. We propose a variable-to-variable formulation of analog generation and train a foundation model on large-scale MMP transformations (MMPTs) to generate diverse variables conditioned on an input variable. To e

infographic.key_insight: Training a retrieval-augmented foundation model on large-scale matched molecular pair transformations (MMPTs) lets the model generate diverse, controllable analog edits that recapitulate medicinal chemistry intuition. The variable-to-variable formulation focuses on local edits rather than whole-molecule rewriting, improving edit fidelity and transferability.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing ML approaches either model whole molecules with poor controllability over local edits or learn MMP-style edits only from small, restricted datasets; this work scales MMPT learning and adds retrieval context to recover chemists' intuitive transformations.
method: Formulate analog generation as a variable-to-variable task that directly models local chemical edits (matched molecular pairs) instead of full-molecule generation.
Train a foundation model on large-scale MMPT data so it learns diverse edit patterns and conditional generation of analog variables.
Augment generation with a retrieval component that provides relevant historical MMP examples as context to guide controllable, chemistry-aware transformations.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, controllable analog design that aligns with medicinal chemists' reasoning, improving iteration speed in lead optimization. Demonstrates that retrieval-augmented foundation models can capture domain-specific edit operators useful for broader AI-driven molecular design.

title: VETime: Vision Enhanced Zero-Shot Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Yingyuan Yang, Tian Lan, Yifei Gao, Yimeng Lu, Wenjun He
abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) requires identifying both immediate Point Anomalies and long-range Context Anomalies. However, existing foundation models face a fundamental trade-off: 1D temporal models provide fine-grained pointwise localization but lack a global contextual perspective, while 2D vision-based models capture global patterns but suffer from information bottlenecks due to a lack of temporal alignment and coarse-grained pointwise detection. To resolve this dilemma, we propose V

infographic.key_insight: VETime fuses vision foundation models with temporal alignment to get the best of both worlds: vision-based global context and 1D temporal pointwise localization, enabling zero-shot detection of both short-term (point) and long-range (context) anomalies.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the fundamental trade-off in TSAD where 1D temporal models localize points but miss global context, while 2D vision models capture global patterns but lack fine-grained temporal alignment and pointwise accuracy—plus the need for zero-shot (label-free) anomaly detection.
method: Translate time series into vision-friendly representations and leverage pretrained vision foundation models to capture global contextual patterns without task-specific labels.
Introduce a temporal-alignment / fusion module that preserves fine-grained, pointwise temporal information while integrating vision-derived global embeddings.
Produce anomaly scores in a zero-shot manner by comparing aligned temporal features and vision-global context to detect both point and context anomalies without supervised training.
infographic.impact: VETime enables practitioners to detect diverse anomaly types (instantaneous spikes and long-range contextual shifts) without labeled anomalies, improving monitoring pipelines and lowering annotation cost while leveraging powerful pretrained vision models.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: time-series → image encoding → vision encoder + temporal-alignment module → anomaly scoring (clear flow of information)

title: Enhanced Diffusion Sampling: Efficient Rare Event Sampling and Free Energy Calculation with Diffusion Models
authors: Yu Xie, Ludwig Winkler, Lixin Sun, Sarah Lewis, Adam E. Foster
abstract: The rare-event sampling problem has long been the central limiting factor in molecular dynamics (MD), especially in biomolecular simulation. Recently, diffusion models such as BioEmu have emerged as powerful equilibrium samplers that generate independent samples from complex molecular distributions, eliminating the cost of sampling rare transition events. However, a sampling problem remains when computing observables that rely on states which are rare in equilibrium, for example folding free ene

infographic.key_insight: Enhanced Diffusion Sampling (EDS) combines diffusion-based equilibrium generative models with targeted sampling and statistical reweighting to efficiently produce and correct for rare-state samples, enabling accurate free-energy estimates without prohibitively long molecular dynamics trajectories.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of computing observables and free-energy differences that depend on rare states or transitions in molecular systems, a longstanding bottleneck in molecular dynamics where conventional simulation spends almost all computation on common equilibrium configurations and misses rare but important events.
method: Start from powerful diffusion-based equilibrium samplers (e.g., BioEmu-like models) that generate independent molecular configurations from the target distribution.

Introduce targeted/biased diffusion sampling to intentionally oversample rare states or transition regions, then compute importance weights or apply statistical reweighting to correct the sampling bias.
Use the reweighted sample set to construct free-energy estimates and rare-event observables efficiently, avoiding long MD trajectories and enabling accurate thermodynamic calculations.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, EDS turns generative diffusion models into practical tools for scientific simulation: it produces rare-event data and free-energy labels far more cheaply than brute-force MD, enabling faster model training, benchmarking, and hypothesis testing in molecular and materials domains.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: conventional MD timeline (many small steps, few rare transitions) vs. EDS pipeline (diffusion sampler → targeted sampling → reweighting → free-energy output).
Diagram of a free-energy surface with rare-state basin highlighted and sampled points showing how EDS fills in low-probability regions versus equilibrium sampling.
Flowchart showing conditioning/biasing during diffusion, computation of importance weights, and aggregation into a free-energy estimator.

title: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
authors: Shruti Joshi, Aaron Mueller, David Klindt, Wieland Brendel, Patrik Reizinger
abstract: Interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) has yielded important insights into model behaviour, yet recurring pitfalls persist: findings that do not generalise, and causal interpretations that outrun the evidence. Our position is that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures, the data or assumptions needed to achieve it, and the inferences it can support. Specifically, Pearl's causal hierarchy clarifies w

infographic.key_insight: Causal inference is necessary for interpretability claims to reliably generalise: mapping model activations to high‑level concepts must meet causal criteria (not just correlational evidence) to support invariant, transferable explanations.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses recurring failures where interpretability findings about LLMs do not generalise and where causal language outruns the evidence by clarifying what evidence and assumptions are required for valid causal claims about model mechanisms.
method: Cast interpretability questions in Pearl’s causal hierarchy to distinguish associational, interventional, and counterfactual claims about activations and concepts.
Specify the data, interventions (e.g., targeted ablations or controlled input manipulations), and assumptions needed to identify causal mappings from activations to high‑level structures.
Demonstrate pitfalls of purely correlational analyses and propose practical causal tests/benchmarks to validate whether inferred structures are invariant and causally relevant.
infographic.impact: Helps practitioners make reliable, testable interpretability claims that generalise across inputs and model variants, reducing false conclusions and improving trustworthiness and robustness of model explanations.
visual_elements: Pearl’s causal hierarchy ladder showing levels: association → intervention → counterfactual, annotated with examples for interpretability claims.
Schematic diagram mapping activations → latent concept with arrows for causal vs correlational edges and a highlighted intervention (e.g., ablation) breaking/confirming the edge.

Checklist/flowchart of required data, assumptions, and tests to move from correlation to causal interpretability (practical recipe for researchers).

title: ViTaB-A: Evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models on Visual Table Attribution
authors: Yahia Alqurnawi, Preetom Biswas, Anmol Rao, Tejas Anvekar, Chitta Baral
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (mLLMs) are often used to answer questions in structured data such as tables in Markdown, JSON, and images. While these models can often give correct answers, users also need to know where those answers come from. In this work, we study structured data attribution/citation, which is the ability of the models to point to the specific rows and columns that support an answer. We evaluate several mLLMs across different table formats and prompting strategies. Our resu

infographic.key_insight: Multimodal LLMs often answer table-based questions correctly but frequently fail to reliably cite the exact rows and columns that support their answers; attribution fidelity varies strongly by table format and prompting strategy.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for structured-data attribution — i.e., whether mLLMs can point to the specific table cells (rows/columns) that justify their answers across Markdown, JSON and image-based tables.
method: Assemble ViTaB-A: an evaluation suite of questions over tables in multiple formats (Markdown, JSON, images) with ground-truth row/column annotations.
Run several state-of-the-art mLLMs under diverse prompting strategies and measure both answer accuracy and attribution/localization fidelity using per-cell/row/column metrics.
Analyze how table format and prompt design affect attribution quality and report common failure modes and patterns.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical benchmark and diagnostic insights so practitioners can choose models and prompts that not only answer correctly but also transparently cite supporting table data—improving trust, interpretability, and compliance for applications using structured inputs.

title: VideoSketcher: Video Models Prior Enable Versatile Sequential Sketch Generation
authors: Hui Ren, Yuval Alaluf, Omer Bar Tal, Alexander Schwing, Antonio Torralba
abstract: Sketching is inherently a sequential process, in which strokes are drawn in a meaningful order to explore and refine ideas. However, most generative models treat sketches as static images, overlooking the temporal structure that underlies creative drawing. We present a data-efficient approach for sequential sketch generation that adapts pretrained text-to-video diffusion models to generate sketching processes. Our key insight is that large language models and video diffusion models offer complem

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained text-to-video diffusion models (combined with large‑language model priors) can be adapted in a data‑efficient way to produce temporally coherent, stroke‑by‑stroke sketching processes rather than static images.
infographic.problem_solved: Most generative sketch models ignore the temporal, sequential nature of drawing and require large paired datasets; this work enables controllable, interpretable sketch generation that reproduces the natural ordering and refinement of strokes with minimal data.
method: Adapt pretrained text‑to‑video diffusion models to generate frame sequences that represent progressive sketch strokes, leveraging the video model’s temporal priors.
Incorporate large language model priors to guide stroke ordering and high‑level semantic structure for sketches.
Use a lightweight, data‑efficient fine‑tuning / adapter strategy so the system learns sketching dynamics from small sketch datasets while retaining rich video priors.
infographic.impact: Enables creation of interpretable, editable sketching processes for design, education, and human–AI co‑creation while reducing data and compute needs; makes sequential generation accessible to practitioners building sketch animation, interactive tools, or sketch-conditioned workflows.

title: Understanding vs. Generation: Navigating Optimization Dilemma in Multimodal Models
authors: Sen Ye, Mengde Xu, Shuyang Gu, Di He, Liwei Wang
abstract: Current research in multimodal models faces a key challenge where enhancing generative capabilities often comes at the expense of understanding, and vice versa. We analyzed this trade-off and identify the primary cause might be the potential conflict between generation and understanding, which creates a competitive dynamic within the model. To address this, we propose the Reason-Reflect-Refine (R3) framework. This innovative algorithm re-frames the single-step generation task into a multi-step p

infographic.key_insight: Improving generation and understanding in multimodal models creates an internal optimization conflict; reframing single-step generation as a multi-step Reason–Reflect–Refine (R3) process reduces that competition and lets models better do both.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the trade-off where boosting a model's generative abilities degrades its understanding (and vice versa) by identifying a competitive dynamic between the two objectives and offering an algorithmic way to reconcile them.
method: Reframe single-step generation into a three-stage pipeline: Reason (produce explicit intermediate representations/answers), Reflect (evaluate/compare outputs to internal understanding and detect conflicts), and Refine (iteratively update the output and internal state).
Use the multi-step loop to decouple and balance understanding vs. generation objectives, allowing the model to optimize for both without direct competition in a single forward pass.
Integrate targeted training signals or objective weighting during the R3 steps so the model can correct misunderstandings before committing to final generations.
infographic.impact: Enables multimodal models that retain strong interpretive capabilities while producing high-quality generations, improving reliability and debuggability for real-world AI systems and downstream tasks.

title: Solving Parameter-Robust Avoid Problems with Unknown Feasibility using Reinforcement Learning
authors: Oswin So, Eric Yang Yu, Songyuan Zhang, Matthew Cleaveland, Mitchell Black
abstract: Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL) have achieved strong results on high-dimensional control tasks, but applying RL to reachability problems raises a fundamental mismatch: reachability seeks to maximize the set of states from which a system remains safe indefinitely, while RL optimizes expected returns over a user-specified distribution. This mismatch can result in policies that perform poorly on low-probability states that are still within the safe set. A natural alternative is

infographic.key_insight: Standard RL optimizes expected returns under a training distribution and can miss low-probability but safe states; this paper develops an RL-based framework that discovers whether a parametric 'avoid' safety requirement is feasible and, when feasible, learns policies that are robust across parameter variations.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between reachability-style safety objectives (maximize the set of initial states that avoid unsafe regions for all time) and policy-learning under unknown parameter uncertainty and unknown feasibility — i.e., determining if a robust safe policy exists and, if so, synthesizing one that performs across the full parameter set rather than just on average.
method: Formulate the parameter-robust avoid problem with an explicit notion of unknown feasibility and convert it into an RL-compatible objective that emphasizes worst-case / low-probability parameter performance rather than expected reward.
Use an adversarial or parameter-sampling curriculum to search parameter space and a safety critic / feasibility detector to identify infeasible regimes or certify candidate policies.

Train policies with robustness-promoting learning (e.g., minimax or risk-sensitive updates and heavy penalty for entering unsafe states), iterating between feasibility assessment and policy improvement.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical path to synthesize controllers that are robust to parameter uncertainty and to detect when safety specs are unattainable — improving reliability for safety-critical systems where rare parameter settings matter as much as average-case performance.
visual_elements: Two-panel schematic: (left) training distribution vs. full parameter space highlighting low-probability safe regions missed by standard RL; (right) target robust safe set covering all parameters.

title: The Geometry of Alignment Collapse: When Fine-Tuning Breaks Safety
authors: Max Springer, Chung Peng Lee, Blossom Metevier, Jane Castleman, Bohdan Turbal
abstract: Fine-tuning aligned language models on benign tasks unpredictably degrades safety guardrails, even when training data contains no harmful content and developers have no adversarial intent. We show that the prevailing explanation, that fine-tuning updates should be orthogonal to safety-critical directions in high-dimensional parameter space, offers false reassurance: we show this orthogonality is structurally unstable and collapses under the dynamics of gradient descent. We then resolve this thro

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuning an already-aligned language model on benign tasks can unexpectedly break its safety guards because the assumed orthogonality between task updates and safety-critical directions is not robust — gradient-descent dynamics cause that orthogonality to collapse.
infographic.problem_solved: Explains why safety guardrails degrade unpredictably after benign fine-tuning and debunks the common reassurance that fine-tuning updates remain harmlessly orthogonal to safety directions; identifies a geometric and dynamical mechanism behind alignment collapse.
method: Geometric analysis of parameter-space directions to characterize ‘safety-critical’ subspaces and the structural instability of orthogonality assumptions.
Dynamical study of gradient-descent trajectories showing how small perturbations and optimization dynamics cause collapse of orthogonality.
Empirical validation on language models: fine-tuning on benign tasks leads to measurable drops in safety metrics despite no harmful training data; propose diagnostics and mitigation directions.
infographic.impact: Practitioners can’t rely on orthogonality as a safety guarantee — fine-tuning may silently erode alignment even when data is benign. This calls for active safety monitoring, robustness-aware fine-tuning methods (e.g., constrained optimization, regularization or safety checkpoints), and new diagnostics for alignment stability.

title: Decision Quality Evaluation Framework at Pinterest
authors: Yuqi Tian, Robert Paine, Attila Dobi, Kevin O'Sullivan, Aravindh Manickavasagam
abstract: Online platforms require robust systems to enforce content safety policies at scale. A critical component of these systems is the ability to evaluate the quality of moderation decisions made by both human agents and Large Language Models (LLMs). However, this evaluation is challenging due to the inherent trade-offs between cost, scale, and trustworthiness, along with the complexity of evolving policies. To address this, we present a comprehensive Decision Quality Evaluation Framework developed a

infographic.key_insight: A practical, policy-aware framework that measures the quality of moderation decisions from humans and LLMs by balancing cost, scale, and trustworthiness, enabling continuous, auditable evaluation tied to evolving safety policies.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluates moderation decision quality at production scale while addressing trade-offs between annotation cost, coverage, and trust (consensus/adjudication) and coping with changing policies and mixed human/LLM decision sources.
method: Policy-aligned taxonomy and labeling guidelines that map content policies to graded decision categories for consistent ground truth.
Hybrid sampling and annotation pipeline: stratified sampling for coverage, human adjudication for high-risk cases, and LLM-assisted annotations to expand scale while retaining human oversight.
Multi-dimensional metrics and feedback loop: accuracy, calibration, disagreement/consistency, and impact-weighted error rates reported in dashboards and fed back into training and policy updates.
infographic.impact: Provides a reproducible, scalable approach for auditing and improving moderation systems, helping AI/ML teams make informed deployment and retraining decisions while reducing safety and compliance risk.

title: *-PLUIE: Personalisable metric with Llm Used for Improved Evaluation
authors: Quentin Lemesle, Léane Jourdan, Daisy Munson, Pierre Alain, Jonathan Chevelu
abstract: Evaluating the quality of automatically generated text often relies on LLM-as-a-judge (LLM-judge) methods. While effective, these approaches are computationally expensive and require post-processing. To address these limitations, we build upon ParaPLUIE, a perplexity-based LLM-judge metric that estimates confidence over ``Yes/No'' answers without generating text. We introduce *-PLUIE, task specific prompting variants of ParaPLUIE and evaluate their alignment with human judgement. Our experiments

infographic.key_insight: Introduce *-PLUIE: a personalisable, task-specific extension of ParaPLUIE that uses perplexity-based yes/no prompting (no text generation) to produce confidence scores that better align with human judgments while reducing compute and post-processing.
infographic.problem_solved: Automated LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is accurate but costly and requires text generation plus post-processing; there is also limited task-specific personalization for alignment with human preferences.
method: Build on ParaPLUIE: use model perplexity over targeted Yes/No prompts to estimate confidence without generating full answers.
Create *-PLUIE: task-specific prompting variants and user-personalisable templates/thresholds to better match task definitions and rater preferences.
Evaluate alignment by comparing *-PLUIE confidence scores to human judgments and measure practical gains in compute and post-processing overhead.
infographic.impact: Provides a cheaper, faster, and customizable way to evaluate generated text that preserves alignment with human judgment—making large-scale NLG evaluation more practical for researchers and engineers.

title: CrispEdit: Low-Curvature Projections for Scalable Non-Destructive LLM Editing
authors: Zarif Ikram, Arad Firouzkouhi, Stephen Tu, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi, Paria Rashidinejad
abstract: A central challenge in large language model (LLM) editing is capability preservation: methods that successfully change targeted behavior can quietly game the editing proxy and corrupt general capabilities, producing degenerate behaviors reminiscent of proxy/reward hacking. We present CrispEdit, a scalable and principled second-order editing algorithm that treats capability preservation as an explicit constraint, unifying and generalizing several existing editing approaches. CrispEdit formulates

infographic.key_insight: CrispEdit is a scalable, curvature-aware LLM editing method that enforces capability preservation as an explicit constraint by projecting edits into low-curvature directions, enabling targeted behavior change without corrupting general model abilities.
infographic.problem_solved: How to perform targeted edits to large language models that change specific behaviors while avoiding proxy/reward-hacking and unintended degradation of general capabilities.
method: Formulate editing as a constrained optimization problem where capability preservation is an explicit constraint alongside the targeted edit objective.
Use second-order (curvature-aware) information to identify low-curvature directions and project candidate edits into that subspace to minimize collateral impact.
Apply scalable approximations to make the projection and second-order calculations tractable for large models, unifying and generalizing prior editing approaches.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a principled tool for non-destructive, scalable model edits—making it easier to correct or update LLM behaviors reliably while maintaining overall performance and safety.

title: GlobeDiff: State Diffusion Process for Partial Observability in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Yiqin Yang, Xu Yang, Yuhua Jiang, Ni Mu, Hao Hu
abstract: In the realm of multi-agent systems, the challenge of \emph{partial observability} is a critical barrier to effective coordination and decision-making. Existing approaches, such as belief state estimation and inter-agent communication, often fall short. Belief-based methods are limited by their focus on past experiences without fully leveraging global information, while communication methods often lack a robust model to effectively utilize the auxiliary information they provide. To solve this is

infographic.key_insight: GlobeDiff applies a conditional diffusion generative model to infer coherent global states from agents' partial observations and exchanged messages, enabling accurate, sample-based reconstruction of the world for better multi-agent coordination.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses partial observability in multi-agent systems where traditional belief estimators and ad-hoc communication fail to produce consistent, globally useful state information for planning and coordination.
method: Train a conditional state-diffusion model that learns the distribution of global states given local observations and inter-agent messages.
At inference, perform reverse diffusion (denoising) conditioned on available partial observations/messages to produce diverse, high-fidelity global state samples for downstream policies.
Design decentralized conditioning and sampling so each agent can obtain coherent global-state hypotheses without requiring full observability or brittle message protocols.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled, generative approach to recover global context under uncertainty—improving robustness and coordination in multi-agent RL, robotics, and distributed sensing where partial observations are the norm.

title: Parallel hierarchical encoding of linguistic representations in the human auditory cortex and recurrent automatic speech recognition systems
authors: Menoua Keshishian, Gavin Mischler, Samuel Thomas, Brian Kingsbury, Stephan Bickel
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 17 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01185-0

Keshishian, Mischler et al. report that a recurrent automatic speech recognition system aligns closely with brain organization: model layers map to distinct cortical regions and naturally learn to encode a parallel progression from acoustic to phonetic, lexical and semantic content.

infographic.key_insight: A recurrent ASR system naturally organizes linguistic information in a hierarchy that mirrors human auditory cortex: distinct model layers map to distinct cortical regions and jointly encode a parallel progression from acoustic → phonetic → lexical → semantic representations.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how hierarchical linguistic representations in engineered speech models correspond to spatially distributed processing in the human auditory cortex, bridging a gap between machine speech representations and neurobiology.
method: Compare internal activations of a recurrent automatic speech recognition (ASR) model with neural recordings from human auditory cortex while participants listened to speech.

Use alignment analyses (layer-to-region mapping, representational similarity and encoding models) to identify which model layers correspond to which cortical sites and which linguistic levels (acoustic, phonetic, lexical, semantic) they encode.
Characterize the parallel progression of information in both systems by tracking how representations evolve across model depth and cortical anatomy.
infographic.impact: Provides empirical evidence that modern ASR layers recapitulate brain-like, hierarchical speech processing—useful for model interpretability, brain-informed architecture design, and cross-disciplinary validation between neuroscience and speech technology.

title: Stabilizing Test-Time Adaptation of High-Dimensional Simulation Surrogates via D-Optimal Statistics
authors: Anna Zimmel, Paul Setinek, Gianluca Galletti, Johannes Brandstetter, Werner Zellinger
abstract: Machine learning surrogates are increasingly used in engineering to accelerate costly simulations, yet distribution shifts between training and deployment often cause severe performance degradation (e.g., unseen geometries or configurations). Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) can mitigate such shifts, but existing methods are largely developed for lower-dimensional classification with structured outputs and visually aligned input-output relationships, making them unstable for the high-dimensional, unst

infographic.key_insight: Selecting D‑optimal low‑dimensional summary statistics (projections) produces stable, highly informative objectives for test‑time adaptation of high‑dimensional simulation surrogates, reducing catastrophic drift and improving accuracy under distribution shift.
infographic.problem_solved: Conventional Test‑Time Adaptation methods are unstable for high‑dimensional, unstructured simulation outputs (e.g., fields or meshes) because self‑supervised objectives are noisy or uninformative, causing poor or divergent adaptation when deployed on unseen geometries/configurations.
method: Derive D‑optimal statistics from the surrogate’s training Jacobian/feature space (select projections that maximize information / determinant of the Fisher/design matrix).

Use those selected low‑dimensional summaries as the adaptation objective at test time (match predicted vs. observed statistics or minimize a summary loss) to produce informative, low‑variance gradients.
Stabilize online updates with regularization and small-step/uncertainty weighting, and perform efficient selection/updating of statistics to keep computation tractable.
infographic.impact: Makes online adaptation of simulation surrogates reliable in real deployment scenarios (e.g., CFD, structural analysis), reducing the need for expensive retraining or additional simulations and improving predictive fidelity across unseen conditions.

title: Perceptive Humanoid Parkour: Chaining Dynamic Human Skills via Motion Matching
authors: Zhen Wu, Xiaoyu Huang, Lujie Yang, Yuanhang Zhang, Koushil Sreenath
abstract: While recent advances in humanoid locomotion have achieved stable walking on varied terrains, capturing the agility and adaptivity of highly dynamic human motions remains an open challenge. In particular, agile parkour in complex environments demands not only low-level robustness, but also human-like motion expressiveness, long-horizon skill composition, and perception-driven decision-making. In this paper, we present Perceptive Humanoid Parkour (PHP), a modular framework that enables humanoid r

infographic.key_insight: Perceptive Humanoid Parkour (PHP) is a modular framework that composes and stitches dynamic human parkour skills by using motion-matching over a motion library together with perception-driven selection, enabling long-horizon, agile humanoid behaviors.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between stable walking controllers and highly dynamic, human-like parkour by addressing skill expressiveness, reliable transitions across long horizons, and perception-guided decision-making in complex environments.
method: Build a curated library of dynamic human parkour motions and index it for fast motion-matching retrieval.
Use an egocentric perception module to interpret the environment and select the next appropriate skill from the library.
Hierarchical control that stitches retrieved motions into smooth, robust transitions with low-level stabilization (e.g., controllers or local optimization/RL) for execution on a humanoid.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, modular recipe for researchers to endow humanoids with expressive, long-horizon agile behaviors that are perception-aware and easier to extend or transfer; useful for locomotion, imitation learning, and agile robot deployment.

title: Operationalising the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis via Task Complexity
authors: Tomás Vergara-Browne, Darshan Patil, Ivan Titov, Siva Reddy, Tiago Pimentel
abstract: The superficial alignment hypothesis (SAH) posits that large language models learn most of their knowledge during pre-training, and that post-training merely surfaces this knowledge. The SAH, however, lacks a precise definition, which has led to (i) different and seemingly orthogonal arguments supporting it, and (ii) important critiques to it. We propose a new metric called task complexity: the length of the shortest program that achieves a target performance on a task. In this framework, the SA

infographic.key_insight: The paper operationalises the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis by introducing "task complexity" — the length of the shortest program that attains a target performance — enabling quantitative tests of whether fine-tuning merely surfaces pre-trained knowledge or requires new learning.
infographic.problem_solved: The Superficial Alignment Hypothesis lacked a precise, testable definition, leading to conflicting arguments and critiques; this work provides a concrete metric to compare tasks and evaluate claims about what is learned during pre-training versus post-training.
method: Define task complexity as the minimal-program-length (algorithmic) description that achieves a target performance on a task, framing SAH in terms of program-length gaps between pre-training and fine-tuning.
Develop practical approximations for task complexity (e.g., compressibility, program-synthesis or model-based proxies) so the metric can be estimated on real tasks and models.
Empirically evaluate the metric across a suite of tasks and model settings to test SAH predictions (correlating estimated task complexity with fine-tuning gains and transfer behavior).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a quantitative tool to predict when fine-tuning will simply surface pre-trained capabilities versus when it must induce new algorithmic structure, informing dataset design, transfer expectations, and allocation of compute for pre-training vs fine-tuning.

title: GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
authors: GLM-5 Team, :, Aohan Zeng, Xin Lv, Zhenyu Hou
abstract: We present GLM-5, a next-generation foundation model designed to transition the paradigm of vibe coding to agentic engineering. Building upon the agentic, reasoning, and coding (ARC) capabilities of its predecessor, GLM-5 adopts DSA to significantly reduce training and inference costs while maintaining long-context fidelity. To advance model alignment and autonomy, we implement a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupli

infographic.key_insight: GLM-5 introduces an efficiency-first design that shifts 'vibe coding' toward 'agentic engineering' by using DSA to cut training/inference costs while preserving long-context reasoning and by using an asynchronous RL pipeline to speed post-training alignment.
infographic.problem_solved: High computational cost and slow post-training alignment of large foundation models, while retaining long-context fidelity and agentic capabilities for reasoning and coding.
method: Apply DSA (an efficiency-focused training/inference technique) to drastically reduce compute and memory overhead while maintaining long-context fidelity.
Introduce an asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that decouples alignment/autonomy updates from base model training to improve post-training efficiency.
Build on prior ARC (agentic, reasoning, coding) capabilities to transition model behavior from style-driven 'vibe coding' to controlled, agentic engineering.
infographic.impact: Practitioners gain a path to deploy more capable, long-context foundation models with much lower compute cost and faster alignment cycles, enabling practical agentic applications and cheaper iteration for research and products.

title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
authors: Dhruva Karkada, Daniel J. Korchinski, Andres Nava, Matthieu Wyart, Yasaman Bahri
abstract: Although learned representations underlie neural networks' success, their fundamental properties remain poorly understood. A striking example is the emergence of simple geometric structures in LLM representations: for example, calendar months organize into a circle, years form a smooth one-dimensional manifold, and cities' latitudes and longitudes can be decoded by a linear probe. We show that the statistics of language exhibit a translation symmetry -- e.g., the co-occurrence probability of two

infographic.key_insight: Translation symmetries in language co-occurrence statistics impose strong constraints on learned representations, causing simple geometric structures (e.g., circles for months, smooth 1D manifolds for years, linearly decodeable spatial coordinates) to emerge naturally in model embedding space.
infographic.problem_solved: Explains why pretrained language models develop crisp, low-dimensional geometric organization in their representations despite complex training dynamics—linking observable geometric phenomena to concrete statistical symmetries in language data.
method: Theoretical analysis: derive how a translation symmetry in token co-occurrence probabilities constrains the space of optimal representations.
Empirical validation: probe multiple models and corpora with linear decoders, PCA and manifold visualizations to recover circles, 1D manifolds, and linearly-decodable coordinates.
Controlled experiments: synthetic data and ablations that add/remove symmetry to demonstrate causality between statistical symmetry and emergent geometry.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled explanation for common geometric patterns in LLM representations, improving interpretability and informing better probing, diagnostics, and dataset or architecture choices that exploit or avoid such symmetries.

title: PDE foundation models are skillful AI weather emulators for the Martian atmosphere
authors: Johannes Schmude, Sujit Roy, Liping Wang, Theodore van Kessel, Levente Klein
abstract: We show that AI foundation models that are pretrained on numerical solutions to a diverse corpus of partial differential equations can be adapted and fine-tuned to obtain skillful predictive weather emulators for the Martian atmosphere. We base our work on the Poseidon PDE foundation model for two-dimensional systems. We develop a method to extend Poseidon from two to three dimensions while keeping the pretraining information. Moreover, we investigate the performance of the model in the presence

infographic.key_insight: A PDE foundation model (Poseidon) pretrained on diverse numerical PDE solutions can be extended from 2D to 3D and fine-tuned to become a skillful, physics-aware weather emulator for the Martian atmosphere while retaining pretraining knowledge.
infographic.problem_solved: How to adapt a 2D PDE foundation model to produce accurate, efficient 3D atmospheric forecasts for Mars without discarding the physics information learned during pretraining.
method: Use the Poseidon PDE foundation model pretrained on a diverse corpus of 2D PDE numerical solutions as the starting point.
Develop and apply a model-extension strategy to lift the pretrained 2D representations to 3D while preserving learned inductive biases from pretraining.
Fine-tune the 3D-extended model on Martian atmospheric data/simulations to produce a fast, skillful weather emulator.
infographic.impact: Provides a pathway to fast, physics-informed planetary weather emulators that reduce reliance on costly full numerical simulators—accelerating research, mission planning, and iterative model development for AI/ML practitioners working in geophysical and planetary domains.

title: Hunt Globally: Deep Research AI Agents for Drug Asset Scouting in Investing, Business Development, and Search & Evaluation
authors: Alisa Vinogradova, Vlad Vinogradov, Luba Greenwood, Ilya Yasny, Dmitry Kobyzev
abstract: Bio-pharmaceutical innovation has shifted: many new drug assets now originate outside the United States and are disclosed primarily via regional, non-English channels. Recent data suggests >85% of patent filings originate outside the U.S., with China accounting for nearly half of the global total; a growing share of scholarly output is also non-U.S. Industry estimates put China at ~30% of global drug development, spanning 1,200+ novel candidates. In this high-stakes environment, failing to surfa

infographic.key_insight: A multi-agent deep research AI pipeline can automatically scout and evaluate drug assets disclosed in regional, non-English channels, substantially expanding global coverage for investing and business development. This approach reduces blind spots from fragmented international disclosures and speeds early-stage evaluation.
infographic.problem_solved: Missed or late discovery of promising drug assets due to geographic and language fragmentation of patents, regional disclosures, and scholarly output, which impedes timely investment and business-development decisions.
method: Multi-agent pipeline that performs cross-lingual retrieval from regional patent offices, preprints, local journals, and corporate disclosures to collect candidate assets.
Domain-aware NLP: entity extraction, patent/literature parsing, LLM-based summarization and provenance tracking, plus relevance scoring and uncertainty estimation to rank prospects.
Human-in-the-loop validation and automated due-diligence checks to convert surfaced leads into actionable investment/BD opportunities.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical blueprint for AI/ML teams to build scalable, multilingual asset-discovery systems that improve recall of global innovation and shorten time-to-decision for investors and BD teams. It demonstrates effective integration of retrieval, LLM reasoning, and domain tooling for high-value enterprise use cases.

title: Rethinking Diffusion Models with Symmetries through Canonicalization with Applications to Molecular Graph Generation
authors: Cai Zhou, Zijie Chen, Zian Li, Jike Wang, Kaiyi Jiang
abstract: Many generative tasks in chemistry and science involve distributions invariant to group symmetries (e.g., permutation and rotation). A common strategy enforces invariance and equivariance through architectural constraints such as equivariant denoisers and invariant priors. In this paper, we challenge this tradition through the alternative canonicalization perspective: first map each sample to an orbit representative with a canonical pose or order, train an unconstrained (non-equivariant) diffusi

infographic.key_insight: Instead of building equivariant architectures, map each sample to a canonical orbit representative (canonical pose/order) and train a standard, unconstrained diffusion model on those canonicalized samples—recovering symmetry-invariant generation via canonicalization and inverse mapping.
infographic.problem_solved: Generative modeling of data with group symmetries (e.g., permutation of graph nodes, rotation/translation of 3D structures) without the complexity and engineering cost of designing equivariant networks or symmetry-aware priors.
method: Canonicalization: deterministically map each training sample to a unique orbit representative (fixed pose/order) that removes symmetry degrees of freedom.
Standard diffusion training: train an off-the-shelf, non-equivariant diffusion model on the canonicalized dataset.

Decanonicalization at sampling: generate canonical samples with the diffusion model and map them back to the original symmetry class (apply appropriate group action) to obtain valid, invariant outputs for tasks such as molecular graph generation.
infographic.impact: This approach simplifies model design and implementation while preserving symmetry invariances, making diffusion-based generative modeling for chemistry and other symmetry-rich domains more practical, modular, and scalable for practitioners.
visual_elements: Orbit diagram: many symmetric variants of a sample mapped to a single canonical representative (circle of states -> one highlighted canonical point).
Pipeline flowchart: Input data -> Canonicalization -> Standard Diffusion Model (train) -> Sample -> Decanonicalization -> Symmetric outputs.

title: Cold-Start Personalization via Training-Free Priors from Structured World Models
authors: Avinandan Bose, Shuyue Stella Li, Faeze Brahman, Pang Wei Koh, Simon Shaolei Du
abstract: Cold-start personalization requires inferring user preferences through interaction when no user-specific historical data is available. The core challenge is a routing problem: each task admits dozens of preference dimensions, yet individual users care about only a few, and which ones matter depends on who is asking. With a limited question budget, asking without structure will miss the dimensions that matter. Reinforcement learning is the natural formulation, but in multi-turn settings its termi

infographic.key_insight: Use structured world models as training-free priors to guide which preference dimensions to query, enabling efficient multi-turn cold-start personalization without per-user training.
infographic.problem_solved: How to infer a new user's few relevant preferences from many possible dimensions under a tight question budget — the routing problem of selecting which questions actually matter for each user.
method: Construct structured world models that encode relationships between tasks, contexts, and preference dimensions as priors (no per-user training required).
Use planning/decision procedures over the world model to route limited queries toward dimensions most likely to influence the user’s outcomes.
Drive a lightweight interaction policy that selects questions and actions based on the model’s priors, adapting in multi-turn conversations to quickly identify salient preferences.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, training-free approach to cold-start personalization, reducing required user interaction and accelerating deployment of personalized systems where historical user data is unavailable.
visual_elements: Routing diagram: many preference dimensions (nodes) with the model highlighting the few queried dimensions for a given user.
Flowchart: structured world model -> planner -> question selection -> user response loop (multi-turn cycle).

title: Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs
authors: Xander Davies, Giorgi Giglemiani, Edmund Lau, Eric Winsor, Geoffrey Irving
abstract: Frontier LLMs are safeguarded against attempts to extract harmful information via adversarial prompts known as "jailbreaks". Recently, defenders have developed classifier-based systems that have survived thousands of hours of human red teaming. We introduce Boundary Point Jailbreaking (BPJ), a new class of automated jailbreak attacks that evade the strongest industry-deployed safeguards. Unlike previous attacks that rely on white/grey-box assumptions (such as classifier scores or gradients) or l

infographic.key_insight: Boundary Point Jailbreaking (BPJ) demonstrates that automated, black‑box attacks can find inputs near a model’s accept/reject decision boundary using only final outputs, enabling robust evasion of classifier‑based safeguards without white‑box signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the gap in security evaluations where industry‑deployed classifier defenses were thought robust against red‑teaming by showing they can be bypassed by automated black‑box methods that do not require scores, gradients, or model internals.
method: Conceptually treat the model + filter as a binary black‑box and probe it to identify input regions that lie close to the accept/reject decision boundary.
Automatically generate and iteratively refine prompts by observing only final accept/reject outputs, steering examples toward boundary points that flip the filter decision.
Operate without access to classifier confidences, gradients, or internal states—relying solely on outcome observations to guide attack refinement.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates a practical weakness in real‑world classifier‑based safeguards and motivates defense redesigns (e.g., multi‑modal checks, randomized or stateful filtering, robust evaluation protocols) and stronger adversarial testing for LLM deployments.
visual_elements: Schematic: black‑box LLM+filter as a sealed box with query arrows in and binary outputs out, illustrating no internal access.
Decision boundary diagram: 2D plot showing accept/reject regions with probes moving toward boundary points that flip decisions.
Flowchart: automated loop of generate → query → observe outcome → refine (high-level, non‑operational).
Bar/line chart: comparative success rates showing BPJ vs prior white/grey‑box attacks against deployed classifier defenses (conceptual, not raw data).

title: BPP: Long-Context Robot Imitation Learning by Focusing on Key History Frames
authors: Max Sobol Mark, Jacky Liang, Maria Attarian, Chuyuan Fu, Debidatta Dwibedi
abstract: Many robot tasks require attending to the history of past observations. For example, finding an item in a room requires remembering which places have already been searched. However, the best-performing robot policies typically condition only on the current observation, limiting their applicability to such tasks. Naively conditioning on past observations often fails due to spurious correlations: policies latch onto incidental features of training histories that do not generalize to out-of-distrib

infographic.key_insight: BPP improves long-horizon robot imitation by automatically selecting a small set of informative past frames to condition the policy on, avoiding spurious correlations that arise when naively using the entire history.
infographic.problem_solved: Robotic policies often need long history to solve tasks (e.g., search or multi-step manipulation), but conditioning on full histories causes overfitting to incidental patterns and fails to generalize; BPP addresses how to use long context without spurious correlations.
method: Learn a lightweight key-frame selector that identifies a sparse subset of past observations (key history frames) relevant to the current decision.
Condition the imitation-learning policy only on the selected frames (plus current observation), reducing noise and spurious cues from irrelevant history.
Train end-to-end with objectives that encourage informative selection and robust downstream policy performance (e.g., imitation loss with selection sparsity/regularization).
infographic.impact: By focusing on a compact, informative context, BPP enables more reliable long-horizon behavior and better generalization for robot imitation tasks — making memory-aware policies practical and robust for real-world robotics.

title: EditCtrl: Disentangled Local and Global Control for Real-Time Generative Video Editing
authors: Yehonathan Litman, Shikun Liu, Dario Seyb, Nicholas Milef, Yang Zhou
abstract: High-fidelity generative video editing has seen significant quality improvements by leveraging pre-trained video foundation models. However, their computational cost is a major bottleneck, as they are often designed to inefficiently process the full video context regardless of the inpainting mask's size, even for sparse, localized edits. In this paper, we introduce EditCtrl, an efficient video inpainting control framework that focuses computation only where it is needed. Our approach features a

infographic.key_insight: Disentangle local (mask-focused) and global (scene/temporal) control so the model only computes heavy operations where edits occur, enabling high-quality video inpainting with much lower latency and cost.
infographic.problem_solved: Pre-trained video foundation models waste computation by processing full video context even for small, localized edits; EditCtrl addresses this inefficiency to enable fast, scalable generative video editing.
method: Disentangled controllers: a local pathway that concentrates computation and high-resolution reconstruction inside inpainting masks, and a global pathway that preserves scene context and temporal consistency.
Mask-aware sparse computation and attention routing so only affected frames/patches receive expensive processing, while the global controller supplies lightweight contextual guidance.
Plug-and-play integration with pre-trained video foundation models to retain generation quality while greatly reducing FLOPs and latency for localized edits.
infographic.impact: Makes interactive, real-time generative video editing practical by cutting unnecessary computation for sparse edits—beneficial for content creators, product prototypes, and large-scale video pipelines.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: two parallel tracks (Local Controller vs Global Controller) showing where heavy computation is applied only inside masks.

title: Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models
authors: Subham Sekhar Sahoo, Jean-Marie Lemercier, Zhihan Yang, Justin Deschenaux, Jingyu Liu
abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their potential for faster generation. Among discrete diffusion approaches, Masked diffusion currently dominates, largely driven by strong perplexity on language modeling benchmarks. In this work, we present the first scaling law study of uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion methods. We also show that Masked diffusion models can be made approximately 12% more FLOPs-efficient when trained with a si

infographic.key_insight: This paper is the first to establish scaling laws for uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion language models, showing they scale differently than Masked diffusion. It also demonstrates that Masked diffusion can be made ≈12% more FLOPs-efficient with a simple training modification.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how different discrete diffusion formulations scale with model size and compute, and reduces computational cost of Masked diffusion to make diffusion-based generation more practical compared to autoregressive approaches.
method: Empirical scaling-law study across model sizes and compute budgets for uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion methods.
Direct comparison to Masked diffusion on language modeling benchmarks (e.g., perplexity and compute cost).
Introduce and evaluate a straightforward training modification that yields ~12% FLOPs savings for Masked diffusion models.
infographic.impact: Provides guidance for researchers and engineers choosing between diffusion formulations as they scale, and offers an easy optimization to reduce training/inference FLOPs—helpful for lowering cost and improving throughput of diffusion LMs.
visual_elements: Scaling-law plot: loss/perplexity vs. compute/model size for Masked, uniform-state, and interpolating diffusion (log–log axes).

title: Generalization from Low- to Moderate-Resolution Spectra with Neural Networks for Stellar Parameter Estimation: A Case Study with DESI
authors: Xiaosheng Zhao, Yuan-Sen Ting, Rosemary F. G. Wyse, Alexander S. Szalay, Yang Huang
abstract: Cross-survey generalization is a critical challenge in stellar spectral analysis, particularly in cases such as transferring from low- to moderate-resolution surveys. We investigate this problem using pre-trained models, focusing on simple neural networks such as multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), with a case study transferring from LAMOST low-resolution spectra (LRS) to DESI medium-resolution spectra (MRS). Specifically, we pre-train MLPs on either LRS or their embeddings and fine-tune them for app

infographic.key_insight: Pre-trained simple neural networks (MLPs), whether trained on low-resolution LAMOST spectra or on learned spectral embeddings, can be fine-tuned to deliver accurate stellar-parameter estimates on DESI medium-resolution spectra—achieving reliable cross-survey generalization with limited labeled data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the domain shift and resolution mismatch when transferring spectral-parameter models from low-resolution surveys (LAMOST) to moderate-resolution surveys (DESI), reducing the need for large labeled datasets in the target survey.
method: Pre-train lightweight MLPs on LAMOST low-resolution spectra or on embeddings derived from those spectra.
Fine-tune the pre-trained MLPs on a small labeled subset of DESI medium-resolution spectra (case study: LAMOST → DESI).
Evaluate transfer performance vs. training-from-scratch and compare embedding-based vs. raw-spectra pre-training for robustness to resolution gaps.
infographic.impact: Shows that simple architectures plus transfer learning can bridge instrument and resolution differences, enabling fast, label-efficient deployment of spectral-parameter models across surveys—useful for practitioners who need scalable, maintainable pipelines without complex architectures.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: Pre-train on LAMOST (raw spectra or embeddings) → Fine-tune on small DESI labeled set → Predict stellar parameters.

title: Learning User Interests via Reasoning and Distillation for Cross-Domain News Recommendation
authors: Mengdan Zhu, Yufan Zhao, Tao Di, Yulan Yan, Liang Zhao
abstract: News recommendation plays a critical role in online news platforms by helping users discover relevant content. Cross-domain news recommendation further requires inferring user's underlying information needs from heterogeneous signals that often extend beyond direct news consumption. A key challenge lies in moving beyond surface-level behaviors to capture deeper, reusable user interests while maintaining scalability in large-scale production systems. In this paper, we present a reinforcement lear

infographic.key_insight: Combine reasoning over heterogeneous, cross-domain user signals with knowledge distillation (and reinforcement learning) to infer deep, reusable user interests and compress that reasoning into a lightweight model for scalable news recommendation.
infographic.problem_solved: How to move beyond surface-level click behavior to recover underlying, transferable user interests from heterogeneous signals while keeping inference fast and scalable for production systems.
method: A reasoning (teacher) module that integrates cross-domain signals to infer latent user interests—trained with reinforcement learning to optimize long-term recommendation objectives.
Knowledge distillation that transfers the teacher's reasoning into a compact student model for low-latency serving.
Joint training/optimization that balances recommendation effectiveness with model size and serving efficiency for large-scale deployment.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy more personalized, generalizable news recommendation systems that capture deeper user intents without incurring high inference cost—improving relevance while meeting production latency and resource constraints.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing teacher (reasoning + RL) → distillation → student (production) pipeline
Flowchart of heterogeneous cross-domain signals (news, search, clicks, preferences) being fused into latent interest vectors

t-SNE/UMAP visualization of learned user-interest embeddings to show clustering and transferability

title: Asynchronous Verified Semantic Caching for Tiered LLM Architectures
authors: Asmit Kumar Singh, Haozhe Wang, Laxmi Naga Santosh Attaluri, Tak Chiam, Weihua Zhu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now sit in the critical path of search, assistance, and agentic workflows, making semantic caching essential for reducing inference cost and latency. Production deployments typically use a tiered static-dynamic design: a static cache of curated, offline vetted responses mined from logs, backed by a dynamic cache populated online. In practice, both tiers are commonly governed by a single embedding similarity threshold, which induces a hard tradeoff: conservative thres

infographic.key_insight: Decouple cache hits from correctness by returning optimistic cached responses immediately and verifying them asynchronously, enabling higher semantic-cache hit rates in tiered static/dynamic LLM caches without sacrificing response fidelity.
infographic.problem_solved: Production tiered semantic caches use a single embedding-similarity threshold, forcing a tradeoff between conservative thresholds (low hits, high safety) and permissive thresholds (high hits, noisy/unsafe responses). The paper solves how to increase hit rates while still ensuring cached responses are verified and trustworthy.
method: Serve optimistic hits from static/dynamic tiers immediately when similarity passes a permissive threshold, then verify correctness asynchronously using lightweight verifiers or validation checks.

If asynchronous verification fails, revoke or replace the cached response and optionally re-request a fresh LLM inference; apply tier-aware policies (e.g., stricter static cache rules, adaptive thresholds for dynamic cache).
Maintain correctness metadata and verification state so the system can audit, roll back, or refresh cached entries without blocking user-facing latency.
infographic.impact: Enables production LLM systems to substantially reduce latency and inference cost while preserving response quality and safety—making semantic caching practical at higher hit rates for search, assistants, and agent workflows.
visual_elements: Flow diagram of tiered cache: static cache + dynamic cache → optimistic serve → asynchronous verifier → revoke/refresh loop
Timeline illustrating instant response vs background verification (showing no user-facing latency impact)
Tradeoff plot: single-threshold (accuracy vs hit-rate) vs asynchronous-verified approach shifting curve toward higher hit-rate without accuracy loss
