title: LongStream: Long-Sequence Streaming Autoregressive Visual Geometry
authors: Chong Cheng, Xianda Chen, Tao Xie, Wei Yin, Weiqiang Ren
abstract: Long-sequence streaming 3D reconstruction remains a significant open challenge. Existing autoregressive models often fail when processing long sequences. They typically anchor poses to the first frame, which leads to attention decay, scale drift, and extrapolation errors. We introduce LongStream, a novel gauge-decoupled streaming visual geometry model for metric-scale scene reconstruction across thousands of frames. Our approach is threefold. First, we discard the first-frame anchor and predict

infographic.key_insight: LongStream removes dependence on a fixed first-frame anchor and introduces a gauge-decoupled, streaming autoregressive representation that preserves metric scale and accuracy over thousands of frames. This prevents attention decay, scale drift, and extrapolation errors common in long-sequence 3D reconstruction.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses failure modes of existing autoregressive visual geometry models on long sequences—specifically attention decay, scale drift, and extrapolation caused by first-frame anchoring.
method: Discard the first-frame anchor and predict poses/states in a gauge-decoupled (scale- and orientation-separable) representation to avoid propagating anchor-induced errors.
Use a streaming autoregressive architecture with bounded-state memory and targeted attention patterns to maintain long-range consistency without attention decay.
Enforce metric-scale constraints and state-decoupling during streaming updates so reconstruction remains accurate across thousands of frames.
infographic.impact: Enables robust, metric-scale 3D reconstruction over very long sequences, improving reliability for robotics, SLAM, AR/VR mapping, and any application requiring long-term spatial consistency.
visual_elements: Before/After comparison: reconstruction with first-frame anchor (drift) vs LongStream (stable scale)
Sequence timeline showing consistent scale across thousands of frames
Architecture diagram: streaming autoregressive block, bounded state buffer, and gauge-decoupled pose representation

title: Learning functional components of PDEs from data using neural networks
authors: Torkel E. Loman, Yurij Salmaniw, Antonio Leon Villares, Jose A. Carrillo, Ruth E. Baker
abstract: Partial differential equations often contain unknown functions that are difficult or impossible to measure directly, hampering our ability to derive predictions from the model. Workflows for recovering scalar PDE parameters from data are well studied: here we show how similar workflows can be used to recover functions from data. Specifically, we embed neural networks into the PDE and show how, as they are trained on data, they can approximate unknown functions with arbitrary accuracy. Using nonl

infographic.key_insight: Embed neural networks as unknown functional components inside PDEs and train them on observational data so the networks converge to the true unknown functions, enabling recovery of function-valued coefficients from data with high accuracy.
infographic.problem_solved: Many PDE models contain unknown spatially or temporally varying functions (e.g., coefficients, sources) that are hard or impossible to measure directly; prior workflows focus on scalar parameters, not full functions—this work provides a practical method to infer those functions from data.
method: Represent each unknown function in the PDE by a neural network whose input is space/time (and optionally solution features) and whose output is the function value.
Embed the neural networks into the PDE solver or physics-informed loss; combine data-misfit and PDE-consistency terms to form a differentiable loss.
Train end-to-end with gradient-based optimization so the networks adapt to reproduce observed solution data and satisfy the PDE, recovering the underlying functions.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to recover spatially/temporally varying model components directly from data, improving prediction and interpretability of physics-based ML models; lowers the barrier to fusing domain knowledge with flexible learnable components in scientific ML.
visual_elements: Schematic: PDE block diagram showing unknown function replaced by a neural network (NN icon inside PDE).
Training loop infographic: observed data → loss (data + PDE residual) → backprop → updated NN, iterated until convergence.
Comparison plots: true vs. recovered function (line or heatmap) and corresponding PDE solution before/after recovery.
Error/residual heatmap or convergence curve showing decreasing PDE residual and data-mismatch during training.

title: Quantization-Robust LLM Unlearning via Low-Rank Adaptation
authors: João Vitor Boer Abitante, Joana Meneguzzo Pasquali, Luan Fonseca Garcia, Ewerton de Oliveira, Thomas da Silva Paula
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning aims to remove targeted knowledge from a trained model, but practical deployments often require post-training quantization (PTQ) for efficient inference. However, aggressive low-bit PTQ can mask or erase unlearning updates, causing quantized models to revert to pre-unlearning behavior. We show that standard full-parameter fine-tuning often induce parameter changes that are too small to survive 4-bit quantization. We propose quantization-robust unlearning via

infographic.key_insight: Applying low-rank adaptation (LoRA-style) for targeted LLM unlearning produces parameter updates that survive aggressive post-training quantization (e.g., 4-bit), avoiding the reversion to pre-unlearning behavior seen with full-parameter fine-tuning.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard full-parameter unlearning updates are often too small and get masked or erased by aggressive post-training quantization, so quantized deployments revert to their pre-unlearning behavior—this work makes unlearning robust to low-bit quantization.
method: Perform unlearning via low-rank adapters (LoRA) instead of full-parameter fine-tuning to concentrate updates in structured, higher-magnitude low-rank deltas.
Design/scale adapters and training objectives so the resulting parameter deltas are quantization-resilient (optionally combined with lightweight quantization-aware tuning).
Deploy by either keeping adapters as runtime patches or merging them into weights with a quantization-preserving merge strategy so the unlearning effect persists after PTQ.
infographic.impact: Enables compliant, privacy-preserving LLM unlearning that survives aggressive low-bit quantization, making unlearning practical for memory- and compute-constrained deployments without full model retraining or retaining full‑precision checkpoints.

title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
authors: Joseph Szymborski, Amin Emad
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 13 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01176-7

The usage of pretrained protein language models (pLMs) is rapidly growing. However, Szymborski and Emad find that pretrained pLMs can be a source of data leakage in the task of protein–protein interaction inference, showing inflated performance scores.

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can introduce subtle data leakage into protein–protein interaction (PPI) inference pipelines, causing artificially inflated performance metrics that overstate real predictive ability.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes how using pretrained pLM embeddings can leak dataset-specific information into PPI models, exposing a blind spot in common evaluation practices.
method: Systematic empirical analysis comparing PPI inference results with and without pLM-derived features to isolate the effect of pretrained embeddings.
Controlled experiments and evaluation splits designed to reveal leakage-driven performance gains vs. genuine generalization.
Quantification of performance inflation and recommendations for stricter data-splitting and validation protocols to avoid misleading results.
infographic.impact: Alerts ML practitioners that off-the-shelf pLM features can mask true model performance on PPI tasks, prompting more rigorous evaluation standards to ensure reliable biological predictions.
visual_elements: Schematic showing how pretrained embeddings can carry information from training/related sequences into downstream PPI predictors (arrow from pLM to leakage icon).
Bar chart comparing reported (inflated) vs. corrected performance scores across models with and without pLM features.
Flowchart of recommended evaluation protocol (dataset split → leakage checks → model training → unbiased evaluation).
Warning/alert icon paired with checklist: data-split controls, sequence-similarity filtering, ablation tests.

title: FlashSchNet: Fast and Accurate Coarse-Grained Neural Network Molecular Dynamics
authors: Pingzhi Li, Hongxuan Li, Zirui Liu, Xingcheng Lin, Tianlong Chen
abstract: Graph neural network (GNN) potentials such as SchNet improve the accuracy and transferability of molecular dynamics (MD) simulation by learning many-body interactions, but remain slower than classical force fields due to fragmented kernels and memory-bound pipelines that underutilize GPUs. We show that a missing principle is making GNN-MD IO-aware, carefully accounting for reads and writes between GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and on-chip SRAM. We present FlashSchNet, an efficient and accurate

infographic.key_insight: FlashSchNet makes GNN-driven molecular dynamics IO-aware: by minimizing and reorganizing reads/writes between GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and on-chip SRAM, it dramatically improves GPU utilization and delivers SchNet-level accuracy at much higher throughput.
infographic.problem_solved: GNN potentials (e.g., SchNet) are accurate but slow because fragmented kernels and memory-bound pipelines underutilize GPUs; the paper addresses this by treating GNN-MD as an IO-bound workload and optimizing memory traffic and kernel structure.
method: Design an IO-aware execution model that explicitly accounts for HBM↔SRAM reads and writes and optimizes data movement.
Apply kernel fusion, on-chip tiling/buffering, and compute/communication overlap to raise arithmetic intensity and reduce memory stalls.
Optimize data layout and batch/neighbor processing to preserve SchNet-level accuracy while maximizing GPU throughput.
infographic.impact: Enables much faster coarse-grained MD simulations with GNN accuracy, making larger and longer simulations cost- and time-feasible for AI/ML practitioners and HPC applications; the IO-aware principles generalize to other memory-bound GNN workloads.
visual_elements: Diagram of GPU memory hierarchy (HBM ↔ SRAM) showing reduced read/write paths after IO-aware optimization.

title: Monocular Markerless Motion Capture Enables Quantitative Assessment of Upper Extremity Reachable Workspace
authors: Seth Donahue, J. D. Peiffer, R. Tyler Richardson, Yishan Zhong, Shaun Q. Y. Tan
abstract: To validate a clinically accessible approach for quantifying the Upper Extremity Reachable Workspace (UERW) using a single (monocular) camera and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Markerless Motion Capture (MMC) for biomechanical analysis. Objective assessment and validation of these techniques for specific clinically oriented tasks are crucial for their adoption in clinical motion analysis. AI-driven monocular MMC reduces the barriers to adoption in the clinic and has the potential to reduce

infographic.key_insight: AI-driven monocular markerless motion capture can accurately quantify the Upper Extremity Reachable Workspace (UERW) from a single camera, making objective biomechanical assessment feasible in routine clinical settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Replaces expensive, complex multi-camera/marker-based motion-capture setups with a clinically accessible, single-camera pipeline that objectively measures UERW, lowering barriers to adoption in clinics and rehab settings.
method: Capture monocular video and apply AI pose-estimation to extract 2D/estimated 3D joint keypoints.
Use a biomechanical reconstruction pipeline to compute the 3D reachable workspace and standardized UERW metrics from keypoints.
Validate the monocular MMC outputs against clinical gold-standard measurements (e.g., marker-based systems) using statistical comparisons and error analyses.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to build and deploy lightweight, validated clinical motion-analysis tools that support remote or low-cost assessment, facilitate larger-scale data collection, and accelerate translational research in rehabilitation and biomechanics.

title: Semantic Chunking and the Entropy of Natural Language
authors: Weishun Zhong, Doron Sivan, Tankut Can, Mikhail Katkov, Misha Tsodyks
abstract: The entropy rate of printed English is famously estimated to be about one bit per character, a benchmark that modern large language models (LLMs) have only recently approached. This entropy rate implies that English contains nearly 80 percent redundancy relative to the five bits per character expected for random text. We introduce a statistical model that attempts to capture the intricate multi-scale structure of natural language, providing a first-principles account of this redundancy level. Ou

infographic.key_insight: Natural language’s low entropy (~1 bit/char) can be explained by a multi-scale statistical process of semantic chunking: words and phrases form hierarchical chunks that create high redundancy across scales, accounting for most of English’s information compression.
infographic.problem_solved: Explains why printed English exhibits ~80% redundancy (far below random-text entropy) by providing a first-principles statistical model that captures multi-scale structure and long-range dependencies in language.
method: Introduce a generative statistical model in which meaning-bearing units form semantic chunks at multiple scales (words, phrases, clauses), with explicit rules for chunk formation and overlap.
Derive entropy-rate predictions analytically and validate with numerical simulations and comparisons to empirical entropy estimates from corpora and modern LLM outputs.
Analyze how chunk-size distributions and inter-chunk correlations reduce per-character uncertainty, linking model parameters to observed redundancy levels.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled explanation of language redundancy that informs compression limits, evaluation benchmarks for LLMs, and architectural choices to better capture hierarchical, long-range dependencies.
visual_elements: Schematic diagram of hierarchical semantic chunking (tokens → words → phrases → clauses) showing information flow and dependencies.

title: CoPE-VideoLM: Codec Primitives For Efficient Video Language Models
authors: Sayan Deb Sarkar, Rémi Pautrat, Ondrej Miksik, Marc Pollefeys, Iro Armeni
abstract: Video Language Models (VideoLMs) empower AI systems to understand temporal dynamics in videos. To fit to the maximum context window constraint, current methods use keyframe sampling which can miss both macro-level events and micro-level details due to the sparse temporal coverage. Furthermore, processing full images and their tokens for each frame incurs substantial computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose to leverage video codec primitives (specifically motion vectors an

infographic.key_insight: CoPE-VideoLM uses video codec primitives (e.g., motion vectors and residuals) as compact, semantically meaningful inputs to Video Language Models, enabling dense temporal coverage with far lower compute than processing full RGB frames.
infographic.problem_solved: Current VideoLMs rely on sparse keyframe sampling or expensive per-frame image processing, which either misses short-lived events or incurs high computational cost and limits temporal context.
method: Extract codec primitives (motion vectors + residual/transform coefficients) from compressed video and convert them into compact tokens/features instead of decoding full frames.
Use motion vectors to propagate and align features across time, and combine residual tokens for appearance/detail, feeding the combined representation into a lightweight VideoLM backbone.
Operate in the compressed domain to increase effective temporal coverage within the same context window and reduce per-frame token/computation overhead.
infographic.impact: This approach enables VideoLMs to cover longer temporal contexts and capture both macro events and micro details while lowering compute and memory needs—making video-language tasks (QA, captioning, retrieval) more scalable and practical.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: raw compressed video → codec primitive extraction (motion vectors, residuals) → tokenization → VideoLM, highlighting avoided full-frame decoding.
Before/after timeline: sparse keyframe sampling missing short events versus dense codec-primitive coverage capturing micro-events.

title: FlexAM: Flexible Appearance-Motion Decomposition for Versatile Video Generation Control
authors: Mingzhi Sheng, Zekai Gu, Peng Li, Cheng Lin, Hao-Xiang Guo
abstract: Effective and generalizable control in video generation remains a significant challenge. While many methods rely on ambiguous or task-specific signals, we argue that a fundamental disentanglement of "appearance" and "motion" provides a more robust and scalable pathway. We propose FlexAM, a unified framework built upon a novel 3D control signal. This signal represents video dynamics as a point cloud, introducing three key enhancements: multi-frequency positional encoding to distinguish fine-grain

infographic.key_insight: Separating appearance and motion using a 3D point-cloud control signal with multi-frequency positional encoding enables flexible, generalizable control over video generation in a task-agnostic way.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a robust, interpretable alternative to ambiguous or task-specific control signals for video generation by explicitly decomposing and independently controlling appearance and motion dynamics.
method: Represent video dynamics as a 3D point-cloud control signal that encodes motion across space and time.
Apply multi-frequency positional encoding to the point cloud so both coarse and fine-grained motion patterns are captured and disambiguated.
Use an appearance–motion decomposition that can be plugged into existing generative pipelines (e.g., diffusion-based video models) to enable independent editing and flexible conditioning.
infographic.impact: Enables precise, reusable control primitives for video synthesis and editing, improving transferability across tasks and making interactive or conditional video generation more practical for practitioners.

title: Imitating What Works: Simulation-Filtered Modular Policy Learning from Human Videos
authors: Albert J. Zhai, Kuo-Hao Zeng, Jiasen Lu, Ali Farhadi, Shenlong Wang
abstract: The ability to learn manipulation skills by watching videos of humans has the potential to unlock a new source of highly scalable data for robot learning. Here, we tackle prehensile manipulation, in which tasks involve grasping an object before performing various post-grasp motions. Human videos offer strong signals for learning the post-grasp motions, but they are less useful for learning the prerequisite grasping behaviors, especially for robots without human-like hands. A promising way forwar

infographic.key_insight: Use simulation to filter which segments of human videos are physically executable by a target robot, then learn modular policies (grasp + post-grasp) from the filtered data so robots can imitate realistic human motions even with non-human hands.
infographic.problem_solved: Human videos provide rich signals for post-grasp manipulation but often contain grasps that robots cannot physically perform; this work solves how to reliably leverage human video data for robot prehensile manipulation by selecting only simulation-feasible demonstrations and training modular controllers.
method: Automatically parse human videos into grasp and post-grasp segments and propose candidate robot grasps.
Simulate candidate grasps and filter out video segments that are not physically executable by the target robot (simulation-filtering).
Train modular policies: a grasping policy (from simulation/robot data) and a post-grasp imitation policy (from filtered human video segments), then combine them for execution.
infographic.impact: Enables large-scale use of widely available human video data for robot manipulation while avoiding infeasible demonstrations, lowering the need for costly robot-specific data and speeding development of practical manipulation policies.

title: Agentic Test-Time Scaling for WebAgents
authors: Nicholas Lee, Lutfi Eren Erdogan, Chris Joseph John, Surya Krishnapillai, Michael W. Mahoney
abstract: Test-time scaling has become a standard way to improve performance and boost reliability of neural network models. However, its behavior on agentic, multi-step tasks remains less well-understood: small per-step errors can compound over long horizons; and we find that naive policies that uniformly increase sampling show diminishing returns. In this work, we present CATTS, a simple technique for dynamically allocating compute for multi-step agents. We first conduct an empirical study of inference-

infographic.key_insight: CATTS (a dynamic test-time compute allocation strategy) improves multi-step agent performance by allocating extra compute to the few hard steps where per-step errors compound, instead of uniformly increasing sampling across all steps.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces error compounding and diminishing returns of uniform test-time scaling for agentic, long-horizon web tasks by making compute allocation adaptive to per-step difficulty.
method: Detect per-step difficulty/uncertainty (e.g., low confidence, disagreement, or low value estimates) during agent execution.
Dynamically reallocate additional inference compute (more samples, larger beam, or extra queries) to high-difficulty steps while keeping cheap processing for easy steps.
Use lightweight heuristics/predictors to decide when and how much extra compute to spend, yielding better trade-offs than uniform scaling.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get a simple, cost-effective way to boost reliability and success rates for multi-step web agents and other agentic systems without linearly increasing inference cost. CATTS enables more robust long-horizon behavior by targeting compute where it matters most.
visual_elements: Flow diagram of an agent performing multiple steps with variable compute icons showing more compute on a few hard steps (CATTS) vs equal compute per step (uniform).

title: Self-Supervised Learning via Flow-Guided Neural Operator on Time-Series Data
authors: Duy Nguyen, Jiachen Yao, Jiayun Wang, Julius Berner, Animashree Anandkumar
abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a powerful paradigm for learning from unlabeled time-series data. However, popular methods such as masked autoencoders (MAEs) rely on reconstructing inputs from a fixed, predetermined masking ratio. Instead of this static design, we propose treating the corruption level as a new degree of freedom for representation learning, enhancing flexibility and performance. To achieve this, we introduce the Flow-Guided Neural Operator (FGNO), a novel framework combining op

infographic.key_insight: Instead of using a single, fixed masking/corruption ratio for self-supervised time-series learning, treat the corruption level as a controllable degree of freedom and learn representations by modeling the entire corruption "flow" with a Flow-Guided Neural Operator (FGNO). This yields more flexible, robust representations across corruption levels.
infographic.problem_solved: Most SSL methods for time-series (e.g., MAE-style) rely on a predetermined, static masking/corruption ratio, which limits robustness, requires costly hyperparameter tuning, and can fail to capture multi-scale temporal dynamics.
method: Introduce FGNO: a neural-operator-style module that models mappings across a continuum of corruption levels (the "flow") rather than a single fixed mask.
Use self-supervised reconstruction / prediction objectives over corrupted-to-clean flows so the model learns representations stable across varying corruption strengths and time scales.
Train end-to-end with flow-guided sampling (varying corruption levels during training) to produce transferable, robust time-series embeddings without per-task masking tuning.
infographic.impact: FGNO reduces sensitivity to masking hyperparameters and produces flexible, robust time-series representations that transfer better across downstream tasks and corruption regimes, simplifying SSL pipelines for practitioners.
visual_elements: Schematic comparing static masking (single ratio) vs. flow-guided corruption (continuum) — arrow showing learned mapping across corruption levels.
Architecture block: FGNO module inserted between corrupted input and representation head, with icons for time-series, operator, and learned flow.

title: Think like a Scientist: Physics-guided LLM Agent for Equation Discovery
authors: Jianke Yang, Ohm Venkatachalam, Mohammad Kianezhad, Sharvaree Vadgama, Rose Yu
abstract: Explaining observed phenomena through symbolic, interpretable formulas is a fundamental goal of science. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools for symbolic equation discovery, owing to their broad domain knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities. However, most existing LLM-based systems try to guess equations directly from data, without modeling the multi-step reasoning process that scientists often follow: first inferring physical properties such as symmetries

infographic.key_insight: A physics-guided LLM agent that reasons like a scientist—inferring physical properties (e.g., symmetries, invariances) then iteratively proposing and testing symbolic hypotheses—discovers interpretable governing equations more reliably than directly guessing formulas from data.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing LLM-based equation discovery systems typically guess equations directly from data and miss the multi-step scientific reasoning and physics constraints, producing spurious or poorly generalizing formulas.
method: Physics-guided LLM agent: infer physical properties (symmetries, invariances, conservation laws) from observations before proposing models.
Iterative scientist loop: generate hypotheses, design targeted experiments or queries, run symbolic regression, then verify and refine using physics priors.
Physics priors and symbolic verification prune the search space and improve robustness and interpretability of discovered equations.
infographic.impact: Enables more data-efficient, interpretable, and physically consistent equation discovery by combining LLM reasoning with domain priors—useful for scientific ML, modeling, and automated discovery workflows.

title: Scaling Verification Can Be More Effective than Scaling Policy Learning for Vision-Language-Action Alignment
authors: Jacky Kwok, Xilun Zhang, Mengdi Xu, Yuejiang Liu, Azalia Mirhoseini
abstract: The long-standing vision of general-purpose robots hinges on their ability to understand and act upon natural language instructions. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made remarkable progress toward this goal, yet their generated actions can still misalign with the given instructions. In this paper, we investigate test-time verification as a means to shrink the "intention-action gap.'' We first characterize the test-time scaling law for embodied instruction following and demonstrate that

infographic.key_insight: At test time, investing compute into verification (sampling + scoring/reranking) reduces instruction–action misalignment more effectively than further scaling the policy model or its training data. A dedicated verifier and more verification compute follow a favorable scaling law for embodied instruction following.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the "intention–action gap" in Vision–Language–Action models by reducing incorrect or misaligned actions produced in response to natural language instructions without retraining or heavily scaling the policy.
method: Characterize test-time scaling laws for embodied instruction following and show verifier compute/size yields larger marginal gains than policy scaling.
Generate multiple candidate action trajectories from a policy, then use a learned verifier to score alignment between each trajectory, the visual observations, and the instruction.
Select or rerank actions at inference based on verifier scores (sampling + reranking / search), allowing better alignment with fixed policies.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to improve robot instruction-following accuracy by allocating inference-time compute to verification rather than costly policy retraining or scaling. This provides a practical, modular path to safer and more reliable VLA systems.

Pipeline diagram: policy generates candidate trajectories → verifier scores each → best action selected (sample-and-rerank)

title: Function-Space Decoupled Diffusion for Forward and Inverse Modeling in Carbon Capture and Storage
authors: Xin Ju, Jiachen Yao, Anima Anandkumar, Sally M. Benson, Gege Wen
abstract: Accurate characterization of subsurface flow is critical for Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) but remains challenged by the ill-posed nature of inverse problems with sparse observations. We present Fun-DDPS, a generative framework that combines function-space diffusion models with differentiable neural operator surrogates for both forward and inverse modeling. Our approach learns a prior distribution over geological parameters (geomodel) using a single-channel diffusion model, then leverages a L

infographic.key_insight: Fun-DDPS couples a function-space diffusion prior over geological fields with a differentiable neural-operator surrogate, enabling fast, accurate forward simulations and efficient inverse (posterior) sampling for subsurface flow in CCS from sparse observations.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses ill-posed, computationally expensive inverse problems in Carbon Capture and Storage where sparse observations and complex geological priors make uncertainty-aware subsurface characterization difficult.
method: Learn a function-space (single-channel) diffusion model as a prior over spatial geological parameters (geomodels).
Train a differentiable neural operator surrogate to approximate the physics-based forward map (PDE solver) for fast, gradient-enabled predictions.
Decouple sampling of geomodels from expensive solvers by combining the diffusion prior with the neural operator in a conditional/inference pipeline for forward and inverse modeling.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, differentiable inference and uncertainty quantification for PDE-governed geoscience problems; practitioners can get orders-of-magnitude faster inversion and easy integration of learned priors into downstream decision workflows.

title: MonarchRT: Efficient Attention for Real-Time Video Generation
authors: Krish Agarwal, Zhuoming Chen, Cheng Luo, Yongqi Chen, Haizhong Zheng
abstract: Real-time video generation with Diffusion Transformers is bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of 3D self-attention, especially in real-time regimes that are both few-step and autoregressive, where errors compound across time and each denoising step must carry substantially more information. In this setting, we find that prior sparse-attention approximations break down, despite showing strong results for bidirectional, many-step diffusion. Specifically, we observe that video attention is not relia

infographic.key_insight: MonarchRT introduces an attention design for diffusion Transformers that preserves essential long-range video context while reducing the quadratic 3D self-attention bottleneck, enabling high-quality, few-step autoregressive video generation in real time.
infographic.problem_solved: Quadratic cost of 3D self-attention makes diffusion-based video generation too slow and memory-intensive for real-time, few-step autoregressive pipelines; prior sparse approximations collapse under the strict information-per-step demands of this regime.
method: Design of a streaming-friendly attention module that combines temporal recurrence/summary with spatially local + selectively global attention to keep key video context while avoiding full 3D quadratic costs.
Attention factorization and compact key/value caching across timesteps so each denoising step reuses compressed global context, yielding near-linear time/memory scaling in practice.
Routing/selection mechanism (learned or structured) that preserves critical cross-frame dependencies for few-step autoregressive diffusion, robust where previous sparse patterns fail.
infographic.impact: Enables practical real-time video generation with diffusion Transformers by dramatically reducing latency and memory without sacrificing generation fidelity—useful for interactive systems, live content creation, and deployment on resource-constrained hardware.

title: Reusability Report: Evaluating the performance of a meta-learning foundation model on predicting the antibacterial activity of natural products
authors: Caitlin M. Butt, Allison S. Walker
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 12 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01187-y

This Reusability Report tests the ability of a foundation model, ActFound, to predict the antibacterial activity of plant natural products. We found that although all models performed poorly on this task, ActFound performed better than similar models.

infographic.key_insight: A meta-learning foundation model (ActFound) outperforms comparable models at predicting antibacterial activity of plant natural products, but absolute predictive performance is low. This indicates limited out-of-the-box reusability for specialized biochemical tasks despite relative gains.
infographic.problem_solved: Evaluates whether foundation/meta-learning models can be reused to predict antibacterial activity of plant-derived natural products without extensive task-specific retraining.
method: Benchmark ActFound against similar foundation models on a curated dataset of plant natural products labeled for antibacterial activity.
Quantify performance using standard classification metrics (e.g., AUROC/accuracy) with cross-validation to assess robustness.
Perform error and chemical-space analyses to identify where models fail and which molecules drive poor performance.
infographic.impact: Shows AI/ML practitioners that meta-learning foundation models can offer a better starting point for niche biochemical prediction tasks but should not be relied on zero-shot; domain-specific fine-tuning, targeted datasets, or model adaptation remain necessary for usable performance.

title: UniT: Unified Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Test-time Scaling
authors: Leon Liangyu Chen, Haoyu Ma, Zhipeng Fan, Ziqi Huang, Animesh Sinha
abstract: Unified models can handle both multimodal understanding and generation within a single architecture, yet they typically operate in a single pass without iteratively refining their outputs. Many multimodal tasks, especially those involving complex spatial compositions, multiple interacting objects, or evolving instructions, require decomposing instructions, verifying intermediate results, and making iterative corrections. While test-time scaling (TTS) has demonstrated that allocating additional i

infographic.key_insight: UniT enables unified multimodal models to perform chain-of-thought style iterative reasoning at test time, using extra inference compute to decompose, verify, and correct multimodal outputs for harder spatial and multi-step tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Unified single-pass multimodal architectures struggle with complex spatial compositions, interacting objects, and evolving instructions because they lack an iterative refinement/verification loop at inference time.
method: Introduce test-time scaling (TTS) for unified multimodal models: run multiple inference steps (decompose → reason → verify → correct) without retraining the base model.
Use a lightweight controller and cross-modal feedback buffer to aggregate intermediate multimodal predictions and guide subsequent reasoning passes.
Leverage multimodal chain-of-thought prompts/representations so the model can expose intermediate decisions (textual and visual) that are checked and iteratively refined.
infographic.impact: Practitioners can improve robustness and accuracy of multimodal systems by allocating extra test-time compute instead of redesigning or retraining models, making high-stakes or compositional tasks (e.g., VQA, scene editing, robotics instructions) more reliable and interpretable.

title: On-Policy Context Distillation for Language Models
authors: Tianzhu Ye, Li Dong, Xun Wu, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei
abstract: Context distillation enables language models to internalize in-context knowledge into their parameters. In our work, we propose On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD), a framework that bridges on-policy distillation with context distillation by training a student model on its own generated trajectories while minimizing reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence against a context-conditioned teacher. We demonstrate the effectiveness of OPCD on two important applications: experiential knowledge distillati

infographic.key_insight: On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD) trains a student on its own generated contexts and aligns it to a context-conditioned teacher by minimizing reverse KL, allowing the model to internalize in‑context knowledge into its parameters.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the distribution mismatch between teacher-generated contexts and student usage: existing context distillation methods struggle to transfer in‑context (experiential) knowledge effectively into model parameters, limiting generalization and requiring large prompts or teacher rollouts.
method: On-policy rollouts: the student generates its own context-conditioned trajectories to train on the distributions it will actually encounter.

Reverse KL alignment: minimize KL(student || teacher) between student-generated conditionals and a context-conditioned teacher to encourage the student to match teacher behavior while using its own outputs.

Context-conditioned teacher targets: use a teacher that provides conditional distributions given contexts so the student internalizes experiential knowledge into weights rather than relying on external prompts.
infographic.impact: Enables language models to absorb in-context knowledge into model weights, reducing reliance on long prompting or teacher rollouts and improving sample efficiency for downstream tasks and model compression/fine-tuning workflows.

title: CM2: Reinforcement Learning with Checklist Rewards for Multi-Turn and Multi-Step Agentic Tool Use
authors: Zhen Zhang, Kaiqiang Song, Xun Wang, Yebowen Hu, Weixiang Yan
abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to solve real-world tasks by reasoning over multi-turn user interactions and invoking external tools. However, applying reinforcement learning to such settings remains difficult: realistic objectives often lack verifiable rewards and instead emphasize open-ended behaviors; moreover, RL for multi-turn, multi-step agentic tool use is still underexplored; and building and maintaining executable tool environments is costly, limiting scale and coverage. We propose CM2,

infographic.key_insight: Introducing checklist-style rewards provides verifiable intermediate signals that make reinforcement learning effective for multi-turn, multi-step agentic tool use without requiring fully executable tool environments.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables RL for open-ended, multi-turn tool-using agents where final rewards are sparse or unverifiable and constructing full tool environments is costly.
method: Design checklist rewards that decompose tasks into verifiable intermediate subgoals and provide dense, structured feedback during multi-turn interactions.
Train agents with RL using these checklist rewards to guide multi-step tool invocations and dialogue policies across turns.
Evaluate agentic tool use without exhaustive executable environments by validating subgoal completion and chain-of-actions instead of relying solely on terminal success signals.
infographic.impact: Makes RL practical for complex conversational agents that must coordinate multiple tools and steps, reducing environment engineering overhead and improving learning stability and interpretability.

title: T3D: Few-Step Diffusion Language Models via Trajectory Self-Distillation with Direct Discriminative Optimization
authors: Tunyu Zhang, Xinxi Zhang, Ligong Han, Haizhou Shi, Xiaoxiao He
abstract: Diffusion large language models (DLLMs) have the potential to enable fast text generation by decoding multiple tokens in parallel. However, in practice, their inference efficiency is constrained by the need for many refinement steps, while aggressively reducing the number of steps leads to a substantial degradation in generation quality. To alleviate this, we propose a trajectory self-distillation framework that improves few-step decoding by distilling the model's own generative trajectories. We

infographic.key_insight: T3D uses the model's own multi-step generative trajectories to self-distill a few-step decoder, combined with a direct discriminative optimization objective, enabling diffusion LLMs to generate high-quality text with far fewer refinement steps.
infographic.problem_solved: Diffusion LLMs can decode tokens in parallel but require many refinement steps for good quality; aggressively reducing steps degrades generation. T3D addresses how to retain high-quality outputs while drastically cutting the number of refinement steps.
method: Trajectory self-distillation: collect the model's multi-step generative trajectories and use them as targets to train a few-step student decoder.
Direct discriminative optimization: apply a discriminative loss to directly encourage the student to prefer higher-quality trajectory states and correct errors from aggressive step reduction.
Jointly align parallel-token diffusion decoding with distilled trajectories so the student learns to reproduce the teacher's final-quality outputs in far fewer steps.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, low-latency deployment of diffusion-based language models by preserving generation quality while reducing inference steps — important for real-time systems and cost-efficient large-model serving.

title: GENIUS: Generative Fluid Intelligence Evaluation Suite
authors: Ruichuan An, Sihan Yang, Ziyu Guo, Wei Dai, Zijun Shen
abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) have shown remarkable progress in visual generation. Yet, existing benchmarks predominantly assess $\textit{Crystallized Intelligence}$, which relies on recalling accumulated knowledge and learned schemas. This focus overlooks $\textit{Generative Fluid Intelligence (GFI)}$: the capacity to induce patterns, reason through constraints, and adapt to novel scenarios on the fly. To rigorously assess this capability, we introduce $\textbf{GENIUS}$ ($\textbf{GEN}$ Fluid

infographic.key_insight: GENIUS introduces a focused benchmark to measure Generative Fluid Intelligence (GFI) — a model's ability to induce patterns, reason under constraints, and adapt to novel, on-the-fly scenarios — revealing gaps that standard 'crystallized' benchmarks miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing multimodal benchmarks mainly test memorized knowledge and fixed schemas; GENIUS fills the gap by providing tasks and metrics that evaluate models' real-time pattern induction, constraint reasoning, and adaptive generative behavior.
method: Design a suite of procedurally generated, multimodal tasks that require pattern induction, rule inference, and constrained generation (novel combinations not seen during training).
Define evaluation metrics targeting generative fidelity, rule-consistency, generalization to novel constraints, and adaptation speed.
Release baselines, evaluation tools, and reproducible workflows to measure and compare UMMs on GFI-specific capabilities.
infographic.impact: GENIUS gives researchers and engineers a targeted way to diagnose and improve models' adaptive generative reasoning, guiding development of UMMs that generalize beyond memorized examples and handle novel constraints in real applications.

title: When large language models are reliable for judging empathic communication
authors: Aakriti Kumar, Nalin Poungpeth, Diyi Yang, Erina Farrell, Bruce L. Lambert
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 11 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01169-6

Kumar et al. show that large language models (LLMs) nearly match expert reliability and outperform laypeople when assessing empathic communication across multiple frameworks. The performance of both LLMs and experts depends on clear and specific evaluation criteria.

infographic.key_insight: Large language models can nearly match experts and outperform laypeople when rating empathic communication — provided the evaluation criteria are clear and specific.
infographic.problem_solved: Human evaluation of empathy is costly, variable, and slow; the paper evaluates whether LLMs can provide reliable, scalable judgments comparable to expert raters.
method: Systematic comparison of ratings from LLMs, domain experts, and lay raters across multiple established empathic-communication frameworks.
Quantified agreement and reliability (e.g., inter-rater metrics) to benchmark LLM performance against humans.
Tested the effect of rubric/prompt clarity and specificity on rater reliability to identify conditions where LLMs excel.
infographic.impact: Shows LLMs can be a scalable, cost-effective alternative for reliable empathy assessment in research and product workflows — but only when paired with clear evaluation rubrics, informing better human-AI evaluation design.

title: YOR: Your Own Mobile Manipulator for Generalizable Robotics
authors: Manan H Anjaria, Mehmet Enes Erciyes, Vedant Ghatnekar, Neha Navarkar, Haritheja Etukuru
abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have generated significant interest in capable platforms that may eventually approach human-level competence. This interest, combined with the commoditization of actuators, has propelled growth in low-cost robotic platforms. However, the optimal form factor for mobile manipulation, especially on a budget, remains an open question. We introduce YOR, an open-source, low-cost mobile manipulator that integrates an omnidirectional base, a telescopic vertical lift, an

infographic.key_insight: YOR presents an open-source, low-cost mobile manipulator that combines an omnidirectional base and telescopic vertical lift to deliver a compact, versatile form factor designed for generalizable robot learning experiments.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of an affordable, reproducible, and task-flexible mobile manipulation platform optimized for research on generalization and real-world robot learning.
method: Design and open-source release of a modular hardware platform focused on omnidirectional mobility plus telescopic reach to maximize workspace in a small footprint.
Standardized interfaces and software integration to plug into learning pipelines (sim-to-real and on-robot evaluation) and enable repeatable experiments.
Cost-performance optimization and empirical validation across representative manipulation tasks to demonstrate practicality for research use.
infographic.impact: Lowers the barrier to entry for robotics and ML researchers by providing an accessible, reproducible platform for developing and evaluating generalizable manipulation algorithms, accelerating iteration and comparison across labs.

title: The Offline-Frontier Shift: Diagnosing Distributional Limits in Generative Multi-Objective Optimization
authors: Stephanie Holly, Alexandru-Ciprian Zăvoianu, Siegfried Silber, Sepp Hochreiter, Werner Zellinger
abstract: Offline multi-objective optimization (MOO) aims to recover Pareto-optimal designs given a finite, static dataset. Recent generative approaches, including diffusion models, show strong performance under hypervolume, yet their behavior under other established MOO metrics is less understood. We show that generative methods systematically underperform evolutionary alternatives with respect to other metrics, such as generational distance. We relate this failure mode to the offline-frontier shift, i.e

infographic.key_insight: Generative MOO methods (including diffusion-based generators) can achieve high hypervolume but systematically fail on other metrics (e.g., generational distance) because they reproduce a dataset-induced Pareto surface rather than the true Pareto frontier — a phenomenon the authors call the "offline-frontier shift."
infographic.problem_solved: Diagnoses why state-of-the-art generative approaches for offline multi-objective optimization perform well under hypervolume yet underperform on other established metrics, by identifying and characterizing a distributional failure mode caused by limited, static datasets.
method: Empirical comparison of generative (including diffusion) and evolutionary baselines across multiple MOO metrics (hypervolume, generational distance, coverage, etc.).
Define and analyze the "offline-frontier shift": how the dataset’s Pareto frontier diverges from the true frontier and biases generated solutions.
Diagnostic analyses linking dataset support and model behavior to metric-specific failures (coverage, closeness, and diversity).
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a clearer evaluation framework and a warning: high hypervolume alone can be misleading for generative MOO. Use multiple metrics and inspect dataset-induced biases when selecting or trusting offline generative optimizers.

title: Beyond VLM-Based Rewards: Diffusion-Native Latent Reward Modeling
authors: Gongye Liu, Bo Yang, Yida Zhi, Zhizhou Zhong, Lei Ke
abstract: Preference optimization for diffusion and flow-matching models relies on reward functions that are both discriminatively robust and computationally efficient. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have emerged as the primary reward provider, leveraging their rich multimodal priors to guide alignment. However, their computation and memory cost can be substantial, and optimizing a latent diffusion generator through a pixel-space reward introduces a domain mismatch that complicates alignment. In this paper

infographic.key_insight: Train reward models directly in the diffusion model's latent space (diffusion-native) instead of relying on expensive pixel-space VLM rewards—this reduces compute/memory costs and removes the domain mismatch between reward and generator.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the high computational/memory cost and domain mismatch that arise when using pixel-space Vision–Language Model (VLM) rewards to steer latent diffusion and flow‑matching generators during preference optimization.
method: Define and train a reward model that operates in the generator's latent space (latent reward modeling) so rewards align with the diffusion representation.
Use preference-driven objectives (e.g., pairwise comparisons or contrastive signals) adapted to latent embeddings to learn discriminative, robust rewards.
Integrate the latent reward into preference optimization loops for diffusion and flow‑matching models to guide generation with lower overhead and tighter alignment.
infographic.impact: Makes alignment and preference optimization for diffusion/flow models more computationally efficient and semantically consistent, enabling faster iteration and deployment of aligned generative models without heavy VLM dependencies.

title: FormalJudge: A Neuro-Symbolic Paradigm for Agentic Oversight
authors: Jiayi Zhou, Yang Sheng, Hantao Lou, Yaodong Yang, Jie Fu
abstract: As LLM-based agents increasingly operate in high-stakes domains with real-world consequences, ensuring their behavioral safety becomes paramount. The dominant oversight paradigm, LLM-as-a-Judge, faces a fundamental dilemma: how can probabilistic systems reliably supervise other probabilistic systems without inheriting their failure modes? We argue that formal verification offers a principled escape from this dilemma, yet its adoption has been hindered by a critical bottleneck: the translation fr

infographic.key_insight: FormalJudge presents a neuro-symbolic oversight paradigm that converts natural-language policies into formal specifications and applies formal verification to certify and correct LLM-agent behavior, reducing reliance on purely probabilistic judgments.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the reliability gap of the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm by overcoming the bottleneck of translating human policies into machine-checkable specifications and providing verifiable, actionable oversight for agentic systems.
method: Neuro-symbolic translation: use neural models plus symbolic parsing to convert natural-language policies and agent intents into formal specifications (e.g., temporal logic).
Formal verification: apply model checking / symbolic analysis to agent plans and behaviors against the formal specs to produce pass/fail decisions and concrete counterexamples.

Corrective loop & monitoring: feed verification counterexamples back to agents for repair (replanning, constraint injection, or retraining) and deploy runtime monitors enforcing the synthesized symbolic constraints.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a practical route to provable, interpretable oversight of LLM-driven agents—improving safety, auditability, and compliance in high-stakes deployments without relying solely on probabilistic judgment.
visual_elements: End-to-end pipeline diagram: Natural-language policy → Neuro-symbolic translator → Formal spec → Verifier → Agent correction loop.

title: SurfPhase: 3D Interfacial Dynamics in Two-Phase Flows from Sparse Videos
authors: Yue Gao, Hong-Xing Yu, Sanghyeon Chang, Qianxi Fu, Bo Zhu
abstract: Interfacial dynamics in two-phase flows govern momentum, heat, and mass transfer, yet remain difficult to measure experimentally. Classical techniques face intrinsic limitations near moving interfaces, while existing neural rendering methods target single-phase flows with diffuse boundaries and cannot handle sharp, deformable liquid-vapor interfaces. We propose SurfPhase, a novel model for reconstructing 3D interfacial dynamics from sparse camera views. Our approach integrates dynamic Gaussian s

infographic.key_insight: SurfPhase recovers sharp, deforming 3D liquid–vapor interfaces from a few camera views by using a surface-aware neural representation and rendering pipeline, enabling accurate interfacial dynamics reconstruction where prior neural methods fail.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing imaging and neural-rendering techniques cannot robustly reconstruct sharp, moving two-phase interfaces from sparse video viewpoints, limiting measurement of interfacial dynamics in experiments.
method: Represent the interface with surface-aware dynamic primitives (e.g., Gaussian surface elements) that capture sharp, deformable boundaries instead of diffuse volumetric fields.
Train a differentiable rendering pipeline that fits the primitives to sparse multi-view video frames, enforcing camera consistency and temporal coherence.
Incorporate physics-informed regularization and geometry constraints (two-phase interface priors) to stabilize reconstruction from limited views.
infographic.impact: SurfPhase provides a practical way to extract 3D interfacial geometry and motion from sparse experimental video, enabling data-driven analysis, validation of simulations, and improved learning of fluid dynamics where direct measurement is impractical.

title: What matters in building vision–language–action models for generalist robots
authors: Xinghang Li, Peiyan Li, Long Qian, Minghuan Liu, Dong Wang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 11 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01168-7

Vision–language–action models recently emerged as a tool for robotics. Here Li and colleagues compare vision–language–action models and highlight what makes a model useful.

infographic.key_insight: A few design choices — especially action grounding, instruction-aligned supervision, and diverse task/data coverage — matter more than raw model scale for building useful vision–language–action (VLA) models for generalist robots. Systematic comparisons show which components most strongly drive real-world robot performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies which architectural, data and training choices actually improve VLA model usefulness for embodied control, resolving uncertainty about whether scale, objectives, or data diversity are the primary drivers of robot generalization.
method: Systematic comparison of multiple VLA model variants across key axes: data composition, training objectives (language-aligned vs task-only), action representations, and model modularity.
Controlled ablation studies and benchmark evaluations spanning simulated tasks and real-world robot experiments to measure transfer and robustness.
Derive practical guidelines from empirical results to prioritize design choices for deploying generalist robotic agents.
infographic.impact: Provides actionable guidance for ML and robotics practitioners on where to invest effort (e.g., grounded action representations and aligned instruction data) to improve robot generalization and reduce wasted compute on unhelpful scaling. Accelerates development of reliable, generalist robot behaviors by focusing on the most effective components.

title: Diffusion-Pretrained Dense and Contextual Embeddings
authors: Sedigheh Eslami, Maksim Gaiduk, Markus Krimmel, Louis Milliken, Bo Wang
abstract: In this report, we introduce pplx-embed, a family of multilingual embedding models that employ multi-stage contrastive learning on a diffusion-pretrained language model backbone for web-scale retrieval. By leveraging bidirectional attention through diffusion-based pretraining, our models capture comprehensive bidirectional context within passages, enabling the use of mean pooling and a late chunking strategy to better preserve global context across long documents. We release two model types: ppl

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion-pretraining gives the language model bidirectional attention that, when combined with multi-stage contrastive fine-tuning, yields dense and contextual multilingual embeddings that better preserve global context across long documents using mean pooling and a late-chunking strategy.
infographic.problem_solved: Produces compact, retrieval-ready embeddings that retain bidirectional and long-range document context for web-scale, multilingual retrieval — addressing loss of global context and suboptimal pooling/chunking in long-document embedding pipelines.
method: Use a diffusion-pretrained language-model backbone to capture comprehensive bidirectional context within passages.
Apply multi-stage contrastive learning to produce both dense and contextual embedding variants optimized for web-scale retrieval.
Employ mean pooling plus a late-chunking strategy to aggregate representations while preserving global context across long documents.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build more accurate multilingual dense-retrieval systems for long documents with simpler pooling and chunking, improving end-to-end retrieval quality and scalability for web-scale search.

title: Just on Time: Token-Level Early Stopping for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Zahar Kohut, Severyn Shykula, Dmytro Khamula, Mykola Vysotskyi, Taras Rumezhak
abstract: Diffusion language models generate text through iterative refinement, a process that is often computationally inefficient because many tokens reach stability long before the final denoising step. We introduce a training-free, token-level early stopping approach that identifies convergence independently at each position. Our method leverages lightweight signals derived from the model's predictions and local context to dynamically determine when individual tokens can be finalized. This yields adap

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion LMs can finish many tokens well before the final denoising step; by detecting convergence at each token during inference, you can stop refining those tokens early without retraining the model.
infographic.problem_solved: Iterative denoising in diffusion language models is computationally inefficient because tokens often stabilize long before the full number of refinement steps, wasting compute, latency, and energy.
method: Training-free, token-level early stopping: monitor each position independently during inference and decide when a token has converged.
Use lightweight signals derived from the model's own predictions and local context (e.g., prediction consistency, local confidence) to detect per-token convergence.
Dynamically finalize tokens as soon as they meet convergence criteria and skip further denoising for those positions while continuing refinement elsewhere.
infographic.impact: Enables lower-latency, more compute- and energy-efficient text generation from diffusion LMs without retraining, making diffusion-based inference more practical for deployment and high-throughput applications.

title: VideoWorld 2: Learning Transferable Knowledge from Real-world Videos
authors: Zhongwei Ren, Yunchao Wei, Xiao Yu, Guixun Luo, Yao Zhao
abstract: Learning transferable knowledge from unlabeled video data and applying it in new environments is a fundamental capability of intelligent agents. This work presents VideoWorld 2, which extends VideoWorld and offers the first investigation into learning transferable knowledge directly from raw real-world videos. At its core, VideoWorld 2 introduces a dynamic-enhanced Latent Dynamics Model (dLDM) that decouples action dynamics from visual appearance: a pretrained video diffusion model handles visua

infographic.key_insight: VideoWorld 2 shows that decoupling action dynamics from visual appearance—via a dynamic-enhanced Latent Dynamics Model (dLDM) combined with a pretrained video diffusion model—lets agents learn transferable knowledge directly from raw real-world videos.
infographic.problem_solved: How to learn transferable, actionable knowledge from unlabeled, visually diverse real-world videos so that policies or dynamics models generalize to new environments without costly labels or simulators.
method: Introduce dLDM that models action dynamics in a latent space separately from visual appearance.
Leverage a pretrained video diffusion model to handle realistic visual generation/appearance, while dLDM focuses on dynamics.
Train on large-scale unlabeled real-world videos to produce dynamics representations that transfer to downstream control or decision tasks.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to use abundant unlabeled video data to pretrain transferable dynamics models, improving sample efficiency and cross-domain generalization for embodied agents and downstream RL/vision tasks.

title: ConsID-Gen: View-Consistent and Identity-Preserving Image-to-Video Generation
authors: Mingyang Wu, Ashirbad Mishra, Soumik Dey, Shuo Xing, Naveen Ravipati
abstract: Image-to-Video generation (I2V) animates a static image into a temporally coherent video sequence following textual instructions, yet preserving fine-grained object identity under changing viewpoints remains a persistent challenge. Unlike text-to-video models, existing I2V pipelines often suffer from appearance drift and geometric distortion, artifacts we attribute to the sparsity of single-view 2D observations and weak cross-modal alignment. Here we address this problem from both data and model

infographic.key_insight: ConsID-Gen combines data-level multi-view augmentation with model-level identity- and view-consistency constraints to generate temporally coherent videos from a single image while preserving fine-grained object identity across changing viewpoints.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses appearance drift and geometric distortion in image-to-video (I2V) generation caused by sparse single-view observations and weak cross-modal alignment, enabling stable identity preservation as viewpoint and motion change.
method: Data augmentation: synthesize or mine pseudo multi-view observations from the single input to densify geometric and appearance supervision.
Model constraints: introduce identity-preserving and view-consistency losses (cross-frame feature matching / perceptual identity regularizers) to prevent appearance drift.
Cross-modal & temporal alignment: strengthen image–text alignment and temporal modeling (e.g., sequence-conditioned generator) so animations follow instructions while remaining consistent over time.
infographic.impact: Makes I2V outputs more reliable for applications that require faithful identity preservation (avatars, digital doubles, AR/VR, visual effects) and reduces common artifacts, improving usability for practitioners deploying generative video systems.
visual_elements: Before/after strip: single input image on the left, generated video frames across time on the right to show preserved identity under viewpoint change.
Pipeline diagram: blocks for multi-view augmentation → consistency & identity losses → temporally-conditioned generator, with arrows showing information flow.

title: A federated graph learning method to realize multi-party collaboration for molecular discovery
authors: Liang Zhang, Juan Zhang, Rui Huang, Yiwen Wang, Linjing Liu
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 10 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01184-1

Zhang et al. introduce FedLG, a federated graph learning framework that leverages Lanczos-based projection to effectively aggregate heterogeneous molecular data. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate its robustness across diverse molecular discovery tasks.

infographic.key_insight: FedLG introduces a federated graph learning pipeline that uses a Lanczos-based projection to align heterogeneous molecular graph embeddings across parties, enabling effective multi-party model training without sharing raw data.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables collaborative molecular discovery across organizations that hold distributed, heterogeneous graph-structured data while preserving privacy and addressing representation mismatch between parties.
method: Federated training of graph neural networks: local GNN updates at each party with periodic secure aggregation.
Lanczos-based projection: low-rank spectral projection to align and compress heterogeneous graph embeddings for efficient, robust aggregation.
Benchmark-driven validation: extensive evaluations across diverse molecular discovery tasks to demonstrate robustness and performance gains over baselines.
infographic.impact: Practitioners can train joint GNN models on decentralized molecular datasets with reduced communication and improved cross-site generalization, enabling privacy-preserving drug discovery collaborations and more robust molecular prediction models.

Illustration of Lanczos projection: spectral decomposition compressing and aligning node/graph embeddings across sites.
Benchmark charts: bar/line plots comparing FedLG vs. baselines across several molecular tasks (accuracy, AUC, robustness).

title: VLA-JEPA: Enhancing Vision-Language-Action Model with Latent World Model
authors: Jingwen Sun, Wenyao Zhang, Zekun Qi, Shaojie Ren, Zezhi Liu
abstract: Pretraining Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies on internet-scale video is appealing, yet current latent-action objectives often learn the wrong thing: they remain anchored to pixel variation rather than action-relevant state transitions, making them vulnerable to appearance bias, nuisance motion, and information leakage. We introduce VLA-JEPA, a JEPA-style pretraining framework that sidesteps these pitfalls by design. The key idea is \emph{leakage-free state prediction}: a target encoder prod

infographic.key_insight: VLA-JEPA trains a latent world model that predicts future task-relevant states without leaking pixel-level cues, so the model learns action-relevant dynamics instead of appearance or nuisance motion.
infographic.problem_solved: Current VLA pretraining objectives get anchored to pixel variation and nuisance motion, causing appearance bias and information leakage that hurt downstream action-conditioned policies.
method: JEPA-style latent prediction: learn to predict future latent states (a compact world model) rather than raw pixels.
Leakage-free targets: design the target encoder and training pipeline so predicted latents cannot access appearance/nuisance signals from target frames.
Action-conditioned dynamics & alignment: condition latent predictions on action/context and align latent space with language and policy objectives for VLA tasks.
infographic.impact: Leads to more robust, generalizable vision-language-action representations that reduce appearance bias and improve performance of action-conditioned policies from internet-scale video pretraining.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: encoders -> latent bottleneck -> JEPA predictor with a 'no-leak' barrier shown between target pixels and target latents.
Before vs after comparison: bar or line charts showing reduced sensitivity to appearance change and improved downstream policy metrics.

title: 4RC: 4D Reconstruction via Conditional Querying Anytime and Anywhere
authors: Yihang Luo, Shangchen Zhou, Yushi Lan, Xingang Pan, Chen Change Loy
abstract: We present 4RC, a unified feed-forward framework for 4D reconstruction from monocular videos. Unlike existing approaches that typically decouple motion from geometry or produce limited 4D attributes such as sparse trajectories or two-view scene flow, 4RC learns a holistic 4D representation that jointly captures dense scene geometry and motion dynamics. At its core, 4RC introduces a novel encode-once, query-anywhere and anytime paradigm: a transformer backbone encodes the entire video into a comp

infographic.key_insight: 4RC introduces an encode-once, query-anywhere-and-anytime transformer that learns a unified dense 4D representation from a monocular video, enabling on-demand reconstruction of geometry and motion at arbitrary spatio-temporal points.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing methods either decouple motion from geometry, produce sparse/limited 4D outputs, or require costly optimization; 4RC addresses the need for a single, efficient feed-forward model that yields dense, joint geometry+motion across space and time from a single camera.
method: Encode-once: a transformer backbone processes the entire video into a compact latent 4D representation in a single forward pass.
Conditional querying: a lightweight query module retrieves dense geometry and motion for arbitrary 3D positions and time instants, enabling anytime/anywhere access to 4D attributes.
End-to-end learning: the model is trained to jointly capture dense scene geometry and dynamic motion, replacing decoupled or sparse reconstructions with a holistic feed-forward solution.
infographic.impact: Enables fast, flexible, and dense 4D reconstruction from monocular video for AR/VR, robotics, and video editing workflows, reducing computation and supporting real-time or on-demand queries of scene dynamics.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: video input → transformer encoder (encode-once) → query module → per-point geometry+motion outputs (encode & query flow).
Space–time volume: 3D scene + time axis showing arbitrary query points and retrieved geometry/motion (query-anywhere/anytime concept).
Comparison panel: prior decoupled/sparse approaches vs 4RC's joint dense reconstruction (qualitative results overlayed on frames).

title: Towards Explainable Federated Learning: Understanding the Impact of Differential Privacy
authors: Júlio Oliveira, Rodrigo Ferreira, André Riker, Glaucio H. S. Carvalho, Eirini Eleni Tsilopoulou
abstract: Data privacy and eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) are two important aspects for modern Machine Learning systems. To enhance data privacy, recent machine learning models have been designed as a Federated Learning (FL) system. On top of that, additional privacy layers can be added, via Differential Privacy (DP). On the other hand, to improve explainability, ML must consider more interpretable approaches with reduced number of features and less complex internal architecture. In this contex

infographic.key_insight: Adding differential privacy to federated learning creates a measurable trade-off: stronger privacy noise reduces accuracy and destabilizes feature-attribution explanations, but model simplification and careful DP tuning can recover interpretable behavior without sacrificing much utility.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how differential privacy affects model explainability in federated learning and provides empirical guidance to balance privacy, accuracy and interpretability in distributed ML systems.
method: Systematic empirical study comparing FL models trained with and without DP across datasets, measuring accuracy, feature-attribution stability (e.g., SHAP/LIME-style metrics) and feature sparsity.
Analysis of model complexity (feature count, architecture depth) and DP noise levels to identify configurations that preserve explainability.
Derive practical recommendations for configuring DP parameters and model design to mitigate negative impacts on explanations.
infographic.impact: Enables ML engineers and researchers to make informed trade-offs when deploying privacy-preserving federated models, helping maintain trustworthy, interpretable predictions in privacy-sensitive applications.
visual_elements: 3‑axis trade-off plot (privacy ε vs. accuracy vs. explanation stability) showing Pareto frontier
Side‑by‑side feature‑attribution heatmaps before and after applying DP to illustrate explanation drift
Bar chart of feature importance stability or sparsity as DP noise increases
Pipeline diagram of a federated learning system with DP injection points and XAI evaluation module

title: Quantum-Audit: Evaluating the Reasoning Limits of LLMs on Quantum Computing
authors: Mohamed Afane, Kayla Laufer, Wenqi Wei, Ying Mao, Junaid Farooq
abstract: Language models have become practical tools for quantum computing education and research, from summarizing technical papers to explaining theoretical concepts and answering questions about recent developments in the field. While existing benchmarks evaluate quantum code generation and circuit design, their understanding of quantum computing concepts has not been systematically measured. Quantum-Audit addresses this gap with 2,700 questions covering core quantum computing topics. We evaluate 26 m

infographic.key_insight: Quantum-Audit introduces a large, focused benchmark (2,700 questions) that systematically measures how well language models understand core quantum computing concepts, revealing concrete reasoning limits beyond code/circuit generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks focus on quantum code and circuit design but do not measure conceptual understanding and reasoning in quantum computing; this paper fills that evaluation gap.
method: Curate a 2,700-question benchmark covering core quantum topics (theory, algorithms, gates/measurement, noise and complexity).
Evaluate a wide set of language models on the benchmark using accuracy and qualitative reasoning/error analyses.
Analyze failure modes to map where models misunderstand concepts versus where they can reliably assist users.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a diagnostic tool to assess and improve LLM reliability on quantum computing tasks, guiding model selection, fine-tuning, and dataset creation for scientific QA and education.

Leaderboard bar chart of model accuracies with confidence/error bars

title: Step-resolved data attribution for looped transformers
authors: Georgios Kaissis, David Mildenberger, Juan Felipe Gomez, Martin J. Menten, Eleni Triantafillou
abstract: We study how individual training examples shape the internal computation of looped transformers, where a shared block is applied for $τ$ recurrent iterations to enable latent reasoning. Existing training-data influence estimators such as TracIn yield a single scalar score that aggregates over all loop iterations, obscuring when during the recurrent computation a training example matters. We introduce \textit{Step-Decomposed Influence (SDI)}, which decomposes TracIn into a length-$τ$ influence tr

infographic.key_insight: Step‑Decomposed Influence (SDI) breaks a single training‑data influence score into a length‑τ vector aligned with each recurrent iteration, revealing when (which loop step) a training example actually affects a looped transformer’s computation.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing influence estimators (e.g., TracIn) aggregate influence across all recurrent iterations, hiding the temporal/iteration structure of influence in looped transformers and preventing step‑level attribution and debugging.
method: Derive SDI by decomposing the TracIn influence score into per‑iteration contributions across the τ recurrent applications of the shared block.
Compute a length‑τ influence trace for each training example (instead of a single scalar), enabling identification of which iteration(s) drive the influence.
Provide practical computation strategy and diagnostics to visualize and compare per‑step contributions for target examples and datasets.
infographic.impact: SDI gives practitioners fine‑grained, step‑level attribution useful for debugging, dataset curation, targeted data editing, and understanding where and when training data steer latent reasoning in looped transformers.
visual_elements: Schematic of a looped transformer showing a single shared block applied τ times with arrows labeled by step index (1..τ).
Example per‑step influence vector: a horizontal bar/line plot showing influence magnitude across steps for one training example.
Heatmap (steps × training examples) highlighting which examples matter at which iterations.
Workflow diagram: compute SDI → visualize top per‑step influencers → apply targeted data edits or diagnostics.
