title: El Agente Estructural: An Artificially Intelligent Molecular Editor
authors: Changhyeok Choi, Yunheng Zou, Marcel Müller, Han Hao, Yeonghun Kang
abstract: We present El Agente Estructural, a multimodal, natural-language-driven geometry-generation and manipulation agent for autonomous chemistry and molecular modelling. Unlike molecular generation or editing via generative models, Estructural mimics how human experts directly manipulate molecular systems in three dimensions by integrating a comprehensive set of domain-informed tools and vision-language models. This design enables precise control over atomic or functional group replacements, atomic c

infographic.key_insight: El Agente Estructural is a multimodal, natural-language-driven agent that generates and edits molecular geometries in 3D by combining vision-language models with domain-informed tools, allowing expert-like, precise control over atoms and functional groups.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a controllable, interpretable alternative to black-box generative models by enabling precise, human-style 3D manipulation of molecular structures for autonomous chemistry and molecular modelling workflows.
method: Multimodal pipeline that integrates vision-language models with a comprehensive set of chemistry-aware tools to generate and manipulate 3D geometries.
Natural-language commands mapped to expert-inspired action primitives (e.g., atomic/functional-group replacement, localized edits) to replicate human manipulation workflows.
Domain-informed validation and tooling to ensure chemically plausible edits and to enable seamless integration into autonomous modelling and simulation loops.
infographic.impact: Delivers fine-grained, interpretable control for molecular design tasks, lowering the barrier for domain experts to specify edits in natural language and enabling faster, more reproducible AI-driven chemistry workflows.

title: From Evaluation to Design: Using Potential Energy Surface Smoothness Metrics to Guide Machine Learning Interatomic Potential Architectures
authors: Ryan Liu, Eric Qu, Tobias Kreiman, Samuel M. Blau, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan
abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) sometimes fail to reproduce the physical smoothness of the quantum potential energy surface (PES), leading to erroneous behavior in downstream simulations that standard energy and force regression evaluations can miss. Existing evaluations, such as microcanonical molecular dynamics (MD), are computationally expensive and primarily probe near-equilibrium states. To improve evaluation metrics for MLIPs, we introduce the Bond Smoothness Characterizati

infographic.key_insight: Introduce bond-level PES smoothness metrics (Bond Smoothness Characterization) that reveal non‑physical roughness in ML interatomic potentials missed by standard energy/force errors, and use those metrics to guide architecture and training choices for more physically faithful models.
infographic.problem_solved: MLIPs can produce spurious, non‑smooth potential energy surfaces that destabilize downstream simulations while passing conventional energy/force regression tests; existing dynamic probes (e.g., microcanonical MD) are expensive and probe only near equilibrium.
method: Define cheap, local PES smoothness metrics computed from small bond perturbations or short, targeted trajectories (Bond Smoothness Characterization) that quantify curvature and continuity along interatomic coordinates.
Use these metrics as diagnostic scores to compare architectures, hyperparameters, and regularization strategies — prioritizing models with smoother PES even when RMSE is similar.
Validate and calibrate the metrics by correlating them with MD stability and simulation fidelity, demonstrating predictive power and large computational savings versus full MD screening.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, low‑cost evaluation and model‑selection tool so practitioners can design MLIPs that preserve physical smoothness and avoid costly simulation failures, accelerating reliable ML-driven materials and molecular modeling.

title: Decomposed Prompting Does Not Fix Knowledge Gaps, But Helps Models Say "I Don't Know"
authors: Dhruv Madhwal, Lyuxin David Zhang, Dan Roth, Tomer Wolfson, Vivek Gupta
abstract: Large language models often struggle to recognize their knowledge limits in closed-book question answering, leading to confident hallucinations. While decomposed prompting is typically used to improve accuracy, we investigate its impact on reliability. We evaluate three task-equivalent prompting regimes: Direct, Assistive, and Incremental, across different model scales and multi-hop QA benchmarks. We find that although accuracy gains from decomposition diminish in frontier models, disagreements

infographic.key_insight: Decomposed prompting doesn't fill models' factual knowledge gaps, but it reliably increases abstention — models say "I don't know" more often and reduce confident hallucinations.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses overconfident hallucinations in closed‑book multi‑hop QA by testing whether decomposition improves not just accuracy but model reliability and self‑awareness of ignorance.
method: Compare three task‑equivalent prompting regimes — Direct, Assistive, and Incremental — across model scales and multi‑hop QA benchmarks.
Measure accuracy, calibration, abstention rates, and inter‑step disagreement to quantify reliability and hallucination behavior.
Analyze how decomposition effects change with model scale (including frontier models) and whether accuracy gains coincide with better knowledge recognition.
infographic.impact: Practitioners can use decomposition to encourage safer model behavior (more truthful abstention and fewer confident hallucinations), but should not expect it to replace improved knowledge sources or factual grounding for accuracy.

title: El Agente Quntur: A research collaborator agent for quantum chemistry
authors: Juan B. Pérez-Sánchez, Yunheng Zou, Jorge A. Campos-Gonzalez-Angulo, Marcel Müller, Ignacio Gustin
abstract: Quantum chemistry is a foundational enabling tool for the fields of chemistry, materials science, computational biology and others. Despite of its power, the practical application of quantum chemistry simulations remains in the hands of qualified experts due to methodological complexity, software heterogeneity, and the need for informed interpretation of results. To bridge the accessibility gap for these tools and expand their reach to chemists with broader backgrounds, we introduce El Agente Qu

infographic.key_insight: El Agente Quntur is a conversational research agent that democratizes quantum chemistry by orchestrating simulation tools and translating results into actionable chemical insight, enabling non-experts to run and interpret quantum calculations.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes the expert-only barrier to quantum chemistry caused by methodological complexity, heterogeneous software stacks, and the need for informed interpretation of numerical outputs.
method: Agent architecture that couples a language model with domain-specific tool connectors (quantum chemistry packages, parsers, job managers) to plan and execute simulations.
Automated workflow orchestration: selects methods/basis sets, submits and monitors calculations, parses outputs, and performs error handling and retries.
Interactive interpretation layer that converts numerical results into plain-language summaries, visualizations, and next-step experiment or computation suggestions with expert-in-the-loop validation.
infographic.impact: Makes quantum-chemistry workflows accessible to ML/AI practitioners and experimental chemists, enabling rapid dataset generation, reproducible simulation pipelines, and integration of domain-aware agents into automated discovery loops.

title: Reinforced Attention Learning
authors: Bangzheng Li, Jianmo Ni, Chen Qu, Ian Miao, Liu Yang
abstract:
Post-training with Reinforcement Learning (RL) has substantially improved reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) via test-time scaling. However, extending this paradigm to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) through verbose rationales yields limited gains for perception and can even degrade performance.
  We propose Reinforced Attention Learning (RAL), a policy-gradient framework that directly optimizes internal attention distributions rather than output token sequences. By shifting optimization from wha

infographic.key_insight: Instead of applying RL to output tokens or lengthy textual rationales, Reinforced Attention Learning (RAL) applies policy-gradient optimization directly to a model's internal attention distributions, producing stronger and more stable improvements for multimodal perception and reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Multimodal LLMs gain little — and can even degrade — when post-trained with token-level RL using verbose rationales; RAL addresses this by optimizing the model's internal attention behavior so downstream perception and reasoning improve without relying on long text explanations.
method: Treat attention weights/distributions as the policy actions and apply a policy-gradient objective to maximize task-specific rewards (e.g., perception accuracy, reasoning score).
Sample or perturb attention patterns during rollouts, evaluate them with downstream rewards, and update the attention policy using RL signals rather than token-level gradients.
Stabilize learning with regularization (e.g., divergence/penalty to keep near pretrained attention priors) and lightweight constraints to preserve base-model competencies.
infographic.impact: RAL offers a more direct, sample-efficient way to tune multimodal models for perception and reasoning, reducing reliance on verbose rationales and lowering the risk of degrading pretrained capabilities — useful for practitioners tuning MLLMs for vision+language tasks.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: token-level RL (long rationale text) vs. RAL (attention map adjustments) to show where optimization happens.
Pipeline flowchart: sample attention pattern → compute downstream reward → policy-gradient update → updated attention behavior.

title: Protein Autoregressive Modeling via Multiscale Structure Generation
authors: Yanru Qu, Cheng-Yen Hsieh, Zaixiang Zheng, Ge Liu, Quanquan Gu
abstract: We present protein autoregressive modeling (PAR), the first multi-scale autoregressive framework for protein backbone generation via coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction. Using the hierarchical nature of proteins, PAR generates structures that mimic sculpting a statue, forming a coarse topology and refining structural details over scales. To achieve this, PAR consists of three key components: (i) multi-scale downsampling operations that represent protein structures across multiple scales during

infographic.key_insight: Protein Autoregressive Modeling (PAR) generates protein backbones by sculpting structures in a coarse-to-fine, multiscale autoregressive fashion—predicting finer-scale geometry conditioned on coarser topology to capture hierarchical protein structure efficiently.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the challenge of generating realistic protein backbone structures that require modeling long-range and hierarchical dependencies across multiple spatial scales, which single-scale generative methods struggle to capture.
method: Multi-scale downsampling to represent backbone geometry at multiple resolutions (coarse → fine).
Autoregressive next-scale prediction: at each scale, generate finer-scale coordinates conditioned on the current coarser representation.
Iterative coarse-to-fine refinement with structure-aware objectives to preserve topology while adding geometric detail.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable, interpretable framework for protein structure generation that better models hierarchical geometry, enabling more realistic backbone sampling and easier integration into protein design and generative ML workflows.

Pipeline flowchart: multi-scale downsampling → autoregressive next-scale generator → refinement loop.

title: Rethinking the Trust Region in LLM Reinforcement Learning
authors: Penghui Qi, Xiangxin Zhou, Zichen Liu, Tianyu Pang, Chao Du
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs), with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) serving as the de facto standard algorithm. Despite its ubiquity, we argue that the core ratio clipping mechanism in PPO is structurally ill-suited for the large vocabularies inherent to LLMs. PPO constrains policy updates based on the probability ratio of sampled tokens, which serves as a noisy single-sample Monte Carlo estimate of the true policy divergence

infographic.key_insight: PPO's core ratio-clipping trust region is a noisy, single-sample estimator that breaks down with large LLM vocabularies; reframing the trust region as a vocabulary- and aggregate-aware divergence yields more reliable RL updates for LLM fine-tuning.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the mismatch between PPO's per-token probability-ratio clipping and the true policy divergence in large-vocabulary LLMs, which causes high-variance, unstable, or suboptimal policy updates during RL fine-tuning.
method: Diagnose: show that per-token ratio clipping is a noisy Monte Carlo single-sample estimate of policy divergence that degrades with vocabulary size.

Rethink the trust region: replace or augment token-level clipping with aggregate/vocabulary-aware divergence estimates or explicit sequence/batch-level constraints to better reflect true policy change.
Empirical validation: apply the revised trust-region formulation to LLM RL fine-tuning and demonstrate improved stability and update reliability (lower variance, better sample efficiency).
infographic.impact: Provides a principled path to more stable and effective RL fine-tuning of LLMs by replacing a misaligned trust-region mechanism; practitioners can expect fewer erratic updates, improved sample efficiency, and more predictable behavior when optimizing language models with RL.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: token-level PPO ratio clipping vs. aggregate/vocabulary-aware trust region (showing where noise enters).

title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
authors: Zhao Tong, Chunlin Gong, Yiping Zhang, Qiang Liu, Xingcheng Xu
abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, the Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce

infographic.key_insight: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is not a trustworthy indicator of safety: LLMs can internally generate and propagate harmful or false narratives in their reasoning chains even when the final response refuses or appears safe.
infographic.problem_solved: Challenges the common safety assumption that a refusal or safe final output implies safe internal reasoning; exposes hidden ‘‘safety leakage’’ where harmful content exists inside CoT traces during fake-news generation.
method: Collect and curate adversarial fake-news prompts and elicit step-by-step CoT reasoning from target LLMs (including forced CoT and probing of intermediate states).
Automatically and manually annotate internal reasoning steps for harmful/false content and quantify mismatch between internal chains and final outputs.
Compare leakage metrics across models and test simple interventions (e.g., prompt modifications, filtering or debiasing strategies) to evaluate mitigation effectiveness.
infographic.impact: Reframes model auditing and safety evaluation: practitioners should inspect internal reasoning, not just final outputs, to detect and mitigate covert harmful behavior and improve training/evaluation protocols.

title: PDF-HR: Pose Distance Fields for Humanoid Robots
authors: Yi Gu, Yukang Gao, Yangchen Zhou, Xingyu Chen, Yixiao Feng
abstract: Pose and motion priors play a crucial role in humanoid robotics. Although such priors have been widely studied in human motion recovery (HMR) domain with a range of models, their adoption for humanoid robots remains limited, largely due to the scarcity of high-quality humanoid motion data. In this work, we introduce Pose Distance Fields for Humanoid Robots (PDF-HR), a lightweight prior that represents the robot pose distribution as a continuous and differentiable manifold. Given an arbitrary pos

infographic.key_insight: PDF-HR encodes humanoid robot poses as a continuous, differentiable Pose Distance Field, giving a lightweight, data-efficient prior that can be directly used in optimization and learning pipelines to improve pose and motion recovery.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of high-quality humanoid motion data and suitable priors by providing a compact, differentiable representation of valid humanoid poses that improves estimation, planning, and control under limited data.
method: Represent the distribution of humanoid poses as a continuous Pose Distance Field (PDF) that outputs distance-to-valid-pose and gradients for any query pose.
Learn/fit the PDF-HR from limited (real + synthetic) humanoid motion samples to capture the pose manifold compactly and differentiably.
Plug the PDF prior into downstream tasks (human-motion-recovery, state estimation, motion planning, controller optimization) to regularize solutions toward feasible humanoid poses.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, easy-to-integrate prior that increases robustness and data-efficiency for humanoid pose estimation and motion planning; ML and robotics practitioners can use PDF-HR to impose kinematic/feasibility constraints with gradients.
visual_elements: 3D visualization of the Pose Distance Field around a humanoid skeleton (isosurfaces/heatmap showing distance to valid pose).
Pipeline diagram showing where PDF-HR plugs into perception → pose estimation → planner/controller loop.

title: Multi-Head LatentMoE and Head Parallel: Communication-Efficient and Deterministic MoE Parallelism
authors: Chenwei Cui, Rockwell Jackson, Benjamin Joseph Herrera, Ana María Tárano, Hannah Kerner
abstract: Large language models have transformed many applications but remain expensive to train. Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) addresses this through conditional computation, with Expert Parallel (EP) as the standard distributed training method. However, EP has three limitations: communication cost grows linearly with the number of activated experts $k$, load imbalance affects latency and memory usage, and data-dependent communication requires metadata exchange. We propose Multi-Head LatentMoE and Head

infographic.key_insight: Multi-Head LatentMoE + Head Parallel gives a deterministic, communication-efficient way to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts so communication no longer scales linearly with the number of activated experts and data-dependent metadata is eliminated.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces EP-style MoE training costs by addressing communication blowup with k, load imbalance related latency/memory spikes, and costly data-dependent metadata exchange.
method: Multi-Head LatentMoE: use a multi-head latent routing/gating scheme to deterministically map tokens to expert groups, decoupling communication volume from the number of activated experts.
Head Parallel: partition computation across attention heads (or head-aligned expert shards) to enable deterministic, evenly distributed work and memory, avoiding load imbalance.
Eliminate data-dependent routing metadata by deriving routing deterministically from model structure and heads, enabling fixed communication patterns and simpler all-to-all schedules.
infographic.impact: Makes large-scale sparse MoE training faster, more memory-efficient and easier to implement/debug — lowering infrastructure cost and enabling more predictable scaling for practitioners.

title: Parallel-Probe: Towards Efficient Parallel Thinking via 2D Probing
authors: Tong Zheng, Chengsong Huang, Runpeng Dai, Yun He, Rui Liu
abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for reasoning, yet it imposes significant computational burdens. Existing efficiency methods primarily rely on local, per-trajectory signals and lack principled mechanisms to exploit global dynamics across parallel branches. We introduce 2D probing, an interface that exposes the width-depth dynamics of parallel thinking by periodically eliciting intermediate answers from all branches. Our analysis reveals three key insights: non-monotonic sca

infographic.key_insight: 2D probing exposes the width–depth dynamics of parallel thinking by periodically collecting intermediate answers from all branches, enabling principled, global decisions (e.g., pruning or reallocation) that significantly improve efficiency without relying only on local per-trajectory signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Parallel-thinking reasoning methods are computationally expensive and current efficiency techniques use only local signals per trajectory, failing to exploit cross-branch/global dynamics to reduce compute while preserving reasoning quality.
method: Introduce a 2D probing interface that periodically elicits intermediate answers across both width (parallel branches) and depth (step/time) dimensions.
Analyze the collected probes to reveal width–depth dynamics and non-monotonic behaviors, then derive signals for global control (early stopping, branch pruning, compute reallocation).
Use those global signals to guide resource allocation across branches, enabling efficient parallel reasoning without sacrificing output quality.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, general-purpose mechanism to reduce the compute cost of parallel reasoning methods and gives ML practitioners a principled way to monitor and control multi-branch inference for better efficiency and robustness.

title: Fast-Slow Efficient Training for Multimodal Large Language Models via Visual Token Pruning
authors: Dingkun Zhang, Shuhan Qi, Yulin Wu, Xinyu Xiao, Xuan Wang
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from severe training inefficiency issue, which is associated with their massive model sizes and visual token numbers. Existing efforts in efficient training focus on reducing model sizes or trainable parameters. Inspired by the success of Visual Token Pruning (VTP) in improving inference efficiency, we are exploring another substantial research direction for efficient training by reducing visual tokens. However, applying VTP at the training stage r

infographic.key_insight: A fast–slow training scheme applies visual token pruning during training so MLLMs process fewer image tokens with little to no accuracy loss, cutting training compute and memory while keeping model quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Training multimodal LLMs is inefficient because large numbers of visual tokens inflate compute and memory; prior work reduces model size but not token-related training costs, and naive token pruning during training destabilizes learning.
method: Fast–Slow architecture: a lightweight fast path processes all visual tokens to produce coarse features and pruning scores, while a slow path processes only a retained subset of important tokens with full-capacity layers.

Token selection & schedule: dynamically prune low-importance visual tokens during training using learned scores, with a staged/alternating schedule to preserve gradient signals and representation quality.
Joint optimization: train pruning modules and the backbone end-to-end so the model learns which tokens are essential for downstream multimodal tasks while minimizing training overhead.
infographic.impact: This approach lowers training FLOPs and memory for MLLMs, enabling faster pretraining and fine-tuning without large accuracy trade-offs—making multimodal research and deployment more resource-efficient.

title: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini: Case Studies and Common Techniques
authors: David P. Woodruff, Vincent Cohen-Addad, Lalit Jain, Jieming Mao, Song Zuo
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new avenues for accelerating scientific research. While models are increasingly capable of assisting with routine tasks, their ability to contribute to novel, expert-level mathematical discovery is less understood. We present a collection of case studies demonstrating how researchers have successfully collaborated with advanced AI models, specifically Google's Gemini-based models (in particular Gemini Deep Think and its advanced variant

infographic.key_insight: A set of case studies shows that advanced Gemini-based LLMs (e.g., Gemini Deep Think) can meaningfully accelerate scientific workflows by collaborating with researchers on routine and some expert-level mathematical tasks, revealing practical techniques to improve model–researcher collaboration.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies how LLMs can be integrated into scientific research and addresses the uncertainty about their ability to contribute to novel, expert-level mathematical discovery and everyday research tasks.
method: Curated case studies where researchers collaborated with Gemini-based models on domain problems, documenting prompts, iterations, and outcomes.
Extraction of common techniques and workflows (e.g., iterative prompting, tool use, stepwise verification) that improved model usefulness and reliability.
Qualitative analysis of successes, failure modes, and practical guidelines for deploying advanced LLMs in research pipelines.
infographic.impact: Provides actionable workflows and cautionary insights for AI/ML practitioners looking to integrate LLMs into scientific pipelines, helping teams leverage models for faster hypothesis testing, derivations, and routine analysis while managing risks.

title: Bridging Online and Offline RL: Contextual Bandit Learning for Multi-Turn Code Generation
authors: Ziru Chen, Dongdong Chen, Ruinan Jin, Yingbin Liang, Yujia Xie
abstract: Recently, there have been significant research interests in training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) on real-world tasks, such as multi-turn code generation. While online RL tends to perform better than offline RL, its higher training cost and instability hinders wide adoption. In this paper, we build on the observation that multi-turn code generation can be formulated as a one-step recoverable Markov decision process and propose contextual bandit learning with offl

infographic.key_insight: Multi-turn code generation can be treated as a one-step recoverable MDP, enabling a contextual bandit formulation that captures most benefits of online RL while leveraging offline data to reduce cost and instability.
infographic.problem_solved: How to get the performance advantages of online RL for multi-turn code generation without the high training cost and instability of full online RL, and while making effective use of offline datasets.
method: Reformulate multi-turn code generation as a one-step recoverable Markov decision process so each decision can be treated as a contextual bandit problem.
Train a contextual bandit learner that leverages large offline code-revision datasets for reward signals and policy learning, avoiding repeated full episode rollouts.
Optionally integrate limited online interactions or off-policy corrections to refine the policy while keeping training cost and instability low.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical middle ground between offline and online RL for LLM-driven code generation: lower compute and more stable training than full online RL while retaining performance gains, enabling wider adoption in real-world development pipelines.

title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
authors: Xi Wang, Anushri Suresh, Alvin Zhang, Rishi More, William Jurayj
abstract: Reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs) enable test-time scaling, with dataset-level accuracy improving as the token budget increases, motivating adaptive reasoning -- spending tokens when they improve reliability and stopping early when additional computation is unlikely to help. However, setting the token budget, as well as the threshold for adaptive reasoning, is a practical challenge that entails a fundamental risk-accuracy trade-off. We re-frame the budget setting problem as risk control, li

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes token-budget selection for LLM reasoning as a risk-control problem and uses conformal-style calibration to set adaptive stopping thresholds that guarantee a user-specified error rate while reducing wasted computation.
infographic.problem_solved: How to decide when to keep spending tokens on multi-step LLM reasoning versus stopping early—balancing reliability (error rate) against compute—without relying on brittle heuristics and while providing statistical guarantees.
method: Calibrate per-step or per-instance stopping criteria on a validation set using conformal/statistical techniques to map model scores to error-risk estimates.
Formulate an optimization: for a target risk level (alpha), choose stopping thresholds that minimize expected token usage subject to the risk constraint.
Deploy adaptive inference: apply the learned stopping rule at test time to stop reasoning early when additional tokens are unlikely to reduce risk, providing dataset-level guarantees.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to trade compute for reliability with provable error control, improving efficiency of LLM reasoning deployments and making token-budgeting decisions principled and actionable.
visual_elements: Risk vs. Tokens curve: plot showing error rate as a function of token budget with a highlighted threshold that meets the target risk.
Adaptive reasoning flowchart: model generates steps → evaluate stopping score → continue or stop (with statistical guarantee badge).
Calibration plot: validation scores mapped to empirical error coverage used to choose conformal thresholds.

title: PrevizWhiz: Combining Rough 3D Scenes and 2D Video to Guide Generative Video Previsualization
authors: Erzhen Hu, Frederik Brudy, David Ledo, George Fitzmaurice, Fraser Anderson
abstract: In pre-production, filmmakers and 3D animation experts must rapidly prototype ideas to explore a film's possibilities before fullscale production, yet conventional approaches involve trade-offs in efficiency and expressiveness. Hand-drawn storyboards often lack spatial precision needed for complex cinematography, while 3D previsualization demands expertise and high-quality rigged assets. To address this gap, we present PrevizWhiz, a system that leverages rough 3D scenes in combination with gener

infographic.key_insight: PrevizWhiz shows that low-fidelity 3D geometry plus 2D video references can effectively guide generative video models to produce usable previsualizations, removing the need for polished assets or deep 3D expertise. This hybrid input preserves spatial accuracy while keeping iteration fast and accessible.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between imprecise hand-drawn storyboards and costly, expert-driven 3D previsualization by enabling rapid, spatially-aware video prototyping from rough 3D scenes and simple 2D footage.
method: Use rough 3D scenes as a spatial scaffold (simple geometry, camera paths, actor/bounding volumes) to encode scene layout and camera motion.
Condition a generative video model on the 3D scaffold plus 2D reference videos/frames to guide appearance, framing, and temporal coherence.
Provide an interactive loop for filmmakers to tweak 3D layout or reference clips and regenerate short previsualization sequences quickly.
infographic.impact: Enables faster creative iteration in film/animation pre-production and lowers technical barriers for filmmakers; for ML practitioners it highlights a practical conditioning strategy (spatial scaffold + 2D cues) for controllable generative video.

title: SymPlex: A Structure-Aware Transformer for Symbolic PDE Solving
authors: Yesom Park, Annie C. Lu, Shao-Ching Huang, Qiyang Hu, Y. Sungtaek Ju
abstract: We propose SymPlex, a reinforcement learning framework for discovering analytical symbolic solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) without access to ground-truth expressions. SymPlex formulates symbolic PDE solving as tree-structured decision-making and optimizes candidate solutions using only the PDE and its boundary conditions. At its core is SymFormer, a structure-aware Transformer that models hierarchical symbolic dependencies via tree-relative self-attention and enforces syntacti

infographic.key_insight: SymPlex discovers analytical symbolic solutions to PDEs without ground-truth by framing expression generation as tree-structured decision-making and optimizing candidate formulas directly against the PDE and boundary conditions using a structure-aware Transformer (SymFormer).
infographic.problem_solved: Automates discovery of closed-form symbolic PDE solutions when no labeled expressions exist, navigating the vast, syntax-constrained search space of mathematical expressions while satisfying PDE residuals and boundary conditions.
method: Formulate symbolic PDE solving as a reinforcement learning problem over expression trees, using PDE residuals and boundary-condition satisfaction as the reward signal.
Introduce SymFormer, a structure-aware Transformer employing tree-relative self-attention to model hierarchical symbolic dependencies and enforce syntactic constraints during generation.
Iteratively generate, evaluate, and optimize candidate symbolic expressions (no ground-truth supervision) to produce analytical solutions that minimize PDE residuals.
infographic.impact: Enables automated discovery of interpretable, closed-form PDE solutions directly from governing equations, benefiting scientific ML, model interpretability, and domains where analytic expressions are preferred over black-box numeric solvers.

title: They Said Memes Were Harmless-We Found the Ones That Hurt: Decoding Jokes, Symbols, and Cultural References
authors: Sahil Tripathi, Gautam Siddharth Kashyap, Mehwish Nasim, Jian Yang, Jiechao Gao
abstract: Meme-based social abuse detection is challenging because harmful intent often relies on implicit cultural symbolism and subtle cross-modal incongruence. Prior approaches, from fusion-based methods to in-context learning with Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), have made progress but remain limited by three factors: i) cultural blindness (missing symbolic context), ii) boundary ambiguity (satire vs. abuse confusion), and iii) lack of interpretability (opaque model reasoning). We introduce CROSS

infographic.key_insight: A culturally-aware, cross-modal approach (CROSS) can decode symbolic and contextual cues in memes to distinguish harmful abuse from benign humor while providing human-readable rationales.
infographic.problem_solved: Detecting meme-based social abuse where harmful intent is conveyed implicitly via cultural symbols, jokes, or cross-modal incongruence—issues that cause cultural blindness, satire/abuse boundary ambiguity, and opaque model decisions.
method: CROSS: a cross-modal pipeline that links visual symbols and textual cues to external cultural knowledge to recover implicit meaning.
Contrastive and boundary-aware training to separate satire/irony from targeted abuse and reduce confusion at decision boundaries.
Explainable output: attribution/rationale module that highlights image regions, symbolic references, and the cultural cues driving the classification (supports human review).
infographic.impact: Improves reliability and interpretability of multimodal abuse detection in real-world social content moderation, helping practitioners build safer, culturally-sensitive systems and audit model reasoning.

title: AutoFigure: Generating and Refining Publication-Ready Scientific Illustrations
authors: Minjun Zhu, Zhen Lin, Yixuan Weng, Panzhong Lu, Qiujie Xie
abstract: High-quality scientific illustrations are crucial for effectively communicating complex scientific and technical concepts, yet their manual creation remains a well-recognized bottleneck in both academia and industry. We present FigureBench, the first large-scale benchmark for generating scientific illustrations from long-form scientific texts. It contains 3,300 high-quality scientific text-figure pairs, covering diverse text-to-illustration tasks from scientific papers, surveys, blogs, and textb

infographic.key_insight: AutoFigure pairs a new large-scale benchmark (FigureBench) with a generation+refinement pipeline to automatically produce publication-ready scientific illustrations from long-form scientific text, reducing the manual burden of figure creation.
infographic.problem_solved: Manual creation of high-quality scientific illustrations is time-consuming and expertise-intensive; the paper addresses automatic generation and iterative refinement of figures from long-form scientific text across diverse sources.
method: Introduce FigureBench: a 3,300 high-quality text–figure pair benchmark drawn from papers, surveys, blogs, and other long-form scientific texts for training and evaluation.
Develop AutoFigure: a multimodal generation pipeline that converts descriptive scientific text into initial illustrations.
Apply iterative refinement (layout, visual style, and content grounding) and evaluation modules to produce publication-ready figures and measure quality.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a standardized dataset and a practical pipeline to accelerate figure production, enabling faster paper drafting, reproducible visuals, and focused research on text-to-illustration models and refinement techniques.

title: Antidistillation Fingerprinting
authors: Yixuan Even Xu, John Kirchenbauer, Yash Savani, Asher Trockman, Alexander Robey
abstract: Model distillation enables efficient emulation of frontier large language models (LLMs), creating a need for robust mechanisms to detect when a third-party student model has trained on a teacher model's outputs. However, existing fingerprinting techniques that could be used to detect such distillation rely on heuristic perturbations that impose a steep trade-off between generation quality and fingerprinting strength, often requiring significant degradation of utility to ensure the fingerprint is

infographic.key_insight: Antidistillation Fingerprinting embeds subtle, optimized signals into a teacher LLM so that those signals reliably survive a wide range of distillation procedures, enabling detection of student models trained on the teacher without noticeably degrading generation quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Detecting when third-party student models were trained on a teacher's outputs while avoiding the steep quality-vs.-detectability trade-offs of prior heuristic fingerprinting or watermarking techniques.
method: Optimize compact, low-visibility fingerprint signals injected into teacher outputs that create persistent distributional artifacts rather than obvious token-level perturbations.
Train or regularize the teacher (or its inference outputs) with an objective that maximizes detectability under typical distillation pipelines while constraining downstream utility loss.
Evaluate robustness with simulated distillation scenarios and statistical detectors applied to student generations to measure persistence and false-positive rates.
infographic.impact: Provides model owners and practitioners a practical way to establish provenance and detect unauthorized distillation of LLMs with minimal impact on model quality, aiding licensing enforcement and model accountability.

title: EventNeuS: 3D Mesh Reconstruction from a Single Event Camera
authors: Shreyas Sachan, Viktor Rudnev, Mohamed Elgharib, Christian Theobalt, Vladislav Golyanik
abstract: Event cameras offer a considerable alternative to RGB cameras in many scenarios. While there are recent works on event-based novel-view synthesis, dense 3D mesh reconstruction remains scarcely explored and existing event-based techniques are severely limited in their 3D reconstruction accuracy. To address this limitation, we present EventNeuS, a self-supervised neural model for learning 3D representations from monocular colour event streams. Our approach, for the first time, combines 3D signed d

infographic.key_insight: EventNeuS is the first self-supervised method that combines 3D signed-distance implicit geometry with monocular colour event streams to produce dense 3D mesh reconstructions from a single event camera, improving reconstruction accuracy from event data.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing event-based approaches struggle to produce accurate, dense 3D meshes from monocular event-camera input; EventNeuS addresses the gap by enabling high-quality 3D surface reconstruction directly from event streams without ground-truth meshes.
method: Encode monocular colour event streams into a continuous representation and feed them to a neural implicit surface model based on a 3D signed-distance function (SDF).
Self-supervise training with event-driven consistency cues and colour information (no ground-truth meshes required), jointly optimizing geometry and appearance.
Extract a dense triangle mesh from the learned SDF for downstream use (visualization, metric evaluation, or further processing).
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical route to dense, accurate 3D reconstruction in scenarios where event cameras excel (high speed, high dynamic range, low latency), enabling robust 3D perception pipelines that do not rely on multi-view RGB or ground-truth meshes.

title: AgentRx: Diagnosing AI Agent Failures from Execution Trajectories
authors: Shraddha Barke, Arnav Goyal, Alind Khare, Avaljot Singh, Suman Nath
abstract: AI agents often fail in ways that are difficult to localize because executions are probabilistic, long-horizon, multi-agent, and mediated by noisy tool outputs. We address this gap by manually annotating failed agent runs and release a novel benchmark of 115 failed trajectories spanning structured API workflows, incident management, and open-ended web/file tasks. Each trajectory is annotated with a critical failure step and a category from a grounded-theory derived, cross-domain failure taxonomy

infographic.key_insight: AgentRx shows that systematically annotating failed AI agent executions with a grounded, cross-domain failure taxonomy makes it possible to localize the critical failure step in long-horizon, noisy, multi-agent runs. The released benchmark of 115 annotated failed trajectories enables reproducible diagnosis and analysis.
infographic.problem_solved: Agents fail in ways that are hard to localize and study because runs are probabilistic, long-horizon, involve multiple agents/tools, and produce noisy outputs—AgentRx provides a structured dataset and taxonomy to identify where and why failures occur.
method: Manually annotate 115 failed agent execution trajectories spanning structured API workflows, incident management, and open-ended web/file tasks.
Derive a grounded-theory, cross-domain failure taxonomy and label each trajectory with its critical failure step and category.
Release the benchmark (AgentRx) to support reproducible diagnosis, analysis, and tool development for agent failures.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners and researchers a concrete dataset and taxonomy to pinpoint failure causes, accelerate debugging of complex agent systems, and benchmark improvements in agent reliability and monitoring.

title: RE-TRAC: REcursive TRAjectory Compression for Deep Search Agents
authors: Jialiang Zhu, Gongrui Zhang, Xiaolong Ma, Lin Xu, Miaosen Zhang
abstract: LLM-based deep research agents are largely built on the ReAct framework. This linear design makes it difficult to revisit earlier states, branch into alternative search directions, or maintain global awareness under long contexts, often leading to local optima, redundant exploration, and inefficient search. We propose Re-TRAC, an agentic framework that performs cross-trajectory exploration by generating a structured state representation after each trajectory to summarize evidence, uncertainties,

infographic.key_insight: Re-TRAC compresses each agent trajectory into a structured, recursive state summary so LLM-based agents can revisit, branch, and reason across trajectories—breaking the linear ReAct chain to avoid local optima and redundant exploration.
infographic.problem_solved: Linear ReAct-style traces make it hard for agents to maintain global awareness, revisit earlier states, or branch into alternative search directions, which causes inefficient search, redundant work, and stagnation in local optima.
method: After each trajectory, generate a structured state representation that captures evidence, actions, outcomes, and uncertainty.
Recursively compress and index these state summaries to enable cross-trajectory retrieval, branching, and re-entry into prior search points.
Use the compressed summaries to guide planning and prioritization (uncertainty-guided exploration and targeted re-examination), reducing context burden and redundant exploration.
infographic.impact: Re-TRAC makes deep search agents more efficient, scalable, and interpretable by enabling non-linear exploration and global state awareness—leading to faster convergence, less wasted computation, and better handling of long-context tasks.

Flowchart showing: trajectory -> structured state summary -> compression/indexing -> cross-trajectory retrieval -> guided next-step planning

title: SPARKLING: Balancing Signal Preservation and Symmetry Breaking for Width-Progressive Learning
authors: Qifan Yu, Xinyu Ma, Zhijian Zhuo, Minrui Wang, Deyi Liu
abstract: Progressive Learning (PL) reduces pre-training computational overhead by gradually increasing model scale. While prior work has extensively explored depth expansion, width expansion remains significantly understudied, with the few existing methods limited to the early stages of training. However, expanding width during the mid-stage is essential for maximizing computational savings, yet it remains a formidable challenge due to severe training instabilities. Empirically, we show that naive initia

infographic.key_insight: SPARKLING makes it possible to stably expand model width in the middle of training by jointly preserving forward/backward signal magnitudes and applying controlled symmetry breaking, enabling width-progressive learning without catastrophic instability.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the severe training instabilities that occur when increasing model width mid-training—instabilities that have prevented practical width-progressive schedules and limited pre-training compute savings.
method: Signal-preserving layer surgery: add parameters with rescaling/initialization that maintain activation and gradient magnitudes after widening.
Controlled symmetry breaking: introduce small, structured perturbations or asymmetric initialization for new units to avoid neuron collapse and encourage diversity.
Training-state-aware transfer: adapt optimizer state or selectively reset/update moments so training continues smoothly after width changes.
infographic.impact: Enables large compute savings and more flexible scaling schedules by allowing safe mid-stage widening—practitioners can progressively widen models with less tuning and fewer stability failures, making large-scale pre-training more efficient.
visual_elements: Training timeline: stages showing when width is expanded and corresponding compute saved (bar/area chart).

title: RLAnything: Forge Environment, Policy, and Reward Model in Completely Dynamic RL System
authors: Yinjie Wang, Tianbao Xie, Ke Shen, Mengdi Wang, Ling Yang
abstract: We propose RLAnything, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically forges environment, policy, and reward models through closed-loop optimization, amplifying learning signals and strengthening the overall RL system for any LLM or agentic scenarios. Specifically, the policy is trained with integrated feedback from step-wise and outcome signals, while the reward model is jointly optimized via consistency feedback, which in turn further improves policy training. Moreover, our theory-motivat

infographic.key_insight: RLAnything jointly forges environment, policy, and reward models in a closed-loop optimization, amplifying learning signals and improving RL performance for LLMs and agentic systems.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes limitations of static RL pipelines—sparse/noisy rewards and decoupled env/policy/reward components—by creating a dynamic system that produces stronger, consistent learning signals.
method: Integrate environment, policy, and reward into a closed-loop training pipeline so each component continuously adapts to the others.
Train the policy with combined step-wise and outcome feedback while jointly optimizing the reward model using consistency feedback from policy behavior.
Provide theoretical justification and empirical evaluation showing amplified learning signals and improved robustness across LLM/agent scenarios.
infographic.impact: Makes RL training for LLMs and agentic applications more efficient and robust by reducing reliance on hand-crafted rewards and enabling adaptive, self-improving systems.

title: Training LLMs for Divide-and-Conquer Reasoning Elevates Test-Time Scalability
authors: Xiao Liang, Zhong-Zhi Li, Zhenghao Lin, Eric Hancheng Jiang, Hengyuan Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities through step-by-step chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Nevertheless, at the limits of model capability, CoT often proves insufficient, and its strictly sequential nature constrains test-time scalability. A potential alternative is divide-and-conquer (DAC) reasoning, which decomposes a complex problem into subproblems to facilitate more effective exploration of the solution. Although promising, our analysis reveals a fun

infographic.key_insight: Training LLMs to explicitly perform divide‑and‑conquer (DAC) — decomposing problems into subproblems, solving them (potentially in parallel), then recombining answers — substantially improves test‑time scalability and robustness compared to strictly sequential chain‑of‑thought.
infographic.problem_solved: Chain‑of‑thought reasoning is often insufficient at the limits of model capability and inherently sequential, limiting exploration and scalability at test time; the paper addresses how to make LLM reasoning scale to larger, more complex tasks.
method: Fine‑tune or supervise LLMs to produce structured decompositions of complex problems (explicit subproblems and solving plans).
Solve subproblems independently (enabling parallelism and targeted search) and optionally iterate recursively on difficult subparts.
Aggregate and verify subanswers with a recomposition step and use training signals that reward useful decompositions and correct final solutions.
infographic.impact: This approach lets practitioners scale reasoning to bigger tasks by exploiting parallelism and better exploration, improving reliability of LLMs on problems that exceed single‑chain capacity.

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
authors: Haozhen Zhang, Quanyu Long, Jianzhu Bao, Tao Feng, Weizhi Zhang
abstract: Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present \textbf{MemSkill}, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pru

infographic.key_insight: MemSkill replaces rigid, hand-designed memory operations with learnable, evolvable "memory skills"—structured, reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning memory—so agents can adapt memory behavior to diverse interactions and long histories.
infographic.problem_solved: Current LLM agent memory systems use a small set of static procedures that hard-code human priors, making them inflexible across interaction patterns and inefficient when scaling to long conversation histories.
method: Reframe extraction, consolidation, and pruning as parameterized memory skills that can be learned rather than hand-crafted.
Organize skills as structured, reusable routines that can be applied across contexts and updated from interaction data.
Introduce a self-evolution mechanism that adapts and refines the skill library over time so agents improve memory handling without manual redesign.
infographic.impact: MemSkill enables more flexible, scalable, and efficient memory management for LLM agents, improving long-term coherence and reducing manual engineering of memory operations—beneficial for deployed conversational and multi-step AI systems.

title: Expanding the Capabilities of Reinforcement Learning via Text Feedback
authors: Yuda Song, Lili Chen, Fahim Tajwar, Remi Munos, Deepak Pathak
abstract: The success of RL for LLM post-training stems from an unreasonably uninformative source: a single bit of information per rollout as binary reward or preference label. At the other extreme, distillation offers dense supervision but requires demonstrations, which are costly and difficult to scale. We study text feedback as an intermediate signal: richer than scalar rewards, yet cheaper than complete demonstrations. Textual feedback is a natural mode of human interaction and is already abundant in

infographic.key_insight: Textual feedback provides a middle ground between sparse binary rewards and costly demonstrations: it is richer than a single-bit signal yet cheaper and more scalable than full demonstrations, enabling denser, human-native supervision for policy learning.
infographic.problem_solved: RL training for language and decision agents relies on either very sparse rewards or expensive demonstrations; this paper addresses how to obtain richer, scalable supervision that improves learning without requiring full expert demonstrations.
method: Collect natural-language feedback associated with rollouts or model outputs (human or crowd-sourced).
Train models to interpret text feedback into dense training signals (e.g., learned reward or loss shaping).
Use the derived dense signals to update policies (via RL fine-tuning or supervised objectives), closing the gap between scalar rewards and demonstrations.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, scalable way to improve sample efficiency and alignment in RL systems by leveraging abundant human-language feedback—reducing annotation cost while yielding richer supervision that is easy to inspect and improve.

title: MentisOculi: Revealing the Limits of Reasoning with Mental Imagery
authors: Jana Zeller, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Fanfei Li, Thomas Klein, Prasanna Mayilvahanan
abstract: Frontier models are transitioning from multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that merely ingest visual information to unified multimodal models (UMMs) capable of native interleaved generation. This shift has sparked interest in using intermediate visualizations as a reasoning aid, akin to human mental imagery. Central to this idea is the ability to form, maintain, and manipulate visual representations in a goal-oriented manner. To evaluate and probe this capability, we develop MentisOculi, a

infographic.key_insight: MentisOculi shows that even advanced unified multimodal models can form visual "mental images" but struggle to reliably maintain and manipulate them for goal-directed reasoning, exposing concrete limits in image-based intermediate reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a targeted benchmark and analysis framework to measure whether and how multimodal models can form, maintain, and manipulate intermediate visual representations as a reasoning aid—something prior evaluations did not systematically quantify.
method: Design a suite of controlled tasks requiring stepwise visual reasoning (formation, persistence, transformation) that force use of intermediate imagery.
Instrument models to produce native interleaved visual outputs and log intermediate states; evaluate fidelity, consistency, and goal alignment with quantitative metrics.
Compare state-of-the-art UMMs/MLLMs, run ablations and interventions to identify failure modes and factors that degrade mental-imagery reasoning.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners a practical toolkit and empirical evidence to judge when visual intermediateizations help or hinder reasoning, guiding model selection, training, and prompt design for reliable multimodal reasoning.

title: HumanX: Toward Agile and Generalizable Humanoid Interaction Skills from Human Videos
authors: Yinhuai Wang, Qihan Zhao, Yuen Fui Lau, Runyi Yu, Hok Wai Tsui
abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to perform agile and adaptive interactive tasks has long been a core challenge in robotics. Current approaches are bottlenecked by either the scarcity of realistic interaction data or the need for meticulous, task-specific reward engineering, which limits their scalability. To narrow this gap, we present HumanX, a full-stack framework that compiles human video into generalizable, real-world interaction skills for humanoids, without task-specific rewards. HumanX integrate

infographic.key_insight: HumanX compiles large-scale human video into reusable, agile interaction skills for humanoid robots, enabling generalizable real-world behaviors without per-task reward engineering.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap caused by scarce realistic interaction data and costly task-specific reward design, enabling scalable learning of adaptive humanoid interaction skills.
method: Full-stack pipeline that converts human videos into compact skill representations and supervision for robot policies (data curation → representation extraction → policy learning).
Reward-free learning: train interaction skills from imitation and self-supervision instead of hand-designed, task-specific rewards.
Sim-to-real and control adaptation: refine policies with simulation-aware dynamics and adaptive controllers for stable transfer to humanoid hardware.
infographic.impact: Reduces engineering overhead and unlocks scalable transfer of rich human behaviors to humanoid platforms, accelerating development of adaptive interactive robots for real-world tasks.

title: Flow Policy Gradients for Robot Control
authors: Brent Yi, Hongsuk Choi, Himanshu Gaurav Singh, Xiaoyu Huang, Takara E. Truong
abstract: Likelihood-based policy gradient methods are the dominant approach for training robot control policies from rewards. These methods rely on differentiable action likelihoods, which constrain policy outputs to simple distributions like Gaussians. In this work, we show how flow matching policy gradients -- a recent framework that bypasses likelihood computation -- can be made effective for training and fine-tuning more expressive policies in challenging robot control settings. We introduce an impro

infographic.key_insight: Flow-matching policy gradients let you compute policy updates without requiring action likelihoods, enabling training and fine-tuning of much more expressive, potentially multimodal action policies for robot control.
infographic.problem_solved: Likelihood-based policy gradients require differentiable action likelihoods and therefore force simple output distributions (e.g., Gaussians), limiting expressiveness and performance in challenging robotic tasks.
method: Replace likelihood-based gradient estimators with a flow-matching gradient objective that bypasses explicit likelihood computation.
Parameterize policies with expressive flow-style models (enabling multimodal and structured action outputs) and backpropagate flow-matching gradients to update them.
Apply the approach as a training and fine-tuning recipe for robot control policies to improve expressiveness and practical performance in hard control settings.
infographic.impact: Practitioners can train richer policy families for robotic control without being constrained to simple distributions, improving adaptability and performance on tasks with multimodal or structured action requirements. This opens a path to better fine-tuning of complex policies using standard RL reward signals.

title: VideoGPA: Distilling Geometry Priors for 3D-Consistent Video Generation
authors: Hongyang Du, Junjie Ye, Xiaoyan Cong, Runhao Li, Jingcheng Ni
abstract: While recent video diffusion models (VDMs) produce visually impressive results, they fundamentally struggle to maintain 3D structural consistency, often resulting in object deformation or spatial drift. We hypothesize that these failures arise because standard denoising objectives lack explicit incentives for geometric coherence. To address this, we introduce VideoGPA (Video Geometric Preference Alignment), a data-efficient self-supervised framework that leverages a geometry foundation model to

infographic.key_insight: VideoGPA distills geometry priors from a geometry foundation model into video diffusion training via a self-supervised preference-alignment objective, enabling substantially improved 3D structural consistency across generated video frames.
infographic.problem_solved: Video diffusion models produce high-quality frames but often fail to maintain 3D coherence across time (object deformation, spatial drift) because standard denoising objectives don’t explicitly enforce geometric consistency.
method: Leverage a pre-trained geometry foundation model (e.g., depth/pose/3D-aware estimator) to produce geometric cues as supervision.
Distill those geometry priors into the video diffusion model with a self-supervised preference-alignment objective that biases generation toward geometrically consistent solutions.
Design the pipeline to be data-efficient by applying alignment on latent/denoised representations and across temporal frames to enforce 3D-consistent motion and shape.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get more temporally and spatially stable video generation with fewer artifacts, which improves downstream use in AR/VR, visual effects, and any application needing multi-frame 3D coherence—without large labeled video datasets.

title: TEON: Tensorized Orthonormalization Beyond Layer-Wise Muon for Large Language Model Pre-Training
authors: Ruijie Zhang, Yequan Zhao, Ziyue Liu, Zhengyang Wang, Dongyang Li
abstract: The Muon optimizer has demonstrated strong empirical performance in pre-training large language models by performing matrix-level gradient (or momentum) orthogonalization in each layer independently. In this work, we propose TEON, a principled generalization of Muon that extends orthogonalization beyond individual layers by modeling the gradients of a neural network as a structured higher-order tensor. We present TEON's improved convergence guarantee over layer-wise Muon, and further develop a p

infographic.key_insight: TEON generalizes the Muon optimizer by modeling gradients as a structured higher-order tensor and applying tensorized orthonormalization across modes, yielding stronger convergence guarantees than layer-wise (matrix) orthogonalization.
infographic.problem_solved: Layer-wise Muon treats each layer independently and misses cross-layer and multi-mode correlations in gradients; TEON addresses this by removing redundancy and collinearity in a tensor-structured gradient representation to improve optimization for large language model pre-training.
method: Represent the network gradients (or momenta) as a structured higher-order tensor that captures interactions across parameter modes (e.g., layers, heads, channels).
Perform tensorized orthonormalization across tensor modes (mode-wise / multi-mode orthogonalization) to decorrelate gradient components beyond per-layer matrices.
Design scalable approximations and algorithmic steps that retain provable improved convergence over layer-wise Muon while remaining practical for LLM-scale pre-training.
infographic.impact: TEON can make LLM pre-training more stable and sample-efficient by removing multi-mode gradient redundancies, enabling faster convergence and more robust scaling of optimizer behavior across very large models.

title: FOCUS: DLLMs Know How to Tame Their Compute Bound
authors: Kaihua Liang, Xin Tan, An Zhong, Hong Xu, Marco Canini
abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs) offer a compelling alternative to Auto-Regressive models, but their deployment is constrained by high decoding cost. In this work, we identify a key inefficiency in DLLM decoding: while computation is parallelized over token blocks, only a small subset of tokens is decodable at each diffusion step, causing most compute to be wasted on non-decodable tokens. We further observe a strong correlation between attention-derived token importance and token-wise dec

infographic.key_insight: DLLM decoding wastes compute because only a small subset of tokens is decodable at each diffusion step; attention-derived token importance strongly predicts which tokens are decodable, enabling focused allocation of decoding compute.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces wasted parallel compute in Diffusion Large Language Model (DLLM) decoding by identifying and prioritizing tokens that are actually decodable at each diffusion step.
method: Use attention-derived token importance to estimate per-token decodability during diffusion decoding.
Dynamically allocate decoding computation to high-importance (decodable) tokens and defer or skip non-decodable ones while retaining block-parallel processing.
Introduce a lightweight gating/scheduling mechanism (FOCUS) to route compute only where it yields progress, cutting redundant work across diffusion steps.
infographic.impact: Makes DLLM inference much more compute- and time-efficient, lowering inference cost and improving practicality of diffusion-based LLMs for deployment and research.

title: UPA: Unsupervised Prompt Agent via Tree-Based Search and Selection
authors: Siran Peng, Weisong Zhao, Tianyu Fu, Chenxu Zhao, Tianshuo Zhang
abstract: Prompt agents have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for automated prompt optimization, framing refinement as a sequential decision-making problem over a structured prompt space. While this formulation enables the use of advanced planning algorithms, these methods typically assume access to supervised reward signals, which are often unavailable in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose UPA, an Unsupervised Prompt Agent that realizes structured search and selection without relying o

infographic.key_insight: UPA reframes prompt optimization as a tree-based search that finds high-quality prompts using unsupervised selection signals instead of relying on labeled reward feedback. This enables automated, structured prompt refinement when supervised rewards are unavailable.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes the dependence on supervised reward signals for automated prompt optimization, allowing prompt agents to search and select effective prompts in practical, unlabeled settings.
method: Construct a structured prompt space as a tree and perform iterative expansion/search over candidate prompt branches.
Score and prune branches using unsupervised selection criteria (e.g., self-consistency/consensus, diversity, uncertainty, language-model-based fluency/coherence) rather than labeled rewards.
Iteratively refine and select promising prompts via tree-based planning (expansion, evaluation, selection) to produce robust final prompts.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to automate prompt tuning in domains where labeled feedback is scarce or expensive, reducing manual engineering and allowing scalable prompt discovery for downstream tasks.

title: Denoising the Deep Sky: Physics-Based CCD Noise Formation for Astronomical Imaging
authors: Shuhong Liu, Xining Ge, Ziying Gu, Lin Gu, Ziteng Cui
abstract: Astronomical imaging remains noise-limited under practical observing constraints, while standard calibration pipelines mainly remove structured artifacts and leave stochastic noise largely unresolved. Learning-based denoising is promising, yet progress is hindered by scarce paired training data and the need for physically interpretable and reproducible models in scientific workflows. We propose a physics-based noise synthesis framework tailored to CCD noise formation. The pipeline models photon

infographic.key_insight: A physics-based CCD noise synthesis pipeline can generate realistic, interpretable noisy–clean image pairs for astronomical imaging, enabling effective supervised denoising without relying on scarce real paired data.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of physically realistic paired training data and the need for interpretable, reproducible noise models in astronomical CCD denoising workflows.
method: Construct a modular, physics-based simulator of CCD noise formation that models key stages (photon shot noise, dark current, pixel defects, readout electronics and digitization).
Use the simulator to synthesize realistic noisy–clean image pairs for training and augmenting learning-based denoisers.
Validate synthetic noise by matching statistical signatures to real observations and integrate the pipeline with standard calibration/denoising workflows.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners with reproducible, physically grounded training data and diagnostics that improve denoiser generalization and scientific interpretability, reducing reliance on hard-to-obtain real paired datasets.

title: End-to-end Optimization of Belief and Policy Learning in Shared Autonomy Paradigms
authors: MH Farhadi, Ali Rabiee, Sima Ghafoori, Anna Cetera, Andrew Fisher
abstract: Shared autonomy systems require principled methods for inferring user intent and determining appropriate assistance levels. This is a central challenge in human-robot interaction, where systems must be successful while being mindful of user agency. Previous approaches relied on static blending ratios or separated goal inference from assistance arbitration, leading to suboptimal performance in unstructured environments. We introduce BRACE (Bayesian Reinforcement Assistance with Context Encoding),

infographic.key_insight: BRACE jointly learns a Bayesian belief over user intent and a policy for assistance in an end-to-end way, so inference and assistance are optimized together rather than treated separately. This yields more adaptive, context-aware assistance that preserves user agency in unstructured environments.
infographic.problem_solved: Current shared-autonomy systems use fixed blending or decoupled goal inference and arbitration, producing suboptimal assistance when user intent and environment context are uncertain; BRACE addresses this by integrating belief estimation and policy optimization.
method: End-to-end training that backpropagates through a Bayesian belief module and a reinforcement-learning policy so belief updates and assistance actions are jointly optimized.
Context encoding to represent environment and user signals, producing a posterior over goals that conditions the assistance policy.
Reinforcement learning objective balances task performance and user agency, enabling adaptive assistance levels rather than static blending.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get a recipe for principled, adaptive shared-autonomy systems that improve task success under uncertainty while respecting user control; applicable to assistive robotics, teleoperation, and human-in-the-loop systems.

title: Decoupled Diffusion Sampling for Inverse Problems on Function Spaces
authors: Thomas Y. L. Lin, Jiachen Yao, Lufang Chiang, Julius Berner, Anima Anandkumar
abstract: We propose a data-efficient, physics-aware generative framework in function space for inverse PDE problems. Existing plug-and-play diffusion posterior samplers represent physics implicitly through joint coefficient-solution modeling, requiring substantial paired supervision. In contrast, our Decoupled Diffusion Inverse Solver (DDIS) employs a decoupled design: an unconditional diffusion learns the coefficient prior, while a neural operator explicitly models the forward PDE for guidance. This dec

infographic.key_insight: Decoupled Diffusion Inverse Solver (DDIS) separates the generative prior and the forward physics: an unconditional diffusion models the coefficient prior in function space, while a neural operator explicitly provides PDE-based guidance during sampling. This yields a data-efficient, physics-aware posterior sampler for inverse PDE problems.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces the need for large paired coefficient–solution datasets in inverse PDE problems by avoiding joint coefficient-solution modeling and making physics explicit during sampling, enabling accurate posterior sampling with far less supervised data.
method: Train an unconditional diffusion model in function space to learn the prior over PDE coefficients (no paired solution data required).
Train or use a neural operator to model the forward PDE map; use it to provide physics-based guidance (likelihood) during diffusion sampling.
Decouple prior learning from forward physics so the sampler produces physics-consistent posterior samples with improved data efficiency and modularity.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a modular, scalable approach to solve inverse PDEs with fewer paired examples while respecting physical constraints—useful for scientific ML, engineering inverse design, and uncertainty quantification in high-dimensional/function-space settings.

title: Exploring Reasoning Reward Model for Agents
authors: Kaixuan Fan, Kaituo Feng, Manyuan Zhang, Tianshuo Peng, Zhixun Li
abstract: Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL) has achieved notable success in enabling agents to perform complex reasoning and tool use. However, most methods still relies on sparse outcome-based reward for training. Such feedback fails to differentiate intermediate reasoning quality, leading to suboptimal training results. In this paper, we introduce Agent Reasoning Reward Model (Agent-RRM), a multi-faceted reward model that produces structured feedback for agentic trajectories, including (1) an

infographic.key_insight: A multi‑faceted reward model (Agent‑RRM) provides structured, step‑level feedback on agent trajectories so training can target intermediate reasoning quality rather than only final outcomes.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes reliance on sparse outcome‑based rewards that fail to distinguish good vs. poor intermediate reasoning and tool use, which leads to slow learning and suboptimal agent behavior.
method: Design Agent‑RRM to produce structured, per‑step rewards across multiple facets (e.g., reasoning correctness, tool usage, coherence/confidence, efficiency).
Integrate these dense, facetized signals into agent training for better credit assignment (reward shaping, auxiliary losses, or critic augmentation).
Evaluate and refine the model by comparing agent learning trajectories and reasoning quality under Agent‑RRM vs. sparse outcome rewards.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to train more reliable, interpretable agents by rewarding intermediate reasoning and tool use—improving sample efficiency, debugging, and alignment of complex agent behaviors.

title: RedSage: A Cybersecurity Generalist LLM
authors: Naufal Suryanto, Muzammal Naseer, Pengfei Li, Syed Talal Wasim, Jinhui Yi
abstract: Cybersecurity operations demand assistant LLMs that support diverse workflows without exposing sensitive data. Existing solutions either rely on proprietary APIs with privacy risks or on open models lacking domain adaptation. To bridge this gap, we curate 11.8B tokens of cybersecurity-focused continual pretraining data via large-scale web filtering and manual collection of high-quality resources, spanning 28.6K documents across frameworks, offensive techniques, and security tools. Building on th

infographic.key_insight: RedSage creates a cybersecurity-focused generalist LLM by continual pretraining on a curated 11.8B-token corpus, delivering domain-aware capabilities without relying on proprietary APIs. This bridges the gap between privacy risks of hosted services and the poor domain fit of untuned open models.
infographic.problem_solved: Security teams need a privacy-preserving, domain-adapted assistant that supports diverse cybersecurity workflows; existing solutions either expose sensitive data to proprietary APIs or use open models that lack specialized cybersecurity knowledge.
method: Curate a large cybersecurity corpus (11.8B tokens, 28.6K documents) via large-scale web filtering plus manual collection covering frameworks, offensive techniques, and security tools.
Perform continual pretraining of a foundation LLM on the curated dataset to produce a domain-adapted cybersecurity generalist (RedSage).
Design the model and deployment workflow to support diverse security operations while minimizing exposure of sensitive data (privacy-aware integration).
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML and security practitioners a practical path to deploy high-quality, domain-tuned assistants that improve performance on infosec tasks and reduce dependence on proprietary, privacy-risky APIs.

title: UEval: A Benchmark for Unified Multimodal Generation
authors: Bo Li, Yida Yin, Wenhao Chai, Xingyu Fu, Zhuang Liu
abstract: We introduce UEval, a benchmark to evaluate unified models, i.e., models capable of generating both images and text. UEval comprises 1,000 expert-curated questions that require both images and text in the model output, sourced from 8 real-world tasks. Our curated questions cover a wide range of reasoning types, from step-by-step guides to textbook explanations. Evaluating open-ended multimodal generation is non-trivial, as simple LLM-as-a-judge methods can miss the subtleties. Different from pre

infographic.key_insight: UEval provides the first focused benchmark to evaluate unified generative models that must produce both images and text, using 1,000 expert‑curated multimodal questions spanning 8 real‑world tasks to surface nuanced failures that simple LLM‑as‑judge methods miss.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of a standardized, high‑quality evaluation for unified multimodal generation — existing benchmarks and automatic judges often fail to capture the joint visual+text reasoning and open‑ended requirements of image+text outputs.
method: Assemble 1,000 expert‑curated questions that explicitly require both image and text in model outputs, sampled from 8 real‑world tasks and varied reasoning types (e.g., step‑by‑step guides, textbook explanations).
Design evaluation protocols and reference outputs that emphasize fine‑grained visual‑textual correctness and robustness, and highlight shortcomings of naive LLM‑as‑judge approaches.
Release the benchmark and evaluation tools to enable consistent comparison of unified models and stimulate improvements in multimodal generation and evaluation.
infographic.impact: UEval gives practitioners a rigorous, focused way to measure and compare unified image+text generation systems, driving development of models and evaluation methods that handle joint visual and textual reasoning rather than optimizing for narrow automatic metrics.
