title: Hybrid Linear Attention Done Right: Efficient Distillation and Effective Architectures for Extremely Long Contexts
authors: Yingfa Chen, Zhen Leng Thai, Zihan Zhou, Zhu Zhang, Xingyu Shen
abstract: Hybrid Transformer architectures, which combine softmax attention blocks and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have shown a desirable performance-throughput tradeoff for long-context modeling, but their adoption and studies are hindered by the prohibitive cost of large-scale pre-training from scratch. Some recent studies have shown that pre-trained softmax attention blocks can be converted into RNN blocks through parameter transfer and knowledge distillation. However, these transfer methods requ

infographic.key_insight: You can get the long-context throughput and memory advantages of RNN-like or linear-attention components while preserving the accuracy of pretrained Transformers by efficiently distilling and transferring parameters into a carefully designed hybrid linear-attention + RNN architecture.
infographic.problem_solved: Training hybrid Transformer–RNN architectures for extremely long contexts from scratch is prohibitively expensive; the paper solves how to convert and distill pretrained softmax-attention blocks into efficient hybrid/linear-attention architectures so models can handle much longer contexts with far less pretraining cost.
method: Design hybrid architectures that combine linearized attention with recurrent state updates to retain expressivity while enabling constant-memory, streaming execution.
Develop an efficient parameter-transfer and knowledge-distillation pipeline to convert pretrained softmax-attention blocks into the hybrid/linear-attention modules without full-scale retraining.

Introduce practical training/regularization and architectural tweaks (e.g., gating, normalization, and state-update schedules) to preserve accuracy across very long context lengths while improving throughput and memory use.
infographic.impact: Makes it practical for researchers and engineers to deploy and fine-tune models that handle extremely long contexts (e.g., millions of tokens) without the compute cost of pretraining from scratch—improving inference speed, memory footprint, and applicability to streaming or long-document tasks.

title: One-step Latent-free Image Generation with Pixel Mean Flows
authors: Yiyang Lu, Susie Lu, Qiao Sun, Hanhong Zhao, Zhicheng Jiang
abstract: Modern diffusion/flow-based models for image generation typically exhibit two core characteristics: (i) using multi-step sampling, and (ii) operating in a latent space. Recent advances have made encouraging progress on each aspect individually, paving the way toward one-step diffusion/flow without latents. In this work, we take a further step towards this goal and propose "pixel MeanFlow" (pMF). Our core guideline is to formulate the network output space and the loss space separately. The networ

infographic.key_insight: Pixel MeanFlow (pMF) enables one-step, latent-free image generation by separating what the network predicts (output space) from how it's trained (loss space), allowing a single-step flow transform from simple noise to high-quality images.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between multi-step latent diffusion/flow models and fully one-step, pixel-space generative models — removing iterative sampling and latent-space dependencies that increase latency and system complexity.
method: Design a flow-based generator whose network outputs live in a tailored pixel-space (the "mean flow" representation) while the optimization/loss is computed in the target image space.
Train the model so a single transformation maps simple base noise directly to images (one-step sampling) without intermediate latents or multi-step denoising.
Separate output & loss spaces to stabilize training and align the model's predictive target with perceptual/image reconstruction objectives.
infographic.impact: Practitioners get a fast, simpler alternative to multi-step diffusion/flow pipelines — enabling real-time or resource-constrained image synthesis and easier deployment while retaining high image quality.
visual_elements: High-level pipeline diagram: single-step mapping from noise to image, highlighting separation between network output space and loss space.

title: Do VLMs Perceive or Recall? Probing Visual Perception vs. Memory with Classic Visual Illusions
authors: Xiaoxiao Sun, Mingyang Li, Kun yuan, Min Woo Sun, Mark Endo
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often answer classic visual illusions "correctly" on original images, yet persist with the same responses when illusion factors are inverted, even though the visual change is obvious to humans. This raises a fundamental question: do VLMs perceive visual changes or merely recall memorized patterns? While several studies have noted this phenomenon, the underlying causes remain unclear. To move from observations to systematic understanding, this paper introduces

infographic.key_insight: VLMs often produce illusion-appropriate answers by recalling memorized associations rather than perceiving visual changes — they persist with the same responses even when illusion cues are inverted, unlike humans.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines whether VLM outputs reflect genuine visual perception or pattern recall, and provides a systematic probing protocol to diagnose non-perceptual behavior on classic visual illusions.
method: Build a controlled benchmark of classic visual illusions paired with inverted/altered variants that flip the perceptual effect while keeping surface statistics similar.
Query VLMs (with standardized prompts) on original vs inverted images and quantify response consistency, agreement with human perception, and failure modes.
Analyze contributing factors (prompting, model architecture, training data artifacts) to separate perception-like responses from memorized pattern recall.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a practical evaluation to detect when VLMs rely on memorized templates rather than visual reasoning, informing model selection, fine-tuning, and dataset curation to improve real visual understanding.

title: Late Breaking Results: Conversion of Neural Networks into Logic Flows for Edge Computing
authors: Daniel Stein, Shaoyi Huang, Rolf Drechsler, Bing Li, Grace Li Zhang
abstract: Neural networks have been successfully applied in various resource-constrained edge devices, where usually central processing units (CPUs) instead of graphics processing units exist due to limited power availability. State-of-the-art research still focuses on efficiently executing enormous numbers of multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations. However, CPUs themselves are not good at executing such mathematical operations on a large scale, since they are more suited to execute control flow logic, i.e.

infographic.key_insight: Neural networks can be transformed into control-flow–style logic programs that replace many MAC-heavy operations with branching and bitwise logic, enabling much more efficient inference on CPU-based edge devices. This conversion yields deterministic, low-power execution tailored to resource-constrained platforms.
infographic.problem_solved: Edge devices often lack GPUs and are inefficient at executing large numbers of multiply-accumulate operations; the paper addresses how to run neural-network workloads efficiently on CPU-centric, power-limited hardware by re-expressing models as logic flows.
method: Quantize and simplify network components (low-bit / binarize activations & weights) to expose Boolean structure.
Translate neuron computations into equivalent logic-flow primitives (bitwise ops, branches, lookup tables) and synthesize a control-flow program representing the model.
Apply pruning and CPU-aware optimizations (instruction-level scheduling, branch fusion, memory reduction) to produce compact, low-latency inference code for edge CPUs.
infographic.impact: This approach enables low-power, predictable ML inference on ubiquitous CPU-based edge devices, reducing energy and latency while improving deployability and interpretability for practitioners working on TinyML and embedded AI.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: trained neural network -> quantization -> logic-flow extraction -> optimized CPU code
Bar chart comparing MAC-heavy inference vs logic-flow inference on latency and power for an edge CPU

title: DynaWeb: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning of Web Agents
authors: Hang Ding, Peidong Liu, Junqiao Wang, Ziwei Ji, Meng Cao
abstract: The development of autonomous web agents, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning (RL), represents a significant step towards general-purpose AI assistants. However, training these agents is severely hampered by the challenges of interacting with the live internet, which is inefficient, costly, and fraught with risks. Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) offers a promising solution by learning a world model of the environment to enable simulated interaction. This

infographic.key_insight: DynaWeb adapts model-based reinforcement learning to web agents by learning a compact world model of the web so agents can train via simulated interactions, greatly reducing the need for costly and risky live-web exploration.
infographic.problem_solved: Training autonomous web agents on the live internet is inefficient, expensive, and unsafe; interacting with real web environments at scale prevents practical RL-driven agent development.
method: Learn an action-conditioned world model of web state transitions (e.g., DOM/API/response dynamics) from limited real interactions and logs.
Use the learned model to generate imagined rollouts for policy learning and planning, interleaving simulated training with occasional real rollouts for grounding.
Mitigate model bias via uncertainty-aware rollouts (ensembles or confidence gating) and selective real-environment fine-tuning.
infographic.impact: Enables sample-efficient, safer, and cheaper training of web-capable agents (including LLM-based assistants), accelerating development and deployment of autonomous web automation and assistance.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: real web -> world model -> simulated rollouts -> policy -> periodic real validation (highlight feedback loop).

title: DynamicVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
authors: Haozhe Xie, Beichen Wen, Jiarui Zheng, Zhaoxi Chen, Fangzhou Hong
abstract: Manipulating dynamic objects remains an open challenge for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which, despite strong generalization in static manipulation, struggle in dynamic scenarios requiring rapid perception, temporal anticipation, and continuous control. We present DynamicVLA, a framework for dynamic object manipulation that integrates temporal reasoning and closed-loop adaptation through three key designs: 1) a compact 0.4B VLA using a convolutional vision encoder for spatially efficient

infographic.key_insight: DynamicVLA enables reliable manipulation of moving objects by combining a compact vision-language-action backbone with explicit temporal reasoning and closed-loop adaptation, allowing fast perception-to-action loops for dynamic scenarios.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between strong static-scene VLA capabilities and real-world dynamic object manipulation that requires rapid temporal anticipation and continuous control.
method: Compact 0.4B VLA backbone with a convolutional vision encoder for spatially efficient perception and low-latency inference.
Temporal reasoning module that predicts short-horizon object motion and integrates past observations for anticipation.
Closed-loop adaptation and continuous control pipeline that updates actions in real time based on streamed visual and language inputs.
infographic.impact: Makes dynamic-object manipulation practical for resource-constrained robots and interactive agents by enabling anticipatory, closed-loop control with a small, deployable VLA model—reducing latency and improving robustness in time-sensitive tasks.

title: FreeFix: Boosting 3D Gaussian Splatting via Fine-Tuning-Free Diffusion Models
authors: Hongyu Zhou, Zisen Shao, Sheng Miao, Pan Wang, Dongfeng Bai
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting have advanced novel view synthesis, yet still rely on dense inputs and often degrade at extrapolated views. Recent approaches leverage generative models, such as diffusion models, to provide additional supervision, but face a trade-off between generalization and fidelity: fine-tuning diffusion models for artifact removal improves fidelity but risks overfitting, while fine-tuning-free methods preserve generalization but often yield lower fidelity.

infographic.key_insight: Pre-trained diffusion models can be used as a non-invasive, test-time corrective supervisor for 3D Gaussian Splatting—boosting extrapolated-view fidelity without fine-tuning and thus avoiding overfitting.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the fidelity vs. generalization trade-off when using generative priors for novel view synthesis: removes rendering artifacts and improves extrapolated views without updating diffusion model weights.
method: Use off-the-shelf diffusion models at inference as a corrective signal for 3D Gaussian Splatting outputs (no fine-tuning of diffusion weights).
Introduce a consistency-preserving guidance/correction pipeline that injects diffusion-based priors into rendered views while maintaining 3D structure and cross-view coherence.
Adaptively apply correction strength (e.g., targeted to high-uncertainty or artifact-prone regions) to maximize fidelity gains without sacrificing generalization.
infographic.impact: Allows practitioners to improve novel-view fidelity and robustness of 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines with minimal engineering and compute overhead, avoiding the risks and costs of fine-tuning large diffusion models.

title: Evolutionary Strategies lead to Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs
authors: Immanuel Abdi, Akshat Gupta, Micah Mok, Alexander Lu, Nicholas Lee
abstract: One of the biggest missing capabilities in current AI systems is the ability to learn continuously after deployment. Implementing such continually learning systems have several challenges, one of which is the large memory requirement of gradient-based algorithms that are used to train state-of-the-art LLMs. Evolutionary Strategies (ES) have recently re-emerged as a gradient-free alternative to traditional learning algorithms and have shown encouraging performance on specific tasks in LLMs. In th

infographic.key_insight: Using Evolutionary Strategies (ES) as a gradient-free way to continue-training LLMs induces severe catastrophic forgetting — ES can rapidly overwrite previously learned behaviors despite being memory-efficient.
infographic.problem_solved: Examines whether ES can be a practical, low-memory alternative for continual learning in deployed LLMs and uncovers its suitability (or lack thereof) for preserving past knowledge.
method: Empirically evaluate ES-based continual fine-tuning on LLM benchmarks/tasks and measure retained vs. lost capabilities over time.
Compare forgetting and performance trajectories between ES and standard gradient-based continual learning baselines.
Analyze failure modes (e.g., parameter drift, distributional shift) to identify why ES induces catastrophic forgetting.
infographic.impact: Alerts practitioners that although ES reduces memory requirements, it can compromise model stability and long-term retention — prompting caution and motivating development of hybrid or mitigative continual-learning strategies.
visual_elements: Line chart: task performance over time showing rapid decline (forgetting) for ES vs. stable or slower decline for gradient-based methods.
Bar chart: final retained accuracy or knowledge retention comparing ES and gradient-based baselines across tasks.

title: Teaching machines to blend electrolyte cocktails

Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 January 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01181-4

Mixtures are ubiquitous in industrial formulations. A framework unifying predictive and generative machine learning now offers a blueprint for data-driven design of multi-component battery electrolytes.

method: Train predictive surrogate models to map multi‑component compositions to target properties (e.g., conductivity, stability).
Use generative/inverse models to propose candidate compositions that meet target property objectives, guided by the predictors.
Iterate search across composition space to prioritize promising electrolyte cocktails for further testing (closed‑loop design).
infographic.impact: Provides a practical blueprint for applying combined predictive and generative ML to accelerate materials/formulation discovery, reducing experimental burden and enabling rapid exploration of complex mixture spaces.

title: A New Dataset and Framework for Robust Road Surface Classification via Camera-IMU Fusion
authors: Willams de Lima Costa, Thifany Ketuli Silva de Souza, Jonas Ferreira Silva, Carlos Gabriel Bezerra Pereira, Bruno Reis Vila Nova
abstract: Road surface classification (RSC) is a key enabler for environment-aware predictive maintenance systems. However, existing RSC techniques often fail to generalize beyond narrow operational conditions due to limited sensing modalities and datasets that lack environmental diversity. This work addresses these limitations by introducing a multimodal framework that fuses images and inertial measurements using a lightweight bidirectional cross-attention module followed by an adaptive gating layer that

infographic.key_insight: Fusing camera images with IMU data using a lightweight bidirectional cross-attention module plus an adaptive gating layer yields more robust, generalizable road surface classification across diverse environmental conditions; the paper also provides a new multimodal dataset to benchmark this setting.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing road surface classification methods struggle to generalize beyond narrow operational conditions because of limited sensing modalities and datasets lacking environmental diversity. This work addresses both limits by supplying a diverse camera–IMU dataset and an efficient fusion framework that adapts to noisy or degraded inputs.
method: Curate a synchronized multimodal dataset of camera frames and IMU readings covering varied road types, lighting and weather conditions (benchmark for RSC).
Fuse visual and inertial features via a lightweight bidirectional cross-attention module to let each modality inform the other.
Apply an adaptive gating layer that dynamically weights modalities to suppress noisy sensors and emphasize reliable cues, followed by a compact classifier for on-device deployment.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical fusion architecture and dataset to build RSC models that generalize to real-world variability and run efficiently on edge platforms—reducing failures in predictive maintenance and autonomous systems.

title: Reward Models Inherit Value Biases from Pretraining
authors: Brian Christian, Jessica A. F. Thompson, Elle Michelle Yang, Vincent Adam, Hannah Rose Kirk
abstract: Reward models (RMs) are central to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values but have received less attention than pre-trained and post-trained LLMs themselves. Because RMs are initialized from LLMs, they inherit representations that shape their behavior, but the nature and extent of this influence remain understudied. In a comprehensive study of 10 leading open-weight RMs using validated psycholinguistic corpora, we show that RMs exhibit significant differences along multiple dime

infographic.key_insight: Reward models inherit systematic value and preference biases from their LLM pretraining priors, producing consistent differences in moral, social, and political judgments across models even after fine-tuning for reward tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and quantifies how pretraining representations shape reward-model outputs, revealing a previously underexplored source of bias in alignment pipelines (RMs initialized from pretrained LLMs).
method: Survey of 10 leading open‑weight reward models initialized from different pretrained LLMs and fine‑tuning procedures.

Evaluation using validated psycholinguistic corpora spanning moral, social, and political value dimensions; statistical comparison of RM responses across dimensions and against pretrained LLM baselines.
Controlled analyses isolating effects of initialization vs. post‑training (e.g., comparing models with different pretraining priors and fine‑tuning histories).
infographic.impact: Practitioners should treat reward-model choice and pretraining history as a critical alignment vector—biases in pretrained LLMs can propagate into RMs and affect downstream RLHF outcomes, evaluation, and deployment safety decisions.

title: Open-Vocabulary Functional 3D Human-Scene Interaction Generation
authors: Jie Liu, Yu Sun, Alpar Cseke, Yao Feng, Nicolas Heron
abstract: Generating 3D humans that functionally interact with 3D scenes remains an open problem with applications in embodied AI, robotics, and interactive content creation. The key challenge involves reasoning about both the semantics of functional elements in 3D scenes and the 3D human poses required to achieve functionality-aware interaction. Unfortunately, existing methods typically lack explicit reasoning over object functionality and the corresponding human-scene contact, resulting in implausible o

infographic.key_insight: Combines open-vocabulary semantic understanding of functional scene elements with contact-aware 3D human pose generation so models can produce plausible, functionality-driven human–scene interactions from language and scene input.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between recognizing object function in 3D scenes and generating realistic human poses that physically and semantically interact with those objects — preventing implausible or non-functional placements.
method: Open-vocabulary semantic grounding: map free-form language and scene geometry to functional element labels/affordances (e.g., 'sit-able', 'graspable') using language–vision priors.
Contact-aware pose generation: produce 3D human poses conditioned on scene geometry and predicted functional regions, enforcing plausible contact points and body support constraints.

Joint optimization/conditioning pipeline: combine scene semantics, contact priors and pose generation (learning-based or diffusion/optimization) to synthesize interactions that respect both function and physical plausibility.
infographic.impact: Enables more realistic, controllable 3D human–scene synthesis for embodied AI, robotics, and content creation pipelines, improving downstream tasks like simulation, virtual staging, and human-centered scene understanding.

title: A unified predictive and generative solution for liquid electrolyte formulation

abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 January 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01173-w

Yang et al. introduce a unified framework for liquid electrolyte design, integrating a forward predictive model with an inverse generative approach, where three generated high-conductivity candidates were identified and experimentally validated.

infographic.key_insight: A single integrated framework couples a forward predictive model with an inverse generative model to design liquid electrolyte formulations, and three high-conductivity candidates proposed by the system were experimentally validated.
infographic.problem_solved: Accelerates and automates discovery in a vast electrolyte formulation space by enabling design-by-performance (inverse design) rather than costly trial-and-error or one-way prediction.
method: Train a forward predictive model to map electrolyte formulations to target properties (e.g., ionic conductivity).
Develop an inverse generative model conditioned on desired properties to propose new formulations, guided by the forward model.

infographic.impact: Demonstrates a transferable AI pattern—coupling predictive and generative models with experimental feedback—that reduces experimental workload and speeds materials/formulation discovery, useful across battery, chemistry, and materials ML projects.

title: SokoBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Planning and Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Sebastiano Monti, Carlo Nicolini, Gianni Pellegrini, Jacopo Staiano, Bruno Lepri
abstract: Although the capabilities of large language models have been increasingly tested on complex reasoning tasks, their long-horizon planning abilities have not yet been extensively investigated. In this work, we provide a systematic assessment of the planning and long-horizon reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). We propose a novel benchmark based on Sokoban puzzles, intentionally simplified to isolate long-horizon planning from state persistence. Our findings rev

infographic.key_insight: SokoBench provides a focused benchmark showing that state-of-the-art Large Reasoning Models exhibit notable deficits on long-horizon planning tasks when state persistence is controlled for, revealing weaknesses not captured by standard reasoning tests.
infographic.problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for long-horizon planning and multi-step reasoning in large language models by isolating planning difficulty from state-tracking confounds.
method: Design a novel Sokoban-based benchmark simplified to remove state-persistence complexity and isolate long-horizon planning demands.
Evaluate multiple state-of-the-art Large Reasoning Models on puzzles of varying horizon length and difficulty using success-rate and plan-quality metrics.
Analyze failure modes and scaling/generalization behavior to identify where models break down on extended multi-step plans.
infographic.impact: SokoBench gives researchers and practitioners a targeted tool to measure and debug long-horizon planning capabilities, guiding model development, evaluation protocols, and few-shot / prompting strategies for multi-step tasks.

title: $\mathbb{R}^{2k}$ is Theoretically Large Enough for Embedding-based Top-$k$ Retrieval
authors: Zihao Wang, Hang Yin, Lihui Liu, Hanghang Tong, Yangqiu Song
abstract: This paper studies the minimal dimension required to embed subset memberships ($m$ elements and ${m\choose k}$ subsets of at most $k$ elements) into vector spaces, denoted as Minimal Embeddable Dimension (MED). The tight bounds of MED are derived theoretically and supported empirically for various notions of "distances" or "similarities," including the $\ell_2$ metric, inner product, and cosine similarity. In addition, we conduct numerical simulation in a more achievable setting, where the ${m\c

infographic.key_insight: A 2k-dimensional Euclidean space (R^{2k}) is theoretically sufficient — and in many formulations tight — to represent subset membership for top-k retrieval, so embedding-based top-k decisions need far lower dimension than the combinatorial number of subsets suggests.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines the minimal embedding dimension required to encode membership of up to k-item subsets from m items (the Minimal Embeddable Dimension, MED), resolving how compactly one can represent exponentially many subsets for top-k retrieval.
method: Formally define MED for m items and all subsets of size ≤ k and derive information-theoretic lower bounds.
Construct explicit embedding schemes and matching upper bounds showing R^{2k} suffices under ℓ2, inner-product, and cosine similarity notions.
Empirically validate theoretical claims with simulations in practical settings (finite m, noisy/approximate distances) to confirm achievability.
infographic.impact: Provides a principled guideline to set embedding dimensionality for top-k retrieval systems — enabling much smaller, more efficient representations without sacrificing exactness under common similarity measures.
visual_elements: Schematic: items and k-subsets mapped into a 2k-dimensional vector space (arrow from combinatorial set to compact vector representation).
Plot: MED (required dimension) vs. k showing the 2k line and comparisons to naive combinatorial complexity.
Table/heatmap: comparison of tight bounds and empirical error across similarity measures (ℓ2, inner product, cosine).

title: Routing End User Queries to Enterprise Databases
authors: Saikrishna Sudarshan, Tanay Kulkarni, Manasi Patwardhan, Lovekesh Vig, Ashwin Srinivasan
abstract: We address the task of routing natural language queries in multi-database enterprise environments. We construct realistic benchmarks by extending existing NL-to-SQL datasets. Our study shows that routing becomes increasingly challenging with larger, domain-overlapping DB repositories and ambiguous queries, motivating the need for more structured and robust reasoning-based solutions. By explicitly modelling schema coverage, structural connectivity, and fine-grained semantic alignment, the propose

infographic.key_insight: Routing user natural-language queries to the correct enterprise database is significantly harder as repositories grow and overlap; explicitly modeling schema coverage, structural connectivity, and fine-grained semantic alignment improves routing robustness.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines which database(s) in a multi-database enterprise should handle a given natural-language query, especially under domain overlap and query ambiguity.
method: Construct realistic multi-database routing benchmarks by extending existing NL-to-SQL datasets to simulate large, overlapping enterprise DB repositories.

Model routing using three complementary signals: schema coverage (which tables/columns are mentioned), structural connectivity (how schemas link across DBs), and fine-grained semantic alignment (query-to-schema meaning matching).
Evaluate routing difficulty and performance, showing degradation with larger/overlapping repositories and motivating structured, reasoning-based routing solutions.
infographic.impact: Improves reliability of NL interfaces to enterprise data platforms by reducing incorrect query dispatch, lowering latency and downstream errors; guides practitioners to design routing systems that combine structural and semantic reasoning rather than relying on surface similarity alone.
visual_elements: Schematic pipeline: user query → routing model (coverage + connectivity + semantic alignment) → selected database(s)

title: Evaluation of Oncotimia: An LLM based system for supporting tumour boards
authors: Luis Lorenzo, Marcos Montana-Mendez, Sergio Figueiras, Miguel Boubeta, Cristobal Bernardo-Castineira
abstract: Multidisciplinary tumour boards (MDTBs) play a central role in oncology decision-making but require manual processes and structuring large volumes of heterogeneous clinical information, resulting in a substantial documentation burden. In this work, we present ONCOTIMIA, a modular and secure clinical tool designed to integrate generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into oncology workflows and evaluate its application to the automatic completion of lung cancer tumour board forms using large la

infographic.key_insight: ONCOTIMIA integrates a secure, modular GenAI pipeline to automatically populate lung cancer tumour board forms, reducing the manual documentation burden for multidisciplinary tumour boards (MDTBs).
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the time-consuming, error-prone process of structuring heterogeneous clinical data for MDTBs by automating extraction and form completion while maintaining clinical workflow integration and data security.
method: Modular, secure pipeline that connects clinical data sources to a tuned large language model for clinical text understanding and generation.
Structured information extraction (NLP) + LLM-driven template filling to auto-complete tumour board forms for lung cancer cases.
Clinician-in-the-loop evaluation within MDTB workflows to validate outputs and ensure safety, relevance and interoperability with existing systems.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates a practical path for responsibly deploying LLMs in clinical workflows, reducing documentation workload and improving MDTB efficiency while highlighting the need for clinician oversight and secure integrations. This informs AI/ML practitioners about design patterns for clinical GenAI applications.

title: EgoHandICL: Egocentric 3D Hand Reconstruction with In-Context Learning
authors: Binzhu Xie, Shi Qiu, Sicheng Zhang, Yinqiao Wang, Hao Xu
abstract: Robust 3D hand reconstruction in egocentric vision is challenging due to depth ambiguity, self-occlusion, and complex hand-object interactions. Prior methods mitigate these issues by scaling training data or adding auxiliary cues, but they often struggle in unseen contexts. We present EgoHandICL, the first in-context learning (ICL) framework for 3D hand reconstruction that improves semantic alignment, visual consistency, and robustness under challenging egocentric conditions. EgoHandICL introduc

infographic.key_insight: Applying in-context learning (ICL) to egocentric 3D hand reconstruction lets a model adapt on-the-fly to new visual contexts (occlusions, objects, lighting) using a few examples, improving semantic alignment and visual consistency without large task-specific retraining.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses depth ambiguity, severe self-occlusion, and complex hand–object interactions in first-person (egocentric) images, improving reconstruction accuracy and robustness in unseen or cluttered scenarios.
method: Introduce an ICL-style reconstruction pipeline that conditions the predictor on a small set of example image–3D pairs at inference to guide pose/shape estimation.
Fuse egocentric image features with context tokens (example-driven prompts) in a geometry-aware model to produce semantically aligned 3D hand pose and shape.

Enforce visual consistency and semantic alignment during training via losses that encourage rendered 3D hands to match input appearance and exemplar structure, improving robustness to occlusion and objects.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable egocentric hand tracking for AR/VR, wearable perception, and HCI by reducing the need for massive labeled datasets or heavy domain adaptation — practitioners can use example-driven conditioning to adapt models quickly to new users or scenes.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: context/examples (image + 3D) → ICL conditioning tokens → egocentric image input → 3D hand output (pose + shape).

title: RHSIA: Real-time Hemodynamics Surrogation for Non-idealized Intracranial Aneurysms
authors: Yiying Sheng, Wenhao Ding, Dylan Roi, Leonard Leong Litt Yeo, Hwa Liang Leo
abstract: Extensive studies suggested that fluid mechanical markers of intracranial aneurysms (IAs) derived from Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) can indicate disease progression risks, but to date this has not been translated clinically. This is because CFD requires specialized expertise and is time-consuming and low throughput, making it difficult to support clinical trials. A deep learning model that maps IA morphology to biomechanical markers can address this, enabling physicians to obtain these mar

infographic.key_insight: A deep-learning surrogate can predict clinically relevant hemodynamic markers for intracranial aneurysms from patient geometry in real time, enabling CFD-level insights without the time and expertise burden of full simulations.
infographic.problem_solved: CFD-derived fluid-mechanical markers are valuable for assessing aneurysm risk but are too slow, specialized, and low-throughput for routine clinical use or large trials—this work provides a fast, automated alternative that works on realistic (non-idealized) patient geometries.
method: Generate training targets by running CFD on a diverse set of non-idealized, patient-derived aneurysm geometries to obtain hemodynamic markers.
Train a deep-learning surrogate model that maps 3D aneurysm morphology to biomechanical markers, optimized for runtime and robustness to realistic geometry artifacts.
Evaluate the surrogate against CFD on held-out cases for marker agreement and measure runtime speedups to demonstrate real-time inference capability.
infographic.impact: Enables scalable, real-time hemodynamic assessment for clinical workflows and trials; for ML practitioners it exemplifies building physics-informed surrogate models that trade minimal accuracy loss for large gains in speed and clinical applicability.

title: Visual Generation Unlocks Human-Like Reasoning through Multimodal World Models
authors: Jialong Wu, Xiaoying Zhang, Hongyi Yuan, Xiangcheng Zhang, Tianhao Huang
abstract: Humans construct internal world models and reason by manipulating the concepts within these models. Recent advances in AI, particularly chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, approximate such human cognitive abilities, where world models are believed to be embedded within large language models. Expert-level performance in formal and abstract domains such as mathematics and programming has been achieved in current systems by relying predominantly on verbal reasoning. However, they still lag far behind

infographic.key_insight: Generating visual representations of intermediate reasoning states turns implicit linguistic world models into explicit, manipulable multimodal world models, enabling more human-like stepwise reasoning and verification.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcoming the limits of language-only chain-of-thought: implicit, hard-to-inspect internal models that struggle on abstract/formal reasoning tasks and offer limited interpretability and corrective affordances.
method: Embed a visual-generation module into the reasoning loop so the model produces images (visual scratchpads) representing intermediate concepts or program/math states.
Train or align multimodal components (language reasoning + visual decoder) to translate symbolic/linguistic states into visual scenes and back, enabling iterative perception–action style reasoning.
Use the generated visuals as explicit checkpoints for verification, hypothesis testing, and iterative refinement during problem solving on abstract and formal domains.
infographic.impact: Makes reasoning more interpretable, debuggable, and robust for practitioners working on math, code, planning, and other abstract domains; opens the door to human-in-the-loop correction and multimodal benchmarks that better reflect human cognition.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: language reasoner ⇄ visual generator loop with arrows showing iterative refinement.
Stepwise example: a 3–5 panel sequence showing a problem, intermediate visual scratchpads, and final solution.
Performance comparison chart: language-only vs. multimodal world models on abstract/formal tasks.

title: M-SGWR: Multiscale Similarity and Geographically Weighted Regression
authors: M. Naser Lessani, Zhenlong Li, Manzhu Yu, Helen Greatrex, Chan Shen
abstract: The first law of geography is a cornerstone of spatial analysis, emphasizing that nearby and related locations tend to be more similar, however, defining what constitutes "near" and "related" remains challenging, as different phenomena exhibit distinct spatial patterns. Traditional local regression models, such as Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) and Multiscale GWR (MGWR), quantify spatial relationships solely through geographic proximity. In an era of globalization and digital connectiv

infographic.key_insight: M-SGWR extends geographically weighted regression by integrating multiscale similarity (both geographic and non‑geographic) into local weighting, so local effects are estimated using the most relevant neighborhood definitions for each phenomenon.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional GWR/MGWR assume proximity only by physical distance, failing to capture non‑local or multi‑scale relationships (e.g., social, economic, network ties) that affect spatial processes; M-SGWR solves how to define and use 'near' and 'related' across scales.
method: Construct multiple similarity measures (e.g., geographic distance, network/flow ties, attribute similarity) that capture different notions of neighborhood.
Combine those measures in a multiscale weighting scheme to build location-specific kernels so each coefficient is estimated using the most relevant scale and similarity mix.
Fit a geographically weighted regression with these multiscale similarity weights to produce spatially varying coefficients that reflect both local and non‑local influences.
infographic.impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners and spatial analysts to model heterogeneous spatial effects more accurately and interpretably by accounting for non‑physical connections and scale-dependent relationships, improving prediction and policy insights in urban, environmental, and socio‑economic applications.
visual_elements: Map overlay showing multiple similarity layers (physical proximity, mobility/flow network, attribute similarity)
Schematic of the M-SGWR pipeline: similarity construction → multiscale weighting → local regression

method: Audit datasets to identify and quantify sources of bias (similarity/leakage between train and test, class/label imbalances).
Apply bias-mitigation strategies—realistic OOD train/test splits, reweighting or resampling, and controlled evaluation on held-out sets—and retrain models to measure true generalization improvements.

title: HexFormer: Hyperbolic Vision Transformer with Exponential Map Aggregation
authors: Haya Alyoussef, Ahmad Bdeir, Diego Coello de Portugal Mecke, Tom Hanika, Niels Landwehr
abstract: Data across modalities such as images, text, and graphs often contains hierarchical and relational structures, which are challenging to model within Euclidean geometry. Hyperbolic geometry provides a natural framework for representing such structures. Building on this property, this work introduces HexFormer, a hyperbolic vision transformer for image classification that incorporates exponential map aggregation within its attention mechanism. Two designs are explored: a hyperbolic ViT (HexFormer)

infographic.key_insight: HexFormer embeds visual features in hyperbolic space and integrates exponential-map-based aggregation into the transformer attention, enabling the model to more naturally represent hierarchical and relational structure in images.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard Euclidean Vision Transformers struggle to compactly represent hierarchical/relational structure present in many image modalities; this work addresses that limitation by moving attention and feature aggregation into hyperbolic geometry.
method: Represent image tokens and features on a hyperbolic manifold to capture tree-like and hierarchical relations more naturally than Euclidean embeddings.
Introduce exponential map aggregation inside the attention mechanism so key/value combination and updates occur on the manifold (preserving geometric consistency).
Explore two architectural variants (including a hyperbolic ViT called HexFormer) and evaluate their behavior for image classification to compare manifold-aware designs.
infographic.impact: Brings geometric inductive bias for hierarchies into transformer-based vision models, offering practitioners a principled way to improve representation fidelity for hierarchical/relational data and potentially yield more compact or semantically structured embeddings.

title: Identifying and Transferring Reasoning-Critical Neurons: Improving LLM Inference Reliability via Activation Steering
authors: Fangan Dong, Zuming Yan, Xuri Ge, Zhiwei Xu, Mengqi Zhang
abstract: Despite the strong reasoning capabilities of recent large language models (LLMs), achieving reliable performance on challenging tasks often requires post-training or computationally expensive sampling strategies, limiting their practical efficiency. In this work, we first show that a small subset of neurons in LLMs exhibits strong predictive correlations with reasoning correctness. Based on this observation, we propose AdaRAS (Adaptive Reasoning Activation Steering), a lightweight test-time fram

infographic.key_insight: A small, identifiable subset of neurons in LLMs strongly predicts whether a reasoning step will be correct, and steering those neurons' activations at test time (via AdaRAS) reliably improves reasoning without expensive retraining or heavy sampling.
infographic.problem_solved: Improves LLM reasoning reliability at inference time while avoiding costly post-training adjustments or computationally expensive sampling strategies.
method: Identify reasoning-critical neurons by measuring predictive correlations between neuron activations and reasoning correctness across examples.

Learn a lightweight, adaptive test-time controller (AdaRAS) that steers those neurons' activations—e.g., rescaling, replacing, or transferring activation patterns—conditioned on confidence/predicted error.
Apply activation transfer/steering across prompts or models as a minimal, deployable intervention to correct likely failure modes without full fine-tuning.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable LLM reasoning with low compute overhead and easy test-time integration, giving practitioners a practical, interpretable tool to reduce failures and cut down on expensive sampling or retraining.

title: An Interpretable Recommendation Model for Psychometric Data, With an Application to Gerontological Primary Care
authors: Andre Paulino de Lima, Paula Castro, Suzana Carvalho Vaz de Andrade, Rosa Maria Marcucci, Ruth Caldeira de Melo
abstract: There are challenges that must be overcome to make recommender systems useful in healthcare settings. The reasons are varied: the lack of publicly available clinical data, the difficulty that users may have in understanding the reasons why a recommendation was made, the risks that may be involved in following that recommendation, and the uncertainty about its effectiveness. In this work, we address these challenges with a recommendation model that leverages the structure of psychometric data to

infographic.key_insight: An interpretable recommender that leverages the inherent structure of psychometric data can produce transparent, risk-aware recommendations suitable for gerontological primary care, improving clinician trust and actionable use.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes barriers to clinical recommender adoption—scarce public clinical data, opaque black‑box outputs, and lack of clear risk/uncertainty information—by producing explanations tied to psychometric questionnaire structure.
method: Leverage psychometric structure (items, subscales, domains) to constrain and inform the recommendation model so outputs align with clinically meaningful constructs.
Generate human‑readable rationales that map specific questionnaire responses to recommended actions, enabling clinician interpretability and auditability.
Incorporate uncertainty/risk awareness into recommendations to prioritize safe, actionable suggestions for gerontological primary care.
infographic.impact: Makes recommendation systems more practical and trustworthy for healthcare settings, helping AI/ML practitioners design models that clinicians can understand, evaluate, and safely act on—especially in geriatrics where risks and interpretability are critical.

title: Neural Neural Scaling Laws
authors: Michael Y. Hu, Jane Pan, Ayush Rajesh Jhaveri, Nicholas Lourie, Kyunghyun Cho
abstract: Neural scaling laws predict how language model performance improves with increased compute. While aggregate metrics like validation loss can follow smooth power-law curves, individual downstream tasks exhibit diverse scaling behaviors: some improve monotonically, others plateau, and some even degrade with scale. We argue that predicting downstream performance from validation perplexity suffers from two limitations: averaging token-level losses obscures signal, and no simple parametric family can

infographic.key_insight: Aggregate validation metrics like perplexity can follow smooth power laws while individual downstream tasks show heterogeneous scaling — some improve, some plateau, and some worsen — so validation perplexity alone is an unreliable predictor of task performance as models scale.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies why using aggregate scaling laws (validation loss/perplexity) to predict downstream task performance fails, and identifies the mechanisms (token-level averaging and lack of a universal parametric mapping) behind that failure.
method: Empirical, task-level scaling study: measure downstream performance across model sizes and compute budgets to reveal diverse per-task trajectories (monotonic improvement, plateaus, degradation).
Diagnostic decomposition: analyze token-level losses and their aggregation to show how averaging obscures task-relevant signal.
Statistical assessment: evaluate parametric fits linking perplexity to downstream metrics and demonstrate that no simple family robustly generalizes across tasks.
infographic.impact: Practitioners should not rely solely on validation perplexity when forecasting gains from scaling; instead, evaluate task-specific metrics and consider token-level or task-aware extrapolations to guide compute allocation and model selection.

title: DuwatBench: Bridging Language and Visual Heritage through an Arabic Calligraphy Benchmark for Multimodal Understanding
authors: Shubham Patle, Sara Ghaboura, Hania Tariq, Mohammad Usman Khan, Omkar Thawakar
abstract: Arabic calligraphy represents one of the richest visual traditions of the Arabic language, blending linguistic meaning with artistic form. Although multimodal models have advanced across languages, their ability to process Arabic script, especially in artistic and stylized calligraphic forms, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present DuwatBench, a benchmark of 1,272 curated samples containing about 1,475 unique words across six classical and modern calligraphic styles, each pai

infographic.key_insight: DuwatBench provides a focused multimodal benchmark for Arabic calligraphy—1,272 curated samples (~1,475 unique words) across six classical and modern styles—enabling systematic evaluation of models on stylized Arabic script that blends visual art and language.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of curated, style-aware datasets for Arabic calligraphy, which has limited multimodal models' ability to recognize, interpret, and preserve artistic forms of Arabic script.
method: Curate and standardize 1,272 high-quality calligraphic samples spanning six classical and modern Arabic styles with approximately 1,475 unique words.
Annotate each sample with word-level transcriptions, style labels and metadata, plus quality control to ensure consistency and cultural fidelity.
Define standardized evaluation tasks and protocols for multimodal models (e.g., stylized text recognition, style classification, image–text retrieval) to enable reproducible benchmarking.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a dedicated resource to train and evaluate OCR and multimodal models on artistic Arabic script, improving robustness for real-world, culturally-rich text and supporting preservation of visual heritage.
visual_elements: Dataset composition chart: bar/pie showing sample counts per calligraphic style and unique-word distribution.
Style mosaic: side-by-side image tiles of example samples from each of the six calligraphic styles with overlaid transcriptions.
Task flow diagram: input image ⇒ annotated data ⇒ benchmark tasks (recognition, style classification, retrieval) ⇒ evaluation metrics.
Performance mock-up/leaderboard: heatmap or table showing model performance across tasks and styles to highlight strengths/weaknesses.

title: When Iterative RAG Beats Ideal Evidence: A Diagnostic Study in Scientific Multi-hop Question Answering
authors: Mahdi Astaraki, Mohammad Arshi Saloot, Ali Shiraee Kasmaee, Hamidreza Mahyar, Soheila Samiee
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) extends large language models (LLMs) beyond parametric knowledge, yet it is unclear when iterative retrieval-reasoning loops meaningfully outperform static RAG, particularly in scientific domains with multi-hop reasoning, sparse domain knowledge, and heterogeneous evidence. We provide the first controlled, mechanism-level diagnostic study of whether synchronized iterative retrieval and reasoning can surpass an idealized static upper bound (Gold Context) RAG.

infographic.key_insight: Synchronized iterative retrieval-and-reasoning loops can outperform an idealized static 'Gold Context' RAG in scientific multi-hop question answering under realistic conditions (sparse domain knowledge and heterogeneous evidence). This shows iteration can assemble complementary evidence that a single static context cannot.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines when and why iterative RAG actually surpasses a static upper-bound RAG for scientific multi-hop QA, isolating the mechanisms and conditions that enable gains.
method: Controlled, mechanism-level diagnostic comparisons between iterative retrieval–reasoning loops and an idealized static (Gold Context) RAG setup.
Systematic ablations varying evidence properties (sparsity, heterogeneity) and synchronization of retrieval+reasoning to identify which factors drive iterative gains.
Quantitative experiments showing stepwise evidence assembly by iteration yields higher accuracy in the settings identified as favorable.
infographic.impact: Provides practical guidance for when to invest in iterative retrieval pipelines versus building larger static contexts, improving design choices for domain-specific multi-hop QA systems and reducing wasted engineering effort.
visual_elements: Side-by-side flow diagram: iterative retrieval→reasoning loop vs static Gold Context pipeline to show procedural differences.
Bar/line chart: accuracy comparison across conditions (homogeneous vs heterogeneous evidence; dense vs sparse knowledge).
Evidence-assembly Sankey or stepwise diagram: how multiple retrieval steps combine complementary snippets to answer a multi-hop question.
Decision flowchart: recommended conditions for choosing iterative RAG vs static RAG (based on evidence heterogeneity and knowledge sparsity).
infographic.paper_title: When Iterative RAG Beats Ideal Evidence: A Diagnostic Study in Scientific Multi-hop Question Answering
infographic.paper_authors: Mahdi Astaraki, Mohammad Arshi Saloot, Ali Shiraee Kasmaee, Hamidreza Mahyar, Soheila Samiee

title: HARMONI: Multimodal Personalization of Multi-User Human-Robot Interactions with LLMs
authors: Jeanne Malécot, Hamed Rahimi, Jeanne Cattoni, Marie Samson, Mouad Abrini
abstract: Existing human-robot interaction systems often lack mechanisms for sustained personalization and dynamic adaptation in multi-user environments, limiting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We present HARMONI, a multimodal personalization framework that leverages large language models to enable socially assistive robots to manage long-term multi-user interactions. The framework integrates four key modules: (i) a perception module that identifies active speakers and extracts multimodal

infographic.key_insight: HARMONI combines multimodal perception, long-term user memory, and LLM-based reasoning to enable socially assistive robots to personalize and adapt interactions across multiple users over time.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing HRI systems struggle to sustain personalized behavior and dynamically adapt in multi-user, real-world settings; HARMONI addresses persistent user modeling and context-aware social adaptation for long-term multi-user interactions.
method: Multimodal perception: identifies active speaker(s) and extracts audio, visual, and behavioral cues for contextual understanding.
Long-term personalized memory: maintains and updates multi-user profiles and interaction history to inform future behavior.
LLM-driven reasoning & policy: uses large language models to fuse context and user profiles into socially appropriate dialogue plans and action policies for the robot.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical blueprint for integrating LLMs into robotic agents that require sustained personalization and social adaptability, improving long-term engagement and real-world deployment potential for ML-driven HRI.
visual_elements: End-to-end system diagram showing Perception → Memory → LLM Reasoning → Policy/Execution loop
Interaction timeline illustrating accumulation of user preferences and personalization across repeated sessions
Before/after comparison chart (engagement, satisfaction, or task success) showing benefits of personalization
Annotated example multimodal turn (audio + gaze + gesture) mapped to model input and resulting robot response

title: Multi-agent AI systems need transparency
authors: Unknown
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 27 January 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01183-2

Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks are in vogue. However, implementing such systems in scientific research workflows requires clear motivations and explanations, given the risk of wasting computational as well as human resources.

infographic.key_insight: Agentic and multi‑agent AI systems are increasingly used, but their benefits are often unclear; demanding explicit transparency—clear motivations, documented decision processes, and resource accounting—prevents wasted computational and human effort and improves trust.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of clear justification, explanations, and reporting for using agentic AI in research workflows, which can lead to wasted resources, irreproducible results, and hidden failure modes.
method: Advocate a transparency‑first workflow: require an explicit, documented rationale for choosing agentic/multi‑agent approaches and expected gains over simpler alternatives.
Mandate explainability and provenance artifacts (decision logs, reasoning traces, resource/cost accounting) for each agent interaction to enable auditing and debugging.
Standardize evaluation and reporting: track resource consumption, failure modes, and reproducibility checks for multi‑agent experiments.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners practical criteria to decide when to use agentic systems, reduces wasted compute and human time, and improves reproducibility, auditability, and responsible deployment.
visual_elements: Decision flowchart: 'When to use agentic AI?' showing criteria and go/no‑go checkpoints
Bar chart: resource (compute + human) cost of agentic system vs baseline methods
Diagram of transparency artifacts: agent interactions → logs, reasoning traces, provenance, cost reports
Icon set: benefits vs risks (efficiency, autonomy, waste, opacity, reproducibility)
infographic.paper_title: Multi-agent AI systems need transparency
infographic.paper_authors: Unknown

title: POPE: Learning to Reason on Hard Problems via Privileged On-Policy Exploration
authors: Yuxiao Qu, Amrith Setlur, Virginia Smith, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Aviral Kumar
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), yet state-of-the-art methods still fail to learn on many training problems. On hard problems, on-policy RL rarely explores even a single correct rollout, yielding zero reward and no learning signal for driving improvement. We find that natural solutions to remedy this exploration problem from classical RL, such as entropy bonuses, more permissive clipping of the importance ratio, or direct optimizat

infographic.key_insight: POPE provides a privileged on-policy exploration mechanism that finds correct reasoning rollouts on hard problems so the learner receives non-zero reward; this converts otherwise signal-less training into effective learning of complex reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: On hard reasoning tasks, standard on-policy RL rarely encounters any correct rollout, producing zero reward and preventing learning; POPE addresses this exploration failure so models can receive learning signals on difficult problems.
method: Introduce a privileged exploration policy that can sample (or guide to) correct/high-reward rollouts on hard training problems during on-policy training.

Incorporate those privileged rollouts into the learner's updates while retaining on-policy update structure (e.g., via controlled importance weighting, constrained updates, or auxiliary losses) so exploration signal transfers without destabilizing training.
Train the main policy to reproduce successful trajectories discovered by the privileged explorer, enabling the learner to perform correct multi-step reasoning without privileged access at test time.
infographic.impact: By breaking the zero-reward deadlock on hard problems, POPE enables RL-based fine-tuning of LLMs to acquire complex reasoning skills more reliably and efficiently, improving sample efficiency and robustness on difficult tasks.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: privileged explorer + learner policy interacting with environment, with arrows showing privileged rollouts providing rewards to learner.
Before vs after bar/line chart: fraction of episodes with non-zero reward and learning curve showing training stagnation without POPE versus improvement with POPE.
Example rollout visualization: token-level or step-level trace highlighting a correct reasoning trajectory discovered by the privileged policy.
Icon set: 'zero reward' stop sign, 'privileged guide' flashlight icon illuminating successful paths, and 'learner' model icon absorbing knowledge.
infographic.paper_title: POPE: Learning to Reason on Hard Problems via Privileged On-Policy Exploration
infographic.paper_authors: Yuxiao Qu, Amrith Setlur, Virginia Smith, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Aviral Kumar

title: Proposing and solving olympiad geometry with guided tree search
authors: Chi Zhang, Jiajun Song, Siyu Li, Yitao Liang, Yuxi Ma
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 26 January 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01164-x

TongGeometry both solves and proposes olympiad-level geometry problems. It uses guided tree search to find hard but concise problems, making advanced mathematical reasoning more accessible.

infographic.key_insight: TongGeometry combines neural guidance with symbolic tree search to both propose and solve olympiad-level geometry problems, discovering hard yet concise problems automatically.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates the discovery and solution of challenging geometry problems that traditionally require expert human creativity and lengthy manual proof search, enabling scalable generation of high-quality math problems and proofs.
method: Neural-guided tree search: learn policy/value models to prioritize construction and proof branches during symbolic search.
Difficulty-conciseness scoring and pruning: rank candidate problems to find problems that are both hard and succinct while keeping search tractable.
Formal verification and synthesis: generate, synthesize and verify geometric proofs to ensure correctness of proposed and solved problems.
infographic.impact: Advances neural-symbolic mathematical reasoning and enables automated benchmark/problem generation for research and education, lowering the barrier to studying advanced geometry with verifiable solutions.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: propose → guided tree search → verify (icons for neural model, search tree, proof checker).
Search tree visualization: highlighted paths showing neural-guided branch selection vs unguided search.
Example olympiad problem: geometry figure with solution steps annotated to show concise proof found by the system.
Scatter plot: difficulty vs conciseness of generated problems, illustrating selection of hard-but-short instances.
infographic.paper_title: Proposing and solving olympiad geometry with guided tree search
infographic.paper_authors: Chi Zhang, Jiajun Song, Siyu Li, Yitao Liang, Yuxi Ma

title: HalluGuard: Demystifying Data-Driven and Reasoning-Driven Hallucinations in LLMs
authors: Xinyue Zeng, Junhong Lin, Yujun Yan, Feng Guo, Liang Shi
abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, and scientific discovery is often compromised by hallucinations. These failures typically stem from two sources: data-driven hallucinations and reasoning-driven hallucinations. However, existing detection methods usually address only one source and rely on task-specific heuristics, limiting their generalization to complex scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Hallucination Risk Bo

infographic.key_insight: HalluGuard presents a unified, model-agnostic framework that separates and detects two distinct hallucination sources—data-driven and reasoning-driven—using a single risk-oriented approach, improving generalization beyond task-specific heuristics.
infographic.problem_solved: Detecting and distinguishing hallucinations in LLM outputs is brittle because existing methods target only one hallucination source or rely on task-specific rules, limiting reliability in high-stakes domains.
method: Taxonomy + risk framing: formally separate data-driven (factual/knowledge gaps) and reasoning-driven (chain-of-thought/logic errors) hallucinations and define a unified Hallucination Risk score.

Dual-check pipeline: combine retrieval- and evidence-based factual verification for data-driven errors with chain-of-thought consistency/self-verification and contradiction-detection for reasoning-driven errors.
Model-agnostic evaluation & calibration: apply the risk estimator across tasks and LLMs, calibrate thresholds, and validate detection/mitigation performance on multi-domain benchmarks.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical, generalizable toolset to detect and prioritize hallucination risks across models and tasks, enabling safer deployment and targeted mitigation strategies in high-stakes applications.
visual_elements: Venn/contrast diagram showing 'Data-driven' vs 'Reasoning-driven' hallucinations with examples for each
Pipeline flowchart of HalluGuard: Input → Retrieval Verification → CoT Consistency Check → Risk Score → Mitigation/Flagging
Bar/line chart comparing detection accuracy/generalization of HalluGuard vs task-specific baselines across multiple domains
Annotated chain-of-thought example highlighting where and why the model hallucinates (evidence mismatch vs logical error)
infographic.paper_title: HalluGuard: Demystifying Data-Driven and Reasoning-Driven Hallucinations in LLMs
infographic.paper_authors: Xinyue Zeng, Junhong Lin, Yujun Yan, Feng Guo, Liang Shi

title: Dep-Search: Learning Dependency-Aware Reasoning Traces with Persistent Memory
authors: Yanming Liu, Xinyue Peng, Zixuan Yan, Yanxin Shen, Wenjie Xu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning tasks, particularly when augmented with search mechanisms that enable systematic exploration of external knowledge bases. The field has evolved from traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks to more sophisticated search-based frameworks that orchestrate multi-step reasoning through explicit search strategies. However, existing search frameworks still rely heavily on implicit natural lang

infographic.key_insight: Modeling and learning explicit, dependency-aware reasoning traces plus a persistent memory module lets search-guided LLMs plan and reuse intermediate facts, yielding more accurate, efficient, and interpretable multi-step reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Search-based reasoning frameworks often rely on implicit natural-language prompts and lack explicit modeling of dependencies and long-lived intermediate facts, causing redundant retrievals, brittle reasoning chains, and poor traceability.
method: Represent multi-step reasoning as dependency-aware traces that record actions, retrieved facts, and directed dependencies between steps.
Train a controller to generate search actions conditioned on the current trace and a persistent memory store that accumulates and indexes intermediate results.
Use the persistent memory to prune redundant searches, resolve dependencies, and enable iterative refinement of answers with explicit, reusable traces.
infographic.impact: Makes search-augmented LLM reasoning more reliable, efficient, and auditable—helpful for practitioners building complex QA, multi-hop retrieval, and decision-support systems that need repeatable, explainable chains of thought.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: controller + dependency-aware trace representation + persistent memory module and search loop
Example reasoning trace timeline: steps, retrieved facts, and directed dependency edges
Bar chart: accuracy/efficiency comparison vs RAG and other search baselines
Memory graph visualization: nodes = facts, edges = dependencies showing reuse across queries
infographic.paper_title: Dep-Search: Learning Dependency-Aware Reasoning Traces with Persistent Memory
infographic.paper_authors: Yanming Liu, Xinyue Peng, Zixuan Yan, Yanxin Shen, Wenjie Xu

title: Modelling drug-induced cellular perturbation responses with a biologically informed dual-branch transformer
authors: Yue Guo, Hao Zhang, Haitao Hu, Jialu Wu, Ji Cao
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 26 January 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01165-w

A dual-branch framework that disentangles cell states from drug-induced regulatory shifts to predict transcriptional responses is presented. It captures nonlinear dose–time dynamics and excels in generalizing to unseen cellular contexts.

infographic.key_insight: A biologically informed dual-branch transformer separates intrinsic cell state from drug-induced regulatory shifts to accurately predict transcriptional responses across doses and times, allowing strong generalization to unseen cellular contexts.
infographic.problem_solved: Predicting how cells' transcriptional programs change after drug treatment is hard because responses mix baseline cell identity with dose- and time-dependent perturbations; this model disentangles those factors to produce accurate, generalizable predictions.
method: Dual-branch transformer architecture: one branch encodes baseline cell state, the other encodes drug-induced regulatory perturbations, with learned fusion to predict post-perturbation transcription.
Biologically informed priors: incorporate pathway/regulatory structure (e.g., gene modules or network constraints) to guide attention and improve interpretability and robustness.
Dose–time modeling: explicit representation of nonlinear dose and time dynamics so the model can predict continuous perturbation trajectories and generalize to unseen conditions.
infographic.impact: Enables more accurate, interpretable in silico prediction of drug responses and improves transfer to new cell types or conditions—useful for ML practitioners building models for perturbation biology, drug screening, and hypothesis generation.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing two transformer branches (cell state vs drug perturbation) and a fusion head producing predicted expression
Schematic illustrating disentanglement: baseline expression vs drug-induced shift vectors
Dose–time response surface/heatmap showing nonlinear predicted trajectories versus ground truth
Bar/line chart comparing generalization performance on seen vs unseen cell contexts

title: Teaching Models to Teach Themselves: Reasoning at the Edge of Learnability
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, John Quan, Ariel Kwiatkowski, Kartik Ahuja, Yann Ollivier
abstract: Can a model learn to escape its own learning plateau? Reinforcement learning methods for finetuning large reasoning models stall on datasets with low initial success rates, and thus little training signal. We investigate a fundamental question: Can a pretrained LLM leverage latent knowledge to generate an automated curriculum for problems it cannot solve? To explore this, we design SOAR: A self-improvement framework designed to surface these pedagogical signals through meta-RL. A teacher copy of

infographic.key_insight: A pretrained LLM can bootstrap its own learning by generating an automated curriculum targeted at problems just beyond its current ability, using a teacher-student meta-RL loop to surface latent knowledge and escape training plateaus.
infographic.problem_solved: Reinforcement learning finetuning of large reasoning models stalls when initial success rates are very low and training signals are sparse; the paper addresses how to create useful training signal automatically when the model cannot yet solve available problems.
method: SOAR framework: maintain a teacher copy of the model that proposes problems/tasks aimed at the student’s current ability.
Meta-reinforcement learning trains the teacher to generate curricula that maximize student improvement — focusing on the "edge of learnability" where problems are solvable with small progress.
Iterative teacher–student loop uses student performance gains as reward to select and refine generated problems, surfacing latent knowledge into actionable training examples.
infographic.impact: Enables efficient self-directed finetuning of reasoning LLMs without extensive human-crafted curricula or dense supervision, helping practitioners overcome low-signal plateaus and improve sample efficiency for hard reasoning tasks.
visual_elements: Teacher–Student loop diagram showing a teacher model generating tasks, a student model learning, and feedback from student success guiding the teacher.
Staircase or frontier graphic labeled "edge of learnability" illustrating tasks increasing in difficulty and the curriculum focusing on the step just above current capability.
Performance curves comparing standard RL fine-tuning (flat plateau) vs SOAR (escape from plateau and rising accuracy over time).
Icon set: brain/gear for latent knowledge, target for curriculum selection, and reward signal for meta-RL feedback.
infographic.paper_title: Teaching Models to Teach Themselves: Reasoning at the Edge of Learnability

title: ctELM: Decoding and Manipulating Embeddings of Clinical Trials with Embedding Language Models
authors: Brian Ondov, Chia-Hsuan Chang, Yujia Zhou, Mauro Giuffrè, Hua Xu
abstract: Text embeddings have become an essential part of a variety of language applications. However, methods for interpreting, exploring and reversing embedding spaces are limited, reducing transparency and precluding potentially valuable generative use cases. In this work, we align Large Language Models to embeddings of clinical trials using the recently reported Embedding Language Model (ELM) method. We develop an open-source, domain-agnostic ELM architecture and training framework, design training t

infographic.key_insight: Aligning a language model to embedding space (using the Embedding Language Model approach) allows opaque clinical-trial embeddings to be decoded into human‑readable descriptions and programmatically manipulated, enabling transparent exploration and generative uses.
infographic.problem_solved: Clinical-trial and general text embeddings are hard to interpret, explore, or invert, which limits transparency, validation, semantic search, and generative workflows in biomedical settings. ctELM provides tools to decode and manipulate those embeddings without requiring access to original training data.
method: Develop an open‑source, domain‑agnostic Embedding Language Model architecture that maps between embedding vectors and LLM token space.

Train the model on clinical‑trial embeddings with reconstruction and contrastive-style objectives plus domain-specific augmentations so embeddings can be decoded to descriptive text and edited in embedding space.
Expose decoding and manipulation primitives (embedding → text, text → embedding, embedding interpolation/perturbation) for search, explanation, and controlled generation.
infographic.impact: Practitioners gain practical tools to inspect, debug, and repurpose embedding spaces for better retrieval, interpretability, and synthetic data generation—while also needing to consider new privacy and inversion risks arising from reversible embeddings.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: embedding vector input → ELM alignment layer → LLM decoder (labels showing reconstruction/contrastive losses).
Embedding-space visualization (t-SNE/UMAP) with points annotated by decoded trial summaries to show semantic neighborhoods and decoding fidelity.
Before/after examples: raw embedding → decoded trial title/criteria → edited embedding → generated variant trial text.
Pipeline flowchart: clinical-trial data → embeddings → ELM training → tools for decode/search/edit → downstream applications (retrieval, generation, auditing).

title: Reuse your FLOPs: Scaling RL on Hard Problems by Conditioning on Very Off-Policy Prefixes
authors: Amrith Setlur, Zijian Wang, Andrew Cohen, Paria Rashidinejad, Sang Michael Xie
abstract: Typical reinforcement learning (RL) methods for LLM reasoning waste compute on hard problems, where correct on-policy traces are rare, policy gradients vanish, and learning stalls. To bootstrap more efficient RL, we consider reusing old sampling FLOPs (from prior inference or RL training) in the form of off-policy traces. Standard off-policy methods supervise against off-policy data, causing instabilities during RL optimization. We introduce PrefixRL, where we condition on the prefix of successf

infographic.key_insight: Reuse previously generated off-policy trajectories by conditioning the policy on successful prefixes, turning old inference/RL FLOPs into useful supervision that boosts learning on hard problems where on-policy successes are rare.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard RL on difficult reasoning tasks wastes compute because correct on-policy traces are scarce, gradients vanish, and training stalls; the paper addresses how to reuse past off-policy computation safely and effectively to restart learning.
method: Condition the policy on prefixes of successful off-policy traces so the model continues from partially successful contexts instead of treating off-policy data as full-target supervision.
Integrate prefix-conditioning into the RL optimization pipeline to convert off-policy sampling FLOPs into actionable learning signals while avoiding typical off-policy instabilities.
Train/finetune the model to complete conditioned prefixes (and then use RL updates), enabling reuse of prior inference or training trajectories to improve sample and compute efficiency.
infographic.impact: Makes RL practical on hard LLM reasoning tasks by converting wasted inference/RL compute into reusable training signal, improving sample-efficiency and accelerating learning where conventional on-policy RL fails.
visual_elements: Schematic: model conditioned on a prefix (highlighted) of a trajectory and generating the continuation — shows prefix→completion flow.
Before/After bar chart: on-policy-only training vs. PrefixRL sample- or compute-efficiency (fewer FLOPs to reach a success rate).
Pipeline diagram: collect traces → extract successful prefixes → conditioned RL updates → improved policy, emphasizing FLOP reuse loop.
Icon set: clock/FLOP reuse, shield for stability (avoiding off-policy collapse), and a rising-learning curve for faster convergence.
