title: Trust, Don't Trust, or Flip: Robust Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Expert Feedback
authors: Seyed Amir Hosseini, Maryam Abdolali, Amirhosein Tavakkoli, Fardin Ayar, Ehsan Javanmardi
abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PBRL) offers a promising alternative to explicit reward engineering by learning from pairwise trajectory comparisons. However, real-world preference data often comes from heterogeneous annotators with varying reliability; some accurate, some noisy, and some systematically adversarial. Existing PBRL methods either treat all feedback equally or attempt to filter out unreliable sources, but both approaches fail when faced with adversarial annotators who syst

infographic.key_insight: PBRL can be made robust to heterogeneous and even adversarial annotators by explicitly modeling each expert's reliability and either trusting, ignoring, or flipping their pairwise labels during joint inference of the reward model. This yields reliable reward learning and downstream policies despite noisy or malicious feedback.
infographic.problem_solved: Preference-based RL methods break down when real-world pairwise labels come from mixed-quality annotators (accurate, noisy, or systematically adversarial); the paper addresses how to learn correct preferences and rewards when some experts cannot be trusted or actively mislabel.
method: Introduce a per-expert reliability model that classifies feedback into trust / ignore (don’t trust) / flip decisions and estimates flip probabilities for adversarial annotators.
Jointly infer true pairwise preferences and train the reward model (e.g., via a probabilistic preference model + EM or robust loss) while simultaneously estimating expert reliability parameters.
Use the inferred robust reward to train downstream RL policies and evaluate robustness across mixtures of honest, noisy, and adversarial annotators.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to use heterogeneous multi-expert feedback without extensive filtering or trusting all labels, improving robustness of preference-based reward learning and making human-in-the-loop RL deployment safer and more reliable.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: annotators (honest, noisy, adversarial) → reliability estimator (trust / ignore / flip) → joint preference inference → robust reward → RL policy
Annotator reliability spectrum: icons for trusted, noisy, and flipped/adversarial annotators with estimated reliability scores
Performance chart: policy return vs. fraction of adversarial annotators comparing baseline PBRL, filtering methods, and the proposed robust method
Illustration of flip mechanism: example pairwise trajectory comparison where an adversarial label is detected and flipped before updating the reward model

title: VisGym: Diverse, Customizable, Scalable Environments for Multimodal Agents
authors: Zirui Wang, Junyi Zhang, Jiaxin Ge, Long Lian, Letian Fu
abstract: Modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) remain poorly characterized in multi-step visual interactions, particularly in how they integrate perception, memory, and action over long horizons. We introduce VisGym, a gymnasium of 17 environments for evaluating and training VLMs. The suite spans symbolic puzzles, real-image understanding, navigation, and manipulation, and provides flexible controls over difficulty, input representation, planning horizon, and feedback. We also provide multi-step solvers t

infographic.key_insight: VisGym provides a unified, configurable suite of 17 environments that reveal how Vision–Language Models perform across long-horizon, multi-step visual interactions by letting researchers control perception, memory, and action variables.
infographic.problem_solved: Current VLMs are poorly characterized in extended, interactive tasks; there is no scalable, customizable benchmark to evaluate and train models on integrated perception–memory–action behavior over long planning horizons.
method: Design and release a gym of 17 diverse environments (symbolic puzzles, real-image tasks, navigation, manipulation) covering varied modalities and interaction types.
Expose fine-grained controls for difficulty, input representations, planning horizon, and feedback to enable targeted evaluation and curriculum learning.
Provide multi-step solvers, training/evaluation protocols, and metrics to measure integrated perception, memory, and action performance across environments.
infographic.impact: VisGym enables reproducible, scalable benchmarking and targeted training for multimodal agents, helping researchers diagnose long-horizon failures and iterate on architectures and training strategies that integrate perception, memory, and action.
visual_elements: Grid infographic showing representative snapshots of the 17 environments grouped by category (puzzle, real-image, navigation, manipulation).
Timeline diagram of a multi-step episode illustrating perception → memory update → action → feedback over several steps.
Control-panel mockup with sliders/icons for difficulty, input representation, planning horizon, and feedback to show configurability.
Radar/bar chart comparing model performance across key axes (perception accuracy, memory retention, planning depth, action success rate).

title: SyncLight: Controllable and Consistent Multi-View Relighting
authors: David Serrano-Lozano, Anand Bhattad, Luis Herranz, Jean-François Lalonde, Javier Vazquez-Corral
abstract: We present SyncLight, the first method to enable consistent, parametric relighting across multiple uncalibrated views of a static scene. While single-view relighting has advanced significantly, existing generative approaches struggle to maintain the rigorous lighting consistency essential for multi-camera broadcasts, stereoscopic cinema, and virtual production. SyncLight addresses this by enabling precise control over light intensity and color across a multi-view capture of a scene, conditioned

infographic.key_insight: SyncLight is the first method that enables controllable, parametric relighting that remains photometrically consistent across multiple uncalibrated views of a static scene, allowing precise control of light intensity and color while preserving cross-view coherence.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing single-view generative relighting methods fail to guarantee rigorous lighting consistency across multiple cameras, which prevents their use in multi-camera broadcasts, stereoscopic cinema, and virtual production pipelines; SyncLight addresses this gap.
method: Accepts uncalibrated multi-view images and explicit lighting parameters (intensity, color) as input and produces relit images for each view with shared lighting behavior.

Learns a joint multi-view representation and enforces cross-view photometric consistency via multi-view consistency losses during training, ensuring coherent shadows, highlights, and color across views.
Provides controllable, parametric edits (e.g., sliders for intensity and hue) so users can precisely and consistently manipulate scene illumination across all cameras.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to perform photorealistic, controllable relighting across multi-camera captures—facilitating virtual production, stereoscopic content, and any pipeline that requires consistent multi-view lighting. It bridges single-view relighting advances with production-grade multi-view requirements.

title: Empowering Medical Equipment Sustainability in Low-Resource Settings: An AI-Powered Diagnostic and Support Platform for Biomedical Technicians
authors: Bernes Lorier Atabonfack, Ahmed Tahiru Issah, Mohammed Hardi Abdul Baaki, Clemence Ingabire, Tolulope Olusuyi
abstract: In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), a significant proportion of medical diagnostic equipment remains underutilized or non-functional due to a lack of timely maintenance, limited access to technical expertise, and minimal support from manufacturers, particularly for devices acquired through third-party vendors or donations. This challenge contributes to increased equipment downtime, delayed diagnoses, and compromised patient care. This research explores the development and validation of

infographic.key_insight: An AI-powered diagnostic and support platform enables local biomedical technicians in low-resource settings to identify, troubleshoot, and repair diagnostic equipment faster and with less reliance on manufacturer support, cutting downtime and improving patient care.
infographic.problem_solved: Widespread equipment downtime in LMICs caused by limited access to technical expertise, delayed manufacturer support, and lack of local maintenance capacity—leading to underutilized or nonfunctional diagnostic devices and compromised clinical services.
method: Multimodal diagnostic models that analyze sensor logs, error codes, and equipment photos to detect faults and suggest root causes.
Interactive decision-support workflows and step-by-step repair guidance (including AR/annotated images and technician-facing checklists) plus secure remote expert escalation.
Lightweight, privacy-aware deployment for mobile/edge devices with continuous learning pipelines to adapt models to local device variants and data scarcity.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners this work highlights building robust, interpretable models for constrained, real-world settings—emphasizing edge deployment, domain adaptation, and human-AI workflows that directly improve healthcare delivery in resource-limited contexts.

title: LoL: Longer than Longer, Scaling Video Generation to Hour
authors: Justin Cui, Jie Wu, Ming Li, Tao Yang, Xiaojie Li
abstract: Recent research in long-form video generation has shifted from bidirectional to autoregressive models, yet these methods commonly suffer from error accumulation and a loss of long-term coherence. While attention sink frames have been introduced to mitigate this performance decay, they often induce a critical failure mode we term sink-collapse: the generated content repeatedly reverts to the sink frame, resulting in abrupt scene resets and cyclic motion patterns. Our analysis reveals that sink-co

infographic.key_insight: The paper identifies a failure mode called sink-collapse—where autoregressive long-form video models repeatedly revert to an attention "sink" frame—and introduces targeted architectural and training fixes that restore long-term temporal coherence, enabling generation that scales toward hour-long videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Mitigates error accumulation and cyclic scene resets in autoregressive long-form video generation by diagnosing and preventing sink-frame driven collapse, improving continuity and realistic long-term dynamics.
method: Diagnose and quantify sink-collapse to reveal how sink-frame attention causes abrupt resets and cyclic motion patterns.
Introduce a sink-aware attention design plus anti-collapse regularization to discourage repeated reversion to the sink frame during generation.
Use hierarchical temporal context (chunked decoding with a persistent latent memory) to preserve long-range dynamics and scale autoregressive decoding to hour-long outputs.
infographic.impact: Makes autoregressive video generators more reliable for long-form outputs, reducing repetitive artifacts and improving coherence across minutes-to-hours—useful for simulation, film/VFX, and long-form content generation research and products.

title: The Trajectory Alignment Coefficient in Two Acts: From Reward Tuning to Reward Learning
authors: Calarina Muslimani, Yunshu Du, Kenta Kawamoto, Kaushik Subramanian, Peter Stone
abstract: The success of reinforcement learning (RL) is fundamentally tied to having a reward function that accurately reflects the task objective. Yet, designing reward functions is notoriously time-consuming and prone to misspecification. To address this issue, our first goal is to understand how to support RL practitioners in specifying appropriate weights for a reward function. We leverage the Trajectory Alignment Coefficient (TAC), a metric that evaluates how closely a reward function's induced prefe

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces the Trajectory Alignment Coefficient (TAC), a metric that quantifies how well a reward function's induced trajectory preferences match desired preferences — and shows TAC can be used both to tune reward weights and to learn reward functions from preference data.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces time-consuming, error-prone reward engineering by providing a principled measure to evaluate and optimize reward functions so they better reflect task objectives.
method: Define TAC to measure alignment between the ordering of trajectories induced by a candidate reward and the target (ground-truth or preference) ordering.
Use TAC to guide reward tuning: search or optimize reward weights to maximize trajectory alignment without relying solely on policy rollouts.
Use TAC as an objective/regularizer for reward learning from preferences, enabling preference-informed reward inference that directly targets aligned behavior.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a compact, actionable signal for diagnosing and improving reward specifications, reducing trial-and-error and enabling more reliable preference-driven reward learning and safer, goal-aligned policies.

title: ColorConceptBench: A Benchmark for Probabilistic Color-Concept Understanding in Text-to-Image Models
authors: Chenxi Ruan, Yu Xiao, Yihan Hou, Guosheng Hu, Wei Zeng
abstract: While text-to-image (T2I) models have advanced considerably, their capability to associate colors with implicit concepts remains underexplored. To address the gap, we introduce ColorConceptBench, a new human-annotated benchmark to systematically evaluate color-concept associations through the lens of probabilistic color distributions. ColorConceptBench moves beyond explicit color names or codes by probing how models translate 1,281 implicit color concepts using a foundation of 6,369 human annota

infographic.key_insight: ColorConceptBench provides the first human-annotated, probabilistic benchmark for how text-to-image models map implicit color concepts to color distributions, enabling evaluation beyond single color names or codes.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing evaluations focus on explicit color labels and ignore the inherent ambiguity of implicit color concepts; this benchmark quantifies color–concept associations as probability distributions derived from human judgments so models can be assessed more realistically.
method: Curate 1,281 implicit color concepts and collect 6,369 human annotations to build ground-truth probabilistic color distributions.
Generate images or color predictions from T2I models for each concept and extract color distributions (e.g., color histograms / palette probabilities).
Compare model-derived distributions to human distributions using distributional similarity metrics to measure alignment with human color expectations.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a practical tool for diagnosing color understanding and generation in T2I systems, guiding model/data improvements for more human-aligned and nuanced color rendering.

title: Information Representation Fairness in Long-Document Embeddings: The Peculiar Interaction of Positional and Language Bias
authors: Elias Schuhmacher, Andrianos Michail, Juri Opitz, Rico Sennrich, Simon Clematide
abstract: To be discoverable in an embedding-based search process, each part of a document should be reflected in its embedding representation. To quantify any potential reflection biases, we introduce a permutation-based evaluation framework. With this, we observe that state-of-the-art embedding models exhibit systematic positional and language biases when documents are longer and consist of multiple segments. Specifically, early segments and segments in higher-resource languages like English are over-re

infographic.key_insight: State-of-the-art long-document embedding models systematically over-represent early document segments and segments in higher-resource languages (e.g., English), reducing the discoverability of later or low-resource-language content; a permutation-based evaluation reveals this positional × language bias interaction.
infographic.problem_solved: Quantifies and diagnoses how different parts of multi-segment, multilingual documents are unequally reflected in a single embedding, exposing biases that harm fair retrieval and discoverability.
method: Permutation-based evaluation: systematically shuffle segment order within documents to probe sensitivity of embeddings to position.
Segment-level diagnostics: measure retrieval/similarity and representational strength per segment across positions and languages.
Cross-model and cross-language experiments: analyze how positional and language-resource effects interact across state-of-the-art embedding models and multilingual content.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners with a reproducible diagnostic to detect representation unfairness in long-document embeddings, guiding model choice, indexing strategies, and training fixes so later or low-resource-language segments become discoverable and fairly represented.

title: A Scalable Measure of Loss Landscape Curvature for Analyzing the Training Dynamics of LLMs
authors: Dayal Singh Kalra, Jean-Christophe Gagnon-Audet, Andrey Gromov, Ishita Mediratta, Kelvin Niu
abstract: Understanding the curvature evolution of the loss landscape is fundamental to analyzing the training dynamics of neural networks. The most commonly studied measure, Hessian sharpness ($λ_{\max}^H$) -- the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian -- determines local training stability and interacts with the learning rate throughout training. Despite its significance in analyzing training dynamics, direct measurement of Hessian sharpness remains prohibitive for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to hi

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a scalable, low-cost estimator of loss-landscape curvature that closely tracks Hessian sharpness for very large language models, enabling curvature-aware analysis during real LLM training runs.
infographic.problem_solved: Directly computing Hessian sharpness (largest Hessian eigenvalue) is computationally and memory prohibitive for LLMs, leaving practitioners without a practical curvature diagnostic to analyze stability and learning-rate interactions during training.
method: Design a stochastic, scalable curvature estimator that uses cheap directional probes (Hessian-vector products or gradient-difference approximations) instead of forming the full Hessian.
Aggregate a small number of randomized directional measurements with lightweight spectral extraction (e.g., power / Lanczos-style steps) to approximate the top eigenvalue with sublinear extra cost.

Implement the estimator to run in distributed/parallel training without large communication overhead and validate it empirically across LLM scales and training phases to show strong correlation with true Hessian sharpness and predictive power for instability events.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical tool for monitoring and diagnosing training stability and learning-rate interactions in LLM training, allowing researchers and engineers to make informed optimization and scheduling decisions without prohibitive compute or memory overhead.
visual_elements: Loss-landscape sketch showing flat vs sharp minima with overlaid directional probes and an arrow indicating the estimated top curvature.

title: GPA-VGGT:Adapting VGGT to Large scale Localization by self-Supervised learning with Geometry and Physics Aware loss
authors: Yangfan Xu, Lilian Zhang, Xiaofeng He, Pengdong Wu, Wenqi Wu
abstract: Transformer-based general visual geometry frameworks have shown promising performance in camera pose estimation and 3D scene understanding. Recent advancements in Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) models have shown great promise in camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. However, these models typically rely on ground truth labels for training, posing challenges when adapting to unlabeled and unseen scenes. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised framework to train VGGT with u

infographic.key_insight: A self-supervised adaptation of VGGT enables large-scale camera localization and 3D scene understanding without ground-truth labels by introducing geometry- and physics-aware loss terms that enforce physically consistent pose and reconstruction signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Removes the dependency on labeled pose/geometry data when deploying Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers (VGGT) to unlabeled, unseen, large-scale scenes, enabling scalable localization and reconstruction.
method: Self-supervised training loop that adapts a pretrained VGGT to new scenes using only image streams (no ground-truth poses).
Geometry-aware loss: enforces multi-view geometric consistency (e.g., epipolar/pose-consistency, reprojection errors) between predicted correspondences and scene geometry.

Physics-aware loss: penalizes physically implausible pose or depth solutions (e.g., scale-consistency, gravity/orientation priors, smoothness and visibility constraints) to regularize ambiguous cases.
infographic.impact: Makes state-of-the-art VGGT models practical for real-world, large-scale localization and 3D tasks by reducing annotation costs and improving robustness on unseen environments, accelerating deployment in robotics, AR, and mapping.

title: Boosting Deep Reinforcement Learning with Semantic Knowledge for Robotic Manipulators
authors: Lucía Güitta-López, Vincenzo Suriani, Jaime Boal, Álvaro J. López-López, Daniele Nardi
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is a powerful framework for solving complex sequential decision-making problems, particularly in robotic control. However, its practical deployment is often hindered by the substantial amount of experience required for learning, which results in high computational and time costs. In this work, we propose a novel integration of DRL with semantic knowledge in the form of Knowledge Graph Embeddings (KGEs), aiming to enhance learning efficiency by providing contextu

infographic.key_insight: Incorporating semantic knowledge via Knowledge Graph Embeddings (KGEs) into Deep Reinforcement Learning significantly reduces the experience (samples) required to train robotic manipulators, enabling faster and more reliable policy learning.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses DRL's sample inefficiency and high computational/time costs in robotic manipulation by providing contextual semantic priors that guide learning and exploration.
method: Encode task- and environment-level semantics as Knowledge Graph Embeddings and integrate them into the agent's observation or latent state.
Use semantic priors to shape exploration and/or augment the policy/value network input, reducing reliance on raw trial-and-error.
Evaluate the combined KGE+DRL pipeline on robotic manipulator tasks to demonstrate faster convergence and improved sample efficiency (with ablation to isolate KGE benefit).
infographic.impact: Makes DRL for robotics more practical by cutting training time and compute needs, improving sample efficiency and facilitating safer, more transferable policies for real-world manipulators.

title: Domain-invariant Mixed-domain Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Clustered Maximum Mean Discrepancy Alignment
authors: Ba-Thinh Lam, Thanh-Huy Nguyen, Hoang-Thien Nguyen, Quang-Khai Bui-Tran, Nguyen Lan Vi Vu
abstract: Deep learning has shown remarkable progress in medical image semantic segmentation, yet its success heavily depends on large-scale expert annotations and consistent data distributions. In practice, annotations are scarce, and images are collected from multiple scanners or centers, leading to mixed-domain settings with unknown domain labels and severe domain gaps. Existing semi-supervised or domain adaptation approaches typically assume either a single domain shift or access to explicit domain in

infographic.key_insight: A domain‑invariant semi‑supervised segmentation framework that automatically discovers latent domains in mixed‑center medical image sets and aligns them using a Clustered Maximum Mean Discrepancy (C‑MMD) loss, removing the need for explicit domain labels.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses scarce expert annotations and severe, unknown multi‑scanner/center domain gaps in medical image segmentation where data come from multiple unlabeled domains (mixed‑domain setting).
method: Automatically cluster samples to infer latent domains from mixed labeled and unlabeled medical images.
Apply Clustered Maximum Mean Discrepancy (C‑MMD) to align feature distributions across the inferred clusters, creating domain‑invariant representations.
Train a semi‑supervised segmentation model jointly with the C‑MMD alignment and unlabeled‑data supervision (e.g., pseudo‑labels or consistency regularization).
infographic.impact: Enables more robust, generalizable segmentation models across hospitals and scanners with fewer annotations, easing real‑world deployment and reducing annotation costs for medical AI projects.

title: Spatial-Agent: Agentic Geo-spatial Reasoning with Scientific Core Concepts
authors: Riyang Bao, Cheng Yang, Dazhou Yu, Zhexiang Tang, Gengchen Mai
abstract: Geospatial reasoning is essential for real-world applications such as urban analytics, transportation planning, and disaster response. However, existing LLM-based agents often fail at genuine geospatial computation, relying instead on web search or pattern matching while hallucinating spatial relationships. We present Spatial-Agent, an AI agent grounded in foundational theories of spatial information science. Our approach formalizes geo-analytical question answering as a concept transformation p

infographic.key_insight: Spatial-Agent grounds LLM-driven geospatial reasoning in formal spatial information science, reframing geo-analytical QA as explicit concept transformations so the agent computes spatial relationships instead of hallucinating them.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses LLM agents' inability to perform reliable geospatial computation — they often rely on web search or pattern matching and hallucinate spatial relations rather than executing verifiable spatial analyses.
method: Formalize geo-analytical question answering as concept transformations using scientific core concepts from spatial information science (e.g., objects, fields, topology, metrics).
Use a hybrid agent pipeline that combines LLM-driven interpretation with symbolic/geospatial operators and explicit grounding to GIS computations to produce verifiable spatial outputs.
Evaluate on geospatial tasks and benchmarks to demonstrate reduced hallucination and improved correctness of spatial relationships and measurements.
infographic.impact: Enables reliable, verifiable geospatial reasoning in AI agents for urban analytics, transportation planning, and disaster response — reducing hallucinations and making outputs actionable for practitioners and domain experts.

title: AnyView: Synthesizing Any Novel View in Dynamic Scenes
authors: Basile Van Hoorick, Dian Chen, Shun Iwase, Pavel Tokmakov, Muhammad Zubair Irshad
abstract: Modern generative video models excel at producing convincing, high-quality outputs, but struggle to maintain multi-view and spatiotemporal consistency in highly dynamic real-world environments. In this work, we introduce \textbf{AnyView}, a diffusion-based video generation framework for \emph{dynamic view synthesis} with minimal inductive biases or geometric assumptions. We leverage multiple data sources with various levels of supervision, including monocular (2D), multi-view static (3D) and mul

infographic.key_insight: AnyView uses a diffusion-based video generation framework with minimal geometric assumptions to synthesize arbitrary novel viewpoints in highly dynamic real-world scenes, by training on heterogeneous supervision sources.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between high-quality generative video and strict multi-view + spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic environments, enabling reliable novel-view synthesis without heavy inductive biases or explicit geometric priors.
method: Diffusion-based video generation conditioned for dynamic view synthesis (time + target viewpoint conditioning).
Leverages heterogeneous supervision: monocular 2D, multi-view static 3D, and multi-view dynamic data to learn from varied annotation levels.
Training objectives and architecture choices that encourage multi-view consistency and temporal coherence while keeping minimal geometric assumptions.
infographic.impact: Enables more reliable, view-consistent video synthesis for AR/VR, telepresence, robotics, and dataset augmentation, lowering the barrier to synthesize novel views in complex, changing scenes without detailed scene geometry.

title: Reward-Forcing: Autoregressive Video Generation with Reward Feedback
authors: Jingran Zhang, Ning Li, Yuanhao Ban, Andrew Bai, Justin Cui
abstract: While most prior work in video generation relies on bidirectional architectures, recent efforts have sought to adapt these models into autoregressive variants to support near real-time generation. However, such adaptations often depend heavily on teacher models, which can limit performance, particularly in the absence of a strong autoregressive teacher, resulting in output quality that typically lags behind their bidirectional counterparts. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach that

infographic.key_insight: Reward-Forcing introduces a reward-based feedback loop for autoregressive video generators that reduces reliance on teacher models and brings output quality closer to bidirectional counterparts, enabling higher-quality near real-time generation.
infographic.problem_solved: Autoregressive video generation frequently depends on strong teacher models and lags behind bidirectional architectures in output quality; this paper addresses how to train autoregressive models to achieve competitive quality without heavy teacher supervision.
method: Propose a Reward-Forcing training objective that supplies scalar/structured reward feedback to the autoregressive decoder instead of relying solely on a teacher model.
Use a learned reward function and/or perceptual metrics to evaluate generated frames/sequences and backpropagate guidance that improves temporal coherence and visual fidelity.
Integrate the reward feedback into the autoregressive sampling loop so the model refines next-frame predictions and reduces dependence on a separate teacher model.
infographic.impact: Makes high-quality, low-latency autoregressive video generation more practical by decreasing dependence on strong teacher models—beneficial for real-time applications, deployment, and interactive generative systems.

title: 360Anything: Geometry-Free Lifting of Images and Videos to 360°
authors: Ziyi Wu, Daniel Watson, Andrea Tagliasacchi, David J. Fleet, Marcus A. Brubaker
abstract: Lifting perspective images and videos to 360° panoramas enables immersive 3D world generation. Existing approaches often rely on explicit geometric alignment between the perspective and the equirectangular projection (ERP) space. Yet, this requires known camera metadata, obscuring the application to in-the-wild data where such calibration is typically absent or noisy. We propose 360Anything, a geometry-free framework built upon pre-trained diffusion transformers. By treating the perspective inpu

infographic.key_insight: A geometry-free framework that lifts perspective images and videos into full 360° equirectangular panoramas by leveraging pre-trained diffusion transformers, removing the need for camera calibration or explicit geometric alignment.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing panorama-lifting methods require known camera metadata or careful geometric alignment between perspective views and ERP space, which prevents application to in-the-wild images and videos where calibration is missing or noisy. 360Anything enables reliable 360° synthesis without camera parameters.
method: Treat input perspective frames as partial observations and condition a pre-trained diffusion transformer to hallucinate the missing 360° content, avoiding explicit geometric warping.
Use learned attention/transformer-based priors to map local image appearance into equirectangular layout, plus temporal conditioning for consistent video lifting.
Train/fine-tune on paired (or synthetic) perspective⇄ERP examples so the model learns how to complete panoramas without relying on camera metadata.
infographic.impact: Simplifies creation of panoramic and immersive content from in-the-wild photos and videos, enabling easier data collection and downstream VR/AR, scene reconstruction, and dataset augmentation without calibration overhead.

title: CamPilot: Improving Camera Control in Video Diffusion Model with Efficient Camera Reward Feedback
authors: Wenhang Ge, Guibao Shen, Jiawei Feng, Luozhou Wang, Hao Lu
abstract: Recent advances in camera-controlled video diffusion models have significantly improved video-camera alignment. However, the camera controllability still remains limited. In this work, we build upon Reward Feedback Learning and aim to further improve camera controllability. However, directly borrowing existing ReFL approaches faces several challenges. First, current reward models lack the capacity to assess video-camera alignment. Second, decoding latent into RGB videos for reward computation in

infographic.key_insight: Introduce an efficient camera-alignment reward feedback mechanism that lets video diffusion models learn stronger, more accurate camera control by assessing alignment without expensive RGB decoding.
infographic.problem_solved: Camera-controlled video diffusion models still struggle to follow desired camera trajectories: existing reward-feedback (ReFL) methods lack a camera-aware reward model and computing rewards by decoding latents to RGB is computationally costly and slow.
method: Design a camera-aware reward model that evaluates video↔camera alignment (trained to recognize trajectory, framing, and motion consistency).
Compute reward signals efficiently in latent space (or via a compact camera encoder) to avoid full RGB decoding for every sample.
Integrate the efficient reward into a ReFL loop to fine-tune the video diffusion model, improving its camera-controllability while keeping compute low.
infographic.impact: Makes camera-conditioned video generation more reliable and practical by improving alignment accuracy and drastically lowering reward-evaluation cost—accelerating research and deployment of controllable generative video systems.

title: LLM Prompt Evaluation for Educational Applications
authors: Langdon Holmes, Adam Coscia, Scott Crossley, Joon Suh Choi, Wesley Morris
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly common in educational applications, there is a growing need for evidence-based methods to design and evaluate LLM prompts that produce personalized and pedagogically aligned out-puts. This study presents a generalizable, systematic approach for evaluating prompts, demonstrated through an analysis of LLM-generated follow-up questions in a structured dialogue activity. Six prompt templates were designed and tested. The templates incorporated esta

infographic.key_insight: A repeatable, evidence-based evaluation pipeline can identify which LLM prompt templates produce personalized, pedagogically aligned follow‑up questions in structured educational dialogues, demonstrated by testing six prompt templates.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of systematic methods for designing and evaluating prompts that reliably generate personalized and educationally appropriate outputs for learning applications.
method: Design a set of six prompt templates targeted at generating follow‑up questions within a structured dialogue activity.
Use LLM(s) to produce responses from each template and collect generated follow‑up questions across conditions.
Evaluate outputs with a mix of pedagogical/persona rubrics and quality metrics (e.g., alignment, personalization, relevance), using human raters and/or automated measures to compare templates.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and EdTech designers a practical framework to iterate on prompt design and select templates that better support personalized learning and pedagogical goals, reducing trial-and-error deployment risk.

title: Why Can't I Open My Drawer? Mitigating Object-Driven Shortcuts in Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition
authors: Geo Ahn, Inwoong Lee, Taeoh Kim, Minho Shim, Dongyoon Wee
abstract: We study Compositional Video Understanding (CVU), where models must recognize verbs and objects and compose them to generalize to unseen combinations. We find that existing Zero-Shot Compositional Action Recognition (ZS-CAR) models fail primarily due to an overlooked failure mode: object-driven verb shortcuts. Through systematic analysis, we show that this behavior arises from two intertwined factors: severe sparsity and skewness of compositional supervision, and the asymmetric learning difficul

infographic.key_insight: Zero-shot compositional action models often succeed by relying on object cues instead of true verb understanding — an overlooked ‘object-driven verb shortcut’ caused by sparse/skewed compositional supervision and asymmetric learning difficulty between verbs and objects.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and mitigates the failure mode where models use object identity as a shortcut to predict verbs, which breaks generalization to unseen verb-object combinations.
method: Systematic diagnosis: quantify shortcutting via analyses of supervision sparsity, class skew, and asymmetric learning dynamics between verbs and objects.

Mitigation strategies: introduce targeted interventions (e.g., reweighting, regularization, representation disentangling or contrastive objectives, and data augmentation/occlusion) to reduce object-driven bias and encourage verb-focused learning.
Evaluation: test interventions in zero-shot compositional splits to verify improved compositional generalization (controlled comparisons against baseline ZS-CAR models).
infographic.impact: Highlights a concrete, actionable failure mode and provides practical mitigation patterns so practitioners can build more robust compositional action recognizers that truly learn verbs independent of object identity.

title: LLM-in-Sandbox Elicits General Agentic Intelligence
authors: Daixuan Cheng, Shaohan Huang, Yuxian Gu, Huatong Song, Guoxin Chen
abstract: We introduce LLM-in-Sandbox, enabling LLMs to explore within a code sandbox (i.e., a virtual computer), to elicit general intelligence in non-code domains. We first demonstrate that strong LLMs, without additional training, exhibit generalization capabilities to leverage the code sandbox for non-code tasks. For example, LLMs spontaneously access external resources to acquire new knowledge, leverage the file system to handle long contexts, and execute scripts to satisfy formatting requirements. W

infographic.key_insight: Placing a pretrained LLM inside a sandboxed virtual computer enables it to autonomously use computing tools (file system, scripts, external resources) to solve non-code tasks, revealing agentic general intelligence without extra training.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes limitations of static LLM outputs by giving models a safe, programmable environment to retrieve knowledge, manage very long contexts, and automate multi-step formatting or processing—without fine-tuning.
method: Run an off-the-shelf LLM with access to a code sandbox that exposes a shell, file system, and controlled network/resource interfaces.
Let the LLM generate and execute scripts, read/write files, and fetch external data to extend memory, perform computations, and satisfy task constraints.
Evaluate emergent behaviors on non-code tasks (knowledge acquisition, long-context handling, formatting automation) to demonstrate generalization.
infographic.impact: Practical pathway to turn pretrained LLMs into capable, self-directed agents for complex workflows—improving flexibility, reproducibility, and real-world utility without additional model training.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: LLM connected to sandbox components (shell, file system, network) with arrows showing read/write/execute actions.

title: Provable Robustness in Multimodal Large Language Models via Feature Space Smoothing
authors: Song Xia, Meiwen Ding, Chenqi Kong, Wenhan Yang, Xudong Jiang
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit strong capabilities across diverse applications, yet remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that distort their feature representations and induce erroneous predictions. To address this vulnerability, we propose the Feature-space Smoothing (FS) and theoretically prove that FS offers certified robustness on the feature representations of MLLMs. Specifically, FS transforms any feature encoder into a smoothed variant that is guaranteed to main

infographic.key_insight: Feature-space Smoothing (FS) converts any multimodal feature encoder into a smoothed variant that provably limits the effect of adversarial perturbations on feature representations, yielding certified robustness for downstream MLLM predictions.
infographic.problem_solved: MLLMs are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that distort intermediate feature representations and cause incorrect outputs; prior defenses lack theoretical guarantees for multimodal feature robustness.
method: Apply smoothing (noise-averaging) directly in the encoder feature space to produce a smoothed feature extractor that reduces sensitivity to input perturbations.

Derive theoretical certificates that bound how much a feature can be perturbed before the smoothed encoder’s output (and thus downstream prediction) can change — i.e., a provable robustness radius in feature space.
Design FS as a plug-in transformation compatible with existing encoders and LLM heads, enabling certified robustness without redesigning the entire MLLM pipeline.
infographic.impact: Gives practitioners a practical, plug-and-play defense with formal guarantees, making multimodal systems more reliable against adversarial attacks and suitable for safety-critical deployments.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: input image/text → feature encoder → Feature-space Smoothing block → LLM head, annotated with a certified radius around smoothed features.

title: HVD: Human Vision-Driven Video Representation Learning for Text-Video Retrieval
authors: Zequn Xie, Xin Liu, Boyun Zhang, Yuxiao Lin, Sihang Cai
abstract: The success of CLIP has driven substantial progress in text-video retrieval. However, current methods often suffer from "blind" feature interaction, where the model struggles to discern key visual information from background noise due to the sparsity of textual queries. To bridge this gap, we draw inspiration from human cognitive behavior and propose the Human Vision-Driven (HVD) model. Our framework establishes a coarse-to-fine alignment mechanism comprising two key components: the Frame Featur

infographic.key_insight: HVD introduces a human-vision inspired, coarse-to-fine alignment that lets a text-video retrieval model focus on salient frames and regions, reducing background noise and improving cross-modal matching.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses 'blind' feature interaction in CLIP-style text-video retrieval where sparse textual queries and noisy backgrounds prevent the model from identifying key visual information.
method: Coarse frame-level alignment: identify and weight video frames that are globally relevant to the text query.
Fine-grained region/patch-level alignment: apply human-vision driven saliency or attention to localize and align important visual regions with textual tokens.
Dual-level contrastive/cross-modal learning: jointly train coarse and fine alignments to produce discriminative, interpretable video representations for retrieval.
infographic.impact: Makes text-video retrieval more accurate and interpretable by focusing modeling capacity on semantically relevant visual cues; useful for practitioners building robust multimodal search and indexing systems.

title: Scaling Text-to-Image Diffusion Transformers with Representation Autoencoders
authors: Shengbang Tong, Boyang Zheng, Ziteng Wang, Bingda Tang, Nanye Ma
abstract: Representation Autoencoders (RAEs) have shown distinct advantages in diffusion modeling on ImageNet by training in high-dimensional semantic latent spaces. In this work, we investigate whether this framework can scale to large-scale, freeform text-to-image (T2I) generation. We first scale RAE decoders on the frozen representation encoder (SigLIP-2) beyond ImageNet by training on web, synthetic, and text-rendering data, finding that while scale improves general fidelity, targeted data composition

infographic.key_insight: Scaling Representation Autoencoder (RAE) decoders on a frozen high-quality encoder (SigLIP-2) for text-to-image generation improves overall image fidelity, but careful dataset composition (web, synthetic, text-rendered) is still crucial for reliable text conditioning and compositional control.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables scaling RAE-based diffusion models from ImageNet to open-ended text-to-image generation while maintaining high fidelity and semantic alignment, addressing whether semantic latent RAEs can generalize to large-scale, freeform T2I tasks.
method: Freeze a pre-trained representation encoder (SigLIP-2) and scale RAE decoders trained in a high-dimensional semantic latent space.
Train on a mixture of web images, synthetic data, and text-rendered examples to improve generalization to freeform captions.
Use diffusion transformers operating in the RAE latent space to generate images conditioned on text.
infographic.impact: Shows a practical path to scale semantic-latent diffusion for high-quality, controllable T2I models while leveraging a frozen encoder—reducing retraining cost and focusing engineering effort on decoder scaling and dataset design.

title: Pay (Cross) Attention to the Melody: Curriculum Masking for Single-Encoder Melodic Harmonization
authors: Maximos Kaliakatsos-Papakostas, Dimos Makris, Konstantinos Soiledis, Konstantinos-Theodoros Tsamis, Vassilis Katsouros
abstract: Melodic harmonization, the task of generating harmonic accompaniments for a given melody, remains a central challenge in computational music generation. Recent single encoder transformer approaches have framed harmonization as a masked sequence modeling problem, but existing training curricula inspired by discrete diffusion often result in weak (cross) attention between melody and harmony. This leads to limited exploitation of melodic cues, particularly in out-of-domain contexts. In this work, w

infographic.key_insight: A curriculum masking strategy for single-encoder masked-sequence transformers encourages stronger cross-attention from harmony to melody, enabling the model to better exploit melodic cues and generalize to out-of-domain melodies.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing training curricula (inspired by discrete diffusion) produce weak cross-attention between melody and harmony, causing generated accompaniments to underuse melodic information and fail to generalize beyond training distributions.
method: Design a progressive masking curriculum that controls which tokens (melody vs. harmony) are masked and how masking difficulty increases during training to prioritize melody–harmony interactions.
Train a single-encoder transformer as a masked sequence model using the curriculum so the model learns to attend to melody tokens when reconstructing harmony.
Evaluate attention patterns and generalization to out-of-domain melodies to verify improved melody-conditioned harmonization and robustness.
infographic.impact: A lightweight, training-time modification that significantly improves how conditional sequence models leverage context—useful for music generation and other conditional generation tasks where strong cross-conditioning is critical.

title: Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning
authors: Moo Jin Kim, Yihuai Gao, Tsung-Yi Lin, Yen-Chen Lin, Yunhao Ge
abstract: Recent video generation models demonstrate remarkable ability to capture complex physical interactions and scene evolution over time. To leverage their spatiotemporal priors, robotics works have adapted video models for policy learning but introduce complexity by requiring multiple stages of post-training and new architectural components for action generation. In this work, we introduce Cosmos Policy, a simple approach for adapting a large pretrained video model (Cosmos-Predict2) into an effecti

infographic.key_insight: A large pretrained video generation model (Cosmos‑Predict2) can be fine‑tuned with minimal changes to serve as an effective visuomotor policy and planner—removing the need for multi‑stage post‑training or new action‑generation architectures.
infographic.problem_solved: Prior attempts to adapt video models for robotics required complex multi‑stage pipelines and added modules to generate actions, making integration brittle and sample‑inefficient; this work simplifies the adaptation so spatiotemporal priors from video models can be directly leveraged for control and planning.
method: Start from a pretrained Cosmos‑Predict2 video model and fine‑tune it end‑to‑end on visuomotor datasets with simple action conditioning (minimal architectural changes).
Train the model to predict future observations conditioned on candidate action sequences and use its predicted futures to select or refine actions (planning / MPC style inference).

Keep training objectives and pipeline lightweight (behavior‑cloning / likelihood‑based fine‑tuning and optional online adaptation) to preserve pretrained spatiotemporal priors and improve sample efficiency.
infographic.impact: Provides a low‑complexity, high‑reuse path for turning large video models into practical visuomotor controllers and planners, lowering engineering overhead and improving long‑horizon reasoning for robotics and embodied AI.

title: Learning to Discover at Test Time
authors: Mert Yuksekgonul, Daniel Koceja, Xinhao Li, Federico Bianchi, Jed McCaleb
abstract: How can we use AI to discover a new state of the art for a scientific problem? Prior work in test-time scaling, such as AlphaEvolve, performs search by prompting a frozen LLM. We perform reinforcement learning at test time, so the LLM can continue to train, but now with experience specific to the test problem. This form of continual learning is quite special, because its goal is to produce one great solution rather than many good ones on average, and to solve this very problem rather than genera

infographic.key_insight: Train the LLM at test time with reinforcement learning so it adapts to the specific problem instance and iteratively discovers a single, superior solution rather than relying on frozen prompting or averaging many outputs.
infographic.problem_solved: How to push a model to discover a new state-of-the-art solution for a specific scientific/test problem by continuing to learn from experience during inference, instead of using a frozen model or search over prompts.
method: Run reinforcement learning during inference: generate candidate solutions, evaluate them against the task objective, and update the model policy using the feedback.
Optimize for a single-best outcome (continual/test-time learning) rather than average-case performance, enabling aggressive exploration-exploitation tailored to the current test instance.
Contrast with prior test-time search (e.g., prompting a frozen LLM): incorporate on-the-fly parameter updates so the model accumulates problem-specific experience.
infographic.impact: Enables automated discovery of higher-quality, instance-specific solutions (useful for scientific tasks, optimization, and benchmarks) by allowing models to adapt and improve at test time rather than relying on static inference strategies.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: Frozen prompt-based search (multiple static outputs) vs. Test-time RL loop (generate → evaluate → update → repeat).

title: Learning to Watermark in the Latent Space of Generative Models
authors: Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Tuan Tran, Valeriu Lacatusu, Pierre Fernandez, Tomáš Souček
abstract: Existing approaches for watermarking AI-generated images often rely on post-hoc methods applied in pixel space, introducing computational overhead and potential visual artifacts. In this work, we explore latent space watermarking and introduce DistSeal, a unified approach for latent watermarking that works across both diffusion and autoregressive models. Our approach works by training post-hoc watermarking models in the latent space of generative models. We demonstrate that these latent watermar

infographic.key_insight: Watermarks can be applied more effectively and efficiently inside a generative model's latent space rather than in pixel space; DistSeal is a unified, post-hoc latent watermarking method that works across diffusion and autoregressive models.
infographic.problem_solved: Pixel-space watermarking of AI images is computationally costly and can introduce visible artifacts; there is a need for a model-agnostic, low-overhead, robust watermarking technique that can be applied to pretrained generative models without retraining them.
method: Train lightweight post-hoc watermarking networks that operate in the generative model's latent space (encode -> watermark latent -> decode).
Design objectives that balance imperceptibility (minimal visual change) and detectability/robustness so the watermark survives generation and common perturbations.
Make the approach model-agnostic and compatible with both diffusion and autoregressive pipelines by working at the shared latent representation level.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to add reliable, low-cost provenance signals to outputs from pretrained generative models with fewer visual artifacts and less compute than pixel-space methods — improving content traceability and stewardship.

title: PyraTok: Language-Aligned Pyramidal Tokenizer for Video Understanding and Generation
authors: Onkar Susladkar, Tushar Prakash, Adheesh Juvekar, Kiet A. Nguyen, Dong-Hwan Jang
abstract: Discrete video VAEs underpin modern text-to-video generation and video understanding systems, yet existing tokenizers typically learn visual codebooks at a single scale with limited vocabularies and shallow language supervision, leading to poor cross-modal alignment and zero-shot transfer. We introduce PyraTok, a language-aligned pyramidal tokenizer that learns semantically structured discrete latents across multiple spatiotemporal resolutions. PyraTok builds on a pretrained video VAE and a nove

infographic.key_insight: PyraTok learns discrete video tokens at multiple spatiotemporal scales and explicitly aligns them with language, producing semantically structured representations that improve cross-modal alignment and zero-shot transfer.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video tokenizers use single-scale codebooks with limited vocabularies and weak language supervision, leading to poor semantic alignment with text and limited zero-shot capability for video understanding and generation.
method: Construct a pyramidal tokenizer on top of a pretrained video VAE to produce discrete latents at multiple spatiotemporal resolutions (a multi-scale codebook pyramid).
Introduce stronger language alignment across scales so tokens become semantically structured and directly comparable to text representations.
Replace single-scale discrete latents with the language-aligned pyramidal tokens for downstream text-to-video generation and zero-shot video understanding.
infographic.impact: PyraTok provides more expressive, language-grounded video tokens that improve cross-modal transfer and reduce reliance on task-specific fine-tuning, benefiting practitioners building text-to-video models, retrieval systems, and zero-shot video classifiers.

title: LuxRemix: Lighting Decomposition and Remixing for Indoor Scenes
authors: Ruofan Liang, Norman Müller, Ethan Weber, Duncan Zauss, Nandita Vijaykumar
abstract: We present a novel approach for interactive light editing in indoor scenes from a single multi-view scene capture. Our method leverages a generative image-based light decomposition model that factorizes complex indoor scene illumination into its constituent light sources. This factorization enables independent manipulation of individual light sources, specifically allowing control over their state (on/off), chromaticity, and intensity. We further introduce multi-view lighting harmonization to en

infographic.key_insight: LuxRemix decomposes complex indoor illumination from a single multi-view capture into individual light sources, enabling intuitive per-light editing (on/off, color, intensity) while enforcing multi-view consistent harmonization for realistic relighting.
infographic.problem_solved: Interactive, per-light editing of indoor scenes is hard because scene illumination is entangled and edits must remain consistent across viewpoints; LuxRemix provides a factorized representation that isolates light sources for independent manipulation and coherent multi-view rendering.
method: Generative image-based light decomposition that factorizes scene illumination into constituent light sources from a single multi-view capture.
Per-source controls for state (on/off), chromaticity, and intensity to enable targeted edits.
Multi-view lighting harmonization and rendering to ensure consistent appearance, shadows, and reflections across all views after edits.
infographic.impact: Makes realistic, interactive relighting and light-level editing practical for applications in AR/VR, interior design, and content creation; simplifies workflows for ML practitioners needing controllable scene illumination in downstream tasks.

title: Walk through Paintings: Egocentric World Models from Internet Priors
authors: Anurag Bagchi, Zhipeng Bao, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Yu-Xiong Wang, Pavel Tokmakov
abstract: What if a video generation model could not only imagine a plausible future, but the correct one, accurately reflecting how the world changes with each action? We address this question by presenting the Egocentric World Model (EgoWM), a simple, architecture-agnostic method that transforms any pretrained video diffusion model into an action-conditioned world model, enabling controllable future prediction. Rather than training from scratch, we repurpose the rich world priors of Internet-scale video

infographic.key_insight: EgoWM retrofits any pretrained video diffusion model into an action-conditioned egocentric world model, enabling controllable and temporally accurate future prediction by leveraging Internet-scale video priors instead of training from scratch.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between generic video generation and actionable, egocentric future prediction—removing the need for costly-from-scratch training and large task-specific datasets while providing control over predicted outcomes via actions.
method: Architecture-agnostic adaptation: add lightweight action conditioning (e.g., conditioning inputs or adapter modules) to pretrained video diffusion models so they accept actions and produce corresponding future frames.

Repurpose Internet priors: leverage rich, pretrained video knowledge from large-scale web data rather than training new generative models from scratch, enabling sample- and compute-efficient adaptation.
Action-conditioned rollout: generate multi-step egocentric rollouts conditioned on specified actions to produce temporally coherent, controllable future predictions for planning and downstream tasks.
infographic.impact: Makes it practical for ML practitioners to convert existing video generators into controllable world models for robotics, planning, and simulation with much lower data and compute cost—accelerating deployment of action-aware prediction systems.

title: StableWorld: Towards Stable and Consistent Long Interactive Video Generation
authors: Ying Yang, Zhengyao Lv, Tianlin Pan, Haofan Wang, Binxin Yang
abstract: In this paper, we explore the overlooked challenge of stability and temporal consistency in interactive video generation, which synthesizes dynamic and controllable video worlds through interactive behaviors such as camera movements and text prompts. Despite remarkable progress in world modeling, current methods still suffer from severe instability and temporal degradation, often leading to spatial drift and scene collapse during long-horizon interactions. To better understand this issue, we ini

infographic.key_insight: StableWorld pinpoints why current interactive video models suffer spatial drift and scene collapse over long interactions and introduces stability-focused design choices that keep generated worlds temporally consistent and controllable.
infographic.problem_solved: Mitigates instability and temporal degradation (spatial drift, scene collapse) in long‑horizon interactive video generation driven by camera movements and text prompts, enabling persistent, coherent video worlds across extended interactions.
method: Analyze failure modes in long interactive sequences to quantify temporal degradation and identify sources of instability.

Incorporate stability-focused components (e.g., temporal-consistency objectives, memory/latent alignment, and explicit conditioning on camera/interaction signals) to preserve geometry and identity over time.
Train and evaluate on long-horizon interactive scenarios to enforce smooth transitions and prevent cumulative drift during prolonged camera or prompt-driven behaviors.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to build more reliable, controllable interactive video systems (virtual production, simulation, embodied AI) that maintain scene integrity over long interactions, reducing artifacts and improving user trust.

title: Towards Understanding Best Practices for Quantization of Vision-Language Models
authors: Gautom Das, Vincent La, Ethan Lau, Abhinav Shrivastava, Matthew Gwilliam
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deliver impressive results for a variety of tasks, but state-of-the-art systems require fast GPUs with large amounts of memory. To reduce both the memory and latency of these systems, practitioners quantize their learned parameters, typically at half precision. A growing body of research focuses on preserving the model performance with more aggressive bit widths, and some work has been done to apply these strategies to other models, like vision transformers. In our s

infographic.key_insight: A focused empirical study shows that vision–language models can be aggressively quantized with minimal performance loss when using tailored recipes — e.g., per-channel weight quantization, activation calibration/outlier handling, and selective mixed-precision for sensitive layers.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides practical, evidence-backed guidelines to reduce memory and latency of large vision–language models while preserving downstream accuracy, removing guesswork from quantization choices.
method: Systematic benchmarking of VLMs across quantization families (post‑training quantization, quant‑aware training) and bit widths to measure accuracy/latency tradeoffs.
Layer‑wise sensitivity analysis to identify which components require higher precision and recommendation of mixed‑precision allocations.
Practical engineering recipes: per‑channel weight quantization, activation clipping/calibration and outlier handling, plus minimal fine‑tuning when needed.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to deploy VLMs more efficiently on constrained hardware and reduces iterative tuning time by offering reproducible best practices for aggressive quantization.

title: Iterative Refinement Improves Compositional Image Generation
authors: Shantanu Jaiswal, Mihir Prabhudesai, Nikash Bhardwaj, Zheyang Qin, Amir Zadeh
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have achieved remarkable progress, yet they continue to struggle with complex prompts that require simultaneously handling multiple objects, relations, and attributes. Existing inference-time strategies, such as parallel sampling with verifiers or simply increasing denoising steps, can improve prompt alignment but remain inadequate for richly compositional settings where many constraints must be satisfied. Inspired by the success of chain-of-thought reasoning in large

infographic.key_insight: Iterative refinement—repeatedly verifying and correcting generated images against decomposed prompt constraints—substantially improves alignment on richly compositional text-to-image prompts. This yields more accurate multi-object, relation, and attribute satisfaction than single-pass sampling or naive step increases.
infographic.problem_solved: Text-to-image models fail to reliably render complex, compositional prompts that require simultaneously satisfying many objects, relations, and attributes; existing inference tricks (more denoising steps or parallel sampling) are insufficient for such multi-constraint scenarios.
method: Decompose complex prompts into smaller constraints (objects, relations, attributes) and use a looped inference procedure that verifies which constraints are unmet.
Apply targeted iterative edits or re-sampling steps guided by a verifier or internal reasoning signal (inspired by chain-of-thought) to progressively satisfy remaining constraints.
Stop when a verifier indicates prompt alignment or after a fixed budget of refinement steps, producing higher-fidelity, compositionally correct images.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to get more reliable, faithful image outputs for complex prompts without retraining models—useful for design, illustration, and downstream evaluation tasks that demand precise compositional control.

title: APPLE: Attribute-Preserving Pseudo-Labeling for Diffusion-Based Face Swapping
authors: Jiwon Kang, Yeji Choi, JoungBin Lee, Wooseok Jang, Jinhyeok Choi
abstract: Face swapping aims to transfer the identity of a source face onto a target face while preserving target-specific attributes such as pose, expression, lighting, skin tone, and makeup. However, since real ground truth for face swapping is unavailable, achieving both accurate identity transfer and high-quality attribute preservation remains challenging. In addition, recent diffusion-based approaches attempt to improve visual fidelity through conditional inpainting on masked target images, but the m

infographic.key_insight: APPLE introduces attribute-preserving pseudo-labeling to supervise diffusion-based face swapping, enabling accurate identity transfer while explicitly preserving target-specific attributes (pose, expression, lighting, skin tone, makeup).
infographic.problem_solved: Face swapping lacks real ground-truth, forcing a trade-off between identity transfer and preserving target attributes; diffusion-based conditional inpainting often degrades those target-specific attributes.
method: Generate pseudo ground-truth attribute labels from the target image (pose, expression, lighting, skin tone, makeup) to serve as conditioning signals.
Condition a diffusion-based inpainting/synthesis model on both source identity features and the target pseudo-attribute labels, with losses that enforce identity fidelity and attribute consistency.
Train end-to-end so the model learns to decouple identity from target attributes, producing high-fidelity swapped faces that retain target-specific appearance and geometry.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to supervise face swapping without real paired data, improving visual fidelity and attribute reliability. This benefits practitioners building realistic synthesis, data augmentation, and evaluation tools in face-related applications.

title: Many Experiments, Few Repetitions, Unpaired Data, and Sparse Effects: Is Causal Inference Possible?
authors: Felix Schur, Niklas Pfister, Peng Ding, Sach Mukherjee, Jonas Peters
abstract: We study the problem of estimating causal effects under hidden confounding in the following unpaired data setting: we observe some covariates $X$ and an outcome $Y$ under different experimental conditions (environments) but do not observe them jointly; we either observe $X$ or $Y$. Under appropriate regularity conditions, the problem can be cast as an instrumental variable (IV) regression with the environment acting as a (possibly high-dimensional) instrument. When there are many environments bu

infographic.key_insight: When experiments produce unpaired X and Y across many environments with few repeats each, the environment labels can act as high-dimensional instruments — enabling identification and consistent estimation of sparse causal effects under suitable regularity conditions.
infographic.problem_solved: Estimates causal effects under hidden confounding from unpaired observational blocks (we either observe X or Y per environment), in the regime of many environments but few samples per environment, where standard methods fail.
method: Recast unpaired-environment data as an instrumental variables (IV) problem with the environment index as the instrument (possibly high-dimensional).
Exploit sparsity in the causal coefficient vector (few nonzero effects) and use regularized/penalized IV estimation (e.g., Lasso-style selection in IV stages) to recover effects.
Provide identifiability conditions and finite-sample/consistency guarantees that link number of environments, repeat counts, and sparsity level.
infographic.impact: Enables causal effect estimation in modern experimental setups with many small experiments or fragmented data (e.g., lab assays, A/B slices, distributed sensors) where X and Y are never jointly measured; offers a practical route to recover sparse causal signals despite hidden confounding.
visual_elements: Schematic DAG: Environment -> X -> Y, with an unobserved confounder between X and Y, and a note that X and Y are observed in disjoint batches.
Block diagram showing unpaired data layout: many environment blocks, some containing only X, others only Y.
Barplot of true vs. recovered sparse coefficients to illustrate sparse-effect recovery.
Performance curve: estimation error vs. number of environments (showing improvement as environments increase) and vs. repeats per environment.

title: Evaluation of Large Language Models in Legal Applications: Challenges, Methods, and Future Directions
authors: Yiran Hu, Huanghai Liu, Chong Wang, Kunran Li, Tien-Hsuan Wu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being increasingly integrated into legal applications, including judicial decision support, legal practice assistance, and public-facing legal services. While LLMs show strong potential in handling legal knowledge and tasks, their deployment in real-world legal settings raises critical concerns beyond surface-level accuracy, involving the soundness of legal reasoning processes and trustworthy issues such as fairness and reliability. Systematic evaluation of LLM p

infographic.key_insight: LLMs show promise for legal tasks but must be evaluated on legal reasoning, fairness, and reliability—not only surface accuracy—to be safely deployed in real-world legal settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the absence of a systematic, domain-tailored evaluation framework for LLMs in legal applications, covering reasoning soundness, normative consistency, bias, robustness, and practical deployment checks.
method: Define a legal-focused evaluation taxonomy covering factual accuracy, reasoning traceability, precedent consistency, fairness, and robustness.
Design mixed evaluation protocols combining automated benchmarks, adversarial tests, and human-expert case-based assessments to measure both outputs and reasoning traces.
Apply protocols in case studies and propose operational guidelines for auditing, continuous monitoring, and dataset/metric design for legal LLM deployment.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners concrete metrics and workflows to audit and improve legal LLMs, reducing deployment risk and improving trustworthiness; guides creation of benchmarks and best practices for responsible LawTech.

Pipeline flowchart from dataset → evaluation tests (automated + adversarial) → human expert review → deployment/monitoring.

title: MolecularIQ: Characterizing Chemical Reasoning Capabilities Through Symbolic Verification on Molecular Graphs
authors: Christoph Bartmann, Johannes Schimunek, Mykyta Ielanskyi, Philipp Seidl, Günter Klambauer
abstract: A molecule's properties are fundamentally determined by its composition and structure encoded in its molecular graph. Thus, reasoning about molecular properties requires the ability to parse and understand the molecular graph. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to chemistry, tackling tasks such as molecular name conversion, captioning, text-guided generation, and property or reaction prediction. Most existing benchmarks emphasize general chemical knowledge, rely on literature

infographic.key_insight: MolecularIQ introduces a symbolic verification framework to directly evaluate AI models' ability to reason about molecular structure encoded as graphs, revealing gaps between text‑based chemical knowledge and true graph‑level chemical reasoning.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing chemistry benchmarks focus on textual or literature knowledge and do not reliably measure whether models can parse, manipulate, and verify structural information in molecular graphs — a core requirement for predicting molecular properties and reactions.
method: Define tasks that require structural reasoning on molecular graphs (e.g., substructure identification, valence checks, functional group inference) rather than only text-based prompts.
Translate molecular graphs into symbolic representations and apply automated symbolic verification to check model outputs against graph-grounded constraints.
Use the verification pipeline to benchmark LLMs and graph models, exposing specific failure modes in symbolic/graph reasoning.
infographic.impact: Provides a targeted evaluation tool that helps practitioners diagnose and improve models' chemical-structure reasoning, guiding model selection, training strategies, and dataset design for molecular applications.

title: RayRoPE: Projective Ray Positional Encoding for Multi-view Attention
authors: Yu Wu, Minsik Jeon, Jen-Hao Rick Chang, Oncel Tuzel, Shubham Tulsiani
abstract: We study positional encodings for multi-view transformers that process tokens from a set of posed input images, and seek a mechanism that encodes patches uniquely, allows SE(3)-invariant attention with multi-frequency similarity, and can be adaptive to the geometry of the underlying scene. We find that prior (absolute or relative) encoding schemes for multi-view attention do not meet the above desiderata, and present RayRoPE to address this gap. RayRoPE represents patch positions based on associ

infographic.key_insight: RayRoPE encodes image patches by their projective camera rays and applies a rotary-style, multi-frequency positional encoding so multi-view attention is uniquely informed by 3D geometry and is SE(3)-invariant.
infographic.problem_solved: Prior absolute or relative positional encodings for multi-view transformers cannot simultaneously (a) uniquely identify patches across views, (b) support SE(3)-invariant multi-frequency attention, and (c) adapt to scene geometry; RayRoPE fills this gap.
method: Represent patch positions using their associated camera rays (ray direction + projective depth/parameterization) so tokens are grounded in 3D geometry.
Apply a projective rotary positional encoding (RayRoPE) to queries/keys to preserve multi-frequency similarity while achieving SE(3)-invariant attention.
Adapt encoding frequencies or scales based on ray depth / local geometry so embeddings remain discriminative across varying distances and viewpoints.
infographic.impact: Makes multi-view transformers geometry-aware and robust to camera motions, improving cross-view feature alignment and generalization for tasks like 3D reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, and multi-view perception.

title: Rethinking Video Generation Model for the Embodied World
authors: Yufan Deng, Zilin Pan, Hongyu Zhang, Xiaojie Li, Ruoqing Hu
abstract: Video generation models have significantly advanced embodied intelligence, unlocking new possibilities for generating diverse robot data that capture perception, reasoning, and action in the physical world. However, synthesizing high-quality videos that accurately reflect real-world robotic interactions remains challenging, and the lack of a standardized benchmark limits fair comparisons and progress. To address this gap, we introduce a comprehensive robotics benchmark, RBench, designed to evalu

infographic.key_insight: Introducing RBench, a standardized robotics-focused benchmark and evaluation suite that reframes video generation for the embodied world—enabling consistent assessment of how well models capture perception, reasoning, and action in real robot interactions.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of a standardized benchmark and evaluation protocol for synthesizing high-quality, realistic robot interaction videos, which has hampered fair comparison and progress in embodied video generation.
method: Curate a diverse robotics video dataset covering real-world interactions, multiple tasks, and varied sensors/angles (RBench).
Define evaluation protocols and specialized metrics that quantify perception fidelity, action/causal consistency, and physical plausibility.
Provide baseline model evaluations and an open framework for reproducible comparisons and future method development.
infographic.impact: RBench enables researchers and practitioners to reliably compare video generation models for robotics, accelerating progress in data synthesis, sim-to-real transfer, and downstream embodied AI tasks by providing standard data, metrics, and baselines.
