title: Fast-ThinkAct: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Reasoning via Verbalizable Latent Planning
authors: Chi-Pin Huang, Yunze Man, Zhiding Yu, Min-Hung Chen, Jan Kautz
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) tasks require reasoning over complex visual scenes and executing adaptive actions in dynamic environments. While recent studies on reasoning VLAs show that explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) can improve generalization, they suffer from high inference latency due to lengthy reasoning traces. We propose Fast-ThinkAct, an efficient reasoning framework that achieves compact yet performant planning through verbalizable latent reasoning. Fast-ThinkAct learns to reason efficie

infographic.key_insight: Fast-ThinkAct compresses lengthy chain-of-thought reasoning into compact, verbalizable latent plans so agents can plan effectively with much lower inference latency while retaining decision quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Long, explicit chain-of-thought traces in vision-language-action tasks improve generalization but incur high inference latency, making real-time action in dynamic environments impractical.
method: Learn a latent planning space where multi-step reasoning is performed compactly, then decode short, human-interpretable verbalizations from those latents.
Train a two-stage pipeline: a latent planner that reasons in compressed space and an action actor conditioned on the latent (and its verbalization) to produce environment actions.
Optimize for a trade-off between plan compactness and fidelity (e.g., via distillation or joint training) so verbalizable latents match the performance of long CoT with much lower runtime cost.
infographic.impact: Enables fast, interpretable vision-language-action agents suitable for real-time robotics and interactive systems by dramatically reducing inference time without sacrificing reasoning quality.

title: Contrastive Geometric Learning Unlocks Unified Structure- and Ligand-Based Drug Design
authors: Lisa Schneckenreiter, Sohvi Luukkonen, Lukas Friedrich, Daniel Kuhn, Günter Klambauer
abstract: Structure-based and ligand-based computational drug design have traditionally relied on disjoint data sources and modeling assumptions, limiting their joint use at scale. In this work, we introduce Contrastive Geometric Learning for Unified Computational Drug Design (ConGLUDe), a single contrastive geometric model that unifies structure- and ligand-based training. ConGLUDe couples a geometric protein encoder that produces whole-protein representations and implicit embeddings of predicted binding

infographic.key_insight: A single contrastive geometric model (ConGLUDe) unifies structure- and ligand-based drug design by aligning geometric protein representations with ligand information, enabling joint training and cross-modal transfer between protein structure and ligand data.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing workflows treat structure-based and ligand-based methods separately because of different data types and modeling assumptions, preventing scalable joint learning and reuse of knowledge across tasks.
method: Contrastive geometric learning to align protein-level geometric encodings with ligand or predicted-binding embeddings in a shared representation space.
A geometric protein encoder that produces whole-protein representations plus implicit embeddings of predicted binding regions, enabling cross-modal supervision without separate pocket annotation.
Unified training procedure that leverages both structural data (protein coordinates) and ligand data (SMILES/graphs) so a single model supports structure- and ligand-centered downstream tasks.
infographic.impact: ConGLUDe enables AI/ML practitioners to train one model that transfers between structure- and ligand-based tasks, improving data efficiency and simplifying pipelines for virtual screening, lead optimization, and generative design.

title: Routing with Generated Data: Annotation-Free LLM Skill Estimation and Expert Selection
authors: Tianyi Niu, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Genta Indra Winata, Shi-Xiong Zhang, Supriyo Chakraborty
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) routers dynamically select optimal models for given inputs. Existing approaches typically assume access to ground-truth labeled data, which is often unavailable in practice, especially when user request distributions are heterogeneous and unknown. We introduce Routing with Generated Data (RGD), a challenging setting in which routers are trained exclusively on generated queries and answers produced from high-level task descriptions by generator LLMs. We evaluate query-a

infographic.key_insight: LLM routers can be trained without human labels by using synthetic queries and answers generated from high-level task descriptions, enabling accurate annotation-free skill estimation and expert selection across heterogeneous, unknown request distributions.
infographic.problem_solved: How to train routers that pick the best expert model when ground-truth labeled routing data is unavailable and user request distributions are diverse or unknown — eliminating dependence on costly human annotations.
method: Use generator LLMs and high-level task descriptions to synthesize diverse query–answer pairs that approximate real user requests.
Train a skill-estimation router on the generated dataset to predict or rank which expert/model will perform best for each input.
Deploy the router to route real queries to selected experts at inference time and evaluate robustness to distribution shifts and heterogeneous tasks.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, annotation-free multi-model routing for ML systems — lowering labeling costs and allowing dynamic, data-efficient selection of the best model per request, improving overall system accuracy and resource use.

authors: Ailin Huang, Chengyuan Yao, Chunrui Han, Fanqi Wan, Hangyu Guo

title: DeepResearchEval: An Automated Framework for Deep Research Task Construction and Agentic Evaluation
authors: Yibo Wang, Lei Wang, Yue Deng, Keming Wu, Yao Xiao
abstract: Deep research systems are widely used for multi-step web research, analysis, and cross-source synthesis, yet their evaluation remains challenging. Existing benchmarks often require annotation-intensive task construction, rely on static evaluation dimensions, or fail to reliably verify facts when citations are missing. To bridge these gaps, we introduce DeepResearchEval, an automated framework for deep research task construction and agentic evaluation. For task construction, we propose a persona-

infographic.key_insight: DeepResearchEval automates the construction of realistic, multi-step web research tasks and provides an agentic, citation-aware evaluation pipeline that reduces annotation overhead and improves the fidelity of evaluating deep research systems.

method: Persona-driven automated task construction: synthesize realistic multi-step research prompts and role-based objectives without intensive manual annotation.
Agentic evaluation pipeline: run agents to execute tasks, capture reasoning traces and retrieved sources, and aggregate outputs for assessment.

title: SCE-SLAM: Scale-Consistent Monocular SLAM via Scene Coordinate Embeddings
authors: Yuchen Wu, Jiahe Li, Xiaohan Yu, Lina Yu, Jin Zheng
abstract: Monocular visual SLAM enables 3D reconstruction from internet video and autonomous navigation on resource-constrained platforms, yet suffers from scale drift, i.e., the gradual divergence of estimated scale over long sequences. Existing frame-to-frame methods achieve real-time performance through local optimization but accumulate scale drift due to the lack of global constraints among independent windows. To address this, we propose SCE-SLAM, an end-to-end SLAM system that maintains scale consis

infographic.key_insight: SCE-SLAM uses learned scene-coordinate embeddings as a global, metric anchor inside a monocular SLAM pipeline to prevent scale drift across long sequences while preserving real-time local optimization.
infographic.problem_solved: Monocular SLAM systems accumulate scale drift over long videos because local frame-to-frame optimization lacks global metric constraints; SCE-SLAM enforces a consistent global scale across independent optimization windows.
method: Learn per-pixel / per-keypoint scene coordinate embeddings that map image observations to a shared metric 3D coordinate space.
Integrate embedding-based global constraints into an end-to-end SLAM pipeline so local windowed optimizers are anchored to a consistent scale and can be globally aligned.
Maintain real-time performance by combining lightweight local optimization with occasional global consistency updates via embedding matches (no heavy full-batch bundle adjustment).
infographic.impact: Provides reliable, scale-consistent monocular 3D reconstruction suitable for long-range mapping, internet-video reconstruction, and resource-constrained robotics — reducing post-processing and improving downstream perception tasks.

title: ShortCoder: Knowledge-Augmented Syntax Optimization for Token-Efficient Code Generation
authors: Sicong Liu, Yanxian Huang, Mingwei Liu, Jiachi Chen, Ensheng Shi
abstract: Code generation tasks aim to automate the conversion of user requirements into executable code, significantly reducing manual development efforts and enhancing software productivity. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has significantly advanced code generation, though their efficiency is still impacted by certain inherent architectural constraints. Each token generation necessitates a complete inference pass, requiring persistent retention of contextual information in memory and escal

infographic.key_insight: ShortCoder combines external code knowledge with syntax-aware representations to compress and restructure code generation so that models emit fewer tokens for the same program, reducing inference passes and compute cost.
infographic.problem_solved: LLM-based code generation is token-inefficient: every generated token requires a full inference step and large context retention, causing high latency, memory use, and cost for producing long or repetitive code.
method: Knowledge augmentation: inject retrieved or pre-learned code patterns, API usage, and idioms to raise the semantic abstraction level the model needs to generate.
Syntax-aware compression: convert code to compact, syntax-preserving representations (e.g., AST-driven tokenization/macros) so that common constructs map to fewer tokens.
Decoder-friendly integration: align the compact representations with the model decoder (scaffolding/caching) to reduce per-token inference and enable multi-token emission of structured blocks.
infographic.impact: By cutting token counts and inference passes, ShortCoder lowers latency and compute cost for code generation systems, making LLM-based coding tools faster, cheaper, and more feasible on constrained hardware or at production scale.

title: Disentangling Task Conflicts in Multi-Task LoRA via Orthogonal Gradient Projection
authors: Ziyu Yang, Guibin Chen, Yuxin Yang, Aoxiong Zeng, Xiangquan Yang
abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) combined with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a promising direction for parameter-efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs). By sharing a single adapter across multiple tasks, one can significantly reduce storage overhead. However, this approach suffers from negative transfer, where conflicting gradient updates from distinct tasks degrade the performance of individual tasks compared to single-task fine-tuning. This problem is exacerbated in LoRA due

infographic.key_insight: Applying orthogonal gradient projection inside a shared LoRA adapter disentangles conflicting task gradients so each task keeps its useful update directions while removing interference, preserving parameter-efficiency with large gains in per-task performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Negative transfer in multi-task LoRA: sharing a single low-rank adapter across tasks causes conflicting gradient updates that degrade individual task performance compared to single-task fine-tuning.
method: Detect gradient conflict directions between tasks in the shared LoRA parameter space.
Project each task's gradient onto the subspace orthogonal to identified conflicting components (Orthogonal Gradient Projection) to remove interference while retaining task-aligned updates.
Integrate orthogonal projection into the LoRA update loop with minimal computational and storage overhead to keep a single shared adapter.
infographic.impact: Enables robust, parameter-efficient multi-task adaptation of LLMs by reducing negative transfer—practitioners can deploy one shared LoRA adapter with near single-task performance across tasks, saving storage and maintenance cost.

title: Benchmarking large language models on safety risks in scientific laboratories
authors: Yujun Zhou, Jingdong Yang, Yue Huang, Kehan Guo, Zoe Emory
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 14 January 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01152-1

Large language models are starting to be used in safety-critical tasks such as controlling robots. Zhou et al. present LabSafety Bench, a benchmark evaluating the ability of large language models to identify hazards and assess laboratory risks.

infographic.key_insight: LabSafety Bench provides the first systematic benchmark that tests large language models on identifying hazards and assessing risks in scientific laboratory scenarios, revealing notable gaps in LLM hazard recognition and risk reasoning that could lead to unsafe outputs if models are deployed in lab settings.
infographic.problem_solved: Fills the evaluation gap for how well LLMs detect and reason about laboratory hazards and risk levels, enabling objective comparison of safety performance across models and prompting safer deployment practices.
method: Constructed a curated benchmark of realistic lab scenarios and prompts covering hazard identification, risk assessment, and recommended actions.
Evaluated multiple large language models across tasks and settings using quantitative metrics (accuracy, calibration, harmfulness) and qualitative analysis of failure modes.
Analyzed systematic weaknesses (misclassification, overconfidence, missing context) and provided recommendations for auditing and mitigation.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners and safety auditors with a practical tool and empirical evidence to quantify LLM safety in laboratory contexts, guiding model selection, prompt design, and risk-mitigation strategies before real-world deployment.

title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning
authors: Zhiyuan Hu, Yunhai Hu, Juncheng Liu, Shuyue Stella Li, Yucheng Wang
abstract: Multi-agent systems have evolved into practical LLM-driven collaborators for many applications, gaining robustness from diversity and cross-checking. However, multi-agent RL (MARL) training is resource-intensive and unstable: co-adapting teammates induce non-stationarity, and rewards are often sparse and high-variance. Therefore, we introduce \textbf{Multi-Agent Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (MATTRL)}, a framework that injects structured textual experience into multi-agent deliberation at inf

infographic.key_insight: MATTRL enables multi-agent LLM teams to adapt at test time by injecting structured textual experience into their deliberation loop, achieving robust reasoning improvements without costly, unstable multi-agent RL training.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the resource intensity, instability (co-adaptation / non-stationarity), and sparse/high-variance reward issues of conventional multi-agent RL for LLM-driven collaborators by shifting adaptation to a lightweight test-time procedure.
method: Run multiple LLM agents in a deliberation loop and log structured textual experiences (dialogue turns, proposed actions, outcomes, and rewards).

Inject these textual experiences back into the deliberation at test time to shape behavior (guided sampling, credit assignment, or reward shaping) so agents adapt on-the-fly without full MARL retraining.
Use cross-checking and aggregated signals from diverse agents to stabilize learning and reduce variance in sparse-reward reasoning tasks.
infographic.impact: MATTRL lets practitioners obtain stronger, more robust multi-agent reasoning with far less compute and training complexity, enabling practical deployment of collaborative LLM systems that adapt in real-world inference settings.

title: Image2Garment: Simulation-ready Garment Generation from a Single Image
authors: Selim Emir Can, Jan Ackermann, Kiyohiro Nakayama, Ruofan Liu, Tong Wu
abstract: Estimating physically accurate, simulation-ready garments from a single image is challenging due to the absence of image-to-physics datasets and the ill-posed nature of this problem. Prior methods either require multi-view capture and expensive differentiable simulation or predict only garment geometry without the material properties required for realistic simulation. We propose a feed-forward framework that sidesteps these limitations by first fine-tuning a vision-language model to infer materi

infographic.key_insight: A feed-forward pipeline fine-tunes a vision-language model to infer both garment geometry and material properties from a single image, producing simulation-ready garments without multi-view capture or costly differentiable simulation.
infographic.problem_solved: Recovering physically accurate, simulation-ready cloth (geometry + material parameters) from a single image — an ill-posed task made harder by the lack of image-to-physics training data and prior methods that require multi-view capture or only predict geometry.
method: Fine-tune a vision-language model to predict garment semantics and material attributes from a single RGB image.
Map predicted semantics/material cues into simulation-ready outputs (meshes/patterns plus material parameters) using learned priors and templates.
Use a fully feed-forward generator to produce ready-to-sim garments, avoiding multi-view capture and expensive differentiable physics during inference.
infographic.impact: Enables fast creation of realistic, physically plausible garments from a single photo—reducing data/capture needs and accelerating workflows for virtual try-on, game asset creation, and cloth-aware simulation in research and industry.

title: 3AM: Segment Anything with Geometric Consistency in Videos
authors: Yang-Che Sun, Cheng Sun, Chin-Yang Lin, Fu-En Yang, Min-Hung Chen
abstract: Video object segmentation methods like SAM2 achieve strong performance through memory-based architectures but struggle under large viewpoint changes due to reliance on appearance features. Traditional 3D instance segmentation methods address viewpoint consistency but require camera poses, depth maps, and expensive preprocessing. We introduce 3AM, a training-time enhancement that integrates 3D-aware features from MUSt3R into SAM2. Our lightweight Feature Merger fuses multi-level MUSt3R features t

infographic.key_insight: 3AM injects 3D-aware features from MUSt3R into SAM2 at training time via a lightweight Feature Merger, producing video object segmentation that is more consistent across large viewpoint changes without heavy 3D preprocessing.
infographic.problem_solved: Memory-based video segmentation (e.g., SAM2) fails under large viewpoint changes because it relies on appearance features; prior 3D-aware solutions need camera poses, depth maps, and expensive preprocessing.
method: Training-time augmentation: integrate multi-level 3D-aware features from MUSt3R into SAM2 to imbue geometric consistency.
Feature Merger: a lightweight fusion module that merges MUSt3R features with SAM2 representations (multi-level, low compute overhead).
Maintain SAM2 inference pipeline while improving robustness to viewpoint change, avoiding explicit pose/depth preprocessing.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to make off-the-shelf segmentation models robust to viewpoint changes with minimal added cost, enabling better video understanding in dynamic camera scenarios without expensive 3D data or pipelines.

title: Multiplex Thinking: Reasoning via Token-wise Branch-and-Merge
authors: Yao Tang, Li Dong, Yaru Hao, Qingxiu Dong, Furu Wei
abstract: Large language models often solve complex reasoning tasks more effectively with Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but at the cost of long, low-bandwidth token sequences. Humans, by contrast, often reason softly by maintaining a distribution over plausible next steps. Motivated by this, we propose Multiplex Thinking, a stochastic soft reasoning mechanism that, at each thinking step, samples K candidate tokens and aggregates their embeddings into a single continuous multiplex token. This preserves the vocab

infographic.key_insight: Multiplex Thinking replaces long, discrete chain-of-thought token streams with a token-wise stochastic branch-and-merge that samples K candidate tokens per step and fuses their embeddings into a single continuous "multiplex" token, enabling soft, high-bandwidth internal reasoning while keeping the model's vocabulary interface.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the inefficiency and low information bandwidth of long CoT token sequences by providing a compact, probabilistic internal reasoning state that captures multiple plausible continuations without emitting long explicit chains.
method: At each decoding step, sample K candidate next tokens (branching) instead of committing to one token.
Aggregate the K candidates' embeddings into one continuous multiplex token via a stochastic/weighted merge, preserving the model's embedding space and vocabulary interface.
Repeat token-wise branch-and-merge across steps to maintain a distributional, soft reasoning trajectory that can be decoded or collapsed when needed.
infographic.impact: Enables LLMs to reason with richer, uncertainty-aware internal states while avoiding verbose CoT outputs—potentially improving reasoning quality, compute-efficiency trade-offs, and integration with existing transformer architectures.

title: Spatial Context Improves the Integration of Text with Remote Sensing for Mapping Environmental Variables
authors: Valerie Zermatten, Chiara Vanalli, Gencer Sumbul, Diego Marcos, Devis Tuia
abstract: Recent developments in natural language processing highlight text as an emerging data source for ecology. Textual resources carry unique information that can be used in complementarity with geospatial data sources, thus providing insights at the local scale into environmental conditions and properties hidden from more traditional data sources. Leveraging textual information in a spatial context presents several challenges. First, the contribution of textual data remains poorly defined in an ecol

infographic.key_insight: Incorporating spatial context when fusing textual information with remote sensing data substantially improves the accuracy and local relevance of maps of environmental variables—text helps, but only when tied to where it matters.
infographic.problem_solved: How to reliably leverage heterogeneous, location-linked textual resources together with remote sensing to map environmental conditions at fine scales, despite ambiguous geolocation, modality mismatch, and unclear contribution of text.
method: Create joint representations of textual and remote sensing inputs while explicitly encoding spatial context (e.g., neighborhood information or location-aware features).
Fuse the spatially-aware text and image representations in a multimodal model and train/evaluate on environmental mapping targets to quantify each modality's contribution.
Compare spatially-aware fusion against baselines lacking spatial context to demonstrate improved mapping performance and interpretability.
infographic.impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners a practical way to augment remote sensing with textual data for higher-resolution, more interpretable environmental maps—enabling better local insights for ecology, conservation, and land management workflows.

title: Uncovering Political Bias in Large Language Models using Parliamentary Voting Records
authors: Jieying Chen, Karen de Jong, Andreas Poole, Jan Burakowski, Elena Elderson Nosti
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become deeply embedded in digital platforms and decision-making systems, concerns about their political biases have grown. While substantial work has examined social biases such as gender and race, systematic studies of political bias remain limited, despite their direct societal impact. This paper introduces a general methodology for constructing political bias benchmarks by aligning model-generated voting predictions with verified parliamentary voting records. W

infographic.key_insight: The paper provides a systematic benchmark that measures political bias in LLMs by comparing model-generated voting predictions to verified parliamentary roll-call records, revealing consistent partisan alignment patterns across models.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of objective, reproducible methods and datasets for quantifying political bias in large language models by leveraging real-world parliamentary votes as ground truth for model behavior.
method: Convert parliamentary roll-call items into standardized prompts and collect LLM voting predictions (labels or probabilities).
Align model predictions with verified voting records to compute partisan-alignment metrics (party-level agreement, bias scores, calibration).
Run sensitivity analyses across countries, time periods, and prompt framings to isolate systematic political leanings.
infographic.impact: Provides AI practitioners and auditors a scalable, verifiable way to detect and quantify political bias in deployed LLMs, supporting model selection, mitigation strategies, and policy-compliant deployment.

title: Near-perfect photo-ID of the Hula painted frog with zero-shot deep local-feature matching
authors: Maayan Yesharim, R. G. Bina Perl, Uri Roll, Sarig Gafny, Eli Geffen
abstract: Accurate individual identification is essential for monitoring rare amphibians, yet invasive marking is often unsuitable for critically endangered species. We evaluate state-of-the-art computer-vision methods for photographic re-identification of the Hula painted frog (Latonia nigriventer) using 1,233 ventral images from 191 individuals collected during 2013-2020 capture-recapture surveys. We compare deep local-feature matching in a zero-shot setting with deep global-feature embedding models. Th

infographic.key_insight: Zero-shot deep local-feature matching achieves near-perfect photographic re-identification of the Hula painted frog without species-specific training, outperforming deep global-feature embedding approaches.
infographic.problem_solved: Enables non-invasive, accurate individual identification for a critically endangered amphibian (Hula painted frog) where physical marking is impractical or harmful.
method: Dataset: 1,233 ventral images from 191 known individuals collected during 2013–2020 capture–recapture surveys.
Approach: zero-shot deep local-feature matching — extract dense local descriptors, match keypoints across images, and spatially verify correspondences to declare identity matches.
Comparison: evaluated against deep global-feature embedding (re‑id) models using identification metrics (top‑1/top‑k accuracy, false positives) to show superior performance of local matching.
infographic.impact: Demonstrates that zero-shot local-feature methods can solve fine-grained re-identification with minimal annotation, reducing data/label requirements and providing a transferable pipeline for wildlife monitoring and other re‑ID problems.

title: APEX-SWE
authors: Abhi Kottamasu, Akul Datta, Aakash Barthwal, Chirag Mahapatra, Ajay Arun
abstract: We introduce the AI Productivity Index for Software Engineering (APEX-SWE), a benchmark for assessing whether frontier AI models can execute economically valuable software engineering work. Unlike existing evaluations that focus on narrow, well-defined tasks, APEX-SWE assesses two novel task types that reflect real-world software engineering work: (1) Integration tasks (n=100), which require constructing end-to-end systems across heterogeneous cloud primitives, business applications, and infrast

infographic.key_insight: APEX-SWE is a practical benchmark that measures whether frontier AI models can perform economically valuable, real-world software engineering work by evaluating end-to-end, system-level tasks rather than narrow micro-tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Current evaluations focus on small, well-defined tasks that do not reflect the long-horizon, heterogeneous responsibilities of real software engineers; APEX-SWE fills this gap by introducing tasks that mirror actual integration and system-engineering work.
method: Define two novel task classes that reflect real-world software engineering workflows, including Integration tasks (n=100) that require building end-to-end systems across cloud primitives, business apps, and infrastructure.
Design benchmark exercises that capture long-horizon, multi-step decision making and end-to-end execution rather than isolated code snippets or unit problems.
Provide standardized evaluation criteria emphasizing economic value, robustness, and cross-component correctness to assess model utility for industry software engineering.
infographic.impact: APEX-SWE helps practitioners and organizations understand which models can deliver real engineering value (not just code completion), guiding model selection, tooling, and deployment for production software workflows.

title: Motion Attribution for Video Generation
authors: Xindi Wu, Despoina Paschalidou, Jun Gao, Antonio Torralba, Laura Leal-Taixé
abstract: Despite the rapid progress of video generation models, the role of data in influencing motion is poorly understood. We present Motive (MOTIon attribution for Video gEneration), a motion-centric, gradient-based data attribution framework that scales to modern, large, high-quality video datasets and models. We use this to study which fine-tuning clips improve or degrade temporal dynamics. Motive isolates temporal dynamics from static appearance via motion-weighted loss masks, yielding efficient an

infographic.key_insight: Motive provides a motion-centric, gradient-based data-attribution method that isolates and quantifies how individual training/fine-tuning clips influence a video generator's temporal dynamics.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies which data samples improve or degrade motion in video-generation models by separating temporal dynamics from static appearance, enabling targeted dataset curation and fine-tuning decisions.
method: Compute gradient-based influence scores per clip for a target video-generation model to attribute effects to training/fine-tuning samples.
Use motion-weighted loss masks to isolate temporal dynamics (motion) from static appearance when measuring influence.
Scale the procedure to modern, large, high-quality video datasets and models to identify clips that improve or harm temporal behavior.
infographic.impact: Makes it practical to debug and curate datasets for better temporal realism in generated video, helping practitioners prioritize or remove clips that positively or negatively affect motion quality.

title: M3CoTBench: Benchmark Chain-of-Thought of MLLMs in Medical Image Understanding
authors: Juntao Jiang, Jiangning Zhang, Yali Bi, Jinsheng Bai, Weixuan Liu
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has proven effective in enhancing large language models by encouraging step-by-step intermediate reasoning, and recent advances have extended this paradigm to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). In the medical domain, where diagnostic decisions depend on nuanced visual cues and sequential reasoning, CoT aligns naturally with clinical thinking processes. However, Current benchmarks for medical image understanding generally focus on the final answer while ign

infographic.key_insight: M3CoTBench provides a targeted benchmark to evaluate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on medical image understanding, showing that CoT prompts reveal strengths and systematic gaps in stepwise clinical reasoning that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing medical image benchmarks focus on final answers and ignore intermediate diagnostic reasoning; there is no standard way to measure the quality, faithfulness, and clinical alignment of CoT outputs from MLLMs.
method: Curate medical image tasks (e.g., radiology, dermatology) with structured questions and expert-annotated CoT reasoning traces as ground truth.
Design evaluation protocol combining automated metrics (answer accuracy, step-level correctness, faithfulness, calibration) with expert human review for clinical alignment.
Benchmark multiple MLLMs and prompting strategies (CoT prompting vs direct-answer) and analyze failure modes, localization alignment, and reasoning depth.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a standardized way to measure and compare MLLM reasoning transparency and safety in clinical imaging, guiding model selection, prompt design, and targeted improvements for diagnostically reliable multimodal systems.

title: To Retrieve or To Think? An Agentic Approach for Context Evolution
authors: Rubing Chen, Jian Wang, Wenjie Li, Xiao-Yong Wei, Qing Li
abstract: Current context augmentation methods, such as retrieval-augmented generation, are essential for solving knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks.However, they typically adhere to a rigid, brute-force strategy that executes retrieval at every step. This indiscriminate approach not only incurs unnecessary computational costs but also degrades performance by saturating the context with irrelevant noise. To address these limitations, we introduce Agentic Context Evolution (ACE), a framework inspired by h

infographic.key_insight: Instead of retrieving external context at every reasoning step, an agentic controller can decide when to 'retrieve' vs when to 'think' (use internal reasoning), reducing noise and cost while improving downstream performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Retrieval-augmented pipelines indiscriminately perform retrieval at every step, incurring unnecessary compute and introducing irrelevant context that can hurt reasoning accuracy.
method: Introduce Agentic Context Evolution (ACE): an agentic controller that dynamically decides whether to trigger retrieval or rely on internal generation at each step.
Evolve the working context iteratively — selectively augmenting it only when utility signals (e.g., uncertainty, information gap, or expected value of retrieval) indicate benefit.
Maintain a compact, high-signal context by avoiding redundant retrievals and by updating context through targeted external lookups and internal synthesis.
infographic.impact: ACE lowers computational cost and context noise, yielding more efficient and often more accurate knowledge-intensive reasoning—beneficial for deploying large-scale LLM systems and building robust retrieval-augmented agents.

title: Rewarding the Rare: Uniqueness-Aware RL for Creative Problem Solving in LLMs
authors: Zhiyuan Hu, Yucheng Wang, Yufei He, Jiaying Wu, Yilun Zhao
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), particularly for complex reasoning tasks, yet it often suffers from exploration collapse: policies prematurely concentrate on a small set of dominant reasoning patterns, improving pass@1 while limiting rollout-level diversity and gains in pass@k. We argue that this failure stems from regularizing local token behavior rather than diversity over sets of solutions. To address this, we propose U

infographic.key_insight: Augmenting RL rewards with a rollout-level uniqueness bonus prevents policies from collapsing to a few dominant reasoning patterns, enabling LLMs to discover rarer, creative solutions and improving set-level metrics like pass@k without sacrificing single-trial quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Exploration collapse during RL fine-tuning of LLMs: policies concentrate on a small set of high-probability reasoning patterns (raising pass@1) but reduce rollout diversity and hurt pass@k and creative problem solving.
method: Uniqueness-aware reward: augment the standard task reward with a rarity/novelty bonus computed over model rollouts so that infrequently seen solutions receive extra credit.
Set-level regularization: evaluate diversity across generated solution sets (batch- or rollout-level) instead of only regularizing token-level behavior, preventing premature mode collapse.
Adaptive rarity estimation: compute online rarity/similarity scores (e.g., inverse-frequency or similarity-based measures) and balance task quality vs. uniqueness during RL updates.
infographic.impact: This approach helps LLMs explore a wider range of valid reasoning paths, improving performance on tasks that benefit from multiple distinct solutions (e.g., code generation, math, creative tasks) and offering practitioners a practical way to trade off quality and diversity during RL tuning.
visual_elements: Before vs After schematic: many identical rollouts (exploration collapse) vs many diverse rollouts (uniqueness-aware RL).
Reward composition diagram: task reward + uniqueness bonus → augmented reward used by RL.

title: MemRec: Collaborative Memory-Augmented Agentic Recommender System
authors: Weixin Chen, Yuhan Zhao, Jingyuan Huang, Zihe Ye, Clark Mingxuan Ju
abstract: The evolution of recommender systems has shifted preference storage from rating matrices and dense embeddings to semantic memory in the agentic era. Yet existing agents rely on isolated memory, overlooking crucial collaborative signals. Bridging this gap is hindered by the dual challenges of distilling vast graph contexts without overwhelming reasoning agents with cognitive load, and evolving the collaborative memory efficiently without incurring prohibitive computational costs. To address this,

infographic.key_insight: MemRec introduces a shared, compact collaborative semantic memory for agentic recommender systems, enabling agents to exchange and evolve social/contextual signals without overwhelming their reasoning capacity or incurring high computational cost.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing agentic recommenders keep isolated memories and thus miss collaborative signals from user-item graphs; MemRec addresses (a) how to distill large graph contexts into small, useful memory units so agents aren't cognitively overloaded, and (b) how to evolve that collaborative memory efficiently without prohibitive compute.
method: Collaborative memory layer: aggregate multi-agent semantic traces into shared memory entries that capture cross-user and cross-item context.
Graph-to-memory distillation: compress large graph context into sparse, high-utility memory tokens/prototypes to limit per-agent reasoning load.
Efficient evolution mechanism: incremental/low-cost update rules (merge, prune, and lightweight synchronization) to keep the collaborative memory current without expensive retraining.
infographic.impact: MemRec enables scalable, socially aware agentic recommenders that leverage collective signals while keeping reasoning and update costs low, making it practical to deploy collaborative memory in production recommender pipelines.

title: Grid-Aware Charging and Operational Optimization for Mixed-Fleet Public Transit
authors: Rishav Sen, Amutheezan Sivagnanam, Aron Laszka, Ayan Mukhopadhyay, Abhishek Dubey
abstract: The rapid growth of urban populations and the increasing need for sustainable transportation solutions have prompted a shift towards electric buses in public transit systems. However, the effective management of mixed fleets consisting of both electric and diesel buses poses significant operational challenges. One major challenge is coping with dynamic electricity pricing, where charging costs vary throughout the day. Transit agencies must optimize charging assignments in response to such dynami

infographic.key_insight: Jointly optimizing charging schedules and bus operations while accounting for dynamic electricity prices and grid constraints cuts operating cost and improves service reliability for mixed electric/diesel transit fleets.
infographic.problem_solved: Determines when and where to charge electric buses and how to assign vehicles to routes under time-varying electricity prices and grid limits, ensuring service requirements are met while minimizing cost and grid impact.
method: Formulate a grid-aware operational optimization that jointly assigns charging slots and route duties for a mixed fleet (mixed-integer/convex program).
Incorporate dynamic electricity pricing and grid capacity constraints via scenario-aware or rolling-horizon decision making to handle temporal uncertainty.
Validate with realistic transit and grid data and compare against baseline heuristics to quantify cost, energy, and service benefits.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical optimization framework AI/ML practitioners can pair with forecasting or learning modules (price, demand, battery degradation) to build hybrid model-based/data-driven operational systems that reduce costs and emissions.

title: Reasoning Matters for 3D Visual Grounding
authors: Hsiang-Wei Huang, Kuang-Ming Chen, Wenhao Chai, Cheng-Yen Yang, Jen-Hao Cheng
abstract: The recent development of Large Language Models (LLMs) with strong reasoning ability has driven research in various domains such as mathematics, coding, and scientific discovery. Meanwhile, 3D visual grounding, as a fundamental task in 3D understanding, still remains challenging due to the limited reasoning ability of recent 3D visual grounding models. Most of the current methods incorporate a text encoder and visual feature encoder to generate cross-modal fuse features and predict the referring

infographic.key_insight: Incorporating explicit multi-step reasoning into 3D visual grounding pipelines enables models to resolve complex, relational referring expressions much more effectively than standard fusion-only approaches.
infographic.problem_solved: Overcomes the limited reasoning ability of current 3D visual grounding models that fail on relational, compositional, or context-dependent referring queries in cluttered 3D scenes.
method: Augment a 3D-text fusion architecture with a dedicated reasoning module that performs iterative, interpretable inference over object-centric 3D features.
Explicitly model spatial and relational priors (e.g., via graph-based reasoning or attention over object relations) to disambiguate referents using multi-step logic.
Use reasoning-aware training objectives and targeted supervision or prompts that encourage stepwise decomposition of complex referring expressions.
infographic.impact: Makes 3D grounding more accurate and robust for real-world tasks—helpful for robotics, AR/VR, and multimodal applications where precise language-to-3D mapping and relational understanding are critical.

Before/after scene examples: challenging queries where baseline fails but reasoning-enabled model succeeds

title: More Images, More Problems? A Controlled Analysis of VLM Failure Modes
authors: Anurag Das, Adrian Bulat, Alberto Baldrati, Ioannis Maniadis Metaxas, Bernt Schiele
abstract: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet their proficiency in understanding and reasoning over multiple images remains largely unexplored. While existing benchmarks have initiated the evaluation of multi-image models, a comprehensive analysis of their core weaknesses and their causes is still lacking. In this work, we introduce MIMIC (Multi-Image Model Insights and Challenges), a new benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate the multi-image capabilities

infographic.key_insight: More images do not always improve LVLM performance: under controlled conditions, adding images frequently exposes systematic multi-image failure modes (cross-image reference errors, aggregation failures, hallucinations) that MIMIC reveals and quantifies.
infographic.problem_solved: Fills the gap in rigorous evaluation and diagnosis of multi-image vision–language models by providing a controlled benchmark and analysis that pinpoints when and why performance degrades as image count and inter-image complexity increase.
method: Introduce MIMIC — a controlled multi-image benchmark with tasks for cross-image reference, comparison, temporal reasoning, and synthesis.
Run controlled experiments varying image count, order, semantic relations and prompts across SOTA LVLMs to measure sensitivity and failure rates.
Diagnose and categorize failure modes (e.g., cross-image confusion, aggregation errors, hallucination) and use ablations to trace root causes.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a focused toolkit and empirical findings to better evaluate, design, and prompt LVLMs for multi-image scenarios; informs dataset creation, model architecture choices, and mitigation strategies to reduce common multi-image failures.
visual_elements: Benchmark schematic: grid of multiple images + prompt → model outputs, annotated to show correct vs. incorrect reasoning pathways.
Failure taxonomy diagram: icons and short labels for main failure modes (cross-image reference, aggregation, hallucination, ordering sensitivity) with example error snippets.
Performance chart: line/bar plot showing model accuracy or error rate as a function of number of images and task type (comparison, temporal, synthesis).
Case-study callouts: side-by-side multi-image examples with highlighted regions and model explanations showing how/why the model failed.

title: PFT: Phonon Fine-tuning for Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials
authors: Teddy Koker, Abhijeet Gangan, Mit Kotak, Jaime Marian, Tess Smidt
abstract: Many materials properties depend on higher-order derivatives of the potential energy surface, yet machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained with standard a standard loss on energy, force, and stress errors can exhibit error in curvature, degrading the prediction of vibrational properties. We introduce phonon fine-tuning (PFT), which directly supervises second-order force constants of materials by matching MLIP energy Hessians to DFT-computed force constants from finite displacement

infographic.key_insight: Phonon Fine-Tuning (PFT) improves ML interatomic potentials by directly supervising second-order force constants: matching the MLIP energy Hessian to DFT-computed force constants corrects curvature errors and greatly improves vibrational/phonon predictions.
infographic.problem_solved: Standard MLIP training on energies, forces, and stresses often yields incorrect curvature (second derivatives) of the potential energy surface, causing poor predictions of vibrational properties (phonons, vibrational density of states, thermal behavior).
method: Compute DFT force constants via finite-displacement calculations to obtain target second-order derivatives (force constant matrix).
Evaluate the MLIP energy Hessian (analytic or finite-difference) and add a Hessian/force-constant matching loss to fine-tune a pretrained MLIP.
Fine-tune with a multi-term loss to preserve original energy/force/stress accuracy while correcting curvature for improved phonon predictions.
infographic.impact: PFT gives ML/Materials practitioners a lightweight, targeted way to fix curvature deficiencies in MLIPs, enabling reliable prediction of vibrational and thermal properties and more stable atomistic dynamics without full retraining.
visual_elements: Schematic energy vs. displacement curve showing curvature mismatch: baseline MLIP vs. PFT-corrected MLIP vs. DFT reference.
Pipeline flowchart: DFT finite displacements → force constants (target Hessian) → MLIP Hessian computation → PFT loss → fine-tuned MLIP.
Before/after phonon dispersion or vibrational density-of-states plots highlighting improved agreement with DFT after PFT.
Bar/line chart comparing second-derivative (Hessian) errors and resulting property errors (e.g., phonon frequencies, specific heat) for baseline vs. PFT.

title: A Framework for Feature Discovery in Intracranial Pressure Monitoring Data Using Neural Network Attention
authors: Jonathan D. Socha, Seyed F. Maroufi, Dipankar Biswas, Richard Um, Aruna S. Rao
abstract: We present a novel framework for analyzing intracranial pressure monitoring data by applying interpretability principles. Intracranial pressure monitoring data was collected from 60 patients at Johns Hopkins. The data was segmented into individual cardiac cycles. A convolutional neural network was trained to classify each cardiac cycle into one of seven body positions. Neural network attention was extracted and was used to identify regions of interest in the waveform. Further directions for expl

infographic.key_insight: A CNN trained on intracranial pressure cardiac cycles can use its attention maps to reveal waveform regions that correlate with patient body position, enabling interpretable feature discovery from physiological waveforms.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the lack of automated, interpretable methods for discovering meaningful features in intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring waveforms and links waveform morphology to patient state (body position).
method: Collected ICP monitoring data from 60 patients and segmented recordings into individual cardiac cycles.
Trained a convolutional neural network to classify each cardiac cycle into one of seven body positions.
Extracted neural network attention maps to identify and localize regions of interest in the waveform for feature discovery and interpretability.
infographic.impact: Delivers a practical, explainable pipeline for physiologic time-series analysis that helps ML practitioners and clinicians discover clinically relevant waveform features and build more transparent models.

Example ICP waveform annotated with attention heatmap showing highlighted regions across a cardiac cycle

title: Predictive Analytics for Dementia: Machine Learning on Healthcare Data
authors: Shafiul Ajam Opee, Nafiz Fahad, Anik Sen, Rasel Ahmed, Fariha Jahan
abstract: Dementia is a complex syndrome impacting cognitive and emotional functions, with Alzheimer's disease being the most common form. This study focuses on enhancing dementia prediction using machine learning (ML) techniques on patient health data. Supervised learning algorithms are applied in this study, including K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and Gaussian Process Classifiers. To address class imbalance and improve model perform

infographic.key_insight: Applying classic supervised ML models (KNN, LDA, QDA, Gaussian Process) together with class-imbalance mitigation improves predictive capability for dementia using routine patient health data, enabling more reliable early-warning signals.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the challenge of accurately predicting dementia from heterogeneous, imbalanced healthcare data where minority (dementia) cases are underrepresented and traditional models may be biased or unstable.
method: Assemble and preprocess patient health records and clinical features relevant to cognitive decline.
Train and compare supervised classifiers: K-Nearest Neighbors, Linear/Quadratic Discriminant Analysis, and Gaussian Process Classifier.
Mitigate class imbalance (e.g., resampling or class-weighting strategies) and evaluate models with robust metrics to improve minority-class detection.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, reproducible pipeline showing that combining interpretable classical models with imbalance-aware training can boost dementia prediction reliability—useful guidance for ML practitioners building clinical decision-support tools.

title: Advancing Multinational License Plate Recognition Through Synthetic and Real Data Fusion: A Comprehensive Evaluation
authors: Rayson Laroca, Valter Estevam, Gladston J. P. Moreira, Rodrigo Minetto, David Menotti
abstract: Automatic License Plate Recognition is a frequent research topic due to its wide-ranging practical applications. While recent studies use synthetic images to improve License Plate Recognition (LPR) results, there remain several limitations in these efforts. This work addresses these constraints by comprehensively exploring the integration of real and synthetic data to enhance LPR performance. We subject 16 Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models to a benchmarking process involving 12 public d

infographic.key_insight: Fusing diverse synthetic license-plate images with real, multinational data substantially improves OCR robustness and cross-country generalization for license plate recognition models; a large-scale benchmark identifies which models and mixing strategies benefit most.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses the scarcity and heterogeneity of annotated multinational license-plate data and the limited understanding of how to best combine synthetic and real images to boost LPR performance across different countries and plate styles.
method: Generate diverse synthetic license-plate images that capture multinational layout, font, color and environmental variations.
Combine (fuse) synthetic and real datasets and train/evaluate 16 OCR models across 12 public datasets to measure performance gains.
Run systematic benchmarking and ablation analyses to quantify the effect of different mixing ratios, augmentation choices, and model architectures on recognition accuracy.
infographic.impact: Provides practical guidance to reduce costly annotation needs and improve real-world, cross-border LPR performance; helps practitioners choose architectures and data-mixing strategies that maximize accuracy and generalization.

title: Exchange Is All You Need for Remote Sensing Change Detection
authors: Sijun Dong, Siming Fu, Kaiyu Li, Xiangyong Cao, Xiaoliang Meng
abstract: Remote sensing change detection fundamentally relies on the effective fusion and discrimination of bi-temporal features. Prevailing paradigms typically utilize Siamese encoders bridged by explicit difference computation modules, such as subtraction or concatenation, to identify changes. In this work, we challenge this complexity with SEED (Siamese Encoder-Exchange-Decoder), a streamlined paradigm that replaces explicit differencing with parameter-free feature exchange. By sharing weights across

infographic.key_insight: Replace explicit bi-temporal differencing with a parameter-free feature exchange inside a Siamese encoder–decoder pipeline (SEED), enabling direct cross-temporal interaction while keeping the model simple and shared-weighted.
infographic.problem_solved: Remote sensing change detection typically relies on bespoke difference modules (subtraction, concatenation) to fuse bi-temporal features, increasing architectural complexity and tuning burden. SEED addresses the need for a simpler, more streamlined fusion mechanism that still discriminates changes effectively.
method: Siamese encoders with shared weights process the two temporal images to produce comparable feature maps.
Parameter-free feature exchange swaps/ merges features across the two temporal streams (instead of computing explicit differences) to enable direct cross-temporal interaction.
A decoder consumes the exchanged features to predict the change map, keeping the overall pipeline lightweight and modular.
infographic.impact: SEED simplifies model design for change detection, reducing architectural complexity and hyperparameter tuning while enabling straightforward incorporation into existing pipelines—useful for practitioners seeking efficient, robust bi-temporal fusion.

title: Failure-Aware RL: Reliable Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning with Self-Recovery for Real-World Manipulation
authors: Huanyu Li, Kun Lei, Sheng Zang, Kaizhe Hu, Yongyuan Liang
abstract: Post-training algorithms based on deep reinforcement learning can push the limits of robotic models for specific objectives, such as generalizability, accuracy, and robustness. However, Intervention-requiring Failures (IR Failures) (e.g., a robot spilling water or breaking fragile glass) during real-world exploration happen inevitably, hindering the practical deployment of such a paradigm. To tackle this, we introduce Failure-Aware Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning (FARL), a new paradigm

infographic.key_insight: FARL enables safe offline-to-online fine-tuning for real-world manipulation by detecting intervention-requiring failures and autonomously triggering a learned self-recovery policy, allowing continued online learning without human rescue.
infographic.problem_solved: Real-world online fine-tuning of RL policies is blocked by intervention-requiring failures (e.g., spills, breakage). FARL addresses the safety and practicality gap by preventing or recovering from such failures during exploration so offline-trained policies can be safely adapted online.
method: Failure-aware monitoring: learn or estimate failure risk / detect IR failures online (uncertainty or classifier) to flag dangerous states before catastrophic outcomes.
Self-recovery policy: a dedicated recovery behavior trained (or distilled) to safely restore the robot from failure-prone states without human intervention.

Conservative offline-to-online updates: risk-aware policy updates and safe-exploration constraints that fall back to recovery/offline policy when risk is high, enabling sample-efficient, safe adaptation.
infographic.impact: Enables practical deployment of RL for delicate manipulation by reducing human interventions and catastrophic events during online fine-tuning, improving safety, robustness, and real-world sample efficiency.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: offline dataset → base policy + failure monitor → online loop with risk check → recovery policy fallback
Sequence illustration: detected risky state → trigger recovery → resume learning (before/after frames)

title: Hiking in the Wild: A Scalable Perceptive Parkour Framework for Humanoids
authors: Shaoting Zhu, Ziwen Zhuang, Mengjie Zhao, Kun-Ying Lee, Hang Zhao
abstract: Achieving robust humanoid hiking in complex, unstructured environments requires transitioning from reactive proprioception to proactive perception. However, integrating exteroception remains a significant challenge: mapping-based methods suffer from state estimation drift; for instance, LiDAR-based methods do not handle torso jitter well. Existing end-to-end approaches often struggle with scalability and training complexity; specifically, some previous works using virtual obstacles are implement

infographic.key_insight: A scalable framework that enables humanoid robots to perform robust hiking and parkour in unstructured environments by combining a local, drift-tolerant exteroceptive perception stream with hierarchical locomotion control, avoiding reliance on full mapping or fragile end-to-end training.
infographic.problem_solved: Integrates exteroception into humanoid locomotion without falling prey to mapping-based state-estimation drift or torso-jitter failures, and without the scalability and complexity issues of prior end-to-end approaches.
method: Ego-centric, local perceptual representation (vision/LiDAR fusion) designed to be resilient to state-estimation drift and torso jitter, avoiding dense global maps.
Hierarchical control: perception-driven footstep/trajectory planning at a higher level + robust low-level stabilizing controllers for contact-aware execution.
Scalable training and deployment pipeline (simulation curriculum, domain randomization and modular transfer) that reduces sample complexity and supports real-world transfer.
infographic.impact: Enables practical, scalable deployment of perceptive humanoid locomotion in real-world, unstructured environments and provides a modular template for research on perception-action integration and hierarchical controllers in robotics.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: sensor inputs → ego-centric perceptual map → footstep planner → low-level controller
Before/after robustness chart: mapping-based vs proposed method under state-estimation drift and torso jitter

title: Smooth Operator: Smooth Verifiable Reward Activates Spatial Reasoning Ability of Vision-Language Model
authors: Siwen Jiao, Tianxiong Lv, Kangan Qian, Chenxu Zhao, Xiuyuan Zhu
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) face a critical bottleneck in achieving precise numerical prediction for 3D scene understanding. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches, primarily based on relative ranking, often suffer from severe reward sparsity and gradient instability, failing to effectively exploit the verifiable signals provided by 3D physical constraints. Notably, in standard GRPO frameworks, relative normalization causes "near-miss" samples (characterized by small but non-zero e

infographic.key_insight: Introduce a Smooth Verifiable Reward that turns discrete, verifiable 3D physical constraints into dense, continuous supervision—eliminating near-miss suppression from relative ranking and thereby activating spatial/numeric reasoning in Vision–Language Models.
infographic.problem_solved: VLMs struggle to produce precise numerical predictions for 3D scene understanding because standard RL-based ranking rewards are sparse, unstable, and discard informative near-miss examples; the paper addresses how to exploit verifiable 3D constraints to provide stable, informative learning signals.
method: Design a Smooth Verifiable Reward (SVR) that maps verifiable 3D constraint violations into a continuous, differentiable reward signal rather than a binary/relative rank.

Integrate SVR into the RL training loop (replacing or adapting relative normalization in GRPO-style pipelines) to preserve gradient information from near-miss samples and reduce reward sparsity/instability.
Use physics- and geometry-based verifiers to generate reliable supervision from 3D scene constraints, providing dense corrective feedback for VLMs' numeric/spatial outputs.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical way to teach VLMs precise spatial and numerical reasoning with stable gradients, improving accuracy on 3D understanding and enabling stronger performance in robotics, AR, and other real-world tasks that require verifiable geometry.
visual_elements: Before/after reward diagram: sparse binary or relative reward vs. smooth continuous SVR curve showing preserved gradient around near-miss samples
Pipeline flowchart: input image+text → verifiable 3D constraint checker → SVR computation → RL update (highlighting change from relative normalization)
Performance bar/line chart: accuracy or error on 3D numeric tasks comparing baseline RL, ranking methods, and SVR

title: OS-Symphony: A Holistic Framework for Robust and Generalist Computer-Using Agent
authors: Bowen Yang, Kaiming Jin, Zhenyu Wu, Zhaoyang Liu, Qiushi Sun
abstract: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly advanced Computer-Using Agents (CUAs), current frameworks struggle with robustness in long-horizon workflows and generalization in novel domains. These limitations stem from a lack of granular control over historical visual context curation and the absence of visual-aware tutorial retrieval. To bridge these gaps, we introduce OS-Symphony, a holistic framework that comprises an Orchestrator coordinating two key innovations for robust automati

infographic.key_insight: OS-Symphony introduces an Orchestrator that coordinates granular visual-history curation and visual-aware tutorial retrieval, enabling vision-language computer-using agents to be robust in long-horizon workflows and to generalize to novel domains.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses brittleness of current Computer-Using Agents caused by uncontrolled historical visual context and lack of visual-aware retrieval of task tutorials, which degrade performance on long workflows and unseen domains.
method: Orchestrator module that selects, prunes, and prioritizes historical visual context for downstream reasoning and action planning.
Visual-aware tutorial retrieval that matches current visual state to relevant external procedures and demonstrations to provide contextual guidance.
Tight integration enabling iterative planning and execution across long-horizon tasks, improving robustness and cross-domain generalization.
infographic.impact: Makes multimodal agents more reliable in real-world, multi-step tasks and easier to adapt to new environments, reducing failure modes and lowering the need for extensive domain-specific fine-tuning.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram showing the Orchestrator, visual-history curator, tutorial retriever, planner, and executor modules.
Timeline/sequence comparison: naive full-history vs. curated-history highlighting reduced noise and improved decision points.

title: MHLA: Restoring Expressivity of Linear Attention via Token-Level Multi-Head
authors: Kewei Zhang, Ye Huang, Yufan Deng, Jincheng Yu, Junsong Chen
abstract: While the Transformer architecture dominates many fields, its quadratic self-attention complexity hinders its use in large-scale applications. Linear attention offers an efficient alternative, but its direct application often degrades performance, with existing fixes typically re-introducing computational overhead through extra modules (e.g., depthwise separable convolution) that defeat the original purpose. In this work, we identify a key failure mode in these methods: global context collapse,

infographic.key_insight: Introducing token-level multi-heads restores the expressivity that linear attention loses (preventing global-context collapse) while preserving the efficiency advantages of linear attention.
infographic.problem_solved: Linear attention methods are efficient but often degrade model performance because they collapse global context or lose multi-head expressivity; prior fixes add extra modules that re-introduce costly computation.
method: Token-level multi-head mechanism: apply lightweight, per-token multi-head projections to recover head-wise expressivity without global quadratic operations.
Architectural design preserves linear time/space scaling by keeping core attention computations in a linearized form and using compact reweighting per token.
Avoids heavy auxiliary modules (e.g., depthwise separable convolutions), achieving a clean trade-off between expressivity and efficiency.
infographic.impact: Makes linear-attention Transformers practical for large-scale or resource-constrained deployments by restoring performance close to standard attention without losing computational benefits. Useful for practitioners needing scalable attention with strong representational power.
visual_elements: Two-panel diagram comparing standard quadratic attention vs linear attention: complexity arrows (O(N^2) vs O(N)) and a callout showing 'global-context collapse' in simple linear attention.
Architecture block showing token-level multi-head module inserted into a linear-attention block, highlighting per-token heads and lightweight reweighting.

title: Beyond External Guidance: Unleashing the Semantic Richness Inside Diffusion Transformers for Improved Training
authors: Lingchen Sun, Rongyuan Wu, Zhengqiang Zhang, Ruibin Li, Yujing Sun
abstract: Recent works such as REPA have shown that guiding diffusion models with external semantic features (e.g., DINO) can significantly accelerate the training of diffusion transformers (DiTs). However, this requires the use of pretrained external networks, introducing additional dependencies and reducing flexibility. In this work, we argue that DiTs actually have the power to guide the training of themselves, and propose \textbf{Self-Transcendence}, a simple yet effective method that achieves fast co

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion transformers can generate and use their own semantic features as internal guidance, removing the need for external pretrained networks while preserving the training acceleration benefits.
infographic.problem_solved: Eliminates dependence on external semantic feature extractors (e.g., DINO) that add complexity and brittle dependencies to accelerated DiT training, enabling faster, simpler, and more flexible model training.
method: Extract semantic signals from intermediate DiT representations (attention maps / feature tokens) and treat them as internal guidance targets.
Introduce a lightweight self-guidance objective (auxiliary loss / self-distillation) that aligns diffusion model features across timesteps or snapshots to bootstrap semantic learning.
Integrate the self-guidance objective into standard DiT training to accelerate convergence without needing pretrained external networks.
infographic.impact: Makes accelerated DiT training more self-contained and reproducible, lowering engineering overhead and improving adaptability to new domains or modalities while keeping training fast.
visual_elements: Side-by-side pipeline diagram: (a) external-guidance setup with a pretrained network feeding features vs (b) Self-Transcendence using internal features as guidance.
Convergence plot: training loss or FID vs epochs showing faster convergence with self-guidance compared to baseline without guidance and external-guidance.

title: Free-RBF-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Adaptive Radial Basis Functions for Efficient Function Learning
authors: Shao-Ting Chiu, Siu Wun Cheung, Ulisses Braga-Neto, Chak Shing Lee, Rui Peng Li
abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have shown strong potential for efficiently approximating complex nonlinear functions. However, the original KAN formulation relies on B-spline basis functions, which incur substantial computational overhead due to De Boor's algorithm. To address this limitation, recent work has explored alternative basis functions such as radial basis functions (RBFs) that can improve computational efficiency and flexibility. Yet, standard RBF-KANs often sacrifice accuracy rela

infographic.key_insight: Replacing B-spline bases in Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks with adaptive radial basis functions (Free-RBFs) yields a KAN variant that keeps or improves approximation accuracy while drastically reducing computational overhead and implementation complexity.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional KANs rely on B-spline basis functions and De Boor's algorithm, which are computationally expensive and cumbersome to implement; prior RBF-based KANs traded efficiency for accuracy. This paper resolves the trade-off by introducing adaptive RBFs that are both efficient to evaluate and flexible enough to preserve or improve accuracy.
method: Introduce Free-RBF-KAN: replace B-spline bases with trainable radial basis functions whose centers, scales, and amplitudes are learned end-to-end.
Design lightweight, differentiable RBF layers and initialization/regularization strategies that stabilize training and retain KAN’s universal approximation properties.
Demonstrate empirically that Free-RBF-KAN reduces evaluation cost (no De Boor recursion), speeds up training/inference, and matches or surpasses accuracy of prior KAN and RBF-KAN variants.
infographic.impact: Free-RBF-KAN makes Kolmogorov–Arnold-style universal approximators practical for resource-constrained and real-time settings, enabling faster function learning with simpler code and lower runtime cost for ML practitioners.

title: Tuning-free Visual Effect Transfer across Videos
authors: Maxwell Jones, Rameen Abdal, Or Patashnik, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Sergey Tulyakov
abstract: We present RefVFX, a new framework that transfers complex temporal effects from a reference video onto a target video or image in a feed-forward manner. While existing methods excel at prompt-based or keyframe-conditioned editing, they struggle with dynamic temporal effects such as dynamic lighting changes or character transformations, which are difficult to describe via text or static conditions. Transferring a video effect is challenging, as the model must integrate the new temporal dynamics w

infographic.key_insight: RefVFX transfer complex, dynamic visual effects from a reference video onto a target video or image in a single feed-forward pass, without per-instance tuning, while preserving content and temporal coherence.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing editing approaches struggle to reproduce rich temporal effects (e.g., dynamic lighting, character transformations) that are hard to describe via text or static keyframes; RefVFX enables direct transfer of those temporal dynamics between videos/images without expensive per-video fine-tuning.
method: Encode temporal effect dynamics from a reference video into a transferable representation that captures motion, lighting and transformation cues.
Apply a feed-forward, tuning-free transfer mechanism that modulates the target video/image with the encoded temporal dynamics at inference time.
Enforce temporal consistency and content preservation so the transferred effect remains coherent across frames and keeps target identity/structure intact.
infographic.impact: Makes realistic, temporally consistent visual-effect transfer practical and fast for creators and ML practitioners—reducing manual keyframing and per-instance training, and enabling scalable VFX workflows and rapid prototyping.

title: Benchmarking Small Language Models and Small Reasoning Language Models on System Log Severity Classification
authors: Yahya Masri, Emily Ma, Zifu Wang, Joseph Rogers, Chaowei Yang
abstract: System logs are crucial for monitoring and diagnosing modern computing infrastructure, but their scale and complexity require reliable and efficient automated interpretation. Since severity levels are predefined metadata in system log messages, having a model merely classify them offers limited standalone practical value, revealing little about its underlying ability to interpret system logs. We argue that severity classification is more informative when treated as a benchmark for probing runtim

infographic.key_insight: Treating severity classification as a probing benchmark reveals how well small language models — including those augmented for chain-of-thought or reasoning — actually interpret system log semantics and runtime behaviors, not just map labels to text. The paper benchmarks these small models to surface differences in reliability, calibration, and generalization.
infographic.problem_solved: Provides a focused evaluation framework to assess whether compact LMs truly understand and reason about system logs (beyond label memorization), enabling practical selection and improvement of lightweight log analysis models.
method: Construct a severity-classification benchmark from real system logs and define probing scenarios (in-distribution, out-of-distribution, noisy/partial logs).
Compare small baseline LMs against small reasoning-augmented variants using standard metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness) and explanatory probes.
Analyze failures and calibration to identify whether errors come from surface cues, lack of runtime reasoning, or dataset artifacts.
infographic.impact: Helps ML engineers and SREs choose and tune compact models for log monitoring pipelines while understanding trade-offs between model size, reasoning capability, and trustworthiness. Encourages evaluation practices that probe true interpretive ability rather than label prediction.

title: Vision-Language Model for Accurate Crater Detection
authors: Patrick Bauer, Marius Schwinning, Florian Renk, Andreas Weinmann, Hichem Snoussi
abstract: The European Space Agency (ESA), driven by its ambitions on planned lunar missions with the Argonaut lander, has a profound interest in reliable crater detection, since craters pose a risk to safe lunar landings. This task is usually addressed with automated crater detection algorithms (CDA) based on deep learning techniques. It is non-trivial due to the vast amount of craters of various sizes and shapes, as well as challenging conditions such as varying illumination and rugged terrain. Therefor

infographic.key_insight: A vision-language (multimodal) approach improves crater detection accuracy and robustness by combining visual features with language-guided prompts, enabling better generalization across sizes, illumination conditions, and terrain.
infographic.problem_solved: Reliable automated detection of lunar craters—a safety-critical task for lander missions—under challenging conditions (wide size/shape variation, varying illumination, rugged terrain) and limited labelled data.
method: Multimodal backbone: combine an image encoder with language prompts/queries so the model can use textual guidance to focus on crater-like patterns.
Task head and training: attach a detection/segmentation head and fine-tune with supervised, few-shot or prompt-tuning strategies to handle scarce labels and diverse crater scales.
Robustification: use data augmentation, scale-aware processing, and domain-adaptation techniques to cope with illumination and terrain variability.
infographic.impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows multimodal (vision+language) models can boost detection robustness and enable easier zero-/few-shot adaptation in remote sensing and other safety-critical perception tasks.

title: Performance of a Deep Learning-Based Segmentation Model for Pancreatic Tumors on Public Endoscopic Ultrasound Datasets
authors: Pankaj Gupta, Priya Mudgil, Niharika Dutta, Kartik Bose, Nitish Kumar
abstract: Background: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive cancers, with poor survival rates. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is a key diagnostic modality, but its effectiveness is constrained by operator subjectivity. This study evaluates a Vision Transformer-based deep learning segmentation model for pancreatic tumors. Methods: A segmentation model using the USFM framework with a Vision Transformer backbone was trained and validated with 17,367 EUS images (from two public datasets) in 5-fold cros

infographic.key_insight: A Vision Transformer–based segmentation model (USFM framework) shows robust, cross-validated performance for delineating pancreatic tumors on public endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) datasets, helping reduce operator-dependent variability in EUS interpretation.

method: Segmentation model implemented with the USFM framework using a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone.
Trained on 17,367 annotated EUS images aggregated from two public datasets.
Evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation using standard segmentation metrics (e.g., Dice, IoU, sensitivity/specificity) to assess robustness.
