title: The World is Your Canvas: Painting Promptable Events with Reference Images, Trajectories, and Text
authors: Hanlin Wang, Hao Ouyang, Qiuyu Wang, Yue Yu, Yihao Meng
abstract: We present WorldCanvas, a framework for promptable world events that enables rich, user-directed simulation by combining text, trajectories, and reference images. Unlike text-only approaches and existing trajectory-controlled image-to-video methods, our multimodal approach combines trajectories -- encoding motion, timing, and visibility -- with natural language for semantic intent and reference images for visual grounding of object identity, enabling the generation of coherent, controllable even

infographic.key_insight: WorldCanvas enables promptable, controllable world-event generation by jointly conditioning on text, trajectories (motion/timing/visibility), and reference images, bridging semantic intent with precise spatio-temporal control and visual identity. This multimodal fusion produces coherent, user-directed simulations that go beyond text-only or trajectory-only image-to-video methods.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing approaches either rely on text alone (lacking precise motion/timing) or on trajectories without semantic/visual grounding. WorldCanvas addresses the challenge of producing coherent, controllable event simulations that honor user intent, object identity, and explicit motion/visibility constraints.
method: Multimodal conditioning: combine natural language for semantic intent, trajectories encoding motion/timing/visibility, and reference images for visual grounding of object identity.
Fuse modalities into a generative simulation pipeline to produce temporally coherent event sequences (image/video) that follow specified trajectories and textual prompts.
Design interfaces/representations that let users specify high-level goals (text) and low-level spatial/temporal constraints (trajectories + reference visuals) for deterministic, controllable outputs.
infographic.impact: This approach gives practitioners fine-grained control over generated events while preserving semantic meaning and visual fidelity, enabling applications in animation, virtual prototyping, interactive storytelling, and realistic simulation. It reduces ambiguity in generation and improves reproducibility of desired behaviors.

title: Depth Any Panoramas: A Foundation Model for Panoramic Depth Estimation
authors: Xin Lin, Meixi Song, Dizhe Zhang, Wenxuan Lu, Haodong Li
abstract: In this work, we present a panoramic metric depth foundation model that generalizes across diverse scene distances. We explore a data-in-the-loop paradigm from the view of both data construction and framework design. We collect a large-scale dataset by combining public datasets, high-quality synthetic data from our UE5 simulator and text-to-image models, and real panoramic images from the web. To reduce domain gaps between indoor/outdoor and synthetic/real data, we introduce a three-stage pseudo

infographic.key_insight: A panoramic metric-depth foundation model trained on a large, mixed dataset (real + synthetic + web) and a data-in-the-loop pipeline can generalize across diverse scene distances and domains for accurate panoramic depth estimation.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges domain and scale gaps in panoramic depth estimation so a single model can produce reliable metric depth across indoor/outdoor scenes and near/far ranges without per-dataset specialization.
method: Assemble a large-scale, mixed dataset by combining public datasets, high-quality UE5 simulator data, text-to-image synthetic panoramas, and real web panoramas.
Apply a three-stage pseudo supervision / domain-reduction pipeline (data-in-the-loop) to reduce synthetic/real and indoor/outdoor domain gaps during training.
Train a panoramic-capable foundation model that outputs metric depth for equirectangular panoramas with multi-scale supervision to improve generalization across scene distances.
infographic.impact: Provides practitioners a robust, general-purpose panoramic depth model and data-construction strategy that reduces the need for scene-specific labeling—beneficial for AR/VR, robotics, mapping, and large-scale 3D scene understanding.

title: Next-Embedding Prediction Makes Strong Vision Learners
authors: Sihan Xu, Ziqiao Ma, Wenhao Chai, Xuweiyi Chen, Weiyang Jin
abstract: Inspired by the success of generative pretraining in natural language, we ask whether the same principles can yield strong self-supervised visual learners. Instead of training models to output features for downstream use, we train them to generate embeddings to perform predictive tasks directly. This work explores such a shift from learning representations to learning models. Specifically, models learn to predict future patch embeddings conditioned on past ones, using causal masking and stop gra

infographic.key_insight: Training vision models to generate (predict) future patch embeddings conditioned on past ones — rather than just learning static representations — yields strong self-supervised visual learners that can be used directly for downstream tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Bridges the gap between generative pretraining successes in NLP and vision by replacing the representation-plus-probe paradigm with a direct predictive objective, simplifying self-supervised pretraining and improving the model's utility for downstream tasks.
method: Next-embedding prediction: train models to predict future patch embeddings given past patches (a generative predictive objective).
Causal masking: enforce autoregressive conditioning over patch sequence so predictions use only past context.
Stop-gradient stabilization: block gradients on target embeddings to avoid collapse and stabilize learning.
infographic.impact: Provides a simple, scalable self-supervised approach that can improve transfer performance and streamline vision pretraining workflows, offering practitioners an alternative to contrastive and representation-only methods.

title: Generative Adversarial Reasoner: Enhancing LLM Reasoning with Adversarial Reinforcement Learning
authors: Qihao Liu, Luoxin Ye, Wufei Ma, Yu-Cheng Chou, Alan Yuille
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with explicit reasoning capabilities excel at mathematical reasoning yet still commit process errors, such as incorrect calculations, brittle logic, and superficially plausible but invalid steps. In this paper, we introduce Generative Adversarial Reasoner, an on-policy joint training framework designed to enhance reasoning by co-evolving an LLM reasoner and an LLM-based discriminator through adversarial reinforcement learning. A compute-efficient review schedule part

infographic.key_insight: Co-training an LLM reasoner with an LLM-based discriminator via on-policy adversarial reinforcement learning reduces process-level reasoning errors (wrong calculations, brittle logic, and superficially plausible but invalid steps) while a compute-efficient review schedule keeps training practical.
infographic.problem_solved: Reduces process errors in explicit chain-of-thought reasoning by making the model produce verifiable, correct intermediate steps rather than superficially plausible but incorrect reasoning.
method: On-policy joint training: a reasoner LLM generates chains-of-thought and an LLM discriminator evaluates step-level correctness to produce reward signals.
Adversarial reinforcement learning loop: the discriminator learns to detect invalid steps while the reasoner adapts to 'fool' the discriminator, improving reasoning robustness.
Compute-efficient review schedule: selective/prioritized evaluation of outputs to limit compute while maintaining effective discriminator feedback.
infographic.impact: Makes LLM reasoning more reliable and verifiable for mathematical and logical tasks, helping practitioners deploy models with fewer process errors and lower post-hoc correction costs.

title: Learning cell dynamics with neural differential equations
authors: Michael E. Vinyard, Anders W. Rasmussen, Ruitong Li, Allon M. Klein, Gad Getz
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 18 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01150-3

Vinyard et al. present a generative method to model cell dynamics using neural stochastic differential equations that learn state-dependent drift and diffusion, outperforming existing approaches and enabling perturbation studies of development and disease.

infographic.key_insight: Neural stochastic differential equations that learn state-dependent drift and diffusion can accurately model and generate single‑cell dynamics, producing realistic trajectories and enabling in silico perturbation experiments. This approach outperforms prior methods by explicitly capturing both deterministic trends and state-dependent stochasticity.
infographic.problem_solved: Modeling the complex, stochastic, and state-dependent dynamics of cells from single‑cell time series data — including realistic uncertainty and the ability to simulate counterfactual perturbations — where prior methods either ignore state‑dependent noise or lack generative/causal simulation capabilities.
method: Parameterize continuous‑time dynamics as neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with neural nets for state‑dependent drift and diffusion.
Train the model on single‑cell trajectory/timecourse data using continuous‑time inference to fit both mean dynamics and noise structure.
Use the learned generative SDE to sample realistic trajectories and perform in silico perturbations by modifying drift/diffusion or inputs to study developmental and disease scenarios.
infographic.impact: Provides ML practitioners a principled, uncertainty‑aware continuous‑time generative framework for systems with stochastic dynamics, enabling higher‑fidelity simulations, interpretable dynamic models, and practical counterfactual experiments in biology and other time‑dependent domains.

title: EasyV2V: A High-quality Instruction-based Video Editing Framework
authors: Jinjie Mai, Chaoyang Wang, Guocheng Gordon Qian, Willi Menapace, Sergey Tulyakov
abstract: While image editing has advanced rapidly, video editing remains less explored, facing challenges in consistency, control, and generalization. We study the design space of data, architecture, and control, and introduce \emph{EasyV2V}, a simple and effective framework for instruction-based video editing. On the data side, we compose existing experts with fast inverses to build diverse video pairs, lift image edit pairs into videos via single-frame supervision and pseudo pairs with shared affine mo

infographic.key_insight: EasyV2V constructs high-quality instruction-driven video edits by combining curated edit pair data (from existing experts and fast inverses) with simple supervision strategies that lift image edits into temporally consistent videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Makes instruction-based video editing more consistent, controllable, and generalizable by addressing limited video training data and temporal inconsistency in prior methods.
method: Data composition: synthesize diverse video-edit pairs by composing existing expert editors with fast inverse transforms to generate plentiful training examples.
Lift image edits to video: use single-frame supervision plus pseudo-paired frames with shared affine motion to extend image-level edits into temporally coherent video sequences.

Design for control & consistency: adopt lightweight architectural and control choices (temporal alignment and instruction conditioning) to preserve per-frame quality while enforcing cross-frame consistency.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, data-efficient framework that lets practitioners build robust, instruction-driven video editing models without massive bespoke video datasets—improving usability and deployment of video editing tools.

title: A psychometric framework for evaluating and shaping personality traits in large language models
authors: Gregory Serapio-García, Mustafa Safdari, Clément Crepy, Luning Sun, Stephen Fitz
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 18 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01115-6

Serapio-García, Safdari and colleagues develop a method based on psychometric tests to measure and validate personality-like traits in LLMs. Large, instruction-tuned models give reliable personality measurement results, and specific personality profiles can be mimicked in downstream tasks.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a psychometrics-based framework that reliably measures and validates personality-like traits in large instruction-tuned LLMs, and shows those traits can be induced to produce target profiles in downstream tasks.
infographic.problem_solved: Lack of a validated, quantitative method to assess and shape personality-like behaviors in LLMs—making it hard to compare models, diagnose behavior, or intentionally design assistant personas.
method: Translate established psychometric instruments (e.g., Big Five style items) into prompts/tests for LLMs and collect model responses.
Validate measurement properties (reliability, construct validity, consistency) across instruction-tuned large models to confirm stable trait-like scores.
Demonstrate shaping: use prompting/conditioning or downstream fine-tuning to induce target personality profiles and evaluate effects on task behavior.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a practical, validated toolkit to quantify, compare, and steer LLM personality traits — useful for debugging, alignment, persona design, and measuring behavioral change after interventions.

title: AdaTooler-V: Adaptive Tool-Use for Images and Videos
authors: Chaoyang Wang, Kaituo Feng, Dongyang Chen, Zhongyu Wang, Zhixun Li
abstract: Recent advances have shown that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) benefit from multimodal interleaved chain-of-thought (CoT) with vision tool interactions. However, existing open-source models often exhibit blind tool-use reasoning patterns, invoking vision tools even when they are unnecessary, which significantly increases inference overhead and degrades model performance. To this end, we propose AdaTooler-V, an MLLM that performs adaptive tool-use by determining whether a visual problem

infographic.key_insight: AdaTooler-V learns when to call vision tools (for images and videos) instead of invoking them blindly, cutting unnecessary tool use while preserving or improving reasoning performance.
infographic.problem_solved: Open-source multimodal LLMs overuse vision tools — invoking expensive vision modules even when not needed — causing higher latency, compute waste, and degraded overall performance.
method: Adaptive tool-use controller that predicts, per query (and per video frame when applicable), whether a vision tool is necessary before invoking it.
Integrates selective tool invocation into multimodal interleaved chain-of-thought reasoning so the model still uses tools when they provide real benefit.
Training with a cost-aware objective (trade-off between accuracy and invocation overhead) and temporal-aware selection for videos to limit frame-level tool calls.
infographic.impact: Reduces inference latency and compute cost while maintaining or improving reasoning accuracy for image and video tasks, making multimodal LLM deployments more efficient and scalable.

title: Multimodal out-of-distribution individual uncertainty quantification enhances binding affinity prediction for polypharmacology
authors: Amitesh Badkul, Li Xie, Shuo Zhang, Lei Xie
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 18 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01151-2

Badkul et al. develop eMOSAIC, a method that improves drug discovery by accurately predicting the interaction mechanics of various compounds with multiple proteins.

infographic.key_insight: eMOSAIC combines multimodal protein–compound representations with per-sample out-of-distribution (OOD) uncertainty estimates to substantially improve binding affinity predictions across multiple targets, enabling more reliable polypharmacology assessment.
infographic.problem_solved: Accurately predicting drug–target binding affinities under distribution shift and for compounds that act on many proteins is undermined by miscalibrated predictions and lack of per-sample OOD awareness; this work addresses unreliable generalization and decision-making in multi-target screening.
method: Multimodal modeling: integrate molecular (compound) and protein representations to predict binding affinity under a unified model.
Per-sample OOD uncertainty quantification: estimate individual prediction uncertainty for each compound–protein pair to detect domain shift and flag low-confidence predictions.
Use uncertainty-aware outputs to improve ranking/prioritization for polypharmacology (e.g., downweight or defer high-uncertainty predictions), yielding more robust affinity predictions.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical blueprint for building uncertainty-aware multimodal models that generalize under domain shift—helpful for ML practitioners deploying predictive models in drug discovery where reliable, per-sample confidence is critical for decision-making.

title: FrontierCS: Evolving Challenges for Evolving Intelligence
authors: Qiuyang Mang, Wenhao Chai, Zhifei Li, Huanzhi Mao, Shang Zhou
abstract: We introduce FrontierCS, a benchmark of 156 open-ended problems across diverse areas of computer science, designed and reviewed by experts, including CS PhDs and top-tier competitive programming participants and problem setters. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on tasks with known optimal solutions, FrontierCS targets problems where the optimal solution is unknown, but the quality of a solution can be objectively evaluated. Models solve these tasks by implementing executable programs rather

infographic.key_insight: FrontierCS introduces a 156-problem benchmark of open-ended computer science challenges where optimal solutions are unknown but solution quality can be objectively measured, shifting evaluation from label prediction to producing and executing programs.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing benchmarks emphasize tasks with known optimal answers and static metrics; FrontierCS addresses the need for evaluating model creativity, algorithmic reasoning, and real-world coding ability on open-ended CS problems.
method: Curate 156 diverse, open-ended CS problems spanning algorithms, systems, theory, and applied areas, designed and reviewed by CS PhDs, top competitive programmers, and problem setters.
Require models to produce executable programs as solutions rather than scalar predictions, enabling objective, automated evaluation via program execution and measurable outputs.
Provide a standardized benchmark framework that captures solution quality (e.g., correctness, efficiency, robustness) even when a single optimal solution is unknown.
infographic.impact: FrontierCS offers a realistic, scalable way to measure and drive progress on model coding, algorithmic creativity, and general problem solving — critical for developers building agents that must produce reliable, executable solutions in open-ended settings.

Pipeline flowchart: model → generated executable program → automated evaluation → quality metrics.

title: Spatia: Video Generation with Updatable Spatial Memory
authors: Jinjing Zhao, Fangyun Wei, Zhening Liu, Hongyang Zhang, Chang Xu
abstract: Existing video generation models struggle to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency due to the dense, high-dimensional nature of video signals. To overcome this limitation, we propose Spatia, a spatial memory-aware video generation framework that explicitly preserves a 3D scene point cloud as persistent spatial memory. Spatia iteratively generates video clips conditioned on this spatial memory and continuously updates it through visual SLAM. This dynamic-static disentanglement desig

infographic.key_insight: Spatia preserves a persistent 3D scene point cloud as spatial memory and uses it to iteratively generate and update video clips via visual SLAM, enabling much stronger long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generated videos.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing video generation models struggle to maintain coherent scene geometry and temporal continuity over long sequences because video signals are dense and high-dimensional.
method: Maintain an explicit 3D scene point cloud as persistent spatial memory that represents static scene geometry.
Iteratively generate short video clips conditioned on the spatial memory, then update the memory continuously using visual SLAM.
Employ a dynamic–static disentanglement design to separate moving content from persistent scene structure, stabilizing long-range consistency.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable way to generate longer, more geometrically and temporally consistent videos, useful for applications requiring persistent scene understanding (e.g., simulation, AR/VR, robotics) and for practitioners building infrastructure for generative video systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: 3D point-cloud memory → clip generator → visual SLAM updater (loop) to show iterative generate+update flow.
3D scene point-cloud visualization annotated as 'persistent spatial memory' vs per-frame pixels.
Before/after frame sequences showing improved long-term consistency (e.g., stable background, coherent object positions).
Illustration of dynamic–static disentanglement: overlayed masks or color-coding separating moving objects from static scene geometry.

title: Solving finite element methods with spiking networks
authors: Wenhao Song, Zixu Wang, J. Joshua Yang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 17 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01158-9

Brain-inspired computing can enhance the finite element method, a cornerstone of scientific modelling, by reducing energy costs and reframing numerical simulation through neural dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Finite element method (FEM) problems can be reformulated and solved by spiking neural networks, enabling event-driven, brain-inspired numerical simulation that substantially reduces energy use compared with conventional solvers.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional FEM solvers are computationally and energy intensive, especially for large sparse linear systems and real‑time/embedded scenarios; there is a gap between numerical methods and low‑power neuromorphic hardware that this work addresses.
method: Map FEM linear systems and mesh connectivity onto a sparse spiking network where synaptic weights encode the stiffness/mass relationships and node states are represented by spike-driven membrane potentials.
Use event-driven spiking dynamics (e.g., integrate‑and‑fire regimes) and tailored encoding/decoding to iteratively converge to the FEM solution, leveraging locality and sparsity for parallelism.
Validate stability and accuracy through network parameter tuning and demonstrate energy/time benefits on neuromorphic hardware or efficient spiking simulators.
infographic.impact: This approach opens a pathway for integrating physics‑based simulation with energy‑efficient neuromorphic platforms, making real‑time, embedded, or large‑scale FEM feasible for AI‑driven engineering and scientific workflows.
visual_elements: Diagram mapping a FEM mesh (nodes/elements) to a spiking network graph showing synaptic weights = stiffness entries.
Comparative bar/line chart of energy consumption and runtime: conventional FEM solver vs spiking network implementation.
Schematic timeline illustrating event-driven spike updates converging to the continuous FEM solution (encoding → spiking dynamics → decoding).
Flowchart of the end‑to‑end pipeline: mesh → network construction → neuromorphic execution → reconstructed field.

title: GateFusion: Hierarchical Gated Cross-Modal Fusion for Active Speaker Detection
authors: Yu Wang, Juhyung Ha, Frangil M. Ramirez, Yuchen Wang, David J. Crandall
abstract: Active Speaker Detection (ASD) aims to identify who is currently speaking in each frame of a video. Most state-of-the-art approaches rely on late fusion to combine visual and audio features, but late fusion often fails to capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions, which can be critical for robust performance in unconstrained scenarios. In this paper, we introduce GateFusion, a novel architecture that combines strong pretrained unimodal encoders with a Hierarchical Gated Fusion Decoder (HiGat

infographic.key_insight: GateFusion replaces brittle late fusion with a hierarchical gated decoder that enables fine-grained, layer-wise cross-modal interactions between strong pretrained audio and visual encoders, improving robustness of frame-level active speaker detection.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing ASD systems using late fusion fail to capture detailed audio–visual interactions across scales and layers, reducing accuracy in unconstrained, noisy, or multi-speaker scenarios.
method: Leverage strong pretrained unimodal encoders for audio and visual streams to extract rich features.
Introduce a Hierarchical Gated Fusion Decoder (HiGat) that applies gating and cross-attention across multiple levels/timescales to selectively combine modalities.
Use the fused representations for frame-level active speaker classification, preserving fine-grained temporal and spatial cues missed by late fusion.
infographic.impact: GateFusion offers practitioners a modular way to fuse pretrained encoders that better models cross-modal dependencies, yielding more robust ASD in real-world video/audio settings and a template for other multimodal tasks.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: parallel pretrained audio and visual encoders feeding into the Hierarchical Gated Fusion Decoder with gated connections illustrated by adjustable valves.
Gating detail inset: close-up showing how gating weights modulate cross-modal feature flow across layers/time.
Performance schematic: conceptual comparison (late fusion vs GateFusion) showing improved interaction capture and robustness (no raw numbers).
Qualitative examples: video frames with audio waveform and detected active-speaker heatmap/overlay to show practical outputs.

title: Skyra: AI-Generated Video Detection via Grounded Artifact Reasoning
authors: Yifei Li, Wenzhao Zheng, Yanran Zhang, Runze Sun, Yu Zheng
abstract: The misuse of AI-driven video generation technologies has raised serious social concerns, highlighting the urgent need for reliable AI-generated video detectors. However, most existing methods are limited to binary classification and lack the necessary explanations for human interpretation. In this paper, we present Skyra, a specialized multimodal large language model (MLLM) that identifies human-perceivable visual artifacts in AI-generated videos and leverages them as grounded evidence for both

infographic.key_insight: Skyra is a multimodal large language model that detects AI-generated videos by spotting human-perceivable visual artifacts and uses those artifacts as grounded, human-readable evidence rather than only producing a binary label.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing AI-generated video detectors give binary outputs with little interpretability; Skyra addresses the need for reliable detection plus grounded explanations that humans and practitioners can inspect and trust.
method: Train a specialized MLLM to recognize and name visual artifacts (e.g., temporal flicker, inconsistent shadows, texture glitches) across video frames and localize them spatially and temporally.
Aggregate artifact detections into grounded evidence and perform reasoning to produce a detection decision accompanied by human-readable explanations and visual highlights.
Leverage multimodal inputs (frame sequences, optical-flow or temporal features, and auxiliary metadata) and curated annotations to align model outputs with human-perceivable artifacts.
infographic.impact: Skyra improves trust and usability of video forensics by giving practitioners actionable, interpretable evidence—enabling better triage, human review, and downstream policy or legal actions instead of opaque automated flags.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: video input → artifact detector (frame & temporal) → evidence aggregator → interpretable verdict
Before/after frame pairs with highlighted artifact heatmaps (e.g., flicker zones, texture seams) to show localization
Artifact taxonomy infographic listing common artifact types with short descriptions and example thumbnails
Flowchart showing how grounded evidence supports a final detection decision and human-readable explanation

title: In Pursuit of Pixel Supervision for Visual Pre-training
authors: Lihe Yang, Shang-Wen Li, Yang Li, Xinjie Lei, Dong Wang
abstract: At the most basic level, pixels are the source of the visual information through which we perceive the world. Pixels contain information at all levels, ranging from low-level attributes to high-level concepts. Autoencoders represent a classical and long-standing paradigm for learning representations from pixels or other raw inputs. In this work, we demonstrate that autoencoder-based self-supervised learning remains competitive today and can produce strong representations for downstream tasks, wh

infographic.key_insight: Revisiting autoencoder-style pixel supervision shows that learning from raw pixels remains a competitive and effective route for visual pre-training when combined with modern training practices, producing strong downstream representations.
infographic.problem_solved: Clarifies whether pixel-level reconstruction objectives (autoencoders) are still viable compared to recent self-supervised paradigms and identifies how pixel supervision can be leveraged for robust visual pre-training.
method: Re-evaluate the classical autoencoder paradigm for visual representation learning under contemporary training recipes and architectures.
Apply pixel-level supervision (reconstruction/masking) with modern optimizers, scaling, and regularization to learn transferable features from raw images.
Perform systematic comparisons and ablations across downstream tasks to isolate the contributions and trade-offs of pixel supervision.
infographic.impact: Shows practitioners that simple, interpretable pixel-supervision objectives can rival complex pretext tasks, offering a strong, lightweight baseline and clearer design choices for visual pre-training.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: raw pixels → encoder → latent representation → decoder (reconstruction) with callouts for key design choices (masking, loss, scaling).
Performance comparison bar chart: autoencoder-based pixel supervision vs popular SSL methods across several downstream tasks (classification, detection, segmentation).
Reconstruction examples paired with embedding visualizations (t-SNE/UMAP) to illustrate how pixel supervision relates to representation quality.
Ablation heatmap/table showing impact of components (mask ratio, decoder size, loss variants) on downstream transfer performance.
infographic.paper_title: In Pursuit of Pixel Supervision for Visual Pre-training

title: Gaussian Pixel Codec Avatars: A Hybrid Representation for Efficient Rendering
authors: Divam Gupta, Anuj Pahuja, Nemanja Bartolovic, Tomas Simon, Forrest Iandola
abstract: We present Gaussian Pixel Codec Avatars (GPiCA), photorealistic head avatars that can be generated from multi-view images and efficiently rendered on mobile devices. GPiCA utilizes a unique hybrid representation that combines a triangle mesh and anisotropic 3D Gaussians. This combination maximizes memory and rendering efficiency while maintaining a photorealistic appearance. The triangle mesh is highly efficient in representing surface areas like facial skin, while the 3D Gaussians effectively h

infographic.key_insight: GPiCA introduces a compact hybrid representation that combines a triangle mesh for smooth surface regions with anisotropic 3D Gaussians for fine, view-dependent detail, enabling photorealistic head avatars that render efficiently on mobile devices.
infographic.problem_solved: How to produce and render photorealistic, multi-view-derived head avatars in real time on resource-constrained devices without huge memory or compute costs.
method: Reconstruct a triangle mesh for large, smooth facial surfaces and fit anisotropic 3D Gaussians to capture fine-scale, view-dependent appearance (hair, eyes, speculars, soft geometry).
Jointly optimize geometry and Gaussian attributes from multi-view images, then use a hybrid renderer that rasterizes the mesh and blends Gaussian primitives for detailed shading.
Design the representation and rendering pipeline for low memory footprint and GPU-friendly execution suitable for mobile real-time rendering.
infographic.impact: GPiCA enables high-quality, real-time avatar rendering on mobile/edge devices, lowering barriers for AR/VR, telepresence, and interactive applications by balancing photorealism with practical memory and performance constraints.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic of the hybrid representation: triangle mesh overlayed with colored anisotropic 3D Gaussians highlighting different roles.
Pipeline flowchart from multi-view capture → joint optimization → hybrid rendering, annotated with compute/memory advantages.
Comparison grid showing visual quality vs. rendering time/memory for GPiCA versus mesh-only and Gaussian-only baselines.
Zoomed detail panels (hair, eyes, specular highlights) demonstrating how Gaussians capture fine, view-dependent effects.

title: Predictive Concept Decoders: Training Scalable End-to-End Interpretability Assistants
authors: Vincent Huang, Dami Choi, Daniel D. Johnson, Sarah Schwettmann, Jacob Steinhardt
abstract: Interpreting the internal activations of neural networks can produce more faithful explanations of their behavior, but is difficult due to the complex structure of activation space. Existing approaches to scalable interpretability use hand-designed agents that make and test hypotheses about how internal activations relate to external behavior. We propose to instead turn this task into an end-to-end training objective, by training interpretability assistants to accurately predict model behavior f

infographic.key_insight: Train end-to-end "interpretability assistants"—Predictive Concept Decoders (PCDs)—that learn to map internal activations to model behavior, producing scalable, faithful explanations without hand-designed hypothesis testers.
infographic.problem_solved: Automates and scales the hard task of relating complex internal activation space to external model behavior, replacing slow, hand-crafted interpretability agents with trained predictors that directly capture useful concepts.
method: Introduce Predictive Concept Decoders (PCDs) that consume hidden activations and predict model behavior or human-understandable concept signals.
Train PCDs end-to-end with objectives that maximize predictive fidelity to the base model, aligning learned concepts with downstream behavior.
Evaluate assistants on fidelity, scalability, and usefulness compared to hand-designed interpretability agents.
infographic.impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a scalable, trainable tool to obtain more faithful internal explanations for debugging, auditing, and alignment workflows, reducing manual effort and improving interpretability fidelity.

title: End-to-End Training for Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Self-Resampling
authors: Yuwei Guo, Ceyuan Yang, Hao He, Yang Zhao, Meng Wei
abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models hold promise for world simulation but are vulnerable to exposure bias arising from the train-test mismatch. While recent works address this via post-training, they typically rely on a bidirectional teacher model or online discriminator. To achieve an end-to-end solution, we introduce Resampling Forcing, a teacher-free framework that enables training autoregressive video models from scratch and at scale. Central to our approach is a self-resampling scheme tha

infographic.key_insight: Resampling Forcing is a teacher-free, end-to-end training framework that uses a self-resampling scheme to close the train–test gap in autoregressive video diffusion models, removing the need for a separate teacher or discriminator while enabling scalable training from scratch.
infographic.problem_solved: Addresses exposure bias in autoregressive video diffusion — the mismatch between training (ground-truth conditioning) and inference (model-generated conditioning) that degrades long-horizon video generation quality and stability.
method: Introduce Resampling Forcing: a training protocol that simulates test-time autoregressive conditioning during training without an external teacher.
Self-resampling scheme: periodically replace ground-truth conditioning frames with the model's own predicted frames (resampled) so the model learns to recover from its own errors.
End-to-end, teacher-free training: integrates resampling into standard diffusion optimization, enabling scalable training from scratch without bidirectional teachers or online discriminators.
infographic.impact: Provides a practical, scalable way to train autoregressive video diffusion models that are more robust at generation time, reducing the need for complex teacher models or adversarial components — useful for researchers and engineers building long-horizon video simulators and generative systems.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: training with ground-truth conditioning vs. training with self-resampling showing reduced train–test mismatch.
Flowchart of the Resampling Forcing loop: predict -> resample -> condition -> train (one-line depiction of end-to-end pipeline).
Before/after sample grid or metrics chart: visual quality and stability improvements over baseline autoregressive training.

title: VLIC: Vision-Language Models As Perceptual Judges for Human-Aligned Image Compression
authors: Kyle Sargent, Ruiqi Gao, Philipp Henzler, Charles Herrmann, Aleksander Holynski
abstract: Evaluations of image compression performance which include human preferences have generally found that naive distortion functions such as MSE are insufficiently aligned to human perception. In order to align compression models to human perception, prior work has employed differentiable perceptual losses consisting of neural networks calibrated on large-scale datasets of human psycho-visual judgments. We show that, surprisingly, state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) can replicate binary

infographic.key_insight: State-of-the-art vision-language models can reliably replicate binary human preference judgments and serve as perceptual judges, enabling image-compression systems to be aligned to human perception without large-scale costly psychophysical datasets.
infographic.problem_solved: Conventional distortion metrics (e.g., MSE) and earlier perceptual losses are poorly aligned with human judgments; collecting and calibrating large human preference datasets for perceptual losses is slow and expensive.
method: Use pretrained vision-language models to predict pairwise human preferences between compressed image variants, effectively acting as a perceptual judge.
Convert VLM outputs into a differentiable or ranking loss/signal (or use them as an evaluation metric) to steer compression model training toward human-aligned quality.
Optionally calibrate or fine-tune the VLM on a small set of human judgments to improve agreement and then integrate it into the compression training/evaluation pipeline.
infographic.impact: Provides a scalable, cheaper route to train and evaluate image compression models that better match human perceptual preferences, reducing reliance on extensive human studies and improving subjective image quality in practice.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: original image → compressor → two compressed variants → VLM judge vs. human vote (showing alignment)
Bar/line chart: correlation or agreement between MSE, prior perceptual losses, and VLM judgments with human preferences

title: Network-aware self-supervised learning enables high-content phenotypic screening for genetic modifiers of neuronal activity dynamics
authors: Parker Grosjean, Kaivalya Shevade, Cuong Nguyen, Sarah Ancheta, Karl Mader
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 17 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01156-x

Grosjean et al. present a network-aware, self-supervised learning approach for screening neuronal activity dynamics. They demonstrate its applicability across a range of neural interventions.

infographic.key_insight: A network-aware self-supervised learning pipeline can learn label-free, biologically meaningful representations of neuronal activity dynamics, enabling high-content phenotypic screening to identify genetic modifiers across diverse neural interventions.
infographic.problem_solved: Scales up detection of subtle, network-level changes in neuronal activity without manual labels or handcrafted features, overcoming limits of conventional single-cell or supervised screening methods.
method: Train self-supervised models that incorporate network structure and temporal dynamics from neuronal activity recordings as pretext tasks.
Produce low-dimensional embeddings that capture network-level phenotypes and similarity between perturbations.
Use embeddings for high-content screening: cluster, compare, and prioritize genetic modifiers across multiple interventions and datasets.
infographic.impact: Offers a general, label-free framework for learning interpretable representations of dynamical biological networks, accelerating scalable perturbation screens and enabling transfer of ML tools to other networked time-series applications.
visual_elements: Pipeline schematic: raw neuronal activity (raster/voltage traces) → network-aware SSL model → embedding space → phenotypic hits
Side-by-side time-series examples mapped to embedding clusters to show phenotypic separation
Heatmap or volcano-style plot of perturbation effects across genes/interventions
Schematic plate/well map or scalability icon to highlight high-throughput screening capability
infographic.paper_title: Network-aware self-supervised learning enables high-content phenotypic screening for genetic modifiers of neuronal activity dynamics
infographic.paper_authors: Parker Grosjean, Kaivalya Shevade, Cuong Nguyen, Sarah Ancheta, Karl Mader

title: mimic-video: Video-Action Models for Generalizable Robot Control Beyond VLAs
authors: Jonas Pai, Liam Achenbach, Victoriano Montesinos, Benedek Forrai, Oier Mees
abstract: Prevailing Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) for robotic manipulation are built upon vision-language backbones pretrained on large-scale, but disconnected static web data. As a result, despite improved semantic generalization, the policy must implicitly infer complex physical dynamics and temporal dependencies solely from robot trajectories. This reliance creates an unsustainable data burden, necessitating continuous, large-scale expert data collection to compensate for the lack of innate phy

infographic.key_insight: Pretraining models on temporally rich video-action data lets policies learn physical dynamics and temporal structure, enabling more generalizable robot control than Vision–Language–Action models built on static web images and text.
infographic.problem_solved: VLAs rely on static vision-language backbones that lack inherent understanding of physical dynamics and temporal dependencies, forcing large-scale expert robot trajectory collection; Mimic-Video reduces that data burden by learning dynamics from video.
method: Pretrain a spatio-temporal video-action backbone on large-scale, dynamics-rich video data to capture motion and physical interaction cues.
Align video-derived representations with robot actions via imitation-style fine-tuning (mimic) on a small set of robot demonstrations, bridging video semantics and control.
Use temporal modeling and cross-modal alignment to enable zero-/few-shot transfer to new manipulation tasks and environments.
infographic.impact: Enables sample-efficient, more robust robot policies that generalize to novel tasks and environments with far fewer expert demonstrations — lowering deployment cost and accelerating real-world robotic learning.

title: Dynamic Rebatching for Efficient Early-Exit Inference with DREX
authors: Xuting Liu, Daniel Alexander, Siva Kesava Reddy Kakarla, Behnaz Arzani, Vincent Liu
abstract: Early-Exit (EE) is a Large Language Model (LLM) architecture that accelerates inference by allowing easier tokens to be generated using only a subset of the model's layers. However, traditional batching frameworks are ill-suited for EE LLMs, as not all requests in a batch may be ready to exit at the same time. Existing solutions either force a uniform decision on the batch, which overlooks EE opportunities, or degrade output quality by forcing premature exits. We propose Dynamic Rebatching, a so

infographic.key_insight: Dynamic Rebatching (DREX) continually reshapes inference batches based on each token's early-exit readiness so tokens that can finish early do not wait for slower tokens, improving latency and throughput while preserving output quality.
infographic.problem_solved: Traditional batching for Early-Exit LLMs either forces a single batch decision (losing early-exit opportunities) or forces premature exits (hurting quality). This paper addresses inefficient resource use and increased latency when mixed-exit requests are processed together.
method: Continuously track per-token/per-request exit readiness and decision signals during inference.
Form and dispatch dynamic micro-batches that group tokens by exit stage, allowing ready tokens to exit immediately while others continue deeper layers.
Lightweight scheduler integrates with the runtime to rebatch with minimal overhead, balancing GPU utilization and per-request quality constraints.
infographic.impact: DREX enables faster, more cost-efficient LLM serving by unlocking early-exit benefits in real-world batched deployments without sacrificing accuracy—useful for latency-sensitive applications and large-scale model serving.

Timeline swimlane comparing static batching vs dynamic rebatching (showing reduced wait times and earlier exits)
Bar chart or heatmap illustrating throughput and latency improvements (relative comparison without exact numbers)

title: DiffusionVL: Translating Any Autoregressive Models into Diffusion Vision Language Models
authors: Lunbin Zeng, Jingfeng Yao, Bencheng Liao, Hongyuan Tao, Wenyu Liu
abstract: In recent multimodal research, the diffusion paradigm has emerged as a promising alternative to the autoregressive paradigm (AR), owing to its unique decoding advantages. However, due to the capability limitations of the base diffusion language model, the performance of the diffusion vision language model (dVLM) still lags significantly behind that of mainstream models. This leads to a simple yet fundamental question: Is it possible to construct dVLMs based on existing powerful AR models? In res

infographic.key_insight: A practical recipe to convert existing autoregressive (AR) language models into diffusion-based vision-language models (dVLMs), enabling diffusion-style decoding while leveraging the capabilities of strong AR backbones.
infographic.problem_solved: Diffusion vision-language models lag behind mainstream AR-based VLMs because base diffusion language models lack comparable capabilities; this work addresses how to build competitive dVLMs by reusing powerful pretrained AR models instead of training new diffusion LMs from scratch.
method: Introduce a translation/interface that maps pretrained AR model behavior into a diffusion-compatible component, allowing the AR backbone to be used inside a diffusion generation loop.

Train lightweight adapters or distill from AR outputs into a diffusion score model so the system preserves AR knowledge while supporting diffusion denoising and conditional image-to-text/text-to-image workflows.
Combine diffusion decoding advantages (e.g., flexible parallel generation, robustness) with AR model strengths via joint conditioning and inference strategies tailored for multimodal tasks.
infographic.impact: Enables practitioners to rapidly build high-performing diffusion VLMs by repurposing existing AR models, unlocking diffusion decoding benefits (robustness, parallelism, flexible conditioning) without sacrificing language and multimodal capabilities.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: AR model + translator/adapters feeding into a diffusion denoising loop (show data flow and conditioning).
Before vs After bar chart: performance gap between native diffusion VLMs and translated AR→diffusion VLMs.
Decoding pipeline illustration: comparison of autoregressive sequential decoding vs diffusion denoising (parallel steps).

title: Native and Compact Structured Latents for 3D Generation
authors: Jianfeng Xiang, Xiaoxue Chen, Sicheng Xu, Ruicheng Wang, Zelong Lv
abstract: Recent advancements in 3D generative modeling have significantly improved the generation realism, yet the field is still hampered by existing representations, which struggle to capture assets with complex topologies and detailed appearance. This paper present an approach for learning a structured latent representation from native 3D data to address this challenge. At its core is a new sparse voxel structure called O-Voxel, an omni-voxel representation that encodes both geometry and appearance. O

infographic.key_insight: Introduce a compact, structured latent learned directly from native 3D data via a new sparse voxel format (O‑Voxel) that jointly encodes geometry and appearance, enabling more faithful generation of complex topology and fine detail.
infographic.problem_solved: Existing 3D representations struggle to represent complex topologies and detailed appearance while remaining compact and generative-friendly; this work addresses representation bottlenecks by providing a native, sparse, appearance-aware voxel latent.
method: Define O‑Voxel: an omni‑voxel sparse 3D structure that stores both geometric and appearance signals at voxel locations.
Learn compact structured latents from native 3D data by mapping into the O‑Voxel space so downstream generative models operate on a dense-yet-sparse, semantically meaningful latent.
Use the O‑Voxel latent as the core representation for 3D generation and reconstruction tasks, reducing memory and improving fidelity for complex assets.

abstract: The core challenge for streaming video generation is maintaining the content consistency in long context, which poses high requirement for the memory design. title: LLM use in scholarly writing poses a provenance problem
authors: Brian D. Earp, Haotian Yuan, Julian Koplin, Sebastian Porsdam Mann
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 12 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01159-8

LLM use in scholarly writing poses a provenance problem

infographic.key_insight: Using large language models in scholarly writing creates a provenance problem: generated text, citations, and edits often lack traceable origin, threatening accountability, reproducibility, and the integrity of the scientific record.
infographic.problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes the challenge of undocumented, non-auditable LLM contributions to manuscripts and proposes a framework of technical and policy measures to restore provenance and accountability.
method: Conceptual analysis that defines provenance dimensions for scholarly outputs (source, transformation, attribution, timestamp).
Illustrative examples/case studies showing hallucinated citations and opaque edits in LLM-assisted drafts.
Prescriptive recommendations combining metadata standards, logging/timestamps, model attribution, and cryptographic/technical controls for auditability.
infographic.impact: Prompts AI/ML practitioners, publishers, and researchers to adopt provenance-first workflows (machine-readable metadata, disclosure, and audit trails) to preserve reproducibility, trust, and ethical accountability in LLM-assisted research.
visual_elements: Provenance chain diagram: human author → LLM (with model/version) → edits → final manuscript, annotated with timestamps and metadata.
Side-by-side example: hallucinated citation vs. verified source to show risk and detection.
Flowchart of technical solutions: metadata standards → logging → cryptographic signatures → publisher ingestion.
Policy checklist / icon set for stakeholders (authors, reviewers, publishers, toolmakers) showing required disclosures and controls.
infographic.paper_title: LLM use in scholarly writing poses a provenance problem

authors: Mohammed El Fallaki Idrissi, Jad Mounayer, Sebastian Rodriguez, Fodil Meraghni, Francisco Chinesta
abstract: This paper presents a novel paradigm in simulation-based engineering sciences by introducing a new framework called Generative Parametric Design (GPD). The GPD framework enables the generation of new designs along with their corresponding parametric solutions given as a reduced basis. authors: Titaya Mairittha, Tanakon Sawanglok, Panuwit Raden, Jirapast Buntub, Thanapat Warunee
abstract: While voice-based AI systems have achieved remarkable generative capabilities, their interactions often feel conversationally broken. This paper examines the interactional friction that emerges in modular Speech-to-Speech Retrieval-Augmented Generation (S2S-RAG) pipelines. authors: Lin Bai, Xiaoyang Li, Liqiang Huang, Quynh Nguyen, Hien Van Nguyen

authors: Kai Yao, Marc Juarez
abstract: Model fingerprint detection techniques have emerged as a promising approach for attributing AI-generated images to their source models, but their robustness under adversarial conditions remains largely unexplored. authors: Sacha Braun, David Holzmüller, Michael I. Jordan, Francis Bach
abstract: Evaluating conditional coverage remains one of the most persistent challenges in assessing the reliability of predictive systems. Although conformal methods can give guarantees on marginal coverage, no method can guarantee to produce sets with correct conditional coverage, leaving practitioners without a clear way to interpret local deviations. authors: Tim Cofala, Christian Kalfar, Jingge Xiao, Johanna Schrader, Michelle Tang
abstract: Therapeutic decision-making in clinical medicine constitutes a high-stakes domain in which AI guidance interacts with complex interactions among patient characteristics, disease processes, and pharmacological agents. authors: Brenda Nogueira, Werner Geyer, Andrew Anderson, Toby Jia-Jun Li, Dongwhi Kim
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in academic writing practices. authors: Yang Fei, George Stoica, Jingyuan Liu, Qifeng Chen, Ranjay Krishna
abstract: Reality is a dance between rigid constraints and deformable structures. For video models, that means generating motion that preserves fidelity as well as structure. Despite progress in diffusion models, producing realistic structure-preserving motion remains challenging, especially for articulated and deformable objects such as humans and animals. authors: Wei Chow, Linfeng Li, Lingdong Kong, Zefeng Li, Qi Xu
abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models (DMs) have achieved exceptional visual quality in image editing tasks. However, the global denoising dynamics of DMs inherently conflate local editing targets with the full-image context, leading to unintended modifications in non-target regions. abstract: Accurately quantifying vitiligo extent in routine clinical photographs is crucial for longitudinal monitoring of treatment response. title: Deciphering RNA–ligand binding specificity with GerNA-Bind
authors: Yunpeng Xia, Jiayi Li, Yi-Ting Chu, Jiahua Rao, Jing Chen
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 12 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01154-z

Xia et al. introduce GerNA-Bind, a geometric deep learning framework designed to predict RNA–ligand binding specificity by integrating multistate RNA–ligand interactions.

infographic.key_insight: GerNA-Bind applies geometric deep learning to explicitly model multistate RNA conformations and their interactions with ligands, enabling more accurate prediction of RNA–ligand binding specificity and highlighting structural determinants of binding.
infographic.problem_solved: Predicting RNA–ligand binding specificity is hard because RNA is highly flexible, adopts multiple conformational states, and existing models often ignore geometric/3D multistate information—GerNA-Bind addresses this gap.
method: Represent RNA and ligand as 3D geometric graphs that capture atomic coordinates, bonds, and multistate conformations.
Use equivariant/geometric neural network layers to learn rotation- and translation-aware interaction features across multiple RNA states.

Integrate multistate interaction modeling and interpretability modules to predict specificity and highlight structural binding determinants; train/evaluate on curated RNA–ligand datasets against baseline models.
infographic.impact: For ML practitioners, GerNA-Bind demonstrates how structure-aware, equivariant models that incorporate multistate representations can substantially improve predictive performance for biomolecular binding tasks—accelerating rational RNA-targeted design and interpretable molecular AI.
visual_elements: Schematic of multiple RNA conformations (states) binding the same ligand to show multistate concept
Architecture diagram: geometric graph input → equivariant layers → interaction module → specificity prediction
Bar/line chart comparing GerNA-Bind performance vs. baselines on binding specificity metrics
Heatmap or attention overlay on RNA structure highlighting learned binding determinants (interpretable features)

authors: Ye Fang, Tong Wu, Valentin Deschaintre, Duygu Ceylan, Iliyan Georgiev
abstract: Large-scale video generation models have shown remarkable potential in modeling photorealistic appearance and lighting interactions in real-world scenes. However, a closed-loop framework that jointly understands intrinsic scene properties (e.g., albedo, normal, material, and irradiance), leverages them for video synthesis, and supports editable intrinsic representations remains unexplored. authors: Yongsheng Huang, Peibo Duan, Yujie Wu, Kai Sun, Zhipeng Liu

authors: Jan U. Müller, Robin Tim Landsgesell, Leif Van Holland, Patrick Stotko, Reinhard Klein
abstract: The recent success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has reshaped novel view synthesis by enabling fast optimization and real-time rendering of high-quality radiance fields. title: Agile Flight Emerges from Multi-Agent Competitive Racing
authors: Vineet Pasumarti, Lorenzo Bianchi, Antonio Loquercio
abstract: Through multi-agent competition and the sparse high-level objective of winning a race, we find that both agile flight (e.g., high-speed motion pushing the platform to its physical limits) and strategy (e.g., overtaking or blocking) emerge from agents trained with reinforcement learning. authors: Minglei Shi, Haolin Wang, Borui Zhang, Wenzhao Zheng, Bohan Zeng
abstract: Visual generation grounded in Visual Foundation Model (VFM) representations offers a highly promising unified pathway for integrating visual understanding, perception, and generation. authors: Liqiang Huang, Rachel W. Mills, Saikiran Mandula, Lin Bai, Mahtab Jeyhani
abstract: Whole-slide multiplex imaging of brain tissue generates massive information-dense images that are challenging to analyze and require custom software. title: A multimodal cell-free RNA language model for liquid biopsy applications
authors: Mehran Karimzadeh, Aiden M. Sababi, Amir Momen-Roknabadi, Nae-Chyun Chen, Taylor B. Cavazos
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 10 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01148-x

Exai-1, a cell-free RNA foundation model that integrates sequence, structure and expression features, advances liquid biopsy diagnostics by denoising noisy data, augmenting limited datasets and improving the generalizability of cancer detection models.

title: Fully analogue reinforcement learning with memristors
authors: Yue Zhang, Xiaojuan Qi, Zhongrui Wang
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 09 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01157-w

Reinforcement learning has a key role in artifical intelligence (AI), but its implementation on neuromorphic hardware typically involves operations executed on conventional digital computers. A study now addresses this issue by implementing an actor–critic network fully in hardware using analogue memristors.

title: Actor–critic networks with analogue memristors mimicking reward-based learning
authors: Kevin Portner, Till Zellweger, Flavio Martinelli, Laura Bégon-Lours, Valeria Bragaglia
abstract:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 09 December 2025; doi:10.1038/s42256-025-01149-w

A framework based on actor–critic temporal difference learning and employing a biologically plausible network architecture that mimics reward-based learning on memristors and enables full in-memory training for navigation tasks is discussed.
